The dancers continued to struggle with the suspect until he was detained by security and eventually taken into custody by Metro officers. The suspect, identified as Michael Maharas but later found to be Joey Kadmiri, was booked into Clark County Detention Center on charges of attempted murder with a deadly weapon, attempted robbery with a deadly weapon, and burglary with a deadly weapon. The show, Thunder From Down Under, remained on schedule for the next performance.

Jonathan J. Pollard, a convicted spy for Israel who has served 29 years of a life sentence, is set to be released from federal prison on November 20, exactly 30 years after his arrest. His parole was granted after a lengthy legal process, with his lawyers arguing that he met the legal standards for parole, including his behavior in prison and his non-threatening nature. The release could help ease tensions between the U.S. and Israel, particularly in the context of the Iran nuclear deal, which President Obama supports but Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu opposes. Despite Israeli lobbying, the White House has stated that Pollard's release is not connected to the Iran deal. The Justice Department and Pollard's pro bono attorneys confirmed the release date, with Pollard's lawyer, Eliot Lauer, informing him of the news. The White House maintains that President Obama has no intention of altering the terms of Pollard's parole, which require him to remain in the U.S. for at least five years. This decision comes after a federal panel denied Pollard's request for parole in July 2014, setting in motion a year-long effort to secure a different outcome.

The otherwise benign-looking DVD hid a brutal double beheading that was stamped with all the hallmarks of Mexico's ultra-violent drug cartels. As the bloody short film booted up in the laptop, a sinister figure in a black balaclava appeared wielding the kind of sub-machine gun favored by drive-by shooters in the US. The hooded man on screen then issued a thinly veiled threat to the audience of two watching the DVD - RJ Cipriani, an American professional gambler, and his Brazilian model and actress wife, Greice Santo. Pay up a $2.5m debt to a US cocaine kingpin with links to Mexican and South American drug cartels or face a grisly fate, warned the man in the DVD. A man holds a gun and threatens RJ Cipriani and his wife, Greice Santo, in the DVD that was sent to them by Owen Hanson. (Supplied) The film then cut away to a pair of shirtless men. Each is savagely beheaded – one with a chainsaw, the other with a butcher's knife. In a San Diego courtroom last Friday, Owen "O-Dog" Hanson, the 35-year-old Californian who had sent that vicious DVD to Cipriani and his wife, was sentenced to 21 years and three months. He pleaded guilty to racketeering conspiracy and conspiracy to distribute drugs - US federal prosecutors also seized upwards of $6.5m of Hanson's cash and property assets. The $2.5m Hanson had been trying to shake out of Cipriani in the beheading DVD had an Australian connection, with the seven-figure sum having been lost in 2011 on VIP blackjack tables inside Sydney's The Star casino. High-roller Cipriani, who also goes by the name Robin Hood 702, had blown the millions in drug money – purposefully he claimed – after realizing he had been set up to launder Hanson's cocaine profits from his lucrative Australian operation. By the time of his arrest in September 2015, Hanson had smuggled hundreds of kilograms of cocaine into Australia through connections in Mexico and Peru. Hanson, a former University of Southern California football player, was able to sell a kilogram of cocaine for $230,000 in Australia, compared to $20,000 in Los Angeles. RJ Cipriani, who also goes by the name Robin Hood 702, pictured with actress and model wife, Greice Santo. (Supplied) The cash flooded in, but Hanson needed to clean it. Enter Cipriani, a pro-gambler well known in Las Vegas betting circles. Around the time Hanson was lining his pockets with Australian drug money, Cipriani was branding himself as Robin Hood 702, a kind of philanthropist who would win money from the casinos to give to the poor. Cipriani had once dated a woman named Crista Velarde, who unbeknownst to him was now married to Hanson. One day she phoned Cipriani out of the blue, and told him she knew of an American businessman who wanted to bank roll Robin Hood 702's charitable efforts. After meeting up, Hanson explained to Cipriani that he loved the Robin Hood 702 vision. Hanson said he would give the high-roller his cash and whatever profits Cipriani made he could give away to the needy. The principle sum would go back to Hanson via a casino cashier's cheque. The plan sounded solid, straight out of a Martin Scorsese gangster flick, but down in Australia Cipriani got spooked. Hanson delivered several large suitcases and a carry bag containing millions of dollars in Australian fifty dollar bills to Cipriani's plush penthouse suite at the five-star Four Seasons Hotel in Sydney. "I can't begin to tell you how many people have offered me money; put up money for me to gamble," Cipriani told nine.com.au, recalling the cash exchange with Hanson. "It wasn't unusual in the slightest for someone to say, 'Here's some money go gamble.'" But the way Hanson handed over millions of dollars like it was no big thing unsettled Cipriani. So, inside The Star casino's VIP room, Cipriani decided to "leave it with the gambling gods" and lay the maximum bet of $20,000 on every hand. In a couple of days, every dollar of the $2.5m was gone. Hanson was furious. He met Cipriani at a bar inside The Star, and he brought with him some extra muscle, a former Australian MMA fighter. Cipriani told nine.com.au how Hanson's snarling henchman said he was going to cut the gambler's throat, and that he was to hand over his passport. Cipriani went back to his hotel room and called security at The Hilton Hotel, where the hired muscle was staying. He falsely told Hilton staff that a man with a gun was inside room 3026. Staff called NSW police, who stormed the room but they didn’t find a gun. Police officers did, however, find a suitcase stuffed full of $702,000. "I was so emotional I was trying to hold back tears. I was talking about my wife and what they did to her. It all came back to me, all the emotions, all the anger. It finally gave me and my wife closure because there was a fear that Owen Hanson was only going to get five years or ten years," Cipriani said, delivering an emotional victim impact statement. This now infamous cash-packed suitcase marked the start of a joint four-year investigation between the NSW Police and FBI that ended with the take down of Hanson and the dismantling of his drug and gambling operation, O-Dog Enterprise. But in the four years leading up to his arrest in the car park of a San Diego golf club, Hanson had tried various methods to try and intimidate Cipriani to hand over the missing $2.5m cash. After Hanson had desecrated his mother's grave, Cipriani went to the FBI and became a source, codenamed Jackpot. During Hanson's sentencing last week, Cipriani delivered an emotional victim impact statement, often fighting back tears. He detailed the threats made against his actress wife, Greice Santo, and the long-lasting impact they had left. "Words cannot describe the horror my wife went through watching every frame of the beheading video. It was gruesome," Cipriani said. "She is so paranoid still today because of what Owen Hanson put her through. She constantly looks over her shoulder … and she can't check her mail without being worried that another package might be sent by Owen Hanson or one of his crew." Cipriani targeted Hanson and Velarde with a personal barb at the end of his victim statement: "While you sit and rot in jail for decades your wife Crista Velarde has moved on with her life, and has been spending your money and having a grand old time." When Cipriani first approached the FBI in Philadelphia, they did not believe his story

Archaeologists have unearthed two 1,000-year-old skeletons holding hands at the Chapel of St Morrell, an ancient site of pilgrimage in Hallaton, Leicestershire. The University of Leicester's Vicky Score, who leads the project, says the pair, believed to be of similar age, were buried in the 14th century. The Chapel of St Morrell, which has been "lost" for centuries, was discovered after local historian John Morrison pieced together historical references. Archaeologists have excavated 11 skeletons, all oriented east-west in the Christian tradition, with nine radiocarbon-dated to the 14th century. Among the findings, a man was killed by a sharp implement, possibly in battle, and another young male was buried in a pit with his legs raised to his chest, suggesting a potential disease. The chapel, located on a hilltop, has been a special place for over 2,000 years, with Roman archaeology beneath it indicating its significance long before the medieval period. The skeletons, now removed to the university for further investigation, add to the mystery of why these individuals were buried in this unique location, possibly as pilgrims or due to special circumstances. The dig, ongoing for four years, continues to uncover new insights into the history and significance of Hallaton.

The U.S. House of Representatives voted Friday to defund Planned Parenthood for a one-year period, passing the Defund Planned Parenthood Act with a 241-187 vote, nearly all of which were Republican supporters. The bill, sponsored by Rep. Diane Black, R-Tenn., would withhold federal health-care funding from the organization for a year, citing the need for a thorough investigation into its practices. The vote came in the wake of undercover videos released by an activist group claiming violations of federal laws prohibiting the sale of fetal tissue for profit and restrictions on certain abortion procedures. Planned Parenthood has denied any wrongdoing, calling the videos a "coordinated, broad-based smear campaign full of distortions and misinformation." The organization, which provides sexual disease testing, contraception, and abortions, receives around $450 million in federal payments annually, mostly through Medicaid reimbursements for low-income patients. While the bill is unlikely to become law due to Senate Democrats' filibuster and President Obama's threatened veto, it has been used by House Republicans to appease conservatives who have threatened a government shutdown over the issue. The Born-Alive Abortion Survivors Protection Act, which imposes criminal penalties on medical personnel who fail to aid infants born after an attempted abortion, also passed with a 248-177 vote. Democrats criticized both bills as attacks on women's health care and noted that other health-care providers would struggle to absorb Planned Parenthood's patients. The votes broke down mostly along party lines, with only two Democrats supporting the defunding bill and five supporting the survivor protection bill. The debate underscored the political and practical challenges facing any attempt to restrict Planned Parenthood's funding, as both parties seek to balance conservative demands with the realities of federal appropriations and funding cycles.

President Donald Trump tweeted Friday afternoon that he had turned down an interview and photo shoot for Time magazine's "Person of the Year" issue, stating that he "probably" would have been named the title for the second year in a row. However, Time magazine responded by saying that Trump's claim was "incorrect." The magazine, which has awarded the Person of the Year title since 1927, explained that the yearly title is an acknowledgment of influence, noting that Adolf Hitler and Joseph Stalin have both been featured in the role. Trump frequently brags about his cover appearances in the iconic magazine, falsely claiming to hold the record of cover appearances. In June, The Washington Post reported that fake covers of Time magazine featuring Trump hang in at least four of his golf clubs. The Person of the Year will be announced on December 6.

A 24-year-old North Korean soldier, identified only by his family name Oh, has become a focal point of worldwide attention after he was shot and badly wounded as he scrambled across the heavily guarded border into South Korea. The doctor treating him, John Cook-Jong Lee, has revealed that Oh is a quiet, pleasant man who has nightmares about being returned to the North. Lee, who has been operating and caring for the soldier, described Oh as a "pretty nice guy" and said he had hair "like a jarhead, like a U.S. Marine," which prompted Lee to joke that Oh might join the South Korean marines. However, Oh expressed a firm commitment never to return to the military system.

The soldier, who joined the North Korean army at 17 after secondary school graduation, has shown signs of depression and post-traumatic stress. He has been recovering in a Seoul hospital, where he can smile, talk, and use his hands. Since his defection, Oh has undergone multiple surgeries to remove the shards of at least four bullets from his body, stitch up his shredded organs, and treat pre-existing conditions including tuberculosis, hepatitis B, and a case of massive intestinal worms. Lee has been playing South Korean pop music and American films and TV shows for his patient, including "The Transporter" and "CSI," to keep him entertained.

Oh's case has drawn significant attention due to the severity of his injuries and the discovery of 10-inch-long parasitic worms in his stomach, a condition that Lee said he had never seen except in medical textbooks. The soldier has also been found to have a collapsed lung, which was treated with a large needle. Lee has been cautious about exposing Oh to any news coverage, fearing it might disturb him.

The incident has prompted North Korea to replace all its security guards on the border, an intelligence source in South Korea told Yonhap news agency. Meanwhile, South Korean and U.S. soldiers who led a daring rescue attempt to drag the gravely injured soldier to safety have been awarded medals. The North Korean defector's escape has also led to the planting of two trees and digging of a trench at the spot where he crossed the line, according to a photograph posted by the acting U.S. Ambassador to South Korea, Marc Knapper.

Despite the soldier's critical condition, Lee is optimistic about his recovery. "He's a quite strong man," Lee said, adding that Oh has expressed gratitude for South Koreans saving his life and giving him so much blood. The doctor is concerned about Oh's psychological well-being and has asked senior South Korean military officials to hold off on questioning him until he is fully recovered.

World of Beer, a chain of taverns with 77 locations nationwide, is offering an unprecedented internship opportunity that could turn your wildest dreams into reality. For four months this summer, three lucky interns will travel the world, visiting breweries and World of Beer taverns to taste beer, attend festivals, and document their experiences. The internship comes with a generous $12,000 stipend to cover all travel, food, and lodging expenses. Anyone over 21 can apply, and applications are due by March 26. To apply, you can either submit a video resume or participate in an in-tavern interview with a live judging panel. The internship is part of World of Beer’s “drink it in” mantra, aiming to provide a global experience. Successful interns will have their work published in Draft Magazine. The process involves interviews, followed by Skype interviews with World of Beer corporate, who will select the final three interns. This unique opportunity promises a summer of beer-filled adventures, but with a catch: you must be prepared to document your experiences and share them with the world.

The trend of American mothers giving birth at older ages and higher levels of education has continued to rise, according to a study by the Pew Research Center. In 2008, nearly 14% of mothers of newborns were 35 or older, compared to 10% in 1990. The study also found that half of mothers surveyed said parenthood "just happened," highlighting the lack of deliberate planning. Among mothers 35 or older, 71% had at least some college education. The number of births to unmarried women reached a record 41% in 2008, up from 28% in 1990, reflecting a shift in societal norms. Improvements in medical care and fertility treatments, along with delayed marriage and childbearing to pursue education and careers, contributed to these changes. The average age of first-time mothers increased to 25, up from 21.4 in 1970. The study also noted that the number of multiple births associated with older mothers had increased significantly, with a 70% rise in twin birth rates from 1980 to 2004. Experts attribute the trend to a combination of factors, including better medical technology, evolving attitudes, and the increasing number of women pursuing higher education and careers.

In 1925, Florida coroner records indicated that Thomas Curry died from a "wound on the forehead: skull crushed from an unknown cause." His remains were shipped home by freight, buried without a headstone at St. Bridget's parish in East Falls, stacked upon his great-grandparents' graves. For nearly 90 years, his family believed he was at rest. However, a recent exhumation in Philadelphia, conducted by forensic anthropologists from the University of South Florida and Pennsylvania authorities, revealed an unsettling truth. The casket, believed to contain Curry's remains, was filled with wooden planks, not human bones. Upon uncovering the remains of his great-grandparents beneath the wooden casket, the team realized the grave had been filled with wood, likely to deceive Curry's family and cover up the truth of his death.

The Arthur G. Dozier School for Boys, a notorious Florida institution that operated from 1900 to 2011, was known for its brutality and numerous deaths. Hundreds of boys died there, with only about half buried on the school grounds. Curry was one of 10 boys who died after fleeing the school. His death was marked by a mysterious train accident, but the coroner's report did not specify the cause. Records from the school and Old Cathedral Cemetery in Philadelphia contradicted each other, with one stating he was killed by a train and the other by blunt force trauma.

Erin Kimmerle, a renowned forensic anthropologist, led the investigation. She had previously worked on identifying remains in the former Yugoslavia and returned American Indian remains to their tribes. Using ground-penetrating radar, Kimmerle's team discovered 55 graves on the former school grounds, nearly double the number previously identified. The exhumation in Philadelphia was part of a broader effort to uncover the truth about the deaths and disappearances at the Dozier School. The team hopes to use DNA from Curry's relatives to identify his remains among the others buried at the school.

The exhumation raised questions about the school's practices and the intentions of those who buried Curry. It also highlighted the ongoing efforts to uncover the truth about the Dozier School's dark legacy. While the exhumation did not provide definitive answers, it brought to light the need for transparency and justice for the victims and their families. The investigation continues, with the team now focusing on matching DNA samples to the remains found on the former school grounds.

Anthony Weiner's wife Huma Abedin faced a new challenge on Wednesday when a young woman came forward, claiming to have sexted with the former congressman after his resignation from Congress. The woman, identified by BuzzFeed as Sydney Elaine Leathers, used the handles "Sydney Leathers" and "sidneyelainexo" on social media platforms. Leathers, who was a field organizer for Obama for America and listed Weiner as one of her heroes, said she wanted to remain anonymous but was quickly identified by BuzzFeed. The young woman revealed that she and Weiner had exchanged raunchy messages and that Weiner had promised to move her to either Chicago or New York. Leathers stated that she felt she was the more important of the two, even topping Huma Abedin in Weiner's affections.

Abedin, who had already penned an essay for Harper's Bazaar, defended her husband once again, stating that he was now "a better man." In the essay, published as an excerpt titled "The Good Wife," she explained her decision to stay with Weiner, saying, "Anthony has always been a smart, caring, and dedicated person, and while he’s the same public servant who wants what’s best for the people he represents, he is now something else—a better man." This revelation came after Abedin had nervously spoken on Weiner's behalf at her first press conference on Tuesday evening, offering a second defense of her husband.

The incident has reignited questions about Abedin's decision to remain with Weiner despite his repeated transgressions. Some observers, like Maureen Callahan of the New York Post, questioned whether Abedin was simply supporting Weiner's political ambitions or if she had a pathological need for public humiliation. Gloria Steinem, a feminist activist, expressed concern, stating, "I have no way of knowing whether Huma, for whom I have great respect, is responding out of new motherhood, the Stockholm syndrome, or a mystery. I strongly object to holding one spouse responsible for the other’s acts. He’s the one who should get out of the race."

The public's reaction to Abedin's continued support of Weiner remains divided. While some, like Jenny Sanford, understand the complexities of marriage, others, like Geena Bale, are puzzled by her decision to promote Weiner's mayoral ambitions. The situation highlights the ongoing tension between personal and political considerations in Weiner's campaign for mayor of New York City.

Former Congresswoman Corrine Brown has been found guilty of 18 out of 22 charges related to a scam that defrauded donors of $833,000 intended for scholarships. The scam involved a sham charity, One Door for Education, which was supposed to award scholarships to disadvantaged students but only distributed $1,200 in scholarships. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tysen Duva and Eric Olshan presented evidence that Brown and her chief of staff, Ronnie Simmons, used the funds for lavish events and personal gain. They alleged that Brown directed the deposit of $37,000 into her personal account and was instrumental in planning nine events costing the charity $330,000. Brown’s defense hinged on the claim that Simmons was the mastermind, but she was convicted of conspiracy, wire/mail fraud, and tax fraud. Her lawyer, James Smith, plans to file motions for a new trial, arguing that Brown was an aging public servant who relied heavily on Simmons. Judge Timothy Corrigan will decide Brown's sentence, which could take up to 90 days, and will also decide the fate of Simmons and One Door for Education President Carla Wiley, who both testified against her. Acting Assistant Attorney General Kenneth Blanco and Acting U.S. Attorney Stephen Muldrow emphasized the importance of holding public officials accountable for their actions, while FBI Special Agent in Charge Charles Spencer highlighted the FBI’s commitment to investigating public corruption. The case underscores the need for transparency and integrity in public service, as Brown, a long-serving representative, was found to have abused her position for personal gain.

A New Orleans woman, Jacqui Stavis, was killed, and two others were injured when lightning struck their tent during the T-Bois Blues Festival in Larose, authorities said. Stavis, a 28-year-old massage therapist, was found unresponsive after the lightning strike occurred around 10:05 p.m. on Friday, March 18. She was pronounced dead the following day at a local hospital. Two other women, both from New Orleans, were also injured and hospitalized; a 30-year-old woman remained hospitalized in Larose, while a 24-year-old woman was transported to University Medical Center in New Orleans. A large Labrador dog in the tent with the women was also killed. The three women had retreated into a small personal tent on the festival grounds during a severe storm. Stavis was a New Orleans transplant who had become deeply involved in the city's culture and music scene. She was described as a joyful, petite sprite who loved music, art, and New Orleans. Friends and colleagues expressed shock and sadness at her sudden death. The T-Bois Blues Festival, held on an alligator farm, is known for its relaxed atmosphere and features home-cooked Cajun food, catfish, crawfish, beer, and camping. The incident highlights the dangers of lightning strikes, with the National Weather Service noting that 10 percent of lightning strikes can result in death, often from cardiac arrest or irreversible brain damage. The festival, headlined by guitarist Anders Osborne, ran from Thursday to Saturday, and the tragic event left a significant impact on the community.

Fargo police announced on Tuesday that the body of 22-year-old Savanna Greywind, who was eight months pregnant when she went missing, was found in the Red River. Greywind's cause of death was determined to be homicidal violence, though details of the autopsy were not disclosed. The body was discovered Sunday evening, wrapped in plastic and duct tape, by kayakers. In the same apartment building where Greywind lived, a newborn girl believed to be Greywind's was found. Prosecutors charged the man and woman who lived there, Brooke Crews, 38, and William Hoehn, 32, with conspiracy to commit murder as part of a scheme to take Greywind's baby. The newborn is currently under the care of social services. Police Chief David Todd described Greywind's death as "a cruel and vicious act of depravity."

The case has taken a complex turn with conflicting statements from the suspects. Crews initially claimed Greywind had given up her newborn daughter but later admitted to taking advantage of Greywind to obtain the child. Hoehn told police he found Crews cleaning up blood in their bathroom on the day Greywind disappeared and that she presented him with an infant baby girl, saying it was their family. Hoehn disposed of bloody shoes and towels in an attempt to cover his tracks. Both suspects are also charged with conspiracy to commit kidnapping and giving false information to police. Their bail was set at $2 million each, though Hoehn objected to the amount as "unattainable for any regular person." The two suspects, who are neighbors of Greywind, were arrested after the newborn was found with Crews.

Family members of Greywind, a member of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa, expressed their emotions and questions during the court hearing. A memorial was set up outside the apartment building where Greywind lived, with flowers, candles, stuffed animals, and a portrait dedicated to her memory. The search for Greywind's body led to the discovery of suspicious items at a farmstead on the Minnesota side of the river, which may indicate a crime scene. The case remains under investigation, with DNA tests being conducted to confirm the identity of the newborn as Greywind's.

NASA has suspended most of its ongoing engagements with Russia, except for operations related to the International Space Station, due to Russia's actions in Ukraine. NASA's associate administrator for international and interagency relations, Michael O'Brien, issued a memo suspending bilateral contacts with Russia, including travel to Russia, visits by Russian officials to NASA facilities, and email and teleconferences. NASA will continue to work with Russia to maintain the safe and continuous operation of the space station. This move highlights the US's growing reliance on Russia for transporting astronauts to the station, as the US space shuttle program ended in 2010. NASA is focusing on developing commercial launch systems to reduce this dependence, but funding challenges have delayed these plans. The decision to suspend cooperation with Russia is seen as a way to pressure Moscow over the Ukraine crisis, but it also underscores the critical role of the space station in international cooperation. Russia's space program is expected to adapt to the new reality, but the move could have broader implications for global space exploration efforts.

A former Marine, Itzcoatl Ocampo, died after ingesting cleaning product Ajax in his jail cell, raising questions about inmate supervision and mental health care. Ocampo, 25, was awaiting trial for the deaths of six people, including four homeless men, a woman, and her son. His lawyer, Michael Molfetta, said Ocampo had mental health issues and should have been under higher scrutiny. Ocampo was found shaking and vomiting in his cell on Wednesday and died the following day at a hospital. Orange County sheriff's Lt. Jeff Hallock stated that Ocampo was not on suicide watch but that jail deputies are required to walk by each inmate's cell at least once an hour. The Orange County district attorney's office will investigate the death, and an independent pathologist will review the autopsy results. Ocampo's death means that relatives of the victims will not see him held accountable, according to district attorney's spokeswoman Susan Kang Schroeder. Ocampo, who was discharged from the Marines in 2010, was accused of targeting homeless men because they were vulnerable and a blight on the community. He was also facing murder charges in the deaths of a school friend's mother and brother. His family said he was troubled after returning from Iraq in 2008 and visited his friend's grave twice a week. Ocampo was placed on suicide watch in March 2012 after exhibiting erratic behavior. His defense attorney, Randall Longwith, declined to comment until all facts were known. The case highlights the challenges in managing inmates with mental health issues and the potential for inadequate supervision.

Google's rebranding as Alphabet has led to some unexpected complications, particularly with the domain name Alphabet.com. The German automaker BMW owns this domain, which Alphabet is now trying to navigate. BMW has no plans to sell the domain, citing its importance to its fleet services business. This issue highlights the challenges of rebranding and the importance of securing key domain names. Alphabet has launched abc.xyz as its new domain, but the confusion and complications surrounding Alphabet.com have sparked discussions about the naming process. The New York Times reports that Alphabet has encountered similar issues with other companies that already use the Alphabet name, such as an Ohio company that manufactures electrical components. Additionally, the @Alphabet Twitter handle is currently owned by Chris Andrikanich, who has gained unexpected attention. Google founders Larry Page and Sergey Brin emphasized the unconventional nature of their company in their original founders' letter, stating that they intended to make "smaller bets in areas that might seem very speculative or even strange." The rebranding to Alphabet aims to separate core products like search, Gmail, and Android from more experimental projects such as Calico and self-driving cars. Alphabet's new structure includes rigorous capital allocation and segment reporting, with Sundar Pichai taking on the role of CEO for Google. The move to Alphabet also includes the company's X lab, which incubates new efforts like Wing, and growing investment arms, Ventures and Capital. Despite the challenges, the rebranding reflects Google's commitment to innovation and its desire to operate more cleanly and accountably.

This weekend marks President Donald Trump’s third consecutive visit to his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, where he has taken to calling it the "Winter White House." The White House initially downplayed Trump's golf game, stating he had only played a few holes, but reversed its stance after professional golfer Rory McIlroy revealed they played 18 holes. White House spokesperson Sarah Sanders confirmed that Trump played a full round and had a full day of meetings, calls, and interviews for the new NSA, adding that he will return to Washington, D.C., later that night. Trump's golfing habits, which he often criticized Barack Obama for, have drawn criticism and praise. McIlroy's participation in a four-ball event with Trump, including Clear Sports CEO Garry Singer, World No. 3 Rory McIlroy, ISM agent Nick Mullen, and Trump friend Rich Levine, has sparked controversy, with some golf fans questioning McIlroy's decision. McIlroy reportedly shot around 80, describing Trump as a "decent player for a guy in his 70s." The golfing encounters with Trump, including with Tiger Woods, Ernie Els, and Lexi Thompson, have been widely reported, highlighting Trump's continued interest in the sport despite his age. The social media backlash against McIlroy's participation in these events underscores the polarizing nature of Trump's presidency and the complex dynamics surrounding his golfing activities.

Police in Charlottesville, Virginia, are intensifying their search for Hannah Graham, a 18-year-old University of Virginia student who has been missing since September 13. Chief Timothy J. Longo announced Thursday that search efforts are expanding into nearby rural areas, urging property owners and real estate agents to assist in the search by reporting any unusual activity or evidence. Graham's parents, John and Susan Graham, have expressed hope that their daughter can be found, despite the two-week search. The parents have offered a $100,000 reward for information leading to her safe return.

The police are particularly interested in locating Jesse L. "LJ" Matthew Jr., 32, who is charged with abduction with intent to sexually assault Graham. Matthew was arrested in Galveston, Texas, after a tip from a local resident who recognized him. He is currently being held in the Albemarle-Charlottesville Regional Jail. Longo said that Matthew is the last known person to have seen Graham, and his car and apartment have been searched for evidence. Matthew's attorney, James L. Camblos III, stated that his client sounded okay after his arrest, though Matthew declined a court-appointed attorney and waived an extradition hearing.

Matthew's presence in Galveston, a popular summer destination, remains unexplained. The restaurant where Graham was last seen, Tempo, reported that she did not enter the establishment with Matthew but waited outside for him while he purchased drinks. The owner, Brice Cunningham, stated that Graham appeared intoxicated and left with Matthew. Surveillance footage showed Graham and Matthew walking together on the Downtown Mall shortly after 1 a.m. on the night of her disappearance.

The search for Graham has been ongoing, with authorities collecting evidence from Matthew's car and apartment. Longo emphasized the importance of finding Graham, stating, "We have no idea where she is, despite our best efforts." The case has garnered significant attention, with a $50,000 reward offered by the city of Charlottesville, the University of Virginia, and local businesses. The search continues, with hopes that the community's help will lead to Graham's safe return.

A Los Angeles entertainment executive, identified only as Jane Doe, has filed a lawsuit against Match.com, the popular online dating site, demanding that it begin screening its members for potential sexual predators. The executive's attorney, Mark L. Webb, plans to ask a Los Angeles County Superior Court judge for a temporary injunction to halt the site's sign-ups until the demands are met. Webb argues that Match.com, with its significant user base and resources, has the capability to implement such a screening process. Match.com officials, reached by KABC-TV Channel 7 last week, stated that they provide safety tips on their website and warn members to be responsible for screening those they meet. They also noted that incidents of this nature are rare but acknowledged that they are still concerning. Jane Doe, an Ivy League graduate working in the film and television industry, claims she was sexually assaulted by a man she met on Match.com. She had agreed to a second date with the man, who then allegedly followed her home and forced himself on her. After the incident, she discovered that the man had a history of sexual battery convictions. Jane Doe's lawsuit seeks to compel Match.com to check its members' names against public sex offender registries, though her attorney acknowledges that such a measure is not a guarantee of safety. "It's not a guarantee, but don't you think something is better than nothing?" Webb said. The case highlights the ongoing challenges in ensuring safety for online daters and the potential for improved measures by major dating platforms.

In Yellowstone National Park, a grizzly bear that fatally attacked a hiker in July was later euthanized after DNA evidence linked it to a second fatal bear mauling in August. Superintendent Dan Wenk stated the decision aimed to protect park visitors and staff. The investigation remains open, as it's unclear if the same bear was responsible for both deaths. Evidence showed multiple bears, including a sow with two cubs, were near the second victim, John Wallace, but it wasn't clear if the sow was involved. The sow was linked to the scene through DNA analysis of hair and scat samples. The cubs were relocated to a discovery center. After Wallace's death, park officials believed the responsible bear was not the same one that killed Brian Matayoshi in July, as no cub tracks were found at the scene. However, investigators now think those tracks might have been washed away by a rainstorm. Since the maulings, park officials have captured and radio-collared at least seven bears in the area. An estimated 600 grizzlies live in the greater Yellowstone region, and human-bear conflicts have reached record levels, with 295 incidents reported in 2010, of which three-quarters involved bears damaging property or livestock for food.

Sen. Chuck Grassley of Iowa, a key player in the Senate Finance Committee, defended the Republican push to eliminate the estate tax, arguing that it rewards savers over spenders. In an interview with the Des Moines Register, Grassley said, "I think not having the estate tax recognizes the people that are investing, as opposed to those that are just spending every darn penny they have, whether it’s on booze or women or movies." This statement drew criticism on social media, with users pointing out that many people struggle to make ends meet and cannot afford to save or invest.

The estate tax, often called the "death tax," applies only to the wealthiest Americans, with an exemption of $5.5 million for individuals and $11 million for couples. The House version of the tax bill would abolish the estate tax entirely in 2024, while the Senate version doubles the current exemption to $11 million for individuals and $22 million for couples. Despite the differences, both bills aim to significantly reduce the tax burden on the wealthy.

Critics argue that the estate tax impacts only a tiny fraction of taxpayers. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities estimates that fewer than 2 in 1,000 estates will owe any estate tax in 2017, or about 0.2 percent. In Iowa, the state most affected by the estate tax, the number of taxpayers subject to the tax is even smaller. According to the Des Moines Register, in 2016, 5,219 tax returns were affected by the estate tax, with only 682, or 13 percent, of those filers owning farm assets. A 2015 report from the Congressional Research Service found that only 65 farm estates annually face an estate tax liability.

Grassley and other Republicans argue that the estate tax creates an undue burden on family farmers and small business owners, forcing them to sell off land or other assets to pay the tax. Grassley stated, "Death should not be a taxable event and families should not have to fear the Internal Revenue Service and more taxes making it more difficult and costly to pass on the farm or family business to the next generation." However, data from the USDA and the Iowa State University Center for Agricultural Law and Taxation suggest that only a small number of farms are actually affected by the estate tax, and the tax liability is generally manageable for those who do owe it.

Some Republicans also claim that the estate tax forces families to spend large sums on lawyers and accountants to avoid its impact, rather than reinvesting in their businesses. Grassley noted, "Family farmers, small businesspeople and others that may be affected by the estate tax understand that it is law, so many are forced into spending large sums of their hard-earned dollars on lawyers and accountants to avoid its impact instead of reinvesting in their business." However, a review of the data shows that the majority of estates that owe the tax do not face a significant financial burden.

The elimination of the estate tax would save billions for the richest Americans. Seventy-two percent of estate tax payments come from the top 1 percent of U.S. taxpayers, and 42 percent come from the top 0.1 percent. Despite the limited impact on most taxpayers, the estate tax remains a contentious issue in the ongoing debate over tax reform.

A New York City real estate agent, Kevin Brown, revealed to China’s CCTV that a Chinese mother purchased a $6.5 million apartment in Manhattan for her 2-year-old toddler, sparking international headlines. Brown stated that the buyer, who remains anonymous, was looking for a central Manhattan location for her daughter, who was expected to attend prestigious universities like Columbia or NYU or even Harvard. Brown expressed shock when the buyer revealed her daughter’s age. The luxury Manhattan building, One57, which is still under construction, boasts a library with a pool table and a 7.3-meter aquarium, a private concert hall, and a pet washroom, along with an enviable location on 57th Street between Sixth and Seventh Avenues. According to Brown, the apartment’s value has already increased to $8.9 million in less than two years. In China, the purchase has sparked speculation, with comments on Weibo, China’s version of Twitter, suggesting the woman might be related to a corrupt government official. As income inequality in China continues to widen, President Xi Jinping has prioritized combating corruption and official abuse of power.

A particularly dangerous type of superbug, known as CRE or carbapenem-resistant Enterobacteriaceae, is on the rise in the United States, according to a report by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). This superbug is concerning because it is resistant to most antibiotics and can be deadly, with up to 50% of patients who become infected potentially succumbing to the illness. Health officials have labeled CRE among the country's most urgent public health threats. The specific strain of CRE highlighted in the report is particularly alarming due to its ability to spread antibiotic resistance through plasmids, which can transfer the resistance gene to other bacteria. This "phantom menace" strain has a lower profile because it is less antibiotic-resistant than other common types of CRE, leading to under-detection by clinical laboratories. Between June 2010 and August 2015, CDC reported 43 patients in 19 states with this type of superbug. The majority of these cases involved patients who had recently traveled internationally, with India being a common destination. However, the majority of identified patients had exposure to healthcare outside the United States, suggesting a need for enhanced detection and prevention strategies. The report emphasizes the importance of modifying clinical laboratory testing to better identify these organisms and implementing transmission-based precautions in healthcare settings. The spread of these superbugs is a growing concern, as they pose a significant threat to public health by reducing the effectiveness of antibiotics and potentially leading to untreatable infections.

The 68-year-old son of Cuba's former leader, Fidel Castro, has taken his own life, according to Cuban state media. Fidel Ángel Castro Díaz-Balart, known as "Fidelito" or Little Fidel, was found on Thursday morning and had been suffering from depression, state-run newspaper Granma reported. The son of the late president, who led Cuba for nearly half a century, had been receiving outpatient medical treatment for several months. His death comes just over a year after the passing of his father, Fidel Castro, who died at the age of 90 in 2016. Fidelito was a nuclear physicist, trained by the former Soviet Union, and served as a scientific adviser for the Cuban Council of State and vice president of Cuba's Academy of Sciences. He headed the island's nuclear program from 1980 to 1992, but his ideas for developing renewable energy were not incorporated into state policy. His last public appearance was in 2015, when he posed with socialite Paris Hilton during the Habanos Festival in Havana. The personal lives of members of the Castro family are generally kept away from the public eye, and his mental health issues were not widely known prior to his death. The TV announcement stated that his funeral would be planned by his family, but no further details were given. His mother, Mirta Díaz-Balart, was the daughter of a prominent pre-revolution politician, and his father managed to bring him back to Cuba after his mother's family fled the island and went to Florida. Fidelito's death has left many wondering about the impact of his famous father's legacy on his own life and career.

A 13-year-old girl named Jayme Closs remains missing since her parents were found shot to death in their home early Monday in Barron, Wisconsin. Barron County Sheriff Chris Fitzgerald said Jayme was in the home when her parents were killed and that she is still in danger. The search for evidence continues, with 800 tips received but none confirmed. Authorities have doubled the reward to $50,000 for information leading to her safe return. Wausau police sent a school resource officer and therapy dog to help students cope with the disappearance and double murder. The state justice department's Office of School Safety plans to send counselors to the community. The sheriff's office has received over 800 tips and is still seeking credible information. Jayme is described as 5 feet tall, 100 pounds, with green eyes and blonde or strawberry blond hair. The FBI has expanded its search nationwide and has agents working on the case. Anyone with information is asked to call the tip line at 1-855-744-3879 or contact the nearest FBI office. The community of Barron, with fewer than 3,500 people, is deeply affected by the tragedy, with residents expressing concern and anxiety. The motive behind the killings remains unclear, and the sheriff stated that he has a 100% expectation that Jayme is alive. The search for evidence continues, with hundreds of volunteers helping in the search for clues. The community is rallying to support the family and the ongoing investigation.

Kylie Jenner is expecting her first child, a baby girl, according to multiple sources who confirm the news to PEOPLE. The 20-year-old reality star and business mogul is due in February, with rapper Travis Scott as the father. Jenner, who has been dating Scott since April, started telling friends about the pregnancy a few weeks ago, with the family being aware for some time. "They are really excited and so is Travis," says a source. Another insider adds, "It is an unexpected but completely amazing turn of events that she could not be more excited or thrilled about." The family is reportedly overjoyed, with Jenner's sister, Kim Kardashian West, also expecting via surrogate. Kim and Kanye West are parents to daughter North, 4, and son Saint, 21 months, and are due in late January. Meanwhile, Jenner's older sister, Kourtney Kardashian, has three children with Scott Disick: Mason, 7, Penelope, 5, and Reign, 2. Jenner's ex-boyfriend, rapper Tyga, posted and deleted a Snapchat of the news with devil emojis, hinting at potential drama. The family is expected to confirm the news soon, with Jenner's social media activity, including old photos of herself and new shots from the chest up, raising suspicions of an impending announcement.

Maroon 5 has been confirmed as the halftime performers for Super Bowl LIII, according to multiple sources. The band, currently on their Red Pill Blues Tour, has a break between a New Year's Eve show in Las Vegas and the Australian leg of their tour, making them available for the February 3rd game. Adam Levine, the band's frontman, has expressed interest in performing at the Super Bowl in the past. The NFL has not yet officially announced the lineup, but a spokesperson stated, "It’s a Super Bowl tradition to speculate about the performers for the Pepsi Halftime Show." The band's recent hit "Girls Like You" featuring Cardi B and their collaboration with Kendrick Lamar on "Don't Wanna Know" suggest they might consider left-field guest appearances. The NFL faces challenges in choosing performers due to past controversies, such as Janet Jackson's 2004 wardrobe malfunction, and the ongoing issues surrounding Colin Kaepernick's decision to protest during the national anthem. Despite these challenges, Maroon 5's selection is seen as a return to a more mainstream act, similar to recent performers like Justin Timberlake and Bruno Mars.

ROME — In a display of fiscal austerity and environmental concern, Rome’s central Piazza Venezia has been adorned with a Christmas tree nicknamed Spelacchio, or Mangy, due to its pitiful appearance. The 72-foot Norway spruce, imported from the Trentino region near Italy’s border with Austria, was estimated to have cost Italian taxpayers 48,000 euros, or $57,000, for transport and decorations. Upon arrival, the tree began to shed its needles, leaving it looking sparse and forlorn. 

Antimo Palumbo, a tree historian, suggested that the concrete poured around the tree's roots to stabilize it might have caused its decline. Despite the tree’s poor condition, there isn’t enough time, money, or political will to replace it, so Spelacchio the Mangy will remain in Piazza Venezia through the holidays. The tree has become a metaphor for the broader issues facing Rome, including chronic traffic congestion, inefficient public transport, and sporadic trash collection. 

Social media users and Roman residents quickly mocked the tree, trading jokes and criticizing its appearance. The Italian media delved into the tree’s costs, questioned its transport, and analyzed its health. One expert declared, “It has clearly been traumatized.” A consumer rights group even asked an administrative court to investigate the situation, describing it as a “shameful spectacle for citizens and tourists” and demanding immediate removal.

The incident has sparked broader discussions about the priorities of the Italian government and the state of the city. Despite early hopes for Mayor Virginia Raggi, who was elected on an anti-establishment agenda, her administration has faced familiar allegations of corruption and nepotism. As the tree stands in Piazza Venezia, it serves as a poignant reminder of the challenges and shortcomings of governance in Rome and Italy more broadly.

Cartman and Kyle are locked in a heated battle over the animated series "Family Guy," with the future of the show hanging in the balance. When the creators announce plans to depict the prophet Muhammad, the network threatens to pull the episode, seeing it as an opportunity to silence the controversial show. Cartman seizes this moment to orchestrate the show's downfall, setting off on a frenzied cross-country chase to be the first to reach Hollywood. Kyle, on the other hand, is determined to defend "Family Guy," racing against time to save the show from cancellation. The fate of "Family Guy" rests on which boy can make it to the network's headquarters first, with the entire cartoon community watching in anticipation. The race is on, and the future of a beloved animated series hangs in the balance.

One person was killed and five others were injured after a large eucalyptus tree fell on a wedding party in Whittier, California, on Saturday afternoon, according to the Los Angeles County Fire Department. The tree toppled over around 4:30 p.m. in Penn Park, trapping up to 20 people. Witnesses reported hearing a crackling sound before the tree fell, and multiple people were injured, including a 4-year-old girl who was hospitalized in critical condition. Chainsaws were used to free those trapped under the tree's branches. The identity of the person who died has not yet been released. A search dog was brought in to search for additional victims, and officials could not confirm if the heavy rains reported Friday evening played a role in the tree collapse. Arborists are expected to investigate why the tree fell. The park will remain closed indefinitely as authorities conduct their investigation. Mayor Joe Vinatieri expressed concern for the families involved and emphasized the community's support. Officials are also checking the integrity of other trees in the park to ensure safety. The incident highlights the ongoing challenges posed by the five-year drought and its impact on local vegetation.

Lois Lerner, the IRS official at the center of the scandal over targeting conservative groups, has been placed on administrative leave. Lerner, who was in charge of the division that oversaw the extra scrutiny, has faced intense criticism for her role and her testimony. She first disclosed the targeting almost two weeks ago during a planted question at a legal conference, leading to a White House surprise. Lawmakers from both parties have called for her resignation, citing her misleading statements and involvement in the controversial rollout of the story. Despite her refusal to resign, Lerner invoked her Fifth Amendment rights at a House Oversight hearing, asserting she had not done anything wrong. The IRS has since announced that Ken Corbin, a 25-year veteran, will take over as acting director of the tax-exempt organizations division. The scandal has also led to the retirement of Lerner’s boss, Joseph Grant, and the pushout of acting IRS Commissioner Steven Miller. The Treasury’s inspector general’s audit revealed that Lerner knew about the targeting as early as June 2011 and ordered changes, but the practice continued. The controversy has further eroded public trust in the IRS and raised questions about the agency’s handling of political groups.

Doctors at Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine in Baltimore have performed the world's most extensive penis and scrotum transplant, a groundbreaking 14-hour procedure on a U.S. military veteran severely injured in an IED blast in Afghanistan. The patient, whose identity was not released, is recovering well and expected to regain both urinary and sexual function. The surgery, led by Richard Redett, involved transplanting a penis, scrotum, and part of the abdominal wall from a deceased donor. The patient did not receive testicles to avoid ethical issues related to potential fatherhood. The donor's family praised the sergeant’s service and noted the donor family includes veterans, stating, "We are so thankful to say that our loved one would be proud and honored to know he provided such a special gift."

The surgery was the most extensive yet, involving a large skin graft and the connection of three arteries, four veins, and two nerves to provide blood flow and sensation. The patient is expected to regain urinary function by the time he leaves the hospital later this week, with sexual function and sensation expected to return within six months. Johns Hopkins covered the cost of the procedure and hopes to complete more in the near future. The patient will have to be on continuous therapy to tamp down his immune system to prevent rejection, with the donor's bone marrow infusion reducing the need for multiple medications to one low-dose drug.

This surgery aims to address the emotional and psychological trauma of losing genitalia, which can affect urination, sexual intimacy, and the ability to conceive a child. The loss of a penis is often emotionally devastating, and many patients suffer in silence due to stigma. The Department of Defense Trauma Registry has recorded 1,367 male service members with genitourinary injuries between 2001 and 2013, though it's unclear how many lost all or part of the penis. Johns Hopkins is screening additional veterans to see if they are good candidates for this type of reconstructive transplant, with finding donors being an additional hurdle. The patient expressed feeling "finally more normal" upon waking, highlighting the transformative potential of such surgeries.

Starting Monday, same-sex marriage became legal in Hawaii, potentially opening the state to a new market for wedding tourism. As a long-standing destination for weddings and honeymoons, Hawaii is now positioning itself to attract same-sex couples looking to marry legally and have their unions recognized by the federal government. Wedding planner Keane Akao, who started his company with his business partner just before the bill passed, reports receiving more than two dozen confirmations from couples planning to marry in Hawaii. Cira Abiseid and Cyrilla Owle, a couple from Conway, Arkansas, are among those planning to marry in Hawaii, citing the state's beautiful scenery and the legal recognition of their union as key factors. Economists estimate that over the next three years, gay marriage could boost tourism in Hawaii by $217 million, with hotels and resorts already adapting to cater to this new market. The Sheraton Waikiki, for instance, is hosting mass ceremonies for anyone wanting to sign up, while a group of clergy is planning a wedding for an openly gay Unitarian minister. Hawaii's marriage laws allow couples to register for a license and be married the same day, a process that is particularly conducive for tourists. The first couples began tying the knot early Monday, shortly after midnight, when the new law took effect. With Hawaii often credited as the starting point for the national gay marriage discussion, the state now hopes to capitalize on this historic change to boost its tourism industry.

Snow shoveling can be a painful experience, but the right tools can make the task easier and safer. MOTUS, a company that manufactures hand grips for snow shovels, claims their products can reduce the risk of low back injuries and other repetitive strain injuries. The D-grip and T-grip are designed to optimize the mechanical advantage of the shovel, making it easier to lift and push snow. The D-grip, mounted mid-way down the handle, provides lifting leverage, while the T-grip, mounted at the upper end, offers control for pushing and pulling. These ergonomic designs adjust to any stature and hand position, ensuring a neutral limb alignment and reducing the risk of arthritis and back pain. A case study by Dean Kriellaars, Ph.D., at the University of Manitoba, found that the straight grip (T-grip) and D-grip reduce the effort required to lift and carry the load, resulting in a 10% overall reduction in the load. This reduction in effort can be substantial for repetitive tasks and can help prevent and rehabilitate low back injuries. The study also found that the hand-grip reduces the potential for blister formation by decreasing skin surface shear. MOTUS offers discounts for bulk purchases, making their products accessible to a wider audience. Whether you're facing a blizzard or just a heavy snowfall, these ergonomic grips can help you stay safe and pain-free.

New archaeological tests have confirmed that the site many Christians believe to be the tomb of Jesus Christ dates back 1,700 years to A.D. 325, the same era when the Romans first identified the place as holy. With invasions, fires, and earthquakes occurring at Jerusalem's Church of the Holy Sepulchre over the centuries, historians had questioned whether the tomb had been destroyed or moved. To date the tomb, known as the Holy Edicule, conservators from the National Technical University of Athens looked at radioactive elements in the architectural glue that fit it together, using ground-penetrating radar and laser scanning. The tomb is the size of a coat closet and was open for just 60 hours while restoration work was also carried out. The results of the tests were first reported Tuesday by National Geographic. "Scientists and archaeologists are very excited about this because, what it does is, it corroborates our historical accounts," said National Geographic archaeology writer Kristin Romey, who was on site during the nine-month renovation project. Experts believe the site was identified around A.D. 325 when the Roman emperor Constantine the Great came to the city with his team to locate places associated with the life of Jesus. The Romans are said to have torn down a temple in Jerusalem where they found the cave that they believed to be his burial site, then built a shrine and a church around that site. Three different Christian denominations—Roman Catholic, Greek Orthodox, and Armenian Orthodox—share custody over the church, and there have been turf wars and brawls in the past over the management of the site. Even the restoration took decades to settle, with various denominations agreeing to conserve the edicule in 1959 but not agreeing on a plan for the restoration until 2016. The same Greek team that restored the Acropolis in Athens was chosen to carry out the project. Archaeologists believe there may be more surprises to come at the site. "There is so much information in the data that was collected by the restorers during the conservation project," said archaeologist-in-residence Fredrik Hiebert. The tomb was opened for the first time in centuries in October 2016, when the shrine that encloses the tomb, known as the Edicule, underwent a significant restoration by an interdisciplinary team from the National Technical University of Athens. Several samples of mortar from different locations within the Edicule were taken at that time for dating, and the results were recently provided to National Geographic by Chief Scientific Supervisor Antonia Moropoulou, who directed the Edicule restoration project. When Constantine's representatives arrived in Jerusalem around 325 to locate the tomb, they were allegedly pointed to a Roman temple built some 200 years earlier. The Roman temple was razed, and excavations beneath it revealed a tomb hewn from a limestone cave. The top of the cave was sheared off to expose the interior of the tomb, and the Edicule was built around it. A feature of the tomb is a long shelf, or "burial bed," which according to tradition was where the body of Jesus Christ was laid out following crucifixion. Such shelves and niches, hewn from limestone caves, are a common feature in tombs of wealthy 1st-century Jerusalem Jews. The marble cladding that covers the "burial bed" is believed to have been installed in 1555 at the latest and most likely was present since the mid-1300s, according to pilgrim accounts. When the tomb was opened on the night of October 26, 2016, scientists were surprised by what they found beneath the marble cladding: an older, broken marble slab incised with a cross, resting directly atop the original limestone surface of the "burial bed." The new test results, which reveal the lower slab was most likely mortared in place in the mid-fourth century under the orders of Emperor Constantine, come as a welcome surprise to those who study the history of the sacred monument. "Obviously that date is spot-on for whatever Constantine did," says archaeologist Martin Biddle, who published a seminal study on the history of the tomb in 1999. "That's very remarkable." During their year-long restoration of the Edicule, the scientists were also able to determine that a significant amount of the burial cave remains enclosed within the walls of the shrine. Mortar samples taken from remains of the southern wall of the cave were dated to 335 and 1570, which provide additional evidence for construction works from the Roman period, as well as a documented 16th-century restoration. Mortar taken from the tomb entrance has been dated to the 11th century and is consistent with the reconstruction of the Edicule following its destruction in 1009. "It is interesting how these mortars not only provide evidence for the earliest shrine on the site, but also confirm the historical construction sequence of the Edicule," Moropoulou observes. The mortar samples were independently dated at two separate labs using optically stimulated luminescence (OSL), a technique that determines when quartz sediment was most recently exposed to light. The scientific results will be published by Moropoulou and her team in a forthcoming issue of the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports.

When the Camp Fire, the deadliest and most destructive wildfire in California history, devastated Butte County, Sierra Nevada Brewing Co. in Chico, California, responded by brewing Resilience Butte County Proud IPA, a fundraiser beer for Camp Fire relief. The initiative, which Sierra Nevada launched in collaboration with more than 1,200 breweries across the United States, aimed to support the recovery efforts of those affected by the fire. Sierra Nevada, which was only partially spared by the fire, lost 15% of its employees’ homes and other properties. To aid the community, Sierra Nevada donated $100,000 to establish the Sierra Nevada Camp Fire Relief Fund through the Golden Valley Community Bank Foundation.

The beer, a classic West Coast-style India Pale Ale, was crafted to evoke a taste of home, featuring Centennial and Cascade hops. Sierra Nevada shared the recipe with other breweries, encouraging them to participate in the fundraiser. Malt and hop suppliers contributed ingredients, and participating breweries agreed to donate 100% of their sales to the relief fund. Resilience Brewing Company allowed Sierra Nevada to use its name temporarily for the beer. The beer will be available in cans and on draught, with an estimated 8.6 million pints to be produced. Sierra Nevada plans to release the beer in late January, while other participating breweries will release it in late December.

The collaborative effort extended beyond the breweries, with malt and hop suppliers, wholesalers, and retailers all contributing to the cause. Sierra Nevada’s website lists more than 1,200 breweries participating in the project. The response was overwhelming, with the initiative doubling Sierra Nevada’s initial goal of 500 participating breweries. The craft brewing community rallied around the cause, with breweries from small, midsize, and regional companies to major brands like Goose Island Beer Co. and Blue Moon Brewing Co. joining in.

The beer’s release will be celebrated with Resilience Night, an event where customers can try the beer at participating breweries. Additionally, Untappd, a social networking platform for beer enthusiasts, will offer a limited-edition badge for users who check in to any Resilience IPA from any participating brewery. Sierra Nevada is hopeful that the beer will raise more than a million dollars for the recovery efforts. The company emphasized that the rebuilding process would take time, but they were committed to supporting their community through this challenging period.

A former associate of Paul Manafort, Sam Patten, pleaded guilty to a lobbying crime, giving prosecutors access to insights from a longtime international political operative whose Russian business partner has already been indicted in Special Counsel Robert Mueller’s probe. Patten, 47, admitted to failing to register in the U.S. as a foreign agent for his work lobbying on behalf of a Ukrainian political party. His plea agreement also included the suggestion that the Trump Inaugural Committee improperly accepted funds from a foreigner, though he wasn’t charged. Patten worked with Manafort and on Ukrainian campaigns, and reportedly worked on microtargeting operations with Cambridge Analytica. The nature of his cooperation with prosecutors isn’t clear, but it may provide valuable information in Mueller’s ongoing investigation. Patten’s plea came as his Russian business partner, Konstantin Kilimnik, was indicted in absentia alongside Manafort on obstruction of justice charges. Kilimnik, identified in filings as having worked for the Russian military’s intelligence service known as the GRU, has denied these allegations. Patten’s work for multiple political parties and office-holders in Ukraine, including his consulting firm Begemot Ventures International Ltd., has raised questions about his role in international political operations. His plea agreement also includes a reference to the Trump Inaugural Committee’s potential acceptance of illegal foreign funds, though he was not charged with this. The case highlights the ongoing scrutiny of individuals associated with Manafort and the broader investigation into Russian influence in the 2016 U.S. election.

Search crews hunting for the missing Malaysia Airlines jet have failed to relocate faint sounds heard deep below the southern Indian Ocean that officials said were consistent with a plane's black boxes, the head of the search operation said. Angus Houston, the retired Australian air chief marshal leading the search, stated that sound locating equipment on board the Ocean Shield has picked up no trace of the signals since they were first heard late Saturday and early Sunday. Time may have already run out to find the devices, whose locator beacons have a battery life of about a month. Tuesday marks one month since the plane vanished. Up to 14 planes and 14 ships are scouring the 30,000-square-mile search zone. The wait has been devastating for weary families, who insist the search continues at all costs, despite frustrations. It is unclear whether a sub on board the Ocean Shield will be deployed to try to chart out any debris on the sea floor when searchers are certain the black boxes' locator beacons have gone silent. If the sub maps out a debris field, the crew will replace the sonar system with a camera unit to photograph any wreckage. Houston's comments about deploying the sub contradicted an earlier statement from Australia's acting prime minister, Warren Truss, who said search crews would launch the Bluefin 21 autonomous sub on Tuesday. The towed pinger locator detected late Saturday and early Sunday two distinct, long-lasting sounds underwater that are consistent with the pings from an aircraft's "black boxes" - the flight data and cockpit voice recorders. Still, officials warned it could take days to determine whether the sounds were connected to Flight 370, which vanished March 8 on a flight from Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, to Beijing with 239 on board. "This is an herculean task - it's over a very, very wide area, the water is extremely deep," Defense Minister David Johnston said. "We have at least several days of intense action ahead of us." Finding the black boxes is key to unraveling what happened to the Boeing 777, because they contain flight data and cockpit voice recordings that could explain why the plane veered so far off-course. "Everyone's anxious about the life of the batteries on the black box flight recorders," Truss said. "Sometimes they go on for many, many weeks longer than they're mandated to operate for - we hope that'll be the case in this instance. But clearly there is an aura of urgency about the investigation." The first sound picked up by the equipment on board the Ocean Shield lasted two hours and 20 minutes before it was lost, Houston said. The ship then turned around and picked up a signal again - this time recording two distinct "pinger returns" that lasted 13 minutes. That would be consistent with transmissions from both the flight data recorder and the cockpit voice recorder. The black boxes normally emit a frequency of 37.5 kilohertz, and the signals picked up by the Ocean Shield were both 33.3 kilohertz, U.S. Navy Capt. Mark Matthews said. But the manufacturer indicated the frequency of black boxes can drift in older equipment. The frequency used by aircraft flight recorders was chosen because no other devices use it, and because nothing in the natural world mimics it, said William Waldock, a search-and-rescue expert. Pressure from being so deep below the surface and the age of the batteries can also affect the transmission level, he said. The Ocean Shield is dragging a ping locator at a depth of 1.9 miles. It is designed to detect signals at a range of 1.12 miles, meaning it would need to be almost on top of the recorders to detect them if they were on the ocean floor, which is about 2.8 miles deep. Meanwhile, the search for any trace of the plane on the ocean's surface continued, with 133 missions completed so far in the hunt from the air for debris that could be from Flight 370, but no debris from the plane has been found.

Prince William and Duchess Kate Middleton have adopted a three-month-old cocker spaniel puppy, marking their first pet together, according to The Telegraph. The puppy, whose name remains undisclosed, is the son of Kate's mother's dog, Ella. The couple initially considered their readiness for pet ownership but decided to keep the puppy after a trial period. "William and Catherine fell in love with the pup instantly and it wasn't long before they decided to keep him," a Palace aide told US Weekly. The new addition will replace Prince William's deceased black Labrador, Widgeon. Spaniels, known for their friendly and affectionate natures, have a long history in the royal family, with the current Queen owning several corgis and dorgis. The puppy's arrival is timely, as William will be posted to the Falkland Islands for six weeks, leaving Kate to spend more time in London and live with her new companion at Kensington Palace.

O.J. Simpson, the former NFL star, appeared before a Nevada parole board on Thursday, marking the first time in four years that the public could witness his parole hearing. The hearing, broadcast live, garnered extensive media coverage, reminiscent of the "trial of the century" from 1995. Simpson, now 70, apologized for his role in the 2007 armed robbery, emphasizing that he had been a model prisoner during his nine-year sentence. He stated, "I've done my time, I've done it as well and as respectfully as I think anyone can." Simpson's energy and demeanor suggested little impact from his time in prison, and he maintained a positive outlook, expressing plans to move to Florida after release. The parole board, consisting of four members, voted unanimously to grant Simpson parole, with Chairman Connie Bisbee noting that he was graded a "low risk to reoffend." 

Simpson's testimony focused on his remorse and his role as a peacemaker in prison. He highlighted his participation in "Alternative to Violence" classes and his relationship with his oldest daughter, Arnelle, who testified that he was "my best friend and my rock." Simpson's friend, Tom Scotto, also supported his release, stating that Simpson was ready to return to his life in Florida. Bruce Fromong, one of the robbery victims, testified in favor of Simpson's release, saying he had forgiven him for the crime.

The parole hearing also featured testimony from Simpson's associates, including Tom Riccio, who claimed Simpson had orchestrated the robbery. However, Simpson maintained that his associates misled him and then turned on him. Despite his efforts to portray himself as a reformed individual, Simpson's legal team argued that the nine-to-33-year sentence was disproportionate to the crime and a form of payback for his controversial acquittal in the 1994 murders of his ex-wife, Nicole Brown Simpson, and her friend, Ronald Goldman. Their families won a wrongful death civil judgment against him in 1997.

Simpson's legal team and supporters emphasized his model prisoner status and his remorse, hoping these factors would influence the parole board's decision. The unanimous vote in his favor suggests that Simpson's behavior and rehabilitation efforts were considered significant. However, the case remains contentious, with some victims' families and legal experts questioning the fairness of his sentence and the potential for him to reoffend.

Five former Ohio State University wrestlers, including UFC world champion Mark Coleman, have come forward to contradict Rep. Jim Jordan’s claim that he had no knowledge of the team doctor’s alleged sexual misconduct against athletes. They allege that Jordan, who was an assistant wrestling coach from 1986 to 1994, was aware of the abuse and failed to act. One of the wrestlers, Shawn Dailey, said he was groped by Dr. Richard Strauss, the team doctor, multiple times in the mid-1990s. Dailey recalled, “I participated with Jimmy and the other wrestlers in locker-room talk about Strauss. We all did. It was very common knowledge in the locker room that if you went to Dr. Strauss for anything, you would have to pull down your pants.” Another wrestler, Dunyasha Yetts, said he and others protested to Jordan and head coach Russ Hellickson after Strauss tried to pull down his wrestling shorts when Yetts sought help for a thumb injury. Hellickson, Jordan's mentor, said in a recent video that he had told Strauss he was being too "hands on" with students. DiSabato, another former wrestler, called Jordan a "liar" and said Jordan had been directly warned about Strauss's behavior. DiSabato said he reached out to Jordan this year, before going to the university, to tell him he planned to go public with his allegations. Jordan denied any knowledge of the abuse and has continued to do so. Former Ohio State wrestlers have accused Jordan of turning a blind eye to the abuse and then lying about it. The university opened an investigation into the abuse in April after DiSabato came forward. The Perkins Coie law firm, which is overseeing the probe, has interviewed more than 150 former students and witnesses. Former athletes from 14 Ohio State sports have reported abuse by Strauss. Jordan, a founder of the House Freedom Caucus and a staunch ally of President Trump, has been floated as a potential replacement for the speaker of the House, Paul Ryan. Ryan's spokesman Doug Andres said, "These are serious allegations and issues. The university has rightfully initiated a full investigation into the matter. The speaker will await the findings of that inquiry." Jordan has received threatening emails from DiSabato, including one that landed in his inbox on Wednesday. Jordan forwarded the emails to the U.S. Capitol Police, which is reviewing them. Dailey said he has spoken twice with investigators from Perkins Coie and that they questioned him about Jordan’s actions at the time. Jordan has denied any knowledge of the abuse and has continued to do so. The case highlights the broader issue of sexual misconduct in sports and the potential failure of institutions to address such issues.

The shift towards chip-enabled credit cards, which are already in use in several parts of Europe, is coming to the United States, where card fraud has more than doubled over the last 15 years. These new cards, featuring a microchip on the front, will replace the traditional magnetic strip and require insertion into a reader rather than being swiped at checkout terminals.
