The microchip contains a user's payment information and generates a unique code for each transaction, significantly enhancing security. According to Visa's Stephanie Erickson, this transition will make it more difficult for criminals to create counterfeit cards, as the chip-based cards are harder to replicate due to their unique transaction codes. Countries that adopted this technology saw a reduction of up to 70 percent in counterfeit card fraud within two years. However, the chip-based cards do have a downside: transactions take longer to process, with dip methods taking between five to ten seconds compared to the three to five seconds for swipe transactions. This could lead to longer lines, particularly during high-traffic periods such as Black Friday. By October 1, merchants who have not upgraded their payment terminals will be liable for fraudulent transactions, shifting the responsibility from card issuers to retailers. While most customers at major banks like JPMorgan Chase and Bank of America will receive their new cards by the end of the year, some will not get them until 2016. Credit and debit cards without chips will continue to work until they expire or until consumers activate their new cards, and they will still function at updated payment terminals. However, new machines will prompt users to dip their cards instead of swiping them. To ensure security, consumers are advised to always use the chip device for transactions.

After a freshman died from consuming beer, rum, and 151-proof liquor during a fraternity initiation ritual in 2010, California Polytechnic State University banned fraternities from recruiting freshmen. The North-American Interfraternity Conference (NIC), representing 75 national fraternities, intervened, conducting a study and launching a three-year campaign to overturn the ban. The university eventually lifted the restriction, allowing freshmen to join fraternities immediately. This decision reflects the NIC's significant influence in higher education, as it opposes proposals to delay fraternity recruitment, often citing the potential risks to freshmen. While some argue that postponing recruitment could save lives and reduce alcohol-related incidents, the NIC maintains that freshmen should have the opportunity to join fraternities right away. The article highlights the ongoing tension between the NIC and educational institutions, with the former advocating for the status quo and the latter seeking to protect freshmen from potential dangers. Despite the ban's lifting, the incident and subsequent events underscore the complex relationship between fraternities and colleges, as well as the broader issues surrounding student safety and alcohol consumption on college campuses.

Researchers have discovered a novel method to transform used coffee grounds into an alcoholic beverage, potentially revolutionizing the spirits industry. By collecting and drying coffee grounds, then heating them in water, adding sugar, and fermenting with yeast, scientists produced a 40% ethanol content drink comparable to vodka and tequila. Eight trained taste testers rated the product, describing it as coffee-scented and bitter, but with the potential for improved flavor with aging. This process, while similar to making other distilled beverages, offers a unique twist by utilizing a common waste product. The caffeine content, which typically causes energy drinks to combine alcohol and caffeine, is significantly reduced during the brewing process. This innovative approach could cater to coffee enthusiasts seeking a new buzz, aligning with America's love for coffee, and potentially opening new markets for the spirits industry.

A 30-year-old Santa Rosa woman, Delia Garcia-Bratcher, is facing felony child abuse charges after allegedly grabbing a 12-year-old boy by the throat on Friday at Olivet Charter Elementary School in Santa Rosa. According to the Sonoma County Sheriff's Office, Garcia-Bratcher came to the school to confront a boy she suspected of bullying her 10-year-old daughter. She approached the boy in front of other students, grabbed him by the neck, and warned him to stop, causing red marks on his neck, authorities said. No adults witnessed the confrontation, and Garcia-Bratcher had not checked in with the school office before coming on campus. The boy ran to a classroom, told a teacher, and the staff took photos of the injuries. Garcia-Bratcher was arrested on Saturday and released on $30,000 bail. The school district is also investigating the bullying claims but has not yet substantiated them. Lt. Mark Essick of the sheriff's department stated that it was unreasonable for a parent to confront a student directly on campus. School Superintendent Jennie Snyder said it is rare for parents to confront students on campus and that the school has safety procedures in place.

Russell Crowe, star of the new Robin Hood film, walked out of a BBC Radio 4 interview after being accused of giving the hero an Irish accent. The 46-year-old New Zealand-born actor, known for his prickly reputation, denied the claim, saying, "You've got dead ears, mate, if you think that's an Irish accent." Interviewer Mark Lawson had suggested there were "hints" of Irish in Crowe's portrayal, but Crowe was unyielding, interrupting with an expletive and waving his cigarette before leaving. The dispute over the accent, which has also drawn criticism from other sources, comes as Crowe has been defending his portrayal of Robin Hood against other critics. In the interview, Crowe stated, "I'm a little dumbfounded that you could possibly find any Irish in that character— that's kind of ridiculous, but it's your show." The controversy highlights the sensitive issue of regional accents in film and the potential for actors to be accused of cultural misrepresentation.

A Duluth, Minnesota, couple, Ron and Mary Tarnowski, were found dead on August 5, eight days after going missing. Ron, 82, and Mary, 78, were discovered in a remote swampy area off Highway 2, about a mile from their hunting camp. The U.S. Border Patrol Helicopter found their vehicle, which was stuck on a trail, with Mary inside and Ron closer to the highway. Ron may have driven onto the trail accidentally before getting his car stuck, according to Lt. Mike Ceynowa of the Duluth Police Department. The couple had been missing since July 29, when they were last seen at a local store. Their disappearance sparked a community-wide search involving hundreds of volunteers, law enforcement, and community members. Ron had early-stage dementia, and Mary had right-sided paralysis, making it difficult for her to move or speak. They spent most of their days confined to their home in Duluth, rarely leaving due to their physical limitations. The couple had been married for 59 years, and their love and commitment to each other were evident in their daily routines. The Tarnowskis' story resonated with families across the state, particularly those with elderly parents, highlighting the dangers vulnerable adults can face when they leave home with no way of being reached or tracked. The couple's sons, Karl and Kurt, and their wives, were tireless in organizing search efforts and checking on possible sightings. The Duluth Police Department's violent crimes unit, which handles missing person cases, had been working on the case since the beginning and had tracked down dozens of leads in six counties and two states. The search efforts were ongoing, and the community continued to support the Tarnowski family with their outpouring of condolences and support.

During a court-martial proceeding, Pvt. Marcus Merritt testified that Sgt. Adam Holcomb, the first of eight soldiers facing prosecution in connection with the suicide of Private Danny Chen, a Chinese American, had taunted him with racial slurs and threatened to "kill me and put me in a body bag and send me home," according to the Fayetteville Observer. Holcomb's hazing of Chen, who died under mysterious circumstances at a remote combat outpost in Afghanistan, is at the center of renewed attention on allegations of hazing and racism within the U.S. Army. Holcomb, 30, is charged with negligent homicide, assault, and other counts. Prosecutors are presenting evidence that Holcomb subjected Chen to relentless racial taunts and physical abuse, including dragging him across rocky ground, in the weeks leading up to his suicide. Holcomb's immediate superior, Staff Sgt. Darren Holt, testified that he confronted Holcomb about the dragging incident and reported it to higher-ups. Chen's death sparked outrage among Chinese American activists in New York City, where he grew up. Holcomb's defense argues that Chen's suicide was due to his parents' disapproval of his military career choice and his poor performance as a soldier. Despite these claims, several former platoon members testified that most of the discipline Holcomb imposed on Chen was justified by his failure to follow orders. The platoon medic, Spec. Zachary Bolin, treated Chen's back abrasions but said Chen denied suicidal thoughts. The court-martial is set to continue, with further testimony expected from other former platoon members as the case unfolds.

A bill in New Jersey aims to crack down on distracted driving by imposing hefty fines and potentially suspending driver’s licenses for those who engage in activities such as eating, drinking, grooming, or using electronic devices while behind the wheel. Assemblyman John Wisniewski, the sponsor of the legislation, seeks to broaden current laws that already prohibit texting or talking without a hands-free device. The proposed law would bar any activity unrelated to the actual operation of a motor vehicle that interferes with safe operation. Offenders could face fines ranging from $200 to $800, with a third offense potentially leading to a 90-day license suspension and motor vehicle points. Wisniewski introduced the measure seven months ago but has yet to bring it up for a vote in a committee he leads. Despite the bill’s broad scope, many are questioning its practicality and whether it goes too far.

The legislation is modeled after a similar law in Maine and is intended to educate drivers about the dangers of distracted driving. Wisniewski argues that the bill is necessary to discourage dangerous behaviors behind the wheel, citing the alarming statistics from the federal government that in 2014, there were 400,000 accidents involving distracted drivers, with 3,000 resulting in fatalities. Critics, however, argue that the bill is an overreach and question how police could effectively enforce such a law. Steve Carrellas, policy and government affairs director for the National Motorists Association state chapter, contends that three existing statutes can be used to address distracted driving without the need for a new law.

Proponents of the bill, like Arnold Anderson, the Essex County Community Traffic Safety Program coordinator, emphasize the importance of breaking the habit of multitasking while driving. They believe that educating the public about the dangers of distracted driving could have a similar effect as seat belt laws, which have increased seat belt usage even without fines. Tracy Noble, AAA Mid-Atlantic spokeswoman, notes that while the legislation may be difficult to enforce, it could still have a positive impact by raising awareness and ingraining safer driving habits.

The bill, which does not specifically mention coffee or other beverages, has sparked controversy and backlash. Wisniewski himself was surprised by the reaction, noting that people were concerned about being pulled over for drinking coffee. He introduced the bill to avoid the need for new legislation every time technology changes. Despite the bill’s potential to change attitudes and behaviors, its future remains uncertain as it has not yet been voted on in a committee.

Adrianne Haslet-Davis, a professional ballroom dancer who lost her left leg below the knee in the 2013 Boston Marathon bombing, announced her intention to run the 120th Boston Marathon this April, training with her "AdrianneStrong" team to raise funds for the Limbs for Life Foundation. Haslet-Davis, who vowed to dance again after the bombing, successfully showcased her skills at the marathon finish line in 2015. She now aims to run the marathon, dedicating her race to those who have supported her and other survivors. "It's just a giant thank you to everyone," she said. "I’m going to cry the whole time." Her return to the finish line, both as a dancer and a runner, symbolizes resilience and triumph over tragedy.

Julia Roberts' half-sister Nancy Motes died in an apparent drug overdose on February 9, 2013, in Los Angeles. Nancy's fiancé, John Dilbeck, found her body in a bathtub, where she had taken an overdose, according to the Los Angeles Coroner's Office. Nancy's family, including her mother, Betty Lou Motes, and her siblings, Eric Roberts and Lisa Roberts Gillan, have been at odds with Julia over the years, with Nancy accusing Julia of bullying her about her weight. Nancy had undergone weight loss surgery in 2012 and had been working as a production assistant on Glee. Nancy had recently been tweeting aggressively about Julia, calling her a "b*tch" and "hag," and had refused Julia's repeated attempts to get her into rehab. Julia's representative stated that the family was shocked and devastated by Nancy's death, and Julia canceled several scheduled engagements. Nancy's fiancé, John Dilbeck, is reportedly considering keeping control of her possessions and asserting his right to be a beneficiary of her estate, which has caused tension with Julia's family. Nancy's death has reignited the long-standing conflict between the two sisters, with Nancy's fiancé claiming that Julia inflicted "pure cruelty" on Nancy and that Nancy's suicide letter contained dark secrets about Julia that she wanted to be made public. Nancy's death has left Julia devastated, and the family is struggling to come to terms with the loss.

Senator Bernie Sanders, who has not yet officially conceded the Democratic presidential primary to Hillary Clinton, is not being considered as a potential running mate for Clinton, a Democrat familiar with the decision tells CNN. Sanders, a self-described democratic socialist, remains committed to transforming the Democratic Party rather than becoming Clinton's partner, according to a person close to him. He would risk being seen as a sell-out by his supporters if he were to join the Clinton ticket, another source adds. During a private meeting with Clinton on Tuesday night, which lasted about 90 minutes, the issue of a potential running mate was not discussed. Sanders, who has been a vocal critic of Clinton on issues such as the Trans-Pacific Partnership and has called for a $15 minimum wage, is still actively campaigning and working to build his platform. His campaign has raised over $4.6 million and has a strong base of supporters who are eager to see him challenge Clinton in the general election. Despite the lack of a formal endorsement, Clinton has been working to unite the Democratic Party and secure the nomination, with endorsements from President Obama, Vice President Biden, and Elizabeth Warren. Meanwhile, Sanders continues to focus on issues such as income inequality, climate change, and campaign finance reform, and has been making the case that his agenda aligns more closely with the needs and concerns of working-class Americans.

The Wisconsin Air National Guard's 115th Fighter Wing will conduct nighttime training flights from Monday through Thursday, potentially causing residents to hear or see F-16 fighter jets taking off or landing until around 10 p.m. These nighttime operations are part of the pilots' and maintenance personnel's readiness training. Frostquakes, or cryoseisms, have also been reported in southern Wisconsin, with a loud boom felt from Columbus to Fox Lake and from Johnson Creek to Oconomowoc. These seismic events occur when frozen ground expands, creating stress that fractures the soil and rock. Meteorologist Justin Schultz confirms that while the frostquake was loud, it did not cause any damage. Wisconsin is among the states that have experienced such phenomena, making this a relatively rare but not uncommon occurrence in the region.

A former U.S. Postal Service worker and three accomplices have been sentenced for their roles in a scheme to cash stolen money orders, according to court documents. Marc Saunders, 40, of Sicklerville, New Jersey, was the mastermind behind the 15-month scheme, using a stolen imprinting machine to produce the money orders and directing others to cash them. Eugene Bowen, 35, of Knoxville, Tennessee, and Andre Sutton, 39, recruited individuals to cash the money orders, splitting the proceeds with Saunders. Saunders pleaded guilty and received a five-year probationary sentence, including eight months of home confinement, and was ordered to pay nearly $100,000 in restitution. Bowen and Sutton were sentenced to 20 months and nine months in prison, respectively, with Bowen ordered to pay $18,470 in restitution and Sutton $4,700. The scheme began when the New Lisbon post office failed to return a machine that printed money orders when the USPS introduced new technology in February 2013. The postmaster, who was transferred in June 2013, also neglected to destroy about 180 loose money orders that could be printed with the outdated machine. The stolen machine was stored in a cabinet at the Pemberton office, where Saunders began working more than a year later. The investigation, led by special agents of the USPS Office of the Inspector General, uncovered that the money orders were cashed in various post offices, with most transactions occurring in the Philadelphia area. Bowen allegedly recruited residents of homeless shelters in Knoxville to conduct the transactions, while Sutton and Bell were involved in cashing the money orders in York, Pennsylvania, and Jersey City. Investigators linked the cellphones and Facebook pages of the lower-level participants to those of Saunders and the middlemen, revealing their connections and shared backgrounds. The case highlights the importance of proper security measures in the postal system and the consequences of negligence in handling sensitive equipment.

A rare German Enigma I cipher machine from World War II, acquired at a Romanian flea market for just 100 euros, sold for 45,000 euros ($51,500) at an Artmark auction in Bucharest, Romania. The machine, which dates back to 1941 and is in almost perfect condition, was initially purchased by a collector who recognized its true value. The Artmark auction house, which specializes in collectibles, put the machine up for sale with a starting price of 9,000 euros, but it fetched a much higher price from an online bidder. According to Cristian Gavrila, the collectible consignment manager at Artmark, the seller was a cryptography professor who identified the machine's historical significance at the flea market. Romania, which was an ally of Nazi Germany until 1944, may still be hiding many other cryptographic machines that have yet to be discovered. The Enigma machine, used by the German military to encrypt messages, played a crucial role in Nazi war efforts. However, it was eventually cracked by a team of cryptologists at Bletchley Park in southern England, a breakthrough credited with shortening the war by at least two years. This sale follows a world auction record set last month by Christie's New York Books, which sold a four-rotor Enigma cipher machine from 1944 for $547,500. The University of Manitoba Libraries, in collaboration with the National Centre of Truth and Reconciliation and the Library and Archives of Canada, is curating a collection of webpages, blogs, news coverage, and PDF files related to Manitoba's involvement with the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, highlighting the ongoing efforts towards reconciliation and healing in the province.

A rare book heist of extraordinary stealth and value has left one London book dealer devastated. Over £2 million worth of antique works, including rare editions of Dante's Divine Comedy and Galileo's scientific writings, were stolen from a West London warehouse. Alessandro Meda Riquier, the book dealer, expressed deep upset over the loss, stating, "I'm very upset because this is not something you can buy everywhere. Behind these books there is a lot of work because we have to search to try to find out where the books are - auction houses, collectors, colleagues - and there's big research behind these books." The books were due to be flown to the United States for the California International Antiquarian Book Fair, but the Metropolitan Police confirmed that a "number of valuable books" had been taken in a commercial burglary between January 29 and 30, 2017. A warehouse in Feltham was broken into, and detectives are investigating. The theft was captured on the warehouse's CCTV cameras, showing a gang of thieves climbing onto the roof, cutting holes through reinforced skylights, and abseiling down to target four containers storing rare books. The thieves reportedly ignored other items, focusing on the books, and then placed the stolen works into holdalls, pulling them onto the roof using ropes before driving away in a van. The stolen books include a 1566 edition of "De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium" by Copernicus, a 1656 Galileo book titled "Opere di Galileo Galilei," and a 1506 edition of Dante's "Divine Comedy." The heist, described as "Mission Impossible"-style, has raised concerns about the rise in rare book thefts, with leading art lawyer Chris Marinello warning that criminals first try to cash out on these crimes, making it difficult to sell them as reputable dealers and collectors will not touch them. The next few days and weeks are crucial for the investigation, and the International League of Antiquarian Booksellers has published lists of the stolen books, urging anyone with information to contact the police.

The saga of illegally obtained nude photos of celebrities has taken a darker turn, with gymnast McKayla Maroney and MTV actress Liz Lee among the latest victims, reports reveal. According to Maroney's lawyers, the photos shared on the Reddit forum r/TheFappening, viewed by 130,000 people, constitute child pornography due to the gymnast's underage status when the photos were taken. The lawyers have demanded that the images be removed from Porn.com and other websites. Meanwhile, Reddit users have been sharing revenge-porn photos of Liz Lee, taken by her 16-year-old boyfriend before she turned 18. The ongoing leak, dubbed #CelebGate or "the Fappening," includes naked photos of A-listers like Jennifer Lawrence and Kate Upton, prompting outrage and legal threats from the women targeted. The Reddit community r/TheFappening has become the main hub for the leaked photos, despite Reddit's decision not to proactively delete links to them. In an urgent post, the subreddit’s moderators warn the community that the site’s admins have informed them that Maroney was underage in the photos and that they need to remove them quickly to avoid subreddit bans. The moderators also caution against sharing Lee’s photos. Redditors have begun panicking, discussing potential legal implications of possessing child pornography. Despite the proliferation of child pornography across the subreddit, Reddit admins have chosen not to ban the community, instead hiding it from r/all. The focus of the subreddit is the potential ramifications community members may face for downloading and sharing child porn. Some Redditors are using the site to instruct one another on how to erase evidence of their criminal activity. The leak's origins remain unclear, with Apple denying early reports that hackers gained access through a vulnerability in iCloud. The bizarre silver lining to the scandal: Redditors have donated thousands of dollars to the Prostate Cancer Foundation in Jennifer Lawrence's honor, a move that only adds to the subreddit's questionable reputation.

France has seen a disturbing rise in infanticide cases over the past three decades, with several high-profile incidents involving mothers allegedly killing newborns and hiding their bodies. In the most notorious case, Vï¿½ronique Courjault, now 41, admitted to murdering three babies and keeping their bodies in a freezer. Other cases include Jean-Pierre and Rolande Leymarie, who were jailed for killing seven newborns, and Rosita Garnier, who murdered three infants. These cases deviate from the typical U.S. pattern, where the mother is usually young and conceals the pregnancy from her parents before killing the child. Experts suggest pregnancy denial, a psychiatric condition where a woman either doesn't realize or cannot accept she's having a baby, as a possible explanation. This condition can result from previous trauma or nonphysical factors, leading women to view the child as an inconvenience and sometimes killing it. The phenomenon raises questions about the broader societal factors that may contribute to this troubling trend.

The world's ugliest color, Pantone 448C, has been chosen to discourage smoking in Australia and other countries. This drab, dark brown hue, dubbed "opaque couché," was selected after three months of research by the marketing firm GfK Bluemoon, which was hired by the Australian government to find a color that would repel smokers. The color was chosen based on its association with negative terms such as "dirty," "tar," and "death." Now, the UK, Ireland, and France have also adopted similar packaging laws, using the same color for their cigarette boxes. The Australian government hopes that this color, combined with graphic health warnings, will reduce smoking rates. The color was chosen through extensive studies involving over 1,000 smokers, who found it to be the most unappealing among options like lime green, beige, white, mustard, and medium olive. The new packaging has already shown promising results in Australia, with tobacco sales declining. The move to plain packaging, using the world's ugliest color, is seen as a significant step in the global fight against smoking. However, not everyone agrees on the color's effectiveness; some find it appealing, while others see it as a necessary measure to combat the health risks associated with smoking. The use of this color in cigarette packaging highlights the ongoing efforts to reduce smoking rates through innovative and sometimes unconventional methods.

A digital director named Cassie Young faced an encounter with a personal trainer who attempted to body-shame her for declining his weight-loss services. The trainer, who remains unnamed, offered to help Young get in shape for her upcoming wedding, suggesting that she should hire someone to ensure she looked her best in her wedding photos. Young politely declined, explaining that she was already happy with her body. However, the trainer's comments took an odd and unwelcome turn, as he began to shame her for not trying to "look her best" in her wedding photos. Young responded by sharing the conversation on Facebook, where she emphasized that one's appearance does not define their self-worth. She wrote, "Life is waiting for you. It's too short to be spent worrying about a belly roll. Go be happy and live it to your fullest."

The post went viral, garnering support from other Facebook users who were disgusted by the trainer's tactics. Young, who has shared her past struggles with body acceptance, explained that it had taken her a long time to love her body, having battled past insecurities and being reminded of her weight. She stated, "I’m sad for you that your self-worth is wrapped up in your appearance. You clearly place a lot of stock in looks but fail to understand that not everyone wants to be chained to that insecurity." The trainer's comments were seen as an attempt to undermine Young's hard-won body-positivity and plant a seed of doubt in her mind during a significant life event.

Young's experience highlights the ongoing issue of body shaming and the importance of self-acceptance. She emphasized that her decision to wear clothes that fit and have modeling photos taken was a step towards rejecting societal pressures and embracing her inner health goals. Despite the trainer's comments, Young refused to publicly name him, stating, "No one should be vilified because they’re ignorant." Her post serves as a powerful reminder that everyone, regardless of their body type, deserves to be treated with respect and love.

Moses Malone, a three-time NBA MVP and one of basketball's most ferocious rebounders, passed away at the age of 60. His impact on the Philadelphia 76ers was profound, as he led the team to its only championship since 1967. In his first season with the Sixers, Malone won MVP honors, averaging 24.5 points and 15.3 rebounds, and the team compiled a 65-17 record. During the 13 playoff games, Malone averaged 26 points and 15.8 rebounds, earning Finals MVP. Billy Cunningham, the head coach at the time, emphasized the physical presence Malone brought to the team, noting that the Sixers needed that presence to reach the next level. Cunningham recalled that Malone was 100% committed to their playing style, expecting him to rebound defensively and get the ball out for fast breaks. Malone's contributions extended beyond the court, as his jovial personality and sense of humor endeared him to fans. His career spanned 19 seasons, during which he was a 12-time NBA All-Star, won three MVPs, and led the league in rebounding six times. The Sixers CEO, Scott O'Neil, expressed deep sadness over Malone's passing, calling him a genuine icon and pillar of the most storied era in the history of the Philadelphia 76ers. Malone's legacy includes his career as the NBA's career leader in offensive rebounds and his induction into the Naismith Memorial Hall of Fame in 2001. His death marks the loss of a basketball legend and a beloved figure in Philadelphia.

Kate Gosselin, once a reality TV star, has landed a new job as a coupon blogger for CouponCabin.com, offering money-saving advice on topics like holiday shopping and stretching budgets for large families. This move marks a shift away from her TV career and provides a way to support her eight children. While some may view this as a step down, it also offers Gosselin a chance to use her expertise in practical ways and potentially find new opportunities. Her first post will focus on navigating Black Friday. This change could be seen as a positive development, keeping Gosselin off TV and providing her with a new platform to share her insights.

Six Sydney women, not bridesmaids, found themselves in a fashion faux pas at a wedding reception, all wearing the same A$160 ($95) dress, sparking amusement and confusion among guests and social media users. The incident, which resembled the 1993 Alan Ball play, Five Women Wearing The Same Dress, unfolded when cousin Debbie Speranza and her friends walked into the reception and saw each other in identical outfits, leading to further discoveries of more women in the same dress. The photo of the six women, dubbed "#backupbridesmaids," quickly gained traction, receiving over 39,000 likes and 9,500 comments on Facebook. The women, initially taken aback by the coincidence, decided to embrace the situation, bonding and dancing the night away. Debbie Speranza humorously noted the improbability of the event, writing, "Imagine the odds," on a post to fashion brand Forever New's Facebook page. The story resonated with many, with friends sharing their own experiences of wearing the same dress as others, some even more dramatically, like Chantel Lopex-Rubio, who found her expensive frock resembled curtains. The incident turned out to be a lighthearted and memorable moment for the women, proving that sometimes, coincidences can lead to unexpected connections and laughter.

Rafe Esquith, a celebrated and decorated elementary school teacher in Los Angeles, has been accused of sexual misconduct, leading to a wave of controversy and outrage. For over three decades, Esquith taught fifth grade at Hobart Elementary School, a high-poverty school with a high percentage of English-language learners. His "Hobart Shakespeareans" nonprofit, which produced an annual Shakespeare play, gained international recognition and earned him numerous awards, including the National Medal of the Arts, Oprah Winfrey’s Use Your Life Award, and the Dalai Lama’s Compassion in Action Award. However, the Los Angeles Unified School District released 66-page documents detailing allegations of inappropriate behavior, including making jokes about nudity, encouraging students to view porn, and making sexually explicit comments to students. The documents also describe incidents of physical contact, such as spanking and tickling, and sending grotesque emails to students. Despite these allegations, Esquith has not been charged with a crime. His lawyer accused the school district of constructing a "fraudulent narrative" and filed a $1 billion class-action lawsuit on behalf of approximately 2,000 LAUSD teachers who were removed from the classroom for unclear reasons, alleging an age-discrimination scheme. The case raises questions about the handling of teacher misconduct and the impact on the careers of educators facing such allegations.

Gwyneth Paltrow, 38, and mother of two, showcases her toned and stretch-mark-free body in a topless photoshoot for Vanity Fair. Wearing only Louis Vuitton jewelry and fishnet tights, she poses demurely, her hair in a French twist and makeup natural. Paltrow, known for her strict yoga and healthy eating routine, maintains her youthful appearance through dedication. Her lifestyle website, GOOP, offers advice on leading a better life, though it faces criticism for being unrealistic. The photos highlight her commitment to health and wellness, despite her busy acting and parenting schedule.

A 25-year-old woman riding a Divvy bike in Chicago's Avondale neighborhood died in a collision with a flatbed truck, believed to be the first fatality involving U.S. bike-share programs. The crash occurred near Sacramento and Belmont avenues, with the truck and the woman's bike both turning east at Belmont from northbound Sacramento. The woman was taken to Advocate Illinois Masonic Medical Center in critical condition but was later pronounced dead. Virginia Murray, 25, from the Wicker Park neighborhood, was identified as the victim. This incident marks the first known bike-share fatality in the U.S., occurring in a city that has seen nearly 8 million rides on the Divvy system since its introduction in June 2013.

The Chicago Department of Transportation and Divvy issued a statement expressing condolences to the rider’s family and loved ones. Advocacy groups, such as the Active Transportation Alliance, emphasized the need for improved infrastructure to enhance safety for all road users. The Alliance is looking forward to the release of the city’s “Vision Zero” plan, aiming to eliminate traffic fatalities. The police department’s Major Accident Investigation Unit was tasked with investigating the incident.

A study by the Mineta Transportation Institute, released in March, indicated that collision and injury rates among bike-sharing participants were lower than those among regular bicyclists. Factors contributing to this lower rate include the shared bike's bulky, heavy design, which limits speed and visibility, and discourages risky maneuvers. This design feature, along with the visibility of the bikes, helps mitigate the conditions that contribute to collisions. Bike-share programs have expanded to over 32,000 bikes in about 100 U.S. cities over the past nine years, including recent additions in Evanston and Oak Park. Despite the growth, bike-share deaths have occurred in other countries, such as Canada and Mexico.

The incident highlights the ongoing challenge of balancing the benefits of bike-share programs with the need for enhanced safety measures. The study's findings suggest that while bike-share systems can be safer for riders, they still pose risks, and the industry and city officials must continue to work towards safer infrastructure and practices.

DES MOINES, Iowa – Hillary Clinton learned her lesson: No rope lines in Iowa. In stark contrast to her 2008 campaign, when she was criticized for seeming too-cool-for-school to mingle with "everyday Americans," Clinton embraced the masses at the Iowa State Fair this weekend. She shook hands, took selfies, listened to personal stories, met a young boy’s show cow, and even munched on a pork chop. Clinton’s approach was a world of difference from her last White House bid, where she was seen as too distant. Given Iowa’s traditional early-state role in presidential elections, its residents are accustomed to, and expect, face-to-face interaction with political candidates. Clinton’s two-day sweep through the Hawkeye State this weekend showed she’s really trying to put her past problems behind her.

Clinton’s absence from the soapbox at the Iowa State Fair drew criticism. While Bernie Sanders got a large crowd, Clinton did not join him, prompting some to wonder why. Clinton’s supporters, however, saw a different side. “She’s doing it. Right here,” said Dan Fredericks of Boone, pointing to the ground. Clinton met with a 3-year-old girl named Quinn, whose mother asked for support to legalize medicinal marijuana. Clinton agreed that more research was needed. Clinton also ran into people she seemed to know, suggesting pre-planning by the campaign. She joked about a straw hat and raved about being a grandmother. By the time she left, Clinton had posed for 42 pictures with fans, many of them selfies.

At the fair, Clinton and her escort, former Sen. Tom Harkin (D-Iowa), chatted with a young boy holding a cow. Harkin praised Clinton for her public service, fighting for early childhood education and ensuring pay equity for women. Clinton addressed the email scandal, reiterating that she used her private account for convenience and vowing that she “never sent any classified material or received any marked classified.” She pushed back, saying it wasn’t something people talk to her about. Clinton’s visit was a stark contrast to her 2008 campaign, where she was criticized for being too cool. This time, she seemed to have fun, engaging with the crowd and showing a more approachable side.

Michael Schumacher's medical files, allegedly stolen from his hospital in Grenoble, are being offered for sale, his manager Sabine Kehm has announced. Kehm stated that the documents, which reportedly contain details of surgical procedures, have been offered for around €50,000 (£40,000) and have been for sale for several days. Kehm emphasized that the documents are clearly stolen and that the theft has been reported to the authorities. She warned that both the purchase and publication of such documents are forbidden and that criminal charges and damages will be pursued against any publication of the content or reference to the medical file. Schumacher, a 45-year-old former Formula One racing driver, sustained life-threatening injuries in a skiing accident in December and has been in hospital for nearly six months. He was transferred to University Hospital Lausanne in Switzerland last week after being kept in a medically induced coma for more than three months. The Grenoble hospital's media office stated that they have initiated an investigation, and a French prosecutor concluded that speed was not a factor in the accident.

At least nine undocumented immigrants have died after being found severely injured in a tractor-trailer parked outside a Walmart in Texas, according to federal authorities. The discovery came after a Walmart employee was approached by someone inside the trailer who asked for water. The employee provided water and then alerted police, who found eight bodies and 31 people suffering from heat injuries. The air conditioning in the trailer was not working, and the temperature in San Antonio was 100 degrees Fahrenheit on the day of the incident. Two of the injured victims were 15 years old. Authorities are investigating the incident, which they believe is a human trafficking case, and are reviewing surveillance video to determine the trailer's origin and how long it was parked at the Walmart. The driver, James Matthew Bradley Jr., 60, of Florida, has been taken into custody and faces state and federal charges. US Immigration and Customs Enforcement acting Director Thomas Homan emphasized the need to pursue and punish human smuggling networks, citing the case as a stark reminder of the issue. The incident has sparked calls for comprehensive immigration reform and renewed efforts to combat human trafficking.

The International Criminal Court (ICC) has initiated a preliminary investigation into allegations of crimes against humanity committed by Philippine President Rodrigo Duterte and other officials during the government's anti-drugs campaign. Fatou Bensouda, the ICC prosecutor, stated that the inquiry would assess whether there is sufficient evidence to build a case, focusing on events since July 1, 2016. The ICC's move is seen as a significant development, marking its first preliminary examination in a Southeast Asian nation. 

Philippine officials, including President Duterte, have expressed skepticism and disagreement with the ICC's decision. Duterte's spokesperson, Harry Roque, described the inquiry as a "waste of the court's time and resources," arguing that many of the allegations predate the Philippines' ratification of the ICC treaty in 2011. Roque also emphasized that domestic courts are functioning and willing to handle such matters. However, Bensouda specifically referenced killings since July 1, 2016, in her statement, suggesting that the ICC is not ignoring recent events.

The anti-drug campaign under Duterte has been marked by widespread violence, with official statistics showing that 4,000 people have been killed by police in anti-drug operations since Duterte took office. However, a 77-page report submitted by a Philippine lawyer, Jude Sabio, alleges that the death toll is over 8,000. The report details evidence of extrajudicial executions and mass murder over three decades, dating back to Duterte's time as mayor of Davao in 1988.

Opposition politicians and human rights groups have welcomed the ICC's decision, seeing it as a step toward accountability for the thousands of alleged victims of the anti-drug campaign. Gary Alejano, an opposition politician who tried to impeach Duterte last year, stated that the move offers "a ray of hope for the victims of his war on drugs, which is still ongoing." Alejano believes that the ICC can provide a platform for impartial investigation and prosecution, unlike domestic courts that are seen as complicit in covering up the crimes.

Duterte has long been critical of the ICC, calling it "bullshit" and "hypocritical," and has threatened to withdraw the Philippines' membership multiple times. Despite this, his administration has not taken any concrete steps to distance itself from the ICC's investigation. Human Rights Watch, which has been calling for an independent international investigation into Duterte's war on drugs, expressed support for the ICC's move, stating that it is essential to investigate the alleged crimes due to the lack of serious attempts to do so by domestic authorities.

The ICC defines crimes against humanity as "serious violations committed as part of a large-scale attack against any civilian population." Since its establishment in 2002, the court has received over 12,000 complaints or communications, with nine cases going to trial. The ICC's preliminary investigation into the Philippine anti-drugs campaign is seen as a critical step in addressing the human rights abuses and potential crimes against humanity that have occurred during the campaign.

Orexigen Therapeutics Inc. saw its stock surge after winning the first U.S. panel recommendation for its long-sought prescription diet pill, Contrave. Outside advisers to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) deemed the weight-loss benefits of Contrave to outweigh the risks of elevated pulse and blood pressure, allowing a large study on cardiovascular risk to wait until after the drug is approved. This decision came after Arena Pharmaceuticals Inc. and Vivus Inc. faced setbacks with their competing drugs, Qnexa and lorcaserin, respectively. Shares of Orexigen rose 84% to $8.77, while Vivus and Arena also saw gains. The approval of Contrave could be worth up to $1 billion in the U.S. market. However, the FDA may delay its decision until January 31 to address concerns about the drug's cardiovascular risks. The approval process highlights the challenges of developing a new weight-loss drug, as the FDA requires rigorous safety evaluations and long-term efficacy data.

Former Berkshire Hathaway executive David Sokol violated the company’s insider-trading rules and misled Warren Buffett when pitching an investment in Lubrizol, according to a scathing report from the company’s board. Sokol, who had a personal stake in Lubrizol worth about $10 million, recommended the company to Buffett as a potential takeover target. The board concluded that Sokol’s “misleadingly incomplete disclosures” violated his duty of candor to the company. Berkshire will cooperate with any government investigations and may sue Sokol to recover his $3 million trading profit from the $9 billion acquisition of Lubrizol. Sokol’s high-profile attorney disputes the board’s findings, arguing that Sokol acted with honesty and integrity. The report, which uses the term “violation” eleven times, may add fuel to an ongoing SEC probe of Sokol. Sokol, seen as a potential heir to Warren Buffett, has maintained he had no aspirations to the CEO role. The board’s statement is likely to relieve some pressure on Buffett as he faces questions about his oversight and faces criticism for not condemning Sokol’s stock trades.

Michele Bachmann's recent accusations against State Department aide Huma Abedin and Rep. Keith Ellison of Minnesota being tied to the Muslim Brotherhood have sparked a mixed reaction. While the Washington establishment swiftly condemned Bachmann's claims as a step too far, her base remains supportive. Bachmann's supporters, including Duane Halstad, a 69-year-old from Elk River, Minnesota, believe she is "the only one telling the truth." The controversy has galvanized Bachmann's base, making it harder for Democrats to unseat her. Bachmann's long-standing belief in the infiltration of the government by the Muslim Brotherhood, even before her intelligence committee role, has been bolstered by private briefings and information she claims to have. Her political star has risen once again on the far right, becoming an annoyance for House Republican leaders who say her conspiracy theories tarnish the party's brand. Meanwhile, Democrats are targeting Bachmann, with Jim Graves, a wealthy businessman, positioning himself as the moderate alternative. Bachmann's claims have also drawn criticism, with Republicans like John Boehner, John McCain, and Marco Rubio condemning her. Despite the backlash, Bachmann insists the matter needs to be investigated, citing a report from the Center for Security Policy that links anti-tax crusader Grover Norquist to the Muslim Brotherhood.

Actor Lou Ferrigno is recovering after a pneumonia vaccination went wrong, sharing his experience on social media. The 67-year-old, best known for his role as The Incredible Hulk, revealed on Instagram that he ended up in the hospital after receiving a pneumonia shot. He posted a photo of himself in a hospital gown with IVs in his arm, warning his 87,000 Instagram followers about the incident. "Went in for a pneumonia shot and landed up here with fluid in my bicep," he wrote, advising his fans to be cautious when receiving shots. Ferrigno also shared the news on his Instagram account, adding relevant hashtags. While his representatives did not immediately respond to PEOPLE’s request for comment, Lou Ferrigno's experience highlights the importance of proper vaccine administration. The CDC recommends two types of pneumonia vaccines for adults aged 65 and older, PCV13 and PPSV23, to avoid infections from pneumococcal diseases. Despite the complication, Ferrigno's acting career remains active, with recent roles in films such as The Avengers, Star Trek Continues, and Enter the Fire. Additionally, his reputation in bodybuilding and fitness has led to the creation of Ferrigno Fit, a family fitness program he co-founded with his daughter Shanna.

The Islamic Penal Code of the Islamic Republic of Iran, specifically Book Five, outlines a comprehensive framework for penalizing a wide array of offenses, from crimes against national and foreign security to public prudency and morality. This code, which has been adopted permanently and is not subject to experimental periods, details stringent punishments for offenses such as espionage, treason, and the production and distribution of counterfeit currency. It also covers crimes against individuals, such as murder, assault, and theft, with varying degrees of punishment based on the severity and circumstances of the crime. The code also addresses offenses related to family and property, including marriage fraud, bankruptcy, and breach of trust. Additionally, it includes provisions for offenses against public order, such as public consumption of alcohol, gambling, and tramping. The punishments range from fines and imprisonment to corporal punishment and, in severe cases, the death penalty. The code emphasizes the importance of maintaining public order, family values, and the sanctity of the state, reflecting the Islamic principles that underpin the legal system in Iran.

Chinese authorities confirmed a case of forced abortion in Shaanxi province, where a woman, Feng Jianmei, was compelled to terminate her seven-month pregnancy due to non-payment of a fine for violating the country's one-child policy. The Shaanxi provincial government acknowledged the case, stating it was "basically true," and vowed to take action against the perpetrators, though it did not specify who was responsible. The incident, which drew widespread condemnation online, highlights the ongoing enforcement of China's strict population control measures, despite the recent relaxation of the one-child policy to a two-child policy. Rights groups have long criticized the policy, alleging forced abortions and other coercive measures. The US State Department has also expressed opposition to China's coercive birth limitation policies, including forced abortions and sterilizations. The case has further damaged the image of China's family planning efforts and sparked outrage among internet users, many of whom compared the forced abortion to historical atrocities. The incident has reignited discussions about the human rights implications of China's population control policies and the need for more humane enforcement methods.

France is preparing to close its embassies and schools in 20 countries on Friday due to the publication of cartoons of the Prophet Muhammad by the satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo, a move aimed at preventing further escalation of tensions. The French weekly, known for its controversial and often provocative content, published the cartoons on Wednesday, featuring a cover with an Orthodox Jew pushing a turbaned figure in a wheelchair, along with several caricatures of the Prophet inside. The decision to close diplomatic missions and educational institutions stems from concerns that the cartoons could spark unrest, especially given the ongoing outrage over an anti-Islam film that has led to violent protests in several Muslim-majority countries.

The publication of these cartoons has drawn criticism from French authorities, who have sent riot police to protect the magazine's offices. French Prime Minister Jean-Marc Ayrault emphasized the importance of free speech while urging restraint, stating that anyone offended could take legal action. However, he also warned against provoking further tensions, saying, "Is it pertinent, intelligent, in this context to pour oil on the fire? The answer is no." The government has called for calm and has stated that a planned protest against the film in Paris will not be authorized.

The move by Charlie Hebdo to publish such content is not without precedent. The magazine's offices were firebombed last year after it released an edition "guest-edited" by the Prophet Muhammad, which was titled Sharia Hebdo. This incident led to an ongoing investigation. The publication of the new cartoons has prompted immediate calls from political and religious leaders for responsible behavior and calm, with the senior cleric at Paris's biggest mosque, Dalil Boubakeur, urging Muslims to avoid exacerbating tensions.

The French government's decision to close embassies and schools is part of a broader effort to manage the delicate situation, balancing the protection of diplomatic and educational institutions with the need to avoid inflaming the current tensions. As the world watches, the French government faces the challenge of navigating the complex interplay between free speech and religious sensitivities.

Catherine Zeta-Jones, 41, has checked into a mental health facility for a brief stay to treat her Bipolar II Disorder, her publicist confirms. After dealing with the stress of the past year, including her husband Michael Douglas' throat cancer diagnosis and legal battles, Zeta-Jones has found herself in need of expert care. Zeta-Jones, who has been by Douglas' side through his treatment, has been outspoken about her frustration with the delayed diagnosis. Douglas' ex-wife also sued him for profits from his "Wall Street" sequel, adding to the stress. Zeta-Jones' rep says, "She's feeling great and looking forward to starting work this week on her two upcoming films." The stress has taken a toll, but Zeta-Jones and Douglas have grown closer, with Douglas noting a new appreciation for life and loved ones.

Vanderbilt University has taken steps to rename Confederate Memorial Hall, a residence hall on its campus that has long been a source of controversy. The university's chancellor, Nicholas S. Zeppos, announced that the building will be renamed Memorial Hall, effective immediately, after raising $1.2 million to repay a 1933 donation from the United Daughters of the Confederacy. The original name, which has been on the building since its construction in 1935, was a symbol that many found deeply offensive and painful. Vanderbilt first attempted to rename the building in 2002 but faced legal challenges from the United Daughters of the Confederacy, which sued to keep the original name. The Tennessee appeals court ruled in 2005 that Vanderbilt could only remove the "Confederate" designation after repaying the donation at its current value. Anonymous donors provided the necessary funds, and the Vanderbilt Board of Trust approved the move this summer.

The decision to rename the building reflects a broader trend among universities to address the legacy of racism and slavery on their campuses. Vanderbilt's announcement comes as other institutions, such as Middle Tennessee State University, grapple with similar issues. MTSU is considering removing the name of Nathan Bedford Forrest, a founder of the Ku Klux Klan, from a campus building. Forrest's name is now facing scrutiny due to his involvement in the slave trade and his role in the formation of the KKK. The Tennessee Board of Regents has approved the change, but it still needs to be approved by a state panel.

Chancellor Zeppos emphasized that the name change is not an attempt to erase history but to create a more inclusive environment for all students. "We are not saying this is not part of Vanderbilt's history," he stated. "I think we teach history by how we talk about these events." The move has been praised by student leaders, such as Ariana Fowler, president of Vanderbilt Student Government, who commended the administration for addressing student concerns and setting a precedent for diversity and inclusion.

The renaming process also highlights the ongoing debate over Confederate symbols and their place in public spaces. In Tennessee, a new law has made it more difficult to remove Confederate symbols and statues from public places, complicating efforts to address historical legacies. Vanderbilt's decision to remove the Confederate name from its building represents a significant step in the university's commitment to fostering an inclusive environment and addressing the complex issues surrounding its history.

Congressional leaders and President Barack Obama called for a return to negotiations to avert the so-called fiscal cliff, a day after talks cratered in a very public fashion when Republicans abandoned House Speaker John Boehner's backup plan. The negotiations had already broken down Monday afternoon in the office of Mr. Boehner, a Wall Street Journal reconstruction shows. Mr. Boehner, irritated with the White House, was finding it hard to keep his troops in line as details of his negotiations with Mr. Obama leaked out. One by one, his top lieutenants came out in favor of Plan B and against the broader deal. House Ways and Means Chairman Dave Camp said the new tax revenue the broader plan called for was too high. Then Budget Chairman Paul Ryan said he couldn't sign on because it didn't make structural changes in entitlements. The speaker went ahead with Plan B, which collapsed Thursday night before he could even bring it to a vote, leaving talks at a perilous standstill just days before the year-end fiscal-cliff deadline. Even if an agreement can be reached by then, both sides expect it to be a small package doing little to tackle the long-term budget woes and deferring the battle until next year. The problems lay in Mr. Boehner's inability to coax his rank-and-file to support a deal that raises taxes on higher-income Americans. Another factor was what Republicans saw as President Obama's unwillingness to bend when a deal was in sight, jamming the speaker with a deal his party couldn't swallow. The negotiations offer little evidence November's election brought the president and House Republicans closer together. If anything, the talks poisoned an already distrustful relationship. Mr. Boehner could soon face a decision whether to call for a vote on some sort of plan that could avert the cliff's spending cuts and tax increases but might imperil his position if he had to rely on Democrats to pass it. Mr. Obama repeatedly lost patience with the speaker as negotiations faltered. In an Oval Office meeting last week, he told Mr. Boehner that if the sides didn't reach agreement, he would use his inaugural address and his State of the Union speech to tell the country the Republicans were at fault. After the election, Boehner aides tried to shape the debate by offering early concessions, including that the GOP would agree to raise new tax revenue. A speech Mr. Boehner planned to give was rewritten 18 times and included input from top Republican leaders. He and Mr. Obama didn't sit down together for another 10 days. The session began genially. But tension quickly emerged over the president's call to include increasing the U.S.'s borrowing limit in any final package. Responded Mr. Boehner: "I've found in my life that everything I've ever wanted has come with a price." Mr. Obama told the speaker he wasn't willing to play games with the debt ceiling. Staffs got to work on the outline of a deal. In their first offer, Republicans wanted to essentially preserve Bush-era rates set to expire Dec. 31 while raising some new revenue through a tax overhaul in 2013. The White House made clear it wouldn't agree to a plan that didn't raise some tax rates immediately. Brett Loper, the speaker's top policy aide, prodded White House officials to look for tax revenue elsewhere. In phone calls and meetings, he steered them to tax shelters and suggested limiting deductions for tax-exempt municipal bonds. National Economic Council Director Gene Sperling told Mr. Loper it was impossible to hit revenue targets without raising tax rates. At one point, Mr. Loper said, "I'm asking you for help. Are you going to help me or not?" The quest to avert the fiscal cliff is as uncertain as ever after rival plans were rejected.

Pregnant women typically undergo routine anatomy scans at 20 weeks, but for Kristine Barry and her husband Christopher Havill, this routine procedure revealed their unborn baby Sebastian Havill had a life-threatening congenital heart defect. Doctors at the Hospital for Sick Children and Mount Sinai Hospital in Toronto diagnosed Sebastian with severe complete transposition of the great arteries (TGA), a condition where the pulmonary artery and aorta are switched, preventing the heart from circulating blood properly. The Barrys were assured by doctors that they could fix the issue through in-utero surgery. 

Sebastian's heart had all its walls closed, meaning he would not receive oxygen after birth, leading to potential severe brain damage or death within minutes. Doctors at Mount Sinai Hospital and Sick Kids Hospital devised a plan to perform the world’s first in-utero balloon atrial septoplasty to treat TGA. On May 18, Barry underwent the procedure, with doctors using ultrasound guidance to insert a needle into Sebastian’s heart to inflate a tiny balloon, creating a hole in the atrial septum to allow blood and oxygen to circulate properly. The surgery was successful, and Barry gave birth to a healthy Sebastian five days later. 

Sebastian underwent a second balloon atrial septoplasty after birth and then had open-heart surgery to switch his aorta and pulmonary artery into their proper positions. Now a two-month-old, Sebastian is healthy and meeting all his developmental milestones. The Barrys credit the doctors at both hospitals for saving their son’s life and allowing him to lead a normal life. The in-utero surgery provided a safe and effective alternative to the high-risk emergency cesarean section that would have been necessary otherwise, ensuring Sebastian’s survival and a normal birth.

A man named Grim LeRogue, who legally changed his name from Joe Rogan, caused a commotion at Yankee Stadium by running onto the field during a game between the Yankees and the Texas Rangers. His actions were fueled by a bizarre mix of jealousy and admiration for Cameron Diaz, whom he reportedly admires and wants to be with. LeRogue carried five photographs, including one of Alex Rodriguez with an X over his face and a gun pointed at his head, along with a message: "You have to go bud, you've ruined too many of our white queens." He also had a picture of Diaz with the message: "We will be together soon." Adding to the bizarre nature of the incident, LeRogue was holding images of Osama bin Laden and Whitney Houston. The al Qaeda leader's picture bore the inscription, "I will serve you," and a caption describing him as his "master." LeRogue's mother expressed disbelief at her son's actions, noting that he had a history of assault and burglary but was 33 years old at the time. He was charged with assault and interfering with a sporting event and taken to Lincoln Hospital for a psychiatric evaluation.

The San Francisco home famous for its role in the 1993 film "Mrs. Doubtfire" was the target of a suspicious fire on Monday night. According to authorities, someone tried to set fire to the home's garage door and front door, possibly using an accelerant like gasoline. The incident occurred around 8 p.m., and police remained on the scene until after 11 p.m. No suspects have been identified. The home, located on Broadway and Steiner Street, has regained notoriety since Robin Williams' death in August 2014, with fans leaving flowers and notes outside. The current owner, Dr. Douglas Ousterhout, a pioneer in facial feminization surgeries, told police he is having problems with a former client, but is unsure of the suspect's identity. The fire department is investigating the incident, and police are urging the public to come forward with any information that could help solve the case. The house, which served as a makeshift memorial site following Williams' death, now faces another troubling chapter.

Richard Carpenter, representing the Carpenters' estate, has filed a lawsuit against Universal Music Group and A&M Records, alleging that the music companies have underpaid them in digital royalties. The lawsuit claims that the record labels have improperly classified revenue from digital downloads of The Carpenters' music as sales of records rather than licensing revenue, resulting in a lower royalty rate. Additionally, the lawsuit alleges that the defendants undercounted digital downloads and applied an incorrect base price to the sales of CDs. The Carpenters are seeking compensatory damages of at least $2 million. According to the lawsuit, the dispute is similar to litigation involving Eminem, where the 9th Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that digital downloads are a licensing of master recordings rather than a sale of records. Richard Carpenter stated, "I regret that I have been unable to amicably resolve this serious royalty dispute with Universal and A&M. The Carpenters' recordings are among the best sellers in the history of popular music and after 48 years continue to contribute a substantial amount to UMG/A&M's annual bottom line. It seems only fair that these companies account fairly to my sister's estate and to me." The Carpenters are represented by Larry Iser and Greg Gabriel at Kinsella Weitzman Iser Kump & Aldisert. Universal Music Group did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The tragic downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight MH17 over Ukraine has sent shockwaves through the global AIDS research community, with the loss of numerous key figures and researchers en route to the 20th International AIDS Conference in Melbourne. The International AIDS Society (IAS) and other organizers are grappling with the loss of colleagues and friends, with the IAS expressing "sincere sadness" and offering condolences to the loved ones of the victims. Among the deceased is renowned HIV researcher Joep Lange, who had been working for 30 years to combat the epidemic. His friend Seema Yasmin described him as a "kind man and a true humanitarian," while former IAS President Chris Beyrer lamented that "the HIV/AIDS movement has truly lost a giant." The conference, which was set to feature prominent speakers including former US President Bill Clinton and Bob Geldof, now faces a somber and sombre mood. The loss of 27 Australians and other attendees has also cast a pall over the event, with US Ambassador John Berry expressing deep sympathy. The tragedy has also highlighted the ongoing conflict in Ukraine, with Russian-backed rebels delaying the recovery of victims' bodies and the handover of the plane's black boxes. The EU and US are pressuring Russia to cooperate fully with the investigation, while France faces criticism for continuing a controversial arms deal with Moscow. The incident has reignited debates about the balance between trade and security, with Lithuania's President Dalia Grybauskaite warning that the EU is "Mistralising" its values to protect business ties. As the world mourns the loss of key figures in the fight against HIV/AIDS, the conference organizers and attendees are left to grapple with the reality of a community that has lost many of its brightest minds.

In Washington, D.C., a debate over customer rights and coffee preferences has sparked controversy at Chinatown Coffee Co., where a barista refused to make an espresso-over-ice drink for a customer. The incident, documented in a Yelp review, highlights the tension between customer expectations and café policies. The barista, citing concerns about the quality of the espresso, refused the request, leading to a brief but heated exchange. This situation echoes a similar incident in 2008 at Murky Coffee, where a customer, Jeff Simmermon, challenged the barista's refusal and poured the espresso into ice, making a viral statement. The debate centers on whether customers should be able to order drinks in unconventional ways and whether coffee shops have the right to dictate how customers consume their beverages. The incident has reignited discussions about the balance between customer autonomy and café standards, potentially influencing how independent coffee shops handle such requests in the future.

A 2006 letter from Cardinal Leonardo Sandri, a top Vatican official, confirms that the Holy See received information in 2000 about the sexual misconduct of now-resigned U.S. Cardinal Theodore McCarrick, lending credibility to accusations of a cover-up at the highest echelons of the Roman Catholic Church. The letter, published by Catholic News Service, mentions a 2000 letter from Father Boniface Ramsay to the then-Apostolic Nuncio in the United States, Archbishop Gabriel Montalvo, reporting complaints from seminarians about McCarrick's inappropriate behavior. Sandri, who was the No. 3 in the Vatican's secretariat of state at the time, wrote Ramsay on Oct. 11, 2006, seeking his recommendation for a former seminarian for a Vatican job, citing the 2000 letter as relevant. This corroborates claims made by Archbishop Carlo Maria Vigano, who served as nuncio to the United States from 2011 to 2016, that the Vatican was informed of McCarrick's misconduct as early as 2000. Vigano accused church officials, including Pope Francis, of failing to act on accusations of sexual abuse and abuse of power by McCarrick. McCarrick resigned as a cardinal in July after a U.S. church investigation found credible an allegation that he groped a teenage altar boy in the 1970s. Since then, several former seminarians have come forward to say that McCarrick routinely invited them to his beach house and into his bed. The letter from Sandri suggests that the Vatican was aware of the allegations and their severity, yet did not act on them for years. This revelation adds to the ongoing scandal of sexual abuse within the Catholic Church and the handling of such cases by church officials.

Steven Spielberg's "Bridge of Spies" is a nuanced and deliberate Cold War thriller that challenges the audience to follow its intricate plot and thematic layers. The film, based on the true story of James B. Donovan, a Brooklyn insurance lawyer, is a slow-burn that rewards multiple viewings. Donovan is tasked with representing Soviet spy Rudolf Abel and later negotiating the release of Francis Gary Powers, the U-2 pilot shot down over Soviet territory. Tom Hanks delivers a nuanced performance as the everyman lawyer, embodying modesty, high principles, and simple fairness. His quiet heroism is the emotional core of the film, which explores themes of patriotism, honor, and duty. Mark Rylance, making his American film debut, steals the show as Abel, a Soviet agent portrayed with subtle and complex humanity. The film's cinematography, by Janusz Kaminski, and production design, by Adam Stockhausen, create a somber and atmospheric Cold War backdrop. While the narrative occasionally falters in East Germany, the film's strength lies in its exploration of moral ambiguity and the personal cost of political decisions. "Bridge of Spies" is a testament to Spielberg's ability to craft a lean, purposeful narrative that resonates with contemporary issues. Critics praise the film for its thoughtful script, strong performances, and Spielberg's masterful direction, which balances historical accuracy with a compelling human story. The film's pacing and thematic depth make it a must-see for those interested in both Cold War history and well-crafted cinema.

Two more suspected drug-smuggling tunnels connecting warehouses in Tijuana and San Diego have been uncovered, marking the sixth and seventh super tunnels found between the two cities since 2010. The first tunnel, discovered in an industrial park in San Diego's Otay Mesa section, was approximately 600 yards long, 70 feet underground, and equipped with lighting, a crude rail system, and wooden trusses. The second, more sophisticated passage, unearthed in Otay Mesa by Mexican investigators, stretched about 700 yards and featured a multi-tiered electric rail system and ventilation equipment. No drugs or other contraband were found in the tunnels or the warehouses on either side of the border. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement announced the discoveries on Friday. Glennys Rodriguez, a 73-year-old U.S. citizen from Chula Vista, was arrested on Wednesday and accused of overseeing logistics for one of the tunnels. She faces federal charges of conspiring with others to maintain a drug-involved premises. The busts eliminated a multi-million dollar drug-smuggling venture and have reduced it to "a colossal waste of money on the part of the drug cartels," according to the Drug Enforcement Administration's San Diego special agent in charge, William Sherman. Since 2006, more than 80 cross-border tunnels in various stages of construction have been found, mostly in California and Arizona. Authorities have found similar settings outside other tunnels, with operators hiring people to occasionally visit the property to make it appear normal to neighbors. The quantity of drugs successfully channeled through the tunnels found this week is unknown.

Ivanka Trump used a personal email account to send hundreds of official White House-related messages last year, according to officials. The Washington Post reported that while most of the emails contained logistical and personal information, some may have violated federal records rules. Trump's lawyer stated she stopped using her personal account for government work after being briefed on the rules. However, critics argue that her practices mirror those of Hillary Clinton, who faced intense scrutiny for her private email server during the 2016 campaign. White House ethics officials learned of Trump’s email use when reviewing emails gathered to respond to a public records lawsuit. Some advisers were alarmed by the volume of official emails sent via personal accounts, fearing a similarity to Clinton's case. Trump's emails did not contain classified information, her lawyer said, and she turned over all relevant emails for preservation. Critics, including Austin Evers from American Oversight, argue that the Trump family is not above the law and that Congress should investigate. The revelation comes as Trump supporters still chant "Lock her up!" at rallies, echoing her father's criticism of Clinton's email practices.

Thais, dressed in black, form long lines outside the Grand Palace to sign condolence books, marking the start of a year-long mourning period for their late King Bhumibol Adulyadej. The Commerce Ministry has warned traders against exploiting the situation by raising prices on black mourning attire. Officials have instructed provincial offices to monitor the market for any price gouging, ensuring supplies of black and white fabric remain available. In Bangkok, traders at wholesale markets, such as Bo Bae and Pratunam, report brisk business, with most customers purchasing black shirts. Despite price increases, many Thais remain focused on their duty to mourn rather than the cost. The government has declared a year of mourning, urging citizens to wear black or white and cancel outdoor festivities for the first 30 days. The Ministry of Commerce has dispatched inspectors to ensure traders adhere to price regulations, with violators facing up to seven years in jail and fines of up to 140,000 baht. As the nation grapples with the loss of its beloved monarch, the focus remains on honoring his memory through traditional practices and adherence to government guidelines.

Many Afghan army units are running out of key equipment, including Humvees, due to their inability to repair or find replacements. After a tough fighting season, Afghan soldiers are finding that a significant portion of their vital equipment is broken and cannot be easily replaced. The Afghan soldiers could not fix any of them, and replacements hadn't come. Seventy-five percent of the battalion's armored vehicles were out of commission. Some soldiers walked for 20 hours to get from base to base. The U.S. military shouldered that responsibility for years. But just as the Afghan army started doing the bulk of the fighting, the Americans stopped repairing Afghan equipment. Afghan commanders are now taking stock of how many vehicles they have lost during the fighting season, which typically lasts from spring until fall, when many Taliban commanders return to Pakistan. Afghan commanders are concerned about how to repair or replace their equipment before the next fighting season, as it could wipe out what's left of their vehicles. The Afghan Defense Ministry has acknowledged the problems but has not provided a solution. The U.S. military has praised the Afghans for their resilience but has not provided spare parts or support. The Afghan army is also facing procurement troubles, such as a lack of rockets that can be used with the launchers they were provided. The Afghan army is also running out of boots and other essential supplies. The U.S. officials say they are aware of the Afghan security forces' logistical problems but that they have seen signs of improvement. NATO forces are redoubling efforts to improve supply processes and prevent waste and fraud in the Afghan Defense Ministry. However, the push comes as the Americans are rapidly withdrawing from Afghanistan, removing advisers working with Afghan battalions and attaching them to higher levels of leadership. At those more-senior levels, officials say, these advisers will be able to identify and monitor systemic problems. But they are less likely to assist when a battalion or platoon is handicapped by an isolated logistical issue, particularly compared with a few years ago, when the Americans were fixing Afghan vehicles themselves. The U.S. is leaving heaps of scrap in Afghanistan, including treadmills, air-conditioning units, and other rudimentary appliances, which are being destroyed before they are offered to the Afghan people to ensure that they are not used to make roadside bombs. The equipment is being destroyed before it is offered to the Afghan people, as many non-military items have timing equipment or other components that can pose a threat. The U.S. is leaving heaps of mattresses, barbed wire, and shipping containers in scrap yards near its shrinking bases. The Bagram scrap yard is owned by Feda Mohammad Ulfat, who helped build the neighboring base more than a decade ago, transporting gravel and concrete. Now Ulfat is helping to dismantle the base, taking in thousands of pounds of American scrap metal every day. Some of the scrap still shows signs of its previous owners, such as vehicles spray-painted with American names, mattresses sunken from 12 years of use, and bumper stickers from Hawaii or Oklahoma. The U.S. drawdown has reached a fever pitch, with dozens of bases being closed, and suddenly, a torrent of scrap metal was being delivered to Ulfat’s farm. The Pentagon has budgeted $5 billion to $7 billion to ship gear back to the United States, but that sum isn’t enough to take everything currently in Afghanistan. Wanting at least a small return on its investment, the U.S. military decided to sell the leftovers for pennies on the pound.
