This incident highlights the dangers of leaving children unattended near firearms and the importance of proper gun storage.

Drew Peterson, the former Bolingbrook police sergeant, is on trial for the murder of his third wife, Kathleen Savio, whose body was found in a bathtub in 2004. A friend of Savio's, Mary Parks, testified that Savio once told her that Peterson had grabbed her by the throat and asked, "Why don't you just die?" during a conversation in 2003. Savio also mentioned that Peterson had told her he could kill her and make it look like an accident. Parks described seeing dark red bruises on Savio's neck, which she believed were from the attack. The testimony, which included graphic details of Savio's alleged assault, was part of the prosecution's case, as physical evidence from the initial investigation was lacking. Peterson, now 58, has pleaded not guilty. The trial has seen other testimonies, including that of Savio's friend Kristen Anderson, who said Savio kept a knife under her mattress for protection. Peterson's defense team has questioned the consistency of the testimonies, but the judge has allowed the hearsay evidence, potentially bolstering the prosecution's case. The trial continues, with the defense expressing disappointment in the judge's rulings.

The master sommelier examination, often called "the hardest test you've never heard of," has a long and prestigious history, with only 274 people having passed it since its inception in 1969. This year, 24 individuals successfully earned the coveted title, but the joy of their achievement was marred by a significant scandal. The Court of Master Sommeliers, Americas announced that the results of the tasting portion of the 2018 examination would be invalidated due to a breach of confidentiality. According to the board chairman, Devon Broglie, MS, a member of the Court disclosed detailed information about the wines to be tasted, compromising the integrity of the exam. As a result, 23 of the 24 newly minted master sommeliers, including four based in the Bay Area, had their titles rescinded. The affected candidates will have two opportunities to retake the tasting exam, with all related fees refunded. The decision was made to protect the reputation of the master sommelier title and maintain the high standards of the examination process. The Court of Master Sommeliers, Americas, which administers the exam, is known for its rigorous and demanding process, with candidates required to pass multiple stages, including theory, practical service, and the challenging blind tasting. The exam, which tests the ability to identify and describe wines accurately, is seen as a pinnacle of wine expertise. The news has sent shockwaves through the sommelier community, highlighting the dedication and years of preparation required to pass the exam. The integrity of the examination process is paramount, as the title Master Sommelier is highly respected in the hospitality industry.

A chilling sequence of events unfolded in a Fort Bend County home, leading to the tragic deaths of a mother and her two daughters. The Fort Bend County Sheriff's Office released 911 calls that captured the harrowing moments before the shooting. In the first call, 17-year-old Madison Sheats pleaded, “Please forgive me, I'm sorry,” and “Please don't shoot, I'm sorry.” Her father, Jason Sheats, could be heard saying, “I promise you, whatever you want,” before the call ended. In the second call, Taylor Sheats’ voice was heard, but the words were indistinct. The third call, made by a neighbor, provided a vivid account of the shooting. He described seeing the mother, Christy Sheats, chasing her daughters outside the home and then standing over them, trying to fire more shots. After the gun was empty, she went back inside to reload, only to return and shoot Taylor again from behind. The neighbor heard more gunshots and then saw law enforcement officers arrive. A Fulshear police officer shot and killed Christy Sheats after she refused to drop her weapon. The daughters, Taylor, 22, and Madison, 17, died of gunshot wounds. Jason Sheats, 45, was unharmed but was taken to the hospital as a precaution. A family friend, Madison Davey, 21, revealed that Christy Sheats had a history of mental illness, having been hospitalized several times after suicide attempts. The Sheats family had been the subject of 14 calls to the Fort Bend County Sheriff's Office over the past four years, including three suicide attempts. The shooting occurred on Jason Sheats' birthday, and Taylor was set to be married on Monday. Taylor had planned to marry her long-term boyfriend, Juan Sebastian Lugo, at the courthouse. Madison was an incoming senior at Seven Lakes High School. The incident has left the community in shock, with neighbors expressing disbelief and sorrow. "That is one of the saddest things I've ever heard," said a neighbor. "That's horrible. ... Just terrible." The tragic events have sparked discussions about mental health and the complexities of family dynamics.

The search continues for Phylicia Simone Barnes, a 16-year-old honor student from Monroe, North Carolina, who went missing in Baltimore three days after Christmas. Phylicia, described as a 5-foot-8-inch, straight-A African-American student, was last seen on December 28th via Facebook, where she posted that she was visiting her half-sister's apartment with her sister's boyfriend. Her disappearance has garnered little media attention, raising concerns about a potential double-standard in how cases involving African-American victims are covered. Her father, Russell Barnes, vowed to "turn this city upside down" to find her, while Baltimore police have deployed FBI helicopters and obtained additional security footage but have yet to find any clues. The investigation is focusing on two scenarios: abduction or murder. The case has highlighted the frustration of local authorities, who believe the national media should give more attention to the case, comparing it to the Natalee Holloway disappearance. The Baltimore Mayor's office expressed concern about the possible double-standard and emphasized the heartbreaking nature of the case. Over 9,000 people have joined a Facebook page praying for Phylicia's safe return, and a vigil was held at her school. Despite the efforts, time is working against the investigation, and authorities are urging anyone with information to come forward.

A Michigan State University medical student, 24-year-old Andrew David Thompson, faces multiple charges for allegedly killing and torturing several dogs in his Meridian Township apartment over several months. Thompson, who was studying to be a doctor, was formally charged with ten counts of killing and torturing an animal and one count of abandoning and cruelty to an animal. Prosecutors say he brought dogs to his apartment and killed them. After a neighbor reported the case, police executed a search warrant and arrested Thompson. He is currently in jail on a $600,000 bond and has been suspended from the MSU College of Osteopathic Medicine. More charges are expected as the investigation continues.

A new study suggests that feeling younger than your actual age could have significant health benefits, potentially lowering your risk of death. Researchers from University College London analyzed data from the English Longitudinal Study of Ageing, involving 6,489 participants with an average chronological age of 65.8 years. The study asked participants how old they felt, dividing them into three groups: those whose self-perceived age was close to their actual age, those who felt more than 1 year older, and those who felt 3 or more years younger. The findings revealed that participants who felt younger than their actual age had a 41% lower mortality rate compared to those who felt their age or older. The study observed this association across all causes of death, with a particularly strong link to cardiovascular disease. The authors noted that baseline health, physical disability, and health behaviors accounted for some of the association but remained significant after adjusting for various factors.

The research highlights the potential of self-perceived age as a health indicator, suggesting that interventions targeting those who feel older than their actual age might promote positive health behaviors and attitudes toward aging. Lead author Isla Rippon stated, "Self-perceived age has the potential to change, so interventions may be possible." The study's findings could inform public health strategies aimed at improving well-being and longevity by encouraging individuals to adopt a more positive outlook on aging. Further research is needed to validate these findings and explore the underlying mechanisms that link self-perceived age to mortality rates.

The cost of the traditional "Twelve Days of Christmas" gifts has risen by 6.1 percent this year, according to the annual Christmas Price Index from PNC Wealth Management. Thrifty shoppers may find some cheer in the fact that six items in the carol have not increased in price, including maids-a-milking, ladies dancing, lords-a-leaping, calling birds, turtle doves, and the partridge. However, the prices of other items have climbed significantly. For instance, the cost of swans has increased by 11 percent to $7,000, while the price of five gold rings has risen by 16.3 percent to $750. The pear tree, which costs $189.99, has seen a 11.8 percent increase from last year's $169.99. The most expensive item, a swan, still costs $1,000 each. The least expensive item, the partridge, remains at $15. The core items in each verse of the carol cost $24,431 in traditional stores, but the same set of gifts costs $40,440 online, with the extra expense of shipping live birds contributing to the higher price. PNC Financial Services Group compiles the list by checking jewelry stores, dance companies, pet stores, and other sources, with some of its sources this year including the National Aviary in Pittsburgh and the Philadelphia-based Pennsylvania Ballet Company. The 2011 drought caused some bird prices to soar, partly due to increased feed costs. Despite the modest economic growth, the rise in the cost of Christmas gifts is larger than expected, with the government's Consumer Price Index rising just 2 percent in the 12 months before September.

UFC Women's Bantamweight champion Miesha Tate and Game of Thrones creators David Benioff and D.B. Weiss join Matt Serra and Jim Norton on Episode 7 of the UFC Unfiltered podcast. Tate discusses her upcoming title defense against Amanda Nunes at UFC 200, while Benioff and Weiss talk about the latest season finale of GoT and what's ahead. The podcast covers various topics, including the show's grim weather, the number of remaining episodes, and the possibility of a prequel. Miesha Tate shares insights into her upcoming fight and her journey to the championship. The creators discuss their UFC fandom and the challenges of adapting the books to the screen. The conversation reveals that the next season of Game of Thrones will debut later than usual due to the need for winter-themed scenes, likely in late 2017. Despite the delay, the final two seasons could still conclude in June, as per usual.

Charlie Sheen disclosed his HIV-positive status on the Today show, aiming to counteract smear campaigns and extortion attempts. He claimed he had trusted people in his inner circle but had to pay out over $10 million to keep his diagnosis private. Sheen stated he was diagnosed about four years ago, with his first symptoms being severe headaches. He insisted he never knowingly transmitted the virus, having unprotected sex only with two people who were informed and under medical care. Sheen's doctor, Dr. Robert Huizenga, noted that while HIV is a lifelong condition, advancements in antiviral drugs have made it manageable. Sheen hoped his public announcement would help reduce the stigma surrounding HIV. He revealed he had informed his ex-wives Denise Richards and Brooke Mueller about his diagnosis, as well as his oldest daughter. Sheen also addressed his history of substance abuse and public meltdowns, expressing a desire to enter a more philanthropic phase. His behavior during his 2011 feud with the creator of Two and a Half Men was not related to his diagnosis, according to Sheen. He maintained that his HIV status would not impact his future career, citing ongoing film and television projects. Sheen's announcement came amidst a broader discussion on HIV, with UNAIDS reporting that the global goal to provide treatment to 15 million people by the end of 2015 had been met, highlighting significant progress. However, challenges remain, including cultural and legal barriers to accessing HIV services and the need for continued financial support to maintain these gains.

British conspiracy theorist and UFO researcher Max Spiers, 39, was found dead in a Warsaw apartment on July 16, with his mother, Vanessa Bates, 63, alleging foul play. Spiers, who had been investigating UFOs and alleged government cover-ups, had warned his mother before his death, "Your boy's in trouble. If anything happens to me, investigate." Polish authorities stated his death was from natural causes, but no post-mortem was conducted, and Bates claims the Polish authorities are withholding paperwork. Spiers was known for his theories on the Fourth Reich, claiming a link between Nazis and Zionists, and his belief in an alien base in New Mexico where children were allegedly used for their "pure energy." His mother described him as "incredibly strong" and "in good health" before his death, suggesting he was unlikely to have died naturally. Conspiracy theorists and UFO researchers are speculating that Spiers may have been targeted due to his investigations, with Scott C. Waring of UFO Sightings Daily stating, "This is really strange. It does seem that UFO researchers are now being targeted, probably to slow the rate of information being leaked to the public." Nick Pope, who investigated UFO phenomena for the UK Government, denied any government involvement in targeting researchers. Spiers was buried in Canterbury cemetery, and the UK coroner's office is conducting an investigation, but Bates is still awaiting the results of toxicology tests. The case has sparked renewed interest in the safety of conspiracy theorists and UFO researchers, with many believing Spiers' death was suspicious.

The Obama administration and the new Iranian President Hassan Rouhani are engaging in a diplomatic dance, with both sides expressing cautious optimism. Rouhani's election has brought a shift in Iran's approach, with the new president emphasizing a path for negotiations and moderation. This is evident in his recent letter to President Obama, which the White House described as positive and constructive. However, the differing interpretations of the letter in Tehran and Washington highlight the political hurdles and legacy of mistrust that both sides must navigate.

Rouhani's letter to Obama, which was answered with a similar length response, has sparked hopes of a genuine diplomatic breakthrough. The Iranian leadership was encouraged by Obama's offer to conduct face-to-face talks, which they prefer to the more bureaucratic negotiating process with the five major world powers. This shift in strategy by the moderate new president is part of a broader effort to restore vitality to Iran's economy and improve relations with the West, following years of hostile relations under the previous president, Mahmoud Ahmadinejad.

Rouhani will present Iran's new face to the world next week with speeches at the United Nations General Assembly and other events. His address to the United Nations, his evening speech to the Council on Foreign Relations and the Asia Society, and television interviews with Charlie Rose and CNN, will be key moments to gauge his intentions. The overtures to the United States are part of a flurry of steps altering the trajectory of the Iranian state, including domestic liberalizations and returning the politically powerful military to the barracks for now.

In his reply to Obama, Rouhani said public opinion in Iran did not favor talks, but he urged the U.S. to prepare the grounds for successful negotiations with a gesture of good faith. The Iranian leadership is convinced that the next six months, before campaigning begins for parliamentary elections in March, represent the best opportunity to reach a nuclear agreement in over a decade. They are hoping that the White House will lift some sanctions as a gesture to show its seriousness about the talks, particularly the ban on Iranian money transfers through the Swift system.

While there is a sense of optimism, there are also concerns that the consensus within Iran's political establishment could break down if there are no results. The world must know that time is not unlimited for solving the nuclear problem, Rouhani said. The Obama administration shares this sentiment, with officials hoping that this time may be different. Dennis Ross, a former adviser to Obama on Iran, said Rouhani is sending signals he wants to deal, and wants to end the sanctions and knows he does not have a lot of time to deliver.

The upcoming U.N. meeting between Obama and Rouhani could be the most historic handshake since the 1979 Revolution. However, a face-to-face meeting is not guaranteed, and the focus will be on Rouhani's address and other engagements. The charm offensive by Iran is part of a broader strategy to address the underlying causes of tension and resolve issues through constructive engagement. The key will be whether Rouhani's overtures yield concrete steps that can lead to a nuclear accord.

Britney Spears' handlers have strict guidelines for radio interviews to promote her upcoming Las Vegas residency, which starts in December. Spears' representatives have instructed stations that their five-minute interviews can only discuss her Vegas show, new single, and her "Britney Jean" album, with no personal questions allowed. However, even when interviewers stick to these rules, the interviews can turn out to be one-sided and unentertaining, according to radio insiders. For instance, deejays Roula and Ryan from Houston's 104.1 KRBE had their taped segment pulled after realizing it was a one-sided conversation. Spears' representatives argue that the provided information is meant to aid in smooth interviews rather than dictate the conversation. Despite these efforts, Spears' handlers have also been facing criticism, as she has been known to give vague or detached answers during interviews, making it seem like she is lip-syncing. In fact, a source told Confidenti@l that Spears does not sing during her performances and is being paid a lot of money to lip-sync. This has been denied by Team Britney, who have not commented on the video evidence that suggests Spears was digitally slimmed down for the "Work Bitch" music video. The article also mentions that the 31-year-old mother of two has given up singing, which has been denied by her representatives. Meanwhile, Spears' father, Jamie, has filed a petition asking for more money for his role in managing his daughter's estate, including an additional $800 per month for office rent and $2,000 per month for an office space. This request comes as Jamie has overseen Britney's life and business for over five years, ensuring she remains under his control for at least two more years, as she is signed to perform at Planet Hollywood for a minimum of $432,000 more.

In the waters off the coast of Gela, Sicily, archaeologists have uncovered 39 ingots of a mysterious metal known as orichalcum, a material once considered more valuable than gold by the ancient Greeks. These ingots, which date back to around 2600 years ago, were likely part of a shipwreck that occurred during the first half of the 6th century BC, as reported by Sebastiano Tusa, Sicily's superintendent of the Sea Office. The ingots, found about 1,000 feet from Gela's coast at a depth of 10 feet, are made of an alloy consisting of 75-80 percent copper, 15-20 percent zinc, and small amounts of nickel, lead, and iron, as analyzed by Dario Panetta of TQ - Tecnologies for Quality. This discovery is unique, as no similar artifacts have been found before, and orichalcum was previously known only through ancient texts and a few ornamental objects.

According to the ancient Greek philosopher Plato, orichalcum was a legendary metal, second only to gold in value, and used to cover the interior walls, columns, and floors of Poseidon's temple in the mythical island of Atlantis. The metal was also said to be mined in Atlantis and was considered a mysterious and valuable material. The ingots recovered from the shipwreck are believed to have been destined for Gela, a wealthy city founded in 689 BC, which had artisan workshops specializing in high-quality decorations. The presence of orichalcum in Gela suggests the city's economic prosperity and advanced metallurgical skills.

However, some scholars, like Enrico Mattievich, argue that the ingots are not properly made from orichalcum but are instead lumps of latone metal, an alloy of copper, zinc, and lead. Mattievich, who has conducted extensive research on the origins and nature of orichalcum, believes that the mysterious metal may have its roots in the Peruvian Andes and the Chavín civilization, which developed from 1200 BC to 200 BC. He claims that a metallic alloy with fire-like reflections, similar to Plato's description, was found in a set of metallic jaguars of Chavín style, made of 9 percent copper, 76 percent gold, and 15 percent silver.

Despite the ongoing debate about the nature and origins of orichalcum, the discovery of these 39 ingots provides valuable insights into the ancient economy and trade routes of the Mediterranean. The Sicilian authorities plan to excavate the shipwreck and uncover the entire cargo, which will offer a wealth of information on Sicily's ancient economic history. This find not only sheds light on the mysterious metal of orichalcum but also highlights the importance of continued archaeological research in understanding the rich cultural and economic heritage of the region.

Lindsay Lohan has joined the cast of Sky comedy Sick Note for its second season, which premieres this fall. The show, starring Rupert Grint and Nick Frost, follows the story of Daniel Glass, a compulsive liar stuck in a failing relationship and dead-end insurance job, under the thumb of his boss, played by Don Johnson. Lohan will portray the boss's daughter. In the first season, Grint's character is wrongly diagnosed with a terminal illness by his incompetent doctor, who convinces him to hide the truth of his misdiagnosis from colleagues, friends, and family in a lie that spirals out of control. The show is part of Sky 1's growing stable of edgier, grown-up comedies, joining other shows like Bliss and Bounty Hunters in the channel's 10 p.m. slot. Produced by British production firm King Bert, the comedy is created and written by Nat Saunders and James Serafinowicz, with Matt Lipsey directing. Executive producer Jo Sargent expressed excitement about Lohan's addition to the cast, calling it a "nail-biting comedy."

A flight recorder revealed that pilots of a UPS cargo jet that crashed short of a runway at Birmingham's airport received warnings about their rate of descent seconds before impact, according to investigators. National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) member Robert Sumwalt told reporters that a recorder captured the first of two audible warnings in the cockpit 16 seconds before the sound of an impact, either with trees or the ground. The warnings indicated the A300 cargo plane was descending at a rate outside normal parameters given its altitude. The aircraft went down less than a mile from the end of Runway 18 at Birmingham's airport before dawn on August 14, 2013. UPS has identified the victims of the crash as Capt. Cerea Beal, Jr., 58, of Matthews, N.C., and First Officer Shanda Fanning, 37, of Lynchburg, Tenn.

Landing on the runway can be tricky for pilots, particularly those flying big jets like the twin-engine UPS cargo carrier. Sumwalt said the plane was being flown by the captain, who had 8,600 hours of flight experience, including 3,200 hours in an A300. However, investigators don't know whether Beal or Fanning had ever before landed on Runway 18. Sumwalt said the NTSB will analyze the airplane's weight to determine whether it should have attempted a landing on the runway, the shorter of two runways at Birmingham Shuttlesworth International Airport. With a large hill and trees at one end, the runway lacks the electronics for a full instrument landing, forcing pilots to make key judgments about altitude while aiming a descending aircraft at a runway that's 5,000 feet shorter than the airport's main runway, which was closed for maintenance work at the time of the crash.

Some pilots simply avoid landing on Runway 18 when possible, said veteran commercial pilot Ross Aimer. The NTSB previously said a preliminary investigation didn't reveal any evidence of engine failure before the plane struck trees about one mile away from the end of the runway. It crashed into the bottom of a hill less than a quarter mile after hitting the trees. The A300, which weighs about 172,700 pounds when empty, was at the end of a 45-minute flight from Louisville, Ky., to Birmingham when it went down. A flight summary from flightaware.com, which tracks airplanes, shows the aircraft made a descent in steps, which Aimer said is a "dive and drive" method common on runways with the same navigational guidance as Runway 18.

The NTSB said the aircraft went down during its first landing attempt. Sumwalt said investigators have not found any problems with the runway's lights or navigation system, which typically provides pilots with information about their lateral position but not about their altitude, unlike those on runways where pilots can land using only instruments. National Weather Service records from the morning of the crash show the plane would have descended through overcast conditions to only a few clouds at 1,100 feet. Within seconds after the plane hit a tree and at least one turbine sucked in wood, the twin-engine plane crashed. It hit the base of a large hill, shearing off pieces of the aircraft and sending them crashing onto two homes along with large pieces of limbs. Keenen Brown, 17, said he witnessed the crash while getting ready for work before dawn. Brown, who lives with relatives across the street from the crash site, said it was unusual to see such a large aircraft attempting to land on the runway.

The transcripts of President Donald Trump’s January 2017 phone calls with Mexican President Enrique Peña Nieto and Australian Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull, obtained by The Washington Post, reveal a president who is deeply concerned about his image and the potential for political backlash, particularly regarding immigration and the controversial border wall. The conversations, which were initially reported in summaries by The Washington Post, provide a stark insight into Trump’s approach to international diplomacy and his handling of sensitive issues.

In the call with Peña Nieto, Trump persistently pressured the Mexican leader to accept financial responsibility for the wall, which he repeatedly emphasized was a political necessity rather than a security measure. Trump suggested that both leaders should issue vague statements to avoid public disagreement, stating, “We should both say, ‘We will work it out.’ It will work out in the formula somehow. As opposed to you saying, ‘We will not pay,’ and me saying, ‘We will not pay.’” Peña Nieto, however, remained firm in his position that Mexico would not pay for the wall, leading to a tense exchange.

Trump’s frustration with the situation is evident, as he expressed his desire to avoid appearing weak or ineffective. He stated, “I look like a dope,” and emphasized the political importance of the wall, saying, “This is the least important thing that we are talking about, but politically this might be the most important.” His comments about New Hampshire as a “drug-infested den” drew criticism from local politicians and the media, highlighting the potential political fallout from his remarks.

The call with Turnbull, on the other hand, was marked by a more heated exchange over an Obama-era agreement to accept 1,250 refugees from Australia. Trump was particularly critical of the deal, stating, “This is going to kill me. I am the world’s greatest person that does not want to let people into the country. And now I am agreeing to take 2,000 people and I agree I can vet them, but that puts me in a bad position. It makes me look so bad and I have only been here a week.” He expressed his belief that the refugees were dangerous, saying, “I hate taking these people. I guarantee you they are bad. That is why they are in prison right now. They are not going to be wonderful people who go on to work for the local milk people.”

Turnbull attempted to appeal to Trump’s business acumen, stating, “There is nothing more important in business or politics than a deal is a deal. You can certainly say that it was not a deal that you would have done, but you are going to stick with it.” However, Trump was unconvinced, expressing his fear that one of the refugees could become a terrorist in the future, saying, “I think it is a horrible deal, a disgusting deal that I would have never made.” He also questioned the Australian policy of detaining refugees who arrived by boat, saying, “What is the thing with boats? Why do you discriminate against boats?”

The transcripts reveal a president who is deeply concerned about his image and the potential for political backlash, particularly regarding immigration and the controversial border wall. His comments about New Hampshire as a “drug-infested den” drew criticism from local politicians and the media, highlighting the potential political fallout from his remarks. The calls also show a president who is struggling to navigate the complexities of international diplomacy, particularly when it comes to sensitive issues such as immigration and border security. The release of these transcripts is likely to anger Trump, as they portray him as acrimonious and uncooperative in his dealings with world leaders.

As Ron Paul's support grows, so does scrutiny of his past, particularly his newsletters published in the 1980s and 1990s. These newsletters contained overtly racist and conspiracy-theory-laden content, raising questions about his values and the nature of his political movement. Paul has disavowed the content, claiming he did not write or authorize it, but critics argue his name on the newsletters makes him responsible. The controversy highlights the tension between Paul's libertarian principles and his association with extremist views. While Paul's campaign manager emphasizes his disavowal, the issue could undermine his credibility. The broader implications include the potential for similar issues to arise with other candidates, as their past statements and affiliations come under greater scrutiny. The media and voters are increasingly focused on these historical elements, potentially limiting support for candidates with problematic pasts.

A 45-year-old man was arrested early Tuesday morning after a standoff lasting over eight hours in Brunswick, Ohio. The suspect, armed with a handgun, was subdued by police after entering a house in the 3300 block of Valley Forge Drive through an unlocked front door. The arrest came after police were aware of the man's presence at the home. During the standoff, residents were advised to remain indoors, and a section of Valley Forge Drive was blocked off. The suspect is a person of interest in the deaths of three women: 45-year-old Suzanne Taylor and her two adult daughters, Taylor Pifer, 21, and Kylie Pifer, 18, who were found dead in their North Royalton home on Sunday evening. The bodies of the three victims were discovered by Suzanne Taylor's boyfriend, who received a call from one of the daughters' boyfriends. Upon arrival, investigators noted no signs of forced entry and believe the daughters were killed elsewhere before their bodies were moved to their mother's bed. Forensic evidence and autopsies are being conducted, but a motive for the murders remains unclear. Detective Dave Loeding stated that all evidence collected would lead to a positive outcome. The stepmother of the daughters expressed that they were great students, with Taylor majoring in fashion design and Kylie in forensic science. The case is ongoing, with police and the Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation continuing their investigation.

A routine traffic stop in South Seattle early Sunday morning turned into a miraculous childbirth event. Around 3:45 AM, Officer Anthony Reynolds pulled over a speeding car for running red lights on Martin Luther King Jr. Way S. The driver, Abdul Abdashiek, immediately informed Reynolds that his wife, Maly Yusuf, was in labor. Reynolds quickly called for an ambulance, but the baby was eager to make her entrance. As Yusuf gave birth to a baby girl in the car, officers Lorissa Johnson, Nicholas Kartes, and Jason Alvord joined Reynolds to assist. After the baby's initial cry, she began struggling to breathe, and Officer Reynolds, with the help of the mother, cleared her airway. An ambulance arrived shortly after, transporting both mother and child to a nearby hospital in stable condition. The family later sent a heartfelt note to the officers, expressing gratitude for their assistance. "You have helped deliver a precious gift," they wrote. The baby was named Hadaya, meaning "gift" in Arabic.

In the wake of the devastating earthquake that struck Haiti, aid began trickling into the country as desperate survivors sought to save the injured and retrieve the dead. An Air China plane landed in Port-au-Prince with a Chinese search-and-rescue team, while three French planes arrived with aid and a mobile hospital. The U.S. and other nations pledged food, water, and medical supplies to assist Haiti, a nation already reeling from the quake's impact. Survivors used pick-up trucks as ambulances and doors as stretchers to transport the injured, while bodies lay scattered in the streets. Doctors Without Borders set up tent clinics, and Cuba dispatched hundreds of doctors to treat the injured. President Barack Obama promised an all-out rescue and humanitarian effort, including military and civilian teams. The aircraft carrier USS Carl Vinson was expected to arrive, and the amphibious assault ship USS Bataan was ordered to sail with a 2,000-member Marine unit. However, the Haitian government's response was limited, with President Rene Preval and other officials scattered by the quake. The streets were filled with people, many without food or medical care, as law enforcement struggled to maintain order. Looting broke out, with people carrying food from collapsed buildings. The U.S. Embassy had no confirmed reports of deaths among the estimated 40,000 to 45,000 Americans living in Haiti, but many were struggling to find a way out. The International Committee of the Red Cross launched a website to help Haitians find missing loved ones. As night fell, thousands gathered outside the crumpled presidential palace, singing hymns and praying. The scale of the disaster was immense, with many buildings, including the president's palace and the cathedral, reduced to rubble. The quake's impact was felt across the city, with survivors using sledgehammers and bare hands to search for victims in the debris. The lack of water and electricity further hampered rescue efforts, and calls for help often went unanswered. Despite the arrival of some aid and rescue teams, Port-au-Prince remained a haunting scene of destruction, with many of its pastel buildings collapsed into death traps. The full extent of the damage and the death toll remained unclear, with estimates ranging from thousands to 50,000.

Moe’s Southwest Grill has surpassed Chipotle Mexican Grill to become America’s favorite Mexican-inspired fast casual restaurant chain, according to a recent Harris Poll. Chipotle, which had topped the poll for the past three years, failed to even make the top four this time. The Denver-based chain has faced numerous food safety issues, including a norovirus outbreak that sickened 386 customers, a salmonella incident affecting 64 people, and E. coli episodes in 11 states, each of which sickened 60 people. As a result, sales have declined by 30 percent, and the company’s stock has dropped 33 percent, to $411.14, in early Friday trading.

Moe’s, a 600-unit chain based in Atlanta, has seen a significant increase in brand equity, with a 13 percent rise. This marks the first time Moe’s has taken the top spot in the Harris Poll’s category of fast-casual Mexican restaurants, unseating Chipotle, which had held the title for three consecutive years. Other chains, such as Taco Bell, Qdoba Mexican Grill, and Baja Fresh Mexican Grill, also outperformed Chipotle in the poll. Harris Poll surveyed 97,120 U.S. consumers aged 15 and over.

Chipotle’s struggles have provided a significant opportunity for Moe’s, which has capitalized on the situation. The company has benefited from a 5 percent increase in foot traffic, partly due to Chipotle’s challenges. Moe’s president, Bruce Schroder, emphasized the importance of listening to customer feedback and meeting their needs. Moe’s is part of Focus Brands Inc., which also operates chains such as Carvel, Cinnabon, and Auntie Anne’s Pretzels.

Chipotle has attempted to recover from its food safety issues by offering free burritos and buy-one-get-one deals. In the first quarter, sales at stores open at least a year fell nearly 30 percent, but transaction volume improved as the quarter progressed. A free burrito offer in February had a 67 percent redemption rate. However, the company has faced criticism for not doing enough to reassure customers about the safety of its food. Chipotle has adopted new food safety protocols but has not communicated these changes effectively to customers.

The fast-casual restaurant landscape has become more competitive as chains introduce healthier menu options and new items. Qdoba Mexican Grill and Taco Bell have gained prominence with their respective offerings. Moe’s is known for its wide selection of ingredients for build-your-own tacos, quesadillas, and burrito bowls, as well as limited-time menu additions. In contrast, Chipotle has rarely introduced new menu items, leading some to question whether the company has done enough to convince customers that its food is safe.

Moe’s has seen a significant increase in brand equity, ranking highest in familiarity, quality, and purchase consideration. The company’s rapid expansion in recent years has given it a stronger position as a Chipotle alternative. Moe’s opened 70 new restaurants last year, with sales hitting nearly $640 million. While Chipotle still holds a larger market share and higher sales, Moe’s has an opportunity to continue converting brand equity into restaurant visits.

The legal battle over the iconic Martin D-18E guitar, played by Kurt Cobain in Nirvana's 1993 "MTV Unplugged" performance, is escalating into a multimillion-dollar dispute. Frances Bean Cobain, Kurt's daughter with Courtney Love, is locked in a contentious legal struggle with Isaiah Silva, her ex-husband and the current possessor of the guitar. Silva claims Frances Bean gifted him the instrument, a left-handed Martin D-18E, as a wedding present when they secretly married in 2014. The guitar, insured for $1 million at the time, is now valued at several times that amount, making it a highly prized artifact. Love, however, maintains that the guitar is a "treasured heirloom" and not Silva's to take, as Frances Bean denies ever giving it to him.

Silva's legal team has been negotiating with Frances Bean's representatives for months, but the talks have reached a deadlock. According to Silva's side, he is taking "extreme and unsupportable positions" and is now pushing the matter to litigation. In September, a judge ordered Frances Bean to pay Silva $15,000 a month in spousal support as part of an interim settlement, pending the resolution of the guitar dispute. Frances Bean's representatives have not commented on the matter.

Meanwhile, Isaiah Silva is also seeking substantial spousal support from Frances Bean, requesting $25,000 a month. Silva argues that he left a stable job to marry Frances Bean and has been covering significant expenses for their child from a previous relationship. He claims Frances has access to substantial funds from her father's estate and is now seeking to renegotiate their financial agreement. Frances Bean's divorce documents state that the Cobain estate money is hers alone, but she is open to paying some spousal support.

The legal and financial complexities of this case highlight the ongoing tensions between Frances Bean and Isaiah Silva, as well as the potential for a high-stakes courtroom showdown. Both parties are now preparing for a legal battle that could determine the future of the guitar and the financial support arrangements between them.

Scarlett Johansson and Ryan Reynolds, known for their private lifestyle, have unexpectedly split after a two-year marriage, shocking friends who had no idea the relationship was troubled. "No one had any idea this was coming," a close friend of Johansson's tells the source. The couple, who rarely spoke about their relationship in public, kept their personal life tightly guarded, with Reynolds admitting he was "a little more guarded" after getting married. Their split statement emphasized love and kindness, while stressing the importance of privacy. Given their desire for secrecy, fans and the media can expect little insight into the reasons behind their separation, with insiders suggesting that questions about Scarlett will be off-limits during Reynolds' promotional tour for "Green Lantern."

A Delaware family's Caribbean vacation took a tragic turn when they became seriously ill after exposure to a banned pesticide at their resort in the U.S. Virgin Islands. The Esmond family, including father Steve Esmond, his wife Theresa Devine, and their two teenage sons, fell ill on March 20, with the sons in critical condition and the father regaining consciousness weeks later. Paramedics were called to the villa, where the family was staying at the Sirenusa resort in Cruz Bay, St. John. The U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) confirmed the presence of methyl bromide, a potent neurotoxin, in the unit where the family was staying. The EPA, which banned the chemical for residential use in 1984, is investigating the use of methyl bromide at the resort, which has reportedly been used in other units over the past year. The Justice Department is also conducting a criminal investigation. Sea Glass Vacations, which manages the rental units at Sirenusa, has terminated its contract with Terminix, the pest control company that reportedly applied the pesticide. The EPA is working with local authorities to ensure the safety of the property and prevent future incidents. The family expressed confidence in their medical professionals and hope for a full recovery. The incident highlights the ongoing challenges in enforcing environmental regulations and the potential for serious health consequences from pesticide misuse.

The 5th Circuit Court of Appeals in Austin ruled that hospital-like structural requirements for Texas abortion clinics can go into effect, which will cause all but seven or eight clinics to close. This decision, part of the state's 2013 law that also banned abortion after 20 weeks of pregnancy, mandated physicians to have hospital admitting privileges, and tightened regulations on abortion-inducing drugs, has been challenged twice. In June 2013, there were 40 abortion clinics in Texas; now, there are 17, with only seven meeting the new building standards. The remaining clinics are located in major cities like Austin, Houston, Dallas, Fort Worth, and San Antonio. Whole Woman’s Health in McAllen won an exception to the building requirements and the admitting privileges for one doctor. The court upheld the provisions requiring doctors at abortion clinics to obtain admitting privileges at nearby hospitals and the regulations that mandate where and when a woman can take abortion-causing pills, stating that these do not impose an “undue burden” on women because they are still within driving distance of clinics. Nancy Northup, CEO of the Center for Reproductive Rights, criticized the decision, saying, "Not since before Roe v. Wade has a law or court decision had the potential to devastate access to reproductive health care on such a sweeping scale." Texas will be able to start enforcing the restrictions in about three weeks unless the Supreme Court steps in and temporarily halts the decision. The ruling is the 5th Circuit's latest in a lawsuit challenging some of the toughest abortion restrictions in the country. Texas currently has about 17 abortion providers, down from 40 clinics in 2012. The new restrictions will leave women in El Paso needing a 1,200-mile round trip to San Antonio or crossing the border into New Mexico for an abortion. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton praised the court's ruling, stating, "Abortion practitioners should have no right to operate their businesses from sub-standard facilities and with doctors who lack admitting privileges at a hospital."

Russian actor Steven Seagal has been appointed as a "special representative" for US-Russian humanitarian ties by the Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, according to a statement on the ministry's official Facebook page. Seagal's role will focus on promoting US-Russia relations in the humanitarian sphere, including collaboration in the fields of culture, public, and youth exchanges. This appointment is similar to the United Nations' goodwill ambassador positions. Seagal, who became a Russian citizen in 2016 and is a close friend of Russian President Vladimir Putin, has been an ardent supporter of Putin, defending his government against allegations of election meddling in the United States. In an interview with Piers Morgan, Seagal praised Putin as "a great world leader" and a "brilliant tactician." In 2013, BuzzFeed reported that Putin suggested Seagal serve as an honorary envoy of Russia to help improve relations between the two countries. Seagal also facilitated meetings for a congressional delegation that visited Russia in the wake of the Boston Marathon bombings to investigate the suspects' backgrounds and discuss intelligence sharing issues. CNN has reached out to Seagal's spokesperson for comment.

A 59-year-old Kansas man was fatally injured when his motorcycle collided with a black cow on a rural road Friday night, according to the Kansas Highway Patrol. James Zordel, of Russell, was driving northbound on a blacktop road about 6.5 miles south of Interstate 70 when the accident occurred. Trooper Brant Birney stated there were no witnesses and it is unclear if Zordel was speeding or if the cow suddenly appeared. "It was dark. He was driving down a blacktop road and he hit a black cow," Birney said, noting that the exact cause may never be known. Zordel, who was not wearing a helmet, died at the scene. No other individuals were injured in the crash.

For 40 years, Bill Bresnan of Toms River, New Jersey, has written his wife, Kris, a love letter every single day. This dedication has resulted in over 10,000 cards and letters, meticulously organized in 25 boxes. Bresnan and Kris met in 1974 when he was teaching a class to license students in the securities industry. Their relationship quickly blossomed, with Bresnan sending notes and cards to Kris on their daily commute. As their marriage approached its 50th anniversary, Bresnan began sending Kris a card 50 days before her birthday, continuing this tradition throughout the milestone year.

Their daily expressions of love extend beyond the written word. Bresnan and Kris maintain a nightly routine of candlelit dinners, romantic music, and a kiss goodnight that starts each morning. Bresnan's commitment to their relationship is evident in his daily rituals, such as playing Boggle over breakfast and sending postcards or letters when they are apart. Their love story includes a memorable reenactment of the 1955 film "Summertime," where they sailed across the Mediterranean and experienced the romance depicted in the movie. Bresnan even had a friendship ring engraved with hieroglyphics, an expression of eternal love, which Kris has worn for over 40 years.

Despite the challenges of their long marriage, Bresnan and Kris have never had a major fight. They prioritize communication and resolving issues before going to bed, ensuring that each day begins with a clean slate. Bresnan's daily letters are more than just declarations of love; they document their shared experiences, from restaurant visits to movie nights. Kris Bresnan describes the letters as "hilarious, very funny, cute, not all mushy mushy, all kinds," emphasizing the variety and humor in their daily expressions of affection.

Bresnan's dedication to their relationship has inspired him to offer advice to younger couples, noting that many seem more engrossed in their gadgets than in each other. He encourages couples to treasure the time they have together, suggesting simple gestures like having a nice dinner, a special bottle of wine, and a piece of chocolate to celebrate Valentine's Day. Bresnan's story is a testament to the power of daily effort and commitment in maintaining a long-lasting and loving relationship.

A former Miss Delaware contestant is suing the state and national pageant organizations, seeking to be reinstated as Miss Delaware and $3 million in damages, reports the Associated Press. Amanda Longacre, who was crowned Miss Delaware in June, was stripped of her title last month for being too old, as she turns 25 in October. The lawsuit, filed in Delaware's Court of Chancery, also seeks a waiver to compete for Miss America in September. Longacre claims that other contestants were also too old but were allowed to compete. The Miss America Organization stated that the lawsuit has no merit and will be defended vigorously. Longacre's attorney argues that the pageant officials recruited her and other contestants, knowing they were too old, for fundraising and appearances, then disqualified them. Longacre lost her crown, scholarships, and potential career opportunities, and the lawsuit details her financial and emotional losses. The Miss Delaware Scholarship Organization did not immediately respond to the lawsuit.

The Arcade Fire's single "We Used to Wait" has been transformed into an interactive website called "The Wilderness Downtown," offering a unique, nostalgic experience. By entering your childhood address, the website uses Google Maps and Street View to create a personalized, interactive music video. The experience includes various windows popping up with videos, animations, and satellite shots of your neighborhood. The song plays throughout, enhancing the emotional journey. This innovative approach to music videos, combining video, interactivity, and web technology, could potentially redefine the medium. Critics and fans alike are intrigued by its potential, seeing it as a future trend in music video creation. While some might find it irritating, the overwhelming sentiment is one of excitement for the possibilities it presents.

The investigation into the killings of eight members of the Rhoden family in Pike County, Ohio, continues to expand, with more than 200 law enforcement officials involved. Autopsy results revealed that seven of the victims were shot multiple times, including one who suffered nine gunshot wounds. Some victims also showed signs of soft tissue bruising, suggesting a struggle before their deaths. The Pike County Medical Examiner stated that the eight victims, all part of the Rhoden family, died from gunshot wounds. The killings, described as "execution-style" and "pre-planned," took place at four different crime scenes. Ohio Attorney General Mike DeWine and Pike County Sheriff Charles Reader confirmed that marijuana growing operations were found at three of the four locations. One of the grow operations was reportedly comprised of over 100 plants, indicating it was for sale rather than personal use. The Ohio Bureau of Criminal Investigation, along with the FBI and DEA, are assisting in the investigation. No suspects have been identified, and the motive remains unclear. Dana Rhoden's father, Leonard Manley, expressed disbelief that his daughter could be involved in any illegal activities and noted that the assailant was able to bypass her two dogs. A $25,000 reward has been offered for information leading to the arrest of those responsible. The investigation is ongoing, and authorities are continuing to serve search warrants and gather evidence.

Google has ventured into the wedding planning domain, launching a dedicated site for couples to create wedding websites, edit photos, and plan their special day using templates from Google Sites, Google Docs, and Picnik. This move is part of Google's strategy to integrate more deeply into consumers' daily lives, following previous attempts like Google Health. The company collaborated with Michelle Rago, a renowned wedding planner, to develop the templates and provide planning tips. To promote the service, Google is hosting a sweepstakes offering a $25,000 prize and the chance to have Rago assist in wedding planning. The initiative showcases Google's ambition to offer comprehensive tools for various life events, potentially blurring the line between providing helpful services and invading privacy. The partnership with Rago highlights Google's effort to combine professional expertise with its suite of productivity tools, aiming to make wedding planning more accessible and user-friendly.

MasterCard is introducing a new security system that allows customers to use selfies and fingerprints instead of passwords for online payments, aiming to enhance security and convenience. The payment processing company confirmed this decision at the Mobile World Congress in Barcelona, following successful trials in the U.S. and the Netherlands. Ann Cairns, head of international markets for MasterCard, stated that the biometric checks have the potential to protect users during payments. The system will be launched in the U.K. and will be rolled out to other countries including the U.S., Canada, the Netherlands, Belgium, Spain, Italy, France, Germany, Switzerland, Norway, Sweden, Finland, and Denmark. Users will need to download an application to their PC, tablet, or smartphone to use the system. When making an online purchase, they will still need to provide their credit card details. However, if a further authentication check is required, they will be asked to use their phone's camera or fingerprint sensor instead of typing in selected letters from their password. To prevent spoofing, users will have to blink into the camera during the selfie process. MasterCard claims that 92% of its test subjects preferred this new system to traditional passwords. Ajay Bhalla, chief of the firm's safety and security division, emphasized the benefits of biometric checks, stating that they are more secure and convenient than passwords. He noted that passwords are often weak and can be easily compromised, leading to security breaches. The company asserts that its other security mechanisms can prevent or detect suspicious behavior, and the facial scans and fingerprint data will not be transmitted in a form that could be intercepted or used by scammers. This move by MasterCard is part of a broader trend in the industry, with other firms also experimenting with facial scans and fingerprint sensors for authentication. The introduction of such biometric tests could potentially reduce fraud and make online payments more secure.

Donald Trump faced immediate backlash Friday morning for his handling of a question at a town hall event in Rochester, New Hampshire, where an audience member asked when the U.S. can "get rid" of Muslims, claiming President Barack Obama is Muslim. Trump, seemingly bewildered, did not correct the questioner and moved on to another audience member. White House Press Secretary Josh Earnest condemned the remarks, but added, "Is anybody really surprised that this happened at a Donald Trump rally?" Democrats, including Hillary Clinton, Bernie Sanders, and Martin O'Malley, denounced Trump's comments, calling them "out of bounds" and "untrue." Rep. Keith Ellison, the first Muslim elected to Congress, criticized Trump for showing "a lack of moral courage." Democratic National Committee Chairwoman Debbie Wasserman Schultz flatly called Trump a racist. While Trump's campaign manager, Corey Lewandowski, claimed Trump did not hear the question about Obama being a Muslim, focusing instead on training camps, Trump canceled his trip to South Carolina, citing a "significant business transaction." New Jersey Gov. Chris Christie stated leaders have an obligation to correct voters on certain issues, suggesting he would have addressed the questioner's assertions. The incident highlights the persistent falsehoods about Obama's background, with 29% of Americans, including 43% of Republicans, believing he is a Muslim.

Ricky Gervais, known for his biting humor and willingness to offend, delivered a scathing monologue at the 73rd Golden Globes, targeting a wide array of celebrities and industry figures. His opening lines immediately set a confrontational tone, with Gervais addressing the male nominees by saying, "This is the first time in three months it won't be terrifying to hear your name read out loud." Gervais did not hold back, mocking Sean Penn, Caitlyn Jenner, Roman Polanski, Jennifer Lawrence, Jeffrey Tambor, and Ben Affleck, among others. He also took a jab at the Hollywood Foreign Press Association, the group responsible for hosting the ceremony, by suggesting they were biased due to their lack of nominations.

Gervais’s jokes were often sharp and pointed, such as his comment on Jennifer Lawrence's advocacy for equal pay, stating, "There were marches on the street with nurses and factory workers saying, ‘How the hell can a 25-year-old live on $52 million?!’" He also made a humorous reference to Mel Gibson, who had previously faced controversy, by asking, "What the f–k does ‘sugar t-ts’ even mean?" Gervais’s introduction of Matt Damon was equally biting, with the line, "He’s the only person Ben Affleck hasn’t been unfaithful to." He also made a pointed comment about all-female remakes, saying, "There’s a female remake of Ghostbusters. There’s going to be a female remake of Ocean’s 11. And this is brilliant for the studios because they get guaranteed box office results and they don’t have to spend too much money on the cast."

Gervais’s monologue was not just about celebrities; he also made references to the broader issues in Hollywood. He criticized the treatment of trans-people, saying, "What a year she’s had! She became a role model for trans-people everywhere, showing great bravery in breaking down barriers and destroying stereotypes. She didn’t do a lot for women drivers. But you can’t have everything, can ya? Not at the same time." He also took a swipe at the film industry’s tendency to remake successful stories, stating, "The excellent Spotlight has been nominated. Yeah. The Catholic Church are furious about the film as it exposes that 5 percent of all their priests have repeatedly molested children and been allowed to continue to work without punishment. Roman Polanski called it ‘the best date movie ever.’"

Gervais’s humor was not without its controversial moments. He openly admitted to NBC that he would say whatever he wanted, stating, "They said I could say what I want — NBC and the Hollywood Foreign Press. I don’t think they know what that means. I won’t break any laws." His comments on the value of the Golden Globes awards were particularly blunt, saying, "Remember if you do win tonight, no one cares about that award as much as you do. Don’t get emotional, it’s embarrassing. That award is, no offense, worthless. It’s a bit of metal some nice old confused journalists wanted to give you in person so they could meet you and have a selfie with you, okay? That’s all it is!"

Gervais’s performance was widely discussed and analyzed, with many stars and industry insiders expressing their reactions. While some found his humor refreshing and relevant, others felt uncomfortable with the level of criticism. The controversy surrounding Gervais’s hosting gig highlighted the ongoing issues in the entertainment industry, particularly regarding gender equality and the treatment of marginalized groups. Despite the backlash, Gervais’s performance remained a talking point throughout the night, with his jokes and commentary continuing to resonate long after the ceremony had ended.

A Pembroke Pines police officer was allegedly denied service at an Arby's restaurant because she is a cop, sparking a controversy and calls for a national boycott from the police union. The incident occurred when a drive-thru employee told a Pembroke Pines Police Sergeant, Jennifer Martin, that the manager refused to serve her because she is a police officer. Sergeant Martin was uncomfortable and left without eating, requesting a refund. The manager, Angel Mirabal, laughed and said the clerk had the right to refuse service. Chief Dan Giustino of the Pembroke Pines Police Department was offended and appalled, demanding an apology from Arby's CEO, Paul Brown. Arby's executives apologized, stating the employee's behavior was unacceptable and not representative of the company's values. However, the Pembroke Pines Police Benevolent Association is calling for the employees involved to be fired, and the Miami-Dade and Broward Police Benevolent Associations are supporting a national boycott. The Arby's manager's grandfather, Thomas McCutcheon, believes the incident was blown out of proportion, saying his grandson was just making a joke. Despite the controversy, Arby's offered free meals to all uniformed cops in South Florida as a gesture of goodwill. The Pembroke Pines Police Department is hopeful that this incident is an isolated case and that the partnership with the community remains strong.

House Speaker John Boehner insists that President Barack Obama must accept significant entitlement cuts and reject any tax increases to secure a debt-ceiling increase from Congress, as top congressional leaders convene at the White House for deficit reduction talks. Boehner, who pulled out of one-on-one discussions with Obama after facing criticism from conservative lawmakers, maintains that the House cannot pass a bill raising taxes on "job creators" and that spending cuts must exceed the debt limit increase. He also calls for a balanced-budget amendment and emphasizes the need for serious entitlement reform. Despite Obama's repeated praise for Boehner's willingness to explore a "grand bargain" that includes tax revenue, Boehner maintains that the gap between the two parties is rooted in policy differences, not personalities. The White House and congressional leaders are working to finalize a deal to reduce spending and raise the borrowing limit before the August 2 deadline.

During a House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology hearing, Alabama Republican Rep. Mo Brooks challenged the consensus view that sea levels are rising due to global warming. Brooks argued that other factors, such as erosion and sediment deposition, are more significant contributors to sea level rise. He cited examples like the White Cliffs of Dover, the California coastline, and major river systems, suggesting that the erosion of cliffs and the deposition of silt from rivers could cause sea levels to rise. Brooks also claimed that Antarctic ice is growing, not shrinking, and that he had received conflicting information from NASA. 

Brooks’ questioning of climate scientists, including Philip Duffy of the Woods Hole Research Center, drew criticism from his colleagues and the media. Duffy maintained that human activities, particularly greenhouse gas emissions, are the primary drivers of sea level rise, citing satellite data that shows a clear trend of shrinking Antarctic ice sheets. Brooks’ comments reflect a broader skepticism among some lawmakers about the scientific consensus on climate change and its impacts. Despite the overwhelming evidence from NASA and other scientific institutions, Brooks insisted that his district’s NASA base was providing him with different information, suggesting a disconnect between scientific data and political perspectives.

After a lengthy closed-door meeting with House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi and other Democratic leaders, Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid expressed hope for a vote on the emerging agreement tonight, though sources indicated that House Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio) was holding up the deal due to potential defense cuts. The Senate failed to break the 60-vote threshold to end debate on Reid’s debt ceiling bill, with 50 senators voting to end debate and 49 opposing it. The mood on Capitol Hill was one of relief, with Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) stating that default was now less likely than the previous day. Senate Republican Leader Mitch McConnell echoed optimism, saying negotiations had made significant progress. Reid emphasized the need to give everyone room to finalize the deal, while Boehner appeared to have had no direct contact with President Obama, despite McConnell speaking to the president and Biden. The biggest issues included matching deficit reductions with borrowing authority increases and ensuring the joint committee meets its $1.6 trillion savings target. Democrats feared their priorities might be lost in the process, and Reid accused McConnell of engaging more for show. Boehner showed signs of running out the clock, hoping for White House concessions. The vote on Reid’s bill was 246-173, with Pelosi urging an end to the "theater of the absurd" and calling for a more serious approach.

New Zealand is considering a significant price hike for cigarettes to combat smoking, with some officials suggesting a pack could cost up to $100 by 2020. The Health Ministry aims for the country to be smoke-free by 2025 and is exploring various strategies, including a 30% immediate increase followed by annual 30% hikes. However, Prime Minister John Key warns that such a drastic price rise could fuel a black market. Associate Health Minister Tariana Turia, however, is open to any measure that helps achieve the smoke-free goal. The Ministry's internal discussion paper also proposes regulating tobacco as a toxic substance, banning smoking in cars with children, doubling anti-smoking media campaigns, and removing tobacco from duty-free sales. While a $100 pack is seen as unrealistic, the government is considering a shock increase followed by smaller annual hikes to reach a $60 pack by 2025.

Virginia officials are warning residents to be vigilant after the first sighting of giant hogweed, an invasive plant capable of causing severe burns and even blindness. The Massey Herbarium at Virginia Tech reported 30 giant hogweed plants discovered in Clarke County, prompting environmental authorities to issue a cautionary alert. The plant, native to the Caucasus region, can grow up to 14 feet tall and features large, umbrella-shaped clusters of white flowers. Its most dangerous attribute is a highly toxic sap found in all parts of the plant, particularly the stems and leaves. This sap, when combined with sunlight, can lead to painful blisters, severe skin reactions, and long-lasting scars. Ingesting the sap can result in blindness if it enters the eyes. To prevent these hazards, experts advise against using weed-whackers or brush cutters, as the sap can splatter and spread. Instead, physical removal or herbicides like glyphosate or triclopyr are recommended. Long-term monitoring is crucial, as hogweed seeds can remain viable in the soil for up to 15 years, necessitating repeated efforts to control and eradicate the plant. Environmental officials stress the importance of reporting sightings to extension agents and taking necessary safety precautions when handling the plant. The plant's massive size and rapid spread pose a significant threat to both human health and local ecosystems, making it a formidable adversary in the battle against invasive species.

PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), the auditing firm responsible for handling the Oscars votes, issued a statement on Monday, February 27, acknowledging their "series of mistakes and breaches of established protocols" during the 89th annual Academy Awards. The firm's partner, Brian Cullinan, handed the wrong envelope to presenters Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway, leading to the incorrect announcement of La La Land as the Best Picture winner. Cullinan's tweet of Emma Stone backstage just before the announcement was cited as a potential policy violation, though PwC stated that Cullinan was instructed not to use social media during the show. PwC's U.S. chairman, Tim Ryan, expressed regret, saying that Cullinan "feels very, very terrible and horrible" about the mix-up. The firm's partner, Martha Ruiz, also failed to act quickly enough to correct the error. PwC's statement apologized to those involved, including Beatty, Dunaway, and host Jimmy Kimmel, as well as the casts of La La Land and Moonlight. The Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences has launched a full-scale review of its relationship with PwC, with the possibility of changes to the voting process. PwC's 83-year-old contract, which has never faced tender because of their "long-term relationship and absolute trust," could be in jeopardy. The review includes considering a new system with two auditors at each stage entrance to prevent future mix-ups. The incident has raised questions about the firm's protocols and the possibility of a policy violation, with the review process continuing as of mid-Tuesday.

A music fan named Craig Mandell has launched a crowdfunding campaign to keep the much-maligned Canadian band Nickelback out of London. Mandell, inspired by a recent Tilt campaign that brought the Foo Fighters to Charlottesville, VA, created the "Don't Let Nickel Back" campaign to discourage the band from playing in the city. The campaign aims to prevent Nickelback from scheduling any gigs in London by sending emails to the band's management. For every $1 donated, Mandell will send one email; a $5 donation gets a "slightly more forceful email," and a $50 contribution includes an email with an attached mp3 of Nickelback's music, potentially leading to the band's immediate retirement. Mandell hopes that thousands of music lovers will contribute to the campaign, ensuring that no one in London witnesses a Nickelback concert. All funds raised will go to charity or therapy for those affected by the band. Meanwhile, a separate crowdfunding effort to bring Foo Fighters to Cornwall has already reached its £150,000 target in just two days, but the organizers now face the challenge of convincing the band to agree to a show in the English county.

True Grit, directed by the Coen brothers and starring Jeff Bridges, Hailee Steinfeld, and Matt Damon, is a beautifully crafted Western that brings Charles Portis's 1968 novel to life with a mix of humor and poignancy. At 14, Mattie Ross hires the one-eyed Marshal Reuben "Rooster" Cogburn to find her father's killer, Tom Chaney. The journey, filled with tense encounters and vivid landscapes, is both a revenge tale and a coming-of-age story. Bridges's portrayal of Rooster is nuanced, balancing toughness and humanity, while Steinfeld brings authenticity to the spirited Mattie. Damon's Texas Ranger, LaBoeuf, adds a layer of complexity. The Coens and cinematographer Roger Deakins create a haunting, poetic atmosphere, making every scene feel significant. The film is a testament to the Coens' ability to blend classic Western tropes with fresh storytelling, resulting in a wonderfully entertaining and visually stunning Western.

Rhonda Thill, a St. Paul woman, lost her husband Randy's wedding ring after he died in a motorcycle accident in June. She couldn't bear the thought of losing his ring, which he wore every day for nearly 19 years. About a dozen bikers, including members of the Sober Soldiers and Los Valientes motorcycle clubs, joined forces to help Rhonda find the ring. They searched a 100-foot stretch of road, using metal detectors and their hands and knees. After persistent searching, Jay Stevens of the Sober Soldiers found the ring pushed into the soil behind a weed where Randy Thill died. The group returned to Rhonda's house, where she held her head down, about to fall over, as Stevens handed her the ring. Rhonda was overwhelmed by the kindness of the strangers who helped her find the ring, saying, "All those people have such kind hearts. They didn't hesitate." The search for the ring brought closure to Rhonda and a chance to remember her late husband. A benefit event, "Riding with Randy," was organized to honor Randy and raise funds for Rhonda.

A California family is dealing with a live-in nanny who refuses to leave their home after being fired. Diane Stretton, 64, was hired in March to care for the Bracamontes' three children in exchange for room and board. After a few months, the family claims Stretton stopped working and refused to leave, even threatening legal action for elder abuse and wrongful termination. The Bracamontes, Ralph and Marcella, have been trying to get Stretton to vacate the premises, but she has remained in the house, driving past the home and keeping her belongings in her room. Now, Stretton has agreed to move out by July 4, but only under certain conditions. She wants to stay for three more nights, use the family bathroom, and have the media leave before she departs. The Bracamontes are skeptical, especially since they have plans to be away for the holiday, and intend to have family members house-sit while they are out. Stretton’s past is also a concern; she has a history of litigation, including lawsuits against her own family members, and is listed as a vexatious litigant in California. The family’s lawyer, Marc Cohen, explains that Stretton has a legal right to the room she was given, and that interfering with her belongings could result in legal repercussions. The case raises questions about the legal obligations of both the family and the nanny, and highlights the complexities of eviction when it involves a live-in arrangement.

A federal judge on Saturday temporarily blocked the deportation of a New York pizza shop worker, Pablo Villavicencio, after he was arrested while making a delivery to a Brooklyn Army base. Villavicencio, a 35-year-old Ecuadorean immigrant and father of two young girls, was detained on June 1 while delivering to Fort Hamilton. A background check revealed an active warrant for his arrest due to immigration law violations. The Legal Aid Society obtained a temporary stay for Villavicencio, which will last until July 20, allowing him to pursue relief from removal. Villavicencio's wife, Sandra Chica, is an American citizen, and their daughters were born in the U.S. The case has sparked outrage from his family and local officials, including New York Governor Andrew Cuomo, who wrote letters to high-ranking officials calling for an investigation into ICE tactics and requesting Villavicencio's release. Villavicencio has been to the base "many times" in the past to make similar deliveries, and his attorney claims he does not have a criminal record. The Legal Aid Society's Gregory Copeland stated that the stay is a victory for Villavicencio, his family, and due process. The case highlights the potential for hasty and cruel decisions by other branches of government and emphasizes the importance of the judiciary serving as a check on such actions.

The Showtime series "The Big C" centers on Laura Linney's character, Cathy, a high school teacher diagnosed with Stage IV melanoma. The show, aiming for a comedic tone, portrays Cathy's life-changing diagnosis with a mix of humor and drama. Linney's performance is praised for its authenticity, capturing the reserved and apologetic nature of Cathy before the diagnosis, and then her transformation into a more assertive and unconventional persona. The series introduces a cast of eccentric characters, including Cathy's husband, Paul, played by Oliver Platt, who is described as childish and self-centered, and her son, Adam, who is insolent. Gabourey Sidibe, known for her role in "Precious," portrays a summer school student who becomes a significant character in the narrative. Despite the strong performances and potential for dark humor, the show's structure and pacing are criticized for being overly chaotic. The series attempts to explore the question of how one would live their life knowing its limited duration but struggles with an abundance of quirky and often distracting subplots. While the show has its merits, particularly in its portrayal of Cathy's character, it faces challenges in balancing its comedic and dramatic elements, leading to a disjointed viewing experience.

A nephew fatally shot his uncle over a prized pet fighting rooster early Wednesday morning in a shootout at a mobile home near Decatur, Tenn., in Meigs County. Timothy Dewayne Johnson, 52, was found dead in the driveway, while Larry Eugene Johnson Jr., 28, was seriously wounded inside the trailer. The rooster, named "Bubba," was unharmed and left with food and water. Timothy Johnson accused Larry of stealing the gamecock and confronted him, leading to a gun battle. Larry Johnson told a bystander his uncle had drawn a gun and that he was trying to grab it when he was shot in the chest. He then retreated and returned fire multiple times. Larry Johnson was armed with a semi-automatic handgun that held 17 shots, and authorities estimated at least 11 gunshots were fired. Timothy Johnson, standing when shot, was struck four times. A single-action .38-caliber revolver and a loaded .22-caliber pistol were found on Timothy. Larry Johnson, flown to the University of Tennessee Medical Center, was listed in stable condition. The district attorney's office will present the case to the Meigs County grand jury after completing the investigative file and toxicology results. Both families claim a good relationship and dispute the exact nature of the conflict.

The death of 17-year-old Kendrick Johnson, found dead in a rolled-up gym mat at Lowndes County High School, has been a source of controversy for his family. State medical examiners initially ruled the death accidental, stating that Johnson suffocated after getting stuck in the mat while reaching for a sneaker. However, his parents, Kenneth and Jacquelyn Johnson, never accepted this explanation and fought for a second autopsy. A private pathologist found that Johnson had sustained a blow to the right side of his neck, consistent with inflicted injury, contradicting the original findings. This new evidence, along with death scene imagery, has led a former FBI agent to question the official account of Johnson's death, suggesting foul play.
