The imagery, including a 15-minute video and nearly 700 photos, reveals Johnson's body wedged in the mat, with blood stains on the nearby wall that investigators claim were not his. A pair of gym shoes and a sweatshirt found nearby also raised questions about the handling of potential evidence. The discovery that Johnson's organs were removed and stuffed with newspaper before burial has added a new layer of distress and suspicion for his family. Federal prosecutors are reviewing the case, but the local sheriff's department has classified the death as an accident. Kenneth Johnson believes his son was murdered and that authorities are not being transparent. The family continues to push for answers, emphasizing their belief that Johnson's death was not accidental.

President Obama demanded daily meetings with House Speaker John Boehner and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid to resolve a budget impasse or risk a government shutdown. At a White House press conference, Obama stated his team was prepared to meet indefinitely until an agreement was reached, threatening to call the leaders back if necessary. Boehner's office countered that the two sides remained far apart, with Republicans insisting on deeper spending cuts. The White House accused Republicans of pushing harmful spending cuts and attaching social policy riders, while Republicans accused the White House of gimmicky budget cuts. As the deadline approached, Obama ruled out a longer extension for negotiations, while Boehner proposed a one-week funding extension. The impasse also highlighted long-term Republican plans to slash the budget deficit by over $5 trillion, including converting Medicare into a private insurance system and transforming Medicaid into a block grant program.

President Donald Trump drew criticism from U.K. officials for his comments on the London subway attack, tweeting, "These are sick and demented people who were in the sights of Scotland Yard. Must be proactive!" British Prime Minister Theresa May and other officials rebuked Trump, stating that it was unhelpful to speculate on an ongoing investigation. May emphasized that the police and security services were working to identify the full circumstances of the attack. Trump's tweet was seen as an attempt to criticize Scotland Yard's handling of the situation, though it is unclear if he had any non-public information to base this claim on. National Security Adviser H.R. McMaster tried to clarify Trump's statement, saying the president was generally referring to law enforcement's focus on terrorism. The tweet also drew ire from other U.S. officials, including former aide Nick Timothy, who called it "unhelpful from the leader of our ally and intelligence partner." In response to the attack, Trump vowed to be "very smart" and "very tough" in the fight against terrorism and North Korea, which had recently launched a missile over Japan. Trump also claimed that the U.S. had made more progress against ISIS in the past nine months than the Obama administration had in eight years. Trump's comments were part of a broader pattern of criticism from British officials, who had previously clashed with the U.S. over intelligence sharing and leaks. Despite the diplomatic tension, the White House stated that Trump had privately offered his sympathies and pledged continued collaboration with the U.K. to combat terrorism. Trump later said he had called May to express his condolences and commitment to eradicating "radical Islamic terrorism." The Islamic State claimed responsibility for the attacks, and Trump used the incident to justify his proposed travel ban on people from predominantly Muslim countries entering the U.S.

The Great Recession has significantly impacted American retirement plans, with about 40% of individuals aged 45 and over delaying their retirement. This shift could have far-reaching consequences, affecting Social Security, financial markets, and workforce demographics. A concerning 54% of those earning less than $25,000 reported having no retirement savings, compared to just 10% of those earning $100,000 or more. Many are adjusting their retirement plans; 36% now plan to retire later than initially intended, while 31% have zero money saved for retirement. Among those not yet retired, 18% expect to continue working full-time, 24% plan to work as long as possible, 18% intend to retire and take up part-time work, and 9% anticipate retiring and becoming self-employed. Despite the shift towards defined-contribution plans like 401(k)s and IRAs, only about a quarter of respondents are actively planning for their retirement. A staggering 25% of all respondents, and 14% of those aged 45 or older, admitted they do not know how they will cover expenses in retirement. Financial resources, particularly for part-time or low-wage workers, are limited, with only 37% of part-time workers having access to a retirement plan. Social Security is the most common resource cited for retirement, with 45% of respondents relying on it. The Federal Reserve's report, based on a survey of over 4,100 people, underscores the ongoing financial struggles of many Americans, with 34% reporting they were worse off than in 2008. Economic growth has been inconsistent, and wage growth remains sluggish, adding to the financial challenges faced by many.

Ariel Winter, the 19-year-old star of Modern Family, has faced criticism for her fashion choices and public persona. Known for her unapologetic approach to social media, Winter recently appeared on Conan's show, where she showcased a baby voice that many found cringeworthy. In a video, Winter explained that her baby voice "creeps out" her boyfriend and friends, but the sound was described as "horrifying" by many. Despite the backlash, Winter remains unfazed, embracing a zero-fucks-given attitude that she believes is empowering. Speaking to Elite Daily, she emphasized the importance of self-love and self-acceptance, stating that she posts photos without caring about trolls or haters. Winter's bold fashion choices, such as a gold minidress to a Modern Family event, have also drawn criticism. Some viewers accused her of being overdressed and "trying too hard," while others went so far as to compare her to Lindsay Lohan. In response, Winter defended her right to wear whatever she wants, stating, "Why do I have to be like everyone else? Why can’t people just let other people feel good about themselves and do what they want?" She concluded, "WEAR WHATEVER YOU WANT PEOPLE!" Winter's stance on self-expression and her defiance of societal expectations have made her a symbol of authenticity in the entertainment industry.

Japanese author Haruki Murakami, known for his surreal and often philosophical works, is set to engage with readers in a unique and unprecedented way. For a limited period, starting from January 15 to January 31, Murakami will answer questions from fans on his publisher Shinchosha's website, a project named "Murakami's Place." This initiative, which follows a similar effort in 2006, offers a rare opportunity for Murakami's vast global fanbase to interact directly with the reclusive author. The questions can be submitted in any language, and Murakami's responses will be published over the following two months. His publisher emphasized that he will address a wide range of topics, from his literary works to his personal interests such as running, cats, and his support for the Tokyo Yakult Swallows baseball team. Murakami, who has lived in self-imposed exile for years and is often critical of his home country, is a global literary sensation, with his books translated into over 50 languages. His most recent novel, "Colorless Tsukuru Tazaki and His Years of Pilgrimage," was an instant bestseller in Japan. Despite his reclusive nature, Murakami has a strong connection with his readers, and this project is expected to provide a platform for him to share insights and advice, potentially offering solace and enlightenment to those seeking answers about life's uncertainties. The project is seen as a significant step in bridging the gap between the author and his audience, allowing for a more intimate and direct form of communication.

In his address to the nation almost two weeks ago, President Obama pledged to use force against the armies of Islamic State "wherever they are," including Syria. However, the recent Monday night airstrikes in Syria came sooner and with more force than anticipated, targeting not only Islamic State but also the Khorasan Group, an Al Qaeda offshoot suspected of plotting attacks on Americans. This major offensive raises questions about the extent of U.S. involvement in Syria, where the leadership did not initially invite intervention. Coupled with Obama's successful lobbying for Congress to allocate hundreds of millions of dollars to train Syrian rebels, the airstrikes mark a significant reversal from his previous stance of avoiding entanglement in Syria's civil war.

Until recently, Obama had assiduously resisted American involvement in Syria, citing the complex and unstable nature of the conflict's factions, which include a secular dictator, Bashar Assad, and a mix of moderate and extremist opponents. The decision to launch airstrikes was influenced by the rapid advance of Islamic State fighters, their brutal attacks on Christians and other minorities, and the beheadings of two American journalists. This led Obama to promise a long-term campaign to "degrade and ultimately destroy" Islamic State, though he maintained that it would not require U.S. combat forces.

However, the airstrikes raise concerns about the potential for an escalating U.S. military role in Syria and Iraq. While the threat posed by Islamic State is serious, questions remain about the necessity of an ever-escalating U.S. military presence and the clarity of the strategy and achievable goals. The case for such an intervention has yet to be fully made.

On the other hand, the initial bombing raids are seen as a welcome offensive against a heinous group that poses a threat to U.S. interests in the Middle East and security at home. President Obama emphasizes that this will be a long campaign, but it will need to be conducted within the limitations he has set for the military. The immediate goal is to stop ISIS assaults on Kurdish civilians in the north of Syria while also targeting the Khorasan branch of Al Qaeda.

The decision to act now, rather than waiting for a more definitive strategy, has been praised by some as a necessary response to the urgent threat. However, others remain troubled by the potential for an expanding U.S. role in the region and the need for a clear and achievable strategy to justify such intervention.

The U.S. Supreme Court declined to intervene in a case where a convicted killer in Illinois argued that prosecutors improperly focused on his failure to testify during his trial. Ronald Mikos, a former foot doctor, was sentenced to death in 2005 for shooting a disabled nurse to prevent her from testifying against him in a Medicare fraud trial. Mikos's defense team claimed his silence did not reflect a lack of remorse. The 7th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals upheld his sentence. In a separate case, federal prosecutors announced they would seek the death penalty for Brendt Christensen, a former University of Illinois graduate student accused of kidnapping and killing visiting scholar Yingying Zhang. Christensen is also accused of a 2013 sexual assault and has a history of making threats. His trial is likely to be delayed. The decision to seek the death penalty, which requires approval from the U.S. Attorney General, marks the third such case in recent weeks. The last federal death sentence in Illinois was given to Dr. Ronald Mikos, who remains in federal prison awaiting execution. The case of Christensen highlights the rare and complex process of seeking the death penalty in federal court.

Wal-Mart de Mexico paid over $24 million in bribes to secure construction permits, according to a New York Times investigation. When a whistleblower alerted top executives in 2005, the company launched an internal investigation but later shut it down, failing to report the findings to law enforcement. This revelation threatens to tarnish Wal-Mart's image as a company committed to ethical business practices. The U.S. Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, which bans companies from paying foreign officials to gain business, has come under scrutiny from business groups, including an arm of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce with ties to Wal-Mart. Wal-Mart de Mexico, the company's largest foreign subsidiary, employs 209,000 people in Mexico, making it the country's largest private employer. The company's shares fell nearly 5% on the news, and it faces potential criminal charges under the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act. Wal-Mart has met with U.S. authorities and is conducting its own investigation, promising to enhance its anti-corruption program. The investigation may slow the company's expansion in Mexico and other markets, and executives, including former CEO Lee Scott, were made aware of the allegations in 2005. Congressional Democrats have called for a probe and a meeting with Wal-Mart executives.

Police in Sparks, Nevada, entered an apartment after a standoff and found Mark and Debby Constantino, a couple known for their appearances on the reality TV show "Ghost Adventures," dead inside. The incident began when Reno police received a call about a man found dead in a northwest Reno home. The couple's daughter, who was living in the apartment near Sparks High School, was missing. Officers tracked her cellphone and found her with her estranged husband, Mark Constantino, inside the apartment. They heard several shots fired when they knocked on the door and heard a man yelling at police to leave, giving them 15 minutes to gather his thoughts or threatening to kill his wife. SWAT teams from Reno and Sparks surrounded the apartment, evacuated the complex, and put it on lockdown. Officers eventually used explosives to open the door and found the couple dead inside. The couple had been featured on the Travel Channel's "Ghost Adventures" and maintained a website, www.spirit-speak.com. Debby Constantino had obtained a restraining order against her husband and was involved in a previous kidnapping and domestic incident. The cause of death was not immediately released. The incident prompted Sparks High School to be put on lockdown as a precaution. Police were not searching for other suspects and had not ruled out any possibilities.

Depending on your depth of feeling about Whitney Houston, the Motown-era musical “Sparkle” will either feel like a fond (and sometimes cringe-inducing) farewell to an old friend, or a wholly unremarkable entry in the already overcrowded star-is-born genre. Houston, who shot the film just a few months before her death in February, does get her moment of glory in a scene so pointed, it’s hard to believe it wasn’t re-edited after she died. Standing at the front of a church, clad in a royal-purple cape and flanked by stained glass and a full choir, the late singer belts out — in a voice substantially huskier than in her “Bodyguard” days — that she’s “singing because I’m happy.” At my screening, I’m pretty sure there wasn’t a dry eye in the house. If you’re still mourning Houston’s death, it’s almost enough of a reason to go. But it does little to redeem the rest of this plodding story, which often seems like a flat, straightforward Supremes biopic in its adherence to seemingly pointless scenes and exposition. Director Salim Akil (“Jumping the Broom”), working from a screenplay by his wife, Mara Brock Akil (TV’s “The Game”), gets the retro visuals just right, and some stage performances do, well, sparkle. But they’re too few and far between, surrounded by cardboard dialogue and a now-well-worn “Behind the Music” trajectory. The remake of a 1976 film starring a young Irene Cara, it’s the story of three sisters, Sparkle (Jordin Sparks), Sister (Carmen Ejogo), and Dolores (Tika Sumpter), who try to make it as a girl group in the burgeoning Detroit Motown scene of 1968. Houston, the girls’ churchgoing single mother, Emma, “used to be a professional singer” who turned to substance abuse before finding God, so they’re doing the singing thing on the down-low, sneaking out to perform in smoky clubs once Mom’s gone to bed. Houston does get a few amusing moments in her supporting role, dancing along with a band on TV before snapping it off and commanding the girls’ Bible club to hit the books, or training a steely eye on her daughter being chatted up by a young man after church. As the group, Sister and the Sisters, begins to make a name for itself, the film briefly takes off with a series of lively performances; Ejogo is a particularly dynamic and gorgeous singer, and all three young actresses wear the increasingly glam period outfits well. But eventually, Sister’s bruises and track marks, courtesy of Satin (Mike Epps), start to show through the cover-up, and her downfall takes center stage in a way that feels awfully close to a Lifetime TV movie. For a movie called “Sparkle,” the absolutely least interesting or central thing about it is Sparkle (and Sparks), although the “Idol” winner does bust out one impressive performance. In any case, I hope not to have to type that name again unless I’m covering a My Little Pony resurgence. Whitney Houston deserved better than to go out onscreen with this botch job remake of a 1976 soap opera that never deserved another thought. Hell, Dreamgirls did a better job of fictionalizing the story of the Supremes into a viable musical. The new Sparkle is a formula job from scene one to dead end. Set in Detroit in the late 1960s with Motown in flower, Sparkle casts Houston as the domineering mother of three daughters who form a girl group behind mama's back. Sister (Carmen Ejogo) is the troubled bombshell who fronts the group, called – ready for it? – Sister and Her Sisters. Dee (Tika Sumpter) doesn't mind singing backup because she has her eye on being a doctor. It's Sparkle (Jordin Sparks), a churchy mama's girl, who does mind. Sparkle writes all the songs and yearns to be a STAR!. In a movie that feels fake to its core, Houston is the genuine article. She will be much missed.

Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, a conservative icon and the longest-serving member of the current court, was found dead at a West Texas ranch on Saturday morning, federal officials confirmed. The 79-year-old justice, who was a guest at the Cibolo Creek Ranch, was discovered by a person involved with the ranch when he failed to appear for breakfast. His body was taken to El Paso, where it was escorted back to Washington by U.S. marshals and Supreme Court police. The cause of death was not immediately known, but a federal official stated there was no evidence of foul play. Texas Governor Greg Abbott and Chief Justice John Roberts released statements mourning Scalia's passing and praising his contributions to the legal world. Scalia's death sets the stage for a contentious political battle over his replacement, with Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell arguing the vacancy should be filled by the next president, while Senate Minority Leader Harry Reid called for a swift nomination. President Obama vowed to nominate a successor, stating he would fulfill his constitutional responsibility to fill the vacancy. The sudden absence of Scalia, who was a leading proponent of originalism and textualism, will have significant implications for the court's upcoming decisions, particularly in cases where a 4-4 split could result in no precedent being set. His death also reignites debates on the role of judges in interpreting the Constitution and the importance of filling judicial vacancies, especially in an election year.

A Catholic priest in the Philippines faced disciplinary action after a video of him using a hoverboard during Christmas Eve Mass went viral. The incident occurred when the unidentified priest, riding a hoverboard up and down the nave of his church with a microphone, sang "May the Good Lord Bless and Keep You." Upon concluding his performance, parishioners gave him a round of applause. However, the Diocese of San Pablo was not amused, issuing a statement condemning the priest's actions. They emphasized that the Mass is the church's highest form of worship and not a personal celebration where one can introduce new elements to gain attention. The priest acknowledged his mistake and promised it would not happen again, leading to his suspension from his parish. He will spend time reflecting on the incident. The diocese's statement referred to the event as a "wake-up call" for the priest. The suspension highlights the strict adherence to traditional practices during religious ceremonies, even in the face of modern technology and its potential to distract from the sacred nature of the Mass.

A 14-year-old girl from Greenwood, Delaware, fell from a stopped gondola ride at Six Flags Amusement Park in Queensbury, New York, on Saturday night, tumbling into a crowd of park guests and employees gathered below in an effort to catch her before she hit the ground. The Warren County Sheriff's Office reported that the girl, who is in stable condition with no serious injuries, was riding the "Sky Ride" with a child relative when she fell about 25 feet from a stationary two-person car. The ride was stopped by an operator after receiving word of the rider in distress. The girl fell from the car, struck a tree, and landed in the crowd. She was treated by park emergency medical staff and transferred by ambulance to Glen Falls Hospital before being taken by helicopter to Albany Medical Center. 

Six Flags Amusement Park stated that the safety of guests is a top priority and that there does not appear to be any malfunction of the ride. The park has closed the attraction until a thorough review can be completed. An unidentified 47-year-old man from Schenectady, New York, who was a guest at the park, was treated and released from a hospital for a back injury sustained when he attempted to catch the falling girl. The park's official statement emphasized the safety measures in place, but the incident has raised concerns about the adequacy of safety protocols and the potential risks associated with stopped rides. The accident has also prompted discussions about the responsibilities of park staff and the public in ensuring the safety of amusement park guests.

Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney released his 2010 and 2011 tax returns, revealing that he paid a lower effective tax rate than many top wage-earners. Romney’s income is primarily from investment profits, dividends, and interest, with his 2010 income at $21.7 million and estimated 2011 income at $20.9 million. His effective tax rate was 13.9% in 2010 and 15.4% in 2011, significantly lower than the 35% top income tax rate on wages. Romney’s tax rate is lower due to the tax code favoring investment income, including the 15% capital gains rate and the “carried interest” provision, which taxes investment income at a lower rate than wages. His wife, Ann, contributed $7 million to charity, mostly to the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Romney’s tax returns are part of his campaign to regain momentum after losing the South Carolina primary to former House Speaker Newt Gingrich. President Barack Obama plans to emphasize the “Buffett rule” in his State of the Union address, aiming to make the tax code fairer and ensure the ultra-wealthy pay their “fair share.” The release of Romney’s tax returns highlights the debate over income inequality and the tax code, with Democrats calling for more transparency and Republicans defending Romney’s financial practices. The tax returns show Romney’s extensive investments in foreign entities, including a closed Swiss bank account, and his use of tax losses to reduce his taxable income. The release of the returns is seen as a political move to address concerns about Romney’s finances and his image as a wealthy financier.

SpaceX launched a classified U.S. spy agency mission, NROL-76, from Kennedy Space Center on May 1, 2017, at 7:15 a.m. ET. The Falcon 9 rocket, after a sensor issue caused a scrub on the previous day, successfully carried the National Reconnaissance Office (NRO) mission into orbit. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk noted that the launch was a good one despite high-altitude wind shear, which was at 98.6% of the theoretical load limit. The first stage of the Falcon 9 rocket returned to Earth and landed at Landing Zone 1, marking the 10th successful landing for SpaceX. This mission was significant as it was SpaceX’s first dedicated launch for the NRO, the intelligence agency responsible for satellites. The launch was part of SpaceX’s ongoing effort to make reusable rockets a reality, with the company planning to launch another Falcon 9 from Kennedy Space Center on May 15. The successful launch and landing demonstrated SpaceX’s progress in reducing launch costs and advancing its goal of colonizing Mars.

Josh Duggar, the former executive director of the Family Research Council and star of 19 Kids and Counting, has been accused of using a model’s face on his Ashley Madison profile, according to Gawker. Matthew McCarthy, a 27-year-old DJ and photographer, claims Duggar used his picture on several dating and social media sites, including Ashley Madison, causing him significant embarrassment. McCarthy has filed a lawsuit against Duggar, alleging wrongful use of his image and seeking damages. The lawsuit highlights the humiliation McCarthy has faced due to the connection between his professional and personal life and Duggar's controversial past. Duggar, who has admitted to a porn addiction and has faced child molestation allegations, has not responded to the allegations. The OkCupid profile in question, which was recently taken down, listed Duggar as a political professional with a $100,000 to $150,000 annual salary, looking for casual sex while claiming to be strictly monogamous. The profile's last activity date coincides with the time Duggar's credit card stopped paying for his Ashley Madison account. The profile's photo, which is not of Duggar, is a common Google search result for "random guy," leading many to speculate that the profile was created using McCarthy's image. McCarthy's DJ career has been affected by the scandal, and he is considering legal action. The case raises questions about the misuse of personal images and the lasting impact of public scandals.

UC Irvine faced criticism after it rescinded admission offers to nearly 500 students this year, contributing to a higher-than-expected number of freshmen accepting spots. Vice Chancellor for Student Affairs Thomas Parham acknowledged that the university took a stricter approach on processing admissions, leading to the withdrawal of 499 admission offers: 299 were transcript-related, with 185 students appealing; another 209 were grade-related, with 110 appeals. As of Friday, 63 students who appealed were reinstated. Parham apologized to those who felt ignored or mistreated, emphasizing that all students who meet the terms and conditions of the admissions offer will be welcomed into the Anteater family. No acceptance will be withdrawn due to over-enrollment, despite external reports to the contrary. The university received more than 104,000 applications from both freshmen and transfer students for the 2017-18 year, one of the highest numbers in the country. UCI offered admission to 31,103 freshmen, with about 7,100 accepting, but the school had planned a freshman class of approximately 6,250 students. Students complained on social media that the university over-enrolled and used any excuse to trim its number. Many of the prospective students who saw their offers rescinded said that either the university or their high school made mistakes, causing them a lot of anxiety. Johnny Wang, 18, of Glendale, is appealing because UCI didn’t receive a transcript from his high school. Simran Chopra, 18, of Los Angeles, locked herself in a bathroom and cried when she learned of the withdrawal, saying she has proof that her transcript was sent via certified mail before the July 1 deadline. Julia Kim, 18, of Claremont, considered community college or taking a gap year after her appeal was denied, as she wanted to stay close to her family and attend UCI. The university increased the number of people reviewing appeals and expects those already on appeal to be completed by the end of next week, with fewer than two months before school starts.

The scandal that led to the resignation of former CIA Director David Petraeus has expanded to involve Marine General John Allen, the U.S. commander in Afghanistan, according to reports. Defense Secretary Leon Panetta has put on hold Allen’s nomination as NATO Supreme Allied Commander, pending an investigation into allegedly inappropriate communications between Allen and Jill Kelley, a Tampa socialite. Kelley, who was a volunteer social liaison at MacDill Air Force Base, had initially complained to the FBI about receiving harassing emails that eventually led investigators to uncover the affair between Petraeus and his biographer, Paula Broadwell. The investigation into Allen’s emails with Kelley, which spanned from 2010 to 2012, has raised concerns about potential ethical lapses and the handling of sensitive information. Pentagon officials say no classified material was found, but the sheer volume of communications, estimated at 20,000 to 30,000 pages, has prompted scrutiny. Allen has denied any wrongdoing, stating he never shared classified information with Kelley and that any communications were innocent. White House Press Secretary Jay Carney said President Obama remains supportive of Allen, though the nomination’s future remains uncertain. Meanwhile, Kelley, who is an honorary consul of South Korea, has invoked her diplomatic status in a 911 call, attempting to invoke protection for her property. The scandal has also revealed that Kelley and her husband, Scott, are in significant debt, with multiple lawsuits and foreclosure proceedings against their properties. Despite their financial troubles, the Kelleys hosted high-profile military events, including Petraeus and Allen, at their home in Tampa. The investigation into Allen’s emails is ongoing, with no definitive conclusions yet reached. Defense officials urge caution, stating that Allen’s nomination may still proceed if the investigation finds no evidence of wrongdoing.

Tony Curtis, the legendary actor who starred in films like "Some Like It Hot" and "Spartacus," disinherited his five children in his final will, written five months before his death from cardiac arrest at age 85. Instead, he left his entire estate to his widow, Jill Vandenberg Curtis. One of his children contested the will in court but was unsuccessful. Jamie Lee Curtis, his daughter with actress Janet Leigh, expressed shock and sadness at the news. In a statement, Jill Curtis said the matter was a private family affair. Curtis made over 140 films over a 60-year career. His children from three marriages include Jamie Lee, Christine Kaufmann, and Leslie Allen.

Four families of American hostages who were killed while in Islamic State custody have issued a joint letter to President Obama, urging the administration to use all appropriate means to find and return missing U.S. journalist Austin Tice. Tice, 34, a U.S. Marine-turned-journalist, vanished in Syria in August 2012, and his whereabouts remain unknown. The families of Kayla Jean Mueller, James Foley, Steven Sotloff, and Peter Kassig, who were also held captive by the Islamic State, have united to call for increased efforts to locate Tice. Mueller, Foley, and Sotloff were beheaded by the group, while Kassig died in a coalition strike. The families' letter, released on Wednesday, highlights the ongoing tragedy and terror experienced by their loved ones and emphasizes the need for the Obama administration to act boldly to bring Tice home. The families have urged the White House to leverage all appropriate means, including diplomatic efforts, to find Tice and secure his release. They have also criticized the administration for not mentioning Tice during a high-profile speech at the White House Correspondents Association dinner. The Tices, who have endured three Christmases without their son and brother, have specifically asked the government to engage in bold action to bring Austin Tice safely home. The families have expressed their hope that the government will not repeat missed opportunities and "deadly silence" that led to the deaths of the other hostages. They have emphasized that they are not asking for any compromise on national security but are asking the president to use his full authority to bring Tice home. The families have also acknowledged the anguish of the Tice family and have expressed unwavering hope that Austin’s parents will not give up.

A controversial video game that allowed players to simulate a school shooting was removed from Steam, the world's largest PC gaming platform, after widespread backlash. The game, "Active Shooter," developed by Revived Games and published by ACID, was set to launch on June 6. Critics, including survivors of the Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School shooting and anti-gun activist Fred Guttenberg, condemned the game, calling it "disgusting" and "vile." Valve Corporation, which runs Steam, removed the game due to the developer, Ata Berdiyev, being a "troll with a history of customer abuse, publishing copyrighted material, and user review manipulation." The game's description attempted to downplay its controversial nature but failed to quell public outrage. This incident highlights the ongoing debate about the ethics of gaming companies profiting from violent content in the wake of mass shootings.

House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif., stated that she will not trade with President Donald Trump for his border wall, calling it a "manhood issue" for him, setting a firm stance ahead of a potential December showdown over the issue. Pelosi emphasized that Democrats support border security but prefer to focus on strengthening existing measures as part of a comprehensive immigration overhaul. She warned that Democrats cannot be forced to support the wall as the only way to secure the border, suggesting it is likely the worst method. Trump is eager for a confrontation over wall funding, with GOP leaders having secured a delay in the battle until after the midterm elections. Pelosi’s stance is unlikely to matter much in the House, where Republicans have enough votes to pass the $5 billion requested for the wall. However, Senate Democrats, particularly Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, may pose a significant obstacle. Pelosi hinted that if Democrats win the House majority in the upcoming election, she could have more leverage. She expressed confidence about being elected speaker but noted that she is prepared for challenges. Pelosi outlined Democrats’ top priorities for next year, including lowering health care costs, increasing paychecks, and improving green infrastructure. She also mentioned that campaign finance reform is likely to be the first bill of the new Congress. Pelosi stressed the importance of holding the Trump administration accountable, but she wants a thoughtful approach to oversight, not a "scattershot" approach.

The 2014 All-Star Game at Target Field in Minneapolis turned into a love poem to Derek Jeter, with National League pitcher Adam Wainwright playing a pivotal role. As Jeter approached home plate, Wainwright stepped back, placed his glove on the mound, and joined the applause, showing respect. However, Wainwright's moment of kindness quickly turned into controversy. After giving up a double, a triple, and a home run, he admitted, "I was going to give him a couple of pipe shots," implying Jeter might not have hit the ball without the pitch. Wainwright's candidness backfired, as his comments were seen as disrespectful and cheapened Jeter's moment. He expressed regret, calling himself a "knucklehead" and "idiot," and acknowledged his words might have detracted from Jeter's big moment. The incident highlighted the issues with the "This One Counts" initiative, which awards home-field advantage in the World Series based on the All-Star Game's outcome. Wainwright's experience suggested the need to reconsider the All-Star Game's format and purpose, as it has too many pitfalls and minefields. The controversy also underscored the changing mindset around the game, where the line between showmanship and respect can blur.

A Chinese tourist visiting Yellowstone National Park was fined $1,000 and a $30 court processing fee for walking off the boardwalk in the Mammoth Hot Springs thermal area on June 14, 2016. According to a witness, the individual collected thermal water and broke through the fragile travertine crust. Park rangers issued a federal violation notice requiring the man to appear in the Yellowstone Justice Center Court. The incident occurred just a week after a 23-year-old Oregon man, Colin Nathaniel Scott, fell into a hot spring in the Norris Geyser Basin and was presumed dead. Scott's death was the second known thermal-related incident in the park during the 2016 summer season. Earlier, six people received $130 citations for walking off the trail in the Grand Prismatic Springs area. Park regulations mandate visitors stay on designated trails and boardwalks for their safety and to protect the park's natural resources. The hefty fine highlights the importance of adhering to these rules, as the thermal features are irreplaceable. Park officials urge visitors to remain on boardwalks and trails to ensure their safety and the preservation of the park's unique natural wonders.

In Taiwan, the betel nut, a small seed harvested from the Areca palm and chewed for its stimulating effects, is causing a significant public health crisis. Chewed with a mixture of slaked lime, a betel leaf, and flavorings, the nut is a common sight among working-age men, who use it to stay awake during long hours of labor. However, the habit, while providing temporary energy, is linked to high rates of oral cancer, with Taiwan ranking among the world's top for oral cancer incidence and mortality. The Taiwanese government is now taking action, offering free screenings and subsidies for farmers to switch to alternative crops, aiming to reduce the domestic supply of betel nuts. Despite these efforts, the tradition remains deeply ingrained in many communities, with nearly all children of workers in the fishing industry admitting their parents or relatives chew the nut. The dangers of betel nut use are not limited to oral cancer; it can also cause gum irritation, tooth decay, and even lead to the incurable condition, oral submucous fibrosis. The WHO has classified betel nuts as a carcinogen, and the U.S. FDA considers them unsafe for consumption. Public health campaigns are ongoing, but the long-term effects of betel nut use mean that many individuals, like Qiu Zhen-huang, a former gravel company worker, are only diagnosed with oral cancer decades after their first taste. His story highlights the devastating impact of the habit, as he underwent extensive surgery and faced significant psychological and physical challenges. The Taiwanese government's efforts to curb the use of betel nuts are crucial, but the cultural and economic factors that sustain the tradition present a formidable challenge. The journey to reduce the prevalence of betel nut use is a complex one, involving not only health education but also addressing the social and economic roots of the habit.

U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton firmly stated that she has no plans to run for president in 2012 or 2016, according to interviews in New Zealand. Clinton, who previously ran for the Democratic nomination in 2008, made it clear she is satisfied with her current role as Secretary of State. In separate interviews with TV3 New Zealand and TV New Zealand, Clinton emphasized that she is not considering another presidential run, even as far as 2016. She expressed that she is enjoying her current position and is not interested in returning to the political arena. Clinton also highlighted that the United States should be ready for a female president, though it will not be her. During her nearly two-week Asia-Pacific tour, Clinton visited New Zealand, where she met with Prime Minister John Phillip Key and Foreign Minister Murray Stuart McCully. Key inadvertently referred to Clinton as "President Clinton" during a speech, leading to laughter and a quick correction. Clinton used the opportunity to defend President Barack Obama, stating that his decisions, though not always popular, were essential for the well-being of the American people. She also acknowledged that the Democrats' losses in the recent mid-term elections were significant but not unprecedented.

The Obama administration faced new scrutiny over its handling of a $535 million loan to Solyndra, a California solar panel maker that declared bankruptcy, with emails revealing possible conflicts of interest and legal concerns. Energy Department official Steven J. Spinner, who had promised to recuse himself due to his wife’s law firm representing Solyndra, pushed for the loan despite these issues. Spinner frequently communicated with Solyndra officials and urged the White House budget office to expedite the approval. Emails show that top officials, including Rahm Emanuel and Carol Browner, were involved in discussions about Solyndra, raising questions about potential conflicts of interest. Despite warnings from the Treasury Department that the loan restructuring might be illegal, the Energy Department proceeded. The restructuring allowed private investors to be repaid before taxpayers in case of default, potentially putting taxpayers at risk. The controversy has intensified as the Justice Department investigates Solyndra for possible financial misrepresentations, and the House Energy and Commerce Committee accuses the administration of a “disturbingly close relationship” between key officials and Solyndra investors. The emails also highlight disagreements between the Energy Department and other agencies over the legality and thoroughness of the loan vetting process. The administration defended its actions, stating that career professionals made the legal determinations. However, the ongoing investigation and new revelations continue to cast doubt on the administration’s handling of the Solyndra loan.

President Obama delivered a speech in Afghanistan outlining his strategy for the war, emphasizing a steady drawdown of U.S. troops and a commitment to the 2014 deadline for turning security over to the Afghan government. The speech, while thoughtful and sober, was criticized for its rushed and perfunctory delivery, with some arguing that it lacked compelling reasons for escalation. Obama's approach was seen as a mix of Third Way realism and national self-interest, avoiding the Wilsonian rhetoric of past interventions. Critics pointed out the limitations of the Afghan government, the uncertain prospects for a "Pashtun awakening," and the potential for increased stratification and backlash in the face of continued U.S. involvement. The speech was also seen as a fulfillment of campaign promises, with some questioning whether Obama's decision was truly a break from the status quo or a continuation of the Bush-Cheney administration's policies. The article concludes by questioning the feasibility of Obama's strategy, suggesting that the war may be a "doom loop" for Western liberalism, leading to economic stagnation and social discontent.

Alvin Cross Jr., an Albany, Georgia man, found himself in a precarious situation after sending a text message to his probation officer asking if he had any drugs, only to have the officer forward the message to the police. The text, "You have some weed?" as reported by WALB, led to a raid on Cross's home, where authorities discovered a bag of cocaine. As a result, Cross pleaded guilty to cocaine possession and will serve one year in prison, with an additional year for violating his probation. This case highlights the potential consequences of digital missteps, especially when dealing with sensitive matters such as probation. The incident serves as a cautionary tale about the importance of careful communication, especially when using mobile devices, as the immediacy of text messages can lead to unforeseen and serious repercussions.

The bipartisan Commission on Wartime Contracting issued a critical report on the overreliance on contractors in Iraq and Afghanistan, highlighting tens of billions of wasted dollars due to poor planning, oversight, and criminal behavior. The report, titled "At What Risk? Correcting Over-reliance on Contractors in Contingency Operations," calls for reforms in how the government awards and monitors contracts, suggesting the creation of special federal oversight teams and restrictions on contractors' roles in hiring others. It also criticizes the current system, where untrustworthy contractors can continue profiting while responsible businesses are denied opportunities. The commission's findings echo previous reports of waste and abuse, with the State Department's cable revealing Afghanistan's vice president carrying $52 million in cash. Despite the Obama administration's recent decision to withhold public access to contractor performance data, the commission's recommendations aim to address the systemic issues that have led to significant financial and operational inefficiencies in military, reconstruction, and training programs.

A mother of two from the United Kingdom died from sepsis after a minor hand scrape while gardening, her family has revealed. Lucinda Smith, 43, went to see her GP after feeling pain in her shoulder following the minor scrape in March last year. The doctor diagnosed a trapped nerve and prescribed anti-depressants to relax her, and she was also advised to see a physiotherapist. Within a few days, Smith's condition worsened, with her fingers and arm becoming red and swollen, and she was also vomiting. Her mother, Shirley, believes her fate was already sealed by then. Three days after the initial visit, Smith went to the accident and emergency department at Basildon Hospital, where a blood test revealed she had sepsis, a form of blood poisoning. She was immediately admitted for emergency treatment but died two days later from organ failure. 

Shirley Smith believes her daughter could have been saved if she had been given the test and had her blood pressure taken when she first complained of feeling unwell. The inquest ruled she died of toxic shock caused by sepsis. The family hopes her story will raise awareness about the importance of recognizing and treating sepsis early. 

Sepsis is a potentially life-threatening complication of an infection, according to Mayo Clinic experts. It happens when chemicals released into the bloodstream to fight the infection trigger inflammatory responses throughout the body, leading to organ damage and failure. Sepsis can also cause septic shock, where the person's blood pressure drops dramatically, potentially leading to death. 

Anyone can develop sepsis, but seniors and people with weaker immune systems are more vulnerable, say Mayo Clinic experts. Early treatment of sepsis, usually with antibiotics and large amounts of intravenous fluids, improves chances for survival. People should know the signs and immediately seek medical care if they notice these symptoms after developing an infection: shivering, fever, or very cold; extreme pain or discomfort; clammy or sweaty skin; confusion or disorientation; shortness of breath; high heart rate. 

In August, a CDC report showed that for nearly 80 percent of patients, sepsis begins outside of the hospital. It is also linked to exposure to medical environments—7 in 10 patients with sepsis had recently used health care services or had chronic diseases requiring frequent medical care. Dr. Tom Frieden, CDC Director, emphasized the importance of recognizing and treating sepsis quickly, as it is a race against time. The most common infections that can lead to sepsis include lung infections, such as pneumonia, urinary tract infection, gut infection, and skin infection.

A 60-year-old man from Leonora, Western Australia, was found dead near Wiluna, 1,000 kilometres north-east of Perth, after abandoning his broken-down vehicle in the remote Outback. The man had walked more than 40 kilometres with only a small container of water to seek help, but his body was discovered only two kilometres from Windidda Station, where he was heading. A woman who left the vehicle about 24 hours later was found by people from Wongawol Station and taken to Windidda Station. The woman had been heading to the same destination and had camped on the roadside for the night before being rescued. Her alarm led to the discovery of the man's body. Police stated there were no suspicious circumstances and a report would be prepared for the coroner. The incident highlights the dangers of traveling in remote areas and the importance of staying with a vehicle if it breaks down. Authorities urged people to carry a three-day supply of food and water, ensure their vehicle is in good condition, and consider carrying emergency equipment like a satellite phone or CB radio. They also advised travelers to inform others of their plans and estimated time of arrival. The maximum temperature in Wiluna reached 41.5 degrees Celsius on the day the woman was found, emphasizing the harsh conditions faced by travelers in the region.

Nearly two dozen Islamist women and girls, some as young as 15, were sentenced to heavy prison terms in a court ruling that came a day after police beat and terrorized prominent female activists in a crackdown on secular demonstrators under a tough new anti-protest law. The harshness of the sentences and the scenes a day earlier were new signs that the military-backed government was becoming bolder in silencing dissent, reminiscent of the Hosni Mubarak era. The 21 young female defendants, including seven teenagers, were convicted of holding a protest in Alexandria demanding the reinstatement of ousted President Mohammed Morsi. They were sentenced to 11 years in prison, while six other Brotherhood members received 15-year sentences for inciting the demonstrations. The sentences were met with shock and criticism, with the Muslim Brotherhood's political arm vowing that the verdict would only increase the determination of the people to get their rights. Meanwhile, hundreds of secular youth activists protested in downtown Cairo against the government's clampdown on dissent. The new protest law, which bans any protests or public political gatherings of more than 10 people without a prior police permit, has been criticized for imposing stiff fines and jail terms for violators. The crackdown is rearranging Egypt's political map, with the government moving against secular youth activists opposed to the military and police. The crisis is fragmenting the loose coalition of liberal and secular groups that supported the military in its July 3 removal of Morsi. The government's actions have been justified as needed to fight terrorism and bring stability, but critics argue that they are exploiting divisions among secular democracy activists. The prosecutor general's office ordered 24 people arrested in Tuesday's activist protest to be held for questioning on possible charges of violating the protest law. The harsh sentences and the government's actions have sparked wide criticism of the way the Interior Ministry and the judiciary have been handling the cases of Morsy supporters.

At least 45 people, including 15 children, have died after an illegal building collapsed in a Mumbai suburb, police say. About 70 others were injured, and many are feared trapped beneath the seven-storey structure. Construction work was ongoing even though four floors were already occupied. Rescue efforts continued through the night, with dozens injured. The collapse is part of a pattern of building failures in India, often due to poor construction practices and illegal structures. The builder used substandard materials and lacked an occupation certificate. Authorities are searching for the builders to arrest them and are questioning officials who supervised the construction. The incident highlights the issue of illegal construction in India, where demand for housing outstrips supply, leading to the proliferation of unsafe buildings. Rescue workers faced challenges due to the building's complex structure, with multiple floors sandwiched together. The collapse underlines the broader issues of corruption and inadequate oversight in the construction sector.

A 12-year-old girl narrowly averted a suicide attempt on a bridge in Southern California, thanks to the calm and patient intervention of Officer Chris Perez, a rookie on the South Pasadena Police force. The girl, who had fled from a group home due to severe emotional distress, was hanging from the 80-foot-high York Bridge, threatening to jump. Officer Perez, who had been on duty for only an hour, approached the girl calmly, asking what was happening and learning that she was upset by her living conditions. He spent time building trust, engaging in back-and-forth conversation, and eventually asked if he could help her over the railing to a safer environment. The girl agreed, and Officer Perez carefully pulled her over the edge, hugging her to safety. Paramedics arrived to assist, and the girl was taken into protective custody for a medical evaluation. Officer Perez, who has only been with the department for a year, expressed reluctance to be called a hero, but emphasized the importance of his parents' support and the training he received. The incident highlights the critical role of empathy and patience in crisis situations, as well as the potential impact of a single officer's actions in saving a life.

Camp John Waters, set to debut in September 2017 in Kent, Connecticut, invites adult fans of the avant-garde filmmaker to immerse themselves in a weekend of debauchery and creativity. This unique summer camp offers a blend of traditional activities like ziplining and canoeing, alongside a rich array of Waters-centric offerings. Attendees can enjoy screenings of his cult classics, participate in 'Blood Mary Bingo,' and engage in Hairspray karaoke. Burlesque lessons, a 'Scotch and Cigars' session, and a costume contest judged by the legendary John Waters himself are also on the agenda. Waters will perform a one-man show, read from his new book "Make Trouble," and host a Q&A session. The camp can accommodate up to 300 participants over the three-day period from September 22-24, 2017, with alcohol available for an additional fee. Each camper will receive an autographed copy of "Make Trouble," a speech-turned-manifesto that has garnered praise for its witty and inspirational content. The book, illustrated by Eric Hanson, is described as a "commencement address I consumed with joy," filled with thought-provoking advice and playful visuals. It's not just a read for recent graduates but a reminder of Waters' ongoing impact on society. The camp promises to be a unique experience, combining the campfire traditions of outdoor living with the irreverent spirit of the "Pope of Trash."

Five children, including 1-year-old twins, died in a late-night fire that swept through a house in Youngstown, Ohio, according to authorities. The only survivor was the children's mother, who managed to jump out of a second-floor window. Youngstown Fire Capt. Kurt Wright said the other three children who died were ages 9, 3, and 2. The fire, which started on the first floor, was accidental, Wright said, as state and local investigators were just beginning to search for a cause. The mother, Deborah Rivera, was taken to a hospital for treatment of her injuries. A neighbor, Justin Viera, said flames were shooting out of the first-floor windows when he arrived. The home, a two-story wood structure built more than 90 years ago, was mostly damaged on the first floor. Youngstown Fire Chief Barry Finley said the tragedy hit the department hard, especially as Christmas was approaching. Firefighters were able to rescue three of the children, but they later died at a hospital. One firefighter was treated at the scene and another was taken to a hospital for treatment and released. A memorial began to grow outside the home, with people leaving stuffed animals in honor of the children. The house, valued at $7,930, was last sold for $10,000 in September 2013. The owners, Lindsey Maggie and Lindsey Henry of Campbell, were neighbors and had just moved into the house six months ago. The fire is the most deadly in Youngstown since a January 2008 arson that claimed the lives of two adults and four children. The family's mother, America Negron Acevedo, was in critical but stable condition at MetroHealth's Burn Center in Cleveland. The fire department and community expressed their condolences and support for the family.

Microsoft unveiled its new motion-sensing controller, Kinect, during a Cirque du Soleil performance at the University of Southern California. The device, which will be compatible with Xbox 360, allows users to play games and interact with the console through gestures and spoken commands. The event, which featured a gospel revival-like atmosphere with audience members wearing white ponchos, showcased various games and applications that utilize Kinect's technology. Among the games demonstrated were a yoga and Tai Chi game, a soccer game, a racing game where players can steer using their hands, and a collection of sports games including boxing, bowling, beach volleyball, track and field, soccer, and table tennis. Additionally, a dance game called Dance Central, developed by MTV Games, was shown. The event also highlighted the integration of Kinect with dashboard apps, enabling users to scroll through photos, start live video chats, and share photos. While the technology demonstrated showed potential, the event left some wondering if it would significantly challenge the Wii and Sony's upcoming motion control system, Move.

Lawyers for Boston Marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev argue his trial should have been held outside the city due to widespread outrage and publicity, and they seek a new trial. In court papers, they cite a recent Supreme Court ruling that could invalidate many convictions, including Tsarnaev's. The defense claims jurors couldn't avoid media coverage and that the venue was improper. Tsarnaev was sentenced to death in June for the 2013 bombings that killed three and injured over 260. His case is part of the rare federal death row, with only three executions in the past 50 years. Despite the dramatic news, his fate will likely take years to resolve due to the lengthy appeals process. Tsarnaev's legal team plans to appeal on prejudicial grounds and insufficient time to present a full mitigation argument.

Democratic presidential candidate Bernie Sanders is set to introduce a bill that would eliminate for-profit prisons, aiming to expand a national conversation on social justice and prison reform. The "Justice Is Not For Sale" Act, co-sponsored by Rep. Raul Grijalva, calls for a ban on federal, state, and local governments using private prisons within three years. The bill also seeks to reduce high fees for prisoner services, reinstate the federal parole system, and decrease the number of immigrants held in detention centers. Sanders argues that the private prison industry creates a "perverse incentive" to keep jails filled, disproportionately impacting black and Hispanic communities. The bill is part of Sanders' broader criminal justice reform plan, which includes ending three-strike laws and minimum sentencing requirements. The move comes as other Democratic candidates, like Hillary Clinton and Martin O'Malley, have also criticized mass incarceration but have not proposed specific reforms. The legislation is expected to face challenges in Congress, but Sanders believes it can gain bipartisan support. The bill aims to address the issue of the United States having the highest incarceration rate in the world, with more than 1 percent of the population behind bars.

A Miami doctor, Arturo Carvajal, filed a lawsuit against Houston's Restaurant in North Miami Beach after allegedly suffering severe abdominal pain and discomfort from consuming an entire grilled artichoke. Carvajal, a doctor with a family practice in Hollywood, claims he had never seen or heard of the dish before and the server failed to explain the proper method of consuming an artichoke, which involves only eating the inside portion of the leaf. Carvajal’s lawyer, Marc R. Ginsberg, states that Carvajal was mystified by the vegetable, thinking it was similar to a food he might have eaten in his native Cuba. After Carvajal courageously gnawed his way through every leaf on his plate, he ended up with artichoke leaves lodged within his bowel, requiring an exploratory laparotomy. Carvajal is seeking unspecified damages for bodily injury, pain and suffering, disability, disfigurement, and loss of capacity for the enjoyment of life. The restaurant's general counsel, Glenn Viers, dismisses the claim as a "silly notion" and states that the company will defend the lawsuit vigorously, arguing that they do not have a duty to post warnings against someone eating an entire artichoke.

Police in Washington state issued an Amber Alert for a 2-year-old boy who was reportedly taken by force, along with his mother, from their home in Des Moines. The situation, involving multiple suspects, has been described as complicated by Sgt. Mike Graddon, who stated, "We’re still trying to figure this all out." According to authorities, the boy's 40-year-old mother was stunned with an electrical device and bound by two female assailants, known to her, before being driven to a house in Fife, where she was tied to a cupboard in the garage. The boy was taken inside. The mother managed to escape around noon the next day but was unable to retrieve her child, who remained in the house. Police were notified around 9:30 p.m. on Tuesday and located the boy's paternal grandmother, 65-year-old Vien Nguyen, who is also missing. The boy's father, Kang Tran, is cooperating with investigators but was not charged. The boy's mother identified both suspects, but the case is still under investigation. The incident unfolded when the grandmother and the girlfriend of the boy's father, Alyssa Chang, allegedly abducted the mother and the child to a home 20 miles away. The boy was found safe when his babysitter, John Truong, recognized him from an Amber Alert and contacted police. Chang was taken into custody, while Nguyen turned herself in later. Both face charges of kidnapping, felony assault, and unlawful imprisonment. The boy was reunited with his mother and father on Wednesday afternoon.

The Hunger Games: Mockingjay — Part 2 maintained its box office supremacy for a fourth consecutive weekend, earning $11.3 million and pushing its domestic total to $244.5 million. In contrast, Warner Bros.’ historical drama In the Heart of the Sea, directed by Ron Howard and starring Chris Hemsworth, struggled at the box office, opening with a disappointing $11 million in its first three days. The film, based on the true story of the 1820 sinking of the whaling ship Essex, received a B+ CinemaScore and a 43% positive rating on Rotten Tomatoes but failed to attract a broad audience, with 68% of viewers being over 35. Despite the weak opening, Mockingjay continued its strong performance, while other holdovers like Pixar’s The Good Dinosaur ($10.5 million) and Creed ($10.1 million) kept the top five positions. The Big Short, a film about the 2008 financial crisis, opened to $720,000 in just eight theaters, achieving a remarkable $90,000 per theater average, driven by positive reviews and award buzz. However, the looming release of Star Wars: The Force Awakens on Friday and the Christmas Day openings of multiple new films are expected to significantly impact the box office landscape in the coming weeks.

Scientists from the U.S. and Denmark are embarking on a groundbreaking study to map the underground hydrothermal plumbing system of Yellowstone National Park, aiming to understand the mechanisms behind famous geysers like Old Faithful and the park's other hydrothermal features. This initiative, set to begin this week, will utilize a unique electromagnetic system, resembling a giant hula hoop, mounted on a helicopter. The device, capable of detecting voltage signals, will help researchers distinguish between solid earth, "rotten" sulfuric rock, and water, providing insights into the depth and flow paths of the hot water beneath the surface. The survey, covering the Mammoth-Norris corridor, is expected to take at least four weeks and will extend to a depth of about 500 meters, or 1,500 feet. By visualizing the geology and water underground, the study seeks to fill in knowledge gaps about the causes of geysers and hydrothermal explosions, potentially aiding future park management and development. This project represents a significant step towards comprehending the complex geological processes at work in one of the world's most famous natural wonders.

In the rugged Central Coast of California, beneath acres of sand dunes, lies the remains of a lost city. In 1982, Peter Brosnan, a freelance journalist, heard a story that seemed too wild to be true: a massive Egyptian temple, a dozen plaster sphinxes, and other monumental structures were buried in the sands, remnants of a 60-year-old Hollywood set from Cecil B. DeMille’s 1923 film The Ten Commandments. Brosnan, inspired by the idea, drove across the country to the Guadalupe coast with a friend to see the ruins for himself. The discovery of the set, if real, promised a documentary that would uncover a forgotten bit of Hollywood’s history. Brosnan, along with his friend, visited local libraries, contacted politicians, and even spoke to a ranch hand who had run cattle through the dunes, eventually finding a chunk of Plaster of Paris statuary poking through the sand.

The set was built for DeMille’s epic, requiring 1,500 workers and over 25,000 pounds of nails. DeMille, already a star in Hollywood, was recovering from a string of critical flops. The film’s production was a logistical nightmare, with DeMille’s tent city covering 24 square miles. The set included a 109-foot-tall Great Gate, two 35-foot-tall statues of Ramses II, and five mammoth sphinxes, each weighing over five tons. Despite the costs, DeMille razed the set, burying it in the sands to prevent rivals from using the same location. Sixty years later, in 1983, Brosnan and his team began their search, using ground-penetrating radar to locate the set. They received funding from Paramount Pictures and the Smithsonian, but faced ongoing issues with permitting and funding. By 1990, the project was halted, leaving much of the set buried.

The dunes, formed about 15,000 years ago, have preserved the set due to the minerals in the sand acting as a natural desiccant. However, powerful storms in recent years have shifted the sands, exposing more of the set. In 2010, Brosnan received an anonymous offer to complete the film, but by then, he was married with children and had been away from the project for two decades. With the help of a Santa Barbara County grant, a team of archaeologists excavated a sphinx, and Brosnan is now working on a final draft of the documentary. The Dunes Center, which runs a small museum and conservation efforts, needs funding to unearth more artifacts before they are lost to the elements. The search continues, with Applied Earthworks planning at least one more flyover to pinpoint the camp’s location and potentially uncover more of the lost city.

The U.S. government's six-month ban on deepwater drilling in the Gulf of Mexico, imposed after the Deepwater Horizon explosion, faced legal challenges and criticism from industry representatives. On Tuesday, Interior Secretary Ken Salazar announced a new order to reinstate the moratorium, emphasizing the need for a pause on deepwater drilling due to ongoing oil spills. However, a federal judge in New Orleans issued a preliminary injunction against the ban, arguing that the moratorium could cause significant economic harm to the Gulf Coast's industries and workers. Salazar's statement highlighted the evidence of the need for a pause, citing BP's inability to stop the oil spill. The judge's ruling acknowledged the government's authority but questioned the scope of the ban, stating that it could not justify the "immense scope" of the moratorium. Industry representatives, including Transocean and Louisiana Governor Bobby Jindal, supported ending the moratorium, while environmentalists and some politicians urged the government to appeal the ruling. Meanwhile, cleanup efforts showed some progress, with oil visibly reduced in some areas, but long-term environmental impacts remained uncertain. BP continued to face financial and operational challenges, with costs reaching $2 billion and ongoing efforts to contain the spill. The incident highlighted the tension between safety concerns and the economic impacts of deepwater drilling bans.

An aircraft carrying 54 people crashed in Indonesia's Papua province on Sunday, the latest in a series of aviation disasters in the country. The Trigana Air Service ATR 42-300 plane, which was flying from Jayapura to Oksibil, was located in the Bintang Mountains after local residents reported a crash. The plane was carrying 44 adult passengers, five crew, and five children and infants. Search efforts were hampered by bad weather and rugged terrain. Trigana Air has a history of safety issues, with 14 serious incidents since 1991 and 10 aircraft written off. The plane, which made its first flight 27 years ago, was on the European Union's list of banned carriers since 2007. Indonesia's aviation safety record is poor, with two major crashes in the past year, including the AirAsia flight that went down in the Java Sea and killed all 162 on board. President Joko Widodo has called for a review of the country's aging air force fleet.

The Thomas Jefferson Memorial's gleaming white dome has been increasingly darkened by a colony of microscopic organisms called biofilm, a problem not unique to the Jefferson Memorial but found on monuments around the world. The blackening effect, first noticed in 2006, has become more pronounced in recent years, raising concerns among National Park Service officials. The biofilm, a combination of algae, bacteria, and fungi, adheres to stone surfaces, creating a protective pigment to shield itself from solar radiation. While it doesn't eat the stone, its presence poses a challenge for preservationists. The National Park Service is testing various chemical biocides and non-traditional methods like ozonated water and laser irradiation to remove the biofilm without damaging the soft marble. The Jefferson Memorial, dedicated in 1943, has undergone several repairs, including a $12.4 million project to stabilize its seawall and address ceiling issues. The black biofilm has also affected other memorials, such as the Lincoln Memorial and the D.C. War Memorial. The National Park Service is studying the biofilm's growth and impact on stone, with no permanent solution yet found. The treatment method ultimately chosen will balance effectiveness, safety, and cost. The Jefferson Memorial's dome, a prominent landmark on the Washington, D.C., skyline, faces the ongoing challenge of biofilm growth, with officials working to restore its original luster while ensuring long-term preservation.

Talia Jane, a customer service representative for Yelp, penned an open letter to CEO Jeremy Stoppelman detailing her struggles with low pay and high living costs in San Francisco. The letter, titled "An Open Letter to My CEO," was published on Medium and quickly gained traction, leading to Jane's termination from her position just two hours later. In her post, Jane outlined her financial challenges, including her $733.24 biweekly salary, which she spent over 80% on rent. She also highlighted the difficulty of affording basic necessities like groceries and utilities, while noting that her coworkers faced similar issues. Jane's letter criticized the company for its low wages and suggested potential solutions, such as offering food assistance from local food banks, matching customer donations to food programs, and reducing unnecessary expenses like flavored coconut waters. Despite the letter's widespread attention, Yelp maintained that Jane was fired for violating the company's terms of conduct, while Jane herself stated that her dismissal was not the primary goal of her post. The incident sparked debate about corporate responsibility, employee welfare, and the high cost of living in the Bay Area. Following the backlash, Yelp announced plans to raise wages for its customer support team, although Jane disputed the claim that such changes were already in the works. The controversy underscored the challenges faced by tech employees in the region and the broader issues of income inequality and corporate accountability.

Texas and surrounding areas faced severe flooding and storms in May 2015, with the state experiencing its wettest May on record, recording 7.54 inches of rain, surpassing the previous high of 6.66 inches set in June 2004. The flooding, triggered by heavy rainfall, caused significant damage, with at least 27 fatalities and 13 people missing. The Blanco River, in particular, surged into vacation homes, including that of the Perez family in Wimberley, Texas, causing extensive damage. The family was rescued by firefighters who were already in the area, highlighting the ongoing challenges faced by emergency services. The flooding also affected numerous other communities, with the Colorado River in Wharton, Texas, spilling over its banks, and the Brazos River in Parker County breaching its banks, leading to voluntary evacuations. In Houston, 1,400 structures suffered severe damage, and six deaths were reported, with additional bodies found in the days following the initial flooding. The National Weather Service issued flash flood watches across a wide area, extending from south of San Antonio to Dallas, Oklahoma, and Kansas, as more storms were expected to hit the region. President Barack Obama pledged federal support, emphasizing the need for continued assistance and recovery efforts. The severe weather also impacted transportation, with over 200 people rescued in Dallas alone, and thousands of residents left stranded due to flooding. The situation highlighted the ongoing challenges of managing extreme weather events and the importance of preparedness and response strategies.

Charlie Sheen, who recently disclosed his HIV-positive status on the Today show, had been developing a new sitcom series before making his announcement. According to industry insiders, Sheen had been meeting with producers from CBS TV Studios and Sony Pictures TV to discuss a half-hour starring vehicle. However, no new series has been set up as of yet. During the interview, Sheen expressed confidence that his HIV status would not impact his career, citing his talks with Sony TV executives. He pointed out that chairman Steve Mosko was "excited about doing a show again" with him, indicating no resistance to his condition. The revelation of Sheen's HIV status has raised questions about potential lawsuits from former sexual partners, but Sheen claims he spent $10 million trying to keep it quiet. Despite his diagnosis, Sheen's previous sitcom, Anger Management, which he completed 100 episodes of, suggests that his condition may not be as detrimental to his career as some might think. The Sony hack email, which revealed an executive's joke about Sheen's ability to complete 40 episodes of the show, indicates that Sheen's diagnosis was known to some in the entertainment industry. Sheen's confident attitude during the interview suggests that his diagnosis may not significantly affect his future career prospects, as evidenced by his ongoing discussions with potential producers and his upcoming film projects.

Two months after their daughter was acquitted of murdering their granddaughter, Casey Anthony's parents, George and Cindy Anthony, have broken their silence and granted an interview to Dr. Phil McGraw, who confronts them about certain aspects of the case. In excerpts that aired Monday on NBC's Today show, McGraw asks Cindy about her distraught MySpace message that began "My Caylee is missing," which she posted on July 3, some 12 days before 2-year-old Caylee Anthony was reported missing. Cindy says, "Caylee was missing in my heart that day. She wasn't missing physically. I thought I knew where she was at. I wanted Casey to know how much she was hurting me. And I thought she was purposely keeping Caylee away from me." McGraw also asks both parents about the smell in the trunk of Casey's car. Cindy responds, "Truthfully, to this day, I don't know, to be honest." George adds, "Do I want to believe Caylee was back there? I don't want to believe it. I'm going by what the investigators have told me. All I know is that Caylee is not with us anymore. I know that. I know that." Cindy defends George against the suggestion that he knew of Caylee's disappearance, stating, "George would have never have put us through those six months of not knowing where Caylee was if he knew where Caylee was. I watched his heart break every single day. And I watched him as frantic as he was." The full interview, for which McGraw's production company reportedly paid a fee to Caylee's Fund, not directly to the Anthonys, will air Tuesday and Wednesday on his TV show.

A tragic accident near Blythe, California, on Wednesday morning sent a bus full of sleeping passengers rolling over the side of the road, killing four people and injuring several others. The bus, carrying 32 passengers from El Paso, Texas, to Los Angeles, struck a load of steel pipes scattered across the freeway after a truck jackknifed and spilled its cargo. The pipes were scattered during an earlier crash involving a flatbed truck that had drifted into the dirt median on Interstate 10. The bus driver reportedly tried to avoid the pipes but was unable to do so in the dark, leading to the crash. Ana Perez, a mother traveling with her 12-day-old baby, described the scene as "really, really bad" and "horrible," holding on tightly to her child as the bus overturned. Perez suffered bruises but was fortunate that her newborn, Daniela, was not injured. Emergency responders helped passengers from the bus through an emergency exit in the roof. Three passengers were airlifted to hospitals, and four others were transported by ambulance. Fourteen others were taken to a hospital for evaluation of minor injuries. The freeway was expected to remain closed into the afternoon. The truck driver and bus driver were unharmed. The truck, operated by VG Transport, had passed three inspections over the past two years but had an expired registration and a driver with an expired medical certificate during a recent inspection.
