The Democratic stranglehold on electing women may start to erode, as evidenced by the numbers of female governors, senators, and representatives. While the Democratic party has six female governors and 59 women in the House, there are only four Republican women in the Senate and 17 in the House. The Republican women appear to have an edge going into November, with three appearing to be at least slightly ahead of their Democratic rivals, and two in dead heats. The documentary "Fire From the Heartland: The Reawakening of the Conservative Woman" capitalizes on this trend, highlighting the role of women in the conservative movement. The film explores the grassroots activists and the more familiar female stars of the conservative movement, including Michele Bachmann, Ann Coulter, and Phyllis Schlafly. The general sense of malaise among Democrats, a volatile electorate, and a growing acceptance of female politicians in both parties contribute to this trend. The documentary aims to capture the essence of the awakening of a new generation of conservative women, reshaping and reenergizing the face of the GOP.

A woman fleeing police through a pasture was caught by more than a dozen cows in Seminole County, Florida, according to the Sanford Police Department. Jennifer Anne Kaufman, 46, was riding in a stolen Subaru SUV being pursued by officers when the vehicle crashed near a pasture after officers attempted to disable it with stop sticks. Kaufman and another occupant, Jamie Michael Young, fled into the pasture, while a third occupant, Erin Thomas, stayed with the vehicle. Young, 46, was chased down by a K9 unit, but Kaufman made it deeper into the field. Video captured by a Seminole County Sheriff's Office helicopter team shows a large group of cows chasing Kaufman, seemingly working together to corral her. The herd chased Kaufman to a fence, where police were waiting on the other side. Kaufman was arrested and charged with petit theft, possession of cocaine, possession of drug paraphernalia, trespassing, resisting arrest, and violation of probation. The Subaru was stolen out of Brevard County, and a search of the vehicle yielded more than a gram of cocaine, a crack pipe, syringes, and a metal spoon. This unusual arrest highlights the unexpected roles animals can play in law enforcement and justice.

A marine biologist at Cal State Long Beach has embarked on a mission to identify the species and origins of all the shells adorning the Watts Towers in South L.A. Meanwhile, the death toll from Japan's devastating earthquake and tsunami surpassed 10,000, with over 17,000 people still missing two weeks after the 9.0-magnitude quake struck the northeastern coast. The crisis has led to widespread anxiety over Japan's food and water safety, with elevated radiation levels detected in raw milk, vegetables, and tap water in Tokyo. The government has restricted shipments of 11 leafy vegetables and advised against giving infants tap water in certain regions. In Tokyo, residents rushed to stock up on bottled water, while farmers faced uncertainty about the demand for their produce. The struggle to contain nuclear fallout at the Fukushima Dai-ichi plant continued, with workers facing setbacks and radiation leaks. The plant's cooling systems remain a critical concern, as engineers work to prevent a full meltdown and manage the radioactive materials.

Amazon has implemented a "Pay to Quit" program, offering fulfillment center employees up to $5,000 to leave their jobs. CEO Jeff Bezos explained in his 2013 letter to shareholders that the initiative aims to ensure Amazon retains only employees who are truly committed to their roles. The program, which Zappos pioneered, offers a $2,000 bonus in the first year, increasing by $1,000 annually until reaching $5,000 in the fourth year. Amazon spokesperson Kelly Cheeseman confirmed that only full-time fulfillment center employees are eligible, and noted that a small percentage of workers opt for the offer. This move reflects Amazon's broader strategy to enhance employee satisfaction and alignment with company goals. The program is part of Amazon's comprehensive approach to employee empowerment, which includes initiatives like Career Choice, where the company subsidizes tuition for employees seeking new skills, and the Virtual Contact Center, which allows customer service support from home. Amazon's commitment to employee welfare extends to its urban campus, designed to be environmentally friendly and promote a healthy work-life balance. The company also emphasizes fast delivery, experimenting with drone delivery and expanding Sunday delivery services. Amazon's diverse portfolio of initiatives, from fashion and groceries to cloud services and voice-activated assistants, underscores its ongoing commitment to innovation and customer satisfaction.

A Minnesota judge overseeing the estate of the late pop star Prince has ruled out nearly 30 potential heirs, ordering genetic testing for six purported family members, including Prince's sister and three half-siblings. Carver County Judge Kevin Eide's order excludes five unidentified individuals with questionable claims of being Prince's biological offspring and dismisses several others who alleged extramarital affairs with his mother or described themselves as descendants of a sister of Prince’s great-grandfather. The judge also ruled there was no credible claim of a surviving spouse. Among those ordered to undergo genetic testing are Brianna Nelson, who claims to be Prince's niece, and possible grandniece Victoria Nelson, whose father is alleged to be Prince's half-brother. The court's decision narrows the pool of potential heirs for the estimated $300 million or more in Prince's estate, which has fallen to the courts due to his death without a will. The special administrator of the estate, Bremer Trust, is now tasked with determining the fair-market value of Prince's assets.

Egypt's political crisis deepened as Islamists and their opponents clashed outside President Mohamed Mursi's palace, with 211 people wounded in the violence. Vice President Mahmoud Mekky proposed amendments to the controversial draft constitution, suggesting a written agreement could be submitted to the next parliament. However, opposition leaders, including Mohamed ElBaradei, demanded Mursi retract his November 22 decree, defer the December 15 referendum, and agree to revise the constitution. Mursi's supporters, confident of winning the upcoming referendum and parliamentary election, showed no signs of backing down. The crisis has polarized Egypt, with many fearing it could lead to further violence. U.S. Secretary of State Hillary Clinton called for dialogue to ensure the new constitution respects all citizens' rights. Meanwhile, state institutions, except the judiciary, have largely supported Mursi, while the army has remained neutral. Despite the tension, Mursi's opponents have yet to organize a mass movement to challenge the Muslim Brotherhood's dominance.

The once-untouchable Tiger Woods is facing a new reality, as evidenced by his performance at the U.S. Open. In the first round at Chambers Bay, he opened with an 80, a score that evoked memories of amateur golfers struggling with their drives. His face betrayed his frustration, mirroring that of his golfing buddies when they hit a poor shot. The hangers-on who still held onto hope for a Woods resurgence are likely to abandon their faith soon. His 2013 season, while impressive, did not translate into major victories, and his game has never recovered since the 2008 scandal. Despite his age, which should still allow for good years, his career has been on hold for seven years, with no major wins since 2014. His performance at the Memorial Tournament earlier this month, where he finished 16 over par, further solidified his current status. Woods' 76 in the second round at the U.S. Open marked his second consecutive missed cut, a rarity for a player of his caliber. His fall from grace is a stark reminder of the unpredictable nature of sports and the challenges faced by elite athletes as they navigate the twilight of their careers.

A Mississippi man, Joshua Vallum, was sentenced to 49 years in prison on Monday for the first-ever conviction under federal hate crime charges for the killing of a transgender woman, Mercedes Williamson, the AP reports. U.S. District Judge Louis Guirola Jr. sentenced Vallum, 29, of Lucedale, for the 2015 murder of Williamson, 17, in a case watched by the LGBT community nationwide. Prosecutors said Vallum shocked Williamson with a stun gun, stabbed her, and beat her to death to prevent fellow Latin Kings gang members from discovering their sexual relationship, as gang rules barred homosexual activity and declared it punishable by death. Vallum pleaded guilty in December and previously faced a life sentence in state court for the same murder, which led to a separate life without parole sentence. In court, Vallum begged forgiveness from Williamson’s family and friends, though none were present, only a few reporters, the judge, and Vallum’s father and stepmother. “Every day, I live with the guilt and regret of my actions,” Vallum said. “If I could bring back Mercedes by giving up my life, I would gladly do so.” U.S. Attorney General Jeff Sessions commented, “Today's sentencing reflects the importance of holding individuals accountable when they commit violent acts against transgender individuals.” The case began under President Obama’s administration, and advocates noted that the outcome was already predetermined when Donald Trump became president. Federal prosecutor Julia Gegenheimer said Vallum lured Williamson into a car in Alabama and drove her 50 miles to his family home near Lucedale, Mississippi, where he shocked her with a stun gun, stabbed her with a pocketknife, and bashed her head with a hammer. Public defenders submitted a sealed brief outlining Vallum’s troubled childhood, characterized by abandonment and neglect. “Mr. Vallum lived through a childhood that was characterized by abandonment and neglect,” said public defender Ellen Allred. “It's difficult to imagine how a mother could lock a two- or three-year-old child in a room for hours on end while adults did drugs.” Vallum initially claimed he found out Williamson was a transgender woman on May 30, 2015, and that he “blacked out” during the crime, a variation of the “trans panic” defense. However, testimony and evidence showed Vallum knew Williamson was transgender before they began dating. A witness testified that Vallum and Williamson had sex multiple times while the witness was a roommate with Williamson. Mercedes Williamson had transitioned from male to female before dropping out of high school in Alabama, leaving her parents' home and drifting from place to place.

Donald Trump’s presidency marks a departure from traditional American values, characterized by an unprecedented embrace of untruth and a disregard for the verifiability of facts. His approach to governance and public discourse is marked by a willingness to fabricate narratives and dismiss evidence, challenging the very foundations of a society premised on the existence and importance of truth. Trump’s presidency is not merely a continuation of the political status quo but a radical shift that threatens the nation’s moral standing and the integrity of its institutions.

Trump’s use of lies and misinformation is not a novel phenomenon; political leaders have long employed deceptive tactics to manipulate public opinion. However, Trump’s approach is more pervasive and less constrained by the norms and checks that typically govern political discourse. His ability to shift between fact and fiction, often through social media, has created a climate of uncertainty and skepticism among the public. This erosion of trust in institutions and the media is particularly concerning as it undermines the ability of citizens to engage in informed and rational debate.

Trump’s presidency is defined by a series of policy decisions that, if allowed to stand, could have severe and long-lasting consequences. From healthcare to climate change, his administration has taken steps that threaten the well-being of the nation and its global standing. The de-insurance of millions of people, the weakening of regulatory agencies, and the expansion of military spending are just some of the policies that, if not reversed, could have catastrophic effects. These actions, while controversial, are not the most alarming aspect of Trump’s presidency. The real danger lies in the man himself.

Trump’s unpredictability, petulance, and self-regard pose a significant threat to the stability and effectiveness of the presidency. His actions are often driven by a desire for personal glory and adulation, rather than a commitment to the public good. This lack of regard for the rule of law and the norms of governance is evident in his frequent disparagement of institutions and his willingness to question the integrity of the electoral process. His embrace of conspiracy theories and racist memes further erodes the fabric of American democracy, fostering a climate of division and distrust.

The challenge for the nation lies in the need to defend the truth and the institutions that uphold it. This requires a collective effort from citizens, the media, and political leaders. The role of the rational opposition is to stand up for the rule of law, the electoral process, and the peaceful transfer of power. It is essential to resist the temptation to accept unverified information and to engage in informed and constructive dialogue. The resilience of American democracy has been tested before, and it will likely endure this latest challenge. However, it requires the active participation of all citizens to safeguard the values that make the United States a beacon of freedom and democracy.

Students returned to Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, for the first time since the Valentine's Day shooting that claimed 17 lives, two weeks prior. The school implemented new safety measures, including prohibiting backpacks, as about 50 armed officers were present to ensure security. Principal Ty Thomas tweeted that the focus was on emotional readiness and comfort rather than curriculum, advising students to leave their backpacks at home. Dick's Sporting Goods announced it would immediately stop selling assault-style rifles and raise the minimum age for purchasing guns to 21, following the tragic event. The company's CEO, Edward Stack, emphasized the need for lawmakers to address the issue, as the existing system failed to prevent the sale to the accused shooter, 19-year-old Nikolas Cruz. Students, like David Hogg, a leader in the anti-assault weapon campaign, expressed fear and determination to push for gun legislation. Meanwhile, teachers and students arrived early, facing a mix of anxiety and resolve as they navigated the return to a routine that had been forever altered. At the school entrance, carnations were handed out by the Broward County Police Benevolent Association, and a long line of cars brought people back to the campus, with the main entrance adorned with flowers and photographs memorializing the victims. The return to school was a poignant reminder of the ongoing impact of the tragedy and the urgent calls for change.

A massive ice jam on the Yukon River in Alaska caused severe flooding in the remote town of Galena, leading to the evacuation of several hundred residents. The ice jam, stretching 30 miles, began to break down on Wednesday, with chunks of ice breaking off, signaling a potential easing of the flood situation. The rising water has already lifted homes off their foundations and threatened to break a dike protecting the airport, leaving the town of 500 people without power, fresh water, and cell phone reception. The National Guard evacuated 32 people and 19 dogs to Fairbanks, while others stayed behind, camping at the airport or in former Air Force barracks. The flooding has caused extensive damage, with cars submerged and sewage systems overwhelmed. The ice jam's weakening was evident by 11 a.m. Wednesday, with water levels already rising downstream. The Weather Service expects the ice jam to break by late Wednesday or Thursday, triggering a surge of water that will flood the downriver community of Koyukuk. The town of Koyukuk, about 14 miles downstream, is preparing for a potential flash flood, with residents hauling water and wood to higher ground and evacuating the sick and elderly. The flood warning issued by the Weather Service indicates that the surge could take about four hours to reach Koyukuk. The situation has left the town of Galena in a state of trauma and vulnerability, with the potential for a disaster declaration to unlock state relief funds. The flooding has been described as the worst in Galena's history, with the ice jam's breaking expected to bring significant challenges to the downstream community.

Los Angeles real estate developer Stephanie Smith, who claims to be California's largest landlord of marijuana businesses, has sued the city of San Bernardino to overturn its new pot regulation ordinance. The ordinance could bar Smith from the industry and prevent her from renting property to pot growers and other marijuana operations. The dispute stems from a December raid where 35,000 marijuana plants were seized from three of Smith's buildings, and 18,000 pounds of marijuana were confiscated from two other properties. Smith was not arrested or charged, but her tenants were detained. The new city ordinance bars anyone who has violated local or state laws related to the marijuana industry or failed to report income from it from operating in the commercial cannabis business. Smith fears this could apply to her company and tenants, as the businesses were in the process of being licensed when shut down. The lawsuit argues the ordinance violates the constitutional right to due process and could create monopolies of certain types of marijuana operating licenses. San Bernardino City Council approved the ordinance in March, allowing only 17 commercial marijuana businesses in the city, despite 19 different types of licenses available under state law. The ordinance also disqualifies businesses that operated prior to the law from getting licenses. San Bernardino is taking a different approach compared to cities like Los Angeles and San Francisco, which have given priority to license businesses that operated under medical marijuana regulations. The lawsuit claims the ordinance is a backdoor ban and violates the will of the voters. San Bernardino Community Development Director Mark Persico says the city is an attractive spot for marijuana businesses, with 50 applications already in the works.

Congressman Allen West, a prominent figure in the Republican Party, spoke at a Florida GOP dinner, issuing a stern warning to Democrats. He declared Florida a "battlefield" where their messages of equality, economic dependency, and enslavement of the entrepreneurial spirit would not resonate. West challenged Democrats, including President Obama, House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, and Florida Representative Debbie Wasserman-Schultz, to take their message elsewhere. He vowed to do everything to prevent President Obama from "destroying" the country and invited Democrats to "bring it on." Meanwhile, the Florida Republican legislature is reportedly planning to redistrict Allen West's congressional district in a way that could jeopardize his re-election, despite West's claims that the maps submitted to the legislature would have kept his district intact. This move, led by one of Mitt Romney's spokespersons, Will Weatherford, has raised concerns among Tea Party supporters, who see it as a betrayal by the establishment. The situation highlights the complex dynamics within the Republican Party and the potential risks faced by Tea Party representatives.

The Buffalo Bills have made history by hiring Kathryn Smith as a quality control assistant, the first full-time female assistant coach in NFL history. Smith, who has been working with the Bills for seven years in various administrative roles, will now officially join the coaching staff under head coach Rex Ryan. Ryan praised Smith, stating, "Kathryn Smith has done an outstanding job in the seven years that she has worked with our staff. She certainly deserves this promotion based on her knowledge and strong commitment, and I just know she’s going to do a great job." Smith will work with special teams coordinator Danny Crossman and will be responsible for a number of coaching duties.

This milestone comes after the NFL has been making strides toward gender equality in recent years. In 2015, the Buffalo Bills hired Sarah Thomas as the first female referee in NFL history. The hiring of Smith is part of a broader trend in professional sports, with the NBA leading the way in female coaching roles. Lisa Boyer served as a volunteer assistant coach with the Cleveland Cavaliers in 2001-02, and the San Antonio Spurs hired Becky Hammon as an assistant coach in 2014. Nancy Lieberman became the second full-time female assistant in the NBA in 2015. The NFL's move is seen as a significant step forward, with head coach Rex Ryan noting the success of female coaches in other leagues and the excitement it brings for women like Smith.

Smith's journey to this role began in 2003 when she started as a gameday/special events intern for the New York Jets. She progressed through various roles, including player personnel assistant and assistant to the head coach, before joining the Bills in 2015. Her appointment is not only a personal achievement but also a testament to the growing recognition of women's capabilities in the coaching profession.

The South Carolina deputy who forcefully removed a student from a classroom by flipping and tossing her across a room has been fired, Richland County Sheriff Leon Lott announced. The incident, captured on video and shared widely online, led to the deputy's suspension and subsequent termination. Lott stated that the deputy's actions were "not acceptable" and did not follow proper training and procedure. Fields, a seven-year veteran of the school resource officer program, was told of his firing late Wednesday morning. His lawyer defended his actions, stating that they were "justified and lawful" and carried out "professionally." Civil rights groups praised the swift action, while critics accused Fields of racial bias. The student, who was black, suffered injuries including a cast on her arm and neck and back injuries, according to her attorney. The incident began when the student was asked to leave her algebra class for texting, and her refusal led to the confrontation. Lott said the student's disruptive behavior did not justify the deputy's actions, but she still needed to be held responsible. The FBI and the Justice Department have opened investigations into whether civil rights were violated. School officials are reviewing their use of police for discipline, and the incident has sparked discussions about the role of school resource officers.

Reactions to the killing of Osama bin Laden by American forces operating inside Pakistan began pouring in from across the globe, including from former U.S. presidents and prominent politicians. Former President George W. Bush, whose presidency was defined by the September 11th attacks, called the operation a "momentous achievement" that marks a victory for America and those who seek peace around the world. Bush congratulated President Obama and the men and women of the military and intelligence communities who devoted their lives to the mission, emphasizing that justice will be done no matter how long it takes. Former President Bill Clinton, who was in office for the first World Trade Center bombing in 1993, also issued a statement congratulating the president, the national security team, and the armed forces on bringing Osama bin Laden to justice. Other notable reactions came from politicians like Senator Charles E. Schumer of New York, who called it a "thunderous strike for justice" and a "massive accomplishment" for the military and intelligence personnel who have been dedicated to the task for the past decade. Mitt Romney, the former Republican governor of Massachusetts, also congratulated President Obama and the military and intelligence communities, expressing hope that the families of the victims of the September 11th attacks will sleep easier knowing that justice has been done. Former Republican governor Tim Pawlenty of Minnesota echoed these sentiments, praising the perseverance of the U.S. military and the American people. Senator John McCain of Arizona, while expressing joy that the world's top terrorist is no longer in it, warned that the fight against radical Islamic terrorism is not over. House Speaker John Boehner of Ohio congratulated the men and women of the Armed Forces and intelligence community for their tireless efforts and perseverance. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid of Nevada and House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi of California both commended President Obama and his team for their leadership in achieving this major accomplishment. Sarah Palin, the former Republican governor of Alaska, expressed gratitude to the brave men and women in the military and intelligence services who contributed to the successful mission. Overall, the reactions underscore the significance of the event for the families of the 9/11 victims, the American people, and the global fight against terrorism.

The Hollywood Sign Trust announced plans to enhance surveillance technology to prevent future pranks after an iconic sign was altered to read "Hollyweed" just before New Year's Day. The prank, which involved hanging tarps over the "O" letters, remains unsolved, with no suspect identified. Chris Baumgart, chairman of the Hollywood Sign Trust, stated that the trust will deploy additional technology to tighten surveillance and deter unwanted visitors. The incident highlights the ongoing challenges of maintaining the landmark, as safety concerns for both the sign and the neighborhood are paramount. The sign, which has been used for political messaging in the past, was restored to its original appearance by mid-morning on January 1, 2017. The prankster left a peace sign and a tribute message on the tarps, possibly referencing California's recent vote to legalize marijuana. The incident has sparked interest from other street artists, including Plastic Jesus, who noted the "great execution" of the prank. The Hollywood Sign has a history of being altered for artistic or political purposes, with notable past incidents including "Hollyweed" in 1976 and "Holywood" in 1987. The current mystery surrounding the prankster adds to the intrigue of the iconic landmark's history.

A senior U.S. Secret Service agent, Kerry O'Grady, is facing scrutiny after posting controversial statements on Facebook during the 2016 presidential campaign, including one in which she said she would rather endure jail time than "take a bullet" for President Donald Trump. O'Grady, who is in charge of the Secret Service's Denver district, made several posts expressing her disdain for Trump and her support for Hillary Clinton. She acknowledged that her posts violated the Hatch Act, which prohibits federal employees from engaging in certain political activities. O'Grady's posts, which included statements like "I would take jail time over a bullet or an endorsement for what I believe to be disaster to this country and the strong and amazing women and minorities who reside here," have led to at least one complaint to the Office of the Inspector General. The Secret Service is reportedly taking "appropriate action" but declined to comment on the matter. O'Grady maintains that her posts were an internal struggle and that she would not shirk her duties to protect the president. She also expressed her commitment to the mission and the institutions of the republic, emphasizing her devotion to the First Amendment rights of free expression. Despite her support for Clinton, O'Grady stated that her devotion to the mission and country is strengthened by the recognition of dissent and the freedom to assemble and voice opposing convictions. The controversy has sparked calls for her dismissal, with critics on social media demanding her firing.

JPMorgan Chase significantly reduced CEO Jamie Dimon's compensation by 50%, reflecting the company's multibillion-dollar trading loss. Despite a record profit of $5.7 billion for the fourth quarter, Dimon’s total compensation dropped to $11.5 million from $23 million the previous year. The board cited oversight failures and Dimon’s responsibility for the trading debacle. The reduction included a 53% cut in his bonus to $10 million, paid in restricted stock, and a delay in his ability to sell $79 million worth of JPMorgan stock for 18 months. While the bank reported strong overall financial performance, including a 53% increase in fourth-quarter profit and a 10% rise in revenue, the trading loss overshadowed these achievements. The board acknowledged Dimon’s forceful response to the trading problems but emphasized his accountability. JPMorgan also faced ongoing legal challenges, including a $8.5 billion settlement with federal regulators and a lawsuit from New York’s attorney general regarding Bear Stearns. The bank’s mortgage banking group saw a $418 million profit, up from a loss the previous year, driven by increased mortgage lending. However, low interest rates and a deposit glut continued to pressure profitability. JPMorgan is also working to comply with international regulatory guidelines, particularly Basel III, to strengthen its capital reserves.

A tragic accident occurred on February 20, 2014, when a film crew was working on train tracks without permission from the railroad, resulting in the death of 27-year-old Sarah Elizabeth Jones and injuries to seven others. The crew, from Savannah-based Meddin Studios, was filming "Midnight Rider," a biopic about singer Gregg Allman. The crash happened at a railroad trestle crossing the Altamaha River in Wayne County, Georgia, about 60 miles southwest of Savannah. The tracks, owned by CSX Railroad, cross private land owned by forest-products company Rayonier. Joe Gardner, the lead detective on the case, stated that the crew had Rayonier's permission to film on its property but not on the train tracks. The train, traveling from Memphis to Savannah, struck some of the crew's equipment and caused injuries, including a fatal one. The film studio, Open Road Films, released a statement expressing condolences and stating that it still plans to release the picture in the U.S. despite earlier reports of potential withdrawal. The investigation is ongoing, with cooperation from CSX Railroad, Rayonier, and the film crew. The incident has raised concerns about safety on film sets and the legal implications of trespassing on railroad tracks.

Johnny Cash's boyhood home in Dyess, Arkansas, has been added to the National Register of Historic Places, recognizing its significance to the legendary musician's early life and career. Initially nominated in December, the nomination was returned by a National Register historian in January, who suggested emphasizing the home's connection to the Dyess Resettlement Colony and its impact on Cash's development as an artist. The nomination was revised, focusing on Cash's formative years and the influence of the colony on his later musical career. The house, built in 1934 as part of the Federal Emergency Relief Administration's Dyess Colony, was restored by Arkansas State University, which spent $575,000 on the project. Cash lived in the five-room farmhouse from age 3 through high school, a period he considered crucial to his musical journey. The home's addition to the National Register highlights the importance of Cash's early experiences in shaping his future as a songwriter and entertainer. The nomination also mentions two of Cash's songs, "Five Feet High and Rising" and "Pickin' Time," which are believed to have connections to his time in Dyess. The Dyess Resettlement Colony, listed on the National Register in 1976, had previously excluded the Cash house due to its location outside the original nomination's boundary. The recognition of Cash's boyhood home underscores the lasting impact of his humble beginnings on his legendary career.

In a California court hearing on June 20, 2018, Louise Turpin and her husband David Tuprin faced preliminary hearings for charges of torture, child abuse, and other offenses, both pleading not guilty. The hearing centered around a 911 call made by their 17-year-old daughter, who described years of abuse and neglect. During the call, the girl detailed the horrific conditions in the family home, including being shackled to beds, choked, and denied basic hygiene. She said two younger sisters and a brother were similarly treated, with the oldest adult child weighing only 82 pounds due to severe malnutrition.

The 911 call was played in court, revealing the girl's plea for help, stating, "They will wake up at night and they will start crying and they wanted me to call somebody. I wanted to call y'all so y'all can help my sisters." The parents, David and Louise Turpin, were arrested after their 17-year-old daughter escaped through a window and alerted authorities. The house where the children were held captive was described as a "house of horrors," reeking of human waste and filled with signs of starvation. The children were locked up as punishment, beaten, and denied food, toys, and games. They were allowed to do little more than write in journals that may corroborate their horrific stories.

The girl's escape was planned for two years, and she was terrified as she made her way to freedom. She couldn't even dial 911 due to her fear, and when she did, she wasn't sure of her address. The children were rarely allowed outside, with the exception of trick-or-treating and family trips to Disneyland and Las Vegas. The girl, who had difficulty pronouncing words and spoke like a child much younger than her age, said she hadn't bathed in about a year and the house was filthy. The girl also recounted an incident where her father choked her and threatened to kill her, saying, "Yes you do, yes you do, you do, you want to die," and "You want to die and go to hell."

The family moved several times, including a stint in Texas, where the girl said they were left on their own for about four years, though her mother bought them food. The children were mostly locked in their rooms and only allowed to leave to eat, use the bathroom, and brush their teeth. Meals were often combined, and the girl said she couldn't stomach peanut butter anymore. If they didn't obey strict rules, they were slapped in the face or had their hair pulled. The case drew worldwide attention, highlighting the severe neglect hidden behind the neat facade of their home in Perris, California, 70 miles southeast of Los Angeles. The Turpins are currently being held on $12 million bail each and will face a trial in the near future.

A week after being struck by lightning in her Dripping Springs home, Lake Travis High School junior Macie Martinez maintains a light-hearted attitude, sharing humorous posts on social media. Macie, who is a softball team trainer, was struck on Memorial Day while opening the refrigerator door, causing a loud explosion and leaving her with a "cool scar." Her mother, Misty Villarreal, recounted how Macie let out a deep, terrifying scream as she was removed from the kitchen. Doctors diagnosed Macie with a "Fern rash," a common symptom of lightning strikes, and noted nerve damage in her arm and hands. Macie's legs were paralyzed for 45 minutes, and she continues to experience fatigue, numbness, and occasional confusion. Despite the pain and uncertainty about long-term effects, Macie's family remains positive, calling her "Sparky" and "Bolt" to lift spirits. The only significant losses were inanimate household items, with the coffee maker being the sole survivor. Macie's mother expressed overwhelming gratitude, stating, "There's so much to be thankful for because for me, it was such a traumatic experience."

Barry Byron Mills, known as "Baron," the notorious leader of the Aryan Brotherhood prison gang, died in his cell at the Florence, Colorado, supermax prison on July 8, just a day after his 70th birthday. His death, while not suspicious, is under investigation. Mills was serving multiple life sentences for murder convictions from 2006. Born in the Bay Area, Mills joined the Aryan Brotherhood during his time at San Quentin State Prison in the 1970s and rose to become its leader, with a strong influence in the Bay Area and Northern California. Mills was known for his brutal killings, including a failed decapitation attempt while in federal custody in Atlanta. His leadership extended beyond California, with his orders distributed coast to coast through couriers, leading to conflicts with other prison gangs and a notorious protection deal with New York mobster John Gotti. Mills was first noticed by authorities for planning and ordering a Central Valley bank robbery from his cell. He faced a RICO indictment in the early 2000s, with 40 members and co-conspirators charged in 14 killings and dozens of attempted hits. Mills and his second-in-command, Tyler Bingham, were convicted based on the testimony of an Aryan Brotherhood dropout, who admitted to a killing and took a plea deal. Mills faced the death penalty but was spared when jurors voted 9-3 in favor of execution. He spent the rest of his life in solitary confinement at the supermax facility in Florence, Colorado. Mills' attorney, Dean Steward, noted that Mills had a complex persona, with admiration and fear among inmates. Mills' death marks the end of an era for the Aryan Brotherhood, a gang that thrived on violence and control within the prison system.

Ambassador J. Christopher Stevens and three other Americans were killed in a planned attack on the U.S. Consulate in Benghazi, Libya, on September 11. The attack, which involved rocket-propelled grenades and gunfire, came as protesters in Cairo, Egypt, stormed the U.S. Embassy in response to an anti-Islam film. U.S. officials stated that the Benghazi attack was not a spontaneous reaction to the film, but rather a premeditated assault. The film, "Innocence of Muslims," produced by Sam Bacile, an Israeli-American real-estate developer, was considered offensive to Islam and sparked protests across the Middle East. The U.S. government condemned the attacks, with Secretary of State Hillary Clinton emphasizing that there is no justification for violent acts that denigrate religious beliefs. President Obama ordered increased security for U.S. diplomatic personnel worldwide. The attack shocked many Americans, who were commemorating the anniversary of the September 11, 2001, terrorist attacks. Libyan officials apologized for the attack and vowed to bring the perpetrators to justice. The incident highlighted the ongoing security challenges in post-revolutionary Libya and the potential for extremist groups to exploit religious tensions.

U.S. President Barack Obama's attendance at the East Asia Summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, thrust him into the heart of the region's most contentious territorial dispute: the South China Sea. The disagreement, involving China and five Southeast Asian neighbors, has become a major impediment to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) as it aims to establish a community of 600 million people by 2015. Despite the summit's focus on economic concerns, the territorial disputes between China and its neighbors, including the Philippines, have once again overshadowed discussions. The dispute sparked a tense moment when Philippine President Benigno Aquino III challenged Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen, who had tried to cut off a discussion of the territorial disputes. Behind closed doors, the Chinese and Philippine leaders pressed their claims, while others called for restraint. Senior Chinese diplomat Fu Ying expressed dismay that the disputes again got the spotlight, stating, "We do not want to bring the disputes to an occasion like this and we do not want to give over-emphasis to the territorial disputes and differences." Washington reiterated its stance of not taking sides but warned against any country resorting to force and blocking access to the South China Sea, a vital commercial and military gateway. The U.S. also called for the early crafting of a "code of conduct" to prevent clashes in the disputed territories. The potentially oil- and gas-rich South China Sea islands and waters are contested by China, Taiwan, and four ASEAN members: Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines, and Vietnam. The last fighting, involving China and Vietnam, killed over 70 Vietnamese sailors in 1988, and fears of a regional conflict have kept governments on edge. The dispute highlights how ASEAN has become a major battleground for influence in Asia, with the U.S. pushing its "Pacific pivot" to the region and China acting to protect its home ground. The lack of consensus among the group over the maritime disputes has pushed much of the bloc's other work to the sidelines. The failure of the July foreign ministers' meeting, hosted by Cambodia, to reach a joint statement on the South China Sea disputes showed that as long as any ASEAN country remains weak and vulnerable to muscling from a major power, the entire group could be compromised.

At a conference in Malmö, Sweden, the Dalai Lama, who won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1989, urged Europe to help refugees but emphasized that they should ultimately rebuild their home countries. Speaking about the moral responsibility of European nations, he said, "Receive them, help them, educate them… but ultimately they should develop their own country." This comes amid Sweden's struggles with a rise in violent crimes linked to an influx of asylum seekers, particularly from predominantly Muslim countries. The Dalai Lama's comments echo his previous statements, including a 2016 remark that "Europe, for example Germany, cannot become an Arab country." His views are likely to resonate with locals, as Sweden has seen an increase in violent incidents involving refugees since 2014.

Zsa Zsa Gabor, the legendary Hungarian-American socialite and actress, passed away at the age of 99, leaving behind a legacy of wit and glamour. Known for her sharp one-liners and frequent marriages, Gabor's memorable quotes continue to entertain and inspire. "I’m a great housekeeper. Every time I get a divorce, I keep the house," she famously said, deflecting questions about her domestic skills. "You can say I’m full of s—t — but don’t say I’m old," Gabor retorted, challenging age stereotypes. Her candid remarks, such as "Husbands are like fires. They go out when unattended," and "I never hated a man enough to give him his diamonds back," showcased her unapologetic approach to life and love. In 1987, Gabor quipped, "Personally, I know nothing about sex because I have always been married," during a speech to the American Bar Association. Her defiance was evident in her response to a 1989 court case, where she said, "He should have apologized and kissed my hand … That’s what a European gentleman would have done." Gabor's memorable quote, "Sorry I’m late, darlings. I had to put on my makeup. I knew you’d want to see the famous Zsa Zsa face," exemplified her larger-than-life persona. These quotes, along with others, highlight Gabor's unique wit and her enduring impact on Hollywood, where she was known for being the first celebrity to become famous for being famous.

On their 9th wedding anniversary, a Michigan couple, Kathy and Brandon Gunn, decided to open a mysterious wedding gift from Kathy's Great Aunt Alison. The gift, a plain white box with a card that read, "Do not open until your 1st disagreement," had been sitting unopened for nearly a decade. Throughout their marriage, they had faced numerous disagreements and even considered giving up a few times, but they never opened the box. They feared that opening it might symbolize their failure and that a worse disagreement might await them in the future. The couple believed the box held the key to saving their marriage, inspired by their Great Aunt and Uncle, who had been married for nearly half a century. However, the contents of the box turned out to be mundane: wine glasses and personal notes with cash for each spouse. Brandon's note instructed him to buy flowers and a bottle of wine, while Kathy's note told her to purchase a pizza or shrimp and get a "bath" ready. Despite the anticlimactic contents, the couple realized that the tools for creating and maintaining a strong, healthy marriage were not within the box but within themselves. Over the years, the unopened box had taught them valuable lessons in tolerance, understanding, compromise, and patience, strengthening their bond and turning them into best friends, partners, and teammates.

President Donald Trump's call for Russia to be reinstated into the Group of Seven (G-7) has sparked controversy and criticism from both Democratic and Republican lawmakers, as well as from G-7 members. Trump made the suggestion on the White House South Lawn before departing for the G-7 summit in Quebec, Canada, where he will meet with allies who are already upset over his decision to impose tariffs on imports from Canada and the European Union. His proposal that Russia should be part of the G-7 group, which was expelled in 2014 for its annexation of Crimea, has heightened tensions at the summit. Trump's support for Russia's re-entry into the group of leading economies has been seen as a softening of his stance towards Russia, despite significant steps taken against the Kremlin, including new sanctions and the expulsion of diplomats. Critics argue that Trump's actions are damaging America's foreign policy and undermining its relationships with allies. The G-7 meeting in Quebec is expected to be tense, with leaders from France and Canada promising to push back against the new U.S. tariffs. Trump's trade policies, which he says aim to "straighten out unfair trade deals," have left him increasingly isolated. His comments on Russia and trade reflect a broader divide between the U.S. and its closest allies, who are already frustrated with his rejection of the Iran nuclear deal and the Paris climate agreement. Sen. John McCain and other lawmakers have criticized Trump, saying his actions are "turning US foreign policy into an international joke" and "doing lasting damage to our country." Despite the controversy, Trump remains focused on his trade agenda, stating that "in the end we'll all get along." His approach to Russia and trade has raised questions about his commitment to long-standing alliances and his "principled realism" in foreign policy.

A new sexual assault claim against Bill Cosby has emerged, alleging he drugged and sexually assaulted an 18-year-old woman at the Playboy Mansion in 2008. Chloe Goins, a model and lap dancer, claims she was invited to a Playboy party in Las Vegas, where she and a friend were introduced to Hugh Hefner. Cosby, known for his close friendship with Hefner, gave Goins and her friend drinks, which she believes were spiked. After becoming unwell, Goins was escorted to a bedroom by Cosby, where she claims he sexually assaulted her, licking her toes and pleasuring himself. Goins, now 24, says she felt compelled to come forward to bring justice for herself and other women. Her lawyer has contacted the Los Angeles Police Department, and Goins plans to make a full statement. This new allegation adds to the ongoing scandal, with over 20 women coming forward with similar accusations. Cosby's lawyer, Martin Singer, has denied the women's claims and questioned their credibility. Meanwhile, Cosby has remained largely silent, issuing a statement urging the "black media" to remain "neutral" on the charges. His wife, Camille, has defended him, praising his "love and strength." The case highlights the complex legal and ethical issues surrounding the statute of limitations and the credibility of long-dormant claims.

Eight-year-old Knuckles, a Jack Russell Terrier, has a unique talent that he performs without fail: whenever he hears the "Law & Order" theme song, he starts to howl along with it. His owner, Daniel Serna of Los Angeles, noticed this behavior shortly after bringing Knuckles home years ago. A YouTube video of Knuckles howling to the theme song has garnered nearly 10,000 views. The phenomenon is not limited to Knuckles, as numerous other dogs have been recorded howling to the same tune, creating a viral trend. Experts suggest that the high-pitched and staccato nature of the music could trigger a response in dogs' auditory nerves, causing them to howl. While some owners are amused by their dogs' unexpected talent, others are concerned about the potential irritation the music might cause. The creator of the theme song, Mike Post, was surprised to learn that dogs were howling along with his music, expressing happiness that the dogs seemed to enjoy it.

In the quest to identify the unique "smell of death," researchers have delved into the volatile organic compounds (VOCs) emitted during the decomposition of human and animal remains. A study published in PLOS ONE sought to pinpoint specific markers that could distinguish human remains from those of other animals, potentially aiding in the training of cadaver dogs and the development of detection devices. Over a six-month period, the researchers monitored the VOCs released by six human and 26 animal remains in a laboratory setting, employing a thermal desorber combined with gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (TD-GC/MS) for analysis. Principal component analysis (PCA) was applied to the data to identify compounds that could serve as markers. Eight compounds, including ethyl propionate, propyl propionate, propyl butyrate, ethyl pentanoate, pyridine, diethyl disulfide, methyl(methylthio)ethyl disulfide, and 3-methylthio-1-propanol, were found to distinguish human and pig remains from those of other animals. Further, five esters—3-methylbutyl pentanoate, 3-methylbutyl 3-methylbutyrate, 3-methylbutyl 2-methylbutyrate, butyl pentanoate, and propyl hexanoate—separated pig remains from human remains. These findings, while promising, require validation in field settings with full bodies to confirm their reliability. The study underscores the complexity of decomposition and the potential for these markers to revolutionize the search for human remains.

For years, The Golden Plough has been a beloved fixture in the heart of the village, offering simple, down-to-earth English fare that has garnered a loyal following. Regulars and newcomers alike eagerly await the Sunday roast, a tradition that has become a highlight of the week. The establishment's charm lies in its unpretentious approach to dining, where the focus is on quality food and warm, friendly service. Despite its lack of formal business training, the team at The Golden Plough has built a reputation for excellence, earning a dedicated customer base that returns time and again.

As the holiday season approaches, The Golden Plough has released its festive schedule, providing a clear roadmap for those planning their holiday feasts. The menu remains open for business on Christmas Eve, offering a limited selection of dishes to cater to last-minute diners. However, the establishment will be closed for the entire Christmas Day, with no plans to reopen until January 2nd. This closure extends to Boxing Day and several days surrounding the New Year, ensuring that patrons can enjoy a well-deserved break during the holiday period. The restaurant's commitment to its community is evident in the warm wishes and holiday greetings that accompany its announcement, reflecting its role as a cornerstone of local tradition and hospitality.

Jessica Hayes, a 38-year-old high school theology teacher from Fort Wayne, Indiana, became the Fort Wayne-South Bend Diocese's first consecrated virgin in 25 years, marking a rare and unique vocation in the Catholic Church. Hayes, who is currently the only consecrated virgin in her diocese, chose to marry Jesus Christ as a public commitment to serve the church and deepen her relationship with God. This decision came after years of prayer and soul-searching, as Hayes sought a path that would bring her the most joy and happiness.

The ceremony, held at the Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, was attended by hundreds of people, including Hayes's students and parishioners. Finding the perfect wedding dress posed a challenge, as Hayes had to ensure it was appropriate for the occasion, with her shoulders covered and a design that still showcased the beauty of a bride. She emphasized the importance of her guests having a good time, as it was a significant moment for others who might be considering this vocation.

Hayes explained that a consecrated virgin is not the same as a nun; she will continue to live her life as a lay person, teaching at Bishop Dwenger High School and being involved in parish life. The vocation allows her to make a total commitment to serve the church, using her gifts and talents to contribute to the community. She hopes her experience will inspire others, especially young women, to consider this path, as the religious life is not as visible in schools today as it once was.

While Hayes will still be called Ms. Hayes by her students, she is now married to Jesus Christ. She believes that everyone is called to be married, but the way of life is different for each person. For her, this vocation represents a deeper commitment to knowing and loving Jesus, which she sees as a step towards the ultimate union with God in heaven. Hayes is excited to begin this new chapter in her life, knowing that it will deepen her commitment to her faith and her service to the church.

LeBron James, the Miami Heat star, recently tied the knot with Savannah Brinson at the Grand Del Mar Hotel in San Diego. Approximately 200 guests attended the private ceremony, part of a three-day celebration that includes a Sunday brunch. James and Brinson, who have been together since high school and have two sons, were seen together in Miami Beach just before the wedding, where James proposed. Security was tight, and even some guests were unsure of the exact details leading up to the event. The Heat, including coach Erik Spoelstra and teammates Dwyane Wade and Chris Bosh, were among the attendees. James ensured that Savannah got everything she wanted on her special day, as he had previously mentioned. The couple's wedding comes less than three months after the Heat won their second consecutive NBA title.

First lady Melania Trump revealed in an exclusive interview with ABC News that she has expressed concerns to her husband about individuals in his administration whom she does not trust. During her first major solo trip to Africa, promoting her "Be Best" campaign against cyberbullying, she stated, "I could say that I'm the most bullied person in the world," before clarifying, "One of them, if you really see what people are saying about me." This admission comes after an anonymous senior Trump administration official's op-ed in The New York Times claimed that many officials are working to frustrate parts of the president's agenda. Trump defended her husband, tweeting that the op-ed was "gutless" and asking, "TREASON?" Her "Be Best" initiative aims to address online bullying, with Trump emphasizing the impact it can have on children, including her son Barron. The first lady's comments highlight the complex dynamics within the Trump administration and her personal stance on the issue of cyberbullying.

In 2002, notorious art thief Octave Durham, also known as "The Monkey," and his accomplice Henk B. carried out a daring heist at the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam, stealing two of Vincent van Gogh's paintings: "View of the Sea at Scheveningen" and "Congregation Leaving the Reformed Church in Nuenen." Durham, now speaking for the first time, revealed that they initially targeted "Sunflowers" and "The Potato Eaters," but the former was too well-guarded and the latter too large to fit through the window they broke to gain entry. The thieves managed to steal the smaller paintings, which they later sold to the Italian mafia. Durham refused to disclose the price, citing potential tax implications.

Durham and B. faced numerous obstacles in selling the paintings. They first approached criminal Sam Klepper, but he was assassinated shortly before the robbery. They then tried to sell to kidnapper Cor van Hout, but he too was killed before the transaction could be completed. After these failed attempts, the paintings were eventually sold to the Italian mafia. Durham, who for years denied any involvement in the theft, was convicted in 2005 and sentenced to 3.5 years in prison.

The stolen paintings remained missing for 14 years until they were recovered by Italian police during a sting operation targeting the Camorra crime syndicate. The paintings were found during an investigation by a specialized team within the Italian Public Prosecutions Department. Upon discovery, the museum's director, Axel Rüger, expressed gratitude to the Italian authorities, stating, "The paintings have been found! That I would be able to ever pronounce these words is something I had no longer dared to hope for."

The recovered paintings, despite their significant historical and monetary value, were initially considered evidence in the Italian authorities' case against the mafia. However, in January 2016, a court ruled that they could be released and returned to the Netherlands. The paintings, which are of inestimable value due to their unique nature and historical significance, are expected to be returned to the Van Gogh Museum.

CBS News revamped "The Early Show" with a complete makeover, replacing co-hosts Harry Smith and Maggie Rodriguez with Saturday anchors Chris Wragge and Erica Hill, starting January 3. Weather forecaster Dave Price is also leaving for Marysol Castro of "Good Morning America." CBS News President Sean McManus believes the new team will help the show grow, though it has consistently ranked behind morning champs "Today" and "Good Morning America." Smith, with 17 years on the show, will stay at CBS as a news reporter. The new anchors' chemistry and familiarity with the morning genre are seen as advantages.

It's a big moment to be a Chicago Cubs fan, as the team aims to win their first World Series title in 108 years. The excitement is palpable, with a host of big-name celebrities turning up at Wrigley Field to support the team. Bill Murray donned the winning shirt, while Pearl Jam's Eddie Vedder was heartbroken by a loud out by David Ross. The Chicago Bulls' Dwayne Wade and Jimmy Butler, along with Blackhawks' captains Duncan Keith, Brent Seabrook, and Jonathan Toews, serenaded the crowd during the 7th inning stretch. Even Vince Vaughn and Parks and Recreation's Nick Offerman, known for their love of the Cubs, made appearances. Meanwhile, Hillary Clinton, born and raised in Park Ridge, has a personal connection to the team. The Curse of the Billy Goat, a sports-related curse supposedly placed on the Cubs in 1945 by Billy Sianis, has been a long-standing belief. Sianis was asked to leave Wrigley Field during the 1945 World Series due to the smell of his pet goat, Murphy, and allegedly declared, "The Cubs, they ain't gonna win no more." Despite numerous attempts to break the curse, including Sam Sianis bringing goats to Wrigley Field, a butchered goat being hung from the Harry Caray statue, and a group of fans consuming a 40-pound goat in 2015, the curse remained intact until 2016. The Cubs finally broke the curse by winning the World Series, ending their 108-year losing streak.

Syrian opposition activists report that the Islamic State group has captured several towns and villages near the Turkish border, displacing other rebel forces fighting against President Bashar Assad. The group has expanded its control, taking over Akhtarin and Turkmanbareh in the Aleppo countryside, as well as three nearby areas. This development highlights the group's growing influence and territorial gains in the region. The Islamic State's control over these areas underscores its ambitions to establish a self-proclaimed caliphate across parts of Syria and Iraq.

In response to the escalating situation, France has announced it will begin supplying arms to Kurdish forces fighting the Sunni extremists. This move comes amid growing concerns about the security of the autonomous Kurdish region in northern Iraq, which is under threat from the Islamic State group. The French decision to arm the Kurds follows the United States' increased involvement in the conflict, with 130 U.S. troops arriving in the Kurdish capital of Irbil to coordinate efforts to aid trapped Yazidi civilians on Mount Sinjar. The U.S. has also reportedly begun directly arming Kurdish fighters, marking a shift in its previous policy of working exclusively through the Baghdad government.

The U.S. and France's actions reflect the urgency of the situation, as the Islamic State group continues to advance rapidly across northern and western Iraq. The group seized Iraq's second-largest city, Mosul, and has displaced thousands of people, causing significant humanitarian crises. The U.S. and France's support for the Kurds is seen as a critical step in bolstering the region's defenses against the extremist group. Meanwhile, the European Union has been called upon to provide additional support, with France pushing other EU members to contribute more resources to aid Christian and other minorities targeted by the Islamic State. A high-level EU diplomatic meeting concluded with a statement that it would consider the Kurdish request for urgent military support, emphasizing the need for coordinated efforts among international partners to address the crisis.

Aimee Copeland, a 24-year-old Georgia graduate student, has spoken for the first time since contracting necrotizing fasciitis after a May 1 fall from a homemade zip line. Her father, Andy Copeland, announced on Facebook that Sunday was "Aimee Day," marking her first words. The infection led to the amputation of her left leg, right foot, and both hands. Aimee began breathing on her own last week and sat up in a chair on Thursday. Her family remains optimistic, with over 100 well-wishers offering encouragement.

Beneath Yellowstone National Park, a supervolcano lies dormant, awaiting the next catastrophic eruption. This supervolcano, capable of spewing more than 1,000 cubic kilometers of material, poses a significant threat, with the potential to blanket much of the United States in ash and even trigger a volcanic winter. The last supereruption occurred 631,000 years ago, but recent research suggests that the process leading to such an eruption can occur much more rapidly than previously thought. Scientists from Arizona State University analyzed phenocrysts, crystals formed in the magma chamber, and found evidence of a significant temperature increase and barium influx in the decades preceding the last supereruption. This suggests that magma injections from deeper reservoirs might trigger such explosive events. While the Yellowstone supervolcano is currently one of the best-monitored in the world, the new findings imply that the warning time before a supereruption might be shorter than anticipated. The U.S. Geological Survey estimates the annual probability of a massive eruption at 1 in 730,000, but the study highlights the need for improved warning systems to mitigate potential catastrophic impacts. The research underscores the ongoing scientific effort to understand the mechanisms behind these rare and powerful events, aiming to better predict and prepare for future eruptions.

Syria's capital, Damascus, is feeling the impact of the ongoing civil war, reports The New York Times. Once a city of all-night parties and routine life, it now faces a growing sense of unease. Sandbagged checkpoints, soldiers searching vehicles for weapons, and the constant threat of shelling and machine-gun fire have transformed the city. "Where is Damascus headed? Are we the next Aleppo?" asks Rifa, a resident, expressing her fears. The city, a stronghold of President Bashar al-Assad, has been shielded from the worst of the conflict until now. However, the reality of war has crept into daily life, with gasoline shortages, food and heating oil worries, and frequent kidnappings. Streets are closed, traffic is diverted, and bridges are shut down, making simple movement difficult. Discussions among friends now focus on the fate of the homeless in city parks and the psychological impact on children. The war's toll is evident in the rise of suicide bombings and the rebels' aim to tighten their grip on the city's suburbs. Even supporters of the government are discussing the city's future, while rebels speak of strangling the government. The city's finest quarters are now under threat, with wealthy Syrians facing kidnapping and fear. The ongoing battles between rebel and government forces are taking their toll on the city, and the government's efforts to maintain an air of normalcy are faltering. The city seems now like a place under siege, where danger is a constant companion for most people. The article highlights the changing nature of life in Damascus, a city that once existed in a bubble of denial but is now facing the harsh realities of a civil war that shows no signs of abating.

Autopsy reports on Christina Anderson and her 8-year-old son, Ethan, whose bodies were found in the burning home of family friend James DiMaggio, have been released. Christina, 44, suffered blunt-force trauma to the head, with multiple impact sites and signs of binding and tape. Ethan's body, found in the charred house, showed signs of burns and possible fractures, though the cause of the fractures could not be definitively determined. The family dog was also found dead, shot. DiMaggio, 40, was shot and killed by FBI agents in Idaho after abducting 16-year-old Hannah Anderson. Hannah was rescued safely. Christina and Ethan's bodies were found on August 4, while Hannah was missing for six days before her rescue. The Medical Examiner’s Office detailed the extensive injuries on Christina, including a neck incision likely inflicted post-mortem, and Ethan's severe burns. The reports provide insight into the brutal nature of the crimes and the tragic loss of the Anderson family.

Two students were shot inside a Philadelphia high school gymnasium, with one in critical condition and the other in stable condition, according to police. A 15-year-old boy charged with aggravated assault was expected to surrender, while another 16-year-old boy was in custody but not charged. Surveillance video and school officials provided information leading to the suspects, but the first teen was cleared. The incident occurred just before 3:30 p.m. at Delaware Valley Charter High School, with the gun reportedly fired accidentally. The school was placed on lockdown, and searches were conducted for the weapon. Parents expressed concerns about safety and recent fights at the school. School officials stated they will continue to prioritize safety and security.

Army Staff Sgt. Robert Bales, a 38-year-old father of two, is accused of killing 16 Afghan civilians in a pre-dawn rampage, leaving nine of the victims as children. His case has drawn attention to the challenges faced by military families and the potential psychological toll of repeated deployments. Bales, who enlisted shortly after the 9/11 attacks, had a commendable military record, serving in Iraq and earning multiple medals. However, his personal life was marked by financial struggles, including a failed investment business and a home in foreclosure. His wife, Karilyn, wrote on her blog about her disappointment over his failed promotion and expressed relief that they could move on. Bales was known in his Washington neighborhood as a mild-mannered, family-oriented man. Legal troubles included a 2002 misdemeanor assault charge and a 2008 hit-and-run incident, where he claimed to have fallen asleep at the wheel. After the killings, Bales allegedly left his base in the Panjwai district of Kandahar province, shooting 16 people, including nine children, and attempting to burn their bodies. He then returned to the base and turned himself in. The incident has strained relations between the U.S. and Afghanistan, with the Afghan government demanding that Bales be tried in an Afghan court. His lawyer, John Henry Browne, has called for a thorough investigation into the factors that may have contributed to the alleged crime. The case has raised concerns about the mental health and well-being of service members, highlighting the need for better support and understanding of the challenges they face.

In his first interview since announcing his "conscious uncoupling" from Gwyneth Paltrow last month, Chris Martin delved into the personal issues that led to the end of their 10-year marriage. Speaking to BBC Radio 1's Zane Lowe, the Coldplay frontman revealed that his own insecurities and challenges played a significant role in the split. "About two years ago I was a mess," Martin admitted. "I can't enjoy the things that we are good at and I can't enjoy the great things around me because I'm burdened by this—I've got to not blame anyone else and make some changes." He elaborated, "I wouldn't use the word breakdown, this was more a realization about trying to grow up. If you can't open yourself up, you can't appreciate the wonder inside. You can be with someone wonderful, but because of your own issues you cannot let that be celebrated in the right way."

Martin's personal issues, he believes, stemmed from a lack of vulnerability. "Up to a certain point in my life I wasn't completely vulnerable and it caused some problems," he said. "If you don't let love in then you can't really give it back. So what Ghost Stories means to me is like, you've got to open yourself up to love and if you really do, of course it will be painful at times, but then it will be great at some point." The new album, which is due out on May 19, is a reflection of his journey towards self-improvement and honesty. "In life everyone needs to be broken in some way," Martin stated. "Everyone in their life goes through challenges, whether it's love or money, kids, or illness. You have to really not run away from that stuff."

The singer also addressed the public's reaction to the split, saying, "The reason I wanted to do this was because I love your Kanye interview. That guy is amazing and I think he is misunderstood by people who only look on the surface. I understand what he is talking about and I understand what he means." Martin's comments came as he discussed his admiration for Kanye West, adding, "That guy is amazing and I think he is misunderstood by people who only look on the surface. I understand what he is talking about and I understand what he means."

Martin's split with Paltrow, who he has been married to for 11 years and has two children with, was a surprise to many. In a blog post on her website, Goop, Paltrow and Martin wrote, "It is with hearts full of sadness that we have decided to separate." The couple cited disagreements over parenting strategies, family plans, and rumors of infidelity as contributing factors. Despite the split, Martin expressed hope for the future, stating, "I think in life everyone needs to be broken in some way. I think everyone in their life goes through challenges, whether it's love or money, kids, or illness. You have to really not run away from that stuff."

The musician also took the opportunity to praise One Direction, saying, "I think One Direction are the biggest band in the world, their songs are great. I’m saying One Direction are brilliant and I’m not kidding. You know why? Because their songs are really good and I don’t think that any of them are going to go solo. I think they appreciate their chemistry from watching their movie." Martin's comments about his split and his new album offer a glimpse into his personal growth and the challenges he faced in his relationship with Paltrow.

For more than five years, the United States has relied on China as the primary market for its recyclable plastic exports, with China taking in a significant portion of the country’s waste. However, China’s recent implementation of Operation Green Fence, which restricts the import of certain types of solid waste, including unwashed plastics, has left American recycling companies scrambling for new buyers. This change has caused a backlog of plastic waste in the United States, as recycling companies in Oregon have stopped accepting certain kinds of plastic due to the cancellation of Chinese orders. The restrictions have left recycling companies across the U.S. without buyers for many of the plastics they have traditionally accepted, limiting the types of plastics that recycling depots will now accept. Far West Fibers, a recycling company in Oregon, has seen 50 trucks worth of mixed plastic pile up after orders from China were canceled, necessitating re-sorting into individual types of plastic before it can be sold. The restrictions do not affect curbside recycling items like milk jugs and yogurt tubs but are limiting the miscellaneous plastics that recycling depots will accept. The lack of alternative buyers has left American cities with a significant problem, as they have made commitments to recycling but did not specify how or where. The U.S. has neglected to develop its own plastic recycling capacity, making it difficult to find new markets for the waste. The challenge now lies in finding new buyers for the recyclable plastics that China won’t take, with recycling companies meeting with officials to explore potential solutions.

A South Carolina woman, Lana Clayton, has been charged with murder after allegedly poisoning her husband, Stephen Clayton, with tetrahydrozoline, a chemical found in over-the-counter eye drops, for three days before his death on July 21. Authorities say she confessed to investigators after an autopsy revealed a high amount of the chemical in his body. Clayton, 52, is also charged with malicious tampering with a drug product or food. Stephen Clayton, 64, was found dead in their home, with police suspecting a fall down the stairs as the initial cause. The couple lived in a $822,000 home on Lake Wylie, and Clayton worked for the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs in Charlotte. This case, shocking to friends and neighbors, marks the second spousal homicide arrest in York County in less than a month.

When Joshua Vandiver, a Princeton Ph.D. student, met Henry Velandia, a salsa dancer from Venezuela, in 2006, they never imagined facing the threat of Velandia's deportation. Velandia, who has been in the U.S. since 2002, risks being sent back to Venezuela due to the 1996 Defense of Marriage Act, which defines marriage as between a man and a woman for federal laws, including immigration regulations. This means no member of a same-sex couple can sponsor a spouse’s visa application. Velandia, who has founded a dance school and appeared on Spanish-language television, faces an immigration hearing in November. The couple is advocating for the repeal of the Defense of Marriage Act and appealing to Congress to halt deportation hearings against foreign-born spouses of U.S. citizens. They have gained support through a Facebook page and hope their case will delay Velandia's deportation until the Supreme Court rules on the constitutionality of the Defense of Marriage Act. Despite their commitment, the couple faces the possibility of being separated, with Vandiver stating, "I never imagined that I would face this kind of discrimination from my own country and potentially have to flee it to be with the one I love."

Rep. Darrell Issa escalated the legal battle over the Fast and Furious scandal by directly accusing President Barack Obama of either abusing his power by withholding information or having his aides conspire with Justice Department officials to manage the aftermath of the failed ATF gun-walking program. In a letter to be released Tuesday, Issa charged that either the White House was involved in advising the Department of Justice regarding the congressional investigation, or Obama was asserting executive privilege unjustly to obstruct the probe. Issa's move is unlikely to force immediate action but is expected to generate significant media attention. The White House has maintained it was not involved in the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives program and has cited long-standing Justice Department precedent to support its position. Democrats are using the situation to portray the Republican contempt motion against Attorney General Eric Holder as an assault on minority rights, with civil rights leaders planning a press conference to highlight the potential impact on voter rights. The House is set to vote Thursday on whether to hold Holder in contempt, with Democrats unlikely to support the measure. The Obama administration invoked executive privilege to prevent Holder from sharing certain documents with the committee, leading to Issa's direct challenge to the president. The legal dispute is likely to continue, with the House considering a contempt vote and the DOJ unlikely to act on such charges. Republicans argue the DOJ has failed to comply with their subpoena, while Democrats contend the move is politically motivated and aimed at suppressing minority voting.

Florida International University's Pi Kappa Alpha fraternity chapter has been suspended following the discovery of a private Facebook page that contained numerous inappropriate posts. The page, which was reportedly accessed by an anonymous individual who shared screenshots with multiple media outlets and university administrators, featured content that violated university policies, including drug sales, hazing, and derogatory comments. One post offered to sell cocaine, while another boasted about selling the prescription drug Adderall. The fraternity's official public Facebook page also included a contact number, but no one answered repeated calls to it. In a statement, the fraternity's national headquarters acknowledged the existence of the private page but assured the university of the chapter's full compliance with the temporary suspension and subsequent investigation. FIU is currently investigating possible violations of its code of student conduct, with the university's on-campus police also involved. The post also highlights a series of previous disciplinary actions against the FIU chapter, including a suspension for serving alcohol to a pledge in June and various offenses such as underage drinking, breaking a student's car windshield, and throwing eggs at a rival fraternity's house since 2006. The penalties have ranged from suspensions to community service hours and a $1,500 donation to Mothers Against Drunk Driving. The article notes that the Facebook posts reflect larger issues within the culture of Greek life, with experts suggesting that universities often overlook such misbehavior due to the benefits these organizations bring to the institution.
