Prager suggests that Jews can celebrate Christmas without renouncing their own traditions, noting that 32% of Jewish households have Christmas trees and 71% of interfaith couples have them. He argues that the holiday has evolved to be more about consumerism and family than religious observance, making it a fitting secular celebration. Prager also highlights Jewish contributions to the holiday, such as Irving Berlin's "White Christmas" and the Rockettes at Radio City Music Hall. He acknowledges concerns from Christians about their religious symbols being co-opted but maintains that a Christmas tree can be a secular symbol for Jews. Ultimately, Prager encourages Jews to embrace the holiday, calling it a way to participate in a national tradition and spread holiday cheer.

Rescue efforts for the missing AirAsia Flight 8501, which vanished on December 28 with 162 people on board, continue in Indonesian waters. The plane was en route from Surabaya to Singapore when it lost contact with air traffic control. The search area, near the islands of Belitung and Borneo, is a busy shipping channel with shallow waters, complicating the search. Indonesian officials believe the plane is likely at the bottom of the sea based on radar data and the plane's last known coordinates. However, the search is hindered by bad weather, including large waves and clouds, which have made it difficult to locate debris and bodies. Despite the challenges, search teams are expanding the search area, now covering 13 zones over 156,000 square kilometers. Several reports of possible signs, such as an oil slick, a faint "ping," and smoke, have been investigated but have not confirmed the plane's location. AirAsia CEO Tony Fernandes stated that weather may have played a role in the disappearance, but the company is not speculating. The search involves over 1,100 personnel from Indonesia, Australia, Singapore, Malaysia, South Korea, Japan, and New Zealand. Families of the passengers have been briefed on the search progress and will be flown over the search area to lay flower wreaths. The Airbus A320-200, which is 6 years old, is being investigated for possible causes of the crash, including metal fatigue and pilot error. The incident has raised questions about the safety of flying in Indonesia and the role of weather in air travel. The article also notes that 2014 was a particularly unlucky year for Southeast Asian aviation, with the disappearance of Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 and the downing of Malaysia Airlines Flight 17. The search for the missing plane continues, with the hope of recovering the flight data and cockpit voice recorders to determine the cause of the crash.

A group of eight U.S. senators is working on a bipartisan immigration bill that includes a path to citizenship for the country's 11 million illegal immigrants, but the plan faces significant opposition from U.S. citizens, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll. The poll, released on Wednesday, shows that 30% of Americans believe most illegal immigrants should be deported, while 23% say all illegal immigrants should be deported. Only 5% of respondents believe all illegal immigrants should be allowed to stay in the United States legally, and 31% want most illegal immigrants to stay. The poll suggests that while most Americans support immigration reform, there is a divide on how to achieve it. Republicans are more likely to support deportation, while Democrats are more supportive of a path to citizenship. The senators' proposal calls for a full path to citizenship for illegal immigrants once they pay back taxes and a fine and wait in line behind others applying to become Americans. However, the senators want any move to relax immigration laws to depend on boosting security on the southern border. The bill, which includes provisions for a high-tech identity card for all U.S. workers, has raised concerns among privacy advocates. The card could use fingerprints or other personal markers to prove a person's legal eligibility to work, but the senators haven't committed to the biometric ID card. The goal is to ensure that employers can learn the legal status of all new hires quickly, part of the effort to dissuade illegal immigrants from entering the country or seeking jobs. While President Obama supports an improved worker-verification system, he doesn't specifically call for a biometric card for all workers. The senators are wary of any element that might split the fragile coalition of Democrats, Republicans, and outside organizations working toward agreement on a broad overhaul of immigration laws.

Morley Safer, the longest-serving 60 Minutes correspondent for 46 years, passed away at 84. His career was marked by groundbreaking reports, including his 1965 exposure of U.S. Marines burning Vietnamese huts, which earned him a George Polk award and angered President Lyndon Johnson. Safer's influential work also included the 1983 "Lenell Geter's in Jail" segment, which overturned a wrongful conviction. He was known for his eloquent, sometimes quirky features and his ability to find unique stories, such as the popularity of tango in Finland. Safer's legacy includes numerous awards and his impact on journalism, as recognized by CBS Chairman Leslie Moonves, who praised him as "one of the most important journalists in any medium, ever." His retirement was celebrated with a special one-hour broadcast, highlighting his remarkable career and the lasting influence of his work on 60 Minutes.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture has approved the commercial planting of a new genetically modified potato called the "Innate" potato, developed by Idaho-based J.R. Simplot Co. The potato is engineered to produce less acrylamide, a chemical suspected to be a human carcinogen, and is also resistant to bruising. However, one of the company's oldest business partners, McDonald's, has stated it does not use genetically modified potatoes and has no plans to change its sourcing practices. McDonald's, along with other fast-food chains and the dehydrated potato industry, has previously resisted GMO potatoes, leading to the discontinuation of Monsanto's "New Leaf" line of genetically modified potatoes. Simplot spokesman Doug Cole stated that the fresh potato market would embrace the Innate potato, and the company expects to increase production after the 2015 harvest. Despite the approval, some growers, like Rupert potato grower Duane Grant, have been told by buyers in the dehydrated potato industry not to plant the GMO potatoes. However, Grant hopes to find willing buyers to plant the biotech potatoes and benefit from their higher yields due to reduced bruising. Food & Water Watch, a consumer advocacy group, celebrated McDonald's decision, stating it marks a milestone in the movement to protect consumers from the potential dangers of GMO foods. The group urged competing fast-food chains to follow McDonald's lead in rejecting GMO potatoes.

A sinkhole that began as a small depression in a backyard in Land O'Lakes, Florida, rapidly expanded and swallowed a boat, destroyed two homes, and prompted officials to evacuate residents from 10 other homes on Friday. The hole, which grew to 200 feet wide and 50 feet deep, was first noticed when someone reported a "depression" under a boat in the backyard of a home in Lake Padgett Estates. Firefighters managed to rescue two dogs and retrieve some belongings from the first home before it started collapsing. By early afternoon, the adjacent home was also destroyed. No injuries were reported. Property records show that a sinkhole had previously opened on the property in 2012 and had been "stabilized," though the effectiveness of the stabilization is unclear. Pasco County officials have tagged 10 other homes in the neighborhood as unsafe and have voluntarily evacuated their residents. Duke Energy cut power to about 100 homes in the area, and the American Red Cross is assisting displaced residents. Kevin Guthrie, Pasco County's assistant county administrator for public safety, described the event as frightening, stating, "Mother Nature is going to take what Mother Nature takes." The rapid growth of the sinkhole, which began as a small depression, highlights the unpredictable nature of these geological phenomena and the challenges in fully stabilizing affected properties.

Hurricane Harvey claimed another victim nearly two months after the storm made landfall in Texas. A 31-year-old man, Josue Zurita, died from a rare flesh-eating bacterial infection known as necrotizing fasciitis after being diagnosed on October 10. Zurita was helping repair homes damaged by the flooding. The Galveston County Health District announced his death, and the Houston Chronicle identified him. Zurita was described as a loving father and hard-working carpenter who had moved to the U.S. from Mexico to help his family and remained to assist in the rebuilding efforts post-Harvey. His death follows that of Nancy Reed, a 77-year-old Houston-area woman who also passed away in September from a similar infection related to Harvey floodwaters. Dr. Philip Keiser, the local health authority, stated that while such infections as necrotizing fasciitis are rare, they should not be surprising given the exposure to construction and potential injuries during the recovery efforts. Keiser explained that the bacteria can enter through a break in the skin and spread quickly, killing soft tissue and potentially leading to death within a short time. Proper wound care is crucial to prevent such infections, including keeping open wounds covered and seeking medical attention for any signs of redness or swelling. The CDC advises against eating or drinking anything contaminated by floodwater and stresses the importance of clean, dry bandages for wounds. The article highlights the ongoing health risks posed by natural disasters, particularly in areas with extensive flooding.

Ford's ambitious $1 billion investment in Argo AI, a previously secretive Pittsburgh-based startup, marks a significant move in the race to dominate the self-driving car market. Argo AI, co-founded by Google's self-driving car veteran Bryan Salesky and Uber's Peter Rander, will operate with substantial independence, allowing Ford to tap into the startup's expertise in artificial intelligence and robotics. The deal, structured as a majority investment rather than an outright acquisition, enables Ford to offer equity stakes to attract top talent, crucial in a highly competitive field. Ford aims to leverage Argo AI's capabilities to develop a fully autonomous vehicle for mass production by 2021, aligning with its broader strategy to transform into a mobility company. This investment underscores Ford's commitment to staying ahead in an industry where tech giants like Google and Apple are also vying for dominance. By combining the agility of a startup with the scale and manufacturing prowess of Ford, the partnership seeks to accelerate the development and commercialization of self-driving technology. The move also reflects Ford's recognition of the critical role that software and AI play in the future of autonomous vehicles, positioning the company to potentially license its technology to other automakers. With other major players like General Motors and Uber also making significant investments in self-driving startups, the stakes are high, and the race to bring autonomous cars to market is intensifying.

When Willie and Carol Fowler's only daughter, Tamara, canceled her wedding 40 days before the scheduled date, the parents faced a dilemma with a venue, food, and entertainment that had all been paid for. Instead of canceling everything and losing their deposits, they decided to repurpose the event into a celebration for 200 homeless individuals. Willie Fowler recounted that his idea was inspired by a vision he had during prayer, and they contacted Hosea Feed the Hungry, a local Atlanta organization that provides services and resources to the homeless.

Carol Fowler explained, "We went home that evening, and my husband woke up the next morning and I was in the process of cancelling out the venue and he said, 'No, what we'll do is donate it to Hosea Feed the Hungry.'" The Fowlers arranged for 200 homeless women, children, and families to be transported to the Villa Christina restaurant for the event. The celebration began with outdoor appetizers and space for the children to play. Inside, the children enjoyed face painting, juggling, and crowns, while the adults were served a meal of salmon and chicken. The event also included a motivational speaker for the adults.

Quisa Foster of Hosea Feed the Hungry shared, "When they first called, the administration thought it was a prank call because it was too good to be true. It's a very creme de la creme wedding venue, so to say that you're going to host 200 homeless individuals at Villa Christina—it sounds like a prank call." The Fowlers persisted and eventually had a meeting with the organization to plan the event. The day was filled with joy and inspiration, with all the plates being empty and no leftover food, demonstrating the value of the experience for the guests.

Carol Fowler stated, "It was a wonderful event. It brought tears to my eyes. You go to weddings sometimes and you see a lot of people really waste food. We take so many things for granted. These clients or guests, they don't." The Fowlers were deeply involved in the event, greeting all the guests, and their daughter, Tamara, found the experience surreal but incredibly rewarding. The family hopes to make the affair an annual event, incorporating educational elements for the participants and seeking sponsors for future years. Willie Fowler added, "There is no way to explain how it makes you feel, but it's wonderful. It's just that wonderful, rewarding feeling. If we could just inspire one youth in that crowd to rise above the situation today and be a very responsible member of society tomorrow, that would be extremely rewarding."

Mitt Romney, the 2012 Republican presidential nominee and current U.S. Senate candidate from Utah, has predicted that President Donald Trump will win re-election in 2020 and secure the Republican nomination easily. Speaking at an event for major GOP donors in Deer Valley, Utah, Romney stated, "I think President Trump will be re-nominated by my party easily, and I think he'll be reelected solidly." He attributed Trump's political prospects to an improving economy and the likelihood of Democrats nominating an outsider. Romney, who previously criticized Trump harshly, now believes Trump's policies have performed better than expected. During a recent interview, Romney acknowledged, "I wouldn't point to the president as a role model for my grandkids on the basis of his personal style," citing instances where Trump departed from the truth and engaged in inappropriate attacks. Despite their past conflicts, Romney's relationship with Trump has mellowed, and he has praised some of the president's actions. Romney's remarks came during the E2 Summit, an annual event he hosts, which drew influential political leaders and donors. Romney also expressed optimism about the GOP's 2018 midterm prospects, predicting that the party would retain control of both chambers of Congress. His favored position in the Utah Senate race, facing a June 26 runoff against Mike Kennedy, a conservative state representative, further underscores his current political standing.

A 23-year-old hotel worker, Jason Garnett, found himself in a highly uncomfortable and embarrassing situation after waking up with an erection that lasted for 17 hours. The condition, known as priapism, is a medical emergency that can cause permanent damage if not treated promptly. Garnett, working in Harrogate, U.K., initially dismissed the persistent erection, but by lunchtime, he realized something was amiss. He tried ice baths and jogging, but nothing helped. His roommate's reaction to the news was one of shock and concern, highlighting the seriousness of the situation.

Seeking medical attention, Garnett was diagnosed with priapism and taken to a local hospital. Doctors drained more than two pints of blood from his penis to reduce the pressure and injected him with medication 24 times to restrict blood flow. The pain was excruciating, Garnett described it as "10 out of 10." After 17 hours of agony, the unwanted erection finally subsided. Garnett's penis, now "black and blue," has fully recovered, though he admits it looks "like it's been through a war." The incident serves as a stark reminder of the importance of recognizing and addressing such medical emergencies.

Kansas's Schlitterbahn Waterparks and Resorts has announced that the 168-foot-tall Verrückt waterslide, which tragically claimed the life of 10-year-old Caleb Schwab, will be permanently removed once the investigation concludes and court permission is granted. The slide, billed as the world's tallest, has been closed since the accident on August 7, 2016, when Caleb died, and two women in the raft with him suffered facial injuries. The park's statement expresses deep sorrow and emphasizes their commitment to safety, noting that this event is unprecedented in their 50-year history. Schlitterbahn maintains that the slide's removal is the only appropriate course of action following the tragedy. The company has been fully cooperating with investigative teams and working with the families, their attorneys, and staff affected by the accident. Caleb's father, Kansas state Rep. Scott Schwab, and his attorneys have been working to ensure the slide's permanent decommissioning. The criminal investigation is ongoing, and it remains unclear if legal action will be taken. In Kansas, personal injury and wrongful death cases have damage limits of $300,000 and $250,000, respectively, which could influence any potential settlement. Independent investigations by the families' legal team and experts continue, focusing on the technical aspects of the slide's design and operation. Schlitterbahn's spokesperson stated that the slide "will never run again— not at any park, anywhere." The company is preparing to dismantle the slide as soon as the court permits, ensuring that it is removed from the tower.

A 36-year-old woman, Marie Joseph, went missing after swimming in the pool at Lafayette Park on Sunday. Her body was found floating on Tuesday night, prompting the investigation into her death. The area was closed and locked when teenagers reported the body to police. Marie Joseph's body has been positively identified, and the cause of death is under investigation. The pool's staff has been placed on administrative leave, and all 30 state-operated deep-water pools will be temporarily closed for safety reviews. A 9-year-old boy, who was at the pool with Joseph, reported that she had an accident on a water slide, but the exact sequence of events is unclear. The investigation is ongoing, and authorities are waiting for the results of an autopsy to determine the cause of death. The Fall River Police Chief, Daniel Racine, emphasized that the investigation is in its early stages, and the circumstances surrounding Joseph's death remain unknown. The state Department of Conservation and Recreation expressed condolences to Joseph's family and friends and pledged to cooperate fully with law enforcement.

Federal authorities in a two-year undercover operation arrested 24 suspected hackers across 13 countries, targeting online financial fraud involving stolen credit card and bank information. The sting, dubbed Operation Card Shop, involved creating a fake carding forum called "Carder Profit," which was monitored by FBI agents. This operation prevented potential losses of over $205 million on more than 411,000 compromised consumer credit and debit cards. Eleven individuals were arrested in the United States, while the rest were apprehended in countries like Britain, Bulgaria, and Norway. Among those arrested, Mir Islam, known as "JoshTheGod," was charged with trafficking 50,000 stolen credit card numbers. The operation also highlighted the growing sophistication of hackers and the need for enhanced security measures, as credit card fraud has surged in recent years.

Nebraska executed Carey Dean Moore on Tuesday morning at 10 a.m. at the Nebraska State Penitentiary in Lincoln, marking the state’s first lethal injection execution since 1997. The execution was conducted using a four-drug cocktail: diazepam, fentanyl, cisatracurium besylate, and potassium chloride. Four media witnesses and Moore’s brother, niece, a friend, and a spiritual adviser were present in the execution chamber. The timeline of the execution began with the arrival of the media witnesses at 10:19 a.m., followed by the lifting of the curtain to reveal Moore on the table, his body covered by a white sheet, with his arm connected to the IV tube. At 10:24 a.m., the first drug, diazepam, was administered. Moore appeared to speak to his witnesses, who were separated from the media by a partition. At 10:26 a.m., a saline cleanse was administered, and Moore’s eyes closed. Fentanyl was delivered at 10:30 a.m., causing him to cough and his diaphragm to move rapidly. At 10:32 a.m., cisatracurium besylate and potassium chloride were administered, and Moore’s face turned red and then purple. At 10:36 a.m., saline was run through the IV tube, and at 10:38 a.m., Moore’s eyelids cracked open slightly. The curtain was lowered at 10:47 a.m., and Moore was pronounced dead by Lancaster County Coroner Pat Condon. The execution chamber was soundproof, and the process was closely monitored by prison officials. Moore’s body was later remanded to the Nebraska State Patrol for an autopsy.

House Majority Leader Eric Cantor (R-Va.) announced his resignation after losing his primary to tea party challenger Dave Brat, setting off a scramble for new leadership within the Republican Party. Cantor, who had been seen as a potential speaker, stepped down at the end of July, leaving Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.) as the frontrunner for the majority leader position. McCarthy, the current majority whip, began building support for his candidacy, while Rep. Pete Sessions (R-Texas), chairman of the powerful House Rules Committee, also emerged as a contender. Sessions argued that he would focus on border security, aligning with conservative priorities. McCarthy, who hesitated to campaign immediately, was seen as the establishment favorite, potentially facing competition from more conservative rivals. Rep. Jeb Hensarling (R-Texas), chairman of the House Financial Services Committee, and Rep. Steve Scalise (R-La.), chairman of the conservative Republican Study Committee, were also considering bids. The leadership elections were scheduled for June 19, with Cantor staying on as majority leader until July 31. Rep. Paul Ryan (R-Wis.), the House Budget Committee chairman, declined to run, while Rep. Peter Roskam (R-Ill.) announced his intention to run for whip. The race highlighted the internal divisions within the Republican Party, with some calling for more representation from red states. The fast-paced developments left many Republicans stunned and scrambling to find a new leadership team to guide the House.

President Donald Trump on Friday tapped Robert Wilkie, the current acting Veterans Affairs Secretary, to become the department’s next permanent leader, according to a White House statement. Wilkie, who has led the VA in an acting capacity since March and was confirmed by the Senate for a Pentagon post last year, will now face the Senate confirmation process. Trump praised Wilkie for an "incredible job" steering the VA in recent months, and the acting secretary shook hands with the president after the unexpected announcement. Wilkie’s path to the VA’s permanent helm is likely to be smoother than the turbulent bid of Ronny Jackson, the president’s former personal physician, who withdrew from consideration amid scandal over his workplace behavior. Jackson’s withdrawal followed the resignation of David Shulkin, who was ousted by Trump amid growing tensions with the White House over a taxpayer-financed trip to Europe and after he openly sparred with conservatives in his agency. The latest leadership development comes as the VA is still reeling from high-profile departures and ethics scandals, with Jackson and Shulkin both leaving the department under controversy. Wilkie’s nomination could face a potential snag due to his connection to the ongoing probe of Trump’s ties to Russia, as he was one of three congressional aides present when the Trump campaign supported the rejection of a tough-on-Russia provision proposed for the GOP’s 2016 platform. Special counsel Robert Mueller’s team is reportedly examining the platform debate, but Wilkie had not been contacted by Mueller as of last fall. Senate Committee on Veterans’ Affairs Chairman Johnny Isakson (R-Ga.) congratulated Wilkie on his nomination and expressed confidence in the confirmation process. Rep. Phil Roe (R-Tenn.), chairman of the House panel on veterans' affairs, also commended Trump’s selection, stating that Wilkie would be an effective permanent secretary. The American Veterans non-partisan advocacy group noted that Wilkie would provide "needed stability" for the VA, as the agency continues to grapple with ongoing issues and controversies.

There is bipartisan agreement that the Secret Service could benefit from more women on the force, according to remarks made by two lawmakers on Sunday. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine) and Rep. Carolyn Maloney (D-N.Y.) both suggested that the presence of more women could have prevented incidents like the recent prostitution scandal in Cartagena, Colombia. Collins noted, "I can't help but wonder if there'd been more women as part of that detail if this ever would’ve happened." Maloney agreed, pointing out that the Secret Service is only 11 percent female and adding, "I can't help but keep asking this question: Where are the women? We probably need to diversify the Secret Service and have more minorities and more women."

In other political developments, Florida Sen. Marco Rubio, who has previously stated his disinterest in the vice-presidential nomination, said he would be "respectful of the process" if Mitt Romney were to select him. Rubio, who was previously dismissive of the VP process, now says, "Up to now it's all been theoretical, we have a nominee now, and our nominee, Mitt Romney, the leader of the Republican Party, has a vice presidential process in place. And I think from this point moving forward, I think it'd be wise for all Republicans to kind of respect that process, myself included, and say moving forward, we're going to let his process play itself out." Rubio expressed support for Jeb Bush, saying, "I hope he'll say yes if future President Romney asks him."

Meanwhile, Independent Sen. Joe Lieberman, who was Al Gore's running mate in 2000 and supported John McCain in 2008, announced that he would stay out of the 2012 race. Lieberman said, "I'm going to try something different this year. I'm going to try to stay out of this one. I'm enjoying not being involved in the nastiness of campaigning in America these days. I think this year, when it comes to the presidential election, I'm just going to do what most Americans do: go in the voting booth on election day and in the privacy of the booth cast my vote."

President Barack Obama is reportedly "apoplectic" about the lavish spending at the General Services Administration (GSA), according to a top adviser. David Axelrod, who spoke on NBC's "Meet the Press," said, "On the GSA issue, he was I think it’s fair to say apoplectic. Because we made a big effort to cut waste, inefficiency, fraud against government, saved tens of billions of dollars doing it on just this very kind of thing. And so this was very enraging to him, and, of course, he acted quickly, the administration acted quickly and changed the management there." The GSA has been in the spotlight recently due to reports of employees spending money on luxury hotel suites and other extravagant expenses.

Finally, conservative Sen. Tom Coburn (R-Okla.) defended the Obama administration's response to the Secret Service scandal, stating, "You know, I'm not critical of what the administration has done thus far. I think what we're seeing is an aberration." Coburn also expressed confidence in Secret Service Director Mark Sullivan, saying, "He has demonstrated in many ways that he is on top of this, and we'll get to the bottom of it. My experience with the Secret Service has been with stellar individuals."

Hillary Clinton’s campaign clarified that her team read every email before deleting or turning it over to the State Department, addressing concerns over how thousands of personal emails were handled. In a statement to Fox News, Clinton spokesman Nick Merrill stated that the team read "every email" before making the decision to discard or retain them. This came after Clinton’s office revealed that while over 30,000 "work-related" emails were turned over to the State Department, nearly 32,000 were deemed "private" and deleted. Critics and lawmakers, including Rep. Trey Gowdy, questioned the criteria used to determine which emails were private and whether Clinton’s lawyers adequately protected public records. House Speaker John Boehner is expected to launch a new investigation into Clinton’s email practices, including the handling of personal emails. Clinton’s team had previously stated that the emails were reviewed in a "multi-step" process, but did not specify if all emails were read. The process included searching for emails from government accounts, organizing emails by sender and recipient, and searching for specific terms like "Benghazi." Clinton said she deleted the personal emails because she felt she had no reason to save them, but this admission raised questions about the thoroughness of the review process. The revelation that the State Department’s email archiving practices for senior officials were not routine until recently further complicated the issue, as it suggested that many emails may not have been automatically saved. State Department officials acknowledged that the archiving process was not in place for all officials until February, and that some emails may still be accessible through technical means. The controversy over Clinton’s email practices continues to raise questions about transparency and the preservation of government records.

A motorcycle-borne suicide bomber killed the deputy governor of Kandahar province, Abdul Latif Ashna, and injured three of his bodyguards as he was driving to work in Kandahar city, raising fears of a renewed campaign of assassinations. The Taliban claimed responsibility, marking the highest-profile strike of its kind in months. The attack, which occurred in Kandahar, the traditional heartland of the Taliban, highlights the ongoing threat to public servants and officials. U.S. Ambassador Karl W. Eikenberry and Afghan President Hamid Karzai condemned the assassination, with Eikenberry calling it a "vicious assassination" and a setback to efforts to stabilize Kandahar. Western military officials hope improving security in Kandahar will pave the way for better governance and public services, but the killing of influential figures undermines this goal. Senior U.S. commanders emphasize the importance of Kandahar in the overall war effort, noting that Taliban fighters usually use winter months to regroup in Pakistan. Despite significant military gains, the Taliban have made inroads in some areas, and their leaders have rejected peace talks.

According to an analysis led by the University of Toulouse's Young-Ho Eom, Frank Sinatra is the most influential person in the English-language Wikipedia, followed by Michael Jackson and Pope Pius XII. Eom's team used methods similar to Google's PageRank algorithm to analyze Wikipedia pages, determining the importance of individuals based on the number of articles linking to them. When considering all 24 major language editions of Wikipedia, Adolf Hitler emerges as the most influential figure, with Michael Jackson in second place and Madonna in third. The study aimed to uncover if Wikipedia is skewed in its attention to various figures based on gender, time, or location. The authors found that most important historical figures across Wikipedia editions were born in Western countries after the 17th century and are male. However, each edition highlights local figures, with most historical figures born in the countries that use the language of the edition. The researchers applied a second method, CheiRank, to measure importance, which considers the number of outgoing links. By combining PageRank and CheiRank, the study arrived at the top 100 for all 24 editions of Wikipedia, with Frank Sinatra at the top. The analysis revealed that Swedish naturalist Carl Linnaeus, known as "The Father of Taxonomy," was the most influential person across all languages due to the extensive use of his system of naming in scientific articles. This unexpected result highlights the importance of Linnaeus' contributions to taxonomy and the specific way the study was conducted.

President Donald Trump's decision to launch airstrikes against a Syrian air base in response to a suspected chemical weapons attack has sparked a divided reaction in Congress, with lawmakers from both parties expressing support and criticism. House Speaker Paul Ryan and Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin called the strikes "appropriate and just" but emphasized the need for further Congressional involvement. Top Democrats like House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi and Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin supported the strikes but stressed the importance of Congressional approval for any escalation. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer also backed the strikes, urging the administration to come up with a strategy and consult Congress. However, libertarian-minded Republicans like Senators Mike Lee and Rand Paul argued that the President needs congressional authorization for military action as required by the Constitution. Similarly, liberal Democrats such as Senator Brian Schatz and Representative Ted Lieu also contended that the use of force requires congressional approval. On the other hand, Republican defense hawks like Senators John McCain and Lindsey Graham praised Trump's decision, stating that it made it clear to Assad that the days of committing war crimes with impunity are over. The article highlights the long-standing debate over the president's constitutional war powers, noting that while the 2001 war authorization against Al Qaeda was passed by Congress, President Obama did not seek authorization for the 2011 military intervention in Libya. The U.S. military has been conducting airstrikes in Syria since 2014, targeting the Islamic State, but Thursday's strike was the first U.S. military action targeting the Bashar Assad regime. Trump's statement emphasized the vital national security interest of the United States in preventing and deterring the spread and use of deadly chemical weapons. The article also mentions criticism directed at MSNBC's Brian Williams for his seemingly euphoric reaction to the missile strikes, with some Twitter users calling his comments insensitive. Williams quoted Leonard Cohen, saying, "I am guided by the beauty of our weapons," during his "11th Hour" show, which drew backlash from viewers.

University of Virginia President Teresa Sullivan suspended all campus fraternities and sororities on Saturday in response to a searing Rolling Stone article detailing an alleged 2012 gang rape at a Phi Kappa Psi fraternity house. The article, which described how a fraternity member led the victim, a student given an alias, upstairs during a party and into a dark room where several men raped her, sparked intense reactions on the 195-year-old university's campus. The suspension, effective until January 9th, was part of a broader effort to address a culture of excessive drinking and sexual misconduct, with President Sullivan calling on the community to come forward with information to the police. The article also highlighted the university's seemingly unconcerned response to sexual assault allegations, raising questions about the handling of such cases. In response, the Inter-Fraternity Council voluntarily suspended social activities through the weekend, while the university's Board of Visitors planned to discuss policies and procedures on sexual assault. President Sullivan urged students, faculty, and alumni to participate in a review of the university’s sexual misconduct policy and to take responsibility for making the community better. The suspension and the article's publication have reignited discussions about the university's tradition of honor and the need for systemic changes to address sexual violence on campus.

Baby names from the TV series "Breaking Bad" like Jesse and Skyler saw significant increases in popularity in 2013, according to BabyCenter's annual list. The name Jesse gained 13%, while Skyler surged 70%. Meanwhile, names from "Duck Dynasty" such as Korie and Silas also rose, with Korie up 89%. The royal baby George and Kanye West's daughter North West also boosted their names' popularity. George for girls saw a 37% increase, while Kanye gained 38%. Other celebrity names like Marnie and Shoshanna from "Girls" rose by 62% and 67%, respectively. In contrast, names associated with negative press, such as Reese Witherspoon and Lindsay Lohan, declined in popularity. Among TODAY show anchors, Al and Hoda's names gained in popularity, while Kathie Lee and Tamron's did not appear in the database. The list, based on 550,000 babies born to registered parents on BabyCenter's website, highlights the influence of personal and celebrity names on parents' choices.

The public school systems in New York and Los Angeles both received bomb threats today, but only one city took it seriously. New York’s students had to spend a lovely 60-degree day in class, while 640,000 California kids got the day off. The discrepancy in responses can be attributed to the level of credulity each city’s officials exhibited. Both threats were similar, if not identical, threatening a multi-pronged, jihadi attack on multiple schools, using bombs and nerve gas. However, several details indicated the threats were hoaxes. The emails were sent by Cockmail, an email host affiliated with 8chan, known for its non-halal domains and inappropriate content. Both emails spelled the word “Allah” with a lowercase “a,” and the Los Angeles email claimed to be from a bullied individual. New York Mayor Bill de Blasio dismissed the threat as a hoax, while Los Angeles Police Chief Charlie Beck defended the decision to close all schools, stating that parents would have made the same decision if they knew the information available to school officials. The threat against the nation's second-largest school district was sent via email to a school board member and traced back to an IP address in Frankfurt, Germany. Despite the threat being deemed not credible after a 12-hour investigation, the Los Angeles school district remained cautious, with all schools being thoroughly searched. The threat was also made against New York City schools, with police believing it to be a hoax. The Los Angeles Unified School District (LAUSD) superintendent, Ramon Cortines, made the decision to close all campuses after consulting with the mayor and local law enforcement. The closure was supported by the mayor, who stated that the decision was his to support. The district serves over 640,000 students and 900 schools, making it the second largest in the nation. The threat was initially characterized as credible, but after a thorough investigation, law enforcement agencies determined it was not credible. Despite the closure, LAUSD officials remained vigilant, ensuring the safety of students and taking steps to restore calm.

A controversial email from the Tennessee Virtual Academy, a for-profit online public school, has raised questions about potential grade manipulation. The email, sent by the school’s vice principal to middle school teachers, instructed them to delete failing grades from the first two months of the semester, replacing them with more recent grades. This practice, if confirmed, could be seen as an attempt to hide poor performance. State Representative Gloria Johnson, a Democrat, expressed concern, stating, "That's cheating in my mind." The email also suggested removing grades of students who failed an assignment, focusing on reading and math while downplaying other subjects. The Tennessee Virtual Academy’s principal defended the practice, saying it was to better recognize students' current progress and differentiate those needing intervention. However, critics argue that this approach could mislead parents and the public about student performance. The Tennessee Virtual Academy, which received state funding of $7.5 million this year, has faced scrutiny over its low standardized test scores. Governor Bill Haslam has proposed legislation to limit the school’s enrollment and potentially shut it down. The controversy highlights the tension between for-profit schools and traditional public education, with some lawmakers questioning the ethics of grade manipulation and the effectiveness of virtual schools.

Houston Texans defensive end J.J. Watt is out for the season after suffering a tibial plateau fracture during the team's 42-34 loss to the Kansas City Chiefs. Watt fell to the ground while engaged in a block on the Chiefs' opening drive, and was taken off the field on a cart before being transported to a hospital. Head coach Bill O'Brien confirmed that outside linebacker Whitney Mercilus will also be out for the remainder of the season due to a torn pectoral muscle. O'Brien emphasized that the team will need multiple players to step up and fill the void left by Watt and Mercilus. Watt, who missed 13 games in the 2016 season due to a back injury, recently used his platform to raise over $37 million for relief efforts following Hurricane Harvey. His absence will significantly impact the Texans' defense, especially considering his dominance in previous seasons. Watt expressed his disappointment and apologized to his teammates and the city of Houston. The team will rely on players like Brandon Dunn, Joel Heath, and Carlos Watkins to contribute more in Watt's absence.

Detectives investigating the attempted murders of Russian double agent Sergei Skripal and his daughter Yulia have said they believe the pair were poisoned with a nerve agent at the front door of his Salisbury home. The highest concentration of the nerve agent was found on the front door, according to police. Counter-terrorism detectives will continue their inquiries around the home for weeks or months. More than 130 people could have been exposed to the chemical weapon in the aftermath of the poisoning. In response, over 150 Russian officials have been expelled from more than 25 countries, and the UK government is considering further measures, including a ban on the City of London from selling Russian sovereign debt. Public health experts are still working to establish whether the nerve agent attack presents a long-term risk to Salisbury’s residents, which will receive a £1m support package from central government to help recover. Deputy Assistant Commissioner Dean Haydon stated that the Skripals first came into contact with the nerve agent from their front door and that officers will continue to search the area. Approximately 250 counter-terrorism detectives are working on the investigation, examining more than 5,000 hours of CCTV and over 1,350 exhibits. Traces of the nerve agent have been found at other scenes but at lower concentrations than at the home address. Surveillance footage shows Sergei Skripal shopping at a convenience store days before he was poisoned. The UK government blames Russia for the attack, while Russia denies any involvement. Diplomatic fallout includes the expulsion of 23 Russian diplomats and the shuttering of British cultural institutions in Russia. British Foreign Minister Boris Johnson thanked countries for standing with Britain, saying the expulsions represent a moment when collective patience has worn to the breaking point. The Skripals may never fully recover, according to UK officials, highlighting the "utterly barbaric nature" of the act and the potential danger to innocent citizens in Salisbury.

Millennial workers, those ages 18 to 35, are just as likely to stick with their employers as their older counterparts in Generation X were when they were young adults, according to recently released government data. This trend is consistent across the board, but particularly notable among the college-educated, where Millennials have longer track records with their employers than Generation X workers did in 2000 when they were the same age. The data from the U.S. Department of Labor's Current Population Survey, which has been collected periodically since the early 1950s, shows that in January 2016, 63.4% of employed Millennials, the generation born between 1981 and 1998, reported that they had worked for their current employer at least 13 months. In February 2000, 59.9% of 18- to 35-year-olds – most of whom are today’s Gen Xers – reported similar job tenure. Among the college-educated, 75% of 25- to 35-year-olds had worked for their employer at least 13 months in 2016, a similar share to their Gen X counterparts in 2000. These figures suggest that the "job-hopping Millennial" characterization does not fit the broad Millennial workforce.

One factor contributing to Millennials staying with employers longer is their relatively high levels of education, which is typically associated with longer tenure. Among 25- to 35-year-old workers in 2016, 38% of Millennial men and 46% of Millennial women had completed at least a bachelor’s degree. In contrast, the Gen X workforce back in 2000 had significantly lower levels of educational attainment: 31% of male 25- to 35-year-old workers had finished college, as had only 34% of female workers. The longer tenure of college-educated Millennials compared with that of Gen X workers does not necessarily translate into higher wages or more job security. They may be sticking with their current employers due to a dearth of opportunities to get a better job with a different employer. However, their reported tenure makes clear that the “job-hopping Millennial” characterization does not fit the broad Millennial workforce.

The trend is different among less-educated young adults. For example, among Millennials with a high school education, 70% of men and 69% of women had been with their employer at least 13 months. These proportions are similar to their high-school-educated counterparts among today’s Gen Xers in 2000 (72% for men and 71% for women). This suggests that educational attainment plays a significant role in job tenure among young workers.

The increasing job tenure of college-educated Millennials is consistent with a decline in employer switching among all working-age adults since the 1980s. The reasons for this decline are not well understood. Recent research indicates that the rise of dual-career households, the decline in middle-skill jobs, occupational licensing, and the need for employees to retain health insurance cannot account for much of the decline in job-switching. This trend is part of a broader shift in how young adults approach their careers and life stages, with many prioritizing education and job stability over early marriage and family.

The generational dynamics continue to evolve, with Millennials now surpassing Baby Boomers as the nation’s largest living generation. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, Millennials, defined as those ages 18-34 in 2015, now number 75.4 million, surpassing the 74.9 million Baby Boomers (ages 51-69). Generation X (ages 35-50 in 2015) is projected to pass the Boomers in population by 2028. The Millennial generation continues to grow as young immigrants expand its ranks. Boomers, whose generation was defined by the boom in U.S. births following World War II, are older and their numbers are shrinking as the number of deaths among them exceeds the number of older immigrants arriving in the country.

Generations are analytical constructs, and developing a popular and expert consensus on what marks the boundaries between one generation and the next takes time. Pew Research Center has established that the oldest “Millennial” was born in 1981. The Center continues to assess demographic, attitudinal, and other evidence on habits and culture that will help to establish when the youngest Millennial was born or even when a new generation begins. To distill the implications of the census numbers for generational heft, this analysis assumes that the youngest Millennial was born in 1997.

The generational projections show that the Millennial population is projected to peak in 2036 at 81.1 million. Thereafter, the oldest Millennial will be at least 56 years of age, and mortality is projected to outweigh net immigration gains, leading to a decline in the Millennial population. By 2050, there will be a projected 79.2 million Millennials. Generation X, the smaller generation born between 1965 and 1980, is projected to remain the “middle child” of generations for a few more years. They are smaller than Millennials because the generational span of Gen X (16 years) is shorter than the Millennials (17 years). Also, the Gen Xers were born during a period when Americans were having fewer children than later decades. When Gen Xers were born, births averaged around 3.4 million per year, compared with the 3.9 million annual rate during the 1980s and 1990s when Millennials were born.

The oldest Gen Xer is now 50, but the Gen X population will still grow for a few more years. The Gen X population is projected to outnumber the Boomers in 2028 when there will be 64.6 million Gen Xers and 63.7 million Boomers. The Census Bureau projects that the Gen X population will peak at 65.8 million in 2018. Baby Boomers, who have always had an outsized presence compared with other generations, peaked at 78.8 million in 1999. There were an estimated 74.9 million Boomers in 2015, and by midcentury, the Boomer population will dwindle to 16.6 million.

These trends reflect broader changes in how Americans view work and family, with more young women delaying marriage and having children to focus on education and career. The share of young women 25 to 34 who opted to forgo outside employment in favor of managing a household plunged from 43% in 1975 to just 14% last year, according to the Census Bureau. This trend is part of a long-running trend of higher educational attainment for women but also a reflection of changing attitudes among Americans.

A young woman who livestreamed the beating and racial taunting of a man on Facebook has been arrested along with three others in connection with the brutal attack, Chicago police said. The disturbing 30-minute video shows a man tied up and his mouth covered, cowering in a room as his attackers laugh and shout racial slurs, kick and punch him, and even cut into his scalp with a knife, leaving a bald patch. The victim, an 18-year-old with special needs, was found wandering a Chicago street in a state of crisis on Tuesday afternoon. He was so traumatized that it took most of the night for him to calm down enough to talk to police. The suspects, two men and two women, all 18, are in custody awaiting formal charges, which are expected to be filed Thursday. Hate crime charges are under consideration due to the racial disparity between the victim and the attackers. The victim's parents reported him missing on Monday after not hearing from him since Saturday, when he was dropped off at a McDonald's in the Chicago suburb of Streamwood. After discovering a Facebook video depicting the victim being verbally and physically abused, Streamwood investigators contacted Chicago police, who found the missing man on Tuesday. The suspects are accused of kidnapping the victim, who might have been with them for at least 24 hours. The attack involved a play fight that escalated, leading to the victim being tied up in a corner for four to five hours. The victim's parents received threatening text messages from people claiming to be holding him captive. When a downstairs neighbor threatened to call 911, the suspects kicked in her door and stole something, giving the victim the opportunity to escape. Police found the victim wandering on Lexington, bloodied and battered, and determined he had been reported missing two days earlier. The victim is now at home and expected to recover, though his family is seeking privacy as they cope. The attack, which had political and racial connotations, sent shockwaves across the nation and was addressed at the White House press briefing. Chicago police superintendent Eddie Johnson emphasized that such actions are reprehensible and have no place in the city.

The weight gain experienced by men after becoming fathers for the first time, whether they live with their children or not, has been quantified in a large, long-term study. Published in the American Journal of Men's Health, the study tracked over 10,000 men from adolescence to young adulthood, revealing that the typical 6-foot-tall man who becomes a first-time father gains an average of about 4.4 pounds, while a 6-foot-tall father who does not live with his child gains about 3.3 pounds. This translates to a 2.6 percent rise in BMI for resident fathers and a 2 percent increase for non-resident fathers. In contrast, non-fathers in the same age group tend to lose weight. The study controlled for factors such as age, race, education, income, daily activity, screen time, and marriage status, highlighting that the fatherhood weight gain is in addition to the increase resulting from marriage.

Lead author Dr. Craig Garfield, an associate professor of pediatrics and medical social sciences at Northwestern University, notes that this weight gain can have significant health implications. "The more weight the fathers gain and the higher their BMI, the greater risk they have for developing heart disease, diabetes, and cancer," he explains. The weight gain may stem from lifestyle changes and shifts in eating habits, such as increased consumption of high-calorie foods and less time dedicated to exercise. Garfield's personal experience includes finishing his children's leftover cheese pizza, a common scenario among new fathers.

The study, which followed participants for up to 20 years, measured BMI at four different time points: early adolescence, later adolescence, mid-20s, and early 30s. Each participant was categorized as a non-father, resident father, or non-resident father, and their BMI was averaged across these time points to determine the impact of fatherhood on weight. The findings suggest that pediatricians, who often see new fathers accompanying their children for medical visits, are in a unique position to counsel them on maintaining their health. Many new fathers, Garfield notes, may not prioritize their own health care, seeing doctors only when their children need medical attention.

Garfield's previous research indicated that new fathers experience an increase in depression symptoms during the early years after their child's birth. "We now realize the transition to fatherhood is an important developmental life stage for men's health," he states. "It's a magical moment where so many things change in a man's life, and now the medical field needs to think about how to help these men of child-rearing age who often don't come to the doctor's office for themselves."

The study underscores the importance of addressing the health needs of new fathers, who are often overlooked in health care systems. Garfield suggests that pediatricians can play a crucial role in providing nutritional counseling and mental health education to new fathers, helping them manage their weight and overall health during this critical period.

The Treasury Inspector General for Tax Administration’s report on the IRS’s handling of 501(c)(4) applications reveals that the agency used inappropriate criteria to identify conservative groups for extra scrutiny, focusing on their names and policy positions rather than their activities. Approximately 15% of the flagged applications included terms like “Tea Party,” “patriots,” or “9/12.” Despite these criteria being deemed inappropriate, the report notes that 69% of the fully documented cases on the list were properly identified as having significant violations of tax policy. The document does not definitively prove that the IRS misled Congress, but it does highlight the agency’s ineffective management, which allowed the use of inappropriate criteria for over 18 months. The report also criticizes the IRS for requesting unnecessary and burdensome information, such as donor lists, which could have revealed confidential information. While the report does not find evidence of intentional bias, it does expose a series of delays and inefficiencies in the application process, with some groups waiting over a year for a decision. The IRS has agreed to implement seven of the nine recommendations made by the Inspector General, but the report raises questions about the consequences for the mid-level employees who created and then recreated the problematic criteria, despite management objections.

In the United States, nonfatal self-inflicted injuries requiring medical attention among youth have seen a concerning rise, particularly among adolescent girls. A study examining trends from 2001 to 2015 found that the overall age-adjusted rate of self-inflicted injuries treated in hospital emergency departments (EDs) increased by 5.7% annually after 2008, reaching 303.7 per 100,000 population in 2015. This trend was more pronounced among females, with a 18.8% annual increase among girls aged 10 to 14 years from 2009 to 2015, and a 7.2% increase among those aged 15 to 19 years during 2008-2015. Rates among males remained stable throughout the period.

Poisoning was the most common method of self-inflicted injury for females, with a 5.3% annual increase after 2007. Sharp object injuries, such as cutting, increased 7.1% annually for females from 2001 to 2015, while blunt object injuries remained stable during 2006-2015. The study, based on data from the National Electronic Injury Surveillance System—All Injury Program, only included ED cases, potentially underestimating the true extent of the issue. The findings align with rising suicide rates among youth, especially young girls, and highlight the need for comprehensive prevention strategies. These strategies should focus on improving access to care for suicidal youth, creating protective environments, promoting youth connectedness, teaching coping and problem-solving skills, and identifying and supporting at-risk youth within communities. The study underscores the importance of addressing the underlying factors contributing to the increase in self-harm among young people, including potential influences such as cyberbullying, substance abuse, and economic stress from the recent recession.

Peaceful protesters in Madison, Wisconsin, took to the streets following the fatal shooting of an unarmed 19-year-old black man, Tony Robinson, by a white police officer, Matt Kenny. The shooting occurred on Friday evening, and the city's police chief, Mike Koval, acknowledged the community's anger, assuring demonstrators that his department would protect their rights while urging restraint. The incident took place in a two-story gray house on Williamson Street, known as Willy Street, where Kenny, a 12-year veteran of the Madison Police Department, had entered the apartment after hearing a disturbance. Koval stated that Robinson was unarmed when shot, which would complicate the investigation and public acceptance. Kenny was injured during the altercation and placed on administrative leave pending an investigation by the state's Division of Criminal Investigation. The department did not have body cameras for the officer involved, which has raised questions about the reliability of the investigation.

Protests began the following day, with several dozen demonstrators holding signs and chanting "Black Lives Matter" before walking toward the neighborhood where the shooting occurred. The slogan was adopted by activists and protesters nationwide following high-profile deaths of unarmed black suspects at the hands of police officers, including the shooting of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri, and Eric Garner in New York City. The shooting came amid ongoing racial tensions and protests across the country. Koval struck a conciliatory tone, expressing understanding for the community's distrust and promising to defend and facilitate peaceful demonstrations. He also emphasized the need for non-destructive protests, as seen in Robinson's family's request for a peaceful response.

Robinson's family, including his mother, Andrea Irwin, expressed their shock and grief, stating that they had not had a chance to see their son's body. Koval visited Robinson's mother's house overnight and spoke with his grandparents, expressing sympathy for the family. The shooting raised questions about the integrity of police investigations, as highlighted by a 2014 Wisconsin law requiring outside agencies to investigate officer-involved deaths. Madison, with about 243,000 residents and 7% of them black, is the state capital and home to the University of Wisconsin's flagship campus. The city's police chief also noted that Kenny had been involved in a previous officer-involved shooting, where he was exonerated and later received a commendation. Kenny's background and the circumstances of the shooting have sparked discussions about the police department's handling of such incidents and the community's trust in law enforcement.

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump, speaking at a campaign rally in Franklin, Tennessee, on Saturday, defended Second Amendment rights and criticized "gun-free zones" in the wake of a shooting at Umpqua Community College in Oregon that left nine dead. Trump's comments represent his most extensive and emotionally charged discussion of firearms since launching his campaign in June. He highlighted his personal gun ownership, stating he has a license to carry a gun in New York, and emphasized self-defense as the primary rationale for gun rights. Trump argued that better mental health care could help curb future shootings, but he also warned that "no matter what you do, you will always have problems" due to "sick people." He criticized President Obama's response to the shooting, calling it "divisive." Trump also defended his new tax plan, claiming he could save significant costs in infrastructure projects, and pushed back against critics who suggested he would benefit financially from the plan. His positions on gun control have evolved, and he now aligns with the National Rifle Association's stance. Trump's comments came as he spoke to a crowd in Tennessee, where he noted the strong response to his remarks, indicating the importance of his message in gun-friendly states.

Anthony Weiner, the former New York congressman whose career and personal life were repeatedly derailed by his compulsive sexting, will appear in federal court on May 19, 2017, to face criminal charges. The saga of Weiner’s downfall began in 1998 when he was elected to Congress and continued through his resignation in 2011, his failed mayoral run in 2013, and his most recent scandal in 2016. In 2011, Weiner resigned after a lewd photograph of his crotch was leaked from his Twitter account. He later admitted to sending the lewd photo and lying about it, causing him to step down from Congress.

In 2013, Weiner launched a bid for New York City mayor but was forced to withdraw when it emerged that he had continued his sexting with women, using the pseudonym “Carlos Danger.” His political career took another hit in 2016 when a 15-year-old girl came forward, alleging that she had been exchanging sexually explicit messages with Weiner. The girl claimed that he had asked her to undress and engage in role-playing scenarios. This revelation led to the FBI seizing Weiner’s electronic devices, including his laptop, which contained emails between Weiner and his wife, Huma Abedin, a close aide to Hillary Clinton.

The investigation into Weiner’s communications with the 15-year-old girl and the discovery of the Clinton-Abedin emails prompted FBI Director James Comey to reopen an investigation into Clinton’s use of a private email server, which may have contributed to her loss in the 2016 election. Weiner pleaded guilty in May 2017 to a single count of transmitting obscene material to a minor, admitting to exchanging explicit messages and encouraging the teenager to engage in sexually explicit conduct. He tearfully apologized in court, acknowledging his “sickness” and the devastation his actions had caused.

Weiner’s plea deal included a sentence between 21 and 27 months in prison, with the possibility of early release for good behavior. His wife, Huma Abedin, separated from him in September 2016, following the revelation of his sexting with the 15-year-old girl. The case highlights the long-lasting impact of Weiner’s actions, from his political career to his personal life, and the broader implications for the 2016 presidential election.

Arizona State University (ASU) expelled the Tau Kappa Epsilon (TKE) fraternity on Thursday, just days after it hosted a party during the Martin Luther King Jr. holiday weekend that depicted racial stereotypes. The university permanently revoked the fraternity's recognition for violating the student code of conduct, which includes engaging in discriminatory activities, violating alcohol rules, breaching earlier disciplinary sanctions, and off-campus conduct posing a risk. The party involved students posing in basketball jerseys and flashing gang signs, drinking from watermelon cups, and using the hashtag #blackoutformlk. ASU President Michael Crow emphasized the university’s commitment to promoting a diverse and inclusive environment, stating that any violations by students may result in disciplinary action. The incident drew swift reaction from civil-rights leaders, who demanded that the university expel the fraternity, discipline students involved, and take steps to create a more accepting environment. This is the second time in less than a year that ASU has expelled a fraternity chapter, the first being Sigma Alpha Epsilon in June after a member nearly drank himself to death. The TKE fraternity had a relatively clean record until November 2012, when a group of its members attacked an African-American fraternity member, leading to aggravated assault charges. The national fraternity organization apologized for any offensive actions by its members and stated that it does not condone or support any actions that would be defined as racist, discriminatory, and/or offensive.

In the 1990s, North Korea released a large group of prisoners from its secret labor camps, but these were not criminals or political enemies. They were, as a defector stated, the grandchildren and great-grandchildren of "landlords, capitalists, collaborators with the Japanese colonial government, and other people with bad family background." These individuals were imprisoned for generations, with some still held in camps today. The regime's harshness and evil nature are so extreme that they defy imagination, and stories of the prison camps are hard to absorb. Many former prisoners, who were "free" but had nowhere to live, stayed in the same prison barracks. Others, possibly tens of thousands, may have died of starvation. The North Korean government has never acknowledged the existence of these camps, and information about them is scarce. Organizations like the Committee for Human Rights in North Korea use satellite photographs and defectors' testimonies to uncover the truth. Escapees often take years to reach South Korea, enduring beatings, rape, and starvation. The harsh reality of the regime's practices is overshadowed by the comedic portrayal of Kim Jong-un in films like The Interview, which only adds to the challenge of addressing the severe human rights abuses.

A 23-year-old Mexican immigrant, Daniel Ramirez Medina, who had been granted a work permit under the Obama administration’s Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, was arrested by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents in Seattle, Washington. This arrest, which took place during a raid targeting his father, has raised concerns among immigrant rights groups and lawmakers that the Trump administration may be targeting DACA recipients. Medina, who has no criminal record, was detained despite his legal status under DACA, which shields young immigrants brought to the U.S. illegally as children from deportation. His attorneys argue that his detention violates his constitutional rights and seek his immediate release. The case has sparked debates about the future of DACA recipients under the new administration. ICE officials claim that Medina admitted to being a gang member, but his attorneys deny this and say he was pressured to falsely admit to gang affiliation. The detention of Medina, who has a three-year-old son, has led to calls for a bond hearing and a review of the administration’s stance on DACA. The incident has also prompted Seattle Mayor Ed Murray and Councilmember M. Lorena González to reaffirm the city’s sanctuary policies and demand details about the arrest. The lawsuit filed by Medina’s attorneys seeks to bar ICE from further actions against him and highlights the potential for broader immigration enforcement under the Trump administration. The case has drawn attention from national leaders, including House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi and Senator Maria Cantwell, who have called for an investigation into the incident.

In 1773, a group of Massachusetts colonists, disguised as Mohawk Indians, staged a midnight raid on three British tea ships in Boston Harbor, dumping 342 chests of tea into the water. This event, known as the Boston Tea Party, was a protest against the British Parliament’s Tea Act of 1773, which aimed to save the East India Company by lowering its tea tax and granting it a near-monopoly on the American tea trade. The act was seen as an example of British taxation tyranny, and the colonists demanded the return of the tea to England. When Governor Thomas Hutchinson refused, Samuel Adams organized the raid with about 60 members of the Sons of Liberty. The dumped tea was valued at approximately $18,000. The British Parliament, angered by the destruction of property, enacted the Coercive Acts, or Intolerable Acts, in 1774. These acts included closing Boston to merchant shipping, establishing formal British military rule in Massachusetts, making British officials immune to criminal prosecution in America, and requiring colonists to house British troops. In response, the colonists called the first Continental Congress to consider a united American resistance to British rule.

Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz remains optimistic about the company's future growth in China despite the country's slowing economy. In an interview with CNN in Shanghai, Schultz emphasized that Starbucks plans to open more than one new store per day for the next five years in China, aiming to reach nearly 5,000 stores by 2021. This ambitious expansion strategy underscores Starbucks' long-term commitment to the Chinese market, which has evolved significantly since the company's first store opened 17 years ago. Schultz highlighted the early challenges of educating Chinese consumers about coffee culture, noting that the business initially struggled to turn a profit. However, the company's persistence paid off, as today, the majority of Starbucks' customers in China are local residents rather than expatriates or tourists.

Schultz's confidence in Starbucks' future in China is bolstered by the strong performance of the company's operations in the country over the past five years. He attributes this success to significant investments in people and systems, which have positioned Starbucks to capitalize on the growing demand for high-quality coffee and tea in China. The CEO also addressed concerns about potential competition from other international brands, such as KFC and McDonald's, which are facing challenges in the Chinese market. Schultz emphasized that Starbucks' model, which relies on local ownership and management, is well-suited to the Chinese business environment and provides a sustainable path for future growth.

Despite the economic headwinds, Schultz remains focused on maintaining Starbucks' reputation as a socially responsible and customer-centric brand. He highlighted the company's efforts to integrate local communities through initiatives like the "Race Together" campaign and the "Come Together" campaign, which aimed to foster dialogue on social issues. These efforts, combined with the company's commitment to innovation in mobile and digital technologies, position Starbucks to continue leading the coffee industry in China and potentially beyond.

Schultz's long-term vision for Starbucks in China is rooted in the belief that the market is still in its early stages of development. He sees the potential for China to eventually surpass the United States as Starbucks' largest market, driven by the increasing affluence of the Chinese consumer base and the growing demand for high-quality, specialized coffee experiences. As the company continues to navigate the complexities of the Chinese market, Schultz remains confident that Starbucks' strategic investments and commitment to local operations will ensure the company's continued success and growth in the years to come.

The debate over 11-year-old Barron Trump's casual attire during public appearances has once again sparked controversy, with conservative media outlets and social media users criticizing his style. Barron, the only child of President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump, often appears in t-shirts, khaki shorts, and loafers when joining his parents for public events, despite the fact that the president and first lady always dress in their finest attire. A recent Daily Caller article criticized Barron, stating that he should dress more appropriately for his father’s position. However, political figures and celebrities have come to Barron’s defense, urging the media to respect his privacy and allowing him to be a normal child. Former First Daughter Chelsea Clinton tweeted, "It’s high time the media & everyone leave Barron Trump alone & let him have the private childhood he deserves." First Lady Melania Trump also thanked Clinton for supporting Barron, tweeting, "so important to support all of our children in being themselves! #StopChildhoodBullying." The controversy has continued, with some users defending Barron’s outfit and others questioning why his clothing choices are being scrutinized. The White House has also asked the media to give Barron privacy, stating, "He is a minor child and deserves every opportunity to have a private childhood." The ongoing debate highlights the challenges faced by the Trump family in balancing public scrutiny with the desire to protect their son’s childhood.

NASCAR has issued a statement asking its fans to refrain from displaying the Confederate flag at its upcoming events, including the Coke Zero 400 at Daytona International Speedway. The statement, signed by 30 tracks, aims to create a more inclusive and welcoming atmosphere for all attendees. NASCAR Chairman Brian France had previously expressed a desire to eliminate the Confederate flag from its events. Daytona International Speedway is offering a flag exchange program, allowing fans to trade their Confederate flags for American flags. This move comes after NASCAR supported South Carolina Governor Nikki Haley's call to remove the Confederate flag from the state's Capitol grounds. While fans are still allowed to bring Confederate flags to the races, NASCAR is emphasizing the importance of mutual respect and a welcoming environment. The statement also highlights NASCAR's commitment to providing a fan-friendly experience and avoiding offensive symbols. The flag exchange program at Daytona is a practical step to align with NASCAR's stance, though its effectiveness in curbing the display of Confederate flags remains to be seen.

Three children in Salinas, California, were found severely abused and neglected in their home by their mothers, Eraca Dawn Craig, 31, and Christian Jessica Deanda, 44, who are domestic partners. The children, ages 3, 5, and 8, were discovered on March 14 during a welfare check, with signs of starvation, malnutrition, and physical abuse. The 8-year-old girl was reportedly chained to the wall to prevent her from obtaining food, and the other children showed signs of bruising and emotional distress. The girls were arrested on multiple felony charges of child cruelty, false imprisonment, and other related offenses. The home was described as cluttered and dirty, with little food available. The children were taken into protective custody, and the 8-year-old girl was hospitalized for about five days. The women, who have no criminal records in Monterey County, were arraigned on Tuesday and are scheduled for a preliminary hearing on March 28. The case has raised concerns about the conditions in which the children were living and the failure of authorities to intervene earlier.

Federal Court Justice Robin Camp, known as the "knees together judge" for his controversial comments during a 2014 sexual assault trial, has resigned following a recommendation from the Canadian Judicial Council to remove him from the bench. Camp, who was appointed to the Federal Court in 2015, faced criticism for his inappropriate remarks, including asking a 19-year-old homeless complainant why she couldn't keep her knees together and suggesting that pain and sex sometimes go together. The Canadian Judicial Council's report stated that Camp's conduct was "so manifestly and profoundly destructive of the concept of impartiality, integrity, and independence of the judicial role that public confidence is sufficiently undermined to render the judge incapable of executing the judicial office." Camp publicly apologized and underwent extensive counseling and training to address his comments. However, the council's majority found that his actions were so antithetical to contemporary judicial values that his resignation was necessary to maintain public confidence in the justice system. The case highlights the need for better training for judges in handling sexual assault cases, with the federal government considering mandatory training. Camp's resignation marks the third time in Canadian history that a judge has been recommended for removal by the judicial council, with both previous cases involving judges who resigned without parliamentary approval.

Three novels, three films, and three marriages on the brink of collapse—such is the premise of "Gone Girl," "The Two Faces of January," and "The Blue Room." David Fincher's "Gone Girl," adapted from Gillian Flynn's novel, delves into the complex relationship between Nick (Ben Affleck) and Amy Dunne (Rosamund Pike), a marriage that begins to unravel on their fifth anniversary.
