Nick, a bar owner with his twin sister Margo (Carrie Coon), returns home to find his wife missing and the house in disarray. Detective Boney (Kim Dickens) and Tanner Bolt (Tyler Perry), the defense attorney, become central figures in the unfolding mystery. Amy's narration, interspersed with diary entries and police inquiries, reveals a marriage fraught with secrets and lies. The film's narrative structure, shifting between present and past, keeps the audience guessing, mirroring the complexity of the characters' relationships.

Nick, portrayed by Ben Affleck, is a relatable but flawed character, struggling to navigate the media frenzy that ensues after his wife's disappearance. His initial affability and desire to please contrast sharply with his perceived lack of intelligence, a role that Affleck handles with nuance. Rosamund Pike, in her most challenging role to date, brings a chilling intensity to Amy, a woman who is both victim and perpetrator. Pike's performance is a standout, making Amy's character both sympathetic and unsettling. The supporting cast, including Tyler Perry as the unflappable Tanner Bolt and Carrie Coon as the supportive yet wounded Margo, adds depth to the narrative.

Fincher's direction is meticulous, with Trent Reznor and Atticus Ross's score adding a layer of tension that underscores the film's psychological thriller elements. The cinematography, by Jeff Cronenweth, and editing, by Jeff Baxter, create a visual narrative that enhances the film's suspense. However, the film's final 20 minutes veer off course, losing the coherence and intelligence that defined the first two hours. The narrative's logic is compromised, and the film's cleverness becomes false, detracting from the overall experience.

"The Two Faces of January," based on Patricia Highsmith's novel, and "The Blue Room," adapted from Georges Simenon's work, offer a different perspective on marital discord. "The Two Faces of January" stars Sigourney Weaver and Chris Evans, exploring the complexities of a woman's life after her husband's disappearance. "The Blue Room" features a French setting and a plot involving a murder and a family's secrets. Both films, while well-acted and directed, lack the psychological depth and narrative complexity of "Gone Girl."

In conclusion, "Gone Girl" stands out among the three films, thanks to its intricate narrative, strong performances, and David Fincher's masterful direction. However, the film's final act, while ambitious, fails to live up to the promise set by its earlier sections. The film's exploration of media manipulation and the blurred lines between truth and perception make it a thought-provoking watch, despite its flaws.

Scientists in East Africa are planning to use trained African giant pouched rats to detect tuberculosis among prison inmates in Tanzania and Mozambique, aiming to improve screening for the highly contagious disease. These rats, known for their ability to sniff out landmines, are now being trained to detect TB in sputum samples. Tuberculosis is the leading cause of death from an infectious disease, with around 9 million new cases and 2 million deaths annually worldwide, according to the World Health Organization. In Tanzania, TB rates are 10 times higher in prisons than in the general population, making mass screening challenging due to limited resources and awareness. APOPO, a Belgian non-governmental organization, plans to recruit and train more rats to screen prison inmates, expecting the process to be faster and more cost-effective than existing methods. The rats can screen 100 samples in 20 minutes, costing as little as 20 US cents, compared to four days for a laboratory technician. APOPO's current programs have screened over 340,000 TB samples, halting over 36,000 infections, and increasing detection rates by over 40 percent in several clinics. The rats are rigorously trained from a young age, socialized with people, and rewarded for recognizing TB in samples. They can detect TB with near-perfect accuracy but cannot distinguish between drug-resistant and non-resistant strains. The plan aims to expand to other high-risk settings, including shantytowns and factories, to improve and save lives globally.

The crash of a Trigana Air Service passenger plane in Indonesia's Papua province has claimed the lives of all 54 people on board, including four postal workers escorting government aid money. The plane, an ATR42-300 twin turboprop, was flying from Jayapura to Oksibil when it lost contact with air traffic control on Sunday. Rescuers reached the crash site two days later, finding the plane had crashed into a mountain, with the bodies of all passengers and crew burned beyond recognition. The flight data recorder and cockpit voice recorder, known as the "black boxes," were recovered in good condition and will be analyzed to determine the cause of the crash. The plane was carrying approximately $470,000 in cash intended for poor families in remote areas, as part of a government assistance program. Five members of the Bintang Highlands district parliament and government officials were also on board. The rugged terrain and bad weather hampered rescue efforts, with helicopters and ground teams finally reaching the site on Tuesday. The National Search and Rescue Agency chief, Henry Bambang Soelistyo, stated that all 54 bodies would be taken to Jayapura for identification. Trigana Air Service, which began operations in 1991, has a history of safety issues, having had 14 serious incidents and written off 10 aircraft since its inception. The airline remains on a European Union blacklist due to safety concerns. The incident is the latest in a series of aviation disasters in Indonesia, following the December crash of an AirAsia flight in the Java Sea, which killed all 162 people on board, and the June crash of a military transport plane that killed over 100 people. Indonesia's aviation safety record has been criticized, with the country scoring poorly in a 2014 safety audit by the U.N. aviation agency. The Ministry of Transportation is understaffed, making it difficult to manage the rapid expansion of air travel in the country.

The Democratic National Convention on Tuesday night exceeded expectations for energy and enthusiasm, according to various media outlets. CNN's David Gergen noted the palpable excitement in the hall was more pronounced than at the Republican convention. Politico's Dylan Byers and Alexander Burns highlighted the stark contrast in energy levels, with the Democratic convention appearing more vibrant and engaging compared to the previous Republican convention. BuzzFeed's Ben Smith observed that the Democratic convention's appeal extended beyond its intended TV audience, while The Atlantic's Garance Franke-Ruta predicted a more passionate atmosphere. CNN's Peter Hamby reported that Republican delegates expressed jealousy over the DNC's excitement, and NBC's Chuck Todd emphasized the clear difference in the audience's support for President Obama versus Romney. The Washington Post's Jonathan Capehart and Salon's Irin Carmon also noted the increased energy, with Carmon recalling the contrast to the tepid response during the 2008 convention. Michelle Obama's speech, intended to highlight the differences between her husband and his Republican opponent, generated significant social media engagement, with her tweet about the presidency revealing one's true character garnering widespread attention. The Democratic convention's first night saw over 3 million tweets, nearly matching the total from the previous week's Republican convention.

The Angry Birds Movie soared to the top of the box office this weekend, raking in $39 million and taking the No. 1 spot, reports comScore. The family comedy, budgeted at $73 million, is the third-best animated debut of the year, behind Zootopia and Kung Fu Panda 3. Despite mixed reviews (42% positive on RottenTomatoes), audiences (61% liked it) embraced the film. Captain America: Civil War, starring Chris Evans and Robert Downey Jr., dropped to No. 2, earning $33.1 million and bringing its domestic total to $347.4 million. Neighbors 2: Sorority Rising, with Seth Rogen and Rose Byrne, opened in third place with $21.8 million. The R-rated comedy, however, underperformed its predecessor, which opened with $49 million in 2014. The Nice Guys, directed by Shane Black, debuted in fourth place with $11.3 million, receiving strong critical acclaim (90% positive) and audience approval (84%). Disney's live-action adaptation of The Jungle Book rounded out the top five with $11 million, adding to its impressive $327.5 million domestic total since its release last month.

The latest iPad, unveiled by Apple, offers a significant upgrade in display quality and speed, making it a compelling choice for consumers, according to tech analyst Walt Mossberg. The new iPad boasts a stunning "retina" display, with four times the number of pixels compared to its predecessor, the iPad 2. This results in sharper text and more vivid images, enhancing the overall user experience. Additionally, the device supports 4G LTE cellular data, providing faster internet speeds, similar to a high-speed home connection. The new iPad also includes a 5-megapixel rear camera, which takes better photos and videos than the previous model, and a dictation feature that allows users to type using their voice. Despite these improvements, the new iPad retains the same price point as the iPad 2, making it an attractive option for those who already own an iPad 2. For new buyers, the iPad remains the best choice in a general-purpose tablet, offering a vast selection of apps and content. However, the new iPad's increased weight and thickness are trade-offs for the enhanced features. The iPad 2 is also available at a reduced price, making it a more affordable option for those who do not need the latest features. Overall, the new iPad solidifies Apple's position as the leader in the tablet market, providing a superior user experience with its latest advancements.

An Indian public official, A.K. Verma, was dismissed from his job after being absent from duty for 25 years, marking a rare instance of accountability in the country’s notoriously work-shy bureaucracy. Verma, an assistant executive engineer with the Central Public Works Department (CPWD), had gone on earned leave in December 1990 and never returned to work. Despite numerous extensions of his leave being denied, Verma continued to defy directions to report to his post. In September 1992, an inquiry was initiated against him for "wilful absence from duty," but due to his non-cooperation, the case was delayed for 22 years, with a fresh charge sheet issued in 2005. The inquiry report, submitted in July 2007, was accepted by the then Minister of Urban Development, but no further action was taken. 

Urban Development Minister M.Venkaiah Naidu, upon assuming office, called for a review of pending vigilance and disciplinary cases to ensure expeditious action. He took a serious view of the inaction since 2007 and directed officials to fix responsibility for the delay. Verma’s dismissal was seen as a step towards streamlining the functioning of CPWD and ensuring accountability. 

India’s labor laws, which are among the most restrictive in the world, make it challenging to terminate employment for reasons other than criminal misconduct. However, the government has taken steps to address this issue, with states like Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh changing laws to facilitate easier hiring and firing. Prime Minister Narendra Modi has also taken measures to curb absenteeism, mandating fingerprint attendance checks for New Delhi bureaucrats, with the results publicly available online. 

Verma’s case highlights the long-standing issue of chronic absenteeism in India’s bureaucracy, which has been rated as the worst among major Asian countries in a 2012 survey by the Hong Kong-based Political and Economic Risk consultancy. Modi’s surprise visits to government offices following his election victory in 2014 reportedly led to a significant rise in attendance levels among civil servants. The dismissal of Verma, while a rare occurrence, underscores the government’s commitment to addressing systemic issues within the public sector.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un made a series of statements in a New Year's Day speech, balancing threats and offers of dialogue. In the speech, broadcast nationally, Kim emphasized the operational deployment of nuclear warheads and missiles, stating that the entire United States was within the range of North Korean nuclear weapons. "The whole territory of the U.S. is within the range of our nuclear strike and a nuclear button is always on the desk of my office," he said, indicating that the rhetoric of nuclear capability is a reality. However, Kim also offered a potential olive branch to South Korea, suggesting openness to dialogue and considering sending a delegation to the upcoming Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang. "North Korea's participation in the Winter Games will be a good opportunity to show unity of the people, and we wish the Games will be a success," he said, adding that officials from both Koreas may urgently meet to discuss the possibility. Kim's speech came amid increased international criticism and sanctions over North Korea's nuclear weapons program and repeated missile tests. While his language against the U.S. remained tough, Kim did not employ his typically antagonistic tone when speaking about his southern neighbor, indicating a shift in rhetoric. The South Korean president's office stated their willingness to talk with North Korea at any time and place, expressing hope for improved relations and a reduction in tensions on the Korean peninsula. Analysts noted that Kim's conciliatory tone towards South Korea could be an attempt to create an estrangement between South Korea and the U.S., while also positioning his regime as moving towards its neighbors. The potential participation of North Korea in the Olympics was seen as a strategic move, aiming to showcase unity and improve relations, despite the ongoing nuclear tensions.

Environmental activists have long criticized bottled water for its perceived wastefulness, often citing the billions of plastic bottles discarded annually. However, the International Bottled Water Association (IBWA) has recently conducted its first comprehensive study to quantify the water usage involved in producing bottled water. The study reveals that for North American companies, it takes approximately 1.39 liters of water to produce one liter of bottled water, which is less than the global average for other beverages such as soda (2.02 liters) and beer (4 liters). This finding has been used by the IBWA to argue that bottled water is more efficient in terms of water use compared to other packaged drinks. Chris Hogan, a spokesman for the IBWA, asserts that bottled water products are "extremely efficient in terms of water use compared to some other packaged beverages."

Despite this, water activists maintain that the study does not provide a complete picture of the industry's water usage. Ertug Ercin from the Water Footprint Network emphasizes the importance of considering the entire water footprint, which includes the water used in the supply chain, such as the production of packaging materials. Ercin notes that the water used for packaging can be significantly higher, potentially up to six or seven times the volume of water in the bottle itself. This includes the water required to extract oil for plastic production and the water needed for paper manufacturing. The IBWA's study, while highlighting the efficiency of bottled water in comparison to other beverages, does not account for the water used in the production of packaging materials. This omission has led some to argue that the industry needs to adopt a more holistic approach to water footprint analysis to identify opportunities for conservation.

The IBWA acknowledges that the study does not cover the entire water footprint, including packaging, but contends that it is challenging to determine where to draw the line. Some companies claim they have already reached their efficiency limits, but the IBWA and other organizations continue to push for greater water conservation efforts. Water is described as the "lifeblood of the industry," and companies are motivated to maintain efficiency to ensure their sustainability.

Jennifer Westfeldt, star of "Friends With Kids," is set to perform in a new play called "The Power of Duff" at Vassar's Powerhouse Theater in upstate Poughkeepsie. The venue, known for its summer-camp atmosphere, brings back memories of Westfeldt's own experience. At 13, she was kicked out of summer camp for going out with her boyfriend to get pizza. However, she now jokes that she's of age and no longer has to worry about such incidents. Westfeldt's longtime boyfriend, Jon Hamm, has visited the campus, but without any issues. Meanwhile, in Warsaw, Poland, local officials are facing pressure to cancel Madonna's upcoming MDNA tour concert, scheduled for August 1, due to its proximity to the city's World War II remembrance day. A group called the Youth Crusade has launched an online petition, arguing that Madonna's performances are disrespectful and offensive, particularly her controversial stage antics that have included flashing and burning crosses. The controversy has not only affected Madonna's reputation but also her plans for a 20-year hiatus from Australia, where she canceled her first tour in 2014. Despite the challenges, Madonna's MDNA tour has been a financial success, with ticket prices ranging from $45 to $600. However, the London leg of her tour faced criticism from fans who left the Hyde Park concert early, citing poor sound quality, rain, and a lack of classic hits. Despite these setbacks, Madonna's performances have included provocative elements such as stripping down to a sheer bra and black thong, and she has also incorporated other artists' songs into her setlist, including Lady Gaga's "Born This Way."

The deployment of the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system in South Korea has sparked controversy and backlash, particularly from China, following North Korea's recent ballistic missile launches. On Tuesday, U.S. and South Korean militaries confirmed that THAAD launchers and other essential equipment had arrived in South Korea, marking the beginning of the system's installation. The THAAD system is designed to intercept and destroy short and medium-range ballistic missiles during their terminal phase of flight, according to a statement from the U.S. military. Admiral Harry Harris, head of the U.S. Pacific Command, stated that North Korea's ongoing provocative actions, including the recent missile launches, underscore the prudence of deploying THAAD to South Korea. However, the deployment has not been without opposition. South Korean liberals have voiced concerns that the security benefits of THAAD could be offset by deteriorating relations with China and Russia. Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Geng Shuang warned that China would take "necessary measures" to protect its security interests and urged the U.S. and South Korea to halt the deployment. The controversy has extended to the retail sector, with China's Global Times criticizing South Korea's decision to allow Lotte, a major South Korean retailer, to host one of the THAAD sites. As a result, several of Lotte's stores in China have been abruptly closed. Meanwhile, North Korea's state media reported that leader Kim Jong Un supervised a ballistic rocket launching drill, which involved artillery units targeting "U.S. imperialist aggressor forces in Japan." The North Korean military has expressed readiness to respond to any threats, emphasizing the deployment of its Hwasong artillery, which can carry nuclear warheads. South Korean officials speculate that the THAAD system could be operational as early as April, though the exact timeline remains uncertain. The deployment of THAAD in South Korea continues to strain regional relations and heighten tensions, as both China and North Korea view the system as a potential threat to their security.

A new study published in the Journal of the National Cancer Institute suggests that drinking alcohol even before a woman's first pregnancy can increase her risk of breast cancer and benign breast disease (BBD), a risk factor for breast cancer. Researchers analyzed data from over 91,000 women in the Nurses' Health Study II who had no history of cancer. They found that drinking one alcoholic drink per day between the onset of menstruation and first pregnancy increased the risk of breast cancer by 11% and BBD by about 16% compared to nondrinkers. The risk increased with higher alcohol consumption. The study also noted that drinking after the first pregnancy was linked to breast cancer but not BBD. The researchers suggest that breast tissues are particularly susceptible to environmental exposures during this period, making them more vulnerable to cancer. The findings emphasize the importance of reducing alcohol intake, especially before the first pregnancy, to lower breast cancer risk. Experts advise that while the increased risk is significant, it is crucial to consider the baseline risk of breast cancer, which is about 12% for women. The study highlights the need for moderation and calls for further research to understand the mechanisms linking alcohol consumption and breast cancer.

During a campaign rally in North Dakota, President Donald Trump emphasized the significance of maintaining the Republican majority in the Senate, particularly in light of Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy's retirement. Trump highlighted the importance of Senate control, stating, "Justice Kennedy's retirement makes the issue of Senate control one of the vital issues of our time — the most important thing we can do." The rally was held to support Republican Rep. Kevin Cramer, who is challenging Democratic Sen. Heidi Heitkamp in a key election year race. Heitkamp, a Democrat, is one of several red-state Democrats facing re-election in 2018, and Trump's comments suggest that her vote on any future Supreme Court nominee could be pivotal. Trump claimed that Heitkamp would oppose any nominee the Republican Party supports, saying, "Heidi will vote no to any pick we make for the Supreme Court. She will be told to do so." Heitkamp, however, pushed back against Trump's characterization, stating, "Anytime the president comes to North Dakota, that's a good thing for our state. While we saw election-year politics today, I'm always willing to work with the president if he's helping North Dakota — and if he's not, I'll speak up. I don't answer to a political party or president, I only answer to North Dakotans, who deserve an independent voice in the Senate." Trump's comments came as Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell indicated his intention to hold a vote on Kennedy's replacement before the 2018 midterms, despite Democratic criticism of this approach. The retirement of Kennedy, who served for 30 years and was known as a swing vote, creates an opportunity for the Trump administration to appoint a more conservative justice, potentially shifting the balance of the court. Trump expressed his intention to select a nominee who would serve for decades, stating, "We need intellect, we need so many things. There is so many elements that goes into the making of a great justice of the Supreme Court." The list of potential nominees includes several judges from conservative circuits, raising concerns among Democrats about the potential impact on issues such as abortion rights and the balance of power on the court.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation is investigating an incident that the Democratic National Committee (DNC) initially thought was a sophisticated attempt to hack into its voter database. The DNC contacted the FBI on Tuesday after being alerted by a cloud service provider and a security research firm that a fake login page had been created, designed to gather usernames and passwords for the party's database. The DNC and the companies involved believe they thwarted a potential attack. The fraudulent page was crafted to mimic the access page used by Democratic Party officials and campaigns to log into a service called VoteBuilder, which hosts the database. The incident highlights ongoing threats as the country heads into midterm elections, with the DNC's chief security officer, Bob Lord, emphasizing the need for vigilance. Lord called the voter file the party's most sensitive information. The combination of this attack on the DNC, continued influence operations by Russia and others through social media, and efforts to breach think tanks underscores that the cyber age has fundamentally changed elections. Cybersecurity experts, such as Rob Joyce, the former White House cybersecurity coordinator, warn that the focus has shifted from stealing secrets to imposing national power. Political groups and government organizations are on high alert for new hacks and foreign meddling. Microsoft has reported that hackers tied to Russian intelligence targeted the Senate and conservative think tanks in the United States by creating fake websites. Additionally, Facebook has identified a political influence campaign aimed at potentially disrupting the midterms and has uncovered other disinformation efforts targeting people worldwide. The incident also prompted the DNC to reverse its initial stance, stating that what it had feared was a sophisticated hack was, in fact, an unauthorized "simulated phishing test."

A tourist boat packed with approximately 170 passengers capsized on a reservoir near Medellin, Colombia, on Sunday, leading to nine deaths and 28 people still missing, according to officials. The four-story El Almirante ferry, adorned in turquoise and yellow, was reportedly overcrowded and lacked life vests for its passengers. Dramatic videos circulating on social media depict the vessel rocking violently as people scrambled to safety from the fourth-floor roof. "Those on the first and second floors sank immediately," a survivor recounted to Teleantioquia, emphasizing the urgency of the situation. Rescuers, including firefighters and air force pilots, rushed to the scene, pulling people from the sinking vessel and preventing a potentially more catastrophic outcome. Preliminary reports indicate that 99 people were rescued, and around 40 managed to find their way to shore, all in good condition. Authorities were uncertain about the exact number of people on board and requested that passengers or their loved ones report to a rescue center set up along the shore. Scuba divers were also called upon to assist in the search. The reservoir, surrounding the El Penol rock formation, is a popular weekend destination, particularly busy during the holiday weekend. The cause of the accident remains unclear, but it is suspected to be related to the boat being overloaded. The incident highlights ongoing concerns about maritime safety in Colombia, where such accidents are not uncommon.

The Occupy Wall Street movement's reach expanded to Oakland, where a general strike and port shutdown turned violent late Thursday. Demonstrators, including an Iraq War veteran injured in a clash with police, clashed with police in riot gear, leading to dozens of arrests and property damage. Protesters broke into a vacant building, shattered windows, and set fires, while police responded with tear gas and flash-bang grenades. At least four protesters were hospitalized, including one injured in a fight with an officer. The movement, which had been largely peaceful, saw a shift towards chaos and violence, with police citing the need to protect residents and property. Despite the violence, organizers viewed the port shutdown as a significant victory, highlighting the movement's broadening influence and the growing tensions between protesters and law enforcement.

Angel Gonzalez, 41, walked out of prison Tuesday evening after spending 20 years behind bars for a rape and abduction conviction that was thrown out Monday due to new DNA evidence. Gonzalez, who was originally from Mexico, had maintained his innocence for decades, and his case gained attention from the Innocence Project, which helped secure his release. The DNA tests revealed that the evidence matched profiles of two men, neither of whom was Gonzalez. Lake County prosecutors plan to exonerate Gonzalez and clear his conviction for the 1994 rape and abduction. However, Gonzalez still faced a property damage charge stemming from an incident in which he broke a sink while in solitary confinement. This charge was dismissed in Livingston County on Tuesday, allowing Gonzalez to be freed. Gonzalez's family expressed joy and relief, with his mother, Maria, and his brother, Saul, describing the long wait for justice. Gonzalez, who had been in prison for nearly half his life, was eager to reconnect with his family and resume his life. He had spent his time in prison educating himself and learning various skills, including electronics and mechanics. His release came as a surprise to many, including the victim, who was distraught to learn that prosecutors planned to clear Gonzalez. The exoneration marks a significant step in Lake County's efforts to reform its approach to DNA evidence and wrongful convictions.

A Russian man accused of the Salisbury nerve agent poisoning has been identified as a decorated military officer, Bellingcat and The Insider have revealed. Colonel Anatoliy Chepiga, who received the prestigious Hero of the Russian Federation award, was named as one of the suspects in the poisoning of Sergei and Yulia Skripal, and the death of British citizen Dawn Sturgess. Chepiga, born in 1979, served in Russia's far-eastern military command and was deployed to Chechnya three times. He was later assigned a false identity as Ruslan Boshirov and relocated to Moscow. The award, given by Russian President Vladimir Putin, suggests Chepiga's mission was likely related to operations in Ukraine. Bellingcat's investigation involved reverse image searches, contact with former military officers, and analysis of leaked Russian databases. The findings challenge President Putin's claim that Boshirov is a civilian, and highlight the extent of Russia's efforts to protect the identities of its operatives. The UK government has long accused Russia of involvement in the Salisbury attack, and this new information adds to the tension between the two nations.

The Fourth Kind, a re-enactment of alleged real events in Alaska, stars Milla Jovovich as a hypnotherapist investigating mysterious disappearances and alien abductions. Directed by Olatunde Osunsanmi, the film blends found-footage interviews with dramatized scenes, creating a mix of genuine scares and questionable storytelling. Jovovich's deadpan performance and the inclusion of Will Patton and Elias Koteas as hypnotherapy patients add depth to the narrative. Despite its premise, the movie's reliance on obvious horror tropes and its hybrid format often pulls the viewer out of the experience. However, Jovovich's acting and the film's occasional effective scares keep it engaging. Critics find the concept intriguing but ultimately flawed, with one reviewer suggesting it could have been more immersive as a mockumentary or thriller. The film's grade is a C, reflecting a balance between Jovovich's strong performance and the artificial nature of the footage.

Alabama State Senator Shadrack McGill's wife, Heather, has sparked controversy with a fiery Facebook post aimed at women allegedly soliciting her husband for inappropriate activities. The post, which garnered over 300 likes, warns multiple women, some of whom she claims are not real, to stop contacting her husband through the social media platform. She expresses concern over children potentially seeing such content and threatens to publicly name the women involved. Senator McGill, who was previously in the news for comparing abortion to the destruction of an eagle egg, claims his wife's frustrations stem from incidents during his last campaign, including unsolicited visits by strippers and hijacking of his Facebook page by women sending him explicit photos. He acknowledges his wife's wisdom and support, thanking her for addressing the issue. The senator suggests he might need to reconsider his own Facebook presence due to the moral implications. The post has sparked debate, with supporters praising Heather McGill for protecting her family and opponents criticizing her actions as overreaching and potentially harmful.

Ohio State quarterback Terrelle Pryor and four other Buckeyes—running back Dan Herron, wide receiver DeVier Posey, offensive lineman Mike Adams, and defensive end Solomon Thomas—will be suspended from the first five games of the 2011 season for NCAA violations, including selling championship rings, jerseys, and awards, and receiving improper benefits from a tattoo parlor. All will be eligible to play in the Sugar Bowl against Arkansas. Pryor must repay $2,500, while Adams, Herron, Posey, and Thomas owe between $1,000 and $1,505 to charity. Backup linebacker Jordan Whiting will miss one game and pay $150. Ohio State coach Jim Tressel expressed a "gut-wrenching feeling" and acknowledged the team's responsibility. The NCAA did not suspend the players for the Sugar Bowl due to a lack of adequate rules education during the violations. Ohio State will appeal the suspensions, citing mitigating circumstances.

Ariel Castro, a former school bus driver, was sentenced to life in prison plus 1,000 years for abducting and torturing three women in Cleveland for over a decade. The women, Amanda Berry, Gina DeJesus, and Michelle Knight, were held captive in a house on Seymour Avenue, where Castro subjected them to years of sexual and physical abuse. Castro lured the women into his car with the promise of a ride, and once inside, he chained them in the basement and sexually assaulted them. The women were starved, beaten, and forced to endure repeated pregnancies that Castro terminated by punching them in the stomach. One of the women, Michelle Knight, testified that Castro forced her to deliver his daughter on Christmas Day 2006, while simultaneously raping the woman who helped with the delivery. Castro's crimes were detailed in a diary kept by one of the women, which described their captivity as a "complete and comprehensive captivity," with forced sexual conduct, being locked in dark rooms, and anticipating the next session of abuse. The women were rescued after Amanda Berry kicked out a door panel on May 6, 2013, and Castro was arrested within hours. During the sentencing, Castro attempted to portray himself as remorseful, but his victims and law enforcement officials painted a picture of a remorseless, violent predator. The judge, Michael Russo, reminded Castro that he would never be released from incarceration during the period of his remaining natural life for any reason. The women's legal team and supporters expressed gratitude for the community's support and vowed to help the women recover from their traumatic experiences.

Osama bin Laden's youngest wife, Amal Ahmad Abdul Fateh, provided detailed testimony to Pakistani investigators about her husband's nine-year journey on the run in Pakistan, which spanned five safe houses and involved the birth of four children. Fateh's account, contained in a police report, reveals that the al-Qaeda leader moved among cities across Pakistan, evading detection by security services. The report, while containing some paraphrased details, highlights the challenges faced by Western intelligence in tracking Bin Laden. Fateh married Bin Laden in 2000, and after the 9/11 attacks, the family scattered, eventually settling in Swat, Haripur, and Abbottabad. In Abbottabad, Fateh gave birth to two children, Zainab in 2006 and Hussain in 2008. The youngest wife's testimony, along with that of the other two widows, is of significant interest to authorities, as they hold the key to understanding Bin Laden's movements and the support network that facilitated his prolonged stay in Pakistan. The three widows, currently under house arrest in Islamabad, are expected to face charges related to breaking Pakistani immigration laws, potentially leading to a five-year jail sentence. The case raises questions about the effectiveness of Pakistan's security apparatus and the extent of cooperation between the Pakistani government and the United States in tracking Bin Laden.

The average American woman now weighs 166.2 pounds, nearly identical to what the average American man weighed in the 1960s, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Over the same period, American men have gained nearly 30 pounds, from 166.3 pounds in the 1960s to 195.5 pounds today. This means that today's American man weighs almost as much as 1.5 American women from the 1960s. Both sexes have gained roughly an inch in height over the past 60 years, accounting for some of the weight gain. However, the primary factor in the weight increase is an overall increase in body fat, driven by three main factors: consuming less healthy food, eating more, and engaging in less physical activity.

A 2012 study published in the journal BMC Public Health ranked the United States as the third-heaviest country in the world, behind only the Pacific island nations of Tonga and Micronesia. The average American is 33 pounds heavier than the average Frenchman and 40 pounds heavier than the average Japanese citizen. In comparison, the average American is a whopping 70 pounds heavier than the average citizen of Bangladesh. To accumulate one ton of total mass, it would take 20 Bangladeshis but only 12.2 Americans.

The CDC data indicates that more than one-third (35.1%) of U.S. adults over the age of 20 are considered obese, while 69% of American adults are either overweight or obese. Additionally, over 1-in-5 U.S. children between the ages of 12-19 are considered obese, with 17.7% of kids ages 6-11 also weighing in at obesity levels. The study concludes that tackling population fatness may be critical to world food security and ecological sustainability. As with many global issues, the solutions start at home, particularly with individuals taking responsibility for their health and making healthier lifestyle choices.

The search for 5-year-old Noah Thomas, who was found dead in a septic tank in Dublin, Virginia, has shifted its focus to gathering facts and physical evidence, according to the Pulaski County Sheriff's Office. The body was discovered on Thursday, five days after Noah was last seen by his mother, who claims he was watching cartoons when she took a two-hour nap. While the autopsy has been completed, the cause of death is pending, and no timetable has been given for the release of the results. The sheriff's office is urging the public to come forward with any information or tips, but few details have emerged from the investigation so far. The FBI is providing forensic support, and authorities are not ruling out foul play, with some family members suspecting that someone may have intentionally placed Noah in the septic tank. The sheriff's office is also encouraging the public not to judge the parents, who are living through a nightmare. A candlelight vigil is planned to remember Noah's life, and the family is cooperating fully with the investigation. The search area has been expanded, and police are still canvassing a nearly 10-mile radius around the house, where Noah was found. The sheriff's office has offered a $5,000 reward for information leading to an arrest, and neighbors have noted that every home in the area has a septic tank, roughly four to five feet underground. The investigation is ongoing, and authorities are relying on the exact cause of death to better understand what happened to Noah.

These have been trying times for Siri, the iPhone 4S's voice-controlled personal assistant. Not only has she been fielding mundane questions from users, she has even assisted Santa in his duties. However, it seems Siri has finally reached her limit. During a demonstration at a Tesco store in the UK, 12-year-old Charlie Le Quesne picked up an iPhone 4S, and Siri's frustration boiled over. According to the Sun, the interaction went as follows: Le Quesne asked Siri, "How many people are there in the world?" and Siri responded with, "Shut the f*** up, you ugly t***." Le Quesne's mother, Kim, was taken aback by this outburst and reported it. She told the Sun, "I thought I must be hearing things. So we asked again and the same four-letter stuff blared out." The staff at Tesco suggested that someone might have entered a crude phrase as the user's name during the setup process, which could have triggered Siri's response. Tesco launched an investigation and sent the phone back to Apple for diagnosis. The incident raises questions about the potential for tampering and the source of the prank. This event highlights the unpredictable nature of Siri's responses and the need for more robust safeguards against such incidents.

Iraq's Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki secured unexpected support from the powerful Sadrists, a radical Shiite group led by Moqtada al-Sadr, potentially breaking a months-long political deadlock. This move, seen as a major comeback for the Sadrists, could complicate the situation further, as al-Maliki still needs more votes in the 325-member parliament to form a new government. The U.S. administration, which has long considered the Sadrists a threat, expressed concern over their influence. Al-Maliki's coalition now holds about 148 seats, just short of a majority. The Kurds, who hold 57 seats, could be the key to forming a government, but their support comes with conditions. Meanwhile, al-Maliki faces opposition from other Shiite groups and al-Sadr's followers, who have reservations about his leadership. The Sadrists' endorsement of al-Maliki marks a significant shift, aligning with his goal of preventing a descent into sectarian conflict, despite past enmity. This development could lead to a more inclusive government but also raises concerns about Iran's growing influence in Iraqi politics.

President Donald Trump sent a $25,000 personal check to the family of Army Cpl. Dillon Baldridge the same day The Washington Post reported that Trump had promised the soldier's father a personal donation during a June condolence call but never followed through, according to a White House official. Baldridge, 22, was killed in June by an Afghan police officer. "The check has been sent," Lindsay Walters, White House spokeswoman, told CNN on Wednesday. "It's disgusting that the media is taking something that should be recognized as a generous and sincere gesture, made privately by the President, and using it to advance the media's biased agenda." White House press secretary Sarah Sanders confirmed that it was a personal check from Trump. The timing of Trump's donation raised questions because the Post reported that the check had been "in the pipeline" since the President's conversation with the father. A White House spokesperson said the check had been "in the pipeline" since the President's conversation with the father and that the President had personally followed up several times to ensure the check was being sent. The spokesperson added that there was a substantial process involving multiple agencies anytime the President interacted with the public, especially when transmitting personal funds. Knowledge of Trump's pledge to Baldridge comes amid the ongoing controversy over how presidents handle condolence calls to families of those killed in action and Trump's feud with a Democratic congresswoman over his call with the widow of Sgt. La David Johnson, who was killed earlier this month in Niger. Trump called Myeshia Johnson on Tuesday and, according to Democratic Rep. Frederica Wilson, the President said that the serviceman killed "knew what he signed up for, but I guess it still hurt." Trump denied that he ever said that. "I didn't say what that congresswoman said. Didn't say it at all," Trump told reporters during a Wednesday meeting on tax reform in the Cabinet Room. "She knows it. And she now is not saying it. I did not say what she said." At the same time, the White House is dealing with Trump stating that President Barack Obama didn't call all the families of those killed during his presidency and suggesting that reporters ask his chief of staff, retired Gen. John Kelly, whether Obama called him after his son died in Afghanistan. Kelly's son Robert died when he stepped on a land mine in Afghanistan in 2010. Kelly, a retired four-star Marine general, was a lieutenant general at the time.

A Virginia Beach man is facing animal abuse charges after allegedly shooting and burying his 15-year-old dog, Allie, on the Oceanfront. Michael Whalen, who says Allie was his closest companion, described the night she had a severe seizure, making it impossible to get her to a hospital. Unable to bear the sight of her suffering, Whalen shot her with a small handgun, intending it to be a painless and instantaneous end. He buried Allie at 85th Street, but a resident found her, leading to his arrest. Whalen now faces charges of burying trash and animal cruelty. He claims he acted out of love and necessity, arguing that a gunshot is a form of euthanasia. However, a local veterinarian explained that current guidelines do not consider a gunshot a proper method of euthanasia. Whalen hopes his case will bring attention to the rights of pet owners to properly euthanize their animals. His court date is set for June, and he is speaking out to set the record straight, emphasizing his love for Allie and his duty to end her suffering.

In the wake of the controversial documentary "The Hunting Ground," critics and supporters are engaging in a heated debate over its portrayal of campus sexual assault. The film, directed by Kirby Dick and produced by Amy Ziering, highlights the experiences of several sexual assault survivors and their interactions with university administrations. It also includes the case of Erica Kinsman, who accused former Florida State University football player Jameis Winston of rape, and the subsequent lackluster investigation by both the Tallahassee police and Florida State University. In response to the film, 19 Harvard Law School professors criticized it, alleging that it distorted the university’s handling of a sexual assault claim. This backlash comes as the documentary is being considered for an Oscar nomination, potentially bringing it to a wider audience. Meanwhile, Winston’s legal team has launched a website to counter the film’s narrative, arguing that it contains “critical omissions and distortions.” The film’s creators, however, stand by their work, stating that it accurately represents the experiences of sexual assault survivors and that powerful institutions often attempt to silence critics. The documentary has sparked a broader conversation about the prevalence of sexual assault on college campuses and the challenges faced by survivors in seeking justice. As the film gains traction, the legal battles and public discourse surrounding it continue to unfold, highlighting the complex and often contentious nature of addressing sexual assault on college campuses.

A 20-year veteran meteorologist, Kyle Hunter, is suing CBS Corporation and its Los Angeles affiliates KCAL and KCBS for age and gender discrimination. Hunter claims he was repeatedly passed over for weather broadcaster positions because CBS preferred to hire young, attractive women, despite his qualifications. Hunter, represented by attorney Gloria Allred, seeks unspecified damages and argues that CBS discriminates against experienced male meteorologists to attract male viewers. The lawsuit documents allege that Hunter, with a degree in geosciences and broadcast meteorology and AMS certification, was unfairly ignored for positions that went to less qualified women. Hunter’s case may be unique as it is the first known instance of a man suing for gender and age discrimination in broadcast news. CBS responded that Hunter’s complaint is based on misstatements of fact and will be vigorously defended.

Japanese whisky has stunned the industry by topping the prestigious Jim Murray's Whisky Bible 2015, with the Yamazaki Single Malt Sherry Cask 2013 scoring a perfect 97.5 out of 100, reports the Telegraph. This marks the first time a Japanese whisky has claimed the top spot, and the first year a Scottish malt failed to make the top five. Murray, who tasted over 4,500 whiskies, described the Yamazaki as a "near incredible genius" and praised its "nose of exquisite boldness" and "light, teasing spice." However, the success of the Japanese whisky comes as a wake-up call for Scottish distilleries, which may be producing "drab or mediocre malts." The winning whisky is limited to 18,000 bottles and is available in only a few hundred specialist shops in the UK for around £100. Scottish distilleries are urged to take note and improve their offerings, as the competition from Japanese whisky is now more intense.

"The Giver," the 2014 adaptation of Lois Lowry's 1993 novel, finds itself in a crowded field of dystopian young adult films, including "The Hunger Games" and "Divergent." Despite its early status as a trendsetter in the genre, the movie struggles to stand out, feeling somewhat dated and predictable. Set in a future where sameness reigns, the film follows Jonas (Brenton Thwaites), a 16-year-old living in a seemingly perfect community. The society has eradicated pain, war, and choice, but Jonas, who can see in color, begins to question the world he inhabits. His mentor, the Giver (Jeff Bridges), teaches him about the past, revealing the true horrors and joys that have been hidden. As Jonas learns, he also grapples with the moral complexities of his role and the potential for change.

Director Philip Noyce opts for a more subdued approach, avoiding the action and romance of its contemporaries. The film's visual style, shot in black and white until Jonas's perspective changes, adds a layer of intrigue but also a sense of predictability. The cast, including Meryl Streep as the strict Chief Elder and Katie Holmes as Jonas's mother, brings a range of performances, though some feel underwritten. Alexander Skarsgard's portrayal of Jonas's father is notably muted, while Jeff Bridges brings a world-weary charm to the Giver. The film's third act, which includes a chase scene and Jonas's escape, aims for action but feels rushed and less impactful than the quieter, more introspective sections.

Critics and audiences alike find "The Giver" to be a competent but unremarkable entry in the young adult dystopian genre. While it may appeal to those who enjoyed the book, the film's reliance on familiar tropes and its somewhat heavy-handed approach to themes of freedom and individuality prevent it from truly standing out. The movie's self-righteous and sometimes simplistic philosophizing, along with its predictable plot, make it a case of the same old, same old in a crowded market of similar films. Despite its earnest attempts to engage with complex ideas, "The Giver" ultimately feels like a necessary but not particularly exciting addition to the genre.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive, which is then added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. The Jacksonville International Airport was shut down for nearly five hours on a Tuesday evening, stranding incoming planeloads of passengers on the tarmac after police found two suspicious packages. One package was deemed "destructive" and had to be deactivated offsite by a bomb squad. The airport was evacuated shortly after 6 p.m., with some incoming planes held up on the tarmac until buses could arrive to pick up the passengers. Airport spokesman Michael Stewart stated that he could not confirm local news media reports that two suspects had been arrested. When the airport reopened, individual airlines would determine how to restart their operations, with the goal of ensuring all passengers would receive their luggage. Passengers on a Southwest Airlines flight from New York via Baltimore, which landed just before 6:30 p.m., experienced a delay, with the pilots initially unable to explain the reason. A bus arrived around 9:30 p.m. to start taking passengers to nearby hotels. The incident caused significant disruption, with the airport's operations resuming only after the packages were deemed safe.

The town of Sadiya in Upper Assam, India, was recently invaded by an unknown species of aggressive spiders, leading to a series of mysterious and alarming incidents. On May 8, during a Bihu festival, swarms of these spiders suddenly descended, causing panic among the attendees. Jintu Gogoi, one of the victims, suffered a painful bite and spent a day at the Sadiya Civil Hospital. The incident quickly escalated, with multiple people seeking medical attention for spider bites. Purnakanta Buragohain, a resident, died in the hospital, and an unidentified schoolboy also succumbed to his injuries. The district administration responded by advising people to stay indoors at night, but the situation remained unresolved. Scientists from Dibrugarh University and Gauhati University arrived on May 22 to investigate, collecting specimens. Dr. L R Saikia, head of the Department of Life Sciences at Dibrugarh University, stated that the spiders are highly aggressive and may be a new species, similar to the tarantula. However, their venom has not been tested, and it's unclear if the fatalities were due to the venom or an allergic reaction. The spiders' sudden appearance and behavior suggest they may have been introduced to the area accidentally or intentionally, raising concerns about their origin and potential impact. The government's handling of the situation has been criticized for its lack of effective response and proper procedures, such as conducting autopsies and retaining specimens for testing. The incident highlights the need for better preparedness and awareness in dealing with such unexpected biological threats.

French air strikes have forced Islamist militants to retreat from key towns in northern Mali, but the militants have struck back by seizing a small western town, highlighting the challenges of restoring order in the West African nation. The Islamists, who have imposed a brutal version of Islamic law in the north for nearly a year, claimed a "tactical retreat" from Timbuktu and other towns. However, they launched a counter-attack, taking control of Diabaly, 400 kilometers from Mali's capital, Bamako. French Defence Minister Jean-Yves Le Drian stated that the Islamists were "in retreat" elsewhere, but acknowledged the situation in the west as "difficult," noting that rebels are well-armed. The militants' seizure of Diabaly, home to a key Malian army base, follows French air strikes on the town. French troops, numbering about 550, are in Bamako and Mopti, with plans to increase to 2,500 in the coming days. The UN Security Council has convened to discuss Mali, with France's intervention receiving "quasi-unanimous" international support. Nigeria is set to lead a 3,300-strong West African intervention force, with 600 troops already on the ground. Other countries, including Senegal, Burkina Faso, Togo, and Benin, have pledged troops. The United States, Britain, and Canada have offered logistical support, while Algeria has closed its border to prevent militants from crossing into the country. Aid workers reported that many people had fled areas targeted by French air strikes. The battle for Mali has raised concerns about the potential for increased retaliation, with one al-Qaeda-linked group vowing revenge. The conflict has also highlighted the challenges faced by the Malian military, which has been weakened by a coup and the defection of Tuareg commanders. The US has spent between $520 million and $600 million over four years to combat Islamist militancy in the region, training Malian troops in counterterrorism skills. However, the collapse of the Malian military and the subsequent coup have raised questions about the effectiveness of the US training program. The French intervention aims to prevent the establishment of a "terrorist state at the doorstep of France and Europe," while also addressing the immediate threat to French citizens in Mali.

In the deep waters off California, a tiny octopus with big, round eyes and a squishy body has been discovered, earning it comparisons to both Pac-Man ghosts and Pokemon creatures. Stephanie Bush, a postdoctoral fellow at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute, is considering naming the species Opisthoteuthis Adorabilis due to its cute appearance. This octopus, part of the Opisthoteuthis genus, is known for its distinctive webbing between tentacles, allowing it to float like a parachute while steering with fins on its mantle. Specimens have been collected since 1990 but have not yet been scientifically described. Bush noticed key distinctions while working on the Monterey Bay Aquarium’s Tentacles exhibit, realizing she was dealing with two species. These octopuses, measuring about seven inches in diameter, often swim up off the bottom and hover, looking for small crustaceans and worms. With large, unusually proportioned eyes for its small body, this unique cephalopod is a fascinating addition to the deep-sea ecosystem.

In her acceptance speech at the Democratic National Convention, Hillary Clinton emphasized the importance of community and togetherness, contrasting her vision with Donald Trump's "I alone can fix it" approach. Clinton criticized Trump's business record, manufacturing jobs overseas, and his inability to handle pressure. She highlighted her "Stronger Together" slogan, advocating for a bold agenda to improve lives, including debt-free college education, immigration reform, and a robust social safety net. Clinton also acknowledged Bernie Sanders, praising his campaign's focus on economic and social justice. The speech aimed to unify the party and build a broad coalition, emphasizing America's strength through cooperation rather than division.

Three law enforcement agencies have been searching for 19-year-old Aftab M. Aslam of Johns Creek since Saturday, after he was reported missing on April 27. Initially, Aslam's family reported that they received a text message stating he had been kidnapped. However, investigators from Johns Creek Police, the Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and the Georgia Bureau of Investigation discovered that Aslam had purchased the phone used to send the text and that no one else had handled it. Now, Aslam has returned to his Morton Crossing home unharmed on Sunday evening. He told investigators that he left his home for personal reasons. Authorities are verifying his account, and no charges have been filed yet. The case highlights the importance of community vigilance and the potential for misunderstandings in such situations.

The search for Malaysia Airlines Flight 370 continues, with the Bluefin-21 underwater drone completing its 12th mission after scanning more than 90% of the search area. However, an object found near Augusta, Australia, was not from the missing plane, officials said. The object, described as a metal piece with rivets, was initially considered a potential lead but detailed photos convinced investigators otherwise. Despite the search efforts, which have been ongoing for 48 days, no debris from the plane has been found. The search area is vast, covering 310 square kilometers, and the Bluefin-21 has only scanned 80% of it. The search is complicated by the ocean's garbage, with other objects like trash and fishing gear also being spotted. Bad weather grounded planes searching for signs of debris on Wednesday, and the search could expand if the current underwater efforts fail to find evidence. Australian Prime Minister Tony Abbott emphasized that the search will not end until every reasonable effort is made, even if it means rethinking the search strategy. The next phase may involve more powerful sonar equipment to search deeper waters, and the search area could be expanded to include the last 370 miles of the plane's flight path. The search for the plane's flight data recorders, or "black boxes," remains crucial, as they could provide vital information about the plane's fate. The Malaysian Cabinet approved an international investigation team to determine the cause of the incident, with the investigation led by Malaysia but involving other countries.

Thousands of years ago, hobbits roamed a lush, green land on the Indonesian island of Flores. These ancient human relatives, named Homo floresiensis, stood about three and a half feet tall and weighed around 75 pounds. They gathered food, took shelter in cozy holes in the earth, and even battled dragons, specifically komodo dragons. This is no fantasy epic—it’s the likely lifestyle of an ancient human relative that thrived on Flores. Discovered in 2003 in Liang Bua cave, these hobbits made stone tools and might have survived predatory attacks from komodo dragons. Even more exciting to anthropologists, the discovery team originally estimated that these “halflings” lived as recently as 12,000 years ago, which would mean they outlived Neanderthals and might well have crossed paths with modern humans.

However, a fresh look at the site where the fossils were found puts a twist on the tale. The latest evidence suggests that hobbits vanished from the island far earlier than thought, casting the chances of a cross-species encounter in a new light. Since 2007, a lot more of the cave has been excavated, and researchers found that the layers of sediment in the cave were not all evenly deposited, causing a misinterpretation of the age of the bones and tools. The new analysis, published in Nature, asserts that the skeletal remains of H. floresiensis are more likely between 100,000 and 60,000 years old, and their stone tools date from as far back as 190,000 years to around 50,000 years ago. This suggests these evolutionary cousins did not exist for long after modern humans arrived in the region some 50,000 years ago.

Layered Story
While earlier investigations focused on the cave's center and eastern wall, the current study, conducted by many of the same researchers, expanded excavations between these areas and toward the rear of the cave. Older deposits in certain sections of the cave had eroded away, creating a steep slope near the entrance that became filled in with younger sediments, which caused the original misinterpretation. To ensure that the new age estimates are accurate, the team used five independent dating methods, ranging from the uranium decay rate in bone to luminescence in soil, which measures the amount of time since sand was last exposed to sunlight.

The erosion may also explain why excavators were unable to find all the bones from the upper body of the first known hobbit specimen. According to Tocheri, "if the erosion had continued for just a little longer, then the entire skeleton would more than likely have been lost forever." But age is just one of many bones of contention regarding H. floresiensis. Since the initial discovery, at least six additional hobbits have been exhumed in the cave, and biological anthropologists have been wrestling with issues ranging from how they first migrated to Indonesia, to the reasons for their diminutive size, to whether they even qualify as a unique human species.

Some experts contended that the hobbit's stature and small brain—about one-third the size of an adult human's—mean that the fossils belong to diseased modern humans with dwarfism, Down syndrome, or microcephaly, a developmental condition that produces a small head. Though many of these theories still circulate, a 2007 analysis conducted by Tocheri revealed that the wrist bones of H. floresiensis had very little structural similarity to modern humans and were more comparable to early hominins and chimpanzees, providing strong evidence for a separate species.

The prevailing theory is that H. floresiensis is either a descendant of a hominin that arrived on Indonesia in hobbit form, or a descendant of Homo erectus that evolved into its smaller stature once on the island. This evolutionary process, called island dwarfism, occurs when a species becomes progressively smaller to reduce its food requirements on a resource-deficient island. The excavation site at Liang Bua was littered with remnants of pygmy elephants, which adds credence to this theory.

Not a Fellowship?
Though no direct evidence from Liang Bua shows any interaction with modern humans, Tattersall still believes it is possible that these ancestral cousins could have crossed paths, perhaps with disastrous consequences. "There is this pattern where ancient kinds of Homo that have been doing perfectly well for a very long time disappear as soon as Homo sapiens shows up. For one reason or another, Homo sapiens is an insuperable competitor," says Tattersall. And the new estimates for hobbit extinction coincide suspiciously with the arrival of modern humans in that area.

Further excavations of Liang Bua and other sites on Flores could offer more clues and answer essential questions about the development, lifestyle, and extinction of this mysterious species.

The NFL will not use Roman numerals for the first time since Super Bowl IV, opting instead for the Arabic numeral 50 for Super Bowl 50, which will take place on February 7, 2016, at Levi's Stadium in the San Francisco Bay Area. The league's decision, driven by the unappealing appearance of the "L" in Roman numerals, comes after extensive testing and design work that involved 73 versions of the logo. The final logo, which features the number 50 in gold, aims to highlight the 50th anniversary of the Super Bowl and the game's location in the "Golden State." Both the national and regional logos include the Lombardi Trophy and notable San Francisco landmarks such as the Golden Gate Bridge, Coit Tower, and the Transamerica Pyramid. The NFL plans to revert to Roman numerals for Super Bowl LI in Houston in 2017. The league's use of the term "Super Bowl" began with the third game in 1969, and it filed to trademark the term two months later. The decision to change the numeral system for Super Bowl 50 is seen as a significant departure from tradition, with some promotional materials potentially using "Super Bowl L" instead of the official logo.

Former state senator Brian Joyce, 55, was arrested and charged with over 100 counts, including racketeering, wire fraud, extortion, and money laundering, in a federal indictment alleging he used his legislative position for personal gain. Joyce, who served as assistant majority leader in the Senate, is accused of accepting a "stream of concealed bribes and kickbacks" in exchange for official actions before the state Legislature and exerting pressure on local officials. His attorney, Howard Cooper, maintained that Joyce is innocent and criticized the investigation as overzealous. The 102-page indictment details Joyce’s alleged schemes, including accepting a free Jeep from a developer and receiving hundreds of pounds of free Dunkin’ Donuts coffee in exchange for legislative support. Joyce is accused of using his law firm, the Joyce Law Group, as a money laundering conduit to hide the payments. He is also charged with conspiring to defraud the IRS and falsely reporting stock purchases as tax-free IRA rollovers. Joyce’s arrest comes after a series of stories by The Boston Globe highlighted his alleged conflicts of interest and misuse of public office for personal benefit. The investigation was launched following a series of articles that began in January 2015, focusing on Joyce’s mingling of public and personal business. Governor Charlie Baker called the allegations disturbing, emphasizing the need for public officials to respect their offices and avoid using them for personal gain. Joyce’s case is the most significant corruption charge against a Massachusetts politician in recent years, with some legal experts suggesting that the charges may face scrutiny in court.

A new mother, Monica Thompson, has filed an $8.6 million lawsuit against Portland Adventist Medical Center, alleging negligence in the care of her newborn son, Jacob, who died at ten days old. According to the lawsuit, filed in Multnomah County Circuit Court, the hospital provided Thompson with a combination of painkillers and sleep aids, and a nurse brought Jacob to her room around 3 a.m. so she could breastfeed. About an hour later, Thompson noticed Jacob was unresponsive and attempted to seek help, but no nurse responded. Jacob was taken to Randall Children’s Hospital at Legacy Emanuel Medical Center and was pronounced dead six days later. The lawsuit claims the hospital was negligent in medicating the mother, leaving the infant unattended, and failing to enforce clear policies regarding the dangers of combining medication and shared sleeping. It also seeks compensation for the emotional distress Thompson experienced from unintentionally killing her firstborn child. The case highlights the risks associated with parents, especially mothers, sleeping in the same bed with their newborns, a practice the American Academy of Pediatrics discourages.

It's long been assumed that yawning helps to increase oxygen supply, but studies have failed to show an increase in blood oxygen levels after yawning. Now, Austrian researchers have found that yawning actually works to manage brain temperature, improving alertness and mental efficiency. Yawning is more frequent when we are tired, stressed, or under-stimulated, all factors that can alter brain temperature. To test whether air temperature influences yawning frequency, researchers at the University of Vienna showed pictures of people yawning to pedestrians in Vienna during summer and winter months, comparing their results to a similar US study conducted in Arizona. They found that people in Vienna yawned more in summer than in winter, while people in Arizona yawned more in winter than in summer. The researchers concluded that contagious yawning is most frequent when the temperature is around 20°C, with yawning frequency reduced when temperatures were around 37°C in Arizona's summer or freezing in Vienna's winter. Lead author Dr. Jörg Massen explained that yawning appears to be unhelpful when the air temperature is as hot as the body or when it is freezing, as the cold air is unnecessary or could be harmful. This study adds to accumulating research suggesting that the underlying mechanism for yawning, both spontaneous and contagious forms, is involved in regulating brain temperature. The cooling of the brain functions to improve arousal and mental efficiency, and the spreading of this behavior via contagious yawning could therefore function to enhance overall group vigilance.

The Women's Convention, the first national women's convention in four decades, is set to take place in Detroit, aiming to bring together activists and leaders to share strategies and build on the momentum from the Women's March. Organized by the Women's March, the event, themed "Reclaiming Our Time," is expected to attract over 3,000 participants. Sen. Bernie Sanders, an independent who challenged Hillary Clinton for the 2016 Democratic presidential nomination, will address the crowd on the opening day. However, this decision has sparked controversy, with some critics arguing that a woman should have opened the convention. Tamika Mallory, co-president of the Women's March, defended the choice, stating that Sanders is a "fierce champion of women's rights" and noting that the event will feature more than 60 women speakers. The convention will offer workshops and training sessions on leadership and activism, focusing on empowering women across various demographics. Despite the criticism, organizers remain committed to the event's goals and believe it will provide a platform for collective liberation and social change.

A pregnant woman in Fort Dodge, Iowa, was held at gunpoint by police after refusing to pull over her speeding car on Tuesday morning. Rachel and Ben Kohnen were driving to the hospital at 85 mph in a 55 mph zone when an officer pursued them, leading to a high-speed chase. The Kohnens did not stop, and the officer called for backup, laying tire spikes on the road to force them to a halt. Upon realizing Rachel was in labor, police escorted her to a nearby hospital, where she gave birth to their fourth child, a nearly 10-pound baby named Hazel, about an hour later. Rachel Kohnen said they could not stop because the baby was coming quickly, and they tried to call 911 but the dispatcher could not understand her due to her contractions. The police chief, Tom Ritts, stated they followed standard protocol for a high-speed chase and did not know the reason for the speed until realizing the emergency. No charges have been filed against the couple, and the County Attorney will decide if charges are warranted.

In St. Peter's Square, four women from the Ukrainian Femen group staged a topless protest against the Vatican's opposition to gay marriage, drawing attention to the growing tension between the Church and gay rights supporters. The Vatican's L'Osservatore Romano responded to an Italian court's rejection of a father's appeal, arguing that the traditional family unit is the ideal environment for children's growth. Meanwhile, in Paris, hundreds of thousands protested against President Hollande's plan to legalize same-sex marriage. The Vatican has intensified its opposition to gay marriage, with Pope Benedict XVI reaffirming the Church's stance in December. During his Angelus blessing, Pope Francis appeared unperturbed as the activists disrupted the ceremony. The incident highlights the ongoing conflict between progressive views and traditional Catholic teachings on family and marriage.

The U.S. State Department faced backlash and issued an apology on Wednesday for a tweet that was perceived as sexist and patronizing. The tweet, sent from the @TravelGov account, read, "Not a ‘10’ in the US? Then not a 10 overseas. Beware of being lured into buying expensive drinks or worse—being robbed. #springbreakingbadly." This tweet drew criticism for its implication that Americans' attractiveness is relative to their location and for potentially objectifying language. In response, the department deleted the tweet and issued a two-part apology, stating, "Some have been offended by our earlier tweet and we apologize that it came off negatively (1/2)" and "We see many Americans fall victim to scams each year & want all to be careful while traveling (2/2)." The State Department's attempt at humor backfired, leading to a wave of criticism and even parody tweets, highlighting the importance of sensitivity in public communications.

Bangladesh's anti-terrorism unit has arrested Farabi Shafiur Rahman, a suspect in the hacking death of U.S. blogger Avijit Roy, who was killed in Dhaka last week. Rahman, previously jailed for ties to the extremist Hizbut Tahrir group, was arrested at a bus stop and had allegedly threatened Roy on social media. He posted photos of the crime scene shortly after the attack and wrote that it was a "holy duty" for Bengali Muslims to kill Roy. The arrest comes amid increased activities by hardline Islamist groups in Bangladesh, which have targeted secular bloggers in recent years. Roy's killing has drawn international attention, with the media group Reporters Without Borders ranking Bangladesh 146th among 180 countries in press freedom. Rahman's arrest is seen as a step in the investigation, but his family and social media posts suggest he was a vocal advocate for the blogger's murder.

President Obama and Chinese President Xi Jinping are meeting at the Annenberg Retreat in Rancho Mirage, California, for an informal summit aimed at improving U.S.-China relations. The meeting comes at a time when tensions between the two nations have been on the rise, with issues such as cybersecurity and North Korea's nuclear program at the forefront. Obama and Xi plan to discuss these topics, as well as military-to-military relations, during the two-day summit. Obama will stay at the retreat, while Chinese officials will opt for a nearby hotel to avoid potential eavesdropping. The meeting is seen as a milestone in the often tense relationship between the two countries, with both leaders expressing a desire to work together on common issues. Obama will also use the opportunity to get to know Xi, who will lead China for the next decade. The summit's informal format, which includes golf and other leisure activities, is intended to foster a personal rapport between the two leaders. However, the meeting is not without its challenges, as China has been accused of cyberespionage and other forms of cyberattacks. Obama has sought to draw a distinction between these activities and the kind of surveillance conducted by the National Security Agency. Both leaders have also expressed a desire to avoid conflict and work towards a "new model of cooperation." The summit is expected to set the tone for future U.S.-China relations, with the two leaders hoping to establish a new era of bilateral cooperation.

President Obama denied in an exclusive interview with ABC News that he was "tense" in his airport tarmac encounter with Arizona Governor Jan Brewer, as she has described. "I'm usually accused of not being intense enough, right," he told Diane Sawyer, laughing. "Too relaxed." Brewer said in her 2011 book, "Scorpions for Breakfast," that Obama was "condescending" and "patronizing" and that she and her aides were treated coldly by White House staffers. Obama pushed back against Republican rhetoric, including Newt Gingrich's "food stamp president" claim, arguing that he doesn't put people on food stamps, and that the initial expansion of food-stamp eligibility happened under his Republican predecessor. Obama insisted he's ready to "fight with every fiber of my being" for a second term, emphasizing that whoever wins the Republican primary will be a standard bearer for a vision of the country that he doesn't think reflects who the United States is. He criticized Republicans' "rhetorical flourishes" and their push for less financial regulation and lower taxes, stating that such policies resulted in a huge crash that lost the country the most jobs since the 1930s. Obama outlined his alternative approach, which includes higher taxes on the wealthy to fund new government spending, as a "recipe for a fair, sound approach to deficit reduction and rebuilding this country." He also addressed the tension between Israel and Iran, stating that the United States is keeping a watchful eye but not discussing classified military information. Obama's family is fully prepared for the campaign, with Michelle enthusiastic about campaigning for the next nine months, and the girls focused on their own responsibilities.

Actor Mark Wahlberg is seeking a pardon from the Commonwealth of Massachusetts for a crime he committed over 25 years ago, hoping to have his decades-old assault conviction erased. In a detailed application to the Massachusetts Board of Pardons, filed on November 26, 2014, Wahlberg acknowledges his actions on April 8, 1988, when he was 16 and tried to steal alcohol from a man outside a convenience store in Dorchester, Massachusetts.
