He hit the man over the head with a stick and assaulted another individual, leading to his arrest and a 45-day sentence for assault. Wahlberg emphasizes his commitment to becoming a better person and citizen since then, stating, "I am deeply sorry for the actions that I took on the night of April 8, 1988, as well as for any lasting damage that I may have caused the victims." He highlights his involvement with various charities and good deeds, including the Mark Wahlberg Youth Foundation, the Dorchester Boys and Girls Club, and his frequent church attendance, to support his application. Wahlberg explains that a pardon would be a formal recognition of his transformation and serve as an example of redemption. He also mentions his desire to obtain a concessionaire's license for his restaurant businesses and to assist law enforcement by working with at-risk kids. The process could take time, as the Board of Pardons needs to investigate the petition and decide on a public hearing before it is recommended to the governor. If approved, the pardon would still require the approval of the governor's council.

Nestle's bid to trademark the four-finger shape of its iconic KitKat bar has been rejected by European judges, leaving the confectionery giant facing a potential setback in its long-running legal battle with Cadbury. The European Court of Justice ruled that Nestle must prove the public relies solely on the shape to identify the snack, a hurdle the company struggled to clear given the prominent brand name "KitKat" displayed on the product. This decision, while not final, could allow other chocolate manufacturers to produce similar-shaped bars without legal repercussions. The case, which has spanned over a decade, began when Cadbury attempted to trademark the purple color of its Dairy Milk packaging, a move opposed by Nestle. In 2013, Nestle successfully blocked Cadbury's attempt to trademark the color, but the court's ruling on the KitKat shape marks a significant development. Both Nestle and Cadbury expressed satisfaction with the outcome, with Nestle indicating it would continue to pursue its case. The ruling could have broader implications for trademark law, setting a precedent on what constitutes a distinctive shape for product protection. A similar bar, the Norwegian Kvikk Lunsj, which translates to "quick lunch," has been on the market since 1937 and shares a similar design, further complicating Nestle's claims. The case will now return to the UK High Court for a final decision, potentially shaping the future of trademark law in the confectionery industry. Intellectual property lawyer Sally Britton noted that Nestle's experience in registering difficult trademarks, such as the "Have a Break" slogan, suggests the company will not easily give up its pursuit. The KitKat's enduring popularity and the legal challenges surrounding its shape highlight the ongoing tension in the chocolate industry, where innovation and brand protection are constantly at play.

U.S. President Barack Obama convened the fourth and final Nuclear Security Summit in Washington, aiming to strengthen global efforts against nuclear terrorism. The summit, attended by over 50 world leaders, focused on securing vulnerable nuclear facilities and preventing "madmen" like Islamic State from obtaining nuclear or radioactive materials. Obama emphasized the persistent threat of nuclear terrorism, despite progress in reducing such risks, and highlighted the need for continued vigilance. He cited the recent Brussels attacks, where militants were found to have videotaped the daily routine of a senior Belgian nuclear plant manager, as a concerning example of the threat.

Obama urged world leaders to do more to safeguard nuclear materials, noting that while 102 countries have ratified an amendment to a nuclear security treaty, 2,000 tons of nuclear material remain vulnerable. He also addressed the issue of cyber attacks on nuclear facilities, emphasizing the need for enhanced security measures. The United States and Japan announced the completion of the task of removing all highly enriched uranium and separated plutonium fuels from a Japanese research reactor, a significant step in nuclear disarmament.

The summit also included a special session to coordinate efforts against Islamic State, with Obama praising gains in Iraq and Syria and calling for increased efforts to stem the flow of foreign fighters. North Korea's recent nuclear and missile tests were a concern, with Obama joining South Korean and Japanese leaders in vowing to ramp up pressure on Pyongyang.

Despite significant strides, Obama acknowledged that much work remains, particularly in areas like the Indian subcontinent and the Korean peninsula. He highlighted the Iran nuclear deal as a "substantial success," though he urged patience as Iran re-integrates into the global economy. Obama also addressed criticism of the deal, particularly from Republicans, emphasizing the importance of the world community carrying out its end of the bargain.

Obama's absence of mention of Russian President Vladimir Putin, who boycotted the summit, underscored the tension between the two countries. Putin's emphasis on building up his military was seen as a setback for Obama's nuclear disarmament agenda. While the summit resulted in mostly technical measures rather than policy breakthroughs, Obama maintained that the world cannot be complacent and must continue to build on its progress in securing nuclear materials.

Katie Couric, who previously worked with Matt Lauer on the Today show, addressed a controversial comment she made on Watch What Happens Live (WWHL) during an interview with Andy Cohen. In 2012, Couric joked that Lauer used to pinch her on the ass, a comment that resurfaced after Lauer was fired in 2017 for alleged sexual misconduct. Couric clarified that the comment was a joke and that she was sorry for any misunderstanding. On The Wendy Williams Show, Couric also spoke about the painful situation, stating that she was treated respectfully and appropriately by Lauer. She believes that the full extent of the allegations against Lauer has not been revealed and that some reports have been misreported. Couric also addressed the claim that Lauer had a button under his desk, which was used to lock his door, saying that it was just a privacy feature and not a nefarious thing. Couric’s comments come as part of the ongoing #MeToo and Time’s Up movements, which have brought to light the prevalence of sexual harassment in the workplace.

Michael Bay's "Pain & Gain" is a two-hour spectacle of sweat, blood, and cheerful, nasty vulgarity, starring Mark Wahlberg as Daniel Lugo, a personal trainer and bodybuilder who lands a job at a Miami gym after serving time for an investment scam. The film, based on a series of articles by Pete Collins, is a gritty, aggressive, and unapologetic portrayal of a group of men obsessed with physical fitness and the American dream. Wahlberg's performance is matched by Dwayne Johnson and Anthony Mackie, who bring their unique talents to the roles of Adrian and Paul, respectively. Johnson, known for his ability to balance tough guy and family man personas, finds the humor in a man roasting severed hands on a grill while also portraying the soul of a guy clinging to redemption. The film's opening scene sets a tone of hectic excess, with Wahlberg running from heavily armed forces of law and order, dashing across rooftops and lumbering through streets and alleys. The camera swirls around him, capturing intimate details like a glob of saliva popping out of his mouth and a peek up his nostrils. The film is punctuated by voice-over ruminations about Jesus, physical fitness, and the American dream, along with a few tactical visits to a strip club. The story follows Daniel, motivated by a self-pitying sense of entitlement, as he enlists two fellow gym rats to kidnap Victor Kershaw, a pigeon-chested blowhard who hires Daniel to help him get into shape. Victor's assets are to be used to torture him into signing over his assets. Adrian dreams of overcoming his steroid-related sexual problems and winning the love of Robin, a nurse specializing in such ailments, while Paul, an ex-convict who has found religion, clings to a sense of his own righteousness. The film is a monumentally stupid movie or a brilliant movie about the nature and consequences of stupidity, leaving audiences to ponder which it is.

A Japanese research student studying rural India was allegedly kidnapped and repeatedly gang-raped by a group of men in Bihar, India, according to police reports. The victim, a 22-year-old woman, was lured by a man posing as a tour guide to Gaya, a city in Bihar, where she was held captive for nearly three weeks. Two of the suspects, identified as brothers, were arrested in Gaya, while another was apprehended in Kolkata. The victim, who had been staying in Kolkata, managed to escape on December 26 and contacted the Japanese consulate, leading to the arrests. The case highlights the ongoing issue of sexual violence against women in India, which has been brought to the forefront following high-profile incidents such as the 2012 gang-rape of a student on a Delhi bus. The Indian government has responded by toughening rape laws, including doubling the prison terms for rapists to 20 years and criminalizing voyeurism and stalking. However, the arrest of these men and the ongoing investigation suggest that the problem of sexual violence remains a significant concern in the country.

A drug-sniffing German shepherd named Sombra, who has become a symbol of Colombia's anti-drug efforts, has been moved to a safer location due to a significant bounty placed on her head by one of the country's most powerful criminal organizations. Sombra, known as "Shadow," has been credited with sniffing out over 200 suspects and nearly 10 tonnes of cocaine, making her a formidable adversary for the Urabeños, also known as the Usuga clan or Gulf clan. This notorious group, considered Colombia's most powerful criminal organization, has put a 200 million-peso ($70,000; £53,000) price on Sombra's head, highlighting the financial impact her work has had on their operations. Her previous base in the Urabá region, a strategic point for traffickers with easy access to the sea, has been deemed too dangerous, leading to her relocation to Bogotá's El Dorado International Airport. The international airport is considered safer due to its location outside the gang's main area of influence. To ensure her safety, Sombra now has additional security personnel accompanying her during deployments. Sombra's handler, Oscar Favian Solarte, has described her as friendly and playful, noting that her approachable nature allows her to interact with children while still being effective in her drug detection role. Despite the high-profile nature of her work, Sombra remains a beloved figure in Colombia, serving as a symbol of the ongoing struggle against drug trafficking. Her story underscores the ongoing challenges faced by law enforcement in combating organized crime in Colombia, where drug cartels continue to wield significant influence and resources.

A 9-year-old girl from Charlotte, Zianna Oliphant, addressed City Council members at a meeting where the community called for changes following the fatal police shooting of Keith Lamont Scott, an African-American man. Her emotional testimony, delivered with tears, highlighted the pervasive issue of racial discrimination and policing. "We are black people and we shouldn't have to feel like this," Zianna said, emphasizing the need for justice and an end to the systemic treatment of African-Americans. Her speech resonated widely, capturing attention globally. Oliphant's mother, Precious, expressed pride in her daughter's courage and highlighted the discrimination her children face, noting that they have been pulled over for trivial reasons. Despite the involvement of police in their lives, the family fears for their children's future. The city has been in turmoil since Scott's death, with protests and conflicting accounts of the incident. While police claim Scott was armed and posed a threat, family members and witnesses dispute these claims, citing a lack of aggressive behavior. The incident has sparked calls for the resignation of Charlotte Police Chief Kerry Putney and the city's mayor. Zianna's speech underscored the ongoing struggle for racial equality and justice in Charlotte, with her words echoing the broader concerns of the community. The city remains divided, with some residents advocating for peaceful demonstrations and others calling for more aggressive action. The case of Keith Lamont Scott has become a symbol of the larger issue of police violence against African-Americans, with similar incidents in other cities fueling national discussions on race and policing.

On a muggy Fourth of July night, Rep. Beto O’Rourke, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate, joined legendary country singer Willie Nelson on stage at Nelson’s annual Fourth of July Picnic, an event that has long been a celebration of music and activism. O’Rourke, who has been making waves in the 2018 Texas Senate race against Republican Ted Cruz, used the event to address the crowd, expressing hope that Texans would help show the rest of the United States that there is no need to be afraid of immigrants, Muslims, or anyone else who might be considered different. His appearance was part of a broader strategy to rally support and energize his base, as he continued to engage in a tight race against Cruz.

The event, held just outside Austin, was met with a mix of wild cheers and booing from the crowd. O’Rourke, who has punk-rock roots, later joined Nelson and the rest of his band for spirited renditions of classic country songs, including “Roll Me Up and Smoke Me When I Die” and “Will the Circle Be Unbroken.” This move was seen as a bold political statement, given Nelson’s long history of political activism and liberal-leaning stances, which have often gone against the norm for country-music culture.

However, O’Rourke’s appearance did not sit well with all of Nelson’s fans. Following Nelson’s announcement that he would be headlining a Sept. 29 rally for O’Rourke in Austin, some of Nelson’s long-time supporters took to social media to boycott and publicly disown the country legend. They accused Nelson of aligning with what they believe to be the “socialist” positions of O’Rourke, questioning his political choices and even offering to sell their tickets to the upcoming Willie Nelson concert. For instance, Dakota Bell tweeted, “I am no longer willing to watch that hippie guitarist who supports that… socialist running for Senate,” while others expressed similar sentiments.

In a press release, Nelson defended his decision to support O’Rourke, stating, “My wife Annie and I have met and spoken with Beto and we share his concern for the direction things are headed. Beto embodies what is special about Texas, an energy and an integrity that is completely genuine.” This support from Nelson, a figure known for his activism and liberal-leaning political stances, has added another layer of complexity to the ongoing Senate race, which has gained national attention in recent months.

The event also highlighted the broader political climate in Texas, where O’Rourke and Cruz are entangled in a tight Senate race described by Cruz as a “dogfight.” O’Rourke’s appearance at Nelson’s concert and the subsequent backlash from some of Nelson’s fans underscored the deep divisions within the state and the country at large. As the race continues to heat up, the support and opposition from influential figures like Willie Nelson will likely play a significant role in shaping the narrative and outcome of the election.

Myanmar's Nobel Peace Prize winner, Aung San Suu Kyi, embarked on her first visit to Europe in nearly a quarter-century, marking a significant milestone in her journey from political prisoner to global stateswoman. The 66-year-old, who spent two decades under house arrest, formally accepted the Nobel Peace Prize that thrust her into the global spotlight two decades ago. Her visit, spanning 17 days, includes stops in Norway, Britain, Ireland, and France. However, the trip was briefly disrupted when she fell ill at a press conference in Bern, Switzerland, and had to cancel an official Swiss dinner in her honor. In Geneva, Suu Kyi urged foreign governments not to engage in joint ventures with her country's state-owned oil and gas company until it improves its business practices, citing a lack of transparency and accountability. She highlighted the need for the Myanmar government to adhere to internationally recognized standards such as the IMF code of good practices on fiscal transparency. Suu Kyi also addressed the issue of responsible investment, emphasizing that it is crucial for helping her resource-rich country along the path to democracy after nearly 50 years of military rule. The visit comes as Myanmar has made progress, including lifting restrictions from the International Labour Organization and a pledge to end forced labor. Suu Kyi's confidence in Myanmar's reforms is evident, as she accepted an invitation to attend the World Economic Forum on East Asia in Thailand. Despite concerns over the transparency of contracts, Suu Kyi expressed support for some Western oil firms, particularly Total, acknowledging their sensitivity to human rights and environmental issues. As sanctions are lifted, Suu Kyi advocates for responsible investment that creates jobs and supports the process of democratisation.

A 54-year-old Florida man, David Benes, was arrested for allegedly trying to forcibly exorcise his 80-year-old girlfriend, facing charges of battery on a person 65 or older and false imprisonment. According to a complaint affidavit, Benes held down his live-in companion late Monday evening, attempting to "get the devil out" of her, while removing phone batteries to prevent her from calling for help and taking her car keys. The woman, who had bruises and scratches on her arms, called 911 when the exorcism resumed. Deputies found Benes passed out on a couch, claiming he was too drunk to remember the incident but alleging that his girlfriend started the fight. Benes, who has a history of battery convictions, was arrested and remains in the Land O'Lakes jail without bail.

Arizona's new abortion law, which bans the procedure after 20 weeks of pregnancy, is set to take effect on Thursday, potentially affecting women carrying fetuses with fatal defects. The law, which defines the start of gestational age from the first day of the woman's last period, effectively pushes the ban back to 18 weeks, making Arizona the only state with such a restriction. According to state records, about 100 abortions are performed annually after 20 weeks, but it's unclear how many are due to fatal fetal abnormalities. The new law mandates that doctors offer information about perinatal hospice services to women considering abortion due to a fatal fetal abnormality, and the state will maintain a website listing organizations that provide such services. Two organizations, MISS Foundation and Embrace, offer comprehensive support to families facing difficult pregnancies, including counseling, birth planning, and funeral arrangements. However, these non-profit groups are concerned about potential overwhelming demand and lack of funding. The law aims to support families in making informed decisions and preparing for every outcome, but critics argue it may infringe on women's rights and could lead to more terminations earlier in pregnancy. The law's constitutionality is currently under appeal, with the Center for Reproductive Rights and another group challenging the decision. Arizona joins a growing trend of states enacting 20-week bans, with other states like Georgia and Louisiana following suit. These laws reflect a broader movement to restrict abortion access and protect fetal rights, despite legal challenges and concerns over their impact on women's health and rights.

Bitcoin's price rebounded above $9,000 on Tuesday following "productive" discussions on cryptocurrency among G-20 finance ministers and central bank governors. The price surged more than 4.5 percent, reaching $9,008 by 4:13 p.m. ET, after dipping to a low of $7,335.57 over the weekend. However, this positive news was overshadowed by a concerning discovery: German researchers found that the Bitcoin blockchain contains hundreds of links to child abuse imagery, potentially rendering the cryptocurrency's possession illegal in some countries. The blockchain, designed to be an immutable ledger of transactions, can also store non-financial data, including links and files. Researchers from RWTH Aachen University and Goethe University identified around 1,600 files within the blockchain, with eight being suspected of containing child abuse content. This revelation poses a significant legal and ethical dilemma, as the blockchain's immutability means that anyone with a copy of the ledger could be in legal trouble. The Bitcoin community has not shown concern over this issue, attributing it to the blockchain's openness and the potential for such content to exist. Meanwhile, the cryptocurrency's price has been bolstered by the G-20 discussions, which indicated a cautious but supportive stance towards cryptocurrencies. The G-20 leaders agreed to propose harmonized global regulations in July, after gathering more information. Despite the positive price movement, the underlying issue of illegal content within the blockchain could hinder Bitcoin's growth and mainstream acceptance.

Lois Riess, 56, a Minnesota grandmother, is now suspected of killing her husband, David Reiss, in March and a Florida woman, Pamela Hutchinson, in April, while using Hutchinson's identity to evade authorities. Riess targeted Hutchinson because the two women looked alike, according to investigators. After killing Hutchinson, Riess stole her cash, credit cards, ID, and car, with Hutchinson's white 2005 Acura TL with Florida license plate Y37TAA believed to be her current vehicle. The car has been spotted in Louisiana and Corpus Christi, Texas. Riess' 2005 white Cadillac Escalade was found abandoned in a Florida park. She is wanted for murder, grand theft of a motor vehicle, and grand theft of personal identification in Lee County. Minnesota authorities have issued a warrant for her arrest in connection with her husband's death. U.S. Marshals are actively searching for Riess, who is considered armed and dangerous. Authorities believe Riess' mode of operation is to befriend women who resemble her and steal their identities. Anyone with information on her whereabouts is urged to contact authorities.

Despite speculation that Al Gore might run against Hillary Clinton in 2016, Gore's advisers and close associates say he has no interest in another presidential bid. Gore spokeswoman Betsy McManus stated, "There’s no truth to it. He’s laser-focused on solving the climate crisis." However, with Clinton facing new iterations of the email controversy, flagging poll numbers, and surging Bernie Sanders support, some Democrats are considering Gore as a potential alternative. Gore, who won the popular vote in 2000 but lost the election, has largely stayed out of politics since then. While Gore has not made any formal moves toward running, some strategists believe he might reconsider, given his experience and the current political climate.

A 15-year study of over 530,000 British women has revealed that those who have had their appendix or tonsils removed may be more fertile, according to a report in Fertility and Sterility. The research, conducted by the University of Dundee, found that women who had undergone appendectomies, tonsillectomies, or both, had higher pregnancy rates and became pregnant sooner than their counterparts who had not had these surgeries. Specifically, the study showed that women who had their appendix removed had a 34% higher pregnancy rate, those who had their tonsils removed had a 49% higher rate, and those who had both had a 43% higher rate. The findings challenge the long-held belief that appendectomies can negatively impact fertility by potentially blocking the fallopian tubes. However, the exact reasons behind the increased fertility are not yet clear. Researchers suggest two possible explanations: one biological, where inflammation from an inflamed appendix or tonsils might strain the body and reduce fertility, and another behavioral, where women who undergo these surgeries might engage in more sexual activity, leading to a higher chance of pregnancy. The study's lead researcher, Dr. Sami Shimi, emphasized that women should not seek these surgeries to improve their fertility prospects. The research is seen as important in reassuring young women that appendectomies do not reduce their chances of future pregnancy. Further investigation is needed to determine the exact mechanism behind this surprising link.

Bryson DeChambeau secured a commanding victory at the Northern Trust golf tournament, winning by four shots over Tony Finau and moving to the top of the FedEx Cup standings. DeChambeau's four-shot triumph was a significant step towards his goals of playing in both the Ryder Cup and the FedEx Cup championship. "I'm a man on a mission right now — two missions, actually," DeChambeau stated, highlighting his ambitions. His victory was marked by a consistent performance, with consecutive birdies sealing the deal. DeChambeau's only notable mistake was a wild drive on the 18th hole, which landed in an unused fairway, but he managed to recover with a par. His victory was his second of the year and solidified his position as a strong contender for the $10 million bonus. 

Tony Finau, who also had the Ryder Cup on his mind, finished alone in second place, closing with a 68 and moving to No. 18 in the world rankings. Finau's strong showing put him in the conversation for a captain's pick, with Jim Furyk making his selections a week later. Tiger Woods, coming off a runner-up finish at the PGA Championship, struggled, finishing 14 shots behind the winner in 40th place. Woods expressed his frustration with his putting, stating, "I'm sure you guys are used to seeing me win five times a year or more. It's not that easy to win out here. What you're seeing is that I'm close, and just one shot here, one shot there per day, flips momentum."

The tournament also featured strong performances from Ryan Palmer and Cameron Smith, who tied for third. Dustin Johnson maintained his No. 1 world ranking, narrowly beating Brooks Koepka by four strokes. Six players, including Nick Watney, secured their advancement to the next stage of the FedEx Cup playoffs. DeChambeau's victory and his recent form have made him a strong candidate for a captain's pick for the U.S. Ryder Cup team, with Tiger Woods advocating for his inclusion. The article concludes with President Donald Trump praising DeChambeau's answers and recent play, highlighting the political and personal dynamics surrounding the golfers.

President Barack Obama has spoken out on the issue of racial equity and social justice, specifically referencing the cases of Michael Brown in Ferguson, Missouri, and Eric Garner in New York City. In a statement, Obama highlighted the "growing awareness" that law enforcement practices are not always applied in a "colorblind" fashion, a sentiment that resonates with the ongoing discussions and protests surrounding police brutality and racial inequality. The President emphasized the importance of addressing these issues head-on, stating that "the arc of the moral universe is long, but it bends towards justice." His comments came in the wake of a series of high-profile incidents involving law enforcement and minority communities, which have sparked national debates and calls for reform. Obama's remarks underscore the administration's commitment to promoting fairness and equality, while also acknowledging the challenges that lie ahead in achieving these goals. The President's statement was part of a broader effort to engage the public in discourse on issues of racial equity and social justice, with the hope of fostering a more inclusive and just society.

James Cameron, the renowned filmmaker, recently made history by becoming the first person to undertake a solo journey to the deepest point on Earth—the bottom of the Mariana Trench in the western Pacific Ocean. This extraordinary feat, which took place over the weekend, involved Cameron descending nearly 7 miles in his 12-ton Deepsea Challenger submersible. Cameron described the descent as a "heckuva ride," but his journey was not without potential hazards. The Mariana Trench, with its extreme pressure and cold temperatures, presented numerous risks, including the possibility of an implosion, freezing, fire, or entanglement with submarine cables. Despite these dangers, Cameron managed to avoid them, surfacing three hours earlier than planned due to hydraulic fluid leakage. His ascent took just 70 minutes, and he was picked up by the support vessel Mermaid Sapphire shortly after. Upon resurfacing, Cameron reported that the ocean floor appeared bleak, resembling the moon, and he did not observe any living creatures other than a few shrimp-like amphipods. He planned to spend six hours collecting samples and conducting extensive studies, but the fluid leak forced him to cut his mission short. Cameron hinted at the possibility of future dives to the trench, stating, "Next dive. Gotta leave something for the next one." His mission, supported by the Deep Sea Challenge team, was a significant milestone in ocean exploration, with National Geographic planning to document the adventure in 3D for theaters and television. Cameron's bravery and preparation, including rigorous physical training, underscore the challenges and risks involved in such an endeavor.

The Pentagon's official Twitter account mistakenly retweeted a call for President Donald Trump to resign, a move quickly disavowed by the Department of Defense. An authorized operator of the account erroneously re-tweeted content from @proudresister, which included a call for Trump, along with Alabama Senate candidate Roy Moore and Sen. Al Franken, to step down or resign due to allegations of sexual misconduct. The Pentagon's official Twitter account, @DeptofDefense, later deleted the tweet, and Pentagon spokesman Col. Rob Manning issued a statement explaining the error. Pentagon press secretary Dana White also tweeted a clarification, stating that the retweet was "erroneously" made and did not reflect the Department of Defense's stance. The incident comes amid ongoing sexual harassment allegations against various figures in Washington and Hollywood, forcing the White House to address similar questions about the president's own behavior.

A remarkable Milwaukee woman, Mary Agnes Mullaney, better known as "Pink," left behind a legacy of kindness and generosity upon her passing earlier this week. Her obituary, posted on social media, was a colorful and inspiring testament to her life. The family wanted to showcase her unique personality and values, so they crafted a whimsical and heartfelt announcement. Excerpts from the obituary include: "Go to church with a chicken sandwich in your purse. Cry at the consecration, every time. Give the chicken sandwich to your homeless friend after mass." "Go to a nursing home. Kiss everyone." "Invite new friends to thanksgiving dinner. Bonus points if they're from another country." "Never say mean things about anybody; they're poor souls to pray for." Her family shared memories of Pink's life, emphasizing her devotion to helping others. "From the Northshore doctor to the homeless person, they were all equal in my mother's eyes," said her daughter, Maryanne. Pink's life was marked by small acts of kindness, such as leaving cold drinks for overheated garbage collectors and mail carriers. Her family and friends were inspired by her story, leading to the revival of a Newsline 9 series, "Someone You Should Know," which encourages community members to share stories of those doing good. The obituary's full content can be found at the provided link, offering a day filled with inspiration and lessons from a life well-lived.

A physical altercation broke out at a Manchester buffet over crab legs, leading to the arrest of a husband and wife on Saturday night. The fight began as an argument at the buffet table and escalated, resulting in a 21-year-old man suffering a cut lip and a broken front tooth after being punched in the face. His mother intervened, using pepper spray on the attackers in self-defense and was not charged. Clifford Knight, 45, and Latoya Knight, 38, both of Windsor, were arrested. Clifford Knight faces charges of third-degree assault and disorderly conduct, while Latoya Knight is charged with disorderly conduct and threatening. Both suspects are husband and wife. Clifford Knight was released on a $5,000 non-surety bond, and Latoya Knight was released on a $2,500 non-surety bond, with both set to appear in court on April 14. The Manchester Fire Department responded to ventilate the restaurant, and the Health Department closed it to check air quality due to the pepper spray. The restaurant reopened as usual on Sunday.

In today's era of image-based social media, the advent and popularity of filters and editing tools have transformed how people perceive and present their appearance. From Snapchat's puppy ears to Instagram's Facetune, these tools allow users to alter their selfies, creating an idealized version of themselves. However, this trend is causing concern among experts, who warn that it may contribute to body dysmorphic disorder (BDD) and negatively impact self-esteem. A recent study published in JAMA Facial Plastic Surgery by Boston University researchers highlights a phenomenon dubbed "Snapchat dysmorphia," where patients seek plastic surgery to look more like their edited selfies. The study notes that these edited selfies often present unattainable beauty standards, blurring the line between reality and fantasy for patients. Assistant professor Neelam Vashi of the Boston University School of Medicine explains that while filters and editing tools can provide an instant fix, traditional cosmetic procedures cannot replicate the same results, leading to unrealistic expectations. The term "Snapchat dysmorphia" was coined by British cosmetic doctor Tijion Esho, who describes it as a form of BDD, a mental disorder characterized by an extreme preoccupation with a perceived flaw in appearance. The study found that 55% of surgeons reported seeing patients who requested surgery to look better in selfies, a 13% increase from the previous year. This trend is exacerbated by the constant exposure to edited images on social media, which can lead to feelings of sadness and, in severe cases, suicidal ideation. The article emphasizes the need for awareness and education to help people recognize the difference between reality and fantasy, and to approach their appearance with a more realistic perspective.

The Baltic Sea, a vast underwater graveyard of shipwrecks, continues to yield hidden treasures. German maritime expert Thomas Dehling, who specializes in charting and preserving these underwater artifacts, shares insights into the region's rich maritime history. According to Dehling, the Baltic Sea is home to approximately 1,000 known shipwrecks, with the majority dating back to the early 20th century, a period heavily influenced by the two World Wars. Notably, one 15th or 16th-century wooden shipwreck, discovered in Finnish waters, has been found, though only a few artifacts remain intact, including copper disks, a rare find so far north.

Dehling's team regularly surveys these shipwrecks, particularly those that pose a risk to maritime traffic, with surveys conducted once a year or every 25 years, depending on the object's significance. However, modern technology enables them to map the seafloor with greater precision, uncovering an average of 10 to 15 new objects annually. The Baltic Sea's shipwrecks include not only those from World War II but also remnants from earlier conflicts, such as English submarines in German waters and a Polish shipwreck in the Baltic.

While the Baltic Sea is popular among recreational divers, the area is fraught with dangers, including fishing nets that can ensnare divers. To mitigate these risks, the German Federal Maritime and Hydrographic Agency (BSH) does not publicly disclose the locations of historically significant shipwrecks, only informing relevant authorities about potential hazards. Despite this, a detailed map is available on their website, but it lacks precision for pinpointing exact locations.

Dehling's team has recently uncovered a fascinating find: a cache of 170-year-old champagne bottles, discovered in 2010 by divers off the coast of Finland. These bottles, found in near-perfect condition at a depth of 160 feet, represent a unique opportunity to study 19th-century winemaking practices. A team of scientists, led by Professor Philippe Jeandet of the University of Reims, conducted a detailed chemical and sensory analysis of the champagne, revealing lower alcohol content and higher sugar levels compared to modern vintages. The researchers attribute these differences to factors such as colder climate, less efficient yeast, and the addition of sugar syrup.

The sugar content analysis suggests that the champagne may have been destined for the Germanic market, where moderate sweetness was preferred. However, the high sugar levels also hint at the possibility of the shipment being intended for the Russian market, known for its preference for extremely sweet champagne. The champagne's unique characteristics, including enhanced levels of iron, copper, sodium, and chlorine, offer insights into the manufacturing processes of the time. These findings not only provide a window into 19th-century winemaking but also raise the intriguing question of whether deep-sea aging could enhance the taste of modern wines.

The Boy Scouts of America (BSA) is proposing to lift the ban on gay youth members but maintain a prohibition on gay adults from leading troops, aiming to end a long-standing controversy. This proposal, to be voted on by the BSA's National Council, seeks a compromise that could end a split within the century-old organization. The BSA cited survey results showing that parents in three out of four U.S. regions oppose the current ban. However, the decision has sparked mixed reactions; gay rights groups see it as insufficient, while conservative groups and some churches oppose it. The BSA's move comes amid a broader cultural shift towards greater acceptance of gay rights. The proposal would allow gay youth to join but force them to resign when they turn 18, creating a situation where they can participate as youths but not as adults. The Mormon Church, with significant influence over BSA, is studying the proposal, adding uncertainty to the outcome. The decision reflects the complex interplay between tradition, modern values, and corporate and religious interests.

Leaving a stable job to pursue fantasy sports full-time may seem like a pipe dream, but for Drew Dinkmeyer, it's a reality. Dinkmeyer, an investment analyst by background, has transitioned into a full-time fantasy sports player, a shift he attributes to his daily engagement in multiple high-stakes games. Unlike traditional fantasy football players who might invest a lump sum once a season, Dinkmeyer's strategy involves daily participation in games where he can wager upwards of $500 per game. This frequent and substantial investment has allowed him to achieve income levels comparable to his former financial sector job, making the transition from day trader to daily fantasy player a viable career path. Dinkmeyer likens his approach to day-trading, where the goal is to identify undervalued assets and capitalize on their true worth. In the context of fantasy sports, this translates to selecting players who are underpriced relative to their potential performance, thereby constructing a team that can maximize points. His earnings from writing for fantasy sports websites and hosting on satellite radio further bolster his financial stability, enabling him to sustain this lifestyle. The Fantasy Sports Trade Association reports that approximately 36 million people in the U.S. and Canada engage in fantasy sports, underscoring the industry's significant reach. Dinkmeyer's success story highlights the potential for fantasy sports to transform from a hobby into a legitimate career, challenging the conventional wisdom that such a transition is unattainable.

Saturday Night Live opened its March 10th episode with a sketch mocking Rush Limbaugh's radio show, starring Taran Killam as the controversial host. Limbaugh, portrayed as irrationally defending his sponsors who abandoned him after his controversial comments about Georgetown law student Sandra Fluke, was given bizarre sponsors like "Depends For Racists." The sketch, though amusing in its premise, felt repetitive and stretched beyond its intended length. Meanwhile, 98 advertisers had pulled their ads from Limbaugh's show and other controversial hosts, including carmakers, insurance companies, and restaurants, due to content deemed offensive or controversial. The radio feed at Limbaugh's flagship station, WABC, increasingly featured public service announcements during his show.

Barnes & Noble may be phasing out its 3G Nook model, according to Engadget, which received "hard evidence" from within the company. The rumor suggests that sales will continue until stock is exhausted, and Barnes & Noble is encouraging retail partners not to place bulk orders for the Nook 3G. This move aligns with the trend of customers preferring WiFi-only models, as data connections are rarely needed for e-reader usage. While the Nook Color remains a focus, industry insiders speculate that Barnes & Noble might refresh its e-ink Nook line to reduce costs, possibly releasing a more affordable 3G-enabled model to compete with Amazon's offerings.

Kris Humphries, the NBA player who was married to reality TV star Kim Kardashian for just 72 days, is reportedly planning to file for a legal separation rather than a divorce, according to sources. Humphries, 26, intends to seek an annulment of the marriage, which would clear his record of ever having been married to Kardashian, 31. This move comes after Kardashian filed for divorce on October 31, citing irreconcilable differences. The couple's troubles began almost immediately after their lavish August wedding, with their issues being on display in the season premiere of Kourtney and Kim Take Manhattan. Humphries' lawyer is handling the divorce proceedings, and the NBA player is reportedly doing fine despite the dramatic split. Meanwhile, Daniel Craig, the actor known for his role as James Bond, has criticized the Kardashian family for making careers out of their private lives. Craig, who managed to keep his marriage to Rachel Weisz a secret, told GQ magazine that he thinks the family "f***ing idiots" for selling themselves to the public and then making demands about their private lives. He expressed dissatisfaction with his own career, stating that he is always trying to figure it out and is never fully satisfied. Despite his criticism, Craig remains in love and happy with his wife. In other Kardashian news, Kourtney Kardashian and her boyfriend Scott Disick are expecting their second child together, according to an exclusive cover story in Us Weekly. Kourtney, 32, took a pregnancy test about five weeks ago and woke Disick up around 7 a.m. to tell him the positive results. The couple, who have a 2-year-old son named Mason, are reportedly not surprised about the pregnancy.

A 25-year-old man, Sidney Bouvier Gilstrap-Portley, was arrested after allegedly posing as a Hurricane Harvey evacuee and enrolling as a freshman at Hillcrest High School in Dallas, Texas. He enrolled under the name Rashun Richardson and claimed to be a displaced victim of the hurricane, which made landfall in the Houston area in mid-August. Gilstrap-Portley had previously enrolled at Skyline High School and re-enrolled at Hillcrest two months later. He played for the Hillcrest basketball team, scoring 17 points in the team’s first-round playoff loss, according to a write-up by the Preston Hollow People. The district spokeswoman, Robyn Harris, confirmed that when a student enrolls and claims to be homeless or an evacuee due to a natural disaster, federal law exempts them from requiring documents they might not have. Gilstrap-Portley was booked into the Dallas County Jail on charges of tampering with government records and has since been released. The school principal, Chris Bayer, stated that the school immediately notified the district and local authorities once it became aware of the student enrolled under false pretenses. Bayer emphasized the importance of ensuring every young person feels safe and secure, especially during times of difficulty. The incident highlights the need for improved procedures when welcoming students in times of need.

The Bank of England’s first plastic banknote, the new Winston Churchill fiver, will be unveiled at Blenheim Palace, Churchill’s ancestral home, on Thursday. This marks the beginning of a transition to polymer banknotes, which will replace the current £5 note featuring prison reformer Elizabeth Fry. The fiver, set to enter circulation in September, will be the first in a series of new plastic notes, with the Jane Austen £10 to follow next year and the JMW Turner £20 by 2020. Polymer banknotes offer several advantages, including durability, security, and environmental friendliness, as they can last up to two-and-a-half times longer than paper notes. The Bank of England claims this durability will offset higher production costs and save an estimated £100 million. However, the switch will cost shops and banks up to £236 million, as ATMs, vending machines, and self-service machines will need recalibration or replacement to accommodate the 15% smaller plastic notes. More than 30 countries, including New Zealand, Canada, and Australia, have already adopted polymer notes, which were first introduced by Australia in 1988. The Churchill fiver will feature a view of Westminster with Big Ben showing 3 o'clock, marking the approximate time when Churchill declared, “I have nothing to offer but blood, toil, tears, and sweat,” on 13 May 1940. This move to polymer notes is expected to spark a new era in British currency, blending historical significance with modern technology.

Amazon's enigmatic delivery system, Amazon Flex, operates behind the scenes, employing a vast network of independent contractors to deliver packages to customers' doorsteps. These couriers, often working in plainclothes and driving their own vehicles, compete for shifts on the company's own Uber-like platform. The program, which has expanded to dozens of cities, is shrouded in secrecy, with few people aware of its existence. Amazon Flex offers a flexible schedule, with opportunities available 7 days a week, and pays between $18 and $25 per hour, according to the Amazon Flex app. However, the work can be unpredictable, with drivers often competing for limited blocks of time and facing physical confrontations when someone tries to jump the line. 

Amazon Flex operates from fulfillment centers, where drivers are required to pass a background check administered by a company called Accurate Background. Training is minimal, with drivers mostly watching videos on their phones. Blocks of work are secured through an app, with associated routes and payouts. The pay varies by location, but averages around $20.50 per hour, making it a viable supplemental income for many drivers. However, it is not enough to support a full-time living in major cities like New York and San Francisco. 

Despite the flexibility, drivers face numerous challenges. Local data can be inconsistent, leading to misalignments between block times and package numbers. Additionally, Amazon caps drivers' hours at 40 per week, but in practice, it has become harder to secure enough hours to meet this limit. Drivers report being reprimanded for returning packages they couldn't deliver, and some fear being "ticketed" for failing to fit all packages into their vehicle. Amazon's systems struggle to estimate door-to-door times, particularly in large apartment buildings, leading to frequent block overruns. 

The program's constant evolution and lack of oversight have led to widespread cheating, with drivers using auto-tapping applications like FRep and Repetitouch to secure blocks more efficiently. Flexbot, a device created by a former driver, allows users to tap blocks more quickly, though Amazon claims it does not violate its terms of service. Drivers often turn to closed Facebook groups, Reddit, and gig economy forums to share information and navigate the program's complexities. 

Amazon's relationship with third-party local courier companies is also contentious. These companies, which Amazon contracts to do last-mile work, are required to use Amazon's software and pass Accurate Background's vetting. However, drivers can be deactivated from the Flex app, and some claim that fulfillment center managers control who can work. The writing on the wall is clear: Amazon is poised to dominate the delivery industry, and its business practices are raising legal and ethical concerns. The legality of the mass-contractor model remains an open question, with labor misclassification and worker exploitation at the heart of the issue. Legal experts warn that Amazon's practices could lead to widespread violations of labor laws, and the lack of regulatory oversight is exacerbating the problem.

A Florida man, William Reiss, 68, survived Hurricane Irma but was killed by a FEMA contractor, 18-year-old Gerjuan Jackson, who he had befriended while Jackson was assessing his home for storm damage. Jackson, along with two accomplices, Kenley Campbell, 22, and Darril Rankin Jr., 22, was arrested for the Jan. 3 slaying of Reiss, who also lost his gun collection. The trio had previously met after Hurricane Irma damaged Reiss’ Polk County home. Jackson, who lived in Mobile, Alabama, had bought two handguns from Reiss for $800 about two weeks after they met. On January 3, Jackson and his accomplices returned to Reiss’ home to rob him of more guns, shooting Reiss four times and wounding his roommate, Kenneth Maier, who later died of his injuries. They stole up to 25 firearms and a television from Reiss’ home, burning his truck and selling most of the guns on the street. Jackson admitted to investigators that he shot Reiss and Maier. All three suspects were charged with first-degree murder and multiple counts of robbery, burglary, and grand theft. Jackson’s arrest left other Polk County residents shocked, as he had been inside their homes. Kenneth Maier, 57, who had been shot several times, managed to flag down three people driving by, who found Reiss deceased. The good Samaritans called for help, and Jackson, Campbell, and Rankin were arrested. Jackson initially knew Reiss as a FEMA contractor. The incident left the Polk County Sheriff’s Office and Reiss’ family heartbroken, with the sheriff’s office stating, “This act of vicious murder should have never happened.”

Milwaukee County is grappling with an unprecedented drug crisis, with the chief medical examiner's son, Adam Peterson, 29, becoming the latest victim. Adam was found face down on a floor at a friend's apartment, with first responders administering Narcan, an opioid antidote, but he did not respond and was pronounced dead around 7:30 p.m. on Monday. His death brings the total number of probable drug overdose deaths in Milwaukee County to 70 in the past seven weeks, surpassing the combined number of homicides for the years 2011 to 2014. The Milwaukee County Medical Examiner's Office reported that this year is on track to outpace the previous five in heroin-related deaths. Dr. Brian Peterson, the county's chief medical examiner, has been at the forefront of addressing the crisis, highlighting the scale of drug-related deaths in the area. At a recent opioid round-table discussion, he emphasized the severity, noting that one out of three cases autopsied in one month were overdose cases, with ages ranging from 1 year old to 63. The office's operations manager, Karen Domagalski, stated that the projected number of total drug-related deaths for 2016 had been revised, with the office now expecting more than the previous record of 254 in 2015. The crisis has left the medical examiner's office overwhelmed, as evidenced by the 71 overdose deaths in the previous seven weeks. The Milwaukee County Medical Examiner's Office is working to provide clean data to help understand the extent of the problem, with Dr. Peterson's office describing the current situation as "unprecedented." U.S. Senator Ron Johnson, who hosted the round-table discussion, offered his condolences to the Peterson family and expressed his commitment to fighting the epidemic.

An Egyptian court has sentenced 528 supporters of ousted President Mohammed Morsi to death for their alleged participation in an attack on a police station in Minya in August, which resulted in a police officer's death. The UN human rights commissioner condemned the decision, calling it "rife with procedural irregularities" and a breach of international human rights law. The defendants were found guilty in a mass trial lasting less than an hour, with most of them not present. Human Rights Watch described the trial as "unprecedented in recent history." The 683 Morsi supporters went on trial on Tuesday for a similar attack on another police station. Defence lawyers boycotted the trial, citing procedural irregularities. The verdicts are subject to appeal, and legal experts expect them to be overturned. The mass trials have raised concerns among human rights activists over the lack of due process as Egyptian authorities push swift and heavy prosecutions against Islamists and the Muslim Brotherhood. Over 16,000 Egyptians have been arrested since the military ousted President Morsi last summer. The government has branded the Brotherhood a terrorist group, a claim it denies. The verdicts have sparked protests and clashes between security forces and Islamist students at Minya University.

In recent days, actor Mandy Patinkin, best known for his role as Inigo Montoya in the 1987 film "The Princess Bride," has been inundated with emails and videos showing scenes from the movie with Ted Cruz's face superimposed over Patinkin's. Cruz, a leading Republican presidential candidate, has been reciting lines from the movie, particularly Inigo Montoya's famous line, "Allo, my name is Inigo Montoya. You killed my father. Prepare to die," during campaign events. Patinkin, however, is concerned that Cruz's interpretation of the movie is incomplete and misses its core message of love and hope. Patinkin points out that Inigo's final line, "I have been in the revenge business so long, now that it's over, I don't know what to do with the rest of my life," is a pivotal moment that underscores the film's theme of moving beyond revenge. Cruz, who has long cited "The Princess Bride" as his favorite movie, has been performing scenes from it on the campaign trail, including at an Iowa Central Community College event. Patinkin, a vocal critic of Cruz's rhetoric, believes that the senator's focus on fear and hatred is at odds with the movie's message of love and optimism. A spokesperson for Cruz's campaign, Catherine Frazier, stated that the senator is a "huge fan of the film and the actors in it," and that the senator's use of the movie for political purposes is "something we can all get behind, politics aside." The incident highlights the complex relationship between popular culture and politics, as well as the potential for misinterpretation and misuse of cultural references in political discourse.

First Lady Michelle Obama made a playful appearance on "The Tonight Show with Jay Leno," promoting her "Let's Move!" campaign to encourage healthy eating habits among children. During the segment, she engaged Leno in a friendly challenge, serving him nutritious snacks like apples and sweet potato fries. Leno, known for his aversion to vegetables, was coaxed into trying various dishes, including a pizza made with whole-wheat crust and vegetables. Obama also brought honey from the White House garden for Leno to enjoy with his apple. The first lady used the opportunity to discuss her husband's upcoming re-election campaign, stating, "There's really no way to mentally prepare for it. You take each day as it comes." She also shared that President Obama has a beautiful voice and sings to her frequently, often performing classic soul and R&B tunes like Al Green and Marvin Gaye. When asked about her husband's recent Apollo Theater performance, she admitted, "I didn't even hear about it until it got on YouTube." Obama maintained a non-partisan stance when discussing Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney's rendition of "America the Beautiful," calling it "beautiful" and noting that it is a song meant for every American. The first lady's visit to California included promoting her health initiative and helping Democrats raise funds for the upcoming elections.

Rapper Kevin Gates was sentenced to 180 days in jail after a jury found him guilty of misdemeanor battery in a case that unfolded before a Polk County courtroom on Wednesday. The incident, which occurred during a concert in Lakeland in August 2015, was captured on video and showed Gates kicking a female fan in the chest. The victim, 18-year-old Miranda Dixon, testified that she had reached out and grabbed his pants several times, trying to get his attention for her friend. Dixon admitted to tugging on his pants during the concert, stating, "I was trying to get his attention for my friend." During the trial, Dixon's friend, Termeral Redding, corroborated her story, testifying that when Dixon grabbed Gates the first time, he kept performing, and the second time, "ran and kicked her with force, and her friend fell back into her." 

Gates, 30, testified that he kicked the woman in self-defense after she repeatedly grabbed his pants. He admitted to kicking the fan but maintained it was in self-defense under Florida's "Stand Your Ground" law. However, the jury of six women convicted him after a day of testimony. Jose Baez, the same defense attorney who represented Casey Anthony, defended Gates during the trial, arguing that Gates' kick was in response to Dixon's battery. Baez also suggested that Dixon's testimony was unreliable and that she was attempting to gain damages in a separate civil trial. 

The judge sentenced Gates to 180 days in the Polk County Jail, with credit for any time served, and imposed fines and court costs. The state had requested 60 days in jail, with one year of probation, and mandatory anger management classes. However, the judge tripled the sentence, ordering a one-year probation after Gates' jail time. Dixon suffered a CT scan after the incident, and her mother, Kristy Irelan, spoke to News Channel 8, recounting how her daughter was kicked in the chest and passed out. The case has garnered significant attention, with thousands of people signing a petition aimed at banning Gates from Florida venues.

Since 1996, Alexa Internet has been contributing their daily crawl data to the Internet Archive, which are then added to the Wayback Machine after a certain embargo period. This practice aims to preserve web pages as they are created and the pages they reference. As referenced pages change or disappear from the web, a link to the version that was live when the page was written is preserved. The Internet Archive hopes to replace broken links with references to these archived pages or provide companion links to help users view the original content. The ultimate goal is to fix all broken links on the web, particularly for "No More 404" sites. Additionally, Twitter users can now add location information to their tweets, either through the web or via third-party applications, with the option to delete their tweet location history at any time. This feature allows for more precise tracking and analysis of user-generated content based on geographical data.

Three years after the Casey Anthony murder trial, the nation still grapples with the aftermath. In July 2008, the 22-year-old mother of 2-year-old Caylee Anthony was arrested for child neglect after the toddler went missing in Orlando, Florida. A massive search ensued, and in December 2008, a utility worker found Caylee's skeletal remains in a wooded area near the Anthony home. Prosecutors sought the death penalty, and a two-month trial began in May 2011. Casey Anthony's defense attorney, Jose Baez, shocked the nation by revealing that Casey was a victim of sexual abuse by her father. The prosecution countered with a largely circumstantial case, while the defense argued that Caylee drowned in the family's pool. After deliberating for 10 hours, the jury acquitted Casey Anthony of first-degree murder and other serious charges but convicted her of four misdemeanors for providing false information to law enforcement. Casey Anthony now lives in an undisclosed location in Florida, constantly under public scrutiny and threats to her life. Her attorney, Cheney Mason, described her current life as "a housekeeper, clerk, secretary and stuff like that," working inside her home. Mason's new book, "Justice in America," delves into the trial and legal issues, revealing behind-the-scenes details and challenging the media's role in the case. The book also addresses the impact of the media and bias in the court, providing a comprehensive look at the case from various perspectives. Despite the acquittal, Casey Anthony remains estranged from her family and faces ongoing public hatred, struggling to navigate her life in the shadow of the case.

An authorized biopic of Lucille Ball is in the works, with Cate Blanchett attached to star as the iconic actress. Aaron Sorkin is set to write the script, though he has not officially committed to the project yet. The film will center on Ball's 20-year marriage to Desi Arnaz and will be produced by Ball and Arnaz's children, Lucie Arnaz and Desi Arnaz Jr., along with Escape Artists. Sorkin, known for his work on The Social Network and Steve Jobs, is currently writing the script for another project, Molly's Game, for Sony. The biopic will cover Ball's career on TV sitcoms such as I Love Lucy and The Lucy–Desi Comedy Hour, highlighting her 13 Emmy nominations and four wins, as well as her Golden Globe Cecil B. DeMille Award in 1979. Social media reactions have been mixed, with some expressing excitement and others questioning the choice of Sorkin as the screenwriter.

When President Barack Obama and Secretary of State John Kerry announced the public terms of the Iran nuclear deal, they portrayed the release of seven Iranian-born prisoners as a modest trade-off for the greater good of the agreement. However, a POLITICO investigation reveals that the deal turned out to be worse than initially imagined. The Obama administration agreed to release or stop pursuing more Iranians than the number of Americans released in return, and some of those freed were accused of posing threats to national security. Three were part of an illegal procurement network supplying Iran with U.S.-made microelectronics, including components for surface-to-air and cruise missiles. Another was serving an eight-year sentence for conspiring to supply Iran with satellite technology and hardware. The administration even dropped its demand for $10 million that a jury said the aerospace engineer illegally received from Tehran. In a series of unpublicized court filings, the Justice Department dropped charges and international arrest warrants against 14 other men, all of them fugitives. The administration did not disclose their names or what they were accused of doing, noting only that the U.S. “also removed any Interpol red notices and dismissed any charges against 14 Iranians for whom it was assessed that extradition requests were unlikely to be successful.”

Senior officials from the Obama White House and Justice and State Departments acknowledged that all but a handful of people were kept in the dark, but said top representatives of the Justice Department and FBI helped vet the 21 Iranian proliferators and that then-Attorney General Loretta Lynch herself participated in blocking some other individuals demanded by Tehran from inclusion in potential prisoner trades. However, many federal investigators scrambled to get Justice and State Department approval to lure top Iranian targets into traveling internationally in order to arrest them, but the requests were not approved, and the targets vanished, depriving the U.S. of some of its best opportunities to gain insight into the workings of Tehran’s nuclear, missile, and military programs. The fallout from the nuclear deal and prisoner swap continues to reverberate through the Justice Department and specialized units at the FBI, Department of Homeland Security, and Commerce Department created to neutralize the threat posed by Iran’s nuclear and military ambitions. Critical momentum has been lost, and the trail of some high-value targets has gone cold. The National Counterproliferation Initiative, created with much fanfare a decade ago, has suffered greatly, even as metrics are hard to come by. The initiative’s efforts are in limbo as the result of stalled or stymied investigations and prosecutions, and key enforcement efforts are in jeopardy.

A newly discovered dinosaur from northeastern China, named Caihong juji, which translates to "rainbow with the big crest," boasts iridescent feathers that may have served as a social or sexual cue, much like the feathers of modern hummingbirds, according to a study published in the journal Nature Communications. The fossil, exceptionally well-preserved and complete, reveals that Caihong had a colorful head and chest, with iridescent feathers that likely shimmered and changed color with the viewing angle, similar to the throat feathers of hummingbirds. This discovery suggests that dinosaurs may have used their feathers not only for flight but also for display, providing a more colorful Jurassic world than previously imagined.

The dinosaur, a small carnivore weighing about a pound, lived in forests and may have glided from tree to tree, preying on small mammals and lizards. Its bird-like body, including the necessary feathers for flight, contrasts with a crested head resembling that of a Velociraptor. The name Caihong, meaning "rainbow," was chosen to reflect the stunningly preserved feathers, which, based on their melanosomes, are believed to have given the dinosaur a rainbow-like glimmer. The melanosomes found in the feathers are long, flat, and organized into sheets, closely matching those in the iridescent throat feathers of modern hummingbirds.

Yang Jan, a local farmer, discovered the fossil in Hebei Province, which was acquired by the Paleontological Museum of Liaoning. Scientists, including Dongyu Hu from Shenyang Normal University, examined the fossil and found traces of pigment in the feathers, allowing them to infer the original colors. The team sampled 66 sites across the fossil, comparing the melanosomes with those from modern bird feathers. The iridescent feathers were primarily found on the head, chest, and parts of the tail, suggesting that Caihong used its colorful plumage for social or sexual purposes.

The discovery of Caihong adds to the growing evidence that dinosaurs, like modern birds, used their feathers for display, not just for flight. Unlike Microraptor, another iridescent dinosaur, Caihong lived 40 million years earlier, indicating two different ways of creating iridescent color in small raptor dinosaurs before the origin of birds. The dinosaur's frond-like tail, with asymmetrical feathers, further highlights its potential use in displays, possibly as a dark background to provide contrast against the iridescent head. The exact functions of Caihong's iridescent feathers, and whether males or females had different plumage, remain subjects for further study, as more bones from Caihong and other feathered dinosaurs could provide additional insights.

A Texas prison escapee, Juan Salaz, who fled 16 years ago, has been apprehended in Mexico and awaits extradition to complete his sentence for attempted capital murder of a police officer. Salaz escaped in 1997 from the Garza East prison in Beeville by scaling three 16-foot razor-wire topped fences. The hunt for him involved U.S. and Mexican law enforcement agencies. Salaz is to be returned to Texas custody once Mexico approves his extradition. His capture leaves Jose Fernando Bustos-Diaz, who fled in 2010, as the sole Texas prison fugitive still at large. Bustos-Diaz is serving a 35-year sentence for a 2005 murder in Harris County. Salaz's evasion of authorities for nearly two decades highlights the challenges in managing prison escapes and fugitives across international borders.

A 25-year-old German man who survived an avalanche and subsequent hypoxia developed unusual seizures triggered by solving Sudoku puzzles, according to a case report published in JAMA Neurology. The man, a physical education student, experienced myoclonic jerks in his mouth and legs after the avalanche, which buried him and caused a ruptured spleen and hip fracture. Upon hospitalization, he began having spontaneous tonic-clonic seizures in his left arm, leading doctors to prescribe anti-epileptic medication. Remarkably, the seizures reappeared when he attempted to solve a Sudoku puzzle, a common activity he enjoyed. The seizures ceased when he stopped solving the puzzles, indicating that the intense three-dimensional visualization required to solve Sudoku triggered the seizures. The seizures were linked to the death of inhibitory fibers in the right centro-parietal region of his brain due to hypoxia, leading to overactivation of this brain area during Sudoku solving. This case highlights the phenomenon of reflex epilepsy, where external stimuli can trigger seizures. The man, now seizure-free for over five years, had to give up Sudoku and similar activities to avoid further seizures. The study underscores the complex interplay between brain function and external stimuli, offering insights into the mechanisms of epilepsy.

The Dallas Morning News, known for its unwavering support of Republican candidates, broke with over 75 years of tradition on Wednesday to endorse Hillary Clinton for president, marking the first time in more than 75 years that the newspaper has chosen a Democrat over a Republican. The endorsement came with a direct and unambiguous statement: "There is only one serious candidate on the presidential ballot in November. We recommend Hillary Clinton." The newspaper’s editorial board, known for its conservative leanings, cited Trump’s divisive rhetoric and lack of preparedness as reasons for their decision, while praising Clinton as a "known quantity" with experience in governance. This move reflects the significant impact of Trump’s campaign on even staunch Republican bastions, as it has forced them to reconsider their long-held voting patterns.

The Dallas Morning News’ decision is not merely a headline-grabbing moment but a potential game-changer. According to a 2011 study by political scientists Chun-Fang Chiang and Brian Knight, unusual endorsements by newspapers can influence voters, especially when they break with the expected pattern. The study found that readers were more likely to support the candidate an unexpected newspaper endorsed, particularly if they had seen the endorsement. Given the Dallas Morning News’ conservative reputation, this endorsement could sway undecided voters and potentially impact the election’s outcome.

The endorsement also highlights the evolving political landscape in Texas, a traditionally Republican stronghold. As the state’s population becomes more diverse, particularly with a growing Latino population, the political dynamics are shifting. This demographic shift is bolstering Democratic efforts to gain ground in Texas, and the Dallas Morning News’ endorsement could further strengthen this trend. Recent polls by the Washington Post and SurveyMonkey showed Clinton and Trump in a dead heat in Texas, a surprising result that suggests the state may be more competitive than previously thought.

The Dallas Morning News’ decision to endorse Clinton is not without its criticisms. Critics argue that the newspaper’s endorsement is driven by political expediency rather than genuine ideological alignment. However, the editorial board maintains that Clinton’s experience and willingness to work across the aisle make her the more competent and reliable choice. They point to her record of bipartisan cooperation and her role in key foreign policy decisions, including her tenure as Secretary of State. Despite these credentials, Clinton faces criticism for her use of a private email server and the Clinton Foundation, which the editorial board believes she should address more transparently.

The Dallas Morning News’ endorsement underscores the complex interplay between political parties, media, and voter behavior. It challenges the notion that voters are strictly aligned with their party’s platform and suggests that unexpected endorsements can have a significant impact on the election’s outcome. As the race continues, this move by the Dallas Morning News could serve as a pivotal moment, potentially influencing not only the presidential race but also the broader political landscape in Texas and beyond.

A method that enables skin to tan without exposure to ultraviolet (UV) radiation has shown promise in human skin samples, potentially leading to a new approach for preventing skin cancer and reducing the signs of aging. Published in Cell Reports, the study from researchers at Massachusetts General Hospital demonstrates that a topical drug can penetrate live human skin and trigger the production of melanin, the skin's natural UV-absorbing pigment. This is a significant departure from current self-tanning lotions, which merely stain the skin and provide limited sun protection. The drug, which mimics the effects of sunlight, activates the production of dark melanin, offering a UV-independent way to tan. The researchers tested the drug on skin samples and mice, with the drug producing a potent darkening effect that could block harmful UV rays. The approach could be particularly beneficial for individuals who struggle to tan, such as those with red hair and fair skin, as it bypasses the genetic mutation that disrupts the normal melanin production process in these individuals. While the drug is not yet ready for commercial use, the team hopes to combine it with sunscreen to provide comprehensive protection against solar radiation. The potential benefits extend beyond cancer prevention, as the drug could also help maintain healthier skin by reducing the visible signs of aging caused by UV damage. The researchers emphasize that the drug is not intended to replace sunscreen but rather to complement it, offering a safer and more effective way to protect the skin from the harmful effects of UV radiation.

The shooting of Stephon Clark by Sacramento police in his grandmother's backyard on March 19, 2018, has left his family and community in mourning. Clark, a 22-year-old black man, was shot 20 times by two officers responding to a call of a man breaking car windows. His family claims he was only trying to enter his grandmother's home. The officers said they feared for their safety, believing Clark had a gun, but no weapon was found at the scene. Instead, Clark was carrying a cellphone. The officers fired multiple rounds, hitting him several times. Clark was pronounced dead at the scene. His girlfriend, Salena Manni, and his two young sons, Aiden and Cairo, are devastated by his loss. Manni said Clark had changed his life recently, but his death was unjust. The city of Sacramento has released body camera footage and aerial video of the incident, showing Clark breaking windows and advancing toward the officers with an object in his hand. The object was later identified as a cinder block and a piece of aluminum. Clark's family and community are demanding justice and transparency from the police. A GoFundMe page has been set up to cover funeral expenses. The Sacramento Police Department is investigating the incident, and a review committee will examine the findings. Mayor Darrell Steinberg called for a thorough investigation and promised to seek appropriate changes. The tragic death of Stephon Clark has reignited the debate over police use of force and racial tensions in the community.

A massive winter storm hit the East Coast, bringing heavy snow, frigid temperatures, and howling winds, causing widespread travel disruptions and safety concerns. The storm, which began overnight, dumped nearly 2 feet of snow in parts of New England and the Midwest, with up to 7 inches falling in New York City by Friday morning. Snow totals reached 21 inches in Boxford, Mass., and 18 inches in western New York near Rochester. The National Weather Service issued blizzard warnings for Cape Cod and coastal areas north and south of Boston, as well as parts of Maine and New York's Long Island, with gusts of up to 30 mph expected, causing wind chills as low as minus 25 degrees, dangerous for exposed skin. 

Governors in New York and New Jersey declared states of emergency, urging residents to stay home and avoid travel. In New York City, Mayor Bill de Blasio closed three major highways and warned residents to stay off the streets. He said, "If you don't need to go out, please don't go out." New York Governor Andrew Cuomo ordered the Thruway between Albany and the Bronx to close overnight, with the Long Island Expressway and Interstate 84 between the Pennsylvania and Connecticut borders scheduled to reopen at 8 a.m. The travel ban in New York City was lifted, but the city urged drivers to use mass transit and stay off the roads if possible. 

Mass transit was affected, with Amtrak running on a modified schedule and Metro-North Railroad operating on a Saturday schedule. U.S. airlines canceled more than 2,300 flights due to the storm, stranding travelers like Heather Krochuk, who had to spend 36 hours in a Boston hotel after her flight from Seattle got canceled. The storm also impacted Chicago, where hundreds of flights were canceled, and up to a foot of snow fell in some northern suburbs. 

In Boston, the Pine Street Inn shelter prepared for a packed house, with vice president Heidi Daniels saying, "We won't turn anybody away. We'll pull out cots and mats and make sure everybody has a warm place to stay tonight." The storm tested the new mayor, Bill de Blasio, and the outgoing mayor, Thomas Menino, as they managed the situation. 

Safety teams were deployed to help the homeless, and workers at a salt storage facility in Falls Township, Pa., were killed when a 100-foot pile of road salt fell and crushed a worker operating a backhoe.
