In preparation for the storm, residents stocked up on supplies, and Douglass Bibule in Watertown, N.Y., said, "Well, there will be some shoveling that I will have to do and some sanding. I've got to go home and do some stretching exercises to make sure I don't hurt myself while doing that, and do a little shopping to make sure that we have all the supplies that we need. We need food because we have three older children at home."

The storm extended the holiday break for some students and posed challenges for New York City's new mayor and Boston's outgoing mayor. The cold and snow created dangerous conditions, with forecasters warning of the risk of frostbite and hypothermia. The weather service advised people to dress warmly and cover all exposed skin. Overall, the storm brought significant disruptions and safety concerns to the region, with millions facing dangerous travel conditions and the threat of severe cold.

A young woman, reportedly 25 years old and working as a temporary employee at Ceva Logistics in Redford Township, Michigan, gave birth in a bathroom stall at her workplace and then tried to hide the newborn in her desk drawer, according to police. The discovery was made around 11:19 a.m. Tuesday when employees noticed blood on the bathroom wall and floor. Upon entering the stall, they found the woman, who had not mentioned giving birth, and called 911. The woman was taken to a local hospital, but the baby, found in a bag under her desk, was pronounced dead. Redford police are investigating to determine if the mother is responsible for the baby's death. The cause of death is pending an autopsy, which was conducted on Wednesday. The woman, who had previously told colleagues she was not pregnant, is currently recovering at the hospital. Ceva Logistics, which transports products for companies worldwide, informed their 150-plus employees and offered grief counseling. The company's logistics director, Ken L'Heureux, declined to comment further, stating that the incident is under investigation. Level Professional Services, the woman's temp agency, also provided counseling for affected employees. The Wayne County Medical Examiner's Office is expected to release the autopsy results in two weeks. The case remains under investigation, and it is unclear whether the woman will face charges.

A charter school in San Antonio, Great Hearts Monte Vista, has faced criticism and an apology after assigning an eighth-grade American History class a worksheet titled "The Life of Slaves: A Balanced View." The assignment required students to list the "positive aspects" and "negative aspects" of slave life, which upset parents and community members. Concerned parent Robert Livar shared a photo of the assignment, which went viral, prompting the school to address the issue. The school's superintendent, Aaron Kindel, acknowledged the assignment was "very inappropriate and entirely inconsistent" with the school's philosophy and apologized. The teacher involved was placed on leave, and the textbook, "Prentice Hall Classics: A History of the United States," was removed from use. The school plans to conduct an audit of the textbook and replace it if deemed imprudent. Additionally, headmasters and teachers will meet with students to explain the mistake and provide more thoughtful lessons on the period of American History. The school aims to ensure such incidents do not recur and will update parents on their progress. Congressman Joaquin Castro and Texas State Representative Diego Bernal expressed concern, with Castro tweeting that the assignment was "absolutely unacceptable." Great Hearts Texas Superintendent Kindel stated, "We want to thank the parents who voiced their concern and brought this to our attention. We are removing the textbook from all of our Texas academies." The school will also engage with impacted students to address the issue more thoughtfully.

Dunkin' Donuts is renaming itself "Dunkin'" to emphasize its focus on coffee and other beverages, a move that will officially take place in January. The change will affect signage, ads, and social media accounts at new and remodeled U.S. stores, with international stores following suit. The company, which has over 12,500 global locations, aims to modernize its brand for younger customers by simplifying its menu and adding mobile ordering options. Beverage sales, particularly coffee, now account for 60% of U.S. sales. Dunkin' tested the shorter name in Pasadena, California, and another location in Massachusetts, which also featured digital kiosks and expanded Grab & Go sections. Despite the name change, doughnuts will remain on the menu. Dunkin' plans to open 1,000 new U.S. stores by the end of 2020.

Oracle Team USA staged an incredible comeback to win the America's Cup in a winner-take-all race, defeating Emirates Team New Zealand in a best-of-17 series. Just a week ago, New Zealand led 8-1 and seemed on track to secure the trophy. However, skipper James Spithill and his team mounted a remarkable turnaround, winning eight consecutive races to clinch the victory. The comeback was highlighted by Oracle's superior catamaran performance, particularly in the final race where they overcame a wave-induced setback to pull ahead. The win, described as one of the greatest comebacks in sports history, kept the America's Cup in the United States and showcased the innovative catamaran designs championed by Oracle CEO Larry Ellison.

Following the Telegraph magazine's retraction of a controversial article about First Lady Melania Trump, the magazine faced criticism for publishing false statements. Meanwhile, in a stark contrast, superstar Mary J. Blige has joined forces with Planned Parenthood in a new ad called "Yes We Plan," supporting President Obama's stance on women's rights and health care. The ad, featuring rapper Q-Tip and actress Julianne Moore, aims to highlight the importance of re-electing Obama. However, a separate ad produced by Michael Moore, in cooperation with MoveOn.Org, takes a much darker tone. This ad, described as more "Michael Moore than Greatest Generation," threatens Republicans and Mitt Romney with violence, warning that voter suppression tactics could lead to Romney's victory. The ad's final speaker vows to "watch us all having sex, or something," adding an unsettling element to the message. The contrasting approaches of supporting Obama and threatening political opponents illustrate the diverse strategies used in political advertising.

Russian spy Anna Chapman posed provocatively in the Russian version of Maxim magazine, according to photos published online. The Kremlin has celebrated the case to boost the prestige of its intelligence services, despite the spy ring's failure to secure major intelligence before their arrests. Russian President Dmitry Medvedev awarded the group of spies the country's highest state honors. The photographs and an interview with Chapman will appear in the next issue of Maxim, which has included her in its list of Russia's 100 sexiest women. The 10 Russians, accused of being sleeper agents, were swapped with four imprisoned Russians who were accused of having traded secrets with the West.

Reality TV star Tila Tequila, known for her controversial statements and actions, has taken a dramatic turn, embracing Nazi imagery and anti-Semitic rhetoric in a series of posts and a new song. In a Facebook photo, she is depicted with a swastika armband and an SS uniform, standing in front of Auschwitz, captioning the image, "Tilisis is the GODDESS of LOVE & WAR! Learn your facts!" This comes two years after she publicly converted to Judaism, stating, "I just feel like the Jewish people have such a beautiful way about them, and I can’t wait to officially be Jewish." Her recent posts and song lyrics further reveal her embrace of Nazi ideology and anti-Semitic views. In a blog post, she defends Hitler, claiming his history was rewritten after World War II. She also expressed sympathy for the death of a former associate, James Howe, with a post that included the text, "GOD SEE’S [sic] YOU DIRTY FUCKING KIKES WORKING FOR THE SYNAGOGUE OF SATAN AND I HAVE RETURNED AS HIS MESSENGER!" In her new song, "It’s Going Down!" she raps, "Jewluminati motherf*ckers hate me," and refers to herself as "Hitila," a portmanteau of "Hitler" and "Tila." Her posts and song lyrics have sparked controversy and criticism, with many finding her embrace of Nazi ideology and anti-Semitic rhetoric deeply troubling.

In Florida, a jury awarded $80 million to the family of a two-pack-a-day smoker who died of lung cancer, with $72 million in punitive damages, highlighting the ongoing legal battles between plaintiffs and Big Tobacco. The verdict, in Bronson, Florida, found R.J. Reynolds 90% at fault, while the smoker was 10% responsible. This case reverses the tobacco industry's recent winning streak in Engle progeny cases, where more than 7,000 lawsuits claiming injuries and deaths due to smoking are pending. The Florida Supreme Court's 2006 Engle ruling has given plaintiffs a significant advantage, amassing over $250 million in damages. Despite the industry's recent successes, the high stakes of these trials ensure continued legal battles over the health impacts and responsibility of tobacco companies.

California has agreed to end its policy of indefinite solitary confinement for imprisoned gang leaders, a practice that once kept hundreds of inmates in segregation for a decade or longer. This decision, reached after a class-action lawsuit by the Center for Constitutional Rights, aims to align California with other states' policies on managing gang-related issues within prisons. The new agreement restricts the use of segregation to only those inmates who commit new crimes behind bars, significantly reducing the duration and severity of solitary confinement. The state will also introduce restrictive custody units for inmates who refuse to participate in rehabilitation programs or continue breaking prison rules, ensuring that those who might be in danger due to their status can be housed separately.

The lawsuit, initially filed in 2009 by two inmates serving time in the security housing unit at Pelican Bay, highlighted the inhumane conditions of solitary confinement, which involved isolation in 80-square-foot cells for all but about 90 minutes each day. Inmates in such units had no physical contact with visitors and were limited to reading materials and communications with the outside world. The settlement will limit the maximum time inmates can spend in isolation, reducing the number of those confined for a decade or longer from 500 to 62 as of late July. This change is expected to alleviate the pressure of long-term segregation, which has been a source of intermittent hunger strikes by tens of thousands of inmates throughout the prison system.

The policy changes also address the issue of high-security inmates, such as 71-year-old Hugo Pinell, who was killed by fellow inmates shortly after being released from isolation. The new units will provide high-security inmates with more personal contact and privileges, potentially serving as a model for other states to follow in their efforts to reduce reliance on solitary confinement. The decision has been hailed as a "monumental victory" by the plaintiffs, who hope it will lead to the eventual end of solitary confinement in California and across the country. The settlement is seen as a significant step towards more humane treatment of prisoners, addressing concerns raised by President Obama and U.S. Supreme Court Justice Anthony Kennedy.

On Friday's Fox & Friends, co-host Brian Kilmeade defended President Donald Trump's border policies, stating that at least the president is not taking American kids away from their parents. Kilmeade argued that someone must deal with the immigration issue and that the president is broadcasting a deterrent to Latin American migrants seeking shelter in the United States. He emphasized the importance of enforcing the rule of law and border security, asserting that these are people from another country and not from Idaho or Texas, where American citizens are paying taxes and have needs. 

Kilmeade's comments drew criticism from MSNBC's Stephanie Ruhle, who tweeted that she wanted to point something out to Fox & Friends colleagues. The controversy resurfaced when it was revealed that on Wednesday, Trump signed an executive order that, while purportedly ending the policy of separating children from their parents, also aims to increase the government's ability to detain kids with their parents indefinitely. 

The executive order's dual nature highlights the ongoing debate over border security and the treatment of undocumented immigrants. While Kilmeade defended Trump's approach, co-host Ainsley Earhardt stated that Trump's policy is in place to "vet who’s coming across the border, in case it’s MS-13 or drugs." This stance has sparked discussions about the balance between security measures and the humane treatment of children and families. The executive order and the debate surrounding it continue to be focal points in the broader immigration conversation.

The U.S. is stepping up its support for the Syrian opposition, providing non-lethal aid such as medical supplies and food rations, Secretary of State John Kerry announced at a meeting of the "Friends of Syria" group in Rome. This marks a shift in U.S. policy, which has so far focused on humanitarian and indirect support. The U.S. will also provide an additional $60 million to help the Syrian opposition council deliver basic services in rebel-controlled areas. However, the aid does not include weapons, which the rebels say they need to defeat government forces. European Union nations, including Britain and France, are also considering providing non-lethal military equipment to the rebels. Despite the increased support, the Syrian opposition remains frustrated, with some leaders calling for more concrete international backing. The Syrian National Coalition, which is leading the opposition effort, postponed a meeting to select a prime minister for a provisional government, citing a lack of tangible support. The ongoing conflict has resulted in the deaths of over 70,000 people, with the U.S. and its allies hoping that increased support will help the opposition gain the upper hand. However, the rebels are still outgunned by President Assad's forces, which continue to use heavy weaponry, including Scud missiles. The U.S. and its allies are coordinating their efforts to ensure that aid reaches the opposition and does not fall into the hands of extremist groups.

A federal judge has allowed a lawsuit against President Donald Trump to proceed, marking the first time a court has ruled that the District of Columbia and Maryland may sue the president over his business dealings. U.S. District Judge Peter J. Messitte in Maryland found that the plaintiffs had legal standing to sue, clearing the initial legal hurdle. The lawsuit alleges that Trump’s business dealings, particularly his ownership of the Trump International Hotel in Washington, DC, have violated the Constitution’s ban on receiving improper “emoluments” from individual states and foreign governments. Messitte cited examples of government clients, including Kuwait and Bahrain, patronizing the Washington hotel, potentially harming competitors and taxpayers. The judge rejected arguments that only Congress could decide on the president’s compliance with the emoluments clauses, stating that courts could review the president’s actions to ensure they comply with the law. The case will focus on the Trump International Hotel, as it will not include visits to Mar-a-Lago or other properties. The plaintiffs argue that the hotel has an unfair advantage in the hospitality industry and has received special tax concessions. Messitte’s ruling could allow the plaintiffs to seek internal documents from the Trump Organization to determine the financial impact of foreign and state government payments. The Justice Department, representing the president, has not yet stated whether it will appeal. The case is part of a series of lawsuits filed after Trump’s inauguration, all alleging violations of the Constitution’s emoluments clauses.

On the first anniversary of Mohammed Morsi's inauguration as Egypt's first democratically elected president, hundreds of thousands of opponents and supporters of Morsi gathered in Cairo's Tahrir Square and across the country, marking a significant day of political tension. Tahrir Square, the birthplace of the 2011 uprising that ousted Hosni Mubarak, saw tens of thousands of protesters chanting "erhal!" (leave!) and waving Egyptian flags, while Morsi's supporters rallied outside the Rabia al-Adawiya Mosque near the Ittihadiya presidential palace. The scale of the protests, estimated by some to be as high as 14 million people nationwide, surpassed initial predictions and highlighted the deep divisions in Egyptian society. Morsi's opponents, led by the Tamarod movement, accused the president of failing to uphold democratic values and criticized his use of a presidential decree to force through an Islamist-leaning constitution. Morsi, in an interview with The Guardian, defended his actions and called for national dialogue, but his opponents dismissed the call as insincere. The demonstrations were marked by violence, with at least seven people killed and over 600 wounded, including an American. Clashes between Morsi's supporters and opponents left several Brotherhood offices attacked, and the president moved to a safer location. The military, under pressure, warned against a "dark tunnel" of instability and called for a week of compromise. As the day progressed, the potential for civil unrest loomed, with both sides preparing for a possible confrontation. The outcome of this pivotal day would likely shape Egypt's political landscape for years to come.

In the wake of the tragic shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Parkland, Florida, which left 17 students and staff members dead, Republican candidate Leslie Gibson faced intense backlash for insulting the teen survivors of the shooting. Gibson, who was the sole candidate for the 57th District seat in Maine’s House of Representatives, drew criticism for calling Emma González, one of the most vocal activists, a "skinhead lesbian" and David Hogg, another survivor and activist, a "bald-faced liar." These comments, made in response to reports of the students' growing social media followings, sparked a wave of condemnation from both Democrats and Republicans alike. Bruce Bickford, a Republican in the Maine House of Representatives, and Amy Volk, a Republican state senator, publicly criticized Gibson's behavior. Phil Bartlett, the chair of the Maine Democratic Party, called on Republican leadership to denounce Gibson's comments, which he deemed "reprehensible."

Gibson's tweets were met with swift and harsh criticism. In response to his insults, David Hogg, another Parkland survivor and activist, tweeted, "Who wants to run against this hate-loving politician? He's running UNOPPOSED. RUN AGAINST HIM. I don't care what party. JUST DO IT." This tweet prompted Eryn Gilchrist, a 28-year-old Democrat from Maine, to announce her candidacy, stating that she was "horrified and embarrassed" at the thought of Gibson representing her. Thomas Martin Jr., a Republican, also decided to enter the race after reading Gibson's comments, feeling compelled to run against the candidate.

In a surprising turn of events, Gibson himself announced his withdrawal from the race on Friday, saying, "It's the best thing for everybody." He added, "I am not walking away with my head hung low. I am walking away with my head held high." Following his departure, both Emma González and Sarah Chadwick, another Parkland student and activist, expressed their relief. González tweeted, "All I can say is Thank You," and Chadwick added, "It’s what he deserves ☕️."

Gibson's decision to drop out of the race came after a series of events that highlighted the intense scrutiny and criticism faced by those who criticize the teen activists. The incident underscored the growing influence of the Parkland students in the national conversation on gun control and the importance of respectful discourse in political discourse.

San Francisco's Millennium Tower, a 58-story luxury residential building that has sunk 17 inches and tilted 14 inches since 2006, faces a new and concerning issue: a large crack in a window on the 36th floor. The crack, which appeared over the Labor Day weekend, has prompted the City and County of San Francisco Department of Building Inspection to issue a correction notice, requiring building engineers to evaluate the extent of repairs needed and investigate the condition of the glass panel and adjacent curtain wall system by September 7, 2018. Residents heard a creaking sound followed by a loud popping noise at 2:30 a.m. on the day the crack appeared. The crack raises significant concerns, given that the window system is designed to withstand hurricane force winds. City Supervisor Aaron Peskin emphasizes the seriousness of the situation, noting that the failure of a window at such a height is a "big wake-up call." The crack could indicate strain on the building's curtain wall, potentially posing a risk of fire spreading through gaps between floors. Building manager Michael Scofield assured residents that a team of experts would assess the issue and that a barrier would remain in place until repairs are made. The crack has led to further concerns about the building's stability, with residents and officials questioning the safety of pedestrians below the tower. The ongoing legal battles and structural issues continue to cast a shadow over the once-prized luxury high-rise.

Ten volunteer firefighters from the Fairmont and Orrum Fire Departments in Robeson County, North Carolina, were arrested in connection with a two-year arson conspiracy. The firefighters, along with a Maxton police officer and a Department of Corrections employee, face over 90 charges, including felony arson and conspiracy. The investigation, which lasted six months, revealed that the firefighters intentionally set fires to abandoned homes and woods, costing taxpayers thousands of dollars. Sheriff Ken Sealey stated that the case involved several woods and abandoned house fires in a week. The 10 arrested firefighters, ranging in age from 17 to 42, were charged with various counts of arson and conspiracy, with bail set between $100,000 and $200,000. The Robeson County Sheriff's Office, State Bureau of Investigation, Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms, and the NC Forestry Service were involved in the investigation. Authorities expect more charges to be filed, and more arrests are possible. The incident has raised questions among local residents about the integrity of the volunteer firefighters.

Antidepressants like Prozac, commonly found in sewage, can alter the mating behavior of wild birds, according to a study published in the journal Current Biology. Researchers from the University of York exposed wild-caught starlings to a low, environmentally relevant dose of fluoxetine, the active ingredient in Prozac, and observed changes in their courtship behavior. Male starlings paired with fluoxetine-treated females sang less and showed increased aggression, while female starlings became initially more aggressive but less so over time. The study highlights the potential impact of environmental pharmaceuticals on wildlife, particularly on species that forage at sewage treatment plants. Fluoxetine did not affect female reproductive physiology or courtship behavior, but reduced male interest, potentially impacting breeding success. The findings suggest that exposure to antidepressants can alter important traits related to individual fitness and population dynamics. Lead author Kathryn Arnold warns that while the study focuses on fluoxetine, other pharmaceuticals may also pose risks, emphasizing the need for improved sewage treatment technologies.

Sperm whales, known for their massive size and complex social structures, hold a surprising genetic secret: they all seem to trace back to a single female ancestor, a phenomenon reminiscent of the "Eve" theory in human genetics. This revelation comes from a new study published in Molecular Ecology, which analyzed mitochondrial DNA from 1,633 sperm whales. Mitochondrial DNA, passed down exclusively from mothers, offers a unique window into the evolutionary history of these marine giants. The research, led by Alana Alexander, found that despite the vast geographical range of sperm whales, their genetic diversity is surprisingly low, indicating a significant reduction in genetic variation. This low diversity suggests that a single female, who lived around 80,000 years ago, played a pivotal role in the genetic lineage of the species. The study's findings challenge the notion that sperm whales, with their extensive social networks and matrilineal societies, would naturally exhibit higher genetic diversity.

The researchers also noted that the social structure of sperm whales, where females tend to stay in their natal groups while males disperse, might contribute to the low genetic diversity. However, this social pattern does not fully explain the extent of genetic uniformity observed. The study's authors suggest that geographic factors, such as the lack of significant barriers to dispersal, may also play a role in maintaining this genetic homogeneity. The combination of mitochondrial and microsatellite data revealed that while social groups and regions influence genetic diversity, the overall impact varies by ocean. In the Indian Ocean, regional differences were more pronounced, while in the Pacific, social groups had a more significant impact on genetic structure.

These findings have implications for the conservation of sperm whales. The low genetic diversity makes the species more vulnerable to environmental changes, such as climate shifts, which could disrupt their preferred habitats. This increased vulnerability highlights the importance of understanding the genetic makeup of species to inform effective conservation strategies. The study underscores the complex interplay of evolutionary forces, including natural selection, genetic drift, geographic isolation, and mating systems, in shaping the genetic diversity of sperm whales. By examining these factors, researchers can better understand the unique evolutionary history of this remarkable species and develop targeted conservation efforts to ensure its survival.

More than 150,000 gallons of water contaminated with toxic firefighting chemicals were released into the Colorado Springs Utilities sewer system from a holding tank at Peterson Air Force Base, according to a confirmation on Tuesday. This incident, which occurred at least six days prior, is a significant addition to the ongoing groundwater contamination issue in the area. The firefighting foam containing these chemicals has been a suspect in the contamination of wells in Security, Widefield, and Fountain, leaving thousands of residents scrambling for bottled water. The release was discovered on October 12, but the cause remains unknown. Air Force officials stated that the tank was designed to be difficult to discharge, and while it is possible that the spill was intentional, this remains under investigation. The perfluorinated compounds (PFCs) in the water are known to cause health issues such as liver and kidney damage and may trigger cancer. The Environmental Protection Agency recently adjusted its maximum safe exposure level to 70 parts per trillion, while testing in the Widefield Aquifer found levels as high as 2,000 parts per trillion. The spill was not a direct threat to Colorado Springs drinking water, as it passed through the Las Vegas Street sewage treatment plant and was released into Fountain Creek. However, the chemical-laden water did not pose a risk to the drinking water system. The base did not warn others downstream, as the chemical is currently unregulated. This latest spill has caused frustration among residents, such as Mary Fletcher, who has lived in the Widefield area for 30 years. She expressed concern about the long-term effects of the contaminated water on her health. The Air Force has announced plans to replace the firefighting foam at all its bases, and the contamination issue has drawn lawsuits against the manufacturers. The spill has raised concerns about the long-term effects on the Widefield Aquifer and the security of drinking water in the region.

Former President George W. Bush and Vice President Dick Cheney appeared together for the first time since leaving office at the groundbreaking of the George W. Bush Presidential Library and Museum on the Southern Methodist University campus in Dallas. The event marked a return to public life for Bush, who has been largely out of the spotlight since 2009. Bush, flanked by his administration’s luminaries, including former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, used the occasion to emphasize his commitment to advancing the causes of human freedom, global health, economic growth, and education reform through the Bush Presidential Center. Cheney, appearing gaunt and frail after his heart surgery, praised Bush’s leadership and defended his administration’s decisions. Bush reaffirmed his support for Cheney, calling him a “great vice president” and a “friend.” The library and policy institute will serve as a forum for Bush’s continued public service, allowing him to shape his legacy without criticizing his successor.

SkyMall, the in-flight shopping magazine that once provided quirky catalogs and wacky products to bored travelers, has filed for bankruptcy, marking the end of an era for a business that thrived for decades but ultimately couldn't compete with the convenience and variety of online shopping. Founded in 1989, SkyMall’s catalogs offered everything from novelty items like personalized socks and dog beds to more practical travel essentials such as passport wallets and wrinkle-free resort wear. The company’s 2014 holiday catalog included items like a $129 Santa Claus Sculptural Glass-Topped Holiday Table and $1,000 Serenity Pods for pets, complete with a wireless sound system and LED lights.

However, SkyMall faced significant challenges. The rise of e-commerce giants like Amazon and eBay, coupled with the increasing use of electronic devices on planes, led to a decline in in-flight browsing. Delta’s contract with SkyMall ended in November 2014, and Southwest Airlines announced it would no longer carry the catalog by April 2015. By December 2014, SkyMall was facing a severe liquidity crisis, with sales from Southwest alone accounting for about 7% of its overall merchandise sales.

In its bankruptcy filing, Xhibit Corp, SkyMall’s parent company, cited in-flight Wi-Fi as a factor that lured shoppers away from the traditional catalog. The company plans to sell off its online retail business and other assets, with Xhibit listing assets of $1 million to $10 million and liabilities of $10 million to $50 million. The bankruptcy filing also noted that SkyMall’s revenue had declined sharply, from $33.7 million in 2013 to $15.8 million in the first nine months of 2014.

Despite the decline, SkyMall’s bankruptcy filing is just one part of a broader trend in the mail-order industry. According to IBISWorld analysts, mail-order businesses generated $71.4 billion in revenues in 2014, down 6% from five years earlier, and are expected to drop to $61 billion by 2019. The main reasons for this decline include a shrinking customer base and increased competition from online retailers. While some mail-order businesses have adapted by embracing online retail and mobile platforms, SkyMall’s fate highlights the challenges faced by traditional catalog companies in the digital age.

For many, SkyMall was more than just a source of quirky products; it was a comfort during long flights, a way to pass the time, and a symbol of the freedom and possibilities of travel. For the author, it was a cherished childhood memory, a way to connect with siblings and parents, and a reminder of the innocence of youth. As the catalog disappeared from the skies, so too did a piece of American travel history, replaced by the cold glow of electronic devices and the endless scroll of the internet.

Rescuers are committed to ensuring the safety of the 12 boys and their soccer coach trapped in a flooded cave in northern Thailand, as heavy rains threaten to exacerbate the situation. The boys, aged 11 to 16, and their 25-year-old coach were found alive on Monday, nine days after they entered the Tham Luang Nang Non cave during a training session, only to be trapped by rising floodwaters. They were discovered on a rock shelf about 4 km from the cave mouth, where they have received their first food and medical treatment in 10 days. Seven divers, including a doctor and a nurse, joined the group inside the caves, providing health checks and treatment, and keeping the boys entertained. The Thai authorities are considering how best to bring the group to safety, emphasizing that no risks will be taken. "We will not rush to take the lads out of the cave," Chiang Rai Governor Narongsak Osoththanakorn told reporters, adding that whoever has zero risk first can leave the cave first. The boys are being monitored for hypothermia and an airborne lung infection known as "cave disease," caused by bat and bird droppings. The Thai military has been pumping water from the underground system to reduce the risk of further flooding, and a phone line is being installed so the boys can talk to their families. The governor said that requests have been made to build "infrastructure" in the cave leading to the pocket where the teenagers and their coach are located. The Thai authorities have appealed for donations of full-face scuba diving masks small enough to fit the boys to reduce the risk of their breathing apparatus coming loose as they travel through flooded passageways. The Thai military has stated that the boys would need to learn to dive or wait up to four months for flooding to recede before they could get out of the caves. However, the governor stressed the urgency of the evacuation, adding that rain was forecast "in the next few days." Attempts are being made to reduce the risk of further flooding by pumping water from the underground system, and other teams are still scouring the mountainside in the hope of finding another way into the cave. The boys' families have been celebrating after hearing the news of their discovery, with the Thai Prime Minister Prayuth Chan-ocha saying, "everybody is a hero." The search for the group had gripped the nation as it was unclear where they were or whether they were even still alive. The boys' coach has sent out a message apologizing to the boys' parents, and the Thai authorities have appealed for donations of full-face scuba diving masks small enough to fit the boys to reduce the risk of their breathing apparatus coming loose as they travel through flooded passageways. The rescue operation is a delicate and dangerous task, with experts cautioning that taking inexperienced divers through the dangerous corridors of muddy, zero-visibility waters would be very risky. The safest option could be to supply the 12 boys and their coach where they are and wait for the water levels to drop. However, the Thai authorities are determined to bring the boys to safety as soon as possible, despite the risks involved.

A new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine has found no direct link between antidepressant use during the first three months of pregnancy and an increased risk of heart defects in babies, challenging previous research that suggested such a connection. The study, conducted by researchers at the Brigham and Women's Hospital in Boston, examined data from over 900,000 women who had given birth between 2000 and 2007, using Medicaid records to track antidepressant use and congenital heart defects. The researchers focused on the first trimester, the critical period for organ development, and found that while antidepressant use was common—13% of women took them while pregnant—the risk of heart defects did not significantly increase among infants born to mothers who used SSRIs like paroxetine (Paxil) and sertraline (Zoloft) during this time. The study controlled for various factors, including maternal health conditions and other medications, to ensure accurate results. However, the findings do not rule out the possibility that antidepressants may pose other risks to fetal development, and the researchers caution that their study only addresses heart defects. The results are significant for healthcare providers and pregnant women, as depression is common during pregnancy, and the use of antidepressants is often necessary to manage symptoms. The study's lead author, Krista Huybrechts, emphasizes the importance of individualized care, suggesting that women should discuss their options with their healthcare providers to make informed decisions about their treatment during pregnancy. The research underscores the need for further investigation into the long-term effects of antidepressants on fetal development and highlights the ongoing debate about the balance between maternal mental health and potential risks to the developing fetus.

Howard Stern, a longtime friend of Donald Trump, expressed his concerns about Trump's mental health should he win the presidency, stating that running the country might not be a healthy experience for the businessman. During an episode of his radio show, Stern emphasized that he wishes Trump had never run for president, citing Trump's desire for people to cheer for him and the potential detrimental impact on his mental well-being. Trump's frequent appearances on Stern's radio program over the past two decades, engaging in crude discussions about women and celebrities, were highlighted. Stern, an advocate for Hillary Clinton, shared his shock at Trump's decision to run and his subsequent political shifts, questioning the sincerity of Trump's stance on issues like abortion. He suggested that Trump's recent anti-Hollywood rhetoric is a strategic move to appeal to his base rather than a genuine change of heart. Stern also noted that Trump's feud with the entertainment industry and the media might not be beneficial for his mental health. Stern concluded by pointing out that every former president leaves office with gray hair, implying that the stress of the presidency can be taxing.

The parents of a 3-year-old girl who went missing after being left outside on Saturday in Richardson, Texas, have hired attorneys and are no longer cooperating with investigators, according to an attorney representing the mother. Sini Mathews, the child's mother, is distraught over the disappearance of her daughter, her attorney Kent Starr said. Starr met with the Mathews family and addressed reporters outside their home, stating that the parents have two attorneys to avoid any potential conflict of interest. However, Richardson police told NBC 5 that both parents stopped cooperating over the weekend.

The girl, named Sherin Mathews, was reportedly last seen at 3 a.m. on Saturday by her father, Wesley Mathews. Mathews told investigators that he directed the child to stand by a tree, 100 feet from their home, after she refused to drink her milk, according to police. He reported the child missing five hours later. Mathews was arrested Saturday on a child endangerment charge and was released Sunday night on $250,000 bond. His wife, Sini, was reportedly asleep during the entire incident and is not facing charges at this time.

The FBI Evidence Response team worked through the night Tuesday to process the Richardson home of the missing 3-year-old girl. An FBI Evidence Response team arrived at about 7 p.m., shortly after Richardson police knocked on the door with a search warrant. The team could be seen combing for clues in the front and back yards. The search for the adopted girl has also expanded beyond the immediate neighborhood, including making contact with sex offenders in the area and businesses that could potentially have useful surveillance video. The girl's father was arrested Saturday on a charge of abandoning or endangering a child.

Three vehicles taken from the home of the missing 3-year-old were examined for possible clues in the child's disappearance. A Lexus, driven by Sini, was returned to her late Wednesday. Two other vehicles, an Audi and a minivan, remain in police custody. The girl's mother, Sini, has hired an attorney and is seeking to regain custody of her 4-year-old biological daughter, who was taken into protective custody after Sherin's disappearance. The 4-year-old remains in foster care at least until a hearing scheduled for next month.

Richardson police provided a more detailed timeline of the disappearance, stating that Mathews returned to get his daughter about 15 minutes later but discovered she was gone. He then went inside his home, hoping she would return on her own, and did a load of laundry. He wanted to wait for daylight to search for her again. The delay in reporting the matter "is certainly concerning to us," said Sgt. Kevin Perlich. The search for the girl has intensified, with an Amber Alert being discontinued due to a lack of new information, but the alert could be re-activated in the future.

Los Angeles has become the largest U.S. city to raise its minimum wage to $15 an hour, with the city council voting overwhelmingly in favor of the legislation. The measure, which passed by a vote of 14-1, will gradually increase the city’s minimum wage to $10.50 in July 2016, with further increases every year until it reaches $15 in July 2020. For small businesses with 25 or fewer employees, the wage hike will come on a modified schedule, with incremental increases starting in July 2017 and the minimum wage reaching $15 by July 2021. The move comes as part of a broader national effort to alleviate poverty, with Maria Elena Durazo, former head of the Los Angeles County Federation of Labor, stating that the wage increase will help spur similar increases in other parts of the country. However, some labor leaders have expressed dissatisfaction with the gradual timeline set by elected leaders for raising base wages. Business groups, including the Los Angeles Area Chamber of Commerce, have warned that the mandate will force employers to lay off workers or leave the city altogether. "The very people [council members'] rhetoric claims to help with this action, it's going to hurt," said Ruben Gonzalez, the chamber's senior vice president for public policy and political affairs. He predicted that many businesses would absorb their new labor costs by laying off employees, reducing work hours, or moving out of the city entirely. "It's simple math," Gonzalez said. "There is simply not enough room, enough margin in these businesses to absorb a 50-plus percent increase in labor costs over a short period of time." Councilman Mitchell Englander, the council's only Republican, cast the lone opposing vote, arguing that the council action could "make it impossible for entire industries to do business" in Los Angeles. "The very last thing that we should be doing as a city is creating a competitive disadvantage for our businesses with those in neighboring cities," said Englander, who represents the northwest San Fernando Valley. The council's vote followed months of public debate and back-room lobbying on an issue that has animated City Hall like few others over the last year. The stakes for some low-wage Angelenos were reflected in testimony from workers such as Juan Moran, a line cook in Little Tokyo, who said the current statewide minimum wage of $9 per hour isn't enough to live on. "Sometimes I have to walk half an hour from work to get to my apartment because money's not enough to pay a ride on the bus," the Boyle Heights resident said. "Or I work 12 hours straight without stop … just to pay rent." The shift toward raising the minimum wage by local lawmakers comes at a time when the fight for $15 movement has swelled into the largest protest by low-wage workers in U.S. history. On April 15, some 60,000 workers in more than 200 U.S. cities participated in the Fight for $15 demonstrations. Advocates for higher minimum wages, including Unite Here and Raise the Wage, attended the Los Angeles city council hearing on Tuesday. The city has commissioned a report from the Institute for Research on Labor Employment from the University of California, Berkeley, which found that by increasing the minimum wage to $15.25 by 2019, as some city council members had suggested in the past, would affect 542,000 workers by 2017. While higher pay may lead to higher prices and a drop in consumer spending, those who will get a pay raise thanks to the new bill are more likely to spend more, according to the researchers. The effects of increasing the minimum wage to $15 an hour on such a large scale remain unknown, which is something that continues to worry Los Angeles lawmakers. "This is an experiment," Paul Koretz said during Tuesday’s hearing. "If anyone tells you they know exactly how this is going to go … they’re not being honest with you." Despite concerns about the possible effects of increasing the minimum wage to $15 an hour, the proposal passed. Worker rights advocates declared the vote a win for the low-wage workers. "By a vote of 14 to 1, the council directed L.A.'s city attorney to prepare legislation setting a $15 wage floor," said Christine Owens, executive director of the National Employment Law Project. "Today, Los Angeles becomes the latest and largest city to throw its support behind the legions of workers who ask for nothing less than to be paid a fair and decent wage."

Ray Lewis and the Baltimore Ravens expressed deep gratitude towards the NFL officiating crew following a game where the officials played a crucial role in securing their victory. The Ravens, who had never felt such appreciation for the referees, highlighted the importance of their performance. The game, which was pivotal for the Ravens, saw the officials make several key calls that favored the home team. These calls included crucial penalties and controversial decisions that shifted the momentum in favor of the Ravens. The team's appreciation extended beyond the game itself, as the officials' performance was seen as a lifeline in a season that had been challenging for the Ravens. Ray Lewis, a veteran linebacker known for his passionate support of the officiating crew, emphasized the critical nature of the officials' decisions. He stated, "The officials made the right calls today, and we couldn't have asked for a better outcome. They played a significant role in our victory." The Ravens' victory, bolstered by the officiating, not only secured their playoff spot but also provided a much-needed boost to the team's morale. The game's outcome highlighted the delicate balance between player performance and officiating, and the Ravens' appreciation underscored the impact of these decisions on the game's outcome. As the season draws to a close, the Ravens are keenly aware of the importance of maintaining a positive relationship with the officiating crew, recognizing that their performance can significantly influence the team's success in the playoffs.

More than 40 people were injured, and seven high school students and one teacher died after an avalanche struck a group of students and teachers during a mountaineering expedition near the Nasu Onsen ski resort north of Tokyo. The incident occurred on Monday morning as 52 students and 11 teachers from seven high schools were participating in a three-day mountaineering event. Avalanche warnings were in effect due to heavy snowfall, with over 33 cm of snow accumulating in the Nasu highlands between midnight and 9 am. An instructor reported seeing a white mass heading towards them, and as everyone tried to get down, they were engulfed. Rescue efforts were hampered by bad weather, but the self-defense force was called in to assist. The scale of the tragedy led to questions about whether the event could have been prevented, and a police inquiry was initiated. The incident highlights the risks of outdoor activities in Japan, especially during unusual snow conditions. The climbing trip began on Saturday, and the group was scheduled to ascend the mountain on Monday, but the climb was canceled due to heavy snow. Instead, the group practiced walking in the accumulated snow. The Tochigi education board stated that the training took place about 500 meters from their hotel at an altitude of 1,300 meters. The avalanche occurred on the upper part of the slope, and rescue workers carried the victims down from the mountain and transported them to hospitals. The incident underscores the need for better crisis management systems and highlights the risks associated with outdoor activities in Japan, particularly during extreme weather conditions.

At a House Oversight Committee hearing, the deputy director of the White House’s Office of National Drug Control Policy, Michael Botticelli, faced intense questioning from Rep. Gerry Connolly (D-VA) regarding the perceived dangers of marijuana. Connolly highlighted the stark contrast between marijuana and other substances, noting that while hundreds of thousands die annually from alcohol-related causes, marijuana-related deaths are extremely rare. Botticelli acknowledged the rarity of marijuana overdose deaths but maintained that marijuana is a dangerous drug, despite its lack of associated fatalities. Connolly pressed Botticelli to address President Barack Obama’s recent comments that marijuana is not more dangerous than alcohol, emphasizing the empirical accuracy of this statement. Botticelli dodged direct answers, focusing on the broader harm associated with marijuana. The hearing underscored the ongoing tension between the White House’s evolving stance on marijuana and the steadfast opposition of the Office of National Drug Control Policy. Despite President Obama’s more lenient views, the administration continues to oppose state-based efforts to legalize marijuana, maintaining that the Controlled Substances Act deems marijuana a harmful drug. This stance puts the administration in an awkward position, given that two states have legalized marijuana for adults, and 20 states and the District of Columbia have approved its use for medical purposes. The hearing also highlighted the potential impact of federal policy on public perception, with Rep. John Mica, R-Fla., suggesting that the president’s comments may contribute to a decline in the perceived risk of marijuana use among adolescents. The debate over marijuana policy further complicated by the recent vote in the D.C. city council to decriminalize marijuana possession, which could face congressional intervention. The summary of the hearing and the broader policy debate reveals a complex landscape where public health considerations, legal enforcement, and evolving societal attitudes toward marijuana intersect.

Researchers have developed sperm-inspired micro-robots that can be controlled using magnetic fields, potentially revolutionizing medical and manufacturing applications. These tiny devices, dubbed "MagnetoSperm," mimic the shape and movement of sperm cells and can be steered with precision, reports BBC News. The robots consist of a flexible tail and a metal-coated head, fabricated using a simple spin-coating method. When placed in a moving magnetic field, the metal head rotates, causing the tail to flap and propel the robot forward. This innovative design allows for precise navigation, making the robots useful for tasks such as targeted drug delivery and in vitro fertilization. Despite their small size, the robots can be steered with a magnetic field no stronger than a fridge magnet. The team aims to further miniaturize the robots and develop magnetic nanofibers for the tails, potentially expanding their applications in nanomanufacturing and medical procedures.

Liverpool manager Rafael Benitez has turned to Serbian horse placenta healer Marijana Kovacevic to address his team's injury crisis. Glen Johnson and Fabio Aurelio, both doubtful for Liverpool's upcoming match against Manchester City, have flown to Belgrade for treatment. This follows Arsenal's Robin van Persie's visit for his ruptured ankle ligaments. Kovacevic, who charges up to €3,000 for her unorthodox therapy, uses horse placenta fluids and electrolysis to treat injuries. Her methods have gained credibility, with players from major clubs like Chelsea and Manchester City also seeking her help. Kovacevic's reputation has grown to the point that even Liverpool's respected club doctor, Mark Waller, has referred players to her. However, the medical community remains skeptical, with Jeremy Laurance of The Independent questioning the scientific basis of her treatment.

A bomb scare turned into a smuggling probe when customs officials found 12 gold bars in two lunch boxes hidden in the toilets of a Jet Airways plane at Kolkata's international airport. The gold, worth 73.68 million rupees ($1.18 million), was discovered during routine cleaning after the plane arrived from Patna. The bars, weighing 1 kg each, are suspected to be from Dubai, as the plane's usual route is between Dubai and Mumbai. This incident, part of a rise in smuggling into India due to increased import duties and restrictions, highlights the challenge faced by customs officials. Over two months, 100 kg of gold has been seized in five cases. Officials believe they catch only about 10% of the total smuggling, with many groups operating undetected. To combat the issue, crews are being educated on identifying suspicious behavior, such as passengers spending unusual amounts of time in the restroom.

A teenager, Shana Grice, was murdered by her ex-boyfriend, Michael Lane, despite multiple complaints to the police over months, according to the Lewes Crown Court. Grice, 19, was found with her throat slit in her bedroom in Portslade, East Sussex, in August. Lane, 27, denies murder. The prosecution outlined a timeline of Grice's interactions with the police, highlighting instances where her complaints were not taken seriously. In February, she reported being stalked and harassed by Lane, who had hidden outside her home, sent unwanted flowers, and left a threatening note on her new boyfriend's car. In March, Lane was denied a charge for allegedly assaulting Grice, and she was issued a fixed penalty notice for failing to disclose their relationship and causing a "wasteful employment of police." On July 9, Lane was cautioned for stealing a key to enter Grice's home and watching her sleep. The next day, Grice reported receiving calls with heavy breathing, but the police did not pursue further action. On July 12, she told the police she had been followed by Lane, but the case was deemed "low risk." Lane admitted to leaving a note on Grice's boyfriend's car and fitting a tracker to her vehicle. He also claimed to have had sex with Grice at her home and met her in a hotel. On the day of her death, Lane said he found Grice's body, went into shock, and did not call 999. He denied torching the room and claimed he had bought petrol for suicide. Lane admitted lying in police interviews. The trial was adjourned until Monday.

Oklahoma Rep. Frank Lucas, who has been in Congress for 20 years, won his Republican primary with 82.8 percent of the vote, defeating his opponent Tim Murray, who received only 5.2 percent. However, Murray has taken his loss to an extreme level, announcing plans to contest the election results on the grounds that Lucas is dead and has been replaced by a look-alike. In a letter to local news station KFOR and on his campaign website, Murray claims that Lucas was executed by the world court in Ukraine on January 11, 2011. Lucas, who has been releasing campaign commercials in the Oklahoma City area, told KFOR that the accusation is "a shock" and "kind of a shock to read that you’re not you." 

The Oklahoma State Election Board representative, Paul Ziriax, stated that Murray has not yet filed a formal petition to challenge the results. The deadline for challenging the qualifications of a candidate was April 15, and Murray has until 5 p.m. on the day of the story to make a decision. Stacy Buck, a representative for Lucas, confirmed that the congressman is alive and has never been to Ukraine, but declined to comment further. 

Murray's campaign website has been promoting his theory for a long time, with a press release sent out after the primary. He asserts that "it is widely known Rep. Frank D. Lucas is no longer alive and has been displayed by a look-alike," and adds that "Rep. Lucas’ look-alike was depicted as sentenced on a white stage in southern Ukraine on or about Jan. 11, 2011." Murray also claims that he will never use a look-alike to replace his message to anyone else, as both other Republican challengers have done. 

This bizarre situation has drawn attention from political analysts, with Keith Gaddie at the University of Oklahoma calling it "the stupidest [he's] ever heard," adding, "Welcome to Oklahoma." The story highlights the unusual and often absurd nature of Oklahoma politics, where a candidate can contest an election based on the premise that his opponent is a look-alike.

Meet Mark Block, Herman Cain's top adviser and the newest YouTube sensation in the 2012 presidential campaign. Block stars in a bizarre new ad for Cain, which was posted to Cain's campaign account. The ad features Block, the former Wisconsin political operative, reflecting on the campaign and puffing on a cigarette. “We’ve run a campaign like nobody’s ever seen,” Block says. “But then, America’s never seen a candidate like Herman Cain.” The ad ends with a dramatic song, and Block reveals in slow motion that he is smoking a cigarette. The ad concludes with a profile of Herman Cain. The inclusion of the smoking scene has sparked much debate, with many speculating on its meaning. Some suggest it could be a defiant response to media scrutiny of Cain's past association with the tobacco industry. Others believe it’s an attempt to appeal to working-class Republicans or to gain viral attention. Block himself has denied any deeper meaning, stating that the ad was meant to show supporters that the campaign is on a roll. However, the ad has become a hot topic of discussion, with many finding it strange and unorthodox. The campaign has defended the ad, claiming it has generated significant attention. The bizarre nature of the ad, combined with Cain's other unconventional moves, has raised questions about the candidate's seriousness and staying power in the race.

In a case spanning over four decades, DNA evidence led to the arrests of two men in connection with the brutal murders of two young girls in California. The 13-year-old Doris Karen Derryberry and 12-year-old Valerie Janice Lane, both from Olivehurst, went missing on November 12, 1973, after failing to return from a shopping trip in Linda, a town near their home. Their bodies were discovered the next day in a wooded area near Marysville, north of Sacramento, where they had been shot at close range with a shotgun. The case remained unsolved for years, with a large-scale investigation yielding no significant leads until 1976, when the case went cold. However, in March 2014, an investigator with the Yuba County Sheriff's Department decided to re-examine the case using advanced DNA testing techniques. Semen samples found on Derryberry’s body were retested, and the DNA matched that of two cousins, Larry Don Patterson and William Lloyd Harbour.

Patterson, 65, was arrested in Oklahoma, while Harbour, also 65, was apprehended in California. Both suspects were living in Olivehurst at the time of the murders. Patterson had a history of raping two women in 1976 and failing to register as a sex offender in 2006, while Harbour had felony drug convictions. The families of the victims, who have endured decades of grief and unanswered questions, were informed of the arrests on Tuesday. The case, which shocked the small community and the nation, was reopened after the DNA evidence matched the suspects’ profiles. The investigation, which involved extensive searches in multiple states, finally brought closure to the families after 43 years. Both suspects are expected to face murder charges, marking a significant milestone in the long-standing cold case.

Yesterday, AllOut.org faced a significant cyber attack on their petition aimed at countering anti-gay boycott groups pressuring Electronic Arts (EA) over the inclusion of gay characters in their games. The petition, launched to support EA's decision, was hit with spam comments and signatures, with estimates of 3,000 to 5,000 fake comments. AllOut.org's Community Manager, Tile Wolfe, confirmed that the site has no contact with EA and that the campaign was launched to counter anti-gay boycotts by groups like the Family Research Council. Despite the spam, AllOut.org maintains that over 60,000 members have signed the petition. The organization is working to remove the spam and update the signature count. Meanwhile, the gaming community and press are divided, with some attributing the spam to EA as a PR move and others suspecting the boycott groups. AllOut.org emphasizes their support for EA's decision and the importance of LGBT inclusion in video games. The incident highlights the ongoing tensions and debates surrounding LGBT representation in the gaming industry and the use of online petitions and campaigns to influence corporate policies.

Sarah Catherine Long, 41, was found dead in her Davidson, North Carolina, townhouse on July 23, with a single gunshot wound above her left ear. Initially classified as a suicide, the case has taken a mysterious turn as authorities noticed inconsistencies. The gun was found in her left hand, despite her being right-handed, and no blood was found on the hand she would have fired with. Long's death is now considered suspicious, and a thorough investigation is ongoing. Among the key points: Long was married but had a secret affair with William Becker, a married man. Documents showed Long left her $1 million fortune to Becker, raising suspicions. Neighbors reported seeing Becker at Long's home on July 19, the last time she was seen alive. One neighbor heard a loud bang. A search warrant revealed Becker claimed Long was depressed and had been diagnosed with cervical cancer, but her doctor refuted this. Long's estranged husband, Christopher Reeves, said she seemed fine on the day she died. Police are also investigating whether Long was drugged and whether gunpowder residue was found on her hands. A person of interest has been identified, but no arrests have been made. Authorities are examining Long's electronic and financial records, hoping to uncover more clues.

Saudi media outlets Al-Hayat and Sabq.org fell for a joke by US satirist Andy Borowitz, reporting his column as a serious statement from President Obama. In the column, Borowitz wrote that Obama might agree he is a Muslim to find common ground with Republicans, and even suggested Obama could claim he was born in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean to satisfy both sides. Despite Obama's repeated assertions of being Christian, the article notes that many Muslims and some US Republicans suspect he is secretly Muslim. The satirical piece was taken seriously by influential Saudi newspapers, highlighting the ongoing tension over Obama's religious identity and its political implications.

Step away from the microwave, iPhone owners. While the newly released iOS 8 boasts several impressive features, including app extensions and improved keyboard options, the software upgrade does not — we repeat, does not — let it be wirelessly recharged in the microwave, contrary to a 4chan hoax. See also: The 18 Most Important Features in iOS 8. The fake "Wave" ads, which have been circulating on Twitter and Reddit since the iOS update debuted last Wednesday, are simply untrue, trolling Apple users into ruining their phones by microwaving them for 60 to 70 seconds. Reddit users are attributing the hoax to a 4chan thread. This isn't the first time a microwaving-your-iPhone hoax has made the rounds. Videos on YouTube have touted the fake feature for years — and most likely, that's where 4chan users got the idea. 4chan has previously attempted similar hoaxes. Last year, a spoof attempted to convince Apple users that iOS 7 would make your phone waterproof. It's unclear how many people fell for the Wave hoax — after all, everyone on the Internet lies and nothing is real and the world is upside down. But several people tweeted about the feature and later posted photos of fried iPhones and burned microwaves; we hope they were joking, too.

Cuba has achieved a significant milestone in global health by becoming the first country to eliminate mother-to-child transmission of both HIV and syphilis, according to the World Health Organization (WHO). This accomplishment, validated by an international delegation from WHO and the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), marks a major victory in the fight against these diseases. In 2013, only two children in Cuba were born with HIV, and five with syphilis, demonstrating the effectiveness of the country's healthcare system. Cuba's success highlights the feasibility of achieving universal access and universal health coverage, even against daunting challenges. The WHO credits Cuba with providing early prenatal care, HIV and syphilis testing, and treatment for mothers who test positive. This achievement is seen as a beacon of hope, potentially inspiring other countries to follow Cuba's lead in addressing similar health issues. Cuba's Communist government views its free healthcare system as a major achievement of the 1959 revolution, though ordinary Cubans have faced declining standards since the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991. The PAHO and WHO have initiated efforts to end congenital transmission of HIV and syphilis in Cuba and other countries in the Americas, with Cuba's success setting a precedent for global health initiatives.

A search warrant revealed that a Minnesota doctor, Dr. Michael Todd Schulenberg, treated Prince twice in the month before his death, including the day before he was found unconscious in a Paisley Park elevator on April 21, 2016. Schulenberg saw Prince on April 7 and April 20, and prescribed him medications, according to the warrant. Schulenberg no longer works at the North Memorial Medical Center in Robbinsdale, where his medical records were searched. The warrant also disclosed that Schulenberg had given Prince a prescription to be filled at a Walgreens. Local and federal investigators returned to Paisley Park on May 10, 2016, to continue their work. Schulenberg's attorney declined to comment, citing patient confidentiality. The investigation also involves Dr. Howard Kornfeld, who dispatched his son to meet with Prince on April 21, along with another doctor certified to prescribe buprenorphine, a medication used in treating opioid addiction. Prince had reportedly been seeking treatment for addiction to painkillers in the weeks before his death. Kirk Anthony Johnson, Prince's close associate, was present when investigators arrived at the death scene. The investigation is examining the means by which Prince received prescription opioids, which are subject to federal regulation. The Midwest Medical Examiner’s Office in Anoka is conducting the investigation to determine how Prince died. Results are pending, and neither foul play nor suicide is suspected. The warrant also mentions that Prince had visited the Highway 212 Medical Center for an illness in 2014 or 2015, where he was given fluids. The Carver County Sheriff’s Office has not disclosed the nature of the tests Schulenberg had planned to deliver at Paisley Park. The investigation continues, with authorities searching for answers about the source of the prescription medications and the circumstances surrounding Prince's death.

When Robert Wang was laid off from his software engineering job in 2008, he turned his attention to a personal challenge: creating a device that could help busy parents prepare healthy dinners. The result was the "Instant Pot," a multi-functional kitchen appliance that can serve as a rice cooker, pressure cooker, steamer, and slow cooker, among other roles. The Instant Pot has since become a top seller on Amazon, with versions regularly ranking as the best in their categories. The device has also received praise from food experts, including J. Kenji López-Alt and Melissa Clark. According to market analyst Joe Derochowski, the growth of the multi-cooker market has been dramatic, with a 68 percent increase in the last year and a 90 percent increase in 2016. Wang, now the CEO of Double Insight, the company that produces the Instant Pot, credits the product's success to its ability to solve the time-crunch faced by many families. The Instant Pot features a burn detection mechanism, multiple sensors, and Bluetooth connectivity, ensuring food is cooked perfectly and remotely monitored. Wang's company became profitable in 2012, and it has doubled in revenue every year since. The Instant Pot has also helped people in need, with customers from Florida and Texas using the device during hurricanes Harvey and Irma. Wang's company has a large cache of new products ready to be launched starting in 2018, and the device continues to gain popularity in the U.S. and Canada. The Instant Pot's promise to make slow-cooked foods faster has proved irresistible to time-strapped home cooks, and its features, including digital controls, modern safety features, and a few extra functions, have made pressure-cooking accessible to a wider audience. The device has also sparked a new wave of cookbooks and cooking classes, with the Instant Pot becoming a must-have in many households.

Authorities have arrested Orlando Tercero, 22, in connection with the homicide of 22-year-old nursing student Haley Anderson from Long Island. Tercero, Anderson's ex-boyfriend, was detained in Nicaragua and is being transferred to the prison in El Chipote, about 40 miles southwest of Managua, the capital. Anderson's body was discovered in a Binghamton off-campus home by police around 1 p.m. on Friday. The circumstances of her death have not been revealed, but police stated that Tercero had a previous domestic/romantic relationship with Anderson. They also noted that he had left the United States by international air travel prior to the discovery of Anderson's body. Tercero is believed to have flown to Nicaragua due to family connections in the country. The investigation revealed that Anderson was last seen alive around 4 a.m. on Thursday, with her roommates. The university community expressed condolences to Anderson's family and friends, noting that she was a nursing student and had recently completed an internship at a local hospital. The case is being handled by the Broome County District Attorney's office, which will present all evidence to a grand jury. If Tercero is indicted, a speedy extradition process will be initiated.

India's foreign ministry has lodged a formal complaint with Saudi Arabian authorities following a "brutal" incident involving an Indian domestic worker named Kasturi Munirathinam, who had her right arm severed by her Saudi employer. The 58-year-old worker was reportedly mistreated and harassed by her employers, who allegedly cut off her arm after she complained to the police. Munirathinam is currently recovering in a hospital in Riyadh, with her sister stating that her spinal cord was also injured in the incident. Her family claims that she was not allowed to speak to her relatives, was given inadequate food, and was forced to work long hours. The Indian government has expressed deep concern over the case, with Foreign Minister Sushma Swaraj tweeting that the incident is "unacceptable" and that the embassy is in contact with the victim. The Indian foreign ministry spokesperson, Vikas Swarup, stated that the embassy has requested strict action and severe punishment for the sponsor and urged for an independent investigation, suggesting that a case of attempted murder be filed against the employer. The incident has drawn attention to the plight of thousands of Indian workers who travel to the Middle East each year for domestic work, often facing harsh conditions and abuse. The family is seeking compensation and financial assistance from the Tamil Nadu state government and the Indian government to cover Munirathinam's medical expenses and to facilitate her return to India. The case has further strained relations between India and Saudi Arabia, following a recent accusation of a Saudi diplomat in India allegedly raping domestic workers.

Electronic construction signs in the Dallas area were hacked, displaying messages targeting Donald Trump and Bernie Sanders. The portable signs along Interstate 30 and elsewhere flashed messages early Tuesday, including "Donald Trump is a ... shape shifting lizard!" and "Bernie for president." Another sign read, "Work is canceled. Go back home." The Texas Department of Transportation (TxDOT) told Dallas-Fort Worth broadcaster KRLD that the messages replaced warnings to motorists about nearby construction zones. TxDOT spokesman Tony Hartzel said the signs have been removed and steps have been taken to secure them. Before the political hack, the signs were altered over the Memorial Day weekend, displaying "Party Hardy Yall!" TxDOT officials are concerned about the "serious issue" that could cause problems if drivers don't get the messages. Hacking these roadside signs is a third-degree felony, punishable by up to 10 years in prison. TxDOT encourages people to report any suspicious activity around portable signs, especially when there is no construction. The signs are meant to warn drivers about road construction in the area, and hacking them is not easy. The perpetrator had to cut a lock off of a box and reset the sign’s passwords. TxDOT is taking the matter seriously and is warning against such actions.

Rescue efforts for survivors in a massive mudslide that killed at least eight people and destroyed dozens of homes in Washington state have yielded no more signs of life, officials said Sunday. The death toll rose to eight with the confirmation of four additional bodies, bringing the total unaccounted for to 108, though officials expect the actual number of victims to be lower. The slide, which occurred on March 22, devastated a mile-wide area, including 30 homes and a mile-long stretch of Highway 530. Despite hearing voices on Saturday night, rescuers were forced to abandon their search due to darkness and shifting debris. By Sunday, they heard no more voices. "We didn’t see or hear any signs of life out there today," said Travis Hots, chief of Snohomish County Fire Districts 21 and 22. Casualties include a 4-month-old baby and her grandmother, who were among the missing. The slide, caused by heavy rainfall, blocked the North Fork of the Stillaguamish River, leading to concerns about downstream flooding. The river began breaking through the mud dam, but officials said it was not a cause for immediate alarm. Governor Jay Inslee warned of grim days ahead, emphasizing the need for empathy and compassion. Over 100 rescue personnel from various agencies joined the search, but the difficult terrain hampered their efforts. The slide's impact was felt by the close-knit community, with many residents still waiting for news of loved ones.

A 18-year-old hiker named Chloe Jakubowski and several others were caught in a deadly ice cave collapse in the Mount Baker-Snoqualmie National Forest on a scorching Monday afternoon. Jakubowski, who had recently moved to Bothell from Napa, California, was among the dozens of people seeking relief from the heat by exploring the Big Four Ice Caves. The caves, a popular hiking destination, can be treacherous during warm weather, as the melting snow and ice can cause sections to collapse. Jakubowski and her friends were inside the cave when a loud crack echoed, followed by ice and debris raining down. Jakubowski described the scene as "extremely gruesome," noting that a woman next to her was unconscious and that nearby hikers lay with cuts and broken bones.

Rescue efforts were delayed for nearly 45 minutes due to a lack of cellphone reception in the area, according to the Snohomish County Sheriff’s Office. One person was killed, and five others were injured, two of whom were in critical condition. The body of the deceased remained at the scene as teams assessed the safety of the ice. Three adults—two men and a woman—were airlifted to Harborview Medical Center in Seattle, where the 25-year-old man was upgraded from critical to serious condition, and the 35-year-old man was upgraded from serious to satisfactory condition. Two girls were treated and released from Providence Regional Medical Center in Everett with minor injuries.

The cave-in occurred as the area experienced a heat wave, with temperatures reaching 80 degrees. The Snohomish County Sheriff’s Office had issued a warning in May, advising visitors to stay on the trail and avoid standing on top of the caves. In 2010, 11-year-old Grace Tam was killed by a boulder of ice that came off the caves, leading to a lawsuit against the U.S. Forest Service. The lawsuit was dismissed, but a sign now warns visitors of the potential danger. The area around the Big Four Ice Caves will remain closed indefinitely as search and rescue teams continue to assess the safety of the site.

A team of students, staff, professors, and alumni from Point Loma Nazarene University (PLNU) is launching a campaign to seed The Beauty for Ashes Fund with $40,000, aiming to bring a college education to survivors of human trafficking. Sex and labor trafficking have reached epidemic proportions in the United States and globally, with PLNU’s Center for Justice and Reconciliation (CJR) actively engaged in the issue both locally and internationally. The CJR works with direct service providers, law enforcement, and other movement leaders, and survivors consistently express a desire for a college education. PLNU believes that a university education is a critical component for the long-term rehabilitation of survivors. The campaign’s goal is to provide survivors with financial support for tuition, room and board, vocational discernment, and administrative support. Even if the $40,000 goal is not met, PLNU will still receive the funds raised, and all will go to the Beauty for Ashes Fund. The campaign emphasizes that donors should focus on the dream of providing education for survivors, rather than perks. The university hopes to fund more than one student and is already working with survivors who are applying. PLNU is a Christian university dedicated to providing higher education in a supportive environment where minds are engaged, character is formed, and service is an expression of faith. The university aims to support the most vulnerable, not just the privileged, and is committed to addressing the issue of human trafficking. Other ways to support the campaign include sharing it on social media or contacting the university at BeautyforAshes@pointloma.edu.
