Facebook has developed several internal systems to enhance user security and introduced two new features: a secured connection and social authentication. The secured connection allows users to access Facebook entirely over HTTPS, ensuring data privacy, especially when using public Wi-Fi. Users can enable this feature in their Account Settings. Social authentication aims to verify user identities through friend recognition, adding an extra layer of security. While these features are steps in the right direction, they require user activation and may not be fully implemented across all platforms. Facebook's commitment to enhancing user security is crucial, given the increasing number of security breaches and the need for robust protection measures.

A pregnant server at a Delaware restaurant became a hero to two Maine families after her Facebook search helped find their missing teenage daughters. Lisa Stephenson, 26, and six months pregnant, noticed two young girls applying for jobs at her Blue Crab Grill in Newark, Delaware, on November 2, 2015. The girls seemed too young to be working and had no home addresses or phone numbers on their applications. Concerned, Stephenson did a Facebook search and found a missing persons post for a 16-year-old girl from Brunswick, Maine, and a 14-year-old from Bath, Maine, who had disappeared together on October 25 after a babysitting job. Stephenson contacted the girls' mothers and local police, who tracked down the girls, who had driven south from Maine, through Boston and New York, in a stolen car. The girls had planned a "Thelma and Louise" style trip, stopping in Washington, D.C., for gas but were warned to leave the city. They ended up panhandling in Waldorf, Maryland, where they were found by police. Upon their return to Maine, the girls were grounded, and the older one was banned from using social media. Stephenson's actions helped ensure the girls' safety and earned her praise from the families. Stephenson, who is six months pregnant, said she just wanted to help, as she would want someone to assist her if her daughter were ever missing.

Britain's Prince Harry and Meghan Markle will marry at Windsor Castle's St. George's Chapel in May, Kensington Palace announced. The 15th-century chapel, west of London, is more intimate than Westminster Abbey, where Harry's older brother William married Kate Middleton in 2011. Markle, an American actress, will be baptized in the Church of England and become a British citizen, though the process will take several years. The couple, who have been dating for about a year and a half, announced their engagement on November 27, 2017. Harry proposed to Markle over a roast chicken dinner at his London home, after months of keeping their long-distance relationship private. Markle's future sister-in-law, the Duchess of Cambridge, expressed excitement for the couple, saying, "It's such exciting news." The couple will live in Nottingham Cottage on the grounds of Kensington Palace, and Markle's two dogs will join them in the UK. Harry and Markle's first official joint engagement event will be in Nottingham on December 1, 2017, to mark World AIDS Day. The Church of England will perform the wedding, and Markle will be asked a series of questions to ensure she is ready for remarriage. The couple's engagement has been hailed as a symbol of a modernizing monarchy, bringing a fresh and diverse perspective to the institution.

Kristina Chesterman, a 21-year-old nursing student, tragically died in September 2013 after being hit by an allegedly drunk driver near Chico State University, where she attended school. Her death left her family and friends devastated, but it also led to a remarkable legacy of life-saving organ donations. Five Northern Californians received the gift of life through Kristina's decision to donate her organs, including Jayden Kirby, a 1-year-old boy who was given months to live before receiving part of Kristina's liver. Jayden's mother, Christine Kirby, met the Chestermans through Facebook and celebrated Jayden's first birthday with them, expressing gratitude for the transplant that saved her son's life. Kristina's mother, Sandra Chesterman, shared that her daughter had written a bucket list in high school, including the desire to save a life, which Kristina fulfilled through her organ donation. The Chestermans have formed a close bond with the Pappachans, a Fremont family who received a kidney from Kristina, and the two families have spent time together, including attending Christmas Eve services. Kristina's legacy extends beyond organ donation; her friends and family have taken on her bucket list, inspired by her desire to join Doctors Without Borders. For instance, Bridget Kline, a Livermore resident, went skydiving over the ocean, knowing it would have meant a lot to Kristina. Sandra Chesterman believes her daughter's spirit continues to guide them, providing signs of inspiration. Kristina's heart was given to Susan Vieira, a 64-year-old retired nurse in Campbell, Calif. Vieira, who had already accomplished many of the items on Kristina's bucket list, met the Chestermans and has pledged to complete the rest of Kristina's list in her honor. Through these actions, Kristina Chesterman's impact continues to grow, touching the lives of many and fulfilling her desire to make a difference.

This year's Christmas advert from Poland's online auction website, Allegro, has gone viral, touching the hearts of millions. The ad tells the story of a grandfather who learns English to reconnect with his family living abroad, symbolizing the longing of many Poles who have moved to other countries in search of work. The campaign, titled "Worlds Apart - #OpenYourWorld," aims to highlight the challenges of maintaining family ties despite physical distance. The grandfather's journey to fluency is depicted through humorous scenes of him sticking Post-It notes around his home with English words, reflecting the universal experience of learning a new language. The ad's message resonates widely, as it can be easily related to by any community facing similar challenges of separation and longing. The slogan, "What are you looking for?" encapsulates the essence of the campaign, encouraging viewers to reflect on their own lives and the importance of family connections. The ad's success is evident in the overwhelming response it has garnered, with over two and a half million views and a significant increase in followers for the grandfather's Instagram account. The story not only showcases the power of technology in bridging gaps but also emphasizes the enduring bond between family members, no matter the distance.

President Obama on Tuesday called for Congress to delay the sequester, a series of automatic spending cuts set to take effect March 1, to allow time for a "smarter solution." Obama urged lawmakers to pass a small package of spending cuts and tax changes to postpone the cuts for several months, emphasizing that without action, the $1.2 trillion in sequester cuts over a decade could harm the economic recovery. The White House stated it would work with Congress to craft such a package. However, House Speaker John Boehner (R-Ohio) rejected the idea of tax increases, maintaining that the sequester should be replaced with spending cuts and reforms aimed at balancing the budget in 10 years. The sequester, designed to force significant deficit reduction, has been postponed twice since its inception in 2011. Obama's proposal to Boehner in December, which included ending tax breaks for the wealthy and industries, remains on the table. Meanwhile, the government faces another deadline to fund itself through March 27, and there is a looming debt ceiling increase in the summer. The Congressional Budget Office projected a federal budget deficit of under $1 trillion by the end of 2013, the first such reduction in five years, largely due to tax hikes and sequester cuts. Democrats in the Senate, like Patty Murray, supported Obama's call for a balanced short-term sequestration replacement. The sequester, which indiscriminately cuts most domestic and defense programs, could deliver a fresh blow to the economy if left in place.

Martin Shkreli, the 32-year-old CEO of Turing Pharmaceuticals, has become the most hated man in America, facing intense backlash for raising the price of the drug Daraprim by 5,000%, from $13.50 to $750 per pill. His aggressive defense of the price increase and brash social media interactions have earned him numerous harsh criticisms, including being labeled a "morally bankrupt sociopath" and a "scumbag." Shkreli's controversial actions stem from his background as a former hedge fund manager who founded Turing Pharmaceuticals after being ousted from his previous company, Retrophin, amid allegations of financial misconduct. Turing's acquisition of Daraprim, a 62-year-old drug for treating parasitic infections, highlighted the broader issue of skyrocketing generic drug prices, which have increased by thousands of percent in recent years. Critics argue that pharmaceutical companies are exploiting their near-monopoly on certain drugs to maximize profits, often at the expense of patients who rely on these medications. The outrage over Shkreli's actions has led to calls for regulatory reform, with Hillary Clinton proposing a plan to address the issue. However, experts debate the effectiveness of such measures, with some suggesting that regulatory changes aimed at speeding up the generic drug approval process could be more impactful. Despite the public pressure, Shkreli ultimately agreed to lower the price of Daraprim to an "affordable level," though the exact new price remains unclear. His actions have sparked a broader conversation about the ethics of drug pricing and the role of pharmaceutical companies in the healthcare system.

Sacha Baron Cohen has stepped in to help six Czech tourists who were fined for wearing mankinis, inspired by his character Borat, in Kazakhstan. The tourists were arrested and fined 22,500 Tenge ($67.7) each for "minor hooliganism" after posing in the capital city of Astana. In a Facebook post, Cohen offered to pay their fines, writing, "To my Czech mates who were arrested. Send me your details and proof that it was you, and I'll pay your fine." The response on Kazakh social media has been mixed, with some users calling for harsher punishment and others praising Cohen for promoting Kazakhstan through his actions. The incident highlights the lasting impact of the Borat character and the mankini, which has become a controversial piece of swimwear in various parts of the world. In 2012, mankinis and other "inappropriate clothing" were banned in Newquay to reduce crime and improve the town's reputation. Cohen's involvement in this case has reignited discussions about the character's influence and the potential for comedy to inadvertently promote tourism or cultural awareness.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) is set to announce his presidential bid on Monday, signaling the start of his campaign to become the first Republican candidate in the 2016 race. Cruz, known for his uncompromising conservative stance, plans to launch his campaign outright without forming an exploratory committee, aiming to raise between $40 million and $50 million. His strategy hinges on rallying his base of tea party and social conservative voters, who supported his Senate campaign in 2012. However, critics argue that Cruz will struggle to secure high-dollar donations, gain establishment endorsements, and escape comparisons to President Obama. Despite these challenges, Cruz believes he can win over enough voters to challenge the Republican establishment candidate, potentially becoming a formidable contender. His campaign will focus on mobilizing conservative voters who oppose the "mushy middle" and are eager for a strong conservative voice. Cruz's announcement comes after months of hints and speculation, with other prominent Republicans like Jeb Bush, Scott Walker, Rand Paul, and Marco Rubio expected to follow suit.

Parliament in Athens appeared close to approving a set of unpopular austerity measures after a day of intense political maneuvering on Tuesday. The measures, which include wage cuts, tax increases, and privatizations, are necessary for Greece to receive the next installment of aid from foreign lenders to avoid default. Prime Minister George A. Papandreou, who has a five-vote parliamentary majority, faces opposition from his Socialist Party base and the center-right New Democracy opposition. A key supporter, Thomas Robopoulos, changed his stance, supporting the measures to "put the national interest above everything else." The nation’s unions began a 48-hour general strike, adding to the political and economic pressure. The European Union, European Central Bank, and International Monetary Fund have said they will release $17 billion if Parliament passes the measures. Demonstrations turned violent as youths threw rocks and set fires, with 23 people detained and five arrested. The measures must pass two parliamentary votes on Wednesday and Thursday to secure the aid. Without the aid, Greece faces the prospect of default next month, potentially dragging down European banks and other financially troubled countries. Prime Minister Papandreou urged lawmakers to fulfill a "patriotic duty" by voting in favor, while European officials stressed the importance of avoiding default. Despite the measures, many Greeks remain opposed, believing the crisis is due to politicians' mismanagement.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet has been donating their daily crawl data to the Internet Archive, which is then added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. This archive captures websites, blogs, and editorials from 17 Russian political and cultural figures who have expressed opposition to Vladimir Putin’s policies, including Rustem Adagamov, Sergei Aleksashenko, and Aleksei Naval’nyi. The archive also includes sites like Civil Platform, dedicated to civil society and economic reform, and Traitor.net, which criticizes Russian actions in Ukraine. Meanwhile, in New York City, a video of birds flying in a formation resembling Vladimir Putin's face has gone viral. While some Russian users see it as a message, others dismiss it as a fake. The video, posted by Sheryl Gilbert, has garnered over a million views, with Russian TV station Zvezda pointing it out and suggesting it could be a warning to the U.S. or a prank. The incident highlights the ongoing tension between Russia and the U.S., and the creative ways in which Russian media uses symbolism to convey messages.

In the aftermath of the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster, wildlife in the exclusion zone surrounding the damaged power plant has shown remarkable resilience, according to a study published in the journal Current Biology. After a fire and explosion released radioactive particles, the area was evacuated, leading to the abandonment of human activities such as hunting, farming, and forestry. Researchers found that the abundance of elk, roe deer, red deer, wild boar, and wolves within the 4,200 km² Chernobyl Exclusion Zone is now similar to that in four uncontaminated nature reserves in the region. The number of wolves living in and around the Chernobyl site is more than seven times greater than in nearby nature reserves, highlighting the impact of human absence on wildlife populations.

The study, led by Tatiana Deryabina from the Polessye State Radioecological Reserve in Belarus, utilized long-term census data and aerial surveys to test three hypotheses: that radiation suppressed mammal populations, that large mammal densities were lower in the exclusion zone compared to uncontaminated reserves, and that mammal densities declined after the accident. The empirical data showed no evidence of long-term radiation damage to large mammal populations, contradicting previous studies that suggested initial drops in wildlife numbers. Instead, the relative abundance of elk and wild boar increased in the early 1990s, coinciding with a decline in these species in other parts of the former Soviet Union due to rural poverty and weakened wildlife management.

The researchers attribute the higher wolf population to the lack of hunting in the exclusion zone, which has allowed the predators to thrive. However, the study does not address potential health effects of radiation on individual animals, such as increased mutation rates, cancers, or other abnormalities. The findings suggest that the absence of human activity, rather than radiation, has had a more significant positive impact on wildlife. This study underscores the importance of considering the broader ecological impacts of human presence on wildlife conservation efforts, even in areas affected by severe environmental disasters.

An elderly couple from South Texas died and their son was injured after a swarm of bees attacked them on their remote ranch, authorities said. The incident occurred on Monday when William Steele, 95, and his wife Myrtle, 92, were cleaning a hunting cabin on their ranch near Hebbronville. Their son, Richard, 67, was also present and was injured during the attack. Richard immediately drove about 15 miles to the nearest road to call for help on a cell phone. William Steele tried to escape the bees by running from the cabin but fell and succumbed to hundreds of bee stings. Myrtle Steele was airlifted to a Corpus Christi hospital, where she died the following day after being stung more than 300 times. Richard Steele was transported to a Laredo hospital and released. Jim Hogg County deputies arrived at the scene and were stung by the bees but managed to locate Myrtle alive inside the home. They were unable to identify the species of bees, which were likely Africanized honey bees, also known as "killer bees," due to their aggression. The Steeles had bought the land to raise cattle and for hunting. The incident left Richard Steele feeling guilty for not doing more to help his parents.

A Michigan nurse, Iris Zink, MSN, RN, went above and beyond the call of duty to save the life of a longtime patient, Ginny Holcomb, reports Fox 47 News. Zink, who has been a nurse for about 18 years and often forms close bonds with her patients, had been treating Holcomb for over 15 years. Holcomb was diagnosed with kidney cancer, and Zink, who had become a close friend of Holcomb, did not hesitate to offer one of her kidneys. After a year of tests, Zink and Holcomb discovered they were a perfect match. The transplant surgery took place in July, and both women have since recovered. Zink says, "There was just no hesitation. I didn't want to see her die. I couldn't watch it." Holcomb adds, "It's a beautiful thing to have someone else's body part in you." The two women now wear necklaces shaped like kidneys to symbolize their life-saving bond. They hope their story will inspire others to consider organ donation. "We're bonded for life; she's got part of me in her," Zink says. "It's a beautiful thing to have someone else's body part in you," Holcomb echoes. Both women emphasize that the other is the hero of their story. For more information on being a donor, visit kidney.org/transplantation/beadonor.

Research In Motion (RIM), the company behind BlackBerry, is expected to report a net loss for its first fiscal quarter, marking a significant downturn for the once-dominant smartphone maker. Analysts predict a loss of 3 cents per share on $3.1 billion in revenue, compared to a profit of $1.33 per share on nearly $5 billion in revenue the previous year. The company's troubles are multifaceted, including plummeting device sales, a confusing leadership structure, and a strategic misstep in overconfidence in its keyboard devices as touch-screen smartphones gained popularity. RIM's dual CEO model, with Mike Lazaridis and Jim Balsillie each having separate fiefs, led to internal disagreements and a lack of cohesive strategy. The company's market share has dwindled, with BlackBerry phones now accounting for only 6% of the global market, down from 20% just three years ago. RIM's market value has shrunk to under $5 billion, with its stock down nearly 70% in the past year. The company is now focused on launching its new BlackBerry 10 OS and devices, but the success of this rollout is uncertain. Former executives and analysts suggest that RIM may need to consider a sale or partnership to secure its future, as the company struggles to adapt to the rapidly changing smartphone landscape.

More than $1 million in jewelry was stolen from a store on a historic plaza in Santa Fe during a holiday tree-lighting festival. Santa Fe police Lt. Michele Williams said 11 items were taken from an unlocked case in a store crowded with shoppers. The suspects, a woman and two men, had scouted the store in the weeks before the theft. Police are distributing images of the suspects taken from security camera footage on the day of the theft and in the weeks leading up to it. The jewelry was removed between 5:15 p.m. and 5:30 p.m. the night after Thanksgiving, and the jewelry store employees discovered the items were missing at about 6 p.m. Santa Fe police are seeking help from the public to crack the case and can be reached at 505-428-3710. The incident has raised concerns among other merchants in the plaza, who fear they could be next.

North Carolina lawmakers have approved a bill that significantly expands where concealed handguns can be carried, sending it to Governor Pat McCrory for his signature or veto. The bill, which passed the House 73-41 and the Senate 32-14, allows concealed handgun permit holders to bring their weapons to bars and restaurants that serve alcohol, provided they do not consume alcohol themselves. It also permits storing firearms in locked cars on college and public school campuses. Additionally, the measure removes information about those with concealed handgun permits from public view, strengthens penalties for violating firearm laws, and increases the amount of information, such as mental health records, in the state's background check system. The bill drops a controversial provision that would have repealed the longstanding requirement for a background check and permit issued by county sheriffs for handgun purchases. While the measure expands carry rights, it maintains the current handgun permit system, albeit with some changes. Local sheriffs will no longer be able to restrict the number of handgun permits an individual can obtain in a year, and they must keep a record and show cause when rejecting a permit application. Rep. Grier Martin, D-Wake, expressed concern about the impact on college campuses, representing a district with several universities. However, Rep. John Faircloth, R-Guilford, argued that the college provision merely legalizes what already occurs. Backers of the bill noted that permit holders undergo additional training and background checks, making them reliable individuals to have firearms.

A 14-year-old boy, known as "El Ponchis," was arrested in Cuernavaca, Mexico, as he attempted to flee to his native California, reports the Associated Press. The teen allegedly worked for the South Pacific drug cartel since the age of 11, admitting to participating in at least four decapitations. He claimed to have been drugged and threatened with execution if he refused to carry out the killings. Edgar, as he is known, was arrested with two of his sisters at an airport, who are accused of helping him dispose of victims' bodies. The boy, who has U.S. citizenship, was born in San Diego and was traveling with a 19-year-old sister who reportedly acted as a decoy to lure victims. Another sister, known as "Chabelas," is said to have been involved in disposing of bodies and was the girlfriend of a drug boss. The arrest of "El Ponchis" highlights the growing involvement of minors in drug cartel activities, with figures from Mexico's attorney general's office showing a steady increase in the number of youth detained for drug-related crimes. The case has sparked concerns about the recruitment of young individuals by cartels, who prefer underage assassins for their shorter sentences if caught.

A British makeup artist, Bethany Townsend, who suffers from Crohn's disease, has gained significant attention after posing in a bikini with her colostomy bags. The 23-year-old, who was diagnosed with the condition at the age of three, had two colostomy bags fitted in 2010 after her bowel ruptured. Initially, she felt insecure about the devices but decided to embrace them after a Christmas vacation in Mexico with her husband, Ian. On a whim, she stripped down and posed in a bikini, sharing the photo on the Crohn's and Colitis UK Facebook page. The image, which shows the first time she dared to bare after the bags were fitted, has since been viewed by over nine million people and garnered 190,000 likes and over 10,000 comments. The response has been overwhelmingly positive, and Townsend now feels confident enough to return to modeling as a full-time career. She credits her husband's support for boosting her self-esteem and helping her accept her condition. The viral photo has not only brought about more awareness of Crohn's disease but has also inspired other individuals to feel more comfortable in their own skin. Bethany's story highlights the power of body positivity and the importance of embracing one's unique qualities.

Charlottesville, Virginia, saw a rally by the Ku Klux Klan and its supporters to protest the city council’s decision to remove a statue honoring Confederate General Robert E. Lee. About 30 Klansmen gathered at Justice Park, where they shouted “white power” and some wore white robes. Police in riot gear escorted the rallygoers to and from the event, which was met with jeers from about 1,000 counterprotesters. The counterprotesters, including professors and community members, expressed their opposition to the Klan’s ideology. The rally was held a block away from Emancipation Park, where the Lee statue still stands. Vandalism was reported on the statue with messages painted in green and red paint. Over 100 law enforcement officers were on standby to maintain order. After the rally, 22 people were arrested, and three were hospitalized. City leaders organized diversionary events and encouraged non-confrontational responses. The council voted to remove the statue but a court order has halted the process until a hearing next month. The rally highlighted the ongoing debate over Confederate monuments and their place in public spaces.

A young schoolteacher with a rare form of amnesia, Hannah Upp, has gone missing in the U.S. Virgin Islands, adding to the chaos and uncertainty following Hurricanes Irma and Maria. Upp, 32, was last seen leaving her apartment on St. Thomas on September 14, 2017, around 8 a.m. Her car was later found in a parking lot at Sapphire Beach, and her sandals, sarong, and dress were discovered on the beach. Upp has a history of disappearing, having experienced two previous episodes of dissociative fugue, a condition that can cause people to forget who they are for days or months at a time. In 2008, she vanished for almost three weeks before being found floating in the water off the southern point of the island. In 2013, she disappeared for about two days in Maryland, again telling police after she was found that she had no memory of where she had been or what she had done while missing. 

Her latest disappearance is especially troubling because it comes while St. Thomas rebuilds from Hurricane Irma and as residents sheltered from Hurricane Maria. Upp’s colleagues filed a police report and the U.S. Coast Guard searched the ocean, but the search had to be called off as Hurricane Maria approached the island. The search for Upp has been complicated and slowed by the hurricane and by poor cellphone service on the island. Her colleagues and friends have hung paper fliers around the island and have checked the hospital and shelters. Upp’s mother reported that she had called after a staff meeting at Virgin Islands Montessori School and said she was safe and planned to stay on the island. However, her colleagues and friends remain concerned, as the last known conscious act of Upp was leaving a note for friends saying she was going for a swim at Sapphire Beach and would then go to school. 

Hannah Upp, a passionate Montessori teacher, has been an example to her colleagues and students. Michael Bornn, the head of the Virgin Islands Montessori School, described her as an energetic and loving teacher who taught 3- to 5-year-old children in both English and Spanish. Upp’s disappearance has left her family and friends in a state of uncertainty and fear. Her family released a statement emphasizing the unknown nature of her present condition, stating, “Our beloved Hannah has disappeared. We do not know what has happened and we are hopeful that she will be found alive and well. Our thoughts and prayers are with Hannah and all those who continue to search tirelessly for her. We know our fear and uncertainty is shared by many others, and our hearts go out to all who wait.” 

The search for Upp is ongoing, with some of her friends and colleagues taking matters into their own hands. Jake Bradley, an emergency medical technician, has led the search for Upp, stating, “We’ve done all the physical searching that I think we can do, other than having her posters put up everywhere.” The hope is that even if Upp is in a fugue state, she will see a poster and recognize that something is wrong. The condition of dissociative fugue can cause people to forget who they are for days or months at a time, and Upp’s colleagues and friends are concerned that she may have drowned at Sapphire Beach, been the victim of a crime, or is wandering around the island, confused and hiding. The uncertainty and fear surrounding Upp’s disappearance have left her family and friends in a state of distress, hoping that she will be found safe and well.

Democrats are embracing super PACs with renewed enthusiasm following their success in 2012, despite lingering concerns about the influence of big money on politics. Shortly after the 2012 election, top Democratic officials and donors gathered for a three-day conference hosted by the Democracy Alliance, an exclusive club of major liberal donors. Presentations by Obama campaign and administration officials highlighted the potential for a permanent network of independent groups to compete with the well-funded Republican shadow party. The conference featured discussions on expanding into state politics, policy fights, and even primaries, with groups like Priorities USA Action and American Bridge 21st Century vowing to remain active. These groups are already reaching out to their 2012 donors for additional funding, capitalizing on the current wave of Democratic optimism. Meanwhile, state regulators are cracking down on tax-exempt advocacy groups that engaged in aggressive political activities without disclosing their financial backers. California's Fair Political Practices Commission forced an Arizona-based group to reveal the source of $11 million it gave for ballot initiative campaigns, while Idaho and Montana courts required disclosure of contributors to nonprofits with significant political activity. These state-level actions contrast sharply with the federal level, where nonprofits that spent hundreds of millions of dollars influencing elections are not required to disclose their donors. The federal Federal Election Commission remains gridlocked, unable to take action, while state efforts to pass new disclosure laws have faced legal challenges. The ongoing tension between transparency advocates and groups seeking to maintain their anonymity highlights the complex landscape of campaign finance reform.

A 22-year-old father, Tony Moreno, jumped into the Connecticut River from the Arrigoni Bridge in Middletown late Sunday night, and police believe his 7-month-old son, Aaden, may have gone into the water with him. Moreno called someone threatening suicide around 11:45 p.m., and 911 was dialed, with the baby's crying heard in the background. Upon arrival, police saw Moreno jump, and Middletown firefighters pulled him to shore. LifeStar medical helicopter airlifted Moreno to the hospital, where he was initially listed in serious condition but was alert and conscious as of Tuesday morning. The search for Aaden began immediately, but he was not seen with his father. Search efforts continued for nearly 24 hours before being called off, and the mission was reclassified as a recovery operation. State police issued a Silver Alert for the baby, but the chances of finding him alive were considered slim. Community members gathered at the Middletown green for a candlelight vigil, and a Facebook group garnered support from over 1,500 people. Moreno's condition improved in the hospital, but he did not disclose information about his son's whereabouts to investigators. Police are still investigating and expect to file charges. The events leading up to this tragedy are not unusual for victims of domestic violence, according to Karen Jarmoc, president and CEO of CT Coalition Against Domestic Violence.

A decomposing body was discovered inside a column at a supermarket in Lancaster, California, on Saturday, leading to a bizarre and unsettling investigation. The body, believed to be that of a suspect who had evaded authorities earlier in the week, was found by a store manager who reported a strong odor emanating from the entrance column of the WinCo Foods store on the 700 block of West Avenue K. Upon breaking bricks from the column, a plumber and a handyman discovered a shoe and a leg, leading to the grim discovery of a decomposing body in a state of advanced decomposition. The Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department, specifically homicide detectives, were called to the scene and are treating the case as a possible escape scenario from a previous chase. The suspect, who was reportedly fleeing after being pulled over for a fake license plate, crashed his car, escaped onto the roof, and vanished. The body was found standing upright, with one arm trapped behind the head, suggesting a struggle or an attempt to hide. The coroner’s office is conducting an autopsy to determine the exact cause of death and identify the victim. The store was temporarily closed as investigators worked to remove the body and the scene was secured. Authorities are seeking any information that could help solve the case, urging the public to contact the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department’s Homicide Bureau or Crime Stoppers. The incident has left the community in shock, with some witnesses describing the scene as a horror film come to life.

A humpback whale that became stranded on a sandbar off Stradbroke Island, east of Brisbane, managed to free itself after hours of being stuck, thanks to the efforts of its calf. Queensland Parks and Wildlife (QPW) received reports on Thursday night of a mother and calf stranded on a sandbar at Dunwich, on North Stradbroke Island. Footage from earlier that morning showed the calf swimming nearby and apparently trying to push its mother into deeper water. About 40 minutes after getting stuck, the mother whale successfully dislodged herself and swam away with her calf. QPWS personnel were dispatched to help the pair and planned to stabilize them until a team from Sea World could arrive to assist. However, incoming tides and the calf's efforts were enough to help the mother get free before the Sea World team arrived. QPWS followed the whales to help them navigate to deep water and avoid re-stranding. The mother whale was described as tired and distressed. This incident occurred at a time when humpback whales are common along the Queensland coast, as many travel there to give birth and rear their calves before returning to Antarctic waters.

President Trump has expanded the definition of "fake news" to include any reporting he disagrees with, a move that has alarmed free-speech advocates and drawn comparisons to the Nixon administration. In a tweet on February 6, 2017, Trump declared, "Any negative polls are fake news," and in another, he linked to an article listing 16 fake news stories. Critics argue that this broadens the term to mean any report that requires correction, unfairly attaching malicious intent to honest mistakes. The article provides examples of reports that were indeed erroneous but not necessarily fabricated, such as a false report about the Quebec City shooting and a misreporting of the status of a Martin Luther King Jr. bust in the Oval Office. Trump's use of the term "fake news" has also extended to journalists who report critically on him, as seen in his tweet against CNN and Chris Cuomo. Trump's critics see this as an attack on the First Amendment, while he argues for more honesty in journalism.

At Busch Stadium on Wednesday night, a tense Interleague game between the Royals and Cardinals took an unexpected turn when a small cat suddenly appeared on the field. Royals reliever Peter Moylan was holding a 5-4 lead in the bottom of the sixth inning when the cat, a surprise guest, approached center fielder Lorenzo Cain, causing a brief moment of confusion and amusement. Cardinals manager Mike Matheny, taken aback by the unexpected visitor, joked, "I didn't see anything until all of the noise. I thought there was a streaker on the field to be honest, but I was happy it was a cat." The cat’s arrival was short-lived, as a stadium employee eventually had to track it down, but not before it had a brief, albeit uncomfortable, interaction with the player. Despite the distraction, the game continued, and the Cardinals capitalized on the situation. Yadier Molina, with the bases loaded, hit a game-changing grand slam, putting the Cardinals ahead 8-5. This victory was crucial, as it allowed the Cardinals to leapfrog the Brewers to take second place in the NL Central, just a game and a half behind the Cubs. Manager Matheny, in good humor, remarked, "I'm not a cat person, but I sure like that one." The incident was reminiscent of the Cardinals' previous "Rally Squirrel" that had inspired them during the 2011 NLDS. Molina recalled, "It was the catcher that told me like, 'You haven't seen something like that before,' I said 'Not with a cat, but a squirrel, yes.'" The cat’s unexpected appearance and the Cardinals' subsequent victory added a memorable and amusing chapter to the game, leaving a lasting impression on the players and fans alike.

Sen. Robert Menendez (D-N.J.) faces a growing controversy amid allegations of a questionable friendship with a Florida eye surgeon, Dr. Salomon Melgen, who is under investigation for Medicare fraud and improper flights to the Dominican Republic. Univision has identified one of the women allegedly hired by Melgen to work as a prostitute, but she and her family deny involvement. Menendez has reimbursed Melgen for flights on his private jet to the Caribbean, and the Justice Department is investigating whether Menendez used his position to benefit Melgen’s business interests. The Senate Ethics Committee is also probing the allegations, which include claims of patronizing prostitutes, including underage girls, while in the Dominican Republic. Despite the allegations, Menendez has denied any wrongdoing, and top Democrats, including Majority Leader Harry Reid, are backing him. Reid stated he has confidence in Menendez but acknowledged that investigations are necessary. Menendez’s aides are quietly working to manage the scandal, with some suggesting he may hire a defense attorney. His political machine in New Jersey, known for its rough and tumble environment, may offer some protection, but the ongoing investigations pose significant challenges.

The three women rescued from a decade-long captivity in Cleveland express gratitude for the community's support and emphasize the importance of privacy as they recover, according to a letter released by their attorneys. The letter, which was sent on behalf of Amanda Berry, Gina DeJesus, and Michelle Knight, thanks the public for the overwhelming outpouring of support, including donations that have reached over $650,000 through the Cleveland Courage Fund. The women, who escaped on May 6, are happy and safe but require time and space to heal and reconnect with their families. Their attorneys, Kathy Joseph, Heather Kimmel, Henry Hilow, and James Wooley, represent the survivors pro bono and are in ongoing discussions with them about their needs. The letter also addresses the community's generosity and the best ways to assist the survivors, urging people to donate to the Cleveland Courage Fund, which will distribute funds directly to the women and their families. The letter acknowledges the community's support and the efforts of law enforcement, including the Cleveland Police Department and the Cuyahoga County Sheriff's Office, in the case. The women's recovery process is ongoing, and their attorneys continue to work with them to address their future needs, emphasizing the importance of privacy and the space they require to rebuild their lives.

The U.N. Security Council issued a statement on Saturday calling for a cease-fire in the Israeli-Palestinian conflict centered on the Gaza Strip. The council's statement, approved by all 15 members, urges de-escalation, restoration of calm, and the resumption of direct negotiations between Israelis and Palestinians aimed at achieving a comprehensive peace agreement based on a two-state solution. The statement references the November 2012 cease-fire brokered by Egypt but does not specify a timeline for its implementation. Palestinian U.N. envoy Riyad Mansour emphasized that the Palestinians expect the cease-fire to take effect immediately, warning that if Israel does not comply, the Palestinian side will take action. British Foreign Secretary William Hague echoed the call for a cease-fire, and a meeting is planned in Vienna on Sunday with U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and foreign ministers from Germany and France. Mansour stated that Arab foreign ministers will convene on Monday to continue efforts to halt the conflict. The U.S., Israel's key ally, has defended its attacks against Hamas rocket fire into Israel, while other council members have criticized the escalating Israeli operations, which have resulted in over 1,000 Palestinian casualties. The council's statement avoids mentioning either the Hamas rocketing or the Israeli response, focusing instead on the protection of civilians and adherence to international humanitarian law. If Israel does not respond to the cease-fire call, the Palestinians may return to the Security Council to pursue a legally binding resolution. Meanwhile, the Israeli military has ordered Palestinians in northern Gaza to leave their homes, warning of heavy force to be used against rocket launching sites. This operation, carried out during the Muslim holy month of Ramadan, risks exacerbating tensions. Both U.S. President Barack Obama and Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel have expressed concern over the escalating violence, urging caution to prevent further escalation. Israel, however, is preparing for all options, including a ground offensive into Gaza, home to 1.7 million people.

On May 2, 2015, a family in Wellington, Florida, witnessed a traumatic event unfold in their backyard. Boyd Jentzsch and his 7-year-old son, Kai, were feeding a family of Muscovy ducks when a landscaper, Jason Falbo, 24, of Royal Palm Beach, intentionally ran over the ducklings with his riding lawnmower. The family was horrified as they watched the blades of the mower slice through the birds, scattering feathers and bones. 

According to the arrest report, Falbo, who was working for a lawn service, swerved his mower towards the ducks, which were perched near a tree in the family's yard. Inside the house, Jentzsch's wife, Laura Gontchar, and their son, Kai, screamed in terror as they witnessed the carnage. "We were horrified," said Jentzsch. "I couldn't believe it was happening. It was totally disgusting." 

The family rushed outside, with Gontchar and Kai becoming increasingly hysterical. "These are our friends. These are our babies, we love to feed them!" Jentzsch screamed at Falbo. The landscaper, however, sat on his mower, backed up, and ran over the ducklings again, smiling and laughing. Four ducklings managed to escape, but two drowned in the lake behind the property. Only two of the 11 ducklings survived.

The family called the police and Animal Care and Control, who found the remains of the birds. Nearly two weeks later, the family was still reeling from the traumatic experience. Kai, in tears, ran from the backyard and back into the house, asking his father, "Is everybody out there like this?" Jentzsch and his wife were struggling to explain to their son why this had happened, using the experience as an opportunity to teach him about the value of life and the cruelty of some people.

Falbo was arrested a few hours after the incident and charged with nine counts of felony animal cruelty. He is being held at the Palm Beach County Jail on $27,000 bail. Records show that Falbo had a history of violence, having been arrested in March for domestic battery and aggravated child abuse. The case highlights the devastating impact of such acts on families and the importance of holding individuals accountable for their actions.

Drivers in California can legally read a map on their hand-held cellphones while behind the wheel, according to a ruling by the 5th District Court of Appeal in Fresno. The court reversed a case where a Fresno man, Steven Spriggs, was ticketed in January 2012 for looking at a map on his iPhone 4 while stuck in traffic. Spriggs challenged the $165 fine and took the case to the appellate court, where he was represented pro bono by a law firm. The court ruled that California's law prohibiting people from talking on cellphones without a hands-free device does not apply to looking at maps on cellphones. The law the California Highway Patrol officer used to ticket Spriggs applies specifically to people "listening and talking" on cellphones, not using their mobile phone in other ways. The ruling is the first appellate interpretation of a 2006 state law that restricts handheld uses of a mobile telephone while driving. Attorney Scott Reddie, who represented Spriggs, said it's now up to the state attorney general's office to decide if it will challenge the ruling to the California Supreme Court. The ruling will have statewide impact if it withstands further appeals. Steven Spriggs, whose son suffered a broken leg from a driver who was chatting on a cellphone, hopes that California legislators will revisit the issue and fix the law. He believes that distracted driving is a serious problem and that the law should be rewritten to allow officers to do their job unencumbered.

Five Paraguayan bus drivers and one of their wives have crucified themselves, driving 38cm nails through their hands into wooden crosses in a union protest over sackings. The gruesome demonstration, which began 20 days ago near the bus terminal at Luque, 12km outside the capital Asuncion, is a stark and desperate plea for their reinstatement. The drivers were reportedly fired after asking for medical benefits and overtime pay, and they have vowed to continue their protest until they are given their jobs back. Union leader Juan Villalba, one of the drivers crucified, said they would not give up their protest until all are reinstated. He claims the drivers had been sacked after asking for overtime pay, medical insurance, and state pension contributions. The drivers' wives are also taking turns to be nailed to crosses alongside their husbands, with one appealing to the country's president to come witness their "inhuman situation." The manager of the Vanguardia bus company, Aufredi Paredes, said five of the drivers would be re-hired, but the group are refusing to return until all eight are reinstated. The protest is a powerful and shocking statement of the drivers' determination to fight for their rights and their livelihoods.

A 24-year-old father, Anthony Powell, has pleaded guilty to the fatal beating of his three-year-old son, Tristan, over potty-training accidents. Powell is set to spend 60 years in prison after the conviction. According to court documents, Powell struck Tristan several times, including one instance where he picked up the child like a rag doll after knocking him to the ground. The case details reveal that Powell's son had experienced multiple potty-training mishaps, which apparently led to this violent outburst. Powell's defense attorney stated that his client was overwhelmed by the stress of caring for a young child and had lost control. The court proceedings highlighted the severity of the father's actions and the tragic outcome for both the child and the family. The case has drawn attention to the challenges of parenting and the potential consequences of stress and frustration.

Donald Trump is set to become the 45th president of the United States despite receiving almost 3 million fewer votes than Hillary Clinton. Clinton won the popular vote by 2.86 million, with 65,844,610 votes compared to Trump's 62,979,636. This margin is the largest in raw numbers for a candidate who lost the presidency. However, the Electoral College, which awarded Trump 306 votes to Clinton's 232, secured his victory. The results have reignited debates about the fairness of the Electoral College system, with some calling for its reform. Clinton is the second Democrat to lose a presidential election while winning the popular vote, following Al Gore in 2000.

On Thursday night, Jimmy Kimmel addressed the sad news that Toys'R'Us would be closing all 735 of its stores. Kimmel joked that Toys'R'Us was closing and Babies'R'Us was up for adoption, noting that people now buy toys online from Amazon. An unexpected visitor, Geoffrey the Giraffe, the Toys'R'Us mascot, stopped by the show. Geoffrey expressed his disappointment, stating that people had abandoned him for buying toys online. Kimmel attempted to comfort Geoffrey, but the mascot became emotional, shouting that people had bought toys on Amazon and left him out of a job. Geoffrey then sobbed and sang the old "I'm a Toys'R'Us Kid" jingle. Kimmel asked his security guard to escort Geoffrey out, telling him to "cheer up." The segment highlighted the emotional impact of Toys'R'Us's closure on both the company and its mascot.

The Republican presidential candidates debated immigration, foreign policy, and other key issues during a Road to Majority 2015 convention. Mitt Romney called for immediate removal of the Confederate battle flag from the South Carolina Statehouse, prompting other candidates to weigh in. Some, like Jeb Bush, expressed personal dislike but deferred to South Carolina's decision. Others, such as Scott Walker and Ted Cruz, declined to comment. The debate over the flag reflects broader tensions within the Republican Party regarding race and heritage. Romney's stance aligned with President Obama and civil rights leaders, while other candidates, including Marco Rubio and Rand Paul, remained silent. The candidates also addressed economic issues, including tax cuts, farm subsidies, and the war in Iraq. Romney defended his record of tax cuts and state police expansion, while others, like Paul, called for eliminating farm subsidies. The candidates differed on abortion, with Romney and Huckabee supporting a federal ban, while Thompson focused on overturning Roe v. Wade. The debate highlighted the candidates' varying approaches to key issues, from immigration to foreign policy, and showcased their willingness to take strong stances or remain silent. The candidates also discussed their views on gun control, with Thompson and Romney emphasizing the importance of the Second Amendment. The debate underscored the challenges each candidate faces in addressing the diverse concerns of the Republican base and the broader electorate.

Tragic baby-shampoo heiress Casey Johnson spent the last months of her life in a suicidal drug haze, living in squalor, surrounded by hangers-on and cut off from her family fortune, those close to her said yesterday. The 30-year-old Johnson & Johnson scion, who was found dead in LA on Monday, had gone from being in line to a multibillion-dollar fortune to living in a garbage-filled, rented house with no electricity, water, or gas— but with rats in the pool—as she battled illness and emotional demons. “She was very sick with diabetes and would often fail to take her insulin correctly, and was rushed to the hospital three or four times in the last six months,” a source close to Johnson told The Post. Still, while a family source acknowledged that Johnson “had two specific incidents in the last year where she was taken to intensive care with diabetic comas . . . it was nothing to do with not taking her insulin.” Her family persuaded her to go into rehab a few months ago, but she checked out early and refused to go back. Friends said Johnson coped by self-medicating—popping copious amounts of OxyContin, Klonopin, and Adderall, as well as drugs such as marijuana, ecstasy, and cocaine. Her family cut her off unless she went into rehab, but she wouldn’t help herself. The notorious shopaholic returned to her rented LA home—where she lived without utilities because she was unable to pay her bills—and kept her Porsche hidden in the garage so it couldn’t be repossessed. All the while, the grounds were overrun by vermin. “It was like ‘Grey Gardens,’ ” a source told Page Six last month. As Johnson sank into a sickening world of drugs, she surrounded herself with an ominous group of lowlifes. Neighbors said there was a revolving door of shady-looking characters at Johnson’s house—whose gate was inscribed with the name “Grumblenot.” In her dark pit of drugs and despair, Johnson claimed she had found love—running into the arms of D-lister Tila Tequila. The two announced last month that they were engaged to be married in a disturbing online video in which both lay in their underwear—Johnson in a noticeable state of stupefaction. “Tila was taking advantage of a sick girl. Casey would never have done that had she been in her right mind,” one friend said. The last anyone heard from Johnson was in the early morning of Dec. 29, when she posted a tweet on Twitter: “Sweet dreams everyone.” Her body was found six days later. The Los Angeles Coroner’s Office said an initial autopsy was inconclusive, although there appeared to be no evidence of suicide or trauma to her body. Toxicology tests could take up to six weeks. Jasmine Ferrard, a former friend, had no love lost for Johnson when Johnson allegedly stole from her and used her vibrator in her bed a few weeks ago, but now that the heiress is dead, Jasmine has only kind things to say— to an outlet that routinely pays its sources for stories. "Casey was a fragile, beautiful, witty, wonderful girl who was desperately looking for love," Jasmine, 24, told RadarOnline.com. "Did I love her? Yes. I tried so hard to save her but I couldn't." Jasmine blames Casey's histrionic fiancée Tila Tequila for thwarting the Johnson family's attempts to put Casey in rehab. "Tila is a sick, sick girl," she told Radar. Additional reporting by Tori Richards in Los Angeles.

J.J. Abrams has assembled an eclectic cast for his take on "Star Wars: Episode VII," which was officially titled "The Force Awakens" on December 18, 2015. The film, directed by Abrams and featuring a mix of returning and new actors, is set to be released on that date. The original stars, Harrison Ford, Carrie Fisher, and Mark Hamill, are expected to reprise their roles as Han Solo, Princess Leia, and Luke Skywalker, respectively. The cast also includes newcomers such as Adam Driver, Daisy Ridley, and Andy Serkis, adding a fresh dynamic to the franchise. 

Among the newcomers, John Boyega, a former Marine and actor known for his role in the HBO series "Girls," and Daisy Ridley, an up-and-coming actress with a small role in "About a Boy," are particularly noteworthy. Andy Serkis, famous for his work with motion-capture technology, is also part of the cast, potentially bringing his expertise to the role of a character that requires extensive CGI. 

The inclusion of established actors like Max von Sydow, known for his role in "The Exorcist," and Oscar Isaac, who gained recognition for his performance in "Inside Llewyn Davis," adds a layer of credibility to the film. The casting choices balance veteran talent with fresh faces, ensuring that the film can appeal to both long-time fans and newcomers to the franchise. 

The choice of these actors, particularly the younger cast members, suggests a deliberate effort to pass the torch to a new generation of actors while honoring the legacy of the original trilogy. This approach is reminiscent of George Lucas's original casting choices, which included both seasoned veterans and relative unknowns. 

The title "The Force Awakens" hints at a return to the core elements of the franchise, focusing on the power of the Force and the awakening of new characters. This title, while familiar, also signals a departure from the more experimental and divisive prequels, promising a more traditional and satisfying experience for fans. 

The production faced some challenges, including an accident involving Harrison Ford that temporarily sidelined him. However, the film is now complete, and the cast and crew celebrated the wrap party, marking the end of principal photography. The film's success will depend not only on the performances of the actors but also on how well Abrams balances the familiar with the new, ensuring that the legacy of "Star Wars" continues to captivate audiences.

Three space travelers safely returned to Earth from the International Space Station on September 2, as their Soyuz MS-04 spacecraft touched down on the steppes of Kazakhstan, bringing an end to a record-shattering mission for one American crewmember. NASA's Peggy Whitson, who set a new record for the most cumulative time in space by an American with 665 days accrued, returned home after an extended 288-day mission to the International Space Station (ISS). Her crewmates, NASA astronaut Jack Fischer and Russian cosmonaut Fyodor Yurchikhin, both spent 136 days aboard the orbiting laboratory. Landing occurred at 9:21 p.m. EDT (0121 on September 3 GMT), though it was Sunday morning local time at the touchdown site. Whitson, who arrived in November with Expedition 50/51, filled the empty seat for the return flight after NASA and Russia's space agency Roscosmos agreed to extend her stay through Expedition 52. Whitson's 288-day mission was the longest single spaceflight by a woman of any nationality, and she set multiple other records, including being the world's oldest spacewoman at 57 and the most experienced female spacewalker, with 10 spacewalks. Expedition 51/52 crewmembers Fischer and Yurchikhin arrived at the ISS in April with an empty seat in their Soyuz. Whitson, who arrived in November, filled that seat for the return flight. The Soyuz MS-04 spacecraft undocked from the space station's Poisk module at 5:58 p.m. EDT (1758 GMT), kicking off the crew's 3-hour and 24-minute journey back to Earth. About three hours later, the Soyuz barreled into Earth's atmosphere traveling at a speed of over 500 mph (800 km/h). Friction with the atmosphere caused temperatures outside the spacecraft to reach a scorching 2,500 degrees Fahrenheit (1,400 degrees Celsius). A heat shield outside the Soyuz helped keep the crew relatively cool during the plunge. A series of parachutes were deployed to slow the spacecraft down about 15 minutes before touchdown, followed by a last-second burn of six soft-landing engines that helped cushion the last few feet of the fall. They successfully touched down on target in a remote area near the town of Dzhezkazgan, Kazakhstan. The Soyuz spacecraft tipped over onto its side, which is common for Soyuz crew landings. Recovery teams watched the landing from helicopters nearby before descending to the landing site to help the space travelers out of their capsule. After the crew gets checked out in a medical tent on-site, the helicopters will carry them back to Kazakhstan's Karaganda airport for a traditional welcoming ceremony before they board planes and head home. While Yurchikhin will go to Russia's cosmonaut center in Moscow, Whitson and Fischer will head to NASA's Johnson Space Center in Houston. Due to the devastating floods brought by Hurricane Harvey, NASA had to come up with a contingency plan for getting the astronauts home. The European Space Agency stepped up to the plate and offered the use of its plane that has been to Karaganda before. They will be poised in Karaganda to await the arrival of Whitson and Fischer. The astronauts will then fly back to the European Astronaut Center in Cologne, Germany, where the NASA Gulfstream jet will pick them up and take them back to Houston. Their return is still scheduled for Sunday night, just about the same time they would have returned to Houston had the NASA Gulfstream jet done this all by itself. Back at the space station, NASA astronaut Randy Bresnik, European Space Agency astronaut Paolo Nespoli, and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Ryazansky will be the only three crewmembers on board until September 12, when the Expedition 52/53 crewmembers arrive. NASA astronauts Joe Acaba and Mark Vande Hei and Russian cosmonaut Alexander Misurkin will then dock at the ISS in their Soyuz MS-05 spacecraft and spend the next six months in space. On Friday (September 1), Yurchikhin handed over command of the ISS to Bresnik. Yurchikhin has now spent a total of 673 days in space over the course of five flights and is now in seventh place on the all-time spaceflight endurance list. He has spent just eight more days in space than Whitson, whose 665 days in space put her at number eight on that list. Whitson's 288-day mission was also the longest single spaceflight by a woman of any nationality. Fischer, a rookie astronaut returning from his first trip to space, has now accrued 136 days in orbit.

A political action committee, dubbed Trump Has Tiny Hands PAC, was launched by Henry Kraemer of Portland, Oregon, to challenge Donald Trump's recent denials about the size of his hands. The PAC's name alludes to a series of exchanges during the Republican presidential campaign, where Marco Rubio mocked Trump's hands, and Trump himself responded by defending their size. Kraemer initiated the PAC after Trump began asserting that his hands are not small. "When a call comes into the White House at 3 a.m., will Donald Trump's tiny baby hands be able to lift the phone receiver? This is something Americans should know before voting," Kraemer stated in an interview. The PAC's launch comes amid ongoing debates about the size of Trump's hands, with Rubio's jab and Trump's subsequent defense becoming a recurring theme in campaign rhetoric. Meanwhile, Yelp has also joined the fray, updating its app with a sly reference to the hand size controversy, humorously stating, "Our latest release easily trumps our old version, it’s usable no matter how small your hands are!" Trump has repeatedly insisted that his hands are not small, even going so far as to boast about his golfing abilities. The hand size debate has become a significant part of the campaign narrative, with both Trump and his opponents engaging in back-and-forth exchanges that highlight the personal nature of the ongoing presidential race.

Vermont lawmakers are using a provocative tactic to push for the legalization of marijuana: a bill that would reinstate alcohol prohibition. Reps. Jean O'Sullivan and Christopher Pearson introduced House Bill 502, which would make alcohol possession punishable by fines up to $500 and up to 30 years in prison for those involved in the sale and distribution. O'Sullivan acknowledges the bill's irony, stating it's meant to highlight the broader argument for marijuana legalization. The pair argue that since marijuana is less dangerous than alcohol, which causes over 80,000 U.S. deaths annually, alcohol should be banned if marijuana is legalized. A Rand Corporation study estimates Vermonters spent between $125 and $225 million on marijuana in 2014, suggesting significant tax revenue from legalization. The bill is part of a broader push for marijuana legalization, with Senate Bill 95 also aiming to legalize the drug. Proponents argue that legalizing marijuana could help bridge Vermont's $113 million budget deficit. While the bill is unlikely to pass, it aims to draw attention to the scientific consensus that marijuana is less harmful than alcohol.

Supporters in Ferguson, Missouri, worked to rebuild a memorial for Michael Brown after it was reportedly destroyed by a vehicle. The memorial, which included flowers, signs, and other tributes, was built in the middle of a street near the site where Brown was fatally shot by a police officer on August 9, 2014. On Christmas Day, the memorial was reportedly run over, with some witnesses believing it was intentionally damaged. However, Ferguson Police Department Officer Timothy Zoll, the public relations officer, stated that no crime had been reported in connection with the incident. He suggested that the department would look at any video evidence, but did not specify whether an investigation would be conducted. Despite this, the memorial was quickly rebuilt by morning. The incident sparked discussions about the treatment of the memorial and the ongoing tensions in Ferguson. Ferguson police officer Zoll was placed on unpaid leave after admitting to misleading his superiors about his comments to The Washington Post, where he referred to the memorial as "trash" in the middle of the street. The city's statement emphasized that the negative remarks did not reflect the department's stance and contradicted efforts to relocate the memorial to a more secure location.

In Thailand, elephants are trained to perform various tasks, including playing soccer and stepping on tourists, as seen at the Maesa Elephant Camp in Chiang Mai. These elephants, often mistaken for baby ones, are used to place their feet on tourists' backs to supposedly "ease stress," despite the inherent danger of being near a large animal capable of crushing a person. The experience is further marred by the sudden switch to an adult elephant for "comic effect," leaving tourists in a state of discomfort and unease. Meanwhile, in a bizarre twist, snakes are known to explore unconventional areas on humans, including faces, adding an unsettling element to the already questionable practice of snake massages. While nonvenomous, the snakes' unpredictable behavior can be alarming, especially when combined with the elephant's presence. These scenarios highlight the questionable ethics and safety of elephant and snake tourism, raising concerns about the well-being of both animals and the unsuspecting humans who participate.

President Obama delivered a speech at American University on Wednesday, urging Congress to support the Iran nuclear deal, framing it as a critical moment in U.S. foreign policy, drawing historical parallels to the 1963 speech by President Kennedy on the nuclear test ban treaty. Obama emphasized that rejecting the deal would not only undermine America’s credibility but also risk another war in the Middle East, a narrative he has been pushing since his first presidential campaign. He warned that those opposing the deal, including Republican presidential candidates and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, are making “common cause” with Iranian hard-liners who oppose the agreement. Obama highlighted the deal as the “strongest nonproliferation agreement ever negotiated,” and argued that a better deal is not possible. He also addressed concerns that lifting sanctions would fund Iran’s military and proxies, asserting that a stronger approach would be to directly confront Iran’s destabilizing activities. The speech was aimed at a few dozen undecided House and Senate Democrats, who control the fate of the deal in Congress. Obama’s strategy included engaging in a fierce lobbying campaign, with his team making the president and other senior administration officials available to answer questions and concerns. The White House also planned to dispatch cabinet members to travel the country, outlining the deal’s provisions. Despite opposition from influential Jewish American groups and a multimillion-dollar ad campaign, Obama maintained that the deal is in the best interest of U.S. security and credibility. The deal, which would ease sanctions against Iran in exchange for limits on its nuclear program, faces a September 17 deadline for Congress to vote. Obama promised to veto any legislation rejecting the deal, setting up a key showdown over whether opponents can secure an override.

Wayne Flynt, a professor emeritus of history at Auburn University and author of numerous books on Alabama history, has written a new book, "Mockingbird Songs: My Friendship With Harper Lee," offering insight into the famously publicity-shy Harper Lee, including her relationship with Truman Capote and her decision to publish "Go Set a Watchman." In an exclusive interview with the New York Times, Flynt revealed several details about Lee's life and her friendship with Capote. Lee, known in her hometown of Monroeville by her given name of Nelle Harper Lee, only asked Flynt not to write about her while she was alive, feeling that the book "allows her to speak beyond the grave and without any risk to her privacy." Lee was also known to be fearful of obsessive fans, having once had a stalker and being concerned with stalkers and assassination. Flynt's book includes a letter from Lee to him, in which she called Capote a "compulsive liar," revealing that Capote was the inspiration for the character Dill in "To Kill a Mockingbird." Lee and Capote were childhood friends in Monroeville and traveled to Kansas together in 1959 so that Capote could cover the Clutter murders for The New Yorker. Lee worked as Capote's "assistant researchist" and later edited his final draft of "In Cold Blood," but Capote gave her no credit for her work. Lee's letters to Flynt reveal that "Capote’s drinking and misery soured their friendship," and that she wrote, "I was his oldest friend, and I did something Truman could not forgive: I wrote a novel that sold. He nursed his envy for more than 20 years." Flynt's book also discusses Lee's nervousness before interviews and speaking engagements, noting that she would vomit. Additionally, Flynt admits that Lee "may not have fully participated in the decision to publish a long forgotten and flawed first novel ('Go Set a Watchman')" because of her age and health issues, but that at the time, Lee welcomed its publication.

A missing California woman, Jamie Tull, 33, was found alive after vanishing for nearly three weeks, reports the AP. Tull, a former public elementary school teacher, was last heard from on July 17 when she crashed her vehicle into a ditch. She was discovered emaciated and badly sunburned, less than a mile from the crash site near the small central California farming community of Le Grand. According to Merced County Sheriff Vern Warnke, Tull survived by eating a few bugs and drinking from a dirty cattle trough. She told rescuers that she did not want to be found and was trying to reach Yosemite. Warnke described the surrounding landscape as desolate grazing land with homes visible in the distance. Tull endured a scorching heatwave and was weak but able to speak when found. She was taken by helicopter to a nearby hospital for medical treatment and will be returned to relatives for care. Her father stated that she has bipolar disorder and has not taken her prescribed medication for about six months due to beliefs that pills lead to demons. The search for Tull was suspended, and her family and friends went looking for her, ultimately finding her alive.

A 71-year-old veteran died after collapsing in the cafeteria of the Raymond G. Murphy VA Medical Center in Albuquerque, New Mexico, 500 yards from the emergency room. Despite being within walking distance, it took 30 minutes for an ambulance to arrive, with the veteran dying before medical help could be provided. The delay occurred because hospital staff followed protocol, calling 911 for a medical emergency outside the main hospital building. Kirtland Air Force Medical Group personnel performed CPR until the ambulance arrived. The VA is under scrutiny for widespread reports of long delays in treatment and medical appointments, with a recent review citing "significant and chronic system failures" in the nation's health system for veterans. The death has sparked debate on the VA's local policies and response times, with some questioning the effectiveness of the policy that required calling 911 for a medical emergency in a different building. Critics argue that the VA should have a more flexible policy to address such situations, while supporters maintain that strict adherence to protocols is necessary to ensure patient safety. The incident has raised concerns among veterans and their families, who are considering legal action. The VA is currently reviewing its policy on handling medical emergencies outside the main hospital building.

The Mexican attorney for "affluenza" teen Ethan Couch, who cited his wealthy upbringing as a defense in a fatal drunken-driving crash, has stated that his client's legal fight against deportation to Texas is an "international law case." Couch, 18, and his mother, Tonya, were detained in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, after a video surfaced allegedly showing Ethan at a party where people were drinking, potentially violating his probation. Tonya Couch was quickly deported and is facing charges of hindering an apprehension of a felon, which could result in up to 10 years in prison if she is convicted. Ethan Couch remains in an immigration detention center in Mexico City, where his lawyer, Fernando Benitez, is arguing that his client's constitutional and civil rights may have been violated. Benitez claims that Couch's crimes in Texas should not affect Mexican officials or courts and that a formal extradition request has not been filed. A judge is considering Couch's detention and possible deportation, with the process potentially taking months. Benitez hopes to meet with Ethan Couch in Mexico City next week and expects the case to be reviewed to its fullest extent. Couch's return to Texas is scheduled for a hearing on January 19, where a decision will be made on whether his case will be transferred to adult court, potentially leading to up to 10 years in prison per death if he violates probation again.

Right-wing news site The Daily Caller is running a controversial gun giveaway, offering new registrants a chance to win a free handgun engraved with the Bill of Rights. The gun's manufacturer, Jim Pontillo, has criticized American progressives for promoting communism and claims that secessionists are acting in the Founding tradition. The Daily Caller's "Guns and Gear" page promotes the giveaway, stating that winners can sign up for the site's email updates. Pontillo's website and columns contain extreme right-wing rhetoric, including attacks on liberalism and support for gun ownership as a means to counter perceived threats. The giveaway has sparked outrage and debate over the site's tactics and the current political climate surrounding gun control.

Clarissa Dickson Wright, the co-star and co-chef of the popular British television show "Two Fat Ladies" with Jennifer Paterson, has passed away at the age of 66. Known for her eccentric personality and outspoken views, Dickson Wright was a champion of hunting and shooting, and she once faced legal trouble for attending an illegal hare coursing event. Her career in television began when producer Patricia Llewellyn recruited her for the show, which aired from 1996 to 1999. Each episode featured Dickson Wright and Paterson traveling the UK in a motorcycle sidecar, cooking and speaking about food in a way that was both entertaining and unconventional. The show was well-received, leading to a book and continued success on the BBC and the Food Network.

Dickson Wright's life was marked by a series of challenges. She grew up in a wealthy family but struggled with alcoholism, which she overcame on her 40th birthday. She later became a barrister and worked as a cook before opening a bookshop called Books for Cooks in London. After Paterson's death in 1999, Dickson Wright continued to appear on television, including in the series "Clarissa and the Countryman" and "Breakfast, Lunch and Dinner." She was also a vocal supporter of the Countryside Alliance and wrote a book called "A History of English Food."

Despite her fame, Dickson Wright maintained a down-to-earth attitude. She was known for her strong opinions and her willingness to speak her mind, often challenging social norms. Her personal life was also marked by tragedy, including the loss of her father and her husband, Clive, who died in 1982. She faced financial difficulties and was declared bankrupt several times, but she remained committed to her passions, including cooking and the countryside. Her death was mourned by many, including television chef Jamie Oliver, who praised her as "always entertaining to watch and was of course a passionate foodie."

A woman with an extremely hard-to-treat form of tuberculosis, known as extensively drug-resistant (XDR) TB, has raised concerns among health officials due to her extensive travel before seeking treatment. The patient, whose identity is not disclosed, traveled from India to the United States, passing through Chicago O'Hare Airport, and also spent time in Missouri and Tennessee. Upon seeking medical attention, she was diagnosed with active TB at a hospital in the Chicago area, where she was placed in isolation. She was then transferred to the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for specialized treatment. The NIH stated that the patient is staying in an isolation room designed for handling patients with respiratory infections, including XDR-TB.

Health authorities, including the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), are now tracing the patient's contacts to identify individuals who may have been in close proximity and at risk of exposure. The CDC emphasized that the risk of transmission is low, but they are taking the situation seriously due to the severity of XDR-TB. The patient's condition is being monitored, and tests are being conducted to determine which drugs may be effective in treating her condition.

XDR-TB is a rare form of tuberculosis that is resistant to at least four of the core anti-TB drugs, including isoniazid and rifampin, as well as at least one fluoroquinolone and one of the three injectable second-line drugs. It is estimated that only about 63 cases of XDR-TB have been reported in the United States between 1993 and 2011. The treatment for XDR-TB is complex and costly, with an average cost of $134,000 for multidrug-resistant TB, which can rise to $430,000 for extensively resistant cases. The patient's treatment costs are yet to be determined.

TB is not as easily spread as diseases like the flu or measles, but it can be dangerous, especially for individuals with weakened immune systems.
