Investigators are re-examining conversations detected by U.S. intelligence agencies in spring 2015 that captured Russian government officials discussing associates of Donald Trump, according to current and former U.S. officials, a move prompted by revelations that the president’s eldest son met with a Russian lawyer last year. In some cases, the Russians in the overheard conversations talked about meetings held outside the U.S. involving Russian government officials and Trump business associates or advisers. The younger Mr. Trump said the meeting with the Russian lawyer yielded no useful information about Hillary Clinton, and instead turned into a discussion about a Russian-American diplomatic dispute. By happenstance or not, in the days and weeks after the meeting with the Russian lawyer, emails purloined from Democratic computers were made public, which investigators tied to Russian hacking. As a candidate, the elder Mr. Trump, who had expressed admiration of President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, took positions that summer that caused head scratching. He expressed openness to lifting sanctions on Russia that were imposed after its annexation of Crimea, and suggested he might not defend NATO allies that did not spend enough money on their own security. The Republican platform at the party convention in July 2016 was crafted to keep out a call to provide arms to Ukraine to fight pro-Russian separatists. The president’s legal team declined to comment about the close timing of some of these events. A White House official said the president’s threat to air allegations about Mrs. Clinton on June 7 was part of a long-planned speech and was not related to his son’s decision to meet with the Russian lawyer. At a briefing on Wednesday, Sarah Huckabee Sanders, a White House spokeswoman, dismissed the latest articles about the emails and meeting as “much ado about nothing.” President Trump said on Wednesday he did not fault his son Donald Trump Jr. for meeting with a Russian lawyer during the 2016 presidential election campaign and that he was unaware of the meeting until a few days ago. Asked if he knew that his son was meeting with lawyer Natalia Veselnitskaya in June last year, the president told Reuters in a White House interview: “No, that I didn’t know until a couple of days ago when I heard about this.” Trump Jr. eagerly agreed to meet the woman he was told was a Russian government lawyer who might have damaging information about Democratic rival Hillary Clinton as part of Moscow’s official support for his father’s campaign, according to emails the son released on Tuesday. Seated at his Oval Office desk, Trump said he did not fault his son for holding the meeting, writing it off as a decision made in the heat of an upstart, non-traditional campaign. “I think many people would have held that meeting,” Trump said. “It was a 20-minute meeting, I guess, from what I’m hearing. Many people, and many political pros, said everybody would do that.” The emails were the most concrete evidence that Trump campaign officials might have been willing to accept Russian help to win the Nov. 8 election, a subject that has cast a cloud over Trump’s presidency and prompted investigations by the U.S. Justice Department and Congress. While U.S. intelligence agencies and even members of Trump’s Cabinet have said Russia meddled in the election, Trump has wavered on the subject, at times suggesting that other actors might have been involved. Trump equivocated on whether he felt he could trust Putin. He said Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping both look out for their countries’ interests, as he looks out for U.S. interests. “I am not a person who goes around trusting lots of people. But he’s the leader of Russia. It is the second most powerful nuclear power on earth. I am the leader of the United States. I love my country. He loves his country,” Trump said. As in the past, Trump said there was no collusion between his campaign and Russia. “There was zero coordination. It’s the dumbest thing I’ve ever heard,” he said.

Chris Brown will return to jail for a month after being arrested on Friday for violating his probation. On Monday (March 17), a judge cited his "inability to stay out of trouble" as grounds to keep him locked up until April 23. Brown, 25, was arrested on Friday based on a warrant issued by probation officials and held without bail until Monday. Though authorities have not yet revealed the cause of the alleged probation violation, TMZ reported that the singer was kicked out of a Malibu rehab center for violating unspecified "internal rules." Brown was ordered to spend 90 days in a residential facility in November for anger-management issues after an incident in which he threw a rock through his mother's car window before being discharged from a rehab facility. Brown spent two weeks in a rehab facility in early October after he was arrested in Washington, D.C., for allegedly assaulting a 20-year-old man. He's due back in court on April 17, when a judge will determine whether he committed criminal assault in that incident. The Malibu rehab facility revealed in court documents that the singer suffered from PTSD and bipolar disorder. Brown was thrown out of the Malibu rehab facility for breaking three rules, including one which allegedly applied only to him and which required him to stay at least two feet away from other women at the rehab. He also reportedly acted out during a rehab group session by making harsh comments. The judge in Brown's probation violation case, Superior Court James R. Brandlin, revoked Brown's probation in December but turned down a prosecutor's request in February to jail the singer again because of the D.C. assault case. Brown was slated to finish his probation in August but with a reported 750 hours of community labor left to complete and possible additional penalties for not completing rehab, it's likely his probation could be extended once again.

Children's author R.L. Stine is set to write a new scary story entirely on Twitter for Halloween, continuing his tradition of tweeting spooky tales, such as a tale about a haunted kitchen. This Halloween, he will write a story live on the platform, engaging with fans and marking his presence in the digital age, despite his preference for physical books.

A 2-year-old boy brought to a Wichita hospital Tuesday night with a small octopus stuck in his throat has shown significant improvement, according to police. The boy, in good condition, does not show signs of long-term injury caused by oxygen deprivation to the brain, Lt. James Espinoza of Wichita police said. Doctors extricated the head of the dead octopus, measuring about 2 inches in diameter, from the child’s throat. The boy’s 21-year-old mother told investigators she returned home from work to find her 36-year-old boyfriend performing CPR on her son, who was not breathing. The boy’s 36-year-old boyfriend was taken to the Exploited and Missing Child Unit offices for questioning and arrested shortly after 5 a.m. Wednesday on suspicion of child abuse. He has since bonded out of the Sedgwick County Jail. The investigation is ongoing, and a detective specially trained to interview young children will visit with the boy. Police have said the octopus was not a pet and was likely intended to be used as sushi. The incident happened around 9:30 p.m. Tuesday in the 4900 block of East Waterman.

In recent years, numerous U.S. companies and the federal government have experienced significant data breaches, compromising over 1.1 billion records. WalletHub analyzed 50 states and the District of Columbia, ranking Nevada as the most vulnerable to identity theft and fraud, followed by Florida and New Jersey. The study considered metrics such as identity-theft complaints per capita, average loss amount due to fraud, and availability of security-freeze laws. Tips for protecting personal information include emphasizing email security, signing up for credit monitoring, leveraging account alerts, and using common sense online.

A Chilean mother, Sindy Melany Ortiz, is facing restrictions on her ability to see her newborn daughter due to her admission of smoking marijuana, a practice currently legal for medicinal purposes in private. Ortiz claims she used marijuana to alleviate pain in her arm and was only allowed to visit her daughter for two hours a day, with no permission to breastfeed. Hospital officials in Talcahuano cited protocol and the potential risk to the baby as reasons for these restrictions. Ortiz argues that her rights as a mother are being violated, stating that she only used marijuana for medicinal purposes and was advised to do so by a medical professional. The hospital's actions have prompted a court order to keep the baby at the Las Higueras hospital until a Thursday hearing.

In July, Chile's Congress approved a bill to decriminalize personal use and cultivation of marijuana, allowing possession of up to 10 grams and growing up to six plants. This legislation aims to stop the persecution of medicinal users and provide them with a legal means to access the drug. Santiago, Chile's capital, has already hosted Latin America's first medical marijuana farm. The bill now moves to the full Chamber of Deputies, potentially facing years of legislative review before becoming law.

A new study presented at the American Heart Association's Scientific Sessions 2016 suggests that repeatedly losing and regaining weight, known as weight cycling or the "yo-yo effect," may increase the risk of death from heart disease among postmenopausal women who were of normal weight at the start of the study. The research, involving 158,063 postmenopausal women, found that women who experienced weight cycling had a significantly higher risk of sudden cardiac death and coronary heart disease deaths compared to women who maintained a stable weight. Specifically, women of normal weight who lost and regained weight had a 3.5 times higher risk of sudden cardiac death and a 66% increased risk for coronary heart disease deaths. Notably, weight cycling did not increase the risk of heart disease among overweight or obese women. The study, while observational and subject to some limitations, highlights the potential dangers of rapid weight fluctuations, even for those who start at a healthy weight. The researchers emphasize the need for further research to understand the underlying mechanisms and to develop appropriate clinical recommendations. In the meantime, the American Heart Association recommends following the Life's Simple 7 program to reduce the risk of heart disease, which includes managing blood pressure, controlling cholesterol, reducing blood sugar, getting active, eating better, maintaining a normal weight, and stopping smoking.

Mitt Romney, the former Massachusetts governor and Republican presidential hopeful, will not participate in the December 27th debate scheduled to be moderated by Donald Trump. Romney informed Fox News' Neil Cavuto of his decision, explaining that he has commitments to two other debates in December and needs to focus on campaigning in key early states like Iowa, New Hampshire, South Carolina, and Florida. Romney called Trump to convey his perspective and received understanding in return. Ron Paul and Jon Huntsman have also declined to participate, while Newt Gingrich and Rick Santorum have confirmed their attendance. Romney's decision underscores his strategic approach to managing his campaign resources and prioritizing his presence in early voting states.

Anonymous, the international hacking collective, has intensified its campaign against ISIS following the Paris attacks, releasing a list of more than 1,000 Twitter accounts suspected of supporting the terror group. This marks the group's latest move in a broader effort to disrupt ISIS's online presence. In a YouTube video, a masked Anonymous member declared, "War is declared. Get prepared," warning that the group would launch its "biggest operation ever" against ISIS. The video, which has garnered over five million views, echoes the group's previous calls to action, including their Operation Charlie Hebdo campaign, which targeted extremist websites and social media accounts.

Anonymous's tactics involve launching distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks to overwhelm ISIS's servers and taking down Twitter accounts through coordinated efforts with social media platforms. Since January, the group has claimed to have shut down 9,000 Twitter accounts and 149 websites linked to ISIS. However, experts question the effectiveness of these actions, noting that ISIS supporters can easily create new accounts and that Anonymous's activities might inadvertently disrupt law enforcement investigations. The Islamic Cyber Army, an ISIS-affiliated group, responded to Anonymous's threats, offering tips to protect against cyber attacks and warning supporters to be cautious online. Despite the challenges, Anonymous remains committed to its mission, aiming to disrupt ISIS's digital networks and hinder the group's ability to communicate and recruit supporters globally.

Former President Bill Clinton enjoyed his most lucrative year on the speaking circuit in 2010, earning $10.7 million from 52 paid speeches, marking a significant increase from the $7.5 million he made in 2009. His total earnings since leaving office in 2001 now stand at $75.6 million, with almost half of his 2010 earnings, $4.8 million, coming from 18 speeches in 13 countries, including Canada, the UK, and Australia. Clinton’s domestic earnings were from 34 speeches in eight states and the District of Columbia. Over the past decade, he has delivered 417 paid speeches, averaging $181,000 per event, with international engagements paying better, accounting for $44.9 million of his total earnings. His most lucrative single event was a $1 million speech in Moscow in 2010, and another $500,000 speech in the United Arab Emirates. Clinton’s earnings have varied, with his lowest year being 2004 when he earned $875,000 due to his focus on writing his memoirs and recovering from heart surgery. His wife, Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, has also earned substantial speaking fees, with her memoir “Living History” bringing in more than $10 million. While former President George W. Bush has earned at least $15 million on 140 paid speaking engagements since leaving office, Clinton remains the highest-earning former president, highlighting the financial benefits of post-presidential activities.

Sometimes even the smallest acts of kindness can make a lasting impression, as demonstrated by a long-standing tradition between a commoner and the Queen. Andrew Simes, inspired by his grandfather's practice of sending Christmas cards to Queen Elizabeth II since 1952, continued this tradition after his grandfather's passing in 2011. In 1972, their paths crossed at a reception in Izmir, Turkey, where the Queen, recognizing the sender of the cards, paused to quip, "So it's you who keeps sending me those lovely Christmas cards." This exchange left a lasting memory of the Queen's kindness and attention to detail. In January 2012, Andrew received a letter from Buckingham Palace, acknowledging his grandfather's passing and expressing condolences to Andrew and his family. The letter, written on behalf of the Queen, conveyed her sadness at the news. Andrew, moved by this gesture, continued the tradition, sending his Christmas cards, with the Queen always at the top of his list. The story serves as a reminder that a simple act of sending a card can leave a significant impact, and perhaps even reach the highest levels of royalty. Wishing everyone a Christmas as magical as this story.

A 10-year-old boy was bitten by a shark in Daytona Beach Shores, Florida, on Wednesday afternoon, marking the fourth shark attack in Volusia County this year. The boy, visiting from Georgia, was in chest-deep water when he was bitten on the calf, suffering minor lacerations. He was treated on the scene and did not require hospitalization. This incident comes as part of a concerning trend, with another 10-year-old boy recovering from significant injuries after an attack off Cocoa Beach a week prior. Dr. George Burgess, director of the Florida Program for Shark Research, suggests that the increase in shark attacks is due to more people in the water and not a rise in shark aggression. He notes that Florida led the nation with 28 shark attacks in 2014, and the 11 reported so far this year is not unusual. Burgess advises staying in groups and avoiding areas near inlets where bait is often used. Meanwhile, in Oak Island, North Carolina, the town is considering a temporary ban on shark fishing following back-to-back shark attacks that left a 12-year-old girl and a 16-year-old boy with severe injuries. These attacks, which occurred within 90 minutes of each other, happened in waist-deep water, 20 yards offshore. Fishing piers can attract sharks due to live bait and fish guts, leading to confusion and potential attacks. Experts suggest that shark fishing bans might not be effective, as shark fishing itself attracts fish and, by extension, sharks. However, some towns, including Virginia Beach and Myrtle Beach, have already banned shark fishing from piers to protect swimmers. The increase in shark attacks, while concerning, is attributed more to better reporting and more people in the water rather than a rise in shark aggressiveness.

After three years together, Derek Jeter and Minka Kelly have called off their relationship, according to sources. The split was amicable, and both remain friends, though they still care for each other. Jeter, 37, is in the middle of his MLB season with the New York Yankees, while Kelly, 31, is busy shooting the ABC reboot of Charlie's Angels in Miami. The couple faced rumors of splits and engagements over the years but couldn't make it work. Jeter recently achieved the milestone of becoming the 28th MLB player to reach 3,000 hits, adding to the bittersweet nature of their breakup.

A New Hampshire woman who disappeared with her 8-year-old daughter a decade ago has turned herself in to face trial, according to U.S. Marshals. Genevieve Kelley, 50, and her husband, Scott Kelley, 49, fled with their daughter, Mary, to Central America in 2004 after Genevieve's attempt to prove her ex-husband, Mark Nunes, had harmed the child backfired. The Kelleys were involved in a contentious custody dispute, with Mark given legal custody of Mary in 2005. Genevieve was indicted for interference with custody, and the case garnered national attention when featured on CNN's "The Hunt" in 2015. The marshals investigated numerous tips through the years, and Genevieve made contact shortly after her daughter turned 18 in February. Her lawyer, Alan Rosenfeld, said she wanted to face a jury and be vindicated. Genevieve's return came after a decade of hiding, and U.S. Marshal David Cargill Jr. expressed hope that Mary would be found safe. Mark Nunes, Mary's father, remains hopeful of being reunited with his daughter and wants to learn more about her. Genevieve's lawyer argued that she would not be a flight risk and hoped for a voluntary return, but the Coos County Attorney, John McCormick, disagreed, noting her history of fleeing during a family court proceeding. Genevieve's daughter, now 18, is expected to be a key witness at the trial, and Mark Nunes expressed his love for his daughter and hope for her safe return.

A 17-year-old high school senior, Jacqueline Gomez, was found dead in a north Houston hotel room the morning after her prom at MacArthur High School. Her boyfriend, who was also staying in the hotel, discovered her unresponsive and called 911. Police are investigating the cause of death, which may be related to alcohol and prescription painkillers found in the room. The prom seemed like any other celebration, but the night took a tragic turn. Friends remember Gomez fondly, describing her as outgoing and hardworking. She spent a lot of time at her job at a Kroger's pharmacy and was looking forward to starting classes at Lone Star College. Gomez's death has left her friends and family devastated, struggling to understand what led to her untimely passing. The investigation is ongoing, with authorities awaiting autopsy results and questioning the boyfriend, who has been cooperative. The incident has raised concerns about the safety of after-prom activities and the potential risks associated with alcohol and drug use.

A letter containing a substance that tested positive for ricin was intercepted at the U.S. Capitol's off-site mail facility in Washington, D.C., according to Senate Sergeant-at-Arms Terrance Gainer. The letter was addressed to Sen. Roger Wicker, R-Mississippi, and had a Memphis, Tennessee, postmark with no return address. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid informed reporters that the letter was tested at the facility and came up positive for ricin. However, the FBI stated that additional testing is necessary as field and preliminary tests can be inconsistent. Laboratory tests at an accredited facility in Maryland confirmed the presence of ricin. The letter was quarantined immediately, and Capitol Police hazardous material personnel responded. The Senate mail facility is closed for testing, and all mail bound for Capitol Hill is now directed through a U.S. House facility. The letter was postmarked on April 16, 2013, and had no suspicious markings or return address. A protective detail has been assigned to Sen. Wicker, and lawmakers were briefed on the incident. The Senate went into recess shortly after the discovery. The letter is part of a broader investigation, with a suspect identified but no arrest made. The process of handling mail at the Capitol has been in place since the 2001 anthrax attacks, and senators were warned to be vigilant for similar letters. Ricin, a highly toxic substance derived from castor beans, can be fatal in small quantities.

Norway's Prime Minister Erna Solberg issued a government apology on Wednesday for the mistreatment of women who had intimate wartime relationships with German soldiers during World War II. The estimated 50,000 Norwegian women labeled "German girls" faced severe reprisals after the country's liberation in 1945, including job dismissals, detentions, expulsions, and removal of nationality. Many of these women were just teenagers when they had relationships with German soldiers, and some considered them the love of their lives. The treatment of these women breached the principle that no citizen should be punished outside the court system. Solberg delivered the apology at an event marking the 70th anniversary of the UN's Universal Declaration of Human Rights. The SS chief Heinrich Himmler encouraged German troops to partner and breed with local women as part of Nazi Germany's white supremacist agenda, leading to the establishment of Lebensborn (Fountain of Life) maternity facilities in Norway from 1941. These facilities were set up to promote the Nazi concept of an Aryan master race. Many of the Norwegian-German children were born in these facilities. Women who had relationships with German soldiers became known as "German girls" and were targeted for reprisals, with punishments including being deprived of civil rights, detained, or expelled to Germany with their children. The government's conclusion is that Norwegian authorities violated the fundamental principle that no citizen can be punished without trial or sentenced without law. The apology was based on a report by the Centre for Holocaust and Minorities Studies. The prime minister's statement acknowledged that for many, the relationships were just teenage love, while for some, they were the love of their lives with an enemy soldier or an innocent flirt that left a lasting mark. The apology also touched on the treatment of the estimated 10,000 to 12,000 children born as a result of these relationships, who were often placed in foster homes or institutions. While many of the directly affected women are no longer alive, the apology was seen as important for their families and the children. The event was attended by individuals like Reidar Gabler, whose mother was expelled in 1945 along with her German husband, highlighting the lasting impact of the government's actions.

An FBI agent was shot in the shoulder while conducting surveillance for a drug investigation in Canarsie, Brooklyn, on Saturday afternoon, sources tell CBS2. The agent was inside a car when a suspect, driving a BMW, drove the wrong way down a one-way street and opened fire, the sources said. The agent was conscious and alert when rushed to Kings County Hospital, where he underwent surgery for non-life-threatening injuries. The agent may have tried to intervene before the shooting began, as he pursued the BMW and fired more than 10 times. The suspect fled the scene, abandoning the BMW at an auto body shop. He was later taken to Kingsbrook Jewish Medical Center for treatment of at least one gunshot wound. His friend was arrested for driving with a suspended license. NYPD Chief of Department Terence Monahan tweeted that there were no outstanding suspects at the time of the incident. The investigation is ongoing, with a large police presence in the area.

The magnitude-6.0 earthquake that struck the Napa Valley early Sunday morning caused significant damage to buildings and infrastructure, leading to a state of emergency declaration by Governor Jerry Brown. More than 250 people were injured, with two people in critical condition, including a 13-year-old boy who was injured by a falling chimney. Damage assessments revealed that 70 buildings were deemed uninhabitable, and 600 properties remained without water due to broken water mains. Schools were closed, and residents faced challenges such as accessing clean water, with some using swimming pools to flush toilets. The earthquake's impact on the wine industry was notable, with shattered bottles and spilled wine at several wineries, but overall damage was not as extensive as initially feared. Cleanup efforts were underway, with volunteers and businesses like Home Depot offering assistance. The event highlighted the need for better earthquake preparedness and early warning systems, as the initial seismic activity led to confusion about the fault responsible. The earthquake, while significant, did not cause as much damage as feared, with many structures showing only minor damage. The recovery process, however, is expected to be lengthy, with the possibility of months of cleanup and rebuilding.

On Friday, April 1, 2016, the U.S. government issued the March jobs report, revealing that employers added 215,000 jobs, marking another solid month of hiring. This figure was driven by significant gains in the construction, retail, and health care industries, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Despite the robust job creation, the unemployment rate ticked up to 5.0 percent from 4.9 percent, but this increase was largely due to more Americans entering the labor force, as many who had given up their job search during the Great Recession began looking again. The rise in the labor force participation rate indicates that the job market remains healthy, as employers remain confident in their business prospects, even as overall economic growth has slowed since last winter. Many analysts estimate that the economy grew at a 1 percent annual rate or below in the first quarter, but steady job gains suggest that the slowdown may be temporary.

Wage growth showed modest improvement, with average hourly earnings rising 2.3 percent from the previous year, reaching $25.43. While this figure has increased since the early years of the recovery, it remains below the peak of 2.6 percent reached in December. Sluggish wage growth has been a persistent issue since the Great Recession ended in 2009, with paychecks typically growing at a 3.5 percent pace in a strong economy. Construction firms contributed significantly to job growth, adding 37,000 positions, likely due to warmer weather. However, manufacturing and mining sectors experienced job losses, with mining particularly affected by low oil prices, which have cost the industry 185,000 jobs since September 2014.

The addition of jobs can help fuel consumer spending, which is a critical driver of economic growth. However, consumer spending has faltered since last winter, with spending ticking up just 0.1 percent in February for the third consecutive month. This tepid trend has caused many economists to revise their growth forecasts downward. Americans appear to be saving more of their savings from lower gas prices rather than spending them, as the savings rate rose to 5.4 percent in February, the highest in a year. Other economic data has been unusually mixed, with some reports suggesting that manufacturers may be stabilizing after a difficult 2015, when weak overseas growth and a strong dollar hurt production. Additionally, home sales fell sharply by 7.1 percent in February, held back by a lack of available supply that has pushed up prices. Overall, the March jobs report provides a mixed picture of the U.S. economy, with job growth continuing but other economic indicators showing signs of weakness.

Pepsi faced widespread backlash and criticism for an advertisement featuring Kendall Jenner that was deemed to trivialize the Black Lives Matter movement. The ad, which showed Jenner leaving a modeling shoot to join a group of smiling protesters who cheerfully accepted a can of Pepsi from a police officer, was pulled by the company, which apologized for "missing the mark." Pepsi clarified that the ad was created by its in-house team and was intended to promote a global message of unity, peace, and understanding. However, the ad's critics pointed out that it appeared to co-opt the serious and often violent protests for commercial purposes, with some even comparing it to a photo of Black Lives Matter protester Ieshia Evans approaching a police officer at a demonstration in Baton Rouge. The ad's messages, such as "Join the Conversation" and heart and peace signs, were seen as comically insincere, and the overall tone was described as "tone-deaf" by many. Late-night comedian Stephen Colbert mocked the ad, highlighting its absurdity and the incongruity of Jenner, a member of the "Keeping Up with the Kardashians" reality TV family, being cast in such a role. The incident was reminiscent of Pepsi's 2013 Mountain Dew ad, which was criticized for racial stereotypes and light-hearted treatment of violence against women. Pepsi's apology and the swift removal of the ad indicate the company's sensitivity to public sentiment, but the backlash suggests that the ad's message was not well-received.

Gretchen Carlson, a former Fox News anchor, settled a sexual harassment lawsuit against Roger Ailes, the network’s former chairman and CEO, for $20 million. In a statement, 21st Century Fox, the parent company, expressed regret for the lack of respect and dignity Carlson and other colleagues experienced. Carlson, who was removed from her 2 p.m. show in 2013, alleged that Ailes made inappropriate comments and terminated her contract in retaliation for refusing his sexual advances. Ailes denied the allegations, calling them "false" and "retaliatory." The settlement included a public apology from the company, acknowledging that Carlson and other Fox News employees deserved respect and dignity. Carlson, in her statement, expressed gratitude for the decisive action taken by 21st Century Fox and her commitment to empowering women in the workplace. The article also mentions that two other women are reportedly in talks for their own settlements, though the exact amount is not specified. The settlement comes amid a broader investigation into sexual harassment allegations against Ailes, which led to his ousting from Fox News. The case highlights the complex dynamics within the network and the broader media landscape, where powerful executives have faced scrutiny and accountability for their actions.

In the wake of the tragic shooting at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Florida, Wayne LaPierre, the executive vice president of the National Rifle Association (NRA), addressed a conservative political conference, emphasizing the need for increased school security and dismissing calls for gun control as a threat to liberty. Speaking at the Conservative Political Action Conference, LaPierre accused gun control advocates of exploiting the tragedy for political gain and warned that Democrats, including potential 2020 presidential candidates, are pushing a "socialist" agenda that aims to undermine the Second Amendment. He called for beefing up school security, including arming teachers, and criticized the FBI for failing to prevent the attack. LaPierre’s remarks came as President Trump and some Republican lawmakers considered modest gun control measures, including raising the age for purchasing semi-automatic weapons to 21 and tightening background checks. Meanwhile, the NRA’s own spokeswoman, Dana Loesch, criticized the media for its coverage, suggesting that it benefits from sensationalizing mass shootings. The NRA’s push for more armed security at schools contrasts with the stance taken by some Republican lawmakers, such as Florida Senator Marco Rubio, who oppose arming teachers and support raising the age limit on purchasing certain firearms. The debate over gun control and school safety continues to polarize American politics, with the NRA maintaining its influential role in the discourse.

Spanish police have arrested at least one person following the discovery of what is thought to be the bodies of Dutch international volleyball player Ingrid Visser and her partner Lodewijk Severin, who disappeared in Murcia on May 13. Their bodies were found buried in a shallow grave in a lemon grove near a house in the village of Alquerías, some 12 kilometers from Murcia. Identification is pending DNA testing, but the bodies are described as extremely tall, which is a good indication they are the missing couple. The couple failed to show up for a hospital appointment in Spain, where some reports suggest they were due for fertility treatment. Their rental car was later found on a street in Murcia. The police raided an apartment in Murcia on Friday, finding evidence of a violent crime and arresting one man. Two other suspects, possibly Romanian nationals, were also picked up in Valencia. Spanish police believe the murders may have been business-related, with an ex-director of a Spanish volleyball club among the three arrested. Murcia's police chief stated there appeared to be "certain business disagreements" between the couple and the suspects, though no details were provided. The case, which dominated Dutch media, has now been solved after two weeks.

Rupert Murdoch met with the family of murdered schoolgirl Milly Dowler and offered a "full and sincere apology," according to Dowler family lawyer Mark Lewis. The meeting, held at a London hotel, came as the long-simmering phone hacking scandal involving Murdoch's News of the World intensified. Dowler's phone was allegedly hacked by the now-defunct tabloid, which was shut down last week. Murdoch's apology was humbly delivered, with him reportedly saying, "I was appalled about what had happened and I apologise." Lewis described the apology as "full and sincere," but noted that "actions are going to speak louder than words." The scandal has led to the resignation of Rebekah Brooks, the editor of the News of the World at the time, and has cast a shadow over Murdoch's British newspaper empire. Brooks resigned as CEO of News International, the British arm of News Corp., amid mounting pressure and allegations of wrongdoing. The resignation was seen as "poetic justice" by Lewis. As the scandal continues to unfold, two U.K. police investigations are ongoing, and the FBI is reviewing claims that News Corp. journalists hacked into the phones of 9/11 victims. Meanwhile, News Corp. shares have fallen, and the company faces the prospect of a public inquiry led by Lord Justice Leveson. The resignation of Brooks and the meeting with the Dowler family highlight the severity of the crisis facing Murdoch and his media empire.

Mark Cuban, the outspoken Dallas Mavericks owner, recently found himself at the center of controversy when he admitted to harboring certain prejudices in a video interview with Inc. magazine. Cuban, known for his candid and often controversial statements, revealed that he sometimes walks to the other side of the street when he sees a black kid in a hoodie late at night and avoids walking near a white man with tattoos. This admission sparked a wave of reactions, with some praising Cuban for his honesty and others criticizing him for perpetuating harmful stereotypes.

Cuban, who has been vocal in his opposition to Donald Sterling's racist comments, acknowledged that everyone has some form of prejudice. He emphasized the importance of recognizing and addressing these biases, stating, "We all have our prejudices and bigotries, but we have to learn that it's an issue that we have to control, that it's part of my responsibility as an entrepreneur to try to solve it." His comments came during a business conference in Nashville, Tennessee, where he also discussed the progress made by minority communities in America, noting that "with that progress comes a price."

CNN commentator LZ Granderson criticized Cuban's analogy, arguing that equating the fear of a black kid in a hoodie with the fear of a white man with tattoos is a poor comparison. Granderson pointed out that the former has a long history of unjust treatment and even killings, while the latter does not. Cuban later apologized to Trayvon Martin's family for using the hoodie reference, but stood by the context of his answers, calling for more tolerance and understanding.

The incident also raised questions about the NBA's stance on race and the potential lack of unity among its owners. Cuban, one of 30 NBA owners who will decide Sterling's fate, expressed regret over the situation but acknowledged that bigotry is a reality. He emphasized the importance of addressing these issues constructively, stating, "It's better to work with them and teach them why their views are wrong."

Cuban's remarks sparked a broader discussion about race and prejudice in the business world and society at large. While some praised his honesty, others criticized him for perpetuating harmful stereotypes. The controversy highlights the ongoing struggle to address and overcome racial biases in both professional and personal contexts.

Seminal new wave band Devo, known for their unique sound and provocative lyrics, have lost a founding member, Bob Casale, who passed away at the age of 61. Bob Casale, often referred to as "Bob 2," was a key figure in the band's early days and continued to contribute to their work, including soundtracks for TV, film, and video games. His brother and bandmate, Gerald Casale, described Bob as "solid performer and talented audio engineer, always giving more than he got." The band, which began after Gerald and Mark Mothersbaugh met as art students at Kent State University, started writing music in May 1970, the same month of the Kent State shootings. Devo's machine-like persona, characterized by flowerpot hats, industrial jumpsuits, and futuristic sounds, made them a significant presence in the new wave scene. Despite not maintaining the mainstream success of their hit "Whip It!" in 1980, Devo's influence remains strong, with their work featured in various media and their continued touring. Bob Casale's death came as a shock to the band and fans, with Mark Mothersbaugh expressing his shock and sadness, noting Bob's extensive work on films, television shows, and video games. Gerald Casale was hopeful about the possibility of Mark Mothersbaugh allowing Devo to play shows again, but Bob's sudden heart failure ended his life prematurely.

A 21-year-old former Stanford University student, Scott Bertics, allegedly built a homemade "ghost gun" using parts he ordered online and used it to kill his former girlfriend, Clare Orton, at her home in Walnut Creek, California. The incident occurred on July 21, around 6:50 a.m., when Bertics showed up at Orton's family home in Holton Court, off Homestead Avenue. He shot Orton, who was home for the summer from San Diego State University, and then turned the gun on himself. Police stated that neither of the guns found at the scene had serial numbers, making them "ghost guns." Lt. Lanny Edwards of the Walnut Creek police explained that anyone can purchase parts online, such as metal, trigger assemblies, and handles, to build a gun, with the cost ranging from $400 to $1,200. Bertics, who was studying engineering, had a history of academic projects related to robotics and neural networks. He took a leave of absence from Stanford after the fall 2014 quarter and did not return. Clare Orton, a 19-year-old honors student at San Diego State, was an active member of the Society of Western Engineers and Eco-Action Club. The shooting raised concerns about the ease of obtaining untraceable firearms through online purchases, as similar legislation proposed by California Senator Kevin de León was vetoed by Governor Jerry Brown in September 2014. The lack of background checks and serial numbers on these "ghost guns" highlights the potential for misuse by individuals with malicious intent.

The Vancouver Maritime Museum, located in Vanier Park, offers a unique and engaging exploration of Vancouver's maritime history, with the centerpiece being the St. Roch, the first ship to circumnavigate North America. Visitors can explore the ship's interior, admire model ships, and enjoy interactive exhibits like Pirates Cove and the Discovery Center, which are particularly popular with children. The museum also features extensive galleries of maritime art and artifacts, including the boiler of the Beaver, the first steamship in the Pacific Northwest. While the St. Roch is the highlight, some exhibits and displays, like the "Scrimshaw" exhibit featuring sexually explicit etchings on whale teeth, have drawn criticism for being inappropriate for children. Despite this, the museum remains a popular destination for families and history enthusiasts, offering a mix of educational and entertaining experiences. Parking is available in a pay lot out front or for free across the street, and admission is $11 for adults, with discounted rates on select days.

A 14-month-old girl named Xania Samuels fell from a fifth-story window at her family's Bronx apartment on Monday, but she is expected to survive, authorities and neighbors said. The child's father stated that she was wearing her favorite pink winter coat, which might have cushioned her fall, as it was the hottest day of the year. The incident occurred when the father was giving the girl's twin brother a bath, while the mother was at a Laundromat. There were no window guards on the upper floors of the six-story building, and the family had previously complained to the landlord, who ignored their concerns. Xania was rushed to Jacobi Hospital with head trauma and was listed in critical condition as of 4:30 p.m. The fall happened at 11:29 a.m., but it was not immediately noticed. Willis Sands, a 57-year-old emergency medical technician, found the baby "laying lifelessly" on a bloody pavement and called 911. Within five minutes, emergency assistance arrived, and two minutes later, the father saw the baby's body and screamed for help. Neighbors described the baby as wearing a diaper, one slipper, and wrapped in a pink blanket. The lack of window guards and the family's complaints to the landlord highlight the importance of safety measures in multi-story buildings with young children.

During the busy summer travel season, Pittsburgh International Airport is making a change that could impact how travelers navigate through the airport. Starting September 5, non-ticketed passengers will be allowed to pass through security checkpoints and access the airside terminal's shops, restaurants, and gates. This move, which the airport claims will return to the "good-old days" of air travel, has sparked criticism from the union representing flight attendants at American Airlines. Bob Ross, the national president of the Association of Professional Flight Attendants, argues that this change will decrease airport safety and lead to longer security lines, potentially causing flyers to miss their flights. The TSA supports the change but notes that no additional staff has been hired for it and there are no plans to expand the program. The decision comes days before the anniversary of 9/11, which Ross believes is an inappropriate timing, as it should be a reminder of the need to remain vigilant. Despite the potential benefits for non-flyers, the move has raised concerns about security and the overall travel experience.

Newark Mayor Cory Booker has easily won the Democratic primary for the U.S. Senate seat vacated by the late Frank Lautenberg, with 59% of the vote compared to his closest opponent, Rep. Frank Pallone, who garnered 20%. The race faced criticism for its compressed schedule, with the primary held just 20 days before the general election, which drew accusations that the governor, Chris Christie, was manipulating the date to avoid a potential strong challenger. Booker's campaign focused on his pragmatic approach and his ability to work across the aisle, contrasting this with the aggressive attacks from his rivals. His victory was seen as a confirmation of his political rise, marked by his unconventional path from community activist to mayor, and his ability to leverage his public profile and media presence to highlight Newark's transformation. Despite facing scrutiny over his business interests, including his stake in an Internet start-up, Booker maintained that his record in Newark demonstrated his effectiveness. His win sets the stage for a campaign against Republican Steve Lonegan, who will face the challenge of countering Booker's well-known public persona and his record of urban renewal.

Billionaire fashion designer Peter Nygard claims he has found a way to reverse his aging process through stem cell therapy, according to reports from the Bahamas Tribune. Nygard, who is 70 years old, says he is receiving stem cell treatments and that a study from the University of Miami suggests he is getting younger. "They are looking at me, and my markers have shown exactly that I have been actually reversing my aging and getting younger," Nygard stated. He adds, "I am taking perhaps more stem-cell treatment than anybody else in the world. I have been doing it for four years now, so I am sort of a testimonial that this stem cell really works." Nygard, known for his advocacy of stem cell research in the Bahamas, has been examining potential sites in Freeport, including the shuttered Port Lucaya Resort, for a stem cell clinic. A local attorney, Fred Smith, expressed support for Nygard's plans, stating that Freeport needs the investment and that Nygard would make an excellent contribution to the medical tourism landscape. However, critics and residents of Lyford Cay, where Nygard has faced opposition for his proposed stem cell facility, remain skeptical. The Bahamas Tribune article highlights the potential benefits of stem cell research, including the possibility of curing diseases and extending life, while also raising concerns about the ethical implications and the motives of those pushing the technology.

Louisville guard Kevin Ware suffered a horrific leg injury during a closely watched NCAA tournament game against Duke, leaving his teammates in tears and national television quickly cutting away from the gruesome scene. Ware's right leg broke in two places, with the bone protruding six inches out of his skin, as he landed awkwardly while attempting to block a shot. Louisville coach Rick Pitino described the injury as one he had never seen before, with Ware repeatedly insisting he was fine to encourage his teammates to continue playing. Ware's injury quickly became one of the top trending topics on Twitter, with video of the incident posted on YouTube. Despite the severity of the injury, Louisville went on to win the game 85-63. Kevin Ware underwent successful surgery to reset his bone, insert a rod, and close his wound, with a recovery time of several months or more expected. Ware hopes to return to support his team in the Final Four in Atlanta, his hometown. The incident sparked discussions about the lack of compensation for injured NCAA athletes, as Ware was playing on a scholarship and would not be eligible for worker's compensation. The debate over the morality of college athletics and the potential long-term impact on Ware's career continued as the tournament progressed.

In the ongoing saga of the JonBenét Ramsey case, Boulder police and prosecutors are planning to conduct new DNA tests on key evidence from the 1996 murder of the 6-year-old beauty queen. This decision follows a joint investigation by the Daily Camera and 9NEWS, which revealed serious flaws in the interpretation of previous DNA testing on the girl's panties and long johns. The new tests will utilize more sophisticated DNA kits required by the FBI's Combined DNA Index System, which will be implemented early in 2017. Boulder County District Attorney Stan Garnett and Boulder Police Chief Greg Testa confirmed they had discussed the issue with the Colorado Bureau of Investigation (CBI) administrators, who are preparing to unveil these new, more sensitive testing methods. The move aims to address ambiguities in the 2008 DNA testing, which were disputed by multiple forensic experts. These experts suggested that the "Unknown Male 1" profile, which was used to clear the Ramseys, may not be a single individual's DNA but a composite of multiple contributors. The presence of a third person's genetic markers on the evidence has never been publicly revealed before. The new testing could potentially exonerate or implicate someone in the case, but experts emphasize that DNA alone is not conclusive. The case remains a complex mix of theories, with former District Attorney Mary Lacy's exoneration of the Ramseys now called into question. The investigation continues, with calls for Y-STR testing on key evidence to focus on male contributors. The case, which has captivated the public for two decades, may see new developments as technology evolves.

After days of escalating violence, Palestinian and Israeli authorities have agreed to a truce and to stop all military operations, an Egyptian intelligence official announced. The agreement, facilitated by Egyptian mediators, comes as seven people were killed in Gaza on Monday, and more than 36 rockets fell into Israel. Israeli airstrikes have targeted militant rocket-launching sites in response to over 200 rocket attacks from Gaza since Friday. Palestinian officials reported 25 people killed in strikes since Friday, while at least 80 were wounded. The latest round of violence, the worst in Gaza this year, has seen 21 people killed and 36 injured in Israel. The conflict has prompted international concern, with UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon expressing grave concern over civilian casualties. Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu stated that the military is ready to expand its operations, while Palestinian militant group Islamic Jihad vowed to continue firing rockets into southern Israel. The truce is the first top-level meeting of the diplomatic Quartet in six months, with US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov, and UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon attending the meeting at UN headquarters in New York. EU foreign affairs representative Baroness Ashton will participate via videoconference. The Quartet's efforts to revive direct talks between Israel and the Palestinians have faced challenges, with the US threatening to veto a UN Security Council resolution on Palestinian statehood. The ongoing violence has strained the health care system in Gaza, with the minister of health warning of potential collapse if hostilities escalate further.

A four-story building being demolished in Philadelphia collapsed early Wednesday, crushing a Salvation Army thrift store and killing six people, including five women and one man. The collapse trapped 13 others, but a 61-year-old woman was pulled alive after 13 hours. The building's demolition was permitted, and no violations were known, though witnesses said the structure was unstable for weeks. Bystanders rushed to help, with some rescuing survivors. Mayor Michael Nutter pledged a wide-ranging investigation, as questions arose about the permits and inspections. The tragedy occurred in a busy area, disrupting nearby businesses and traffic. The Salvation Army sent a disaster response team and asked for prayers. The collapse raised concerns about the city's oversight of demolition sites.

When Huguette Clark's will was filed six months ago, art lovers in Santa Barbara were delighted: The reclusive 104-year-old copper heiress had left her bluff-top estate to be transformed into a museum. However, the possibility of this museum being established by Clark's longtime attorney and accountant—whose ethics had been questioned—diminished when a New York City judge suspended them as Clark's executors, citing accusations of massive tax fraud. The public administrator's office alleged that attorney Wallace Bock and accountant Irving Kamsler caused Clark's estate to lose over $50 million through false tax returns, charging her for unfiled returns, and allowing her to make over $56 million in gifts to individuals, including themselves and Clark's nurse, Hadassah Peri. The public administrator contended that Bock and Kamsler were "unfit for the execution of their office" due to their "dishonesty, improvidence, waste, and want of understanding." Bock and Kamsler, who stood to make millions in fees, had already been under investigation by the Manhattan district attorney for alleged mismanagement of Clark's finances. The case is further complicated by the fact that Clark had signed two wills six weeks apart, with the second will cutting out her family and bequeathing significant sums to Bock and Kamsler. The family of the heiress has challenged the second will and requested to intervene in the case. The public administrator is also seeking to claw back any gifts deemed invalid. The case highlights the complex and often murky financial dealings of the wealthy and the challenges faced by their relatives in managing their estates.

Sandy Hook Elementary students returned to class on Thursday at a nearby middle school in Monroe, Conn., where they will remain until their old school is no longer designated a crime scene. The 400-plus students, who had not been back to school since Adam Lanza's shooting on December 14, were thrilled to reconnect with their friends and teachers. Attendance was robust, with most school buses full as they rumbled down streets decorated with balloons and welcome signs. The new school, formerly known as Chalk Hill Middle School, was refurnished for the students, with their old desks, backpacks, coats, and lunch boxes brought in. The new principal, Donna Page, who retired from Sandy Hook in 2010, agreed to come back after her successor, Dawn Hochsprung, was killed. Security was very visible, with police officers and counselors on hand, and parents allowed to stay in the building for the day. Children cuddled with therapy dogs, and the atmosphere was described as cheerful. While security measures were in place, officials aimed to make the day as normal as possible, with teachers trying to recreate familiar classroom settings. The reopening was seen as a step towards normalcy, with Connecticut Governor Dannel Malloy announcing a commission to spearhead legislative and policy reforms to ensure no other children face similar horrors. The commission will focus on school security, mental health services, and gun laws, with Malloy emphasizing the need to address the availability of high-capacity ammunition clips.

Bodybuilder Rich Piana, a former Mr. California bodybuilding champion, had 20 bottles of steroids in his Florida home at the time of his medical emergency, according to a police report obtained by TMZ Sports. On Monday, at 1:30 PM, Piana suddenly collapsed in his bathroom while getting a haircut from his girlfriend, Chanel. Unable to catch him, Chanel witnessed him strike his head during the fall. Emergency operators instructed Chanel to perform CPR, but they were unable to revive him. Paramedics found crushed white powder, a credit card, and a straw at the scene, leading them to administer two doses of Narcan, a drug often used to treat opiate overdoses. Chanel, who claims Rich had battled opiate addiction in the past but believed he was clean, stated that Rich had been using steroids for over 20 years. Rich was transported to a nearby hospital and placed into a medically induced coma. The police report also noted that Rich had suffered from a slightly enlarged heart at one point in his life, though it's unclear if this contributed to the medical emergency. Chanel, who is asking for prayers for Rich, says he is still alive and fighting.

The half marathon has seen a significant surge in popularity, becoming the fastest-growing standard distance among U.S. road races in 2013. According to data from Running USA, an industry trade group, there were approximately 1.96 million finishers in U.S. half marathons, marking a 6% increase from the previous year and setting a new record. This growth is largely attributed to increased female participation, with women making up 61% of finishers, up from 53% in 2006. The race's popularity extends beyond the U.S., with the largest events occurring in Sweden and Great Britain. Since 1990, the number of half marathon finishers in the U.S. has increased more than sixfold, from 303,000 to 1.96 million, highlighting the enduring appeal of this distance among runners.

Portland police have reopened their investigation into sexual assault allegations against former Vice President Al Gore, citing procedural mistakes in the original 2009 handling of the case. The bureau's command-level supervisors should have reviewed the case and made the decision on whether to proceed, according to Chief Michael Reese. In 2006, an attorney representing massage therapist Molly Hagerty contacted Portland police, but detectives failed to contact Gore and did not consult with the Multnomah County district attorney's office. The case was initially cleared due to Hagerty's lack of cooperation. Reese emphasized the bureau's commitment to a thorough, fair, and timely investigation, urging public patience. Detectives will be assigned appropriate resources to ensure an expedited and complete investigation.

On Friday, the Svalbard Global Seed Vault, a facility designed to safeguard global food supplies against natural or man-made disasters, faced a significant challenge when water from melting permafrost leaked into the tunnel leading to the vault. This incident, which occurred in October 2016, highlighted the facility's vulnerability to climate change, despite its robust design. According to Hege Njaa Aschim, the communications director of the Norwegian Government-led organization Statsbygg, the leak happened during a period of high temperatures and unusual rainfall in the Svalbard area. The water intrusion, which reached about 15 meters into the 100-meter tunnel, did not affect the seeds stored in the vault, which are kept at a temperature of -18°C. However, the incident prompted the organization to take measures to waterproof the tunnel.

The Svalbard Global Seed Vault, located on an Arctic island 1,300 kilometers from the North Pole, holds over 860,000 samples of seeds from almost all nations. The facility was built to protect crop seeds against catastrophic events such as nuclear war or disease. The entrance to the vault is designed to be water-tight, but the permafrost near the tunnel entrance, which was disturbed during construction, has become more susceptible to water intrusion due to climate change. The tunnel runs at a slight downward slope, with two pumping stations installed to remove any water that might enter. Despite the recent leak, the vault's design ensures that the seeds remain safe for at least 200 years, even in the event of a power failure.

The incident at the Svalbard Global Seed Vault serves as a reminder of the ongoing challenges posed by climate change to facilities designed to preserve biodiversity. While the seeds themselves are safe, the vulnerability of the tunnel entrance highlights the need for continuous monitoring and adaptation to ensure the long-term preservation of the world's crop diversity. The vault's operators are committed to addressing the issue and enhancing the facility's resilience to environmental changes, emphasizing the importance of global cooperation in safeguarding our agricultural heritage.

A 30-year-old hospital technician in Uganda has died of the Marburg virus, a hemorrhagic fever closely related to Ebola. Health officials have quarantined approximately 80 people who came into contact with the victim, including 60 health-care workers. Among those tested, the brother of the deceased and several others showed early symptoms but tested negative. The virus has a high fatality rate, ranging from 23% to 90% in previous outbreaks, but Uganda has experience in handling such threats. The Marburg virus was first identified in 1967, with an outbreak in Germany and Yugoslavia linked to laboratory monkeys imported from Uganda. Since then, the virus has appeared sporadically, often involving just one patient. Symptoms begin with fever and weakness, progressing to nausea, vomiting, chest pain, and abdominal pain. Severe cases can lead to jaundice, inflammation of the pancreas, massive hemorrhaging, and multi-organ dysfunction. There is no specific treatment or vaccine for Marburg, and hospital care focuses on supportive therapy. The CDC highlights the importance of early detection and response networks, as seen in Uganda's recent containment efforts. The extensive contact tracing, including tracking an embalmer back to Kenya, demonstrates the effectiveness of these measures. While the risk of a large-scale outbreak remains, Uganda's experience and preparedness give reason for cautious optimism.

In a bizarre case that left doctors in Amritsar, Punjab, stunned, a 42-year-old police head constable named Jarnail Singh admitted to eating 40 knives over a period of two months, claiming he "felt like eating them." The unusual situation came to light when Singh visited a hospital with complaints of stomach pain, weight loss, and a decreased appetite. A 5-member medical team spent 5 hours conducting a complex surgery to remove the metallic objects from his stomach. Dr. Jatinder Malhotra, a member of the surgical team, expressed his shock, stating, "In my 20 years of practice, this is the most dreadful surgery I have ever seen or done." The knives, of various sizes, were found to be either opened, broken due to rust, or lying closed inside the patient's stomach. The patient's condition is now stable, but the incident highlights a unique psychological issue that led to such an extreme behavior. Dr. Malhotra further emphasized the severity, saying, "This was very unnerving, I have not witnessed something like this in my career as a doctor."

French prosecutors have filed preliminary murder and terrorism charges against Abdelkader Merah, the 29-year-old brother of Mohamed Merah, who was killed by police after claiming responsibility for attacking a Jewish school, a rabbi, and three paratroopers. Abdelkader Merah, known to security services for helping smuggle Jihadist militants into Iraq, denies complicity but acknowledges being present when his brother stole a scooter used in the attacks. He claims he was not proud of his brother's actions and fears becoming a scapegoat. Abdelkader was questioned several years ago about alleged links to a network sending Toulouse-area youths to Iraq but was not charged. The mother of the brothers, Zoulika Aziri, was released without charge. Meanwhile, several thousand people marched in Toulouse and Paris, urging unity and tolerance.

The United States finally broke through a 75-year losing streak against Mexico, winning 1-0 in Mexico City in a friendly match on August 15, 2012. Michael Orozco Fiscal scored the only goal in the 80th minute, and goalkeeper Tim Howard made crucial late saves to preserve the lead. The victory ended a 24-game losing streak in Mexico, including 23 losses and one tie. Coach Jurgen Klinsmann praised the team's defensive resilience and Howard's crucial saves. Despite Mexico dominating possession and having a 10-0 corner-kick advantage, the U.S. maintained their shape and focus. Key players like Brek Shea and Michael Orozco Fiscal contributed, while Geoff Cameron's defensive performance was highlighted. The win provided a significant psychological boost for the U.S. team, marking a historic achievement in their rivalry with Mexico. The victory also underscored the importance of mental fortitude and the ability to compete in hostile environments, as the U.S. team faced the pressure of playing in the Azteca Stadium. This result, along with a previous victory against Italy, demonstrated the team's potential to compete against top-tier opponents.

California is revising its sex-offender residency rules, allowing parolees to live within 2,000 feet of schools and parks on a case-by-case basis. This change follows a state Supreme Court ruling that found the previous blanket restrictions unconstitutional in San Diego County. The new policy aims to address the issue of thousands of sex offenders becoming homeless due to the stringent residency laws, which made it difficult for them to find housing in urban areas. Under the revised rules, high-risk offenders with a history of sexually abusing children will still be prohibited from living within a half-mile of K-12 schools. However, for those who do not pose a significant risk, the restrictions will be relaxed. The California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation is currently reviewing the cases of over 2,300 homeless sex offender parolees to determine if the residency law should still apply. This process is expected to take about two months. The move is seen as a compromise between public safety concerns and the practical challenges faced by sex offenders in finding suitable housing. Critics argue that the new policy is too lenient and could compromise public safety, while supporters believe it will help reduce homelessness among parolees and improve their chances of rehabilitation.

China is significantly bolstering its defenses along its 880-mile frontier with North Korea, amid escalating tensions on the Korean Peninsula and concerns over potential U.S. military action against Pyongyang. Recent reports published on Chinese military and government websites indicate that Beijing has initiated these changes in recent months, following their initial implementation last year. The North Korean-Chinese border, which includes North Korea, Russia, and Mongolia, is now under heightened surveillance, with new border defense brigades conducting patrols and intelligence gathering. The region is of strategic importance to China, having experienced conflict during World War II and the Korean War. However, the primary concern for Beijing is not a military invasion but a mass movement of North Korean civilians across the border into China. Analysts warn that a conflict on the peninsula could result in hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of refugees, straining China's economy and security. The Syrian refugee crisis serves as a stark reminder of the potential strain such a scenario could place on China. In March, retired PLA Major General Wang Haiyun suggested setting up an international refugee camp in North Korean territory to manage the influx of refugees. The United States has sought to pressure China to take a harder stance against North Korea, but despite repeated condemnations, little progress has been made. The Trump administration's rhetoric on the issue has led to frustration, with U.S. officials, including CIA Director Mike Pompeo, indicating support for regime change in Pyongyang. China's Ministry of Foreign Affairs has maintained that military means should not be an option to resolve the Korean Peninsula issue, while the Defense Ministry has declined to comment on China's war contingency plans. The situation has led to growing tensions, with China's military maintaining a normal combat readiness and training status along the border.

A new report by She Should Run and the Center for Responsive Politics reveals that women's political contributions have decreased, making up only 26% of total federal political contributions in 2010, down from 31% in 2008. This decline coincided with a decrease in women's representation in Congress, where women now make up just 17% of the members, despite representing over 50% of the population. Female candidates are better fundraisers, with incumbents raising $100,000 more on average than their male counterparts, and challengers raising over $74,000 more. However, women are less likely to donate, with only four out of 2,215 candidates relying on women for more than 50% of their contributions. The report suggests that women are less motivated to donate because they do not see the connection between politics and social change, and find the political process distasteful. It recommends emphasizing the impact of contributions on specific issues and framing political giving as a civic responsibility. The decrease in women’s political giving is concerning, as it may hinder progress on issues important to women.

Trouble at the summit of Mount Everest has intensified, with the deaths of 16 Sherpa guides in a deadly avalanche last year and the subsequent decision by Himalayan Experience (Himex), one of the largest commercial operators on Everest, to cancel its expedition in 2012, drawing attention to the mountain's increasing dangers. The avalanche, which struck the Khumbu Icefall, a notoriously unstable section of the route, highlighted the risks faced by Sherpas, who carry the majority of the physical burden for climbers. The fatality rate for Sherpas working on Everest has been alarmingly high, with a death rate of 1,332 per 100,000 full-time equivalents from 2000 to 2010, and a staggering 4,053 per 100,000 from 2004 to 2014, making it far more dangerous than even combat in Iraq from 2003 to 2007.

In 2012, Russell Brice, the owner of Himex, faced a critical decision when a massive ice bulge threatened the main route up the mountain. His clients, guides, and Sherpas repeatedly had to climb beneath the ice, and some of his most experienced Sherpas broke down in tears, confessing their fear for their lives. Brice's decision to pull all his guides, members, and Sherpas off the mountain and head home was met with criticism and backlash, but it now seems justified in light of the avalanche that killed 16 Sherpas in 2014. The avalanche struck the same ice bulge that had earlier frightened Brice, and it was the worst climbing accident in Everest's history.

The incident has sparked a debate over the working conditions and compensation for Sherpas. The Nepali government's offer of 40,000 rupees (approximately $408) to the families of the deceased has been met with outrage, and Sherpas have demanded better compensation, including an increase to $1,041 per family, a permanent relief fund, and a monument in Kathmandu to honor the deceased. The Sherpas' demands reflect their frustration with the lack of recognition and fair compensation for the risks they take. The situation has led to a potential work stoppage, which could disrupt or cancel the 334 expeditions planned for the 2014 climbing season. The Sherpas' anger and the economic pressures they face highlight the complex and dangerous reality of working on Everest.

The climbing season on Everest has become increasingly dangerous, with the Khumbu Icefall, a treacherous section of the route, becoming more unstable due to climate change. The icefall is known for its unpredictable seracs, which can collapse at any moment, and the Sherpas spend 30 to 40 round trips through the Icefall during the climbing season, carrying heavy loads. The Nepali government is considering changing the climbing route to avoid the Icefall, but this may not fully address the underlying issues. The growing number of climbers and the deteriorating conditions have expanded beyond anyone's control, making it nearly impossible to reverse course once teams are committed to the summit push.

The commercial guiding industry on Everest is in trouble, with the fatality rate for Sherpas being far higher than that for traditionally dangerous professions such as commercial fishing, wilderness aviation, and military combat. The increasing number of climbers and the deteriorating conditions have made the mountain more dangerous, and the Sherpas' demands for better compensation and working conditions reflect their frustration with the current system. The situation on Everest underscores the need for better management and a more equitable distribution of risk and reward among all those involved in the climbing industry.

Newt Gingrich, a long-time presidential hopeful, launched his latest campaign with the slogan "Win the Future," which eerily mirrors President Obama's own campaign slogan. The Atlantic discovered that Gingrich registered "American Solutions for Winning the Future" with the IRS back in 2006, years before Obama adopted it. Despite the overlap, Gingrich's campaign spokesman, Rick Tyler, said they are "great" that Obama used the slogan. Gingrich's campaign continues to use the phrase, now as a jab against Obama. The former House speaker's website, Newt.org, prominently features the slogan. Meanwhile, Obama frequently uses "Winning the Future" in his speeches and campaign materials. The White House Correspondents Association dinner even featured jokes about the slogan, with Jon Stewart and Stephen Colbert making light of it. Gingrich's campaign sees this as an opportunity to debate whose policies will truly win the future.

Bill Cosby's sexual assault trial opened on June 5, 2017, in Norristown, Pennsylvania, with a stark contrast between the once beloved "America's Dad" and his current legal predicament. Keshia Knight Pulliam, who played his daughter Rudy Huxtable on "The Cosby Show," accompanied him into the Montgomery County courthouse. The comedian, now 79, faces three counts of aggravated indecent assault for allegedly drugging and assaulting Andrea Constand, a Temple University employee, in 2004. Constand claims she was given pills that incapacitated her, leading to a sexual assault. Cosby has always denied the allegations, portraying the encounter as consensual and claiming he gave Constand two Benadryl pills to help her relax. He has pleaded not guilty and has sued some of his accusers for defamation.

The trial will hinge on the testimony of just two women: Constand and a prior alleged victim known as "Kacey," who worked for Cosby's late agent. Kacey alleges that in 1996, after Cosby insisted she take a pill, she woke up in bed with the half-naked entertainer. Cosby's defense team will likely use Kacey's testimony to cast doubt on Constand's account. The prosecution will also call a psychologist to discuss the behavior of sex-abuse victims and explain why Constand waited a year to report the alleged assault to police. They will also present evidence from pharmaceutical experts to discuss the effects of the pills Cosby allegedly gave to women.

The trial's outcome is crucial for Cosby, who has no plans to testify. If found guilty, it could set a significant precedent in the #MeToo era, potentially encouraging other victims to come forward. However, the case also highlights the challenges in prosecuting such cases, especially when the statute of limitations has expired for many of Cosby's accusers. The trial will resume the national dialogue about sexual assault, including the statutes of limitations, which make these cases so hard to bring. Advocates argue that the Cosby case has led to a national conversation about the arbitrary nature of these laws, with some states already beginning to expand or eliminate them.

The high-profile nature of the case has drawn significant attention, with dozens of women coming forward to accuse Cosby of sexual misconduct. The trial will not only determine Cosby's fate but also shape how America talks about rape, race, and celebrity. The defense will likely use Cosby's status as a beloved public figure to argue that he is the victim of a media witch hunt, while the prosecution will focus on establishing a pattern of behavior. The outcome could have far-reaching implications, potentially emboldening victims to come forward and changing the public's perception of Cosby and other powerful men accused of sexual assault.

A small bowl purchased at a garage sale for $3 by a New York family recently sold for $2.2 million at Sotheby’s, marking a significant windfall for the family. The bowl, dating back to the 10th or 11th century, is a rare example of early-era Ding ware, known for its thin potting, fine near-white body, and ivory-colored glaze. Only one other bowl of the same form and decoration is known, currently housed in the British Museum. The bowl’s value lies in its exceptional craftsmanship and historical significance, aligning it with the ‘five great wares’ of the Song dynasty. The family kept the bowl on their mantle for years before consulting experts, who brought it to Sotheby’s for appraisal. The bowl’s intricate design, mimicking precious metals, and its official ware status further enhance its value. The high-profile sale underscores the potential for unexpected discoveries in everyday objects.

A fugitive murder suspect, Masaaki Osaka, has been arrested after more than 45 years on the run from authorities in Japan. Osaka, now 67, was arrested on Wednesday for five offenses, including the murder of a 21-year-old police officer during a Tokyo street protest in November 1971, according to public broadcaster NHK. The officer was allegedly set on fire using a Molotov cocktail. Osaka was first arrested in May when police raided a communist hideout in Hiroshima City, where he was living under an assumed identity. He was initially arrested for a minor offense—obstructing a police officer—but his true identity was only confirmed through DNA tests, as fingerprints were not available at the time of the crime. Osaka had been wanted by police for over four decades, his face appearing on wanted posters in Tokyo. The arrest marks the longest time spent evading arrest in Japan's history, with the country having no statute of limitations for murder due to a 2010 law revision. Osaka was a former high-ranking member of the Japan Revolutionary Communist League (JRCL) and reportedly received assistance from sympathetic party associates, allowing him to remain hidden for such a long period. The JRCL, established in the late 1950s, was known for staging violent street protests during the 1960s and 1970s, including the one where Osaka allegedly committed the murder.
