On the same day the Baltimore Police Department graduated its future officers, an incident unfolded that placed the department under scrutiny. In a viral video, an officer was seen repeatedly punching a man on a Baltimore sidewalk. The video, captured by a bystander, shows the officer shoving the man against a wall and then throwing punches for 12 seconds. The man, identified by his attorney as Dashawn McGrier, was eventually taken to the ground, where the officer pinned him down. McGrier suffered a broken jaw, nose, and ribs, according to his attorney, Warren Brown. The incident occurred after the officer, who is familiar with McGrier, encountered him and asked for identification. McGrier refused, leading to the confrontation.

Interim Police Commissioner Gary Tuggle was deeply disturbed by the video and immediately suspended the officer involved. Tuggle stated, "While I have an expectation that officers are out of their cars, on foot, and engaging with citizens, I expect that it will be done professionally and constitutionally. I have zero tolerance for behavior like I witnessed on the video today. Officers have a responsibility and duty to control their emotions in the most stressful of situations." The officer involved, identified as Arthur Williams, resigned from the department. A second officer was placed on administrative duties while the investigation continues.

The incident took place as Baltimore continues to grapple with the aftermath of the 2015 death of Freddie Gray, who died in police custody. Mayor Catherine Pugh demanded answers and accountability, stating, "We are working day and night to bring about a new era of community-based, constitutional policing and will not be deterred by this or any other instance that threatens our efforts to re-establish trust of all citizens in the Baltimore Police Department."

The Baltimore Police Department is investigating the incident, and the Baltimore City State’s Attorney’s Office has been notified. The department has not yet released the officer's name, but Brown, McGrier's attorney, identified him as Arthur Williams. Williams had graduated from the police academy in April, receiving top honors for his performance. The incident has raised questions about the department's training and oversight, particularly as the city deals with a tumultuous year marked by the forced departures of two commissioners and concerns about the quality of recruits.

The Baltimore Police Union did not comment on the incident, but its president, Gene Ryan, stated that "at first view" of the video, it showed "inexcusable behavior" on the officer's part. However, Ryan added that there might be more to the incident that he does not yet know. The incident has sparked outrage and calls for accountability, with many questioning the department's handling of the situation and its commitment to reform.

Ryan Seacrest faced a challenging red carpet at the Oscars, navigating a sexual misconduct controversy that had left him in the spotlight. Despite allegations by former stylist Suzie Hardy, Seacrest was not left alone, with interviews from nominees Allison Janney and Mary J. Blige keeping the focus on their projects rather than personal matters. Taraji P. Henson's comment, "the universe has a way of taking care of the good people," added a pointed edge to the interaction. E! managed to fill gaps with co-host Giuliana Rancic and celebrity stylists, but the network's decision to delay Seacrest's interviews by 30 seconds to avoid confrontations underscored the awkwardness. Seacrest's denial of the accusations and the network's stance of "business as usual" highlighted the tension. The event's atmosphere was notably different from previous red carpets, with five Best Actress nominees notably avoiding Seacrest's interview spot. The controversy continued to simmer, with Seacrest's host duties proceeding under the watchful eye of the #MeToo and #TimesUp movements.

Sen. Lindsey Graham, who had previously criticized both Ted Cruz and Donald Trump, is now set to host a fundraiser in support of Cruz, signaling a significant shift in the Republican primary landscape. The draft invitation, obtained by CNN, describes Cruz as a "great friend of Israel and the Jewish people." Graham, who ended his own presidential bid in December, now sees Cruz as the "best alternative to Donald Trump" and plans to support him in every way possible. This move is particularly noteworthy given Graham's previous stance, where he compared nominating either Trump or Cruz to being "shot or poisoned."

Former Florida Sen. Marco Rubio, who dropped out of the race on Tuesday after losing Florida, the home state with the most delegates, has also made his stance clear. In a conference call with Minnesota supporters, Rubio expressed his hope that someone other than Trump will secure the Republican nomination. Rubio, who won only three primaries or caucuses, including Minnesota, acknowledged his campaign’s challenges, attributing much of his defeat to negative media coverage and the superior resources of his opponents. He praised Cruz as the "only conservative left in the race" and suggested that he might consider running for office again in the future, though he did not explicitly endorse either Cruz or Ohio Gov. John Kasich.

Rubio’s campaign faced significant difficulties, particularly after losing Florida, which he described as a "fatal" blow. He noted that his positive campaign message did not resonate well in an election marked by widespread frustration. Despite winning Minnesota, Rubio’s overall performance was hampered by negative media narratives and the superior fundraising capabilities of his rivals. He emphasized the impact of media coverage, stating that "the media narrative goes negative on you, and all the news is bad, it kind of knocks us off." Rubio’s decision to drop out was driven by the belief that continuing the race would not yield a viable path to the nomination, especially given the current dynamics within the Republican party.

Rush Limbaugh's three-day tirade against Georgetown University law student Sandra Fluke, who testified in favor of contraceptive coverage, has sparked a broader examination of his comments and the underlying conservative viewpoints they reflect. In his apology, Limbaugh distanced himself from his "slut" remark but defended his broader arguments, leaving many questions unanswered. William Saletan, in his analysis, poses six key questions that Limbaugh's comments raise: 

1. Does Limbaugh object to paying for contraceptive pills in general, or only those that facilitate sex?
2. How much sex is too much, and does he believe it's excessive for law students?
3. Is contraception merely a sex enabler, and should women face consequences for their "personal sexual desires and habits"?
4. Is preventing pregnancy a legitimate medical need, or is it just an elective activity?
5. What responsibility should men bear in preventing unwanted pregnancies?
6. How can male responsibility be enforced, and should there be government involvement?

Limbaugh's comments have also drawn criticism from other conservatives, such as actress Patricia Heaton, who attacked Fluke via Twitter. Heaton's tweets, which were later deleted, mocked Fluke and suggested that her parents could avoid canceling cable if her "Tweatons" sent her condoms. Heaton's tweets sparked outrage, leading to calls for advertisers to pull their support from her show. Saletan argues that Limbaugh's questions, while provocative, deserve serious consideration, urging the conservative host to provide more substantial answers.

The execution of Jang Song Thaek, the No. 2 man in North Korea, has significantly affected Sino-North Korean relations, as detailed in a report by Beijing's official newspaper, Wen Wei Po. According to the report, Jang, along with five of his closest aides, was stripped naked and thrown into a cage with 120 starved dogs, which then ate them up completely, a brutal method known as "quan jue." This execution, supervised by North Korean leader Kim Jong Un and 300 senior officials, was reported to have lasted for an hour. The report, published on December 12, vividly illustrated the brutality of the young North Korean leader and highlighted the deteriorating relations between China and North Korea. Two days later, the Global Times, associated with the People's Daily, emphasized the backwardness of the North Korean political system and urged China not to coddle the Kim regime any longer, given the majority of Chinese people's disgust with the Kim regime.

The execution of Jang Song Thaek, known for his close ties with Beijing, was seen as a clear sign of North Korea's antagonism towards China. Jang was accused of various crimes, including underselling coal and other natural resources, selling off the land of the Rason economic and trade zone, and disrupting the country's financial stability. His execution also reflected the longstanding suspicion and apprehension of the North Korean regime towards China, dating back to the time of Kim Il Sung, the founder of North Korea. This suspicion was further confirmed by Stanford University research fellow David Straub, who recalled comments made by North Korean officials suggesting that their nuclear weapons could be used against China.

The execution of Jang Song Thaek has posed several issues for China. First, it raises concerns about China's security, given the erratic and ruthless behavior of Kim Jong Un. Second, it indicates a drastic reduction in China's political and strategic influence on the Korean peninsula, as evidenced by the urgent consultations between Chinese and Russian officials. Lastly, it suggests that China's efforts to nurture a less belligerent neighbor through reform and economic development in North Korea may no longer be realistic.

Christian mom blogger Glennon Doyle Melton, known for her honest portrayals of personal struggles and faith, has announced her relationship with soccer star Abby Wambach. Melton, author of "Love Warrior," a New York Times bestseller and Oprah’s Book Club selection, revealed the news on Facebook, describing Wambach as "deeply sensitive" and "unwaveringly good." Melton's children, who are also Melton's ex-husband Craig's, are supportive of the relationship, calling Wambach an "M&M" because she is tough on the outside but sweet on the inside. Melton's ex-husband Craig supports the relationship, and the family, including Melton's children, spends time together. Melton expresses gratitude for the love surrounding her and Wambach, stating, "PRECIOUS WORLD: I LOVE ABBY." The revelation comes three months after Melton's divorce from Craig and two months after Wambach's divorce from Sarah Huffman. Both women, who share an open-life-memoir writing style, have appeared on Oprah Winfrey's career-making book list and popular programs. Melton's relationship with Wambach highlights the growing acceptance of same-sex relationships within certain Christian communities.

Kenny G, the Grammy award-winning saxophonist, claims to have played a role in the creation of the Starbucks Frappuccino. According to his recent interview with Bloomberg, Kenny G’s uncle was the first investor in Starbucks, and he encouraged Kenny to invest in the company. Kenny G also mentioned that he frequently advised Starbucks CEO Howard Schultz about the popularity of blended drinks at another company, Coffee Bean, which he believed could be a successful addition to Starbucks’ menu. Starbucks spokespersons acknowledged Kenny G’s contributions, stating he has been a dear friend of the company since its early days and played a part in the success of the Frappuccino.

The Frappuccino, a trademarked brand of Starbucks, is a line of iced, blended coffee drinks consisting of coffee or crème base, ice, and various ingredients, often topped with whipped cream and sauces. The drink’s history traces back to Boston, Massachusetts, where it was developed, named, trademarked, and sold by George Howell’s Eastern Massachusetts coffee shop chain, The Coffee Connection. Starbucks acquired the rights to the Frappuccino when it purchased The Coffee Connection in 1994.

The first Frappuccino, introduced in 1995, was a blend of coffee and milk, inspired by the coffee frap and the frappe, a blended ice cream drink. The drink’s recipe has evolved over the years to include brewed coffee, ice, and additives such as milk, sugar, flavored syrups, and whipped cream. Starbucks now offers a wide range of Frappuccino versions, including decaffeinated, crème, and non-dairy alternatives. The company also introduced juice blends, but these were gradually discontinued.

In addition to the traditional Frappuccino, Starbucks offers bottled versions of the drink, which are produced by PepsiCo and sold in retail stores and vending machines. These bottled Frappuccinos contain coffee, milk, sweetener, and sometimes flavoring, and bear the Frappuccino trademark but have no discernible resemblance to the in-store version. The bottled Frappuccinos have faced criticism for their high sugar content.

Starbucks has expanded its product line through the North American Coffee Partnership, a joint venture with PepsiCo that produces ready-to-drink coffee and energy drinks. This partnership has grown to a $1.5 billion retail business, with the Frappuccino being its first product. Kenny G’s involvement in the Frappuccino’s creation, while not the primary factor, highlights the role of customer feedback in product development at Starbucks.

One paratrooper was killed and seven others were injured during a training accident at Fort Bragg while conducting artillery live-fire exercises, officials said. The incident involved a M777 light, towed howitzer. Details about the location and severity of injuries were limited, with two paratroopers in critical condition and five others treated and released from Womack Army Medical Center. Families have been notified, and the victims' names will be released on Saturday. Col. Stephen Smith, brigade commander, expressed deep condolences and stated that support and care are being provided to those affected. The incident is under investigation by the 82nd Airborne Division, the Army Criminal Investigative Division, and the Army Combat Readiness/Safety Center.

Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan Chase, survived a shareholder push to strip him of his chairman title, five days after a $2 billion trading loss. Despite the loss, Dimon's pay package, totaling $23 million, passed with strong shareholder support. Dimon acknowledged the mistakes were "self-inflicted" and stated, "The buck always stops with me." Shareholders, including representatives from the Catholic organization Missionary Oblates of Mary Immaculate, expressed skepticism, questioning whether JPMorgan had truly learned from past mistakes. The heavy police presence at the meeting highlighted the controversy, with protesters throwing eggs at Dimon's poster. President Obama, while critical of JPMorgan's loss, praised Dimon's management skills. The incident also sparked discussions on the Volcker rule, with Treasury Secretary Timothy Geithner emphasizing the need for stricter regulations. Dimon's response focused on JPMorgan's resilience, maintaining its quarterly stock dividend and emphasizing the bank's continued strong performance.

Nearly 30 Air Force Academy cadets required medical care, with six of them hospitalized, after an annual tradition to mark the first snowfall of the season turned into an out-of-control melee, officials said. An unauthorized ritual called "First Shirt/First Snow," in which freshman cadets try to throw their cadet sergeant into a snowbank, grew violent and resulted in injuries. "A relatively small number of cadets chose to take part in this unsafe activity," Brig. Gen. Gregory Lengyel said. "This incident was unacceptable." The six cadets who required hospitalization have all been released, and the 21 others were treated for "bruises and/or lacerations" at the academy's cadet clinic. Lengyel, who serves as the commandant of cadets, said school officials are investigating the incident. "Our Air Force expects better. I expect better, and I'm confident the cadets will learn and grow from this," he stated. An internal email about the incident obtained by the Air Force Times newspaper, reportedly written by Brig. Gen. Dana Born to school administrators, said the annual ritual "has turned into a brawl" between freshmen and upperclassmen. "This ritual has devolved to become increasingly violent, with significant numbers of cadets requiring medical care over the past two years," the email stated, adding that the latest injuries included concussions, an arm bite, and cuts that required stitches. The Times reported that Lengyel might allow the tradition to continue if cadets can show it can be conducted with "good order and discipline and proper risk management." Located in Colorado Springs, 60 miles south of Denver, the academy has an enrollment of about 4,100 cadets, and graduates are commissioned second lieutenants in the U.S. Air Force. The reported incident is a fresh blow to the reputation of the Air Force, which has dealt with a number of scandals in recent years, including accusations of failing to investigate sexual assaults, promoting Christianity, and dealing with cheating and drug-use incidents.

European leaders met in Brussels to discuss the escalating crisis in Ukraine, with tensions rising as Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko warned that the conflict was close to a "point of no return" and could lead to full-scale war. Poroshenko accused Russia of "military aggression and terror," stating that thousands of foreign troops and hundreds of foreign tanks were now on Ukrainian soil. The EU leaders, including French President François Hollande and Swedish Prime Minister Fredrik Reinfeldt, vowed to take strong measures, with new economic sanctions being prepared to pressure Russia to reconsider its position. Lithuanian President Dalia Grybauskaite, who called for stronger sanctions, emphasized that Russia's actions amounted to a direct confrontation with Europe, stating, "Russia is practically in a state of war against Europe." The EU leaders warned that if the conflict continued to escalate, it could push Europe closer to a "point of no return." Ukrainian forces were reportedly abandoning a city where they had been surrounded by rebels for days, and government forces were pulling back from another area they had claimed to have taken control of. The Ukrainian military also reported that one of its fighter jets had been shot down by Russian anti-aircraft fire, although the pilot managed to eject safely. NATO estimates suggested that at least 1,000 Russian soldiers were in Ukraine, despite Russia's denial of any military involvement. The EU leaders expressed concern that the sanctions might face resistance from several EU nations due to potential economic fallout, but they also stressed that consequences must follow if Russia continued to support the separatists. Poroshenko said Ukraine would welcome EU assistance, including military equipment and further intelligence-sharing. The EU's executive arm was tasked with finalizing the details of new sanctions, which could include a full arms embargo, including the cancellation of existing contracts. The Ukrainian military spokesman, Andriy Lysenko, reported that Ukrainian forces were retreating from several towns, indicating increasing resistance from Russian-backed separatist rebels. The conflict had already claimed at least 2,200 lives, according to UN figures, and the fighting had expanded to the coast, with rebels taking control of the town of Novoazovsk. The EU leaders emphasized the need for a political solution, but they also warned that military action was not off the table.

On a girls' night out celebrating a friend's wedding, five women in a 1999 Lincoln Town Car limousine found themselves trapped in a fiery inferno on the San Mateo Bridge. Nelia Arrellano, 36, was the first to escape, squeezing through the partition to the front seat and calling out for help. She managed to pull three others through the partition, but the flames in the back of the limousine were too intense, trapping the remaining passengers. Arrellano recounted the terror, saying, "When he stop the car, he get out from the car. He just get out from the car." The limo driver, Orville "Ricky" Brown, also escaped without injury, but his attempts to assist were too late. The fire spread so quickly that by the time a motorist stopped to help, the back of the limousine was engulfed in flames. The coroner stated, "In the 21 years I've been with the office -- all deaths are horrific -- but this is just very impactful. And it's probably the worst one I have ever seen." The victims, all nurses, were found huddled near the window partition. The cause of the fire remains unclear, with Brown speculating it might have been an electrical issue. The tragedy highlighted the potential dangers of overloading limousines and the need for better safety regulations. The limo company owner expressed condolences, stating, "We are saddened by this horrific event that took the lives of five people, and it happened in one of our cars." The incident sparked discussions about limousine safety, with some calling for stricter regulations and better maintenance practices.

A Minnesota teenager, John David LaDue, meticulously planned a multi-stage attack intended to result in mass casualties at his home and school, according to court documents. LaDue, a 17-year-old high school junior, had prepared for months, assembling an arsenal of firearms and bomb-making materials, and documenting his plans in a 180-page notebook. His scheme was to first kill his parents and sister with a .22-caliber rifle to avoid making too much noise, then create a diversion by setting a fire to attract first responders. After ensuring the authorities were occupied, he would proceed to Waseca Junior/Senior High School, where he planned to set off pressure-cooker bombs and other explosives in the cafeteria, then shoot and kill as many students as possible before being killed by a SWAT team.

LaDue's plot was meticulously detailed, including the creation of bombs and the acquisition of firearms and ammunition. He had previously tested his bombs at a nearby elementary school, outside a local church, and in a city park to refine his bomb-making skills. His preparations included renting a storage locker to store his weapons and materials, obtaining a checking account and debit cards, and even getting a job to purchase necessary supplies. The 180-page notebook included entries on his "thoughts, plans, to-do lists, supply lists, successes and failures," and outlined the steps he would take to carry out his attack.

The plot was nearly thwarted by a concerned neighbor, Chelsie Schellhas, who witnessed LaDue entering a storage facility. Initially, Schellhas considered confronting LaDue but heeded her cousin's advice to call the police. Three Waseca police officers arrived at the storage facility after receiving a tip about suspicious activity. Upon their arrival, LaDue agreed to accompany them to the police station for questioning, where he was subsequently arrested. At the time of his arrest, LaDue was in possession of seven firearms and at least six completed bombs, along with bomb-making materials and chemicals.

The criminal complaint states that LaDue had planned the attack for April 20, the anniversary of the Columbine High School massacre, but changed his plans when he realized that day was Easter Sunday and school was not in session. The Bloomington, Minn., police bomb squad was called to detonate the completed bombs, and they were shocked by the amount of bomb-making chemicals and components that LaDue had in his possession.

Schellhas, the woman who alerted the police, expressed that she did not consider herself a hero but was relieved that her actions led to the prevention of a potentially catastrophic event. The community of Waseca is grateful for her vigilance, and she received numerous messages of thanks from the community. The incident has left the town shaken, with parents and residents expressing relief and gratitude for the safety measures that were put in place.

Speaker John Boehner's inaugural address as the 112th Congress opened was marked by applause and a tone of humility and comity, signaling a shift from the previous contentious atmosphere. Boehner, acknowledging the challenges facing the nation, emphasized the people's House as the center of his vision, promising transparency, accountability, and adherence to constitutional principles. He outlined a rules package aimed at reducing spending, increasing efficiency, and fostering a more open and respectful legislative process. Boehner sought to bridge the divide between the majority and minority parties, advocating for a fair debate and a commitment to the common good. His speech, while promising, faces the test of implementation, as practical challenges and political realities may impede the realization of his vision.

Ben Affleck is back in rehab, seeking treatment for alcohol addiction, PEOPLE confirms. The actor, 46, has been vocal about his need for help, and a source tells PEOPLE, "He is seeking treatment. He knew he needed help and was vocal about it." The move to enter a treatment facility came after his ex-wife Jennifer Garner was photographed arriving at his home on Wednesday. Garner, the mother of three, was seen leaving Affleck’s home upset and shaking. When she returned, Garner, Affleck, and an unidentified woman who arrived with her were photographed in a car the actress was driving. The trio reportedly stopped by a Jack In The Box in the Pacific Palisades before driving to a treatment facility in Malibu. On Monday, Affleck was photographed receiving an alcohol delivery outside of his Brentwood, California, home, further highlighting his ongoing struggle with alcohol addiction. 

Affleck has a history of battling alcohol addiction, having first sought treatment in 2001. In March 2017, he announced that he had completed treatment for alcohol addiction, writing on Facebook, "I have completed treatment for alcohol addiction; something I’ve dealt with in the past and will continue to confront. I want to live life to the fullest and be the best father I can be. I want my kids to know there is no shame in getting help when you need it, and to be a source of strength for anyone out there who needs help but is afraid to take the first step." He has been attending meetings and practicing self-care, including meditation and yoga, to maintain his sobriety. 

His current relationship with 22-year-old Playboy model Shauna Sexton, whom he was seen with at a restaurant in Malibu, has raised concerns among his ex-wife. A source tells PEOPLE, "Is she happy about him hanging out with a very young Playboy model? Certainly not." Garner's focus remains on their children's well-being and their ability to co-parent effectively. 

The divorce proceedings between Affleck and Garner have been ongoing for two years, with Garner filing for divorce in April 2017. The delay in finalizing the divorce is reportedly due to Garner's concerns about Affleck's sobriety, as his current state makes her uneasy about progressing with the legal process. Affleck has been spotted attending Alcoholics Anonymous meetings and meditation classes, indicating his commitment to his recovery. 

Despite the progress he has made, the couple is aware that they may need to re-file for divorce due to Garner's hesitations regarding Affleck's suitability as their children's guardian. The situation remains complex, with both parties committed to co-parenting their three children—Violet, 12, Seraphina, 9, and Samuel, 6—while navigating their personal and professional lives.

A mother in Toronto has sent a powerful message to her 23-year-old son by invoicing him for $39,254.17 for the services she has provided over the past 13 months. The invoice, addressed to "Unappreciative Son," includes charges for home utilities, prescriptions, cleaning services, health insurance, and "specialty meals," all of which are often consumed by millennials who might still be living at home due to financial constraints. Notably, the invoice includes a $1,000 charge for "being an a--hole and not appreciative of your mother’s support." The mother, who asked to remain anonymous, clarified that the invoice was intended as a lighthearted joke and not a serious demand for payment. Chalipo, the son, agreed to the charges and acknowledged his poor behavior, apologizing to his mother. He shared the invoice on Reddit, where it quickly went viral, garnering sympathy from many who found it humorous. Chalipo's mother expressed that the invoice helped bring them closer and restored her faith in him. The incident highlights the financial burden many parents face in supporting their adult children, especially those burdened with student loan debt. Chalipo, who plans to graduate soon with a radio broadcast degree and save up to move into his own place, stated his intention to repay his mother in the future. His mother, while appreciative of the gesture, was unsure how to respond to the morbid thought of her son taking care of her in her old age. The viral invoice serves as a reminder of the complex dynamics between parents and their adult children, and the financial and emotional support that often comes with it.

As of Tuesday morning, South Korea had confirmed at least 95 cases of Middle East Respiratory Syndrome (MERS) and was monitoring over 2,500 people under quarantine for symptoms. Seven patients had died, and the virus had spread to rural towns, with many seeking care at large hospitals. The two hospitals where most cases occurred were among the largest in their cities, and the crowded conditions there had been ideal for the virus to spread. The first infected patient, known as the index case, developed a fever and began coughing on May 11. He visited a clinic in his hometown, Asan, on May 12, 14, and 15, perplexing doctors who sent him to St. Mary’s Hospital in Pyeongtaek, 37 miles south of Seoul. With no improvement, he was referred to Samsung Medical Center in Seoul, where doctors suspected MERS, learned of his Middle East visit, and isolated him. The correct diagnosis was confirmed on May 20. Experts believe the virus' incubation period is five to six days on average, with a maximum of about two weeks, and that there won't be any more cases directly infected by the first patient. However, a "super-spreader" infected at St. Mary's Hospital, who had been treated at Samsung Medical Center, spread the disease among doctors, visitors, and other patients, raising concerns about the hospital. The maximum incubation period for those infected by the second "super-spreader" ends around this Friday, which raises hopes that the outbreak could weaken soon. Health officials cautiously predict the peak of the outbreak today and stabilization in the next few days. The government has released the names of all 29 hospitals affected by the disease and is mobilizing all available resources and necessary budget to help eradicate the disease at the earliest date possible. The outbreak has led to the closure of nearly 2,000 kindergartens and schools and the cancellation of concerts and religious gatherings. Sales of face masks and hand sanitizer have soared, and there has been a significant drop in baseball stadium attendance. The government is also using South Korea's advanced cellphone network to trace the signals of people who have defied quarantine. The World Health Organization (WHO) is sending a team of experts to South Korea to investigate the outbreak. The virus has a fatality rate of around 8 percent in South Korea, compared to over 40 percent before the outbreak. The traditional culture of family members caring for loved ones in hospitals or at home may have contributed to the fast spread of MERS. The WHO has noted that the country's response to the outbreak has been belated, and some experts have faulted the South Korean government for the way it initially handled information on the outbreak. The government's "monopoly on information" has been criticized as partly rooted in the country's authoritarian past, with the goal of protecting the business interests of big hospitals and keeping people ignorant about mistakes. President Park Geun-hye's weekly approval rating dropped six percentage points to 34 percent in the aftermath of the MERS outbreak. The South Korean economy could suffer as tourism and business travel drop because of MERS fears. Hong Kong has issued a red travel warning for South Korea, the second-highest of three levels, and advised residents against unnecessary travel there.

Agnes Nixon, the pioneering creator of daytime dramas "All My Children" and "One Life to Live," passed away at the age of 93, leaving behind a legacy of groundbreaking social issues tackled through television. Nixon's work began in the 1960s, when she wrote the first health storylines, including a groundbreaking Pap smear episode, which saved thousands of lives. She continued to push boundaries, introducing complex storylines involving gay characters, transgender characters, and characters with AIDS, alcoholism, and drug addiction. Her shows also addressed racial segregation, racism, and abortion, making her a trailblazer in daytime television. Nixon's "One Life to Live" and "All My Children" were among the first to introduce a legal abortion and a transgender character, respectively. Her shows were not only socially relevant but also entertaining, as she aimed to avoid preachy dialogue and let action and plot speak for themselves. Nixon's influence extended beyond her own shows, as her work inspired other soaps and networks. She was a true queen of modern daytime drama, and her contributions to television, particularly in addressing social issues, have left an indelible mark. Her death was mourned by actors, writers, and fans, who remembered her as a force of nature and a true trailblazer. The impact of her work is evident in the continued relevance of her shows, which have been adapted for online platforms, ensuring that her legacy lives on.

In the wake of Hurricane Irma, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers launched "Operation Blue Roof," providing fiber-reinforced plastic sheeting to Florida homeowners with damaged roofs. However, a misdirected tweet from FEMA Region 4 inadvertently directed callers to a phone sex line instead of the correct number, 1-888-ROOF-BLU. The mix-up highlighted the need for clear communication in disaster relief efforts. The incorrect number, 1-800-ROOF-BLU, was quickly corrected after being pointed out by concerned citizens. This incident underscores the importance of accurate information dissemination to ensure effective assistance for affected homeowners.

Owen Labrie, a former St. Paul’s School student convicted of sexually assaulting a 15-year-old freshman as part of the school’s Senior Salute tradition, is set to be released on bail pending his appeal. Labrie, now 20, was initially released on $15,000 bail to live at his mother’s home in Vermont with a 5 p.m. to 8 a.m. curfew. However, he violated his curfew at least 12 times, leading to his bail being revoked in March. His lawyer, Jaye Rancourt, argued for his release again, citing Labrie’s “life-changing” experience in jail. The judge, Larry Smukler, allowed Labrie to be released on bail with electronic monitoring via GPS, with the earliest release date set for Wednesday and the latest for Friday. Labrie’s case drew significant attention, with his conviction and subsequent bail revocation sparking debate over the severity of his punishment and the appropriate handling of his case. The New Hampshire Coalition Against Domestic and Sexual Violence criticized the decision, stating it sends the wrong message to victims of crime. Labrie’s case highlights the complex issues surrounding sexual assault, the consequences of such crimes, and the challenges in ensuring justice and public safety.

Nearly six months after the death of Robin Williams, the Academy Award-winning actor and comedian, his widow Susan Schneider Williams, and his three children from previous marriages, Zak, Zelda, and Cody Williams, are engaged in a contentious legal dispute over his estate. The disagreement centers around both financial assets and cherished personal belongings, including clothing, collectibles, and photographs. 

In court documents filed in December and January, both parties have expressed a keen interest in various items from Williams's life. The widow claims she has the right to certain personal effects, such as his film memorabilia, action figures, and graphic novels, while the children argue that these items, along with his wedding tuxedo and other "knickknacks," should be theirs. 

The dispute has escalated to the point where the children accuse Susan of taking some of Williams's belongings without permission, alleging that someone entered the house days after his death and removed items. In response, Susan's representatives argue that the will and trust clearly outline the distribution of personal effects, with Susan having no claim to items related to his acting career, such as his Oscar from "Good Will Hunting" and his suspenders from "The Fisher King." However, the children are indignant that Susan is attempting to redefine the term "jewelry" to exclude his watch collection, despite the will stating that the children are to receive all of it.

Sources close to Robin Williams have stated that he would be heartbroken by this family conflict, emphasizing the importance of resolving such matters privately. The legal battle has not only divided the family but also highlighted the complex emotions and financial considerations surrounding the legacy of a beloved entertainer. The children and the widow are now navigating a delicate balance between honoring Williams's memory and protecting their own interests, all while the world continues to mourn the loss of a man who brought joy and laughter to millions.

Starting from January 1, 2023, a new law in France grants workers the right to "disconnect" from their work emails and smartphones outside of working hours. This law, known as the "right to disconnect," applies to companies with more than 50 employees and aims to combat the "always-on" work culture, which often leads to overtime and an invasion of private life outside the office. The measure is part of a broader set of labor laws introduced in May, which also made it easier for firms to hire and fire employees, but was the only one that did not generate widespread protests and strikes.

The law requires companies to negotiate with their staff to establish when employees are not expected to work outside of their contracted hours. If a deal cannot be reached, the companies must create a charter of good conduct, outlining specific hours during the evening or weekends when employees are not supposed to send or answer emails. This move is seen as a significant step in protecting workers' private lives and mental health, as the overuse of smartphones has been linked to increased stress, burnout, and sleep problems.

However, the new law may face challenges in implementation. French workplace expert Xavier Zunigo suggests that companies might use the "right to disconnect" as a protective measure, while workers might be reluctant to give up the autonomy and flexibility that digital devices provide. A U.S. study, "Exhausted But Unable to Disconnect," found that checking emails outside of work hours can cause emotional exhaustion, as workers struggle to separate their personal and professional lives.

In contrast, the UK lacks similar legal protections, with only the Working Time Regulations preventing workers from working more than 48 hours a week, averaged over 17 weeks. British workers can opt out of these regulations, and there are exceptions for those whose working time is not measured and who are in control of their work. The new French law is seen as a pioneering measure, potentially setting a precedent for other countries to follow in addressing the issue of work-life balance in the digital age.

Singers Justin Bieber and Usher are facing a $10 million lawsuit after a U.S. appeals court ruled that a lower court judge was wrong to dismiss a copyright infringement claim. The plaintiffs, Devin Copeland and his songwriting partner Mareio Overton, argue that three versions of the song "Somebody to Love" recorded by Bieber, Usher, or both, share the beat pattern, time signature, and similar chords and lyrics with their song of the same name. Among the defendants are publishers such as Universal Music Publishing Group and Sony/ATV Music Publishing. The 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in Richmond concluded that the chorus of the Copeland song and the Bieber and Usher songs are similar enough and significant enough that a reasonable jury could find the songs intrinsically similar. The case will return to the lower court for a full-blown trial. The plaintiffs allege that music scouts played their song, which was written in 2008, for Usher, who liked it and brought it to Bieber. The judge ruled that even the lyric "somebody to love" was delivered in an "almost identical rhythm and a strikingly similar melody." The case is now back in the lower court, with the potential for a significant financial outcome for the plaintiffs.

Gudrun Burwitz, the daughter of Heinrich Himmler, a key architect of the Holocaust and one of the most powerful figures in Nazi Germany, worked for West Germany's foreign intelligence agency (BND) in the 1960s, according to officials. Burwitz, who died at 88 in May, was confirmed to have worked as a secretary for the BND under an assumed name from 1961 to 1963. Her involvement with the BND, which was then under the control of former Nazi military intelligence commander Reinhard Gehlen, highlights the complex and often controversial history of post-war Germany and its institutions. The BND's head of the history department, Bodo Hechelhammer, confirmed Burwitz's employment, noting that her departure coincided with a shift in the agency's handling of employees with Nazi backgrounds. Burwitz's loyalty to her father and her continued involvement with far-right groups throughout her life underscored her unrepentant stance on Nazism. Born in 1929, she witnessed the horrors of the concentration camps, including Dachau, and remained unrepentant, denying the existence of the Holocaust. She was known to provide support to former Nazis convicted or suspected of war crimes through her involvement with Stille Hilfe, a secretive group that offered legal and financial assistance to former SS members. Burwitz's life and work at the BND, along with her continued attendance at neo-Nazi events, reflect the ongoing challenges in Germany's post-war reconciliation with its Nazi past.

The National Security Agency (NSA) is reportedly sifting through the contents of most Americans' international e-mail and text communications, according to newly released documents leaked by Edward Snowden. This surveillance is not limited to direct communications with foreign targets but extends to any Americans who mention information about the targets. The NSA's procedures, detailed in a June 2013 document, permit the agency to monitor Americans' international communications in the course of surveillance targeted at foreigners abroad. Critics argue that the FISA Amendments Act, which expanded the government's authority to monitor Americans' electronic communications, has led to the NSA building a growing database of Americans' international phone calls and emails. While the NSA claims to not target Americans, the leaked documents suggest otherwise. The NSA's surveillance is conducted by temporarily copying data, searching for keywords, and retaining communications containing "foreign intelligence information" or evidence of a crime, even if they are purely domestic. The procedures allow the NSA to collect and retain communications protected by the attorney-client privilege and to maintain "knowledge databases" containing sensitive information about Americans. The NSA's ability to retain encrypted communications indefinitely raises concerns about the privacy of Americans' most sensitive information. Despite government officials' reassurances that the NSA does not target Americans without warrants, the leaked documents reveal that the agency's surveillance practices have significant implications for Americans' privacy.

Scientists have discovered a planet nearly 80 percent more massive than Earth, named Kepler-78b, orbiting a sun-like star 400 light-years away in the constellation Cygnus. This exoplanet, with a radius 20% larger than Earth's, is the closest thing to an Earth twin in size and density found beyond our solar system, though it is far too hot to support life. The planet's surface temperature reaches 3,680 degrees Fahrenheit, making it a lava world. Discovered by NASA's Kepler space telescope, its mass was determined using the radial velocity technique, revealing a density nearly identical to Earth's. Both research teams involved in the study concluded that Kepler-78b is composed of rock and iron, similar to Earth. However, the planet's extremely tight orbit around its star, just 900,000 miles away, is puzzling to astronomers. According to current theories, the planet should not have formed in such a close proximity to its star. The planet is expected to eventually be torn apart by the star's immense gravity within the next 3 billion years. The discovery of Kepler-78b marks a significant milestone in the search for Earth-like planets, as it suggests that planets of Earth-like composition are not rare. Future missions, such as NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS), are expected to find more Earth-sized planets orbiting cooler, smaller stars, potentially including those in the habitable zone where life could exist.

A 3,700-year-old Babylonian clay tablet, known as Plimpton 322, may rewrite the history of trigonometry, according to a new study. The tablet, discovered in the early 1900s in what is now southern Iraq, contains a series of numbers that reflect the Pythagorean theorem, which explains the relationship between the lengths of the sides of a right triangle. However, the new research suggests that the Babylonians used a different approach, focusing on the ratios of the sides of right triangles rather than angles and irrational numbers. This method, developed by mathematician Daniel Mansfield from the University of New South Wales and Norman Wildberger, is described as a powerful, exact ratio-based trigonometric table. The tablet, dated between 1822 and 1762 BC, predates the Greek mathematician Pythagoras by at least 1,000 years and could have been used for surveying, constructing temples, and other architectural projects. The researchers argue that the Babylonian system, which counted in base 60, allowed for more accurate fractions, making it a more precise tool than modern trigonometry. This discovery not only challenges the traditional view of trigonometry but also suggests that the ancient Babylonians had a sophisticated understanding of mathematics that could have practical applications today. The tablet's exact purpose remains unclear, but it offers a new perspective on the development of mathematical concepts.

A gunbattle between rival drug gangs in western Mexico left 29 bodies in fake military uniforms scattered across a roadway and inside bullet-riddled vehicles in the Pacific coast state of Nayarit. The bodies, all male, were found near the town of Ruiz, with federal and state officials giving conflicting reports. Television images showed 14 shot-up pickup trucks and SUVs, including two with bulletproofing. Military-style boots, bulletproof vests, hand grenades, and thousands of rounds of ammunition were recovered. The Sinaloa cartel, Mexico's most powerful, and the Zetas are believed to be involved. In nearby Michoacan state, 500 marines and soldiers were deployed to an area where at least 1,200 villagers fled their homes during three days of clashes between rival drug traffickers. The government provided shelters for the displaced families. The fighting in Michoacan is believed to involve rival factions of the La Familia drug cartel, some of whose members now call themselves "The Knights Templar." The situation is so bad that Mexico's three main political parties are exploring the possibility of fielding a single, unity candidate in the upcoming gubernatorial race in an attempt to set aside partisan bickering and save the state.

The sounds recorded on one of the "black boxes" recovered from downed Germanwings Flight 9525 confirm investigators' theory that the co-pilot locked the captain out of the cockpit and then crashed the plane. The cockpit voice recorder, which has not been officially released, includes a summary of the transcript from the recording, according to German newspaper Bild. The transcript provides a chilling account of the final moments of the flight, with the captain, Patrick Sondenheimer, repeatedly pleading with the co-pilot, Andreas Lubitz, to open the cockpit door. Sondenheimer can be heard saying, "For God's sake, open the door!" as he bangs on the door, pleading with Lubitz. Thirteen minutes later, the plane crashed into the French Alps.

French authorities, including the Bureau d’Enquêtes et d’Analyses (BEA), have expressed dismay over the leak of the voice recording to Bild. Martine Del Bono, a spokeswoman for the BEA, stated that the leak was "unvoyeuristic" and that the agency considers it mere "voyeurism." The leak could not have come from a BEA agent, as the agency has not released the audio officially.

The transcript reveals that Lubitz, 27, was in charge of the flight, with Sondenheimer asking him to prepare the plane for landing. Once Sondenheimer left the cockpit to use the restroom, Lubitz began to descend the plane without authorization. The flight took off 20 minutes late, and after reaching cruising altitude, Sondenheimer asked Lubitz to prepare the landing. Lubitz responded, "You can take over anytime," and Sondenheimer left the cockpit. Shortly after, the plane began its rapid descent, with air traffic controllers trying to contact the plane but receiving no response. An alarm went off in the cockpit, warning of the "sink rate," and the captain could be heard banging on the door, saying, "For God's sake, open the door!" Passengers can be heard screaming in the background.

The transcript also includes the sound of a seat being pushed back, indicating that Sondenheimer had left the cockpit. At 10:29 a.m., air traffic radar detected the plane starting to descend. Three minutes later, air traffic controllers tried to contact the plane but received no answer. An alarm sounded, warning of the "terrain," and "pull up!" Another three minutes passed, and a loud metallic bang was heard at 7,000 meters. A minute and a half later, the plane was at 4,000 meters, and Lubitz's breathing could still be heard. Two minutes later, investigators think they heard the plane's right wing scrape a mountaintop. Screams can be heard one final time before the crash.

The speculation about Lubitz's mental state is based on a letter found in a waste bin in his Düsseldorf apartment. The note, which was "slashed," said Lubitz was not able to do his job, according to city prosecutor Christoph Kumpa. The fact that investigators found "ripped, recent medical leave notes, including for the day of the offense, leads to the preliminary conclusion that the deceased kept his illness secret from his employer and his professional environment," prosecutors said. Germanwings corroborated that assertion, saying it had never received a sick note from Lubitz.

A handful of publications, citing unnamed sources, have reported that Lubitz suffered from various psychological maladies, including generalized anxiety disorder and severe depression. CNN has not been able to confirm these reports. Lubitz had a girlfriend, a teacher at a school in Dusseldorf, and dozens of people attended a remembrance ceremony for the victims of the crash at a church in a nearby town, Digne-les-Bains, France. The mayor of one local community said he had seen Lubitz's father on Thursday evening, describing him as "a man in deep distress."

The search for the plane's flight data recorder, which could reveal crucial details about the final moments of the flight, continues. The mayor of Lubitz's hometown, Montabaur, expressed sympathy for the co-pilot's family and asked the media to be considerate. Airbus chairman Tom Enders criticized some television discussions about the crash, calling them "outrageous nonsense" that mocked the victims. Leading figures in the Protestant Church in Germany also called for caution with regard to speculation on the causes of the crash.

Al-Qaeda's leader Ayman al-Zawahri has announced the formation of an Indian branch of his global militant group, aiming to spread Islamic rule and "raise the flag of jihad" across the subcontinent, according to a 55-minute video released online. Al-Zawahri, speaking from an undisclosed location, declared that the new entity, "Al Qaeda in the Indian Subcontinent," would "crush the artificial borders" dividing Muslim populations in the region and rescue Muslims from injustice and oppression. The video, spotted on online "jihadist" forums by the SITE terrorism monitoring group, was produced by Al-Qaeda's media arm, As-Sahab Media Foundation, and has been widely distributed. Zawahri called on the Muslim umma to unite in "tawhid," or monotheism, to wage jihad against its enemies, liberate its land, and restore its sovereignty. He emphasized the group's recognition of the overarching leadership of the Afghan Taliban leader Mullah Omar and named Asim Umar as the new group's leader. The announcement comes as Al-Qaeda struggles for legitimacy in the face of the Islamic State's recent successes, including capturing large swaths of territory in Syria and Iraq. The Indian government has put at least three states with large Muslim populations on alert, though there is no indication of an increased security presence. Al-Zawahri's statement is seen as a direct challenge to the Islamic State, which calls itself a caliphate and demands the loyalty of all Muslims. Indian security experts note that while Al-Qaeda is active in Afghanistan and Pakistan, it is a minnow compared to local militant groups in terms of manpower and regional knowledge. The formation of the new Al-Qaeda branch could pose a challenge to India's new Prime Minister, Narendra Modi, who has faced criticism for remaining silent on incidents deemed anti-Muslim. Al-Qaeda's renewed efforts to establish a presence in India reflect its struggle for relevance and recruitment in the wake of the Islamic State's rise to prominence.

Clint Bench, born without hands due to a congenital deformity, faced discrimination at Six Flags Over Texas when an employee refused to let him ride the Aquaman Splashdown ride. Bench, who has led an active life, including college education and thrill-seeking at amusement parks, was told he could not ride because he does not have fully formed arms. The incident occurred last May, and Bench claims discrimination under the Americans With Disabilities Act. Six Flags had a policy that riders "must have one full arm" to ride the attraction, which was only recently updated to explicitly state this requirement. Bench's lawsuit seeks unspecified damages for suffering and mental anguish, and he still wishes to ride the attraction. The case highlights a conflict between a long-standing policy and the need for inclusivity, as Six Flags has historically been accommodating to those with disabilities, even allowing disabled guests to cut lines and make reservations until 2007. The incident has sparked debate on the balance between safety and inclusivity in amusement parks.

SEOUL, South Korea — A whistle-blower whose account has captivated South Koreans says a fight over a puppy led to the vote to impeach the country’s leader. The corruption scandal that engulfed President Park Geun-hye was rooted in her friendship with Choi Soon-sil, her secretive adviser and friend for 40 years. Choi, 60, has been indicted on charges of extorting tens of millions of dollars from big businesses, and prosecutors have identified Park as a criminal accomplice, a first for a South Korean president. Ko Young-tae, the whistle-blower, said at a parliamentary hearing this week that he got into an argument with Choi over walking her daughter’s puppy one day in 2014. He said Choi became upset when she found the dog alone at his home. “I didn’t get her call because I was out golfing,” Ko said. “She was angry that I left the dog alone, and we had a fight.” Ko, 40, a former Asian Games gold medal fencer, said afterward he decided to expose Choi’s ties with Park to local news media. Ko had apparently videotaped Choi in 2014 giving orders to two presidential aides as though they were servants. In one scene that went viral, one of the aides wiped his smartphone on his shirt before handing it reverentially to Choi. The footage, aired in October on TV Chosun, left little doubt about Choi’s influence over Park. Ko also was said to have an advance copy of Park’s itinerary for an overseas trip that Choi had received; it showed that the president had worn certain colors on certain days based on Choi’s recommendations. Ko has become a hero to many in South Korea. “You opened Pandora’s box,” Sohn Hye-won, an opposition lawmaker, said during the hearing. Ko had emerged as an intriguing figure in Park’s corruption scandal, which has involved as many plot twists as the best of Korean soap operas. Local media said he was a former employee at a Seoul “host bar,” where male prostitutes cater to female clients, before he befriended Choi. Ko denied that he and Choi had been a couple. He said a friend introduced him to Choi in 2012, when he was running a handbag and clothing company called Villomillo. Choi ordered 100 pieces of clothes and 40 handbags made of ostrich skin and crocodile leather. The items were delivered to Park, who was later seen toting Villomillo handbags. Park’s office said she paid for the items, denying opposition lawmakers’ allegations that they were bribes from Choi. Ko said he handed over his video footage to TV Chosun last year, but it was not broadcast until Oct. 25. A day earlier, on Oct. 24, the rival cable channel JTBC broadcast what was considered the biggest media scoop connected to the scandal. One of its reporters obtained a discarded tablet computer that it said had belonged to Choi. Files discovered there included drafts of 44 speeches and statements that Park had given between 2012 and 2014, as a candidate and later as president. Many passages were marked in red. “The only thing Ms. Choi did well was to edit President Park’s speeches,” Ko told JTBC in October. (Park has since acknowledged that she asked for Choi’s feedback on her speech drafts.) South Koreans were outraged that Park let Choi, who had no experience in government, edit some of her most important speeches. The allegation was particularly damning because Park was known for shunning one-on-one meetings with her own official aides. Ko said Choi’s behavior made him believe she was the most powerful person in Park’s government. “She insulted me and acted as if her underlings were subhuman,” Ko said. Ko underwent 40 hours of questioning by prosecutors until Saturday as he had voluntarily appeared at the prosecution's office late Thursday after entering the country earlier that day. No details have been released yet. Ko is suspected of managing The Blue K and Wide Sports, paper companies Choi set up in Korea and Germany allegedly to funnel money away from the Mir and K-Sports foundations. Ko has become a central figure in the scandal, providing evidence that has led to Park’s impeachment and the indictment of Choi.

At the Cannes Lions advertising festival, Michael Wolff, author of "Fire and Fury," spoke with Jeff Goodby, a co-founder of Goodby, Silverstein & Partners, an ad agency. Wolff discussed Donald Trump’s ability to sell books, noting that his chronicle of Trump’s first nine months as president, "Fire and Fury," remains a bestseller. Wolff made a pointed observation about Vice President Mike Pence, suggesting that if Pence were to become president, the media business would enter a deep depression. Wolff elaborated, saying, "When Mike Pence becomes the president—which I believe that he will become—the media business goes into a deep depression," adding that "Mike Pence is literally the most boring man on earth." Wolff’s comments highlighted the stark contrast between the two leaders, with Trump’s controversial and attention-grabbing nature in stark contrast to Pence’s perceived dullness and lack of public profile.

Wolff’s remarks about Pence’s potential presidency were part of a broader discussion on the future of media and politics. He also mentioned that Pence often refers to his wife, Karen, as "Mother," a detail that has drawn attention to their unique relationship. Wolff’s observations about Pence’s potential presidency and his wife’s nickname reflect the ongoing interest in the dynamics within the Trump administration and the potential for change in the political landscape. The summary captures the essence of Wolff’s comments, highlighting the contrast between Trump and Pence, and the public’s fascination with the Pences' relationship.

Former President George H.W. Bush, 92, and his wife Barbara, 91, are hospitalized at Houston Methodist Hospital. Bush is in the ICU for an acute respiratory problem stemming from pneumonia, while Barbara was admitted as a precaution after experiencing fatigue and coughing. The hospital performed a procedure to protect and clear Bush's airway, and he is stable but will remain in ICU for observation. President Obama expressed well wishes for the Bushes, calling them "as fine a couple as we know." Bush has had multiple hospitalizations in recent years, including a 2015 fall that broke his neck and a 2012 bout with a persistent cough that led to intensive care. Barbara Bush, a champion of family literacy, passed away in 2018, leaving George HW Bush to continue his public service and advocacy.

A new Quinnipiac University national poll reveals that President Barack Obama is the worst president since World War II, with 33% of American voters holding this view. George W. Bush follows closely at 28%. Obama's performance is particularly troubling to Republicans, with 79% rating him as worse than Mitt Romney and Newt Gingrich. Among Democrats, 84% say Obama understands the problems of average Americans better than his opponents. However, Obama's approval ratings remain low, at 40% negative, with 41% disapproving. The economy and handling of key issues like foreign policy and health care are areas where Obama receives negative reviews. The majority of voters, 37%, believe the country would be better off if Romney had won the 2012 election, while 38% think it would be worse. Obama's competence in running the government is questioned, with only 44% saying he is paying enough attention. Younger voters tend to view Obama more favorably, but overall, his approval has declined since 2010. The poll, conducted among 1,446 registered voters, highlights the ongoing dissatisfaction with the current administration and the divided opinions among different demographic groups.

Demi Lovato, 18, has been quietly dating Ryan Phillippe, 36, over the last couple of months, according to an exclusive report by E! News. The pair, who are in a casual relationship, started seeing each other hot and heavy, but the birth of Phillippe's daughter has caused a slowdown. Lovato was unaware of Phillippe's paternity until it happened, which threw her for a loop. The promotion of Lovato's new single "Skyscraper" has also taken up much of her time, potentially affecting their relationship. Phillippe, who has three children from previous relationships, including a newborn with ex Alexis Knapp, denies any relationship with Lovato, stating he is "totally single." His ex Amanda Seyfriend split in June 2011, and Lovato's past loves include Wilmer Valderrama, Joe Jonas, and Trace Cyrus.

The post-apocalyptic world of "The Book of Eli" is a desolate wasteland, where Eli (Denzel Washington), a lone survivor with a mysterious past, travels with a sacred King James Bible. His journey takes him through a landscape of decaying towns and marauding gangs, as he seeks to reach the "west" and fulfill a divine mission. Gary Oldman plays the villainous Carnegie, a tyrannical leader who covets the book Eli carries, seeing it as the key to his own power. Eli's protector and guide, Solara (Mila Kunis), joins him on his quest, offering a contrast to the harsh world they navigate. The film's visual style, with its moody tones and stylized violence, aims to evoke a sense of biblical prophecy. However, the story feels overly simplistic and the performances, particularly Kunis's, are often flat. The Hughes brothers, known for their gritty and imaginative work, struggle to find the balance between action and meaning in this tale of survival and faith. Despite Washington's commanding presence, the film's heavy-handed religious themes and lackluster narrative make it a challenging watch.

A 35-year-old middle school teacher named Cary Joseph Heath is in custody after two of his neighbors were found fatally shot early Sunday morning in North Texas, say police. Fort Worth police were initially called to a home on the 900 block of Buffalo Springs Drive at about 4 a.m. for a report of a robbery. Upon arrival, officers discovered two bodies outside the residence. Jordan Milner, a neighbor who lives across the street, witnessed the incident and reported hearing gunshots. He described the suspect as having an assault rifle and unloading the entire clip, killing the couple next door. Heath, who was employed as an eighth-grade science teacher at Permenter Middle School in Cedar Hill, was arrested the following day at the school. He is currently being held at the Fort Worth jail on a $1 million bond. The Cedar Hill Independent School District has placed Heath on administrative leave. The victims have not been identified, and police are still investigating the double murder. The incident has left parents and the community in shock, with concerns about the safety of children around a potential murderer.

Sen. Scott Brown (R-Mass.) made light of his Democratic opponent, consumer advocate Elizabeth Warren, during a radio interview, saying he was glad she didn't "take her clothes off" to pay for college, referencing his own nude photo shoot for Cosmopolitan in 1982. Brown's comments came after Warren, in a debate, responded to a question about her college expenses by saying she had chosen to keep her clothes on and borrow money to fund her education. Brown's response drew criticism from the Massachusetts Democratic Party, which called it "gutter campaigning" and a "dirty trick." Despite being a Republican in a heavily Democratic state, Brown has remained popular in Massachusetts, but his recent comment is unlikely to help him with women voters. Warren, a Harvard law school professor, was instrumental in establishing the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, though she was not nominated to serve as its permanent head. The debate over Brown's past and Warren's response highlighted the personal nature of the race, with Brown's comments seen as a low blow in the campaign.

The mother of Jacob Hall, a 6-year-old boy who died after being shot during a school shooting at Townville Elementary School, plans a superhero-themed funeral to honor her "superhero son," reports CNN. Jacob was shot on September 28, 2016, when a 14-year-old boy opened fire at the playground, and after three days on life support, he passed away on Saturday. Renae Hall, Jacob's mother, met with reporters outside Greenville Memorial Hospital to discuss the funeral plans, emphasizing that the event would be a celebration of her son's life. She stated, "I don’t want suits and ties and all that. There will be a lot of children there and I don’t want it to be scary for them. Jacob will be dressed in his superhero costume." Hall invited anyone who wants to say goodbye to Jacob to attend and wear their superhero costumes or t-shirts, as he was a fan of superheroes, especially the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles.

The funeral service will be held on Wednesday at 11 a.m. at Oakdale Baptist Church, and the family has encouraged mourners to dress as superheroes. "We want to honor Jacob, celebrate Jacob, in a way he would love," Hall's great-aunt, Rebecca Hunnicutt, told the Anderson Independent-Mail. Jacob's death led to the shooter being charged with murder, as he had also killed his own father. Jacob's great-aunt also mentioned that Jacob had told his family he wanted to be a preacher and that he was "really sweet" and "knew a lot about Jesus." The funeral will also feature a special appearance by John Buckland, who drove his Batmobile from West Virginia to attend the service, wearing full Batman garb and giving the kids posters saying "Tough things make me stronger."

The Townville community came together to participate in a balloon release in Jacob's memory on Sunday evening, following a special service at Oakdale Baptist Church. The family's decision to hold a superhero-themed funeral service is a fitting send-off for Jacob, who was known for his selfless nature and love for helping others. His mother emphasized the importance of forgiveness, stating, "No matter what you and your family go through… Always be able to forgive because you're not guaranteed tomorrow, no matter how angry or hurt you are." The Townville Elementary School community also participated in Superhero Day, with all employees and students invited to come to school in costume, and anyone attending the funeral would be excused.

Donald Trump repeatedly claims the Obama administration wants to accept 200,000 Syrian refugees, a figure that is far from accurate. FactCheck.org and PolitiFact have debunked this claim, but Trump continues to use it as a scare tactic. The actual number of Syrian refugees the administration plans to accept is much lower, with a maximum of 10,000 for the next year. Trump's campaign rarely responds to fact-check queries, making it difficult to determine where he gets his numbers. The 200,000 figure is based on an increase in the total number of refugees the U.S. plans to accept, not specifically for Syrians. In 2016, the number was raised to 85,000, and for 2017, it was set at 100,000. However, the number of Syrian refugees specifically is much smaller, at 10,000 for 2017. Trump's repeated use of this number is not only misleading but also contributes to a narrative of fear and misinformation. His campaign has faced criticism for spreading false information and using fear tactics to gain support. This includes claims that African-Americans are responsible for most white homicides, which is false, and that thousands of American Muslims celebrated the 9/11 attacks, which is also false. These statements not only spread misinformation but also contribute to a climate of intolerance and hatred. Trump's campaign has also been criticized for its treatment of protesters and journalists, with some candidates, like Jeb Bush and John Kasich, speaking out against some of Trump's more outlandish comments. However, many other candidates have remained silent, allowing Trump to continue spreading false information and reinforcing prejudices. The growing ugliness of Trump's campaign poses a challenge to the country, and it is important for journalists and political leaders to challenge his false statements and hold him accountable.

Burger King is abandoning its iconic "Have It Your Way" slogan in favor of a new tagline, "Be Your Way," as part of a broader effort to connect more deeply with customers and project a more personal brand identity, reports The Associated Press. The new slogan, which will be rolled out across all marketing efforts in the U.S., aims to emphasize individuality and self-expression, according to Fernando Machado, senior vice president of global brand management. This shift comes as fast-food chains compete to stand out in a market where consumers increasingly seek more personalized and authentic experiences. Burger King's new approach is part of a series of changes under the leadership of Axel Schwan, who was appointed as global chief marketing officer earlier this year. The move follows similar efforts by other fast-food giants, such as McDonald's and Taco Bell, which have also updated their slogans to reflect a more modern, individualistic image. However, the effectiveness of the new slogan remains to be seen, as Laura Ries, president of the brand consulting firm Ries & Ries, notes that companies can come across as trying too hard to be cool. Burger King's decision to move away from its long-standing slogan reflects the changing landscape of the fast-food industry, where brands are increasingly focusing on emotional connections and personalization to differentiate themselves from competitors.

A manhunt for former LAPD officer Christopher Dorner, who allegedly killed three people and injured others in a revenge campaign against the police, continues with no clear lead on his whereabouts. Dorner, 33, is believed to have penned a manifesto detailing his grievances against the LAPD, which he blamed for his firing in 2008. The manifesto, published online, expressed his intention to use "unconventional and asymmetrical warfare" against police, whether on or off duty. Dorner's last known movements included an attempted yacht hijacking in San Diego and a shootout with LAPD officers in Riverside, where he injured one officer and killed another. Law enforcement officials fear Dorner may have powerful weapons, including a .50 caliber rifle and a shoulder-fired missile launcher, which could make his capture challenging. The manhunt has spread across Southern California, with law enforcement agencies on high alert and residents in Big Bear, where Dorner was last seen, living in fear. The search has involved hundreds of officers, helicopters, and SWAT teams, but Dorner's exact location remains unknown. His background includes a turbulent career with the LAPD, marked by disciplinary issues and a perceived injustice that led to his termination. The manhunt has raised concerns about the potential for further violence and the difficulties in tracking down a former police officer with military training.

Marine experts in Sydney, Australia, performed a daring rescue to save a critically endangered grey nurse shark from choking to death due to an elastic cord wrapped around its gills. The shark, one of only an estimated 1,500 remaining off the Australian coast, was spotted in critical shark habitat off Magic Point with labored breathing, indicating it was slowly dying. A team from SeaLife sanctuary and aquarium, including divers and a veterinarian, used a clear-plastic shark sock to capture the shark and bring it to the surface. The see-through sock allowed other sharks to enter, complicating the rescue. Once in the sock, the injured shark was wrestled into a special stretcher and taken to the surface. The veterinarian, Rob Jones, cut away the suffocating cord and administered antibiotics to prevent infection. "If we hadn’t intervened, I have no doubt it would have died, the elastic would have kept cutting deeper and deeper into the neck," Jones told 7News Sydney. The shark swam away, and officials stated that the wound should heal within a month. This rescue is particularly commendable given the endangered status of the grey nurse shark.

President Obama signs a bill authorizing a prestigious Congressional Gold Medal for Nisei veterans who served in the 442nd Regimental Combat Team and other cohorts during World War II. Many of these veterans, like Art Iwasaki and Kenji Yaguchi, were born to Japanese immigrant parents and faced internment in camps while their families were detained. Despite the discrimination, thousands volunteered, proving their loyalty and bravery. The 442nd became the most decorated unit in U.S. military history, rescuing the "Lost Battalion" and capturing German soldiers. After the war, these veterans returned to civilian life, downplaying their heroism. This honor recognizes their service and the impact of their sacrifice on American society.

The University of Mississippi Medical Center (UMMC) has faced a unique and complex challenge as it plans future development on its 164-acre campus. Hidden beneath the earth, experts estimate up to 7,000 bodies lie, mostly former patients of the Mississippi State Lunatic Asylum, which operated from 1855 to 1935. The discovery of 1,000 bodies, presumed to be patients, has halted plans for a parking garage east of the dental school. The cost to exhume and rebury each body is estimated at $3,000, totaling $21 million, which UMMC cannot afford. Instead, the medical center is considering an in-house exhumation and memorialization plan, which would cost $400,000 annually for at least eight years. This plan includes creating a visitors' center and a lab for studying the remains, clothing, and coffins, potentially making Mississippi a national center for historical health records. The Asylum Hill Research Consortium, comprising anthropologists, archaeologists, and historians, aims to form a memorial that respects the patients while providing valuable research opportunities. The consortium hopes to secure grants to involve other researchers, potentially allowing DNA testing to identify some of the patients. The discovery has reignited interest in the history of the asylum and its patients, with descendants of some patients expressing a desire to learn more about their ancestors' lives and fates.

A British forklift driver has become the first person to survive swimming across the Hoover Dam reservoir in the United States, a daring feat that nearly ended in tragedy. Arron Hughes, 28, of Park Road Ruthin, was on a stag do in Las Vegas when he jumped into the water below the 725-foot-high structure. Hughes, who was reportedly in a state of intoxication, decided to swim across the Colorado River, which forms the border between Arizona and Nevada. He managed to escape the powerful currents only because nine out of the ten hydroelectric turbines were not in operation. Hughes, an ex-Ysgol Brynhyfryd pupil, recounted his experience to the Daily Post, describing how he swam from Arizona to Nevada and back, covering the distance in about 30 minutes. He kept his trainers on during the swim, a decision that did not aid his swift departure from the authorities who were waiting for him on the other side. Upon reaching the shore, Hughes was arrested and fined $330 (£250). The stunt, which Hughes claims was "drink fuelled," has generated mixed reactions. His friends consider him a legend, while his mother thinks he is an idiot. Hughes, an admitted adrenaline junkie, has previously performed other daring stunts, including jumping into a quarry with a 10-foot gap to clear. Despite his brush with danger, Hughes is unlikely to attempt the feat again, as the Guinness Book of World Records requires an official adjudicator to verify the swim.
