Dallas Cowboys coach Jason Garrett's news conference was dominated by questions about recently cut wide receiver Lucky Whitehead, who was wrongly implicated in a shoplifting arrest in Virginia. Garrett repeatedly defended the team's decision, stating it was in the best interest of the Dallas Cowboys and that he would not address the matter further. Whitehead, whose actual first name is Rodney, was cleared by Prince William County police, who confirmed that the identity provided during the arrest was falsely given. The incident occurred when a suspect was wrongly identified at a Wawa convenience store, leading to a summons for Whitehead, who was unaware of the arrest. Whitehead maintained his innocence, stating he was in Dallas at the time of the alleged incident. The Dallas Cowboys had given Whitehead multiple chances, but ultimately decided to cut him. Whitehead's agent, David Rich, expressed disappointment in the law enforcement's handling of the case, stating it cost his player his job. The incident has raised questions about the team's decision-making process and its treatment of players involved in controversy.

Google's security bounty programs have been quite lucrative for researchers who discover problems, as evidenced by the company's recent "Google Security Rewards - 2015 Year in Review" report. In 2015, Google paid out over $2 million to more than 300 people, with the largest single payment being $37,500 to an Android security researcher. The report highlights several interesting cases, such as Sanmay Ved, who briefly owned Google.com before it was taken back by the company. Google rewarded him with a $6,006.13 payment, which spelled out "Google" when viewed as a number. After Ved donated his reward to charity, the amount was doubled. Tomasz Bojarski topped the charts as the most prolific researcher, discovering 70 bugs on Google in 2015. The report also mentions the introduction of Vulnerability Research Grants, which provided researchers with funds to carry out their work, even if they didn't find a vulnerability. One example is Kamil Histamullin, a researcher from Kasan, Russia, who received a VRP grant and later found an issue in YouTube Creator Studio, earning an additional $5,000. Android was added to the Security Reward program in 2015, resulting in over $200,000 in payments. The report concludes with Google's plans to continue growing its Security Reward Program in 2016, indicating further changes throughout the year.

A Minnesota restaurant owner sparked controversy by posting a sign outside his establishment that read "Muslims Get Out" in support of St. Cloud, where a man stabbed several people at a mall, allegedly targeting Muslims. The sign, which has generated backlash, has also boosted business for Dan Ruedinger's Treats Family Restaurant in Lonsdale, Minnesota, so much that he had to call in extra workers. Ruedinger believes it is time for people to stand up against what he perceives as a politically correct crowd and expressed his support for his stance. However, Payten Estepp, part of a group protesting the sign, argues that it tarnishes the image of the community and could deter potential customers. Ruedinger maintains no plans to remove or alter the sign, despite the criticism. The article also includes a detailed review of the restaurant's food quality, service, and overall experience, noting issues with the burgers, cheese curds, and soda, while praising the ice cream and the owner's wife's customer service. The review suggests calling ahead or using the drive-thru to avoid long wait times and a less-than-pleasant dining environment.

Retired federal judge Vaughn Walker, who ruled California's Proposition 8 ban unconstitutional, shared his reflections for the first time, stating the trial should have been televised and he never considered recusing himself due to his sexuality. Walker, known for his independent thinking and groundbreaking rulings, said his decision was correct and hopes higher courts review the case. He discussed the case in his first media interview since announcing his retirement in September. Walker's sexual orientation, revealed during the trial, sparked accusations of bias, but he maintained he never thought it appropriate to recuse. He also advocated for televised trials, arguing they expose the public to the judicial process. Walker is now practicing law, specializing in mediation and arbitration. His ruling has thrust his personal life into the spotlight, raising questions about the relevance of a judge's sexuality in deciding cases involving same-sex marriage.

Even in Alabama, where diabetes is rampant, the rate of new cases has begun to decline, marking the first significant drop in decades. According to the CDC, 1.4 million new cases were diagnosed in 2014, down from 1.7 million in 2008. This marks a promising reversal, as the number of adults between 18 and 79 with newly diagnosed diabetes cases more than tripled from 493,000 to over 1.4 million annually. The total number of Americans living with diabetes now stands at 21.9 million. The CDC attributes this decrease to a gradual diffusion of science and education over the past decade, though there is still a long way to go. In Eutaw, Lynette Carpenter, inspired by her cousin's amputation, lost 42 pounds and has remained diabetes-free for two years. Robin Williams, a music teacher in Birmingham, lost 33 pounds by cutting out candy and fast food, and now uses an app to track her calorie intake. The Black Belt region, known for its fertile soil and historical poverty, has seen particularly devastating effects, with racial violence and sharecropping contributing to the health crisis. Despite these efforts, the incidence rate remains 60% higher than in the early 1990s, indicating that much work remains to be done in preventing and managing diabetes.

Bolivia has rejected a generous donation of 100,000 chickens from Bill Gates, citing the country’s self-sufficiency in poultry production and expressing that the billionaire philanthropist should apologize for not understanding Bolivia’s current capabilities. Minister César Cocaric of Bolivia’s development ministry stated that the chickens are an “offensive” gift and that Bolivia already has enough poultry to meet its needs. Gates had announced the initiative earlier this month, emphasizing the benefits of chickens for those living in extreme poverty, such as being inexpensive, providing a good investment, and contributing to better nutrition. The donation aimed to help high-poverty countries, but Bolivia’s rejection highlights the complexities of international aid and the potential for such initiatives to be seen as patronizing.

The rejection of the gift underscores Bolivia’s agricultural progress. According to a report from the Bolivian Institute of Foreign Trade, the poultry industry, including both eggs and chickens, grew by 35% from 2008 to 2014. The Cooperativa Agropecuaria Integral San Juan de Yapacaní (CAISY) is a significant player in the poultry sector, with 71 poultry partners producing an average of 20 million eggs per month, which are sold in major cities. This represents approximately 30% of the domestic market supply.

In terms of chicken meat production, Bolivia saw a 35% increase from 2008 to 2013, with the production of broilers reaching 180 million in 2013. The department of Santa Cruz is the largest egg producer, contributing 59% of the total production, followed by Cochabamba with 522 million units. The Cooperativa Agropecuaria Integral San Juan de Yapacaní focuses on the poultry sector, with the sector representing about 80% of the cooperative’s economic movement. The cooperative imports genetic line ISA Brown directly from Brazil to ensure high-quality production.

Despite the rejection, the Gates Foundation’s initiative highlights the potential of chickens as a tool for poverty alleviation. Chickens are often referred to as “the ATM of the poor” due to their ability to provide a steady source of income, which can be used by women to invest in their families. Studies show that when women control the family’s income, their children are 20% more likely to survive past the age of five. This underscores the importance of gender equality and women’s empowerment in addressing poverty.

The Gates Foundation’s campaign to promote chicken farming in developing countries aims to support women’s economic empowerment and improve nutrition. While Bolivia’s rejection of the gift indicates a level of self-sufficiency, the initiative highlights the broader context of international aid and the potential impact of such programs on poverty reduction and women’s empowerment.

Rescue efforts in Genoa have concluded with the recovery of the last three bodies from the collapsed Morandi bridge, raising the death toll to 43. The bridge, a key artery connecting Genoa to the A10 motorway and the French border, collapsed during heavy rainfall on Tuesday, trapping vehicles and debris 50 meters below. The search for survivors and the cleanup operation continued for five days, with nine people still hospitalized, four in critical condition. The Italian government and the bridge's operating company, Autostrade per l'Italia, have pledged substantial funds to assist victims and those displaced by the disaster. Prime Minister Giuseppe Conte confirmed that legal proceedings are underway to revoke Autostrade's contracts, aiming to compel companies managing Italy's infrastructure to invest more in maintenance and safety. The government plans to launch a comprehensive infrastructure safety plan next month, focusing on motorways, bridges, and public buildings, with an estimated cost that the prime minister claims will not be constrained by fiscal rules. The collapse has reignited debates about Italy's aging infrastructure and the need for better maintenance. Engineers have highlighted concerns about the bridge's concrete-encased stay cables, which were used in several of the bridge's designs. A report by the bridge's designer, Riccardo Morandi, from 1979 warned of the risk of corrosion and the need for constant maintenance, suggesting that the bridge's condition may have been a factor in the disaster. The families of the victims have expressed anger and frustration, with some opting for private funerals and criticizing the government's response. The incident has prompted a thorough investigation into the cause of the collapse, with preliminary findings pointing to a complex series of potential factors. As the investigation continues, the focus remains on ensuring that similar tragedies are prevented in the future.

Inmates at the Century Regional Detention Facility are reportedly growing increasingly frustrated with Lindsay Lohan's presence, according to a source. "She's not treated like if it was anyone else going to jail," Maria Medina, a relative of an inmate, tells PEOPLE. "Like, if they even want to bring her new clothes or bring her anything, they put the whole facility on lockdown. It happens all the time." Medina says that residents at the jail, located in Lynwood, California, find it unfair that Lohan, who is serving a 90-day sentence for violating her probation, is exerting so much control over their stay. "All the inmates are sick of Lindsay," Medina says. "It's almost like Lindsay Lohan's here, but she's not. Like if she even moves, they put the whole facility on lockdown. It happens all the time." Los Angeles Sheriff's spokesman Steve Whitmore denies Medina's claims, stating that "It's business as usual. Lindsay's getting no special treatment." Lindsay's lawyer, Shawn Chapman Holley, tells PEOPLE that his client is now in a better state of mind, saying, "She's doing well, she's doing fine. Her outlook is definitely more positive." Despite the rumors, Whitmore earlier told PEOPLE that Lohan received her visits during the week to avoid disrupting other families visiting on the weekend with ensuing TV crews and photographers.

In a blog post, Max Schireson, the CEO of MongoDB, announced his decision to step down from his position to spend more time with his family. Schireson, a male CEO, often wondered how he balanced his demanding job with his role as a father. He highlighted the fact that his wife, a doctor and professor at Stanford, worked hard to support their family while he was away on business. Schireson stated that he would remain with the company as Vice Chairman, supporting the new CEO, Dev Ittycheria. Schireson's decision to prioritize family life over his career drew positive responses, with his daughter even expressing happiness about the change. However, the article notes that if a woman were to make a similar decision, she might face criticism from other women who view career sacrifices as a negative. This situation highlights the ongoing struggle for both men and women to balance work and family life, with men often facing less scrutiny for taking time off to be with their families. Schireson's decision to speak openly about his choice to spend more time with his family could potentially encourage other male executives to do the same, thereby helping to level the playing field for both genders.

New Jersey Governor Chris Christie and former Arkansas Governor Mike Huckabee have been excluded from the main debate stage for the upcoming Republican presidential debate, as Fox Business Network set a threshold of 2.5 percent in four major polls for the top candidates. Both Christie and Huckabee, who had previously appeared on the main debate stage, will participate in the undercard debate, a move that could significantly impact their campaigns. Christie, who received 2 percent support in Fox News’s latest poll, and Huckabee, with 4 percent, barely missed the mark. The main debate will feature eight remaining candidates: Donald Trump, Ben Carson, Marco Rubio, Ted Cruz, Jeb Bush, Carly Fiorina, John Kasich, and Rand Paul. Candidates like Sen. Lindsey Graham and former New York Governor George Pataki missed the undercard debate as well, failing to poll at one percent in any of the four considered polls. Despite the setback, Christie remained defiant, tweeting that he would still speak out on important issues.

The NBA's swift and decisive action against Donald Sterling has sent ripples through the league and beyond. Commissioner Adam Silver announced a lifetime ban and a $2.5 million fine for Sterling, who made racist remarks in a secretly recorded conversation with his girlfriend, V. Stiviano. This punishment was met with immediate support from NBA owners, players, and sponsors, who had been calling for strong action. The decision was particularly significant given that Sterling's remarks were recorded in private, raising questions about the precedent it sets for disciplining owners. Sterling's wife, Rochelle Sterling, filed a lawsuit against V. Stiviano, alleging an affair and seeking to reclaim assets. However, V. Stiviano's lawyer, Mac Nehoray, insisted that Sterling and Stiviano never had a romantic relationship and that the recordings were released for financial gain. The NBA's move to force Sterling to sell the Clippers was seen as a necessary step to address the controversy. Sterling's potential sale could bring in significant profits, with estimates placing the team's value at $1 billion. Among potential buyers, Hollywood mogul David Geffen expressed interest. Despite the controversy, the Clippers' players and staff staged a silent protest, wearing red shirts inside-out to hide the team logo, and the home crowd of 18,000 supported the team. Clippers coach Doc Rivers praised Silver's decision, saying it was "the right one" and that it would create a "safe haven" for all involved. The NBA's swift action also had a broader impact, with sponsors like State Farm and Samsung renewing their partnerships. NBA legend Magic Johnson, who was mentioned in the recordings, expressed dismay but later commended Silver's leadership. The incident highlighted the delicate balance between personal values and professional responsibilities in the sports world, and it remains to be seen how this will play out in the coming weeks and months.

A Playmobil pirate ship set has ignited a controversy over a figurine that resembles an African American slave wearing a neck shackle, with instructions directing users to place the shackle around the figure's neck. Ida Lockett of Sacramento, California, expressed outrage after her 5-year-old son received the toy as a birthday present. The set, which retails for $89.99 but is currently on sale for $62.99, includes a dark-skinned doll wearing no shoes and tattered pants, with instructions to attach a silver shackle to its neck. Lockett stated, "This right here was found on his neck," and argued that the toy is "definitely racist" and "obscene," given the historical context of slavery. She emphasized that the shackle is a "slave collar" and criticized the toy's depiction as offensive. The Playmobil company defended the toy, stating that the figure was intended to represent a 17th-century pirate who was a former slave and not meant to offend anyone. However, Lockett's concerns have resonated with the Sacramento NAACP, which called for the toy to be banned, with President Stephen Webb stating, "This is deplorable; this cannot be accepted, and it needs to be pulled off the shelf." The controversy has sparked a broader discussion about the representation of historical slavery in children's toys and the potential impact on young children. Meanwhile, some Playmobil users defended the toy, arguing that pirates took slaves and prisoners of all races and that children can use their imagination to reinterpret the characters. The debate continues, highlighting the complexities of historical representation in toys and the sensitivity around such issues in the 21st century.

A 3-year-old boy and his 1-year-old brother survived a single-vehicle crash that killed their mother in south Arkansas, reports CNN. The older boy, identified as Kylen Holliman, managed to escape from the wreckage and walk for two days before being found by authorities on a state highway near Camden, Arkansas. The boys’ mother, Lisa Holliman, 25, was not seen since going grocery shopping on Thursday. Kylen was found covered in cuts and scrapes, appearing to have been outside for an extended period. He had managed to climb out of the car seat through the sunroof and up a small hill filled with bushes. When found, the 1-year-old brother was still strapped into his car seat nearby. The car was discovered with the mother’s body nearby, and both boys were taken to the hospital where they were treated for dehydration. The one-year-old is recovering at Arkansas Children’s Hospital and is expected to survive. The cause of the wreck remains under investigation. James Holliman, the boys’ grandfather, expressed disbelief at the tragedy, saying, "I'll never get up and see her, I'll never get to talk to her, laugh with her. My baby's gone." He also revealed that Lisa was four weeks pregnant at the time of the accident. "We just found that out at the hospital that she was pregnant. We didn't know. We lost two," he said. James Holliman described the boys’ ordeal as a "pure hell" and praised Kylen for his bravery, saying, "When he climbed out of that car, seeing his mother dead like that like she was, he tried to wake his mom up." The miraculous survival of the two young boys, who managed to survive for two days without food or water, highlights the severity of the accident and the resilience of the children.

The internet has experienced a significant slowdown due to a massive cyber-attack, described as the largest of its kind in history. The conflict between a spam-fighting group, Spamhaus, and a Dutch web host, Cyberbunker, has escalated into a global internet disruption. Spamhaus, based in London and Geneva, maintains blocklists to filter out spam and other unwanted content. Recently, Spamhaus blocked servers managed by Cyberbunker, leading to retaliation attacks affecting the wider internet. Sven Olaf Kamphuis, a self-proclaimed spokesman for Cyberbunker, criticized Spamhaus for abusing its position and suggested that the attack is a response to Spamhaus's actions. Spamhaus has accused Cyberbunker and "criminal gangs" from Eastern Europe and Russia of orchestrating the attack.

The attacks utilize a Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) tactic, flooding Spamhaus's Domain Name System (DNS) servers with massive amounts of traffic. The DNS infrastructure, crucial for directing web addresses to their correct servers, is the primary target. Spamhaus's chief executive, Steve Linford, emphasized the unprecedented scale of the attack, stating that it could take down government internet infrastructure, with peak traffic reaching 300 gigabits per second, compared to typical bank attacks at 50 gigabits per second. Linford also highlighted the involvement of five national cyber-police forces in the investigation, citing concerns that their infrastructure might also be targeted.

Experts warn that the attack could escalate to affect banking and email systems. The attack's power and the number of involved servers make it difficult to mitigate. Arbor Networks, a firm specializing in DDoS protection, confirmed that this was the largest attack they had seen, with the previous record set in 2010 at 100 gigabits per second. The attacks are intermittent, targeting various parts of the internet infrastructure, and Spamhaus has distributed its infrastructure across multiple countries to cope with the assault.

Spamhaus has received support from major internet companies, including Google, which has made its resources available to help "absorb all of this traffic." The attacks are not limited to Spamhaus; they have also targeted the data connections of both Spamhaus and CloudFlare, a company that provided assistance. Cyberbunker's representative, Sven Olaf Kamphuis, acknowledged the scale of the attack, stating that it is one of the largest DDoS attacks the world has seen, and that Cyberbunker is retaliating against Spamhaus for abusing its influence.

The core issue, according to several internet engineers, lies in the security vulnerabilities of the Domain Name System (DNS). Many large internet service providers have not adequately secured their networks to prevent unauthorized traffic from leaving their systems. This flaw has long been known but has only recently been exploited to threaten the internet infrastructure. The only effective solution, according to security researchers, is to identify and arrest the individuals responsible for the attacks.

Archaeologists have finally pinpointed the location of San Marcos, one of several 16th-century Spanish forts built on the Santa Elena settlement, now part of Marine Corps Recruit Depot Parris Island. The search, which spanned over two decades, utilized advanced technology such as ground-penetrating radar and magnetometers, with significant improvements in data interpretation methods. The general location was initially noted using historical documents archived in Spain, which included a drawing of the fort and a written description, but lacked specific details. Traditional digging methods had failed to locate the fort, prompting the use of high-tech equipment. University of Georgia archaeologist Victor Thompson and University of South Carolina archaeologist Chester DePratter, who began searching in 1993, employed these tools to map the fort’s outline and other structures within the 15-acre Santa Elena settlement, believed to include around 60 homes, a church, shops, and taverns. The breakthrough came in June, after extensive mapping and the exclusion of Native American artifacts and 20th-century Marine structures. The fort, founded in 1577 by Pedro Menendez Marquez, was constructed in just six days with pre-made wooden pieces to protect against Native American attacks. It was a two-story structure with 11 mounted cannons, including the largest weighing over 5,400 pounds. After the wooden posts rotted, a new fort was built nearby. The restored Santa Elena settlement grew to nearly 400 residents and was named the capital of Spanish Florida in 1571. However, it was abandoned in 1587 due to attacks by English privateer Sir Francis Drake. The new findings will be published in the Journal of Archaeological Science: Reports and will be included in future exhibits at the Santa Elena History Center, which opened this year in downtown Beaufort. The discovery offers a unique glimpse into the early colonial history of the region, providing insights into the competition between European powers for control of the New World.

Florida Representative Brad Drake, a Republican, has proposed a bill that would replace lethal injection with electrocution or a firing squad for death row inmates. Drake's idea came from a conversation he had with a constituent at a Waffle House regarding the legal battles surrounding the execution of Manuel Valle. Drake believes that lethal injection allows convicted killers to die in their sleep, while a firing squad or electrocution would force them to contemplate their fate every morning. He argues that the government should not spend time listening to advocacy groups and instead implement a death sentence that would make the condemned think about their punishment. The bill is part of the 2012 legislative session and has sparked controversy, with critics calling it barbaric and suggesting it would cause embarrassment for Florida. Supporters of the bill argue that it would ensure that convicted murderers face a more severe form of execution, forcing them to consider their actions. The debate over the method of execution has reignited discussions about the death penalty and its effectiveness in deterring crime.

In Anhui province, China, an elderly woman named Zhang Wenying hanged herself in front of her family home to ensure a proper burial before a city-wide ban on burials took effect. The ban, which went into effect on June 1st, was implemented in Anqing to save land, but it has sparked outrage and public debate. Zhang was not the only one to take drastic measures; her neighbor Wu Xiuli starved himself to death, and four others also committed suicide to avoid the new regulations. Reports of these suicides have incited public outrage, with some netizens questioning the motives behind the ban and suggesting that it is driven by local governments' reliance on land transfers for revenue. "As the value of land goes up," one netizen observed, "the value of human lives goes down." 

The ban has forced residents to destroy wooden coffins that they had prepared for years, leading to a sense of loss and anger. The traditional belief in "entering the earth and being at peace" (rutu wei'an) has deep roots in Chinese culture, emphasizing the importance of a proper burial. However, in Hong Kong, where cremation has been the norm for a long time, traditional ancestral veneration has survived more intact. In Hong Kong, burials in government-run cemeteries are disinterred after six years, and the remains are either collected for cremation or reburied in urns or niches, a practice known as "digging up bones" or jian'gu. This tradition reflects the southern Chinese practice of cleaning and rehousing ancestors' bones after some years.

The heavy-handed approach in Anhui contrasts sharply with the market-driven transition in Hong Kong, where the shift from burials to cremation was decided by market forces rather than official fiat. While Hong Kong residents can still opt for burials if they can afford it, the prohibitive cost of grave plots has led most people to adapt to the new reality. The Anhui ban has highlighted the tension between traditional cultural practices and modern land-use policies, raising questions about the balance between economic development and cultural preservation.

The Obama administration announced a one-year delay in enforcing the employer mandate of the Affordable Care Act, a significant revision that will affect businesses with 50 or more full-time workers. The mandate, which requires companies to provide health insurance or face a penalty of at least $2,000 per employee, will now be implemented in 2015 instead of 2014. This delay, announced by the Treasury Department, was made to give employers more time to adjust to the new system, according to White House officials. The decision, which reflects pressure from businesses, will delay the requirement beyond the 2014 midterm elections, when the GOP is likely to use the Affordable Care Act as a vehicle to attack vulnerable Democrats. Critics, including Senate Republican leaders and some Democrats, argue that the delay shows the law is fatally flawed and that the administration is acknowledging the law's complexity for businesses without offering a similar break to individual workers who still have to buy insurance. The delay could have significant implications for the implementation of other aspects of the law, particularly the establishment of health insurance marketplaces. While some employer groups welcomed the news, health policy experts warn that the delay could significantly reduce the number of people who gain coverage in 2014. The political effects of the delay could be more severe than the effect on the law's expansion of healthcare coverage, as it could help vulnerable Democrats in 2014. The decision also raises concerns about the administration's commitment to fully implementing the healthcare law.

Digital match-making services have transformed the way we form relationships, breaking down traditional social barriers and potentially fostering stronger connections. For over half a century, social networks have been characterized by a mix of strong and weak ties, with weak ties acting as bridges between closely connected groups. However, the advent of online dating platforms in the 1990s, and the subsequent rise of apps like Tinder in the 2010s, have introduced a new dynamic. These platforms have significantly altered the landscape of how people meet partners, with online dating becoming the second most common way for heterosexual couples to connect, and the most popular for homosexual couples.

Researchers Josue Ortega and Philipp Hergovich from the University of Essex and the University of Vienna, respectively, have conducted a study that delves into the implications of this shift. They argue that online dating introduces a large number of weak ties, which can dramatically change the structure of social networks. By modeling society as a network of interlinked nodes, where individuals are nodes and connections represent relationships, the researchers demonstrate that online dating can lead to a more integrated and diverse society. This is particularly evident in the rise of interracial marriages, which have increased significantly since the introduction of online dating platforms.

The study suggests that the emergence of online dating has facilitated the formation of new, strong ties between individuals from different racial backgrounds. This is because online platforms allow people to connect with strangers, bypassing the traditional social networks that often limit interactions to close friends and acquaintances. The researchers' model predicts that even a small number of new connections can lead to substantial changes in the overall network structure, promoting greater social integration.

Moreover, the study indicates that marriages formed through online dating may be more resilient and less likely to end in divorce. A 2013 study supports this hypothesis, showing that couples who meet online have lower rates of marital breakup compared to those who meet traditionally. This finding is consistent with the researchers' model, which suggests that the weak ties formed through online dating can create stronger, more stable relationships.

The implications of these findings are profound. As online dating continues to grow in popularity, it has the potential to significantly impact social structures and relationships. By breaking down barriers and fostering new connections, online dating platforms may contribute to a more integrated and harmonious society. However, the study also highlights the need for further research to fully understand the long-term effects of these changes.

Syrian President Bashar al-Assad has expressed interest in visiting North Korea and meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, according to North Korea's state-run news agency KCNA. Assad made the comments on May 30 while receiving the credentials of North Korean Ambassador Mun Jong Nam. This potential meeting could mark the first visit by another head of state to North Korea under Kim's leadership since 2011. North Korea and Syria maintain close diplomatic and military ties, with North Korea providing military support to Syria during the Arab-Israeli war in 1973. Kim has recently engaged in a series of high-level diplomatic meetings, including a summit with U.S. President Donald Trump scheduled for June 12 in Singapore. Assad praised Kim's leadership, stating, "I am sure that he will achieve the final victory and realize the reunification of Korea without fail." The Syrian government did not immediately respond to a request for comment. This development comes as international attention is focused on the upcoming summit between Kim and Trump, and highlights the complex web of relationships and alliances in the region.

Republican presidential candidate Ted Cruz faced criticism and issued an apology after making a joke at the expense of Vice President Joe Biden, whose son Beau died of brain cancer. Cruz, speaking at a Republican gathering in Michigan, used an old line: "Joe Biden … You know what the nice thing is? You don't even need a punch line." He added, "I promise you it works. The next party you're at, just walk up to someone and say, 'Vice President Joe Biden' and just close your mouth. They will crack up laughing." The joke, which had been a staple of Cruz's stump speeches, drew immediate backlash on social media, with many pointing out Biden's recent loss. Cruz later apologized on Facebook, stating, "It was a mistake to use an old joke about Joe Biden during his time of grief, and I sincerely apologize. The loss of his son is heartbreaking and tragic, and our prayers are very much with the Vice President and his family." Cruz's campaign chair, Saul Anuzis, defended the timing, saying, "Timing could have been better." However, Michigan Democratic Party chairman Lon Johnson criticized Cruz, stating, "When it counted, and it always does for someone attempting to become the leader of our nation, Sen. Cruz demonstrated a true lack of Christian compassion for a father mourning a son." Cruz's comments came during his first campaign event in Michigan since launching his presidential bid, where he also called for a federal flat tax, abolishing the Internal Revenue Service, and repealing Obamacare.

On the evening of Tuesday, November 17, and into the morning of Wednesday, November 18, the Leonid meteor shower will peak, creating a moderate number of shooting stars. The annual event, caused by bits of ice and rock burning in Earth’s atmosphere, will appear to originate from the constellation Leo. For the best viewing, head out after sunset on Tuesday, November 17, and look east, away from city lights. NASA predicts one meteor every four minutes, with a darker sky due to a crescent moon. However, cloud cover may obstruct views for a significant portion of the U.S. The Leonids occur annually around November 17 as Earth passes through the debris field of the comet Tempel-Tuttle, with the next peak expected in 2032.

The largest diamond ever found in North America has been discovered at the Diavik mine in Canada’s frozen north by Dominion Diamond Mines and Rio Tinto Group. Weighing in at 552 carats, the yellow gem is almost three times the size of the next largest stone ever found in Canada. This discovery marks the seventh-biggest diamond find of the 21st century, according to Bloomberg calculations, and would place it among the 30 largest diamonds ever unearthed. The largest diamond ever found, the 3,106-carat Cullinan, was discovered near Pretoria in South Africa in 1905 and was cut into several polished gems, with the two largest stones set in the Crown Jewels of Britain. 

The Diavik mine, 60% owned and fully operated by Rio, is known for producing high-quality diamonds but is not typically associated with such large finds. The diamond was found in October and is gem quality, suitable for jewelry, but Dominion CEO Shane Durgin provided few details on its value. Yellow diamonds typically sell at a discount to Type IIa top whites, often found in the best African mines, but the highest quality fancy vivid yellow or fancy intense yellow stones can command a premium. 

Durgin noted that the diamond's rough nature and abrasions from the processing facility made it difficult to estimate its value. "It’s very hard to give a ballpark estimate. It all depends on, again, the cutting and the resulting stone it ends up," he said. The discovery is significant for Dominion, which has been experiencing a management shakeup since billionaire Dennis Washington bought the company for $1.2 billion last year. There have been at least five senior personnel changes, including the recent departure of CEO Patrick Evans after just over a year. Dominion needs to decide if it will proceed with expansion projects that would extend the life of the Ekati mine. 

The Diavik mine is located 135 miles south of the Arctic Circle in Canada’s Northwest Territories, an area known for its challenging diamond mining conditions. There are no permanent roads, and access is by air or ice roads that must be rebuilt each winter. The global diamond market has been under pressure, especially for smaller and lower-quality stones, due to an oversupply and weaker demand in India, where about 90% of diamonds are cut and polished. Major cutting centers have also been squeezed by low margins and a drop in trade finance. The 552-carat yellow Canadamark diamond is a significant milestone for diamond mining in North America and showcases the unique geological journey of natural diamonds from their formation to their discovery.

In a small Ohio town, a long-standing feud has escalated into a relentless campaign of horn honking, with one man claiming he has been the target of over 5,000 honks in the past seven years. Rick and Cindy Krlich, longtime residents of Hubbard, Ohio, say that after a failed real estate bid in 2007, the Clemente family, including the former fire chief, retaliated by organizing a "vast conspiracy" of honking. The Krlichs have installed surveillance cameras to document the honking, capturing video of a fire truck, a police officer, and other residents honking their horns. They have even sued 40 alleged honkers, including the Clementes. 

John Clemente, now retired, denies instigating the honking. He says that his son's girlfriend and her friends would honk their horns as a way of saying goodbye, but he acknowledges that the Krlichs have been targeted. "Why wouldn't you be against him … and what he is doing to everybody?" Clemente told ABC News' "20/20." "Do you realize he has got 700 cases going to court?" Marlene Clemente added, "Just a regular beep or just to beep at the neighbors across the street, he'll take you to court."

In an attempt to bring the community together, "20/20" organized a "Peace and Reconciliation Barbecue," inviting the Krlichs, the Clementes, and the town of Hubbard. However, the event did not seem to bring about the hoped-for reconciliation. The Krlichs continued to express their frustration, while the Clementes defended their actions. The town's police chief, James R. Taafe, has been criticized for not taking the Krlichs' complaints seriously, despite evidence of honking incidents involving police and fire department vehicles. Garrick Krlich has filed a lawsuit against the town, the police chief, and Trumball County, alleging a violation of the Equal Protection Clause, seeking compensatory damages and punitive damages.

North Korea's Kim Jong Il has appointed his youngest son, Kim Jong Un, as a four-star general, a significant promotion seen as a confirmation that he is the country's chosen successor. State media announced Kim Jong Il's re-election as leader of the ruling Workers' Party, with Kim Jong Un and other family members receiving top posts. The North Korean capital was decorated with banners and placards celebrating the historic political convention, the country's biggest in 30 years. Kim Jong Un, believed to be in his late 20s and educated in Switzerland, has remained largely unknown to the outside world. Analysts suggest his promotion is the start of his formal succession to power, with Kim Jong Il committed to maintaining control within his family. The appointment aims to solidify the "songun" or military-first policy, with Kim Jong Un expected to take up other top military jobs. His sister, Kim Kyong Hui, was also promoted to general, potentially acting as an adviser during his rise. The convention, initially delayed, appears to address concerns over Kim Jong Il's health and the need for a smooth power transition.

Germanwings co-pilot Andreas Lubitz researched suicide methods and cockpit door security measures on his tablet device in the days leading up to the crash, according to Düsseldorf prosecutors. The analysis of Lubitz's tablet, retrieved from his Düsseldorf apartment, revealed searches for suicide methods and cockpit door security terms from March 16 to March 23. Lubitz, 27, is suspected of deliberately crashing Germanwings Flight 9525 into the French Alps, killing all 150 people on board. The cockpit voice recorder showed that Lubitz locked the captain out of the cockpit before guiding the plane into the mountains. Investigators have also found 40 damaged cellphones at the crash site, though their usefulness is questionable due to their condition. The discovery of the second black box, the flight data recorder, should provide more details on Lubitz's actions during the final moments of the flight. German authorities are considering changes to cockpit door controls and pilot medical assessments in response to the tragedy. The investigation continues as authorities aim to understand Lubitz's motivations and prevent similar incidents in the future.

About 80% of the migrants in the caravan are from Honduras, fleeing poverty, political unrest, and violence following the contested election of Honduran President Juan Orlando Hernández. They chant "out with JOH" and "we aren't immigrants, we're international workers" as they march. The group, organized by Pueblos Sin Fronteras, aims to help migrants safely reach the United States, bypassing authorities and gangs. The number of participants caught organizers by surprise, overwhelming towns they've stopped in. Upon reaching the U.S., some hope for asylum, while others plan to cross illegally. The caravan's sheer size is intended to deter authorities and criminals. Organizers have established security, food, and logistics committees, empowering the migrants. Some, like Yonis, aim to legalize their status in Mexico and reunite with their families. The journey is fraught with risks, but migrants see it as a safer alternative to solo travel. The group uses various methods to move, including hitching rides on trucks and practicing boarding freight trains. Despite the challenges, the caravan continues, driven by the hope of a better life in the United States.

Mel B's journey to healing and self-acceptance continues, but her hand still clings to a symbol of a tumultuous past. The 43-year-old Spice Girl, who recently filed for divorce from Stephen Belafonte, was spotted in Los Angeles wearing a $300,000, 7-carat diamond ring, despite the couple's separation since December. This behavior has raised questions about her emotional state and the depth of her commitment to the divorce. Mel B's legal troubles with Belafonte have been well-documented, with her filing for a restraining order, alleging physical and emotional abuse. She claims that Belafonte, a film producer, would demean her, destroy her self-esteem, and even threaten to release sex tapes to ruin her career. The abuse reportedly escalated to the point where Mel B attempted suicide by swallowing an entire bottle of aspirin. Her story has gained significant attention, with many around her witnessing her injuries but not reporting the abuse to authorities. Mel B's legal battle with Belafonte includes his alleged threats to use a gun, which is a violation of his domestic violence conviction. Despite the ongoing legal and emotional challenges, Mel B remains focused on her personal growth and plans to enter a UK-based treatment center to address her PTSD and other issues.

After 27 years in prison, Krishna Maharaj, a British businessman, now has a chance to prove his innocence in the double murder of his business partners Derrick Moo Young and his son Duane in a Miami hotel. Maharaj's lawyers claim new evidence could free him, alleging he was framed by the Medellin drug cartel to cover up their involvement in the killings. The case is set for a full evidentiary hearing in April, where Maharaj's legal team will present 53 witnesses and 498 documents to support their claims. Maharaj asserts that the Moo Youngs were laundering money for the cartel, which led to their murder. Among the evidence, his lawyers have identified former cartel members who claim to have carried out the killings. However, prosecutors argue that much of the new evidence is inadmissible hearsay. Maharaj, 75, has maintained his innocence throughout his imprisonment, and his wife Marita has been a constant support, visiting him every Sunday. Despite the significant evidence against him, including fingerprints found at the crime scene, Maharaj's legal team believes they have a strong case for his exoneration. The judge will decide whether the new evidence is compelling enough to warrant a retrial.

Posters featuring Meryl Streep with the text "She knew" appeared in several locations in Los Angeles, following Streep's denial of knowing Harvey Weinstein's alleged predatory behavior. The posters, hung before sunrise, were spotted near Streep's Pasadena home, the SAG-AFTRA building, and the 20th Century Fox studio lot. Streep's statement, sent to USA TODAY, clarified that she did not know about Weinstein's crimes and that she was not deliberately silent. Rose McGowan, who alleges she was raped by Weinstein, criticized Streep for her professional relationship with the producer, suggesting that Streep knew about Weinstein's alleged misconduct. McGowan's tweets sparked a response from Streep, who denied knowing about Weinstein's alleged behavior. Actress Amber Tamblyn, a friend of McGowan, defended Streep, stating she does not support shaming other women's movements. The controversy highlights the ongoing debate and accusations surrounding Weinstein's alleged misconduct and the responses of those who worked with him.

Two women, Lizandra Cosme, 32, and Susana Gonzalez, 27, have been charged in connection with an incident at the Children’s Learning Place daycare in Chicago, where five toddlers were allegedly injured with a hot glue gun. According to surveillance footage, Cosme, who was working with 16 children, applied hot glue to the hands and arms of the five 2-year-olds, causing visible pain and distress, as the children winced and whined during the process. Gonzalez, an assistant at the daycare, was seen laughing nearby. Prosecutors stated that each child victim winced and some whined at the application of the hot glue, and Cosme attempted to apply neosporin to one of the children after noticing circular burn marks. The incident occurred on December 1st, and the extent of the children's injuries is currently unknown. During a court appearance, Cosme's defense attorney claimed that her actions were not malicious, citing her 12 years of experience working with young children. However, prosecutors alleged that Cosme brought the hot glue gun to the daycare to use on a Christmas project. The Children’s Learning Place, a licensed child-care facility serving children between 6 weeks and 6 years, has four locations in Chicago. Upon learning of the alleged incident, the daycare immediately terminated the two employees involved. The Department of Children and Family Services is investigating the case, and the two women are facing serious charges. Cosme was arrested on Sunday and charged with five counts of aggravated battery of a child under 13 years old causing great bodily harm, while Gonzalez was charged with five misdemeanor counts of causing the circumstances of child endangerment. Both women are scheduled to appear in court on December 26th.

Burberry has announced it will stop destroying unsaleable products and will no longer use real fur, marking a significant step towards sustainability. This move builds on the company's existing responsibility agenda and aligns with its commitment to reducing waste and environmental impact. Burberry will expand its efforts to reuse, repair, donate, or recycle unsaleable items. The company has also partnered with Elvis & Kresse to repurpose leather offcuts into new products, and supports the Burberry Material Futures Research Group to develop sustainable materials. Burberry's CEO, Marco Gobbetti, emphasizes the importance of social and environmental responsibility in modern luxury. The company's initiatives include sourcing 21% of its cotton through the Better Cotton Initiative and working with Teach First to support young people in disadvantaged communities. These actions reflect Burberry's broader goal of positively impacting one million people and becoming carbon neutral in its operations.

In 1983, during the NCAA tournament, Benny Anders, a key player for the University of Houston's Phi Slamma Jamma team, delivered a memorable dunk against Louisville that has since become legendary. Anders, known for his flamboyant style and eccentric personality, had a significant impact on the team's identity, even though he played primarily as a reserve. His most iconic play came during a crucial game against Louisville, where he executed a daring dunk that left defenders in the dust. Anders's contributions extended beyond the court, as he was a frequent source of colorful quotes and antics, earning him the nickname "The Outlaw."

After Anders's college career, his life took an unexpected turn. He quit the team in 1985, citing a disagreement with the coach, and disappeared from the public eye, vanishing for over three decades. Despite numerous rumors and speculations about his whereabouts, including suggestions that he had undergone a sex change or was living in Asia, his true location remained a mystery. His family and former teammates were unable to locate him, leading to a persistent "Where in the world is Benny Anders?" question among basketball enthusiasts.

In 2013, a documentary filmmaker named Chip Rives embarked on a quest to find Anders, eventually tracing him to the Detroit area. Anders was working at a restaurant, and he looked good, having slimmed down from his 350-pound days. The documentary, "Phi Slama Jama," which aired later that year, featured Anders's candid admission that "A brotherly love is a very powerful thing." Anders's appearance in the film provided closure to a decades-long mystery, confirming his continued existence and allowing basketball fans to see the man behind the legend.

President Donald Trump indicated for the first time on Wednesday that he is open to a path to citizenship for some younger undocumented immigrants, known as "dreamers," as part of an immigration deal being negotiated by Congress. Trump's remarks, made in an impromptu discussion with reporters, came with conditions, including securing $25 billion for a border wall and $5 billion for additional border security upgrades. This potential shift represents a significant change from Trump's campaign promises and his previous rejection of a bipartisan Senate proposal that included citizenship for dreamers. Trump emphasized that the path to citizenship would be contingent on the dreamers meeting certain conditions and would take 10 to 12 years. He also stressed that his support for the deal is contingent on the funding for the border wall and other security measures.

The White House plans to release a complete "framework" on Monday, which is expected to grant immediate provisional legal status to those immigrants covered by the Obama-era Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program. This group, which includes about 690,000 immigrants, would then be eligible to pursue full citizenship over the 10 to 12-year period. Trump's proposal would be limited to the DACA recipients and would not extend to a larger group of dreamers, as some Democrats and Republicans have pushed for. The White House official stated that the framework would give lawmakers a clearer set of guidelines to help break the impasse in the negotiations.

The announcement comes as Congress faces a February 8 deadline for a must-pass spending bill to keep the government open, with immigration being a major sticking point. Democrats and some Republicans have said they will not support a long-term deal that does not address the future of the DACA program. The impasse over immigration led to a brief, partial government shutdown this week before lawmakers agreed on a three-week funding extension. White House officials said Trump's proposal for citizenship would be limited to the 690,000 who were enrolled in DACA when he terminated the program.

Trump's statement was welcomed by some lawmakers, such as Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), who drafted the bipartisan immigration plan along with Sen. Richard J. Durbin (D-Ill.). Graham said the president's support for a pathway to citizenship would help them get strong border security measures as they work to modernize a broken immigration system. However, Democrats expressed exasperation that Trump has not clearly articulated his demands and have criticized his past vacillations on the issue. The White House announcement on immigration came as 35 senators gathered to figure out how the chamber will proceed on its immigration debate. The group of Democrats and Republicans asked Sens. John Cornyn (R-Tex.) and Durbin to serve as a clearinghouse and sort out the parameters and timetable for the debate.

The White House plan is expected to include a path to citizenship for the 690,000 DACA recipients, contingent on securing $25 billion for a border wall and $5 billion for additional border security upgrades. Lawmakers face the challenge of negotiating the details of the plan, including how much money for the wall is enough, how strict the limits on relatives should be, and what new powers to provide. Additionally, a major question is how many dreamers to cover, with the number potentially ranging from about 700,000 to some 2 million. The White House's framework is seen as a compromise that members of both parties can support, and the administration encourages the Senate to bring it to the floor.

The Hope Diamond, one of the world's most famous and enigmatic gems, has been a part of the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History collection for 53 years, and the institution has managed to avoid any of the supposed misfortunes associated with the stone. Despite its legendary curse, the Smithsonian has thrived, with increased attendance and a world-renowned gem collection. However, the true history of the diamond is far more complex than the tales of misfortune would suggest. The gem's origins trace back to the 17th century, when French merchant Jean Baptiste Tavernier acquired the original 115-carat blue diamond in India. The story goes that Tavernier stole the gem from a Hindu idol, leading to his untimely death by dogs. However, this account is a myth, as Tavernier sold the diamond to King Louis XIV for a significant sum and retired peacefully in Russia. The diamond was later stolen during the French Revolution and resurfaced in Britain in 1812, where it was cut down and renamed the Hope Diamond. It passed through several owners, including financier Henry Philip Hope, Lord Francis Hope, and American socialite Evalyn Walsh McLean, each of whom experienced tragic events, but none of these can be definitively linked to the diamond's supposed curse. Pierre Cartier, who acquired the diamond from McLean's estate, managed to avoid any misfortune. The Smithsonian eventually purchased the diamond in 1958, and while the museum has thrived, the postman who delivered it did face some misfortunes, including a truck accident and the loss of his wife and dog. Recent scientific discoveries have shed new light on the diamond's history, revealing that it was likely cut to resemble a sun at its center during the reign of King Louis XIV. This unique cut was designed to create a golden sun in the center of the deep blue stone, symbolizing the Sun King's power and status. The Hope Diamond continues to captivate visitors and researchers alike, with its mysterious history and scientific intrigue making it a focal point of the Smithsonian's collections.

A video of CBS Evening News anchor Katie Couric preparing to go on air on the day John McCain announced Sarah Palin as his running mate has resurfaced, and it’s being used by Palin allies to suggest Couric was mocking Palin. The video, which appears to be raw and unedited, shows Couric commenting on the names of Palin’s children, saying, “where the hell do they get these [names]?...” The producer running the sound board shut off the sound at that point, likely due to Couric’s disdainful tone. The video also includes Couric making comments about female basketball players and Palin’s hometown, which is described as one of the fastest-growing areas in Alaska and the fifth-largest city in the state. 

Critics of the video argue that it is a small sample and that Couric’s comments may have been made in a private setting. They point out that Couric was not the only one to make snide comments about the names of Palin’s children, and that Palin herself acknowledged the difficulty in finding unique names for her children during the campaign. The video is being used by Palin supporters to highlight what they see as bias and mockery from Couric, but defenders of Couric argue that the video is just a snippet and that it’s possible Couric made more positive comments that were not captured.

The controversy comes at a time when CBS is facing criticism for its coverage of the 2008 election, with some arguing that the network focused on Palin’s personal life rather than her policy achievements. Palin allies are using the video to argue that CBS was biased against Palin and that her approval ratings were unfairly low. However, defenders of Couric and CBS argue that the video is not representative of her overall demeanor and professionalism, and that it is unfair to draw conclusions based on a single, unverified clip. The video has sparked a broader debate about media bias and the role of journalists in shaping public perception of political figures.

A new, classified unmanned aircraft, the RQ-180, developed by Northrop Grumman, is now flying, marking a significant leap in combining stealth and aerodynamic efficiency for intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance (ISR) missions. According to defense and intelligence officials, the RQ-180, funded through the Air Force’s classified budget, is scheduled to enter production for the U.S. Air Force and could be operational by 2015. The Air Force and Northrop Grumman have remained tight-lipped about the project, with Air Force spokeswoman Jennifer Cassidy stating that the program details are not for public discussion. The RQ-180 is equipped with advanced sensors, including active, electronically scanned array (AESA) radar and passive electronic surveillance measures, and may also be capable of electronic attack missions. This aircraft is designed to operate in contested or denied airspace, shifting ISR assets away from permissive environments such as Iraq and Afghanistan. The RQ-180 is expected to replace a version of the RQ-4B Global Hawk after 2014, and its stealth design and improved aerodynamics will enable it to conduct longer missions over restricted airspace. The program is managed by the Air Force’s Rapid Capabilities Office and will likely be jointly controlled by the Air Force and the CIA, similar to the RQ-170 Sentinel. Northrop Grumman’s financial reports and satellite imagery of its facilities in Palmdale, California, and Area 51 suggest that the RQ-180 is in flight testing. The RQ-180’s capabilities are seen as a response to the retirement of the SR-71 in 1998, addressing the need for a stealthy, long-range ISR platform that can operate in hostile environments.

Scientists recently revealed that Earth narrowly avoided a catastrophic solar storm in July 2012, which could have plunged the planet into a technological blackout lasting years. The storm, described as the most powerful in over 150 years, was nearly Earth-directed but instead hit NASA’s STEREO-A satellite, providing valuable data. If it had hit, the storm would have delivered a geomagnetic disturbance of -1200 nT, comparable to the 1859 Carrington Event, which destroyed telegraph networks and caused widespread disruptions. The National Academy of Sciences estimates the economic impact of such a storm could exceed $2 trillion, with critical infrastructure like power grids and satellites potentially crippled. A study by physicist Pete Riley of Predictive Science Inc. found that there is a 12% chance of a similar storm hitting Earth in the next decade. The July 2012 event was part of a series of eruptions, with multiple coronal mass ejections (CMEs) clearing a path, making it more intense. The STEREO-A satellite, orbiting outside Earth’s magnetosphere, survived the storm, providing unprecedented data. This event highlights the need for better preparedness and monitoring of space weather to mitigate potential impacts on modern technology.

A Florida couple, Chris and Dana White, recently shared their harrowing experience on a Carnival Cruise, revealing the discovery of a hidden recording device in their stateroom. The Whites were aboard the Carnival Fantasy for a three-day Caribbean cruise in October 2018 when they noticed the device, which they say was hidden among TV wires and pointing directly at their bed. In an exclusive interview set to air on Inside Edition, the couple expressed their shock and dismay, stating they will never set foot on another Carnival Cruise ship again. Upon discovering the device, Chris and Dana immediately contacted Carnival security, and Chris filmed an employee inspecting and dismantling the device. The employee confirmed the presence of a video transmitter, but Carnival's response was initially that it was not a camera. However, Chris and Dana insisted that the device was functional, warm to the touch, and clearly a recording device. 

Carnival acknowledged a "video transmitter" was found during a full investigation by the shipboard team. In a statement, the company noted that the device "was not connected to an electrical source and not capable of recording." Despite this, the Whites remain unconvinced, maintaining that the device was operational. The couple emphasized the invasion of their privacy and the unsettling experience. The device was subsequently turned over to the FBI for further inspection, and Carnival also notified the U.S. Customs and Border Protection. 

This incident is not the only bizarre occurrence on Carnival Cruises. Earlier this month, reports surfaced of a Royal Caribbean International cruise, which left from Sydney, Australia, being overrun with approximately 1,300 men from a tobacco company, Kamla Pasand, who held wild parties featuring women dressed as Playboy bunnies. Passengers described the situation as akin to a large bachelor party, with the men taking over pool decks, bars, and buffets. The men were said to have brought burlesque dancers onboard and filmed young girls, leading to a chaotic and uncomfortable environment for many passengers. Families were forced to take refuge inside as the scantily clad women danced on the decks. The workers also brought crates of their own food, leading to extensive refurbishments of the ship. Royal Caribbean International issued full refunds to passengers and is currently investigating the incident to prevent future occurrences.

A West Virginia Department of Transportation worker, Thomas Keith Henderson, was arrested on Wednesday night for driving a state snow plow while intoxicated. Deputy R.L. Jones pulled Henderson over on Burke Mountain near Keystone due to a non-functioning headlight, and observed signs of alcohol use. Henderson's blood alcohol level was 0.09, more than twice the legal limit for commercial drivers. He was charged with DUI (CDL) and defective equipment. Despite being released on $500 bond, Henderson's employment with the DOT remains an ongoing legal matter.

A controversial video featuring ants crawling over a crucifix has been exhibited at the New Museum in New York, sparking debates on freedom of expression. The video, titled "A Fire in My Belly, A Work in Progress," was originally shown at a Smithsonian museum but was later removed after protests led by the Catholic League President, Bill Donohue. Donohue criticized the artistic community for being insensitive to Christians and called for the institution's funding to be cut. In response, the New Museum's director, Lisa Phillips, defended the exhibit, stating that the museum would not yield to censorship. The video now screens in the museum's lobby and is accessible to the public free of charge, drawing requests from numerous galleries to show the controversial work. This exhibit highlights the ongoing tension between artistic freedom and religious sensitivities in a city renowned for its avant-garde art scene.

Russian authorities have expressed disappointment over the death of Vladimir Katriuk, a 93-year-old former SS officer suspected of involvement in a 1943 massacre of civilians in Belarus. Katriuk, a Ukrainian-born beekeeper who lived in Quebec, passed away after years of health issues, according to his lawyer. The Russian Embassy in Ottawa criticized the Canadian government for allowing Katriuk to retain citizenship while residing in the country, stating that employing legal or politically motivated loopholes to avoid trying or extraditing Nazi war criminals is unacceptable. Katriuk was No. 2 on the Simon Wiesenthal Center’s list of most wanted Nazi war criminals and was suspected of participating in the Khatyn massacre, where he allegedly operated a machine-gun outside a burning barn, killing civilians attempting to escape. The Canadian Centre for Israel and Jewish Affairs urged Ottawa to ensure Katriuk be held accountable for alleged war crimes. Meanwhile, the Ukrainian Canadian Congress argued that Katriuk should be left alone, citing the Federal Court’s 1999 ruling that found no evidence of his direct involvement in atrocities. Despite Moscow’s demand for Katriuk’s extradition, the Canadian government has maintained its stance against recognizing Russia’s annexation of Crimea and its interference in Ukraine. Katriuk’s case has become a pawn in the strained relations between Canada and Russia, highlighting the ongoing tension between justice for historical crimes and diplomatic considerations.

Twenty-two states and the District of Columbia are backing Montana in its legal bid to preserve state-level regulations on corporate political expenditures, challenging the U.S. Supreme Court's 2010 Citizens United decision. New York's attorney general's office has filed a brief with the high court, arguing that Montana's state-level ban on corporate campaign spending should be upheld as it differs significantly from the federal issues addressed in Citizens United. The states contend that local election regulations are necessary to prevent corruption, particularly at the state and local level, where the risk of corporate influence is greater. Montana Attorney General Steve Bullock argues that the state's ban is not a complete ban on corporate political speech but rather a regulation requiring the formation of political action committees. Critics, including the Virginia-based American Tradition Partnership, argue that such state laws unfairly restrict corporate political engagement. The brief emphasizes that Montana's ban is rooted in a history of corporate corruption and aims to protect the integrity of local elections. The case has garnered support from U.S. Senators John McCain and Sheldon Whitehouse, who argue that evidence since Citizens United shows that large independent expenditures can lead to corruption. Legal experts are skeptical of the Supreme Court reconsidering Citizens United, but the states are hopeful that a clarification could be issued to allow the Montana law to stand. The Supreme Court has blocked the Montana law until it can review the case, and a decision is pending.

Minnesota Congresswoman Michele Bachmann has withdrawn her Swiss citizenship, a move that has sparked debate and raised questions about her political stance and judgment. Bachmann, who was born in America and considers herself a proud American, requested the withdrawal of her dual citizenship, stating, "I was born in America and I am a proud American citizen. I am, and always have been, 100 percent committed to our United States Constitution and the United States of America." The decision came after news broke that she and her children had recently applied for Swiss citizenship, a move that caused controversy. Bachmann's initial explanation was that her husband, Marcus, a dual American and Swiss citizen, had passed on the citizenship to their family. However, this contradicts earlier statements from Bachmann's spokeswoman, Becky Rogness, who said the family had sought the citizenship "recently." Bachmann's withdrawal of Swiss citizenship aims to clarify her allegiance to the U.S., but it has led to speculation about potential security clearance issues and raised questions about her decision-making. Critics argue that her actions are hypocritical, given her past questioning of President Obama's loyalty and her constant harping on Democratic opponents' supposed lack of American patriotism. Some suggest that her actions might be politically motivated, while others see it as a simple mistake. The controversy highlights the complex and often misunderstood nature of dual citizenship in the United States, where holding such status is not uncommon but can sometimes lead to complications, especially in the political arena.

A 22-year-old man, Isaiah Thompson, has been arrested for subway surfing, a dangerous and thrill-seeking activity that involves riding on the exterior of a moving subway train. This was at least the third time Thompson was caught doing so, with previous incidents occurring in March and November 2017. The latest incident was captured on video by straphanger Matt Beary, who documented Thompson hanging on to the C train between the Clinton-Washington and Lafayette Street stations. Thompson's nonchalant approach to the dangerous activity, including letting one arm down and pressing tightly against the door, alarmed some passengers. The NYPD Transit Bureau chief, Andy Byford, emphasized the extreme danger of the behavior, stating that it can result in death or major delays. Thompson was charged with reckless endangerment and disorderly conduct. His repeated offenses highlight the ongoing challenge for authorities to deter such risky behavior, which has claimed lives in the past.

A new survey has revealed that the number of Americans who were "totally sedentary" last year has risen to its highest level since 2007, with approximately 83 million Americans, or about 28% of the population, reporting that they did not participate in any of the 104 specific physical activities listed in the survey for the entire previous calendar year. This concerning statistic highlights a significant shift in the nation's physical activity levels, as the percentage of sedentary individuals has increased by nearly 4% compared to the previous year's findings. The survey, which covered a wide range of activities including walking, gardening, and even housework, paints a troubling picture of a growing sedentary lifestyle among Americans.

Experts have long warned about the dangers of a sedentary lifestyle, linking it to a host of health issues such as obesity, diabetes, and heart disease. The rise in sedentary behavior has been attributed to various factors, including the increasing prevalence of desk jobs, the rise of technology and screen time, and the overall shift towards more sedentary leisure activities. The survey results underscore the need for public health initiatives aimed at promoting physical activity and combating the sedentary lifestyle epidemic.

The findings also raise questions about the effectiveness of current public health campaigns and policies. While many programs have been launched to encourage physical activity, the survey suggests that these efforts may not be reaching the intended audience or may not be as effective as hoped. Some experts argue that more targeted interventions, such as workplace wellness programs and community-based initiatives, are needed to address the root causes of sedentary behavior.

Moreover, the survey results highlight the disparities in physical activity levels across different demographic groups. For instance, older adults, women, and those with lower incomes tend to be more sedentary, raising concerns about health inequalities. Addressing these disparities will require tailored approaches that take into account the unique challenges faced by different populations.

In conclusion, the survey's findings serve as a wake-up call for policymakers, health professionals, and the general public. The rising number of sedentary Americans underscores the urgent need for comprehensive strategies to promote physical activity and improve overall public health. As the nation grapples with this growing issue, it is clear that a multi-faceted approach will be necessary to reverse the trend and ensure a healthier future for all Americans.

At least 717 people have lost their lives in a tragic stampede during the final ritual of the Hajj pilgrimage near the holy city of Mecca, Saudi Arabia. The incident, which occurred as two million pilgrims were participating in the stoning of the devil ritual in Mina, has been the deadliest disaster at Mina in 25 years. King Salman has ordered an urgent review of this year's Hajj plans to improve organization and management. The stampede reportedly began when two large groups of pilgrims converged from different directions onto one street, causing a sudden surge and leading to a large number of people falling. Eyewitnesses described a chaotic scene with people climbing over each other just to breathe, while others fell and were trampled. The Saudi civil defense directorate deployed 4,000 workers, along with 220 ambulances and other vehicles, to Mina in response to the disaster. The stampede has drawn criticism, with Iran's supreme leader blaming Saudi Arabia's "mismanagement and improper actions." Saudi authorities have stated that many pilgrims moved "without respecting the timetables" established by authorities. The incident highlights the ongoing challenges in managing the massive crowds during the Hajj, which has seen previous tragedies including a crane collapse that killed 107 people and injured 238 others just two weeks earlier. The stampede serves as a stark reminder of the risks involved in one of the most significant religious events in the Islamic calendar.

In a surprising twist to Tiger Woods' ongoing scandal, porn star and escort Devon James claims the golfer fathered her secret love child. Born in early 2001, before Woods and Elin Nordegren's marriage, the child bears a striking resemblance to the world's top golfer. James, one of approximately 15 women linked to Woods in secret affairs, recently revealed her claim on a porn movie set in Los Angeles. RadarOnline.com has seen photographs of the purported love child and reports that Woods has not taken or been asked to take a paternity test. James claims she had a two-and-a-half year affair with Woods, during which she became pregnant. Six years later, she allegedly told Woods she believed her son was his. The claims resurface just a day after other reports emerged about Tiger's secret child, though those did not name the alleged mother. RadarOnline.com has found no evidence that Woods has paid James. The story reignites speculation about Tiger's fidelity and his potential fatherhood.

During 2011, the United States experienced 222 measles cases, marking a significant increase from the median of 60 cases reported annually during 2001 to 2010. Importations of measles from other countries accounted for 90% of these cases, with 72 cases linked to U.S. residents who had traveled abroad, 67 linked epidemiologically, 39 with virologic evidence suggesting recent importation, and 22 linked to cases with virologic evidence of recent importation. The majority of patients were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status, and 200 cases were associated with 17 outbreaks. The report highlights the ongoing risk of measles among unvaccinated individuals and the importance of vaccination to prevent outbreaks and sustained transmission. Health-care providers play a crucial role in maintaining measles elimination by maintaining a high awareness of the disease, suspecting measles in patients with a febrile rash and compatible symptoms, and promptly reporting suspected cases to limit spread. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) emphasizes the need for high MMR vaccination coverage to prevent large, sustained outbreaks and reestablishment of endemic transmission. The article also notes that despite the relatively small number of reported cases, vigilance is necessary to prevent a drop in vaccination coverage, which could increase the risk of large outbreaks. Health-care providers are encouraged to remind their patients, especially those traveling internationally, of the importance of vaccination to prevent measles.

Republican House Speaker Paul Ryan has firmly rejected speculation that he might become the party's presidential nominee, stating that he has no intention of running for the presidency. Ryan, speaking to The Times of Israel after arriving for a visit, emphasized that he had made a conscious decision not to run for president and that he believes in the importance of starting a presidential campaign in Iowa and running to the finish line. He cited personal reasons, such as his phase of life with a young family, as well as the strength of the Republican field with 17 candidates vying for the nomination. Ryan also addressed the rise of Donald Trump and Bernie Sanders, attributing their success to the deep anxiety among Americans regarding the stagnant economy and national security threats. Despite the ongoing speculation, Ryan remains focused on his role as co-chair of the upcoming Republican National Convention, maintaining a neutral stance on the race. His comments come as Donald Trump is expected to secure the nomination in Wisconsin, while Ted Cruz is gaining momentum, potentially leading to a contested convention.
