Ryan's visit to Israel marks his first overseas trip since becoming Speaker, underscoring the importance of reinforcing the alliance between the U.S. and Israel.

At least 13 people, including several children, died after a tourist boat capsized and sank on Table Rock Lake in Branson, Missouri, during a severe thunderstorm, authorities said. Stone County Sheriff Doug Rader reported that 14 people survived, with seven injured, including two in critical condition. The National Transportation Safety Board and the Coast Guard were investigating the incident. Four adults and three children were treated for minor injuries at Cox Medical Center Branson. The boat, operated by Ride the Ducks, was carrying 31 passengers and two crew members when it was overwhelmed by the storm. Sheriff Rader said the boat capsized because of the weather, while another duck boat on the lake safely returned to shore. The National Weather Service had issued a severe thunderstorm warning for the area, with winds reaching over 60 mph. The captain of the boat survived, but the driver, identified as Robert "Bob" Williams, 73, was killed. The mayor of Branson, Karen Best, identified Williams as a local resident who was a significant part of the community. The duck boat tragedy involved nine members of the Coleman family from Indiana, with only two survivors. The boat, originally used by the U.S. military in World War II, was a popular tourist attraction in Branson, known for its amphibious capabilities. The National Transportation Safety Board noted that duck boats have been involved in other deadly incidents, including one in Seattle in 2015 where five college students died, and another in 1999 near Hot Springs, Arkansas, where 13 people were killed. The boat was one of two on the lake; the other made it back to shore safely. The incident raised questions about the safety of the boats and the adequacy of weather warnings and responses.

Two men from the Jersey Shore are facing criminal charges after police say they allegedly took a taxi to rob a house and then did not pay their fare, officials said. The Asbury Park Police Department responded to a possible robbery in Deal Township, New Jersey, around 10:30 p.m. on Nov. 4. A taxi driver called authorities after Kenneth Burke, 46, from Asbury Park, and Timothy Foote, 38, of Ocean Township, are accused of taking the car to a house and asking the driver to wait in the car. They returned with a television set and some liquor bottles, but did not pay the fare when dropped off at an apartment in Asbury Park. The stolen items were later returned to the homeowner. Burke and Foote are charged with burglary, conspiracy to commit burglary, criminal trespass, and theft. They were taken to Monmouth County Correctional Institution and their bail was set at $20,000, with court dates pending.

A tragic accident occurred on the Chesapeake Bay Bridge-Tunnel (CBBT) in Virginia Beach, Virginia, where the driver of a tractor-trailer, identified as 47-year-old Joseph Chen from Greenville, North Carolina, died after falling into the water. The incident took place on Thursday afternoon, with the Medical Examiner’s Office confirming Chen’s death to be accidental, resulting from drowning and hypothermia. The driver was hauling a load of seafood for Evans Transports, based in Washington, North Carolina. A relative of Chen’s in Greenville shared that he was a father and husband and the founder and president of Turn-N-Burn Motorcycle Club.

The tractor-trailer plunged into the water on the southbound side of the CBBT at mile marker 15 around 12:30 p.m. A Navy crew from HSC 2 in Norfolk, which was training in the area, responded to the call for assistance and used an MH-60 Sierra helicopter to rescue the driver. Video footage from Chopper 10 showed a large section of damaged guardrail on the side of the bridge. CBBT officials initially closed both sides of the bridge-tunnel due to the incident but reopened it before 2 p.m.

Bridge officials had issued Level 2 wind restrictions on Thursday, with winds exceeding 47 mph. At the time of the accident, the restriction was at Level 1. Under a Level 2 restriction, tractor-trailers must be hauling a gross payload of 30,000 pounds, in addition to the weight of the rig. Charles Lattimore, a truck driver from Chesapeake, shared that he and about 30 other truck drivers on the Eastern Shore were cleared to cross before learning of the crash on the radio. He was headed to Norfolk but pulled over about a mile north of the bridge-tunnel, worried his own truck would be too light.

Super Doppler 10 Meteorologist Ashley Baylor reported that the water temperature was 45 degrees with wave heights between five and seven feet at the time of the accident. The Virginia Trucking Association issued a statement expressing their condolences to the family, friends, and fellow employees of the victim. This incident is reminiscent of previous accidents on the CBBT, including a similar event in January 2016 where the driver was rescued and survived, and a more fatal accident in May 2014 where a tractor-trailer hit a maintenance truck on the bridge, resulting in the death of the driver. The CBBT continues to operate under Level 2 wind restrictions, with winds exceeding 47 mph.

Taxi drivers across Europe staged large-scale protests against ride-hailing services like Uber, disrupting traffic in major cities and challenging the tech company’s expansion. In London, thousands of black cabs and private hire cars blocked tourist hubs, while in Paris, drivers blocked airports and highways. Madrid saw 5,000 drivers strike, and Berlin’s taxis lined up in columns. The protests highlight the tension between traditional taxi services and the disruptive influence of apps like Uber, which operate without the same stringent regulations. Uber defended its service, stating it provides cheaper and more convenient transportation. Despite the backlash, Uber has expanded rapidly, operating in 128 cities across 37 countries, and recently secured $1.2 billion in new funding, valuing the company at $18.2 billion. However, local authorities in Europe are grappling with how to regulate this new form of transportation. The protests underscore the broader debate over technological innovation versus traditional industries and the need for regulatory adaptation. Uber argues that its services offer choice and lower prices, while taxi drivers claim they are being unfairly undercut. The European Union’s Commissioner for Digital and Telecoms Policy, Neelie Kroes, urged dialogue rather than strikes, acknowledging the challenges posed by such innovations.

A species of Darwin's finch, the medium ground finch (Geospiza fortis), faces a looming threat of extinction due to a parasitic fly, Philornis downsi, which was first documented in the Galápagos in 1997. This fly infests finch nests, with its larvae feeding on nestlings, often leading to their death. A new study, published in the Journal of Applied Ecology, forecasts the potential extinction of the medium ground finch within the next four decades, depending on environmental conditions. Researchers from the University of Utah gathered five years of data from the island of Santa Cruz, documenting the detrimental effects of the fly on the finch's reproductive success. Using this data, they developed mathematical models to predict the finch's long-term survival under different scenarios: "good" years with favorable conditions, "bad" years with unfavorable conditions, and "neutral" years with a mix of both. The models predict that the medium ground finch could face extinction in 43 to 57 years under "bad" conditions, and in 65 to 95 years under "neutral" conditions, with only the "good" scenario showing potential for the species' survival. The study's lead author, Dale Clayton, warns that the problem may extend to other Darwin's finch species, as they share the same fly problem. However, there is hope. Reducing the fly infestation by 40 percent could significantly lower the risk of extinction. Potential solutions include the use of insecticides, the introduction of fly-parasitizing wasps, the breeding of sterile male flies to suppress egg production, and the hand-rearing of at-risk chicks. Additionally, the finches might develop their own defenses through rapid evolutionary adaptation. Clayton notes, "That happens in other animals. The question is: Will these finches have enough time to develop effective defenses before they are driven to extinction by the fly? It’s an arms race."

A New Hampshire farm that posted a video of a newborn Scottish Highland calf named Pitcher Diego is facing backlash from animal rights supporters who oppose the idea of slaughtering the animal. The video, posted on Facebook, has garnered nearly 13 million views and sparked a heated debate about eating meat. In the video, the calf, tied up with a red rope, is seen being warmed by an off-screen hair dryer as he quietly mooes. The calf's birth occurred during a snowstorm, adding to the emotional appeal of the video. However, the positive response has been overshadowed by negative comments from people who believe the calf will be slaughtered or has been separated from its mother. Some individuals have even offered to adopt the calf to save it from its presumed fate. The video's popularity has led to a significant shift in the farm's online ratings, with a large number of one-star reviews from those opposed to the farm's practices. Despite the controversy, the farm's owner, Brian Farmer, maintains that the animals on his farm, including the Scottish Highland cattle and American buffalo, are raised ethically, with free access to pastures and no use of antibiotics or hormones. Farmer explains that the calf has been returned to its mother and is a good candidate for breeding, not for slaughter. He emphasizes that his approach to raising animals is designed to ensure their health and happiness, and the resulting products are healthier for consumption. Farmer is committed to continuing to share updates about his animals to educate the public on ethical farming practices.

An 86-year-old woman in New Cumberland, Pennsylvania, died after tripping and her medical alert necklace got caught on her walker, leading to strangulation. The Cumberland County Coroner's Office reported that Roseann J. DiFrancesco was found dead in her bathroom on February 15, 2016, by a visiting nurse who entered the home after receiving no response. The coroner stated that the lanyard of the medical alert device, lacking a breakaway feature, caught on the walker, causing DiFrancesco's upper torso to be suspended above the floor, cutting off air and blood flow. This incident highlights the potential choking hazard associated with non-breakaway lanyards of personal emergency response systems, which are commonly used by seniors living independently. Between 1998 and 2009, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) documented at least six cases of serious injury or death related to such devices, primarily involving users with mobility limitations. The FDA advises users to consult healthcare providers to determine the most appropriate type of emergency button, whether worn around the neck or wrist, to ensure safety. The agency also recommends considering devices with breakaway features to mitigate the risk of choking.

In the isolated Black Sea village of Kuşköy, nestled among steep hills and tea fields, a unique whistled language called "bird language" or "kuş dili" thrives. For decades, linguists and curious visitors have been intrigued by this distinctive form of communication, which adapts standard Turkish syllables into high-pitched whistles audible from half a mile away. The phrase "Do you have fresh bread?" becomes a sequence of six whistles, each representing a different syllable. This language, though unusual, has been documented in various regions with challenging terrain, such as the Atlas Mountains and the Brazilian Amazon, where it aids in long-distance communication.

Onur Güntürkün, a Turkish-born German biopsychologist, conducted a study to explore how the brain processes this whistled language. He recruited thirty-one volunteers fluent in both spoken and whistled Turkish, who listened to pairs of different syllables played simultaneously through headphones, one in each ear. When presented with spoken Turkish, the participants generally understood the syllable played through the right speaker, indicating that the left hemisphere was processing the sound. However, when presented with whistled Turkish, both hemispheres played significant roles in comprehension, suggesting a more balanced processing of the language.

Güntürkün's findings are significant as they challenge the long-held belief that the left hemisphere dominates language processing. His results imply that the way information is presented can alter the brain's structure and function. He speculates that people with damaged left-hemisphere speech comprehension might be able to learn to understand a whistled dialect, similar to how some people with speech damage can communicate through singing.

However, the whistled language in Kuşköy is at risk of disappearing. In 1964, a stringer for the Times reported that children learned to communicate by whistling before starting school, and both men and women used it for daily communication. Yet, Güntürkün found that few young women had learned the language, and only some young men mastered it as a form of pride, not necessity. The village has organized a whistling contest to promote tourism and cultural preservation, but the language is increasingly being replaced by modern communication methods like texting. Despite this, the whistled language occasionally comes in handy, as villagers can use it to communicate with a secretary who speaks a different language.

The International Monetary Fund chief, Dominique Strauss-Kahn, is being held in special conditions at New York's Rikers Island jail complex following his arrest on charges of sexually assaulting a hotel maid. Strauss-Kahn, 62, is being monitored 24 hours a day and has his own wing of the jail, typically reserved for inmates with contagious diseases. He has been placed on suicide watch as a precautionary measure due to his high-profile status and the sensitive nature of the case. Strauss-Kahn, who is not required to wear a prison uniform, has been given a CPAP machine to address his sleep apnea and is allowed limited recreational time outside his cell. His next court appearance is scheduled for Friday, and his lawyer denies the charges, stating there is no evidence of a forced encounter. The maid's lawyer has said her client is in hiding due to the ordeal. Strauss-Kahn, a prominent political figure, was considered a strong potential challenger to President Nicolas Sarkozy in the upcoming French elections. His arrest has raised concerns about the safety and security measures in place for high-profile inmates at Rikers Island.

A new study, published in the journal Science, suggests that many published psychology results cannot be replicated, raising concerns about the reproducibility of research. The study, part of the Reproducibility Project: Psychology, attempted to recreate 100 studies recently published in major psychology journals and found that only 39 of these studies' results could be replicated. The replication efforts, conducted by a large, collaborative team, included working closely with the original researchers and using their original materials. The replication results showed a significant decline in effect sizes, with 83% of the replicated studies having smaller effects than the original reports, often by about 50%.

The researchers identified three possible reasons for the discrepancies: the original result might have been an artifact, the researchers might have failed to detect a real effect, or both studies might have been accurate but had slightly different methodologies. The study highlights the importance of reproducibility in science, as it is a defining feature that ensures the reliability of scientific findings. However, the findings also suggest that the current emphasis on novelty in scientific research may be problematic, as it can discourage replication efforts. The researchers argue that the incentives in the scientific community should shift to prioritize both innovation and replication to ensure the robustness of scientific knowledge.

The study's corresponding author, Brian Nosek, emphasized that the results present an opportunity for self-correction within the scientific community. He noted that the project demonstrates science's ability to address its own challenges and improve the quality of research. Despite the disappointing replication rates, Nosek and his team view the findings as a call for action rather than a failure. They suggest that the variation in the strength of initial evidence, as measured by the original P values, was a better predictor of replication success than the characteristics of the original and replication teams. This finding underscores the need for more rigorous replication efforts and better guidelines for ensuring the reproducibility of research.

University of Cincinnati President Santa Ono, 53, recently revealed to a fund-raising audience and his 70,000-plus Twitter followers that he twice attempted suicide in his youth, aiming to erase the stigma attached to mental illness and encourage those suffering to seek help. Ono, who attended the Indian Hill fundraiser for a group called 1N5, which focuses on helping teenagers, shared his experiences of depression and recovery, emphasizing that depression is treatable and that sufferers can move on with their lives. He stated, "Someone was there for me to help me work my way through that with medication and also seeing a professional to help me through very dark times in my life. There's light at the end of the tunnel. If you have the proper counseling and support, it's really possible for you to move past that and move back into functioning life."

Ono's revelation came after the tragic death of University of Cincinnati student Brogan Dulle in 2014, which prompted Ono to be instrumental in providing resources for students to access mental health counseling. Following Dulle's death, Ono met with mental health care providers at the university and was instrumental in arranging for University Health Services to provide five free counseling sessions to students. If students needed more help, they could be referred to other resources. Ono's actions have been praised by Dr. Phil Diller, who oversees the University Health Service, for his courage and commitment to addressing mental health issues on campus.

Ono's openness about his struggles with depression and suicide attempts has been met with positive responses on social media, with many users thanking him for his leadership and vulnerability. His story has motivated students to seek help and has encouraged legislators to support more mental health programs. Ono's passion for suicide prevention stems from his research into mental illness during his time at Emory University, where he studied the high suicide rates among Korean students who felt extreme shame in failure. Since then, he has been committed to addressing mental health issues and promoting mental health awareness among students.

Ono's revelation has had a significant impact on the University of Cincinnati community, with his support and advocacy for mental health services being seen as a positive step towards addressing the issue. His message of hope and encouragement has been particularly important in a time when college students are particularly vulnerable to depression and suicide. The University of Cincinnati offers various resources for mental health services, including the University of Cincinnati Counseling & Psychological Services, the National Suicide Prevention Lifeline, and the Crisis Text Line, among others. These resources are available to help students address and resolve personal issues so that they can make the most of their educational opportunities at the university.

Control of Virginia's House of Delegates hung in the balance on Wednesday after a three-judge panel declined to certify the recount of a key House race, leaving the race tied between Republican Del. David Yancey and Democrat Shelly Simonds. The panel's decision came a day after a recount erased a 10-vote lead Yancey held on Election Day. The outcome of the race could determine whether the state's legislature ends 17 years of Republican dominance or sees a 50-50 split between Republicans and Democrats. The judges ruled that a questionable ballot should be counted in favor of Yancey, despite the fact that the ballot contained marks for both candidates. This decision came as a shock to Democrats, who had celebrated their unlikely rise to power in the House of Delegates. The closeness of the race was seen as a rebuke to President Trump and a lesson in the importance of every vote. The state law mandates that a tied race will be decided by a coin toss, with the winner chosen by placing names on slips of paper into two film canisters and drawing the canisters from a glass bowl. The drawing is scheduled for December 27 at 11 a.m. at the elections board in Richmond. However, the process is complicated by the need for both a Democratic and Republican representative of the three-member elections board to be available during the holidays. If the loser of the coin toss is unhappy, they can seek a second recount. The outcome of the race could have significant implications for the balance of power in the House of Delegates, as the state Senate has a 21-to-19 edge in favor of Republicans, with ties broken by the incoming Democratic lieutenant governor. The House Democratic Caucus vowed to fight the judges' decision, calling it "erroneous." Republicans, who had previously conceded the seat and pledged to share power, issued a new statement after the turn of events. The race's outcome remains unclear, as two other recounts are ongoing, potentially reshuffling the political landscape in Richmond. House Democrats were meeting to elect their own leadership, but held off due to the uncertainty. The state's political climate is in flux, with the potential for a power-sharing arrangement between the parties.

Dozens of concertgoers were hospitalized during a show by superstar DJ Avicii in Boston on Wednesday night, according to CNN affiliates. Local media reported between 30 and 80 patients were treated. Massachusetts General Hospital received 13 patients, all under 20, for dehydration, drug, and alcohol-related issues. Avicii, whose real name is Tim Bergling, performed at the TD Garden as part of his True Tour. Dozens of ambulances lined up outside the venue, and frazzled parents searched for their children. Concertgoers attributed the issue to heat and drug use. Boston EMS stated that most patients had heat and alcohol-related symptoms. TD Garden was cited for the incident, implementing increased precautions such as restricted alcohol sales and additional security. Mayor Walsh criticized the venue for allowing intoxicated young people inside. Boston EMS noted that heavy alcohol consumption at such concerts is common. Concert promoter Live Nation stated that most patients were stopped before entering the venue. Avicii tweeted his concern for everyone's safety, hoping all were okay. Boston EMS reported that most patients were between 16 and 25 years old, and no injuries were serious. TD Garden has been cited multiple times in the past few years for various issues, which officials said is not unusual for an entertainment venue.

Burger King has introduced a new menu item called the Whopperito, which takes the classic Whopper and wraps its contents in a tortilla. The Whopper-burrito hybrid features flame-grilled beef, American cheese, tomatoes, lettuce, mayo, ketchup, pickles, and white onions, all stuffed into a tortilla. This new offering is currently being tested at several Burger King locations in Pennsylvania, with Grub Grade first spotting the sign advertising the Whopperito.

The Whopperito concept is a natural evolution of Burger King's recent Whopper Dog, which placed the Whopper's ingredients on a hot dog instead of a bun. This new creation aims to provide a more calorie-conscious option for customers while still delivering the familiar Whopper flavor. However, the reaction from social media users has been largely negative, with many expressing disappointment or outright disgust at the idea.

The Whopperito has sparked a range of reactions on Twitter, with some users expressing their distaste, while others humorously suggested that it might be a healthier alternative to the traditional Whopper. One user even joked that they would eat the Whopperito, while another described it as a "fast food abomination." The idea of combining a burger with a tortilla is not entirely new; some Twitter users recalled a previous, unofficial version where customers would create a Whopperito by combining a Burger King Whopper with a Taco Bell burrito.

Despite the mixed reviews, Burger King seems to be moving forward with the Whopperito, as the item is currently available at a Burger King in Hermitage, Pennsylvania. The company has not yet announced whether the Whopperito will be rolled out to other locations or if it is just a temporary test. The Whopperito represents Burger King's ongoing efforts to innovate and adapt to changing consumer preferences, particularly those seeking healthier options without sacrificing the taste and convenience of fast food.

China has called on the United States to bar a Taiwanese delegation from attending Donald Trump's inauguration, citing concerns that the incoming president might seek to redefine relations between Beijing, Taipei, and Washington. The Taiwanese delegation, led by former Premier Yu Shyi-kun, includes a national security adviser and some lawmakers, and plans to meet with U.S. politicians, academics, and representatives of the overseas Chinese community. China considers Taiwan a breakaway province and opposes any official contact with the island. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Hua Chunying urged the U.S. to prevent the Taiwanese delegation from attending the inauguration and avoid any official exchanges with Taiwan. This comes after Trump broke with decades of precedent by taking a congratulatory telephone call from Taiwanese President Tsai Ing-wen and questioning the "one China" policy. The U.S. has no formal relations with Taiwan but maintains robust informal ties and sells arms to the island. Tensions across the Taiwan Strait have risen since Tsai's election, with Beijing cutting off contacts and working to deepen Taiwan's diplomatic isolation.

Palau, a small island nation in the Pacific known for its pristine beaches and rich marine life, is considering a new tourism strategy to shift from mass tourism to a more exclusive, high-end market. President Tommy Remengesau Jr. has proposed a law that would limit new hotel developments to only five-star establishments, aiming to attract wealthier visitors who will likely spend more. This move is part of a broader effort to preserve the natural beauty and environment of the islands, which have faced issues such as overcrowding and damage to coral reefs due to increased tourism. The president envisions a scenario where high-end investors would be incentivized through tax breaks and other benefits, provided they handle their own infrastructure needs, such as building roads and water treatment systems. This strategy is expected to generate more revenue and align with Palau’s goal of sustainable development. While Palau currently has a handful of five-star resorts, the new law could significantly alter the tourism landscape, potentially reducing the number of visitors but increasing the overall economic impact. The government hopes this approach will not only boost the economy but also respect the local culture and natural resources.

The Supreme Court on Monday maintained the stringent reach of a federal law prohibiting individuals with misdemeanor domestic violence convictions from owning firearms. In a 6-2 decision, the justices dismissed arguments from two Maine men who argued their convictions for misdemeanor domestic violence, which stemmed from incidents of hitting their partners, should not bar them from gun ownership. The court's ruling reinforces the interpretation that the law applies broadly, covering not only intentional acts of abuse but also reckless behavior. Advocates for victims of domestic abuse argue that the law should encompass such reckless behavior, while gun rights groups contend that the men should not forfeit their constitutional right to bear arms due to misdemeanor convictions. The case, which drew attention from various interest groups, underscores the ongoing debate over the scope and enforcement of gun control measures.

Nigeria's military has arrested Babuji Ya'ari, a suspected Boko Haram intelligence cell leader linked to the abduction of more than 200 schoolgirls in April, according to a military statement. Ya'ari, described as a businessman who actively participated in the abduction of the girls and the killing of a traditional leader, had been using his role in a civilian vigilante group to cover his work for the militants. The military also arrested women from the intelligence cell. Meanwhile, suspected Boko Haram extremists have attacked churches and killed at least 30 people in Kwada village, just miles from Chibok, where the girls were kidnapped. The extremists also attacked villages in the area, including Kautikari, and burned down several church buildings. The government claims to know the whereabouts of the girls but fears a military rescue could lead to their deaths. Boko Haram has demanded the release of imprisoned militants in exchange for the girls. The group has increased its activities, including bombings in several northern towns and the capital, Abuja, in central Nigeria, targeting a shopping mall that killed 24 people. The Nigerian government faces criticism for its response to the abductions and failure to swiftly rescue the girls. The U.S. is flying drones to help locate the girls, while other nations have sent experts to assist. The ongoing conflict has resulted in more than 2,000 deaths this year, with Boko Haram expanding its operations to several northern states.

Russia's track and field athletes are banned from the 2016 Rio Olympics due to a state-sponsored doping scandal, a decision without precedent in Olympic history. The International Association of Athletics Federations (IAAF) announced the ban in a unanimous vote, citing Russia's failure to restore global confidence in the integrity of its athletes. The ban affects 18 medals won by Russia in the last Summer Olympics, including eight golds. Individual athletes can still compete as neutrals if they can convincingly show they have been subject to effective anti-doping systems and have not been tainted by the Russian system. However, the IAAF task force monitoring the verification process found that a deep-seated culture of tolerance for doping remains unchanged. The task force also highlighted significant obstacles in testing athletes in Russia, with the Russian Anti-Doping Agency 18-24 months away from compliance with the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) code. Pole vaulter Yelena Isinbayeva plans to file a discrimination case in the court for human rights, while the Russian Ministry of Sport appeals to the International Olympic Committee, claiming it has met the IAAF's criteria and that clean athletes' dreams are being destroyed. The decision is expected to face legal challenges, with the crack in the door for individual athletes being narrow. The culture of doping in Russia is deeply entrenched, with athletes and officials openly dismissing the independent commission report and obstructing testing efforts. The IAAF's decisive action has drawn praise from athletes and anti-doping officials, marking a significant step in the fight against doping. However, the decision also raises questions about the effectiveness of sport organizations in responding to widespread doping scandals.

The United States and its allies are reportedly preparing to launch a military strike against Syria, a move that has sparked intense debate and criticism. The Obama administration is reportedly considering limited cruise-missile or bomber strikes against regime targets, possibly for three days, as a response to alleged chemical weapons attacks in Damascus. Critics argue that such a move could escalate the conflict, potentially drawing in Hezbollah and other regional actors, and could lead to civilian casualties. Some also warn that a limited strike might not deter Assad from using chemical weapons again, given the potential for regime change or other non-military options.

The decision to bypass Congress and the United Nations, as well as the lack of clear evidence, has raised questions about the administration’s credibility and the potential consequences of a unilateral action. Some, like John McCain, have criticized the administration for not acting forcefully enough in the past, while others, like Bill Clinton, have called for a more robust response. The administration’s reluctance to engage Congress and the War Powers Act has also been highlighted, with some arguing that a formal authorization process could help clarify the administration’s objectives and ensure a more deliberative approach.

The debate over Syria extends beyond the immediate military action. Critics argue that a limited strike would be ineffective and could exacerbate the conflict, while supporters believe that such a move is necessary to uphold international norms against the use of chemical weapons. The potential for a broader regional conflict, involving Iran and other powers, adds another layer of complexity to the situation.

The article also questions the credibility of the evidence presented by the administration, suggesting that the alleged chemical weapons attacks may have been carried out by rebel groups. It highlights the lack of reliable evidence and the potential for intelligence to be manipulated or misinterpreted. The article argues that a more effective approach would be to support a United Nations investigation and to work towards a political settlement that addresses the root causes of the conflict.

The decision to strike or not to strike Syria is not just a military decision but also a political and diplomatic one. The potential for a broader regional conflict, the credibility of the evidence, and the effectiveness of a limited military strike are all factors that need to be carefully considered. The article concludes that a more nuanced and comprehensive approach, involving diplomacy and a focus on human rights, would be more effective in addressing the crisis in Syria.

A Christmas carol service in Sri Lanka mistakenly printed the lyrics to Tupac Shakur's "Hail Mary" instead of the traditional Hail Mary prayer, causing shock among attendees. The incident occurred during the Joy to the World 2016 service, one of the country's largest carol services. Attendee Andrew Choksy recognized the song and shared pictures of the booklet on social media, which quickly went viral. The printed lyrics, which include lines like "Makaveli in this … Killuminati, all through your body. The blows like a twelve-gauge shotty," are from Tupac's 1997 track, not the Christian prayer. The service organizers did not provide any explanation for the mistake, and many attendees were initially taken aback but later took it in good humor. The incident highlights the cultural impact of Tupac's work, even in contexts far removed from his original audience.

On December 22, 2017, a 22-year-old customer in Madison, Wisconsin, found himself in a shocking situation at Ruby's Salon when he sought a simple haircut, only to have his head and ear subjected to a bizarre and violent incident. According to the Madison Police Department, the customer, who was not named, went to the salon to get a No. 2 on the sides and an inch taken off the top with scissors. However, the experience took a dark turn when the barber, 46-year-old Khaled A. Shabani, allegedly began complaining about the customer fidgeting and moving his head, leading to a dispute. Shabani then allegedly grabbed a "zero" clipper and snipped the customer's ear, before shaving a line down the middle of his head. The victim, visibly bloodied, got up and left the salon, with Shabani allegedly shouting, "You want a zero right?" The customer called the police upon returning home, and Shabani was subsequently arrested on suspicion of mayhem and disorderly conduct while armed. Shabani pleaded not guilty to the disorderly conduct charge, which is a violation of a county ordinance, not a criminal charge. The incident left the victim with a striking resemblance to Larry from the Three Stooges, as the police spokesman Joel Despain described. The Madison Police Department clarified that while it is not a crime to give someone a bad haircut, intentionally snipping someone's ear with scissors is a different matter entirely.

Rockies shortstop Trevor Story made history in Colorado's home opener against the San Diego Padres by homering for the fifth and sixth times in his first four games. According to Elias Sports Bureau, Story is the first player in 100 years to achieve this feat, and the fifth player since 1900 to hit a home run in each of his team's first four games in a season. Story, 23, has already hit six home runs and driven in 11 runs in his first 19 major-league at-bats, showcasing a powerful swing that has impressed his teammates and opponents alike. "It's legendary what he's doing," Rockies slugger Carlos Gonzalez said. "He's fearless. He's playing like a Hall of Famer right now." Story's home run surge continued on Friday, with two more dingers off San Diego's Colin Rea and Ryan Buchter. Despite the Rockies' 13-6 loss, Story's performance was a bright spot, and his manager, Walt Weiss, called him "one of the few bright spots today." Even the Padres acknowledged his talent, with outfielder Matt Kemp praising his swing. Rockies owner Dick Monfort, however, expressed concern about the domestic abuse incident that led to Reyes' suspension, stating, "If he did something wrong, he should pay for it." Story's remarkable start has put him on pace for 243 home runs in 2016, a feat that has already drawn comparisons to the Hall of Fame. His success at Coors Field, where the fences have been raised, has made his home runs even more impressive.

Following Donald Trump's convincing Republican primary win in South Carolina, pundits and political rivals are beginning to shift their view on the billionaire's candidacy from unlikely outsider aberration to a very real GOP challenger for the White House. Fittingly, as some begin nervously considering how the U.S. might elect a reality TV star as president, a brilliant parody of Trump's rise has appeared, deftly using the lore of Game of Thrones as the backdrop. Titled "Winter is Trumping," the clever clip by Huw Parkinson uses real Trump footage and speech audio and merges it almost seamlessly with key Game of Thrones scenes. We get to see Trump negotiating with Littlefinger, facing down the queen of dragons, Daenerys Targaryen, and even preparing for battle alongside Tyrion Lannister. And yes, these people thought of everything, we even see Trump defending against invaders from atop The Wall. Sure, comparing Trump to the characters in a world in which the good guys often get decapitated and no one's innocence lasts for long is a bit harsh. But as this video shows, it's hard to deny just how well the would-be president might fit into the ruthless world of The Seven Kingdoms. The clip offers a satirical glimpse into a future where the unpredictable and controversial businessman could indeed become the leader of the free world, navigating treacherous alliances and deadly conflicts much like his fictional counterparts. As the political landscape continues to evolve, this parody serves as a reminder that the path to the White House may be more complex and unpredictable than ever before.

A large Libyan military convoy has entered Niger, raising speculation that ousted leader Moammar Gadhafi or one of his sons might be among the desert-bound troops. The convoy, consisting of several dozen vehicles, arrived in Agadez from Arlit and headed towards Niamey, the capital. Gadhafi's spokesman, Moussa Ibrahim, declared that the dictator is "in excellent health, planning and organizing for the defense of Libya," and remains in the country. Meanwhile, tribal elders in Gadhafi strongholds are attempting to persuade regime loyalists to surrender, aiming to avoid bloodshed. In Bani Walid, rebel negotiator Abdullah Kanshil reported that tribal elders are seeking assurances from the rebels before encouraging Gadhafi loyalists to lay down their arms. The convoy's arrival in Niger coincides with ongoing negotiations and a push by rebels to secure the surrender of Gadhafi loyalists in several towns, including Bani Walid. NATO has not confirmed any information about the convoy, which is believed to be a protection team rather than a large number of soldiers. The situation in Libya remains tense as the country transitions to a new government.

Jonathan Trappe, a balloonist aiming to cross the Atlantic Ocean using only helium-filled balloons, was forced to land in a remote area of Newfoundland's west coast after his journey was cut short. Trappe, who left Caribou, Maine, near the New Brunswick border, in a small boat suspended below more than 300 balloons, expressed relief at being rescued by a CBC-chartered helicopter on Friday afternoon. "I've never been so glad to see the media," he told CBC News videojournalist Lindsay Bird. Trappe explained that he was burning through ballast too quickly to make it across the Atlantic and had to choose between landing in the isolated woods on Thursday night or ditching over the ocean on Friday. He landed in a remote area south of the small Bay of Islands community of Lark Harbour, where much of the surrounding area is impassable, with no roads leading to the location. Residents had been trying to reach him on ATVs without success. Trappe, known for his adventurous use of cluster balloons, including flying in a house as depicted in the Disney-Pixar animated film Up, emphasized that the journey was about more than reaching a specific destination. "We set out on this expedition for the adventure, and we got the adventure," he said. "The destination was always unknown, and it's pretty grand where we've come in to. It's not the destination I set out for, but it's kind of the way with real adventure — adventure isn't what you planned on, it's what you find, and that's what we have today." Despite not achieving his goal of crossing the Atlantic, Trappe reflected on the unexpected beauty of his landing site, noting, "Hmm, this doesn't look like France."

Chicago police officer Jason Van Dyke, charged with murder after shooting 17-year-old Laquan McDonald 16 times in 2014, has been hired by the Fraternal Order of Police (FOP) as a janitor and "jack-of-all-trades," union president Dean Angelo confirmed. Van Dyke, who is currently suspended without pay and on unpaid status, now makes $12 an hour at the FOP hall in the West Loop. Angelo stated that the decision to hire Van Dyke was made "weeks ago" to assist the officer and his family, citing financial difficulties due to his notoriety and the closure of his wife's business following threats. The union president emphasized that such arrangements are not unique, noting that the FOP has hired over 100 officers in similar situations. Critics, including Father Michael Pfleger, condemned the move, calling it a "disgrace" and demanding Van Dyke's immediate firing. Demonstrations were planned outside the FOP office, with activists arguing that the union's actions undermine public trust in law enforcement. Van Dyke has pleaded not guilty and faces first-degree murder charges, with his case drawing national attention and sparking ongoing debates about police accountability and the treatment of officers involved in controversial incidents.

Oliver Stone’s "The Putin Interviews" offers a four-part series of conversations between the American filmmaker and Russian President Vladimir Putin, providing a unique insight into the Russian leader’s perspective on various geopolitical issues. The series, created from over 30 hours of footage spanning 12 different interviews, presents a dynamic that often feels like a game of chess, with Stone and Putin engaging in a subtle dance of mutual respect and strategic maneuvering. Stone, known for his controversial and often revisionist take on historical events, approaches the interviews with a mix of skepticism and admiration, while Putin, a master of self-presentation, is keen to present himself as a competent and strategic leader.

The interviews delve into a range of topics, including the history of American dominance in the post-Vietnam era, the role of NATO, and the U.S. strategy in the Middle East. Stone and Putin often find common ground, agreeing on issues such as American overreach and the need for a more balanced approach in international relations. However, Stone’s documentary is criticized for its one-sided approach, as it aids and abets Putin’s narrative while failing to challenge his more dubious claims and omissions.

One of the most striking aspects of the series is its use of multiple camera angles and hand-held shots, creating a sense of intimacy and immediacy that draws the viewer into the room with Putin. This technique, combined with Stone’s often deferential questioning, allows Putin to present himself as a multifaceted figure, with a wide-ranging skill set that has enabled him to navigate the complexities of international politics.

However, the documentary is also seen as problematic for its failure to critically engage with some of Putin’s more controversial actions and policies. For instance, Stone’s presentation of Putin’s rise to power and his handling of the Chechen Wars is sanitized and incomplete, omitting crucial details about the role of powerful anti-communist forces and the impact of these conflicts on Russian society. Additionally, the series avoids discussing Putin’s involvement in the 2016 U.S. election, focusing instead on broader themes of American interference in Russian affairs.

Critics argue that Stone’s approach is misguided and even harmful, as it provides a platform for Putin to spin his narrative without meaningful challenge. The documentary’s reliance on Putin’s own account, coupled with its avoidance of critical perspectives, raises questions about its true value as a tool for understanding the complex dynamics of Russian-U.S. relations.

Overall, "The Putin Interviews" is a complex and often controversial piece of work, offering a unique window into the mind of a powerful world leader while also raising important questions about the nature of documentary filmmaking and the responsibility of the filmmaker to present a balanced and accurate account of the subjects they interview.

A species of snake that had been "lost" for nearly 80 years has been rediscovered on a remote Mexican island, a discovery that sheds light on the fragility of island ecosystems and the importance of historical data and museum collections in solving modern biodiversity mysteries. The Clarion nightsnake, first spotted by American naturalist William Beebe in 1936, was found again on one of the Revillagigedo Islands, more than 400 miles off Mexico's Pacific coast. Subsequent visits failed to find more nightsnakes, and the species was largely struck from taxonomic registries due to a presumed labeling error. However, Daniel Mulcahy, a researcher from the National Museum of Natural History in Washington, and Juan Martinez Gomez, an expert on the Revillagigedo Islands, set out to find it. Martinez Gomez, using Beebe's original field notes as a guide, noted that the islands change significantly from season to season, so they timed the expedition last May to replicate Beebe's steps. Graduate student Juan Alberto Cervantes was the first to spot one of the snakes, which had a distinctive pattern of spots and blended in with the island's rock formations, largely active at night. DNA analysis confirmed that the Clarion nightsnake was genetically distinct from other snakes found in mainland Mexico and is now recognized as a full species. The re-discovery of the Clarion nightsnake highlights the importance of preserving historical data and museum collections, as it was only through these resources that the species could be rediscovered. The National Museum of Natural History stated that the rediscovery is an incredible story of how scientists rely on historical data and museum collections to solve modern-day mysteries about biodiversity. The Clarion nightsnake is now recognized as a full species, and efforts will continue to monitor its role in the delicate Clarion Island ecosystem.

A New Jersey driver who hit a fire hydrant and a mailbox on Edwards Road fled the scene, leaving behind a trail of water that led police to his vehicle and the damaged hydrant in a nearby trash bin. The 27-year-old, Domingo Moreno, was arrested at a nearby diner and faces multiple charges including criminal mischief, tampering with evidence, hindering apprehension, failure to report an accident, unlicensed driving, and reckless driving. Moreno, of Parsippany, was remanded to the Morris County Correctional Facility pending a court appearance. Police are still investigating the cause and other details of the crash.

An Ohio couple married for 69 years died eight hours apart, ending a lifelong partnership. Gene Warrington, 88, and his wife Pat, 86, passed away on December 27 in Findlay, with their son Phil noting their lifelong togetherness. In hospice care, Gene visited Pat's room and held her hand before recognizing her critical condition. He then willed himself to die, passing away eight hours before Pat. The couple, who met in junior high and secretly wed before Gene's World War II service, raised three children and had seven grandchildren and 12 great-grandchildren. Throughout their long marriage, they were inseparable, even in their final hours.

Georgia Senator Saxby Chambliss, facing potential primary challenges, announced his retirement in 2014. Chambliss cited frustration with the White House and Congress, particularly the debt-ceiling and fiscal-cliff issues. His decision leaves the seat open, with several Republicans interested, including former presidential candidate Herman Cain, who would likely pose the greatest threat. Democrats are also eyeing the opportunity, with Atlanta Mayor Kasim Reed and Rep. John Barrow as potential candidates. Polls show Chambliss is vulnerable to primary challengers, with conservative voters more likely to want a replacement. The race could become a top priority for Democrats, potentially leading to a Democratic pickup. The outcome hinges on who emerges from the crowded Republican primary field.

Reality TV star Mitchell Guist, a key figure in The History Channel's "Swamp People" series, tragically died while filming in Louisiana's Atchafalaya Swamp. The incident occurred around 9 a.m. in St. Martin Parish along the Belle River, where Guist, a Cajun alligator hunter, suffered a fall in the boat and experienced seizures. Witnesses called for help, but efforts to revive him were unsuccessful. The History Channel confirmed his passing, expressing deep sadness and respect for the Guist family's privacy. The channel stated that all planned episodes of "Swamp People" would continue as scheduled, with plans to honor Guist's memory. Fans of the show, who appreciated the genuine and hospitable nature of the cast, expressed their condolences and admiration for Guist's character. The incident highlights the dangers and risks involved in reality TV productions, especially those set in challenging environments.

Tunisian Prime Minister Mohammed Ghannouchi resigned on Sunday, fulfilling a key demand of protesters. Ghannouchi, seen as too closely linked to the old regime, defended his decision, stating it would serve the revolution and Tunisia's future. He was replaced by 84-year-old Beji Caid-Essebsi, a former government minister. The resignation came as violent protests continued, with at least five deaths since Friday. Ghannouchi warned of unspecified forces trying to undermine the democratic transition. The change aims to quell unrest and restore order, but protesters remain skeptical. Meanwhile, authorities imposed a temporary ban on traffic in central Tunis to maintain calm.

In the aftermath of the Boston Marathon bombings, the region's Muslim community has distanced itself from the suspects, raising questions about their Islamic burial. The Boston area's Muslim leaders have refused to conduct funerals for the suspects, citing their alleged crimes. Imam Talal Eid of the Islamic Institute of Boston stated that Tamerlan Tsarnaev, the older brother, should not be buried as a Muslim due to his actions. Similarly, the Islamic Society of Boston Cultural Center in Cambridge has not been contacted about a funeral. The next-of-kin, Tamerlan's wife Katherine Russell, has not responded to inquiries about a funeral. Meanwhile, Tamerlan's father Anzor Tsarnaev, who claims his sons were framed, has expressed his intention to travel to the U.S. from Russia to attend a funeral but has not specified if it includes his son. Islamic tradition mandates a prompt burial, preferably before sunset, with a ritual washing and shrouding. Boston has at least two facilities for Islamic burials. The next step in the process is the release of Tamerlan Tsarnaev's body for forensic examination. The situation is unprecedented, with few precedents in U.S. history for such a case. The community grapples with the ethical dilemma of whether to accept the brothers as Muslims despite the allegations.

Oklahoma State Senator Ralph Shortey, a conservative who once aspired to be a missionary, faces serious charges of offering to pay a 17-year-old boy for sex, according to police reports. Shortey, 35, was arrested last Thursday in a hotel room in Moore, Oklahoma, with the teenager, who was not charged due to his age. The case has sparked calls for Shortey to resign from his Senate seat. The evidence against Shortey includes a graphic online conversation where he discussed sex and marijuana with the teenager, using the online name "Jamie Tilley," according to a court affidavit. Shortey, who has been a senator since 2010, was stripped of most of his privileges at the Capitol, including his office and parking space, by the state Senate. The charges against him include engaging in child prostitution, engaging in prostitution within 1,000 feet of a church, and transporting a minor for prostitution, with a maximum sentence of 25 years in prison if convicted. The incident occurred on March 9, when police were called to a Super 8 hotel after the teenager’s girlfriend reported seeing him being picked up by a white Jeep Cherokee. The teenager, who has a history of soliciting himself on Craigslist and drug abuse, told police he needed money for spring break. Shortey, who studied to do mission work in Uganda but later entered politics, has been a vocal advocate for law-and-order issues. His wife is his high school sweetheart, and they have three children. The case has drawn strong condemnation from Governor Mary Fallin and Lieutenant Governor Todd Lamb, who called for Shortey to step down. The senator, who had initially refused to open the hotel room door, later admitted to police that he and the teenager were inside.

Authorities are on high alert after a man named Jesus Henry Kong, also known as Jessie Eloah Calix and Jesus Matute, posted threatening messages on Twitter, warning of plans to shoot students and place pipe bombs in Orange County schools. The FBI, Orlando Police Department, and Orange County Sheriff's Office are investigating the threats, though they do not believe them to be credible. Kong, a 23-year-old transient with a history of law enforcement encounters, has lived in Florida, California, Virginia, and Maryland. The threats, which began on July 24, targeted William R. Boone High School, Edgewater High School, Colonial High School, Colonial Ninth Grade Center, and Liberty Middle School. The posts included explicit encouragement to shoot students and detailed plans to place bombs in two schools. Orange County Public Schools alerted parents and students, and many students stayed home, with 379 students absent at Liberty Middle School, 357 at Boone High School, and 174 at Edgewater High School. The FBI and local law enforcement are actively searching for Kong, who is described as a transient with a history of law enforcement interactions.

The relationship between income and life expectancy in the United States is stark, with higher incomes associated with greater longevity, according to new research from Stanford University. Analyzing over one billion tax and Social Security records from 1999 to 2014, the study reveals that the gap in life expectancy between the richest 1% and the poorest 1% of the population is 14.6 years for men and 10.1 years for women. This disparity has been increasing over time, with life expectancy for the wealthiest 5% of men rising by 2.3 years and for the wealthiest 5% of women by nearly 3 years. However, the study also highlights significant geographic variations in life expectancy, with poor individuals living longer in prosperous urban areas such as San Francisco and New York City compared to more rural and industrial Midwest regions. Factors contributing to these differences include health behaviors, such as smoking rates, and local area characteristics like the presence of college graduates, government expenditures, and public health policies. For instance, San Francisco's ban on smoking in public places and its strong social services for the poor contribute to a 3-year longer life expectancy for the poor compared to those in Detroit. The research underscores the importance of local policies and community support in mitigating health disparities, suggesting that targeted interventions could help reduce the income gap in life expectancy.

The British election results have delivered a resounding victory for Prime Minister David Cameron and his Conservative Party, securing a majority government and ending weeks of political uncertainty. Cameron's unexpected success, with his party winning at least 324 of the 650 seats in the House of Commons, has sent shockwaves through the political landscape, with significant implications for the UK and its global standing. The exit poll, which predicted a Conservative majority, was accurate, with Labour trailing far behind with 229 seats, a sharp decline from their 258 seats in 2010. The Scottish National Party (SNP) emerged as the third-largest party, capturing almost all of Scotland's 59 seats, marking a historic shift and raising concerns about the future of the United Kingdom. The SNP's surge, coupled with Labour's losses, has left the Labour Party in a precarious position, with leader Ed Miliband expected to step down, and the party facing a significant overhaul. The Liberal Democrats, once a key coalition partner, suffered a crushing defeat, with their leader Nick Clegg likely to resign, and the party losing most of its seats. The UK Independence Party (UKIP), despite gaining support, failed to win any seats, leaving the party's future uncertain. The election results have also highlighted the growing divide between England and Scotland, with the SNP's success in Scotland likely to intensify calls for Scottish independence. This could potentially lead to a dis-united Kingdom, with Scotland seeking to join the European Union, further complicating the UK's relationship with the bloc. The outcome of the election also brings into focus the looming Brexit referendum, with Cameron promising a vote on Britain's membership in the EU. This decision, which could significantly impact the UK's economy and global influence, is now more pressing than ever. The Conservative Party's victory, while providing political stability, also means that Cameron will face significant challenges, including dealing with the SNP and managing the UK's relationship with the EU. The election results have not only reshaped British politics but have also set the stage for a potentially tumultuous period ahead, with the country facing major decisions on its future.

The Australian radio hosts responsible for a prank call to the hospital treating the Duchess of Cambridge broke their silence after the apparent suicide of nurse Jacintha Saldanha. Mel Greig and Michael Christian, from Sydney station 2Day FM, expressed deep regret and offered condolences to Saldanha's family. Greig described the call as the "worst phone call I've ever had in my life," while Christian said they were "shattered, gutted, heartbroken." The prank, where the DJs posed as Queen Elizabeth II and Prince Charles, led to Saldanha transferring the call to a colleague, who then provided information about the Duchess's condition. Saldanha was found dead three days later, and her family has demanded answers from the radio station and the hospital. 2Day FM has suspended all prank calls, ended the show the DJs presented, and halted advertising. The incident has sparked calls for stricter media regulation, and the Australian Communications and Media Authority is considering an investigation. The hospital chairman criticized the prank as "truly appalling" and "extremely foolish," stating it humiliated dedicated nurses. The case has also drawn attention to Saldanha's own struggles with depression, as her family revealed she had attempted suicide twice in the past year.

In a stark warning, former White House speechwriter Jon Favreau argues that House Republicans are acting like "anarchists" and "terrorists" by threatening an economic shutdown to force their agenda, drawing parallels to the 2011 debt ceiling crisis. Favreau recounts how the 2011 standoff nearly led to a catastrophic default, causing financial turmoil and economic damage. He contends that the current situation is even more perilous given the weak economy, and that a debt default would be far more devastating than a government shutdown. Favreau calls for the White House to use the term "economic shutdown" more frequently to highlight the severity of the situation. He criticizes Republicans for equating a debt ceiling vote with increased spending, and suggests that they need to find a more apt description for their tactics. Favreau argues that the president should not negotiate on this issue, as it would be a dangerous precedent. He concludes that the current political system is irrational, with a significant number of Republicans believing they can force concessions through threats of shutdowns or defaults, and that this could lead to a constitutional crisis.

Former International Monetary Fund chief Dominique Strauss-Kahn and the Guinean maid who accused him of sexual assault have reached a settlement, likely ending their legal dispute, reports The Associated Press. The agreement, reached within recent days, was facilitated by Bronx Supreme Court Justice Douglas McKeon, who also helped resolve a separate lawsuit filed by the maid against the New York Post. Details of the settlement, likely involving a confidentiality agreement, remain undisclosed. Strauss-Kahn's lawyers argue that the encounter was consensual, while the maid maintains it was a brutal attack. The case, which forced Strauss-Kahn's resignation and opened a floodgate of accusations, was dropped by prosecutors in August 2011 due to concerns about the maid's credibility. Strauss-Kahn now faces additional charges in France related to a suspected prostitution ring. The settlement aims to bring closure to a high-profile legal saga that tarnished his reputation and political prospects.

A British Royal Marine killed by a Taliban bomb in Afghanistan left behind a generous legacy, including a $400,000 insurance policy that will send 32 of his friends on a Las Vegas vacation. David Hart, 23, who was described as "the perfect Marine," took out the policy before his deployment and instructed that $150,000 of it should go toward a holiday for his friends and their girlfriends, as he always looked forward to "lad's holidays." Hart's friends, including Andy Hare, praised his generosity, saying, "He said, 'Go and have a good time and spend all this money.' All the lads said, 'What a guy.'" Hart's parents, Chris and Dilys, were supportive of their son's friends, who have been visiting them since his death. Additionally, $80,000 of the insurance money will go to a charity for injured Marines, and $160,000 will be given to Hart's family. Hart's sister, Sarah, expressed pride in her brother's career and his character. His commanding officer, Lt Col Paul James, described Hart as "a perfect commando," noting his courage and selflessness. In memory of Hart, his family and friends plan to embark on a 170-mile charity bike ride to raise funds for the Royal Marines Charitable Trust Fund.

Thailand's Prime Minister Abhisit Vejjajiva declared a state of emergency Wednesday, hours after anti-government demonstrators stormed the parliament, intensifying the political crisis. The measure, effective in Bangkok and nearby provinces, bans gatherings of more than five persons deemed to instigate an emergency situation, publishing threatening information, and staying in certain areas. Authorities can summon, arrest, and detain people, and access communications. The emergency was declared a few hours after protesters stormed the parliament and regrouped at main gathering places. The cabinet extended the Internal Security Act for two weeks to maintain order. The unrest, involving supporters of former Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, who was ousted in 2006, has paralyzed parts of Bangkok and could affect tourism by about 10 percent. The state of emergency and the ongoing protests have intruded on a summit of Southeast Asian leaders, with concerns about potential violence. The Thai upheaval overshadowed other regional issues, including Myanmar's upcoming elections, as leaders focused on the domestic political situation.

In December 2004, a devastating tsunami in Aceh, Indonesia, claimed the lives of nearly 170,000 people and left 130,000 missing. Wati, an 8-year-old girl, was believed to have been swept away by the waves. For nearly seven years, her parents thought she had perished. However, on Wednesday, Wati returned home, reportedly found by an acquaintance in a coffee shop where she had been sitting silently, unrecognized. Her grandfather, Ibrahim, recognized her by a mole and a scar. The girl, now 15, was unable to recall her relatives' names except for Ibrahim. This miraculous reunion occurred nearly seven years to the day after the tsunami that devastated the coastlines of more than 10 countries.

The Oklahoma Department of Corrections is in a dispute with the city of McAlester over ownership of the state’s electric chair, which may be reactivated if challenges to Oklahoma’s lethal injection procedures are upheld. The electric chair, nicknamed Old Sparky, was last used in 1966 and has been in storage since then. Oklahoma law permits the use of the electric chair or a firing squad only if lethal injection is declared unconstitutional, a situation that has arisen following the botched execution of Clayton Lockett in April 2014. Lockett, who died after writhing and groaning during the execution, suffered what corrections director Robert Patton described as a massive heart attack, 43 minutes after the procedure began. This incident led to a halt in all executions in the United States.

The McAlester city council and its mayor, Steve Harrison, argue that the electric chair should be on public display as a historical artifact. Harrison stated, “I would like to get it displayed somewhere since it is a historical artefact. I don’t think it does anybody any good for it to sit in storage somewhere.” The chair, first used in 1915, was employed in 82 executions before its retirement. McAlester, a town of about 18,000 people that houses the state’s death chamber, had the electric chair in a museum until the corrections department reclaimed it. Harrison expressed uncertainty about the legal ownership of the chair and suggested that if the electric chair were to be used again, the state would likely acquire a new one due to the chair’s age and lack of recent use.

The dispute over the electric chair predates the current execution crisis. Corrections spokesman Jerry Massie stated that the department has not had much discussion about the chair’s ownership, but acknowledged that it is possible the chair could be rewired and used again if lethal injection procedures are declared unconstitutional. However, Massie emphasized, “There is not much possibility of that, unless lethal injection is declared unconstitutional.” As states across the country grapple with a European-led boycott of lethal injection drugs, some have proposed returning to older methods such as the electric chair and the firing squad. Tennessee’s governor recently approved the use of the electric chair for executions where drugs cannot be acquired, and states like Florida, Alabama, and Virginia have long listed electrocution as an optional execution method. The last US inmate to die by electrocution was Robert Gleason, who chose this method over lethal injection and was executed in Virginia on January 16, 2013.

Two Nebraska children, 14-year-old Mackenzie and 12-year-old Ethan Behrens, texted 911 to alert police that their drunken father, 44-year-old Jason Behrens, was driving them on a family vacation. The kids described multiple near-misses and swerves, with one incident almost resulting in a head-on collision. They urged their father to pull over at a Burger King, where officers caught up to the family. Jason Behrens was arrested for drunk driving and was found to have nearly three times the legal limit of 0.08%. The children, who had previously experienced similar incidents, expressed relief and gratitude to the officers who intervened. They stated that it was the hardest decision they had ever made but that they felt compelled to act to ensure their safety. Their mother, Amy Brooks, expressed both anger and relief, noting that the children were now in her care. The incident highlights the effectiveness of the Text 911 program in Buffalo County, Nebraska, which has been operational for over a year. The children's message to the officers was clear: "I just want to thank them, because they really, really saved our lives."

Federal health officials are warning about a new outbreak of E. coli linked to romaine lettuce, affecting at least 32 people and hospitalizing 13. The CDC advises consumers to discard any romaine lettuce in their homes and not to eat it, even if some has already been consumed and no one has fallen ill. This warning includes all types of romaine lettuce, such as whole heads, hearts, and precut mixes. The outbreak, which does not appear to be linked to the 2018 E. coli outbreak in romaine lettuce, is believed to be from romaine lettuce harvested from specific counties in the Central Coastal growing regions of northern and central California. The FDA, along with CDC and state partners, investigated farms and cooling facilities in California, finding the outbreak strain of E. coli O157:H7 in sediment within an agricultural water reservoir on an Adam Bros. Farming, Inc. farm. The strain isolated from ill people in this outbreak is closely related genetically to the strain from a 2017 outbreak linked to leafy greens in the U.S. and romaine lettuce in Canada. The FDA is continuing its investigation into how the E. coli bacteria entered the agricultural water reservoir and ways romaine lettuce from the farm could have been contaminated. As of January 9, 2019, this outbreak appears to be over. The CDC and FDA are emphasizing the importance of proper cleaning of refrigerators after a food recall, including steps to clean and sanitize shelves, drawers, and the inside of the refrigerator.

Marvel Studios and director Joe Johnston are intensifying their search for the perfect actor to star as Captain America in The First Avenger, with Chris Evans among the new contenders. The studio is considering actors like Chris Evans, who previously played Johnny Storm/Human Torch in Fantastic Four films. Two actors, Mike Vogel and Garrett Hedlund, remain in serious contention. Hedlund was initially on the list but was not initially cast due to scheduling issues and concerns over his salary, which was only around $300,000 for the role. Other actors who tested, including Chace Crawford, John Krasinski, Scott Porter, Michael Cassidy, and Patrick Flueger, will not be moving forward. The film is set for release on July 22, 2011, and Hedlund is currently seen in Disney's new trailer for Tron: Legacy.

After decades of decline, the prevalence of smoking in China has held steady in recent years, leading to a significant increase in the number of smokers, according to a new study published in the Journal of the American Medical Association. Despite a decrease in smoking prevalence from 30.4% to 24.2% between 1980 and 2012, the number of smokers in China has surged by almost 100 million, reaching 281 million in 2012, which is about one-third of the world's smoking population. The study, conducted by researchers at the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, highlights the "absolute need for China to awake and really grasp the political nettle of tobacco control," as stated by Judith Mackay, senior adviser to the World Lung Foundation. The leveling off of smoking prevalence in China and globally can be attributed to varying degrees of addictiveness, and the average number of cigarettes consumed daily per smoker has increased from about 15 in 1980 to 22 in 2012. China's health authorities estimate over a million deaths from tobacco-related diseases annually, and the WHO warns that these deaths could increase to 3 million by 2050 if tobacco use is not decreased. The Chinese government has taken steps to ban indoor smoking in public areas by the end of 2014, but enforcement has been lax. In 2011, the health ministry issued guidelines to ban smoking in hotels and restaurants, but they have not been strictly enforced. The skewed gender ratio of China's smoking population has also become more pronounced, with only about 4% of smokers in 2012 being female, down from about 8% in 1980. This trend is puzzling, as greater independence and improved economic conditions have not led to an increase in smoking among Chinese women, unlike in the West. The increase in the number of smokers in China has significant economic and health implications, including medical and healthcare costs, family costs, and the costs of secondhand smoke.

A new study challenges the conventional wisdom that blue families are stronger and more stable than red families, suggesting that conservative regions across the country may actually have an advantage in fostering stable family life. The research, conducted by sociologists W. Bradford Wilcox and Nicholas H. Wolfinger, analyzed data from the General Social Survey (GSS) and found that married Republicans are more likely than Democrats to report being "very happy" in their marriages, a difference that persists even when demographic factors are controlled for. This finding adds to a growing body of research that questions the notion that liberal family values lead to more stable family lives.

The study reveals that, on average, Republicans are more likely to be married and less likely to be divorced compared to Democrats. Among married individuals aged 20 to 60, 67% of Republicans report being "very happy" in their marriages, compared to 60% of Democrats. The gap narrows to three percentage points when demographic differences are accounted for, but it does not disappear entirely. Wilcox and Wolfinger suggest that this difference could be due to a variety of factors, including optimism, a tendency to look at marriages through "rose-colored glasses," or the influence of cultural and religious norms that emphasize the importance of marriage.

While the study provides compelling evidence that married Republicans are happier on average, it does not definitively explain the underlying reasons for this difference. The researchers acknowledge that other factors, such as race, education, and religious practice, could play a role. For instance, higher levels of education and religiosity are associated with greater marital satisfaction, and these factors are more prevalent among Republicans. However, even after controlling for these factors, a significant gap remains.

The findings challenge the prevailing narrative that liberal values, such as gender equality and sexual freedom, are better suited to creating stable family environments. Instead, the data suggest that conservative values, which place a higher emphasis on marriage and family stability, may be more effective in promoting family well-being. This conclusion is significant given the ongoing debate about the role of political ideology in shaping family life and social policies.

However, the study also highlights that the difference in family stability between red and blue families is modest. Only about half of all teens in both red and blue counties are living with their biological parents. This suggests that while conservative values may contribute to greater marital stability, they do not guarantee a stable family environment for all children.

In conclusion, the research by Wilcox and Wolfinger provides a nuanced view of the relationship between political ideology and family stability. It challenges the assumption that liberal family values are inherently superior and suggests that conservative values, while not a panacea, may offer some advantages in fostering stable family lives. The findings underscore the complexity of family dynamics and the need for further research to understand the multifaceted factors that influence family stability in different political contexts.

Thirty-two years after the AIDS virus was first discovered, a new study from Kaiser Permanente in San Francisco has shown that HIV is 100 percent preventable, reports the San Francisco Chronicle. Since the drug Truvada was approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration in 2012, Kaiser Permanente has been giving the drug to its patients, with even better results than in clinical trials. In a real-world study, more than 650 patients have been on the drug for nearly three years, and none has tested positive for HIV. The results of the clinical trials showed that Truvada was effective in more than 90 percent of patients, and since then, Kaiser Permanente has been giving the drug to its patients for more than two years with even better results. Doctor Jonathan Volk put Kaiser Permanente patients at risk for HIV on the medication, such as gay and bisexual men, as well as heterosexuals and injection drug users. Patients like Paul Marcelin were put on a daily regimen of the drug Truvada, which has proved in clinical trials to protect a vast majority of people from HIV infection.
