"It's wonderful to have less worries about HIV. It's something that is always lurking in the back of one's mind," Marcelin said. Kaiser researchers found that the drug has been 100 percent effective, with their patients having been taking it since the drug was approved. Patients are tested every three months for HIV and monitored for any possible side effects, such as kidney and liver problems. The study suggests that HIV is very close to being managed like any other chronic disease, such as diabetes or asthma. However, the drug, which costs Kaiser patients about $50 a month, is not without controversy. PrEP was criticized early on by health providers and other advocates over concerns that the drug would encourage unsafe sex because of a false sense of security. The Kaiser study did find a significant decrease in condom use among the participants. But the CDC and public health advocates disagree, recommending the drug as a prophylactic for those at highest risk of becoming infected. The CDC last summer recommended the drug as a prophylactic for those at highest risk of becoming infected—sex workers, men with HIV-positive partners or those who engage in high-risk behaviors, such as IV drug use—and under careful watch by their doctors. San Francisco health advocates have also recognized Truvada as an important tool for the city's Getting to Zero program, which aims to make the city the first in the country to have no new HIV infections, deaths, or stigma. "We have a fantastic new tool we can be using to help our patients protect themselves from HIV," Kaiser's Volk said. "I don’t think PrEP is right for everybody. But for the folks who need it, it works."

A 40-year-old DreamWorks animator, Young Song, has been accused of brutally beating a puppy with a hammer, an incident captured on surveillance video. The alleged attack occurred in Pasadena when Song, who worked on films like "Kung Fu Panda" and "Madagascar 2," scaled a fence into a neighbor's yard and chased a muzzled 16-month-old German shepherd with a pellet gun. He then hit the defenseless dog repeatedly with a hammer until it lay senseless. The Humane Society described it as one of the worst cases of animal abuse they've ever seen, with the dog now missing and presumed dead. Song, charged with felony animal cruelty and theft of the animal, appeared in court and pleaded not guilty. The incident has shocked authorities and animal welfare advocates, with one officer in tears upon viewing the video. Song faces potential years in state prison if convicted.

In an interview published in Turkey's Cumhuriyet newspaper, Syrian President Bashar al-Assad expressed his regret over the downing of a Turkish F-4 Phantom jet over the Mediterranean, but maintained his stance that the plane was in Syrian airspace. Maj. Gen. Robert Mood of Norway, who commands the UN monitors, stated that the escalating violence has hindered their ability to observe and report on the situation. The bodies of the two Turkish pilots were recovered from the Mediterranean and sent to Turkey for a memorial service. Turkey claims the plane was shot down over international waters, while Syria asserts it was in its airspace. Assad, however, did not show any willingness to heed cease-fire calls or Kofi Annan’s transitional government plan. He blamed outside terrorist agitators, including Islamist militants, for the uprising, and suggested his own support from the majority of Syrians. Assad also criticized Turkey’s Prime Minister Recep Tayyip Erdogan, saying he had burned his bridges with him. Meanwhile, Iraq’s Foreign Minister, Hoshyar Zebari, warned of al-Qaeda militants crossing from Iraq into Syria, citing solid information and intelligence. He stated that Iraq has reinforced its border with Syria and is concerned about the spillover of violence and the establishment of extremist groups in neighboring countries.

A nine-year-old girl in Edmonton, Canada, capitalized on the first day of legal cannabis sales by selling Girl Guide cookies outside a nearby cannabis store. Elina Childs, part of the Girl Guides Canada Brownies program, sold out of 30 boxes of cookies, each priced at $5, in just 45 minutes. Her father, Seann Childs, came up with the idea a day before legalization, as selling cookies door-to-door in their neighborhood had been slow. Elina's father used the opportunity to teach her about the legalization of cannabis, explaining its benefits and demystifying the topic for her. Elina's father noted that smoking is usually harmful for her due to her cystic fibrosis, but this was "the one day she could benefit from smoking." The experience was a teaching moment for Elina, as she learned about the legal sale of cannabis and its impact on the community. The viral social media post about Elina's entrepreneurial venture sparked questions from other parents about the legality of selling cookies near cannabis stores, with the Girl Guides praising Elina's strategy.

A 19-year-old man has been arrested by the Metropolitan Police Central e-Crime Unit in connection with network intrusions and distributed denial-of-service attacks against international businesses and intelligence agencies, according to a statement from the Met. The teenager, currently in custody at a central London police station, was arrested on suspicion of offenses under the Computer Misuse Act and Fraud Act. The investigation involved the FBI, and some reports suggest the attacks may correlate to those perpetrated by the LulzSec and Anonymous activist groups. LulzSec has a history of hacking high-profile targets, including the US Senate, the CIA, the NHS, and an FBI partner company. On Sunday, the group teamed up with Anonymous to launch an operation called AntiSec. The first AntiSec victim appears to have been the UK's Serious Organised Crime Agency (Soca), which confirmed it came under DDoS attack on Monday. However, new information from a self-proclaimed Anon member suggests the arrested individual, named Ryan, has little to do with LulzSec and that all six members of LulzSec are fine and safe. Another Anon Twitter account downplayed the significance of the arrest, stating that if it is Ryan, "they're alright. lol #LulzSec." LulzSec's official Twitter account joined in, tweeting, "Seems the glorious leader of LulzSec got arrested, it's all over now... wait... we're all still here!" This arrest has created some confusion, as Ryan was previously associated with attacking Anonymous in an attempted "coup d'etat," and his place in the current situation seems tense. LulzSec clarified that Ryan is not part of LulzSec, but they do use his IRC server for one of their chatrooms.

The U.S. and coalition forces trained and equipped Iraq's military, yet when insurgents attacked several cities this week, Iraqi soldiers surrendered without a fight, raising questions about the effectiveness of the training and equipment. The U.S. has been flying unmanned surveillance aircraft over Iraq to collect intelligence, but the program proved little use when the insurgents seized Mosul and Tikrit. The U.S. is considering all options, including military action, to help Iraq fight the Islamist militants, but insists it has no intention of sending ground troops. Defense contractors working with the Iraqi military have been evacuated from Balad air base to Baghdad due to security concerns. The Islamic State in Iraq and the Levant (ISIS) is believed to be planning to push further south to Baghdad and regions dominated by Iraq's Shia Muslim majority, who they regard as "infidels." Fears of a wider Sunni uprising have increased with reports that former Baath Party members loyal to Saddam Hussein have joined forces with the jihadists. ISIS has taken control of Mosul, Tikrit, and other cities, and is advancing on Baghdad. The U.S. and the United Nations Security Council have condemned the attacks and called for a united Iraq. However, the fragmented state of Iraqi politics, with only 128 out of 325 MPs present for a parliamentary vote to grant emergency powers to Prime Minister Nouri Maliki, highlights the challenges in forming a cohesive response. Kurdish forces have claimed control of Kirkuk, an area they historically claim as theirs, and have been locked in a dispute with Baghdad over its incorporation into their autonomous region. The U.S. is considering air strikes, but its limited options in the Middle East are seen as potentially inflaming tensions. The success of ISIS could lead to a break-up of Iraq on sectarian lines, deepening the sectarian conflict between Sunnis and Shias in the Middle East.

Researchers have developed a new atomic clock that sets a new record for stability, potentially revolutionizing timekeeping and various scientific fields. The ytterbium optical lattice clock, developed at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in Boulder, Colorado, demonstrates a groundbreaking level of stability, with its ticking rate varying by less than one part in 10^18. This means that if the clock were to run for the age of the universe, its accuracy would only deviate by a few nanoseconds. The clock operates by using yellow light from a laser to excite electrons in ytterbium atoms, providing a more precise measurement of time compared to traditional cesium clocks. The ytterbium clock's stability is about 10 times better than the previous best results for other atomic clocks, making it a significant advancement in timekeeping technology.

The new clock's stability has several potential applications. It could be used to more accurately measure how time is affected by gravity, improving the precision of global positioning systems (GPS) and other navigation systems. Scientists could also use it to test alternative theories about the relationship between time and gravity. The clock's high stability also means that precise results can be achieved very quickly, which could be beneficial in rapidly changing environments, such as factory floors or natural settings. Additionally, the development of this clock is part of a broader effort to create next-generation atomic clocks worldwide, including at NIST and the joint research institute operated by NIST and the University of Colorado Boulder.

To achieve this level of stability, NIST scientists made several improvements to the clock, including developing an ultra-low-noise laser to excite the atoms and discovering a method to cancel disruptive effects caused by collisions between atoms. While the ytterbium clock currently requires a table-sized setup, efforts are underway to miniaturize the technology, potentially leading to its use in space. The high stability of the ytterbium clock opens the door to numerous practical applications, from improving timekeeping to advancing scientific research, making it a significant milestone in the field of atomic clocks.

An Odessa woman's wedding ring was stolen from a deceased mother's hand at Sunset Memorial Gardens & Funeral Home, causing her family immense grief. The theft occurred on April 8th, when an unknown woman entered the funeral home, parked her red or maroon 4-door Saturn, and stole the ring from the body of Lois Hicks, who had passed away three years ago at the age of 88. Surveillance video captured the thief's actions, including her heavy-set, white appearance, brown long-sleeve sweater, black sweatpants, and black sandals. The ring, symbolizing the deceased woman's love and devotion to her husband, was forcibly removed, causing injury to the deceased's hand. The family is devastated and is urging anyone with information to contact the Odessa Police Department or Odessa Crime Stoppers. The incident, described as the first of its kind in the funeral home's 19-year history, has left the community in shock. The investigation is ongoing, and the family hopes for swift resolution to this brazen crime.

Republicans on the House Intelligence Committee have voted to release a classified memo alleging misconduct by senior FBI officials involved in the Russia probe, despite objections from the Department of Justice. The GOP-led panel voted along party lines to release the secret document, which was written by Republicans, and against making public a competing memo crafted by Democrats. The memo addresses a dossier of allegations against Trump compiled by a former British spy and questions over whether it was used to obtain surveillance warrants. Rep. Adam Schiff, the top Democrat on the committee, says Democrats voted against releasing the memo, arguing it mischaracterizes intelligence and aims to distract from special counsel Robert Mueller's investigation into Russia's interference in the 2016 election. The House committee's decision to publish the document came after committee Republicans, led by Chairman Devin Nunes, pushed for its disclosure. The memo's release is part of a growing partisan tension in Congress, with the panel voting to publish the document only a day after sharing it with the FBI director, who was appointed by the president. Schiff criticized the committee's actions, saying they politicized the intelligence process and selectively released the memo. The White House has not yet decided whether to authorize the release, with President Trump having five days to either object or clear the way for the memo's release. The memo is alleged to accuse senior FBI officials of abusing a classified surveillance program, known as FISA, to spy on a Trump campaign foreign policy adviser. Obtaining a warrant under FISA requires the FBI to present an application to a court with evidence that the target is acting on behalf of a foreign power. The GOP has complained that the FBI included in its evidence material from a dossier compiled by former British spy Christopher Steele, which described illicit connections between Trump and Russia. The memo also reveals that Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein approved an application to extend the surveillance of a former Trump campaign aide in early 2017. Rep. Trey Gowdy, a former federal prosecutor who helped craft the memo, urged the FBI to see the document before its release and said it should not be used to interfere with Mueller's probe. Rep. Will Hurd, a member of the House intelligence committee and a former CIA officer, expressed concerns about the potential national security risks of releasing the memo without DOJ review.

President Donald Trump blamed Democrats for the policy of separating immigrant children from their parents at the border, stating, "The Democrats forced that law on the nation." However, this claim is inaccurate. The policy is a result of the Trump administration’s "zero-tolerance" approach, which mandates the criminal prosecution of all individuals crossing the border illegally, including parents. This leads to the separation of children from their parents, as they cannot be held in adult detention facilities. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has stated that they do not have a policy of separating families, but the increase in separations is due to the administration’s decision to prosecute all illegal border crossers. Critics argue that the policy is inhumane and has led to the separation of hundreds of families. Despite the administration's claims, there is no single law that mandates the separation of families. Instead, the policy is a result of a combination of existing laws and the administration's enforcement priorities. The Trump administration has faced significant backlash, with many lawmakers and advocacy groups calling for an end to the practice. The House Republicans unveiled a compromise immigration bill that includes a measure to end the separation of migrant children and parents, but the White House has indicated it would not support this bill. The controversy continues to highlight the complex and contentious nature of immigration policy in the United States.

In Champion, Wisconsin, a small chapel has recently gained the status of a significant religious site after being officially validated by the Roman Catholic Church for apparitions of the Virgin Mary. In 1859, Adele Brise, a Belgian immigrant, reported being visited three times by Mary, who appeared between two trees in a bright light, dressed in white with a yellow sash and a crown of stars. Brise dedicated her life to teaching Catholic beliefs to children. After a two-year investigation by theologians, Bishop David L. Ricken of Green Bay declared with moral certainty that Brise had encounters of a supernatural character that are worthy of belief. This validation makes the chapel one of only a dozen worldwide, and the first in the United States, where such apparitions have been officially recognized.

Since the validation, a growing number of visitors, some traveling several hours, have come to pray and experience the presence of Mary. The local church is considering expanding its parking lot, which currently has only 75 spaces, to accommodate the influx of pilgrims. Debbie Banda and her mother, Mary Young, came for the first time and felt the presence of Mary, with Banda weeping and hugging her mother after praying in the chapel. The validation is seen as a source of hope and healing, especially in light of the Catholic Church's ongoing struggles with sex abuse scandals. Bishop Ricken noted that the church has a tradition of taking its time with such cases, and the validation does not influence his decision, but if the shrine can become a source of hope and healing for people, including victims of errant priests, "that would be beautiful."

The validation process involves careful consideration by local bishops and adherence to guidelines set by the Vatican. The church is generally reluctant to investigate claims, but increasingly uses psychiatric examinations and brain scans to ensure the credibility of claims. The chapel's grounds and the terrified crowd who gathered there were spared the flames of the Great Peshtigo Fire of 1871, adding to the credibility of the apparitions. The validation has brought a sense of joy and purpose to the local community, with families and individuals expressing their belief in the authenticity of the apparitions.

D.C. police have released video images of a person of interest in the deaths of four people in a house in an upscale neighborhood in Northwest Washington. The incident occurred on Thursday, and the victims were identified as Savvas and Amy Savopoulos, their 10-year-old son, Philip, and housekeeper Veralicia Figueroa. The fire at the large, red brick home on Woodland Drive NW was intentionally set, and the deaths are being investigated as a homicide arson. D.C. Police Chief Cathy Lanier said the fire is suspicious, and ATF agents, evidence collectors, and police investigators are working both inside and outside the house. Neighbors reported seeing a man banging on the door of one home, an aggressive vacuum cleaner salesman at another house, reports of a prowler, and what a witness said could have been the Savopoulos' blue Porsche speeding down the street the day before the deaths were discovered. The family's extensive and valuable art collection, which was on display a couple of years ago during the Christmas house tour put on by St. Albans school, where Phillip was a student, adds to the mystery. The Savopoulos family had been having a busy week, with Savvas trying to get a new martial arts center in Chantilly, Va., ready for a grand opening, and Amy being ill. The police have been sorting through a great deal of potential evidence, including the missing blue Porsche 911, which was found burned in a church parking lot in Hyattsville, Md. The deaths have shocked the Upper Northwest Washington and the District’s society circles, with the family known for their active donations to social and political causes. Gutierrez, the housekeeper who received messages from Savvas Savopoulos, said the series of messages left her with the impression that something was amiss. The police are still working on a timeline and looking for a motive, and they are asking anyone who saw the blue Porsche on Wednesday or Thursday to contact them.

Former White House chief strategist Stephen Bannon faces a challenging future as he steps away from his roles at Breitbart News and SiriusXM. Fox News and CNN have both confirmed they will not hire Bannon, leaving him without a prominent media platform. Bannon’s departure from Breitbart was announced on Tuesday, following controversial remarks he made to Michael Wolff, the author of "Fire and Fury: Inside the Trump White House." The book revealed Bannon’s harsh comments about Trump’s family, including calling Donald Trump Jr. "treasonous" for his meeting with a Russian lawyer. President Trump responded by characterizing Bannon as having "lost his mind," and the White House has distanced itself from him. Bannon’s influence waned after his ouster from the White House in August 2017, amid rising tensions with the president and his association with controversial figures like Roy Moore and Milo Yiannopoulos. His position at Breitbart became untenable following the release of Wolff’s book, which featured Bannon as a key source. Despite attempts to smooth over the incident, Bannon’s financial patron, Rebekah Mercer, severed ties with him, and Breitbart’s board reportedly debated firing him. Bannon’s career trajectory highlights the precarious nature of his role in the Trump administration and the challenges he faces in the media landscape post-White House.

The worst mass extinction in Earth's history, which occurred 252 million years ago at the end of the Permian period, may have been caused by a microscopic methane-producing microbe named Methanosarcina, according to a new study. This microbe, part of the archaea kingdom, dramatically increased its methane production, releasing vast amounts of the potent greenhouse gas into the atmosphere. This led to a rapid increase in global temperatures and ocean acidification, causing the extinction of 90% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrates. The researchers suggest that while massive volcanic eruptions in Siberia may have contributed to the extinction, they were not the primary cause. Instead, the sudden proliferation of Methanosarcina, which gained the ability to produce methane through a gene transfer, played a crucial role. The eruptions likely introduced nickel, a vital nutrient for Methanosarcina, into the ocean, allowing the microbe to thrive and produce methane at an unprecedented rate. This scenario contrasts with the asteroid impact that led to the extinction of the dinosaurs, highlighting the complex interplay of biological and geological factors in shaping Earth's history. The findings, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, suggest that microbial life can have a profound impact on the planet's environment and climate, potentially offering insights into the current climate crisis.

U.S. judges in multiple states issued rulings blocking federal authorities from enforcing President Donald Trump’s executive order restricting immigration from seven Muslim-majority countries. The order, which halted travel by people with passports from Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, and Yemen for 90 days, and stopped the resettlement of refugees for 120 days, sparked confusion and outrage. Legal challenges from states and individuals continued, with lawsuits filed on behalf of more than 100 travelers. In Boston, U.S. District Judge Allison Burroughs temporarily blocked the removal of two Iranians from the University of Massachusetts, who were detained at Logan International Airport. In Los Angeles, U.S. District Judge Dolly Gee ordered the return of Ali Khoshbakhti Vayeghan, who had been sent back to Iran. In Alexandria, Virginia, U.S. District Judge Leonie Brinkema barred the Homeland Security agency from removing an estimated 50 to 60 legal permanent residents detained at Dulles Airport. In Seattle, U.S. District Judge Thomas Zilly barred the government from removing two people, scheduling a hearing to decide if the stay should be lifted. Meanwhile, protests erupted at major U.S. airports, with thousands of demonstrators voicing opposition. The order also affected international travelers, with some green card holders and artists like Iranian director Asghar Farhadi facing uncertainty about their ability to enter the U.S. The White House defended the order, stating it was aimed at preventing potential terrorists and that green card holders would not be affected. However, the growing number of judicial rulings and protests suggested that the administration’s efforts to enforce the order were facing significant challenges.

A British Airways flight from Geneva to Heathrow Airport was reportedly struck by a drone on Sunday, April 17, 2016, at an altitude of 1,700 feet while approaching the London airport. The Airbus A320, carrying 132 passengers and five crew members, was hit as it flew over Richmond Park in southwest London. The pilot reported an object striking the front of the aircraft, but no damage was found, and the plane landed safely. The British Airline Pilots Association (Balpa) emphasized the "very real dangers" of drone use near airports, and the Civil Aviation Authority (CAA) stated that flying drones near airports is "totally unacceptable." The incident, believed to be the first such case in the UK, highlights the growing concern over potential drone strikes on commercial aircraft. The CAA and Balpa called for stricter enforcement of existing rules and possibly new regulations, such as mandatory registration and geo-fencing to prevent drones from flying in restricted airspace. The UK Air Proximity Board reported several serious near-misses involving drones at UK airports, including incidents where drones narrowly missed passenger planes and helicopters. The incident also follows warnings from the International Air Transport Association (IATA) about the "real and growing threat" posed by drones to civilian aircraft. While the threat of bird strikes has been well-researched, there is little data on the potential damage a drone could cause to an aircraft. The British government's Civil Aviation Authority admitted they have no live test data on the effects of a drone strike on a jet engine, although a computer model by Virginia Tech suggested significant damage. The UK government is considering a consultation on future drone regulations, while the US has introduced a registration scheme for drones to help trace owners in case of accidents. The increasing number of close calls between drones and aircraft, including incidents at Gatwick, Heathrow, and other UK airports, underscores the need for better enforcement and regulation of drone use.

Retired General David Petraeus, former CIA director, has not been following the media storm surrounding his resignation, according to a former aide. Petraeus, 60, and his biographer, Paula Broadwell, 40, ended their affair about four months ago but remained in contact, mostly professionally. Broadwell is unlikely to face prosecution for potential release of classified information, a law enforcement official says. Meanwhile, General John Allen, commander of U.S. and NATO forces in Afghanistan, was cleared of wrongdoing by the Pentagon’s inspector general after an investigation into potentially inappropriate emails with Tampa socialite Jill Kelley, who initially complained about harassing emails from Broadwell. Allen’s nomination to NATO commander was temporarily delayed, but he retains the White House’s confidence. President Obama declined to investigate the FBI’s handling of the affair, stating he has confidence in the bureau. Petraeus will testify before the House Intelligence Committee on Friday regarding the Benghazi attack, amid ongoing investigations into the affair and potential national security implications.

Tampa's interim police chief, Brian Dugan, addressed the media on Friday, expressing frustration and anger over the third murder in 11 days in Seminole Heights. The latest victim, Anthony Naiboa, 20, was shot while walking home from work, ending his bus ride at the wrong stop. His body was found near the intersection of 15th Street N. and E. Frierson Avenue, just 200 yards from where he left the bus. Dugan emphasized that Naiboa should not have been in that part of the neighborhood. The police response was swift, with officers arriving within minutes, but the shooter had already fled the scene. The three victims—Naiboa, Benjamin Edward Mitchell, 22, and Monica Caridad Hoffa, 32—are connected by proximity and time frame, but authorities have not yet identified any suspect or motive. Dugan stated that the victims were all alone and did not appear to have any connection, making the killings appear to be part of a larger, unexplained pattern. The police chief released surveillance video from the first murder, hoping to identify the person seen walking in the area. He urged residents to stay vigilant, keep their porch lights on, and avoid walking alone. The hunt for the perpetrator continues, with the FBI, Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office, and St. Petersburg Police offering support. Crime Stoppers and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives are offering a $25,000 reward for information leading to an arrest. The community is on edge, with businesses and residents concerned about the safety of the area. The shootings have led to a significant increase in police presence and a call for residents to remain cautious. Dugan emphasized that the killings are not random and that the community should not be held hostage by the perpetrator. The chief also warned that the shooter is an "animal and a terrorist," but stopped short of calling the case a serial killer. The incident has shaken the neighborhood, with residents and family members of the victims expressing their grief and fear.

A Detroit-area grandmother, Sandra Layne, was convicted of second-degree murder for fatally shooting her 17-year-old grandson, Jonathan Hoffman, in May 2012. Jennifer Hoffman, Jonathan's sister, called her mother a "monster" and said the verdict was a "vindication" for her son. Layne claimed self-defense, arguing that Jonathan, who had a history of drug use, had threatened her with violence. However, the jury rejected her defense, finding her guilty of second-degree murder and using a gun during a felony. Prosecutors highlighted a 911 call where Hoffman pleaded for help, stating, "My grandma shot me. I'm going to die. Help. I got shot again." This call, along with other evidence, convinced the jury that Layne had left Hoffman bleeding and then returned to shoot him again. Hoffman's father, Michael, praised his son's "amazing courage" in his final moments. Layne faces at least 14 years in prison, and her defense attorney Jerome Sabbota said she was devastated by the verdict.

A Florida teenager, Tyler Hadley, 17, is accused of brutally murdering his parents, Blake and Mary Jo Hadley, with a hammer before hosting a wild house party for 40 to 60 friends. Hadley allegedly told his best friend, Michael Mandell, that he was on ecstasy and possessed by the devil when he committed the murders. Mandell recounted to WPTV that Hadley admitted to planning the attack and taking three ecstasy pills before the killings. He described seeing bloody sheets and Blake Hadley's leg during the party. Hadley's father, Blake, was reportedly murdered first, and his mother, Mary Jo, was hit with a hammer. Mandell called the police, who found the bodies in a locked bedroom with a 22-inch framing hammer between them. Hadley, who is on suicide watch, made his first court appearance and was charged with second-degree murder, facing life in prison. His attorney, Mark Harllee, filed a not guilty plea. The case has shocked the community, with relatives and friends struggling to comprehend the tragedy.

Police discovered 18 dismembered and beheaded bodies in two vans near Lake Chapala, a tourist destination in western Mexico, authorities said. The Jalisco state Prosecutor Tomas Coronado confirmed the gruesome find, noting 15 severed heads were among the body parts. The area has been a battleground between the Jalisco New Generation gang, allied with the Sinaloa cartel, and the Zetas drug cartel. The victims were likely targeted by the Zetas, as handwritten messages found in the vans indicated conflict between rival groups. A woman detained in connection with the separate kidnapping of 12 people in the same area admitted the abductions were a response to events in Tamaulipas, where 23 people were found decapitated or hanging from bridges. The Zetas, known for their brutal tactics, are battling the Jalisco New Generation gang for control of the drug trade in eastern Mexico and the north. The bodies, which appear to have been refrigerated after death, were found in two vans on a dirt road near Lake Chapala, a popular spot for tourists and American retirees. The prosecutor stated, "They are clearly messages between rival groups that are in conflict," highlighting the escalating violence between the cartels.

The United States is home to an estimated 70 to 80 million pet dogs, making up 37 to 47 percent of all American households. These dogs, known as Canis familiaris, are the first species to be domesticated by humans from Eurasian gray wolves, a process that began at least 15,000 years ago. However, the exact location of this domestication has long been a subject of debate. A new genomic study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, offers strong evidence that domesticated dogs originated in Central Asia, specifically around modern-day Nepal and Mongolia.

Previous genetic studies have suggested that domestication occurred in Southern China around 16,500 years ago, while the earliest archaeological evidence of domesticated canines is found in Europe and Siberia. This conflicting evidence has led to significant debate. One key factor that was largely neglected in previous studies is the inclusion of "village dogs," which are free-roaming and breeding populations that have lived alongside humans since the first domestication of wolves. These village dogs, despite their varied appearances, are genetically diverse and carry a more authentic genetic signature of the original dog populations.

Adam Boyko, from Cornell University, led a team that analyzed 185,800 genetic markers in 5,392 dogs, including 549 village dogs from 38 countries, making this the largest study of worldwide canine genetic diversity. The team found that genetic diversity is highest in Central Asia, specifically Nepal and Mongolia, with genetic diversity then spreading out like ripples, with areas like Afghanistan, Egypt, India, and Vietnam having the next highest levels. This pattern mirrors how humans spread out of East Africa.

The study also revealed that dogs studied in regions farther away, such as the South Pacific and Americas, were almost exclusively of European origin. This is likely due to the spread of modern Western culture and the appeal of pure breeds. Boyko notes that village dogs with indigenous traits have not been overcome by foreign gene flow in Central Asia because they originated there and have large populations, suggesting they are better adapted to that environment.

The research suggests that hunter-gatherers in central Asia domesticated dogs from gray wolves. A combination of increasing human population density, better hunting methods, and climate change may have reduced the availability of prey, pushing some wolves towards scavenging. This favored tameness and smaller size, reducing their hunting prowess and setting them on the path to domestication. Other researchers have welcomed the tracing of domestication to the neighborhood of central Asia, although some dispute the precise site. Peter Savolainen of the Royal Institute of Technology in Solna, Sweden, compliments the thoroughness of the study but notes the lack of DNA from southern China, where he believes dogs originated.

The study's conclusion is important because it provides a clear origin that can be tested further. Olaf Thalmann at Uppsala University praises the scale of the study and says its conclusion is reasonable. However, he doubts that the study is the final word on where dogs were tamed, suggesting that the only way to shed further light on the topic is by analyzing ancient remains. A consortium led by Greger Larson of the University of Oxford is now working on this, collecting more than 1500 ancient dogs and wolves to compare with morphological data from over 4000 specimens going back into the late Pleistocene.

Two weeks after the devastating earthquake in Haiti, the situation remains dire for many, with international aid groups struggling to reach all those in need. Yet, in the midst of despair, a small act of kindness is bringing hope to the people of Port-au-Prince. Muncheez, a pizza restaurant on the outskirts of the capital, has transformed into a community hub, serving free meals to those in need. Co-owner Gilbert Bailly explains that the idea to serve food began the day after the earthquake when he realized his ingredients would spoil before anyone could afford to buy a pizza. "So instead of losing the food, we said let's cook the food and give it away to people that need it," he says. As donations from other businesses in the neighborhood ran out, Bailly's nephew brought in a truckload of food from the Dominican Republic. Now, with the help of a Facebook page, Bailly is trying to get additional support. Muncheez is feeding about 1,000 people a day, with lines wrapping around the building when the restaurant opens its doors in the late afternoon. Leonce Bell, 40, who lost his house and job in the earthquake, has been served a plate of spaghetti and a cup of water. He says he hasn't eaten in three days and is saving his meal for his child. World Vision, an international aid group, has recently found out about the improvised soup kitchen at Muncheez and is bringing trucks carrying sacks of dry food. Now, along with their meal, people get bags of bulgur and lentils to take back to their families. Bailly hopes this will ease some of the pain and provide a glimmer of hope in the midst of the ongoing crisis.

Tech firms are known for their lavish meals, but cities are now clamping down on campus cafeterias in an attempt to support local restaurants. In a highly unusual mandate, city officials have barred Facebook from serving free food to its employees when the tech company moves into a new office in Mountain View later this year – and the city of San Francisco hopes to follow suit. The restriction was enforced after local restaurants complained that free meals at Google, the city’s largest employer, had damaged their business. Facebook employees have access to high-end restaurants with pizza ovens, sushi counters, and freshly baked pastries. However, the rules for Facebook’s new office are designed to encourage the thousands of tech workers to spend some money in and integrate with the local community, rather than arriving in a bus each day and never leaving the building. In San Francisco, a city proposal, announced on Tuesday, would ban on-site workplace cafeterias. If approved, the measure would alter city planning laws to ban workplace cafeterias in any new developments, but would not be retroactive. The rule is designed to get workers to engage with the local community. The Silicon Valley paradox: one in four people are at risk of hunger. Axing company cafeterias also means axing jobs that, depending on the company, can come with good pay and benefits. In March, cafeteria workers at Facebook’s Menlo Park headquarters unionised, a move that secured $4.75 an hour in raises, affordable healthcare, and a pension plan. The ban on having a free cafeteria in the Mountain View complex could mean losing well-paid jobs to minimum-wage jobs in nearby restaurants. Contact the author: olivia.solon@theguardian.com. The daily banquets at big tech companies have become legendary. Google hired its first chef about 20 years ago, when the company had just 50 employees. Reviews of its corporate cuisine popped up on Bon Appetit, Serious Eats, and Yelp. New companies such as Facebook and LinkedIn matched the perk as they tried to lure employees away. Staffing the cafeterias became a booming business for the formerly sleepy field of corporate catering. But the in-house eating places have drawn customers and potential employees away from neighboring businesses, and city officials are concerned that local restaurants struggle and potentially bustling streets are empty as a result. Under Mountain View’s rules for the Village complex, meals within the offices can’t be subsidized by more than 50 percent on a regular basis. Facebook can fully subsidize employees if they go to restaurants that are open to the public. Mountain View has been seeking other concessions from tech giants. A November ballot measure proposes a per-employee tax that would hit Google the hardest. Last year, a new Google campus called Charleston East will be partially open to the public, including restaurants that anyone can dine in. While the cafeteria provision only applies to the Facebook site, it’s possible Mountain View could seek to impose similar conditions on Google’s next major expansion in the North Bayshore area, where it has its headquarters campus. Mountain View Councilwoman Margaret Abe-Koga said it’s possible Google could help subsidize the rent for small businesses on its property or have agreements with retailers to patronize their businesses. Mountain View’s neighbors don’t have plans to impose similar requirements on employee cafeterias. Cupertino Vice Mayor Rod Sinks said it’s already common to see Apple employees dine at local restaurants; the company charges employees for meals, making outside offerings relatively more attractive. Apple is more concerned with secrecy: It built a glassy restaurant that resembles one of its gadget stores on Alves Drive in Cupertino. A stand-alone building, it’s in walking distance of some Apple offices. Though the building is on a commercial street, the public can’t enter unless they’re the guest of an employee. In San Jose, there are no prohibitions on businesses offering free food, with the exception of its City Hall. When it was designed more than a decade ago, there were concerns that a cafeteria there would compete with local food businesses, so the city didn’t build one. Adobe’s downtown headquarters has partially subsidized cafeterias. Near San Jose’s Diridon Station, Google is planning another huge development. There has been no talk of restricting subsidized meals there, said Nanci Klein, San Jose’s assistant director of economic development. Chris Foley, co-owner of the Market, a food hall underneath Twitter’s headquarters in San Francisco, hopes that one day the city will follow Mountain View’s lead. Restaurants have opened in the Mid-Market neighborhood in hopes of gaining customers from the tech companies there, but a number have shuttered and struggled. If there were no meals served inside those offices, that would greatly benefit restaurants and food vendors like those in the Market. Having (tech workers) in their offices and not engaging with the community isn’t really good for the community or these small businesses.

A 17-year-old Dutch girl, Vera Mol, died after misunderstanding her instructor's instruction during a bungee jumping session in northern Spain in August 2015. The incident occurred when the instructor, who was from the UK and spoke poor English, told the group "no jump," which the teenager misinterpreted as "now jump." As a result, she leaped from a 130-foot-high bridge before her harness was properly secured, leading to her fatal fall. The Spanish court has ruled that the instructor's poor English contributed to the tragedy, and the company organizing the bungee jump may face criminal charges, including accidental homicide. The court's decision was based on the fact that the instructor's command could have been misinterpreted, and he should have used the correct phrase "don't jump" to avoid confusion. Additionally, the judge noted that the instructor should have verified the teenager's age, as bungee jumping is legally restricted to those over 18 in Spain. The case highlights the potential dangers of language barriers in adventure sports and the importance of clear communication to prevent accidents.

The "horrific" slaying of a Chinese herbal medicine practitioner, his wife, and their 5-year-old daughter in their California home does not appear to be random, authorities say. The crime was discovered Wednesday when sheriff's deputies responded to a welfare check on the residence in a modern neighborhood just outside Santa Barbara. Early Thursday, detectives entered the home and coroner's investigators collected the remains, identified as 57-year-old Dr. Weidong "Henry" Han; his 29-year-old wife, Huijie "Jennie" Yu; and their daughter, Emily Han, a kindergartner. The Santa Barbara Herb Clinic, founded by Han in 1991, provided traditional treatments including acupuncture, acupressure, and herbal formulas. Han, a co-author of books on the combination of Chinese and Western medicine, came from a family of doctors in China and earned medical degrees in Beijing. The Sheriff's Office stated that early indications suggest this was not a random attack, and detectives are working around the clock to determine the responsible party. The next-of-kin notification process is underway, and anyone with information is asked to call the Sheriff's anonymous tip line. The tragic incident has left the Foothill Elementary School community in shock, with kindergarten families consulting the school psychologist on how to discuss the event with their children.

A $1 million lawsuit filed by a Dallas pet-sitting company against a Plano couple who wrote a one-star review has been dismissed. Prestigious Pets and its owner filed the lawsuit against Michelle and Robert Duchouquette, accusing them of defamation, business disparagement, and a breach of contract after the couple posted the negative review on Yelp. The Duchouquettes argued the case should be dismissed based on the Texas Anti-SLAPP statute, meant to allow judges to dismiss frivolous suits filed against people who speak out about a matter of public concern. Prestigious Pets sought between $200,000 and $1 million in damages, up from an initial $6,700, which the company's attorney said was made to reflect a loss in business. The company said the Duchouquettes violated a non-disparagement clause in their contract by posting the review, and that their statements were false and defamatory. The complaint alleged the family did not initially tell the company it had a fish and that the sitter agreed to feed the betta for free after the Duchouquettes "demanded" it. The sitter did not agree to clean the fish bowl or change the water and was told to feed it less, according to court documents. The review stated, "The one star is for potentially harming my fish, otherwise it would have been 2 stars." The family said in the review that the care for their dogs "was fine." The company's attorney provided documents showing only two pets on the contract—dogs Bogey and Barley. The complaint also said the company's owner and her husband "have had to deal with numerous rape and death threats" and other forms of harassment. The case attracted the attention of advocates for consumers and free expression, with attorney Paul Alan Levy from Public Citizen taking on the task of asking the court to dismiss the case, arguing that the petsitter’s complaint is a frivolous SLAPP. The judge granted the couple's motion to dismiss the case, and the company is now responsible for paying court costs and reasonable attorney fees. The couple expressed their relief and gratitude regarding the ruling, stating that they should have the opportunity to express their opinions without fear of a lawsuit.

A 21-year-old University of Washington student, Casey Henderson, has been arrested and charged with homicide after allegedly attacking his 22-year-old girlfriend, also a UW student, in their University District apartment. The incident occurred around 2 p.m. on Sunday, and neighbors reported hearing a male yelling, "You wanna die?" and "I will kill you." Police arrived and found Henderson strangling his girlfriend, leading to a struggle. They pulled Henderson off the woman, who was then taken to Harborview Medical Center with life-threatening injuries. She later died. Henderson told police he and his girlfriend had taken LSD, which led to him becoming paranoid and believing she was plotting against him. He admitted to punching her in the face and head, then strangling her. The case is now being investigated as a homicide, with Henderson facing a $1 million bail and scheduled to appear in court on Wednesday. Both victims were students at the University of Washington. A neighbor who called 911 described the incident as extremely violent, with the suspect continuously yelling threats. While the woman's name has not been released, the Seattle police stated that she was undergoing treatment at Harborview Medical Center with life-threatening injuries.

Target's CEO, Gregg Steinhafel, defended the four-day delay in notifying customers of the security breach during a CNBC interview, stating that the delay was necessary for the investigation and preparation for consumer reaction. The breach, which occurred between November 27 and December 15, affected as many as 110 million customers, including names, mailing addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses. Steinhafel explained that the first day focused on securing the environment, the second day on initiating the investigation, the third on preparation, and the fourth on notification. While Steinhafel defended the delay, critics questioned the timing, especially since similar breaches occurred at other retailers like Neiman Marcus and an unnamed retailer. The breach involved malware infecting Target's point-of-sale terminals, leading to the theft of 40 million credit card records and 70 million other records. Steinhafel emphasized the company's commitment to improving security, advocating for the adoption of chip-and-PIN technology, which stores customer information on computer chips and requires users to type in personal identification numbers. The incident highlights the increasing vulnerability of retailers to cyber attacks and the need for enhanced security measures. Retailers and card processing companies have reported a steady stream of security breaches, but the Target breach may mark a turning point, leading to stricter security standards and potentially more spending on security measures.

The Celebrity 100 list, compiled by Forbes, ranks the most powerful people in the entertainment business based on a combination of earnings and media visibility. Earnings are calculated from May 1, 2011, to May 1, 2012, and include pretax income from film and television, music, endorsements, and other ventures. Media visibility is measured through print, television, radio, and online exposure, along with social media presence. Jennifer Lopez tops the list for the first time, earning $52 million and leveraging her platform for various endorsement deals and a clothing line. Oprah Winfrey ranks second, making $165 million from her empire of spin-offs and media ventures. Justin Bieber, at 18, is the youngest celebrity on the list, earning $55 million through touring and record sales, and he's also a budding venture capitalist. Kim and Khloe Kardashian make the cut, with Kim ranking seventh and Khloe 73rd, thanks to their reality TV shows and business ventures. Ashton Kutcher, who took over Two and a Half Men, debuts at 51st place with $24 million, reflecting his earnings and tech investments. The list highlights the evolving landscape of celebrity success, where acting, singing, and sports are no longer enough; a celebrity must also excel in endorsements, social media, and business ventures.

In the aftermath of the Camp Fire, which claimed 88 lives and devastated Paradise, California, a cleanup worker named Rob Freestone faced criminal charges after posting inflammatory images on his Facebook page. Freestone, who worked for Pacific Gas and Electric Co. as a third-party contractor, shared photos that some found disrespectful, including one of cleanup workers posing with a burned-out RV, another of a dead cat with a beer bottle placed near its mouth, and a third of him jumping on a trampoline with the caption, "Trampolines are stupid. (By the way), it used to be called a Jumpoline until your mom got on it." The Town of Paradise shared these screenshots on their Facebook page, drawing attention to Freestone's actions. Paradise police stated they would pursue criminal charges, possibly for being in an evacuated area, as Freestone was operating outside his cleanup responsibilities. Bigge Crane and Rigging, the company Freestone worked for, terminated his employment and those of two other employees involved in the incident, issuing a statement that such behavior was inconsistent with their company values and ethical code. The company expressed regret for the residents of Paradise and Butte County, who had already suffered a devastating loss. Pacific Gas and Electric Co. also issued a statement, confirming that Freestone had been removed from the Camp Fire recovery effort. The incident highlights the sensitivity required in disaster recovery work and the consequences of insensitive behavior during such times.

Stephanie Clifford, known professionally as Stormy Daniels, has publicly distanced herself from her lawyer, Michael Avenatti, over several issues, including his handling of legal and financial matters. In a statement to The Daily Beast, Daniels expressed gratitude for Avenatti's efforts to support her in her legal battle against President Donald Trump but criticized his actions. She alleged that Avenatti ignored her requests for financial transparency regarding a legal defense and safety fund, which has received substantial donations. Daniels also criticized Avenatti for starting a new crowdfunding campaign without her consent, using her name and face without her permission. Avenatti, on the other hand, defended his actions, stating that he has always been transparent with Daniels and that the money raised has been used for her security and legal expenses. He also clarified that he has not received any personal fees from the crowdfunding efforts. The dispute highlights the complex relationship between Daniels and Avenatti, with Daniels seeking to regain control over her legal representation and financial management. The controversy adds another layer to the ongoing legal saga involving Daniels, Trump, and Avenatti, as both parties continue to navigate the legal and financial implications of their interactions.

SpaceX, led by billionaire entrepreneur Elon Musk, has announced its first private passenger for a moon voyage, Japanese billionaire Yusaku Maezawa, founder of online fashion retailer Zozo. Maezawa, a 42-year-old entrepreneur, is set to embark on a lunar flyby in 2023 aboard SpaceX’s Big Falcon Rocket (BFR), a super heavy-lift launch vehicle designed for moon and Mars missions. Maezawa plans to invite six to eight artists to accompany him on this historic trip, aiming to make a significant impact on the development of the BFR, which Musk estimates will cost around $5 billion. The mission, relying on the yet-to-be-built BFR, represents a significant step in commercializing space travel. Maezawa’s significant deposit underscores the potential market for such luxury space trips. SpaceX has already disrupted the space industry with its reusable Falcon 9 rockets, completing over 50 successful launches and securing billions in contracts with NASA and the U.S. Department of Defense. The BFR, standing 118 meters tall and capable of lifting 150 tonnes into low-Earth orbit, is expected to revolutionize space travel. Musk has previously set ambitious timelines for the BFR, aiming for an unpiloted Mars mission in 2022 and a crewed flight in 2024, though these goals have faced delays. Maezawa’s journey, while risky, aligns with his history of extravagant purchases and ventures, including his $110 million acquisition of a Jean-Michel Basquiat painting. His participation could bring significant publicity to Zozo, his fashion company, and potentially revolutionize the fashion industry through his Zozosuit, a made-to-measure clothing technology. Meanwhile, other space companies like Blue Origin and Virgin Galactic are also vying to offer space tourism, with Virgin Galactic’s suborbital flights costing around $250,000. While Maezawa’s trip is not a landing mission, it marks the first private citizen to venture beyond Earth’s protective magnetic shield since 1972, making it a historic and potentially lucrative endeavor for SpaceX.

A recent Colorado Tourism Office survey reveals that legal recreational marijuana is increasingly influencing travel decisions to Colorado, challenging the state's tourism officials who have long attributed record visitation and spending to marketing alone. The survey, conducted by Strategic Marketing and Research Insights (SMARI) and presented to the Colorado Tourism Office's board of directors, found that 48 percent of potential summertime visitors cited marijuana laws as a significant motivator for their travel plans. This contrasts with the state's "Come to Life" campaign, which has been highly successful, generating a $2.6 billion economic impact and 2.1 million leisure trips, with a return on investment of $490 for every dollar spent. However, only 8 percent of Colorado tourists reported visiting a marijuana dispensary during their trips, with 85 percent of those who did visit considering marijuana a primary motivator.

The survey, which targeted tourists from Chicago, Dallas, Houston, Indianapolis, Milwaukee, San Diego, St. Louis, and other cities, showed that while marijuana was a significant factor, its influence varied. Twenty-two percent found it "extremely influential," and 20 percent said it was "very much influential." The data also indicated that the impact of marijuana laws on tourism decisions is likely to diminish as other states legalize recreational marijuana, with nine states considering similar measures for 2016. Despite the survey's findings, the Colorado Tourism Office has not promoted marijuana, adhering to state regulations that prevent pot businesses from advertising outside the state. However, the office's new chief, Cathy Ritter, acknowledges the growing influence of marijuana on tourism and suggests the state should embrace this industry, comparing it to the wine industry in Napa Valley and Sonoma County.

Tourism leaders, like Danny Schaefer of My420Tours, see this as an opportunity to educate visitors about the modern cannabis industry, noting that many tourists are seeking information on marijuana but find none on Colorado's official tourism website or at welcome centers. Schaefer advocates for the state to take a more proactive role in promoting marijuana tourism, arguing that it could become a significant economic driver. Meanwhile, local tourism boards, such as Telluride's, are beginning to incorporate marijuana into their marketing strategies, recognizing its potential as a tourism amenity. The survey's director, Denise Miller, acknowledges the need for better questions to capture a more comprehensive understanding of marijuana's impact on tourism. As the debate continues, the influence of legal marijuana on Colorado's tourism industry appears to be growing, challenging traditional tourism strategies and prompting a reevaluation of how the state positions itself in the cannabis market.

Israeli police faced off with thousands of ultra-conservative Jews who tried to drive liberal women worshippers from the Western Wall on Friday, marking a significant shift in the authorities' handling of a long-standing religious schism. The clash erupted after a court ruling last month that allowed the Women of the Wall group to pray at the site without fear of arrest for wearing prayer shawls, a practice reserved for men under Orthodox tradition. Ultra-Orthodox protesters, including yeshiva students and community leaders like rabbis Ovadia Yosef and Aharon Leib Shteinman, threw chairs, water, and coffee at the women, and even stoned their buses. Two policemen were injured in the scuffle, and three ultra-Orthodox men were arrested. This incident highlights the growing tension between a secular majority and an ultra-Orthodox minority over religious practices in Israel, where institutions such as marriage, divorce, and burial are controlled by religious authorities. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has tasked former cabinet minister Natan Sharansky with seeking a compromise to permit the Women of the Wall to hold prayers without exacerbating tensions. Sharansky's proposed solution includes widening a separate zone at the Western Wall for egalitarian prayer, a suggestion neither side nor the government has yet embraced. The dispute also underscores the role of religion in modern Israel, with the Western Wall serving as both a place of Jewish prayer and a site for national ceremonies. Women of the Wall's Catherine Leff, 17, said the events actually strengthened the group and encouraged them to sing and pray even louder. The clash between the Women of the Wall and ultra-Orthodox protesters has sparked further debate on the role of religious authorities in the modern State of Israel, with some calling for a more inclusive approach.

Scientists at the European Organization for Nuclear Research (CERN) have reported a perplexing result that could challenge one of the cornerstones of modern physics: the speed of light as the ultimate speed limit. In a groundbreaking experiment, a neutrino beam fired from CERN to a lab 454 miles away in Italy was found to travel 60 nanoseconds faster than light, a finding that, if confirmed, would require a fundamental rethink of Einstein's theory of special relativity. The OPERA collaboration, which conducted the experiment, has meticulously checked their results and now invites the broader physics community to scrutinize their findings. The potential implications are enormous, as the speed of light is a fundamental constant in physics. However, the team is cautious, emphasizing the need for independent verification. If confirmed, this could open doors to new physics, including the possibility of faster-than-light travel and a deeper understanding of the universe's most elusive particles.

A New Jersey housewife, Tova Gerson, is suing Century 21 for $5 million over what she claims is a 80-cent coupon fraud. Gerson bought items worth over $100 on January 10, using a $5-off coupon. A week later, she returned a $17.97 children's outfit, but Century 21 only refunded $17.17, pro-rating the coupon. Gerson argues this practice deprived her of the full coupon benefit. Her lawyer, Harry Katz, has previously sued retailers like Dick's Sporting Goods and The Children's Place for similar issues. The case, filed in Manhattan federal court, seeks class-action status, alleging that hundreds of other shoppers could have been similarly affected. Century 21 did not immediately comment.

The only surviving animals from Mosul Zoo, located in the war-torn Iraqi city, have been rescued from horrific conditions and are now beginning a new life in Jordan, thanks to the efforts of Four Paws International. Simba, a lion, and Lula, a bear, were found abandoned at the privately-owned zoo in February, still in their cages and covered in dirt and excrement. Four Paws International's mission to rescue these animals was a challenging one, as they had to secure the necessary permits from the Iraqi authorities, which took weeks. Their first attempt to transport the animals was thwarted when a lorry carrying them was detained at a checkpoint for nine days, during which time Simba developed a respiratory problem. Amir Khalil, the Egyptian-Austrian vet who led the mission, reported that both Simba and Lula were suffering from many diseases caused by malnutrition and lack of care. They had very bad teeth, Lula was suffering from pneumonia, and Simba from ill joints. Khalil stated, "This is a beginning of a new life for the animals," and they will no longer be part of the ongoing war. The Montazah al-Morour Zoo, where the animals were found, was nearly destroyed during the battle for the eastern half of the city earlier this year, and most of its animals, including a lioness, monkeys, and rabbits, were killed or died of starvation. The rescue mission highlights the ongoing struggles of animals in conflict zones and the importance of international organizations in providing aid and care.

David Cameron, facing a General Election within 18 weeks, is determined to secure another five-year term as Prime Minister, or risk a political career cut short before he turns 50. Cameron, known for his "competence" message, is launching his campaign with a focus on the economy, warning that Labour's budget plans could cost £13.5 billion extra in interest payments on the deficit, more than the police budget. The Prime Minister is preparing for tough negotiations with Angela Merkel over Britain's future in the EU, stating he is prepared to take Britain out if his demands are not met. Cameron's relationship with Barack Obama is strong, with the US President calling him "bro." The election is seen as a choice between "competence or chaos," with Cameron promising to introduce reforming legislation on education and welfare within the first 50 days of a re-election. He faces challenges from potential Tory rebels and the prospect of stepping down halfway through his next term if he wins. Cameron's wife, Samantha, supports his political ambitions, and he is confident in his message, despite the looming threat of a potential leadership challenge from within his party. The election will also see the increased influence of social media, with Cameron embracing the platform to reach voters beyond traditional campaign trails.

Bill Hudson, a former husband of actress Goldie Hawn and father to five children, including actors Kate and Oliver Hudson, is left heartbroken and angry after his eldest children posted a Father’s Day Instagram photo that cut to the core of his fatherhood. The photo, posted by Oliver, showed him with Kurt Russell, Goldie’s long-term partner, and the caption read, “Happy Abandonment Day....@katehudson.” Kate responded with a picture of herself with Kurt Russell, saying, “Pa, just simply... thank you. Happy Father’s Day. I love you to the moon and back.” Bill, now 65, has vowed to sever all ties with his eldest children, describing their actions as “malicious, vicious, and premeditated.” He claims that Goldie, his ex-wife, has been “wilfully alienating” him from his children for decades, using their fame and financial power to distance him from their lives. Bill says he considers himself a father of only three children now, as he no longer recognizes Oliver and Kate as his own. He demands that they stop using the Hudson name and that they are no longer a part of his life. Bill’s relationship with his children has been fraught with tension for years, with Goldie’s claims of his alleged absence as a father and her desire for an open marriage. Bill maintains that he was always a present father, sending birthday cards and making efforts to stay involved in his children’s lives. However, he says that Goldie’s actions, particularly after her relationship with Kurt Russell, made it increasingly difficult for him to see his children. The article details the complex family dynamics and the emotional toll on Bill, who has removed photographs of his children from his home and thrown away their baby booties. His decision to cut ties with his eldest children comes as a shock to many, as Bill has always maintained a dignified silence in the face of public attacks on his fatherhood.

For nearly six months, Andrew Shirvell, an assistant attorney general for the state of Michigan, has waged an internet campaign against Chris Armstrong, the openly gay student assembly president at the University of Michigan in Ann Arbor. Shirvell, using the online moniker "Concerned Michigan Alumnus," launched his blog in late April, accusing Armstrong of various misdeeds, including going back on a campaign promise to minority students, engaging in "flagrant sexual promiscuity," and hosting a gay orgy in his dorm room. Michigan Attorney General Mike Cox has declined to comment directly, stating that Shirvell's personal opinions do not reflect the views of the Michigan Department of Attorney General. Shirvell has protested outside Armstrong's house, calling him "Satan's representative on the student assembly." Armstrong, who supports gender-neutral housing for transgender students, has hired an attorney and may pursue legal action for harassment. Shirvell maintains his actions are a matter of exercising his First Amendment rights as a Christian citizen.

Is sexual addiction the real deal? A new study challenges the notion of hypersexuality or sexual addiction as a mental disorder. Nicole Prause, a researcher at the Semel Institute for Neuroscience and Human Behavior at UCLA, led the study, which measured brain responses to sexual images in individuals who reported problems controlling their viewing of such images. Contrary to expectations, the brain's response to sexual stimuli was not related to the severity of hypersexuality but was instead linked to the level of sexual desire. The study involved 52 volunteers, 39 men and 13 women, who reported difficulties in controlling their use of pornography. Using electroencephalography (EEG), researchers monitored brain activity while participants viewed a set of images, including sexual and neutral ones. The P300 response, a brain measure of interest, was higher in those with higher libidos but showed no correlation with measures of sexual compulsivity. Prause suggests that hypersexuality does not explain brain responses to sexual images more than high libido does. This finding challenges existing theories of sex addiction and raises questions about categorizing hypersexual behavior as a mental disorder. The study, published in Socioaffective Neuroscience and Psychology, provides a significant challenge to the addiction model of hypersexuality, though the debate continues. Further research is needed to fully understand the underlying mechanisms of hypersexual behavior.

Around 6:30 p.m. on February 17, 1864, eight Confederate sailors boarded the H.L. Hunley, a 40-foot-long iron submarine, and embarked on a historic but fateful mission. The Hunley set out to become the first combat submarine to sink an enemy ship, the USS Housatonic, a Union warship patrolling the waters off Charleston, South Carolina. After a successful torpedo attack, the Hunley mysteriously sank, leaving its crew of eight men unaccounted for. For over 150 years, the cause of the submarine's demise remained a mystery, with theories ranging from suffocation to a lucky shot from the Housatonic.

In 2016, biomedical engineer Rachel Lance, with no prior experience in archaeology or forensics, began to unravel the mystery. Using computational models and scaled-down experiments, Lance proposed that the explosion from the Hunley's own torpedo likely caused the submarine's sinking. The torpedo, filled with 135 pounds of black powder, was attached to the end of a 16-foot spar. Lance's experiments, conducted in a pond and using scaled models, demonstrated that the blast wave from the explosion could have instantly killed the crew by causing catastrophic injuries to their lungs and brains.

Lance's research involved constructing a 6.5-foot-long model of the Hunley, nicknamed the CSS Tiny, and exposing it to underwater blasts. The experiments showed that the blast wave, traveling through the submarine's thin iron hull, would have caused immediate and fatal injuries to the crew. The findings were published in the journal Plos One, providing a compelling explanation for the Hunley's sudden and mysterious sinking.

Despite the compelling evidence, the Hunley Project scientists at Clemson University, who have been studying the submarine for over a decade, remain cautious. They acknowledge the possibility of the blast wave theory but point out that previous computer modeling studies suggested the blast would not have harmed the crew. The Hunley Project's Michael Scafuri notes that the scenario is complex, akin to reconstructing a car accident with limited information. However, Lance's experiments offer a new perspective, challenging previous theories and potentially solving a century-old mystery.

The Hunley's sinking remains a significant event in American history, marking the first successful submarine attack. The mystery of the crew's fate, solved through modern scientific methods, sheds light on the dangers and ingenuity of Civil War-era engineering. The findings not only provide closure for historians but also offer insights into the human body's response to explosive blasts, applicable to modern injury biomechanics.

Barbara Walters, a veteran ABC News journalist and co-host and co-creator of "The View," will step down in the summer of 2014, ending a career spanning more than five decades. Walters, who will turn 84 in September, intends to remain on "The View" through the next season and will step down after the season wraps in summer 2014. She will continue to be a co-executive producer of the show and will be involved in selecting new co-hosts to replace Joy Behar and Elisabeth Hasselbeck, who have both announced their departures. Walters' retirement will be marked by a series of retrospectives and specials celebrating her long and storied career, which began in 1961 when she was hired as a researcher for NBC's "Today" show. She has since become the first woman to host an evening newscast when paired with Harry Reasoner on the ABC Evening News in 1976, and has interviewed numerous world leaders, celebrities, and newsmakers, including Anwar Al Sadat, Margaret Thatcher, Vladimir Putin, and Monica Lewinsky. Walters' decision to retire comes after more than 40 years at ABC News and nearly 40 years at "The View." In a statement, she expressed her happiness with her decision and her excitement for the year ahead, stating, "I am very happy with my decision and look forward to a wonderful and special year ahead both on 'The View' and with ABC News. I created 'The View' and am delighted it will last beyond my leaving it." ABC News president Ben Sherwood added, "There's only one Barbara Walters. And we look forward to making her final year on television as remarkable, path-breaking, and news-making as Barbara herself."

One woman died, and dozens were hospitalized after smoke filled the L'Enfant Plaza Metro station in Washington, D.C., on Monday afternoon. The incident occurred when a Virginia-bound Yellow Line train stopped just south of the station around 3:20 p.m. for unknown reasons, causing the tunnel to fill with thick, black smoke. Passengers described the scene as harrowing, with people barely able to breathe and some in critical condition. Firefighters gained access to the tunnel at the Ninth Street and Maine Avenue SE evacuation point, and one injured firefighter was transported from there by ambulance. A total of 84 patients were taken to hospitals, with three in critical but stable condition, two at George Washington University Hospital. One passenger, Denzel Hatch, recounted the chaos, saying, "People could barely breathe. They had to evacuate us through the tunnel and walk back through the front. No electricity, no visibility, nothing. Couldn't see anything at first." Adjoa Adofo, a passenger, described the panic, noting, "You're hearing other people crying, you're seeing people passing out... it was a horrific thing to witness." The cause of the smoke and fire remains unknown, with NTSB investigators saying there was an electrical arcing involving the third rail and power supply cables prior to the fire. The smoke spread along the third rail due to water nearby. The incident involved a fatality, leading the Metropolitan Police Department to be involved in the investigation. Metro service was disrupted, with Green and Yellow line service suspended between the Gallery Place and Navy Yard/Pentagon stations. The station was evacuated and closed for several hours, and some service was restored by the end of the day. The Metro General Manager, Richard Sarles, announced his retirement, effective Friday. The probe into the case continues, with the NTSB expected to take six months to a year to complete.

Crystal Matrau-Belt, 24, from Michigan, delivered her son, Jeremiah James Matrau-Skokan, at Bronson Medical Hospital in Kalamazoo on Saturday, only to find out later that her fiancé, Emil Skokan III, and her mother, Peggy Nichols, had been killed in a car accident. Matrau-Belt had called her fiancé before the emergency cesarean section, telling him they were going to deliver the baby. "He said, 'Do you need anything?' and that he would come up shortly and that he loved me and all that and stuff," she recalled. "It was the last time I talked to him." Her family, including her stepfather and stepmother, were present during the delivery. Matrau-Belt named her son Jeremiah, a name she and Skokan had agreed on just before her delivery. "Our entire pregnancy we could not agree on a name. Everybody kept asking what's the name and we said we don’t know yet," she said. "I said 'What about Jeremiah?' He loves the name. ... The first time we agreed on a name was Friday." Matrau-Belt sees a lot of her fiancé's personality in her young son already, noting that "The looks he gives if something is annoying him, he gives this wrinkled up nose look," similar to her fiancé. "They have the same kind of expressions. When I look at him I see a lot of Emile in him." Matrau-Belt is expected to get out of the hospital tonight so that she can attend the funerals for her fiancé and mother later this week. "Don’t take life for granted," Matrau-Belt told ABC News. "You’ve got to cherish every moment. You don’t know when things are going to happen, especially if you’re on the way to the birth of your child and grandchild. You’ve got to be able to slow down and look at every part of life and cherish it." Matrau-Belt and Skokan had plans for their future together, with Skokan wanting to get married and make sure Matrau-Belt was ready before they could all have the same last name. Skokan was handy around the house and had been helping Matrau-Belt's mother and stepfather work on their house, which had caught fire in February 2015. "He loved helping my mom," Matrau-Belt said. "He loved my mom." Matrau-Belt described her fiancé as "caring, hard-working, really smart." She could not wait for him to be here, as her mother had been excited to meet her first biological grandchild and had bought "his entire wardrobe," a car seat, and a stroller. Matrau-Belt called Nichols "the most caring person I've ever met." Funeral arrangements for Skokan and Nichols are set, with Skokan's funeral at 11 a.m. Wednesday, Dec. 16, at Langeland Family Funeral Homes, Memorial Chapel, 622 S. Burdick St., and Nichols' funeral at 11 a.m. Friday, Dec. 18, with interment following at Mt. Ever-Rest Memorial Park South.
