Archaeologists are set to conduct a ground scan at Waltham Abbey Church in Essex, on the 950th anniversary of the Battle of Hastings, to investigate the possibility that King Harold II, the last Saxon king of England, survived the battle and lived for another 40 years as a hermit. The same team that discovered King Richard III's remains under a Leicester car park is now leading the search. According to Peter Burke, an amateur historian and author, the alternative theory is based on a 12th-century document called Vita Haroldi, which is housed in the British Museum. This document suggests that Harold Godwinson, who is traditionally believed to have been killed by an arrow to the eye and hacked down by four Norman knights, may have escaped death and lived until 1090. Burke believes that Harold was taken to Winchester for treatment and that his wife, Edith, may have used an unknown headless knight's grave to conceal his fate. The scan, funded by Burke and supported by Oval Films, the production company involved in the Richard III discovery, will take place in the Abbey gardens. If the scan reveals the presence of Harold's remains, a DNA test will be necessary to confirm his identity. The search could potentially rewrite history, as it challenges the widely accepted narrative of Harold's death at the Battle of Hastings. Burke, who has lived within 200 meters of Waltham Abbey for the past 29 years, has been researching this theory for the past five years. He hopes that the scan will uncover the body of a 6-foot-1-inch old man with scarring on his temple and cheek, which could be Harold. The scan is set to take place on October 14, the anniversary of the Battle of Hastings, and will be filmed for a documentary exploring this alternative history. While some members of the Waltham Abbey Historical Society doubt the likelihood of finding Harold's remains due to frequent disturbances at the site, Burke remains optimistic. He emphasizes the importance of questioning historical narratives and suggests that if the scan confirms his theory, it could lead to a significant reevaluation of the events surrounding the Battle of Hastings.

Kim Kardashian West was robbed at gunpoint in a private Paris residence, with millions of pounds worth of jewellery stolen by men disguised as police. The incident took place early Monday morning, with Kardashian West "badly shaken but physically unharmed" after being tied up in the flat’s bathroom. Five armed men, still at large, handcuffed the concierge and forced him to show them where Kardashian West was staying. They escaped on bicycles with a jewellery box valued at €6m (£5.2m) and a ring worth €4m. The 35-year-old had been in Paris for fashion week and had attended the Balenciaga show earlier on Sunday. Her husband, Kanye West, had abruptly ended his performance at the Meadows music and arts festival in New York on Sunday night, citing a “family emergency.” The reality star has remained silent on social media since the incident, though her name was trending on Twitter and Facebook. The robbery sparked criticism from political opponents to the Socialist government, with Nathalie Kosciusko-Morizet, a right-wing member of Paris council, saying the incident proved there is a "general emergency on security" in the French capital. Paris has been a special place for Kardashian West and her husband, who spent the weekend there before marrying in Florence in May 2014. The incident has raised questions about the security of the private apartment where Kardashian West was staying, located in the chic eighth district of Paris.

Boston Marathon bombing suspects Tamerlan and Dzhokhar Tsarnaev, ethnic Chechens from Russia, befriended a brain-damaged anti-U.S. government conspiracy theorist, Donald Larking, through their mother's health care aide job years before the deadly attack, according to a lawyer representing Larking. Larking, who has suffered brain damage since being shot in the head in 1974, shared radical publications with the brothers, including theories that the 9/11 attacks and the Newtown school shooting didn't happen or that the U.S. government was behind them. The brothers, who were helpful to the Larkings, reportedly attended the mosque with Larking, where Larking converted to Islam and still attends. The Tsarnaev brothers' apartment contained publications advocating violence to terrorize Islam's perceived enemies and bomb-making instructions. The relationship between the Tsarnaevs and Larking suggests that the brothers may have been influenced by Larking's views, though the lawyer believes Larking did not directly help them formulate ideas. The case highlights the complex social dynamics that may have influenced the Tsarnaev brothers' radicalization.

A fire in an Air Route Control Center in Aurora, Illinois, caused significant disruptions to air traffic, leading to the cancellation of hundreds of flights and delays at Chicago's O'Hare and Midway International Airports. Brian Howard, 36, of Naperville, has been charged with destruction of aircraft or aircraft facilities after allegedly setting the fire, cutting radar feeds, and damaging communications systems, which forced a ground stop at both airports. Howard, a contract employee with intimate knowledge of the facility, entered the building at around 5:06 a.m. and left a Facebook message referencing the facility's three-letter call number before starting the blaze. He was found lying on the floor, having inflicted self-inflicted stab wounds. Howard's actions caused extensive damage, including to the host computer and radar lines, leading to a reduced rate of flights in the Great Lakes region. The incident resulted in over 1,550 cancellations at O'Hare and 470 at Midway, with ripple effects on flights across the nation. Airlines urged travelers to check flight statuses, as the impact on the economy was significant. The FAA is assessing the damage and planning repairs, but it is unclear when operations will resume at full capacity. Howard's motive remains unclear, and he faces a possible sentence of up to 20 years in prison and a $250,000 fine if convicted. The incident highlights the critical role of air traffic control centers and the potential for individual actions to cause widespread disruptions.

United Airlines has introduced a new boarding process to reduce congestion and improve efficiency at the gates. The change, which went into effect this week, involves reducing the number of boarding lanes from five to two, with elite and priority passengers boarding through lane 1, while other passengers board through lane 2. This streamlined approach aims to alleviate the overcrowding and delays that have been reported at United gates, particularly during peak travel times. The airline is also implementing push notifications for passengers who have the United mobile app, allowing them to be informed when boarding begins, thus reducing the need for passengers to wait in line for extended periods. United claims that customer feedback played a significant role in the development of this new boarding process, with the goal of reducing wait times and improving the overall boarding experience. The new system is expected to benefit not only passengers but also the airline by ensuring that flights depart on time and minimizing delays. While the change is designed to be more efficient, it remains to be seen how well it will be received by passengers, especially those who are used to the previous five-lane boarding system. The new process is part of a broader effort by airlines to address the challenges of boarding in a congested and increasingly busy environment.

Ireland became the first country to legalize same-sex marriage via a popular vote, with 62% of voters supporting the measure, marking a significant social shift in a traditionally Catholic country. The referendum, which had the highest turnout in two decades, was celebrated with joy and national pride. Prime Minister Enda Kenny hailed the result as a "social revolution" and a "beacon of light" for the world. "Yes" supporters gathered at Dublin Castle to witness the results, with many breaking into the national anthem. The Catholic Church, which had opposed the measure, saw its influence wane, with Archbishop Diarmuid Martin acknowledging the challenge ahead. The victory was seen as a triumph for the "Yes" campaign, which received support from all political parties, big employers, and celebrities. The "No" campaign, which focused on religious and moral arguments, conceded defeat. The result was a clear victory across the country, with only one constituency voting against same-sex marriage. The referendum also highlighted the changing attitudes among younger voters, who traveled from across the country to cast their ballots. The victory for "Yes" was seen as a step towards equality for all, with Senator Averil Power stating that gay campaigners had helped change Ireland for everyone. The result was celebrated internationally, with US Vice President Joe Biden tweeting his support for Ireland's stance on equality.

California fish market owner Giovanni DeGarimore recently purchased a 70-pound octopus, named Fred, from a crab fisherman in San Luis Obispo County, with the sole intention of releasing him back into the wild. The purchase, costing "a couple hundred dollars," was made by DeGarimore, who owns Giovanni's Fish Market in Morro Bay. He released Fred the following day, driven by his personal belief that octopuses, known for their intelligence and unique nature, deserve to live freely in the ocean. DeGarimore, an avid diver and lover of the ocean, had previously sold octopus but found it increasingly difficult to justify after a close encounter with one while diving in Fiji. The octopus's story gained traction on the business's Facebook page, where it was shared hundreds of times. Despite the high cost, DeGarimore felt it was a meaningful act, stating, "It might not change the world, but I'm going to do one thing and if it only makes me and Fred happy, that's okay too." This incident highlights the complex relationship between humans and marine life, particularly as concerns about overfishing and the welfare of intelligent creatures like octopuses continue to grow.

House Republicans have moved to impeach IRS Commissioner John Koskinen, accusing him of violating the public trust and misleading Congress during the investigation into the agency's improper scrutiny of conservative groups. Oversight Committee Chairman Jason Chaffetz (R-Utah) introduced an impeachment resolution, arguing that Koskinen failed to comply with a congressional subpoena, destroyed 422 backup tapes containing potentially relevant documents, and misled lawmakers about the availability of emails from former official Lois Lerner. Chaffetz stated, "Commissioner Koskinen violated the public trust. He failed to comply with a congressionally issued subpoena, documents were destroyed on his watch, and the public was consistently misled." The resolution claims that Koskinen's actions have undermined public confidence in the IRS and the legislative branch. However, the IRS maintains that it has fully cooperated with all investigations and disputes the allegations. House Democrats have denounced the move as political grandstanding, with Rep. Elijah Cummings (D-Md.) calling the impeachment resolution "ridiculous" and a waste of taxpayer money. The impeachment process, while unusual, is a significant step beyond previous attempts to hold IRS officials accountable through contempt charges.

On August 9, 2014, Port St. Lucie police officers captured a 12-foot, 120-pound Burmese python that neighbors suspected was preying on their cats. The snake, found hiding in waist-high brush, killed one cat and may have been responsible for the recent disappearances of several others. Sgt. John Holman discovered the dead cat before locating the large python. Despite Florida's ban on Burmese pythons in 2012, the snake was owned by an individual with a license to keep it. This incident highlights the ongoing issues with invasive species in the area and the potential risks they pose to local wildlife.

A former physician, Dr. Henry Bello, who was fired from Bronx Lebanon Hospital in 2015 amid a sexual harassment scandal, opened fire at the hospital on June 30, 2017, killing one person and injuring six others. Dr. Kamran Ahmed, who worked with Bello, expressed shock at being singled out by the shooter. Bello, 45, had a history of conflict with colleagues and had previously warned Ahmed that he would return to the hospital to kill him. On the day of the shooting, Bello entered the hospital with an assault rifle hidden under his lab coat and approached Dr. Roger Green, who was not his intended target. Green managed to escape, raising the first alerts of an active shooter. Bello then proceeded to the 17th floor, where he encountered Dr. Tracy Sin-Yee Tam, 32, a family medicine doctor who was covering a shift as a favor. Tam was killed, and Bello set fire to the nurse’s station before committing suicide. The six injured individuals were hospitalized, with one remaining in critical condition. Bello had purchased the assault rifle in Schenectady a week before the incident. His former co-workers described him as aggressive and threatening. The shooting left the hospital staff in shock, with Ahmed noting, "It makes you think that anything can happen to anybody." The incident also highlighted the hospital's vulnerability to such attacks, with Ahmed's neighbor, Alena Khaim, expressing her grief over Tam's loss.

Al Qaeda's leader Ayman al-Zawahiri claimed responsibility for the kidnapping of Warren Weinstein, an American aid worker in Pakistan, and issued demands for his release in a video message. Weinstein, a 70-year-old development expert, was abducted by armed men from his home in Lahore on August 13. Al-Zawahiri demanded the release of all al-Qaeda and Taliban suspects worldwide and the cessation of U.S. airstrikes in Afghanistan, Pakistan, Somalia, and Yemen. Weinstein, who worked for J.E. Austin Associates, a U.S.-based consulting firm, had been in Pakistan for several years and spoke Urdu. His health had been deteriorating, with a detailed list of medications, many for heart problems, provided by his employer. The U.S. government and his family pushed for his release, but he was killed in a U.S. drone strike targeting an al-Qaeda compound in January, along with another hostage, Italian aid worker Giovanni Lo Porto.

The Boy Scouts of America has revoked the charter of a Seattle-area church-sponsored troop after the church refused to fire its openly gay Scoutmaster, Geoff McGrath. The Boy Scouts, which recently voted to allow gay youth but not gay adult leaders, informed leaders and parents of the children in Troop 98 and its Cub Scout pack that Rainier Beach United Methodist Church is no longer authorized to be a charter partner. Boy Scout troops require a charter partner for meeting space and financial support, and the organization's policies ban gay adults from membership. Deron Smith, a Boy Scouts spokesman, stated that the church no longer agrees to the terms of the BSA chartered organization agreement, including following BSA policies. The church's pastor, Rev. Monica Corsaro, expressed that her congregation’s anti-discrimination beliefs were not respected and called the decision a "unilateral" action by the BSA. She said the church would still offer a youth program but had not had a chance to discuss the details. The Boy Scouts have been grappling with their controversial membership policy, which allowed gay youth to join but not adults, since last May's vote. Troop 98 got its start shortly after the contentious ballot, formed to address the lack of youth programs in the area. McGrath, a married Eagle Scout, was believed to be the first openly gay adult to be dismissed from the Boy Scouts of America since the policy change. He expressed shock at the BSA's decision and stated that discussions were already underway about the future of the youth organization. The Boy Scouts have identified a new chartered organization to sponsor the units and are contacting the parents and leaders to inform them of the change.

In El Salvador prior to President Obama’s 2011 visit, a U.S. government subcontractor witnessed about a dozen Secret Service agents and a few military specialists drinking heavily and engaging in sexual activities with strippers at a strip club. The subcontractor claims the agents were "wasted" and "heavily intoxicated" and paid for VIP access to the club, where they received sexual favors. Despite warnings, some agents reportedly bragged about their actions. The strip club owner confirmed a large number of U.S. Secret Service agents and military escorts visited his establishment over multiple nights. He stated his club is known for "security" and "privacy," catering to high-ranking U.S. embassy employees and visiting FBI and DEA agents. The Secret Service is investigating the claims, which are similar to recent incidents in Colombia that led to a widespread probe. House Oversight Committee Chairman Darrell Issa and Sen. Chuck Grassley called for an independent investigation, citing the need to address rumors of misconduct by Secret Service agents and other law enforcement and military personnel in various locations. The Secret Service maintains there is no evidence of additional misconduct, but the incident has raised concerns about the agency's culture and oversight.

On the first day of his tenure as President Trump’s national security adviser, Michael Flynn found himself in a precarious position. He was summoned by FBI agents for questioning about his conversations with Russia’s ambassador, a meeting that any White House official would dread. While the exact details of what Flynn said remain undisclosed, current and former government officials reported that investigators believed he was not entirely forthcoming. This led to a chain of events that culminated in Flynn’s resignation, thrusting the Trump administration into a fresh crisis.

Flynn’s rapid rise and fall mirrored the typical pattern in Washington, where ambitious figures often secure high positions only to lose them due to contradictions, recriminations, and scandal. Flynn’s case, however, was unique in its brevity; he held his post for just 24 days. His resignation raised questions about what President Trump knew and when, particularly regarding the relationship between the Trump administration and Russia.

Conservative radio host Rush Limbaugh accused the media of orchestrating Flynn’s ouster, claiming they were trying to secure a “scalp” and would continue to impede the Trump administration. This sentiment was echoed by others, including Trump himself, who tweeted about the “illegal leaks” coming out of Washington.

Leading members of the Republican Party called for a wide investigation into Flynn’s alleged ties with Russia. The White House initially stated that President Trump was unaware of the issues with Flynn’s interactions with the Russian ambassador until a Washington Post report revealed the extent of the problem. However, it later emerged that Trump was informed of the concerns as early as January 26, more than two weeks before Flynn’s resignation.

Flynn’s resignation was precipitated by his alleged misleading of Vice President Mike Pence about whether he had discussed US sanctions during pre-inauguration phone calls with the Russian ambassador. Flynn claimed he “crossed no lines” in his conversation with the ambassador, but acknowledged that he had given “incomplete information” to Pence. He also expressed concern over the “unprecedented” leaks of classified information, which he believed were part of a broader disinformation campaign.

The FBI had interviewed Flynn in the early days of the administration about the calls to the Russian ambassador, adding to the intrigue surrounding his interactions with Moscow. Flynn’s departure did not end questions about contacts between Trump’s campaign and Russia. Democrats and some Republicans called for congressional probes into Trump’s ties to Moscow, despite resistance from some House Republicans.

The controversy also raised questions about the relationship between the Trump administration and Russian President Vladimir Putin. Many Washington insiders were astonished by Trump’s frequent defenses of Putin and his determination to improve relations with the Kremlin, despite Moscow’s Cold War-style confrontational policies. This situation prompted Republican senators to call for investigations, while the White House pushed back, focusing on the source of the leaks.

The Flynn affair added to the confusion and internal strife within the Trump administration as it struggled to find its footing. It also highlighted the ongoing uncertainty about the relationship between the United States and Russia, particularly in light of intelligence reports of Russian intervention in the 2016 election. As the administration faced multiple controversies, the Flynn case thrust Trump’s admiration for Putin back into the spotlight, prompting further scrutiny from both allies and critics alike.

Venezuela’s political crisis took a dramatic turn on June 27, 2017, when a police helicopter, allegedly piloted by Oscar Pérez, launched an attack on the Supreme Court and Interior Ministry in Caracas. The incident, which President Nicolas Maduro called a “terrorist” attack, left the country in shock. Pérez, a former police captain, identified himself as the mastermind in a video posted on Instagram, where he declared a coalition of military employees, policemen, and civilians against what he called a “criminal government.” He claimed to be acting against “tyranny” and “impunity,” and urged Venezuelans to join the fight.

The helicopter, which carried a banner reading “350 Freedom,” dropped four Israeli-made grenades on the Supreme Court and fired 15 shots at the Interior Ministry. Despite the intensity of the attack, no one was injured, and one grenade failed to detonate. The government immediately launched a manhunt for Pérez, who was last seen in Washington, D.C. Venezuela’s vice president, Tareck El Aissami, urged the public to help find the pilot, calling him a “fanatic, extremist terrorist.”

Opposition leaders were quick to suspect the attack might have been staged by the government to justify further repression. They pointed to the timing of the incident, which coincided with a judicial measure weakening the powers of the opposition-aligned chief prosecutor, Luisa Ortega. Ortega, who had broken with the government, was accused of “serious offenses” by the Supreme Court. The helicopter attack also came as the opposition was preparing to block a vote on July 30 for a new constituent assembly, which Maduro sees as a way to rewrite the constitution and maintain power.

The incident exacerbated the already tense situation, with opposition supporters taking to the streets and clashing with security forces. President Maduro condemned the violence and warned that if the opposition failed to accept the results of the vote, the government would use force. The government accused Pérez of links to the CIA and former Interior Minister Miguel Rodriguez, who denied any involvement. The attack underscored the deep divisions in Venezuelan society and the ongoing struggle for power in a country grappling with severe economic and political crises.

A Moldovan dancer who was on the bridge of the Costa Concordia with Captain Francesco Schettino during the ship's grounding off the Italian coast has admitted to being his lover during his trial. Domnica Cemortan testified that she was with the captain when the cruise ship ran aground on a reef, killing 32 people. She faced intense media scrutiny, with local press speculating about the distraction or even the captain showing off during the incident. Cemortan stated she had worked for the cruise line for about three weeks in December 2011 and had met the captain previously. She claimed she helped other passengers evacuate the ship before getting into a lifeboat herself. The trial of Captain Schettino, who faces multiple charges including manslaughter and abandoning ship, is expected to hear evidence from around 1,000 survivors and crew members. Schettino has admitted fault but blames his Indonesian helmsman for steering the ship onto the rocks and ignoring orders to slow down. An Italian naval expert testified that the helmsman's actions were not crucial to the crash. The captain also blamed the ship's watertight doors for not functioning. The Costa Concordia was righted in September 2013 after a complex salvage operation, and the remains of one of the two missing individuals, Maria Grazia Trecarichi, were recovered. Plans are underway to remove the wreckage next year.

Nick Stoeberl, a 24-year-old artist and comedian from California, USA, has claimed the world record for the longest tongue, with his impressive 10.1 cm (3.97 inches) lingua. This achievement is featured in the latest Guinness World Records 2015 book, marking the 60th anniversary edition of the world’s best-selling record book. Stoeberl’s father was a big fan of KISS, and young Nick would imitate Gene Simmons’ iconic tongue pose, realizing early on that his tongue was notably longer than most. He boasts that he can not only lick his nose but also his elbow, though he admits to spending extra time brushing his tongue in the morning. This record-breaking feat surpasses the previous holder, British man Stephen Taylor, whose tongue measured 9.8 cm. The 2015 book is packed with incredible feats and achievements, including new Augmented Reality technology that brings record-breakers to life in stunning 3D. Readers can explore more about the book on the official Guinness World Records website. For the latest on all things world record, including the 2015 book, follow Guinness World Records on Facebook, Twitter, Google+, and Instagram. The YouTube channel also features the latest record-breaking videos, including the world's longest usable golf club and the largest collection of James Bond memorabilia.

ABC has announced a revival of the iconic family sitcom Roseanne, bringing the Connor clan back to the network that made them household names. Network president Channing Dungey confirmed the plans for the new eight-episode revival during a conference call with reporters ahead of ABC's 2017 Upfronts week in New York City. The reboot, set to air midseason, will find the Connors continuing to deal with the economic challenges of living paycheck to paycheck in 2018. Original cast members Roseanne Barr, John Goodman, Sara Gilbert, Laurie Metcalf, Michael Fishman, and Lecy Goranson are all set to return, with Sarah Chalke also joining the cast in a different role. The revival is expected to debut sometime midseason, with a formal date to be announced later. The series will again be a multicamera comedy, produced by independent studio Carsey-Werner Television and exec produced by Gilbert, original exec producers Barr, Tom Werner, and Bruce Helford, as well as Whitney Cummings and Tony Hernandez. The pickup comes almost 20 years after the Emmy-winning multicam went off the air and as networks have worked to better appeal to working-class middle America in the wake of Donald Trump's stunning victory in the 2016 presidential election. Roseanne will be one of two revivals on the Disney-owned broadcaster, alongside American Idol, which was resurrected only a year after Fox opted to cancel the singing competition. The network will start the fall 2017-18 season without a single multicamera comedy on its schedule, as pilot Household Name, starring Carol Burnett, is being redeveloped.

In a segment on Last Week Tonight, host John Oliver critically examines Donald Trump’s proposal for a border wall between the United States and Mexico. Oliver highlights several key issues with the plan, including its escalating cost, which has been estimated by experts at around $25 billion, significantly higher than Trump’s previous estimates of $4 billion to $12 billion. He also questions the feasibility of Mexico paying for the wall, noting that Mexican officials have rejected the idea. Oliver points out the geographical challenges, such as the Rio Grande river, which cannot be obstructed by the wall due to a 1970 treaty, leading to potential logistical nightmares. The effectiveness of the wall is also scrutinized, as nearly half of unauthorized immigrants enter legally and then remain in the country without authorization. Additionally, Oliver suggests that a $75 electric waffle iron for every American would be a more effective and less costly solution, arguing that it would achieve similar goals of keeping out immigrants and drugs without harming the relationship with Mexico. The segment humorously concludes with a poll question about which dog would make the best Merrick Garland on a hypothetical Dog Supreme Court, underscoring the absurdity of the wall proposal.

A Cobb County police lieutenant has been fired after being caught on dashcam video during a traffic stop in 2016 saying "we only shoot black people," the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reports. Cobb County Police Chief Mike Register announced the firing at a news conference, emphasizing that "there's really no place for these types of comments in law enforcement." The video, obtained by WSB-TV through an open-records request, shows Abbott, a white officer, interrupting a woman who was scared to move her hands to retrieve her cellphone and saying, "But you're not black. Remember, we only shoot black people. Yeah. We only shoot black people, right?" Register stated that Abbott, who had been on the force for 28 years, was placed on administrative leave pending an investigation. Abbott's attorney, Lance LoRusso, said Abbott was cooperating with the investigation and that his comments were meant to "de-escalate a situation involving an uncooperative passenger." Register, who has been chief since June, acknowledged that several seconds of video could potentially damage the department's relationship with the community. "It's sad to think that several seconds of video has the potential of tearing that apart," he said. Black community leaders applauded Register's quick action, with Deane Bonner of the Cobb County chapter of the NAACP stating that the officer's comments were "particularly troubling and may be systematic, a deeper issue in the department." Ben Williams, chairman of the Cobb County chapter of the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, emphasized that "the real story here, in my opinion, is the behavior of this police chief in Cobb County, Georgia." Register maintained that Abbott was trying to be sarcastic and address the situation as he perceived it, but admitted that "it's inexcusable."

Cypriot officials are investigating reports of a meteor that reportedly exploded with a loud bang, causing the ground to shake, over the island. Eyewitnesses described a blue glow and a series of loud noises heard in Nicosia and Limassol districts. Police received hundreds of calls from the south coast and inland areas. The Cyprus Geological Department suggests the object likely exploded in the sky and is searching for any debris. Civil aviation authorities report no unusual activity in the airspace. Meteors, which are pieces of comet or asteroid that create fireballs as they enter the Earth's atmosphere, may have caused the phenomenon. If confirmed, this would be the first meteorite fall in Cyprus in recent history, providing valuable information about the early solar system.

The mayor of Venice, Luigi Brugnaro, has vowed to get justice after four Japanese tourists complained about an eye-watering €1,100 bill for a meal at a restaurant near St Mark's Square. The four students, who are actually from Bologna, say they were charged for four steaks, a plate of fried fish, water, and service. Italian media report that even the three women who chose another restaurant ended up paying €350 for three plates of seafood pasta. The mayor has promised to thoroughly examine the case and punish those responsible if the complaint is confirmed. Marco Gasparinetti, spokesman for a Venice residents' forum called "Gruppo 25 Aprile," has taken up the case and plans to post advice for tourists on Facebook to help them avoid similar scams. The mayor has faced criticism for his response to tourists who claim they were overcharged. He called a British family who complained about a €500 bill "cheapskates" and said they should have known better. The mayor also tweeted a photo of an €11 bill for four coffees from a café in Austria, questioning why he should write to the mayor of Vienna about it. A citizens' group claims the mayor is "selling Venice by the pound" and that his attitude towards visitors is unacceptable. The city has long struggled with overtourism and the mayor has introduced measures to reduce the number of tourists, including limiting tourist accommodation and installing automatic people-counters in high-traffic areas. Last week, Italy's national government approved plans to ban cruise ships from the center of Venice.

Experts from the UN's cultural body Unesco have concluded that a wreck off the coast of Haiti is not the long-lost remains of the Santa Maria, the flagship of Christopher Columbus's first voyage to the Americas. Unesco's team, led by the former head of the Spanish National Museum on Underwater Archaeology, Xavier Nieto Prieto, examined the site and found that the artefacts and construction techniques do not match those of the 15th century Santa Maria. The report states that the ship is more likely from the late 17th or 18th century, based on the nature of the fasteners found at the site. Barry Clifford, an American marine archaeologist, had previously announced that he believed he had found the Santa Maria, citing geographical and underwater topography evidence, as well as the presence of what he thought was a 15th-century cannon. However, the Unesco experts found that the metallic tube Clifford had seen was no longer at the site, and that the wreck was further from shore than expected. They also noted that the site was not consistent with historical accounts of the Santa Maria's location and condition. Unesco now plans to search for the Santa Maria in other areas, including coastal marshlands near En Bas Saline and La Petite Anse, as well as on the seabed. The report's rejection of Clifford's site has sparked controversy among scholars, who argue that the evidence from his 2003 expedition, including photographs of what may be 15th-century cannons, should be re-evaluated. The Santa Maria was Columbus's flagship, which ran aground near Haiti in December 1492, and its discovery would be a significant archaeological find. The Unesco report may also have implications for the US public's perception of the organization, as the US has been in a strained relationship with Unesco for the past three years.

Tiffany & Co., the renowned luxury jeweler, has cited protests and security measures around Trump Tower as a factor in its recent sales slump, according to its latest financial report. The company noted a 2% decline in comparable store sales for the quarter ending October 31, 2016, attributing some of the drop to "recent election-related activity" near its flagship Fifth Avenue store. This store, immortalized in the 1961 film "Breakfast at Tiffany's," has been the site of numerous protests and heightened security since the election. Despite the store's symbolic importance, it only accounted for less than 10% of Tiffany's global sales, according to the company. However, Tiffany remains cautious about the potential long-term impact of the protests and security measures on its sales. The company reported a 1% increase in worldwide net sales to $949 million, with a 2% decline in comparable store sales. Sales in Japan and China showed improvement, driven by a stronger yen and increased tourist spending. Tiffany's strategy to attract younger customers and boost sales through new product lines and marketing efforts appears to be showing some success, as fashion jewelry sales performed well. Nevertheless, Tiffany's outlook for the current quarter remains cautious, as the company cannot predict the impact of ongoing protests and security measures on its flagship store's performance.

A significant proportion of the weapons in the "Islamic State" (IS) arsenal were manufactured in the European Union, according to a 200-page study published by Conflict Armament Research (CAR). The weapons, recovered from IS frontline positions in Syria and Iraq between 2014 and 2017, included guns, ammunition, and components used to make explosive devices. More than 30 percent of the arms used by IS were manufactured in Bulgaria, Romania, Hungary, and Germany, while Russia and China produced more than half of the weapons held by the terror group. The study highlighted that most IS weapons were looted from Iraqi and Syrian armies, but arms purchased from eastern European nations by Saudi Arabia and the United States and then supplied to Syrian opposition forces also ended up in IS hands. CAR found that many of these transfers violated the terms of sale and export agreements between weapon exporters and recipients. The report emphasized the contradictions in supplying weapons to conflicts with multiple competing non-state armed groups. CAR's findings underscore the risks of supplying weapons to unprepared or poorly trained groups, as evidenced by the diversion of weapons from intended recipients to IS. The study also revealed that IS had stockpiled weapons, including 122 Chinese-made light machine guns, with amphetamines attached for performance enhancement. The report concluded that IS's arsenal, combined with its global reach, logistical capacity, and willing recruits, posed a significant threat beyond the region.

John McCone, an industrialist and engineer, took over as director of the CIA in 1961, succeeding Allen Dulles, following the Bay of Pigs fiasco. McCone’s primary mission was to restore order at the CIA, which faced significant challenges. After President Kennedy’s assassination in 1963, McCone remained in his position, becoming a key witness for the Warren Commission. He testified that the CIA had no evidence of a conspiracy and portrayed Lee Harvey Oswald as a lone assassin. However, a 2013 CIA report, declassified in 2014, reveals that McCone and other senior officials may have withheld critical information from the Warren Commission. The report suggests that McCone was involved in a "benign cover-up" to keep the commission focused on Oswald’s lone-wolf status, while concealing CIA plots to assassinate Fidel Castro, some of which involved the Mafia. This omission may have prevented the commission from investigating potential Cuban or Soviet involvement. Despite the CIA’s assertion that the Warren Commission’s findings were accurate, the report highlights the agency’s role in misleading the commission. It also mentions that McCone had frequent, informal contacts with Robert Kennedy, the attorney general, during the days following the assassination, raising questions about possible connections between the administration’s anti-Castro activities and the president’s death. The CIA’s decision to declassify the report, albeit with some redactions, indicates a willingness to address past improprieties, even if it came decades after the events.

Rosie O'Donnell recently experienced a "widow maker" heart attack but kept it secret until now, revealing the ordeal in a poem on her blog. On Tuesday morning, while walking in a parking lot, she heard a woman asking for help, which turned out to be a sign of her own impending heart attack. She experienced chest pain, nausea, and vomiting but did not call 911, relying on a TV commercial to remember to take aspirin. The next day, after an EKG, doctors found her left anterior descending artery 99% blocked and inserted a stent. O'Donnell warns other women to know the symptoms and to call 911, emphasizing the importance of recognizing and addressing heart attack signs.

Pacific Coast News reports that Neal McDonough, a married Catholic father of three, recently left a role on the ABC show Scoundrels after the script required him to participate in a sex scene, a decision he made to adhere to his principles. This incident highlights McDonough's steadfast refusal to engage in any sex scenes throughout his career. The article draws attention to the broader issue of marital stability and the challenges of modern monogamous relationships, as discussed in the book "Sex at Dawn" by Christopher Ryan and Cacilda Jethá. According to the authors, the current understanding of marriage and monogamy is at odds with human evolutionary history, which suggests that pre-agricultural humans lived in less sexually possessive cultures. They argue that the nuclear family and lifelong monogamy are recent social constructs, not natural human behaviors. The book challenges the notion that love and sex are inherently intertwined, proposing that the insistence on monogamy in modern society leads to significant emotional and psychological distress. Ryan and Jethá use evidence from human physiology, archaeology, primate biology, and anthropological studies to support their claims, suggesting that humans are naturally inclined towards non-monogamous relationships. The authors also discuss the implications of human testicle size and penis design, which they believe indicate a history of sperm competition and non-monogamous behavior. They caution that the modern emphasis on strict monogamy, exemplified by the Bill Clinton-Lewinsky scandal, may be counterproductive and suggest that a more open and tolerant approach to human sexuality could lead to healthier relationships.

U.S. District Judge Denise Cote ruled that Nomura Holdings Inc. and Royal Bank of Scotland Group Plc may face $500 million in damages for selling defective mortgage-backed securities to government-owned mortgage companies Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. In a 361-page opinion, Cote criticized the banks for making false statements in offering documents, stating, "The magnitude of falsity, conservatively measured, is enormous." The ruling may encourage other banks to settle similar claims related to the 2008 financial crisis. Cote ordered the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) to propose damages, with the agency entitled to $624.4 million, minus over $178 million in payments received since the lawsuit began in 2011. Nomura and RBS plan to appeal, arguing they were "confident that they were consistently candid, transparent and professional in all of their dealings with Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac." The case was the first to reach trial out of 18 filed by the FHFA over $200 billion in mortgage-backed securities sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Judge Cote noted that the securities were supported by loans with "materially defective" mortgages, and that the banks' misconduct exacerbated the collapse of the housing market.

A judge in Phoenix, Arizona, on Tuesday reduced the bond for Leslie Merritt Jr., allowing him to be released from jail amid ongoing questions about evidence linking him to freeway shootings that caused panic in the area last year, the Associated Press reports. Merritt, who has pleaded not guilty to drive-by shooting and aggravated assault charges, was initially held on a $1 million bond but was released after the judge set his bond to zero, permitting his return home under electronic monitoring. Defense lawyers argued that ballistic tests cast doubt on the claims by authorities that Merritt was responsible for the four freeway shootings. "With all due respect your honor, there's no evidence against him to show he's responsible for this," defense lawyer Jason Lamm said, adding that Merritt was "no more the I-10 shooter than, respectfully, you are." Merritt's family celebrated his release, hugging and shaking hands with his legal team. The judge, Warren Granville, imposed a gag order on the case, preventing lawyers from discussing the evidence that prompted the bond reduction. Merritt's lawyers have raised questions about ballistics information and phone records they claim provide an alibi for their client. They also pointed to other road rage incidents that occurred after Merritt's arrest, suggesting the real culprit was still at large. The freeway shootings, which targeted 11 vehicles in August and September, led to heightened patrols and surveillance by authorities. Governor Doug Ducey declared "We got him!" on Twitter shortly after Merritt's arrest. Merritt's case is set for a May 18 court date, and the judge emphasized the importance of his attendance. Merritt responded, "I'll be here sir," showing his commitment to facing the charges.

In the chaotic final days of Moammar Gaddafi’s rule, desperate prisoners in Libya faced unimaginable horrors. Muneer Masoud Own, 33, survived the harrowing ordeal of nearly 150 detainees being slaughtered as rebels approached Tripoli. He and his brother were detained for 18 days in a warehouse, where they endured abuse, starvation, and the stench of human waste. On the day of promised release, guards instead threw a grenade and opened fire, killing dozens. Own barely escaped, but his brother’s fate remains unknown. Meanwhile, Faraj, a 25-year-old rebel, and thousands of others went missing during the six-month conflict. The Transitional National Council has freed thousands from Gaddafi’s prisons but has accounted for only about 10,000, leaving families to fear the worst for the missing. The Abu Salim prison, notorious for its brutality, was reopened, and freed prisoners shared harrowing stories of torture and abuse. The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Gaddafi and his aides, intensifying the pressure on the regime. As the conflict rages on, the search for the missing and the truth about their fate continues.

Libyan leader Moammar Gaddafi, in an interview with the BBC, denied any protests in Tripoli and insisted that his people would die to protect him. Gaddafi laughed at the suggestion he would leave Libya, stating he could not step down as he did not have an official position and that power was with the people. He accused Western countries of abandoning Libya and said they had no morals, wanting to colonize the country. US Ambassador to the UN Susan Rice described Gaddafi as "delusional" and "unfit to lead," noting his comments while civilians were being killed. World foreign ministers condemned attacks on Libyan civilians, and the European Union imposed sanctions including an arms embargo, asset freeze, and travel ban on Gaddafi and his close entourage. Gaddafi accused al Qaeda of encouraging young people to seize arms and claimed protesters were under the influence of drugs. He denied using force against his people, but protests in eastern Libya had secured towns, and there was fighting in Misrata. The UN estimated 100,000 people had fled the unrest, with long queues at banks in Tripoli as the government tried to quell the unrest. Libyan air force planes reportedly attacked ammunition depots in eastern towns. Deputy Foreign Minister Khaled Kaim said authorities would attempt to talk to protesters but would use force if necessary. Gaddafi's defiant stance contrasted with the reality on the ground, as anti-government forces still controlled Zawiya and repelled a government counter-attack in Misrata.

The Syrian regime faces potential U.S. intervention if it deploys its chemical weapons arsenal, with Pentagon contingency plans in place to secure or destroy these weapons. President Obama warned Assad that any use or movement of chemical weapons would cross a "red line" and invite U.S. military action. However, officials stress that a large-scale U.S. intervention is unlikely unless part of an international coalition. The White House is considering sending special operations teams to secure chemical weapons depots, focusing on preventing them from falling into the hands of rebel fighters or extremist groups. U.S. intelligence suggests Syria has produced or acquired hundreds of tons of sarin nerve agent and mustard gas, with some stockpiles near key cities. Despite the threat, Pentagon officials note that the Syrian stockpiles seem well guarded for now, and no detailed plans have been made for securing the facilities. The U.S. is closely monitoring the sites but acknowledges the risk of some materials, like small artillery shells, being relocated undetected. The Syrian government denies using chemical weapons against civilians, claiming they would only be used in response to foreign intervention. Meanwhile, the conflict continues to intensify, with heavy shelling in Damascus and ongoing urban warfare in Aleppo. The U.S. and Israel express concerns about the potential loss of control over chemical weapons, while Russia believes Syria has no intention of using them and can safeguard them. The situation remains volatile, with the U.N. mediator, Lakhdar Brahimi, meeting with the Free Syrian Army to discuss ways to end the violence.

New details have emerged about the events leading up to Demi Moore's hospitalization for "exhaustion" on Monday night. According to E! News, the 49-year-old actress hosted a birthday dinner party for a close friend, Heather Parry, a former MTV executive, in her Beverly Hills home. The party, attended by a small group of Moore's girlfriends, including Jennifer Meyer, wife of Tobey Maguire, was described as a "few girlfriends" gathering, not a "big rager," with no male guests present. Moore was reportedly "pretty hyper" and "acting crazy" throughout the evening, leaving and returning several times. After dessert, Moore reportedly began convulsing and acting "like she was having a seizure," prompting a friend to call 911. Paramedics rushed her to a nearby hospital. Moore's representatives have stated that she is seeking treatment for anorexia and substance abuse, including the use of Adderall. Her publicist has said that her exhaustion and health issues are being addressed. Meanwhile, Ashton Kutcher, her ex-husband, has been partying in Brazil and has not commented publicly on Moore's hospitalization. A source close to Kutcher insists that he is "deeply concerned" for Moore's well-being.

Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway, and JPMorgan Chase have partnered to tackle the high costs of healthcare for their combined 1.1 million U.S. employees, aiming to improve services and reduce expenses. The trio announced the formation of an independent company that will focus on technology solutions to simplify healthcare, with the ultimate goal of providing high-quality, transparent care at a reasonable cost. The project, spearheaded by executives from each company, seeks to address the complex and costly healthcare system, which has been a significant burden on the American economy. 

Warren Buffett, CEO of Berkshire Hathaway, emphasized the urgent need for innovation in healthcare, stating that the rising costs act as a "hungry tapeworm" on the economy. Jeff Bezos, CEO of Amazon, and Jamie Dimon, CEO of JPMorgan Chase, echoed this sentiment, expressing their commitment to finding solutions that benefit not only their employees but potentially all Americans. The new company will operate independently and will not be driven by profit-making incentives, ensuring a focus on the well-being of employees and their families.

The move has sent shockwaves through the healthcare sector, with shares of major healthcare companies falling sharply. Analysts and experts view this partnership as a significant step towards disrupting the traditional healthcare system, which has been criticized for its complexity and lack of transparency. However, the success of the initiative remains uncertain, as the details of the project are still in the early planning stages. The companies hope to leverage their collective resources and expertise to develop innovative solutions that could lead to meaningful improvements in healthcare delivery and cost management.

In April 2012, just days before George Zimmerman was arrested for the shooting death of 17-year-old Trayvon Martin, his fellow neighborhood watch volunteer Frank Taaffe emerged as a vocal supporter, giving numerous interviews and defending Zimmerman on national television. Taaffe portrayed Martin as a drug-addled hoodlum and Zimmerman as a community-minded do-gooder, while accusing Zimmerman’s critics of a witch hunt. However, Taaffe's own history is marked by a lengthy criminal record, including charges of domestic violence and burglary, and he has aired virulently racist views. He appeared on a white supremacist podcast, where he argued that whites and blacks should not mingle and that young black males were responsible for burglaries in their neighborhood. Taaffe’s Twitter feed also contained racially charged comments. Despite his support for Zimmerman, Taaffe testified before a grand jury that he received a call from an unknown number two years earlier, in which the caller made racist comments about Martin. Taaffe now believes that Zimmerman may have racially targeted Martin. His change of heart came after the deaths of his two sons, which allowed him to identify more strongly with the Martin family. Taaffe hopes his testimony will make amends with the Martin family and clear his conscience. His support for Zimmerman had caused his daughter, a U.S. Marine, to be ostracized, damaging their relationship. Taaffe's testimony is part of a federal investigation into whether Zimmerman violated Martin's civil rights.

The condition of Yulia Skripal, the daughter of a former Russian double agent, has improved significantly since she was poisoned with a nerve agent in Salisbury, according to doctors. Yulia, 33, is no longer in critical condition and is described as stable, though she continues to receive expert clinical care. Her father, Sergei Skripal, 66, remains in critical but stable condition. Dr. Christine Blanshard, the medical director for Salisbury District Hospital, expressed gratitude to the hospital staff for their care and highlighted the improvement in Yulia's condition. The hospital stated that Yulia has responded well to treatment but still requires 24-hour expert care.

Meanwhile, Russian authorities are retaliating against the expulsion of their diplomats by expelling an equal number of British diplomats and closing down the British Council in Russia. This tit-for-tat action by Russia follows the UK's expulsion of 23 Russian diplomats in response to the poisoning incident. The UK government has accused Russia of being behind the attack, which used the nerve agent Novichok, and has imposed a series of sanctions, including the expulsion of Russian diplomats and the closure of the Russian consulate in St. Petersburg. In response, Russia has expelled 60 US diplomats and closed the US consulate general in St. Petersburg.

Detectives investigating the case have placed a cordon around a children's play area near Sergei Skripal's home as a precautionary measure. The police are continuing to focus their inquiries around the Skripals' home address. The investigation involves examining over 5,000 hours of CCTV footage and 1,350 exhibits, with 500 witnesses identified. The nerve agent Novichok, which was used in the attack, is known to work by attacking the nervous system, preventing chemical messages from being transmitted around the body, causing the heart to slow and airways to constrict.

The Skripals were found collapsed on a bench at the Maltings shopping centre in Salisbury on March 4. Forensic tests revealed that the highest concentration of the nerve agent was found on the front door of Sergei Skripal's home. The nerve agent was also detected at other locations in the town, but in lower concentrations. A police officer who was exposed to the nerve agent, Det Sgt Nick Bailey, was treated in hospital but was discharged on March 22. The case is being treated as an attempted murder, and the investigation is expected to continue for months.

County officials in San Juan, Utah, have declared a state of emergency and are preparing to take control of national park areas within their jurisdiction, reopening them to the public despite federal park closures. The San Juan County Commission has decided to mobilize local law enforcement, search and rescue volunteers, and other resources to manage the parks, with an estimated 60 people involved. The move is driven by the economic impact on local businesses, which heavily rely on visitors to national parks, monuments, and public lands. Approximately 70 percent of the county's businesses depend on these visitors, and 91 percent of the land is state, federal, or Indian reservation land. The commissioners are seeking financial assistance from the state of Utah and are prepared to provide toilet facilities, collect garbage, conduct search and rescue operations, and staff park entrances. They plan to explain their actions as being in the best interests of the public. Governor Gary Herbert has pledged to support the county's efforts and has asked President Obama for immediate authorization to fund or staff the reopened parks. The county's actions, while described as civil disobedience, are seen as a response to the closure of national park areas and the potential economic harm to local communities.

A Bronxville resident, 43-year-old William McCormack, is suing Lawrence Hospital Center, alleging that he underwent an appendectomy in the Adirondacks last month, a year after a supposed appendectomy at a Bronxville medical facility. According to a lawsuit filed in state Supreme Court, McCormack experienced severe stomach pain in early March and was taken to Adirondack Medical Center in Saranac Lake, where he underwent emergency surgery. The lawsuit claims that during this second operation, it was discovered that McCormack's appendix was never removed and was still inside him. Dr. Michael Kerin, who performed the Bronxville surgery and is listed on his website as former director of surgery at Lawrence Hospital, is also named as a defendant. The lawsuit includes a copy of a 2013 Operative Report from Lawrence Hospital stating that McCormack's appendix had been removed, signed by Kerin. However, a report from Lawrence Hospital's Pathology Department indicates that the specimen marked "appendix" was not actually an appendix. The lawsuit alleges that Lawrence Hospital never notified McCormack about the discrepancy, despite being aware of the error. McCormack's attorney, Mitchell Baker, claims that the hospital and the surgeon may have been faced with more than medical malpractice if McCormack's appendix had not been removed during the second surgery. The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages for the pain and suffering, as well as the need for two surgeries. Lawrence Hospital has stated it is investigating the claim and will not comment on pending litigation.

Actor George Takei sparked controversy by referring to Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas as a "clown in blackface" on his Facebook page, igniting a debate over the meaning and implications of the term. Takei sought to clarify his statement, explaining that "blackface" is a theatrical term and not inherently racist, though many found his defense lacking. Critics argued that Takei's attempt to downplay the term's historical significance was condescending and dismissive of the serious issues it represents. Takei's assertion that Justice Thomas has "abdicated and abandoned his African American heritage" further fueled the outrage, with many questioning his right to make such a claim. The incident highlighted the ongoing tensions within Hollywood and among people of color regarding cultural appropriation and the use of historically offensive terms. Takei's supporters defended his intentions, emphasizing the importance of context and the actor's history as a survivor of Japanese American internment. However, others pointed out that Takei's stubbornness and refusal to acknowledge the misrepresentation of Thomas' views were problematic. The controversy also brought to light the lack of significant backlash from prominent figures in the entertainment industry and the left, with Marc Lamont Hill being one of the few to publicly condemn Takei's comments. The discussion underscored the complexities of race and identity in the public sphere, where actors and public figures must navigate the delicate balance between artistic freedom and cultural sensitivity.

A Jacksonville, Florida, pediatric dentist, Dr. Howard Schneider, is now the target of a class-action lawsuit and state investigation, following allegations of physical and psychological abuse of children in his dental practice. Four plaintiffs have filed a lawsuit in the 4th Judicial Circuit Court in Duval County, Florida, accusing Dr. Schneider of assault, battery, false imprisonment, and intentionally inflicting "severe emotional distress." The lawsuit, filed in response to ongoing protests outside Schneider's office and complaints from parents, claims that his practice has been a "house of horrors," where children were allegedly strapped down, left with visible injuries, and subjected to non-medically necessary procedures. The plaintiffs, represented by attorney John Phillips, are seeking damages exceeding $15,000 and a jury trial, alleging that Schneider's methods were "sadistic and systematic" and that he preyed on low-income, uneducated, and non-English speaking clients. They claim he choked children to the point of unconsciousness, performed unnecessary extractions, and threatened parents to avoid exposure.

Schneider, 78, has been practicing for over 40 years and has never been charged with a crime in connection with the allegations. However, he has faced two previous malpractice suits and was called to his practice by the Jacksonville Sheriff's Office twice, in 2001 and 2013, to deal with complaints about excessive force on young patients. In 2014, Brandi Motley brought her 6-year-old daughter, Bri-el, to Schneider's office for a tooth extraction. After waiting three hours, Motley was informed of an "accident" and saw her daughter, hyperventilating and covered in blood, with visible injuries. Motley claims Schneider extracted all eight of Bri-el's front teeth, despite only being scheduled for one. Motley's case, along with others, was initially dismissed by an attorney, but after the viral spread of her Facebook post, she was able to secure representation and begin legal action.

The Florida Attorney General's Office is investigating Schneider for Medicaid fraud, alleging that he billed the government program hundreds of thousands of dollars for procedures he did not perform. The state's evidence includes accounts from parents of children who experienced injuries, screaming, and unnecessary procedures. The investigation has led to Schneider's voluntary surrender of his dental license, avoiding a full board investigation. Despite the allegations, Schneider maintains that the claims are false and that he used appropriate anesthesia, arguing that giving up his practice was not an admission of guilt. His trial on Medicaid fraud charges is set for November, with a defense motion to declare him incompetent to stand trial currently pending.

Lindsay Lohan's on-again-off-again girlfriend, Samantha Ronson, was arrested on suspicion of DUI early Monday morning in Baker, California. Ronson, a 33-year-old DJ, was pulled over at 10:30 am for speeding and refused a breathalyzer test on the scene, leading to her arrest and transport to the Barstow jail. After being released several hours later, the District Attorney’s office will decide within a day or two whether to file charges against her. Ronson had been traveling back from Las Vegas, where she had spun at the Lavo nightclub. This incident adds to Lohan's concerns about her girlfriend's behavior, following past reports of Lohan's worries about Ronson's partying.

Brevard County Hall of Fame president John Tice wants to move Jim Morrison's remains from his Paris gravesite to Melbourne, Florida, the birthplace of the controversial "Lizard King" lead singer of The Doors. Morrison, born James Douglas Morrison on December 8, 1943, at the former Brevard Hospital, was born in Melbourne, though his connection to the city is not widely recognized. Tice, who founded the Brevard Hall of Fame in 2012, hopes to contact Paris cemetery officials to move Morrison's remains for display at the Brevard Hall of Fame. The nonprofit organization, located inside the Liberty Bell Memorial Museum, currently features a modest Morrison display with posters, records, and a framed copy of his last will and testament. Tice believes Morrison, a popular public figure from the area, should be honored more prominently. He heard that French cemetery officials offered to move Morrison’s remains to Melbourne, but the homeowner declined the offer. Tice plans to organize a fundraising drive if cemetery officials agree, and any legal issues are resolved. Morrison left the United States for Paris after an arrest warrant was issued for him out of Miami for indecent exposure during a concert. While not everyone in Brevard County would support Morrison's possible return, Tice argues that Morrison ought to be where he was born. He is still waiting to hear back from officials in Paris.

A Michigan woman, Kimberly Pappas, 25, faces trial for the murder of her newborn son, who she allegedly suffocated and hid in a desk drawer at work. Pappas, who was charged with homicide in April for delivering the baby in a bathroom stall at CEVA Logistics, 24450 Glendale in Redford, is now facing more severe charges, including first-degree premeditated murder, felony murder, and first-degree child abuse. The baby was found in a plastic bag inside another bag at Pappas's desk on March 31, and an autopsy revealed the child had lived 20 to 30 minutes before dying of suffocation. Kimberly Pappas's lawyer argued for manslaughter charges, citing her client's alleged lack of intent to kill, but Judge Karen Khalil found the evidence compelling and ordered Pappas to stand trial. Khalil noted the case as "very difficult" and maintained the same bond conditions. Kimberly Pappas's sister, Cassie Pappas, testified that Kimberly had gained weight without disclosing a pregnancy, and that she had asked Kimberly if she was pregnant, to which Kimberly denied. Kimberly's attorneys sought to prove her mental health issues, but Pappas was found competent to stand trial. The case highlights the complexities of such tragic incidents and the legal challenges they present.

President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, appeared before Senate Intelligence Committee staff for a closed-door meeting on Monday, following a series of inquiries into his contacts with Russian officials. In a brief statement upon his return to the White House, Kushner reaffirmed his stance that he did not collude with Russia and that his interactions with foreign governments were proper. He detailed four meetings with Russian officials during the campaign and transition, including a June 2016 meeting with a Russian lawyer that Trump Jr. had initially believed would provide damaging information about Hillary Clinton. Kushner maintained that the meeting was a waste of time and that he had no prior knowledge of its purpose. He also addressed a Reuters report claiming he had two calls with the Russian ambassador, Sergey Kislyak, during the campaign, stating that he did not recall these calls and that his phone records did not confirm their existence. Additionally, he discussed his December 2016 meeting with Russian banker Sergey Gorkov, noting that the meeting was brief and focused on general economic statements. Regarding his security clearance form, Kushner explained that it was submitted prematurely due to a miscommunication and that he had since provided a more comprehensive list of foreign contacts. The summary of his interactions with Russian officials, combined with his denial of collusion, sets the stage for ongoing scrutiny from congressional and federal investigators.

Did You Hear About the Morgans? is a romantic comedy that has critics and audiences alike scratching their heads. The film, starring Hugh Grant and Sarah Jessica Parker, is a typical rom-com with a twist: it's so painfully awkward that it's hard to watch. As Jeff Goldstein of the Chicago Tribune puts it, "Each of its theoretical punch lines is preceded by an eerie second or two of dead air, followed by the jokelike 'payoff,' guiltily delivered by one of its game cast members, followed by a longer awkward pause." The premise, where a Manhattan power couple on the brink of divorce witness a murder and are forced into the federal witness protection program, seems promising. However, the execution is far from it. The characters' dependency on their BlackBerrys and general sense of privilege should be the source of humor, but the script fails to deliver. Instead, the film relies on forced blue state versus red state humor, which falls flat. Grant, who is usually reliable, is pained in his role, and Parker's character is not given enough depth to carry the film. The supporting cast, including Sam Elliott and Mary Steenburgen, try their best but can't save the movie. The film's director, Marc Lawrence, has previous work in the genre, including Music and Lyrics, but this seems to be a step down. Overall, the movie is a "throwaway" in the truest sense, a disposable comedy that doesn't quite hit the mark. Critics are unanimous in their dislike, with Jeff Goldstein calling it "multiplex meringue compared to the meat-and-potatoes cinema at this most award-whoring time of year." While some may find it entertaining, it's unlikely to be a standout in the crowded rom-com genre.

Nearly a year before Attorney General Jeff Sessions fired senior FBI official Andrew McCabe for what Sessions called a "lack of candor," McCabe oversaw a federal criminal investigation into whether Sessions lacked candor when testifying before Congress about contacts with Russian operatives, sources familiar with the matter told ABC News. Democratic lawmakers have repeatedly accused Sessions of misleading them in congressional testimony and called on federal authorities to investigate, but McCabe's previously-unreported decision to actually put the attorney general in the crosshairs of an FBI probe was an exceptional move. Sessions was not aware of the investigation when he decided to fire McCabe, according to a lawyer representing Sessions. McCabe authorized the criminal inquiry after a top Democrat on the Senate Judiciary Committee, Sen. Patrick Leahy, D-Vermont, and then-Sen. Al Franken, D-Minn., wrote a letter in March 2017 to the FBI urging agents to investigate "all contacts" Sessions may have had with Russians, and "whether any laws were broken in the course of those contacts or in any subsequent discussion of whether they occurred." Sessions recused himself from the FBI’s probe of Russia’s meddling in the 2016 presidential election, giving Deputy Attorney General Rod Rosenstein oversight of the growing effort. Two months later, Rosenstein appointed special counsel Robert Mueller to take over the investigation and related inquiries, including the Sessions matter. Sessions was interviewed by Mueller's team, and the federal inquiry related to his candor during his confirmation process has since been shuttered. Sessions called any suggestions that he misled lawmakers "false." Nevertheless, charges subsequently brought by Mueller raised more questions over Sessions' testimony to Congress. In November, former Trump campaign adviser George Papadopoulos admitted to federal authorities that during the campaign he was in frequent contact with Russian operatives about setting up a meeting between Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin, and Papadopoulos pitched the idea to Sessions and Trump at a meeting of the then-candidate's foreign policy team in March 2016. Sessions later told lawmakers he "always told the truth," insisting he didn’t recall the March 2016 meeting when first testifying to Congress. He later remembered the meeting after reading news reports about it, he said. Sessions was fired by McCabe, who was fired Friday after the Justice Department's inspector general concluded that McCabe misled investigators looking into how Justice Department and FBI officials handled matters associated with the 2016 presidential election. McCabe vehemently denies misleading investigators, saying in his own statement that he is "being singled out and treated this way because of the role I played, the actions I took, and the events I witnessed in the aftermath of the firing of James Comey." McCabe's critics point to his ties to Democrats, particularly his wife's failed Democratic run for state senate in Virginia nearly three years ago. But in an interview with ABC News, McCabe insisted politics was "absolutely not" a factor in any of the decisions he made, noting he has considered himself a Republican all his life.

A great white shark named Mary Lee has been tagged and is being tracked as she cruises the East Coast of the United States. The tracking can be followed on the Ocearch website, which provides real-time updates on the shark's movements. Ocearch, a non-profit organization dedicated to shark research and conservation, uses advanced technology to tag and monitor sharks, contributing valuable data to scientific understanding and public awareness. The organization aims to protect sharks and their habitats by gathering information on their behavior, migration patterns, and health. By following Mary Lee's journey, enthusiasts and researchers alike can gain insights into the lives of these magnificent creatures. The tracking data helps in studying the impact of human activities on shark populations and supports conservation efforts aimed at preserving marine biodiversity.

Democratic presidential candidate Bernie Sanders and presumptive nominee Hillary Clinton engaged in a series of strategic moves to bridge their policy differences, particularly in the realm of healthcare, ahead of Sanders' possible endorsement of Clinton. At a meeting of the Democratic Party draft platform committee in Orlando, Florida, on Saturday, supporters of Sanders were unable to secure a strong condemnation of the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) trade pact, marking a significant setback for Sanders' efforts to push the party further to the left. Instead, the committee adopted language opposing “trade agreements that do not support good American jobs,” a compromise that disappointed Sanders' supporters. Clinton, meanwhile, announced a healthcare plan aimed at expanding investments in community health care centers, doubling funding for primary care services at Federally Qualified Health Centers, which serve populations with limited access to healthcare. She also affirmed her commitment to providing Americans with the choice of a “public-option” insurance plan and allowing people to opt into Medicare at age 55. These proposals were seen as a significant step forward in addressing healthcare access and costs, aligning more closely with Sanders' priorities. Clinton's campaign stressed that the proposals would be fully paid for with savings, innovations, and tax reform that closes loopholes and ensures the wealthiest pay their fair share. Sanders praised the updates, indicating they were an important step toward universal, quality, and affordable healthcare. Both candidates' actions reflect a growing compromise between their campaigns, with Clinton working to secure Sanders' support and Sanders acknowledging the importance of Clinton's healthcare initiatives. The announcements come as the two prepare for a joint campaign event in Portsmouth, New Hampshire, where Sanders is expected to endorse Clinton. This strategic move by Clinton aims to win over Sanders' supporters and solidify her position as the Democratic nominee.

Donald Trump's hopes for a "big surprise" at the Republican National Convention were dashed as Tropical Storm Isaac forced the postponement of Monday's events. Trump was set to deliver a speech, but the real estate mogul now faces scheduling conflicts for the rest of the week. The convention, originally planned for four days, is now reduced to three, with full proceedings scheduled to begin on Tuesday. Despite the shortened schedule, Republican officials aim to maintain their focus on criticizing President Obama's leadership and promoting Mitt Romney. The storm also affected other convention participants, such as Louisiana Governor Bobby Jindal, who will not attend due to the approaching hurricane. Meanwhile, Republican strategists emphasize the need to highlight Romney's managerial skills and economic policies, while the Obama campaign counters with a video highlighting Romney's inconsistent positions. The convention faces additional challenges, including the fallout from controversial comments by Rep. Todd Akin regarding rape and abortion, and the ongoing debate over Romney's Medicare reform plan. Despite the disruptions, the convention remains a critical platform for both parties to define their candidates and policies for the upcoming election.

Archaeologists have uncovered a 4,300-year-old house on the edge of Marden Henge, a giant ditch and bank enclosure in Wiltshire, England, that has almost vanished from view due to rich farmland covering it. The house, one of the best-preserved from the Neolithic period ever found in the UK, was part of a monument that was once one of the biggest and most impressive in Britain. The rectangular building, made to look smarter with tonnes of white chalk brought from miles away and stamped into a kind of plaster, is as neatly levelled and regular as nearby postwar bungalows. The house, believed to be connected with great gatherings for feasts, has already produced finds including beautifully worked flint arrowheads and blades, decorated pottery, shale and copper bracelets, and a Roman brooch, as well as the tiny jawbone of a vole. Analysis of the mass of seeds and charred grains recovered will reveal what the people were growing and eating. Pig bones, scorch marks from a charcoal firepit, and evidence of a massive workforce suggest the house was never a permanent residence but part of a larger monument. The structure originally stood on a terrace overlooking a mound, within a small earth-banked circle, in turn part of the enormous Marden Henge. Ramparts three metres high enclosed a vast space of 15 hectares, far larger than the Avebury or Stonehenge circles, and too large for any imaginable practical use. Dr Jim Leary, director of this summer’s excavation with the Reading University archaeology summer school, believes the purpose must have been status, showing off wealth and power in the ability to mobilise a massive workforce. The site is so vast that it takes Leary and fellow director Amanda Clarke 40 minutes to walk from the team working on the house to the diggers who have uncovered a previously unrecorded Roman complex including the foundations of an impressive barn. The outer ring of Marden Henge enclosed a complex of smaller monuments, including the Hatfield Barrow, which was once 15 metres tall, and now survives only as a 15cm ripple in the field. The site, which is open to visitors, will welcome them next weekend for an open day as part of the national festival of archaeology. The aim is to gain a better understanding of the people who lived in the areas surrounding Stonehenge.
