The three-year Vale of Pewsey dig is a partnership between the University of Reading, Historic England, the Arts and Humanities Research Council, and Wiltshire Museum. The best discoveries are often revealed last, and the house at Marden Henge is part of a larger story that is still unfolding.

Four people, including a prominent East Hampton builder known for his work with celebrities, were presumed dead after a small plane crashed off the coast of Long Island, reports the AP. Bernard Krupinski, 70, his wife Bonnie, 70, their 22-year-old grandson Will Maerov, and 47-year-old pilot Jon Dollard were on board the Piper PA31 Navajo twin-engine aircraft when it went down about 3 p.m. Saturday, about a mile and a half south of East Hampton. The plane was en route to East Hampton Airport when it encountered severe thunderstorms, according to local pilot Bill Gardiner. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the cause of the crash. Bernard Krupinski, a builder to the stars, had crafted luxury mansions for clients such as Martha Stewart and Billy Joel. Known as "Bennie and Bonnie" to locals, the couple was well-respected for their charitable work and philanthropy. Their real-estate empire, worth an estimated $150 million, included the popular East Hampton restaurant Citta Nuova, where workers and patrons gathered in shock after the news of the crash. The restaurant was closed, with a sign explaining the closure was due to a family emergency. The couple's only child, Laura Krupinski, 52, was a former model who once publicly accused her father of having an affair with Stewart. Grandson Will Maerov had just started a job with ad agency Chandelier Creative. The tragedy was the second small-plane crash on Long Island in less than a week, following a World War II-era plane that crashed into the woods of Melville, killing its sole occupant.

A 17-year-old Orofino, Idaho, high school student, Kristian Perez, has been missing since April 15th, sparking a search and investigation by local police. Kristian left the Orofino High School prom at 9:32 p.m. on Friday, April 15th, and his family reported him missing after he failed to return home. The last known location of Kristian was near the National Guard Armory, where the prom was held, as his tuxedo jacket, one shoe, and a broken cell phone were found in the vicinity. A canine tracking team was deployed, and while the initial track suggested Kristian may have walked west from the prom location to a nearby parking lot along U.S. Highway 12, the trail was lost after a short distance. 

Orofino Police Department launched a search warrant for Kristian’s cellular phone records, hoping to uncover any clues that could lead to his whereabouts. The police are also investigating a possible sighting of a person matching Kristian’s description at the Zip Trip on Main Street in Lewiston, though surveillance video later revealed it was not him. Despite the efforts, as of April 17th, no family or friends have heard from Kristian since he left the prom. The police are urging the public to come forward with any information that could assist in locating Kristian, and the community is rallying to support the family and the search efforts.

The Orofino High School principal stated that Kristian is a good, quiet student, and the school has implemented a crisis prevention program to support students and staff. The superintendent, Robert Vian, emphasized the protocols in place to address any concerns that may arise from this unique situation. The community remains vigilant, with a heavy police presence in the neighborhood, and the search continues as the investigation progresses.

The Accountant, starring Ben Affleck, opened at No. 1 at the weekend box office with $24.7 million, beating out Kevin Hart's live comedy concert film Kevin Hart: What Now?, which took second place with $11.98 million. The Accountant, a moderately budgeted film at $44 million, received a 51% positive rating from critics but an A grade from audiences at CinemaScore. In third place, The Girl on the Train, starring Emily Blunt, earned $11.97 million, bringing its total to $46.6 million in two weeks. Tim Burton's Miss Peregrine's Home for Peculiar Children placed fourth with $8.9 million, adding to its $65.8 million total. Mark Wahlberg's disaster drama Deepwater Horizon rounded out the top five with $6.4 million, reaching $49.3 million in three weeks. The weekend's other major release, Max Steel, a sci-fi adventure based on a toy, failed to make the top 10, earning only $2.2 million. The film received a 0% positive rating on Rotten Tomatoes and a B from audiences at CinemaScore. The Birth of a Nation, an Oscar hopeful, dropped 61% in its second weekend, earning $2.7 million, for a total of $12.2 million. Despite strong marketing for The Accountant, its modest opening numbers suggest a more cautious approach to future releases.

A Wisconsin woman, Cindy Cox, has filed a lawsuit against the online retailer Accessory Outlet, alleging that the company used unfair terms and threatened her to prevent her from complaining about a bad purchase experience. Cox, a disabled veteran and substitute teacher, ordered an iPhone case from Accessory Outlet on July 6, 2014, but the item never arrived. After checking the tracking number, Cox contacted the company, requesting a refund. Accessory Outlet refused, claiming the order had shipped. Cox then threatened to dispute the charge with her credit card company, which prompted the company to threaten a $250 penalty and even send her account to collections. Accessory Outlet's Terms of Sale, buried at the bottom of the website, state that customers agree not to file any complaint, chargeback, claim, or make any public statement regarding the order or the company's website for 90 days, or to threaten to do so, creating liability for damages in the amount of $250, plus additional fees. Cox's lawsuit argues that the terms are unenforceable, both because they are unconscionable as a matter of law and because she never agreed to them. The terms also claim that the sole method of dispute resolution is binding arbitration in New York City, with all expenses paid by the respective parties. Cox's case highlights the problematic practices of Accessory Outlet, which has faced scrutiny for its deceptive practices and unscrupulous methods of handling customer complaints. The company's "A+” rating from the Better Business Bureau has been called into question, as the BBB states that the firm is not currently a BBB-accredited business and has been served a cease-and-desist order. The lawsuit seeks to have Cox's alleged debts voided and to declare the company's terms unenforceable.

Alabama voters are deciding between Republican Roy Moore, a former chief justice of the Alabama Supreme Court, and Democrat Doug Jones in a closely watched U.S. Senate election. The race has drawn national attention due to allegations of sexual misconduct against Moore, who denies the accusations. President Donald Trump and the Republican National Committee supported Moore, while Democrats rallied behind Jones, hoping to break their 0-5 streak in special elections for Republican-held seats in 2017. With Jones' victory, the Democratic Party aims to build momentum heading into the 2018 midterm elections. Security measures are heightened, and voter turnout is expected to be high, especially among young people and black voters, who could help Jones. Moore's supporters remain optimistic, while Jones expresses confidence in his campaign. The race has significant implications for the Senate's composition and the broader political landscape.

McDreamy, star of Grey's Anatomy, Patrick Dempsey, and his wife of 15 years, Jillian Fink, are ending their marriage, according to Page Six. "It is with careful consideration and mutual respect that we have decided to end our marriage," the couple stated, prioritizing the wellbeing of their three children. Fink, who filed for divorce citing irreconcilable differences, is seeking joint custody and spousal and child support. The couple, worth around $40 million, has three children together: 12-year-old Tallula and twins Darby and Sullivan. While Dempsey is known for his privacy, the divorce has brought their family life into the spotlight.

Pete Davidson's proposal to Maggie Rogers during a "Saturday Night Live" promo video has sparked a new round of tension between the comedian and his ex-fiancée, Ariana Grande. In a series of now-deleted tweets, Grande took aim at Davidson, writing, "For somebody who claims to hate relevancy, you sure love clinging to it, huh." She followed up with the phrase "thank u, next," a reference to her hit song. The proposal, which came just hours after the SNL promo aired, saw Davidson jokingly ask Rogers, "Hey Maggie, I’m Pete. You wanna get married?" Rogers quickly declined, and Davidson playfully noted his "0 for 3" record with failed relationships. Grande, who has been dealing with the loss of her ex-boyfriend Mac Miller, has been keeping busy with her "Sweetener" world tour. The couple, who met on SNL and became engaged in June after dating for just a few weeks, have since called it quits. Sources close to the pair told TMZ the split was a mutual choice, as both felt the timing wasn't right. Grande's team stated that she would be taking time to heal and work on new music without deadlines. Davidson has previously mined his relationship with Grande for comedy, including at the Judd & Pete for America benefit, where he joked about finding a new roommate. Despite the tension, Grande's team has noted that the couple is moving on, with both covering matching ink that outlived their engagement.

For the first time in history, complications from preterm birth have surpassed all other causes as the world's leading killer of young children, according to new findings published in The Lancet by a research team coordinated by Robert Black, M.D., of the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, together with the World Health Organization and the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine. In 2013, of the estimated 6.3 million deaths of children under five, complications from preterm births accounted for nearly 1.1 million deaths, with direct complications from preterm births causing 965,000 deaths during the first 28 days of life and an additional 125,000 deaths between the ages of one month and five years. Other main causes for young child deaths include pneumonia, which killed 935,000 children under-five, and childbirth complications, which caused 720,000 deaths (662,000 in the neonatal period, most on the first day of life, and 58,000 in the post-neonatal period).

The countries with the highest numbers of children under-five dying from preterm birth complications each year are: India (361,600), Nigeria (98,300), Pakistan (75,000), Democratic Republic of the Congo (40,600), China (37,200), Bangladesh (26,100), Indonesia (25,800), Ethiopia (24,400), Angola (15,900), and Kenya (13,300). Some of the highest rates of preterm deaths are in West Africa, particularly in countries currently being decimated by Ebola, where the risk is now even higher given the challenges faced, notably Sierra Leone and Liberia.

The 10 countries with the highest percentage of under-five deaths directly resulting from preterm birth complications are: Macedonia, 51.0 percent; Slovenia, 47.5 percent; Denmark, 43.0 percent; Serbia, 39.8 percent; the United Kingdom, 38.7 percent; Hungary, 37.4 percent; Slovakia, 34.9 percent; Poland, 34.8 percent; Republic of Korea and Switzerland, 32.7 percent. All of these exceed the global average of 17.4 percent of under-five deaths, partly because of success in reducing infectious diseases.

In the U.S., 28.1 percent of under-five deaths are from direct complications due to preterm birth, which translates to 8,100 deaths of children under-five. The U.S. ranks 141st worst on the list of 162 countries, followed by Oman, Georgia, Egypt, Canada, Germany, and Qatar. The epidemic of prematurity has been moving higher up on the global agenda. In addition to new research to solve the problem, global health partners are intensifying joint efforts to advocate for investment and policy approaches to reduce preterm birth and improve newborn health. A key moment in this effort is World Prematurity Day (WPD), which will be celebrated for the fourth time on November 17th.

More than 200 countries, non-government organizations, UN agencies, medical and health organizations will participate in WPD activities, reaching 1.4 billion people via radio, TV, print, Internet, and social media. The global public service announcements featuring Celine Dion and Thalia reached more than a billion people on CNN International and CNN en Español. The partners of WPD also hosted a 24-hour Twitter relay that involved nearly 30 million people. WPD reached another 7.3 million people via Facebook through a collection of more than 3,000 personal family stories about prematurity.

National parent groups affiliated with the European Foundation for the Care of Newborn Infants and the US-based NGO March of Dimes lit some of the world's most famous buildings and landmarks purple, the representative color of WPD: Empire State Building (New York), Niagara Falls (New York/Canada), Brandenburg Gate (Germany), Peace Bridge (New York/Canada), Belfast City Hall (Ireland), First Direct Arena (England), CN Tower (Canada), Singapore Flyer, National Museum (Poland), Bratislava Castle (Slovakia), El Moro (Mexico City), the Bosphorus Bridge (Turkey), General Motors Headquarters (Detroit), and the Las Vegas Strip (Nevada).

The Every Women Every Child initiative, spearheaded by the UN Secretary-General, was created to rapidly advance the UN Millennium Development Goals (MDGs) 4 and 5, to reduce under-five child and maternal mortality by two-thirds and three-fourths, respectively. The initiative has grown to include 300 partners and 400 financial, policy, and service delivery commitments, such as training midwives. In total, $27.3 billion has already been disbursed.

Adding to the successful Every Woman Every Child movement, WHO and partners have been working on two complementary approaches: the Every Newborn Action Plan (ENAP), led by WHO and UNICEF and adopted by 194 countries at the World Health Assembly this year, and Ending Preventable Maternal Mortality (EPMM). ENAP and EPMM have articulated strategies and set targets to improve maternal and child health in the post-MDG era and both have attracted unprecedented commitments from countries and development partners.

Four major research initiatives, with some $250 million in funding, are now underway. Researchers seek to discover the unknown causes of prematurity and find effective ways to prevent or delay preterm births. The Global Coalition to Advance Preterm Birth Research (GCAPR) is a new partnership initiated by the National Institute of Child Health and Human Development (NICHD), the March of Dimes, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, and the Global Alliance to Prevent Prematurity and Stillbirth (GAPPS). Some 16 institutions are now members of the coalition.

The March of Dimes has launched a $75 million Campaign to End Premature Birth, a "medical Manhattan Project" to create a specialized network of five research centers conducting team-based research to discover the unknown causes of prematurity. Two of these research programs are well underway. The remaining three will be named by the end of 2014.

The University of California at San Francisco's (UCSF) Preterm Birth Initiative (PTBi) has launched a 10-year global initiative to slow the epidemic of preterm births and improve the health of preterm babies. PTBi is currently in a planning phase to determine where UCSF and its partners can have the greatest impact. The Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and Marc and Lynne Benioff are co-funding this $100 million initiative.

The last research effort led by the Global Alliance to Prevent Prematurity and Stillbirth (GAPPS), a program started by Seattle Children's Hospital, is focusing its research on discovering the causes and mechanisms of prematurity, work that may lead to interventions to prevent it. IKEA is recalling approximately 27 million chests and dressers due to the risk of tipping and potentially crushing children if not properly anchored to the wall. Two children have died from Malm chests tipping over since 2014, and IKEA is aware of three additional deaths involving other models since 1989. The company's new repair program involves offering free wall anchoring kits to consumers to secure the furniture, but consumers are not expected to return the products. Instead, they should either order or pick up the kits from an IKEA store or register online. Consumers are advised to move unsecured chests and dressers to storage or other areas inaccessible to children until the furniture is properly anchored.

The Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) and IKEA have collaborated on this recall, with CPSC Chairman Elliot Kaye calling for more stable furniture designs and urging the industry to lead the way. IKEA's U.S. commercial manager, Patty Lobell, expressed deep sadness over the deaths and emphasized the company's commitment to preventing further tragedies. However, Kaye highlighted that the current U.S. standard for furniture stability is less stringent than Europe's, and IKEA acknowledged that many consumers may not be aware of the risk or properly secure their furniture.

The CPSC has been addressing furniture and TV tip-overs for several years, noting that a child dies every two weeks and one is injured every 24 minutes in the U.S. due to these incidents. IKEA has distributed over 300,000 anchoring kits since the recall was announced, but critics argue that this is insufficient. Safety advocates have called for a more comprehensive approach, including a mandatory recall and buying back of potentially dangerous furniture. The American Home Furnishings Alliance, representing over 200 large furniture manufacturers, has been working on improving safety measures.

The recall affects about 7 million Malm chests and 20 million other IKEA chests and dressers. Consumers can obtain a free anchoring kit by visiting an IKEA store, registering online, or calling the company's toll-free number. IKEA remains committed to raising awareness about this home safety issue and providing tools and knowledge to prevent accidents. However, some safety advocates argue that IKEA's efforts are inadequate and that more needs to be done to ensure the safety of children.

Reality TV star Tila Tequila, known for her flat Earth beliefs and controversial statements, attended an alt-right conference in Washington DC, where she gave a Nazi salute and praised Adolf Hitler, sparking outrage. Tequila, who has a history of making inflammatory remarks, defended her actions, claiming it was just "trolling" and a "fun" way to "get a rise out of people." She also expressed concerns about the entertainment industry being "owned by Jews" and criticized what she perceived as a "biased" media. Tequila, who has previously stated that the earth is flat, defended her beliefs, saying she left the "fake world" in 2014 and now lives in an "alternate universe." She also discussed her support for Donald Trump, saying she was one of the first to publicly back him, and expressed excitement about his presidency. Maggiano's Little Italy, the restaurant where the event took place, issued an apology after protesters confronted attendees, and the restaurant pledged to donate $10,000 to the Anti-Defamation League. The incident highlights the growing tensions between the alt-right movement and mainstream society, as well as the potential for reality TV personalities to inadvertently or deliberately promote extremist views.

George Talley, a 71-year-old retired resident of Detroit, thought his 1979 Corvette was gone for good after it was stolen more than three decades ago. However, the car was recently found in Mississippi, sparking a story of unexpected good fortune. Michigan State Police, working with the Mississippi Bureau of Investigation, traced the vehicle back to Talley, who initially reported the theft to his insurance company. The car, with 47,000 miles on it, was located at a residence in Columbia, Mississippi, and is currently at the Hattiesburg police station. Talley, a Corvette enthusiast who has owned four different models, was initially skeptical when he received a call from his insurance company about the car’s recovery. When Michigan State Police confirmed the news, he was shocked and overjoyed. General Motors, Talley’s former employer, heard about the situation and offered to pick up the car and deliver it to him, covering all expenses. Talley, now worried about how to transport the car, was relieved when GM’s Executive Vice President, Mark Reuss, appeared on a radio show and offered to bring the Corvette home. Talley expressed gratitude, saying, “GM is paying for all of that, which is beautiful.” The journey of the 1979 Corvette from theft to recovery and eventual return to its rightful owner is a testament to the power of persistence and the kindness of strangers.

Bob Schieffer, the anchor of CBS News' "Face the Nation," announced his retirement this summer after 50 years in journalism. CBS News President David Rhodes praised Schieffer as an inspiration and mentor to many colleagues. Schieffer, who has interviewed every U.S. president since Nixon, has won numerous awards, including eight Emmys. His decision to retire is partly due to his pride in CBS News' current state, with a focus on hard news and foreign reporting. Two of his colleagues, Major Garrett, the network's chief White House correspondent, and Norah O'Donnell, co-anchor of "CBS This Morning," are among the likely candidates to replace him. CBS is also considering outside talent, such as CNN's Jake Tapper and ABC's Jonathan Karl. The search for a new host of "Face the Nation" is ongoing, with no final decision yet made.

A queen bee's unexpected journey led to a two-day chase through the streets of Haverfordwest, Wales, as a swarm of around 20,000 bees followed her from the back of a 4x4 vehicle. The incident began when the queen bee, possibly attracted by something sweet inside the car, became trapped in the boot. Upon realizing the situation, Roger Burns, a 65-year-old beekeeper, and other beekeepers carefully transferred the bees into a cardboard box. However, a gust of wind blew the box off the car, and the queen returned to the boot, restarting the chase. The swarm was spotted by park ranger Tom Moses, who noticed a "brown splodge" on the car's back. Moses, along with beekeepers, spent about three hours managing the swarm, with Moses receiving five stings. The bees eventually settled in a box, but the queen's return to the car prompted the swarm to follow the vehicle. The owner, Mrs. Howarth, drove home believing the problem was resolved, only to find the bees had followed her the next morning. The incident, while amusing to some, highlighted the importance of bee conservation and the need for people to handle such situations carefully to avoid harming both humans and bees.

Tom Hanks has continued his tradition of providing the White House press corps with a new espresso machine, this time replacing the one he gifted during the Bush administration in 2010. The Oscar-winning actor left a note with the new machine, encouraging the press to "Keep up the good fight for Truth, Justice, and the American Way. Especially for the Truth Part." The note, featuring an illustration of American troops, was accompanied by a new espresso cup set. Hanks first noticed the need for a coffee maker during a visit to the White House in 2010, when he saw the press corps relying on vending machine coffee. His gesture has become a symbol of support for the media, especially during President Trump's first 40 days in office, keeping the press corps well caffeinated and perhaps a bit more productive. The new machine and note serve as a reminder of Hanks's long-standing commitment to the press, providing a small but meaningful gesture of encouragement and support.

JPMorgan Chase & Co. disclosed a $5.8 billion trading loss in its chief investment office, significantly larger than analysts' estimates, which has complicated efforts by CEO Jamie Dimon to restore investor confidence. The loss, caused by traders potentially hiding problems in a portfolio, has driven the bank's second-quarter profit down 9%, reducing net income to $4.96 billion. Dimon faces scrutiny over his management, with the bank restating first-quarter earnings and being probed for potential market manipulation. The loss may increase by up to $1.6 billion, and JPMorgan has already overhauled CIO management. Ina Drew, the chief investment officer, retired after a $57.5 million severance package, while Dimon plans to claw back compensation from those responsible. The bank is also grappling with historically low interest rates and weak trading revenue, with consumer credit showing some resilience. Despite these challenges, JPMorgan benefited from mortgage lending, with mortgage fees and related revenue up significantly.

President Donald Trump's ongoing feud with Rosie O'Donnell has spanned over a decade, with both parties trading insults and public jabs. The animosity began in 2006 when O'Donnell criticized Trump's decision to allow Tara Conner, a Miss USA contestant, to keep her crown despite allegations of drug use and underage drinking. Trump retaliated, calling O'Donnell "a real loser" and "a woman out of control." Their relationship took a turn in 2011 when O'Donnell announced her engagement to Michelle Rounds, and Trump tweeted, "I feel sorry for Rosie's new partner in love whose parents are devastated at the thought of their daughter being with @Rosie—a true loser." O'Donnell responded with a tweet calling Trump "an a--."

In 2012, O'Donnell suffered a heart attack, and Trump sent well-wishes, which O'Donnell found surprising. Trump continued to criticize O'Donnell's show "Rosie" and her new co-host Lawrence O'Donnell, tweeting, "Same last name, same bad ratings- @lawrence and @rosie." In 2014, O'Donnell underwent weight-loss surgery, and Trump tweeted, "Rosie O'Donnell just said she felt 'shame' at being fat—not politically correct! She killed Star Jones for weight loss surgery, just had it!" O'Donnell responded, "Donald—go away."

In 2015, O'Donnell returned to "The View," but Trump remained critical, tweeting, "Rosie is back on the View which tells you how desperate they must be. It is the standard short term fix and long term disaster." He followed up, "Rosie is crude, rude, obnoxious and dumb—other than that I like her very much!" When O'Donnell left the show in 2015, Trump commented, "Well, it's very sad what's happened to 'The View' and I predicted that with Rosie O'Donnell it would fail. I guess the prediction is correct, but, I mean she's a total trainwreck, so let's see what happens and I hope it works out well. ... I like the show a lot, but let's face it, Rosie is a loser."

During the 2016 Republican primary debate, Trump referenced O'Donnell, saying, "Only Rosie O'Donnell," generating applause from the audience. O'Donnell responded, "try explaining that to your kids." Trump's comments about O'Donnell continued during the first presidential debate, where he said, "I said very tough things to her and I think everybody would agree she deserves it and nobody feels sorry for her." O'Donnell, a vocal critic of Trump, tweeted, "HE WILL NEVER BE PRESIDENT" and called on people to "shame the Donald." Despite their long-standing feud, O'Donnell was one of the few celebrities to travel to the White House in February to protest Trump's first joint address to Congress.

Lindsay Lohan, currently in rehab at Cliffside Malibu, had an unexpected visitor in the form of actor and producer Ben Affleck, RadarOnline.com reports. Affleck, known for his own struggles with substance abuse, dropped by the treatment center late at night just a few days before Lindsay’s birthday, staying for about an hour. Lohan, 27, was reportedly excited about the possibility of a role in Affleck’s upcoming film, Live by Night, revealing to a former patient that she would have dark hair and an Irish accent in the movie. However, a source close to the project maintains that Lohan “isn’t being considered and won’t be in the movie,” though they didn’t deny the visit. Meanwhile, as Lohan prepares to sit down with Oprah Winfrey for an interview, a 15-second sneak peek of the interview has been released, showing Winfrey asking, "Do you think you can turn it around?" and "What is it that you are addicted to?" Lohan responded, "I'm my own worst enemy and I know it." Winfrey, who described Lohan as "honest" and "authentic" during their interview, also grilled her with questions such as, "What's going to be different this time?" and "When you get the first DUI, is that a wake-up call?" The full interview, which aired on OWN on August 18, 2013, showcased Lohan’s determination to turn her life around.

In 2015, a 61-year-old Chicago police officer, William Whitley, paid for sex with multiple underage girls, including a 14-year-old and a 16-year-old, according to court records. Whitley's case highlights the technical elements that can justify federal charges for human trafficking. The FBI complaint against Whitley, a 20-year veteran of the Chicago Police Department, points to the interstate nature of the condoms he used, which came from outside Illinois. This interstate commerce factor, combined with his use of a phone and other factors, allowed prosecutors to charge him in federal court, where he pleaded guilty to one count of sex trafficking a minor. Whitley admitted to using Trojan Magnum and LifeStyles condoms, which are manufactured outside Illinois, as well as taking sexually explicit photos of the girls and discussing prices and meeting times with other underage girls. Whitley's defense that braces on the 14-year-old's teeth did not indicate her age was dismissed by the judge. Whitley's case also involved the use of a loaded firearm, and he admitted to paying for sex acts with three other teenage girls. He faces a minimum of 10 years in prison and must register as a sex offender. The federal charge carries a mandatory minimum sentence, which could explain why prosecutors sought federal charges over state ones. Whitley's case underscores the broader issue of human trafficking, particularly involving law enforcement officials, and the technical aspects that can lead to federal prosecution.

Administration lawyers have presented President Barack Obama with four potential restructuring options for the National Security Agency's (NSA) phone-surveillance program, according to officials familiar with the discussions. The options range from retaining the current program to significant changes. The first option involves phone companies controlling the data and allowing the NSA to access certain information upon request. The second option proposes another government agency, such as the FBI or the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, to retain the data, providing a separation of power. The third option suggests a non-telecommunications and non-government agency to manage the data, though Obama has previously dismissed this as impractical due to increased expense, legal ambiguity, and public confidence issues. The final option is to scrap the program entirely, which Obama has deemed unrealistic. The options were submitted well ahead of the March 28 deadline set by the President, with the Office of Director of National Intelligence and the Justice Department completing the task early. Obama's own remarks last month leaned towards one of the first two options, but the decision on which path to take remains uncertain. The debate over the NSA's phone-surveillance program continues, with various stakeholders weighing in on the potential impacts of each restructuring option.

The U.S. government is on the brink of a shutdown, with Congress working through the weekend to avoid a 17-year first-time occurrence. House Speaker John Boehner’s latest move to delay the Affordable Care Act (ACA) for a year and repeal its medical device tax has set the stage for a potential impasse. Senate Democrats and President Obama are resolute in their stance against any changes to the ACA, viewing such moves as a non-negotiable demand. Boehner’s strategy, driven by his party’s conservative base, aims to delay the ACA’s implementation and repeal the medical device tax, but this could lead to a government shutdown if the Senate rejects the amendments. The Senate is not scheduled to reconvene until Monday, leaving little time to resolve the impasse. 

Democrats, led by Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, are pushing a hardline approach, refusing to negotiate on any short-term funding bills that include anti-ACA provisions. Reid’s strategy is to force Republicans to choose between a shutdown or passing a clean funding bill that funds the ACA without changes. This approach is seen as politically risky for Republicans, who could face backlash if a shutdown occurs. However, Democrats are also wary, as a shutdown could harm their Senate majority, especially in red states. 

The White House and Democrats are united in their refusal to negotiate on the debt ceiling, viewing it as a non-negotiable issue. The looming deadline for raising the debt ceiling on October 17 adds another layer of complexity to the budget negotiations. If the government does shut down, the economic impact on the Washington region, which hosts the largest concentration of federal workers, could be severe. The region could lose an estimated $200 million a day and see more than 700,000 jobs affected. Federal services, including child-care centers and research facilities, could be suspended, and the Smithsonian museums and other attractions might close. 

Local officials are preparing for the worst, with cities like Washington, D.C., attempting to declare all employees essential to avoid service disruptions. Del. Eleanor Holmes Norton has introduced legislation to exempt the city from a potential shutdown, recalling the disastrous impact of the 1995 shutdown. The region’s economy, already weakened by sequestration cuts, could suffer further. Air traffic controllers, considered essential, will continue to work, but other support staff might be furloughed, leading to delays in services. Veterans’ benefits and new patient enrollments at the NIH could be delayed, and courts might operate for only two weeks. 

Republicans, however, are pushing back, accusing Reid of deliberately seeking a shutdown to hurt their political standing. They argue that the burden will be on Boehner to pass a clean funding bill or risk a shutdown. Despite the risks, Democrats and the White House are confident that Boehner will eventually have to acquiesce to their demands to keep the government funded. The political landscape is tense, with the potential for a shutdown looming as the clock ticks down.

Premier Wen Jiabao of China encouraged North Korea to allow market mechanisms to revamp its economy, recommending improvements in laws and regulations, business investment, and customs services. These suggestions came after Wen's meeting with Jang Song-thaek, the powerful uncle of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, in Beijing. Jang's visit to China, the highest-profile by a North Korean official since Kim's ascension, signals a potential thaw in relations between the two countries. China's President Hu Jintao also met with Jang, underscoring Beijing's support for the North's new leadership. China and North Korea are working to intensify economic cooperation through development zones in Rason and Hwanggumphyong, with North Korea receiving around $300 million in non-financial direct investment from about 100 Chinese companies. Despite these efforts, China faces challenges in managing its relationship with North Korea, which it views as a strategic buffer between itself and U.S. military forces in South Korea. North Korea's nuclear weapons program and past border incidents, such as the seizure of Chinese fishermen, have strained Sino-North Korean relations. Beijing supports international sanctions against North Korea but is hesitant to impose harsh measures that could destabilize the regime and lead to a refugee crisis. The development zones aim to boost economic growth and reduce North Korea's reliance on Chinese aid, aligning with China's interests in a more prosperous and stable North Korea.

Dove, a brand known for its "Real Beauty" campaigns, has ventured into a new form of advertising that has sparked both praise and criticism. The company recently launched a limited edition of body wash bottles, each designed to represent a different body shape, from curvaceous to slender. Unilever, the parent company, claims the bottles celebrate diversity and individuality, aligning with Dove's long-standing mission to promote real beauty. According to the company, these bottles are part of a broader effort to empower women to embrace their unique body types, reflecting the belief that beauty comes in all shapes and sizes.

However, the initiative has not gone down well with many consumers. Social media users have mocked the bottles, pointing out that they are more likely to highlight body insecurities than to promote body positivity. One Twitter user quipped, "thanks Dove but I already have a body wash that matches my natural curves :)" Another added, "who at Dove thought this was a remotely good idea?" The bottles, with their exaggerated and sometimes comical shapes, have been compared to everything from a wine jug to a blender, highlighting the absurdity of the concept. Critics argue that Dove's attempt to sell body wash by emphasizing body shape is not only ineffective but also potentially harmful, as it could reinforce rather than challenge societal beauty standards.

The campaign has also been criticized for its incoherence and contradiction. By creating bottles that mimic the shapes of different body types, Dove risks making women feel even more self-conscious about their own bodies. A pear-shaped woman, for example, might find herself choosing between bottles that represent her ideal body type and one that does not. This could turn a simple trip to the store into a reminder of her body image struggles. Additionally, the functional differences between the bottles—such as their unwieldy shapes—could inadvertently suggest that there is a "best" body type, undermining the message of diversity and inclusivity.

Dove's statement that the bottles are intended to remind women of their individuality and uniqueness has been met with skepticism. Some argue that the company's true motive is to sell more products, rather than genuinely promote body positivity. The campaign's failure to address the underlying issues of body image and the pressure to conform to unrealistic beauty standards has led many to question the effectiveness of Dove's approach. While the company claims to be celebrating diversity, the practical implications of the bottles suggest a more superficial and potentially counterproductive strategy.

The backlash against the Dove Real Beauty Bottles highlights the complex relationship between advertising and body image. While companies like Dove aim to use their platforms to promote positive messages, the execution can often fall flat, especially when it relies on gimmicks that may do more harm than good. As the debate continues, Dove faces the challenge of balancing its marketing goals with the need to genuinely support body positivity and self-acceptance.

In San Antonio, Texas, a man named Gilbert Flores was fatally shot by two Bexar County Sheriff deputies after a 20-minute struggle, according to a video captured by a passerby. The incident unfolded following a domestic disturbance call at Flores's home in northwest San Antonio on Friday. When deputies arrived around 11:30 a.m., they found a woman with a cut on her head and a baby who appeared to be injured. Flores, who had a criminal past and was armed, resisted arrest and was shot by the deputies after non-lethal weapons proved ineffective. The video shows Flores standing with his hands up next to a sheriff's SUV as two deputies, Greg Vasquez and Robert Sanchez, take aim from about 10 yards away. Suddenly, Flores doubles over and goes down, dying moments later. Sheriff Susan Pamerleau acknowledged the video as a cause for concern but emphasized the need for a thorough investigation. District Attorney Nicholas LaHood described the video as troubling and confirmed that two separate recordings were being reviewed. Both deputies were placed on administrative leave pending the outcome of the investigation, which is ongoing. The incident has sparked community outrage and raised questions about the use of force by law enforcement. With a history of criminal activity, including a 2003 aggravated robbery charge and a 1999 criminal trespass charge, Flores's background adds complexity to the situation. The Bexar County Sheriff's Office and the District Attorney's office are currently investigating the circumstances leading to Flores's death.

A St. Louis jury recently awarded a California woman over $70 million after finding that Johnson & Johnson's baby powder caused her ovarian cancer, the latest in a series of lawsuits raising concerns about the health risks of talcum powder use. The jury's decision came after a nine-day trial that began on September 26, during which the plaintiff, Deborah Giannecchini, testified that she used Johnson & Johnson's baby powder for feminine hygiene for over four decades before being diagnosed with ovarian cancer in 2012. Giannecchini, now 62, has an 80% chance of dying within the next two years and has undergone extensive medical treatments, including surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy.

The jury found that Johnson & Johnson, through its subsidiary, was responsible for $65 million in punitive damages, while the talc supplier, Imerys Talc America, was ordered to pay $2.5 million in punitive damages. The plaintiffs' attorney, Jim Onder, expressed satisfaction with the verdict, stating, "They once again reaffirmed the need for Johnson & Johnson to warn the public of the ovarian cancer risk associated with its product." Onder's firm has represented plaintiffs in all three St. Louis cases that have gone to trial, with the two previous verdicts totaling $127 million.

Johnson & Johnson, however, maintains its stance that talcum powder is safe and that the science supports its safety. A company spokeswoman, Carol Goodrich, stated, "We deeply sympathize with the women and families impacted by ovarian cancer. We will appeal today's verdict because we are guided by the science, which supports the safety of Johnson's Baby Powder." The company also noted that two other lawsuits in New Jersey were dismissed by a judge who found insufficient evidence linking talcum powder to ovarian cancer.

The case highlights the ongoing debate over the health risks associated with talcum powder use. While much research has found no link or a weak one between ovarian cancer and using baby powder for feminine hygiene, some studies suggest that women who regularly use talc on their genital area face a 40% higher risk of developing ovarian cancer. This has led to numerous lawsuits, with about 2,000 women filing similar suits and lawyers reviewing thousands of potential cases.

The verdict in this latest trial is part of a growing trend of lawsuits against Johnson & Johnson, which faces hundreds of claims in St. Louis state court, as well as about 300 suits in Los Angeles and a growing number of federal cases. A New Jersey state court judge recently dismissed two talc cases, finding inadequate scientific support for the claims. Despite the company's denials, the repeated jury verdicts suggest that the public may be increasingly concerned about the potential health risks of talcum powder use.

Scientists have discovered that interbreeding between two major African malaria mosquitoes, Anopheles gambiae and Anopheles coluzzii, has resulted in a hybrid mosquito that is resistant to insecticide-treated bed nets, posing a significant challenge to malaria control efforts. This hybrid mosquito emerged during a period of hybridization between the two species in Mali, coinciding with the start of a major insecticide-treated bed net campaign. The hybrid mosquito inherited an entire genomic island of divergence from A. gambiae, which includes a suite of insecticide-resistance alleles. This event suggests that increased insecticide exposure acted as a selective force, driving the introgression of an entire genomic island across the reproductive barrier separating these two species. The study provides a rare example of adaptive introgression in an animal species and highlights the dynamics of how insecticide resistance evolved in A. coluzzii. This finding underscores the need for the development of new and effective malaria vector control strategies, such as new insecticides, biological agents, and genetic manipulation of mosquitoes. The research, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, emphasizes the importance of understanding the evolutionary dynamics of mosquito populations in response to environmental changes, including the introduction of insecticides.

Steven Spielberg's adaptation of Roald Dahl's children's book, The BFG, debuted with a disappointing $22.2 million in the U.S., falling short of expectations and marking a significant box office underperformance for the usually reliable director. The film, produced by Disney, had a $140 million budget, making it a substantial gamble. Despite positive reviews and a solid CinemaScore, the movie struggled to attract audiences, especially in the face of competition from Pixar's Finding Dory, which took in $50 million over the same weekend. Several factors contributed to the film's poor performance. First, the sentimental and emotional storyline, while heartfelt, lacked the awe-inspiring visuals that typically draw in families. Second, the film's lukewarm critical reception and mixed reviews from critics may have deterred potential viewers. Additionally, the lack of recognizable stars and the absence of flashy spectacles in the marketing campaign did not help. Lastly, the film's release timing coincided with a weak overall box office performance during the holiday weekend, further dampening its prospects. The BFG's failure raises questions about the future of children's book adaptations in the current market, where franchises like Minions and Disney's own fairy-tale adaptations dominate. While the film may still find success overseas, its domestic performance suggests that Spielberg's once-unquestionable box office draw may be waning, especially for family-friendly, fantasy-oriented projects.

A Washington, D.C., police officer challenged a teenage girl to a dance-off, holding her own as the two did the "Nae Nae" dance. The incident occurred in a park on K Street SW when a female officer arrived to break up a fight and saw 17-year-old Aaliya Taylor dancing to the popular Silentó song "Watch Me (Whip/Nae Nae)." Surprised by the officer's unexpected challenge, Aaliya, a senior at Ballou High School, accepted. The officer, whose identity the Metropolitan Police Department declined to disclose, matched Aaliya step for step, much to the amusement of onlookers. The dance-off was recorded and posted on Facebook, where it garnered over 279,000 views in less than 24 hours. Aaliya said the encounter changed her perception of the police, noting, "She gave me a hug and was like, 'What's your name?' and she was smiling. I was like, 'Oh yeah, we need more cops like you.'" The officer and Aaliya called the dance-off a tie, and D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser tweeted, "DC has innovative ways to keep our community #saferstrongerDC," highlighting the officer's initiative. The video's viral success suggests a positive shift in community-police relations, as Aaliya's tweet, "We need more cops like you," indicates a newfound appreciation for the officer's approach.

The Toronto Zoo is investigating after a YouTube video surfaced showing a woman jumping over a protective fence to retrieve a hat that fell into a tiger's enclosure. The video, posted on Saturday, depicts the woman climbing down the fence and reaching for the hat while a tiger, separated by a second barrier, lunges towards her. After recovering the hat, she hops back over to a group of onlookers. A man is heard criticizing her actions, calling her a "moron" and a "bad example." The zoo's spokesperson, Jennifer Tracey, stated that the incident was very irresponsible, as the woman could have injured herself or the tiger. No zoo staff were present at the tiger's pen when the incident occurred. According to Tracey, the staff member assigned to the tiger's area was likely attending to other animals. The zoo is seeking witnesses to help clarify what happened. Violations of the zoo's by-laws, which prohibit climbing or entering restricted areas, could result in bans or fines. The zoo is encouraging anyone with information to come forward.

A 29-year-old Southern California man has been charged with murder in the fatal mauling of 63-year-old Pamela Devitt, who was attacked by a pack of pit bulls while jogging in the Mojave Desert on May 9. Devitt suffered approximately 150 to 200 puncture wounds and died en route to the hospital. When the first deputy arrived at the scene, one of the dogs was still attacking Devitt. The deputy fired two shots, but the dogs continued to approach. The Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department and animal control officials obtained a warrant and searched Jackson's home, located about a block from the attack site. Eight dogs, including six pit bulls, were taken into custody and are likely to be euthanized. Jackson, who authorities say was running a marijuana operation from his home, faces additional charges of cultivating marijuana, possession of marijuana for sale, and assault with a deadly weapon. Since January, the district attorney's office received at least three reports of Jackson's pit bulls attacking people. Pamela Devitt's husband, Ben Devitt, expressed shock and fear, stating, "The fact that there's animals out there roaming around with that kind of killer instinct, it's just something I can't shake." The case is rare, as murder charges in dog attack cases are extremely uncommon, with only six such cases documented in the past year.

A ceremony at Florida Memorial University, a historically black university, honored Trayvon Martin and his parents, Sybrina Fulton and Tracy Martin, by opening the headquarters of the Trayvon Martin Foundation. The foundation, established after Martin’s 2012 death at the hands of neighborhood watch volunteer George Zimmerman, now has a physical space where it can host events and meetings. The foundation focuses on helping families affected by violent crime and aims to promote non-violent solutions. During the ceremony, the Martin family and university officials emphasized the importance of education and leadership development for young men, drawing parallels between Trayvon and the university’s Black Male College Explorers Program. The program provides academic and leadership training to at-risk black males. The university president, Roslyn Artis, highlighted the space as a place for reflection and remembrance. Attendees included local politicians, state representatives, and community members. The event concluded with a ribbon-cutting ceremony and a tour of the facility, where attendees could view artwork depicting Trayvon and learn about the foundation’s mission. Despite the racial tensions surrounding Martin’s death, the foundation’s work is seen as universal, addressing violence and its impact on families. The ceremony underscored the ongoing efforts to honor Trayvon’s memory and promote positive change.

A member of the Sackler family, which owns Purdue Pharma, has been awarded a patent for a new formulation of buprenorphine, a medication used to treat opioid use disorder. The patent, issued in January, concerns a wafer that could dissolve faster than existing forms when placed under the tongue, potentially reducing the risk of drug diversion. Critics argue that the patent could enable the Sackler family to benefit financially from the addiction crisis that their company is accused of fueling. Purdue Pharma, which faces over 1,000 lawsuits from cities, states, counties, and tribes, has denied allegations of wrongdoing. The lawsuits target the company for its alleged role in seeding the opioid crisis with its pain medication, OxyContin. In addition to the lawsuits, Congress has requested a copy of a deposition from Richard Sackler, a member of the Sackler family, as part of a lawsuit brought by Kentucky against Purdue. Meanwhile, the company has been trying to show it is taking steps to address the addiction crisis by backing safer prescribing efforts and donating money to the National Sheriffs’ Association to purchase naloxone and train law enforcement on its use. The Sackler family has donated hundreds of millions of dollars to museums, schools, and hospitals around the world, but has increasingly come under scrutiny amid the opioid crisis. The patent's description warns that people addicted to drugs sometimes commit crimes to feed their habit, highlighting the public safety and law enforcement costs associated with addiction.

Downsizing has hit the toilet paper aisle as rolls become narrower, cardboard tubes grow in diameter, the number of sheets per roll falls, and the sheets get smaller. Manufacturers, aiming to save costs, have introduced "desheeting"—reducing the number of sheets per roll. Kimberly-Clark, for instance, recently launched a new Kleenex tissue that claims to be 15% "bulkier" but actually contains 13% fewer sheets than before. This trend has sparked debate among consumers, who argue that they should decide for themselves how much toilet paper to use and prefer transparency from manufacturers.

Consumer Reports has tested various brands for strength, softness, disintegration, and tearing ease, identifying two top performers. White Cloud 3-Ply Ultra, sold at Walmart, was named a CR Best Buy, scoring excellent marks for strength and softness, with very good disintegration and tearing ease. At 25 cents per 100 sheets, it offers good value. Charmin Ultra Strong, at 41 cents per 100 sheets, excels in strength but falls short in softness and disintegration, making it a close second. However, other brands like Scott 1000, Marcal Small Steps, and Cottonelle CleanCare with Touch of Soft Cotton, despite their names, do not perform as well. Scott 1000, at 8 cents, is neither soft nor strong, while Marcal Small Steps, at 25 cents, is harsh and doesn’t tear easily. Cottonelle CleanCare, at 44 cents per 100 sheets, is less soft than many and costs more than most other tissues tested.

Consumers are advised to choose wisely, considering not just brand but also performance and price. The article suggests that while some brands may claim to be softer or stronger, their actual performance may not justify the higher cost. Therefore, it’s crucial to read reviews and test the products to ensure they meet individual needs.

An iguana electrocuted itself on a power line, causing a fire that knocked out electricity to The Palms Care Center in Lauderdale Lakes, Florida, forcing 20 patients to be moved to hospitals as a precaution. Battalion Chief spokesman Michael Kane of Broward Sheriff Fire Rescue said the facility was running on generator power but only cooling half of the building effectively. Firefighters moved residents to parts of the facility with working air conditioning units. Electricity was restored late Friday, and patients were expected to be returned to the nursing home by Saturday. The facility, licensed for 120 beds, was left with half its cooling capacity due to the iguana incident.

Hillary Clinton has embarked on a new phase of her career as the co-leader of the Clinton Foundation, alongside her husband Bill and daughter Chelsea. This marks the first time the two elder Clintons have worked together in a similar capacity since the 1992 campaign. The foundation has undergone an internal review, driven by Chelsea, which has led to recommendations for tightening structure and management. Clinton’s arrival provides her with a formal platform to focus on issues she cares about, potentially laying the groundwork for a presidential campaign in 2016. Her role at the foundation offers a buffer from the daily political grind, allowing her to work on specific issue sets while maintaining a high profile. The foundation’s mission includes improving global health, strengthening economies, promoting health and wellness, and protecting the environment through partnerships among governments, businesses, NGOs, and private citizens. Clinton plans to focus on issues related to women and girls, early childhood development, and economic development. Her work at the foundation will be closely scrutinized, but it also provides a stress-free path to being an influential public figure. The foundation’s projects include the Clinton Climate Initiative, the Clinton Health Access Initiative, and the Alliance for a Healthier Generation, among others. This new phase of Clinton’s career offers both opportunities and challenges, as she balances her public profile with the demands of leading a major philanthropic organization.

Jamaican lawmakers have passed legislation decriminalizing the possession of small amounts of marijuana and establishing a licensing agency to regulate a lawful medical cannabis industry. The new act, which passed after several hours of debate in the lower house, makes possession of up to 2 ounces of marijuana a petty offense, punishable by a fine but not a criminal record. Cultivation of five or fewer plants on any premises is also permitted. The law paves the way for a licensing authority to oversee the cultivation and distribution of marijuana for medical, scientific, and therapeutic purposes, as well as for religious use by Rastafarians, a spiritual movement founded in Jamaica in the 1930s. Tourists prescribed medical marijuana abroad will be able to apply for permits to legally purchase small amounts of "ganja," the local term for marijuana.

The move is part of a broader international trend towards easing restrictions on marijuana for medical or personal use. More than 20 U.S. states now allow some form of medical marijuana, and last year, Colorado and Washington legalized personal use. On Tuesday, Alaska became the third U.S. state to legalize the recreational use of marijuana for adults. In the Americas, Uruguay was the first nation to create a legal marijuana market, while Argentina decriminalized personal possession of marijuana in 2009. Jamaica's decision to decriminalize marijuana and establish a regulated medical cannabis industry is seen as a significant step, given the drug's long-standing cultural significance on the island. However, the national security minister, Peter Bunting, emphasized that the legislation does not mean Jamaica plans to soften its stance on transnational drug trafficking or illegal cultivation. The U.S. assistant secretary for counter-narcotics affairs, William Brownfield, noted that while Jamaica has the right to make its own laws, the trafficking of marijuana into the U.S. remains illegal.

The new law is expected to have significant economic implications for Jamaica, which has long been a major supplier of marijuana to the U.S. and regional islands. The Jamaican commerce minister, Anthony Hylton, stated that the cannabis industry holds "great potential" for the island, which is currently grappling with economic challenges. Local scientists have already developed marijuana-derived products, such as "Canasol," which helps relieve pressure in the eyes of glaucoma patients. The establishment of a licensing authority and the development of a medical marijuana sector will need to be refined in the coming months. For now, Jamaican cannabis crusaders are celebrating the amendments, viewing them as a significant step in the right direction.

The Houston Rockets have been sold to local billionaire Tilman Fertitta for a record-breaking $2.2 billion, pending approval from the NBA's Board of Governors. Fertitta, a native of Galveston, Texas, expressed his excitement and called it a "dream come true." The sale comes as Houston recovers from Hurricane Harvey. The Rockets were valued at $1.65 billion and received multiple offers starting at $2 billion. Fertitta, who owns Landry's, Inc., and Golden Nugget Casinos and Hotels, plans to keep the Rockets in Houston. Current owner Leslie Alexander, who bought the team in 1993 for $85 million, will pass the torch to Fertitta, who will also operate the Toyota Center. Fertitta's purchase means Beyoncé's hopes of buying the Rockets with an investment group have been dashed.

A woman in Somerset County, Michele Leonard, 47, was arrested for two separate drunken-driving incidents in the same day, according to Pennsylvania State police. Troopers from Somerset reported that Leonard crashed her car around 5 p.m. on a Saturday, was arrested, tested for blood-alcohol levels, and then released. The trooper investigating the case was unavailable on Monday, leaving details about her release unclear. After being released, Leonard allegedly offered a stranger $3 for a ride back to her crashed vehicle, which she then began driving again. Leonard lost control of the car and sideswiped a parked car in Somerset Township around 6 p.m., then crashed into a shed belonging to Stanley Fisher. Fisher described the incident, saying he saw a car fly down his driveway, past his truck, and heard a big crash before looking out and seeing Leonard's car slam into his shed. Fisher stopped Leonard, took her keys, and heard her say, "I can't get another DUI. I already have one today." Charges for both incidents are pending once police receive blood-alcohol test results. Fisher reported that most of the costly tools in his shed were destroyed, as was the shed itself. Crews were on his property Monday moving what was salvageable from the shed to a truck, where the items will be put into a storage unit until a new shed is built. Fisher expressed that no one should have to go through such an ordeal and emphasized that Leonard should never have been driving a second time.

Democrats have struggled with the issue of stagnant wages during the Obama administration, a vulnerability that Republicans have yet to fully exploit. According to Census data, median household income in 2014 was $1,656 lower than in January 2009, when President Obama took office. While incomes have risen slightly since the end of the Great Recession, the overall trend has been negative. This wage stagnation presents a significant challenge for Democratic candidates, particularly Hillary Clinton, who has benefited from the economic recovery. 

Stuart Stevens, a senior strategist in Mitt Romney’s 2012 campaign, suggests that Democrats have been reluctant to address wage issues, as it could undermine Obama’s record. However, the Republican candidates have been vocal about the need for wage growth. At the recent GOP debate, candidates like Bobby Jindal, Rick Santorum, and Jeb Bush highlighted the issue, citing the hollowing out of the middle class and the decline in disposable income. 

Despite the consensus on the problem, the Republican candidates struggle with how to address it. Rick Santorum is the only candidate to support a specific minimum wage increase, proposing to raise it to $8.75 over three years. Other candidates, like Ben Carson, have expressed support for an unspecified increase but have since backed away from the idea. Donald Trump clarified that his statement about wages being too high referred to the minimum wage, not wages in general. 

The minimum wage issue highlights the Republicans’ dilemma: while they advocate for wage growth, they oppose increasing the minimum wage, which could be seen as a contradiction. Instead, they favor economic policies like tax cuts and deregulation, which have had limited success in the past. 

Democrats, on the other hand, have embraced the Labor Department’s proposed overtime rule, which would significantly expand the number of workers eligible for overtime pay. This rule has received support from Clinton and Sanders, but Republicans have opposed it, arguing it would be burdensome for businesses. 

The debate over wage growth and the minimum wage is likely to become more prominent as the election progresses, especially as the Labor Department prepares for a final rule. However, with the rule not expected until late 2016, it may not be a significant campaign issue yet.

Thousands of Native Americans gathered outside TCF Bank Stadium in Minneapolis on a Sunday to protest the Washington Redskins' name, marking what organizers called the largest-ever protest of the team’s moniker. The event took place as the Redskins faced the Minnesota Vikings in a game at the University of Minnesota’s stadium, which was built with a $10 million donation from the Shakopee Mdewakanton Sioux Community, a tribe that opposes the Redskins' name. Demonstrators chanted and waved banners, with one man holding a sign that read “RACIST.” The estimated crowd of 3,500 to 4,000 included Native Americans, students, and other activists, who expressed their opposition to the name, while Redskins fans, some of whom had their caps and jerseys hidden, walked past the protesters. The interactions between the two groups were often tense, with protesters confronting fans and some fans expressing their support for the name. Rep. Betty McCollum of Minnesota addressed the rally, emphasizing the offensive nature of the name and calling for its change. Despite the protest, the Redskins continued to use their name and logo for the game, with the team’s spokesman stating that the accident involving the buses transporting the team would not affect the game. The University of Minnesota had asked the Vikings to limit the use of the Redskins' name and logo inside the stadium, but the Vikings were still considering how to comply with these requests. The controversy surrounding the name has grown more intense, with Native American leaders, lawmakers, and civil rights activists continuing to call for its change.

Since 1998, every Apple keynote and product launch has seen the company make bold moves, from removing the CD drive in the Macbook Air to the 30-pin connector in the iPhone 5. However, the decision to eliminate the 3.5mm headphone jack from the iPhone 7 has garnered widespread criticism. Phil Schiller, Apple's marketing chief, justified the move by invoking "courage," but the term has been widely mocked. Critics argue that the decision is more about hubris and greed, as Apple will likely sell millions of $9 aux-to-Lightning cable dongles. The elimination of the headphone jack is seen as a step backward, as wired headphones generally provide better sound quality than wireless options. Apple's rationale that space inside the iPhone is at a premium and that users want stereo speakers and Taptic engines is met with skepticism, as the majority of iPhone users are unaware of Taptic engines. Furthermore, the move impacts various accessories that plug into the headphone jack, such as credit card readers and temperature sensors, forcing users to purchase expensive, proprietary Lightning connectors. The removal of the headphone jack also means users cannot charge and use headphones simultaneously, unless they opt for inferior wireless options. The old Apple mantra of "it just works" is now dead, as compatibility with any set of headphones is no longer guaranteed. This decision is seen as a retreat into a walled garden, with users paying the price. Critics argue that Apple's move is not courageous but rather a source of frustration and potential rage.

A San Francisco judge has ordered Wells Fargo to pay $203 million to its California customers, citing the bank's manipulation of debit transactions to maximize overdraft fees. The 90-page ruling, penned by Judge William Alsup, accuses Wells Fargo of profiteering by processing transactions from highest to lowest amount, thereby accelerating account depletion and increasing the number of overdrafts. This practice, known as "high-low" resequencing, has been in place since 1998 and has generated over $1.4 billion in overdraft fees for Wells Fargo in California alone from 2005 to 2007. The judge's decision may influence a similar case in Florida, which includes claims against 30 other lending institutions, including Bank of America, Citibank, Chase, Union Bank, and U.S. Bank. Wells Fargo argues that its practices were consistent with regulatory guidelines and that many transactions lack timestamps, necessitating a reordering for processing. The bank plans to appeal the decision. The ruling also criticizes Wells Fargo for inadequate disclosure of its policies, noting that relevant information was buried deep within lengthy documents. New federal regulations will require banks to obtain explicit customer consent for overdraft protection, potentially limiting the practice's future effectiveness.

President Donald Trump criticized the FBI and opened the door to potentially pardoning former national security adviser Michael Flynn just before speaking at the FBI's National Academy. Trump, speaking to reporters on the White House lawn, said, "We're going to rebuild the FBI" after what he described as "really, really disgraceful" documents. He appeared to refer to text messages the Justice Department provided Congress this week, in which a senior agent described candidate Trump as an "idiot" and made other political remarks. Trump's comments are the latest in a series of criticisms he has directed at the bureau, with earlier tweets calling the FBI's reputation "in Tatters — worst in History!" and labeling former FBI Director James Comey a "liar" and "a leaker." Trump also accused the FBI of illegally wiretapping Trump Tower in 2016 and continued to cast doubt on the bureau's conclusion that Russia interfered in the 2016 presidential election.

During his speech at the FBI's National Academy, Trump refrained from directly attacking the bureau, focusing instead on his "law and order" agenda and praising law enforcement. He promised to work with law enforcement to combat drug cartels and gangs, such as MS-13, which he referred to as "savages." Trump also echoed Attorney General Jeff Sessions, stating, "With me as your president, America's police will have a true friend and loyal champion in the White House. More loyal than anyone else can be." However, his earlier comments hung over his appearance, as it was unusual for a president to criticize the FBI, which is the premier law enforcement agency in the country. Trump's pick to lead the FBI, Christopher Wray, also defended the bureau, stating, "There is no finer institution than the FBI and no finer people than the men and women who work there and are its very beating heart."

Trump's remarks came as special counsel Robert Mueller's investigation into possible coordination between the Trump campaign and Russia continued, with Flynn pleading guilty to lying to the FBI and other campaign officials being indicted. Trump's lawyer, Ty Cobb, denied any consideration of pardoning Flynn, stating, "There is no consideration at the White House of a pardon for Michael Flynn." Trump's comments and actions have raised questions about his relationship with the FBI and the integrity of the bureau, particularly given the recent disclosures about biased agents and the handling of the Hillary Clinton email investigation. The FBI Agents Association defended the workforce, stating, "Every day, FBI special agents put their lives on the line to protect the American public from national security and criminal threats."

President-elect Donald Trump met with Martin Luther King III, son of the late civil rights leader, at Trump Tower in New York on January 16, 2017. The meeting took place on the holiday marking the life of Martin Luther King Jr., and King III expressed that he believes Trump's intent is to represent all Americans. This interaction comes days after Trump had engaged in a fierce Twitter exchange with Rep. John Lewis, a prominent civil rights leader, over the legitimacy of Trump's election. The meeting highlights the ongoing efforts by Trump to project a message of unity and inclusiveness, despite facing criticism and low approval ratings. Meanwhile, Russian President Vladimir Putin accused the outgoing Obama administration of trying to undermine Trump's legitimacy through unverified claims, including a dossier alleging sexual misconduct and other activities by Trump. Putin dismissed the dossier as "fake" and "nonsense," and criticized the new sanctions imposed by the Obama administration on Russia. Putin also expressed concern over the "media frenzy" surrounding Trump, suggesting that it reflects the "degradation of US political elites." Trump, for his part, has dismissed the dossier as "fake news" and "phony stuff," aligning with Putin's stance. These developments underscore the complex political landscape as the United States transitions to a new administration.

A woman named Avital* faced a humiliating encounter with Southwest Airlines on June 5th. She was boarding a 6 AM flight from Las Vegas to New York in a casual outfit, including a cotton dress, loose flannel shirt, and colorful scarf, when a representative informed her that her cleavage was "inappropriate" and she would not be allowed to board unless she covered up. Avital, however, decided to board the plane anyway, stating, "I didn't want to let the representative's Big Feelings about my breasts change the way I intended to board my flight." She noted that the plane took off safely, and her cleavage did not interfere with the aircraft's functionality. Avital described the situation as "slut shaming" and highlighted the irony of a man on the same flight wearing a shirt with a Trojan condom applique and boarding without issue. Southwest Airlines offered Avital an apology and a refund as a gesture of goodwill. The airline's spokesperson explained that their Contract of Carriage allows them to refuse transportation to customers whose clothing is deemed lewd, obscene, or patently offensive. However, this incident is part of a broader pattern of Southwest Airlines enforcing arbitrary and often discriminatory dress codes, leading to numerous complaints and lawsuits.

Rapper Andre Johnson, known by the stage name Christ Bearer, recently spoke to E! News about his shocking incident from April 2018, where he cut off his own penis and survived a fall from a second-story balcony. Johnson, 41, claims he was in full control while under the influence of drugs and that he severed his penis as a means to end his struggles with sex. He explained, "That was the root of all my problems. My solution to the problem was the realization that sex is for mortals, and I am a god." Johnson also addressed reports that doctors had reattached his penis, stating, "Doctors didn't reattach it, but I definitely have some penis left." He emphasized that the sensation is still there, and he can still get aroused, but he believes his actions were a blessing. Johnson was not attempting suicide but was under the influence of PCP, a drug he had stopped using for years. He had been studying literature about monks and vasectomies when he took the knife to his genitals and jumped. Johnson survived the fall, which he described as a fortunate outcome, as he was only on the second floor. He welcomed a new daughter, Kennedy, into his life two weeks after the incident and has two older daughters, Lana, 2, and Lauren, 8.
