European counter-terror operations have thwarted a significant plot aimed at targeting police officers and buildings in Belgium, leading to the arrest of 15 suspected jihadis in Belgium and France. In the Belgian town of Verviers, near the German border, two suspected terrorists were shot dead by police, and another was wounded during a shootout. The operation targeted an active terror cell spanning both countries, with the intention of averting an imminent attack. Belgian federal magistrate Eric van der Sypt disclosed that 13 suspects were arrested in Belgium, while two were detained in France. Nine of the suspects were apprehended in Molenbeek, two in Brussels, one in Berchem, one in Verviers, and two in France. The Verviers address yielded ammunition, weapons, including four Kalashnikovs, smaller firearms, and explosives, along with police uniforms, walkie-talkies, radios, mobile phones, false documents, and a substantial amount of money. In Molenbeek, police discovered ammunition, a knife, mobile phones, and other items crucial to the investigation. The operation aimed to dismantle a terrorist cell and its logistic network, with evidence suggesting that the group intended to kill several police officers in the street and at police stations. Belgian authorities have increased security measures, with 150 troops on standby for anti-terror operations, and the country will remain at its highest terrorism threat level for at least one month. Meanwhile, several Jewish schools in Belgium have been closed amid warnings of potential attacks by radical Islamists. Across Europe, authorities are on high alert for further potential terrorist attacks, with concerns about sleeper cells and the evolving threat landscape. European Union and Middle East intelligence agencies have identified an "imminent threat" to Belgium and possibly the Netherlands. The threat is characterized by a large number of radicalized Islamic extremists, their lack of a clear command structure, and the growing sophistication of their operations, making it extremely challenging for law enforcement agencies to prevent every attack.

At least 19 people have perished and dozens remain missing following the collapse of a hydroelectric dam in southeastern Laos, state media reported. The Xepian-Xe Nam Noy dam, under construction by a joint venture led by South Korean companies, collapsed on Monday evening, releasing a massive volume of water that swept away homes and left over 6,600 people homeless. Rescue operations are underway as top government officials rushed to the site, and public appeals for aid have been launched. The dam, still under construction, was designed to generate 1,879 gigawatts of power annually, with 90 percent intended for export to Thailand. The project, costing an estimated $1.02 billion, was a key part of Laos' plan to become the "battery of Southeast Asia," generating significant revenue through electricity exports while providing local benefits. However, the disaster has raised concerns about the environmental impact, particularly on the Mekong River and its communities. As the project was still under construction, the full extent of the damage and the number of casualties remain unclear. The Red Cross has staff and volunteers on the ground, providing assistance to those affected. The incident has caught many unawares, highlighting the risks associated with such large-scale infrastructure projects.

The 2019 Golden Globe nominations included several surprises and snubs. Notably, NBC's The Good Place was honored for best comedy series, while Sacha Baron Cohen and the BBC/Netflix series Bodyguard unexpectedly received nods. However, The Handmaid's Tale and Westworld were snubbed in their respective categories. In the acting categories, Sterling K. Brown, John Krasinski, Liev Schreiber, Milo Ventimiglia, and Bob Odenkirk were all left out, with new additions like Stephan James and Billy Porter. Other notable snubs included Sam Elliott for A Star Is Born, Mary Poppins Returns for best original song, and "Atlanta" for best comedy series. The nominations also highlighted the H.F.P.A.'s preference for network comedies and up-and-coming shows, while overlooking established series like Atlanta, This Is Us, and Westworld.

A Baltimore County police officer, Amy Caprio, was tragically killed during a confrontation with a 16-year-old boy and three other suspects in Perry Hall, Maryland, on Monday, May 21, 2018. Caprio, a 29-year-old officer with four years of service, was responding to a call about a suspicious vehicle when she encountered the suspects. According to witness accounts, Caprio was struck by a vehicle, likely a black Jeep Wrangler, and was pronounced dead at MedStar Franklin Square Hospital. The 16-year-old boy, Dawnta Anthony Harris, has been charged with her murder, and three other suspects are still at large. The incident prompted a massive manhunt and a lockdown of the surrounding community, with nearly 2,000 students stranded in their schools for hours. The search was ongoing as night fell, with police using body camera footage and advanced technology to track the suspects. The Baltimore County Police Department praised Caprio as a dedicated and promising officer, noting her contributions to closing a significant holiday package theft investigation. Her death was a shock to the community, with Governor Larry Hogan offering condolences and stating that U.S. and Maryland flags would fly at half-staff until Caprio’s funeral service. The department also highlighted Caprio’s personal life, including her love for outdoor activities and her husband, Tim, with whom she was planning a trip to celebrate their third wedding anniversary. Caprio’s legacy as a dedicated officer who made the ultimate sacrifice was honored through a viewing and funeral service, attended by many colleagues and friends who expressed their support and grief.

President Donald Trump held a 77-minute press conference on Thursday, marking his first solo event of its kind since taking office, and it quickly became a showcase of his combative and unorthodox style. The event, which was initially announced with just an hour’s notice, was ostensibly to announce the nomination of Alexander Acosta as the new Labor Secretary, but it soon devolved into a platform for Trump to address a myriad of issues and controversies surrounding his administration. The president’s performance was characterized by a mix of bravado, defensiveness, and a relentless attack on the media, which he repeatedly labeled as “fake news” and “dishonest.”

At the outset, Trump took a jab at the media, stating, “I turn on the TV, open the newspapers, and I see stories of chaos. Chaos. Yet it is the exact opposite. This administration is running like a fine-tuned machine.” This statement was quickly contradicted by a fact-check, which revealed that his administration had not accomplished as much as he claimed, and that his Electoral College victory was not the largest since Ronald Reagan as he had boasted. The president’s assertion that “zero chaos” exists in his administration was also challenged by reports of internal strife and the forced resignation of his national security adviser, Michael Flynn, due to his misleading statements about conversations with the Russian ambassador.

Trump’s defense of his administration was met with skepticism as he repeatedly dismissed reports of his campaign’s alleged ties to Russia, stating, “Russia is fake news. Russia — this is fake news put out by the media.” He also downplayed the significance of the travel ban, saying, “The failing New York Times story on alleged campaign contact with Russian officials is a joke and fake news.” This was in stark contrast to the ongoing investigations and public scrutiny of these claims, which had already led to the resignation of Flynn and the appointment of a special counsel to investigate potential collusion.

The president’s approach to the media was particularly aggressive. He accused CNN of poor ratings and mocked the BBC, saying, “That’s another beauty.” He also engaged in a back-and-forth with CNN reporter Jim Acosta, who pressed the president on several points. Trump’s response was to call Acosta “very fake news” and to suggest that the network’s ratings aren’t “good right now.” This exchange highlighted the tension between the administration and the press, with Trump repeatedly using the term “fake news” to dismiss unfavorable reports.

Trump’s defense of his administration extended to other areas as well. He boasted about the economic performance, saying, “Jobs have already started to surge,” but this was countered by data showing that unemployment was higher when he took office than when Obama left. He also claimed that the Islamic State had spread like cancer, another mess he inherited, but this was disputed by reports showing that the group had begun to lose ground before his administration.

During the press conference, Trump took the opportunity to address a range of other issues, including his stance on anti-Semitism. He dismissed reports of anti-Semitic incidents, saying, “They'll do signs, and they'll do drawings that are inappropriate. It won't be my people. It will be the people on the other side to anger people like you.” This response was seen as an attempt to deflect responsibility for the actions of his supporters and to blame them on his opponents.

The president also addressed the upcoming travel ban, stating that it would be revised and tailored to address objections from the appeals court. He also promised to have a health care replacement by mid-March and to roll back Obama-era regulations on mining near streams. However, these promises were met with skepticism given the lack of substantive legislative progress so far.

Throughout the press conference, Trump’s tone was often confrontational and combative. He interrupted reporters, refused to answer certain questions, and even suggested that the media was biased and dishonest. This approach was designed to assert his control over the narrative and to bolster his base, which has been critical of the media’s coverage of his administration.

The event was a stark contrast to the traditional format of a presidential press conference, which is typically more formal and less confrontational. Trump’s performance was reminiscent of his campaign style, characterized by a willingness to take on the media and to use the platform to address a wide range of issues. However, it also highlighted the challenges he faces in governing and the ongoing scrutiny of his administration.

In the end, Trump’s press conference was a mixed bag. While it allowed him to address a range of issues and to assert his control over the narrative, it also underscored the challenges he faces in dealing with the media and in managing his administration. The event was seen as a test of his ability to handle the pressures of the presidency and to navigate the complex relationship between the executive branch and the press.

Scientists have uncovered the mechanism by which animals, including sheep, link the change in seasons to their fertility, a discovery that could help farmers adjust the timing of lambing seasons. This groundbreaking research, led by academics from the Universities of Nottingham and Bristol and published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS), reveals how melatonin, a hormone produced during long winter nights in the pineal gland of the brain, signals to a specific region of the pituitary gland to control sex hormones. David Bates, a joint senior author and Professor of Oncology at the University of Nottingham, explains that changes in sex hormones, which control breeding, horn growth, and coat thickness, are regulated by the length of the day. However, the exact link between melatonin and the pituitary gland had eluded scientists for nearly three decades. The research team, including PhD student Dr. Jennifer Castle-Miller and Dr. Domingo Tortonese from the University of Bristol, discovered that melatonin controls the production of two different forms of a protein called vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) within a specific region of the pituitary gland. In winter, sheep produce a form of VEGF that blocks blood vessel growth, isolating the region that detects melatonin from the area that produces sex hormones. This isolation allows VEGF to act as a messenger, controlling the production of sex hormones and thus the onset of fertility. In summer, a different form of VEGF promotes blood vessel growth, facilitating communication between the two regions and inhibiting fertility. This mechanism, which has been elusive for decades, could help farmers manage the timing of lambing seasons, potentially improving the survival of lambs. The findings also have broader implications for understanding how animals, and potentially humans, use this system in health and disease. Professor Bates notes that this discovery could assist in controlling breeding seasons, particularly as climate change leads to more extreme winters, allowing farmers to delay lambing to increase survival rates. Andrew Loudon, a professor of animal biology at the University of Manchester, highlights the importance of this research, suggesting that similar mechanisms might play a role in human biology, particularly in the regulation of hormone secretion and immune function. This study not only solves a long-standing scientific mystery but also opens new avenues for agricultural and medical research.

The Bank of England has confirmed Jane Austen as the new face of the £10 note, reversing a decision that had sparked public outrage by excluding women from British currency. Austen, the beloved novelist of "Pride and Prejudice" and "Sense and Sensibility," will replace Charles Darwin, possibly from 2017, in a move that addresses concerns raised by a high-profile campaign and an online petition with over 30,000 signatures. Mark Carney, the new governor of the Bank of England, announced the decision at a press conference at Austen's former home in Hampshire, emphasizing the need for a diverse representation of historical figures on banknotes. The choice of Austen, a prominent figure in English literature, highlights her enduring and universal appeal. The Bank of England also pledged to review the selection process for future banknotes, ensuring a more inclusive approach. Caroline Criado-Perez, who led the campaign for women's representation, expressed delight over the decision and the commitment to transparency in the selection process. The announcement marks a significant step towards addressing the imbalance in historical representation on British currency.

President Obama's public approval rating has dipped back to 50 percent, reflecting growing economic concerns among Americans, according to a recent Washington Post-ABC News poll. The poll highlights a significant shift in public sentiment, with a majority now expressing confidence in neither Obama nor congressional Republicans to handle the economy. While a slim majority disapproves of the sequester, most Americans expect it to harm the economy, military, and government services. The desire for bipartisan cooperation to address these issues is widespread. Obama's support has eroded among political independents, liberals, and women. His overall job-approval rating is lower than that of most second-term presidents at this stage. Congress remains deeply unpopular, with only 16 percent approving of its performance. The poll also reveals that while there is majority support for a path to citizenship for illegal immigrants, the divide on gun control and the appropriate balance of government spending persists. Notably, there is strong opposition to cuts in popular social programs like Medicaid and raising the Medicare eligibility age.

In a TechCrunch interview, Stanford University student Josh Browder discusses his innovative applications of blockchain technology and his app, DoNotPay, which helps users contest parking tickets. Browder, who got 30 parking tickets at the age of 18, created DoNotPay as a chatbot that guides users through the appeals process, achieving a 64% success rate and contesting over $4 million in fines within 21 months. Browder explains that the app aims to help the most vulnerable in society, who are often exploited as a revenue source by local governments. The app's success has led Browder to consider expanding it to Seattle and tackling new legal challenges such as flight delay compensation and refugee legal guidance. Additionally, Browder envisions a developer platform that requires only legal knowledge, not coding skills, to create further useful chatbots for legal advice. During the interview, Browder also discusses his innovative use of blockchain for HIV disclosure records, allowing those who are HIV positive to prove disclosure through a permanent and anonymous record on the blockchain. Browder emphasizes the potential of blockchain technology to change the legal landscape, while also expressing skepticism about the role of government in innovation. He believes that governments should stay away from innovation as much as possible, citing the example of Texas banning Uber. Browder's innovative approach to technology and law highlights the potential for young entrepreneurs to drive positive change, even as he acknowledges the challenges posed by the current political and legal systems.

President Barack Obama will not attend the funeral of Supreme Court Justice Antonin Scalia, the White House confirmed, opting instead to pay his respects on Friday when Scalia’s body lies in repose in the Great Hall of the Supreme Court building. Vice President Joe Biden and his wife Jill will attend Scalia’s funeral at the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception. The White House defended Obama’s decision, stating that the president believes it is important to honor Scalia’s life and service. However, the decision has drawn criticism from some, including Fox News host Sean Hannity, who tweeted that Obama should have attended the funeral. The White House made it clear that the Constitution gives the president the right to select a "well qualified candidate" to the Supreme Court, despite pushback from Republicans who say Obama shouldn't nominate a replacement in an election year. Obama called Scalia a "brilliant legal mind" and said he will nominate a successor, though he has not yet announced any candidates. The bench chair of Scalia, draped in black, and the courtroom doors hung with black drapes, honored the justice. The White House press secretary, Josh Earnest, emphasized that the president's decision was not a snub but a matter of honoring the Supreme Court's tradition and the importance of the institution. There is no substantial historic precedent for presidents attending the funerals of sitting justices, with the last one being in 1954. The decision to skip the funeral has been seen as a political move, with some arguing that Obama should have attended to show respect and others defending his choice to focus on the nomination process. The political landscape surrounding the vacancy is complex, with Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell calling for the replacement to be delayed until the next president is in office. However, some Republicans, like Nevada's Dean Heller, have called for a consensus candidate. The White House also clarified that Obama regrets his decision to filibuster against President Bush's Supreme Court nominee, Samuel Alito, in 2006, suggesting that the situation was different.

This week's LOOK magazine reveals that Tom Cruise has penned an "emotional letter" to Katie Holmes, nearly a year after their divorce. Sources say the letter, written as Cruise recognized that Katie will always hold a special place in his heart, aims to rekindle their friendship or perhaps more. Friends of the couple report that Cruise took this surprising step around July, when the anniversary of their split approached. The letter, though not overly dramatic, was crafted with care, given that Holmes, now 34, would likely not be receptive to a sudden reconciliation. In the letter, Tom expressed his enduring feelings for Katie and hoped she was well, aiming to open a dialogue. This gesture reportedly had a profound impact on Holmes, who was genuinely touched by the heartfelt message. The letter served as a reminder of the old, romantic Tom that Katie once fell for, though she has since moved on and settled in New York City with their daughter, Suri. This emotional exchange underscores the lingering affection between the former couple while highlighting Holmes' focus on building a new life.

The defense of George Zimmerman, the neighborhood watch volunteer charged with the second-degree murder of Trayvon Martin, hinges on a violent altercation that occurred before he fired the fatal shot. According to Richard Kurtz, the funeral director who prepared Martin's body for burial, no signs of a fight were visible. "We could see no physical signs like there had been a scuffle or there had been a fight," Kurtz stated. "The hands— I didn't see any knuckles, bruises or what have you. And that is something we would have covered up if it would have been there." 

Surveillance video from 40 minutes after the shooting shows George Zimmerman in handcuffs, with no apparent injuries. However, Zimmerman claims Martin beat him and threatened his life, so he shot the teenager in self-defense. Ben Crump, the lawyer for Martin's parents, argues that the video demonstrates Zimmerman's guilt. "Look at that video," Crump said. "Do you see any blood on his head? He said he broke his nose. Look at that video. And look at how easy he walks out of the car." 

Zimmerman, a crime watch volunteer, initially found Martin suspicious and called the police. He followed Martin along a street and around a corner. Robert Zimmerman, George's father, told WOFL-TV in Orlando that Martin suddenly confronted his son, punching him in the nose and knocking him to the concrete. Trayvon then got on top of George and started beating him in the face and nose, hitting his head on the concrete. Police reports noted Zimmerman was "bleeding from the nose and the back of the head." However, a closer look at Zimmerman shows no obvious head or face injuries. At one point, an officer does check the back of his head.

Martin's family contends that this video proves the police never wanted to arrest Zimmerman. Cheryl Brown, a family member, identified Chris Serino as the lead investigator who questioned people in the neighborhood. "Detective Serino— did you have the sense when he interviewed you that he thought it was a killing in self-defense?" Anderson Cooper asked Brown. "No, because he actually stated to me in my family room that 'we do not believe it was self-defense and we need to prove it,'" Brown responded. 

A special prosecutor will now decide whether Zimmerman deserves to be charged. Robert Zimmerman insists his son is also a victim here, stating, "They are just making up stuff that are not true about George. How he is being portrayed is an absolute lie." He claims Martin beat his son for more than one minute and that George had no choice but to fire his .9-mm weapon.

Since 2010, scientists have known that people of Eurasian descent carry 1 to 4 percent of their DNA from Neanderthals, leading to numerous hypotheses about the impact of this genetic legacy on modern humans. Now, the first study to directly compare Neanderthal DNA in the genomes of a significant population of adults of European ancestry with their clinical records confirms that this archaic genetic legacy has a subtle but significant impact on modern human biology. According to John Capra, an assistant professor of biological sciences at Vanderbilt University, "Our main finding is that Neanderthal DNA does influence clinical traits in modern humans: We discovered associations between Neanderthal DNA and a wide range of traits, including immunological, dermatological, neurological, psychiatric and reproductive diseases."

The study, published in the Feb. 12 issue of the journal Science, found that Neanderthal DNA variants influence skin biology, particularly the risk of developing sun-induced skin lesions called keratosis. Surprisingly, a specific bit of Neanderthal DNA significantly increases the risk of nicotine addiction. The researchers also found that Neanderthal DNA influences the risk of depression, with some variants positively and others negatively affecting this trait. The pattern of associations suggests that Neanderthal DNA may have provided modern humans with adaptive advantages 40,000 years ago as they migrated into new non-African environments with different pathogens and levels of sun exposure. However, many of these traits may no longer be advantageous in modern environments. For example, a Neanderthal variant that increases blood coagulation could have helped our ancestors cope with new pathogens by sealing wounds more quickly, but in modern environments, this variant increases the risk of stroke, pulmonary embolism, and pregnancy complications.

To discover these associations, the researchers used a database containing 28,000 patients whose biological samples have been linked to anonymized versions of their electronic health records. By comparing the unique set of Neanderthal DNA that each person carried with their medical conditions, the researchers could test whether each bit of Neanderthal DNA individually and in aggregate influences risk for the traits derived from the medical records. This work establishes a new way to investigate questions about the effects of events in recent human evolution. Capra and his colleagues are working on analyzing other information contained in the medical records, such as lab tests, doctors’ notes, and medical images, in a similar fashion. The research was funded by National Institute of Health grants and National Human Genome Research Institute grants to members of the eMERGE Network.

The Philae lander, after a successful attempt to nudge itself into a sunnier position, has apparently run out of power, bringing an end to its historic mission on Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko. Despite a last-ditch effort to optimize its solar exposure, the lander’s batteries, which were expected to charge with more sunlight, failed to sustain its systems. Philae’s official Twitter account confirmed a rotation of 35 degrees, but this came too late to save its energy reserves. The lander had been experiencing a challenging position, lodged in the shadows of a cliff or large boulder, receiving only 1.5 hours of sunlight instead of the anticipated 6-7 hours. This limited exposure left it with insufficient power to continue operations.

Mission controllers had hoped to use the lander’s drill to collect samples and analyze them in onboard instruments, but the dwindling battery life made this increasingly unlikely. Engineers considered various strategies, including rotating the lander to maximize solar exposure and potentially using the internal flywheel to generate a small upward motion, but these were risky and uncertain. The lander’s primary mission, designed to last around 60 hours, was always intended to be extended by secondary batteries charged by solar panels. However, the awkward landing left Philae in a position where solar power was insufficient.

Despite the challenges, the lander managed to perform several key tasks, including deploying its arm and drill, and sending back valuable data and images. Scientists estimated that 80% of the mission’s objectives had been achieved, with the drilling operation potentially raising that to 90%. The COSAC instrument, chosen for its lower power requirements, was used to study the comet’s surface, while the PTOLEMY instrument continued to analyze gases released from the comet.

The mission team remains hopeful that Philae might reboot when the comet approaches the sun in August 2015, as increased sunlight could charge its batteries. For now, Philae has gone to sleep, with the lander’s final tweet expressing a desire to share more about its new home, Comet 67P, when it wakes up again. The hunt for Philae’s exact location continues, with scientists using triangulation and high-resolution images from the Rosetta orbiter to narrow down its position. The Rosetta mission, launched in 2004, has been a groundbreaking endeavor, providing insights into the origins of the solar system and the potential role comets played in delivering water and organic molecules to Earth.

Matthew McConaughey, the Oscar-winning actor and UT Austin alumnus, is set to return to his alma mater this fall to teach a filmmaking class, the university announced. McConaughey will co-teach the upper-level division course with Hunger Games director Gary Ross and university lecturer Scott Rice. The class, part of the Moody College of Communications, will take students behind the scenes of their recently released film, Free State of Jones, through recorded videos and at least one on-campus visit. This is the second time McConaughey is coteaching this course; during the spring 2016 semester, he and Rice showed students the filmmaking process for Free State of Jones but required students to sign nondisclosure forms and forbade photos and videos since the film had not yet been released. McConaughey, who frequently visits the campus for football games, will be joined by Ross to explain their creative decisions and the filmmaking process. The class, open to juniors and seniors, requires no prerequisites or fees and meets once a week.

An 81-year-old Sebring woman, Mary H. Musselman, has faced multiple legal issues related to feeding black bears, according to a report. Initially placed on diversion for two counts of feeding black bears in January 2023, she was later placed on probation after violating the agreement. The Florida Fish and Wildlife Conservation Commission (FWC) had been dealing with Musselman since November 2012 due to reports of her feeding bears, eventually euthanizing one bear deemed problematic. As part of her probation, she was ordered not to put out food for animals for a year. However, an FWC officer found numerous bowls and trays with birdseed and corn, hanging birdfeeders, and other food outside her house, leading to her arrest on a violation of probation charge. She was also charged with resisting an officer with violence and battery on a law enforcement officer. The FWC spokesperson, Gary Morse, explained that feeding bears can result in the animals losing their fear of humans, making them more likely to seek food in residential areas. Once a bear has been fed and lost its fear, it cannot be relocated and must be euthanized. The issues with Musselman began in early November 2022 when FWC officers visited her home and warned her to stop feeding the bears. Despite several visits and warnings, she continued the practice. After being placed on probation, a judge ordered FWC officers to check her residence weekly. On January 29, 2023, officers found evidence that she was still feeding bears, leading to her arrest. During the arrest, she threatened to kill the officers and resisted. Musselman's former students described her as gentle and harmless, fearing that she did not fully comprehend the seriousness of her actions. They are working to find a mental health advocate to assist her in court. The FWC has been actively educating the community about living with bears and promoting safe practices to prevent such incidents.

Director Brian Henson's "The Happytime Murders" is a raunchy comedy that tries to distance itself from the Muppets and "Sesame Street" but ultimately fails to deliver on its promise. Set in a world where puppets and humans coexist, the film centers on Phil Phillips, a former puppet cop turned private investigator (voiced by Bill Barretta), and his human partner, Connie Edwards (Melissa McCarthy). Their uneasy alliance is reignited when a series of murders among the cast of the popular TV show "The Happytime Gang" threatens to unravel their partnership. The plot is riddled with clichés and cliché-ridden dialogue, making for a dull and unengaging experience. McCarthy's sharp wit and comedic timing are wasted in this unfunny and overlong film, which relies heavily on shock value and crass humor. The puppet characters, while well-crafted, are generic and lack the charm and creativity of the Muppets. Maya Rudolph and Elizabeth Banks have small roles that offer little to no comic relief. The film's attempts at social commentary on puppet discrimination feel forced and underdeveloped. Overall, "The Happytime Murders" is a disappointing entry in the comedy genre, failing to capitalize on its unique premise and instead opting for a formulaic and unoriginal approach. With a running time of about 90 minutes, it feels even longer due to its lack of substance and humor. While it may appeal to those seeking a raunchy experience, it is unlikely to find much of an audience beyond a niche group of viewers.

Move over Emma Stone, Tinseltown has a new highest-paid actress. Scarlett Johansson leads this year's ranking with $40.5 million in pretax earnings between June 1, 2017, and June 1, 2018, making her the top-earning female lead. Playing Black Widow in Marvel's Avengers movies has become a lucrative role for Johansson, who quadruples her 2017 earnings to bump Stone from the top spot. "The percent of budget cost have certainly skewed heavy, particularly on the Avengers movies, to cast now, whereas maybe in the early ones it was more visual effects or below the line," said Kevin Feige, Marvel Studios President and producer last year. "But that's okay because [the actors] are the best effects." Johansson edges Angelina Jolie (No. 2; $28 million) who returns to the ranking thanks largely to her upfront pay for Maleficent 2. Jennifer Aniston (No. 3; $19.5 million) still earns big bucks 14 years after the conclusion of Friends, making most of her money by endorsing the likes of Emirates airlines, Smartwater, and Aveeno. Expect her paycheck to skyrocket next year when production begins on her forthcoming Apple series with Reese Witherspoon (No. 5; $16.5 million), for which the pair will receive an estimated $1.25 million an episode. Just ahead of Witherspoon, who rejoins the list with movie earnings and Big Little Lies paychecks, is Jennifer Lawrence. The Hunger Games actress' two most recent movies, Mother! and Red Sparrow, underperformed at the box office. But she still commands big bucks for her turns in the X-Men series and a high-paying Dior contract. Together, the world's 10 highest-paid actresses tallied a combined $186 million between June 1, 2017, and June 1, 2018, before fees and taxes. Earnings estimates are based on data from Nielsen, ComScore, Box Office Mojo, and IMDB, as well as interviews with industry insiders. All figures are pretax; fees for agents, managers, and lawyers are not deducted. Overall, the cumulative total is up 16% from $172.5 million in 2017. The list examined actresses the world over, including Australian Cate Blanchett (No. 8; $12.5 million) and Israeli Gal Gadot (No. 10; $10 million). Gadot, whose turn as Wonder Woman catapulted her to fame, is the only newcomer on the ranking. The Patty Jenkins-directed blockbuster tallied $821.8 million at the box office and scored a sequel, which accounts for the majority of Gadot's payday this year. Though she only made an estimated six figures for the first installment, her increased quote, coupled with a Revlon endorsement, launched her among the highest-paid. "There was such an obsession in the industry that teenage boys were the primary target box office," said Jenkins, who helmed the smash hit and will be directing and writing its sequel for an estimated $7 million. "The industry has had a hard time shifting to acknowledging that they need to hit a more diverse audience." Currently, female characters fill only 28.7% of all speaking roles in film, according to a 2016 study. That lack of roles means that there are fewer opportunities for female stars to earn big bucks. This year, only two women broached the $20 million mark, down from three in 2017 and four in 2016. Notably absent: Amy Adams, Emma Watson, Charlize Theron, and last year's top-ranked Emma Stone, who all failed to earn above the $10 million cut off for this year's list and dropped off the ranking. Roles for women who are no longer young ingenues are few and far between. Yet the highest-paid actresses buck that trend: 60% of this year's list members are over the age of 40. Some have forged their own roles to build opportunities for themselves: Witherspoon cofounded her Pacific Standard production company and Hello Sunshine media house to option rights for female-led parts. Others, like Aniston, supplement acting income with hefty endorsement deals.

The California Attorney General is reportedly conducting a preliminary evaluation, termed an "inquiry," into former Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger’s alleged misuse of taxpayer funds to cover up sexual liaisons. According to RadarOnline.com, the Office of the Attorney General, a branch of the Department of Justice, is investigating whether Schwarzenegger used his state-funded security details, including California Highway Patrol officers and vehicles, to escort women into his hotel suite at the Sacramento Hyatt Regency. Veteran hotel security officer William Taylor claims he witnessed the governor using CHP officers to ferry women into his suite, where they would stay for two to four hours before leaving. Taylor passed a polygraph test about his claims. However, Schwarzenegger's attorney, Martin Singer, denies the allegations, calling them "completely false." Retired CHP Sergeant Mark Hammond and Officer Manny Trevino both state they never witnessed any inappropriate behavior from Schwarzenegger during their time on his protective detail. The Hyatt Regency Sacramento General Manager, Ulrich Samietz, also denies any knowledge of such claims. The investigation comes after Schwarzenegger admitted to fathering a love child with his former housekeeper and faces calls for an official inquiry into his finances.

Dawn Wells, the beloved actress who played Mary Ann Summers on the iconic TV show Gilligan’s Island, is in dire need of financial assistance, according to a GoFundMe campaign created by her friend Dugg Kirkpatrick. Wells, 79, has been struggling since the 2008 financial crisis, which decimated her life savings. She recently faced a life-threatening surgery and an unexpected accident that required hospitalization for two months, significantly impacting her financial stability. The campaign aims to raise $194,000 to cover IRS penalties, which are compounded daily, and to pay for her hospital bills. As of September 13, the fundraiser has already garnered nearly $120,000 in just 10 days, a testament to the outpouring of support from fans and admirers.

Kirkpatrick, a hair stylist who has worked with Wells, explains that she is currently living in one of the greatest fears many Americans face: an uncertain future. Wells has no family to support her and has already lost her home. She wishes to move to a smaller assisted living facility that caters specifically to people in the film and TV industry but was denied due to her debt. The campaign has been widely shared, with over 6,600 shares on Facebook, highlighting the public’s desire to help a woman who has brought joy to countless lives over the years. Wells and her agent have not yet responded to PEOPLE’s request for comment, but the overwhelming support from the community suggests that her story has touched many hearts.

Ukrainian forces withdrew from the strategic railway hub of Debaltseve, despite a recent ceasefire agreement, as pro-Russian rebels overran the town, causing widespread condemnation. Ukrainian President Petro Poroshenko claimed his troops left the area in an organized manner, while Russian officials disputed the claim, insisting the town was already under rebel control when the agreement was signed. The withdrawal has raised concerns about the broader peace agreement and prompted calls for a firm response from the international community. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov urged rebels to respect the ceasefire and ensure the safety of surrendered troops. The situation in Debaltseve has left about 7,000 civilians trapped, with the city's strategic position on a railway line connecting rebel-held areas. The ceasefire, effective since Sunday, has been largely observed elsewhere, but the events in Debaltseve have raised doubts about its sustainability.

Harper Lee, the Pulitzer Prize-winning author of "To Kill a Mockingbird," spent a significant portion of her adult life in New York City, far from her hometown of Monroeville, Alabama. This choice was not merely a matter of convenience but a strategic move that allowed her to focus on her writing without the public eye. The Browns, a New York couple, played a crucial role in Lee's literary journey. In 1956, on Christmas Eve, the Browns gifted Lee a year off from her job, enabling her to write "To Kill a Mockingbird" without financial worries. This act of kindness was a pivotal moment in Lee's career, as the initial printing of the book was only 5,000 copies, a far cry from the eventual 30 million copies sold worldwide.

The Browns, Michael and Joy, had met Lee through her friend Truman Capote. Michael, a Broadway lyricist, contributed lyrics to a song in the 1954 Broadway musical "House of Flowers," with a book by Capote and music by Harold Arlen. This connection led to the Browns' involvement in Lee's life. Michael had received a lump-sum payment, and Joy, a former ballerina, immediately thought to give it to Lee. Joy Brown recalled that she and her husband never foresaw the book's massive success. "They published 5,000 copies for heaven's sake. Who was going to buy 5,000 copies of this book?" she wondered.

Lee's time in New York City was marked by anonymity and a retreat from public life. She worked as an airline reservations clerk, writing "To Kill a Mockingbird" in an airless, one-bedroom apartment in Yorkville. The Browns' gift allowed Lee to concentrate on her writing, and the result was a novel that would become a cornerstone of American literature, winning the Pulitzer Prize in 1961 and inspiring the Oscar-winning film starring Gregory Peck.

Despite the book's success, Lee remained reclusive, avoiding public appearances and media attention. Her reluctance to engage with the public was a testament to her desire to maintain the privacy and solitude that had been crucial to her writing process. The Browns' role in Lee's career is a reminder of the often-overlooked support systems that can make a significant difference in the lives of writers. Their gift not only provided Lee with the financial freedom to write but also gave her the confidence to pursue her literary dreams.

Dick Clark, the iconic host of "Dick Clark's New Year's Rockin' Eve," is set to celebrate the 40th anniversary of his annual New Year's Eve special. The show, which will air on ABC, will feature Ryan Seacrest alongside Clark, who is 82 and has been hosting the program since 1972. Seacrest, who has co-hosted the show since 2005, will continue to share the spotlight with Clark, who has faced health challenges, including a stroke that impaired his speech. Despite these difficulties, Clark remains deeply involved in the production and considers the show one of his "children." The 2012 special will include performances by Lady Gaga, Justin Bieber, Pitbull, and other popular artists, and will pay homage to the show's history with clips from previous years. Clark, who hopes to continue hosting, says the show is "very important" to him, and he looks forward to the countdown, even if his speech is sometimes impaired. The special will air from 8 p.m. to 12:15 a.m., with a break for local news, and is expected to draw a large audience, with nearly 19 million viewers tuning in last year.

A Warren man with a rare genetic disorder, Jahmel Binion, has sued NBA star Shaquille O’Neal, former Michigan basketball player Trey Burke, and rapper Waka Flocka Flame for over $25,000 in damages. Binion, who has ectodermal dysplasia and does not sweat, took a selfie that was mocked on social media by the celebrities. Binion created an antibullying campaign called "Hug Don't Judge" after the incident. The lawsuit alleges invasion of privacy, intentional infliction of emotional distress, defamation, and general negligence. Binion claims the mocking communications publicly disclosed embarrassing private facts and lowered his reputation. O’Neal, Burke, and Waka Flocka Flame reside in Florida, Utah, and Georgia, respectively.

Nearly 50 years after the 1964 Winter Olympics in Innsbruck, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) has finally clarified the official medal standings for the pairs figure skating event. The West German pair of Marika Kilius and Hans-Jürgen Bäumler were initially declared the silver medalists, while the Canadian pair of Debbi Wilkes and Guy Revell won bronze. The American pair of Ronald and Vivian Joseph finished fourth. However, it was later revealed that Kilius and Bäumler had signed a contract with a professional ice show before the Games, violating amateurism rules. In 1966, the IOC ordered the West Germans to return their medals, elevating Wilkes and Revell to second place and the Josephs to bronze. In 1987, the IOC quietly reinstated the West Germans' silver medals, leaving the Josephs' bronze status in limbo. Now, the IOC has officially confirmed the Josephs as the bronze medalists, while the Soviets remain the gold medal winners. Vivian Joseph, 66, and her brother Ronald, 70, have long struggled with the uncertainty surrounding their Olympic achievement. Ronald Joseph, an orthopedic surgeon, expressed mixed feelings, saying, "I'm ecstatic it has been changed, but to tell you the truth, that Olympic medal is not our proudest achievement, because we were just handed it." Vivian Joseph added, "I am prouder of the world silver medal and the U.S. title we won in 1965." The case highlights the complex and often politically charged nature of Olympic records and the challenges faced by athletes in maintaining their rightful place in history.

Iraq’s president, Fouad Massoum, appointed Haider al-Abadi as the new prime minister, aiming to form a government and potentially address the crisis with the Islamic State militants. However, incumbent Prime Minister Nouri al-Maliki, who has faced criticism for his sectarian policies, challenged the appointment, arguing that his State of Law coalition, which won the most seats in the April elections, should have the right to nominate the prime minister. Al-Maliki’s supporters rallied in Baghdad, denouncing the move and asserting their loyalty to him. The U.S. administration, concerned about Iraq’s stability, publicly backed Abadi, who is a seasoned member of Maliki’s party and has experience as a communications minister. Meanwhile, the appointment has raised fears of political infighting, as Maliki’s forces remained on high alert, and his State of Law coalition crumbled, with 38 of its 96 parliamentarians supporting Abadi. The new prime minister will face the daunting task of curbing the influence of the Islamic State, while also trying to bridge the country’s sectarian divides and bring the disaffected Sunni minority back into the political process. The Obama administration has deployed top officials to encourage a smooth transition and coordinate with a new Iraqi government to combat the militants. Despite the U.S. support, Maliki’s stance and the potential legal challenges to Abadi’s appointment underscore the complex and volatile political landscape in Iraq.

In 1935, Hessy Taft, a six-month-old Jewish baby, became the poster child for Nazi propaganda. Her photograph was chosen as the image of the ideal Aryan baby and featured on the cover of the Nazi family magazine Sonne ins Haus. However, the photographer, Hans Ballin, had a different intention. He deliberately submitted the photograph to mock the Nazi ideology of racial purity. Despite the photograph being widely distributed, the Nazis never discovered the true identity of the baby. When Hessy's mother, Pauline Levinsons, saw the photograph, she was terrified that their family would be exposed as Jews. She rushed to the photographer, who revealed that he had known the family was Jewish and had submitted the photograph to ridicule the Nazi racial theories. The photograph won the contest, and Hessy's image was believed to have been chosen personally by Nazi propaganda minister Joseph Goebbels. The family fled Germany in 1938, first to Latvia and then to Paris, where they were eventually helped to escape to Cuba. After the war, Hessy Taft, now a 80-year-old professor of chemistry, donated her yellowing copy of the magazine to Yad Vashem, the Holocaust Memorial in Israel. She expressed a sense of satisfaction and revenge for the role she unknowingly played in mocking Nazi ideology. The story of Hessy Taft's photograph highlights the ironic and tragic ways in which Jewish families were caught in the crosshairs of Nazi propaganda, and the lengths they went to protect their identities.

An Algerian man has been sentenced to two years in prison after dangled his baby cousin out of a 15th-floor window in Algiers, a capital city, as part of a social media stunt. The defendant posted a photo of the incident on Facebook with the caption, "1000 likes or I will drop him," which garnered significant attention. In the video, the baby appears to be in a state of fear and bewilderment. Following the incident, many Facebook users demanded that the man be tried on child abuse charges. The defendant later claimed that the image was photoshopped, stating that the balcony had protective bars that were removed by Facebook users in the viral image. However, the court was not convinced by his explanation. The case highlights the potential dangers of social media stunts and the impact of viral content on public perception.

A 14-year-old Chilean girl named Valentina Maureira, suffering from cystic fibrosis, has made a video plea to President Michelle Bachelet, asking for permission to be euthanized. The video, uploaded to her Facebook page, has garnered significant attention and sparked a debate in Chile about the legality and ethics of euthanasia. Valentina, who has already undergone five operations and is currently in a stable condition, expresses her desire to end her life due to the constant pain and suffering caused by her illness. Her father, Freddy Maureira, shared that Valentina's older brother also passed away from cystic fibrosis, adding to the emotional weight of the situation. The girl's plea highlights the ongoing struggle for better medical treatment and quality of life for those with chronic illnesses in Chile.

The government's response has been cautious. Alvaro Elizalde, a government spokesman, stated that the health ministry is in contact with the family to ensure Valentina receives the necessary psychological and medical support. However, he firmly ruled out euthanasia as an option, citing the current Chilean law, which does not permit such actions. Chile is one of the few countries with a strict ban on euthanasia, reflecting the strong influence of the Catholic Church in the country. This ban extends to other sensitive issues, such as abortion, which is also illegal under any circumstances in Chile.

President Bachelet, who has introduced reforms to relax the abortion law, has not addressed euthanasia in her agenda. Her visit to Valentina in the hospital on Saturday underscores the public interest in the case and the broader discussion it has sparked. The debate is not limited to the Maureira family but extends to the wider Chilean society, where opinions are divided on the issue of assisted suicide. While some advocate for the right to die, others argue that the current legal framework should remain in place to protect vulnerable individuals from potential coercion or exploitation.

The case of Valentina Maureira has brought to light the challenges faced by families dealing with terminal illnesses and the complex ethical considerations surrounding end-of-life decisions. It also highlights the ongoing tension between personal autonomy and societal norms in Chile, a country where traditional values and religious beliefs continue to play a significant role in shaping public policy and public opinion.

A Minnesota couple, Pete and Alisha Arnold, 30, have created a website called Birthornot.com, where visitors can vote on whether the couple should keep their unborn child or have an abortion. The Arnolds, both tech professionals, have been married for 10 years and are expecting their third child. They have been blogging about their pregnancy and posting ultrasound pictures and videos. However, at the top of their blog is a poll hosted by PollDaddy.com, asking readers to vote on whether the Arnolds should give birth or have an abortion. The "Have an Abortion" option currently leads with 54% of the vote, while "Give Birth" has 46%. The Arnolds plan to check the poll results on December 7th, the last day Alisha can legally terminate the pregnancy, and use them to decide whether to keep the baby. They say the poll will influence their decision but won't be binding. Pete, a self-described Libertarian, believes this experiment can teach people about the importance of voting. However, many question the sincerity of the Arnolds' intentions, speculating that this could be a prank, a pro-life stunt, or a genuine attempt to decide their future by public vote. The Arnolds' actions raise ethical concerns about the rights of the unborn and the appropriateness of using public opinion to make such a personal decision.

Bill Ayers, a controversial figure known for his involvement in the Weather Underground, has been engaging in a long-standing game of cat and mouse with those who believe he ghostwrote Barack Obama's memoir, "Dreams from My Father." According to John Hawkins, a conservative blogger, Ayers has been deliberately baiting people with this claim for years, often in a mocking manner. In October 2009, a conservative blogger encountered Ayers at Reagan Airport and initiated a conversation about the book. Ayers, unprompted, offered that he had written the book, suggesting that Michelle Obama had orchestrated the situation and even went so far as to propose splitting the royalties with the blogger if she could prove his involvement. His response was met with skepticism, and Ayers continued to mock those who believed the ghostwriting theory, often insisting that he wrote the book to see if his audience would fall for it. This behavior has been documented multiple times, with Ayers maintaining his stance that he wrote the book to test the credulity of his listeners. His approach seems to be a deliberate strategy to mock and toy with those who entertain the ghostwriting theory, making it clear that he is not serious about the claim.

Multiple sources tell The Federalist that The New York Times is preparing a new article to attack Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh for his party planning efforts in the 1980s. The Times is reportedly seeking to corroborate a letter Kavanaugh allegedly wrote to a classmate to organize a week-long beach party, detailing costs and guest lists. Classmates confirm Kavanaugh organized "Beach Week," a popular rite of passage for D.C. area students. The letter, described as innocuous and filled with inside jokes, notes Kavanaugh's role in maintaining order and securing the event. Critics argue the Times is attempting to smear Kavanaugh for his past party planning, having previously reported on alleged ice-throwing incidents. Kavanaugh's defenders maintain he was known for his organizational skills and conservative behavior among his peers. The Senate awaits the FBI's background check before voting on Kavanaugh's confirmation. White House spokeswoman Kerri Kupec criticized the Times, saying it is "committed to embarrassing Judge Kavanaugh with three-decade-old stories of adolescent drinking."

President Obama unveiled a $3.8 trillion budget request for fiscal year 2013, aiming to cut $4 trillion in deficits over a decade through spending reductions and higher taxes on the wealthy. The budget emphasizes investments in infrastructure, education, and domestic manufacturing, while proposing cuts to discretionary spending and entitlement programs. Obama's plan includes a $1.5 trillion tax hike, primarily by allowing the Bush tax cuts to expire for high-income earners and implementing the Buffett Rule, ensuring that households earning over $1 million annually pay at least 30% of their income in taxes. The budget also calls for a year-long extension of the payroll tax cut and unemployment insurance. Defense spending will be reduced, with the Pentagon planning to spend $487 billion less over 10 years. The White House projects a deficit for fiscal year 2012 of $1.33 trillion, with the deficit projected to fall to $901 billion in 2013 and continue decreasing to $575 billion by 2018. However, the budget does little to address the long-term growth in entitlement spending, which critics argue will lead to unsustainable deficits beyond the next decade. Republicans criticized the plan, saying it fails to tackle the nation's deep fiscal problems and that Obama is campaigning instead of governing. The budget is expected to intensify the partisan divisions between the two parties, with the debate likely to continue through the election year.

Texas Rangers catcher Yorvit Torrealba has found himself in hot water after a video of him striking an umpire in the face during a winter league game in Venezuela went viral. General manager Jon Daniels confirmed the Rangers are aware of the incident and are investigating. The video shows Torrealba, playing for Leones del Caracas, striking out and then throwing his hand up towards the umpire, leading to an immediate ejection. After a brief face-to-face confrontation, Torrealba is seen pushing the umpire’s facemask with his open hand. The incident has raised questions about potential disciplinary action, though Daniels stated it would depend on the circumstances. Torrealba, entering his second year of a two-year, $6.25 million contract, has been a respected player for the Rangers, known for his passion and leadership. However, this incident has brought his character into question, as it is an inexcusable and disappointing display of behavior. The Rangers will need to decide how to handle the situation, as it could impact Torrealba's reputation and his playing time in the future.

Allison Williams, known for her role as Marnie in HBO's critically acclaimed series Girls, has recently addressed her father Brian Williams' six-month suspension from NBC News in a public Q&A with Seth Meyers at 92Y in New York City. During the event, Allison defended her father, emphasizing his integrity and commitment to journalism. She expressed that the experience has not shaken her trust in him, calling him a "really good man" and "honest man." Despite Brian's admission of being untruthful about an incident in Iraq in 2003, Allison maintains her belief in his character and values. She shared a personal anecdote about her ninth-grade year, when Brian's unexpected call about a father-daughter dance brought her immense relief. Allison also spoke about her father's resilience, noting the "outreach from people you love, family, friends, and then people we don't even know, strangers, just reaching out saying we want him back on TV." She expressed hope for her father's return to television and reassured the audience that he will work hard to regain viewers' trust. Allison's comments come at a time when her own career is flourishing, with her starring role in the NBC live-action event Peter Pan Live! and the upcoming fourth season of Girls. Her public support for her father, while maintaining her own professional success, highlights the complex dynamics of family and public life.

A packed Aeromexico-operated Embraer jetliner crashed just after takeoff from Durango, Mexico, on Tuesday, injuring dozens but leaving no fatalities, according to Reuters. The plane, carrying 103 people including two infants and four crew members, was nearly full when it crashed at about 4 p.m. local time. Passengers and crew managed to escape via emergency slides before the plane was engulfed in flames. Jackeline Flores, a passenger, described the plane crashing shortly after takeoff in heavy rain. She and her daughter escaped through a hole in the fuselage as the aircraft filled with smoke and flames. "A little girl who left the plane was crying because her legs were burned," Flores said. Passenger Alejandro Cardoza of the state’s civil protection agency stated that around 85 people had suffered mostly light injuries, with 37 hospitalized and two in critical condition. Durango Governor José Rosas Aispuro said a gust of wind rocked the plane before it plunged suddenly, citing air traffic control at the airport. The plane’s left wing hit the ground, knocking off two engines, before it came to a halt 300 meters from the runway. The pilot was the most severely hurt but was in a stable condition. Grupo Aeroportuario Centro Norte, the airport operator, also attributed the crash to bad weather. Aeromexico said in a statement, "We deeply regret this accident. The families of all those affected are in our thoughts and in our hearts." The U.S. will send two people to assist the Mexican investigative team. The plane, flight number 2431, was bound for Mexico City when it crashed. Among the passengers was Chicago-born priest Esequiel Sanchez of the Shrine of Our Lady of Guadalupe. The Embraer 190, involved in one fatal crash in 2010, was leased from Republic Airlines in the U.S. in 2014. Embraer sent a team of technicians to the scene and stood ready to support the investigation. The cause of the crash is still under investigation, and it could take months to determine the exact cause.

The US Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) has faced criticism for live-tweeting the raid that killed Osama Bin Laden, five years after the event. The agency's Twitter account has been sharing details of the mission that led to the capture of the leader of al-Qaeda, who was thought to have ordered the 9/11 attacks, as if it were happening today. The tweets, hashtagged #UBLRaid, began at 1:25 pm EDT with President Obama, DCIA Panetta, and JSOC commander Admiral McRaven approving the operation. Helicopters departed from Afghanistan for a compound in Abbottabad, Pakistan, and just under 90 minutes later, two helicopters descended on the compound, with one crashing but the assault continuing. At 3:39 pm, Osama Bin Laden was found on the third floor and killed. The last tweet at 7:01 pm confirmed the high probability of positive identification of Usama Bin Ladin to President Obama. The tweets have sparked a significant backlash on social media, with many users calling the move "grotesque and embarrassing" and posting memes and gifs of people reacting negatively. Some were more supportive, but the overall reaction has been largely negative. The CIA's usual tweets mostly concern historical trivia and artefacts, making this unusual move stand out. The raid had a great symbolic and strategic effect on al-Qaeda, and CIA director John Brennan said it was important to do the same thing with Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, head of the so-called Islamic State (IS). However, he also noted that IS is a "phenomenon" with influence in many countries, so the agency must remain focused on destroying all the elements of that organization.

Bryan Singer, the director of the Freddie Mercury biopic "Bohemian Rhapsody," has been fired by 20th Century Fox due to a series of conflicts and his prolonged absence from the set. Singer's rep stated that he was terminated because of his "unexpected unavailability," but Singer has disputed this, claiming that he was fired due to the studio's refusal to allow him to attend to a gravely ill parent and his own health. Singer's absences from the set, which included multiple no-shows, led to a production shutdown on December 1, described as the "unexpected unavailability" of the director. This decision came after a series of confrontations between Singer and Rami Malek, who stars as Freddie Mercury. Malek had complained to the studio about Singer's unreliability and unprofessionalism. Singer was warned by Fox executives Stacey Snider and Emma Watts about the consequences of unprofessional behavior before production began, and a representative from the Directors Guild of America was also present to monitor the situation. Despite a reported reconciliation between Singer and Malek, the director's prolonged absence, particularly after the Thanksgiving break, was the final straw. Singer claims that he and Malek had resolved their differences and continued to work together until just before Thanksgiving. The studio, which still has about two more weeks of principal photography remaining, is expected to name a new director soon. Singer's firing has sparked a public dispute, with his statement suggesting that the termination was not his decision and was beyond his control. The film, starring Rami Malek as Freddie Mercury and featuring Ben Hardy, Joe Mazzello, and Gwilym Lee as other members of Queen, is still expected to be released in December 2018 as planned.

Donald Trump’s legal team has faced a backlash after one of his lawyers, Michael Cohen, claimed it is not a crime to rape your spouse. The controversial statement came during an interview with The Daily Beast, where Cohen was defending Trump from a decades-old allegation that he once forced himself upon his ex-wife Ivana. Cohen argued that legally, a spouse cannot be raped, and threatened to sue the publication if they published the story. This assertion has drawn criticism, as New York state previously had a marital rape exemption that was struck down in 1984. Ivana Trump, in a statement provided during their divorce proceedings, described the incident as an emotional violation but clarified that it was not meant in a criminal sense. Trump’s campaign spokesperson dismissed the allegation as old news and a tactic to exploit him during their divorce. Cohen’s comments have sparked outrage, with critics pointing out the legal and ethical implications of his stance. The controversy adds another layer of complexity to Trump’s already contentious campaign, as his history of controversial remarks about sexual assault comes under scrutiny.

Polish historians have compiled and published an extensive online database of Nazi SS commanders and guards at the Auschwitz concentration camp, aiming to bring some of them to justice. The project, spearheaded by the state-run Institute of National Remembrance and historian Aleksander Lasik, includes over 8,500 entries based on data from archives in Poland, Germany, Austria, the United States, and Russia, though access to Russian archives is limited. Lasik, who has spent over three decades researching the topic, claims that up to 200 former Auschwitz guards might still be alive, and that only about 12% of the guards were previously tried by courts in Poland and other countries. The online list, available in Polish, English, and German, provides detailed information on the guards, including dates and places of birth, nationalities, educational backgrounds, military service, and party affiliations. Some entries also feature photographs and judicial documents from trials held in Poland. For instance, the entry for Rudolf Höss, the camp's commander from 1940 to 1943, includes a photocopy of the death sentence he received in Krakow in 1947. The publication of these names is seen as a significant step toward holding former Auschwitz guards accountable, with Nazi hunter Efraim Zuroff emphasizing its importance and potential practical implications for ongoing investigations. The database also includes information on other German-run camps, with a total of over 25,000 names. The project's verification process is ongoing, with the exact dates of service at Auschwitz still being confirmed. The database aims to honor the memory of the 1.1 million people, including 1 million Jews, 75,000 Poles, 21,000 Roma, and 15,000 Soviet prisoners of war, who perished in the camp during World War II.

North Charleston, South Carolina, has grappled with a complex history of mistrust and tension between the police and the community, particularly concerning the treatment of black residents. The shooting of Walter Scott, an unarmed black man, by a white police officer, Michael Slager, in April 2015, highlighted these issues. Slager was charged with murder, and the incident sparked protests and calls for police reform. The city's mayor, Keith Summey, vowed to address community concerns and improve police policies, including the purchase of 150 body cameras. The shooting, captured on video by a bystander, showed Slager shooting Scott eight times as he ran away, with all shots hitting Scott from behind. Scott's family and attorney, L. Chris Stewart, emphasized the importance of the video in bringing charges against the officer. The case drew comparisons to other high-profile police shootings, such as those in Ferguson, Missouri, and New York, and raised questions about the use of force and racial bias in law enforcement. North Charleston, with a population that is 45 percent black, has struggled to balance public safety with civil rights, as evidenced by past incidents like the 2000 shooting of Edward Snowden and the 2003 shooting of Asberry Wylder. The city's police department, while nationally accredited, has faced criticism for its methods, particularly in the use of deadly force against black residents. Despite the swift condemnation of the shooting by the mayor and police chief, the incident damaged the relationship between the police and the community, highlighting the challenges of restoring trust.

Two sailors died and a third went missing after a Navy helicopter crashed into the Atlantic Ocean about 20 miles east of Cape Henry, Virginia Beach. Lt. Wesley Van Dorn, 29, and Petty Officer 3rd Class Brian Collins, 25, died at Sentara Norfolk General Hospital, while the missing pilot, Lt. Sean Christopher Snyder, 39, was identified late that evening. The Navy and Coast Guard searched an area of over 600 square miles before suspending the active search for Snyder. Four crew members were rescued and taken to Norfolk General, where two died and one was in stable condition. The crash occurred when one of two MH-53 Sea Dragons from Helicopter Mine Countermeasures Squadron 14, based at Norfolk Naval Station, made a distress call around 10:45 a.m. and then crashed. The second helicopter dropped a raft, and two crew members were rescued. The crash site was a challenging environment, with a large debris field and cold water temperatures. The Navy launched an investigation into the cause of the crash, which is the fourth major accident involving a Sea Dragon since 2012. The MH-53 Sea Dragons, a critical but aging airframe, are expected to continue flying through 2025. The Navy has invested in upgrades and better maintenance to address safety concerns. The families of the deceased and the injured were offered support and prayers.

Lena Dunham's $3.7 million book deal with Random House, after a bidding war involving all of the major publishers, is emblematic of what is wrong with corporate publishing today, argues an editor. The deal, which smacks of a search for the "Barton Fink" touch, highlights the bottom-line-driven nature of the publishing industry. While Dunham is an easy target—only 26, from an artsy New York family, and the creator, star, and director of her own HBO show—the backlash against her deal includes an element of sexism. Critics argue that the advance, coupled with Random House's marketing of the book as the next "Bossypants," sets unrealistic expectations for Dunham's book to sell. The author points out that even if the book sells well, it is a short-sighted approach to running a publishing company. Instead, the editor envisions a scenario where a publisher like Barney Rosset, the late founder of Grove Press, would have invested $3.7 million in 370 writers, potentially producing cultural touchstones that would outsell Dunham's book. The article contrasts this with the success of small publishers, like Graywolf and McSweeney's, which are thriving and winning awards. The deal with Dunham is seen as the rule, not the exception, in a publishing industry that is losing cultural relevance and solvency. The editor concludes by highlighting the valuable ideas Dunham's book could offer, particularly in addressing issues of gender and age discrimination in the workplace, rather than relying on generic advice.

Pope Francis condemned a "culture of waste" in an increasingly consumerist world during his Wednesday general audience in St. Peter's Square, emphasizing that discarding good food is akin to stealing from the poor. He noted that grandparents used to carefully avoid wasting leftovers, but consumerism has normalized daily food waste. "Throwing away food is like stealing from the table of those who are poor and hungry," he stated. Since his election in March, Pope Francis has advocated for greater austerity and financial reform within the Roman Catholic Church, aiming to defend the poor. Approximately one-third of the food produced for human consumption is lost or wasted globally, with much of this occurring in the industrialized world due to consumer overbuying and oversized portions. Francis highlighted the stark contrast between financial market dips and the daily suffering of the hungry, warning that too much focus on materialism has made human suffering seem normal. He urged people to care for the environment and reduce waste, stating that cultivating and caring for creation is a responsibility given by God. The Pope's speech resonated with Coldiretti, Italy's largest agricultural organization, which welcomed his recognition of farmers' contributions and acknowledged the negative impacts of globalized markets.

Amanda Carpenter, former communication director for Sen. Ted Cruz, found herself in a predicament back in February when she was trapped in an Amtrak elevator at Baltimore–Washington International Airport. With a certificate of compliance well past its expiration date, the situation seemed dire. Carpenter turned to her 90,000+ Twitter followers for help, tweeting, "Guys. I'm trapped in an amtrak elevator at Bwi airport. Help?" Nearly seven months later, on September 7, 2016, Amtrak finally responded, asking if she was still trapped. Amtrak clarified that the tweet had been re-tweeted, leading to a delayed response. The incident garnered attention, and Amtrak offered Carpenter a free ride on its Acela service as compensation. While Amtrak acknowledged that their response in February was prompt, the delay in addressing the situation led to a humorous and somewhat embarrassing situation for the railroad company. The internet was amused by the incident, highlighting the importance of consistent social media monitoring.

Rioting prisoners in a jail in Cascavel, Brazil, have killed four fellow inmates and injured several others, according to Brazilian authorities. The victims were decapitated or pushed off the roof of the building, while guards were taken hostage. The uprising, involving up to 800 inmates, began when guards delivering coffee were overpowered, leading to the ransacking and burning of much of the facility. Prisoners are reportedly unhappy with the jail's management, food quality, and hygiene conditions. Negotiations to end the stand-off resumed on Monday, with authorities aiming to transfer the rioters to another jail and release the hostages. The prison, which houses 1,140 inmates, has a capacity of 1,181, but the union states the true capacity is only 900, indicating overcrowding. The riot highlights the broader issue of prison conditions in Brazil, where 548,000 inmates are held in facilities designed for 300,000. The UN High Commissioner for Human Rights has called for an investigation into the high number of violent deaths in Brazilian prisons, citing previous incidents where dozens of people were killed. The situation underscores the need for improved investment and resources in the prison system to prevent further tragedies.

A prominent Manhattan doctor, Dr. David Newman, appeared in court late Tuesday on charges of sexually abusing two female patients while they were being treated at Mount Sinai Hospital. Newman, a 45-year-old emergency room physician, showed no emotion and declined to speak as he was escorted into the NYPD Manhattan Special Victims Division. He surrendered after days of knowing police were investigating claims by the two women. Newman was ordered held on $150,000 bond, or $50,000 cash. The doctor is accused of drugging and sexually abusing a 22-year-old woman in his care, allegedly knocking her out with morphine and leaving DNA on her body. The woman kept her hospital gown and bedding for evidence, and police are still awaiting lab results on the DNA. Newman has not volunteered his DNA. In court, an assistant district attorney said only nurses are given access to morphine, concluding that Newman must have had his own stash. Newman’s lawyer stated that his client does not have a criminal record or any claims of malpractice against him. Newman was immediately suspended from Mount Sinai after the allegations surfaced. Hospital officials released a statement saying Newman “has not provided care to patients at Mount Sinai since the investigation began” and that they “take the nature of these allegations very seriously and continue to conduct our own extensive internal inquiry.” Some Mount Sinai employees were upset by the news, finding it “disappointing when people abuse their power or position.” Police believe there may be more victims and are urging those patients to come forward. A second woman, also 22, claimed she was seeking treatment for a cold when Newman allegedly groped her during a chest exam. She contacted police Saturday and reported the earlier attack, which occurred in September. The patient alleged Newman fondled her breasts and ejaculated on her face after giving her a morphine shot. Newman has yet to make any comment on the vile charges against him. Authorities want a court order for a sample of Newman’s DNA to compare it with evidence taken from the gown that his alleged second victim was wearing. The woman used the gown to wipe the semen off her face and placed it, along with a blanket she used to clean up, inside a plastic bag. Newman’s home in Montclair, New Jersey, is under scrutiny, and his wife skipped the arraignment. The doctor, described as a leading voice for health care reforms and an Iraq War veteran, is expected to surrender on Tuesday morning. His case has sparked a debate on the ethics and safety of medical professionals, with some colleagues defending him and others expressing shock and disappointment.

A Missouri appeals court judge, Roy L. Richter, was appointed to Ferguson's municipal court to implement reforms following a critical U.S. Department of Justice report on the city's police and court systems.
