She expressed frustration that the media focused heavily on this issue, which she described as a "nothingburger," at the expense of substantive policy discussions. Additionally, she criticized the state of the Democratic Party, citing its financial struggles and lack of effective data operations as contributing to her difficulties. Clinton lamented that the party was not well-organized or well-informed, particularly regarding the economic policies of the Obama administration.

The former secretary of state also took aim at sexism, suggesting that her career was unfairly scrutinized for the speeches she gave, while male counterparts were not similarly criticized. She defended her decision to accept speaking fees, stating that it was part of her career and not a significant factor in her campaign's success or failure.

Clinton's comments on the Trump campaign were largely indirect, focusing more on the broader political and technological landscape. She questioned how the Trump campaign and the Russians coordinated to maximize the impact of leaked information, suggesting that domestic political operatives were involved in guiding the timing and content of the leaks.

Throughout the interview, Clinton maintained a tone of resilience and determination, expressing a commitment to staying active in politics and advocating for her beliefs. She emphasized the importance of organizing and building institutions within the Democratic Party, particularly in the realm of content and communication.

Clinton's remarks reflect a nuanced understanding of the complex factors that contributed to her defeat, placing significant blame on external forces while acknowledging the challenges she faced as a candidate. Her comments underscore the ongoing debate about the role of technology, misinformation, and political strategy in modern elections.

Serena Williams, 35, revealed her pregnancy to the world via a Snapchat photo of her baby bump in April, but the announcement was accidental. Williams, who is engaged to Reddit co-founder Alexis Ohanian, 34, explained to Gayle King at the 2017 Ted Talks conference that she had been checking her pregnancy status every week and taking pictures, but had kept it a secret from most people. "On social media, you press the wrong button and… 30 minutes later, I missed 4 calls and I’m like, ‘That’s weird,'” Williams said. The photo, which was later deleted, showed Williams in a yellow La Blanca Anniversary suit with the caption "20 weeks." Williams' representative confirmed to PEOPLE that the couple would welcome their first child in the fall. Despite the accidental announcement, Williams is not worried about future social media posts, stating, "Every week I just take a picture and save it and I've been so good about it and this was the one time I slipped, but it's okay." At the Ted Talks event, Williams also shared her plans for getting back in championship caliber shape post-baby, saying, "Roger Federer is older than me and he's still winning everything." She expressed excitement about her baby joining the stands to cheer for her.

Katie Holmes and Tom Cruise's high-profile divorce concluded swiftly, with the court papers sealed just a month-and-a-half after Holmes filed for divorce on June 28, seeking sole custody of their six-year-old daughter, Suri. The couple, who dated since April 2005 and married in November 2006, reportedly reached a settlement in a matter of days. Tom Cruise's lawyer, Bert Fields, confirmed that the actor is relieved to be moving forward, prioritizing his role as a good father. The deal includes restrictions on Suri's exposure to Scientology, which Cruise follows. Despite the quick resolution, fans remain eager for details, but they will have to wait as the papers remain sealed.

Scientists have discovered that the larvae of the Argentine horned frog, a species known for its aggressive and carnivorous behavior, emit a "brief, clear and very audible metallic-like sound" when threatened. This is the first evidence of sound production by anuran larvae (frogs and toads). The discovery, reported in the Swedish journal Acta Zoological, was made by Dr. Guillermo Natale of the National University of La Plata in Buenos Aires and his colleagues. They found that the horned frog tadpoles produce the sound by pushing air out of their lungs, which develop very early, even in tadpoles just three days old. The researchers believe the sound serves as a distress call to prevent cannibalism among the tadpoles. This finding raises the possibility that other tadpole species may also produce sounds underwater. The ability to communicate through sound so early in life is remarkable and could have significant implications for our understanding of amphibian behavior and ecology.

Comic Relief's Red Nose Day Actually, a 10-minute special featuring stars from the 2003 rom-com Love Actually, aimed to revisit the beloved characters 14 years after the original film. The special, directed by Richard Curtis and produced for the BBC, was a mix of callbacks and new storylines, with some characters finding happiness while others remained in their original predicaments. Hugh Grant reprised his role as the Prime Minister, now re-elected and performing sultry dance moves to Drake's music, much to the chagrin of his wife, Martine McCutcheon. Keira Knightley and Andrew Lincoln's characters, Juliet and Mark, were still happily married, with Mark having married Kate Moss, who made a cameo. Bill Nighy's character, Billy Mack, was still working at Radio Watford, while Colin Firth's character, Jamie, remained in a loveless marriage with his Portuguese wife, Lucia Moniz, who was now pregnant for the fourth time, much to Jamie's frustration. Liam Neeson's character, Daniel, was still spending his days on park benches, but his son, Sam, had grown up to date Joanna, the girl he had loved since childhood. The special also featured appearances from Rowan Atkinson, who worked at Sainsbury's, and Marcus Brigstocke, who interviewed Billy Mack. Despite the nostalgic charm, the special was criticized for its structural clumsiness and the absence of some original cast members, notably Alan Rickman and Emma Thompson, due to their deaths. The highlight of the special was Ed Sheeran's rescue of Liberian street children, a moment that stood out in a show that was otherwise seen as a "poor man's Four Weddings and a Funeral" that delivered little. The special's format and content were seen as a fun, albeit imperfect, way to revisit the characters and keep the spirit of the original film alive, with Richard Curtis joking that he hoped to see who had aged the best. The special was well-received by fans, who praised the cameo appearances and the return of familiar faces, but the overall execution was criticized for its lack of originality and the technical issues that plagued the broadcast.

At the 90th Academy Awards, three of Harvey Weinstein's most outspoken accusers—Ashley Judd, Salma Hayek, and Annabella Sciorra—presented a powerful video montage advocating for equality and representation. Sciorra began, "It's an honor to be here tonight. This year, many spoke their truth, and the journey ahead is long, but slowly a new path has emerged." Judd echoed, "The changes we are witnessing are being driven by the powerful sound of new voices, of different voices, of our voices, joining together in a mighty chorus that is finally saying, time's up." Hayek added, "So we salute those unstoppable spirits who kicked ass and broke through the biased perceptions against their gender, race, and ethnicity to tell their stories." Sciorra continued, "And on this 90th anniversary evening when the Oscars celebrates timeless classics, we also look forward as well."

The video montage featured other advocates like Mira Sorvino, Kumail Nanjiani, and Greta Gerwig, emphasizing the importance of representation in Hollywood. Judd, one of the first to speak out against Weinstein, recounted her experience, where Weinstein showed up to their business meeting in a bathrobe and later asked her to watch him shower, saying, "I said no, a lot of ways, a lot of times, and he always came back at me with some new ask." Hayek detailed her experiences, including a terrifying encounter where Weinstein threatened to kill her when she refused his advances. Sciorra shared her harrowing story of being forced into sexual intercourse by Weinstein, recounting how he locked her arms over her head and attempted oral sex.

The video montage also highlighted the broader impact of the #MeToo and #TimesUp movements, with Judd stating, "This entire fall, the Time's Up movement, everyone is getting a voice to express something that has been happening forever, not only in Hollywood, but in every walk of life." Hayek emphasized the need for change, saying, "The range of his persuasion tactics went from sweet-talking me to that one time when, in an attack of fury, he said the terrifying words, 'I will kill you, don't think I can't.'"

The powerful message from these women at the Oscars reflected the growing movement against sexual harassment and inequality. Sciorra concluded, "And we look forward to make sure that the next 90 years empower these limitless possibilities of equality, diversity, inclusion, intersectionality. That's what this year has promised us." The video montage served as a reminder of the journey ahead and the ongoing struggle for justice and equality.

One of the most intriguing features of Wolfram Alpha is its ability to identify objects in images, a capability that extends beyond its usual text-based queries. The system, accessible via ImageIdentify.com, allows users to upload photos and receive computer-generated guesses about the contents of the image, often within seconds. This tool, while not infallible, demonstrates remarkable accuracy in many cases. For instance, it correctly identified a picture of a cow as "black angus" and recognized two cups of ice cream as "frozen yogurt," showing a level of detail that goes beyond simple object recognition. However, it occasionally makes humorous mistakes, such as identifying Yosemite National Park's Half Dome as "elevation" and a gecko as a "night lizard."

Stephen Wolfram, the creator of Wolfram Alpha, asserts that the system's errors are often surprisingly human-like, which adds to its charm. The technology behind this image recognition was trained on a vast dataset of tens of millions of images, which Wolfram claims is comparable to the number of distinct views humans encounter in their early years. The system has been tested with challenging images, such as cats in spacesuits and sloths wearing party hats, and while it occasionally fails, these errors are gracefully handled, indicating a sophisticated understanding of visual complexity.

Wolfram envisions the potential of this technology to be applied to large collections of images for identification and categorization purposes. This could revolutionize how we process and understand visual data, potentially leading to applications in various fields, from travel documentation to nutritional analysis. The system's ability to recognize about 10,000 common objects is a testament to its advanced capabilities, although it still struggles with specific people, art, and non-real-world objects.

The new image recognition tool joins other rapid identification services like Google Goggles and Amazon's Firefly, but it stands out for its focus on providing information rather than selling products. Users can contribute to the system's improvement by indicating when the tool is correct or incorrect, and choosing from a few next-best guesses or typing in the correct identification. This interactive feature not only enhances the tool's accuracy but also makes it a fun and engaging experience for users.

While the current implementation is more of a curiosity than a practical tool, its potential applications are vast. Developers can leverage Wolfram's programming and cloud computing tools to build sophisticated applications based on this technology. For example, a program could provide statistical insights on a large number of images, helping users document their travels or translate images of food into nutritional information. The basic ImageIdentify site is just the beginning, with the system poised to improve over time as more data is fed into its training process.

A young Syrian boy, Omran Daqneesh, whose image of sitting alone, dazed, and bloodied in the back of an ambulance became an iconic symbol of civilian suffering in besieged Aleppo, has appeared in new footage posted by a pro-Syrian government television presenter. The video, taken by Kinana Allouche, a reporter for Al-Alam TV, shows Omran and his father in Aleppo, now under the control of President Bashar al-Assad's forces. Omran's father told the reporter that his son was in good health and that he had changed his son's name and hairstyle to protect him from being kidnapped and accused rebels of intimidating the family. However, Valerie Szybala from the Syria Institute, an independent research organization, suggested that the family may have been coerced into the interview, given the government's history of arresting and torturing those who speak out against it.

The original image of Omran, taken by the Aleppo Media Centre (AMC) after an airstrike, showed the five-year-old boy sitting alone in the ambulance, his face covered in dust and blood, and quickly went viral, highlighting the suffering of civilians in the besieged city. His older brother, Ali, died from his wounds after the same airstrike. The AMC reported that the airstrike was conducted by Russian forces, but the Syrian government has since claimed that the family was used as "propaganda" by the opposition and international media. Omran's father, Mohammed Daqneesh, told the reporter that he had been sitting with his son when their home was hit and that Omran had only suffered minor injuries, with the blood on his face having dripped from one of his own wounds. He added that he had taken Omran to an ambulance despite there being no need, as he believed the rebels were intimidating the family.

The new footage marks the first time Omran has been seen publicly since his injuries, and it comes as the Syrian government has regained control of Aleppo after years of fighting and months of bitter siege and bombardment. The Syrian civil war, which erupted in 2011, has killed an estimated 465,000 people. The appearance of Omran in the new video has raised questions about whether the family was coerced into the interview and whether the government is using the boy for a pro-Assad agenda. The Syrian government has a history of disinformation efforts, promising benefits to defectors or displaced civilians if they speak out against alleged rebel crimes.

Ron Paul's declaration that "we are all Austrians now" puzzled many, as he refers to a school of economic thought that is highly critical of government intervention. Paul's statement highlights the divide within the libertarian movement, with his own beliefs aligning more closely with the Austrian school, which advocates for strict free-market principles and rejects government regulation. This contrasts sharply with the mainstream economic consensus, which has largely embraced the ideas of Friedrich Hayek. The article delves into the nuances of Austrian economics, explaining how it differs from standard free-market thinking by rejecting the idea that the government can stabilize the economy or that cutting taxes can boost growth. Critics argue that the Austrian theory, which posits that low interest rates lead to unsustainable bubbles, lacks empirical support and fails to explain the complexities of economic cycles. Despite its flaws, the article suggests that the gap between the natural interest rate and the actual rate is narrowing, signaling a potential economic recovery. This recovery is expected to be driven by increased bank credit, higher employment, and a return to normal levels of construction and durable goods consumption, leading to a period of rapid growth from a low base.

The U.S. Department of Labor has filed lawsuits against the Fundamentalist LDS Church and some of its leaders for alleged child labor violations during the 2012-13 pecan harvest season. The lawsuits target Bishop Lyle Jeffs, member Dale Barlow, and the church’s two operating branches, seeking back wages for 1,400 workers, many of whom were children under 13. The Department of Labor also accuses Paragon Contractors Corporation and its owner, FLDS member Dan Jessop, of violating a 2007 injunction related to child labor. According to the lawsuits, the church pulled children from school to work for weeks without pay, engaging them in various agricultural tasks. The department aims to collect $1.9 million in penalties for these violations. David Weil, the Wage and Hour Division administrator, emphasized that such violations, especially concerning children, will not be tolerated. The department hopes these actions will deter future illegal practices and protect the rights of workers, including children.

The crisis in Ukraine continues to impact Russia's economy and international relations, with sanctions from the U.S. and Europe pushing Russia toward a potential recession. Russian President Vladimir Putin's popularity surged after annexing Crimea, but the economic costs are becoming evident. Russia's stock market, represented by the Micex index, has fallen 13.7% this year, compared to a 5% decline for the broader MSCI Emerging Markets Index. The ruble has weakened 9%, and capital outflows from Russia may reach $70 billion in the first quarter. Sanctions on Russian officials and businesses have led to disruptions in financial services, with Visa and MasterCard suspending services for some sanctioned banks. While average Russians fear the impact of sanctions, experts suggest they may have a limited effect on Putin, whose approval ratings have increased. The U.S. and Europe have expanded sanctions, targeting Russian industries and individuals, but Russia has retaliated by banning 13 Canadians from entering the country. The G8 summit in Sochi was canceled, reflecting international condemnation of Russia's actions in Ukraine. The crisis highlights the growing tension between Russia and the West, with the U.S. and Europe warning of further economic penalties if Russia does not change course. Despite the sanctions, Russia's major energy and financial sectors remain largely unaffected, and the Russian government has expressed reluctance to fully isolate itself from the global economy.

A mass email sent by a Calgary student to 246 women named Nicole led to the formation of a network of like-named women at the University of Calgary. First-year student Carlos Zetina was at The Den, a campus pub, when he met a woman named Nicole from the Netherlands. After she gave him the wrong number, Zetina decided to send a specific email to all women with the name Nicole to find the correct one. He wrote, "If you (sic) name is Nicole and you’re from Holland and you think Nietzsche is depressing then text me," and included his phone number. By 11 a.m. the next day, PhD candidate Nicolette Little received the email and shared it with other women named Nicole, leading to the creation of a Facebook group called "Nicole From Last Night." The group organized a meetup, dubbed the "Congress of Nicoles," where about 20 women gathered at Side Street Pub in Kensington. The event went viral on Twitter with the hashtag #nicolefromlastnight, with users expressing amusement and support. The intended Nicole eventually revealed herself as "the real Nicole" and connected with Zetina, who was surprised by the outcome. The women plan to continue meeting monthly and have formed a "little girl gang" out of their unexpected friendship.

A quick-thinking individual managed to extinguish a fire on a boat, likely saving lives and property, according to a Reddit post. Despite others expressing doubt, the brave bystander used a fire extinguisher effectively, putting out the flames and ensuring everyone's safety. This incident highlights the importance of having fire safety equipment on boats and the potential impact of quick action in emergencies.

A 47-year-old man from Ludhiana, Punjab, India, has been arrested for selling his newborn grandson on Facebook, according to news reports. The baby was allegedly kidnapped by the grandfather shortly after birth and sold for 45,000 rupees to a nurse, who then sold him for 300,000 rupees to a hospital lab assistant. The lab assistant put the baby up for sale on Facebook, where a businessman from New Delhi offered 800,000 rupees for the child. Police recovered the baby and arrested five individuals, including the grandfather and the lab assistant. This case is seen as the "tip of the iceberg" in a larger child-trafficking scandal, with tens of thousands of children trafficked annually in India for various forms of exploitation.

Mobile app development has become a crowded field, with countless ideas vying for attention. Fueled, a New York-based app development company, has compiled a list of ideas that, while well-intentioned, are often doomed to fail. The company's Director & Chief Strategist, Ryan Matzner, polled his staff and clients to identify trends and pitfalls in the app market. Among the "general terrible" ideas are selling public parking spaces, a Tinder for dogs app, GPS-based chat, and a pee break app. These ideas often fail because they require too much effort for too little return, such as the hassle of managing a parking space bidding platform or the low demand for location-based chat. Other ideas, like shock therapy or emoji apps, are technically feasible but lack a clear market need. Apps requiring a massive user base, like point-of-sale systems, are also challenging to implement. Additionally, Fueled frequently receives calls from individuals with "million-dollar ideas" that they are willing to sell, but the company typically dismisses these pitches due to the lack of interest or means to pursue them. The reality is that building a successful app is a complex and resource-intensive process, and many ideas that seem promising on paper often fall flat in practice.

President Obama addressed crises both domestic and foreign from his vacation in Martha's Vineyard, Massachusetts, on August 14, 2014. He called for calm amid violent protests in Ferguson, Missouri, following the shooting of 18-year-old Michael Brown. Obama urged police and protesters to "take a step back" and focus on moving forward. He called the death "heartbreaking and tragic" and asked for healing and peace. The president criticized police for detaining journalists during protests and called for transparency in the investigation. He also announced a limited military mission to rescue religious minorities in Iraq, stating that a full-scale rescue operation was not needed. Obama praised the military's humanitarian operation and expressed hope for progress in Iraq. The situation in Ferguson continued to escalate, with protests and looting, prompting Missouri Governor Jay Nixon to name an African-American captain of the Missouri Highway Patrol to oversee security. The new approach included a pledge to use less heavy-handed tactics and to respect peaceful protests. The shooting raised questions about racial tensions and police practices in Ferguson, with civil rights groups and Anonymous hackers calling for greater transparency and accountability.

Sen. John McCain's column criticizing Russian President Vladimir Putin is set to appear in Pravda, a Russian news site known for its anti-Western stance, after an agreement was reached between the senator's office and the site's editors. McCain's communications director, Brian Rogers, confirmed the senator's willingness to contribute, stating, "Senator McCain would be glad to write something for Pravda." The arrangement comes in response to Putin's recent op-ed in The New York Times, where he criticized the United States. Pravda's English editor, Dmitry Sudakov, expressed interest in publishing McCain's piece, noting that the senator has been "an active anti-Russian politician for many years." McCain's column is expected to address issues such as democracy and human rights in Russia, as well as Putin's regime's support for the Syrian regime, which has killed 100,000 of its own people. The agreement marks a significant development in U.S.-Russian relations, as Pravda, which is not the official Pravda of the Soviet era, is known for its critical stance towards the West. McCain's column will be published in English and then translated into Russian, allowing all Pravda readers to engage with the senator's views. The move is seen as a bold step, considering the restrictive press policies in Russia, where the site ranks 148th out of 179 countries for press freedom according to Reporters Without Borders.

Twenty-five years after the infamous 1990 theft of 13 priceless artworks from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston, law enforcement officials are seeking the public’s assistance in identifying an unauthorized visitor who entered the museum the night before the robbery. This visitor, captured on surveillance video, entered the museum through the same door as the thieves 24 hours before the heist. The video, released by the U.S. Attorney’s Office, shows a security guard admitting an unidentified man to the museum at 12:49 a.m. on March 17, 1990, nearly exactly 24 hours before the heist. The man is seen getting out of a car matching the general description of one reported to be parked outside the museum minutes before the theft. The museum’s Director of Security, Anthony Amore, stated that the video could provide new information that could lead to the recovery of the stolen artworks, worth at least $500 million. The FBI and the museum have offered a $5 million reward for information leading to the recovery of the stolen artwork in good condition. The video footage does not directly implicate any specific individual, but it raises questions about the events that transpired the night before the robbery. The Gardner Museum has been working with law enforcement to ensure that all avenues are explored in the continuing quest to recover the stolen artworks.

The U.S. and China have introduced new sanctions against North Korea at the United Nations, aiming to impede the development of Pyongyang’s nuclear and missile programs following its recent atomic bomb test. Simultaneously, IBM's Sequoia supercomputer has taken the top spot on the list of the world's fastest supercomputers, marking the first time the U.S. has claimed the lead since it was overtaken by China two years ago. Sequoia, installed at the U.S. Department of Energy's Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory in California, scored 16.32 petaflops, significantly outperforming Japan's K Computer, which fell to second place with 10.51 petaflops. IBM, the leading manufacturer in the top 10, prepared for this achievement over two years, with Sequoia using over 1.5 million processor cores and being 1.55 times faster than the K Computer. Sequoia is also more energy efficient, consuming 7.9 megawatts compared to the K Computer's 12.6 megawatts. The supercomputer will be used for simulations to extend the life of aging nuclear weapons, avoiding the need for underground tests. Sequoia's capabilities provide increased confidence in the nation's nuclear deterrent and represent continued American leadership in high-performance computing. The machine will support stockpile life extension programs, enhance the assessment of the stockpile, and address nonproliferation and counterterrorism issues.

Jonathan Porter, 41, was arrested and charged with malicious assault in the attack, which took place in Logan County. Senior Trooper J.E. Garren told the Associated Press that Porter attacked Ojeda after asking the candidate to put a bumper sticker on Porter's truck. However, Ojeda believes the attack was politically motivated. Ojeda suffered multiple fractures to his head and face and was transported to a hospital in Charleston. His campaign page stated that he was "tough as woodpecker lips" and would pull through the attack. Ojeda wanted to return home in time for the primary election and planned to delay surgery until later that week. An update on his campaign page noted that he was resting but would have to spend another night in the hospital. Ojeda's primary opponent, incumbent state Sen. Art Kirkendoll, said in a statement that he wished Ojeda a speedy recovery and condemned violence in politics. Ojeda, a military veteran, wrote that he had "dealt with the Taliban and Al Qaeda" and had been threatened before. He stated that he would continue his campaign despite the attack. Habeas corpus, or the Great Writ, is a legal procedure that prevents the government from holding individuals indefinitely without justification. This fundamental right, enshrined in the U.S. Constitution, ensures that the executive branch must provide a neutral judge with reasons for detaining someone. However, the Military Commissions Act (MCA) of 2006, passed in the waning days of the last Congress, revoked habeas corpus rights for detainees at Guantanamo Bay and for any foreigner labeled an "enemy combatant," including legal residents of the U.S. This provision has significant implications, as it allows the government to detain individuals without legal recourse.

The majority of Guantanamo detainees were not captured on battlefields but were sold by Northern Alliance and Pakistani warlords for substantial bounties. Only 10 out of nearly 800 detainees have ever been charged with any crime. Despite numerous legal victories affirming the detainees' right to challenge their detention, the Bush administration has managed to prevent fair hearings in the courts. In 2007, the Supreme Court agreed to hear a case challenging the detention of many Guantanamo detainees, who have faced indefinite detention, sham trials, and rapidly deteriorating psychological conditions for nearly six years. The coming Supreme Court term will hear these cases again, with the hope of holding the administration accountable and upholding habeas corpus.

The MCA extends the second-class system of justice beyond Guantanamo to any non-citizen, including legal permanent residents of the U.S., who the executive unilaterally declares an "unlawful enemy combatant." This compromise of habeas corpus has eroded the foundational legal and constitutional framework of the U.S. If this right is not defended, it could have far-reaching consequences for everyone. The Nonhuman Rights Project has recently filed a case seeking habeas corpus for two research chimpanzees at Stony Brook University, marking the first time an animal has been granted this legal protection. This case could potentially force the university to release the chimpanzees and could influence other judges to grant similar rights to other research animals.

The MCA's revocation of habeas corpus rights has significant implications for both Guantanamo detainees and potentially for anyone the executive branch deems an "unlawful enemy combatant." The legal battles over this issue continue, with the hope that the Supreme Court will uphold habeas corpus as a fundamental right essential for preserving liberty, justice, and democracy.

A controversial four-lane highway will be constructed under Stonehenge, planners announced, aiming to address a decades-old traffic issue at the ancient British monument. The 1.8-mile tunnel would remove the sight and sound of traffic for visitors, enhancing the experience of the prehistoric landmark. Stonehenge, one of Britain’s top tourist attractions, draws over 1.3 million visitors annually. The busy A303 trunk road, which runs past the site, has created a notorious bottleneck, causing drivers to slow down for a look. Plans for a tunnel at the Wiltshire site were first proposed nearly 30 years ago but have faced repeated delays due to environmental concerns. The latest scheme, which would carry two lanes in each direction, has been met with criticism from the Stonehenge Alliance, which claims the tunnel would cause "irreparable damage" to the landscape. Supporters of the government plan include heritage charity, the National Trust. Helen Ghosh, the director general, stated that the tunnel would restore tranquility and improve the visitor experience, allowing people to hear skylarks singing rather than the constant noise of traffic. The Department for Transport said the Stonehenge tunnel was part of a $2.45 billion program to reduce traffic congestion in the region. A public consultation on the scheme will run until March 5, 2023. Archaeologists are divided, with some concerned that the tunnel could harm the rich and complex archaeology of the area. The A303 has long been a blight on Stonehenge, making it difficult to appreciate the monument’s grandeur. The tunnel is expected to make the site more peaceful, romantic, and emotionally powerful, enhancing its unique historical and cultural significance. However, campaigners argue that a tunnel shorter than 2.7 miles would do "irreparable damage" to the landscape. The project’s history is marked by a long and chequered past, with previous plans for a tunnel having faced significant opposition. The latest proposal, which resurfaced in 2014, has now been given the green light by the government. The tunnel is part of a broader £2 billion scheme to upgrade the A303 between the M3 and M5. The public consultation aims to gather feedback from drivers and residents, ensuring that the project aligns with the needs and concerns of the local community.

YouTube is undergoing a significant shift in its content strategy, with plans to cut programming deals for at least 60 percent of its channels. The video giant has been funding around 160 channels as part of its effort to make the platform more TV-like, but it will now focus on renewing contracts with only a portion of these creators. Starting this week, YouTube will offer new deals to some of the channels that launched in the past year, while others will not receive renewed funding. The decision on which channels to continue supporting is based on engagement metrics, such as total watch time, and cost efficiency. Channels that do not get renewed will still remain on the platform, but their creators will need to find alternative ways to generate revenue. YouTube aims to reinvest in up to 40 percent of its original channels, with the goal of fostering a more sustainable ecosystem. The company's approach to renewals is part of a broader strategy to change perceptions among content creators and advertisers, positioning YouTube as a serious player in the premium content space. While some channels have already shown success, with the top 25 averaging over a million views per week, many producers are still struggling to recoup their initial investments. The renewed funding will be similar in scale to the first round, with most channels receiving between $1 million and $5 million to produce exclusive content for a year. This move reflects YouTube's growing ambition to compete with traditional TV and attract more advertisers, as it aims to increase viewer engagement and time spent on the platform.

House Democratic leader Nancy Pelosi of California rejected the idea of linking funding for President Donald Trump's border wall to legal protections for so-called Dreamers, young immigrants brought to the U.S. as children. Pelosi stated, "They're two different subjects," indicating that the two issues should not be intertwined. The House and Senate approved a two-week stopgap bill to keep the government funded through December 21, with the measure now headed to the White House. Trump has insisted on including at least $5 billion for his proposed wall in any funding package, a demand that Democrats have firmly rejected. Pelosi is seeking to become House speaker in January and called for the lame-duck Congress to pass six government funding bills and a separate measure for the Department of Homeland Security, which oversees border security. Pelosi emphasized that funding for border security does not necessarily include a wall, noting that the wall is "immoral, ineffective, and expensive." Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer echoed Pelosi's stance, stating that the bipartisan Senate plan for $1.6 billion in border security funding does not include money for the 30-foot-high concrete wall Trump envisions. Schumer called the wall a "nonstarter" for Democrats, who face increasing pressure from outside groups and liberal lawmakers to resist Trump's push for the barrier. Trump warned of the potential for "Big danger" at the U.S.-Mexico border in Arizona, demanding that Pelosi and Schumer approve border security and the wall. The administration has not spent more than $1 billion approved for border security in the budget year that ended September 30, and Schumer noted that the idea of demanding such a huge amount this year, without spending last year's money, makes no sense. Senate Appropriations Committee Chairman Richard Shelby preferred to include Homeland Security in an omnibus package containing seven unresolved spending bills for the current budget year. Missouri Sen. Roy Blunt, a member of Republican leadership, warned that a shutdown could occur if Trump signs a bill without funding for the wall, as he has given every indication that he would be willing to have a shutdown over this issue.

The 16-day government shutdown and the near-default on the federal debt ceiling in October 2013, orchestrated by House Republicans, left the White House and Senate Democrats with a series of complex negotiations to avert a fiscal crisis. House Speaker John Boehner’s initial strategy to strip funds from the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare) failed, and he was ultimately sidelined by Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, who orchestrated a bipartisan deal. However, the negotiations were fraught with tension and political maneuvering. 

Boehner’s initial approach was to avoid a shutdown by focusing on the debt ceiling, but he was overruled by his own party’s hard-line members, who demanded a showdown over Obamacare. This resulted in a government shutdown, which was the first in nearly two decades. The shutdown lasted 16 days, and the potential for a default on the federal debt was averted only hours before the deadline. 

President Barack Obama confronted Boehner at the White House, questioning why they were in the second day of a shutdown that Boehner had repeatedly pledged to avoid. The shutdown was a result of a series of complex relationships, internal Republican conflict, and Democratic unity. The House Republicans, led by Boehner, were outmaneuvered by McConnell, who negotiated a bipartisan agreement. 

The shutdown was particularly damaging to the Republican Party, as it forced them to confront their own members who were pushing for a shutdown to defund Obamacare. This internal conflict weakened Boehner’s position and ultimately led to his inability to pass the necessary legislation. McConnell, who had previously negotiated deals with Democrats, stepped in to broker a solution, but his efforts were complicated by the Democrats’ unity and their desire to put the tea party in its place.

The negotiations were further complicated by the release of private emails that showed Boehner had been deeply involved in fixing an Obamacare glitch, which made him appear hypocritical. This, combined with the Democrats’ refusal to negotiate, put additional pressure on Boehner. Despite his efforts, Boehner was unable to secure the necessary votes in the House, and the shutdown continued.

The final deal, brokered by McConnell and Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, included an extension of the debt ceiling until February 7, 2014, and a continuation of government funding until January 15, 2014. The deal was criticized by some Republicans as a capitulation to Democratic demands, but it was seen as a necessary compromise to avoid a default on the federal debt.

The shutdown and the negotiations highlighted the deep divisions within the Republican Party and the challenges of governing in a divided Congress. The episode also underscored the importance of bipartisanship in addressing major fiscal issues and the potential consequences of inaction. The political fallout from the shutdown was significant, with Boehner facing criticism from both his party and the public. The episode also raised questions about the future of the Republican Party’s strategy on healthcare and fiscal issues.
