The three-year competition involves teams deploying devices that can operate at depths up to 4,000 meters, tasked with creating high-resolution maps, taking high-definition images, and identifying specific features like shipwrecks or geological anomalies. Participants must also complete a "bonus" $1 million challenge for technology that can monitor chemical and biological compounds in the water column or follow a chemical or biological signal back to its source. The initiative aims to address critical ocean challenges and inspire innovation, with the ultimate goal of creating a healthier, more understood ocean. The competition is open to anyone, with registration now open until September 2016, and the first tests are scheduled for a year after that. This new challenge is a partnership between XPRIZE, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), and Shell Oil Company, aiming to uncover the mysteries of the deep sea and enhance our understanding of the ocean's crucial role in global food, energy, and economic security.

The North American Aerospace Defense Command (NORAD) has switched from Google to Microsoft Bing for tracking Santa's journey this Christmas Eve, marking a significant technological break-up after five years of collaboration. NORAD, which has been tracking Santa since 1955, now uses four high-tech systems—radar, satellites, Santa Cams, and fighter jets—to monitor his sleigh ride. The switch will see NORAD's tracking site run on Microsoft's Windows Azure cloud-computing platform and Bing Maps, with apps available for Windows 8, Windows Phone 8, and Android. Meanwhile, Google continues its own Santa-tracking efforts, building a new route algorithm to chart Santa's journey on its Earth platform. Both organizations will offer live updates through various channels, including websites, apps, and phone calls. The tradition, which has grown to involve 25 million people annually, continues to engage children and families worldwide, blending technology with holiday magic.

A Bronx woman, Liana Barrientos, 39, who is accused of marrying 10 men over an 11-year period without ever divorcing any of them, was arrested after failing to pay a subway fare. Barrientos, who is also charged with criminal trespass, is believed to be currently married to four men, with some of the 10 marriages occurring simultaneously. The case came to light when Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Department of Homeland Security's Investigation Division informed the Bronx County District Attorney's Office that seven of the men she allegedly married were from "red-flagged" countries, including Egypt, Turkey, Georgia, Pakistan, and Mali. One of the men, Rashid Rajput, was deported to Pakistan after an investigation by the Joint Terrorism Task Force. Barrientos, who is accused of filing false marriage applications, is also charged with theft of service for not paying her subway fare. She is facing up to four years in prison if convicted. The motive behind her multiple marriages remains unclear, with one source suggesting it was not driven by love. Barrientos has two children with different men, and one of them, Carlos Garcia, has reportedly kicked her out of his Bronx apartment. Her lawyer, Chris Wright, declined to comment.

Texas native Peggy Sue Gerron, who inspired Buddy Holly's 1958 hit "Peggy Sue," passed away at the age of 78 in a Lubbock hospital on Monday. Gerron Rackham, as she was later known, unveiled her autobiography "Whatever Happened to Peggy Sue?: A Memoir by Buddy Holly's Peggy Sue" in 2008 to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the iconic song. The book, which Gerron wrote based on about 150 diary entries she kept during her time with Holly, offered a personal account of their friendship. Born in Olton, Texas, Gerron moved to Lubbock, where she attended high school and met Holly and his friends. She married drummer Jerry Allison, a member of Holly's rock 'n' roll band The Crickets, but the couple later divorced. Holly, who penned several other popular songs including "That'll Be the Day" and "Maybe Baby," tragically died in a plane crash in Iowa in 1959, along with Ritchie Valens and J.P. "The Big Bopper" Richardson. In 1978, Gary Busey portrayed Holly in the film "The Buddy Holly Story," while Kathleen Turner starred as a character named Peggy Sue in the 1986 movie "Peggy Sue Got Married." The Buddy Holly Center in Lubbock continues to honor the singer, musician, and songwriter, often referred to as "Lubbock's most famous native son."

In the remote Inyo Mountains of California, near Death Valley, the ghost town of Cerro Gordo, known as "fat hill," has been sold for $1.4 million, a price that reflects the high value of historical properties in the region. The town, which includes 22 structures such as a hotel, church, and bunkhouse, was listed for $925,000 and closed on Friday the 13th, a date that the listing agent, Jake Rasmuson, of Bishop Real Estate, described as "very coincidental but fitting for the property." The sale was made to a group of Los Angeles investors, including Brent Underwood, founder of the youth hostel HK Austin, and Jon Bier, who runs a public relations firm catering to athletes. They plan to preserve the town's history and potentially open it to the public, with plans to add amenities like overnight accommodations and events such as writing retreats, concerts, and photo shoots. The town, which was once a bustling mining hub with a population of 5,000, fell into decline when silver prices dropped in 1877. It has been privately owned for decades but was open to the public for tours. The new owners hope to maintain the historic nature of the property while introducing modern conveniences that will allow more people to experience this piece of American history. The sale garnered 12 serious offers, with the final price reflecting the unique opportunity to own a significant piece of the Wild West. The town's rich history and preserved state make it an attractive investment for those interested in preserving and developing unique properties.

Jordan Peele's "Get Out" is a masterful blend of horror and social commentary, making it a standout in the genre. The film's premise, a young black man visiting his white girlfriend's family estate, immediately sets the stage for a terrifying and thought-provoking experience. Peele's direction is both meticulous and daring, seamlessly weaving together the conventions of horror films with a sharp critique of racial dynamics in America. The opening scene, where Chris (Daniel Kaluuya), a 26-year-old photographer, walks down a dimly lit suburban street, fumbling for directions, is a powerful metaphor for the everyday anxieties faced by black individuals. This scene, along with the subsequent interactions with the Armitage family (Catherine Keener and Bradley Whitford), perfectly encapsulates the microaggressions and subtle racism that permeate society.

Peele's screenplay is a tour de force, drawing inspiration from classic horror films like "Rosemary's Baby" and "The Stepford Wives," while also incorporating elements of science fiction and psychological thriller. The Armitages, a seemingly liberal and well-meaning family, are revealed to be harboring dark secrets that challenge Chris's perceptions of reality. The film's pace is deliberate, allowing the audience to fully immerse themselves in Chris's experiences and the escalating tension. Peele's use of handheld camera work and strategic editing keeps the audience on edge, heightening the sense of dread and unease.

The performances are uniformly strong, with Kaluuya delivering a nuanced and compelling portrayal of Chris. His expressive face conveys a range of emotions, from fear and confusion to determination and anger. Allison Williams, known for her role in "Girls," brings a layered performance as Rose, a character who initially appears to be a supportive partner but gradually reveals her own complicity in the family's sinister plans. The supporting cast, including Betty Gabriel and Marcus Henderson, also excel in their roles, bringing a chilling authenticity to their characters.

Peele's direction is nothing short of brilliant, with a keen eye for detail and a masterful understanding of the genre's tropes. His ability to subvert expectations and create a sense of unease is evident throughout the film. The climax, a tense and harrowing sequence, is a testament to Peele's skill as a storyteller. The film's exploration of the black experience in America is both poignant and timely, making it a must-see for anyone interested in contemporary cinema.

Get Out is a film that challenges its audience to confront uncomfortable truths about race and society. It is a powerful reminder that the fight for equality and justice is far from over, and that the horror of racism is not something we can simply ignore. Peele's debut feature is a triumph of craft and vision, a film that will be remembered as a landmark in horror and social commentary.

Share your story or create an It Gets Better video to inspire others. Take the pledge to spread hope and purchase merchandise or books to help the cause. For just $25, you can even donate a book to your local library or school, ensuring the message reaches more young people in need.

From the labyrinthine security checkpoints to the cramped seats and limited overhead storage, air travel often ranks among the most grueling experiences. Airbus aims to alleviate these issues with its A350 XWB jet, integrating the latest design and engineering advancements to enhance the flying experience for passengers, airlines, and pilots. One of the primary goals is to combat jet lag, a common complaint among frequent flyers. The A350 XWB features LED lights that change color to mimic the sun's natural glow, timed to align with the body's circadian rhythms, offering a more comfortable journey. Additionally, the plane's air filtration system refreshes the air every two to three minutes, and it is pressurized to 6,000 feet, which Airbus claims improves passenger comfort and reduces jet lag upon arrival.

The A350 XWB's design also focuses on reducing weight and improving aerodynamics. Over 50% of the aircraft's structure is composed of carbon fiber-reinforced plastic, making it lighter and more durable. This material is less susceptible to corrosion compared to traditional aluminum, further enhancing the plane's longevity. The wings are 20% larger and 10% wider, inspired by birds' wings, which reduce drag and noise while improving performance at low speeds. The flap system has been redesigned to follow the flight path direction rather than the wind, resulting in a smoother ride and a 25% improvement in fuel economy compared to similar models from competitors.

Passenger comfort is another key aspect of the A350 XWB. The fuselage is wider, allowing for larger passenger seats in economy class and easier movement down the aisles. The interior design is adaptable, allowing airlines to swap out seats and tweak configurations more easily. This philosophy extends to the integration of computer hardware, making avionics and software upgrades less cumbersome. Airbus emphasizes that the A350 XWB is designed to be relevant for the future, with an open architecture that can evolve to accommodate new functions and technological advancements.

Qatar Airways was the first to introduce the A350 XWB to its fleet, with the first US landing in early 2015. Despite lengthy delivery times, the A350 XWB has faced fewer technical and mechanical issues compared to the Boeing 787 Dreamliner. With $15 billion in research and development, the A350 XWB is expected to be in service for the next 30 years, offering a more efficient, comfortable, and adaptable flying experience.

Britain is set to ban the sale of new gasoline and diesel cars starting in 2040, aiming to tackle air pollution and embrace cleaner technologies. This decision, part of a broader plan to reduce emissions and improve public health, comes as similar measures are being considered globally. Environment Secretary Michael Gove emphasized the necessity of embracing new technology, stating, "We can't carry on with diesel and petrol cars." The move is expected to have significant implications for the automotive industry, society, and the environment. However, the transition will be challenging, as electric and fuel cell cars, along with plug-in hybrids, currently account for less than 3% of the market. Industry experts suggest that the shift will require substantial planning and investment, with concerns over affordability, range, and charging infrastructure. The government plans to invest £1.4 billion to ensure that all vehicles on British roads produce zero emissions by 2050. This commitment aligns with France's similar pledge and reflects a growing global trend towards cleaner transportation. Critics argue that the 2040 deadline is too distant, while others question the feasibility of the transition. The plan also includes measures to improve air quality in specific areas, such as retrofitting buses and altering road layouts, with a total investment of £3 billion. Despite these efforts, some experts believe that the timeline is too long and that more immediate actions are needed to address the health risks posed by air pollution. The government's strategy faces challenges, including the need to avoid measures that could be seen as punitive for motorists. As the plan is unveiled, it remains to be seen how effectively it will be implemented and whether it will set a precedent for other countries to follow.

On November 29, 2018, the office of Jewish professor Elizabeth Midlarsky, who teaches and researches the Holocaust at Columbia Teachers College, was vandalized with swastikas and anti-Semitic slurs. Midlarsky discovered the graffiti—two swastikas alongside the derogatory term “Yid”—when she arrived at her office around 1 p.m. The incident remains under investigation by the NYPD Hate Crimes Task Force and is being treated as an aggravated harassment. Midlarsky’s office had been previously vandalized in 2007, when a swastika was spray-painted on her door and anti-Semitic flyers left in her mailbox. This prior incident was “horrifying but not surprising” due to her “relatively visible status as a Jew” at the time, citing her numerous published papers and articles on subjects related to the Holocaust.

Midlarsky’s office is not shared with other staff, and the graffiti was drawn in the entryway. The NYPD was notified, and a different staff member who entered the room at approximately 11:47 a.m. did not observe anything unusual. The incident is part of a broader national rise in anti-Semitic crimes and a changing cultural landscape. Midlarsky, a professor of psychology and education, is known for her research interests in altruism, religiousness, and the Holocaust.

In response, the Office of University Life and Barnard College issued statements strongly denouncing the anti-Semitic act and showing support for Jewish students. Columbia University’s Teachers College president, Thomas Bailey, released a statement, unequivocally condemning any expression of hatred, which has no place in their society. He expressed outrage and horror at the act of aggression and use of the vile anti-Semitic symbol against a valued member of their community. The college is working with police to discover the perpetrator of this hateful act and reaffirmed their commitment to providing a respectful and welcoming environment for all members of their community.

The NYPD Hate Crimes Unit is leading the investigation, and no arrests have been made. The 2007 incidents involving the same professor were also not resolved, and the NYPD declined to say if they believe there is a connection between the two cases. The vandalism has sparked concern and condemnation from the university community, highlighting the ongoing issue of anti-Semitism in New York and beyond.

Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell has stated that he believes the allegations against Alabama Republican Senate nominee Roy Moore and that Moore should step aside from the race, according to CNN. McConnell's comments, made in Kentucky, come after The Washington Post published a report based on interviews with over 30 people, alleging that Moore pursued relationships with teenage women in his 30s. One woman claimed Moore initiated sexual contact with her when she was 14. Moore has denied the allegations and threatened to sue The Post. McConnell's position brings his stance a step further, as he now believes the allegations and is calling for Moore to leave the race. Moore's tweet in response accused McConnell of failing conservatives and needing to be replaced, using the hashtag #DrainTheSwamp. The pressure on Republicans to disavow Moore has increased, with some like Arizona Senator John McCain calling for him to drop out of the race. The National Republican Senatorial Committee, one of the party's main campaign arms, has cut its fundraising ties with Moore. The Senate Majority Leader's office is also exploring a write-in option as a potential strategy. The race, set for December 12, is closely watched as it could impact the Senate's balance of power.

President-elect Donald Trump ignited a debate over flag-burning when he tweeted on November 29, 2016, that burning the American flag should be a crime, potentially punishable by a year in jail or loss of citizenship. Trump's tweet, which drew immediate criticism from legal experts and politicians, came as some protesters had already set fire to American flags in response to his election. Trump's statement contrasted sharply with the Supreme Court's 1989 and 1990 rulings, which established that burning the flag is a form of protected free speech under the First Amendment. In the 1989 case Texas v. Johnson, the Supreme Court ruled that the federal and state laws prohibiting flag desecration were unconstitutional. The following year, in United States v. Eichman, the Court again upheld the right to burn the flag, striking down the Flag Protection Act of 1989. Justice Antonin Scalia, who supported the 1989 decision, later said he would have jailed flag burners if he were king. However, he acknowledged that the flag is a symbol of free speech, stating, "Burning a flag is a form of expression—speech doesn't just mean written words or oral words—burning a flag is a symbol that expresses an idea." Trump's tweet also drew support from some conservative leaders, including Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell, who wrote an op-ed in 2006 defending the right to burn the flag. McConnell argued that "No act of speech is so obnoxious that it merits tampering with our First Amendment." Despite Trump's tweet, legal experts pointed out that flag burning is constitutionally protected and any attempt to criminalize it would likely be unconstitutional. Jason Miller, Trump's senior communications adviser, struggled to defend the president-elect's stance, insisting that flag burning should be illegal even as he tried to pivot to other topics. Trump's tweet reignited the debate over flag-burning and highlighted his willingness to push back against fundamental democratic principles.

This daily flow of data is added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period, preserving web pages and ensuring that broken links can be fixed. Alexa Internet, known for their web traffic data, has been a valuable contributor to the Internet Archive's mission to archive the web. This partnership has allowed the Internet Archive to maintain a comprehensive record of the web's evolution, providing a valuable resource for researchers, historians, and the general public.

These include Hulk Hogan's Pasta Joint, which struggled due to sub-par food and a niche customer base. The XFL, a short-lived extreme football league, also made the list, failing due to lack of talent and poor management. Other notable failures include the music industry ventures of celebrities like George Michael, who struggled with his Fubar label, and the ill-fated business ventures of Axl Rose, Paris Hilton, and many more.

In contrast, the article highlights the success of Jay-Z, who has transformed himself from a rapper into a multi-billionaire businessman. He has built a vast business empire that extends beyond music into clothing, fragrances, sports, and entertainment. The article also touches on Jay-Z's complex journey from the Marcy Projects in Brooklyn to the upper echelons of the music and business worlds. President Donald Trump, under pressure in Washington, defended his administration's record at a raucous rally in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, on Wednesday, emphasizing his achievements and criticizing ongoing investigations. Trump, who arrived in Iowa for the first time since taking office, faced a backdrop of legislative challenges and a declining approval rating. He highlighted job growth and an improving stock market, praising his economic policies and wealthy appointees like Gary Cohn and Wilbur Ross. Trump also vowed to eventually secure funding for a border wall with solar panels, despite congressional resistance. The rally, similar to those he held during his presidential campaign, included protesters escorted out by police and supporters waving "Drain the Swamp" signs, reflecting his ongoing conflict with the media and his critics. Trump criticized the Russia investigation as a "witch hunt" and dismissed Democrats as "unbelievably nasty." He also praised Republican victories in special congressional elections, particularly Georgia's Karen Handel, and mocked her opponent, Jon Ossoff. Trump's visit to Iowa, a battleground state he won in the 2016 election, underscored his comfort in a campaign setting and his efforts to maintain support from his base. The event highlighted Trump's resilience despite the cloud of investigations and declining approval ratings, as he focused on his legislative successes and economic policies.

Newcomers "Project Almanac" and "Black or White" had quiet openings during the football-focused weekend. Clint Eastwood's "American Sniper" earned a strong $30.7 million over Super Bowl weekend, just missing the record for the biggest Super Bowl weekend gross. The film, now in its third weekend, has grossed $247.98 million, becoming the biggest war-themed film of all time. "Project Almanac," a found-footage thriller, opened with $8.5 million, while "Black or White," a racially charged drama starring Kevin Costner and Octavia Spencer, debuted with $6.5 million. "The Boy Next Door" held strong in fifth place with $6.1 million. "The Loft," a thriller, struggled with a soft $2.9 million opening. "American Sniper" continues to dominate, while new releases faced tough competition from long-running hits.

Federal prosecutors have recommended that charges be filed against David Petraeus for mishandling classified information, according to federal officials. Attorney General Eric Holder now holds the decision to bring charges, as no charges have been filed yet. The scandal began when Jill Kelley, a Tampa, Florida socialite and friend of the Petraeuses, complained to the FBI about receiving threatening emails from Paula Broadwell, who was writing a biography of Petraeus at the time. The FBI traced the emails to Broadwell and discovered evidence of an affair between her and Petraeus. The affair reportedly began in 2011, shortly after Petraeus took the CIA director position, while Broadwell was interviewing him for her book. Petraeus resigned from the CIA three days after President Obama's re-election, admitting to the affair and stating that he showed "extremely poor judgment." The recommendation for charges comes despite President Obama's statement that the affair did not harm national security, emphasizing that it still constituted a significant security breach. The case has raised questions about the handling of the investigation and the potential for a quick resolution, as lower-ranking officials have been prosecuted for lesser offenses.

Ford has unveiled its new F-Series Super Duty Limited, a high-end pickup truck designed for luxury and capability, setting a new benchmark in the heavy-duty truck segment. Starting at $80,835 for the F-250, the Super Duty Limited series can reach up to $94,455 for the loaded F-450, a price point that rivals luxury sedans like the Mercedes-Benz S-Class. This truck is not just about towing capacity; it comes with a host of luxury features, including two-tone Camelback leather seats, heated and ventilated front seats, and a hand-finished dark ash wood trim. The interior is further enhanced with a panoramic moonroof, a leather-wrapped steering wheel, and a laser-etched serial number on the center console armrest, making each truck feel unique.

Technologically advanced, the Super Duty Limited is equipped with features such as a 360-degree camera, adaptive cruise control, lane-keeping alerts, and forward collision warnings, all standard across the lineup. These features are designed to make driving easier and safer, catering to both work and leisure. The truck is powered by Ford's 6.7-liter Power Stroke diesel V8, capable of towing up to 30,000 pounds, roughly the weight of an F-35 fighter jet. This capability, combined with its luxury features, positions the Super Duty Limited as a premium choice for high-end heavy-duty truck customers, from boat captains to captains of industry.

Ford's decision to introduce this luxury segment is part of a broader strategy to cater to a growing trend of premium truck buyers. Over 50% of Super Duty sales this year are already from high-end models like the Lariat, King Ranch, and Platinum series. Todd Eckert, Ford Truck Group marketing manager, emphasizes that the Super Duty Limited is created to meet the demands of customers seeking both luxury and capability. The Super Duty Limited is expected to arrive at dealerships this winter, offering three configurations: F-250, F-350, and F-450, all in single or dual-rear-wheel setups. This move by Ford underscores its commitment to providing a wide range of options to meet the diverse needs of its customer base, from work-ready F-250 XL starting at $32,890 to the luxury-focused Super Duty Limited.

Hungarian-born Sebastian Gorka, a former adviser to President Donald Trump and a controversial figure in the White House, faced a legal challenge in his home country during his tenure. An arrest warrant issued in September 2016, first reported by Hungarian online outlet 444 and BuzzFeed News, indicates that Gorka was wanted in Hungary for "firearm or ammunition abuse." The exact nature of the alleged crime remains unclear, with 444 suggesting it might have occurred as early as 2009. Despite this, Gorka served as a deputy assistant to the president, a role whose specifics were not entirely clear. He was reportedly forced out of the White House in August 2017, reportedly by the chief of staff, John Kelly. Gorka, a former Breitbart writer and Trump campaign surrogate, had a history of interest in firearms, admitting to carrying multiple weapons daily. In February 2016, he was caught attempting to bring a gun through Washington's Reagan National Airport. His connections to the "alt-right" in the US and fringe right-wing groups in Hungary raised questions about his credentials and background, particularly his work in counter-terrorism. Gorka's response to the warrant was dismissive, tweeting that it was "more #FAKENEWS" and that he moved to the U.S. in 2008, though he did not clarify if he could have been in Hungary in 2009. His presence in the White House during the entire period of the warrant's existence, including a meeting with Hungarian Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó, highlights the potential legal and ethical issues surrounding his employment.

Target was unprepared for its massive data breach in November, despite having installed a $1.6 million malware detection tool from FireEye months prior, according to a Bloomberg Businessweek report. The retailer had a group of security specialists in Bangalore monitoring the system 24/7. On November 30, FireEye's Bangalore team received an alert and notified Target's security team in Minneapolis. However, for some reason, Target did nothing to address the alert, which would eventually lead to the theft of up to 40 million customers' credit card data, with 70 million people's personal information, including email addresses and phone numbers, also compromised. The article, based on a two-month investigation, contradicts Target's previous statements that it only learned of the attack in mid-December. It claims that computer logs show FireEye alerts from November 30 and December 2, indicating a second attack. Target's security team disabled the automatic malware deletion feature, according to the report. The company's President and CEO, Gregg Steinhafel, issued a statement saying the company is conducting a company-wide probe to determine what happened. Additionally, the article speculates that the perpetrator of the hack may be Andrey Khodyrevskiy, a 22-year-old Ukrainian hacker known as Rescator, who operates in Odessa, a city described as a haven for "carders," or dealers in stolen credit card information. However, Businessweek cautions that there is no definitive proof that Rescator and Khodyrevskiy are the same person.

Samantha Anderson, a 40-year-old businesswoman and mother of three, experienced a sudden and terrifying loss of her ability to swallow, a condition known as dysphagia. Initially misdiagnosed as stress, Sam’s condition worsened, leading to malnutrition and a dramatic weight loss from 60 to 45 kilograms. Doctors eventually traced the cause to a case of shingles that had damaged four of her cranial nerves, affecting her swallowing mechanism. Her life became a daily struggle, with each meal turning into an exhausting ordeal of non-stop chewing, swallowing, and managing her airway. She had to eat in a specific position and could not eat alone due to the danger of choking. Sam’s condition was so severe that she had to rely on a feeding tube for 18 months to ensure she received adequate nutrition.

The journey to recovery was long and challenging. Sam turned to a specialist in the United States, Professor Peter Belafsky, who diagnosed her condition as “like being constantly waterboarded.” Under his guidance, Sam learned to eat some foods that could be chewed with water until they became liquid, such as mashed potato and cake without grains. However, she still cannot eat mincemeat or anything fibrous. Her husband now accompanies her for every meal, helping her navigate the complex process of eating. The emotional toll of the condition was significant, with Sam feeling judged and betrayed by those who should have understood her better. Despite the challenges, she has made progress, learning to manage her condition and even signing up for stem cell trials with Professor Belafsky, which she hopes will further improve her ability to swallow.

Anderson’s story highlights the devastating impact of dysphagia and the importance of accurate diagnosis and specialized care. Her determination to regain her strength and return to a normal life, even after four years, serves as an inspiration to others facing similar challenges. The joy of simple pleasures, like eating a meal with her family, has become a precious part of her recovery journey.

The Pentagon announced on Friday that it will delay the implementation of a policy allowing transgender troops to join the military until January 1, 2018, due to concerns about the impact on military readiness. Defense Secretary Jim Mattis approved the recommendation from the armed services to defer the accession of new transgender applicants until the specified date, as the services will review their plans and provide input on the potential effects on force readiness. This decision comes just hours before the July 1, 2017, deadline set by the Obama administration for the military to recruit transgender enlisted troops and accept new officers. While the policy change will not affect the estimated 15,500 transgender troops already serving, it has faced criticism from gay-rights advocates who argue that it undermines the military's goal of recruiting the best talent. The American Military Partner Association and OutServe-Service Members Legal Defense Network have expressed disappointment, stating that delays beyond January 2018 could negatively impact military readiness. The move has also drawn support from some lawmakers, such as Rep. Vicky Hartzler, R-Mo., who believes the policy was "ill-conceived and contrary to our goals of increasing troop readiness." Despite the delay, the Pentagon maintains that the decision was made to ensure the military remains "the finest fighting force the world has ever known."

In 1996, Alexa Internet began donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive, adding to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. This data, including references to a controversial ancient papyrus fragment, has recently been the subject of new scientific tests. The papyrus, known as the "Gospel of Jesus’s Wife," contains text suggesting that some early Christians believed Jesus was married, specifically to Mary Magdalene. Harvard professor Karen L. King introduced this fragment to the world in 2012, but many scholars and the Vatican dismissed it as a modern forgery. The latest findings, published in the Harvard Theological Review, support King's argument that the document is authentic.

Carbon dating tests indicate the papyrus dates to the eighth century, about 400 years later than initially thought, but still within ancient times. Chemical analysis of the ink reveals it is consistent with carbon-based inks used by ancient Egyptians, and microscopic imaging shows no signs of modern ink application. These results suggest the text is genuine, though a highly skilled modern forger could theoretically create a similar document.

King maintains the fragment is part of a broader debate among early Christians about the role of women, family, and celibacy in spiritual life. The text includes phrases like "My mother gave me life" and "She will be able to be my disciple," suggesting Jesus affirmed the discipleship of wives and mothers. Critics argue the text is a poorly executed pastiche of the Gospel of Thomas, containing grammatical errors and stylistic inconsistencies. Leo Depuydt, an Egyptologist at Brown University, believes the document is a modern forgery, pointing to the text's grammatical blunders and suggesting it reflects contemporary theological concerns.

King hopes the debate can move beyond forgery questions to focus on the document's historical significance. The controversy over the fragment's authenticity is likely to continue, with ongoing scientific tests and scholarly debate. The latest findings, while supportive of the document's authenticity, do not definitively prove it. The text remains a valuable addition to the study of early Christianity, offering insights into the complex debates surrounding Jesus's marital status and the role of women in the faith.

Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg is set to sell 41.35 million 'B' shares, worth approximately $2.3 billion, to cover taxes on the exercise of an option that enabled him to obtain 60 million additional 'B' Facebook shares. These shares, each with 10 voting rights, will allow Zuckerberg to maintain significant control over the company. The sale will also benefit Zuckerberg’s philanthropic efforts, as proceeds will be used to pay taxes. Zuckerberg’s wife, pediatrician Priscilla Chan, will also donate 18 million shares to the Silicon Valley Community Foundation, part of their pledge to give away more than half of their wealth to philanthropic causes. The donation is the largest in the foundation’s history. Zuckerberg’s reduced stake in Facebook will still give him about 62.8% of the voting power, down from 65.2%. Facebook is raising $1.5 billion through the sale of 27 million new shares, taking advantage of the high stock price. The company’s stock has surged, with advertising revenue from mobile devices driving growth. Zuckerberg’s tax obligations highlight the growing dependence of government revenues on the stock sales of the ultra-wealthy, a trend that could reverse if the stock market experiences a downturn.

Sen. Ted Cruz (R) holds a slight lead over his Democratic challenger, Rep. Beto O’Rourke, in their Texas Senate race, according to a new poll from Emerson College. The survey, released on Monday, shows Cruz leading O’Rourke by just 1 point, with Cruz at 38% and O’Rourke at 37%. Four percent of voters favor a different candidate, while 21% remain undecided. This latest poll comes as O’Rourke continues to gain momentum, with recent NBC News–Marist survey data showing Cruz leading by 4 points. The Cook Political Report has also shifted the race from its “likely Republican” column to “lean Republican.” O’Rourke is viewed favorably by 37% of registered voters, while Cruz has the advantage among voters aged 55 and older. The Emerson College survey, conducted from August 22 to 25 among 550 voters, has a margin of error of 4.4 percentage points. The tight race highlights the ongoing challenge for Republicans to maintain control of the Senate, as Texas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate in three decades. Despite the current lead, Cruz’s narrow margin and the shifting landscape of the race suggest that the outcome remains uncertain.

The long-running saga of the highest-priced home in the U.S. is nearing its conclusion. Candy Spelling, widow of late TV producer Aaron Spelling, has agreed to sell her 57,000-square-foot Los Angeles mansion, known as "The Manor," to 22-year-old heiress Petra Ecclestone, daughter of billionaire Formula One racing boss Bernard Ecclestone. The sprawling property, built in 1991 and spanning five acres, boasts a bowling alley, beauty salon, several gift-wrapping rooms, and parking for 100 cars. The home, which had a $150 million asking price, was listed in 2008 and officially in March 2009. Spelling, who has been downsizing, sold a 15,555-square-foot condominium in Century City for $35 million in December 2010. The sale to Ecclestone, who will split her time between London and Los Angeles after her August wedding to entrepreneur James Stunt, underscores the importance of foreign buyers in the U.S. real-estate market. Meanwhile, the broader U.S. real-estate market continues to struggle, with prices sinking to 2002 levels in the first quarter, according to the S&P/Case-Shiller National Index. The property is listed with Rick Hilton and David Kramer of Hilton & Hyland, a Christie's International Real Estate affiliate, and Sally Forster Jones of Coldwell Banker.

In his commencement address to Howard University graduates on Saturday, President Barack Obama highlighted the progress made by black Americans since his graduation from Columbia University in 1983, while also emphasizing the need for ongoing systemic change. Obama specifically praised a new generation of black activists, including those involved in Black Lives Matter and "black Twitter," for raising national awareness about inequality in the criminal justice system. He urged activists to engage in electoral politics and compromise, advocating for "changes in law, changes in custom" to bring about lasting change. Obama stressed the importance of being confident in one's heritage and embracing a broad understanding of racial authenticity, quoting Zora Neale Hurston and singer Prince. He also encouraged graduates to expand their moral imaginations to empathize with all people who are struggling, including refugees, immigrants, the rural poor, and even middle-aged white men who feel powerless due to economic and cultural changes. Obama advised graduates to be passionate but also to participate in the political process, emphasizing the need for "not just awareness, but action. Not just hashtags, but votes." His speech also included a candid discussion of his inability to pass certain initiatives due to lack of cooperation from Congress and a reminder of the barriers his predecessors faced, which pale in comparison to those faced by his grandparents and great-grandparents. Obama concluded by urging graduates to recognize that compromise is necessary even when they believe they are 100% right, and to allow others to speak, even if they disagree. The speech was widely praised, with many attendees and observers noting its unapologetic embrace of blackness and its call for civic engagement.

New Jersey faces a critical shortage of road salt as winter storms continue to hit the state, leaving local municipalities scrambling to find alternative solutions. The Obama Administration has refused to grant a waiver for the 1920 Jones Act, a federal maritime law requiring all cargo and passengers moving between U.S. ports to be transported on American vessels. This refusal has prevented New Jersey from accessing 40,000 tons of salt stored in Searsport, Maine, which could have been transported within days. New Jersey Department of Transportation spokesman Joe Dee confirmed that a waiver from the Jones Act appears unlikely, stating, "We were pursuing a waiver, but we’ve been advised we wouldn’t get one." The state now plans to make multiple trips to transport the salt, which could take a longer time. New Jersey Governor Chris Christie emphasized the urgency of the situation, writing in an executive order that rock salt is essential for maintaining safe travel on roads during winter storms. The state's salt supplies are critically low, with some municipalities, such as Randolph, Fort Lee, and Englewood, having to leave roads untreated. Salting in South Bergen was also curtailed due to the shortage. Monmouth County, Middletown, and Morris County were running low on salt and advised their towns to conserve it. The situation has raised concerns about the potential risks to public safety. While the Obama Administration faced criticism for not granting a Jones Act waiver during the Gulf Oil spill, they did provide one to New York in 2012 to replenish fuel supplies after Hurricane Sandy. The refusal to grant a waiver in New Jersey has highlighted the challenges of navigating a century-old law in the face of urgent needs.

Investigators have identified Tannerite, a legal product primarily used for target practice, as the explosive residue found in the bomb that exploded in Chelsea, New York, on Saturday. The incident injured 29 people. Tannerite is a binary explosive, meaning it consists of two inert components that are not explosive on their own. When mixed, it creates a high explosive that reacts when struck by a high-velocity bullet. The manufacturer, Tannerite, is skeptical that their product was used in the bombing, stating that it can only be detonated by a bullet's impact and not by other means like a fuse or electrical charge. The company claims this makes it a very stable product. However, federal authorities have confirmed that Tannerite residue was found in the New York bomb. The ATF, which does not regulate the sale of the two chemicals that make up Tannerite, issued an advisory warning that these products are high explosives and should be handled with caution. In response to the incident, the company’s Facebook page expressed abhorrence at the unintended use of their product for violence and hate. Indiana is considering legislation to regulate the sale of Tannerite, proposing restrictions on sales to minors and requiring retailers to store the product securely. The incident has raised concerns about the accessibility and potential misuse of such explosives, highlighting the need for better regulation and public awareness.

PGA legend John Daly recently shared his thoughts on the golfing skills of former President Barack Obama, comparing him to another presidential golfer. While Daly acknowledged that Obama is "pretty good" at the sport, he asserted that George H.W. Bush is the "all-time GOAT" (greatest of all time) when it comes to presidential links mastery. Daly's comments come as a reminder of the unique blend of politics and sports, particularly in the realm of golf, which has long been a pastime for many U.S. presidents.

In the freezing cold of 1988, a newborn boy named David Paul was found dead in Meriden, Connecticut, wrapped in a blanket near a tree, marking a tragic event that has been remembered annually by the local police department and community. David Paul, a full-term baby with blonde hair and blue eyes, was officially adopted by the Meriden Police Department, which took up a collection for his burial. The police department has commemorated the child each year, symbolizing their commitment to protecting all children, especially in light of the Sandy Hook tragedy a year ago. This year, a memorial service was held at Walnut Grove Cemetery, attended by about 20 members of the Meriden police department and the Rev. Alden Barnes from the First United Methodist Church. Barnes read a prayer for children, emphasizing the vulnerability of children in society. The service also highlighted the Safe Haven law passed in Connecticut in 2000, which allows mothers to voluntarily drop off infants under 30 days old at hospitals without identifying themselves, ensuring the safety of newborns.

BMX icon Dave Mirra, who died in February from a self-inflicted gunshot wound, was found to have chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) in his brain, making him the first action sports athlete to be diagnosed with the condition, reports ESPN. The diagnosis was confirmed by multiple neuropathologists, including Dr. Lili-Naz Hazrati of the University of Toronto, who examined Mirra's brain posthumously. Mirra, who was 41 at the time of his death, had a history of head injuries that likely contributed to his CTE. He suffered a fractured skull in a car accident at age 19 and also competed in boxing, though his primary sport was BMX. Mirra was a pioneer in freestyle BMX, holding the record for the most X Games medals with 24. His widow, Lauren, received the diagnosis in March and spoke to ESPN about the changes she noticed in her husband's behavior, including mood swings and difficulty in conversations. "I started to notice changes in his mood. And then it quickly started to get worse," she said. "He wasn't able to be present in any situation or conversation, so it was hard to be in a relationship with him to any degree. He was lost. I looked straight through him on a few occasions. And I was like, 'Where are you? Where are you? What is wrong?'"

Mirra's diagnosis highlights the potential risks of repeated head trauma in action sports, similar to those faced by football and hockey players. "It validates what we have been thinking about brain injuries in boxers and football players," Hazrati said. "The key is brain injury. Regardless of how you get it, through BMX or hockey, you are at risk for this." Mirra's family plans to use his legacy to create a platform for CTE awareness and research. Mirra will be honored at the National BMX Hall of Fame induction in Chula Vista, California, on June 11, and during the X Games in Austin, Texas, with a new event named after him, the Dave Mirra BMX Park Best Trick competition. The winner will be awarded the Mirra Golden Pedal and prize money.

In an upcoming Dateline NBC special, Marcia Clark, the former prosecutor who led the O.J. Simpson murder case, reveals her personal reflections on the controversial outcome of the trial. Clark, played by Sarah Paulson in the FX series "The People v. O.J. Simpson: American Crime Story," admits to blaming herself for Simpson’s acquittal. "It was physically painful," Clark tells Dateline host Josh Mankiewicz, "and I thought of Ron and Nicole, and I thought, 'This is wrong.'" Clark also discusses her reluctance to allow Simpson to try on the gloves during the trial, a pivotal moment that significantly impacted the prosecution's case. "That was not my call," Clark asserts, "I did not want him to try on the evidence gloves. I never did." The iconic moment, when the glove appeared to not fit, dealt a massive blow to the prosecution. Clark's reflections come as the double homicide remains a topic of conversation, with the recently launched FX series reigniting interest in the case. The Dateline special will also feature interviews with Kris Jenner, Denise Brown, Fred Goldman, Alan Dershowitz, and Kato Kaelin, among others. The special is set to air on Sunday, bringing viewers a comprehensive look at the case that captivated the world over two decades ago.

A video of a fox in the Chernobyl exclusion zone, Ukraine, has gone viral, showcasing the animal's resourcefulness and lack of fear of humans. The fox, filmed by RFE/RL Ukrainian Service journalists, is seen carefully stacking meat and bread to create a five-decker sandwich, which it carries away. This behavior, captured in the abandoned area since the 1986 nuclear disaster, highlights the resurgence of wildlife in the zone. The Chernobyl exclusion zone, once evacuated by humans, now hosts an increasing population of foxes, wolves, and bears. The video, with over 1 million views, demonstrates the resilience of nature in the face of human absence. Despite the area's lingering radioactive contamination, the fox's bold actions indicate a gradual recovery of the ecosystem. The incident has sparked interest in the ongoing ecological changes in the region, where nature continues to find a way to thrive.

The Library of Virginia, serving as the Commonwealth's archival agency, the reference library at the seat of government, and one of the nation's premier research institutions for Virginia history, politics, and culture, attracts researchers from across the country and worldwide to its Richmond location and to its digital resources available on the web. Meanwhile, millions are being spent on SMS messaging campaigns, with mobile marketing becoming an increasingly integral advertising tool for small businesses to find new and exciting ways to reach current and potential customers. Through these campaigns, businesses can leverage the power of text messages to engage with their audience, provide timely updates, and promote their products or services. By integrating location-based services, businesses can further enhance their marketing strategies, ensuring that their messages reach the right people at the right time. The Library of Virginia, while focusing on preserving and providing access to Virginia's rich historical and cultural heritage, is also part of a broader trend where institutions and businesses are adapting to the digital age, utilizing technology to connect with their audiences in innovative ways.

On October 19, Modoc County Sheriff's Deputy Jack Hopkins was fatally shot while responding to a disturbance call, marking a tragic incident in the region. According to Modoc County officials, Deputy Hopkins was killed instantly as he entered a property about eight miles south of Alturas when confronted and shot by Jack Lee Breiner, a 47-year-old man. The deputy was responding to a disturbance call when he encountered Breiner, who then engaged in a gun battle with another deputy. Breiner was shot and wounded during the altercation, but the deputy was killed on the scene. Breiner has been charged with murder and other crimes in connection with the killing. The incident highlights the dangers faced by law enforcement officers in the line of duty, as Deputy Hopkins was responding to a disturbance call when he was fatally shot. The details of the confrontation and the circumstances leading up to the shooting are still under investigation, but the tragic outcome has left the community in mourning. The Modoc County Sheriff's Department has not yet released additional information about the case, and the investigation is ongoing.

Sarah Palin's influence in Republican politics this election cycle, as measured by her 60 endorsements, yielded mixed results. Of the 34 House candidates she backed, only 15 won, a less-than-stellar performance for a political kingmaker. Her most notable successes included Vicky Hartzler and Michael Grimm, who defeated veteran Democrats. However, in the Senate, only five of her 12 choices prevailed, with her home-state pick, Joe Miller, facing a tight race with Lisa Murkowski. Despite the uneven outcomes, GOP strategists emphasize that Palin's endorsements were not solely based on electability but on ideological alignment. This approach bolstered her brand, making her a star among conservatives and increasing her name recognition. Her high-profile, grassroots campaigning drew significant media attention, overshadowing other potential 2012 presidential hopefuls. While her influence may not have translated into electoral success, it significantly boosted conservative candidates across the country and fueled excitement among her supporters for her potential future role.

A new study from researchers at two universities has revealed that 98% of participants would sign away their firstborn child without reading the terms of service, highlighting the widespread disregard for lengthy and complex legal documents. The study involved creating a fictitious social networking site, NameDrop, with a privacy policy and terms of service modeled after those of LinkedIn, totaling approximately 8000 and 4000 words respectively. These documents included clauses that could share user data with the NSA and other security agencies, as well as third parties, potentially impacting employment, financial services, university admissions, and more. Additionally, the terms of service included a "gotcha" clause promising free access to the site in exchange for assigning a first-born child, which 98% of participants missed. The study found that 543 participants signed up for the site, with 399 skipping the fine print entirely. The remaining 144 participants spent an average of 73 seconds on the privacy policy and 51 seconds on the terms of service, far less than the time required to comprehend the documents. This behavior is not limited to young adults; a similar experiment in the UK in 2014 and a 2010 UK-based retailer study found the same results. The researchers also noted that even those who read the documents did not process the information effectively, with information overload being a significant negative predictor of reading the terms of service upon signup, when they changed, and when privacy policies changed. The implications of this study are concerning, as it suggests that users are vulnerable to data sharing and other terms they fail to notice or understand.

Singapore has taken the top spot as the world's most expensive city to live in, according to the latest Worldwide Cost of Living index from the Economist Intelligence Unit. This ranking is primarily due to the strong Singapore dollar, along with high costs for cars, utilities, and clothing. Despite a 40% currency appreciation over the last decade and consistent price inflation, Singapore's cost of living compared to New York City has actually declined over the past year. The survey, which compares more than 400 individual prices across 160 products and services, is designed to help human resources and finance managers calculate cost-of-living allowances and build compensation packages for expatriates and business travelers. All cities are compared to a base city of New York, which has an index set at 100. The Economist Intelligence Unit, renowned for its comprehensive global coverage and rigorous analysis, provides this bi-annual study to empower business leaders to make strategic decisions with trusted business intelligence.

Mitt Romney secured the Republican presidential nomination at a storm-delayed convention in Tampa, Florida, with delegates overwhelmingly voting for him. Ann Romney's speech aimed to present her husband in a soft and likable light. The convention approved a conservative platform focusing on tax cuts and opposing Obama's health care and Wall Street regulations. Romney's victory was seen as a strong position heading into the general election, with the economy remaining the top issue. Romney criticized Obama as a failed president, while Obama campaigned in Iowa, emphasizing his likability and economic record. The convention highlighted Romney's strong position, but his rivals' continued presence underscored the close race. Security was stringent, and the convention faced challenges from Hurricane Isaac.

A Morro Bay Burger King is set to reopen Tuesday morning after pranksters caused $35,000 worth of damages by smashing all the windows. The incident began when employees received a call Saturday night from someone pretending to be from the fire department, instructing them to ventilate the business. In response, employees smashed the windows, and even the manager used a car to ram into the building. The owner of the fast food restaurant has since suspended the individual responsible. The Morro Bay Police Department is seeking anyone with information, pictures, or video of the incident, urging the public to contact them at (805) 772-6225 or Detective Mark Martin at (805) 772-6233. Crews are currently working to repair the damages, with the restaurant expected to reopen at 6:30 AM on Tuesday.

Former President Bill Clinton delivered a powerful endorsement of President Barack Obama at the Democratic National Convention, delivering a speech that was both passionate and policy-driven. Clinton’s address aimed to highlight the differences between the two parties, emphasizing that Obama’s policies lead to broad prosperity, while Republican policies favor the wealthy. Clinton praised Obama’s 2009 stimulus package, his expansion of college aid, and his efforts to boost renewable energy. He also defended the Affordable Care Act, explaining how it would benefit ordinary Americans and warning that Republican healthcare cuts would hurt the poorest and most vulnerable. Clinton addressed the question of whether Americans are better off than they were four years ago, arguing that the answer is yes, but many people are not feeling it yet. He tackled Republican attacks on Medicare spending and welfare, arguing that proposed cuts would harm the poor and disabled, not just the middle class. Clinton also warned that Republican policies would deepen the country’s fiscal woes and prevent more people from voting. His speech was seen as a template for other Democrats, with many analysts praising his ability to communicate complex policy issues in a way that resonated with voters. Clinton’s performance was described as the best speech he has delivered in years, with many political pundits, including former Republican strategist Steve Schmidt, acknowledging his unmatched political prowess. Clinton’s speech was seen as a significant moment in the Democratic Party’s campaign strategy, potentially sealing Obama’s re-election.

For the past four years, Martin Gill and his partner have been raising two foster children in their North Miami home, providing a stable and loving environment for the brothers, now aged four and nine. Despite the termination of parental rights in 2006, the couple hoped to adopt the children. However, since 1977, Florida law has automatically banned adoptions by gay people, even though the state allows gay and lesbian couples to serve as foster parents. With the assistance of the ACLU, Martin Gill challenged this ban, and in November 2011, a juvenile court judge granted the adoption. The case, however, is not yet settled, as Florida's attorney general immediately appealed the lower court's decision. For now, the brothers remain in the care of Martin and his partner. This ongoing legal battle highlights the complex and often contradictory policies surrounding gay adoption in Florida, and the challenges faced by families like Martin's in seeking to provide a permanent home for the children in their care.

President Barack Obama stated that the United States does not plan to send U.S. troops into Yemen or Somalia, where Islamic militants pose a significant threat, according to remarks published in People magazine. Obama emphasized the intention to work with international partners to ensure the safety of American citizens. The U.S. has increased its security assistance funding to Yemen from $70 million to at least $150 million this year, aiming to support the Yemeni government in combating al Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula. General David Petraeus, head of U.S. Central Command, met with Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh and discussed strengthening security, military, and economic cooperation. Al Qaeda in Yemen has become more active, with the group claiming responsibility for the failed Christmas Day airliner bombing and threatening embassies. Despite concerns, Petraeus noted that Yemen does not want American ground troops, and the U.S. plans to honor this request. The U.S. military does not intend to send ground troops to Yemen, emphasizing the importance of host nations in addressing security issues. The general also highlighted the need for increased resources and a significant commitment to counterinsurgency operations, noting that progress has been made but al Qaeda still poses a threat.

Mitch Carter, a former student at Bakersfield High School, is set to receive $10.5 million in a settlement from the Kern High School District after suffering a violent beating during a 2010 pep rally. The incident occurred when Carter, wearing a chicken costume, was mobbed by students during a skit meant to mock the opposing team’s mascot. Carter’s attorney, Nicholas Rowley, emphasized the severity of the injuries, including brain damage, that Carter sustained. A jury had already found the district liable, and the settlement was seen as a compromise to avoid a potentially higher jury award. The Kern High School District acknowledged responsibility and agreed to reevaluate its safety policies. The settlement includes a significant portion from the district’s insurance company, Everest National Insurance Company. Carter’s lawyer, Ralph Wegis, expressed dissatisfaction with the settlement, calling the district’s actions “despicable” and demanding firings of those involved in the incident. The case highlighted issues of school safety, administration accountability, and the culture surrounding football at Bakersfield High School. The district’s defense attorney, Michael Kellar, defended the actions of the school staff, stating that the incident was a “total surprise” and not intentional. The settlement marks a significant step in addressing the concerns raised during the trial, with both sides agreeing on the need for improved safety measures.

Abortion rights advocates in Texas made a final push against proposed state rules that would require cremation or burial of fetal remains from abortions and miscarriages. The rules, introduced by the Department of State Health Services in July, faced significant opposition, with over 5,500 signatures collected by pro-choice groups like NARAL Pro-Choice Texas. Critics argued that the rules would create unnecessary costs and obstacles for women seeking abortions, potentially infringing on their rights. The rules, if adopted, would require all medical facilities, hospitals, and clinics to cremate or bury fetal remains, regardless of the gestational period. Health officials claimed that the new rules would not increase total costs for healthcare facilities, as the expenses would be offset by current disposal methods. However, opponents highlighted the potential financial burden on abortion providers and hospitals, with some estimating costs to be several thousand dollars per case. The rules faced scrutiny from the medical and funeral industries, who questioned the practicality and costs associated with the new disposal methods.

The Department of State Health Services held public comment periods and conducted research to address concerns, extending the comment period until Monday. The rules would not apply to miscarriages or abortions that occur at home, nor would they require birth or death certificates to maintain confidentiality. Despite these clarifications, reproductive rights activists argued that the rules were unnecessary and aimed at restricting access to safe, legal abortions. They predicted legal challenges, as the rules fall under the state health department’s rulemaking authority and do not require legislative approval. However, Republican lawmakers have already filed legislation to incorporate the rules into statutory law when the legislature reconvenes in January.

Texas is not the only state grappling with such regulations. South Dakota made it illegal to use aborted fetal tissue in research, while Idaho and Alabama prohibit buying, selling, donating, or experimenting on such remains. Indiana’s similar law, which also banned abortions sought because of potential fetal disabilities, was suspended by a federal judge, citing violations of Supreme Court precedents. Legal guidelines for organ and tissue use remain murky, raising complex questions about ownership and legal status. These regulations continue to spark debate, highlighting the ongoing tension between pro-choice and pro-life advocates.

The Arlington, Va. parking garage where Washington Post reporter Bob Woodward met FBI official Mark Felt, known as "Deep Throat," during the Watergate scandal is set for demolition as part of a redevelopment project by Monday Properties. The company plans to replace two aging office buildings at 1401 Wilson Blvd. and 1400 Key Blvd. in Rosslyn with a 32-story apartment or condo building and a 29-story office building. The parking garage, built in the early 1960s, will be razed, though the historical marker outside the garage erected by Arlington County will likely be stored during the redevelopment. Monday Properties hopes to preserve some part of the garage’s history, possibly incorporating the historical marker into the new development. The project, which includes 500,000 square feet of office space, 385,000 square feet of residential space, and a full-service grocery store, will undergo Arlington’s site plan process, which usually takes 1-4 years. The company expects approval and construction to begin in 2016 or 2017, pending county approval.

Rep. Louie Gohmert and Attorney General Eric Holder got into a contentious exchange during a House hearing, with Gohmert pressing Holder for Justice Department documents related to an Islamic charity in Texas. Despite the heated exchange, Gohmert insisted there was no personal bad blood between the two. Gohmert accused Holder of not doing his job, stating, "He is the highest law enforcement officer in the country, and he is obviously choosing, making personal choices, rather than objective choices, on who he prosecutes and persecutes and who he doesn’t." Gohmert's comments came a day after the two faced off during a hearing, with Holder reportedly snapping at Gohmert, "You don’t want to go there, buddy." Holder, however, defended himself, emphasizing the challenges he faces, saying, "What Attorney General has ever had to deal with that kind of treatment?" During a speech to the National Action Network, Holder took a more direct swipe at Gohmert, highlighting the "unprecedented, unwarranted, ugly, and divisive adversity" faced by the Obama administration. Holder's comments came after Republican Blake Farenthold also criticized Holder, saying he should be in jail. The back-and-forth between Gohmert and Holder highlights the ongoing tension between lawmakers and the Justice Department, with Gohmert using the opportunity to criticize Holder's handling of various investigations and Holder defending his position and the administration's broader efforts.

In northern India, police are investigating a case involving a young girl believed to have been living with a group of monkeys in a forest. The girl, estimated to be between 10 and 12 years old, was found in January in Bahraich, Uttar Pradesh, by woodcutters who reported her as naked, crawling on all fours, and eating food off the floor. She was unable to speak and displayed "monkey-like" behaviors, according to the chief medical superintendent of the government-run hospital, D.K. Singh. After being taken to the hospital, she has begun walking normally and eating with her hands, though she still cannot speak and understands what is said to her, smiling in response. A police officer rescued the girl from the forest, where she was being guarded by monkeys, and she was taken to a police car while the monkeys chased after them. Singh stated that the girl's condition is improving, but it remains unclear how long she had been in the forest. Police are reviewing missing children reports to identify her, and she will be transferred to a children's home in Lucknow for further care. Some locals suspect she was abandoned by her family due to her gender, while others draw parallels to the character Mowgli from Rudyard Kipling's Jungle Book. The case highlights the challenges faced by authorities in identifying and caring for such cases, as well as the broader issue of missing children in India.

Sen. Orrin Hatch secured victory in the GOP primary in Utah, defeating a tea party-backed challenger, Dan Liljenquist. Hatch, 78, and a six-term senator, faced a formidable challenge from Liljenquist, who had survived a 2008 plane crash. However, Hatch's substantial financial and organizational advantages, including a $10 million campaign, ensured his triumph. The race highlighted Hatch's longevity and his ability to adapt, as he garnered support from Republican presidential candidate Mitt Romney, who endorsed Hatch's re-election. Despite facing criticism for his long tenure, Hatch emphasized his role as Senate Finance Committee chairman and his commitment to a seventh term. Liljenquist, a relative newcomer, focused on the national debt, but his campaign was hampered by Hatch's extensive resources and strategic alliances. The primary victory positions Hatch for a strong general election against Democratic candidate Scott Howell. The article also mentions other primary results, such as Rep. Charles Rangel's re-election in New York, despite health and ethics concerns, and Rep. John Sullivan's defeat in Oklahoma to a tea party-backed challenger. These races underscore the ongoing political dynamics and challenges faced by long-serving incumbents and the rise of new, conservative voices within the Republican Party.

Bob Dylan discusses his recent album "Triplicate," released exclusively on his website, offering insights into his songwriting process and the themes of the three-disc set. Dylan explains that the interconnected stories on the album, each about 32 minutes long, were crafted to build a narrative journey. He reflects on the influence of earlier music styles, noting the loss of cross-genre influences and the compartmentalization of music genres over the past five decades. Dylan shares personal anecdotes, such as his encounter with John Wayne and his friendship with Frank Sinatra, and discusses the impact of the deaths of legendary figures like Muhammad Ali and Merle Haggard. He also delves into his interactions with other musicians, including a recording session with George Harrison, and shares his thoughts on the evolution of American music, emphasizing the importance of maintaining a broad musical perspective.

Attorney General Eric Holder announced the results of a federal investigation into the Cleveland Police Department, revealing a pattern of "unreasonable and in some cases unnecessary force" that included shootings, blows to the head, and excessive force against the mentally ill. The investigation, launched in March 2013, examined nearly 600 cases of use of force between 2010 and 2013 and found that Cleveland officers were not given adequate training and supervision. Among the incidents cited were a 2011 chase where an unarmed man was kicked in the head after surrendering and being handcuffed, and a 2012 high-speed chase where over 100 officers fatally shot two unarmed civilians, firing 137 shots in total. The report highlighted the unreasonable practices, including unnecessary and excessive use of deadly force, unnecessary or retaliatory use of less lethal force, and excessive force against persons in mental health crises. The Justice Department and Cleveland agreed on a statement of principles, leading to a consent decree that will include an independent monitor to oversee necessary reforms. Holder invoked the names of Michael Brown, Eric Garner, and 12-year-old Tamir Rice, noting the ongoing federal civil rights investigations for each of these incidents. The agreement aims to address the issues and improve relations between law enforcement and the communities they serve.

Chicago's congressman Danny Davis faced the grim reality of gun violence when his 15-year-old grandson, Javon Wilson, was shot and killed in his Englewood home. The fatal shooting occurred on November 18, 2016, as Javon, along with his siblings, was at home when two teenage assailants entered the residence. The incident began as an argument over a pair of basketball shoes, Davis recounted. One of the attackers, a 15-year-old boy, pulled out a gun and fired, striking Javon in the head. The other assailant, a 17-year-old girl, was also involved. Davis expressed his grief and frustration, stating, "It's almost, just the way it is. People think nothing of it." He also questioned the availability of guns to minors, asking, "The question becomes where does a 15-year-old obtain a gun? Who let the 15-year-old have a gun and under what circumstances?" Davis, a 20-year member of the House of Representatives and former Chicago alderman, emphasized the prevalence of gun violence, noting that he had attended multiple funerals for slain teenagers. 

The shooting has drawn attention from national figures, including former House Speaker Newt Gingrich, who tweeted, "The murder of Congressman Danny Davis' 15-year-old grandson in a Chicago home invasion is a reminder we need a federal strategy to save lives." However, police clarified that the incident was not a home invasion but a targeted attack. The two suspects, identified as juveniles, are in custody and facing first-degree murder charges. Davis's son, Stacey Wilson, was present during the shooting and had just given his son money for a haircut, adding to the emotional impact of the tragedy. 

The incident highlights the ongoing issue of gun violence in Chicago, where the number of shootings and homicides has surged, with August 2016 marking the deadliest month in two decades. The city recorded 673 homicides by the end of the year, including the fatal shootings of the cousin of Chicago Bulls star Dwyane Wade, a police officer's son, and the son of a renowned percussionist. Davis, who was re-elected to his 11th term in the 7th Congressional District, vowed to continue his efforts to combat gun violence, stating, "It's going to take me some time to grieve." His family and friends, including Charles Raymond, a 74-year-old family friend, emphasized the need for community involvement and a more personal relationship with law enforcement to address the root causes of such senseless killings.

The Democratic primary for New York City mayor concluded with Bill de Blasio emerging as the frontrunner, despite initially being a distant fourth in a crowded field. With 97 percent of precincts reporting, de Blasio secured about 40.2 percent of the total vote, narrowly avoiding a runoff against Anthony Thompson, who garnered 26 percent. The race was marked by unexpected twists, including the late surge of de Blasio, who focused on economic inequality and criticized the Bloomberg era. His campaign capitalized on his biracial family and a series of controversial incidents, including his arrest while protesting hospital closures. Exit polls showed that de Blasio's message resonated across all boroughs and demographics, particularly with black voters and women. His proposal to raise taxes on the wealthy to fund universal prekindergarten and overhaul police practices garnered support from voters frustrated with the Bloomberg administration's policies. Christine Quinn, the former City Council Speaker and a close ally of Bloomberg, finished third with 16 percent of the vote. Quinn's defeat was seen as a blow to her political career, as her efforts to become the first woman and openly gay mayor were overshadowed by her role in helping Bloomberg secure a third term. The Republican nominee, Joseph J. Lhota, a former chairman of the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, won the primary with 52 percent of the vote against John Catsimatidis, a billionaire grocery magnate. Lhota, who supported Bloomberg's policies, will face de Blasio in the general election on November 5. The election comes at a critical time for New York City, facing challenges such as income inequality and the need to maintain low crime rates. De Blasio's victory suggests a shift in the city's political landscape, with voters eager for a break from the Bloomberg era.

Since the late 1970s, China has transformed from a centrally planned economy to a more market-oriented one, playing a significant global role. Economic reforms, including the liberalization of prices, fiscal decentralization, and the development of a modern banking system, have driven rapid growth. From 2013 to 2017, China's economy grew at an average of over 7% annually, and in 2017, its economy, measured by PPP, became the world's largest. China is the world's largest exporter and trading nation. However, challenges persist, such as reducing high domestic savings, managing corporate debt, and controlling local government debt. The Chinese government aims to boost domestic consumption and innovation to reduce over-reliance on government investment and heavy industry. In 2017, China's economy showed a slight acceleration, providing more room for reforms, including financial sector deleveraging and supply-side structural reforms.

China plans to increase its defense spending by 11.2% in 2018, reaching approximately 670 billion yuan, making it the second-highest in the world after the U.S. This increase is driven by expanding global commitments and territorial disputes, including those with Vietnam, the Philippines, Japan, and India. China's defense spending has more than doubled since 2006, tracking the growth of its economy. The government emphasizes that its military spending is reasonable and appropriate, citing rapid economic and social development and increased fiscal revenues. However, U.S. analysts estimate China's true defense spending is 50% higher than the official budget. China's military modernization, including the development of precision ballistic missiles and modern fighters, has raised concerns among its neighbors and the U.S. Despite its claims of non-confrontational approach, China's military buildup and territorial claims continue to alarm its neighbors.

Halle Berry and Gabriel Aubry's contentious shared custody arrangement over their 6-year-old daughter, Nahla, has hit another snag. Berry, who is of mixed-race and considers Nahla to be black, is furious that Aubry, who is white, is allegedly straightening Nahla's naturally curly hair and giving it highlights to make her appear less African-American. Berry's lawyer, Steve Kolodny, took the case to court, where a judge ruled that neither parent could alter Nahla's hair and ordered it to grow back naturally. This is just the latest in a series of disputes between the former couple, who have joint custody and have been embroiled in a bitter custody battle since 2010.
