By the time police arrived, several drivers had slowed down to form a protective barrier around the child, who was in the far right lane of the parkway, with cars speeding by at 45 mph. "It seemed like the child wanted to continue driving, he was trying to merge on the middle lane of the highway," Rubio said. The boy had driven about two miles from the park on his blue battery-powered toy ATV, heading towards the parkway. Witnesses say the boy's mother had been frantically calling for him as she searched the area. The boy was taken to Montefiore Mount Vernon Hospital for observation and was found to be OK. He was safely reunited with his family. The incident is under investigation.

For classic car enthusiasts, Ford has introduced a brand-new body shell for the 1967 Mustang Convertible, marking the fourth such restoration part available, joining the 1965 convertible, 1967 and 1969 fastbacks. Manufactured by Dynacorn, the body panels are made from modern automotive-grade steel, slightly thicker than the original, and reinforced in key areas for added strength. At $15,995, this part is ideal for those looking to restore or build a new 1967 Mustang Convertible, with over 90% of the necessary parts available as Ford-licensed reproduction components. This means enthusiasts can recreate the iconic muscle car with the assurance that their build will match or exceed the quality of the original. As the value of classic Mustangs has increased, finding a restorable, rust-free 1967 model has become increasingly difficult, making this new body shell a valuable resource for restorers.

The Audubon Zoo in New Orleans faced a tragic incident on Saturday, July 14, 2018, when a 3-year-old male jaguar named Valerio escaped from his enclosure and killed six animals, including four alpacas, one emu, and one fox. Valerio was eventually captured and returned to his night house after being sedated by a vet team. By Sunday, two more animals, an alpaca and a fox, had succumbed to their injuries, bringing the total deaths to eight. Despite the incident, the zoo reopened on Sunday, though the alpaca paddock was empty, with a sign explaining the exhibit was "under repair" due to the "recent incident." Zoo staff and visitors alike grappled with the event, with some questioning the necessity of zoos and expressing concern for the workers who had to clean up the aftermath. The zoo announced the availability of grief counselors for impacted staff members.

China on Sunday began a suspension of all coal imports from North Korea for the rest of the year, as it increases pressure on its communist neighbor to abandon its nuclear and ballistic missile programs. This ban, in line with UN Security Council sanctions imposed in November in response to North Korea's fifth nuclear test two months earlier, marks a significant escalation in Beijing's efforts to curb Pyongyang's activities. China had already banned coal imports from North Korea in April last year, but those restrictions allowed some imports for civilian use. With China being North Korea's largest source of trade and aid, Sunday's suspension will deprive the North of a crucial source of foreign currency. Despite facing pressure from President Donald Trump to exert more influence over North Korea, Beijing maintains that its influence is limited. However, the Chinese government has grown increasingly frustrated with North Korea's defiance of UN demands to halt missile tests and nuclear weapons development. The latest move comes after North Korea conducted its most recent ballistic missile test a week ago, further straining relations between the two countries. Beijing's decision to fully ban coal imports signals a more assertive stance, but experts question whether it will be enough to change North Korea's behavior.

Retailers Walmart, Sears, and Amazon faced backlash over the holiday weekend after selling home decor posters featuring a photo of the notorious Dachau concentration camp's main gate. The gate bears the infamous Nazi slogan "Arbeit macht frei," which translates to "work makes you free." The poster, which was sold by a third-party seller on Walmart's website, was quickly removed after the company issued an apology, stating they were "horrified" to see the item on their site. Similarly, Sears and Amazon also pulled the poster from their websites, with Sears noting that the item violated their guidelines. The incident shocked many, particularly members of the Facebook group Grandchildren of Holocaust Survivors, who expressed outrage. The poster's description on Walmart's site suggested it would make a "great addition to your home or office," further fueling the controversy. While Sears has removed the specific poster, it still lists more generic signs featuring Dachau's ovens as "similar items," raising additional concerns. The sale of Nazi-related items continues to be a sensitive issue for retailers, as evidenced by past controversies, including eBay's handling of Holocaust memorabilia and the sale of Holocaust denial literature on Amazon.

The article from Fortune presents a mix of optimistic and cautious predictions for the U.S. economy in 2018. Despite the passage of corporate tax reforms, the GDP is forecasted to grow by only 2.5%, constrained by an aging population and an under-skilled workforce. The Federal Reserve is expected to raise the Federal Funds Rate to 2.25% by year-end, with wage and price pressures leading to the first rate hike since the 2008 financial crisis. Oil prices are predicted to stabilize at $55 per barrel, driven by U.S. shale oil production. Home prices are projected to rise by 4.1%, slower than the current 6.9% growth rate. The U.S. IPO market is anticipated to rebound significantly, with projected proceeds of $70.9 billion, fueled by a strong stock market and tech companies. These predictions reflect a nuanced view of economic challenges and opportunities in the coming year.

Washington, D.C., is leading the nation in English-language World Cup ratings, with the Ghana vs. USA match on ESPN earning an impressive 11.8 overnight rating in the D.C. market, the highest ever for a World Cup group-round match. This trend has been consistent throughout the tournament, with D.C. topping the list for average ratings on ESPN networks. The highest ratings in the U.S. for World Cup games are being set in D.C., surpassing even the ratings for some NFL games. In contrast, the Washington Redskins continue to dominate local viewership, with their games averaging a 25.8 rating on three networks. The U.S. vs. Ghana match drew 15.9 million viewers combined on ESPN and Univision, setting new viewership records for both networks. This highlights the growing interest in soccer among American viewers, especially when the U.S. team is involved.

This was the year everyone went gaga for Lady Gaga. The shape-shifting pop star took home Billboard's top artist of the year honors, just a year after she earned top new artist applause. Since 1981, only seven women have claimed this title, including Gaga. Her first two albums, "The Fame" and "The Fame Monster," ranked 4th and 13th, respectively, on the year-end Top Billboard 200 Albums tally. Four singles from these albums appeared on the Hot 100 Songs roundup, led by "Bad Romance" at No. 8. Swift, who nabbed the top spot in 2009, was the year's No. 2 artist of the year, marking the first time an act was one of the top two in successive years since Destiny's Child in 2000 and 2001. Gaga's success overshadowed Swift, who, along with Justin Bieber, dominated the year-end Billboard 200 albums tally with their respective albums.

Sean "Diddy" Combs, the 49-year-old rapper and entrepreneur, publicly mourned the death of his ex-partner Kim Porter, who passed away at the age of 46 on Thursday. Combs, who has been in a relationship with Porter for over a decade, expressed his deep sorrow and shared a heartfelt tribute on social media. "For the last three days I’ve been trying to wake up out of this nightmare. But I haven’t. I don’t know what I’m going to do without you baby. I miss you so much," he wrote. "Today I’m going to pay tribute to you, I’m going to try and find the words to explain our unexplainable relationship. We were more than best friends, we were more than soulmates. WE WERE SOME OTHER S—!! And I miss you so much. Super Black Love 🖤," he continued. Law enforcement sources told TMZ that authorities were called to Porter’s home in Toluca Lake, California, with a 911 call reporting "a patient in cardiac arrest." A source also revealed that Porter had been experiencing flu-like symptoms for several weeks. A representative for Diddy confirmed to Page Six on Thursday that Porter had passed away. Diddy and Porter were a couple for more than a decade and remained close after they parted ways in 2007. They had twin daughters and a son together, and Diddy also adopted Porter’s son Quincy from her relationship with music producer Al B. Sure. The summary of Combs' tribute highlights the deep bond between the two, emphasizing their unique relationship beyond typical romantic partners.

During a 1,700-mile road trip across Iran, Nicholas Kristof encountered a complex and divided nation. The journey, which began with a gushing welcome to America, highlighted the contrasting views of Iranians towards their government and the United States. In Mashhad, a former military commando expressed his love for America, blaming his own leaders for economic hardships due to Western sanctions. However, Kristof also met Iranians who strongly supported the Iranian authorities and resented American government actions. The warmth of the Iranian people towards him, despite occasional "Death to America" signs, underscored the country's pro-American sentiment at the grassroots level. Yet, Kristof noted a shift in public behavior, with many Iranians being wary of speaking freely or being filmed, reflecting the post-2009 crackdown on activism. Kristof interviewed various Iranians, from a farmer who believed the government was the source of economic woes to a shopkeeper who supported the leadership. The trip revealed a nation where public opinion is difficult to gauge, with many expressing dissatisfaction with the government while others remained loyal. Kristof's observations suggest that Iran's system may be on the verge of collapse, but a potential war with the West could stabilize the regime.

The U.S. government plans to order emergency inspections of 80 older Boeing 737s, similar to the Southwest Airlines jet that suffered a 5-foot tear in its roof, to search for possibly dangerous cracks. The FAA order will cover 737-300s, 737-400s, and 737-500s built in the 1980s and 1990s, with more than 30,000 flights. About 175 of these aircraft are worldwide, with 80 registered in the U.S., including 78 operated by Southwest Airlines and two by Alaska Airlines. The inspections will use electro-magnetic processes to detect cracks, with more sophisticated tools if needed. The incident highlights the risks of aging aircraft, potentially leading to broader inspection requirements. Southwest has inspected 90% of its 737-300s, finding fatigue cracks in three planes and grounding the affected jets. The tear occurred at a seam where two thin bands of aluminum skin were joined, with evidence of corrosion and enlarged rivet holes. The FAA and Boeing are reconsidering their inspection programs for aging aircraft, with Southwest expecting further action from Boeing and the FAA.

The U.S. Department of Justice filed a lawsuit against North Carolina on Monday, alleging that the state’s new voter ID requirement discriminates against African-Americans, violating the Voting Rights Act. Attorney General Eric Holder announced the lawsuit, emphasizing that such limits on voting rights disproportionately affect minority voters and contradict the nation’s democratic ideals. The lawsuit seeks to bar North Carolina from enforcing the new voter ID law and demands that the entire state be placed under a requirement to preclear any changes to voting laws, procedures, or polling places with either the Justice Department or a federal court. This move follows the Supreme Court’s June decision to strike down the formula used to subject certain states to preclearance under the Voting Rights Act, but it leverages the “bail in” provision to recreate a similar regime. North Carolina’s new voter ID law, signed by Governor Pat McCrory, also eliminates seven days of early voting, ends same-day voter registration during the early voting period, and prohibits counting provisional ballots cast at the wrong polling place. Critics argue that these provisions disproportionately impact African-American and elderly voters, while supporters claim the law aims to prevent voter fraud. The Justice Department maintains that there is no evidence of widespread voter fraud and that the voter ID requirement and other provisions lack logical connections to fraud prevention. This lawsuit marks the second state the Obama administration has sued since the preclearance list was overturned, following a similar action against Texas. Civil rights advocates and the NAACP have been actively challenging the law in federal and state courts, with the NAACP’s study indicating that more than 300,000 registered voters in North Carolina lack a Department of Motor Vehicles-issued ID, with African-Americans making up a disproportionate share of this group. The lawsuit underscores the ongoing debate over voter ID laws and their potential impact on minority voter turnout, highlighting the tension between security measures and access to the ballot.

The US rock band Bloodhound Gang has faced a series of repercussions after one of its members, Jared Hasselhoff, allegedly desecrated a Russian flag during a concert in Odessa, Ukraine. Hasselhoff reportedly stuffed the flag down his pants and wiped his buttocks with it, an incident that sparked outrage in Russia and led to the band's ban from performing at the Kubana rock festival in Anapa, southern Russia. Upon arrival at the Anapa airport, the band members were attacked by a group of self-described Cossacks, who attempted to strangle Hasselhoff with an American flag, later stomping on it. The Russian Interior Ministry has opened a criminal case against the band for flag desecration, which can result in a one-year prison sentence. The incident has also prompted investigations into the band by Ukrainian authorities, who are looking into a similar alleged flag desecration during a concert in Kiev. US Ambassador Michael McFaul condemned the act of violence against the band but defended Hasselhoff's actions as protected under the First Amendment of the US Constitution. Russian lawmakers have proposed permanently banning the band from entering Russia and Ukraine. The controversy highlights the tense geopolitical climate between Russia and the US, with the incident potentially serving as a symbol of broader cultural and political tensions.

The Supreme Court on Friday rejected the Trump administration's request to halt a lawsuit brought by youths seeking to hold the government accountable for failing to do enough to fight climate change. The administration had argued the lawsuit was "misguided" and a "radical invasion of the separation of powers." In an unsigned order, the court said the government had not reached the high bar necessary to stop the lawsuit for now. However, the justices suggested the government might seek relief from the 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals at a later stage of the litigation. Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch would have ruled in favor of the administration. The 21 young plaintiffs, ranging in age from 11 to 22, argue that the government's inaction on climate change violates their constitutional rights to life, liberty, and property. They are seeking a plan from the federal government to reduce atmospheric carbon dioxide levels to 350 parts per million by 2100. The Obama and Trump administrations had repeatedly asked lower courts to dismiss the lawsuit, questioning its merits and arguing that it would usurp the authorities of Congress and federal agencies. The plaintiffs' lawyers argued that the government would not suffer "irreparable" harm if the case proceeded to trial. Julia Olson, the attorney for the youths and executive director of Our Children’s Trust, said they were confident they would get to trial and that the case had overcome everything the government had thrown at them. The Supreme Court's decision leaves the case to proceed in a federal district court in Oregon, where a long trial is expected. The case, Juliana v. United States, is seen as a landmark challenge to the government's role in addressing climate change and could have significant implications for future legal battles over environmental policies.

Rick and Morty fans, fueled by the show's recent season three premiere, are clamoring for a return of the Szechuan dipping sauce that McDonald’s briefly offered in 1998 to promote Disney’s Mulan. The sauce, a cult favorite among the show’s die-hard fans, has sparked a bidding war on eBay, with one seller recently selling a 19-year-old packet for $14,700. This high price tag is a testament to the show's influence and its fans' dedication. The Rick and Morty team, recognizing the potential for a viral marketing campaign, launched a Change.org petition and engaged with McDonald’s on social media, hoping to bring back the sauce. The show’s creators even included a reference to the sauce in the episode, further fueling the excitement. McDonald’s, while not officially announcing plans to bring the sauce back, did hint that they would consider the request if customers spoke up. The sauce, which was only available for a limited time, has since become a symbol of nostalgia and a testament to the show's ability to connect with its audience. Fans continue to search for the sauce, with some even hoarding expired packets, while others are willing to pay a premium to own a piece of the show’s history. The high price of the sauce on eBay, coupled with the show’s recent revival, has reignited the debate over whether McDonald’s will eventually relaunch the sauce, or if it will remain a cherished memory for Rick and Morty fans.

Federal prosecutors are investigating Anthony Weiner, the former New York Democratic congressman, for potential child pornography charges stemming from alleged sexually explicit exchanges with a 15-year-old girl. Law enforcement agencies in New York and North Carolina have opened preliminary investigations into the allegations, with the U.S. Attorney's Office in Manhattan and the FBI involved. The girl claims she engaged in explicit text and video chats with Weiner, who reportedly sent her photos of himself and encouraged her to undress and engage in sexual acts. She said the relationship lasted several months, during which she felt pressured to lie to her parents and teachers about the nature of their interactions. Weiner, who resigned from Congress in 2011 amid a sexting scandal, has acknowledged the allegations, stating he likely was the victim of a hoax. His attorneys are attempting to negotiate a plea deal to avoid serious charges. The case has reignited concerns about Weiner’s past behavior and his wife, Huma Abedin, who serves as Hillary Clinton’s chief of staff. The investigation has prompted calls for Weiner to seek help, with his critics accusing him of manipulation and self-pity. The girl’s father expressed outrage, stating he would be in jail if he ever came into contact with Weiner again. The ongoing legal proceedings and public scrutiny have raised questions about the impact of Weiner’s actions on his family and political career.

Donald Trump's planned endorsement event with 100 black pastors at Trump Tower in New York on Monday quickly turned into a tense meeting as many black faith leaders demanded an apology for his past comments and actions. The event, initially promoted as an endorsement, was canceled and transformed into a private meeting where pastors issued demands for an apology to the black community and Mexicans for his inflammatory rhetoric. Bishop Orrin Pullings, a Richmond, Virginia-based pastor, reported that the pastors asked Trump to apologize and noted that he listened but remained noncommittal. Other pastors advised Trump not to apologize, suggesting he should maintain his tough stance as it has boosted his poll numbers. Trump defended his rhetoric, stating, "The tone has taken me to first position in every single poll," and that the pastors did not ask him to change his tone. The meeting was marred by disagreements, with some pastors criticizing Trump's mocking impression of a New York Times reporter's physical handicap and his handling of the Black Lives Matter protester incident in Alabama. The event highlighted the challenges Trump faces in appealing to the black community, despite his efforts to engage with black religious leaders. The controversy underscores the tension between Trump's aggressive campaign style and the expectations of a candidate seeking to broaden his support base.

The Alberta government has condemned a controversial hunting practice after a U.S. hunter posted a YouTube video showing him killing a bear using a spear. The video, believed to have been shot in May northeast of Edmonton, features Josh Bowmar, a personal trainer and former competitive javelin thrower, hitting the bear with the hand-thrown spear. Alberta's Ministry of Environment and Parks stated that the type of archaic hunting seen in the video is unacceptable and plans to introduce a ban on spear hunting this fall. Fish and wildlife officers have also been directed to investigate the incident to see if charges are warranted under existing laws.

Bowmar's spear, equipped with a 40-centimeter blade, was launched at the bear as it approached food left as bait. The spear lodged in the bear's side, and Bowmar celebrated the kill, stating that the bear "died immediately." However, conservation groups argue that the risk of an injured animal running off and suffering for an extended period is a significant concern. Wayne Lowry, president of the Alberta Fish and Game Association, emphasized the need for the most ethical means of harvesting an animal and expressed doubt that spear hunting would be legal in the future.

The video has garnered over 200,000 views, with many viewers, including some hunters, denouncing the kill as "barbaric" and "unnecessary." British tabloids and online discussion groups have been particularly critical, with headlines such as "Warped Hunter Kills Starving Bear with Seven-Foot Homemade Spear" and "Hunters in Sick New Low as Black Bear is Stabbed with 7 ft Spear then Left to Die." Despite Bowmar's defense of the kill as humane and ethical, the incident has sparked outrage and calls for a ban on spear hunting in Alberta. The government has promised to introduce a spear ban in the fall as part of its ongoing updates to hunting regulations.

The Samsung Galaxy Note 7, once hailed as the best smartphone of its time, is now a cautionary tale of technological hubris and consumer safety. In a series of events that unfolded rapidly, Samsung was forced to halt production and issue a global recall of the device, following reports of the phones catching fire and exploding. The initial recall, involving over 2.5 million units, was deemed insufficient, and Samsung was compelled to halt production entirely. The issue was traced to battery defects, with errors in both design and manufacturing contributing to the problem. Samsung's investigation revealed that insufficient insulation and inadequate battery space were key factors, leading to potential overheating and fire risks.

The Note 7's demise highlights the challenges of balancing innovation with consumer safety. Despite its numerous advanced features, including a powerful processor, large AMOLED screen, and innovative S Pen stylus, the phone's battery flaws overshadowed its merits. The recall not only damaged Samsung's reputation but also cost the company billions of dollars. The incident forced Samsung to reassess its quality control processes and prioritize consumer safety moving forward. The company's response, including a thorough investigation and a commitment to improving battery safety, demonstrated a willingness to learn from the crisis. However, the lasting impact on consumer trust and the company's brand remains a significant concern. The Note 7's legacy serves as a reminder of the critical importance of rigorous testing and quality assurance in the development of high-tech products.

Tracy Fain, a mother of two, suffered a brain aneurysm and stroke on August 7th while taking her son Ethan to Egelston hospital for stitches from a vicious dog attack on Christmas Eve. She collapsed in the hospital lobby and was rushed to Emory for emergency surgery. Tracy is now in a medically induced coma but shows signs of brain activity, and the road to recovery is long. Her mother, Sandra Moore, is heartbroken and struggling to cope with the loss. Just eight months prior, Ethan was severely injured by two dogs, losing an ear in the attack. The family held on to hope for Tracy's recovery, but she took a turn for the worse, leading to her declaration as brain dead. Moore pleaded with Tracy to fight harder, but the family is left with unanswered questions and the devastating reality of their loss. The family has set up an online account at https://www.gofundme.com/496vn2w for donations to help with medical expenses and support during this difficult time. Prayers for Tracy and her family are greatly needed and appreciated. The sudden death of Tracy, just months after Ethan's attack and the death of her nephew, has left the family reeling. Moore's words, "I just wonder why?" encapsulate the heartache and uncertainty they are facing.

Last summer, Democrats argued the Tea Party was a corporate creation, but now progressive groups like the Agenda Project are countering by launching "F*ck Tea," aiming to dismiss the movement and promote progressive causes. The project, founded by Erica Payne, includes merchandise, polling statistics, and a mocking video. It highlights Tea Party activists' views, such as 64% believing America's best years are behind us, 57% supporting George W. Bush, and 40% seeing Sarah Palin as a potential president. The group also targets Tea Party members' skepticism about global warming, support for stricter abortion laws, and opposition to gay rights, all part of their strategy to undermine the movement.

Emerson College is set to launch a Bachelor of Fine Arts degree in Comedic Arts, offering students a unique opportunity to pursue their comedic talents in a structured academic environment. Starting in September 2016, undergraduates can major in this program, which promises a hands-on learning experience. Martie Cook, Emerson’s associate chairwoman of the visual and media arts department, emphasized the practical nature of the curriculum, stating, "This is going to be a hands-on program. If you want to be a sitcom writer, we are going to take you through sitcom writing, and you will walk out of here with several scripts in your hand that you can then show to agents and producers, so you actually have a portfolio."

The program will cover a wide range of topics, from the history of comedy dating back to the Greeks and Romans to the art of perfecting a sketch comedy performance. Students will learn to write jokes for both the stage and the screen, helping them find their voices as comedians. Additionally, the curriculum includes production courses, comedy editing courses, and classes focused on the art and theory of laughter. Cook highlighted the college's track record of producing top industry talents, including Jay Leno, Bill Burr, Harris Wittels, and Denis Leary. She expects the new major to attract famous guest lecturers, many of whom have had experience in the industry and continue to work in it.

Emerson will utilize both its Boston and Los Angeles campuses for the new initiative, aiming to bring its distinctive strengths to the forefront. Doug Herzog, an Emerson alumnus and president of Viacom Music and Entertainment Group, which oversees Comedy Central, praised the program, saying, "Some schools develop NFL quarterbacks. We develop great comedic talent." He emphasized the importance of combining academic focus with hands-on opportunities, noting that the program will offer master classes and events with industry speakers.

The new major is particularly relevant for millennials and Generation Z, who are immersed in a comedy-driven world. Noah Garfinkel, who graduated from Emerson in 2006 and now writes for the Fox sitcom New Girl, highlighted the academic experience's potential benefits, such as teaching students to write comedy scripts before entering the field full-time. However, aspiring stand-up comics like Ryan Doon, who rose to fame using Twitter's six-second video app, Vine, suggested that hands-on experience is crucial, recommending that aspiring comedians work at a Starbucks and do open mikes every night. Despite this, the program is seen as a valuable resource for those who want to pursue a career in comedy, offering a blend of academic rigor and practical training.

The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church) has a complex history with plural marriage, a practice introduced to early members through revelations to Joseph Smith in the 1840s. Plural marriage was seen as a commandment from God, intended to increase the number of children born into the faith and to strengthen the community. For many, it was a trial of faith, as it violated cultural and legal norms, leading to persecution. However, it also brought about significant social changes, such as greater access to marriage for women and increased ethnic diversity within the Church. By 1890, under pressure from the U.S. government, LDS President Wilford Woodruff issued the Manifesto, officially ending the practice of plural marriage in the United States. Despite this, a few continued to practice it in Canada and Mexico. Since then, Church leaders have consistently emphasized that plural marriage is no longer authorized, though some historical records and practices related to sealing families together for eternity continue to be observed. The article explores the origins, challenges, and impacts of plural marriage on the early Church, emphasizing the spiritual experiences and testimonies of those who accepted this practice. It also highlights how the introduction of plural marriage, though difficult, contributed to the growth and cohesion of the faith community.

Miss America 2015 Kira Kazantsev's win last year has come under scrutiny, as she was expelled from her Alpha Phi sorority at Hofstra University for alleged hazing. According to a tipster, Kazantsev and her friend were exceptionally harsh towards pledges, berating them for perceived physical flaws and making them perform exhausting tasks. The university's code of conduct clearly defines hazing as any action that endangers mental or physical health, including forced consumption of liquor, physical abuse, and verbal harassment. Despite these rules, social silence among sorority members allowed such practices to continue. After an investigation, Kazantsev and her friend were expelled from Alpha Phi in late 2013. However, neither the national Alpha Phi organization nor the Hofstra chapter publicly acknowledged her achievement, nor did the local chapter or the affiliated foundation recognize her significant accomplishment. The Miss America organization defended Kazantsev, stating she had been transparent about her expulsion and highlighting her academic achievements and commitment to serving her community. Kazantsev herself denied the allegations, explaining that she was kicked out due to a misinterpreted email chain and that she had never been involved in any name-calling or physical hazing. The controversy highlights the ongoing issue of hazing in college sororities, despite university policies, and raises questions about the transparency and support provided by organizations like Miss America.

Kim Kardashian's latest social media post of riding captive dolphins has drawn criticism from PETA, which calls her actions "intrusive," "dangerous," and "harmful" to the animals. The animal rights organization, Senior Vice President Lisa Lange, told RadarOnline.com that dolphins in captivity are "a lifetime sentence" and that public interaction with them can be stressful and even dangerous. PETA argues that touch tanks and "swim-with" programs, like the one Kardashian participated in, invade the dolphins' already diminished worlds and can cause them to become anxious, aggressive, and ill due to constant interaction with humans. The organization points out that dolphins, including orcas, have distinct personalities, a strong sense of self, and the ability to consider the future, making their captivity in tanks a form of suffering. PETA also highlights the physical and psychological harm captive dolphins often face, such as damaged teeth from chewing cage bars and collapsed dorsal fins. The group emphasizes that wild dolphins and orcas live in large, complex social groups and swim vast distances, which is impossible in captivity. They advocate for the end of dolphin captivity, citing the tragic consequences for the animals, including injuries, illness, and shortened lifespans. PETA encourages people to avoid visiting marine parks, zoos, or aquariums that keep ocean animals in captivity and to support legislation that prohibits the capture or restricts the display of marine mammals.

Nike has finally brought to life the self-lacing shoes that sneaker fans have dreamed of for decades, with the release of the HyperAdapt 1.0. This innovative shoe, inspired by the Back to the Future II's Air Mag, uses a battery-powered system of pulleys and sensors to automatically adjust the fit as you step into it. When you insert your foot, sensors detect your weight and the position of your foot, then a series of tiny pulleys tighten the throat of the shoe around your foot. The wearer can manually adjust the tightness with buttons on either side of the shoe. Nike's goal is to eventually make the micro-adjustments more automated, reacting to biometric data to create a hyper-personalized platform. The shoes will be available during the holiday season in three colors, but you'll only be able to buy a pair if you're a member of Nike+'s fitness portal. While the adaptive laces can be manually controlled, Nike envisions a future where the shoes can sense when you need a tighter or looser fit and adjust on the fly. The shoes will operate on a battery that lasts for two weeks on a single charge, and they will be priced to be accessible to regular customers. The HyperAdapt 1.0 represents a significant step towards the integration of technology and fashion, but it also raises questions about the potential trade-offs of relying on technology for everyday wear.

Veteran race car driver David Steele, 42, died in a wreck during a sprint car race at Desoto Speedway in east Bradenton, Florida. Known for his multiple USAC national championships and victories in various series, Steele was competing in the Southern Sprint Car Shootout Series race on Saturday night. His death quickly drew tributes from fellow racers, including Alex Bowman and Tony Stewart Racing. The incident occurred when Steele’s car and another vehicle hooked wheels, sending Steele’s car airborne and into the retaining wall. Despite immediate medical attention, Steele was pronounced dead on the track. Desoto Speedway owners and staff expressed their condolences, and the race was red-flagged. Steele was survived by his wife and three young children. His racing career included 100 Florida victories, making his loss a shock to the racing community.

The National Security Agency (NSA) is reportedly collecting millions of photos daily as part of a major facial recognition effort, according to a New York Times report based on leaked documents. The NSA harvests about 55,000 images per day considered to be of "facial recognition quality," raising concerns about privacy and the potential for racial bias. Current US privacy and surveillance laws do not specifically protect against the use of facial recognition technology to identify individuals. The NSA's facial recognition program is separate from its bulk metadata collection program, which requires court approval to collect information from American citizens. The agency's use of facial recognition technology has grown significantly under the Obama administration, coinciding with the rise of online self-portrait culture. The NSA relies on both in-house and commercially available facial recognition software, including PittPatt, a company owned by Google. The agency considers facial images, fingerprints, and other identifiers as important as written and oral communications. While the NSA does not have access to US state databases of driver's licenses or passport photos, it can likely obtain this information from other sources, such as social media platforms. The NSA's approach to gathering intelligence involves digitally exploiting clues left behind by targets in their regular online activities. Commercial efforts, like Facebook's DeepFace project, which has achieved near-human accuracy in identifying faces, provide valuable data for the NSA. US privacy laws do not offer express protection for facial recognition data, and the NSA would require court approval for imagery of Americans collected through its surveillance programs. However, cross-border communications could be exempt, depending on the location of the target.

Queen Elizabeth II has surpassed her great-great-grandmother Queen Victoria as Britain's longest-reigning monarch, marking a milestone on September 9, 2015, at approximately 5:30 p.m. local time. The Queen, now 89, expressed gratitude for the "touching messages of kindness" she received from well-wishers at home and abroad. In Scotland, she officially opened the new £294 million Scottish Borders Railway, while in London, a flotilla of historic vessels participated in a procession along the Thames. Prime Minister David Cameron praised her "rock of stability" during a period of significant change. The Queen's reign has spanned 63 years, seven months, and 21 days, including 12 prime ministers. Buckingham Palace released official photographs of the Queen and Prince Philip, showcasing their daily routine and official engagements. The Queen, who will take her traditional summer break at Balmoral, celebrated the occasion privately. Her reign has been marked by significant events, such as the opening of the Scottish Borders Railway, and she has maintained a consistent presence in British life, often described as a "rock of stability."

Patton Oswalt, 48, has married his fiancée Meredith Salenger, 47, at the Jim Henson Company lot in Los Angeles on November 4, 2017. The couple confirmed the news on social media, sharing pictures of their ceremony. Salenger captioned a photo of walking down the aisle with her step-daughter Alice and her new husband, saying, "True love," "True happiness. Forever and Always. The Oswalts. November 4, 2017. Jim Henson Studios." Oswalt, who had been widowed after his first wife, Michelle McNamara, died in 2016, proposed to Salenger in July 2017, sharing a playful Instagram post with a photo of himself and Salenger, along with a caption that read, "What’d you guys do yesterday?" The proposal came after the couple had been dating for about a year and a half, with their relationship gaining public attention after the premiere of Baby Driver in June 2017. 

Oswalt had previously opened up about his relationship with Salenger in an interview with Playboy, stating that they had started talking through Facebook in February 2017 and had been in constant communication for three months. He described their connection as if they had known each other since their teenage years, sharing that he had unrequited crushes on her since they were 14. He also expressed that while he was experiencing joy he hadn't felt in a long time, he wouldn't recommend going through the extremes he did to find happiness. 

Oswalt's journey to finding love again was not easy. After Michelle McNamara's unexpected death in 2016, he became a widower and single parent. He removed his wedding ring from his finger and kept it in a box of keepsakes, symbolizing his denial of his new reality. However, he eventually decided to remove the ring, symbolizing his acceptance of his new life. 

In the wake of his first marriage, Oswalt faced criticism for getting engaged to Salenger just 15 months after McNamara's death. He defended his decision, saying that he was going through intense therapy and grieving, and that finding love again helped him climb out of the depths of grief and find joy. He also noted that Alice, their daughter, was happy and felt loved, which was a priority for him. 

Oswalt continued to focus on his daughter's well-being, stating that if he hadn't had Alice, he might have shut down after his wife's death. He and Salenger chose to stay in their family home, as moving would have been more painful and felt like running away from Michelle's ghost. Overall, the couple's marriage is a testament to their resilience and commitment to each other and their daughter.

A New York man named John Caltabiano Jr., 49, was sentenced to almost five years in prison for disability fraud, reports ABC News. Caltabiano claimed he lost his sight in a workplace accident in 2006 and was unable to drive, cook, exercise, or even shave without help. However, investigators caught him on video driving a vehicle, shopping, and working out at the gym, all behaviors inconsistent with a person claiming to be blind. His girlfriend, Colleen McCarten, 43, also helped him by leading him into disability hearings. The fraud was discovered when investigators obtained videos of Caltabiano performing everyday activities without assistance. Caltabiano was on track to collect over $1 million in benefits before being caught. He was sentenced to 57 months in prison, and his girlfriend was sentenced to three years of probation. Assistant U.S. Attorney Richard S. Hartunian stated, "If Caltabiano had not been stopped, he would have been able to steal more than a half a million dollars based on his life expectancy." The case highlights the serious issue of disability fraud, with the U.S. Social Security Administration receiving 90,000 allegations to investigate last year.

Underwater pumping operations began on the Costa Concordia, nearly a month after the cruise ship ran aground off Tuscany, to remove 500,000 gallons of fuel. The process, expected to take 28 days, aims to prevent environmental contamination in the protected waters off the island of Giglio. Dutch salvage firm Smit is overseeing the operation, which involves attaching valves to fuel tanks and pumping oil into a crane barge for transfer to an oil tanker. The operation is crucial as fears of a fuel leak have persisted, and the ship has already claimed 17 lives, with 15 more missing. The captain, Francesco Schettino, faces charges of manslaughter and abandoning ship. The fuel extraction is part of a broader effort to address the environmental and legal consequences of the disaster.

Astronomers investigating a star in the constellation Hercules, designated HD 164595, have detected a mysterious radio signal, sparking speculation about its extraterrestrial origins. The signal was first observed on May 15, 2015, by the RATAN-600 radio telescope in Zelenchukskaya, Russia, but was initially kept secret. The star, located about 95 light-years from Earth, is similar to the Sun in terms of mass and metallicity, and is known to host a single Neptune-like planet. However, the possibility of additional planets, including potentially habitable ones, cannot be ruled out.

The signal's strength and characteristics suggest it could be from an advanced civilization. If it were an isotropic beacon, it would require a Kardashev Type II civilization, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its star. If it were a targeted signal, it would indicate a Kardashev Type I civilization, able to use all the starlight falling on its home planet. The signal's detection by the RATAN-600 telescope is significant enough to warrant permanent monitoring, according to the researchers.

The SETI Institute and METI International are now using the Allen Telescope Array in Northern California and Panama's Boquete Optical Observatory to investigate the signal further. The signal was observed only once in 39 attempts, raising doubts about its extraterrestrial origin. However, the signal's characteristics are intriguing enough to keep the scientific community engaged. The signal's detection will be discussed at the 67th International Astronautical Congress in Guadalajara, Mexico, on September 27, 2016.

While the signal is not definitive proof of extraterrestrial intelligence, it remains a compelling candidate for further study. The possibility of terrestrial interference cannot be entirely ruled out, but the signal's unusual nature and the efforts to confirm its origin underscore the ongoing search for evidence of life beyond Earth.

Actress Amy Adams, 39, made headlines on a Delta flight from Detroit to Los Angeles by giving up her first-class seat to an American serviceman. Co-host of ESPN's "Numbers Never Lie," Jemele Hill, shared the story on Twitter, recounting how Adams, while waiting to board, glanced at the soldier and spoke with a companion. Once on the plane, Adams was upgraded to first class, while the soldier was seated in her original seat. Hill noted that Adams must have spoken to a flight attendant, as the change happened before takeoff. Adams' act of kindness was captured in a selfie with passenger Ernest Owens, who praised her for the gesture. Upon landing, Adams stated her intention was to draw attention to the troops. This act of generosity earned her praise from fans, who admired her class and thoughtfulness.

A U.S.-Russia-brokered ceasefire aimed at ending the five-year Syrian civil war began at sundown on Monday, but its effectiveness remains uncertain. The deal, set to last a week, calls for a halt to fighting between the U.S.-backed opposition and the Russian-supported Syrian government, with the U.S. and Russia to establish a joint center to coordinate strikes against militant groups such as ISIS and Jabhat Fateh al-Sham. However, the Syrian army announced a seven-day "freeze" on military operations, while rebel factions have expressed mixed reactions, with some cautiously welcoming the truce and others voicing concerns that it could benefit the government. The ceasefire is seen as a test of the improved relationship between the U.S. and Russia, which struggled to find common ground during the early years of the conflict. Despite early reports indicating a reduction in violence, the success of the truce is uncertain, as previous attempts have often unraveled. The cessation of hostilities is set to be renewed every 48 hours, with humanitarian aid deliveries to besieged areas expected to resume. However, the deal excludes terrorist groups, and the Syrian government's continued air strikes on rebel areas raise doubts about the agreement's long-term viability. The truce comes as the Syrian government has intensified its military operations, with reports of air strikes in several rebel-held areas. The outcome of this latest attempt at peace will be closely watched, as it could either mark a pivotal moment in the Syrian civil war or another brief respite in the ongoing violence.

A judge declared a mistrial in the second trial for the murder of Jessica Chambers, a 19-year-old who was burned alive in her car in Courtland, Mississippi, on December 6, 2014. Quinton Tellis, 29, faces capital murder charges for Chambers' death, and this is the second time a jury failed to reach a verdict. The first trial ended with a hung jury in 2017, and the second trial began on Sunday. When first responders arrived, Chambers was still alive but severely burned, and she later died from her injuries. She reportedly told medical personnel that "Eric did this to me." The case garnered national attention, and the investigation expanded to include officials from the FBI, US Marshals Service, and the US Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms. A $54,000 reward was offered, but no suspects were arrested until investigators analyzed "technological data," leading to Tellis's arrest and indictment. Chambers' father, Ben Chambers, said his daughter "is at peace now" and had never mentioned Tellis's name to the family. The judge has not indicated whether there will be a third trial, but Tellis has "some time limits running on some things in Louisiana" that require his return for another case. Tellis is also charged in the 2016 murder of a University of Louisiana Monroe exchange student, Ming-Chen Hsiao, and is serving time in Louisiana for using her debit card. The case remains a focus of public interest and internet sleuthing.

Adele reportedly declined an offer to perform at the 2017 Super Bowl halftime show, citing her inability to dance and stating, "That show is not about music." During a concert in Los Angeles, she directly addressed the rumors, saying, "I’m not doing the Super Bowl. They were very kind, they did ask me, but I said no." The NFL and Pepsi Co. responded by confirming they had not yet extended a formal offer to Adele or any other artist, emphasizing their focus on assembling a fantastic show for Houston. The 2017 Super Bowl is set for February 5 at NRG Stadium, leaving fans to speculate about who will headline the event.

Former U.S. President Barack Obama, in his first interview since leaving office, discussed the responsible use of social media and the potential for its misuse in shaping public understanding and spreading misinformation. Obama, during an interview with Prince Harry on BBC Radio 4's Today programme, emphasized the importance of creating a common space online where diverse voices could coexist and find common ground. He warned against the internet's ability to create echo chambers that reinforce existing biases, advocating for face-to-face interactions to counteract these effects. Obama highlighted the role of social media as a powerful tool for people with shared interests to connect, but stressed the necessity of offline engagement to foster deeper understanding and empathy.

Reflecting on his presidency, Obama shared his perspective on the pressures of being in the public eye, noting the vulnerability of his loved ones and the challenges of maintaining a public image. He expressed gratitude for his wife Michelle's support throughout his tenure and the serenity he felt upon leaving the White House, despite the unfinished work. Obama described his time in office as a relay race, where he aimed to pass the baton successfully, citing the Affordable Care Act as a significant achievement, bringing health insurance to 20 million Americans.

During the interview, Prince Harry, who was guest-editing the programme, posed a series of light-hearted questions, including whether Obama wore boxers or briefs, and which of two singers, Aretha Franklin or Tina Turner, he preferred. Obama humorously stated, "Aretha is the best," in reference to the Queen of Soul. He also expressed his preference for retired basketball star Michael Jordan over current star LeBron James.

Prince Harry and Obama also discussed the future, with Obama remaining an optimist, believing that the world is healthier, wealthier, and more tolerant than ever before. He emphasized the importance of individual responsibility and community engagement in addressing global challenges. The interview touched on various topics, including climate change, the military, and mental health, with Prince Harry using his guest editor role to highlight these issues.

The conversation concluded with Prince Harry's reluctance to reveal whether Obama would be invited to his upcoming wedding to American actress Meghan Markle, maintaining that the guest list had not yet been finalized. The interview provided a unique insight into the transition from public life to private reflection, showcasing the enduring bond between Obama and Prince Harry and their shared commitment to addressing global challenges.

A top U.S. Navy admiral, Adm. John Richardson, has called for a swift and thorough investigation into the collision of the USS John S. McCain with an oil tanker near Singapore, marking the second deadly mishap in the Pacific in three months. Richardson ordered an operational pause in all fleets worldwide to determine the factors behind the collision, including the possibility of "cyber intrusion or sabotage." Adm. Phil Davidson, the head of the Navy's Fleet Forces, will lead the investigation. Richardson made clear that there is no evidence of a hacking at this point, but some cyber experts have raised the possibility given the location of the warships. The USS John S. McCain suffered significant damage to its hull, flooding nearby compartments including crew berthing, machinery, and communications rooms. Ten sailors remain missing, and five were hospitalized in Singapore after being evacuated by helicopter. A multinational search and rescue effort involving Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, and the U.S. is underway. The 7th Fleet reported that damage to the guided missile destroyer's hull flooded adjacent compartments, including crew berths and machinery and communication rooms. The collision occurred in the Strait of Malacca, a busy commercial waterway. The USS John S. McCain was returning from a freedom of navigation exercise in the South China Sea, during which it sailed within six nautical miles of Mischief Reef, an artificial island created and claimed by China. The incident has sparked speculation about the possibility of cyber espionage, with some experts suggesting that the USS McCain and the USS Fitzgerald, which collided in June, may have been the victims of GPS spoofing or a malware attack. The Navy has ordered a comprehensive review of the 7th Fleet, including personnel, navigation capabilities, maintenance, equipment, surface warfare training, munitions, certifications, and how sailors move through their careers. The review will also consider the possibility of cyber intrusion or sabotage. The collision has raised concerns about the safety and security of U.S. Navy ships, particularly as they operate in increasingly congested and contested waters.

Algeria's prime minister accused a Canadian of coordinating the raid on a desert gas plant where 38 mostly foreign hostages, including three Americans, were killed. Seven Americans survived. The FBI recovered the bodies and notified their families. The Canadian, named Chedad, is among 29 gunmen killed. Algerian forces stormed the complex, resulting in 37 foreign deaths. The attack aimed to take hostages to Mali but failed. Prime Minister Sellal pledged to resist al-Qaeda and vowed not to succumb to terrorism. The incident raised questions about Algeria's security capacity and highlighted the region's growing threat from Islamists. Western powers, including Britain and the U.S., defended Algeria's actions, citing the need to act decisively against fanatics. However, some criticized the harsh response, arguing for a more cautious approach.

Congress is setting records for its most unproductive legislative year since World War II, with only 61 bills passed out of 3,914 introduced, according to a USA TODAY analysis. This contrasts sharply with the 111th Congress, which passed 383 laws, and the 110th, which passed 258. The 112th Congress, covering 2011-2012, is the least productive two-year gathering on Capitol Hill since the end of World War II. Even the infamous "do-nothing Congress" of 1948, led by President Truman, passed more laws than the current Congress. The 112th Congress has been defined by partisan divisions and legislative failures, including the failure of a bipartisan "Super Committee" to enact $1.2 trillion in deficit reduction. Issues like the expiration of the Bush tax cuts, a budget plan to replace $109 billion in automatic spending cuts, a drought-relief plan, and a bill to overhaul the U.S. Postal Service remain unresolved. The inertia continues to fuel Congress' historically low approval ratings, with a mere 10% of Americans thinking members of Congress are doing a good job, a Gallup poll found. This approval rating has been consistent among party affiliations, with Democrats, Republicans, and independents all giving Congress low marks. The 112th Congress has consistently registered low approval ratings, with the highest mark coming in May 2011, when 24% of Americans gave a thumbs-up to Congress. The 10% approval rating from Tuesday's Gallup poll was the same as in February of this year, which was the lowest in Gallup’s history.

President Donald Trump recently dismissed the notion of Oprah Winfrey running for president in 2020, stating, "Yeah, I'd beat Oprah," during a meeting with lawmakers on immigration. However, Winfrey's recent speech at the Golden Globes, where she passionately addressed the #MeToo movement, has reignited speculation about her potential presidential run. Best friend and CBS "This Morning" co-anchor Gayle King confirmed that Winfrey is "intrigued by the idea" of a bid and is seriously considering it. Her powerful speech has thrust her into the political spotlight, potentially disrupting the Democratic primary process. Despite Trump's assertion that he knows Winfrey well and would easily defeat her, the former talk show host has a significant following and could pose a formidable challenge. Trump, who has praised Winfrey in the past, noted that he appeared on her show in its final weeks, saying, "She had Donald Trump -- this is before politics -- her last week and she had Donald Trump and my family, it was very nice." The possibility of Winfrey entering the race has sparked discussions and anticipation in political circles, with some suggesting she could be a game-changer in the 2020 election.

The United Nations Human Rights Committee has ruled that Ireland's strict abortion laws violate the human rights of women, particularly in cases involving fatal fetal abnormalities, according to a report from the Irish Times. The committee found that Ireland's prohibition on abortion subjects women to discriminatory, cruel, and degrading treatment. Amanda Mellet, a Dublin woman who was denied an abortion in 2011 after being informed her fetus had a fatal heart defect, filed a complaint with the UN. The committee determined that Mellet was forced to choose between continuing a non-viable pregnancy or traveling abroad for an abortion, which caused her significant emotional and financial distress. The committee called for Ireland to amend its laws to provide accessible procedures for pregnancy termination and to compensate Mellet for the harm she suffered. Ireland is obliged to prevent similar violations in the future. The ruling is expected to set an international precedent and could influence other countries with restrictive abortion laws. Critics argue that the ban on abortion, enshrined in the Irish Constitution, should be maintained to protect the right to life of the unborn. Supporters of reform argue that the ban is cruel and inhumane, leading to unnecessary suffering for women. The Irish government has resisted calls to directly loosen the laws, instead establishing a citizens' assembly to recommend any changes. The committee's findings have put pressure on the government to address the legislative shortcomings and potentially amend the Constitution.

In 2012, the Rich Earth Institute in Brattleboro, Vermont, began collecting human urine to test its potential as a natural fertilizer. The project, which has since grown to involve over 170 volunteers, aims to divert essential plant nutrients from waterways to farms, turning a potentially harmful substance into a boon for crop production. Urine contains nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium, essential for plant growth, and Rich Earth hopes to double the amount of urine collected this year to 6,000 gallons, enough to fill a third of an average American swimming pool. The collected urine is then used to fertilize crops, with some initial success seen on farms like Fair Wind Farms, where urine-treated fields showed twice the productivity of unfertilized controls. The institute has received funding from the USDA to expand trials, and is developing methods to sanitize urine, such as solar pasteurization and long-term storage in greenhouses, to eliminate the risk of pathogens. However, the project faces challenges, including public perception and the need to address pharmaceutical residues that can end up in urine. Despite these hurdles, the potential for urine as a sustainable and cost-effective fertilizer is significant, with studies from Sweden, Nepal, and other countries showing promising results.

Sen. Al Franken's amendment to the FY 2010 Defense appropriations bill, which aimed to bar the government from contracting with companies that prevent their employees from bringing workplace sexual assault cases to court, has survived and remains intact, according to an aide to Franken. The amendment, which passed 68 to 30, now includes a national security waiver, meaning the Department of Defense could prevent a case from coming to court if it imperils safety measures, but the Secretary of Defense would have to explain the use of the waiver to Congress and make it public. The amendment applies to all contracts totaling $1 million or more and includes a Title VII provision allowing an employee to sue not only the alleged perpetrator but also the perpetrator's employer. This solid amendment will prevent contractors from carrying out some of the most despicable business practices, according to a statement from Franken's aide. The amendment's survival marks a significant step in protecting employees from workplace sexual assault.

A gray two-piece ensemble worn by Vivien Leigh as Scarlett O'Hara in "Gone With the Wind" has fetched $137,000 at an auction, marking a significant sale in the ongoing Heritage Auctions event in Beverly Hills, California. The dress, part of a collection amassed by James Tumblin, who worked at Universal Studios for 22 years, was discovered in the 1960s when Tumblin spotted it on the floor of the Western Costume Company. Initially valued at just $20, the dress was destined for disposal, but Tumblin recognized its historical significance and negotiated a purchase. His collection, now numbering over 300,000 pieces, has grown through word-of-mouth and inter-office connections, reflecting the close-knit nature of Hollywood during the film's production. Other notable items from the auction include a straw hat worn by Leigh and a suit worn by Clark Gable as Rhett Butler, both selling for $52,500 and $55,000, respectively. The collection, spanning 75 years, includes various costumes, props, and behind-the-scenes artifacts, with the auction expected to raise up to $1 million. Tumblin, who has toured his collection across the United States, including a visit by former President Jimmy Carter, plans to share the collection with the public through museum exhibitions. Despite not being his favorite film, Tumblin's passion for "Gone With the Wind" remains unwavering, as evidenced by his extensive collection and the sale of these iconic items.

A 58-year-old teacher at Broward Community Charter School in Coral Springs, Florida, was arrested after police alleged she forced a 10-year-old student to clean a clogged urinal with his bare hands. Jennifer Forshey, a third-grade teacher, was charged with battery of a child by exposure to urine. The boy told police that Forshey accused him of clogging the urinal and ordered him to use his hands to remove the paper towels. His hands became saturated with what smelled like urine, and the bathroom lacked soap. The boy's mother, Jenay Roberts, expressed concern about the incident, stating, "The only reason we are bringing this story to the public is to find out if any other child has been treated in this way before. We want to protect this child and possibly any other children that may have been subjected to this form or corporal and unmoral punishment." While some parents defended Forshey, believing she used poor judgment but was otherwise a good teacher, a close family friend and co-worker described her as a dedicated mentor who spent her own money on educational materials. Forshey was released on $1,000 bond and acknowledged her actions, saying, "She only thinks what she did was wrong because she is in trouble for it." The incident has raised questions about the teacher's methods and the school's response.

On the eve of George Washington's birthday, AP writer Jesse Washington delves into the enigma of the "blackest name" in America: Washington. The 2000 U.S. Census revealed that 163,036 people bore the surname, with 90% being African-American, a figure unmatched by any other common name. This phenomenon began with slavery and took a sharp turn after the Civil War, when all blacks were allowed to choose their surnames. Some historians theorize that the name Washington might have been chosen by Reconstruction-era blacks as a symbol of pride in the nation's history, honoring the revered first president. However, the connection to George Washington himself may be a coincidence, as only a handful of his slaves bore his name, and he recorded most as having only first names.

Washington's complex relationship with slavery is a key factor. He owned hundreds of slaves, but his will eventually freed them, with some exceptions. As president, he worked to evade a law that would have freed his slaves by shuttling them between his Philadelphia residence and his Virginia estate. His actions were contradictory, as he was opposed to slavery in theory but fiercely protected his own interests. This duality is reflected in the name's current demographics, with many black Washingtons feeling a sense of pride and connection to the nation's history, while some white Washingtons have experienced discrimination due to their name.

The name's history is further complicated by the fact that many enslaved people had surnames that went unrecorded or were kept secret. Some chose the name Washington as a mark of community identity, maintaining ties to plantation owners who remained powerful figures after the war. Others may have chosen the name for practical reasons, such as the fame and respect George Washington enjoyed at the time. The name's significance extends beyond its demographic makeup, as it represents a complex interplay of history, identity, and the ongoing legacy of slavery in America.

At least 27 people were killed and nearly 100 wounded in twin car bombings that struck intelligence and security buildings in Damascus on Saturday, according to state media. The blasts, which targeted a customs office and air force intelligence, were the latest in a series of attacks on the regime's military and security installations. State TV aired gruesome images of the scene, showing mangled and charred corpses, bloodstained streets, and twisted steel. The government blamed the attacks on "terrorists," while the opposition accused loyalist forces of orchestrating the bombings to tarnish the uprising. U.S. intelligence officials also pointed to al-Qaida in Iraq as a possible culprit, raising concerns about the group's involvement. The attacks come amid ongoing violence and a year-long uprising against President Bashar Assad. The Syrian government denies there is a popular will behind the protests, blaming foreign extremists and gangs. The U.N. estimates that more than 8,000 people have been killed since the uprising began. Diplomatic efforts to resolve the crisis have so far been unsuccessful, with the U.N. envoy Kofi Annan urging the Security Council to speak with one voice. The bloodshed fuels sectarian tensions, as the military's top leadership is dominated by Alawites, while Sunnis make up the majority of the opposition. The attacks highlight the challenges facing the Arab League monitoring mission, which has been criticized for its effectiveness.

Facebook has taken a heavy-handed approach to eliminating any mention of a competing social media platform, Tsu.co, from its platforms. Tsu.co, with its unique business model of sharing advertising revenue with users, has faced a significant backlash from Facebook. The social media giant blocked any link to Tsu.co on its platforms, including Facebook, Messenger, and Instagram, and even deleted over 1 million posts that mentioned the site, affecting both native and cross-posted content. Tsu users were unable to share links to their Tsu pages on Facebook, and any attempt to mention Tsu.co resulted in a warning that the content was unsafe. Sebastian Sobczak, the founder of Tsu.co, argues that the move is not about spam but rather an attempt to stifle competition. Tsu users can earn money by sharing content that generates ad revenue, a model that Facebook, which keeps 100% of ad profits, finds threatening. Facebook's actions have drawn criticism, with some users and Tsu supporters claiming that the move is unfair and aimed at suppressing a more equitable platform. Claudia Everest, a cancer survivor who uses Tsu to sell her artwork, is particularly vocal about the impact of Facebook's ban, stating that the company is trying to prevent users from realizing the value of their content. The dispute highlights the power of social media giants in shaping the landscape of online interaction and the potential for such companies to act against potential competitors. Tsu's temporary opening of its invite-only policy to the public suggests a desire to test the waters and gain more users, despite the challenges posed by Facebook's actions. The situation underscores the complex dynamics between social media platforms, user engagement, and the broader implications for content creation and monetization.

Former professional wrestler Bret "The Hitman" Hart has entered a new battle in his life, revealing on Monday that he is fighting prostate cancer. The 58-year-old, who previously survived a stroke in 2002, shared his determination and fearlessness in an Instagram post, stating, "I now face my toughest battle. With hesitation and fear, I openly declare myself in my fight against prostate cancer." Hart, a WWE Hall of Famer, has won world heavyweight titles with both the WWF/WWE and WCW, including five world heavyweight championships and two U.S. heavyweight titles. He retired after suffering a concussion in 1999, marking the end of his career. The Hart family, known for their wrestling legacy, includes his father, Stu Hart, a trainer and former wrestler, and his brother Owen Hart, who tragically died in 1999 after falling from an apparatus during a match. Despite the challenges, Hart vows, "I make a solemn vow to all of those that once believed in me, the dead and the living, that I will wage my fearsome fight against cancer with one shield and one sword carrying my determination and my fury for life, emboldened by all the love that's kept me going this long already." Bret Hart's journey and resilience continue to inspire many in the wrestling community and beyond.

A 33-year-old Marine died during a skydiving trip to Australia with his wife, a special education teacher, after his parachute failed to open, reports the Jacksonville Daily News. Brandon McGraw, who had recently returned from Afghanistan, was skydiving with his wife Cherilyn, who had won the trip on The Ellen DeGeneres Show. The couple was with members of Euroa Skydive, an Australian skydiving school, when McGraw, an experienced skydiver with "many" jumps under his belt, descended flawlessly for three to four minutes before suddenly veering left and right and crashing to the ground. He was pronounced dead at the scene. Cherilyn McGraw, a special education teacher from Huntington, paid tribute to her husband, calling him her "hero" and "angel" and sharing the final photo of him smiling on the plane just before jumping. The Marine was based at Camp Lejeune in North Carolina and had served in both Afghanistan and Iraq. The skydive school, Euroa Skydive, is investigating the incident, which was the first fatality in its 30-year history. McGraw's wife, who won the "Stuff Your Down Under Pants" contest on The Ellen DeGeneres Show, took the prize to Australia with a stop-over in New York City. The couple was married in 2011 and was celebrating their dream vacation with a trip that Cherilyn had won. McGraw's death has left his wife and the skydiving community in mourning, as he was known for his love of extreme sports and his adventurous spirit.

In the Republican presidential race, Newt Gingrich has positioned himself as a conservative stalwart, often invoking Ronald Reagan's legacy. However, critics argue that Gingrich's record and character raise serious questions about his authenticity. Gingrich has been a long-time figure in Washington, and his political career has been marked by controversies, including his role in the House and his leadership style. His supporters argue that he is a dynamic and inspiring figure, while opponents highlight his past criticisms of Reagan and his role in the House impeachment process. The debate over Gingrich's candidacy has also centered on his record on issues like abortion, immigration, and entitlement reform. Mitt Romney, Rick Santorum, and Ron Paul are presented as more genuine conservatives, with Romney especially praised for his executive experience and conservative credentials. However, Gingrich has capitalized on the media's focus on the "elite" and "establishment," portraying himself as an outsider. His supporters argue that he is the true conservative, while his critics contend that he is a Clintonian figure, lacking in character and principles. The controversy surrounding Gingrich has intensified, with conservative media outlets and political figures like Bob Dole and Ann Coulter criticizing his candidacy. The article concludes by emphasizing that while Gingrich may appeal to those seeking an outsider, Romney is the most conservative and electable candidate, with a track record of conservative principles and a self-made background. The debate over Gingrich's candidacy highlights the challenges of balancing authenticity and conservatism in the current political landscape.

Jennifer Aniston recently introduced her new boyfriend, Justin Theroux, to some of her close friends, including Courteney Cox and Chelsea Handler, during a party last Friday night. The couple, who met while working on the upcoming film 'Wanderlust,' are reportedly doing well together. However, this party may have reignited tension between Aniston and Cox, who have been best friends since the 1994 debut of Friends. Sources tell People that Aniston is upset with Cox for running around with other men, such as Brian Van Holt and Josh Hopkins, while she is still married to David Arquette. Aniston reportedly believes Cox is playing mind games with Arquette. Cox's trial separation from Arquette in September 2010 after 11 years of marriage has led to a rift in their friendship, reminding Aniston of her own past with ex-husband Brad Pitt, who started dating Angelina Jolie just weeks after their split. Despite the tension, Cox and Pitt recently dined together at a Hollywood hotspot, celebrating their manager's birthday. The two hugged and kissed when they greeted each other, and appeared to be catching up happily.

International Monetary Fund Managing Director Christine Lagarde emphasized the need for a balanced solution to avoid the fiscal cliff, advocating for a compromise that includes both increasing revenue and cutting spending. Her comments came during an interview on CNN's "State of the Union," where she warned that going over the fiscal cliff would lead to widespread lack of confidence in the U.S. economy and a swift market reaction, with stock markets taking a significant hit. Lagarde urged for a comprehensive fix rather than a quick fix, suggesting that any deal, even a temporary one, is better than nothing before the year's end.

Former Sen. Alan Simpson (R-Wyo.) predicted that tax rates for the wealthy will likely increase in 2013. Speaking on CBS’s “Face the Nation,” Simpson, co-chairman of the Simpson-Bowles deficit commission, stated that he and Erskine Bowles, the other co-chairman, believe taxes will rise for the rich. Bowles, however, noted that raising taxes alone would not be enough to address the nation’s deficit. He argued that spending cuts must be made, particularly in healthcare, to slow the rate of growth to the rate of economic growth. Bowles estimated that 2 million people could lose their jobs and the unemployment rate could climb to 9 percent if the U.S. goes over the fiscal cliff. He expressed optimism about a deal getting done, saying, “I’m a little more encouraged than if you would have asked me about it a week ago.”

Republicans may need to concede the current tax fight to President Barack Obama, who holds the "upper hand" in that battle, according to Sen. Bob Corker (R-Tenn.). Corker suggested that ceding to Obama and preserving current tax rates for 98 percent of Americans while allowing rates to rise to Clinton-era levels on the top 2 percent would allow Republicans to focus on spending and entitlements next year. Corker also noted that the GOP will have more leverage in the spending and entitlements debate next year because it can use the threat of not raising the debt ceiling to craft a favorable deal with Obama.

Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and MSNBC's Lawrence O'Donnell predicted that if Secretary of State Hillary Clinton decides to run for president in 2016, it would be "virtually impossible" for any Democrat to beat her for the Democratic nomination. Bloomberg News Chief White House Correspondent Julianna Goldman agreed, noting that Clinton would clear the field. Gingrich, who sought the Republican presidential nomination this year, added that Clinton was the nominee in 2008 and suggested that if she won the Democratic nomination, she could potentially face off against former Republican Florida Governor Jeb Bush, creating a family rematch of the 1992 presidential election.

Newark Mayor Cory Booker said he is considering running against Republican Governor Chris Christie in New Jersey next year and is also mulling a run for the Senate. Booker stated he is committed to making a decision about a gubernatorial race soon so that other Democrats can step up if he decides to pass. He also expressed serious thought about a Senate bid, noting that Sen. Frank Lautenberg (D-N.J.) will be 90 in 2014, raising the possibility that his seat might come open.

Former White House chief of staff Erskine Bowles, co-chairman of the Simpson-Bowles deficit commission, expressed optimism about a deal getting done, crediting both President Obama and House Speaker John Boehner for helping to lay groundwork for a possible deal. Bowles praised Boehner for not including potential deal breakers in his recent proposal, noting that the speaker's offer does not mention block granting Medicaid, premium supports, or deep cuts in income support programs.
