Trained to detect electronic data devices, Bear, one of only five such dogs in the nation, found a thumb drive that investigators had missed during a search of Fogle's Indiana home in July, several weeks before Fogle agreed to plead guilty to having X-rated images of minors and paying for sex with teenage girls. Bear's skills were also instrumental in the recent arrest of gymnastics coach Marvin Sharp. The dog has been sold to the Seattle Police Department to aid in investigations of Internet crimes. His handler, Todd Jordan, demonstrated Bear's abilities by hiding electronic devices in a room and having the dog locate them in less than ten minutes. Jordan emphasized that Bear's training is similar to that for narcotics or explosives detection, focusing on rewarding the dog for indicating on the odor. Bear's transition to Seattle marks the fifth case he has worked on, and Jordan is currently training two more dogs with similar capabilities.

After months of skepticism, Republican insiders now concede that Donald Trump could win two of the first four early voting states, though his hold on Iowa remains uncertain. According to a POLITICO analysis of seven months of responses from strategists, operatives, and activists in Iowa, New Hampshire, South Carolina, and Nevada, roughly three-quarters of GOP insiders in New Hampshire and South Carolina now believe Trump would win their states if the primaries were held today. This shift reflects the growing acceptance of Trump as a formidable contender, despite his recent controversies. In Iowa, insiders are divided, with Ted Cruz nudging ahead of Trump. However, insiders still view Trump as having the best ground game and organization in the state. In Nevada, insiders are split between Trump and Marco Rubio, with Rubio having a more established structure among Mormon voters. The article notes that before Trump entered the race, Scott Walker was the favorite in Iowa, and Jeb Bush was leading in New Hampshire. The latest Reuters/Ipsos poll shows a significant decline in Trump's support among Republicans, dropping 12 points in less than a week. This decline follows criticism over his comments on Muslims and his mocking of a disabled reporter. Despite this, Trump remains the front-runner, with Ben Carson trailing significantly. Cruz and Rubio are tied for third place, while Jeb Bush trails with 7 percent. The poll also highlights the evolving dynamics within the Republican race, with insiders increasingly recognizing Trump's staying power and the challenges he poses to the party establishment.

This year's champagne harvest in France is down 40%, the worst yield in at least four decades, due to hailstorms, wet weather, and fungus. Despite the poor crop, champagne drinkers need not worry as producers have a three-year supply of champagne in reserve, typically made from a mixture of grapes from several harvests. However, French champagne sales have been declining, falling 2% in 2011, including an 8% drop during the Christmas and New Year holiday season. The French economy is struggling, with unemployment at a 13-year high, dampening holiday spirits. While larger producers have cushioned themselves by exporting, smaller producers are suffering, and some distributors are lowering prices to clear their inventories, damaging the image of champagne.

The Secret Service has faced yet another scandal, this time involving the unauthorized access and dissemination of sensitive personal information about Rep. Jason Chaffetz, a prominent critic of the agency. An inspector general's report revealed that between March 24 and April 2, 2015, 45 Secret Service employees accessed Chaffetz’s 2003 job application nearly 60 times, despite only four having a legitimate need to do so. The leaks were highly unusual, as they violated federal privacy laws and involved a widespread dissemination of private information. Assistant Director Edward Lowery, in an email, encouraged the release of unflattering information about Chaffetz, stating, “Some information that he might find embarrassing needs to get out. Just to be fair.” The leaks occurred just days after Chaffetz had criticized the agency for a series of security lapses. Chaffetz described the leak as “a tactic designed to intimidate and embarrass me,” and called it “scary to think about all the possible dangers in having your personal information exposed.” The Secret Service apologized for the misconduct, with Director Joseph Clancy stating, “I again apologize to Representative Chaffetz for this wholly avoidable and embarrassing misconduct. Additionally, I will continue to review policies and practices to address employee misconduct and demand the highest level of integrity of all our employees.” Rep. Elijah Cummings, the committee's top Democrat, called for those who are “unwilling or unable to meet the highest of ethical standards” to be removed from the Secret Service. The incident has raised concerns about the agency's culture and its commitment to privacy and ethical standards.

Scientists are embarking on a mission to explore a newly revealed ecosystem beneath the Larsen C ice shelf in Antarctica, an area that has been hidden for 120,000 years. This expedition, led by the British Antarctic Survey, aims to investigate marine life as it responds to a dramatic environmental change following the calving of a massive iceberg, A-68, which broke off the Larsen Ice Shelf in July 2017. The 1 trillion-ton iceberg, roughly the size of Delaware, left a 2,200-square-mile area of the seafloor exposed to sunlight for the first time in centuries. The team, comprising a diverse group of scientists, will spend three weeks aboard the research ship RRS James Clark Ross, battling harsh Antarctic conditions, including temperatures around 15°F and treacherous sea ice. Their primary goal is to collect samples of seafloor animals, microbes, plankton, sediments, and water, to understand the ecosystem before it undergoes significant changes. Katrin Linse, a marine biologist from the British Antarctic Survey, emphasizes the urgency of the mission, stating, "It’s important we get there quickly before the undersea environment changes as sunlight enters the water and new species begin to colonize." This expedition is part of a broader effort to protect the Antarctic region, with Greenpeace advocating for the establishment of the world's largest ocean sanctuary. The research is crucial for understanding the impact of climate change on polar regions and the resilience of Antarctic ecosystems.

A former Intermex employee is suing the company for wrongful termination, alleging that she was fired after refusing to use a tracking app that monitored her every move, both on and off the clock. Myrna Arias, a sales executive for the money transfer service, claims she was monitored by her boss, John Stubits, using the Xora app, which tracked her location 24/7. Arias expressed concerns about the app's privacy invasion, comparing it to a "prisoner's ankle bracelet," and informed Stubits that his actions were illegal. Stubits allegedly responded that she should tolerate the monitoring for the higher salary she was earning. Arias uninstalled the app, and Stubits reportedly scolded her for it. Arias was fired shortly after, and her attorney, Gail Glick, argues that the termination was retaliation for her refusal to be monitored. The lawsuit, filed in Kern County Superior Court, also alleges invasion of privacy, unfair business practices, and retaliation. Arias seeks damages in excess of $500,000 and claims she was monitored even during her non-working hours. The case highlights the tension between employer monitoring and employee privacy, especially in the context of a globalized workforce.

Democratic senators Heidi Heitkamp of North Dakota and Joe Donnelly of Indiana recently endorsed same-sex marriage, marking a significant shift as they represent deeply red states. Heitkamp stated, "I have concluded the federal government should no longer discriminate against people who want to make lifelong, loving commitments to each other or interfere in personal, private, and intimate relationships." Donnelly, on Facebook, emphasized his support for equality and diversity, saying, "In doing so, I have concluded that the right thing to do is to support marriage equality for all." Their endorsements bring the total number of Democratic senators supporting same-sex marriage to 14, with only four remaining holdouts: Mark Pryor, Joe Manchin, Mary Landrieu, and Tim Johnson. Notably, Heitkamp and Donnelly's support is particularly noteworthy because they come from states that voted for Mitt Romney in 2012. However, both are not up for re-election until 2018, potentially reducing the political risk associated with their stance. The shift in support among senators mirrors the broader public opinion trend, with 50 senators now backing same-sex marriage, up from just 16 in 2010 and eight in 2008. This rapid increase in support among senators could be attributed to a combination of strategic calculations and the perception that public opinion has reached a majority status, making it politically advantageous for many senators to align with the growing consensus.

Wesley Snipes, 48, began serving a three-year federal prison sentence on Thursday for failing to file income tax returns. He arrived at the Federal Correctional Institution McKean in Lewis Run, Pennsylvania, shortly before noon. Snipes, known for his roles in films like 'Blade' and 'Undisputed,' faces a stark contrast between his life outside and his new reality. The minimum-security prison lacks fences, offering inmates two-man rooms, daily showers, and double-feature movie showings on Fridays and weekends. However, Snipes will have to adjust to earning just pennies an hour on campus chores and spending only $290 a month at the prison commissary. Snipes has attempted to delay his sentence, filing an emergency motion for a new trial, but the judge has rejected his request. At McKean, Snipes can participate in various activities like sand volleyball, indoor basketball, and spiritual groups. The daily routine includes five head counts, three during the night, and a strict wake-up call at 6:35 AM. Snipes has expressed his belief that there were irregularities in his case and plans to seek a Supreme Court review. His celebrity status does not grant him special treatment, as officials insist on treating all inmates equally. Snipes, who once described himself as an "idealistic, naive, passionate, truth-seeking, spiritually motivated artist," faces the challenges of prison life with a mix of determination and disappointment.

Robin Roberts returned to the "Good Morning America" (GMA) anchor desk on Wednesday, five months after undergoing a bone marrow transplant to treat myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS), a rare blood disorder. Roberts, 52, expressed gratitude to her family, friends, and colleagues during her return, emphasizing the role of faith, family, and friends in her recovery. Her co-hosts and the studio audience welcomed her with warmth, and she appeared in good spirits, despite some initial concerns about her vision due to the bright studio lights. GMA's executive producer, Ben Sherwood, noted that ABC was determined not to repeat the departure of Peter Jennings, who abruptly announced his lung cancer diagnosis and never returned to "World News Tonight." Roberts will gradually increase her appearance frequency on GMA, depending on her doctors' recommendations and her own well-being. Her return was celebrated by fans, with tens of thousands sending well-wishes on social media. The milestone visit also included a special appearance at the Oscars, where Roberts was set to interview First Lady Michelle Obama. Roberts' journey will be featured on a special edition of "20/20," offering a behind-the-scenes look at her recovery and the impact of her story on others. Her return to GMA signifies a significant moment in the network's ongoing ratings battle with NBC's "Today" show, as GMA has been closing the gap in recent weeks.

A family of five, including three young children, was found dead in their home in Sinking Spring, Pennsylvania, on Saturday, August 6, 2016, in what authorities described as an apparent murder-suicide. The victims, identified as 40-year-old Mark Jason Short Sr., his 33-year-old wife Megan L. Short, and their three children Liana, 8, Mark Jr., 5, and Willow, 2, were discovered in their home on Winding Brook Drive. A dog was also found dead. The bodies bore gunshot wounds, and a handgun was found near one of the adults. A handwritten note, described as a "murder-suicide" note, was also discovered in the home. The district attorney's office confirmed that the couple had been experiencing "domestic issues." A concerned relative called police to check on the family, as Megan Short had not shown up for a lunch date and did not answer her phone. Upon arrival, responding officers broke a window to gain entry and found the tragic scene. Megan Short had planned to move out of the home to Yardley, Bucks County, the day of the incident, according to a neighbor. The couple had been active in raising awareness for congenital heart disease, with their youngest daughter Willow, 2, having undergone a heart transplant at 1 week old. The family's struggles with obtaining necessary medications and dealing with post-traumatic stress were highlighted in a blog post by Megan Short. The tragedy has left the community in shock, with neighbors expressing sadness and confusion over the events. Counseling services were made available at the local school to support those affected.

An international operation led by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) aimed at child pornography and sexual abuse has resulted in the arrest of 245 suspects, with 123 child victims identified, in a five-week operation that spanned 46 states and six countries. The operation, dubbed "Operation Sunflower," was executed in November and December, targeting both child exploitation and the distribution of new child pornography online. Of the 123 victims, 44 were directly rescued from their abusers, while 79 were identified as being exploited by others outside their homes or are now adults who were victimized as children. The youngest victims were as young as 3 years old, and the oldest were 17. The operation resulted in 37 arrests in California, the most of any state, including 14 in the Fresno area, with one suspect remaining at large. The suspects ranged in age from their early 20s to early 50s. ICE Director John Morton emphasized the critical role of forensic analysis technology in identifying the locations of abuse and tracking down victims and perpetrators. The agency is calling on the public to provide tips and is working on additional rescues and identifications. "Operation Sunflower" was chosen to commemorate a case from 2011 where Danish law enforcement identified a 16-year-old boy planning to rape an 11-year-old girl, leading to the rescue of the victim. ICE's Victim Identification Program has identified or rescued 292 victims and arrested 1,655 child predators in the previous fiscal year.

Undecided voter Ken Bone, known for his red sweater, gained internet fame after attending the second presidential debate in St. Louis. Bone, who asked a question about energy policy, described the debate as "almost feeling like watching mom and dad fight," due to the "bickering and name calling" that dominated the 90-minute event. Despite the contentious atmosphere, Bone praised the moderators, Martha Raddatz and Anderson Cooper, for their handling of the debate. He noted that while the rhetoric was difficult to wade through, there were substantive answers to be found. Bone's red sweater, which he wore as a backup plan after his olive suit split, became a symbol of the debate's unexpected charm. His Twitter account saw a surge in followers, and he joked that the sweater was more famous than he was. Bone expressed that while the debate did not significantly sway his voting decision, he found Hillary Clinton's composure and answers impressive. He also criticized Donald Trump for inviting women to the debate who claimed to have been wronged by the Clintons, calling it "uncalled for." Bone's story highlights the unexpected moments that can emerge from political events, capturing the public's imagination and providing a human face to the often-difficult political discourse.

A new study published in the journal Science Advances suggests that the modern world is experiencing a "sixth great extinction" of animal species, even when the lowest estimates of extinction rates are considered. The rate of extinction for species in the 20th century was up to 100 times higher than it would have been without human impact, according to researchers from the National Autonomous University of Mexico and Stanford University. This rate is far higher than in the last five mass extinctions, indicating a massive loss of species. The study, which employed better knowledge of natural or background extinction rates, found that 468 more vertebrates have gone extinct since 1900 than would have if the background rate had persisted. The extinction of amphibians, particularly, has been especially severe. The researchers emphasize that the current extinction pace is unprecedented and could lead to a true sixth mass extinction, which would take millions of years to recover. They argue that rapid, greatly intensified efforts are needed to conserve threatened species and alleviate pressures on their populations, such as habitat loss, overexploitation, and climate change. The study's authors warn that if the current trend continues, humanity itself could eventually fall victim to the sixth extinction. However, they also hold out a ray of hope, suggesting that if richer countries can afford to reforest and embark on serious conservation efforts, the problem could decline rapidly.

Back-to-back explosions rocked two churches in Las Cruces, New Mexico, on Sunday morning, causing minor damage but no injuries. The first blast occurred at 8 a.m. at Calvary Baptist Church, where a device placed in a mailbox near the administrative entrance went off, shattering the mailbox and startling worshippers who were just beginning to gather. About 30 people were inside the church at the time. Dennis Llewellyn, a former special forces member, recognized bomb parts among the debris. The second explosion, about 20 minutes later, hit Holy Cross Catholic Church, where a device in a trash can outside the entrance went off during a Mass, breaking the church’s glass front and interrupting communion. Monsignor John Anderson described the loud noise and feeling of the building shaking. Parishioners were evacuated, and the church was closed for the day. Both explosions were being investigated by multiple law enforcement agencies, including the FBI, ATF, and the Department of Homeland Security. Governor Susana Martinez called the act cowardly and vowed that the responsible party would be caught. The blasts, occurring so close in time and place, raised suspicions of a connection, though authorities were cautious about confirming a link. The church community vowed to remain vigilant and continue their services, emphasizing the strength of their faith and fellowship.

Instagram photos could serve as a window into a person's mental health, according to new research from Harvard University and the University of Vermont. Analyzing over 43,950 images from 166 participants, the study found that certain visual characteristics of Instagram posts could indicate depression. The researchers trained a computer to recognize patterns in the photos, such as hue, brightness, and saturation, which were more common among depressed individuals. These patterns included darker, bluer, and grayer images, as well as a higher number of comments and a greater use of the "Inkwell" filter, which converts photos to black and white. Interestingly, depressed users tended to post more photos with faces, though each face in the photo was fewer in number, potentially indicating smaller social circles.

When compared to human raters, the computer's analysis was more accurate, correctly identifying 70% of depression cases. The study's authors suggest that this method could be used for early screening and detection of mental illness, potentially allowing for earlier intervention. However, they caution that the findings need further validation and that the technology should complement, rather than replace, the expertise of human clinicians. The researchers believe that such a tool could be used in the future to augment professional diagnostic decision-making, providing a non-intrusive and cost-effective way to monitor mental health through social media.

Far-right French National Front leader Marine Le Pen praised the suicide of Dominique Venner, a writer and activist opposed to gay marriage, as an "eminently political act" following his dramatic death at Paris's Notre Dame Cathedral. Venner, 78, shot himself in front of the altar, leaving behind statements criticizing the legalization of gay marriage and immigration from North Africa. In a final essay, he called for new, symbolic gestures to awaken consciences and protect French and European identities. Le Pen's statement garnered attention, with some critics questioning the normalization of such acts. Meanwhile, Notre Dame Cathedral's rector expressed shock and concern, stating it was the first time someone had committed suicide inside the historic site. Venner's publisher noted the symbolic power of his death, comparing it to the suicide of Japanese author Yukio Mishima. The incident highlights ongoing tensions within French society regarding immigration, gay rights, and the far-right's influence. The cathedral, a major tourist attraction, was evacuated safely after the incident. The suicide took place on Tuesday, shortly before the final passage of the gay marriage law, adding to the political and social significance of the event.

Indiana man James Wesley Howell, 20, faces felony weapons charges in Los Angeles after authorities found assault rifles and explosive chemicals in his car in Santa Monica, California, on June 12, just before a major gay pride parade. Howell, who told police he was headed to the West Hollywood event, was arrested early Sunday morning and appeared in court on June 14. He has pleaded not guilty to the charges, with a bail set at $2 million. The arrest came just hours after a mass shooting at a gay nightclub in Orlando, Florida, which left 49 people dead. Authorities initially said Howell intended to do harm at the gay pride event, but the Santa Monica Police Chief later clarified that Howell only said he intended to attend the festival. The Indiana man, a known gun enthusiast, was on probation for an incident involving intimidation with a firearm. He was convicted in April of misdemeanor intimidation for an incident with his neighbor, under the terms of which he was not allowed to have weapons or leave Indiana. Court documents reveal that Howell, a member of a car club, took a 12-year-old girl to a state forestry property and had sex with her after she developed a crush on him. The girl's mother reported the allegations to police on June 2. Clark County Prosecutor Jeremy Mull said it's a "logical conclusion" that Howell traveled to California to flee the child molestation investigation. Howell's lawyer, Bobby Boyd, and his public defender, Pamela Jones, did not respond to requests for comment. Federal agents searched Howell's home in Jeffersonville, Indiana, but declined to release any details. The case highlights the complexities of cross-state investigations and the potential consequences of a suspect's actions.

The son of the former Penn State University assistant football coach Jerry Sandusky, Jeffrey Sandusky, 41, pleaded guilty on Friday to 14 counts of child sexual abuse, including solicitation of statutory sexual assault and solicitation of involuntary deviate sexual intercourse, reports CNN. The plea deal comes one week before his scheduled trial, and nearly six years after his father was arrested in a child molestation case that significantly impacted Penn State and continues to be processed through criminal and civil courts. Jeffrey Sandusky will spend up to six years in state prison, but the judge has the discretion to impose a sentence of up to eight years. As part of the deal, the younger Sandusky admitted to pressuring a teenage girl to send him naked photos and asking her teenage sister to provide him with oral sex. The charges involved incidents with two girls, one in 2013 and another in 2016. Jeffrey Sandusky's lawyer did not immediately respond to a call for comment. The Centre County district attorney's office stated that the younger Sandusky will be classified as a Tier III sex offender, the highest level in Pennsylvania. The plea deal effectively ends the younger Sandusky's trial, which was set to begin the following week.

Bill Cosby's spokesperson, Andrew Wyatt, accused both Cosby and Supreme Court nominee Brett Kavanaugh of being victims of a "sex war" during a fiery press conference outside the courthouse after Cosby was sentenced to three to 10 years in prison for drugging and sexually assaulting a woman, Andrea Constand, in 2004. Wyatt claimed the trial was "the most racist and sexist trial in the history of the United States," and that Cosby, once a beloved actor and comedian, had endured an "unjust" conviction. He also criticized the psychologists who testified against Cosby and alleged that audio footage played in the courtroom was falsified. Wyatt drew parallels between the trial and accusations against Kavanaugh, suggesting that both were part of a broader "sex war" being waged in Washington. The sentence also declared Cosby a "sexually violent predator," subjecting him to mandatory counseling for the rest of his life. Cosby was processed at the Montgomery County Correctional Facility before being moved to State Correctional Institution at Phoenix, where his health and other needs would be evaluated for a period of weeks to months as officials determined his final placement. Cosby, who is legally blind, was housed in a single cell adjacent to the infirmary and would be allowed phone calls and visitation in accordance with policy. The Department of Corrections stated that Cosby's safety and general welfare would be ensured, and his long-term goal was to be placed in the general population to receive the programming required during his incarceration.

Rotisserie chickens have become a common sight in grocery stores, often priced lower than buying and preparing a whole chicken at home. A few years ago, Cat Vasko noticed that the rotisserie chickens were cheaper than purchasing and roasting a whole chicken. Intrigued, she decided to investigate why. Her findings revealed that grocery stores use unsold, near-expiration chicken to create rotisserie chickens, making a profit from food that would otherwise be discarded. This practice is part of a broader strategy to reduce spoilage and waste in the supermarket industry. By repurposing produce and meat that are past their prime, supermarkets can offer a wider range of prepared foods at lower prices. This approach not only benefits consumers but also contributes to more efficient use of resources. For instance, a rotisserie chicken at Gelson's costs $6.99, while a whole chicken from the butcher counter at the same store is $12.67 per pound. The economic rationale behind this practice is clear: it allows stores to maximize their profits while providing consumers with convenient, affordable meal options. However, it also raises questions about the quality and safety of these products. Despite the potential for food waste, the practice of using near-expiration produce and meat to create prepared foods has become a significant part of the modern grocery store business model.

A U.S. government agency report has warned that the Islamic State (ISIS) has the ability to create fake Syrian passports, a federal official confirmed. The report, issued by the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agency, warned that ISIS has access to Syrian government passport printing machines and blank passports, raising the possibility that the travel documents could be faked. The report also expressed concern that because ISIS has access to biographical and fingerprint data on Syrian citizens, there is a possibility of identity theft. The State Department and FBI have acknowledged the threat, with State Department spokesman John Kirby stating that government officials are "mindful" that terrorists could be making false passports. FBI Director James Comey testified before a Senate committee that the intelligence community is concerned that ISIS has the capability to manufacture fraudulent passports. The report, which was issued to U.S. law enforcement in recent weeks, notes that since more than 17 months have passed since Raqqa and Deir ez-Zour fell to ISIS, it is possible that individuals from Syria with passports "issued" in these ISIS-controlled cities or who had passport blanks may have traveled to the U.S. The report's primary source was rated at "moderate confidence," the second-highest rating given for source assessments. The report includes an example of a Syrian passport discovered in Turkey that was printed with a designator number indicating it had been printed in an ISIS-controlled area earlier this year. The HSI report's last page contains a warning that if ISIS's ability to produce passports is not controlled, their operations will continue to increase and expand outside of their operational controlled areas. The threat of fake ISIS passports has already been discovered in Europe, most notably two used by suicide bombers in the Paris terrorist attack last month.

On Christmas Day, the French Laundry restaurant in Yountville suffered a significant theft of valuable wines, estimated to be worth at least $300,000. The thieves, who broke into the wine room by jimmying a door, targeted specific bottles from the renowned Domaine de la Romanée-Conti, including those from the Romanée Conti vineyard, which are worth up to $15,000 each. Chef and proprietor Thomas Keller, in a tweet, appealed to the wine community for assistance in identifying the culprits. The stolen wines also included several bottles of California cult Cabernet Sauvignon Screaming Eagle, with prices ranging from $2,100 to $7,500. The French Laundry, which recently closed for a kitchen remodel, is known for its exceptional wine program and is one of only 13 restaurants in the U.S. to have earned three Michelin stars. The restaurant's statement expressed confidence in the authorities and a commitment to rebuilding their cellar.

Sinn Féin leader Gerry Adams was arrested and questioned by police regarding the 1972 IRA murder of Jean McConville, a widow of 10. Adams criticized the timing of his arrest during an election campaign and claimed he was innocent. He voluntarily met with detectives and was released without charges. The IRA's involvement in the abduction and killing of McConville, one of the "disappeared," remains a contentious issue. Adams' arrest has sparked debate over the timing and political implications. Meanwhile, other suspects, including former IRA leader Ivor Bell, have also been charged based on Boston College tapes. The McConville family vows to continue their fight for justice.

Jeb Bush, who entered the fourth GOP debate with the most on the line, turned in his strongest performance to date, rising above his previous struggles and showing a more assertive and commanding presence. Bush's improved performance, marked by fewer gaffes and more concrete answers, offered a much-needed boost to his campaign, though it is unlikely to fundamentally alter his position in the broader field. Bush's strategy of focusing on Hillary Clinton and presenting himself as a viable general-election candidate seemed to resonate with the audience, as evidenced by his repeated references to the Clinton campaign's reaction to his immigration policies. His interactions with other candidates, particularly Marco Rubio, were more controlled, and he managed to avoid the confrontational style that had previously backfired on him. Bush's debate coach, Jon Kraushar, played a significant role in refining his performance, helping him to appear more confident and less jangled. Despite the improvements, Bush still faced moments of awkwardness, such as his double-Washington wordplay, but overall, his performance was seen as a positive step forward.

Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz again outshone their rivals, showcasing their mastery of the facts and ease under the bright lights. Rubio's line about welders making more money than philosophy majors quickly became a memorable quote, and his exchanges with Rand Paul on foreign policy and defense spending were particularly noteworthy. Cruz's performance was consistent with his previous debates, with his denunciations of Washington's "crony" culture resonating with the audience. Both candidates displayed a strong command of policy and appeared more relaxed and confident than in previous debates.

Ben Carson struggled with the debate format, which focused more on substantive policy questions, and took up the least amount of speaking time despite his position in the center of the stage. His performance was marked by a lack of engagement with the other candidates and a tendency to veer off topic with anecdotes, which, while intended to connect with voters, often came across as trite and cliched. Carson's defense of his past exaggerations and inaccuracies regarding his life story, while addressing some of the criticism he faced, did little to improve his standing in the race.

Carly Fiorina, known for her ability to communicate effectively, turned in a solid performance, inserting herself into various discussions and leaving a positive mark. Her focus on the need to challenge vested interests in the political system resonated with the audience, and she appeared more engaged and less rote than in previous debates. However, the suspicion that her moment in the sun had passed after the second GOP debate in September continued to linger, and there was no clear indication that she could reverse this trend.

Donald Trump, the front-runner, faced a more understated debate format and seemed to struggle with the policy questions. His attempts to challenge other candidates on foreign policy and immigration were met with resistance, and his repeated references to his business acumen and past successes often fell flat. Trump's performance was marked by a lack of substantive policy discussion and a tendency to revert to his familiar lines, which, while effective in the past, seemed less impactful in this debate.

John Kasich, who entered the debate with a strategy to install himself in the center of the conversation, struggled to find his footing. His attempts to interrupt and engage with other candidates often backfired, and he appeared peevish and short-tempered. His positions on immigration and Wall Street banks were met with boos from the audience, and his overall performance was seen as a mixed bag, with moments of effectiveness but also clear areas for improvement.

The debate format itself was criticized for its lifelessness and lack of candidate exchanges, with many answers coming from repeated talking points. The decision to limit the number of candidates on the main stage to eight, the smallest primetime grouping to date, was seen as a positive change, as it allowed for more focused and substantive discussions. However, the debate moderators were praised for their smooth running and substantive questions, which helped to keep the conversation on track and avoid the "gotcha" moments that had marred previous debates.

Overall, the fourth GOP debate in Milwaukee was a more policy-focused affair, with the candidates engaging in substantive exchanges on issues such as immigration and defense spending. While it did little to alter the trajectories of individual candidates or the broader narrative of the race, it provided a more focused and substantive discussion of policy, which may have been more in line with the expectations of the Republican base. The debate highlighted the strengths and weaknesses of each candidate, with some, like Rubio and Cruz, maintaining their positions as the strongest contenders, while others, like Carson and Kasich, faced challenges in maintaining their standing in the race.

Shia LaBeouf has quit his role in the Broadway revival of "Orphans" due to "creative differences," leaving the production with Alec Baldwin as the only confirmed cast member. The play, directed by Daniel Sullivan, is set to open at the Schoenfeld Theater on April 7, with previews beginning on March 19. LaBeouf, known for his action movie roles, joined the cast with little theater experience, having started his career in stand-up comedy and Disney Channel shows. His departure comes after he expressed a desire to focus on more indie projects. The production continues despite the change, with no replacement announced for LaBeouf's role. Meanwhile, Tom Hanks is making his Broadway debut in the play "Lucky Guy," directed by George C. Wolfe. Hanks plays Mike McAlary, a muckraking columnist from the 1980s and '90s, a character that challenges his usual wholesome image. Hanks, who won Oscars for "Philadelphia" and "Forrest Gump," is embracing the role of an unlikable character, aiming to portray McAlary's rough edges and determination. The play, originally written by Nora Ephron, has undergone several revisions and is dedicated to her memory after her recent passing. Hanks sees his involvement as a reinvention, a chance to prove himself in a new genre. Both productions highlight the evolving nature of Hollywood stars stepping into the theater world, each bringing their unique perspectives and experiences to the stage.

Afghanistan's High Peace Council has outlined conditions for engaging the Taliban in peace talks, emphasizing no foreign power can interfere without its consent. The council, responding to concerns that the U.S. and Qatar, with German assistance, secretly agreed to open a Taliban office in Doha, has set ground rules for negotiations. These include the Taliban stopping violence against civilians, severing ties with al-Qaeda, and respecting Afghanistan's constitution, which guarantees civil rights, including those for women. The Afghan government prefers the office to be in Saudi Arabia or Turkey, but is open to Doha as long as it does not undermine the state's authority. The council also requires the involvement of well-known figures from both sides and insists that talks can only proceed after the Taliban cease attacks. The U.S. supports Afghan-led reconciliation, while Pakistan, which hosts many Taliban members, is seen as crucial for the process. However, the Taliban, confident in their ultimate victory, have stated they will not engage in talks while foreign troops remain in Afghanistan. The council's demands reflect the complex and challenging nature of the peace process as NATO prepares to withdraw most combat troops by 2014.

The Supreme Court ruled unanimously on Monday that farmers could not use Monsanto’s patented genetically altered soybeans to create new seeds without paying the company a fee. The decision, in the case Bowman v. Monsanto Company, No. 11-796, has implications for many aspects of modern agriculture and businesses based on vaccines, cell lines, and software. Justice Elena Kagan, writing for the court, emphasized that the decision was narrow, addressing the situation before them rather than every case involving self-replicating products. However, the ruling protected biotechnology entrepreneurs like Monsanto from patent infringement by farmers who might use seeds in a way that would undermine the company’s patent.

The case involved an Indiana farmer, Vernon Hugh Bowman, who had signed a contract for his main crop but sought a loophole for his second, riskier crop later in the season. Bowman bought seeds from a grain elevator, hoping they contained Monsanto’s patented Roundup Ready gene, and planted them, spraying them with Roundup. Many plants survived, and Bowman replanted their seeds. Monsanto sued, and a federal judge ordered Bowman to pay the company more than $84,000. The United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit upheld that decision, saying Bowman had infringed Monsanto’s patents.

Justice Kagan agreed, suggesting Bowman had been too clever for his own good. She noted that the exhaustion doctrine allowed Bowman to resell the patented soybeans he purchased from the grain elevator or consume them himself or feed them to his animals. However, the exhaustion doctrine did not apply to the way Bowman used the seeds, as he had infringed Monsanto’s patents by planting them and creating new seeds. Kagan emphasized that allowing Bowman’s tactic would destroy the value of Monsanto’s patent, as it would result in a patent monopoly extending only for one transaction. She also rejected Bowman’s argument that soybeans naturally self-replicate, stating that Bowman controlled the reproduction of Monsanto’s patented invention.

The ruling is significant for the biotechnology industry, as it bolsters the argument that self-replicating products can be protected from patent infringement even if their challengers go through third parties. However, the decision also has implications for consumers, as it may lead to higher prices for patented products. Critics argue that the ruling is a setback for farmers, as it improperly attributes seeds' reproduction to farmers rather than nature. The decision stops short of determining how self-reproducing inventions should be handled in all cases, leaving the court or Congress to address the issue in the future.

Facebook analyzed one million status updates from English speakers in the U.S. to uncover patterns in how people use status updates and how their friends interact with them. Using the LIWC Dictionary, the company categorized words into 68 word groups, such as pronouns, past-tense verbs, and emotional content. Older users tend to use more religious terms, social processes, and family-related words, while younger users are more likely to swear and express anger. People are most positive in the morning and use more time-related words. Negative emotions peak after 10 p.m., and updates with negative emotions receive more comments. People who have more friends tend to use more second-person pronouns and write longer updates. The study found that people use similar words in their status updates as their friends do, especially when referring to family, religion, or swearing. This research could help advertisers and marketers tailor their content to specific demographics.

One day before the 2014 Winter Olympics opening ceremony in Sochi, Google made a strong statement in support of LGBT rights by featuring a rainbow-colored Google Doodle on its homepage, including the Russian version. The Doodle, which includes silhouettes of athletes and the text from the Olympic Charter emphasizing the right to practice sport without discrimination, aims to promote the Olympic spirit of mutual understanding, friendship, solidarity, and fair play. This move comes in response to Russia's controversial anti-gay "propaganda" law and President Vladimir Putin's discriminatory statements. While Olympic sponsors like AT&T and American Apparel have also voiced their support for LGBT rights, none of the official sponsors, including Coca-Cola, Visa, Samsung, and McDonald's, have yet made any public statements in favor of LGBT rights in Russia. The Doodle serves as a clear message to Putin and the world, highlighting the contradiction between the Olympic values and Russia's current policies.

A Georgia mother found out her 18-year-old son, Mackean Robertson, had died in a car crash after she pulled up to the scene of the wreck unaware of what had unfolded. Nicole Bahret of Cumming said she was on her way home in mid-July when she noticed her son's car involved in an accident. "I knew when I saw his car," Bahret told WSB-TV. "So, I actually pulled up to the scene. That's how I found out." The Forsyth County Sheriff's office released a press statement on July 17, detailing that a white 2010 Mercedes SUV, driven by a 17-year-old Natalie D’Allen from Suwanee, collided with a white 2005 Honda Accord driven by an 18-year-old male from Cumming, Mackean Robertson. The Honda slid sideways into the path of a westbound green Nissan Pathfinder, which was also involved in the crash. The driver of the Honda, Mackean Robertson, was pronounced deceased at the scene. Hundreds of people attended Robertson's funeral, with the Forsyth Central High School marching band escorting his body from the church. Robertson was a student at Forsyth Central High School from 2013 to 2016, after which he withdrew to attend Georgia Cyber Academy. His aunt, Baylee Robertson, described him as "an amazing person who was liked by everyone he came into contact with." Robertson's passions included music, spending time with family and friends, and traveling. A fundraising page for Robertson's family to help cover funeral costs has raised more than $15,000 as of Wednesday. Nicole Bahret said she had a conversation with her son just an hour before the crash, and he had asked if he could hang out with friends. "He actually asked and said, ‘Can I hang out with some friends tonight?’ And I was like, ‘Yeah, that sounds great,'" Bahret said. "He was precious." The crash occurred just past the entrance to the Sawnee Mountain Preserve in Forsyth County. The driver of the Mercedes SUV, Natalie D’Allen, turned herself in to law enforcement on July 23 and posted bond. No charges have been filed yet but are pending the results of an investigation, which remains ongoing. The tragedy has left the family and friends of Mackean Robertson deeply affected, with Nicole Bahret sharing that she is finding comfort in the support of close friends and family.

Ten individuals were apprehended in connection with the unlawful killing and dismemberment of a wild giant panda, which had its skin, bones, and 22 pounds of meat seized in a raid on a residence in Yanjin, Yunnan province, according to state television. The suspects, including two brothers, claimed they shot the panda after it injured their goat. DNA analysis confirmed the victim to be an adult female panda. This incident has sparked intense debate on social media, with some expressing outrage over the cruelty towards the adorable animals, while others argue that the existence of buyers fuels the poaching. With only about 1,800 wild pandas left in China, the poaching of these endangered species remains a significant threat, despite efforts to protect them. The black market value of panda parts, driven by their rarity, has led to such heinous acts. The authorities have emphasized the need to intensify law enforcement to combat the illegal trade in rare animal parts.

A new study suggests that body odor can reveal details about a person's personality, adding a new dimension to first impressions. Participants wore cotton t-shirts for three nights without using fragrances or odorous products, and their shirts were later assessed by 100 men and 100 women. Judges rated the shirts based on five personality traits: extroversion, neuroticism, and dominance. The ratings correlated reasonably well with the self-assessments of the shirt wearers, particularly for extroversion and neuroticism. Judgments of dominance were most accurate when the rater was of the opposite sex, hinting at its importance in mate selection. While the match was not perfect, the findings suggest that our sense of smell plays a significant role in perceiving personality traits, alongside visual and auditory cues. The study, set to appear in the European Journal of Personality, opens up new avenues for understanding how we form impressions of others.

Taylor Swift has reemerged on social media with a cryptic video, hinting at a potential new album. On August 21, 2017, Swift posted a 10-second video of a snake's tail on Instagram and Twitter, her first posts since deleting all her social media accounts on Friday. The snake imagery, which Swift fans have long associated with her, has sparked speculation about a new album. Joseph Kahn, Swift's music video director, added a smiley face to the post and joked about the upcoming solar eclipse, suggesting Swift may use the event as a metaphor for her return. Swift's return comes three years after the announcement of her last album, 1989, and coincides with the three-year anniversary of a feud with Kim Kardashian, further fueling theories about a new project. Swift's fans have been quick to react, with some embracing the snake imagery and others speculating about the nature of the new music. The post has also led to a flurry of Game of Thrones references, with some fans joking that Swift is the new "Mother of Dragons." Meanwhile, Swift has been associated with a new single called "Timeless," with a website for the song reportedly coming soon. The timing of Swift's return, amid a political climate and ongoing feuds, has made the speculation even more intense.

When a 10-mile stretch of Los Angeles's Interstate 405 is closed this weekend, the city is preparing for a potential traffic disaster dubbed "Carmageddon." The closure, part of a $1 billion widening project, will last 53 hours and begin at midnight on Friday, closing a major artery that connects the San Fernando Valley with the Los Angeles shoreline. The California Department of Transportation plans to partially demolish a bridge to create a new lane for high-occupancy vehicles. Officials fear the shutdown will overwhelm smaller highways and surface streets, cutting off the San Fernando Valley from communities like Santa Monica and Venice. The event has sparked a flurry of business deals and creative solutions to cope with the anticipated gridlock. Local merchants are offering discounts and special deals, hoping to lure customers away from their homes. For instance, Kim Rodgers, co-owner of Bark Pet Photography, is offering 20% off pet portraits to those stuck at home. T-Man Tattoo is providing 15% off any piercing or tattoo, and Lance Strumpf's Briles Wing & Helicopter is offering a "Fly Over the 405" deal for $150, allowing passengers to view the traffic from above. Meanwhile, businesses are offering various discounts and deals, such as free rides at the Santa Monica Pier and special "Caltrans Orange" cotton candy. Despite the potential for chaos, the closure has also brought about some unexpected benefits, like lower diamond prices at Fifth Generation Readers Fine Jewelers. However, many businesses remain concerned that the deals won't be enough to offset the economic impact of the shutdown. The 405 Freeway has a long history of serving as a critical link in the region's transportation network, with its origins dating back to the 18th century. Over the years, it has evolved from a horse trail to a four-lane boulevard and eventually to the eight-lane freeway it is today. The project to widen the 405 is part of a larger effort to address the region's ongoing traffic challenges, but the upcoming closure has reignited fears of a major traffic catastrophe. As Angelenos prepare for the weekend, the hope is that this "Carmageddon" will be a temporary inconvenience rather than a permanent nightmare.

Occupy Wall Street protesters on Thursday marked the two-month anniversary of their movement with a citywide day of demonstrations, testing both the movement's resilience and the city's ability to handle decentralized protests. The day began with a plan to disrupt the New York Stock Exchange, resulting in hundreds of arrests and sporadic violence. At Zuccotti Park, police clashed with protesters, arresting 242 people, including five for assault, and injuring 10, with seven officers also hurt. The NYPD reported that protesters had deliberately pursued violence, but Mayor Bloomberg stated that most protesters had acted responsibly. Protesters attempted to shut down the stock exchange by surrounding it, leading to a confrontation with police. At Zuccotti Park, a man named Brandon Watts was arrested after allegedly throwing batteries and a pen at officers and attempting to knock down metal barricades. The day also saw protests on the Brooklyn Bridge, with City Councilman Jumaane Williams among those arrested. Demonstrators chanted "Whose bridge? Our bridge?" as cars honked in support. The movement's efforts to disrupt Wall Street operations were met with mixed results, as the stock exchange opened on schedule. Throughout the day, protesters faced challenges from law enforcement, with some using creative tactics to avoid arrest, while others, like a disabled woman, were arrested despite their intentions. The day highlighted the ongoing tension between the Occupy Wall Street movement and authorities, as well as the determination of protesters to continue their cause despite the challenges.

On Saturday, February 17, a man camping at Little Harbor Campground on Catalina Island was unexpectedly gored by a bison, sustaining injuries that required immediate medical attention. According to Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department Sgt. Ray Ward, the incident unfolded around 5:15 p.m. when the man was sitting on a log, and a bison, which was grazing nearby, suddenly charged and gored him in the left arm. Sgt. Ward noted that bison are common and freely roam the back side of Catalina Island, where the campground is located. However, he emphasized that such attacks are extremely rare, as people often forget that bison are wild despite their seemingly domesticated appearance. The man was treated at the scene by Los Angeles Fire Department officials and was later airlifted to Harbor-UCLA Medical Center for further care. Details about the nature and extent of his injuries were not immediately available.

A judge in North Carolina is currently deciding whether to grant a new trial for the man convicted of murdering basketball legend Michael Jordan's father, James Jordan. The case, which took place in March 1996, saw Daniel Green sentenced to life in prison for the murder. Green's co-defendant, Larry Martin Demery, testified that he and Green planned to rob James Jordan, and that Green shot him after the victim awoke from a nap and saw the two men outside his car. Green's legal team, Scott Holmes and Ian Mance, have now filed a motion for a new trial, presenting new evidence that they claim could exonerate their client. This evidence includes a sworn statement from the jury forewoman in the original trial, who claims she conducted her own investigation into the murder, which was against the judge's orders. Additionally, a former newspaper editor from Robeson County, North Carolina, has provided a sworn affidavit stating that Demery admitted to committing the murder. The defense also challenges the forensic evidence presented by the state, specifically questioning the presence of James Jordan's blood in Green's car. The state of North Carolina has until the end of April to respond to the motion, after which Judge Robert Floyd will make a decision on whether to grant a new trial. The outcome of this case could potentially lead to a re-evaluation of the conviction for the murder of Michael Jordan's father, and could have significant implications for the case's history and the justice system's handling of such cases.

The death of internationally renowned hairdresser Fabio Sementilli, 49, in his Woodland Hills home on January 23, 2017, has shocked the beauty industry. Sementilli, who served as vice president of education for Wella and Coty Inc., was found dead on the patio of his gated home in the 5000 block of Queen Victoria Road, with multiple stab wounds to his neck and upper torso. Paramedics arrived shortly after 5 p.m. to find him bleeding profusely and pronounced him dead at the scene. His 2008 black Porsche 911 Carrera, with paper license plates, was missing from the property. Homicide detectives are investigating the case, with initial reports suggesting a break-in and the theft of the car. Sementilli's wife and daughters discovered his body, leading to a somber scene in the upscale neighborhood. His death has left a devastated family and thousands of professional hairdressers worldwide in mourning. Sementilli was known for his mentorship and positive impact on the industry, with colleagues recalling his dedication and generosity. His passing has prompted a renewed focus on his legacy and the support he provided to aspiring stylists. The case remains under investigation, with detectives seeking any information that may help solve the mystery.

Former Rhode Island Governor Lincoln Chafee, a struggling Democratic presidential candidate, officially ended his campaign on Friday. Chafee, who had been advocating for "Prosperity Through Peace," decided to drop out after a "good week" for Hillary Clinton. During this period, former Virginia Senator Jim Webb withdrew from the race, Vice President Joe Biden declined to run, and Clinton withstood intense questioning at the Benghazi hearing. Chafee's decision came after a disappointing performance in the Democratic presidential debate, where he struggled to make a compelling case for his candidacy. The announcement was made at the Democratic National Committee’s Women’s Leadership Forum, where Chafee expressed his intention to continue advocating for peace but acknowledged the long odds against his campaign's success.

The first vice-presidential debate between Joe Biden and Paul Ryan is set to take place on Thursday night in Danville, Kentucky, with high stakes for both candidates. Biden, who has been criticized for his gaffes, is preparing to mount a strong attack on Romney, particularly on Romney's comments about the 47% of Americans who pay no income taxes. Biden's campaign hopes that a robust performance could help shift the momentum of the race slightly back toward Obama. Meanwhile, Ryan and his team are working to ensure a strong showing, aiming to present a clear contrast to Biden and the Obama administration. The debate is expected to be a crucial moment in the campaign, potentially influencing voter perceptions and momentum.

Five key areas to watch include:
1. **Biden's Aggressive Approach**: Biden is expected to be more aggressive than Obama was in the previous debate, aiming to highlight Romney's policies and past statements. His campaign believes he should take the offensive to counter Romney's passive performance. Biden's team hopes he will effectively draw contrasts, particularly on issues like Medicare and tax policy, which are crucial for battleground states.
   
2. **Ryan's Wonkiness**: Ryan is known for his detailed, numbers-driven approach, which can be both an asset and a liability. His debate prep is meticulous, but there's concern that he might get bogged down in complex policy discussions. Ryan must balance presenting his ideas clearly with avoiding the appearance of being too academic or disconnected from voters.

3. **Social Security**: Biden might try to raise the issue of Social Security privatization, which has been a key Democratic talking point. However, Obama appeared to downplay this issue in the previous debate, suggesting that Biden's strategy could face challenges.

4. **Age Gap**: Biden, at 69, is significantly older than Ryan, 42. This age difference could be exploited by both sides, with Biden potentially using it to highlight his experience and Ryan's inexperience. The debate will likely play into broader themes of continuity versus change.

5. **Ryan's Presidential Qualifications**: Ryan needs to demonstrate his readiness to assume the presidency, should something happen to Romney. His role as House Budget Committee chairman and his command of fiscal issues are seen as key assets. However, some strategists argue that the pressure to prove readiness is less significant given the relatively young age of both candidates.

The debate is not just about the candidates but also about their broader campaigns. Biden's performance could bolster the Democratic base, while Ryan's success could reinforce the Republican narrative. The outcome could have significant implications for the overall race, potentially shifting voter perceptions and momentum.

On a bleak February day in 1944, a French gendarme's actions in the eastern French village of Gemeaux inadvertently preserved a poignant reminder of a tragic past. Two Jewish sisters, Denise and Micheline Lévy, aged 10 and 9, were about to be deported to Auschwitz when a gendarme snatched a pair of dolls from them, flinging them to the ground. The sisters, along with their parents, grandparents, an aunt and uncle, a cousin, and other Jewish families, were lined up in the snow, a scene that would soon be etched in history. However, the gendarme's abrupt and seemingly accidental act of defiance left the dolls behind, a small act of defiance in a sea of tragedy.

For three generations, the dolls remained in the village, cared for by a family who kept the story of the Lévy sisters and their family alive. Frédérique Gilles, a teacher from Gemeaux, whose grandmother carefully preserved the dolls, recently presented them to the Holocaust museum in Paris, the Shoah Memorial. The pink and blue dolls, now symbols of resilience and memory, were given a new home, ensuring that the story of the Lévy sisters and their family would not be forgotten. The act of the gendarme, though brief, became a moment of humanity amidst the horrors of the Holocaust, a small gesture that inadvertently preserved a piece of history. The dolls, now in the Shoah Memorial, serve as a testament to the enduring memory of those who perished and a reminder of the importance of remembering the past to prevent its recurrence.

During their season-opener against Fresno State, Nebraska honored its late punter, Sam Foltz, who was killed in a car crash in July. In a poignant moment, the team came out with 10 men in punt formation without a punter, clapping and cheering to remember Foltz and former Michigan State punter Mike Sadler, who also died in the crash. After a minute, they punted the ball away, taking a delay of game penalty. Foltz, the Big Ten Punter of the Year last season, led the conference with 44.2 yards per punt and was on the Ray Guy watch list for the nation's best punter. The gesture highlighted the team's deep respect and admiration for their fallen teammate.

The film "Show Dogs," starring Ludacris and Will Arnett, has faced backlash and subsequent re-editing due to scenes perceived as promoting sexual abuse. The production company, Global Road Entertainment, decided to remove two scenes after concerns from parents and advocacy groups that the film sent inappropriate messages to children. These scenes involved the main character, Max the Rottweiler, having his testicles inspected by dog show judges, a process that made him uncomfortable. Parents, such as Terina Maldonado, compared these scenes to grooming tactics used by sexual predators. The National Center for Sexual Exploitation also criticized the film, stating that it normalizes unwanted genital touching and endorses a confusing message to children. In response, Global Road Entertainment released a statement apologizing for any inappropriate message and clarified that the scenes were depicted accurately as common practice in dog shows. The company stated that the film was "heavily rewritten" by 13 other writers, with Max Botkin, one of the main writers, denying involvement in the rewrites. Despite this, the film will be re-released with the revised version available this weekend. Botkin expressed his condemnation of non-consensual touching and understanding of the parents' concerns. The controversy highlights the importance of maintaining high standards in children's entertainment and teaching children about bodily autonomy and safety.

While "American Sniper" has been a massive box office success, generating record-breaking opening weekend numbers and six Oscar nominations, including best picture and best actor for Bradley Cooper, the film has sparked controversy among some Hollywood figures for its perceived pro-war stance. Seth Rogen, whose comedy often challenges societal norms, tweeted that the film reminded him of a Nazi sniper scene from Quentin Tarantino's "Inglourious Basterds," comparing it to Nazi propaganda. Rogen later clarified that he actually liked the film but found the comparison relevant. Director Michael Moore, known for his anti-war stance, also weighed in, tweeting that snipers are cowards and that invaders are worse. Moore, who famously criticized the Iraq War in his 2003 Oscar acceptance speech, later tweeted a lengthy explanation on his Facebook page, praising Cooper's performance and the film's anti-war sentiment but criticizing Eastwood for conflating Vietnam and Iraq in the story and for characters calling Iraqis "savages." Moore's comments came as the film was enjoying unprecedented success, grossing over $100 million in its opening weekend. Despite the controversy, Jane Fonda, who was once protested for her anti-Vietnam stance, supported the film, tweeting that it was "powerful" and that Cooper and Eastwood did a "sensational" job. The film, based on the life of Navy SEAL Chris Kyle, who served four tours in Iraq and was called the most lethal sniper in U.S. military history, aims to provide insight into the lives of soldiers and their families, according to Bradley Cooper. The film's success and critical acclaim have drawn attention to the ongoing debate over the portrayal of war and its impact on public perception.

Russell Armstrong, the estranged husband of "The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" star Taylor Armstrong, was found dead in an apparent suicide in his Los Angeles home. The news was first reported by TMZ, and the coroner is still conducting an investigation. Armstrong's friend Tom Vickers told RadarOnline that Armstrong was "down in the dumps over the latest allegations that he had abused Taylor" and blamed reality TV for ruining his life. The couple's relationship had been rocky, with Taylor filing for divorce on July 15, citing irreconcilable differences. In an interview with People magazine, Russell admitted, "Did I push her? Yes, maybe things happened in the heat of the moment, but it was during a time in our lives that was not characteristic of who we were. This show has literally pushed us to the limit." Industry insiders say that reality TV often exaggerates conflicts and can put participants under immense pressure. Armstrong leaves behind a daughter, Kennedy, and two sons from a previous relationship. The second season of "The Real Housewives of Beverly Hills" was scheduled to premiere on September 5, but a decision had not been made on whether the season would be postponed or episodes re-edited. Through her manager, Taylor Armstrong issued a statement, saying she was "devastated by the tragic events that have unfolded" and requesting privacy.

A disturbing new study has linked a common chemical found in head lice treatments to behavioral difficulties in children. The research, published in the journal Occupational & Environmental Medicine, found that children with higher levels of certain pyrethroids—synthetic chemicals used in insecticides like head lice treatments and some mosquito repellents—in their system were more likely to display abnormal behaviors at age 6 than those who didn’t. Pyrethroids work by damaging the nerves of insects, killing them in the process, and scientists wanted to see if they had a negative impact on children as well. For the study, the researchers measured levels of five pyrethroid metabolites in the urine of women in the early stages of pregnancy and, later, in their 6-year-olds to see if there was a link between being exposed to the chemical in utero and childhood, and behavior that could suggest neurodevelopmental damage. Nearly 300 women filled out a questionnaire about socioeconomic factors, lifestyle, their child’s behavior, and various things their child had been exposed to. Psychologists visited the families at home to do behavioral assessments of the children, and also took urine and dust samples. Behavior was rated using the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire, a validated behavioral screening test for children, with a focus on altruism (how social children are), internalizing disorders (the inability to share problems and ask for help), and externalizing disorders (being defiant and disruptive). Three of the pyrethroid metabolites showed up most often in the urine of mothers and their children: trans-DCCA, cis-DBCA, and cis-DCCA. Here’s what researchers determined: Mothers with higher levels of cis-DCCA in their urine during pregnancy were more likely to have children with a higher risk of internalizing behaviors. Higher levels of another metabolite, 3-PBA, in the children’s urine were linked with a higher risk of externalizing behaviors. Overall, children with the highest levels of metabolites in their urine were three times more likely to have abnormal behavior than those with lower levels. As a result, the researchers concluded that pyrethroids might alter neurochemical signaling in the brain. The news is understandably disturbing for parents who have treated their children with pyrethroids for lice— and there are a lot of them. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that up to 12 million head lice infestations happen each year among children aged 3 to 11. Lice are parasites that live in human hair, eyelashes, and eyebrows and feed on the blood of their host, and they’re not easy pests to get rid of. Hence, the common use of chemical shampoos and treatments for lice infestations—many of which contain pyrethroids. Before you panic, know this: The study found that there was a correlation between pyrethroids and behavioral issues in children—not a causation. That means they determined that children who have behavioral issues also have high levels of certain pyrethroids in their system, but didn’t actually find that using pyrethroids causes behavioral problems in children. “The findings should be considered preliminary and prompt more rigorous studies,” Amesh A. Adalja, MD, a board-certified infectious disease physician and affiliated scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security, tells Yahoo Beauty. Shahrouz Ganjian, MD, a board certified pediatrician at Providence Saint John’s Health Center in Santa Monica, Calif., tells Yahoo Beauty that he’s not shocked by the findings. “In the past 15 years, there’s been a lot more research that has found pesticide exposure is linked to ADHD in boys and pediatric cancer,” he says. The study that found a link between ADHD and pesticides was published in the journal Environmental Health. It found a link between pyrethroid pesticide exposure and ADHD, particularly in the areas of hyperactivity and impulsivity. While girls were affected, the link was stronger in boys. However, this was also a correlational study. Pyrethroids are among the most common treatments for lice, but other compounds can be used, like alcohol-based treatments and an anti-parasitic drug called ivermectin, Adalja says. However, pyrethroids are “the main recommended treatments for lice,” he adds. Ganjian also recommends Sklice lice treatment, which doesn’t contain pyrethroids and Licefreee, which he calls “more natural.”

Cigarette smoke, long known for its harmful effects, now faces a new accusation: it fuels the virulent spread of superbugs, particularly MRSA. According to a study published in the journal Infection and Immunity, researchers from the University of California, San Diego School of Medicine found that MRSA bacteria exposed to cigarette smoke become significantly more resistant to the body's immune defenses. Pulmonologist Dr. Laura E. Crotty Alexander led the study, which tested MRSA's response to cigarette smoke extract in human cells and whole mice. The findings revealed that smoke-exposed MRSA were four times more resistant to macrophage killing and more resistant to antimicrobial peptides. Moreover, the smoke-exposed bacteria adhered better to human cells, enhancing their invasion capabilities. The study highlighted that the effects persisted for 24 hours post-exposure, suggesting potential inheritance. Notably, the smoke-exposed MRSA were more lethal to mice, underscoring the increased risk they pose. The research also compared the effects of e-cigarette vapor, finding it less impactful than cigarette smoke. Dr. Crotty Alexander emphasized that cigarette smoke not only harms smokers but also assists pathogens in becoming more resilient. This dual threat presents a compelling reason to discourage smoking, as it exacerbates the already severe health risks associated with MRSA infections. The study's implications extend beyond individual health, potentially influencing public health policies and strategies to combat antibiotic-resistant bacteria.

A newborn boy survived after being tossed into a trash can in Greenville, South Carolina, and was listed as stable Monday night, police said. Sharon Lenise Ferguson, 28, was charged with attempted murder and child abandonment and arrested after the baby was found about 4:30 p.m. ET in the family's backyard. Ferguson had wrapped the baby in a pink blanket and placed him in a plastic grocery bag before putting him in a trash can. The baby was discovered by a neighbor who followed a trail of blood to the trash can. Emergency crews treated the newborn at the scene, and by Monday night, he was reported to be stable. Ferguson remained in the Greenville County jail on a $125,000 cash bond. A Department of Social Services official said the newborn was now in foster care. Ferguson told investigators she gave birth on April 21 and abandoned the baby. Neighbors described Ferguson as having unusual behavior and being homeless, but said they did not believe she would intentionally harm the baby. Ferguson has a diagnosed mental illness and her family did not know she was pregnant. A family spokesperson plans to ask for the attempted murder charge to be downgraded.

Sen. David Perdue (R-Ga.) sparked controversy at a conservative Christian event when he quoted a passage from Psalms 109, suggesting prayers for President Barack Obama's days to be "few" and another to take his office. Perdue, speaking at the Faith and Freedom Coalition’s “Road to Majority” event, joked, "We should pray like Psalms 109:8 says. It says, 'Let his days be few, and let another have his office.'" The first-term senator's office clarified that he was not wishing harm on the president, but critics, including Democratic Senate Minority Leader Harry Reid's spokeswoman, Kristen Orthman, accused Perdue of wishing for Obama’s death. Perdue’s use of the imprecatory psalm, which is traditionally a prayer for divine retribution, drew criticism from both sides of the political spectrum. The passage, which includes harsh curses on the psalmist’s enemy, has a long history of being used by conservatives to express their dissatisfaction with Obama. The controversy highlights the delicate balance between political discourse and religious expression in American politics.

New Jersey Governor Chris Christie is poised to make a decision on whether to enter the 2016 presidential race, a move that could be complicated by the looming political calendar and the challenges of launching a late campaign. Christie, who has been weighing his options, spent much of the weekend consulting with his aides and family, according to sources close to his inner circle. Despite not directly addressing questions from reporters, Christie attended an event honoring the New Jersey National Guard on Sunday afternoon. His decision could have significant implications for the Republican primary race, as he is seen as a formidable candidate with a strong organizational base. However, concerns within his close circle about the tight schedule and the difficulties of mounting a last-minute campaign effort are reportedly influencing his deliberations. As Christie's decision approaches, political operatives and insiders are closely watching his move, with some expressing uncertainty about the timing and strategy of a potential late entry. The governor's announcement could reshape the dynamics of the Republican primary, potentially altering the landscape for other candidates and their supporters.

The closure of a neighborhood bar in Molenbeek, Brussels, due to drug dealing and smoking, has raised questions about the transformation of its owners from seemingly ordinary individuals to suicide bombers. Brahim Abdeslam, 31, who ran the bar Les Beguines, and his younger brother Salah, now Europe's most wanted man, have become central figures in the investigation into the Paris attacks. The brothers' journey from running a marijuana-scented beer joint to becoming suicide bombers remains a mystery, with their neighbors describing them as regular guys who enjoyed a laugh and smoked. The closure notice, posted on the bar's door, revealed that the premises had been used for drug consumption and smoking. The brothers sold the business just six weeks before the Paris attacks, with Salah taking over as manager. Legal documents show that Brahim, a French citizen, formed the company in March 2013, while Salah, who has the nom de guerre Abu Omar al-Belgiki, was previously linked to a robbery conviction. Belgian media have described Molenbeek as a "breeding ground for radical violence," suffering from high youth unemployment and overcrowding. The area has been associated with plots including the 2004 Madrid bombing and the 2014 Jewish Museum shooting. Brahim's suicide attack at the Comptoir Voltaire in Paris injured several people, while Salah was reportedly seen in a Volkswagen car near the Bataclan with Belgian plates. Mohammed, Salah's brother, was released after two days in custody, stating that his family was in shock and had no idea about Brahim's involvement or Salah's whereabouts. The case highlights the complex transformation of individuals from ordinary lives to violent extremism, with the brothers' activities and background raising questions about their radicalization process and the role of their neighborhood in this phenomenon.

The House passed legislation on Friday that allows insurance companies to offer health plans that were cancelled for not meeting new requirements under ObamaCare. Thirty-nine Democrats broke with their party's leaders and backed the bill despite a veto threat by the White House, highlighting the political problem the issue has come for President Obama’s party. Only four Republicans opposed it. The House approved the "Keep Your Health Plan Act" in a 261-157 vote. Obama on Thursday announced he would take executive action that would allow insurance companies to offer the old plans for an additional year. That likely prevented a larger wave of Democratic votes in favor of the bill sponsored by Rep. Fred Upton (R-Mich.). The vote is a further blow to Obama, who was forced on Thursday to admit that new standards under the healthcare law are forcing millions of people into new and often more expensive health insurance plans.
