Obama repeatedly said that under ObamaCare people could keep their plans if they liked them. Most of the Democrats who defected from their party face tough reelection campaigns next year. Republicans have promised the 2014 midterm elections will be all about the healthcare law, which polls show is unpopular. The House vote also puts immediate pressure on Senate Democratic leaders to take action. Seven Senate Democrats have backed a bill that would require insurers to offer the cancelled plans. During debate on the House bill, Upton accused Obama of knowing that his signature law would force millions of people out of plans they liked. He said Obama's promise that “if you like your healthcare plan, you can keep it” would go down in history as a line people forever associate with Obama. “For last three years, the president repeated this promise in selling his signature law, and he did so with the knowledge it would not be met,” Upton said. Upton and other Republicans also accused Obama of once again using administrative procedures to fix ObamaCare, when he should be working with Congress. “For the last six weeks, the White House stood idly by, ignore the pleas of millions,” he said. “But as the administration's allies in Congress panicked, the White House went from attacking our thoughtful bill to making an end-run around Congress with a universal fix."” Others noted that Obama continues to refuse legislative fixes to the law, even as he makes administrative fixes. Rep. Michael Burgess (R-Texas) said Congress has no reason to trust that Obama will put the change into effect. “Can we really trust the administration that wrote this disastrous missive in the first place, and so mishandled the implementation, do we trust them to now fix it?” he asked. “Do we trust them not to change their minds in two or three weeks time, when perhaps winds are blowing from a different direction?” House Majority Leader Eric Cantor (R-Va.) agreed that Obama’s promise is now “a promise he has broken,” and said Obama's plan raises too many questions. “The White House doesn't even know how they're going to implement the plan they announced yesterday,” Cantor said. “This proposal that we're talking about here… aims to help Americans keep their health insurance and give their neighbors a chance to buy the same plans, rather than forcing them onto a faulty website to buy new coverage they may not like or cannot afford.” Obama's proposal was to allow state insurance commissioners to allow soon-to-be canceled health plans to be sold for another year, or possibly longer. Upton's bill would allow people to have permanent access to these plans. That prompted Democrats to argue that Upton's bill would drastically undermine ObamaCare, since it would let people keep what they say are substandard plans, and let them avoid buying new plans under the ObamaCare exchanges. “This one on the floor today really takes the cake, because it [would], essentially, pull the plug on the Affordable Care Act,” said Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.). Rep. Rob Andrews (D-N.J.) explained the problem by equating the canceled plans to old cars without modern safety features, and said allowing these plans to exist would make ObamaCare unworkable. “If anyone who wants to can buy one of these cars without an air bag, or cars without seat belts — and that's what these plans are — then you will find that the new marketplaces don't have enough people in them,” he said. “And when they don't have enough people in them, the rates will rise.” House Energy & Commerce Committee ranking member Henry Waxman (D-Calif.) said this would allow a “shadow market” of old plans to undermine ObamaCare plans. But Republicans said that “shadow market” is just another term for the market that sells more affordable plans that people want. “It's forcing people to choose healthcare they do not want, cannot afford, and isn't right for themselves and their families,” said House Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy (R-Calif.). Just before the final vote, Democrats tried to substitute Upton's bill with a Democratic alternative that would extend canceled plans for just a year, similar to Obama's time-limited administrative fix. But the GOP-led House was able to kill that proposal by raising a point of order against it, which argued the Democratic alternative was not germane. That was upheld in a 229-191 vote to turn away the Democratic appeal of that ruling. With their first attempt ruled out of order, Democrats tried again with an amended proposal, but this was also turned away in a 187-230 vote. The proposal goes further than the administrative fix announced by President Obama Thursday, which would only allow insurers and state insurance commissioners to extend those policies through most of 2014. It faces an uphill climb in the Senate and Obama has said he would veto the bill. But both efforts, as well as another crafted by Democrats in the Senate, are aimed at addressing the same issue: The political backlash over letters received by millions of Americans whose private health insurance policies are being canceled because of the health-care law. Republicans have seized on the letters, as well as promises by President Obama that “if you like your health plan, you can keep it,” as evidence that the health-care law is flawed and that the president has not been honest about its downsides. “We knew this was a promise [Obama] could not keep, and now it is a promise he has broken,” House Majority Leader Eric Cantor (R-Va.) said in floor remarks. But the remarkable support from Democrats underscored the widespread political ramifications of Obama’s broken promise. The bill’s co-sponsors included more than 80 Republicans and three swing-district Democrats facing tough reelection contests next year: Reps. John Barrow (Ga.), Mike McIntyre (N.C.) and Patrick Murphy (Fla.). Nervous about other potential defections, Democratic leaders dispatched several senior aides in the hours before the vote, and were seen and heard at one point talking about the vote in the hallways outside the House Chamber with Reps. Brad Schneider (D-Ill.) and Dan Maffiei (D-N.Y.), two freshmen who won tight races last year. Both ended up voted in favor of the legislation.

Facebook has launched its App Center, a centralized platform for discovering and accessing a wide range of mobile applications across various platforms, including iOS, Android, and the web. The App Center aims to enhance user engagement by offering personalized app recommendations based on users' and their friends' activity on the social network. With over 600 apps available, including popular titles like Pinterest, Draw Something, and Nike+, the App Center promises to expand Facebook's role as a key entertainment and utility platform. Users can access the App Center through the Facebook app on mobile devices or via the website, where they can explore categories such as games, entertainment, music, and news. The platform leverages user data and friend activity to provide tailored suggestions, making it easier for users to find and download apps that align with their interests. Additionally, the App Center facilitates seamless integration by allowing users to send app links directly to their mobile devices, streamlining the app discovery and installation process. While the App Center is currently available to US users, it will gradually expand to include all of Facebook's 901 million users. The move reflects Facebook's strategic focus on mobile apps and its ambition to become a central hub for app distribution, potentially generating significant revenue through app downloads and in-app purchases. Despite the App Center's potential, some critics argue that it may contribute to a "walled garden" approach, limiting the diversity and openness of the app ecosystem.

A series of disturbing incidents at St. Michael’s College School, a prestigious private all-boys Catholic school in Toronto, has led to the arrest of six students and the expulsion of eight others. The school, known for its strong sports programs and alumni, including National Hockey League players, has faced a severe crisis after a video depicting a sexual assault was posted online. Police arrested six students, aged 14 and 15, charging them with assault, gang sexual assault, and sexual assault with a weapon. The incident, captured in a 22-second video, shows a teen boy being held down in a locker room and allegedly assaulted with a broomstick. The school’s principal, Gregory Reeves, acknowledged the seriousness of the situation, stating, “These incidents are clearly indicative we have a problem. We need to do much better at our culture and our students' ability to talk to us.” St. Michael’s College School has expelled eight students and suspended another in connection with at least two other incidents captured on video. The school has initiated an independent investigation into the underlying attitudes and behaviors that may have contributed to these incidents. The investigation, led by a three-member independent committee, will examine the school’s traditions, rituals, and social practices, with recommendations to be implemented by the start of the 2019-20 school year. Meanwhile, the school is facing scrutiny over its handling of the initial video, which was only reported to police after it was shared on social media. Principal Reeves defended the delay, stating that his focus was on protecting the victim, but the school’s response has been criticized for its tardiness. The incident has sparked a broader conversation about the culture and practices within private schools and the importance of immediate reporting of such incidents to authorities. The school’s actions and the community’s response highlight the ongoing challenges in addressing and preventing such behaviors in educational institutions.

The New York Jets secured their first playoff victory in five years with a 24-14 win over the Cincinnati Bengals, advancing to the AFC divisional round. Rookie quarterback Mark Sanchez and his teammates, dubbed the "Cincinnati Kids," delivered a strong performance, overcoming an early 7-0 deficit and maintaining turnover-free football. Coach Rex Ryan, emotional after the win, honored team owner Woody Johnson, who had recently lost his daughter. Ryan's confident predictions about the Jets' potential were vindicated, and the team faces either the Colts or Chargers next, with the opponent determined by today's Patriots-Ravens game. Sanchez, praised for his play, became the fourth rookie quarterback in NFL history to win a playoff game. Despite the victory, the Jets remain focused, with linebacker Calvin Pace declaring there is "no ceiling" for their advancement.

Michigan Governor Rick Snyder apologized for the Flint water crisis during his State of the State address, promising to take full responsibility for fixing the "catastrophe" that has affected the town. Snyder called the situation a crisis that no citizen should have to endure and vowed to release all of his emails from 2014 and 2015 regarding Flint to the public. He outlined immediate actions taken in response, including daily door-to-door distribution of bottled water, water filters, filter replacements, and water testing kits, which have visited over 21,000 homes. Snyder also proposed a $28 million budget to fund various initiatives such as replacing fixtures in schools, treating children with high lead levels, providing additional support for children’s health, and conducting infrastructure integrity studies. He emphasized that Michigan will not let Flint down and that individuals responsible for the crisis will be held accountable. However, critics argue that the $28 million is insufficient, with Flint Mayor Karen Weaver estimating the costs to undo the damage could be between $1 billion and $1.5 billion. Protesters gathered outside Snyder's apartment, calling for his resignation. Snyder acknowledged that the state failed to prevent the crisis and broke the trust of Flint residents. The crisis began in April 2014 when Flint switched its water source to the Flint River to save money, leading to lead contamination due to improperly treated water. The state's Department of Environmental Quality failed to treat the water for corrosion, in violation of federal law. As a result, residents faced health issues, and the state is now providing filters and bottled water with the help of the National Guard. Flint residents continue to demand accountability and financial aid, highlighting the ongoing public health emergency.

In a case that has captivated Indonesian media and public attention, Wayan Mirna Salihin, 27, a newlywed, died after drinking a cyanide-laced iced coffee with her friends Jessica Kumala Wongso and Hani at a Jakarta cafe on January 6. The Indonesian police have arrested Wongso, who denies any involvement in the death, and named her as a suspect. The police have gathered around 20 witness statements, including evidence from experts, and conducted a re-enactment of the incident. Chief Detective Krishna Murti stated that Jessica's statement is inconsistent with the facts they have gathered and that they will confirm whether her statement as a suspect is still consistent with her one as a witness or if she will give another statement. The case has drawn attention due to the involvement of Australian universities, as Mirna and her friends studied together at Sydney’s Billy Blue College of Design and Swinburne University of Technology. The Australian Federal Police (AFP) is assisting the Indonesian police in investigating the relationship between Mirna and her friends. Mirna’s uncle, Yudi Wibowo, has questioned the autopsy process and denied rumors of a love triangle between his client and Mirna’s husband, Arief Soemarko. The AFP is considering the request by Jakarta police for assistance, as they seek to uncover the truth behind Mirna’s suspicious death. The police have also taken SR, Wongso’s servant, into police protection as a key witness, as she is believed to have disposed of Wongso’s ripped pants after Mirna’s death at Wongso’s request. The case is ongoing, with the police planning to hold a case expose before prosecutors on Tuesday, where investigators will present evidence and information from three experts involved in the investigation.

Cardinal Jorge Mario Bergoglio, known as Pope Francis, emerged as the clear front-runner in the first round of voting before the conclave to elect a new pope. His election was confirmed on the fifth ballot, with 77 votes, surpassing the required two-thirds majority. Carlo Marroni, a Vatican correspondent for Il Sole 24 Ore, reported that Bergoglio, Cardinal Scola, and Cardinal Marc Ouellet of Canada were the leading candidates. Private conversations and informal chats in the evening helped focus the cardinals on Bergoglio, according to analysts. Ignazio Ingrao, a Vatican expert for Panorama, noted that while Cardinal Scola initially had a strong block of support, including many Americans and Europeans, his candidacy faltered due to opposition from Cardinal Tarcisio Bertone, the powerful secretary of state under Benedict. The final tally was kept secret, but sources indicated that Bergoglio's age of 76, while unexpected, did not significantly impact the decision. Some cardinals believed his age would motivate him to act quickly, while others hoped for a shorter papacy. The choice of Francis was historic, making him the first pope from the Americas and the first from a continent other than Europe in over a millennium. His election stunned many, as few predicted he would be chosen to replace Pope Benedict XVI. The conclave process involved private meetings and voting, with support for other candidates waning as Bergoglio's candidacy strengthened. His humility and focus on reform were key factors in his selection. Upon his election, Francis declined an elevated throne, instead joining the cardinals on a bus back to their residence. His simple speech and silent prayer on the St. Peter's Basilica balcony, and his return to his hotel to pay the bill, showcased his down-to-earth style. Many cardinals praised his ability to inspire action and his potential to bring unity to the church.

Rep. Anthony Weiner faces a new, potentially damaging development in the ongoing scandal. Conservative activist Andrew Breitbart, who first reported the crotch photo sent from Weiner's Twitter account, now threatens to release an even more explicit image as a form of insurance against any future retaliation from the congressman. Breitbart told NBC's "Today" show that he considers the image "an insurance policy" to protect himself from any potential backlash. The married Democrat has admitted to inappropriate contact with six women over three years through social networking sites. This latest twist could significantly worsen the situation for Weiner, as the fully uncensored photo, though not shown on television, will likely spread widely online, potentially sealing his political fate. The image's availability on the internet could engage more people in the scandal, intensifying public scrutiny and pressure on Weiner.

Nashua police believe they have found the body of Jacob Goulet, a 16-year-old missing teen who was feared to have fallen down a storm drain during a storm on Friday night. The body was discovered in the Merrimack River in Tyngsboro on Sunday, according to Nashua police. Jacob’s parents reported him missing around 8:48 a.m. on Saturday after he failed to return home from a friend’s house on Friday night. His family and friends had been searching for him, including by yelling into storm drains throughout the city. Jacob is described as 5 feet 8 inches tall, weighing around 200 pounds, with short, black hair on the sides and longer hair on top, and wearing a denim vest with metal studs, a gray T-shirt, black shorts, and black Converse All-Star sneakers. Nashua police stated that the body appears to be Jacob’s, but a positive identification will be made by the Massachusetts Medical Examiner’s Office. Jacob might have fallen down the storm drain near 75 Main St. in Nashua during the storm on Friday evening. Nashua police believe he could have ended up in the river through the overflow of water through the system following the storm. The storm drain in question is described as an "interceptor" that connects to the waste water treatment plant over several miles of pipeline. It is said to have a steep drop and could be 20 feet deep. Nashua officials are unsure how the cover came off the storm drain, and it is unclear if there was direct flow to the Merrimack River from the drain. The Nashua Fire Department, the city of Nashua Waste Water Department, the Division of Public Works, New Hampshire State Police, Massachusetts State Police, and New Hampshire Fish and Game assisted in the search. Nashua Mayor Jim Donchess said that approximately 1,000 feet of the sewer system had been searched as of Sunday afternoon. Goulet’s friends and family are reeling from the news, and Nashua North High School is providing grief counselors to support students. The community is shocked and grieving the loss of Jacob, who was described as a sweet boy with a great heart. A GoFundMe page has been set up to raise money for Goulet’s funeral costs, and as of Sunday evening, it had raised more than $3,000 toward a goal of $8,000.

Secretary of State John Kerry's offhand suggestion that Syria could avoid American military action by giving up its chemical weapons has created a diplomatic opportunity for President Obama, who has insisted that a military strike is the only way to respond to the alleged use of poison gas in the civil war. Russia, Syria’s arms supplier and ally, immediately embraced Kerry’s proposal and proposed that President Bashar al-Assad hand over his chemical weapons for international control and eventual destruction. The United Nations Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon and Britain’s Prime Minister David Cameron also supported the idea, showing the world’s eagerness to avoid a military showdown. While the Obama administration is skeptical of any promises from the Assad regime or its Russian backers, the proposal could offer a pause in the conflict and a path to a political settlement between Assad and the rebels. The removal and destruction of chemical weapons would ensure greater safety for the Syrian people and have longer-lasting deterrent effects than limited strikes. To have credibility, Assad must allow monitors into the country immediately, and the Russians must work closely with the United States and the United Nations to create a plan for cataloging and verifying Syria’s chemical weapons and setting a specific timetable for their removal and destruction under international auspices. Russia and the United States should propose a formal resolution by the United Nations Security Council to condemn the use of chemical weapons, support this plan, and establish consequences if Syria reneges. However, critics argue that this proposal is a dishonest ploy by Russia and Syria, designed to box in the United States and make any relief for Syria’s civil war far less likely. Michael Doran, a Middle East expert at the Brookings Institution, raises several concerns, including the likelihood that Assad will never truly relinquish his chemical weapons and the potential for the United States to be left in a difficult position if Assad cheats. Doran suggests that Obama should play the proposal aggressively, making serious demands for compliance, or pursue a more aggressive policy of arming the Free Syrian Army as an alternative to both al-Qaeda and the Assad regime. The diplomatic proposal could mean that the United States would not have to go it alone in standing firm against the Syrian regime, but it could also be a boon for Obama, personally, as he could take credit for pushing Syria and Russia into making this move.

Middlesex County Sheriff's Major Michael Sampson said it was too soon to determine if the disappearance of 23-year-old TerriLynn St. John, a mother of two, was an abduction, as the search for her extended into its second day. St. John was last seen around 7:30 a.m. Tuesday when she went to her car in her front yard, with family members believing there was a struggle. Her children, ages three and one, were found alone and unharmed in the home by their grandfather. Jewelry was broken off and her cellphone was found in the bushes. The search involved a K9 unit and air surveillance. Four persons of interest have been interviewed, and they have submitted DNA samples to investigators, who are testing the evidence at the crime lab in Richmond. Major Sampson said a person of interest could be an acquaintance, friend, or family member, including her boyfriend, who is also a person of interest. The community is being asked to call the Middlesex Sheriff's Office at 804-758-5600 with any information. Social media is being used to gather tips, but Major Sampson urged people to call the office directly instead. TerriLynn is described as a white female, 5'6" tall, 130 pounds, with blonde hair and blue eyes, and she was last seen wearing a blue Outer Banks hoodie. The search will resume Wednesday morning, with Virginia State Police on standby if needed. Family members are urging the community to come forward with any information that could help in the search.

State-linked Saudi news websites reported an explosion near the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, one of Islam's holiest sites, on Monday, as two suicide bombers struck in different cities without causing casualties. The explosion, reportedly caused by a suicide bomber near a security building outside the Prophet Muhammad's mosque, left several cars ablaze. Local media showed images of a fire outside a building overlooking the Prophet's Mosque, though it was unclear if anyone was injured. The sprawling mosque, visited by millions of Muslims during pilgrimages, was packed with worshippers for sunset prayers during the final days of Ramadan. The Interior Ministry could not immediately comment.

In a coordinated attack, a suicide bomber and a car bomb exploded near a Shiite mosque in the eastern Saudi Arabian city of Qatif, while another suicide bomber targeted the U.S. Consulate in Jiddah. The attack in Qatif did not result in any injuries, according to resident Mohammed al-Nimr, whose brother is a prominent Saudi Shiite cleric. Al-Nimr stated that the bomber detonated his explosives when most residents were breaking their fast, and a car bomb also went off around the same time. The attack in Qatif, heavily populated by Shiites, highlights the ongoing threat from extremist groups targeting minority communities.

The Islamic State group's local affiliates in Saudi Arabia have previously attacked Shiite places of worship, including a bombing in Qatif in May 2015 that killed 21 people. Earlier in the day, the Interior Ministry reported a suicide bomber detonating his explosives near the U.S. Consulate in Jiddah, killing a bomber and wounding two security guards. The attack on the U.S. Consulate came amid heightened security and a wave of Islamic State attacks targeting Westerners and Saudi security posts.

The U.S. Embassy in Saudi Arabia confirmed no casualties among consular staff and remained in contact with Saudi authorities. The Interior Ministry did not specify the bomber's nationality, stating that an investigation was underway. The attacks on the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, the second-holiest site in Islam, and the U.S. Consulate in Jiddah, a Western-allied institution, underscore the complex security challenges faced by the Saudi government.

King Salman of Saudi Arabia warned his country would respond with an "iron hand" against those preying on youth vulnerable to religious extremism during a speech marking Eid al-Fitr. The attacks, timed to coincide with the end of Ramadan, targeted U.S. diplomats, Shi'ite Muslim worshippers, and a security headquarters at a mosque in Medina. The U.N. human rights chief described the bombing outside the Prophet's Mosque as an "attack on Islam itself," highlighting the shock and concern among Muslims worldwide. The attacks, unprecedented for the city, reflect the ongoing threat from extremist groups targeting minority communities and Western interests in the region.

In an effort to boost voter turnout, The Philadelphia Citizen, co-founded by Larry Platt, is offering a $10,000 lottery to one lucky voter on Election Day. This initiative aims to address Philadelphia's historically low voter participation rates, with only 27% of registered voters participating in the May 2015 primary. Platt, along with the Pamela and Ajay Raju Foundation, which is providing the funds, argue that the scheme is legal and not a direct endorsement of any candidate. The lottery will randomly select a voter from all 1,686 voting divisions, with the winner receiving a surprise $10,000 check upon exiting the polling place. The plan also includes voter education efforts, such as encouraging people to familiarize themselves with candidates and even creating their own ballots. While some view the lottery as a creative and necessary approach, others criticize it as a gimmick that may demean the value of voting. The success of a similar program in Los Angeles, where voter turnout increased from 46% to 80%, offers hope that such a strategy could have a positive impact. However, the effectiveness of this method remains to be seen, especially given the limited awareness of the offer among the general public. The initiative highlights the ongoing challenge of civic engagement in Philadelphia, where the 1971 mayoral race saw 77% voter turnout, a stark contrast to the current 27% figure. This experiment in incentivizing voting underscores the need for broader reforms, such as mandatory voting, automatic registration, and same-day voter registration, to address the declining trend in voter participation.

A 63-year-old postal worker, Peggy Frank, died in her mail truck in Woodland Hills on a day when temperatures reached 117 degrees, according to the Los Angeles Daily News. Frank, who had worked for the U.S. Postal Service for 28 years, was found unresponsive by a neighbor and pronounced dead at 3:35 p.m. by paramedics. Her family believes the extreme heat may have contributed to her death, as the mail trucks are not equipped with air conditioning. An excessive heat warning was issued for the region on the day of her death. The cause of death is pending further tests, but an autopsy has been completed. Frank was just months away from retirement and had recently returned to work after suffering a broken ankle. Her family and coworkers remember her as a friendly and hardworking employee. The U.S. Postal Service stated that the safety of employees is a top priority and that all employees are reminded daily to stay hydrated, wear appropriate clothing, and take sufficient water and ice on their routes. However, some family members and coworkers argue that more needs to be done to protect workers from the heat. In a related case, federal investigators launched a probe into Frank's death. The U.S. Postal Service has a history of heat-related incidents, including a 2012 case where a mail carrier died after collapsing during his route, leading to a willful citation and a $70,000 penalty. In 2016, OSHA cited the Postal Service for two employees who suffered heat-related illnesses while delivering mail. The incident has sparked discussions about the safety measures in place for postal workers during extreme heat conditions.

A knife-wielding man, Usaamah Rahim, who was under 24-hour surveillance by anti-terrorism authorities, was fatally shot by law enforcement officers in Boston after he waved a military knife at them. Rahim, a 26-year-old security guard suspected of being radicalized by ISIS, initially planned to behead activist Pamela Geller, president of the American Freedom Defense Initiative, but instead targeted "boys in blue" as the "easiest target," according to court documents. Rahim had purchased three military fighting knives and allegedly told his associate, David Wright, that he would start randomly killing police officers. Wright, 25, was charged with obstructing a federal investigation and faces up to five years in prison if convicted. Surveillance video shows Rahim approaching officers with a large knife, prompting them to retreat and eventually shoot him. Rahim's brother, Imam Ibrahim Rahim, initially claimed his brother was shot in the back, but later retracted this statement after viewing the video. The FBI-led task force had been monitoring Rahim and two associates, and had searched a home in Rhode Island in connection with the investigation. The shooting has sparked debate over the use of lethal force and the handling of surveillance, with community leaders urging transparency and caution.

General Motors is recalling over one million late-model pickup trucks and large sport-utility vehicles in the U.S. for a steering defect, marking the latest issue stemming from the industry's increasing reliance on software to control car functions. The defect, which has been linked to 30 crashes and two injuries, can cause the vehicles to temporarily lose their electronically controlled power steering, making it difficult for drivers to steer, especially at low speeds. This problem increases the risk of accidents. The recall, announced by GM on Thursday, affects certain 2015 Chevrolet, GMC, and Cadillac pickup trucks and SUVs, with approximately 1.02 million vehicles in the U.S. being impacted. GM dealers will update the power steering module software for free. In 2017, the company had already recalled nearly 800,000 pickup trucks worldwide due to the same issue. The recall is part of GM's ongoing efforts to address safety concerns and adapt to the complex nature of modern vehicles.

The latest leak from Edward Snowden's files, published early by the German newspaper Der Spiegel, reveals a trove of classified documents that paint a vivid picture of the United States’ global diplomatic relations, according to The New York Times. The documents, which include 251,287 cables, offer unprecedented insight into the inner workings of U.S. foreign policy. Among the revelations are details on North Korea’s health issues, the personal lives of world leaders, and the U.S. stance on various international issues.

The documents detail that North Korean leader Kim Jong-il suffers from epilepsy, while Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi’s full-time nurse is described as a “hot blond.” German Chancellor Angela Merkel is referred to as “Angela Teflon Merkel,” and Afghan President Hamid Karzai is described as driven by paranoia. U.S. officials refer to Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin as an “Alpha Male,” while President Dmitry Medvedev is described as “afraid, hesitant.” The State Department is quoted as saying that President Barack Obama “prefers to look East rather than West,” and “has no feelings for Europe.”

The cables also contain sensitive information about U.S. operations, such as a dangerous standoff with Pakistan over nuclear fuel, where the U.S. has unsuccessfully tried to remove highly enriched uranium from a Pakistani research reactor. The documents reveal that Saudi donors remain the chief financiers of Sunni militant groups like Al Qaeda, and that Qatar, despite being a generous host to the U.S. military, is “the worst in the region” in counterterrorism efforts.

The cables also highlight the close relationship between Russian Prime Minister Vladimir Putin and Italian Prime Minister Silvio Berlusconi, including “lavish gifts,” lucrative energy contracts, and a “shadowy” Russian-speaking Italian go-between. The U.S. is also concerned about the deal between Italian energy firm ENI and Russian gas giant Gazprom over the South Stream pipeline.

The leaks also detail the U.S. struggle to prevent Syria from supplying arms to Hezbollah in Lebanon, and the U.S. failing to prevent Pakistan from hosting Al Qaeda. The cables show the U.S. managing relations with a rising China and a retreating Russia, and the Obama administration’s efforts to prevent Iran from building a nuclear weapon.

The documents also contain frank comments behind closed doors, such as the Saudi king’s scathing remarks about the leaders of Iraq and Pakistan. The cables reveal that the Yemeni government has sought to cover up the American role in missile strikes against Al Qaeda, and that the Libyan leader, Muammar Gaddafi, was rarely without his “senior Ukrainian nurse,” described as “a voluptuous blonde.”

The leak has raised concerns about the potential damage to U.S. relations and national security. The U.S. state department has warned that the release of the cables could put lives at risk, but WikiLeaks founder Julian Assange argued that the U.S. was afraid of being held to account. The cables offer remarkable details and insights into U.S. diplomacy, providing a global snapshot of the U.S. government’s interactions with other nations and their leaders.

Greenland's ice sheet melted at an unprecedented rate this month, with virtually the entire ice sheet showing signs of thaw over just four days, according to satellite data from NASA. This rapid melting, captured by three satellites, has alarmed scientists and deepened concerns about the pace and future consequences of climate change. The melting, which expanded from about 40% of the ice sheet surface to 97% within four days, was attributed to a heat dome or a burst of unusually warm air that hovered over Greenland from July 8 to 16. Scientists, including glaciologist Jay Zwally, who has made nearly yearly trips to the Greenland ice sheet for over three decades, were taken aback by the extent of the melt, noting it was unprecedented in their observations. The rapid melt, while exceptional, should be viewed alongside other evidence of climate change, such as earlier melting and more frequent melting at lower elevations. This event, which could contribute to sea-level rise, highlights the potential impacts of continued global warming and greenhouse gas emissions.

Awe, the feeling of being in the presence of something vast that transcends your understanding of the world, is not just a fleeting emotion reserved for extraordinary experiences. It can significantly impact your health and well-being, according to a new study published in the journal Emotion. Researchers from the University of California, Berkeley, and other institutions recruited 94 Berkeley students to fill out questionnaires about their positive and negative emotions over the past month and collected saliva samples to measure interleukin-6 (IL-6), a molecule linked to inflammation and poor health. The study found that students who reported experiencing more positive emotions generally had lower IL-6 levels, with awe emerging as the most potent emotion for reducing inflammation. Participants who felt awe more frequently had lower IL-6 levels, suggesting that awe could be a powerful tool for improving health.

The researchers then expanded their study to 119 students, who completed more detailed questionnaires about their emotional states and provided saliva samples. While all positive emotions were associated with lower IL-6 levels, awe showed the strongest correlation. This finding is particularly significant because awe is a common emotion that can be experienced daily. On average, the students reported feeling awe three or more times a week, indicating that it is not a rare occurrence. Dacher Keltner, a professor of psychology at UC Berkeley and the senior author of the study, suggests that people should seek out awe more often. He notes that awe can be experienced in various ways, such as watching a sunset, listening to music, or observing a child play, highlighting that awe is accessible to everyone.

The study's findings suggest that awe has a profound impact on decision-making and well-being by altering perceptions of time. Awe helps bring people into the present moment, which can influence their decisions and make life feel more satisfying. Keltner explains that awe can expand people's perception of time, making them more patient and less materialistic. This shift in perspective can lead to increased volunteering and a greater willingness to help others. The researchers also found that awe can reduce the negative effects of poverty on health, as awe deprivation may contribute to the pernicious effects of poverty on the immune system.

In summary, the study emphasizes the importance of incorporating awe into daily life. By seeking out awe-inspiring experiences, individuals can improve their health, enhance their well-being, and foster a more collaborative and altruistic mindset. As Keltner concludes, adding "seek more daily awe" to your New Year's resolutions could be a transformative step towards a healthier and more fulfilling life.

A large UPS cargo plane crashed near an airport in Birmingham, Alabama, just before dawn on Wednesday. The Airbus A300-600F, en route from Louisville, Kentucky, did not issue a distress call prior to the crash. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) reports that the pilot and co-pilot died in the crash. The plane broke into pieces, scattering debris over an area of about 300 yards. NTSB investigators are working to retrieve the cockpit and voice recorders, which are still smoldering. No buildings were hit, and no one on the ground was injured. The crash site is about a half-mile north of the runway, and the Birmingham Airport Authority Chairwoman confirmed the deaths of the crew. The incident is the second fatal accident involving a large jet in the U.S. since early July, following a crash in San Francisco.

Bobby Fuller, the rock 'n' roller who recorded the iconic song "I Fought the Law" in 1965, died 32 years ago on July 18, 1966, in Hollywood. His death, attributed to inhalation of gasoline, has long been a mystery to his friends and family. Found slumped in his car outside his apartment, the case remains contentious. Police concluded it was either a suicide or an accident, but friends and family dispute these findings. Rod Crosby, a rival musician, suggests Fuller met the wrong person and couldn't escape the situation, while Randy Fuller, his brother, firmly believes it was neither suicide nor accident. Crosby’s theory posits that Fuller was having a fling with a girlfriend of a low-level mobster, leading to a violent encounter. Lorraine Fuller, Bobby’s mother, also refutes the suicide theory. Despite the mystery, E, the Entertainment Channel, is producing a program on Fuller, with shooting set to begin in the late fall. The documentary aims to unravel the enigma surrounding the rock star's death, which continues to haunt his loved ones. The article also mentions various events happening in Los Angeles, including PaleyFest, a midnight screening of Hackers, a Celtic Faire, and a Holi Festival of Colors, among others. These events, while not directly related to Fuller’s death, provide a vibrant cultural backdrop against which the enduring mystery of his demise is set.

In a surprising turn of events, an 81-year-old man in Grand Rapids, Michigan, learned about a son he never met after finding a hidden letter his late wife had kept for decades. Tony Trapani discovered the 1959 letter when he was cleaning out his wife’s filing cabinets after her death. The letter, from the mother of his then-unknown son, Samuel Childress, revealed that the boy was his son. Trapani had always tried to have children but thought his goal was unfulfilled. Samuel, now 61, grew up in Pennsylvania believing his father never wanted to meet him. The unexpected news came as a shock to both men, with Trapani tearfully saying, "He's my full son that I've had my whole life, but why my wife hid that letter is beyond me." Trapani's wife, who was unable to have children, may have intercepted the letter and hidden it to keep the father from learning of his son. The family plans to undergo a paternity test to confirm the identity. The long-awaited meeting between father and son on Monday marked the beginning of a new chapter in their lives, as they catch up on lost time and make the most of their newfound bond.

As part of the "Tech Surge" to address HealthCare.gov's numerous bugs, the government has recruited engineers from leading tech companies including Google, Oracle, and Red Hat. Michael Dickerson, a site reliability engineer from Google, is working with QSSI, the general contractor, to improve the site's reliability and performance. Greg Gershman, a former Presidential Innovation Fellow, is focusing on optimizing the site to enhance user experiences and making the development process more agile. Dozens of software engineers, developers, designers, and analysts are also working around the clock to address performance and functionality issues. The White House has brought in key personnel from both government and private sectors to strengthen the team addressing the problems. Despite these efforts, concerns remain among lawmakers about the site's reliability and the need for an extension of the enrollment period.

After months of anticipation, Lady Gaga's highly anticipated music video for "Telephone" finally premiered on Thursday night, and it certainly did not disappoint. The video, directed by Jonas Åkerlund and co-written by Gaga, is a nine-minute spectacle that combines elements of pop culture, dance, and product placement. Opening in a women's prison, the video introduces Gaga's character, stripped of her clothes and left nude, before transitioning to scenes of her life behind bars, including make-out sessions and catfights. The song kicks in after nearly three minutes, with Gaga's voice and Beyoncé's vocals blending into an electro-pop track. Beyoncé's character arrives in a "P---y Wagon" from "Kill Bill," and the two engage in a series of campy and stilted dialogues before driving off into the desert. 

The video then takes a turn into a diner scene, where Gaga, dressed in a telephone-head costume, performs a dance number while making a sandwich, complete with product placement for Wonder Bread and Miracle Whip. After poisoning the diner's patrons, including Tyrese Gibson's character, Gaga and Beyoncé continue their dance, joined by the Semi Precious Weapons. The video concludes with the two zooming off into the horizon, leaving behind a trail of dead bodies. 

What makes "Telephone" particularly noteworthy is its ambitious scale and the sheer amount of detail packed into the video. From the elaborate costumes to the product placements, the video is a work of art that showcases Gaga's ability to wow audiences. It is the best big-budget clip since her last one and is likely to be remembered as one of the standout videos of the year. The video's success cements Gaga's status as a pop icon, capable of delivering a show-stopping performance that is both electric and excellent.

A court hearing for Dominique Strauss-Kahn, accused of sexually assaulting a maid at the Sofitel hotel in Manhattan in May, has been delayed until August 1, reports The Wall Street Journal. Both the Manhattan District Attorney's office and Strauss-Kahn's legal team agreed to the two-week postponement to allow for further investigation. Strauss-Kahn has pleaded not guilty, and prosecutors have raised doubts about the credibility of the accuser, who has admitted to lying to authorities. Meanwhile, a French lawyer for Strauss-Kahn filed a slander complaint against Tristane Banon, a French novelist who has accused him of attempted rape in 2003. Banon was interviewed by Paris police for the first time as part of a preliminary inquiry. Her case and the New York charges against Strauss-Kahn continue to complicate his legal situation.

An Ohio man named Doug "Deo" Odolecki was ticketed for warning drivers about an upcoming drunken-driving checkpoint, despite police being required by law to notify the public. Odolecki stood on a street corner with a sign reading "Check point ahead! Turn now!" but was told by Parma Police Lt. Brian McCann to remove the part instructing drivers to turn, as it obstructed police business. When Odolecki refused, Officer James Manzo issued him a ticket. Manzo, involved in a $40,000 police brutality lawsuit earlier this year, was also the officer in that case. Odolecki's attorney, John Gold, supports his client and argues that the sign's content is protected speech under the First Amendment, as Odolecki had used the same sign for two years without incident. The case highlights the tension between police operations and public safety awareness, with a pending bill in the Ohio House of Representatives that would allow drivers to warn others of upcoming checkpoints by flashing their headlights.

A Georgia sheriff, Scott Berry, declared Valentine’s Day canceled in his county due to an ice storm, exempting men in the affected area from buying Valentine’s Day items until February 18, 2014. Berry’s Facebook post, which covered a zone north of I-16 to the Georgia/Tennessee border, went viral, garnering over 1,500 shares. Berry cited closed stores as his reason for the cancellation, aiming to give men a break from running errands. His chief deputy, Lee Weems, noted that Berry’s actions were not unusual, given his history of “hijinks.” Despite the decree, Berry admitted he would not enforce it and would not follow it himself. The decision drew criticism from outside Georgia, with a Michigan resident calling the sheriff’s office to protest. Berry’s unconventional move highlighted the impact of severe weather on local economies and the creative ways officials respond to such challenges.

Flappy Bird, the once-instantly-popular mobile game, has been removed from both the Apple App Store and Google Play. Creator Dong Nguyen announced the removal 22 hours in advance, citing personal reasons and the pressure of success. Fans, who had become deeply attached to the game, reacted with shock and anger, threatening to harm Nguyen or themselves. The game, which had been downloaded over 50 million times on Android and garnered half a million reviews, was a sensation due to its simplicity and difficulty. Despite its sudden rise, the game's creator opted to remove it, leaving players to either continue playing if they already had the game or to grapple with the loss of a game that had become a cultural phenomenon. The decision to take down the game also sparked discussions about the pressures of success in the gaming industry and the challenges faced by independent developers.

President George W. Bush accepted the Ice Bucket Challenge, involving his wife Laura Bush, and challenged former President Bill Clinton to follow suit, raising awareness for ALS. The challenge, trending on social media, has generated nearly $22.9 million for the cause in the last three weeks. Bush's daughter, Jenna Bush Hager, a correspondent for NBC's "Today" show, arranged the challenge. While President Obama has not participated, he made a donation to an ALS charity. The Ice Bucket Challenge, which involves dousing oneself with ice water, has seen participation from celebrities like Rory McIlroy, Woody Johnson, and Coach Jim Harbaugh. The challenge aims to raise awareness and funds for amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or Lou Gehrig's disease. Bush's video, posted on his Facebook page, encouraged Clinton to take the challenge, marking a significant moment in the challenge's spread among political figures.

A chartered plane carrying the Brazilian soccer team Chapecoense crashed near Medellin, Colombia, on its way to the Copa Sudamericana final, killing 76 people and leaving five survivors, including three players. The British Aerospace 146 short-haul plane, operated by LaMia Airlines, declared an emergency at 10 p.m. due to an electrical failure. The team, which had recently won two significant matches against Argentina's San Lorenzo and Independiente, was scheduled to play the first leg of the final in Medellin. The crash site, near La Union, was difficult to access due to heavy rainfall, complicating rescue efforts. Three survivors, including Alan Ruschel, a defender, were taken to local hospitals. The plane was carrying 72 passengers and nine crew members. Chapecoense's president, Luis Dominguez, was on his way to Colombia, and all soccer activities in Brazil were suspended. The team's fairy-tale season, which included promotion to Brazil's top division and victories over strong Argentine teams, added to the tragedy. The club's stadium was deemed too small for the final, and the match was moved to a larger venue. Soccer legends like Lionel Messi and Pele sent condolences. The Colombian and Brazilian governments declared three days of mourning. The team planned an open wake at their stadium, and Atletico Nacional, the opposing team, wanted the trophy to be awarded to Chapecoense in honor of the deceased.
