Chun also addressed the North Korean regime's nuclear and cyber warfare capabilities, noting that while the U.S. and South Korea have the air power to inflict significant damage, the sheer number of North Korean troops and the regime's willingness to use chemical and biological weapons make the conflict complex. He expressed confidence that the alliance would prevail, but warned that the North Korean regime's ability to hack systems worldwide should not be underestimated.

The general's comments come amid reports that the Trump administration is considering a pre-emptive strike on North Korea over its pursuit of nuclear weapons, while also exploring the possibility of diplomacy. Chun's insights highlight the challenges facing the international community in addressing the North Korean threat, emphasizing the need for both preparation and diplomacy.

Former South African President Nelson Mandela, 94, is responding positively to treatment for a recurring lung infection, according to the presidency. Mandela, who has been hospitalized multiple times in recent years, remains under treatment and observation. South African President Jacob Zuma asked the world to pray for Mandela and his family, emphasizing the importance of privacy for the medical team. Mandela's health has been a source of concern, with his hospitalizations reflecting his declining health. Despite his frailty, Mandela's legacy as a symbol of reconciliation and the end of apartheid continues to inspire. President Obama sent his best wishes, calling Mandela a leader whose character embodies qualities of strength and leadership. Mandela's hospitalization highlights the ongoing challenges of his health, but also the enduring respect and admiration he commands.

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has unveiled the first stunning high-resolution images from its newly launched GOES-16 satellite, marking a significant leap forward in weather forecasting capabilities. Launched on November 19, 2016, from Cape Canaveral, Florida, GOES-16, formerly known as GOES-R, is heralded as a "game changer" by NOAA, boasting an image resolution four times greater than that of existing GOES satellites. This enhanced resolution allows for more accurate forecasts, enabling forecasters to provide more advanced warnings for severe weather and tropical systems. Situated in orbit approximately 23,000 miles above Earth, GOES-16 can generate a full image of the Earth every 15 minutes and a detailed image of the continental U.S. every five minutes, significantly outperforming its predecessors.

The first images released by GOES-16 showcase the satellite's advanced capabilities. One image reveals the moon and Earth, while another captures an expansive ice storm that caused widespread damage and fatalities across the U.S. On January 15, 2017, GOES-16 captured a dust plume moving off the coast of Africa, with Florida and parts of the Caribbean visible in the background. The satellite's ability to photograph the entire Western Hemisphere is demonstrated in an image of Argentina, showing storm activity in the northeast and mountain wave clouds in the southwest. Another image captures clouds moving over the west coast of the U.S. and the Baja Peninsula in Mexico, while a subsequent image shows a storm moving into the Northeast, which would bring wet and wintry weather to the region on January 16-17.

GOES-16's Advanced Baseline Imager (ABI) provides a full-disc view of the Earth in high detail, with five times greater coverage, four times the spatial resolution, and three times the spectral channels compared to earlier GOES satellites. This advanced technology allows for more detailed imagery and multi-tasking abilities that previous GOES imagers could not achieve. GOES-16 can provide a full image of Earth every 15 minutes and one of the continental U.S. every five minutes, and it can target regional areas experiencing severe weather, hurricanes, wildfires, volcanic eruptions, or other high-impact environmental phenomena as often as every 30 seconds.

NOAA's GOES-16 satellite is expected to significantly enhance the nation's weather observation network and improve prediction capabilities, leading to more accurate and timely forecasts, watches, and warnings. The satellite's six new instruments will generate new or improved meteorological, solar, and space weather products. In May, NOAA will announce the planned location for GOES-16, with the satellite operational as either GOES-East or GOES-West by November 2017. Following GOES-16, the second satellite in the series, GOES-S, is undergoing environmental testing at Lockheed Martin's facility in Littleton, Colorado, and will be moved into the other operational position as GOES-17 after launch and initial checkout, approximately nine months after GOES-16.

Pat Boone, the 79-year-old legendary singer, finds himself in a peculiar predicament as a warrant has been issued for his arrest, reports TMZ. The warrant stems from a lawsuit involving a condominium he purchased on a luxury cruise liner. The company building the boat was sued by some of its investors and lost the case, resulting in a court order for the company to pay over $800,000 in attorney's fees. However, the lawyers have not received their payment and are now attempting to recover the money from the condo buyers, including Pat Boone. Boone was subpoenaed to testify but failed to appear, leading to the warrant. Despite the serious nature of the situation, Boone maintains a lighthearted attitude, joking that the warrant is "nonsense" and referencing his famous status, saying, "Is this the way I got so famous?" His lawyer assures that Boone intends to attend the court hearing, but warns that the litigant will be "very disappointed" to learn how little Boone knows about the project.

The renowned heart transplant program at Baylor St. Luke’s Medical Center in Houston has faced significant challenges in recent years, according to an investigation by ProPublica and the Houston Chronicle. The program, which once held a stellar reputation, has struggled with an unusually high number of transplant-related deaths and complications, leading to a decline in patient outcomes. Despite its storied history, the hospital has seen a series of top surgeons leave, including world-renowned transplant surgeon O.H. "Bud" Frazier, and has scaled back its ambitions for treating high-risk patients. The program's one-year survival rate now ranks near the bottom nationally, with twice as many patients dying within a year as would be expected based on patient characteristics and illnesses.

In 2015, the program experienced a particularly troubling period, with five out of 14 patients who received heart transplants dying within a year. This prompted the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services to cite the program for significantly worse-than-expected outcomes, threatening to cut off Medicare funds. The program submitted a plan of correction and narrowly avoided losing federal funding. Several doctors and nurses raised concerns about the program's declining quality, including Dr. Roberta Bogaev, who left the hospital in 2017 after observing a decline in patient care and the loss of experienced staff. Dr. Jeffrey Morgan, the program's surgical director, was hired in 2016 and has overseen a series of incidents, including a patient's death due to a blocked major vein and another patient's prolonged hospital stay and complications following a heart transplant. Despite these issues, the hospital continued to market itself as a national leader in heart transplants, boasting above-average survival rates and high transplant volume.

The story of James "Lee" Lewis, a 52-year-old pipefitter, highlights the program's struggles. Lewis had waited years for a new heart and was finally given one in 2018. However, his transplant went poorly, and he endured a series of complications, including a stroke and the need for an artificial heart. Dr. Masahiro Ono, the surgeon who performed the initial transplant, admitted that a defibrillator malfunction during the surgery likely caused significant damage to the donor heart. Despite these setbacks, Lewis's family struggled to get answers about what went wrong, with the hospital initially withholding key details about his care. Lee Lewis passed away on March 23, 2018, after enduring multiple surgeries and procedures. His wife, Jennifer, chronicled their journey on social media, sharing updates and expressing frustration with the transplant program. The case of Lee Lewis and others like him raises questions about the quality of care at St. Luke’s and the broader implications for patients seeking heart transplants.

In the late 1940s, Dr. Theodore Woodward, a professor at the University of Maryland School of Medicine, coined the medical adage "When you hear hoofbeats, think of horses, not zebras," advising medical students to consider common diagnoses first. This phrase, which has since spread widely in medical circles, serves as a caution against the availability heuristic and the tendency to favor striking and novel diagnoses over more common ones. However, diagnosticians emphasize that "zebra" diagnoses, though rare, must still be considered until ruled out by evidence. The term "fascinoma" is used for obscure and rare medical diagnoses. Examples include misdiagnosing necrotic skin lesions as loxoscelism, even in areas where recluse spiders are rare. The television series "House" and the music video "IT'S NOT A ZEBRA!" from Harvard Medical School highlight the importance of this principle. The adage underscores the need for clinicians to maintain a broad diagnostic approach, ensuring that rare conditions are not overlooked in favor of more common ones.

Marc Anthony and Shannon de Lima, married for two years, have confirmed their divorce in a joint statement to Us Weekly. The couple, who dated from 2012 before tying the knot in 2014, share 8-year-old twins Emme and Max. While rumors about their split circulated after Anthony kissed ex-wife Jennifer Lopez at the Latin Grammy Awards, the pair ask for privacy during this difficult process. Anthony and de Lima have no plans to reconcile, with Anthony currently focused on his relationship with Lopez.

The Super Bowl, an event that has become a spectacle of its own, faces a peculiar marketing challenge: how to avoid putting a big, fat "L" on souvenir T-shirts in the future. The NFL, which is four years away from its 50th Super Bowl, is already considering how to navigate this issue. The Roman numerals used for the Super Bowl, a tradition dating back to 1971, have become part of the league's mystique. However, the numeral "L," which represents 50, has become a symbol of losing, thanks to the "loser gesture" depicted in movies and TV shows. This gesture, often forming the letter "L" on one's forehead, has become a secret handshake for fans of the show "Glee." Brand experts suggest that the NFL might emphasize Arabic numerals more in the future, or find creative ways to incorporate the 50th anniversary. The NFL has not announced the host city for the 50th Super Bowl, but the league is already discussing potential solutions. For instance, the logo could stand for "learning" or "love," or the event could be promoted as the largest Super Bowl ever. The official Super Bowl logo has evolved over the years, and the NFL might consider hosting the game in a city that can integrate the Roman numeral into its logo, such as London or Los Angeles. The challenge of the "L" symbol is just one of many issues the NFL must address as it plans for the future of America's favorite sporting event.

California Governor Jerry Brown signed a bill on Thursday allowing immigrants in the U.S. illegally to obtain driver's licenses, marking a significant step in expanding immigrant rights. The measure, dubbed AB 60, is expected to become available by January 2015 and will be issued to anyone passing the written and road tests, regardless of immigration status. The licenses will feature a special designation and cannot be used to prove eligibility for employment or public benefits. Governor Brown, who has enjoyed strong support among Latino voters, hailed the bill as a first step, predicting it would set a precedent for other states. Ten other states have already enacted similar measures, with varying degrees of success. While some immigrant advocates initially raised concerns about racial profiling, the new law bans discrimination based on the license and states it cannot be used as a basis for arresting someone for being in the U.S. illegally. The bill has the backing of police chiefs and insurance authorities, who argue that it will make the streets safer. State officials estimate that 1.4 million drivers will apply for licenses during the first three years. The measure is part of several immigrant-friendly bills passed by the Legislature this year, including efforts to scale back collaboration between local law enforcement and federal immigration officials.

A group led by former Florida Governor Jeb Bush and former New York Yankees captain Derek Jeter has emerged as the winner of the auction for the Miami Marlins baseball team, with a $1.3 billion bid, according to a source familiar with the deal. The sale is pending Major League Baseball (MLB) approval and other details, including the identities of the other investors in Bush’s group, who are expected to be vetted and approved by MLB. The group’s bid was selected over offers from Quogue Capital LLC founder Wayne Rothbaum and Solamere Capital co-founder Tagg Romney, who included former All-Star pitcher Tom Glavine in his group. The Marlins, owned by New York art dealer Jeffrey Loria since 2002, have struggled with sparse crowds and a low regional television contract revenue. Loria, who bought the team for $158 million, is expected to leave with a profit of more than $1.2 billion. Bush plans to be the Marlins’ “control person,” while Jeter intends to play an active role in the franchise. The new ownership group faces the challenge of turning around the Marlins, who have not enjoyed significant success since winning the World Series in 2003. The team’s new owners hope to capitalize on Jeter’s popularity and Bush’s political connections to improve the team’s financial and on-field performance.

Law enforcement in the area received several calls on Monday regarding disoriented birds flying into buildings and cars. The unusual behavior was attributed to an early frost, which causes berries to convert starch into sugar, allowing yeast to enter and accelerate fermentation, producing alcohol. As a result, birds consuming these berries can become intoxicated. Laura Erickson, a Duluth birding expert, confirmed that waxwings, robins, and thrushes are particularly susceptible to this phenomenon. The Gilbert Police Department issued a humorous advisory, listing various bird behaviors that might occur due to intoxication, such as Heckle and Jeckle-like antics or Big Bird operating a motor vehicle unsafely. While occasional reports of inebriated birds are not uncommon, the weather conditions this fall have led to a higher incidence of avian alcoholism. The police department advises against calling law enforcement for these cases, as the birds should sober up within a short period. However, they recommend reporting any birds that appear intoxicated after midnight or show signs of distress, especially those that might collide with windows. Experts also warn that birds that overindulge on fermented berries may face head trauma, either from window collisions or falls. The phenomenon of birds becoming intoxicated from fermented berries is not unique to this incident, with similar cases reported in various regions. While there are few studies confirming the role of alcohol, the conversion of starch to sugar during early frosts and the subsequent fermentation process are key factors. Climate change may exacerbate this issue due to more frequent frosts and thaws, potentially leading to more frequent instances of avian inebriation.

The Kurdish region of Iraq is gearing up for a historic referendum on independence, with a collection of news and social media sources reflecting the anticipation and debate surrounding the upcoming vote. Leading up to September 25, 2017, various political parties and influential figures in the Kurdish region have been actively engaged in discussions and advocacy for the referendum. News outlets from different factions have been reporting on the preparations, the rationale behind the push for independence, and the potential implications of the vote. Social media accounts of key figures have also been instrumental in shaping public opinion, with some emphasizing the historical and legal right to self-determination, while others caution about the economic and political challenges that might arise from the separation. The referendum is seen as a significant step towards realizing the long-held aspirations of the Kurdish people for an autonomous state, but it also faces opposition from the central Iraqi government and international actors concerned about the stability of the region. As the date draws near, the tension and anticipation are palpable, with the outcome potentially reshaping the geopolitical landscape of the Middle East.

Superintendent Nancy Kotowski of Monterey County hopes the revelation of her long-term relationship with a priest will open a dialogue within the Catholic Church about its clerical celibacy requirements. Kotowski, 59, and the Rev. Mike Manning, 70, a prominent figure in the church in Southern California, had a relationship that ended about three years ago, with the "physical aspect" having concluded. Manning has taken a leave of absence from his ministry, and Wordnet, a worldwide Catholic television ministry based in San Bernardino, has confirmed this. The relationship between Kotowski and Manning began when they were young, with their families knowing and even welcoming them at family gatherings. Kotowski believes their relationship was a lifelong commitment, not an "affair" as described by the media. She hopes the discussion about obligatory celibacy will lead to a more open conversation about the church's mandates. Superintendent Kotowski, who has never married and has no children, maintains that she has done nothing wrong or illegal. She is now embracing celibacy, supporting Manning's calling, and facing the struggle with faith. The San Bernardino Sun and The Herald reported on their relationship, and Kotowski hopes this will lead to a broader discussion within the church.

Russian President Vladimir Putin announced the development of a new array of nuclear-capable weapons during his annual address to lawmakers and political elites, signaling a potential new arms race with the West. The ICBM, with a longer range than any other, can reach almost any target in the world, Putin said, and missile defenses will be useless against it. Other new technologies include supersonic missiles and drone submarines that cannot be stopped. The speech came 17 days before Putin's presidential election, where he is seeking an unprecedented fourth term. Putin accused the West of ignoring Russia and sought to reassure his audience that Russia's strong military is a guarantor of peace. He boasted that Russia's new ICBM is "powerful and modern, and defense systems will not be able to withstand it," he said. Other new weapons include the Avangard, an intercontinental hypersonic missile, and the Kinzhal, a weapons system already deployed in southern Russia. Putin insisted Russia had "no plans to be an aggressor" and warned that any use of nuclear weapons against Russia or its allies would be regarded as a nuclear attack against Russia, and in response, Russia would take action instantaneously. The display of military prowess came amid heightened tensions, with the Pentagon releasing a new nuclear arms policy that followed a promise by US President Donald Trump to develop an arsenal "so strong and powerful that it will deter any acts of aggression." The speech was widely viewed as Putin's first campaign speech for the March 18 election, with the Kremlin primarily concerned with boosting turnout, as Putin is expected to cruise to a fourth term. Putin promised to improve the lives of Russians by cutting poverty by half, boosting pensions, and creating more daycare places. He also called for spending on urban infrastructure to be doubled over the next six years. Putin's message was one of defiance, as he portrayed Russia's modernizing arsenal as an adversarial response to US policy since 2001. The Pentagon played down Putin's speech, saying Moscow's weaponry had already been factored into US assessments. Putin's address, which generally lasts around an hour, is given to an audience of lawmakers from the state Duma and federation council, judges, ministers, and other members of the political establishment, and generally focuses on domestic issues such as the economy and corruption.

After 16 years of wrongful imprisonment, Luis Vargas was exonerated on November 23, 2015, by a Los Angeles judge. Vargas, who was convicted in 1999 for three sexual assaults, was cleared when DNA evidence linked the crimes to a notorious "teardrop rapist" suspected of over 30 rapes in the Los Angeles area since 1996. The teardrop rapist, known for his distinctive teardrop tattoo and methodical attacks, had evaded capture for years. Vargas, living near the area where several assaults occurred, was misidentified due to a similar tattoo. Despite his conviction, Vargas maintained his innocence and reached out to the California Innocence Project in 2012. The project, after reviewing his case, filed a motion for post-conviction DNA testing. The tests revealed that Vargas was not the rapist, but the teardrop rapist was. Vargas, 46 at the time, was taken back into custody due to his revoked green card, but his lawyers were hopeful of his imminent release. His daughter, Cristal Nora Vargas, expressed relief and gratitude, stating, "This is all I've ever wanted, and I thank God for this one because God knows the truth behind all of this." Vargas's exoneration came after years of appeals and petitions, with the district attorney's office conducting a careful review before approving his release. The case highlighted the flaws in eyewitness identifications and the importance of DNA evidence in exonerating the innocent.

An anti-Islam group in the Dallas, Texas, suburb of Irving published the names and addresses of over 60 Muslims and Muslim "sympathizers" on its Facebook page, targeting those who spoke out against a controversial Irving City Council vote on Islamic tribunals. The Bureau of American Islamic Relations (BAIR) posted the information, which was copied from an Irving city document containing the personal information of people who signed up to speak against a state bill targeting the influence of Islam in America. The list was published on Wednesday by David Wright III, the spokesman for BAIR, who also organized an armed protest outside the Islamic Center of Irving, where a ninth-grader was arrested for bringing a homemade clock to school, which was mistaken for a bomb. Wright's group, which includes members who tote shotguns and hold signs stating "Stop the Islamization of America" and "The solution to Islamic terrorism," believes that the U.S. is due for violent conflict with Muslims. The names and addresses of those who supported the city's efforts to limit Muslim influence were also included on the list. Alia Salem, executive director of the Dallas/Fort Worth branch of the Council on American-Islamic Relations, expressed concern over the publication of the list, stating that it could lead to harm. The list has since been removed from Facebook, and a pro-Muslim rally is planned to show support for the Irving mosque. The incident has drawn attention to the increase in Islamophobic incidents since the November 13 attacks in Paris, including the defacement of a mosque in Pflugerville, Texas, with feces and torn pages of the Quran, and a mosque in Ontario, Canada, being set on fire.

The ratings for the new Celebrity Apprentice, hosted by Arnold Schwarzenegger, did not impress NBC on its premiere. The show, which previously featured Donald Trump as host for over a decade, debuted with 4.9 million viewers, a 22% decrease from the ratings of Trump's final season. This poor performance contrasts with the 6.6 million viewers that ABC's The Bachelor drew and the 6 million viewers CBS garnered from four half-hour sitcoms. Schwarzenegger's hosting debut also underperformed in the key 18-49 demographic, with ratings 46% lower than Trump's final season. Despite heavy promotion, the show faced stiff competition, including The Bachelor and the Rose Bowl game on ESPN. NBC had hoped for a better start, especially considering the controversy over Trump's continued executive producer credit on the show. While some early reviews were not favorable, NBC's ratings guru, Tom Bierbaum, noted that the show still provided a strong lead-in for the network's new game show, The Wall, in the 10 p.m. time slot. The network is now deciding whether to order more seasons of the reality competition series, with Schwarzenegger's hosting performance raising questions about the show's future.

A dam burst at an iron-ore mine in southeastern Brazil, causing mudslides that killed at least 15 people and devastated a nearby town, reports AP. The Germano mine, operated by Samarco, a joint venture between BHP Billiton and Vale, experienced the disaster, with 45 people still missing. Video footage showed houses and vehicles destroyed by floodwaters and red mud. Samarco stated it was prioritizing care for people and mitigating environmental damage, but the cause of the breach was unclear. The disaster occurred as both companies faced a downturn in iron ore prices. Rescue teams searched for survivors or bodies, and authorities evacuated residents from the village of Bento Rodrigues, located 7 kilometers below the dam. The Civil Defense agency confirmed dead and missing but did not provide numbers. The dam was built to hold back water and mining residue, raising concerns about potential water contamination.

Jessica Simpson and Eric Johnson, a former NFL player, have tied the knot, reports Us Weekly. Just days after Simpson's ex-husband, Nick Lachey, proposed to his live-in girlfriend, Vanessa Minnillo, the 30-year-old singer and reality TV star announced her engagement to Johnson. Their relationship gained momentum when Johnson accompanied Simpson to Italy to celebrate her 30th birthday in July. Following Johnson's divorce from his wife of five years, Keri, Simpson expressed her happiness on Twitter, writing, "So very happy for Jess and Eric," and wished them a lifetime of joy and happiness. The engagement was confirmed when Simpson was spotted wearing a large ruby and diamond ring during a shopping trip in Kansas City. This engagement marks the second marriage for both Simpson and Johnson, with Simpson's previous marriage to Nick Lachey ending in 2006, and Johnson's previous marriage to Keri Johnson finalized in October. Simpson's father, Joe, also expressed his joy on Twitter, adding that he hopes his daughter and Johnson will have a lifetime of happiness together.

As Ryan Gosling prepares to embark on his Ph.D. studies, he reflects on the end of his time running the Feminist Ryan Gosling book, expressing gratitude to all who supported and read the site. Gosling's Golden Globe acceptance speech for best performance by an actor in a motion picture - musical or comedy, was widely praised for its heartfelt and sincere tone. During his acceptance speech, Gosling acknowledged his wife, Eva Mendes, for her unwavering support during his time filming La La Land. He highlighted the challenges Mendes faced, including raising their daughter, expecting their second child, and assisting her brother in his battle with cancer. Gosling emphasized that without his wife's dedication, he would not have been able to achieve this success. "You don’t get to be up here without standing on the shoulders of a mountain of people," he said, "and there’s just no time to thank everyone. I would like to try and thank one person properly and say that while I was singing and dancing and playing piano and having one of the best experiences I’ve ever had on a film, my lady was raising our daughter, pregnant with our second and trying to help her brother fight his battle with cancer. If she hadn’t have taken all that on so that I could have this experience, it would surely be someone else up here other than me today. So, sweetheart, thank you." Gosling also dedicated the award to his daughters, Amada and Esmeralda, and the memory of his brother-in-law, Juan Carlos Mendez, who passed away last April at the age of 53. His speech resonated with many, including Maria Shriver, who tweeted, "Ryan Gosling's speech just blew me away. Attractive, smart & so generous to his partner. What a man." Gosling's speech not only showcased his humility and appreciation for his partner but also highlighted the importance of recognizing the sacrifices made by those who support our endeavors.

A federal judge in Virginia has ruled in favor of a transgender student, Gavin Grimm, in a legal battle against a school district's bathroom policies. Grimm, who identifies as male, was barred from using the boys' restrooms at his high school in Gloucester, Virginia, before graduating in 2017. Grimm, represented by the American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU), filed a lawsuit claiming the school board's policy violated his constitutional rights and federal protections against sex discrimination under Title IX. The case was initially sent to an appeals court, which in September 2017, argued that the case should be dismissed. However, U.S. District Court Judge Arenda Wright Allen in Norfolk declined the school board's request to dismiss the case. The judge concluded that Grimm has sufficiently pled a Title IX claim of sex discrimination under a gender stereotyping theory. This ruling aligns with a similar decision made by a federal appeals court based in Chicago in May 2017. The school board now faces the task of scheduling a settlement conference with Grimm's legal team. This case highlights the ongoing debate over transgender rights and the application of federal anti-discrimination laws in educational settings.

A woman from Stockport, Jane Wilson, fell to her death while attempting to find a safe route down from the peak of Tryfan in Snowdonia, an inquest heard. She and her husband, Gary, had decided against climbing the summit due to the approaching dusk. Using only Gary’s smartphone to navigate, they headed across the mountain’s west face, known for its loose rocks and steep inclines. Gary described to the inquest that Jane, a fit and active 53-year-old academic engagement librarian at the University of Manchester, went ahead to look for a suitable route and asked if it was safe. Gary heard a series of sounds, including an exclamation, followed by a rock fall, realizing Jane had fallen. With limited first-aid knowledge, Gary climbed to a safer ledge and raised the alarm, deciding not to go down in case he was also injured. Members of the Ogwen Valley Mountain Rescue Team eventually found Jane’s body over 150 meters lower down. Detective Constable Tim Bird, the leader of the rescue team, stated that Jane had apparently fallen 20-30 feet down a vertical cliff, then tumbled about 150 meters down into an area known as Notch Arrete. He noted that the weather was dry, but the light boots worn by Jane were unsuitable for such rough terrain, increasing the risk of slipping. After abseiling down two days later, DC Bird himself was hit by falling rocks. He suggested that the couple’s change in route to avoid the summit was a mistake, recommending that they should have retreated the way they had come or chosen the North Ridge instead. The inquest highlighted that the smartphone app used by Gary had limited detail compared to a traditional map. Andy Simpson, a spokesman for Mountain Rescue England and Wales, also advised that walkers should use a map and compass in addition to electronic navigation aids. The coroner recorded a conclusion of accidental death, emphasizing the potential dangers of relying solely on smartphone apps for navigation in challenging terrains.

Rocker Ted Nugent, known for his controversial statements, including calling Hillary Clinton a "devilbitch," visited President Donald Trump at the White House on Wednesday night, accompanied by former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin and musician Kid Rock. Photos shared on social media show the trio in the Oval Office, including one where they mockingly posed with a portrait of Hillary Clinton. The visit highlights a shift in White House policies, as it did not release visitor logs for the first time since the Trump administration. Nugent's presence at the White House, given his past anti-Obama rhetoric, including saying he would be "dead or in jail" if Obama were re-elected, has sparked debate. Palin, an early Trump supporter, thanked the president for the invitation and shared multiple photos of the meeting, which has ignited online discussions. The visit underscores the changing dynamics in the White House and the enduring political impact of Nugent's outspoken nature.

Vice Admiral Scott Stearney, a 36-year Navy veteran and commander of U.S. Naval Forces Central Command and U.S. 5th Fleet in Bahrain, was found deceased in his residence on Saturday. No foul play is suspected, and the Naval Criminal Investigative Service and the Bahraini Ministry of Interior are cooperating in the investigation. Stearney, a decorated naval warrior, served in various roles, including commanding the Golden Warriors of Strike Fighter Squadron VFA-87, the Knighthawks of Strike Fighter Squadron VFA-136, and Carrier Air Wing Seven. He also held flag assignments such as commander of U.S. Transportation Command’s Joint Enabling Capabilities Command, commander of Strike Force Training Atlantic, and commander of Carrier Strike Group 4. Stearney's last position was overseeing more than 20,000 U.S. and coalition sailors, Marines, Coastguardsmen, and civilians in the Middle East. His death is a significant loss for the Navy, and Chief of Naval Operations Admiral John Richardson expressed his condolences, stating, "This is devastating news for the Stearney family, for the team at Fifth Fleet, and for the entire Navy. Scott Stearney was a decorated naval warrior, a devoted husband and father, and a good friend to all of us." Rear Admiral Paul Schlise has assumed command, and Vice Admiral Jim Malloy is preparing to take command in the interim.

A 93-year-old American World War II veteran, Norwood Thomas, traveled 10,000 miles to Australia to reunite with his long-lost wartime girlfriend, Joyce Morris, after they reconnected online. The pair, who first met in London in 1944, spent 70 years apart, each marrying other people. Thomas, a U.S. paratrooper, flew to Australia to finally embrace his first love, sharing a warm hug and kiss. "This is about the most wonderful thing that could have happened," Thomas said, as they reunited on Valentine's Day. Their story began when Thomas, 21, and 17-year-old Morris met in London just before the 1944 invasion of Normandy. Morris, now 88, said, "I would have had a totally different life … and probably a much happier one." The reunion was made possible by donations from hundreds of well-wishers and Air New Zealand's assistance in arranging Thomas's first-class flight.

A federal survey of student experiences in U.S. schools reveals that many students are not being adequately challenged, despite popular perceptions of overburdened students. According to the National Assessment of Educational Progress (NAEP), 37% of fourth-graders find their math work too easy, and 72% of eighth-grade science students report not being taught engineering and technology. High school seniors rarely write about what they read in class, with 39% stating they hardly ever do so. These findings, which come from the student questionnaire of the Nation’s Report Card, highlight a significant gap between student expectations and actual classroom experiences. The data suggest that students from disadvantaged backgrounds are less likely to have access to rigorous learning opportunities, with 74% of higher-income fourth-grade students understanding their science teacher compared to 56% of lower-income students. In math, 80% of higher-income middle-school students report understanding their teacher, compared to 70% of low-income students. These disparities raise concerns about the quality of education and the preparedness of students for college and the modern workforce.

The report, conducted by Ulrich Boser and Lindsay Rosenthal, also finds that many students are not engaged in rigorous learning activities. Only 51% of eighth-grade civics students and 57% of eighth-grade history students report that their work is often or always too easy. Similarly, 37% of fourth-grade students find their math work too easy, and 21% of 12th-graders report their math work as too easy. These findings are consistent across subjects and grade levels, indicating a systemic issue in the U.S. education system. The lack of engagement in writing and reading activities, such as writing long answers to reading questions and identifying main themes, further underscores the problem. Only 33% of eighth-grade students read five or more pages a day, and 33% of 12th-graders write about what they read in class only twice a year or less.

The report calls for policymakers to push for higher, more challenging standards to ensure all students are ready for the global economy. Policymakers should work towards implementing the Common Core standards and other measures to improve the quality of education. Additionally, researchers and educators should continue to develop and refine student surveys to better understand the student experience and identify areas for improvement. The findings suggest that the current education system is not adequately preparing students for the demands of the modern workforce, and significant changes are needed to address these gaps.

An eight-year-old boy in Canada developed severe allergies to fish and nuts after receiving a blood transfusion, according to a new case report published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal. The boy had no history of food allergies and was undergoing treatment for medulloblastoma, a type of brain cancer. A few weeks after the transfusion, he experienced anaphylaxis within 10 minutes of eating salmon, leading doctors to suspect the transfusion had triggered the reaction. After treating him with an antihistamine, doctors advised him to avoid fish and carry an epinephrine injector. Four days later, he had another reaction after eating a chocolate peanut butter cup, leading to a diagnosis of temporary allergies to peanuts and salmon. The researchers believe the boy received antibodies from the blood donor that caused the allergic reactions. The antibodies, called immunoglobulin E, are associated with food allergies. These antibodies cause immune cells to release chemicals like histamine, leading to allergic reactions. The boy's immunoglobulin E levels to salmon and peanuts returned to normal within five to six months, and he was able to reintroduce these foods into his diet with medical supervision. This case highlights the rare but possible transfer of food allergies through blood transfusions. While it is extremely uncommon, doctors recommend being vigilant for the development of allergies after blood transfusions. The case also raises questions about how to prevent such incidents, as current blood donation policies do not typically screen for allergies. The incident prompted Canadian Blood Services to trace the problematic blood product, identify the donor, and bar them from making future donations.

In a 2010 interview with The Wall Street Journal, fashion designer Thom Browne criticized President Obama’s wardrobe, stating that the president could dress much better. Browne argued that Obama’s clothing did not fit well and seemed to be a result of political concerns rather than a desire to look his best. Browne used the example of Queen Elizabeth II during World War II, who continued to dress formally to maintain the expectations of her subjects. The fashion designer suggested that Obama should dress well because it is what the public expects to see from a leader.

The article also highlights a notable error from President Obama’s 2013 inauguration. During the ceremony, Chief Justice John Roberts mistakenly omitted the word “States” from the oath of office. Obama seemed to notice the mistake and appeared to pause, but the error was not corrected. This incident, along with the 2009 swearing-in where Roberts misstated the oath, underscores the challenges in ensuring a flawless inauguration ceremony. Despite extensive rehearsals, the oath of office remains a critical and sometimes problematic moment in the presidential transition.

New York's highest court will hear arguments on whether nude dancing at adult entertainment clubs qualifies for a state tax exemption as a form of art. The case involves Nite Moves, a strip club in suburban Albany, which contested a tax bill of over $124,000 following a 2005 audit. Nite Moves claims that its performances, including cover charges and lap dances, should be exempt under state law as "live dramatic or musical arts performances." The club is relying on testimony from a cultural anthropologist who has studied exotic dance and visited Nite Moves. However, the state Tax Appeals Tribunal and a mid-level court have previously ruled against Nite Moves, finding insufficient proof that the dances are choreographed performances and noting that the dancers do not require formal dance training. New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman's office argues that some pole tricks are difficult to perform, but others have no prior dance experience. The legal battle highlights the broader trend of cash-strapped statehouses targeting strip clubs, with Illinois recently passing a law forcing clubs to pay a $3-per-customer fee to fund rape crisis centers. Nite Moves' lawyer, Andrew McCullough, describes the club as a place where dancers work hard, executing complex routines. He argues that the dancers should be treated like ballerinas, exempt from sales tax. The case is seen as pivotal, potentially setting a precedent for similar legal challenges across the country.

The American Cancer Society has updated its guidelines for the prevention and early detection of cervical cancer, emphasizing the importance of regular screening to catch the disease early and prevent its formation. Starting at age 21, women should undergo cervical cancer testing every three years with a Pap test, or every five years with a Pap test combined with an HPV test, known as co-testing. For women aged 30 to 65, co-testing is the preferred method, while those under 30 should have a Pap test alone every three years. Women with a high risk due to a suppressed immune system or exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES) may need more frequent screening, following their healthcare provider's advice. Women over 65 who have had regular screening in the past 10 years and no history of serious pre-cancerous conditions can stop screening, while those with a history of pre-cancer should continue testing for at least 20 years after the abnormality was found. Women who have had a total hysterectomy, particularly without the cervix, should follow the guidelines for those with a cervix. The guidelines advise against annual screening, emphasizing that follow-up tests may be necessary if initial results are abnormal. The updated guidelines also highlight the importance of continued screening regardless of HPV vaccination status, as the vaccine does not protect against all cervical cancer-causing HPV strains. The study published in the journal Cancer found that the death rate from cervical cancer is higher than previously estimated, with black women dying at a rate 77% higher and white women at 47% higher than previously thought. This discrepancy is attributed to the exclusion of women who have had their cervix removed in hysterectomies, which eliminates the risk of cervical cancer. The findings underscore the need for better access to screening programs, HPV vaccinations, and standard care treatments to address the racial disparity in cervical cancer mortality.

John Travolta, the Hollywood actor and Qantas ambassador, has lent his talents to a new in-flight safety video for the airline, which has been met with mixed reactions. The three-minute video, shown on every domestic and long-haul Qantas flight, features Travolta dressed in a pilot's uniform and hat, delivering a safety message. However, the video has angered Qantas cabin crew, who are annoyed that Travolta refers to them as "the team" instead of "crew." They believe that a "real pilot," such as Captain Richard de Crespigny, who saved 466 lives on the QF32 flight from Singapore, should be the one to deliver the safety message. Cabin crew have expressed their frustration through anonymous posts on online chat forums, calling the video "corny" and "tacky." One staff member even went as far as saying, "The whole thing seems to make the safety message seem trite." Despite the negative feedback, a Qantas spokeswoman stated that they have received only positive feedback from staff and customers, and that they are "really happy with the video and we think it's really engaging." The video, which opens with Travolta saying, "This is your captain speaking—well, maybe not today," aims to emphasize the importance of safety and the dedication of Qantas pilots. However, the use of Travolta, who is not a "real" pilot, has raised concerns among staff about the effectiveness of the message.

A restriction on abortion coverage, added late Saturday to the health care bill passed by the House, has energized abortion opponents, marking their biggest victory in years, reports the New York Times. The provision blocks the use of federal subsidies for insurance that covers elective abortions, which advocates on both sides are calling the biggest turning point in the abortion battle since the ban on partial birth abortions six years ago. The provision applies only to insurance policies purchased with federal subsidies and to a government-run insurance plan. Abortion rights advocates argue that insurers may drop abortion coverage from their plans to sell them in the newly expanded market of people receiving subsidies. The subsidies would be available to anyone earning less than $88,000 for a family of four. While some women who undergo abortions file private insurance claims, the number is small, and many may avoid leaving a record. Only about half of those with insurance coverage from their employers have coverage for abortion. The provision has emboldened abortion opponents, who have been facing a series of incremental defeats in the courts and in Congress. The president and Democratic leaders have long promised that their proposed health care overhaul would not direct taxpayer money to pay for elective abortions. However, the president has not clarified how to apply this standard to the new program of offering insurance subsidies or a government-run plan to millions of poor and middle-class Americans. The House Democratic leaders had sought to resolve the issue by requiring insurers to segregate their federal subsidies into separate accounts. However, the House speaker, Nancy Pelosi, was unable to hold on to enough moderate and conservative Democratic votes to pass the health bill using that approach, forcing her to allow a vote on the amendment containing the broader ban. Five states already bar private insurance plans from covering elective abortions, and the federal employees' health insurance plan and most state Medicaid programs also ban coverage of abortion. The bishops' role was pivotal, as they had pushed for decades for universal health insurance but now see the abortion-financing issue as a deal-breaker. The provision has now been incorporated into the House bill, and some Senate Democrats are pushing to include similar restrictions in their own bill.

The Powerball jackpot has reached a record $550 million, with the odds of winning being 1 in 175,223,510, which is slightly better than the chance of winning a Mega Millions jackpot (1 in 175,711,536). Despite the astronomical odds, the excitement and frenzy surrounding the lottery continue to grow. The article highlights a few unlikely scenarios that are more likely than winning the jackpot, such as dying from a bee sting (1 in 6.1 million) or a lightning strike (1 in 3 million). 

The Powerball jackpot could potentially rise even higher, as the current jackpot is part of a plan by lottery officials to boost jackpots faster by doubling the ticket price to $2. With the jackpot at $500 million, an estimated 105,000 tickets are being sold every minute nationwide. This surge in ticket sales has led to the anticipation of a winner, with a 60 percent chance that the winning combinations have already been sold. 

The article draws on the story of the Lohse family, who won $202 million in Powerball just two months ago. They faced financial struggles before their win, including the threat of foreclosure and car repossession. After winning, they sought legal and financial advice, and have since shared their fortune with their community by planning to help build a new football stadium at their local high school. The Lohses continue to play the lottery every week, including tonight's drawing, where the winner could take a cash option of $327 million before taxes.

Financial expert Jack Ford advises lottery winners to assemble a team of financial advisers and lawyers to manage their newfound wealth. He emphasizes the importance of signing the ticket, securing it in a safe place, and taking time to settle in before making any major decisions. The article concludes by cautioning winners to avoid the pressure of sharing their wealth with strangers and to take the time to understand their financial situation before making any significant moves.

Shia LaBeouf, known for his volatile behavior, recently found himself in another public altercation at a London pub called Hobgoblin. The incident, which occurred in a rough part of South London, escalated into a headbutt after a heated argument over his girlfriend's mother. LaBeouf, appearing drunk, was heard screaming, "What are you saying about my girl's mom? Are you f---ing kidding me bro?" A woman, presumably his companion, could be heard pleading for him to stop. This is not the first time LaBeouf has found himself in a bar fight; he previously engaged in a brawl at the same pub in 2012 and was involved in a street fight outside a Vancouver bar in 2011. In a drunken apology following the incident, LaBeouf claimed he is "super normal" and just like anyone else, despite his history of public disputes.

Whole Foods CEO John Mackey argues that the U.S. health-care system is moving towards a form of fascism, not socialism, due to increased government control. Mackey, a self-described libertarian, criticizes the Affordable Care Act (Obamacare), suggesting it infringes on individual freedom and market choices. He advocates for reforms that reduce government intervention, such as removing legal obstacles to high-deductible health insurance plans, equalizing tax benefits for employer and individual health insurance, and repealing state laws that prevent insurance companies from competing across state lines. Mackey emphasizes the importance of personal responsibility for health, promoting a plant-based diet and preventive lifestyle choices. He also supports voluntary, market-based health-care solutions, contrasting them with government-mandated health-care systems in countries like Canada and the U.K., which he claims ration care through long waiting lists. Mackey's views reflect a broader debate on the role of government in health care, with critics like him arguing for more individual empowerment and less state control.

A bomb blast in St. Petersburg's subway system on April 3, 2017, killed 11 people and injured over 40, causing widespread panic and fear among the city's residents. The attack, which occurred during President Vladimir Putin's visit to the city, coincided with a series of recent terror incidents in Russia, including the Moscow subway bombings in 2010 and the Domodedovo airport attack in 2011. The explosion happened in the middle of a rush hour, as a train traveled between stations on one of St. Petersburg's north-south lines. The driver chose to continue to the next stop, Technological Institute, which facilitated evacuation efforts and reduced the danger to passengers who would have had to walk along electrified tracks. The death toll was 11, with 45 others hospitalized. Amateur video broadcast by Russian TV showed people lying on the platform of the Technological Institute station, and others bleeding and weeping after the damaged train arrived. Within two hours, authorities found and defused another explosive device at Vosstaniya Square station, a major transfer point for passengers on two lines and serving the railway station to Moscow. The National Anti-Terrorism Committee said the suspect, a 23-year-old from Kyrgyzstan, had rented an apartment in St. Petersburg a month before the blast and was linked to radical Islamist groups. The apartment search revealed household containers with an unidentified powder inside, and security cameras showed the suspect leaving home with a bag and a rucksack. The attack drew condemnation from President Donald Trump and the U.S. White House, as well as from Lebanon's militant Hezbollah group, which said the incident was the type of "terrorism" Russia was fighting in Syria. The bombing highlighted the ongoing threat of terrorism in Russia, with the last confirmed attack being the downing of a Russian airliner by Islamic State militants in 2015, killing all 224 people on board. The incident also raised questions about the effectiveness of Russia's counter-terrorism efforts, as the St. Petersburg subway system was shut down and evacuated, and security was immediately tightened at all key transportation sites across the country.

A comprehensive study by The Wirecutter, involving objective sound measurements and real-life testing with children, reveals potential hearing risks associated with popular kids' headphones. The study aimed to evaluate the safety of various models, focusing on their ability to restrict volume and reduce ambient noise. Key findings indicate that many headphones can produce dangerously high volumes, particularly when used with powerful amplifiers like those found in AV receivers or dedicated headphone amps. Passive headphones, which rely on resistors to reduce volume, often fail to limit sound effectively, while active headphones with digital limiters perform better but are less common.

The Puro BT2200 emerged as the top pick for children, offering excellent sound quality, noise cancellation features, and adequate volume control. However, the corded Onanoff Buddyphones Explore and JLab JBuddies Studio were also well-received by younger and older children, respectively. These models provided good fit and sound quality, though they lacked the noise cancellation features of the Puro BT2200.

The study also assessed the headphones' ability to reduce ambient noise, crucial for use in noisy environments like car back seats or airplanes. Only a few models, including the Etymotic ETY-Kids3 and Puro IEM200, demonstrated effective noise isolation, significantly blocking low-frequency sounds. These models, however, were not among the favorites of the child test panel.

Experts advised that the human ear and brain cannot accurately assess volume, necessitating volume-limiting headphones. The study used an iPhone as the source device, as it produces the loudest sound among common devices. Tests with pink noise and a diffuse-field calibration curve ensured accurate measurements, with 88 dBA set as the threshold for safe headphones. The findings highlight the importance of both volume control and noise isolation in safeguarding children's hearing.

In a shocking courtroom confession, Karl Smith admitted to a crime that his identical twin brother, Kevin Dugar, has been serving a 13-year prison sentence for. The brothers, who share the same name and appearance, made their first public appearance together in a Chicago courtroom, with Karl testifying that he was the one who committed the 2003 murder that Kevin was convicted of. The revelation came as a surprise to many, including the judge, who heard Karl's testimony that he and his brother were active gang members and had impersonated each other for years. Karl, who changed his name to his mother's maiden name, is currently serving a 99-year sentence for an armed robbery that ended in a six-year-old boy being shot. He claims he wrote his brother a letter in 2013, confessing to the murder, but only took the stand after an appeals court upheld his own conviction. Assistant State's Attorney Carol Rogala expressed skepticism, arguing that Karl's admission doesn't align with eyewitness accounts. However, Kevin's lawyer, Karen Daniel, maintains that the evidence against Kevin was weak, relying on the testimony of two witnesses, one of whom recanted. Despite the case's complexity, the brothers' mother, Judy Dugar, expressed faith in Karl's honesty, stating, "He wouldn't lie about that." The brothers' case highlights the challenges in distinguishing between identical twins in legal proceedings and the potential for wrongful convictions. The judge has not yet ruled on whether Kevin will receive a new trial.

Former First Lady Michelle Obama spoke at the American Institute of Architects' annual conference in Orlando, discussing her post-White House life and future plans. She expressed that she would not seek political office again, stating, "It’s all well and good until you start running, and then the knives come out. Politics is tough, and it’s hard on a family. I wouldn’t ask my children to do this again." Obama highlighted the challenges of life in the White House, mentioning the burden of political baggage and the impact on her family. She emphasized the importance of continuing to support young girls and women globally, citing the Let Girls Learn initiative. Obama also touched on her adjustment to life outside the White House, noting the freedom to open windows, travel without a motorcade, and answer the front door. She discussed the upcoming Barack Obama Presidential Center, which will be in Jackson Park on the south side of Chicago, and the programming plans for the center. Despite her reluctance to run for office, Obama affirmed that public service will always be in their blood. The Obamas have maintained a low profile since leaving the White House, with details of their post-presidential vacation in Central Florida surfacing recently. Obama's speech reflected on the difficulties of the White House years and her commitment to social causes.

Researchers have reported new evidence strengthening the association between Zika virus and a spike in birth defects, citing the presence of the virus in the brain of an aborted fetus of a European woman who became pregnant while living in Brazil. The fetus showed microcephaly or small head size, as well as severe brain injury and high levels of the Zika virus in fetal brain tissues, exceeding levels typically found in blood samples. The findings help “strengthen the biologic association” between Zika virus infection and microcephaly, according to researchers from the Harvard School of Public Health and Massachusetts General Hospital in Boston, who wrote an accompanying editorial in the New England Journal of Medicine. For definitive proof, however, more studies are needed.

The mother, a 25-year-old European volunteer working in Natal, Brazil, showed signs of Zika infection during her 13th week of pregnancy. Ultrasounds during her 14th and 20th week were normal. It was not until she returned to Europe that researchers found ultrasound evidence of severe fetal abnormalities during an ultrasound in her 29th week. The woman chose to get an abortion at 32 weeks, and doctors performed an autopsy, where they found viral replication of Zika in the fetus's brain. The fetus was negative for 13 other viruses that may cause fetal abnormalities, and the woman had no history of genetic abnormalities in her family. The autopsy also showed severe structural abnormalities in the fetus's brain, including a total absence of brain folds and fluid buildup in the brain.

The virus appeared to particularly favor neurons, and damage from the virus may have halted brain development at 20 weeks. Some structures found at autopsy showed that the virus was reproducing in the fetus's brain. The case provides support for the Brazilian minister of health, who first suggested the link between Zika and microcephaly. However, microcephaly can be caused by a number of viruses, including rubella and toxoplasmosis, as well as by malnutrition or maternal alcoholism. Some scientists have suggested the growth in cases is due to doctors keeping an eye out for microcephaly, as well as its relatively broad diagnosis criteria. The Slovenian team tested for so many other viruses to make sure Zika wasn't accompanied by another infection.

The discovery of viral particles and a high load of Zika virus RNA in the brain samples, coupled with the absence of other possible pathogens, and a complete viral genome present “strong evidence” of the Zika virus’ potential for causing birth defects, according to the researchers. The case is the first documented evidence of virus transmission from mother to child, though it is not a definitive link between Zika and fetal abnormalities. Until now, there was no evidence of virus transmission from a pregnant woman to her fetus. The findings help “strengthen the biologic association” between Zika virus infection and microcephaly, according to the accompanying editorial. The CDC has advised pregnant women to stay away from countries where Zika is newly spreading; the World Health Organization has declared the outbreak of microcephaly to be a global public health emergency and Brazilian authorities are working to eradicate as many of the mosquitoes that carry Zika as possible. Scientists are also teaming up to see what connection there is between Zika and microcephaly and whether the infection is causing a paralyzing neurological condition called Guillain-Barre syndrome in some patients. There’s no specific treatment and no vaccine for Zika, which was considered an extremely mild infection before Brazil called the alarm last year. About 80 percent of people who are infected don’t even know it. Symptoms in the other 20 percent are usually mild and include a rash and fever.

St. Louis, Missouri, marked a somber day with the funeral of Michael Brown, an 18-year-old black man shot and killed by a white police officer. The service at Friendly Temple Missionary Baptist Church drew thousands, including celebrities, civil rights leaders, and local residents, reflecting the national attention and emotional impact of the case. The church’s sanctuary, seating 2,500, was filled to capacity, with overflow rooms also packed. Family members and friends honored Michael, known as "Big Mike," through heartfelt tributes and memories. His father, Michael Brown Sr., urged peace and healing, asking protesters to observe a "day of silence" to allow the family to grieve. The Rev. Al Sharpton delivered a powerful eulogy, emphasizing the need for change in policing practices and condemning the violence that followed Brown’s death. Another eulogy was given by the Rev. Charles Ewing, who drew parallels between Brown’s death and broader issues of racial injustice. The funeral also served as a call to action, with family members and friends urging the community to vote and advocate for reform. The event highlighted the ongoing tension and division in St. Louis, with the city slowly returning to a sense of normalcy as children returned to school. The federal and state investigations into Brown’s death continued, facing challenges from conflicting witness accounts and media influence. The funeral underscored the complex and enduring issues of race, policing, and community healing in the wake of the tragic event.

A pineapple pesticide that contaminated milk in Hawaii in the 1980s may be linked to signs of Parkinson's disease in people today, according to a new study. The research, published in the journal Neurology, found that Japanese-American men who drank more than two cups of milk daily at the start of the study had 40% fewer brain cells in an area of the brain called the substantia nigra 30 years later, on average, compared to men who drank less milk. The substantia nigra is damaged in Parkinson's disease. The study, conducted by Dr. Robert Abbott of the Shiga University of Medical Science in Japan, involved 449 men who were part of a larger study on aging. These men provided details on their milk consumption and later donated their brains for study after death.

The researchers also detected residues of the pesticide heptachlor epoxide in the brains of 90% of the men who drank the most milk, compared to 63% of those who drank no milk. Heptachlor epoxide was present in the milk supply in Hawaii due to its use in pineapple farming. The chemical was banned for most agricultural uses in the U.S. by 1988 but can still be used today for controlling fire ants in electrical grid machinery. The researchers noted they do not have direct evidence that the milk the men drank contained the pesticide but considered it a reasonable explanation.

Interestingly, the study found that men who smoked and drank milk showed no brain cell loss, suggesting a possible protective effect of smoking against Parkinson's disease. Previous research has shown that smokers have a lower risk of developing Parkinson's disease. The findings suggest that diet may play a role in the development of Parkinson's disease, but the study does not establish a cause-and-effect relationship. The Parkinson's Disease Foundation stated that the potential link between drinking milk, pesticides, and developing Parkinson's disease needs further investigation.

The study's authors recommend that people be vigilant about the food they eat, considering not just its nutritional value but also potential contamination. While the data do not indicate that drinking several cups of milk a day increases the risk of Parkinson's, they do highlight the importance of considering environmental factors in understanding the disease. Abbott hopes his findings will fuel continued research into how chemicals in the environment might affect health in indirect and not always obvious ways.

The remains of 21-year-old Jessica Runions, who disappeared in 2016, were positively identified on Wednesday, bringing closure to her family. Runions was last seen leaving a party with Kylr Yust, a friend of her boyfriend, on September 8, 2016. Her burned vehicle was found the next day in a wooded area. Yust, 28, was arrested and charged with intentionally burning her vehicle, though he pleaded not guilty. His arrest came after he was already a suspect in the 2007 disappearance of 17-year-old Kara Kopetsky, whose case remains unsolved. Kopetsky's mother, Rhonda Beckford, and Runions' mother, Jamie Runions, have worked together to search for their daughters and raise awareness about both cases. The second set of remains found in the same area as Runions' could belong to Kara Kopetsky, but it will take time to identify them. Yust has a history of legal trouble, including a domestic violence charge in 2011. The search for answers continues as the families remain united in their quest for justice. Capt. Kevin Tieman of the Cass County Sheriff’s Office stated that investigators are still searching for additional remains at the scene. Yust's attorney, Molly Hastings, has not commented on the new developments. The families hope that the identification of Runions' remains will bring closure and that they will finally find answers for both their daughters.

John Sandoval, whose first-degree murder conviction for the death of his estranged wife was overturned in 2016, led investigators to her remains in exchange for a plea deal. Kristina “Tina” Tournai Sandoval's body was found buried beneath the grave of a World War II veteran at Sunset Memorial Garden cemetery in Greeley, Colorado. Sandoval, 52, pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and will serve 25 years in prison, with five years on parole, with his sentence dating back to August 2010. Tina Sandoval, 45, was reported missing on October 19, 1995, after failing to return from a meeting with Sandoval to settle a debt. Her body was discovered wrapped in plastic and buried 21 inches below the bottom of a grave. Sandoval, a convicted peeping Tom, was arrested shortly after the incident and initially charged with first-degree murder, but his conviction was overturned due to evidence of stalking other women and expert testimony linking stalkers to murderers. The case remained unsolved for 22 years until Sandoval revealed the location of his wife's remains in March 2017. His plea deal was reached after discussions with the Weld County District Attorney's office and family members, who initially refused to accept a reduced sentence. The family eventually agreed to the plea deal, citing the need for closure and the potential danger to other women. The exhumation of the World War II veteran's grave caused controversy, but the family and authorities believed it was necessary to finally lay Tina Sandoval to rest. The Weld County coroner conducted a forensic autopsy, but the cause of death has not yet been determined. Sandoval expressed condolences to the Tournai family and acknowledged the difficulty of the situation.

A new study from China has found that drinking hot tea can significantly increase the risk of esophageal cancer, particularly for those who also regularly consume alcohol and smoke. The research, published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, analyzed data from over 456,000 Chinese adults, aged 30 to 79, who did not have cancer at the study's beginning. Participants were asked to report their tea, alcohol, and cigarette consumption habits, and the researchers followed them for an average of 9.5 years.

The study revealed that drinking at least one alcoholic beverage and a "burning hot" cup of tea daily increased the risk of esophageal cancer by five times compared to those who drank tea less than once a week at a lower temperature. For smokers, drinking hot tea was associated with a roughly two-fold increase in esophageal cancer risk, compared to those who smoked but drank tea less frequently or at cooler temperatures. The findings suggest that the combination of hot beverages and harmful habits like smoking and excessive alcohol consumption can exacerbate the risk of developing esophageal cancer.

Dr. Jun Lv, a professor at Peking University Health Science Centre, explained that drinking very hot tea can harm the cells in the esophagus, and when combined with smoking and alcohol, the risk of cancer increases. He noted that boiling hot tea can irritate the esophageal lining, potentially leading to increased inflammation and faster cell turnover, which may make the tissue more susceptible to damage from other carcinogens. The study highlights the importance of avoiding very hot beverages, especially for those who engage in other risky behaviors.

While the study focused on hot tea, it is worth noting that the temperature of other hot beverages, such as coffee, could also pose a risk. The World Health Organization has classified hot beverages above 149 degrees Fahrenheit as "probably carcinogenic to humans." However, the study's lead author emphasized that the most effective way to prevent esophageal cancer is to avoid smoking and limit alcohol consumption. Despite the potential risks, tea still offers numerous health benefits, such as antioxidant properties that may protect against other types of cancers.

The U.S. Supreme Court declined to hear cases brought by Republican-led states seeking to defund Medicaid funding for Planned Parenthood and other organizations that provide women's reproductive health services, reports CNN. The cases, which were brought by Kansas and Louisiana, did not involve federal money for abortion-related services, which is barred by federal law. Instead, the states sought to block Medicaid funding for organizations that provide other services, such as cancer screenings, prenatal services, birth control, and ultrasounds, but also separately provide abortion services. The Supreme Court's decision not to hear the cases suggests that a majority of justices, led by Chief Justice John Roberts, want to avoid high-profile abortion-related issues for now. Three conservative justices—Clarence Thomas, Samuel Alito, and Neil Gorsuch—dissented, arguing that the court should have heard the challenges brought by the states. The decision leaves in place conflicting lower court rulings, with five federal appeals courts ruling in favor of Planned Parenthood and other similarly affected organizations, and one ruling against them. The Supreme Court's action allows the split decisions to stand in different federal circuits, meaning that Medicaid enrollees in the 8th Circuit, which includes Arkansas, Iowa, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, and South Dakota, can't challenge a decision by their state to terminate Planned Parenthood's Medicaid funding. However, in the rest of the country, Medicaid beneficiaries still have access to Planned Parenthood. The case highlights the ongoing efforts by anti-abortion groups to defund Planned Parenthood, despite the organization's role in providing essential health services to low-income women.

While Seattle's 2018 New Year's Day brought celebration, the city also imposed a 1.75 cent per ounce tax on sweetened beverages, aiming to reduce sugar consumption, fund community college, and assist low-income families. Former Mayor Ed Murray deemed it a "cutting edge piece of legislation," setting an example for the nation. However, critics argue that soda taxes are ineffective, driving revenue outside city limits and uniting diverse groups against them. The tax's impact is evident: a case of Gatorade now costs $26.33, up 64% from $15.99. Retailers like Costco have posted signs directing customers to nearby suburbs to avoid the tax, with some stores seeing significant sales declines. The tax does not apply to milk-based drinks, such as flavored coffee beverages, and Starbucks has rejected the hometown tax. A study by the Mercatus Center at George Mason University ranks California, Oregon, and Washington among the most paternalistic states, highlighting the west coast's trend of social engineering. Opponents argue that the tax disproportionately affects low-income families and fails to address health concerns effectively. The tax's implementation has faced challenges, including lawsuits and administrative issues, with Cook County's tax being repealed after a public outcry. Despite these issues, Seattle's policymakers continue to defend the tax, emphasizing its potential to improve public health and fund important projects.

A male who was reportedly wielding a broomstick was shot and critically injured by Salt Lake City officers on Saturday night, leading to several hours of unrest in the downtown area. The Salt Lake Tribune and Deseret News reported that the male, identified as a teenager by a bystander, was hit twice in the torso by officers responding to a fight near a homeless shelter. Salt Lake City police confirmed that one officer, and possibly a second, was involved in the shooting but did not provide additional details. The shooting sparked hostility from onlookers, who threw rocks and bottles at police, prompting the deployment of almost 100 officers, including those from neighboring departments like Unified Police Department, West Valley City, Sandy, and University of Utah police. Salt Lake City police closed the Trax Blue Line before the Old Greektown stop, causing difficulties for fans leaving a Utah Jazz game. Detective Ken Hansen with the Unified Police Department stated that the male was involved in a fight with another person and tried to attack an officer with the broomstick, leading to the shooting. Bystander Selam Mohammad told the newspapers that his friend was holding the broomstick at his side when officers arrived and that police shot him as soon as he turned around. Detective Greg Wilking with Salt Lake City Police said that there were "a lot of hostile people upset about what had taken place" and that the area was barricaded with a strong officer presence. The incident lasted for several hours, with pockets of disturbance continuing even after the initial shooting.

Emojipedia, the organization that designs sample emoji images, has addressed public feedback by updating three emoji designs: the skateboard, DNA, and lobster. Skateboard legend Tony Hawk was consulted to improve the skateboard emoji, resulting in a design more reflective of modern skateboarding. The DNA emoji was corrected to be right-handed, and the lobster emoji gained two legs to accurately represent the crustacean. These changes, made in response to public criticism, ensure the 2018 emoji release will be more accurate and better received. The updated designs are part of Emojipedia 11.1 and will be implemented by various vendors, with the new emojis expected in the second half of 2018.

The United States and China, the world’s two largest economies, energy consumers, and greenhouse gas emitters, are jointly announcing ambitious targets to reduce carbon emissions in the post-2020 period. This announcement, made by President Obama and Chinese President Xi Jinping, is significant as it aims to inject momentum into global climate negotiations, which will resume in Lima, Peru, and culminate in Paris next year. By setting these targets, both countries are encouraging other nations to put forward their own ambitious emissions reduction plans, thereby overcoming traditional divisions and fostering a strong global climate agreement. The joint announcement is a milestone in the U.S.-China relationship, the outcome of a concerted effort that began last year in Beijing, when State Councilor Yang Jiechi and Obama initiated the United States-China Climate Change Working Group. This effort is driven by the belief that the world’s largest economies, energy consumers, and carbon emitters have a responsibility to lead in the fight against climate change.

The United States intends to reduce its net greenhouse gas emissions by 26 to 28 percent below 2005 levels by 2025. This target is ambitious and feasible, doubling the pace of carbon reductions in the period from 2020 to 2025 compared to the period from 2005 to 2020. It puts the U.S. on a path to transform its economy, with emissions reductions on the order of 80 percent by 2050. The target is grounded in an extensive analysis of the potential to reduce emissions in all sectors of the economy, with significant added benefits for health, clean air, and energy security.
