A Spanish court has ruled that a doctor stole a newborn child nearly five decades ago, one of many abducted during Spain's 20th-century dictatorship, but cleared him because the statute of limitations had expired. The Madrid court found 85-year-old gynecologist Eduardo Vela responsible for abducting Madrigal in 1969, faking her birth by her adoptive parents, and forging official documents. However, the court could not punish Vela as the statute of limitations had expired, despite acknowledging that one of those stolen, plaintiff Ines Madrigal, did not make her complaint until 2012, more than a decade after the crime. Vela, the director of a Madrid clinic considered central to the scandal, denied the accusations during the trial. Madrigal, now 49, learned she wasn't living with her biological parents at 18 and only discovered the scheme in 2010 when her adopting mother disclosed details. DNA tests confirmed her account, but Madrigal's biological parents were never found. The court's verdict was described as "bittersweet" by Madrigal, who announced she would appeal to the country's Supreme Court. This was Spain's first ruling in the "stolen babies" scandal, which began shortly after Franco's victory in the civil war and continued until well after his death in 1975. Estimates suggest as many as 300,000 babies may have been taken from their birth mothers and placed with families supporting the Franco regime. Among those targeted were single mothers, those with "degenerate" political views, or those from poor backgrounds. The trial was a test case for the thousands of families caught up in the illegal practice, with Madrigal's case being the only one to reach the trial stage. Her mother, who died two years ago at 93, supported her efforts to find justice and answers. Madrigal hoped her legal action would be the first of many brought by stolen babies and their families, arguing that people like her had been torn from their parents, trafficked, and ignored for too long.

To boost sales of its Big Mac, McDonald's is giving away 10,000 bottles of its special sauce, a first in the U.S., as it introduces two new sizes: the Mac Jr. and the Grand Mac. The Mac Jr. is a smaller version, while the Grand Mac features a larger patty. This move comes as McDonald's faces declining U.S. sales, down 1.3% in the last quarter, with the All-Day Breakfast program credited for some of the growth. The special sauce giveaway aims to reignite interest in the Big Mac, particularly among younger consumers, as internal data suggests only one in five Millennials have tried it. The bottles will be available Thursday at participating U.S. locations, with McDonald's tweeting about the event and hinting at where and when customers can get their free bottles.

An eastern South Dakota farm with 1.3 million egg-laying chickens has become the first in the state to be infected with a deadly flu virus despite extensive biosecurity measures. Dakota Layers, accounting for nearly half of South Dakota's egg-laying chickens, noticed an unusually high number of dead birds in one of its barns and contacted the state veterinarian. A South Dakota State University lab confirmed the presence of the highly pathogenic H5 avian influenza virus, possibly the H5N2 strain, which has already affected more than 33 million chickens and turkeys in the Midwest, primarily in neighboring states. The farm will begin euthanizing the chickens, and the state veterinarian, Dustin Oedekoven, stated that it was disappointing to see a large-scale operation lose birds after taking all appropriate precautions. The U.S. Department of Agriculture was on-site to evaluate the operation and assist in determining the best course of action. The state has primarily been burying turkey carcasses and composting them. The farm produces over 90,000 dozen eggs daily and ships about 70% of its eggs to California, with officials stressing no danger to the supply and very low risk to humans.

The outbreak has led to record prices for liquid eggs, with the cost more than doubling in the past three weeks. The culprit is the worst-ever American outbreak of the bird flu virus, affecting more than 33.5 million chickens, turkeys, and other birds, with Iowa losing 40% of its laying hens. The government forecasted the first annual drop in egg production since 2008. Greco, a bakery owner near Chicago, has been racing to buy extra supplies and saw prices for liquid eggs jump 28% last week. He is concerned about higher costs and may need to start buying eggs still in shells to crack by hand. The highly concentrated industry in Iowa increases the chances of greater supply impact, with about 1% of the state's farms accounting for 97% of egg capacity. The liquid eggs are a staple in industrial food production for everything from imitation crab meat to ice cream. Governors in Minnesota, Nebraska, Wisconsin, and Iowa have declared states of emergency, and the USDA has authorized $330 million for bird-flu assistance to farmers. Warmer weather is expected to slow the outbreak, but the industry faces significant challenges as the disease continues to spread.

Award-winning musician Prince will play a concert in Baltimore to promote peace following violent protests over the death of Freddie Gray, a 25-year-old man who died in police custody after being arrested for carrying a knife. Prince's concert, scheduled for 5 p.m. Sunday at the Royal Farms Arena, will feature special guests and attendees are being asked to wear something gray. Prince has recorded a new song in response to Gray's death and the protests, which addresses the unrest in Baltimore and broader socio-political issues. The song, titled "Baltimore," is a tribute to the city and all those recently lost in the violence. Prince's performance is part of a "Rally 4 Peace" and is expected to include other stars. The concert aims to be a catalyst for pause and reflection following the outpouring of violence that has gripped Baltimore and areas throughout the U.S. Attendees are encouraged to wear something gray in tribute to those lost in the violence. Prince's new song, "Baltimore," addresses the absence of peace and the need for change, with lyrics such as "Are we gonna see another bloody day? We're tired of cryin' and people dyin'. Let's take all the guns away. Absence of war—you and me. Maybe we can finally say ‘enough is enough.' It's time for love. It's time to hear, it's time to hear, the guitar play!" The event is part of Prince's ongoing efforts to address social and political issues through his music and performances.

"The Lovely Bones," directed by Peter Jackson, is an adaptation of Alice Sebold's best-selling novel, blending elements of warmth, horror, and science fiction. The film, starring Saoirse Ronan as the murdered 14-year-old Susie Salmon, navigates a complex narrative that oscillates between the real world and Susie's afterlife. Ronan's performance is a standout, bringing naturalness and depth to Susie's character, making her both relatable and ethereal. However, the film struggles with its uneven tone and pacing, as it emphasizes its most unsettling and grotesque elements, which can overshadow the emotional core of the story.

Jackson's direction, known for its grand scale and intricate visual effects, is evident in the film's depiction of Susie's in-between world, a fantastical realm filled with magical imagery and special effects. This imaginative setting, while visually stunning, sometimes feels out of place, disrupting the narrative's emotional flow. The film's decision to foreground the killer, George Harvey, played by Stanley Tucci, with a prominent role, adds a layer of tension and horror that can be jarring. Tucci's performance, while unsettling, is not always well-integrated, and his presence can disrupt the film's emotional balance.

The performances of Mark Wahlberg and Rachel Weisz as Susie's parents, Jack and Abigail Salmon, are solid but occasionally struggle to maintain the emotional intensity required by the story. Susan Sarandon, as Abigail's mother, Lynn, provides comic relief but often feels out of place, detracting from the film's overall coherence. The film's handling of Susie's murder is handled delicately, avoiding explicit content, which can leave a sense of incompleteness for those familiar with the book.

While "The Lovely Bones" aims to capture the essence of Sebold's novel, it often falls short, with its focus on horror and special effects overshadowing the more poignant and emotional aspects of the story. The film's structure, which emphasizes Susie's observations from her afterlife, can feel overly sentimental and preachy, detracting from the narrative's impact. Despite these shortcomings, the film retains moments of genuine emotional resonance, particularly in Ronan's performances, which offer a glimpse of the novel's original power.

Poland's Senate has approved a controversial bill making it illegal to accuse the Polish nation or state of complicity in the Nazi Holocaust, a move that has sparked outrage from Israeli officials and lawmakers. The bill, which sets fines or a maximum three-year jail term as punishment, must be signed off by President Andrzej Duda before becoming law. President Duda has defended the bill, stating Poland has the right "to defend historical truth." However, the bill's critics argue it could stifle academic discourse and historical research. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has called the bill an attempt to rewrite history and deny the Holocaust. Israeli lawmakers are now seeking to strengthen their own Holocaust denial laws. The bill's passage has also strained Poland's relationship with the United States, which has urged the Polish government to reconsider the legislation. Polish politicians argue the bill is necessary to protect the nation's historical narrative, which they claim has been unfairly tarnished by phrases like "Polish death camps." Critics, including some Polish historians and Jewish organizations, warn the bill could act as a "muzzle" on those seeking to uncover the full complexity of the Holocaust. The bill's timing, coming just before International Holocaust Remembrance Day, has been criticized as insensitive. Poland's ruling Law and Justice party authored the bill, which calls for up to three years in prison for any intentional attempt to falsely attribute the crimes of Nazi Germany to the Polish state or people. The U.S. State Department has expressed concerns that the legislation could "undermine free speech and academic discourse" and have "repercussions" on Poland's strategic interests and relationships, including with the United States and Israel. The bill's approval has reignited debates about the role of individual Poles during World War II, with some historians arguing that while the Polish state was not complicit in the Holocaust, many Poles were complicit through acts such as denouncing their Jewish neighbors to the Germans. Polish officials argue that the bill is not about denying individual Poles' actions but about protecting the nation's historical narrative. The controversy highlights the complex and often contentious relationship between Poland and Israel, as well as the broader debate over how to remember and teach the Holocaust.

Imagine transforming your bathroom into a confectionary masterpiece: Bathrooms.com and U.K.-based chocolatiers Choccywoccydoodah have collaborated to create a unique chocolate-furnished bathroom suite, complete with a bathtub made from 8 million calories of Belgian chocolate. Dubbed the Maderno Sweet bathroom, it features a 210,000-calorie chocolate bidet and a 210,000-calorie chocolate sink, along with a 980,000-calorie chocolate toilet. The entire set, listed for $133,040, is designed to add a whimsical touch to your bathroom decor, though it's not meant for actual use. The chocolate pieces are crafted fresh, ensuring a two- to three-month wait time. Bathrooms.com's CEO, Ian Monk, was inspired to create this sweet bathroom suite after noticing frequent misspellings of "bathroom suites" as "bathroom sweets" in online searches. While the chocolate bathroom won't withstand direct sunlight, radiator heat, or hot liquids, it can be preserved with a layer of varnish for a shelf life of up to six months. This unique offering is perfect for those who dream of indulging in a bathroom experience that is both visually appealing and, of course, sweet.

Notre Dame football star Manti Te'o claims he was the victim of a cruel hoax after it was revealed that his girlfriend, Lennay Kekua, never existed and her death was faked. Katie Couric's show has released recordings of voicemails Te'o received, which he believed were from Lennay. The voicemails, left on Te'o's phone by Ronaiah Tuiasosopo, reveal Te'o's belief in the hoax, with calls sometimes lasting hours. Phone records show "dozens of calls" to one number, believed to be Lennay's. Te'o maintains he was unaware of the deception until recently, describing his relationship with Lennay as one filled with hope and inspiration, despite the now-proven falsehood.

The New England Holocaust Memorial in Boston was vandalized for the second time in two months when a 17-year-old suspect shattered a glass panel just before 7 p.m. on Monday, police said. The suspect, from Malden, was quickly tackled by two bystanders and held until police arrived. He is charged with willful destruction of property and is due to be arraigned in Boston Municipal Court. The vandalism, which occurred two days after a violent white nationalist rally in Charlottesville, Va., and less than two months after a 21-year-old with a history of mental illness shattered a glass panel at the Boston memorial, has sparked outrage and concern. The glass towers of the memorial, installed in 1995, had never been vandalized before the June incident. Robert Trestan, regional director of the Anti-Defamation League, said it was a reminder that the community needs to be united in opposition to all forms of hate and in the important role that memorials play in the community. Boston Mayor Martin J. Walsh wrote on Twitter that the city stands up against hate and condemned the despicable action. Boston Police Commissioner William Evans said the behavior will not be tolerated in the city. The memorial reopened around 9 p.m., with at least one officer posted there throughout the night. Jeremy Burton, executive director of the Jewish Community Relations Council, noted that the panels are made from resilient glass, and it takes a very conscious effort to break it. The timing of the vandalism, coming as it does in a week when many watched Nazis march in Virginia, has been particularly distressing for the community. Boston residents and visitors expressed shock and sadness at the act, with one family explaining to their 6-year-old child that the memorial was for "grandpa."

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) has dismissed claims of genocide by Serbia and Croatia against each other during the Croatian war of secession from Yugoslavia. The Croatian government had accused Serbia of committing genocide in the town of Vukovar and elsewhere in 1991. Serbia, in turn, filed a counter-claim over the expulsion of more than 200,000 Serbs from Croatia. About 20,000 people died during the 1991-1995 war, mostly Croats. The court's ruling, delivered by Judge Peter Tomka, dismissed both the Croatian claim and the Serbian counter-claim, stating that neither side had provided sufficient evidence to demonstrate the "specific intent required for acts of genocide." The court acknowledged that forces on both sides had carried out violent acts during the war but found that neither side had met the threshold for genocide. The ruling, posted online, marks the end of a 16-year legal saga between the two nations. Serbian Justice Minister Nikola Selkovic stated that the ruling would "start a new and blank page in our relationship with Croatia," while Serbian President Tomislav Nikolic expressed hope for "a period of lasting peace and prosperity" in the region. Croatian Prime Minister Zoran Milanovic, while not satisfied with the court's ruling, accepted it in a civilised manner. The case highlights the difficulty in proving genocide, as the UN 1948 Genocide Convention requires a specific intent to destroy a national, ethnical, racial, or religious group. The ruling is final, and both Croatia and Serbia will now focus on improving their bilateral relations.

Democratic candidate Dan Adler's bizarre and possibly offensive ad campaign is drawing significant attention. In one ad, Adler hangs out with a multi-ethnic crowd, attempting to appeal to Asian voters by mentioning his marriage to a Korean and his Jewish heritage. A heavily-accented Korean immigrant woman in a laundromat awkwardly interrupts him, asking "What's a mensch?" This ad, along with others featuring former Disney CEO Michael Eisner, former child star Patty Duke, and even Adler's young son, is spreading online due to their shock value or sheer weirdness. In another video, Adler's son delivers a foul-mouthed catchphrase while making a special effects-assisted basketball dunk that would impress professional players. These ads highlight the unconventional and often bizarre nature of Adler's campaign strategy.

A mummified monk found in Mongolia has been baffling and astounding those who uncovered him. Senior Buddhists say the monk, found sitting in the lotus position, is in a deep meditative trance and not dead. Forensic examinations are under way on the remains, found wrapped in cattle skins in north-central Mongolia. Scientists have yet to determine how the monk is so well preserved, though some think Mongolia's cold weather could be the reason. Dr. Barry Kerzin, a physician to Tibetan spiritual leader the Dalai Lama, told the Siberian Times that the monk is in a rare state of meditation called "tukdam." "If the meditator can continue to stay in this meditative state, he can become a Buddha," Dr. Kerzin said. Over the last 50 years, there are said to have been 40 such cases in India involving meditating Tibetan monks. The mummified remains, covered in cattle skin, were found on January 27 in the Songinokhairkhan province. However, there is more to the story, and now police have revealed that the monk had been stolen from another part of the country and was about to be sold off. An unnamed official said that it was taken from a cave in the Kobdsk region by a man who then hid it in his own home in Ulaanbaatar. He had then been planning to sell it on the black market at a "very high price," with local media claiming he wanted to take it over the Mongolian border. Police uncovered the plot and quickly arrested a 45-year-old, named only as Enhtor. According to Article 18 of the Criminal Code of Mongolia, smuggling items of cultural heritage are punishable with either a fine of up to 3 million roubles ($43,000) or between five and 12 years in prison. The monk is now being guarded at the National Centre of Forensic Expertise at Ulaanbaatar. Initial speculation is that the mummy could be a teacher of Lama Dashi-Dorzho Itigilov, who was also found mummified. Born in 1852, Dashi-Dorzho Itigilov was a Buryat Buddhist Lama of the Tibetan Buddhist tradition, best known for the lifelike state of his body. In 1927, the then-75-year-old told his students he planned to die and instructed them to "look at" his body in 30 years. As the story goes, Itigilov got into the lotus position and started to meditate and chant, then died. Roughly 30 years later, his followers did indeed exhume his body and reportedly found it still in the lotus position and undecayed. It was transported to a Russian monastery where it is said to remain. At the time, a scientist said the soil, the condition of the coffin, and salt placed in the coffin could help explain how the body remained so well-preserved, but suggested Itigilov may have had a defect in a gene related to decomposition, or was perhaps embalmed in some way. The mummified monk's discovery has raised questions about the preservation process and the possibility of a "tukdam" state. The body is now under guard at the National Centre of Forensic Expertise in Ulaanbaatar, where further investigations will be conducted.

President Obama abruptly left his golf game on O'ahu to check on a friend's injured son, causing a flurry of activity at the Luana Hills Country Club. The first family was unharmed, according to White House spokesman Bill Burton. The injured child, Eric Whitaker's son, suffered a minor beach injury that did not require stitches. Obama quickly returned to the golf course after ensuring the boy was with his parents. His departure and return were marked by a dramatic, high-speed motorcade. The incident raised concerns among the press, who were initially unaware of the situation. Despite the urgency, the White House initially did not provide details to protect the family's privacy. The president's day began with a workout at the Marine Corps Base Hawai'i gym and a private tennis session with his wife. He then addressed the press, discussing the Detroit bombing attempt and condemning the Iranian government's crackdown on protesters. His interactions with Marines and their families highlighted the informal nature of his O'ahu vacation.

A scuba diver and South Florida resident, Christopher Le Cun, is suing Florida Power and Light (FPL) after being sucked into an intake pipe at the St. Lucie Nuclear Power Plant. On July 12, 2015, Le Cun and his best friend, Robert Blake, were scuba diving off Hutchinson Island when they encountered a yellow buoy marking three large submerged structures. Despite no visible warnings, the pair decided to investigate. Le Cun, who was diving with his family, swam towards the structures and was suddenly pulled into one of the pipes. Blake, who stayed on the boat, witnessed the terrifying event, screaming to his family that his friend was being pulled in. Le Cun spent about five minutes tumbling through the darkness, feeling the intense pressure and considering the worst. He eventually emerged into a canal, covered in bruises and battered, and was found by a worker. Le Cun’s wife, Brittany, was unaware of the incident until Le Cun called her on a borrowed phone. FPL claims the intake pipe has a protective cap and a buoy warning to stay 100 feet away, but Le Cun argues the cap is ineffective. This is not the first incident; a diver named William Lamm was also sucked into the pipe in 1989 and survived. Both incidents have raised concerns about safety measures at the plant. Le Cun hopes his lawsuit will lead to improved safety protocols to prevent such tragedies from recurring.

All roads running through Valley Forge National Historical Park were closed Tuesday after a sewer main break caused extensive flooding, with some reports estimating the volume of spilled raw sewage to be about 5 million gallons. The break occurred in the Valley Creek Trunk Sewer Force Main near the intersection of Routes 252 and 23 in Upper Merion Township, drawing a multi-agency response that included contractors and environmental and engineering consultants. The 30-inch main, shared by several local municipalities, sent 5,000 gallons of sewage per minute into the creek. Overnight crews worked to remove the pipe, with a new one expected to arrive around 7 a.m. Wednesday. The following roads are closed: Route 23 eastbound from Davis Road to Route 252, Route 23 westbound from N. Gulph Road to Route 252, Route 252 northbound from the Pennsylvania Turnpike, North and South Outer Line Drives, Gulph Road from Thomas Road to Route 23, and Yellow Springs Road at the Covered Bridge. Public works officials expect these sections of road to remain closed for several days as construction crews repair the damaged water main and resurface portions of the street. The leak doesn't pose a threat to humans but could be a safety concern for wildlife in the area.

Ricky Gervais hosted the 2010, 2011, and 2012 Golden Globe Awards, each year delivering increasingly biting and controversial jokes. In 2010, Gervais opened with a jab at cosmetic surgery, making light of the attendees' appearances, and went on to mock Angelina Jolie, Johnny Depp, and the Golden Globes' writing category, suggesting actors are more important than writers. He also poked fun at Mel Gibson, referencing his DUI arrest, and joked about Bruce Willis being "Ashton Kutcher's dad." In 2011, Gervais took aim at Sean Penn, Caitlyn Jenner, and "The Martian," which he included in the comedy category. His monologue was filled with zingers, such as "Actors aren't just loved here in Hollywood, they are loved the world over," and "It's going to be a night of partying and heavy drinking – or as Charlie Sheen calls it: breakfast." Gervais also made a homophobic comment about Jodie Foster and engaged in a brief exchange with Madonna. In 2012, Gervais toned down his act but still managed to offend, particularly with a joke about Jodie Foster's film "The Beaver," suggesting he hadn't seen it. He also swore while discussing Salma Hayek and Antonio Banderas, though his profanity was bleeped out for home audiences. Meanwhile, Mel Gibson was set to present an award at the 2012 ceremony, adding to the awkwardness. Gervais's hosting style, marked by his acerbic humor and willingness to offend, became a defining feature of the Golden Globes during his tenure.

ISIS has released a new propaganda video featuring two deaf-mute militants delivering a sign language message, aiming to recruit Muslims in Europe and threaten enemies. The video, subtitled in Arabic and English, starts with the fighters declaring, "We, the deaf and mute, direct our message to the Islamic world." One fighter describes his role as a traffic policeman in the Islamic State, while the other shows them directing traffic in Mosul. They claim that deafness or disability is no excuse for not waging jihad. The video ends with the pair launching two rockets, targeting nearby Peshmerga fighters. This campaign underscores ISIS’s efforts to expand its reach by involving individuals from diverse backgrounds, challenging the notion that physical limitations can hinder participation in their cause.

Researchers have unveiled the genetic blueprint of a kangaroo species for the first time, marking a significant milestone in the study of mammalian evolution. An international team of scientists, publishing their findings in the Biomed Central journal, Genome Biology, have sequenced the genome of the tammar wallaby (Macropus eugenii), a small species inhabiting islands off Australia's south and western coasts. The tammar wallaby is the third marsupial to have its genome decoded, following the Tasmanian devil and the South American opossum. This breakthrough provides insights into key marsupial traits, such as the unique development of young in the mother's pouch and the genetic basis for the kangaroo's distinctive hopping ability. The study also explores how genes are activated at different stages of the animal's life cycle and in various parts of its body, potentially offering new avenues for understanding and addressing human diseases. The project, led by Australian scientists, has been a long-term effort, reflecting advancements in genome sequencing technologies. By comparing the tammar wallaby's genome with those of other mammals, researchers hope to gain a deeper understanding of the evolutionary divergence between marsupials and other mammals, which occurred at least 130 million years ago.

Tim Tebow, the New York Jets backup quarterback, has canceled a scheduled appearance at the Dallas megachurch of controversial pastor Robert Jeffress, who has faced criticism for his views on other religions and homosexuality. Tebow, who was set to deliver two sermons at the $130 million building of First Baptist Dallas Church on April 28, tweeted that he would no longer honor the commitment due to new information that had been brought to his attention. He stated, "While I was looking forward to sharing a message of hope and Christ's unconditional love with the faithful members of the historic First Baptist Church of Dallas in April, due to new information that has been brought to my attention, I have decided to cancel my upcoming appearance. I will continue to use the platform God has blessed me with to bring Faith, Hope and Love to all those needing a brighter day. Thank you for all of your love and support. God Bless!" In response, First Baptist Church stated that Tebow called Dr. Jeffress on Wednesday evening, saying he needed to avoid controversy at this time but would like to come to First Baptist Dallas to speak at a future date. Jeffress, known for his critiques of other religions and lifestyles, has made headlines for his statements, including describing Islam as a religion from the "pit of hell" and Mormons as a cult. The cancellation of Tebow's appearance drew intense criticism, with some suggesting it was a tacit endorsement of Jeffress' beliefs. However, Tebow's polite cancellation is seen as an effective rebuke of intolerance, maintaining his principled stand against Jeffress' controversial views.

Elton John and his partner David Furnish plan to get married in May in England, where gay marriage is now legal. The pair will wed quietly in a registry office, bringing their two children, Zachary and Elijah, along with a few friends. They have been in a civil partnership since 2005, which solidified their relationship more than they anticipated. David Furnish, 51, shared that they initially entered the partnership to support the movement for equality and to acknowledge their commitment. Now, they feel it's important to take the next step legally. Elton John, 67, expressed his joy at the change in legislation, stating, "We will get married." The couple hopes to celebrate their union with their children and a few close friends, maintaining their commitment to a quiet celebration. Furnish, who has the names of their children tattooed on his arms, believes the world is changing, and people are becoming more accepting of gay relationships due to increased exposure through media. He credits shows like "Will & Grace" for helping to shift public opinion.

Republican presidential contender Ben Carson has maintained a business relationship with Alfonso A. Costa, a dentist convicted of defrauding insurance companies, despite Carson's past calls for harsh penalties for such crimes. In 2008, Carson testified on Costa's behalf, describing him as a "very close friend" and vouching for his personal integrity. Costa avoided prison time, receiving a one-year house arrest and 100 hours of community service, along with a $294,000 fine and restitution. The two men have continued to maintain business ties, including investments through corporations they co-founded. Carson's actions have raised questions about the consistency of his tough-on-crime stance. In his 2013 book, "America the Beautiful," Carson advocated for severe penalties for health care fraud, including amputation of fingers as a deterrent. However, his support for Costa's lenient sentence contradicts this position. The article also highlights how Costa's dental practice was investigated and charged with fraud, and how the government's approach to such cases can lead to disproportionate penalties. Despite the controversy, Carson's business relationship with Costa continues, raising ethical concerns about his campaign's integrity and his stance on criminal justice.

A teenage suspect, Erich Nowsch, has been arrested in connection with the fatal shooting of a mother of four in a road rage incident that occurred last week. Nowsch, 19, was apprehended after a brief standoff at a home a block away from the scene of the February 12th shooting, where 44-year-old Tammy Meyers was shot outside her home around 11:22 p.m. He faces charges of murder, attempted murder, and discharging a gun in a vehicle. The shooting unfolded after Meyers was confronted by an angry driver earlier that night as she was driving her daughter home from a night-time driving lesson. According to police, after Meyers got home, she and her 22-year-old armed son went out looking for the driver involved in the earlier incident and followed a car they believed was the same. They stopped following the car and returned home, only to be confronted by a silver or gray car that began shooting. Meyers' son, Brandon, returned fire, and when the shooting stopped, they found their mother mortally wounded. Nowsch has told friends he was in a park near the school when he thought someone was following him in a green car, leading him to call a friend with a silver Audi to pick him up. He claims he started shooting when he thought he saw someone in the green car waving a gun from the window, and he was sure he hit someone when he fired again in the cul-de-sac. The driver of the silver car has not been identified. Tammy Meyers' husband, Robert, said the family knew Nowsch and his father had committed suicide in 2010. "We know this boy. I couldn't tell you this before," Robert Meyers told reporters. "He knew where I lived. We knew how bad he was, but we didn't know it was this bad. That he'd gotten to this point, and his friends." Robert Meyers added that his wife had spent countless hours at the park consoling Nowsch, feeding him, and giving him money, urging him to "pull his pants up and to be a man." The family is now seeking answers and justice for the loss of Tammy Meyers, who was a nurse and mother of four.

As the controversy over the death of Cecil the lion, one of Africa's most famous and beloved lions, continued to escalate, two Zimbabwean men who allegedly assisted in the hunt faced poaching charges. Theo Bronchorst, a professional hunter, and Honest Trymore Ndlovu, a landowner, appeared in court in Zimbabwe on Wednesday, facing allegations that they lured Cecil outside Hwange National Park using bait, allowing American dentist Walter James Palmer to kill the lion. Both men were granted bail of $1,000 each and ordered to return to court for further proceedings. Zimbabwean authorities have confirmed that Palmer, who paid $50,000 for the hunt, could also face poaching charges. The Zimbabwe Parks and Wildlife Management Authority stated that Palmer shot Cecil with a bow and arrow, injuring it, and later tracked the lion for 40 hours before finishing it off with a gun. Cecil's death has sparked outrage, with his head reportedly skinned and beheaded. Conservationists fear that Cecil's death could lead to infanticide as other males invade the prides he led. The incident has also reignited debates about trophy hunting and its impact on wildlife populations. Walter Palmer, who has not been charged but is under investigation, expressed regret for the killing and claimed he relied on his local professional guides to ensure a legal hunt. His dental practice in Minnesota has been temporarily closed, and protesters have placed stuffed toys outside his office. The death of Cecil, who was part of a long-term study by Oxford University, has highlighted the complex issues surrounding conservation and the ethics of trophy hunting.

A 37-year-old female caretaker was fatally mauled by a Bengal tiger in a zoo in Benidorm, Spain. The incident occurred around 5 pm when she was inside the tiger's cage at Terra Natura zoo, which is described as an "immersion park" with over 1,500 animals from 200 species. Local reports suggest the woman may have left a door open inadvertently as she performed her duties. Emergency services, including the Red Cross and medics, were called but arrived to find the victim already deceased. The tiger was sedated to allow for the recovery of the body. The park was open at the time, but the cage was not in the public view, and no visitors witnessed the attack. Staff are reportedly "appalled and deeply affected" by the tragedy. An investigation into the circumstances of the death is underway, with the zoo spokesperson stating the accident occurred in a shelter area accessible only to authorized personnel. The latest incident comes after a zookeeper was killed by a Sumatran tiger in 2013, prompting a fine of nearly half a million pounds. The park's website emphasizes its commitment to authentic habitats and interactions with wildlife, yet this tragic event highlights the inherent dangers in such environments.

A stretch of the Bronx River Parkway near the Bronx Zoo has become a dangerous area, with seven people killed in a crash on Sunday, according to an attorney who sued the city and state on behalf of some of the victims. The lawyer, Eric Buckvar, described the area as the "Bermuda Triangle of the Bronx River Parkway," citing multiple accidents where cars have hit the median and gone out of control. Traffic tends to slow suddenly, and officials considered adding a new lane but ultimately decided against it. In 2006, a family of six, including a 6-year-old girl, died in a similar accident. Last June, a car hit the median and sailed into the air, landing on a street below. The latest crash involved a speeding driver who clipped the concrete barrier, damaging a tire and causing the SUV to plunge off the highway and into a ravine. All seven occupants, including three generations of a family, were killed. The crash site, near the Bronx Zoo, was difficult to see, with contents of the SUV scattered on the ground. The family, which had just picked up grandparents from the Dominican Republic for a family party, is struggling to afford the cost of burying everyone at once. The area remains a concern for safety, with family members and officials calling for potential solutions.

More than 6,000 tins of Heinz baked beans with sausages have been stolen from a parked lorry in Worcestershire, UK. Thieves cut a large hole in the curtain-sided vehicle, targeting nearly two pallets of the tins during the night. The driver, asleep in the cab, was unaware of the theft. Police are seeking information, particularly from anyone trying to sell large quantities of Heinz baked beans in suspicious circumstances. The incident occurred on the A441 at Cookhill, near Redditch, and involved a white Scania lorry.

A nine-year-old boy named Kieran Sorkin, born without fully formed ears, underwent a groundbreaking surgery at Great Ormond Street Hospital, where doctors crafted a pair of ears from his rib cartilage. Kieran, from Bushey, Hertfordshire, was born with bilateral microtia, a rare congenital deformity where the external ear is underdeveloped, and is also deaf. He has gradually been able to hear thanks to previous operations and a hearing aid, but the new ears will significantly boost his confidence and appearance. Kieran's father, David Sorkin, said, "We could not have wished for a better result," adding that Kieran's reaction was "just a 'wow'." The surgery, led by Neil Bulstrode, a consultant plastic and reconstructive surgeon, involved harvesting cartilage from Kieran's ribs, shaping it into frameworks, and grafting them onto his head. The procedure, while major, brings substantial psychological benefits, as Kieran's father noted, "If you can change the confidence of a patient at this young age, you can change their whole trajectory in life." Kieran's mother, Louise, expressed relief that he would no longer be bullied because he looks different. The operation is primarily cosmetic, not to improve hearing, but researchers at the University College London Institute for Child Health are exploring the use of stem cells from a child's own fat to create new ear frameworks, potentially making the procedure less invasive. Kieran will need a follow-up operation in six months to ensure his ears stand out more from his scalp.

A historic 85-year-old wooden schooner, the Nina, has gone missing with seven people on board, raising grave concerns for their safety. The vessel, 70 feet long, left New Zealand bound for Australia on May 29 but stopped communicating on June 4. The last known contact was a satellite phone call to a meteorologist, who advised the crew to ride out a storm. No distress signals were sent, and the emergency beacon was not activated. Search efforts escalated this week, with an Air Force plane searching the area but finding no signs of the Nina. The crew includes six Americans and one Briton, with varying levels of sailing experience. The boat is equipped with modern tracking and communication devices, yet none have been heard from since early June. The Nina is a well-maintained racing yacht that had recently received a new engine, which reportedly caused some initial leaking issues. The vessel was last known to be 400 miles northwest of New Zealand in the Tasman Sea. Authorities are considering various scenarios, including the boat losing communications, drifting off course, or the crew taking to lifeboats. The possibility of a catastrophic failure leading to the Nina's sinking before anyone could react is also being explored. The search continues, with authorities emphasizing their concern for the safety and wellbeing of the missing crew.

Rapper 50 Cent faced backlash Tuesday after posting offensive memes mocking actor Terry Crews, who testified before the Senate Judiciary Committee about his own sexual assault experience. The post, which included a split photo of Crews flexing and holding a rose, with the top caption reading "I got raped … My wife just watched" and the bottom "Gym time," garnered nearly 125,000 likes and a crying-laugh emoji from Russell Simmons, who has faced sexual assault allegations. The post was swiftly deleted, but not before generating intense criticism. "Im not surprised at Curtis Jacksons trash a—but Russell commenting is a disappointment," dancer Destiney Bleu tweeted. "As someone who was a fan of 50 cent since I was a kid, I’m disgusted at his ignorance and insensitive response to Terry Crew’s sexual assault story," another user wrote. "To laugh and make jokes about such a serious matter is one of the main reasons why sexual assault victims are afraid to speak up." Terry Crews, however, took the high road, stating, "I prove that size doesn’t matter when it comes to sexual assault." Crews, who testified in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee to advocate for the Sexual Assault Survivors’ Bill of Rights, called out the culture of toxic masculinity. His testimony highlighted the systemic issues faced by sexual assault survivors, including the pressure to remain silent and the belief that men are more valuable than women. The bill aims to remove the burden from victims, providing them with access to counseling and proper legal support. 50 Cent's comments have sparked a broader conversation about the treatment of sexual assault survivors and the need for empathy and understanding.

On the night of October 8, a series of wildfires erupted simultaneously across the North Coast region of California, driven by powerful winds and fueled by the extreme dryness of the landscape, causing unprecedented destruction. The Tubbs Fire, which originated near Tubbs Lane north of Calistoga, spread rapidly, engulfing homes and neighborhoods with ferocious intensity. Battalion Chief Gino DeGraffenreid of Cal Fire recounted how he rescued a couple who had managed to stay alive in a pool for an hour, their clothes soaked and their bodies freezing. The fire's speed and intensity were extraordinary, with flames racing across 12 miles in just over four hours, reaching Santa Rosa's Fountaingrove and Coffey Park neighborhoods. The fire's destructive force was so powerful that it flipped over cars, uprooted trees, and tore apart homes, leaving a trail of devastation in its wake.

The fire's rapid spread was attributed to the Diablo winds, which reached gusts of up to 73 mph, creating a vortex of air that turned into a fire whirl, or fire tornado. This phenomenon, which is rare but not unheard of, occurred when the heat from the fire rose, creating a powerful suction that pulled in more air and debris, forming a vortex that could reach hurricane-force speeds. The fire whirls were responsible for the fire's ability to spread sideways into neighborhoods, causing massive damage to homes and infrastructure. Fire scientists noted that the fire's intensity and the formation of fire whirls were unprecedented, with Scott Upton, the northern region chief for the California Department of Forestry and Fire Protection, describing the damage as akin to a hurricane but with fire instead of rain.

The Tubbs Fire, which has claimed at least 22 lives and burned 36,432 acres, is part of a larger pattern of wildfires that have been exacerbated by climate change, leading to hotter and drier conditions. The fire's behavior was compared to the 2003 Cedar Fire, which also spread rapidly due to strong winds and created its own weather patterns. The fire's intensity was so great that it melted cars and lifted vehicles off the ground, creating a scene of apocalyptic destruction. The fire's spread was not limited to Santa Rosa; it also affected other areas, including Napa Valley, where the Atlas Fire caused significant damage to wineries and homes.

The destructive force of the fire whirls was not limited to the Tubbs Fire; similar phenomena were observed in other fires across the state. In California, fire tornadoes have been known to lift all-terrain vehicles and even entire homes, causing significant damage. The phenomenon is more common in open spaces, but the Diablo winds created conditions that allowed for the formation of fire whirls in densely populated areas. The intensity of the fires was further exacerbated by the lack of resources and the difficulty in containing the rapidly spreading flames. The fires also posed a significant threat to the safety of emergency responders, who had to navigate dangerous conditions to save lives and property.

The aftermath of the fires has left a trail of destruction, with recovery teams working to assess the damage and search for remains in the rubble. The experience of the residents who fled their homes in the middle of the night has been harrowing, with many recounting the terrifying experience of running into a blast furnace of heat and embers. The fires have also had a significant economic impact, with the destruction of homes, businesses, and infrastructure. The response to the fires has been a coordinated effort involving multiple agencies and resources, but the scale of the disaster has highlighted the need for better preparedness and resources to combat the increasing threat of wildfires in the region.

North Korean leader Kim Jong Un has agreed to allow nuclear inspections and to permanently dismantle a key missile test site in the presence of international experts, subject to final negotiations. Kim also pledged to close his main Yongbyon nuclear complex if the United States takes reciprocal actions. South Korean President Moon Jae-in announced these agreements during a joint press conference with Kim after their three-day summit in Pyongyang. The two leaders also agreed to reconnect rail and road links, restart a joint factory park, and allow South Korean citizens to visit the Mount Kumgang tourist region for the first time since 2008. Kim stated his intention to visit Seoul in the near future, making him the first North Korean leader to do so. The United States appeared eager to resume talks with North Korea, with U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo inviting North Korea’s foreign minister to meet in New York next week. However, critics expressed skepticism about the progress on denuclearization, noting that North Korea’s commitments were conditional and lacked specific details. The U.S. and South Korea remain concerned that North Korea may use these steps to drive a wedge between Washington and Seoul, potentially undermining the rationale for U.S. troops in South Korea. Despite the positive rhetoric and agreements, analysts warned that North Korea’s actions so far did not constitute irreversible movement toward denuclearization and that the process would likely be long and complex.

American rock band Bon Jovi faces a significant setback in its plans to perform in China, with concerts in Beijing and Shanghai canceled just a week before their scheduled dates. The cancellations, attributed to the band's inclusion of a picture of the Dalai Lama in a 2010 video backdrop during a concert in Taiwan, highlight the complex and often opaque nature of China's cultural policies. This incident marks Bon Jovi as the latest in a long line of Western artists to run afoul of Chinese authorities, following in the footsteps of Maroon 5, Björk, and even British band Oasis, who had to cancel tours due to their perceived political leanings. The Ministry of Culture, known for its stringent control over cultural content, appears to have taken issue with the band's past performance, leading to the cancellation of the concerts. Promoter AEG Live Asia announced that the shows would be postponed due to "unforeseen reasons," promising refunds to ticket holders. The cancellation has left fans disappointed, with some expressing frustration and others speculating about the political implications. The incident underscores the challenges faced by international artists in navigating China's sensitive political landscape, where even seemingly innocuous actions can have far-reaching consequences. The band's frontman, Jon Bon Jovi, had previously celebrated the prospect of performing in China by recording a Mandarin version of a famous Chinese love song, a move that endeared him to Chinese fans. However, the recent cancellation suggests that the band's relationship with the Chinese market may be more complicated than initially thought. The band's upcoming album, titled "Burning Bridges," hints at themes of individual freedom and expression, which may now face significant obstacles in the Chinese market.

This year’s Academy Awards nominations have sparked renewed discussions about diversity, with seven actors of color earning nods, including Denzel Washington and Viola Davis for “Fences,” Mahershala Ali and Naomie Harris for “Moonlight,” Ruth Negga for “Loving,” Dev Patel for “Lion,” and Octavia Spencer for “Hidden Figures.” The nominations have brought a more inclusive tone to the awards season, with #OscarsLessWhite trending on social media. However, several notable snubs have also emerged, including Martin Scorsese for his film “Silence,” despite its critical acclaim and strong box office performance. Taraji P. Henson, who starred in “Hidden Figures,” was overlooked for a Best Actress nomination, while Amy Adams, despite her critically acclaimed performance in “Arrival,” did not secure a Best Actress nomination. The animated film “Finding Dory” also missed out on a nomination for Best Animated Feature, despite its commercial success and positive reviews. Other notable omissions include Viggo Mortensen for his role in “Captain Fantastic,” Michael Keaton for his performance in “The Founder,” and Matthew McConaughey for his role in “Gold.” The film “Sully,” which starred Tom Hanks and Clint Eastwood, was also snubbed in the major categories, despite its box office success and critical acclaim. The lack of nominations for “The King’s Choice,” “Eye In The Sky,” and “Trolls” further highlights the diversity gap in the Academy’s selections. Despite these snubs, the nominations have brought a more inclusive tone to the awards season, with a record number of actors of color receiving nods, marking a significant shift in the industry’s approach to diversity.

Twitter has faced criticism for its handling of online abuse after Robin Williams' daughter, Zelda, was bullied off the platform following her father's death. Zelda Williams, 25, received messages blaming her for her father's suicide and images of the comedian with alleged bruises. In response, Twitter promised to improve its policies and suspended accounts responsible for the abuse. Twitter's vice president of trust and safety, Del Harvey, stated, "We will not tolerate abuse of this nature on Twitter. We have suspended a number of accounts related to this issue for violating our rules and we are in the process of evaluating how we can further improve our policies to better handle tragic situations like this one. This includes expanding our policies regarding self-harm and private information, and improving support for family members of deceased users." However, Zelda Williams decided to stay off Twitter and Instagram for a "good long time" due to the messages. The incident highlights the broader issue of online harassment, with Imani Gandy, a senior legal analyst, describing the constant abuse she faces on Twitter due to her race, gender, and medical condition. Gandy has blocked thousands of accounts and reported them using Twitter's "Report Abuse" form but notes that the measures do not fully address persistent attackers who often create new accounts. Twitter's commitment to free expression may be seen as a barrier to addressing the problem, according to Soraya Chemaly, a media critic and feminist activist. Chemaly suggests that Twitter should adopt features from third-party software like "Block Together" to better protect users. The article concludes by noting that while Twitter's policies may be updated, the issue of online harassment remains a significant challenge for the platform.

An oil platform exploded and caught fire off the Louisiana coast, the second such disaster in the Gulf of Mexico in less than five months. All 13 crew members were rescued from the water in protective "Gumby suits." The Coast Guard initially reported an oil sheen a mile long and 100 feet wide from the site of the blast, but hours later, crews were unable to find any spill. The platform, owned by Houston-based Mariner Energy, was producing 58,800 gallons of oil and 900,000 cubic feet of gas per day, according to a company report. The platform, in about 340 feet of water, was 100 miles south of Louisiana's Vermilion Bay, making it easier to respond compared to the deep-water operations of the BP spill. The crew was found floating in the water, huddled together in the Gumby suits. The Coast Guard said one person was injured, but Mariner Energy reported no injuries. The platform had seven active production wells, which were shut down shortly after the fire broke out. Mariner Energy has a history of accidents, with 10 incidents reported to the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, Regulation and Enforcement over the past four years. The incident prompted swift reactions from environmentalists, who cited the risks of offshore oil exploration. Meanwhile, efforts to permanently plug BP's well continued, with plans to remove the well's blowout preventer from the seafloor.

Seth Meyers, 44, and his wife Alexi Ashe welcomed their second child, a son named Axel Strahl, into the world on April 8, 2018, in a dramatic fashion. The Late Night with Seth Meyers host shared the story of his baby's birth on his show the following day, detailing the unexpected and somewhat chaotic circumstances. Meyers recounted how his newborn son Axel couldn't wait to make his entrance, with the baby being born in the lobby of their apartment building before the family could even reach the hospital. The NYPD arrived just after the birth and assisted in cutting the umbilical cord, while neighbors provided towels to keep the baby warm. Meyers expressed gratitude to the emergency responders and his supportive wife, who was seen lying on the ground holding their son, with emergency personnel administering oxygen. The proud father's emotional moment was further highlighted by a photo shared on the show, capturing the intimate scene. Social media users praised Meyers, with one user tweeting, "Congratulations to you and your growing family. Welcome Axel. A beautiful story to erase all the bad news from my head." The middle name, Axel, honors Meyers' wife's grandparents, who met in a hospital in Austria after being liberated from a concentration camp. This heartwarming story of birth and resilience resonated with viewers, showcasing the joy and challenges of parenthood.

The U.S. military has no plans to indefinitely suspend major military exercises with South Korea, according to Defense Secretary Jim Mattis, despite the June decision by President Donald Trump to halt the "very expensive" annual drills as a good-faith gesture following his summit with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Trump's unilateral suspension of the drills, which included the Ulchi Freedom Guardian exercise, caught many American military planners off guard and was criticized as a premature concession. Mattis stated that no decisions had been made about major exercises for next year and that smaller, exempted exercises were ongoing. This announcement comes at a time of stalled diplomatic efforts with North Korea, as the Trump administration seeks tangible steps toward denuclearization. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo's planned trip to North Korea was canceled, with Trump blaming China for the lack of progress. North Korea's state media accused the U.S. of "double-dealing" and "hatching a criminal plot," but did not mention Pompeo's canceled visit. The traditional U.S. calendar for major drills does not pick up again until the following spring, potentially offering time for negotiations. The U.S. has about 28,500 troops in South Korea, and Mattis avoided characterizing future U.S.-South Korean exercises as provocative or not. The resumption of regular U.S.-South Korea military exercises may indicate growing impatience from the Trump administration regarding the concessions made while North Korea gains time and space.

More than 50 women have accused Harvey Weinstein of sexual misconduct, with allegations spanning decades and involving various high-profile actresses, models, and industry professionals. Among the most notable claims, Asia Argento alleges that Weinstein raped her in 2004, while Lysette Anthony says she was raped by Weinstein in her London home in the late 1980s. Both women's accounts highlight the power dynamics and fear that often accompanied these encounters. In 2011, Weinstein allegedly forced Melissa Thompson, a tech start-up founder, to perform oral sex during a business meeting, an incident captured in a video that aired on Sky News. 

Actress Gwyneth Paltrow described a terrifying encounter with Weinstein in 1997, where he suggested she give him a massage, an experience she kept secret out of fear of losing her job. Angelina Jolie recounted a similar incident in 1998, where Weinstein made unwanted advances in a hotel room. Other victims include Mira Sorvino, who was allegedly groped by Weinstein in 1995, and Myleene Klass, who claims Weinstein offered a "sex contract" at a film festival in 2010. 

The accusations extend beyond the United States, with international stars like Léa Seydoux, Eva Green, and Cara Delevingne all sharing their experiences of Weinstein's inappropriate behavior. Sophie Dix, an English actress, described a traumatic encounter in a London hotel in the 1990s, while Lupita Nyong’o detailed several instances of Weinstein's alleged harassment, including an incident where he asked to take off his pants. 

Weinstein has denied many of these allegations, maintaining that all relationships were consensual. However, he has faced criminal charges in New York for alleged incidents involving two women, leading to his arrest in May 2018. His fall from grace has sparked a broader conversation about sexual harassment and assault in the entertainment industry, with women using social media platforms to share their stories under the #MeToo hashtag. This movement has brought to light the pervasive nature of sexual misconduct and the need for systemic change.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren grilled Wells Fargo CEO John Stumpf during a Senate Banking Committee hearing, accusing him of "gutless leadership" and calling for his resignation and a criminal investigation. The hearing centered on the massive cross-selling scandal where Wells Fargo employees created millions of fake accounts and enrolled customers into unwanted financial products. Warren highlighted Stumpf's role in promoting cross-selling as a key driver of the company's success, citing his emphasis on achieving eight accounts per customer. She produced transcripts from 12 Wells Fargo earnings calls where Stumpf repeatedly cited cross-selling as a reason to buy more stock in the company. Warren argued that Stumpf's actions were tantamount to fraud, noting that his stock holdings had gained over $200 million during the period in question. Stumpf defended his actions, stating that cross-selling was about deepening relationships. The hearing also touched on the compensation of former executive Carrie Tolstedt, who retired with nearly $125 million, and the bank's efforts to help customers affected by the fake accounts. Stumpf's responses were often evasive, citing his lack of expertise in legal, compensation, and credit matters. His bandaged right hand, which he claimed was injured while playing with grandchildren, drew attention. The hearing underscored the public's growing outrage over the scandal and the need for greater accountability in the banking industry.

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have detailed plans for their upcoming wedding, including the roles of their parents and the memory of Princess Diana. Meghan's parents, Doria Ragland and Thomas Markle, will visit the British royal family before the wedding, including Queen Elizabeth II and the Duke of Edinburgh, to spend time with their daughter. On the day of the ceremony, Thomas Markle will walk Meghan down the aisle at St. George's Chapel. The couple plans to honor Princess Diana by having one of her sisters, Jane Fellowes, read a passage during the service. Meghan will not have a maid of honor, and all bridesmaids and pageboys will be children, potentially including Prince George and Princess Charlotte. The exact location of their honeymoon will remain a secret, but they will make their first public appearance as a married couple a week after the wedding. The royal photographer for their engagement photos, Alexi Lubomirski, will capture the special day.

The Navy has recommended that future security reviews include any available police reports, even if they did not result in charges or convictions, after the shooting deaths of 12 Navy personnel by a gunman who had an honorable discharge, a Secret-level clearance, and at least two firearms incidents in law enforcement files. The recommendation came as the Navy completed a detailed review of the military career of Aaron Alexis, the gunman who was killed at the Washington Navy Yard after last week’s shooting rampage. The review, ordered by Navy Secretary Ray Mabus, included an assessment of whether events in Mr. Alexis’s military career should have raised alerts about his violent potential. In 2004, three years before enlisting as a Navy reservist, Mr. Alexis brandished a .45-caliber pistol and fired at the tires of a construction worker’s car. In another incident, in September 2010, after he was in uniform, commanders halted efforts to force Mr. Alexis out of the Navy with a less-than-honorable discharge because the police declined to pursue a case and it was not entered into his military file. The Office of Personnel Management knew of Alexis' Seattle arrest because of a fingerprint check when he joined the Navy Reserve in 2007 and interviewed him about it, but Alexis had not disclosed the offense on his security questionnaire. Alexis said that he had an altercation with a man doing construction work near his home and that the men had been "taking retaliatory action toward each other's parked cars," according to the investigative document that the personnel office gave to the Navy. Alexis said the construction worker had put a foreign substance in Alexis' gas tank, and Alexis retaliated by "deflating the male person's tires," according to the report. That account "reads very different from the police account of what took place that day," a senior Navy official said. The Seattle police report says Alexis shot out the tires and was charged with malicious mischief. The Navy cleared Alexis based on all the information it had, and there is no way to know "how they would have adjudicated knowing the events we know now." The construction worker did not press charges and the case was dismissed. Sometimes personnel office investigations include police documents, the Navy official said, but in this case the report sent to the Navy did not. A recent memo sent to Navy Secretary Ray Mabus from Assistant Navy Secretary Juan M. Garcia included a recommendation that all personnel office investigative reports include "any available police documents related to the subject being investigated for clearance eligibility." The recommendation has been sent to Defense Secretary Chuck Hagel. Alexis was found to be eligible for the security clearance in March 2008 after the Navy reviewed the personnel investigation. The only concern was Alexis' credit history, according to a timeline released by the Navy. His clearance was valid for 10 years. In September 2008, Alexis was arrested in DeKalb County, Ga., on suspicion of disorderly conduct and jailed for two nights, resulting in an unauthorized absence. The Navy gave Alexis an administrative punishment. In July 2009, he was punished again for being "drunk and disorderly," according to the timeline. But there was no police involvement, and Alexis successfully appealed the punishment, which was removed from his record. In September 2010, he was arrested in Fort Worth for discharging a firearm in his home after an altercation with a neighbor. Alexis told police the gun accidentally went off as he was cleaning it. No charges were filed. After the Fort Worth incident, Alexis' commander began the process "to administratively separate him from the Navy," according to the timeline. But when Alexis was not charged, the matter was dropped. Alexis left the Navy three months later with an honorable discharge.

Over the holiday weekend, a group of predominantly white militiamen took up guns and began occupying the government's Malheur National Wildlife Refuge headquarters in Oregon, culminating in a tense standoff with law enforcement. Media outlets initially treated the situation with a relatively calm tone, characterizing it as a "peaceful protest" despite the armed nature of the occupation. The Associated Press and Fox News both reported on the events with a subdued approach, focusing on the occupation rather than the potential for violence. However, social media reactions were markedly different, with many users expressing concern and calling for a more serious response, particularly when compared to how similar events involving minority groups were covered in the past.

The coverage of the Oregon occupation was notably less intense than the media's response to Black Lives Matter protests or the Baltimore and Ferguson riots. In those instances, media narratives often suggested an increase in violence and crime, linking it to the protests. Critics argue that the media's handling of the Oregon situation reflects implicit biases, favoring white, armed protesters over minority groups. These biases can influence how journalists and the public perceive and react to events, potentially leading to a more lenient response to predominantly white, armed groups.

The implicit bias phenomenon, as evidenced by studies, shows that people, even those without conscious prejudice, can subconsciously dehumanize or superhumanize individuals based on race. This can impact how law enforcement and the media approach situations involving different racial groups, leading to disparate treatment and coverage. The case of the Malheur National Wildlife Refuge occupation highlights the need for media outlets to be aware of these biases and strive for balanced, unbiased reporting.

The Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) has filed a federal lawsuit against Florida Gun Supply, which declared itself a "Muslim-free zone" after a shooting at two military facilities in Chattanooga, Tennessee. CAIR Florida's Chief Executive Director, Hassan Shibly, stated that American Muslims have the right to purchase guns, take gun safety classes, and use the range without discrimination. The lawsuit seeks an injunction to prevent Florida Gun Supply from discriminating against Muslims or implementing any policies that segregate people based on religion. CAIR Florida Civil Rights Director Thania Diaz Clevenger emphasized that the policy violates federal law and that American Muslims are entitled to their rights. Andy Hallinan, the owner of Florida Gun Supply, announced the "Muslim-free zone" policy in response to the Chattanooga shootings, claiming a moral and legal responsibility to ensure the safety of his community. Hallinan's attorney, Robert Muise, called the lawsuit "completely frivolous" and said it contains no factual allegations, potentially seeking sanctions against CAIR for filing a frivolous lawsuit. Hallinan's decision to rescind an invitation to Shibly for a meeting after receiving threats about CAIR's alleged ties to terrorism highlights the tension between public safety concerns and civil rights. The lawsuit aims to counter what CAIR sees as an illegal policy of discrimination against Muslims, emphasizing the need to prevent segregation and protect constitutional rights.

A new study from Germany has linked the use of proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), commonly prescribed for heartburn and acid reflux, to an increased risk of dementia in seniors. The research, published in JAMA Neurology, analyzed data from 73,679 patients aged 75 or older, with no prior history of dementia, over the period from 2004 to 2011. Participants who regularly used PPIs had a 44% higher risk of developing dementia compared to those who did not use these medications. The study's lead author, Britta Haenisch, from the German Center for Neurodegenerative Diseases, noted that while the findings are concerning, they do not establish a definitive cause-and-effect relationship. The increased risk of dementia was observed in both men and women, and the study controlled for potential confounding factors such as age, sex, and comorbidities.

PPIs, including popular brands like Nexium, Prilosec, and Prevacid, work by reducing stomach acid production. The study’s results are supported by recent mouse models showing that PPIs can increase levels of beta-amyloid in the brain, a protein associated with Alzheimer’s disease. Additionally, PPI use has been linked to vitamin B12 deficiencies, which are also associated with cognitive decline. However, the study’s limitations include the lack of data on lifestyle and diet, both of which can significantly impact the risk of dementia.

Experts caution that the findings do not warrant immediate changes in medical practice. Keith Fargo, director of scientific programs and outreach for the Alzheimer's Association, emphasized that the study does not provide sufficient evidence to advise patients to stop taking PPIs. He noted that the risk of dementia is multifactorial, and PPIs may be necessary for some patients to manage their symptoms. The study highlights the need for further research, particularly randomized, prospective clinical trials, to explore the connection between PPI use and cognitive decline in more detail.

Clinicians are advised to follow guidelines for PPI prescription, avoiding overprescribing and inappropriate use. For patients currently using PPIs, the decision to continue or discontinue use should be made in consultation with their healthcare provider, considering the potential benefits and risks. The findings suggest that for some patients, particularly those without severe acid reflux, the risk of overuse might outweigh the benefits, and they may be able to reduce their PPI use without significant health risks.

President-elect Donald Trump has faced a significant challenge as the Washington Post reported that the Central Intelligence Agency concluded Russia intervened in the U.S. election to help him win. This revelation has set off a flurry of reactions and counter-reactions. Trump, known for using Twitter to address controversies, lashed out at the media, tweeting indignantly about the reality TV show, The Apprentice. His team issued a statement attacking the CIA’s credibility, citing past intelligence failures. 

The situation has escalated with the New York Times reporting that Russian actors hacked the Republican National Committee but did not release any documents, raising questions about potential leverage. Trump’s transition team’s response was brief and dismissive, calling the allegations “ridiculous” and “FAKE NEWS.” Trump himself tweeted that he has “nothing to do” with The Apprentice and will devote no time to it.

The implications of this revelation are profound. If true, it suggests a foreign government may have determined the outcome of a presidential election, a scenario previously unimaginable. McConnell, the Senate Majority Leader, played a crucial role in keeping the information under wraps, reportedly voicing doubts about U.S. intelligence and threatening to accuse the Obama administration of partisanship if challenged publicly. His wife, Elaine Chao, was appointed as Transportation Secretary, raising questions about potential conflicts of interest.

The Obama administration is pushing for a definitive report on Russia’s cyber-intrusions before leaving office, aiming to ensure the transition of power is peaceful and informed. However, Trump’s team has dismissed these concerns, aligning with his broader skepticism of intelligence agencies. This stance has raised fears that Trump might ignore evidence of Russian meddling, potentially setting a precedent for future administrations.

Congressional Republicans are divided on how to respond. Some, like Senator Lindsey Graham, are calling for investigations into Russia’s role. They see an opportunity to hold Russia accountable while avoiding an intraparty conflict. Congress has the power to hold hearings, take action on sanctions, and engage in a war of words with Trump. However, these steps risk confrontation and could be seen as partisan attacks.

Ultimately, the challenge for Republicans is to steer Trump away from a potentially friendly relationship with Russia, a move that could be both effective and politically risky. The stakes are high, as this situation could redefine U.S. foreign policy and the balance of power within the Republican Party.

President Obama emphasized the need for a thorough investigation of the prostitution scandal involving 11 U.S. Secret Service agents who were sent home from Cartagena, Colombia, after allegations of misconduct. The incident has overshadowed the economic summit Obama attended, with lawmakers and officials calling for more details on the investigation. Obama highlighted the importance of dignity and probity for the Secret Service, stating that if the allegations prove true, he would be "angry." The scandal involves both Secret Service agents and military personnel who violated curfew, with the controversy stemming from a dispute over payment. The incident has sparked outrage in Colombia, where the country has been trying to project a new image of itself as a major regional player. Lawmakers, including House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chairman Darrell Issa, are pushing for a higher number of agents involved. The Secret Service agents are from both the special agents and uniformed division, and their actions have raised concerns about the security of other high-level officials. The scandal has also prompted questions about the effectiveness of systems in place to prevent such breaches in the future.

Donald Trump is set to receive his first classified briefing as the Republican Party's presidential nominee tomorrow, according to sources. The briefing, which will cover major global threats, is expected to be led by career staffers from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (DNI) and will take place in a secure room at the FBI's New York Field Office. Accompanying Trump will be New Jersey Governor Chris Christie and retired Lt. Gen. Michael Flynn, both of whom have publicly supported Trump. The decision to brief Trump, despite calls from some party leaders to limit access to sensitive information, is part of a long-standing tradition that dates back over 60 years. Trump's upcoming session comes after he outlined plans for "extreme vetting" of immigrants and temporarily blocking immigration from dangerous regions. The briefings are expected to be similar to the annual Worldwide Threat Assessment, focusing on current events and leaders rather than highly classified details. Despite concerns about Trump's fitness to receive classified information, DNI Director James Clapper and the White House have expressed confidence in the briefings' security.

A 49-year-old woman with the last name of Crook was arrested on Friday for allegedly stealing ladies' undergarments from a Kohl's department store in Alhambra, police said. Crook, whose bail was set at $20,000, was taken into custody around 7:15 p.m. and booked at the Alhambra Police Department. She is suspected of commercial burglary and possession of burglary tools, as she was allegedly in possession of wire cutters and scissors. Crook allegedly concealed the items in an empty purse and failed to pay for them. The Alhambra Police Department announced the arrest on their Facebook page. Crook is scheduled to make her first court appearance on Wednesday at the Alhambra Municipal Court.

Over 1,000 meters of overhead cabling was stolen overnight in Lincolnshire, leaving a village without power for several hours. The theft occurred on land off the A1133 near Newton-on-Trent, marking the second such incident in the county this year, with a similar theft taking place at Normanby-Le-Wold in August. Police are warning of the extreme dangers associated with this type of crime and are appealing for anyone with information to come forward. The thefts are prompting concerns about the vulnerability of the region's infrastructure and the potential risks to public safety. Officers are urging the public to remain vigilant and to contact them on 0300 111 0300 if they have any information that could help solve the case.

Russian hackers infiltrated Dow Jones & Co.'s servers, seeking stock tips, according to Bloomberg. The Federal Bureau of Investigation, Secret Service, and Securities and Exchange Commission are investigating, with the probe beginning at least a year ago. Dow Jones stated it has received no information from authorities about the alleged hack and is investigating the claims. The breach is described as more serious than a lower-grade intrusion disclosed a week ago, where hackers sought contact and payment information of about 3,500 customers. The FBI and SEC are consulting financial and market experts to determine how the hackers could profit from the stolen information. Dow Jones publishes the Wall Street Journal and provides information through services like Dow Jones Newswires. The hack investigation highlights the new vulnerability in financial markets, where business journalists and data providers are targeted by hackers who can steal sensitive information and sell it to traders. Law enforcement officials are struggling to keep pace with the rapidly evolving schemes of cyber-criminals.

Katie Holmes, after filing for divorce from Tom Cruise, has continued to maintain a busy schedule, focusing on her career and personal life.
