She has recently begun production on a new film, Molly, which she co-wrote and is co-producing, and is set to star in the romantic comedy Responsible Adults. Holmes has also planned her first-ever show at New York's Fashion Week for her clothing line, Holmes & Yang. Meanwhile, her lawyers are working on a divorce settlement with Cruise, with both parties aiming to avoid a public dispute. Holmes has also kept up with her daughter Suri, taking her on outings and attending events, such as a visit to an ice cream parlor, which she shared with the media, providing a glimpse of her more relaxed side. The article also delves into Tom Cruise's past, revealing that before embracing Scientology, he was a devout Roman Catholic. It details his time at the St. Francis Seminary in Cincinnati, Ohio, where he attended from 1976 to 1977, as a freshman. Cruise's classmates recall him as a good kid who was always smiling but also prone to trouble. The article highlights how Cruise's time at the seminary, along with his personal struggles, may have influenced his later life and career choices. His former manager, Eileen Berlin, provides insight into Cruise's early years, describing him as moody and prone to anger, but also as someone who had a charming side and a strong sense of pride in his physical appearance. The piece concludes by noting that Cruise's relationship with Holmes, despite its duration, may have been doomed due to his history of difficulty in forming deep friendships and his tendency to prove his worth through relationships.

Karl Lagerfeld's modern and innovative spirit has merged with Faber-Castell's reputation in crafting fine art and graphic products to create the limited edition Karlbox, a unique art supply storage box. This elegant black box, launched exclusively at Gump's of San Francisco, Faber-Castell stores, Karl Lagerfeld boutiques worldwide, and Harrods in London, holds 350 Faber-Castell art tools for drawing and painting. Designed by Lagerfeld, the box's exterior resembles a Chinese wedding cabinet, while inside, well-crafted removable drawers store the art supplies. The shades of colors included were personally selected by Lagerfeld to represent his aesthetic and the relationship between fashion, art, and design. 

Since his childhood in Germany, Faber-Castell has been known for its especially good quality, a reputation that remains true today, particularly for artist pencils. During his long career, Lagerfeld has used Faber-Castell products to produce countless works of art, stating that drawing is like breathing and writing. The lacquered beech wood Karlbox holds a varied selection of premium artists' tools, including Albrecht Dürer and Polychromos color pencils, highly pigmented Pitt Artist ink pens, Castell 9000 graphite pencils, and Pitt crayons and pastels. Watercolor brushes and accessories, such as a foldable water cup, an eraser, and sharpeners, are also included. Shades are sorted by primary and secondary colors, ranging from soft pastels to vibrant and intense hues. According to Lagerfeld, his favorite product line is the Albrecht Dürer artist range of water-soluble color pencils, and all 120 shades are included.

Karl Lagerfeld is known for a wide range of luxury goods, including ready-to-wear for men, women, and children, accessories, bags, watches, and eyewear. These collections are complemented by "Lagerfeld," a line of casual urban menswear and premium fragrances, which were added to the portfolio in 2014. In 2015, the company announced the launch of its online global women’s flagship store on Karl.com. Faber-Castell, founded as a pencil factory in 1761 in Stein, Germany, is a family-owned company embracing more than eight generations. As one of the world’s oldest manufacturers of writing instruments, it is renowned for its high-end pens in its Graf line and its Art & Graphic product range, which embodies 255 years of experience in the design and manufacture of exclusive artist products. Renowned artists including Vincent van Gogh, Paul Klee, Oskar Kokoschka, and Neo Rauch were fans of the brand’s assortment of color products and the quality they exemplified.

Each one-of-a-kind Karlbox includes a serial number and certificate of authenticity, making each completely unique. Only 2,500 have been produced, individually priced at $2,850, which seems like a bargain considering its size and provenance. The KARLBOX unites the traditional values of the family-owned company Faber-Castell with the modern, unique, and innovative spirit and style of Karl Lagerfeld, symbolizing the long-term relationship of both brands and representing the symbiosis of the fashion, art, and design worlds.

Archbishop Charles Chaput of Philadelphia has issued new guidelines for the Archdiocese of Philadelphia, which took effect on July 1, 2016. These guidelines, in line with Pope Francis’s Amoris Laetitia, aim to balance greater acceptance of Catholics living outside traditional church teachings with adherence to church doctrine. The document calls on priests to help Catholics with same-sex attractions find chastity and encourages frequent penance. It acknowledges that same-sex attraction can take diverse forms and that some can still pursue heterosexual marriage with children. However, the guidelines are strict for those who are divorced and civilly remarried, cohabitating unmarried couples, and those in active, public same-sex relationships. They must refrain from sexual intimacy to receive Holy Communion, and are required to live as “brother and sister.” The document also restricts roles in parish councils and other leadership positions to those who adhere to church teachings. While Pope Francis has urged bishops to show greater mercy and flexibility, the guidelines reflect a more traditional interpretation of his document. They emphasize that those in “irregular” relationships, no matter how sincere, offer a serious counter-witness to Catholic belief, potentially causing moral confusion in the community. The guidelines also direct priests to consider the readiness of cohabitating couples to marry, urging separation if one person is not capable of or willing to commit to a marriage. This approach aims to guide those who fall short of church teachings toward holiness, while maintaining the church’s stance on marriage and chastity.

An adult film star who partied with actor Charlie Sheen hours before he was rushed to the hospital claims she saw him splattered with wine stains, had "tennis ball size" chunks of cocaine delivered, and was consuming so much booze and coke that she feared he was on a "suicide binge." Kacey Jordan, who attended Sheen's party, described his disheveled appearance and his heavy drug use, including smoking chunks of cocaine every two minutes. Sheen reportedly offered Jordan a deal to move into a mansion with him and babysit his children. Sheen is in an undisclosed rehab center and production on his sitcom "Two and a Half Men" has been put on hold indefinitely. His publicist stated that Sheen was rushed to the hospital with "severe abdominal pains" on Thursday. Despite his public image, Sheen's partying and substance abuse have been well-documented, with his ex-wife Denise Richards reportedly barring him from being alone with their daughters until he completes his rehab. Jordan's claims have pushed Richards to take a tougher stance, emphasizing the need to protect their children from the negative influences of Sheen's lifestyle.

A growing trend of women buying breast milk online poses significant health risks to infants, according to a study published in the journal Pediatrics. Researchers from Nationwide Children's Hospital analyzed 101 samples of breast milk purchased from public milk-sharing websites and found that 75% of the samples contained high levels of bacteria, including harmful pathogens like salmonella and E. coli. The study also revealed that 3% of the samples were contaminated with salmonella, a finding not observed in samples from non-profit milk banks. The samples from milk banks, which strictly adhere to guidelines set by the Human Milk Banking Association of North America, were generally cleaner, with only 25% containing staph and 20% containing strep bacteria. 

The study's lead author, Sarah Keim, emphasized that while some bacteria are naturally present in breast milk and are beneficial for infants, the high levels of harmful bacteria found in the online-purchased samples pose a significant risk. Keim noted that the contamination could be due to poor hygiene during collection, unclean storage containers, or compromised shipping practices. The researchers also found that 19% of sellers did not use cooling methods during shipping, which can further compromise the safety of the milk.

Despite the risks, many new mothers are turning to online milk-sharing platforms to supplement their own breast milk supply. A 2011 study by Keim found that there were over 13,000 postings on leading milk-sharing websites. While some women rely on informal networks or milk banks, the high cost and limited availability of banked milk often drive parents to seek alternative sources. Websites like OnlyTheBreast and EatsonFeets facilitate these transactions, but the lack of regulation and oversight means that buyers have no way of knowing the quality or safety of the milk they are purchasing.

The Food and Drug Administration discourages the buying and selling of breast milk online, citing safety concerns. Dr. Anne Eglash, a family medicine physician and co-founder of the Academy of Breastfeeding Medicine, advises against purchasing breast milk online, stating that it is "totally normal" for there to be some bacteria in breast milk, but the presence of harmful pathogens is a serious concern. Eglash also emphasizes that while sharing milk among friends or relatives can be safe, buying breast milk from unknown sources online is not recommended.

In conclusion, while breast milk is generally safe for healthy infants, the study highlights the potential dangers of purchasing breast milk online. Parents are encouraged to use screened and pasteurized milk from milk banks or consult with healthcare professionals for safe alternatives.

A blood test can detect the presence of beta-amyloid plaques in the brain, potentially indicating a higher risk of Alzheimer's disease, according to research presented at the Alzheimer’s Association International Conference. These plaques, sticky clumps of beta-amyloid, are one of the hallmarks of Alzheimer’s, though their exact role is not yet fully understood. Traditionally, detecting these plaques has required expensive PET scans or invasive spinal taps, but a new, simpler blood test could make early screening more accessible. Developed by researchers at Washington University in St. Louis, the test measures the relative amounts of different beta-amyloid types in the blood, providing an indication of plaque buildup in the brain. The test was validated by comparing blood samples with PET scan results from 41 individuals, showing promising accuracy.

Early detection of beta-amyloid could lead to earlier interventions, potentially slowing the progression of the disease. However, experts caution that a positive test does not definitively diagnose Alzheimer’s, as some people without the disease can also have beta-amyloid plaques. Conversely, a negative test can definitively rule out the presence of these plaques. The findings could significantly impact the way doctors diagnose and treat patients with mild cognitive impairment or dementia, potentially saving resources by avoiding unnecessary medications. The test could also help identify individuals who might benefit from lifestyle changes or other preventive measures.

The research is part of a larger effort to develop non-invasive methods for Alzheimer’s diagnosis, including a $20 million clinical trial by the Alzheimer’s Association to explore the effects of lifestyle changes on cognitive health. These changes, which include physical exercise, nutritional counseling, social and cognitive stimulation, and improved self-management, could potentially delay or prevent cognitive decline in older adults. The trial, known as POINTER, will involve 2,500 participants aged 60 to 79, with results expected in two years.

Meanwhile, a major study called IDEAS (Imaging Dementia—Evidence for Amyloid Scanning) is testing over 18,000 Medicare beneficiaries with mild cognitive impairment or dementia to determine the impact of amyloid-detecting PET scans. Initial findings suggest that a significant number of patients may not actually have Alzheimer’s, as PET scans revealed that only 54.3% of MCI patients and 70.5% of dementia patients had the plaques. These results could influence Medicare’s decision on whether to cover such scans, which are currently not reimbursable due to insufficient evidence of their clinical utility.

The development of a blood test for Alzheimer’s could revolutionize early diagnosis, making it more accessible and less invasive. However, it is crucial to validate the test’s accuracy and reliability in larger, more diverse populations before widespread implementation. As the field continues to advance, the hope is that these tools will help identify those at risk, allowing for earlier interventions and potentially slowing the progression of the disease.

Parents in Windsor, Vermont, have expressed shock and concern after their children, as young as 10, were asked about their sexual history, orientation, and gender identity in a survey conducted by WISE, a domestic violence prevention and advocacy group. Vanessa Beach, whose daughter took part in the survey, was particularly dismayed, noting that a sexual partner at 10 years old would be considered sexual abuse. Beach felt the survey questions were inappropriate for her daughter's age group and that she never received the opt-out form. While WISE officials stated that students were informed they were not required to take the survey, Beach and other parents have raised concerns about the appropriateness of the questions and the lack of communication regarding the survey. School administrators are working to address these complaints, and WISE representatives hope to use the concerns as an opportunity to open a dialogue with parents about their work. Despite the controversy, Beach acknowledged the value of WISE's efforts in promoting awareness and education around domestic violence. The survey, developed with researchers from the University of New Hampshire, has sparked a broader discussion about the balance between education and privacy in elementary schools.

Jon Huntsman's daughters, Mary Anne, Abby, and Liddy, known for their snarky tweets at @Jon2012girls, recently sang karaoke with a mischievous, off-the-cuff energy that contrasts with their campaign's stage-managed image. They discussed using technology to reach disillusioned young voters and explained they're not aiming to be the "Kardashians of politics." Despite their supportive role, they hope to make a difference by campaigning for their father. A brief mention of Mary Anne's past date with Kris Humphries, Kim Kardashian's ex-husband, adds a personal touch to their candid, down-to-earth demeanor.

A suspect in five homicides in Ohio contacted a local television reporter shortly before his arrest, police said. George Brinkman, 45, exchanged Facebook messages with a WOIO-Channel 19 reporter in the hours before and during a nine-hour standoff. The news station notified the police department, which asked the reporter to stop talking to Brinkman. Brinkman was identified as a suspect in the murders of Lake Township residents Rogell Eugene John, 71, and his wife Roberta Ray John, 64, and North Royalton resident Suzanne Taylor, 45, and her daughters Taylor Pifer, 21, and Kylie Pifer, 18. The three women were found dead in their home on Ridge Road in North Royalton, with Taylor stabbed and her daughters likely killed in the same manner. Brinkman was a squatter who had been house-sitting for the Johns before their deaths and was previously in a relationship with their daughter. He was also suspected in the deaths of the Johns, found dead in their home on Mt. Pleasant Street NE in North Canton. Brinkman was arrested after a standoff in Brunswick, where he was holding a gun. He was charged with murder in connection with the deaths and is being held in custody. His criminal history includes misdemeanor convictions for passing bad checks, criminal mischief, and disorderly conduct. The murders shocked the community, with neighbors unaware of the relationships between the victims and the suspect. A vigil was planned for the North Royalton victims.

Republicans pulled their Obamacare repeal bill just before a scheduled vote, dealing a significant setback to President Donald Trump and House Speaker Paul Ryan. The decision came after a day of losing votes and despite Trump’s ultimatum for Republicans to support the bill. The American Health Care Act was short of the necessary votes to pass, with Trump admitting he was 10 to 15 votes shy of victory. Ryan acknowledged that if the bill had been voted on, it would have failed by a larger margin, protecting Trump from a bigger political defeat. Democrats celebrated the outcome, viewing it as a victory for the American people, especially for those with disabilities and veterans. The Freedom Caucus, which opposed the bill, remained committed to repealing Obamacare, while moderate Republicans like Virginia Rep. Barbara Comstock and Ohio Rep. David Joyce joined the opposition. The White House, while disappointed, insisted on the vote, but ultimately Ryan prevailed. The failure highlights the challenges Republicans face in passing major legislation and the internal divisions within the party.

Police in Munich evacuated two train stations, the main station and Pasing station, after receiving hints of a possible bomb attack, specifically targeting these locations. Both stations were reopened hours later after a sweep by off-duty officers who found no suspicious items. Authorities are advising people to avoid crowds, public transportation, and train stations as this is a developing story.

Federal prosecutors in Massachusetts have seized approximately $20 million in cash hidden inside a mattress in a Westborough apartment, part of a wide-ranging investigation into TelexFree, an internet telecom company that was actually a massive international pyramid scheme. The cash was found after investigators followed a Brazilian man, Cleber Rene Rizerio Rocha, from New York, who was charged with conspiring to commit money laundering. Rocha, acting as a courier for Wanzeler's nephew, had transferred $2.2 million to a cooperating witness in a scheme to move millions of dollars of hidden TelexFree assets to Brazil. TelexFree, based in Marlborough, Massachusetts, sold voice-over-internet telephone service but made most of its revenue from people buying into the company with a promise of payouts for posting online ads. The company, founded by James Merrill and Carlos Wanzeler, filed for bankruptcy in 2014, owing $5 billion to its participants, with 965,225 victims worldwide losing $1.76 billion. Merrill pleaded guilty to conspiracy and wire fraud charges, while Wanzeler fled to Brazil and remains at large.

Actor Scott Wilson, best known for his role as Hershel Greene on AMC's "The Walking Dead," has died at the age of 76 due to complications from leukemia. Wilson's career spanned over five decades, with notable roles in films like "In Cold Blood" and "The Ninth Configuration," where he earned a Golden Globe nomination. His character Hershel, a beloved veterinarian and farmer, was a central figure in the show's early seasons, but his death was one of the most shocking and heart-wrenching moments for fans. The show's cast and producers paid tribute to Wilson, with many sharing personal messages of gratitude and remembrance. AMC aired a tribute at the end of the season premiere, honoring Wilson's legacy and the impact he had on the series and its fans.

A video purportedly showing the execution of an Israeli Arab man accused by ISIS of spying for Israel's Mossad intelligence agency has emerged online. The 19-year-old, identified as Muhammad Musallam, was shot dead by a young boy in a field, according to the video, which was posted by ISIS's Furqan media outlet. In the footage, Musallam is seen sitting in a room wearing an orange jumpsuit, talking about his recruitment and training by Mossad. He claims his father and brother encouraged him to join ISIS. The video, approximately 13 minutes long, shows Musallam kneeling in a field as a boy, described as one of the "cubs of the caliphate," shoots him in the head with a pistol. The boy then fires three more shots into his body and chants "Allahu Akbar!" Musallam's family denies he was an Israeli spy, stating he had gone missing while on a trip to Turkey and was recruited by ISIS. His father, Said Musallam, says ISIS forced his son to confess to spying before executing him. The video has not been independently verified, and Israeli officials could not confirm its authenticity. ISIS claims Musallam was a spy, but his family maintains he was recruited by the group. The video highlights the group's alleged use of propaganda and the potential manipulation of their victims.

Bernie Sanders declared that the Democratic Party's convention in Philadelphia will be "contested" unless Hillary Clinton secures enough pledged delegates to win the nomination outright. Sanders, speaking at a press conference in Washington, D.C., emphasized that superdelegates will be crucial in determining the outcome, as Clinton currently holds a lead of 520 to 39 in superdelegate support. The Vermont senator argued that superdelegates should reflect the popular vote in their states, particularly in places where he won by significant margins, such as Washington and Minnesota. His campaign manager, Tad Devine, highlighted battleground states where Sanders outperforms Clinton against Republican candidates, suggesting that superdelegates should consider supporting him. However, the current delegate count shows Clinton with a substantial lead, making it challenging for Sanders to catch up. Sanders acknowledged that he needs to win 65% of the remaining pledged delegates to surpass Clinton, but his campaign remains optimistic about the prospects in key states. Despite these efforts, the math suggests that Sanders faces a tough road, as Clinton's lead among pledged delegates is significant and likely to remain unchanged. The article concludes by noting that, even if Sanders wins the remaining pledged delegates, he still trails in actual votes by an insurmountable margin, making it unlikely that superdelegates will shift their support.

The U.S. military's efforts to screen soldiers for traumatic brain injuries (TBIs) through the Automated Neuropsychological Assessment Metric (ANAM) have fallen far short of expectations, according to an investigation by NPR and ProPublica. Despite spending over $42 million, the program has failed to reliably detect brain injuries, potentially delaying treatment and exacerbating damage. Key issues include the selection of ANAM, which was developed by military researchers and licensed to outside contractors, and its flawed implementation. The test was chosen despite warnings from military medical experts about its unreliability and potential for misdiagnosis. Moreover, the military has not administered the test as recommended, rarely using its results, and has issued orders that limit follow-up evaluations for soldiers with low scores. Critics argue that this approach undermines the program's effectiveness and fails to adequately protect soldiers. The NHL, in contrast, uses a more robust test for its athletes, highlighting the potential for better solutions. Congress mandated comprehensive testing, but the military's approach has been criticized as inadequate, with some lawmakers calling for more thorough evaluations and better follow-up care. The program's shortcomings raise serious questions about the military's commitment to addressing the long-term health needs of its service members.

A 73-year-old man's clean driving record nearly saved him from a citation during a traffic stop in Seattle's Colman neighborhood on Tuesday night, until he attempted to snort cocaine in front of an officer. Officer Nic Abts-Olsen was patrolling the area when he noticed a silver Toyota with its headlights off driving past. After pulling the vehicle over, the officer checked the driver's license and registration before walking back to the car. There, he observed the driver portioning out a scoop of cocaine from a small glass vial. When the officer approached the window, the driver's actions led to a spill of cocaine on his hands and the vehicle's floor. Initially denying possession, the driver eventually admitted to having "vitamins" and then confessed to snorting cocaine during the traffic stop, praising the officer's keen detection skills. Despite his clean driving record, the officer decided to arrest the man for narcotics possession, booking him into the King County Jail. The incident was captured on in-car video, serving as a stark reminder of the consequences of drug use in public.

A Pennsylvania fugitive's social media overshare led to his arrest, highlighting the unintended consequences of posting police mugshots on personal Facebook pages. Anthony J. Lescowitch, 35, of Drifton, was wanted by Freeland police for aggravated assault and other charges since November 27, 2013. Freeland police posted his picture on their Facebook account on Monday, hoping to track him down with community help. Multiple people shared the information on their own pages, but to the surprise of officers, Lescowitch shared the information on his own page to mock police. An undercover officer posed as a female on Facebook and engaged in conversation with Lescowitch for about 30 minutes, gathering key information that eventually led to his arrest. Lescowitch agreed to meet at an undisclosed location, but when he arrived, police were waiting and took him into custody without incident. Lescowitch was charged with aggravated assault and numerous other charges related to the incident, including robbery, access device fraud, and reckless endangerment. He was arraigned and unable to post bail, leading to his detention at the Luzerne County Correctional Facility. The case serves as a cautionary tale about the potential risks of sharing sensitive information online.

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump has called for the United States to consider racial profiling as a preventative measure against terrorism, stating that it is something the country "will have to start thinking about as a country." Trump, who has previously called for a temporary ban on Muslims entering the U.S., said that profiling is a practice used by other countries and is "not the worst thing to do." His comments come in the wake of the Orlando mass shooting, which left 49 people dead. Trump also suggested that attacks like Orlando would stop if those in the Muslim community would "report" suspicious things, citing the San Bernardino shooting as an example where "bombs were all over their apartment floor and people saw it and nobody reported them." Trump defended his stance, saying that the shooter, Omar Mateen, had "definite red flags" and that "you look at his past, I mean? I've never seen a past quite like that." The presumptive GOP nominee is working with the National Rifle Association on a policy that would ban people on the no-fly list from purchasing guns, though he acknowledged there are "problems" with the no-fly list. Trump also criticized Republican leaders for "talking so much" and suggested they should focus on their jobs, such as working on budgets and getting the military the money it needs.

A Connecticut man, Derek Benson, 30, found himself in hot water after a stolen sweatshirt from a Glastonbury home in 2014 was spotted in his mug shot, leading to his arrest on new burglary charges, reports the Glastonbury Police Department. The sweatshirt, a Coco Libre organic coconut water logo sweatshirt, was stolen during a burglary in July 2014, but the case was suspended due to lack of leads. Recently, the homeowner recognized Benson in a mug shot wearing his sweatshirt and contacted police. Benson, already facing multiple burglary charges for stealing expensive golf equipment, was arrested last week on burglary, larceny, and criminal mischief counts. He is currently held in jail on a $125,000 bond.

Apple is set to launch the iPhone 4S in mainland China on January 13, marking the device's entry into the world's largest mobile market. The iPhone now accounts for nearly half of Apple's annual revenue and is expected to earn over 60% of its profits. China has a massive cellphone user base, with estimates suggesting nearly a billion users. Apple currently partners with China Unicom, one of the larger carriers, but has no current plans to announce a partnership with China Mobile, the country's largest carrier. Siri, Apple's voice-activated assistant, won't be able to understand Mandarin when the phone launches next week, but the company plans to add official language support, including Chinese, in 2012. Despite the lack of a partnership with China Mobile, analysts predict a significant demand for the iPhone 4S in the Chinese market, with the device expected to sell out quickly. China's increasing importance in Apple's revenue has made the launch a strategic move, with the smartphone market in China estimated to be worth $70 billion. The iPhone 4S will be available in 20 countries, including Bolivia, the Dominican Republic, Jamaica, and Senegal, on the same day.

A California settler, Granville P. Swift, left behind a legendary mystery: $100,000 in gold, buried somewhere around the Bay Area. Swift, a Kentucky native who came to California in 1840, quickly struck it rich during the Gold Rush. He amassed a fortune, which he buried in various locations, primarily in the Sonoma area, due to the lack of a banking system at the time. Despite his wealth, Swift was known for his forgetfulness, making it difficult to remember the exact locations of his buried treasure. Over the years, some of the gold was discovered, including $7,000 in 1903 and $42,600 in 1914. However, the remainder of the treasure has remained undiscovered, leaving a tantalizing mystery for treasure hunters. Swift's life was marked by both success and tragedy. After losing most of his wealth through investments and financial misfortunes, he moved to Solano County in 1864, where he died in a tragic fall from a mule in 1875. His life story, filled with adventure and financial ups and downs, continues to intrigue historians and treasure seekers.

Wiz Khalifa's video for "See You Again" featuring Charlie Puth became the most-watched video on YouTube, surpassing Psy's "Gangnam Style" with over 2.896 billion views. Justin Bieber's "Sorry" ranks third, with more than 250 million views behind the leaders. Charlie Puth expressed surprise at the milestone, noting his goal to reach 10,000 views when he joined YouTube in 2007. The video was released in 2015 as a tribute to Paul Walker, a late "Fast and the Furious" star. The song and video have inspired and impacted many lives, according to Wiz Khalifa. The University Library at Washington and Lee University supports the institution's teaching, learning, and research mission by providing materials and resources. The library's website offers convenient access to resources, and its two buildings, Leyburn Library and Telford Science Library, are open 24 hours daily when classes are in session. The library participates in a strong resource-sharing system, allowing access to needed materials from other libraries nationwide. The library's Special Collections Department includes rare books, manuscripts, and the University archives, focusing on the history of the University, Rockbridge County, Generals Lee and Washington, and the Shenandoah Valley. Through the Internet, students and faculty have 24-hour access to the library's website and electronic resources.

Students at Anderson High School in Southgate are facing consequences after nearly the entire class was caught cheating on a final exam. Two juniors took photos of the exam's answer key while the teacher was out of the room, sharing the answers via group text. The teacher noticed unusually high grades and alerted administration, leading to the entire class retaking the exam during summer break. School officials are considering disciplinary action, with the superintendent stating, "Consequences are forthcoming," and noting this is the first incident of this magnitude at the school.

U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) Chair Mary Jo White unveiled comprehensive proposals to regulate high-frequency trading (HFT) and monitor dark pools, aiming to enhance market transparency and address concerns over potential unfair advantages. The SEC plans to require registration for proprietary traders who use computers to execute trades in milliseconds, subjecting them to oversight. Operators of dark pools, which compete with exchanges by not publishing bid and ask prices, must disclose their order-matching rules. White emphasized the need to assess whether specific elements of the HFT environment work against investors, cautioning against rolling back technology but considering measures to minimize speed advantages. The SEC will also review stock exchanges' order types, criticized for complexity, and address issues related to order and price data dissemination. These proposals, which align with ongoing investigations by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission and state attorneys general, reflect growing concerns about the impact of HFT on market integrity. While some industry players support increased transparency, others argue against excessive regulation that could stifle innovation.

A Fairfield couple, Ina Rogers and Jonathan Allen, faces multiple charges including child neglect and torture after their 10 children were found living in squalor. The children, ranging from 4 months to 14 years old, were rescued by police after a six-week investigation. Ina Rogers, defending herself and her husband, claims they did not abuse their children and that the squalid conditions were due to her searching for her missing 12-year-old son. Jonathan Allen, 29, was arrested on May 11 and charged with nine felony counts of child cruelty and seven counts of torture. Ina Rogers, 30, was arrested in March and is currently out on $10,000 bail. The children have been placed in the custody of Rogers' sister and mother in the Bay Area. The investigation revealed a long history of severe physical and emotional abuse of the children. Jonathan Allen's bail was set at $1.5 million, while Ina Rogers' bail was set at $5.2 million. The case has drawn attention due to the severity of the alleged abuse and the number of children involved.

Netflix has introduced a new, groundbreaking parental leave policy, allowing employees to take unlimited leave during the first year after the birth or adoption of a child. This policy, detailed in a blog post by Tawni Cranz, Netflix’s Chief Talent Officer, aims to provide flexibility and support to new parents while ensuring they can balance family and work responsibilities without financial or work-related stress. The policy allows parents to return to work part-time, full-time, or even take subsequent leave periods as needed, with their salaries continuing during their absence. This move underscores Netflix’s commitment to fostering a “freedom and responsibility” culture, where employees can make their own decisions about their work and personal lives.

The new policy is part of Netflix’s broader strategy to attract and retain top talent by offering comprehensive support during life’s significant transitions. Cranz emphasizes that this policy, combined with Netflix’s existing unlimited time-off program, will help employees focus and be more dedicated to their work. By removing the need to switch to state or disability pay, the company ensures a smoother transition for parents, allowing them to return to work more focused and prepared.

This initiative builds on similar policies implemented by other tech giants, such as Yahoo, which doubled its maternity and paternity leave in 2013. Such policies have proven to be crucial in retaining talent and supporting work-life balance. However, while unlimited leave policies can offer significant benefits, they also come with potential challenges, such as the need for employees to coordinate with their managers and teams to manage their absence effectively.

Netflix’s new policy highlights the growing trend among companies to prioritize work-life balance and support for new parents, recognizing that a supportive environment can lead to better employee performance and retention. By offering such generous benefits, Netflix aims to not only support its employees but also to set a new standard in the tech industry and beyond.

Steven Seagal, the 65-year-old American action movie star, has joined a growing list of cultural figures barred from entering Ukraine, making him the latest in a series of celebrities to face restrictions from the country. Ukraine's security service has forbidden Seagal entry for five years, citing his national security threat status. This decision comes after Seagal was granted Russian citizenship and voiced support for Russia's annexation of Crimea. The Ukrainian security service's letter, published by news site Apostrophe, states that Seagal has "committed socially dangerous actions that contradict the interests of maintaining Ukraine’s security." Seagal, whose grandmother was from Vladivostok, has a long history of visiting former Soviet countries, including Belarus, Kyrgyzstan, and Chechnya. His support for Putin and Russia's policies, particularly regarding Crimea, has earned him the enmity of Ukrainian authorities. In 2014, Seagal called Russia's annexation of Crimea "very reasonable," and he later played with his blues band at a concert in Crimea, supporting a pro-Putin biker club. Seagal's support for Russia has not gone unnoticed; in 2015, he was included in a proposed blacklist of foreign cultural figures who "speak out in support of violating the territorial integrity and sovereignty of Ukraine," alongside French actor Gérard Depardieu and many Russian artists. Ukraine has also banned more than 100 Russian films and, in a recent move, prevented Russia's Eurovision entrant from performing in Crimea. The cultural war between Ukraine and Russia continues to escalate, with Ukraine hosting Eurovision in Kiev on May 13, 2017, despite Russia's ban on its performer.

The Gulf of Mexico oil spill rapidly expanded, nearly tripling in size in just a day, raising concerns that the environmental disaster could become far worse than initially thought. The slick, initially estimated to cover an area the size of Rhode Island, grew to an area comparable to Puerto Rico, according to satellite images. Environmentalists fear the spill could devastate wildlife and fisheries, with the potential to surpass the Exxon Valdez disaster in scale. The Coast Guard estimated that 200,000 gallons of oil were leaking daily, suggesting 1.6 million gallons had spilled since the April 20 explosion. Frustrated fishermen faced challenges as rough seas hindered efforts to deploy booms and contain the spill. President Obama planned a visit to the Gulf Coast to assess the damage. BP's use of dispersants to break up the oil underwater, while potentially reducing surface slicks, could create new environmental issues, including the potential for toxic compounds to concentrate in the water and harm marine life. The spill threatens hundreds of species, including birds, dolphins, and various fish, shrimp, oysters, and crabs, impacting one of the nation's most abundant sources of seafood. The incident also highlights BP's underestimation of potential risks, with internal documents suggesting a low likelihood of a catastrophic accident.

A hiker died on Monday after falling from the cables near the summit of Half Dome at Yosemite National Park, the National Park Service announced on Tuesday. The incident occurred during thunderstorm activity when a male hiker slipped and fell, while two others were ascending the final 400 feet of the 14-mile round trip trail. Rangers were promptly contacted and assisted the other hiker, who was unharmed. The cables, installed each summer to aid the steep ascent, were in place at the time of the accident. The fallen hiker's body was recovered on Tuesday afternoon, and his identity will be released after notification of his family. This is the first fatal fall from Half Dome since 2010. The park requires hiker permits to manage the popular trail during peak summer seasons, aiming to prevent overcrowding. The NPS is still investigating the exact circumstances of the fall, with uncertainty about whether the trail was wet from rain. The cables are crucial for assisting the thousands of hikers who attempt the ascent each year, though only a minority clip safety harnesses to them.

President Donald Trump's legal team has not heard back from special counsel Robert Mueller's office in nearly three weeks, according to Rudy Giuliani, the President's attorney. Giuliani said that Mueller's office has informed them it is "still studying" the latest letter from Trump's team, which was only five to six pages long. Giuliani suggested several potential next steps for Mueller's office, including issuing a report without speaking to the President, issuing a subpoena, or negotiating with the terms Trump's team offered. Giuliani also mentioned that the battle over a subpoena could occur during the run-up to the midterm elections. Roger Stone, a longtime associate of President Trump, predicted that Mueller would soon indict him as part of the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 presidential election. Stone claimed he was being targeted not because he committed a crime, but because the "deep state" wanted to silence him and pressure him to testify against the President. Stone's prediction came after the conviction of Paul Manafort and the guilty plea of Michael Cohen, both stemming from Mueller's investigation. Stone told The Guardian that Mueller may frame him for a bogus charge to silence him or induce him to testify against the President. Stone has made similar predictions before, stating in June that it was possible Mueller would indict him. The article also notes that Mueller's team has met with Kristin Davis, who once ran a high-end prostitution ring, regarding her relationship with Stone. This ongoing investigation and the potential for further legal action against Stone and others continue to cast a shadow over the Mueller probe.

Silicon Valley startup Bloom Energy unveiled its Bloom Box, a fuel cell system designed to provide clean, affordable electricity for homes and businesses. The company's first product, a box the size of a filing cabinet, currently costs $700,000 and can produce 400 kilowatts of electricity, enough to power 40 homes. Bloom Energy aims to reduce the price to a few thousand dollars for home use within a decade. CEO K.R. Sridhar claims the Bloom Box can produce more energy with less environmental impact than other fuel cells, as it can use a variety of fuels, including natural gas, wind, and solar. However, the company has not disclosed many details about its technology, such as the life span of the system, potential downtime, and heat management. The Bloom Box is currently being tested by major corporations like Google and eBay, which report significant savings from the federal tax credit and subsidies. While the technology is not revolutionary, Bloom Energy hopes to drive down costs enough to eliminate the need for subsidies. The company faces competition from other fuel cell manufacturers, and experts are cautious about the long-term reliability and efficiency of the Bloom Box.

The Netflix series 13 Reasons Why, based on Jay Asher's 2007 young adult novel, has been officially renewed for a 13-episode second season, set to premiere in 2018. Season 2 will delve into the aftermath of Hannah Baker's suicide and the characters' journeys toward healing. Executive producer Selena Gomez will take the lead as the sole showrunner, with Diana Son stepping down. The first season, which garnered critical acclaim and social media attention, follows teenager Clay Jensen as he discovers cassette tapes recorded by Hannah, explaining her reasons for ending her life. The series tackles sensitive issues like teen suicide, bullying, and rape in graphic detail, sparking debate and criticism from mental health experts who warn it could pose risks to vulnerable viewers. In response, Netflix enhanced content warnings. The show is directed by Oscar winner Tom McCarthy and written by Tony and Pulitzer Prize-winner Brian Yorkey, with a star-studded cast including Kate Walsh, Brian D’Arcy James, and Katherine Langford. With a second season confirmed, the series continues to be a topic of discussion and controversy.

A large study published in The New England Journal of Medicine has found that patients treated by certain emergency room doctors for pain are significantly more likely to become long-term users of opioids. The research, which analyzed data from about 375,000 Medicare patients treated in several thousand hospitals from 2008 to 2011, revealed that the prescribing habits of the doctor who initially treated a patient had a substantial impact on their future opioid use. Patients treated by doctors who prescribed opioids more frequently within their department were at a higher risk of becoming long-term opioid users, even when other factors such as the patient’s age, sex, and existing conditions were accounted for.

The study defined high-intensity and low-intensity opioid prescribing physicians based on the proportion of emergency department visits after which an opioid prescription was filled. Physicians were categorized into quartiles of prescribing rates, with the top and bottom quartiles being classified as high-intensity and low-intensity prescribers, respectively. The researchers also considered the median dose of prescriptions filled after an emergency department visit as an alternative measure of prescribing intensity.

The primary outcome of the study was long-term opioid use, defined as 180 days or more of opioids supplied in the 12 months after an index emergency department visit, excluding prescriptions within 30 days after the index visit. Secondary outcomes included rates of hospital encounters, including those related to adverse effects of opioids and those associated with specific medical conditions. The study also measured rates of repeat emergency department visits at 14 and 30 days that resulted in the same primary diagnosis as the initial visit.

The study controlled for patient characteristics such as age, sex, race, Medicaid eligibility, and disability status, as well as the presence of chronic conditions. The researchers used multivariable logistic regression to estimate the adjusted odds ratios for each outcome, with the key explanatory variable being whether a patient was treated by a high-intensity or low-intensity prescriber. The results showed that patients treated by high-intensity prescribers were more likely to become long-term opioid users, with the number needed to harm (NNT) estimated to be 112, meaning that 112 patients would need to be prescribed an initial opioid for one to become a long-term user.

The findings suggest that the initial exposure to opioids in the emergency department can have lasting effects on a patient’s opioid use. This is particularly concerning given the ongoing opioid epidemic, as it highlights the critical role that emergency room doctors play in shaping a patient’s future opioid use. The study’s authors recommend that efforts to address the opioid crisis should include educating emergency room doctors about the risks of prescribing opioids and promoting more conservative prescribing practices.

Amazon.com Inc. is set to open its first physical store in New York City, marking a significant step into traditional retail after 20 years of purely online operations. The Manhattan location, set to launch in time for the holiday shopping season, will serve as a "mini-warehouse" for same-day delivery, product returns, and pickups of online orders, according to a Wall Street Journal report. This move aims to provide a physical presence for Amazon, which has long relied on competitive pricing and online convenience. The store will likely feature Amazon's own tech products, including Kindle e-readers and tablets, as well as the underperforming Fire set-top box and Fire smartphone. Analysts believe that the New York location, with its high foot traffic, could offer a valuable opportunity for Amazon to gather customer feedback and potentially expand its physical footprint. Richard Doherty, an analyst with the Envisioneering Group, suggests that the store could attract foreign tourists who shop on Amazon and find many products only available in the U.S. Meanwhile, Amazon has been experimenting with same-day delivery in 12 cities, including New York, Los Angeles, Atlanta, and Phoenix. By opening in New York, Amazon can showcase its products to a broader audience and test the waters for future brick-and-mortar expansion. The store's address, 7 West 34th Street, is strategically located across from the Empire State Building and a block east of the busy Herald Square, home to Macy's flagship store. This location, reminiscent of the classic 1947 Christmas movie "Miracle on 34th Street," could provide Amazon with a unique opportunity to connect with customers in the physical world.

Former South Carolina Governor Mark Sanford’s political comeback bid has hit several roadblocks in recent weeks, and the candidate has responded with an unconventional move. His ex-wife, Jenny Sanford, filed a court complaint alleging that he trespassed at her home in early February, which could be seen as an attempt to keep the focus on his personal life rather than his policy proposals. National Republicans have also abandoned their support for Sanford’s campaign, with the National Republican Congressional Committee stating they will not be engaged in the special election. Polls show Sanford trailing his Democratic opponent, Elizabeth Colbert Busch, by a significant margin. In an attempt to draw attention away from these setbacks, Sanford organized a debate with a cardboard cutout of House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi, a move reminiscent of Clint Eastwood’s infamous speech at the 2012 Republican National Convention. Sanford accused Colbert Busch of running a “stealth campaign” by avoiding public debates. He argued that the debate with Pelosi was a legitimate alternative, as he posed a question to the cutout regarding a National Labor Relations Board lawsuit that sought to block Boeing from building a new plant in South Carolina, a move he claimed was politically motivated and would have denied the state much-needed jobs. This tactic, while creative, may not be enough to salvage Sanford’s campaign, especially given the ongoing legal issues and the strong lead his opponent currently holds.

Triple suicide bombers hit a pair of mosques in Sanaa, Yemen, on Friday, killing 46 and injuring 100 others, according to medical officials. The attackers targeted mosques controlled by Shiite rebels, specifically the Badr and al-Hashoosh mosques, which were crowded with worshippers during midday prayers, the most crowded time of the week. Eyewitnesses reported that at least two suicide bombers attacked inside the Badr mosque, with one detonating his device as panicked worshippers rushed to the outside gates, followed by a second suicide bomber amid the fleeing crowd. At the al-Hashoosh mosque, a witness said he was thrown two meters away by the blast. The attacks left a small child among the dead, and corpses were lined up on the mosque floor, carried away in pick-up trucks. The Houthis, known as Shiite rebels, control at least nine of Yemen's 21 provinces and have recently taken control of the capital, Sanaa. They put President Abed Rabbo Mansour Hadi under house arrest and forced him to flee to the southern city of Aden, where he established a temporary capital. There was no immediate claim of responsibility, but ISIS purportedly claimed the bombings, marking the group's first major attack in Yemen. The attacks come amid ongoing conflicts between the Houthis and supporters of ousted President Abdu Rabu Mansour Hadi, as well as a growing presence of al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula. The United States, which had a long relationship with Yemen's leader and worked with the regime to target AQAP militants, strongly condemned the mosque bombings and expressed condolences to the victims' families. The U.S. State Department called on the Houthis, former President Ali Abdullah Saleh, and their allies to stop their violent incitement and undermining of President Hadi, emphasizing the need for a political solution. The U.S. also continued its anti-AQAP drone program in Yemen, with a recent strike killing a senior AQAP cleric and three others.

India has elected its first president from the Dalit, or "untouchable," caste, marking a significant milestone in the country's history. Ram Nath Kovind, a member of the ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), won the election with 2,930 votes, defeating the Congress party's candidate, Meira Kumar. Kovind, 72, is the second Dalit to hold the presidency, following K. R. Narayanan, who served from 1997 to 2002. The election highlights the growing influence of the BJP, which has been pushing for greater representation of lower-caste communities. Kovind, a lawyer and former governor of Bihar, lacks a popular mandate but his selection is seen as a strategic move by Prime Minister Narendra Modi to consolidate support among India's 200 million Dalits. Analysts suggest that Kovind's role will be largely ceremonial, but his appointment could help Modi navigate parliamentary challenges. The election comes amid rising tensions over religious and caste divisions, with the BJP's Hindu nationalist agenda facing criticism for exacerbating social tensions. Kovind's victory is viewed as a signal of the BJP's commitment to inclusive governance, though concerns remain about the ongoing marginalization of Dalits in rural areas.

In a first, a humanoid robot named Athena boarded a commercial airline flight at Los Angeles International Airport, marking a significant step in the integration of robots into everyday life. Athena, created by the Salt Lake City engineering and robotics company Sarcos and purchased by Germany’s Max Planck Society, embarked on her journey to Germany as a paid passenger on Lufthansa. The robot, designed to perform dangerous tasks like cleanup after the Fukushima nuclear disaster, attracted attention at the Tom Bradley International Terminal as she was pushed up to the Lufthansa counter for ticket pickup. Athena, equipped with a head, hands, and feet, and wearing stylish red sneakers, received special treatment, including a cut to the front of the ticket line in the first-class lane. Despite not needing to go through the regular metal detector, she still underwent a special electronic pat-down by TSA. Upon boarding, Athena was strapped into a seat like any other passenger, but was accompanied by her creators, Alexander Herzog and Jeannette Bohg, to her new laboratory home in Germany. This event highlights the potential for robots to travel alongside humans and the growing acceptance of such technology in commercial settings.

A vast medieval cemetery, containing approximately 1,300 burials, was discovered beneath the Old Divinity School at St John's College, Cambridge University, during recent refurbishments. Archaeologists from the Cambridge Archaeological Unit uncovered the site, which was far larger than expected and included around 400 complete skeletons. The cemetery, used from the 13th to 15th centuries, served the Hospital of St John the Evangelist, which cared for the poor and sick in the community. Notably, many skeletons did not fit their graves, suggesting some graves were pre-dug in anticipation of winter deaths when ground conditions would have been more challenging. The majority of burials were without coffins or shrouds, indicating the cemetery primarily served the poor. Grave-goods, such as jewelry and personal items, were rare, with only a few found, including a jet crucifix and a woman's head. The cemetery had gravel paths, a water well, and seeds from flowering plants, suggesting it was a place for people to visit their loved ones. The remains showed a roughly equal gender balance, with most individuals dying between 25 and 45 years old, and a lack of young female remains, likely due to the Hospital's exclusion of pregnant women. Despite local rumors linking the cemetery to the Black Death, no evidence of this disease or large burial groups from that period was found. The site, one of the largest medieval hospital cemeteries in Britain, provides significant insights into life and death in medieval Cambridge.

Vincent van Gogh's infamous act of self-mutilation—cutting off his ear—has long been shrouded in mystery. The exact motivation behind this act, whether it was love, jealousy, or rage, has remained unknown for over a century. However, a new study of his time in Provence suggests that the incident was actually triggered by the news that his brother Theo, his most loyal confidant and financial supporter, was about to marry after a whirlwind romance. According to Martin Bailey, author of Studio of the South, the news of the marriage was delivered to Van Gogh in a letter from Theo on December 23, 1888, just days before the incident. Bailey’s research indicates that Van Gogh learned of the impending marriage before the event, which could have threatened the closeness of their relationship and left Theo with a wife and family to support, unable to fund a struggling brother who had yet to sell a single canvas.

The study reveals that Van Gogh was distressed by the news, and later that night, there was a quarrel with fellow artist Paul Gauguin, who had spent the day working with him. However, Bailey believes the trigger for Van Gogh’s despair was not the quarrel but the news from his brother. Van Gogh’s letter to Theo, written after the incident, mentions that the fine days would soon come, and he would start painting again. Despite a further collapse and another spell in hospital, he continued to paint until he left Arles in April.

The act of self-mutilation left Van Gogh bleeding copiously, and he wrapped the piece of ear in paper and walked to his favourite brothel, where he gave it to a young woman he knew. Another recent book, by Bernadette Murphy, suggests that this woman was not a prostitute but a local farmer’s daughter working there as a servant. Murphy also uncovered a drawing, made by a doctor long after the event, suggesting that Van Gogh had cut the entire ear off, and not just the lobe. In any event, the poor woman opened the parcel, fainted on the spot, Van Gogh fled, and the police were called.

Gauguin returned to the house the following morning, Christmas Eve, where he found the police on the doorstep, and the artist lying in his blood-soaked bed. Theo, who had been hoping to spend a first Christmas with his fiancée, arrived on Christmas Day to visit his brother in hospital. Van Gogh was briefly locked in an isolation room but was discharged on January 7, 1889. He wrote to Theo: “Soon the fine days will come and I’ll start on the orchards in blossom again.” Despite a further collapse and another spell in hospital, he continued to paint until he left Arles in April.

The paintings from this desperate period in his life are among his best-loved works. Bailey has also traced the surprising afterlife of the bed in Van Gogh’s famous The Bedroom. The actual bed depicted in the painting survived until after the Second World War, and it was donated to a community in the Netherlands in 1945. The twin pillows in the painting suggest that Van Gogh still had a lingering hope that he might eventually share his bed with a woman. Ensconced in the first comfortable home of his own as an adult, he proudly completed a picture of his newly furnished bedroom.

All five Republican members of the House ethics committee are calling for ethics trials for Reps. Charlie Rangel (D-N.Y.) and Maxine Waters (D-Calif.) to be scheduled before the November elections, despite Democrats' desire to avoid the spectacle. Rep. Jo Bonner (R-Ala.), the committee's ranking member, and his four Republican colleagues issued a public statement urging Chairwoman Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.) to resolve the Rangel and Waters matters transparently. Bonner accused Lofgren of stalling, stating that the trials should be completed before the elections. Democrats are privately upset by the public criticism, seeing it as a partisan move. The ethics committee has struggled to set a trial date, with last Thursday's meeting ending in an impasse. Bonner emphasized that the scheduling is within Lofgren's authority and that the committee members have expressed willingness to meet in October. Rep. Rangel and Rep. Waters have publicly demanded a pre-election trial to ensure a fair resolution.

The $43,000 phone booth installed in Scott Pruitt’s EPA office saw limited use, according to newly released records. Records show Pruitt made only one five-minute call to the White House using the booth. Previously, Pruitt had claimed the booth was necessary for secure communications with the White House and other sensitive matters. The booth’s cost escalated from an initial $25,000 to $43,000 due to additional work, including concrete pouring and room modifications. Despite the high cost, the Government Accountability Office found Pruitt violated federal spending laws by not notifying Congress before the purchase. The EPA’s decision to maintain the booth after Pruitt’s resignation has raised questions about its necessity. Acting Administrator Andrew Wheeler stated he would keep the booth, citing the expense of dismantling it. Meanwhile, the Sierra Club continues to scrutinize Wheeler, seeking more emails and documents from his tenure, aiming to ensure the agency remains accountable to environmental interests.

A great white shark attacked a 50-year-old Denver man named Christopher Myers off Ballston Beach on Cape Cod, Massachusetts, on Monday, prompting a media frenzy and renewed concerns about shark safety. Myers and his 16-year-old son, J.J., were swimming 400 yards offshore when the shark grabbed Myers' left foot, causing serious injuries that required 47 stitches and severed tendons. Myers believes he kicked the shark's snout, which led the shark to release him. The attack, the first in 76 years on Cape Cod, has raised awareness about the growing seal population and the return of great white sharks. State officials have confirmed the presence of at least nine great whites off the coast, with the nearest sightings being in Truro, about 40 miles south of the attack. The shark surfaced between Myers and his son, leading to a tense moment. Myers, despite his injuries, expressed a desire to return to Ballston Beach, stating, "It’s my favorite beach in the world, and I’m sure I’ll be back swimming, but maybe with a bit more care." The incident has heightened concerns among beachgoers and lifeguards, who are on high alert. Massachusetts tourism officials are working to reassure visitors that the risk is minimal, though they advise staying away from seal colonies. The attack has also prompted discussions about the balance between human activities and marine life, with experts emphasizing the importance of respecting the natural environment.

Oakland, California, has seen a series of tragic events in recent years, with a community activist and father, Melvin Johnson, becoming the latest victim of gun violence. Johnson, 39, was fatally shot on December 27, 2016, while driving near a street memorial for his slain family members. His son, Andrew "Drew" Thomas, and grandson, Drew Leon Deon Jackson, were killed in August 2013, when a shooter fired into their home while they slept. Despite the unsolved nature of the killings, Johnson had been a vocal advocate for an end to violence in Oakland, urging the community to "stop the violence" and "put the guns down" after his family's tragic loss. He had moved his son to Fresno to protect him from Oakland's street violence, but the young men were killed while visiting Oakland for a birthday party. Johnson's mother, Carolyn Smith, described him as a kind and helpful individual who had dedicated himself to helping others after his family's tragedies. His business, Drewski Designs, which produced T-shirts and clothing for various events, was noted for its community service. Johnson's death, along with the ongoing investigation into his son and grandson's killings, has brought renewed attention to Oakland's high rates of gun violence. The city, with a population of about 410,000, has seen a significant drop in overall shootings and violent crime in recent years, but poverty and gang-related activity remain major issues. Oakland police have offered up to $10,000 for information leading to the arrest of Johnson's killer, while a reward of up to $30,000 remains for anyone with information on the unsolved murders of Thomas and his grandson. The community continues to mourn the loss of Johnson, who was remembered as a gentle and loving figure who had dedicated his life to helping others in the face of adversity.

Mexican drug kingpin Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzman was transferred to a prison in Ciudad Juarez, near the US border, on Saturday, according to a senior Mexican law enforcement source. The move, which comes one month after a Mexican lawyer requested Guzman's extradition to the US, is said to be aimed at preventing any escape attempts during planned renovations at his maximum-security prison in Altiplano. Guzman, known for his two dramatic escapes from high-security prisons, including a 2015 breakout through a tunnel, faces extradition requests from US courts in California and Texas for charges of homicide and drug trafficking. His transfer to Ciudad Juarez, a city with a low-rated federal prison, has raised questions about its suitability for housing such a high-profile prisoner. Despite the move, Guzman's lawyer, Jose Refugio Rodriguez, claims the transfer is illegal and that his client is willing to plead guilty to drug trafficking charges in the US in exchange for a lighter sentence and confinement at a medium-security prison. The transfer has surprised US authorities, who were not notified in advance. Guzman, the former leader of the Sinaloa drug cartel, is accused of smuggling tons of drugs into the US by various means, including boats, submarines, and extensive tunnel networks. His extradition process, which President Enrique Pena Nieto has said will happen "as soon as possible," may take a year or more due to legal and political considerations.

Los Angeles (CNN) Lonnie David Franklin, Jr., a former garbage truck driver and LAPD garage attendant, was found guilty of murdering nine women and one girl over a span of three decades, making him one of the most prolific serial killers in California history. The verdict, reached after a three-month trial with 61 witnesses, took less than two days, with jurors finding him guilty of all charges, including the attempted murder of a woman who survived an 1988 attack. Franklin, 63, known as "The Grim Sleeper" due to a 13-year gap between some of his killings, remained silent and composed during the reading of the verdicts. Family members of the victims, instructed by the judge to avoid emotional displays, quietly celebrated with each "guilty" verdict, showing relief and gratitude.

The trial, which began in March 2016, featured a detailed account of the crimes, including DNA evidence linking Franklin to the victims. Prosecutors highlighted the common characteristics of the crime scenes, all within a few miles of Franklin's home, and the "body dump" nature of the killings. They also presented testimony from a surviving victim, Enietra Washington, who recounted being shot and left for dead by Franklin. The defense, led by attorney Seymour Amster, argued that the case was circumstantial and lacked sufficient evidence, suggesting an unnamed relative of Franklin could be responsible. However, Amster's arguments were met with frustration from the judge, who reminded him to "just do your job."

The case hinged on DNA evidence, which emerged in 2010, linking Franklin to the crimes through a familial DNA search. Detectives placed Franklin under 24-hour surveillance and collected DNA from a pizza crust left behind, confirming his involvement. Franklin's home was raided, and detectives found numerous photos and videos of unidentified women. The trial also revealed that Franklin had been charged with the attempted murder of another woman in Germany while serving in the U.S. Army in the 1970s.

Outside the courtroom, the sister of Franklin's youngest victim, Samara Herard, expressed her gratitude for the verdict but emphasized remembering her sister, Princess Berthomieux, as a sweet, innocent girl rather than a victim. The verdict marks a significant milestone in the long-standing investigation into the "Grim Sleeper" case, bringing closure to the families and communities affected by Franklin's crimes.

A judge ruled that the three siblings of a 19-month-old girl who died in a Houston apartment fire will remain in foster care. The 5-year-old girl, two 3-year-olds, and their 19-month-old sister, J'Zyra Thompson, were left alone in the apartment when J'Zyra managed to get into the oven, which was turned on, and died from severe burns. CPS believes the 5-year-old claims to have been sleeping when it happened, while one of the 3-year-olds reportedly took responsibility for putting the baby in the oven. The mother, Racquel Thompson, was at work and left the children with her boyfriend, who was questioned by police. CPS has concerns about the mother's previous reports and her leaving the children home alone for an extended period. The next hearing on the custody of the children is set for December 2. The children's attorney stated that the 5-year-old is in one home and the other two children are in another. The case is ongoing, and it is unclear if charges will be filed against the mother or her boyfriend.

The U.S. government has taken a step back from Arctic offshore oil and gas drilling, canceling two potential lease sales off the Alaskan coast in the Beaufort and Chukchi seas. This decision, attributed to "current market conditions and low industry interest," follows Shell's announcement that it will halt exploration in the Chukchi Sea for the foreseeable future. Interior Secretary Sally Jewell stated, "In light of Shell's announcement, the amount of acreage already under lease and current market conditions, it does not make sense to prepare for lease sales in the Arctic in the next year and a half." Environmentalists have welcomed this move, with Miyoko Sakashita of the Center for Biological Diversity calling it "great for the Arctic and its polar bears." She emphasized, "We need to keep all the Arctic oil in the ground." The existing leases in the Beaufort Sea are set to expire in 2017, while those in the Chukchi Sea will expire in 2020. Shell, which has invested approximately $7 billion in Arctic offshore development, cited "disappointing" tests as the reason for ending exploration. The U.S. Geological Survey estimates that the Arctic holds about 30% of the world's undiscovered natural gas and 13% of its oil. However, environmental groups argue that offshore drilling in the Arctic would damage a natural wilderness and contribute to climate change. The Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement also denied lease extension requests from Shell and Statoil, stating that the companies did not demonstrate a reasonable schedule of work for exploration and development. This decision reflects the current low price of oil, making Arctic exploration less attractive for oil companies.

A jury in San Francisco found Jose Ines Garcia Zarate, a Mexican immigrant, not guilty of murder in the 2015 shooting death of Kate Steinle, an incident that sparked a national debate over immigration policy. Zarate, who had been deported five times, was accused of shooting Steinle, 32, as she and her father strolled on a popular San Francisco pier. The jury convicted Zarate of being a felon in possession of a firearm, which could result in a three-year sentence. During the trial, prosecutors argued that Zarate intentionally shot Steinle, while defense attorneys maintained it was an accident. Zarate claimed the gun went off accidentally when he picked it up, which had been found wrapped in a shirt on a pier bench. The verdict was met with strong reactions, with President Donald Trump calling it "disgraceful" and citing the case during his campaign to support his stance on stricter immigration policies. Attorney General Jeff Sessions criticized San Francisco's sanctuary city policy, stating it contributed to the "preventable and heartbreaking death" of Steinle. The Steinle family expressed disappointment and shock, saying justice was rendered but not served. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) announced plans to deport Zarate, while the Justice Department considered additional charges. The case highlighted the ongoing tension between immigration policies and the rights of sanctuary cities, as well as the emotional impact on the victim's family.

Two Sumatran tiger cubs, Bandar and Sukacita, were born at the Smithsonian’s National Zoo in Washington, D.C., on August 5, 2013, marking a significant conservation success for the critically endangered species. The cubs, born to first-time mother Damai and father Kavi, weighed about two pounds each at birth and had not yet opened their eyes. Keepers monitored the cubs closely, ensuring they received proper care and nutrition. Damai, a 4-year-old tiger, exhibited natural maternal behavior, grooming and nursing her cubs. The cubs will not be on exhibit for several months, as they undergo a series of health exams and vaccinations. Their public debut is anticipated in late fall, and visitors can watch their growth on the zoo’s live webcams. The birth of these cubs is crucial for the survival of the Sumatran tiger, with fewer than 500 of them remaining in the wild.

Professor Tyler Cowen of George Mason University was pepper-sprayed and detained by an unknown white male during a class on vigilante justice, sparking a bizarre incident that left the academic community in shock. The suspect, who entered the classroom and declared he was making a citizen's arrest, pepper-sprayed Cowen before following him into the hallway, where two students managed to detain the intruder until police arrived. Students initially thought the arrest was part of the class, given the current topic. Cowen, a popular blogger advocating libertarian beliefs, refused medical treatment and continued his work. Police are unsure of the motive behind the attack, but some speculate it may be related to Cowen's online advocacy. This incident highlights the thin line between academic discourse and real-world consequences, raising questions about the safety of educators and the potential for vigilante justice.

High Street shoe chain Barratts and DVD rental chain Blockbuster have both entered administration, putting over 3,000 UK and Irish jobs at risk. Barratts, which has 75 stores and 23 concessions, is reviewing its financial position and seeking a sale, while Blockbuster, employing 2,000 across 264 stores, may survive as parts of the business are sought after by interested parties. Despite their closures, both companies aim to continue trading temporarily. Barratts has a chance to emerge as a smaller entity, while Blockbuster administrators hope to save jobs and secure a future for the brand. The closures mark the end of an era for both retail giants.

J.K. Rowling, the author of the Harry Potter series, recently revealed her secret writing life as Robert Galbraith with the release of "The Cuckoo's Calling," a crime novel published under a pseudonym. The book, featuring a private investigator named Cormoran Strike, quickly climbed the bestseller lists after Rowling's identity was revealed by The Sunday Times. The novel's success was swift and significant, with the physical edition ranking No. 1 on both Barnes & Noble's and Amazon's online stores by Sunday afternoon. Despite mixed reviews, the book's popularity surged, making it a top seller in the U.S. and the U.K. Mulholland Books, an imprint of Hachette Book Group, published the book in the U.S., while a sister imprint in the U.K. handled the release. The book's success led to a second installment in the series being planned for the following summer. Rowling's desire for a clean slate and the freedom to write without expectations from her audience were cited as motivations for her pseudonymous writing. The revelation of her true identity as the author of "The Cuckoo's Calling" also spurred a reevaluation of her first adult novel, "The Casual Vacancy," which had been released earlier that year. Despite mixed critical reception, "The Casual Vacancy" proved popular with readers, selling over a million hardcover copies in North America. The article concludes with a brief mention of the Stolen Valor Act, a new law signed by President Obama aimed at protecting real military heroes from fraudulent claims.

Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel filed a lawsuit against the Trump administration, challenging the Justice Department’s new conditions on federal law enforcement grant funding, which the city argues are unconstitutional. The new conditions require cities to share immigration status information with federal officials, provide unfettered access to police stations for immigration enforcement, and give 48-hour notice of an arrested person’s release in cases of potential immigration violations. The city contends these conditions violate the 10th and 4th Amendments and the Congressional power of the purse. Emanuel’s move gained support from immigrant rights groups but faced criticism from those who argue the city should do more to prevent police from assisting in deportations. The lawsuit could affect other local Illinois governments and has broader implications for sanctuary cities nationwide. Attorney General Jeff Sessions responded harshly, accusing Chicago of adopting a policy that obstructs the country’s lawful immigration system and harming public safety. Sessions argued that federal funds should be withheld from cities that do not cooperate with immigration officials. However, the city maintains that undocumented immigrants are not driving Chicago’s crime surge and that the policies benefit public safety by encouraging cooperation. The lawsuit is part of a growing legal challenge against the Trump administration’s efforts to punish sanctuary cities, with Seattle and several California cities also filing similar suits.
