Among the revelations, Jasmine Li, granddaughter of powerful Chinese leader Jia Qinglin, was found to be the sole shareholder of two British Virgin Islands companies while studying at Stanford University. Other prominent figures with offshore companies include the brother-in-law of President Xi Jinping and the son-in-law of Zhang Gaoli, a member of China’s Politburo Standing Committee. These offshore entities are often used to hide or transfer assets, raising concerns about the wealth and influence of China’s political elite.

The documents also highlight the extensive use of offshore services by Mossack Fonseca, with the firm being the world’s fourth largest provider of such services, generating about $42 million annually. Mossack Fonseca has offices in eight Chinese cities, serving clients from Hong Kong and China linked to 40,000 companies. The firm claims to have a strong compliance record and has policies to handle politically exposed persons (PEPs), but critics argue that the documents show a lack of thorough due diligence. The leak has sparked debates about the global tax evasion and corruption, with some economists estimating that at least $7.6 trillion is stashed offshore, and as much as $1 trillion is illegally funneled from developing countries.

The scandal has led to political fallout, with Iceland’s Prime Minister Sigmundur Gunnlaugsson resigning after it was revealed he owned an offshore company. The leak has also prompted Panama to create an international panel to improve transparency in its offshore financial industry. Despite the firm’s claims of being hacked, Mossack Fonseca faces scrutiny over its role in facilitating offshore companies for the rich and powerful, raising questions about the effectiveness of current regulations and the need for global cooperation to address tax evasion and corruption.

Police in Mexico's southern Chiapas state found 513 migrants packed inside two trailer trucks, bound for the United States, on Tuesday. The migrants, from Central and South America and Asia, were crammed in dangerously crowded conditions, some suffering from dehydration after hours of travel. The trucks had air holes punched in the tops, but migrants said they lacked air and water. The smugglers were charging about $7,000 per person. None of the migrants said a drug gang was involved in the mass smuggling scheme. Authorities arrested four people accused of smuggling the migrants. The National Immigration Institute identified 410 Guatemalans, 47 Salvadorans, 32 Ecuadorans, 12 Indians, six Nepalis, three Chinese, one Japanese, one Dominican, and one Honduran. There were 32 women and four children among them. This was the largest shipment of migrants detained in Mexico in recent years. In January, 219 migrants were found squeezed into a trailer truck in Chiapas. The use of X-ray scanners by border security and police to inspect vehicles on the road revealed the harrowing scene, drawing attention to the increasing use of this technology for human smuggling detection.

A photo of John Goodlett, a 25-year-old employee at Enterprise Rent-A-Car, holding one of his customer’s twin infants while processing her rental car is going viral, after the mother posted the picture on her Facebook page, TODAY reports. Coty Vincent, 25, a mother of 11-month-old twins, was picking up her car after a hit-and-run accident and needed help carrying both boys. Goodlett, who is a twin himself, simply picked up one of the infants while processing the rental, allowing Vincent to focus on the other tasks at hand. “He grabbed one of the boys out of his car seat and I grabbed the other and we went inside,” Vincent said. “So I kind of moseyed on over to where he was working, playing with one son while he had the other one. He was working away, holding him like a champ, like he’s done it his whole life,” she added. The small gesture moved Vincent, who snapped a photo of Goodlett, typing on the computer with one hand while holding her son with the other. She posted the picture to Facebook that evening, writing, “While he helped me with my rental due to a hit and run accident, he held one of my twin sons as I don't have a double stroller. One of the most compassionate and caring people I've ever met. We need more people like John who go that extra step. #BeAJohn.” The post received more than 224,800 reactions and 24,600 shares. Goodlett, who was surprised by the attention, said, “I’m still blown away. It just makes you wonder: What did I do so special? This was something that’s part of my instinctual way to do. It’s kind of shocking to see the world took it as such a big motion.” Goodlett noted he has something in common with Vincent: He's a twin himself. He lives with a sister, and jokes about their “love-hate relationship.” “Just like any sibling, one moment we got each other’s back, one moment we’re yelling at each other’s throats,” he said. “But it’s a real thing. It’s a natural love and it’s deep.” Goodlett chose to donate the funds from a reward offered by Enterprise’s corporate office to his favorite charity, a local Boys & Girls Club run by the Salvation Army. Vincent also received a double stroller from Enterprise’s corporate office, which ordered her one after hearing about the incident. Vincent is just as excited that her post about "a simple act of kindness" has touched so many hearts around the world. “There are a lot of great Americans in this country and that’s what we really need to see, because people are getting depressed and hearts are getting so heavy from everything going on right now,” she said. “It’s up to us to turn this around. So many have forgotten we are humans and we do kind things and we do treat with each other with respect, and smile and hold doors open and do these little things. I want to remind people they can be kind to one another.”

Trooper Miguel Rincon was conducting a traffic stop on State Route 80 near Bisbee when a woman approached him, stating she was rushing her granddaughter to the hospital. Courtney Benavidez, who was in labor, had called her grandmother for a ride to the hospital after her water broke. Her husband, Adrian Borquez, was in Phoenix for the night, unaware of the impending birth. Benavidez was only about an hour and a half into labor when she couldn't make it to the hospital and pulled over when she saw Trooper Rincon's patrol car. Rincon, a seven-year veteran of the Arizona Department of Public Safety, quickly realized the situation and left his traffic stop to assist. He helped Benavidez deliver her baby boy, Carter Jett, on the side of the road. Rincon wrapped the newborn in a blanket and cared for both mother and child until medics arrived. The family was discharged from Canyon Vista Medical Center the next day, in good health. Trooper Rincon described the experience as his best since joining the force, noting the surprise factor. Benavidez, a third-grade teacher, was shocked by the speed of the delivery, which she compared to her own birth experience. She named her son Carter Jett, a reference to his rapid arrival. Both mother and child are doing well, and Benavidez expressed gratitude for Trooper Rincon's assistance.

A new investment vehicle called Fantex Holdings has emerged, offering fans the chance to buy shares in professional athletes, marking a significant shift in the world of sports and finance. Fantex, backed by executives from Silicon Valley, Wall Street, and the sports world, plans to create stocks tied to an athlete's financial performance, including earnings from playing contracts, corporate endorsements, and appearance fees. The company's inaugural initial public offering (IPO) focuses on Arian Foster, the Pro Bowl running back of the Houston Texans. Investors will receive stock linked to Foster's future earnings, with potential upside if he performs well and secures more sponsorships. However, the investment is highly speculative, with numerous risk factors, including the possibility of a career-ending injury or a performance slump. Fantex aims to capitalize on the popularity of the National Football League and fantasy football, where fans draft players and score points based on their performance. Critics argue that such investments could lead to insider trading violations and compliance issues with federal securities laws. Despite these concerns, the IPO is intended to provide athletes with a large upfront payment for giving up a certain percentage of their future earnings, potentially acting as a hedge against an unexpected downturn in their careers. While some athletes and their agents might view this as a compelling proposition, others might be wary of the risks involved. Fantex's ambitious plans to sign up more football players and other athletes, as well as celebrities, could reshape the landscape of sports investments, but the long-term outlook for these investments remains uncertain.

The parents of First Lady Melania Trump, Viktor and Amalija Knavs, have become U.S. citizens through the sponsorship of their daughter, a process that aligns with the family visa system President Trump has criticized. They obtained permanent residency and lived in the U.S. for over a decade before naturalizing, a journey described by their lawyer as similar to that of millions of others. Despite the administration's efforts to end family-based migration, the Knavses' path to citizenship was typical. Their status as frequent travelers with the Trump family, including visits to Mar-a-Lago and Bedminster, New Jersey, has raised questions about the administration's stance on immigration. Viktor and Amalija, now 73 and 71, respectively, have expressed support for family reunification, countering the administration's push for a merit-based system. Their naturalization highlights the complexity of the family visa system and its role in U.S. immigration policy.

Gwyneth Paltrow’s lifestyle brand, Goop, has faced criticism for promoting unproven health remedies and supplements. Dr. Jen Gunter, an obstetrician and gynecologist, has been a vocal critic of Goop, highlighting its questionable health claims and practices. Goop has marketed products such as jade eggs for vaginal health, which Gunter deems as “the biggest load of garbage” she has read on the site. Other controversial claims include the suggestion that wearing bras increases the risk of breast cancer and the promotion of goat’s milk cleansing to ward off parasites. Despite Goop’s attempts to vet its content, Gunter’s blog has garnered significant attention, with her posts generating over 157,000 page views. Goop has responded to Gunter’s criticisms with a blog post titled “Uncensored: A Word from Our Doctors,” which included a section attributed to “Team Goop” and another by featured doctors, including Dr. Steven Gundry, who criticized Gunter for using profanity. This exchange has escalated into a public debate over the legitimacy of alternative health practices promoted by Goop. The controversy highlights the tension between traditional medical practices and the growing popularity of alternative wellness approaches, with Goop facing scrutiny for its marketing practices.

CIA Director John Brennan held a rare press conference to address the controversy surrounding the agency’s past use of aggressive interrogation techniques, as detailed in a recently released Senate Intelligence Committee report. Brennan defended the integrity of his agency’s workforce, acknowledging that some personnel used techniques that “had not been authorized, were abhorrent and rightly should be repudiated by all.” He praised the agency’s efforts to keep the country safe post-9/11, stating that “the overwhelming majority” of the CIA’s workforce carried out their responsibilities faithfully. However, he conceded that the agency fell short in holding officers accountable for their mistakes. Brennan maintained that detainees subjected to enhanced interrogation techniques provided “useful and valuable” information, though he admitted that it is “unknowable” whether the harsh treatment yielded that information. He did not support the Senate report’s characterization of the techniques as torture and expressed concern over the report’s claim that the CIA misled the White House and Congress. Brennan’s press conference came two days after the Senate report’s release, which detailed the CIA’s abuse of detainees and severe mismanagement of its interrogation program. The report suggested that the CIA misled officials, including President Obama, about the program’s effectiveness. While Brennan acknowledged some aspects of the report’s findings, he criticized its methodology and suggested there was “more than enough transparency” already. His appearance aimed to quell public concern and support the agency’s personnel, but critics, including Senator Mark Udall, called for his resignation. The White House maintained its full confidence in Brennan, who emphasized that he was not in the chain of command during the post-9/11 years when the controversial interrogation program was in place.

CNN is reformatting "Parker Spitzer" into "In the Arena," dropping conservative co-host Kathleen Parker and adding conservative E.D. Hill and Will Cain. The move aims to boost ratings for CNN's struggling 8 p.m. slot, which has seen limited success since its October debut. Parker cited the need to focus on her syndicated column as the reason for her departure. The new format will feature an ensemble of guests from various viewpoints, reflecting CNN's attempt to balance its neutral image with more opinion-based programming. Despite initial challenges, CNN hopes this change will help the channel compete more effectively against Fox News and MSNBC in the prime-time viewership race.

The recent cold snap in various parts of the world, including Beijing, Britain, and Florida, has sparked debates about the validity of global warming predictions. Critics argue that such extreme weather contradicts the notion of a warming planet, while experts emphasize that these events are part of natural variability and do not negate long-term climate trends. Gerald Meehl, a senior scientist at the National Center for Atmospheric Research, explains that record cold temperatures will still occur, but they will become less frequent as the Earth continues to warm. Deke Arndt from the National Climatic Data Center notes that 2009 was among the 10 warmest years since 1880, reinforcing the overall warming trend. Meteorologists attribute the current cold snap to a pronounced zigzag pattern in the atmosphere, which has brought Arctic air southward, causing record lows in some areas. This pattern, while unusual, is not unprecedented and is expected to weaken in the coming weeks. Despite the recent cold, the overall climate trend remains one of warming, with increased potential for severe weather events due to man-made climate change.

Chelsea Manning, the transgender former U.S. Army intelligence analyst who was imprisoned for leaking classified documents to WikiLeaks, is featured in Vogue magazine's September issue, photographed in a red swimsuit by Annie Leibovitz. Manning, who was released from Fort Leavenworth prison in May 2017 after serving seven years, now lives in New York City and has become a social media celebrity. She came out as transgender the day after her sentencing in 2013 and publicly announced it on NBC's "Today" show, expressing surprise at the "outpouring of love and support" she received. Since her release, Manning has embraced her femininity, teaching herself programming languages like Rust, and is working on a memoir. Her life story, including her decision to leak classified information, has sparked controversy. While some praise her photo shoot as "simply lovely" and "brave," others criticize Vogue for featuring a controversial figure. Manning's case highlights the complex intersection of radical identity politics and the rule of law, as she has become a symbol for both transgender rights and the debate over government transparency. Her story is a testament to the resilience and determination of those who challenge societal norms and the systems that govern them.

The bittersweet romantic musical "Once" has emerged as the big winner at the 2012 Tony Awards, taking home eight awards, including the best new musical prize. Based on the 2006 indie film, "Once" tells the story of an unlikely love affair between a Czech flower seller and an Irish street musician in Dublin, using songs by Marketa Irglova and Glen Hansard, including the Oscar-winning "Falling Slowly." The musical stars Steve Kazee and Cristin Milioti and beat out "Newsies," "Nice Work If You Can Get It," and "Leap of Faith." "Once" also won awards for actor Steve Kazee, director John Tiffany, and playwright Enda Walsh. The night also saw Audra McDonald win her sixth Tony for best lead actress in a musical for her portrayal of Billie Holiday in "Lady Day at Emerson's Bar & Grill," making her the most decorated actress in Tony history. Neil Patrick Harris hosted the ceremony at the Beacon Theatre in New York. Other notable winners include "The Gershwins’ Porgy and Bess" for best revival of a musical and "Venus in Fur" for best play. Click for a full list of winners.

A 400-pound Siberian tiger named Bashuta at the Bronx Zoo did not face euthanasia after it mauled a man who jumped from a moving monorail train and fell over a protective fence. The incident occurred in the Wild Asia exhibit, where a monorail train with open sides takes visitors over the Bronx River and through a forest. The 25-year-old man, alone with the tiger for about 10 minutes, suffered bites and punctures on his arms, legs, shoulders, and back, breaking an arm and a leg. After being rescued by zoo officials, who used a fire extinguisher to chase the tiger away, he was instructed to roll under an electrified wire for safety. The tiger was returned to a holding area where it usually sleeps at night and will not be euthanized, as the zoo director, Jim Breheny, stated, "The tiger did nothing wrong in this episode." Breheny praised the quick response by the staff, saying, "We were able to prevent a bad situation from turning into a real tragedy." The tiger, 11 years old and at the zoo for three years, will be back on exhibit the next day. The zoo will review safety procedures but emphasized that the situation was unusual. "We review everything, but we honestly think we provide a safe experience," Breheny said. "And this is just an extraordinary occurrence... somebody was deliberately trying to endanger themselves."

Nora Ephron, a celebrated essayist, novelist, and screenwriter, passed away at the age of 71, leaving behind a legacy of witty and insightful work that spanned multiple decades. Born on May 19, 1941, in Manhattan, she was the eldest of four sisters, all of whom became writers, a family tradition that shaped her early life. Her mother, a Broadway playwright and Hollywood screenwriter, instilled in her a sharp wit and the ambition to turn everyday experiences into compelling narratives. Ephron's writing career began with journalism at the New York Post and Esquire, where she honed her distinctive voice, often blending humor and personal reflections. She became a prominent voice in the women's movement of the 1970s, using her platform to advocate for women's rights through humor and insight.

Ephron's screenwriting career took off in the 1980s with her Academy Award-nominated screenplay for "Silkwood," a biographical drama about Karen Silkwood. Her best-known films include the romantic comedies "When Harry Met Sally" and "Sleepless in Seattle," which remain cultural touchstones. Her novel "Heartburn" was a scathing account of her tumultuous marriage to Watergate journalist Carl Bernstein, and her later works, such as "You've Got Mail" and "Julie & Julia," continued to explore themes of love, relationships, and personal growth. Throughout her career, Ephron was known for her sharp wit and her ability to tackle complex themes with a light touch. She delivered a powerful commencement address at Wellesley College in 1996, encouraging graduates to break the rules and make trouble on behalf of women. Her final book, "I Feel Bad About My Neck," explored the indignities of aging with humor and honesty. Ephron's passing marks the end of an era, but her work continues to inspire and entertain, reminding us of the power of words and the importance of staying true to oneself.

Russell Brand and Katy Perry's divorce is now a topic of back-to-back interviews and public comments. Just a day after tabloids reported that Brand had made his first public dig at Perry during a taping of his new show, "Brand X," the comedian had only nice things to say about his ex-wife in interviews with Piers Morgan and Howard Stern. On Tuesday night, Brand told Morgan, "Of course I still feel great feelings of compassion and warmth for Katy," echoing the love and goodwill he extended to the "Fireworks" singer in an interview with Ellen DeGeneres back in May. In a back-to-back interview with Howard Stern, Brand took the high road again, saying, "When we got married, I just thought, ‘I’ve got to marry her, I just love her so much.' And then we got married and I thought, ‘Okay, this isn’t really working out.' " According to MTV.com, Brand even dished to Stern about tabloid reports that disagreements over starting a family played a role in the split. Brand acknowledged that they had discussed having children but refused to say anything more for Perry's sake. "I don't want anything to hurt her," he reportedly told Stern. "She's younger than me, she's a young woman and she's beautiful and she's sensitive and I care about her deeply... I don't want to be too glib... She'll read it and she'll be sad and I don't want that." Brand also confirmed to Stern that he's in a relationship with Isabella Brewster, the younger sister of "Dallas" star Jordana Brewster. "Ah, yes, yes, and some things in the newspaper are true," Brand joked. The article also provides a slideshow of scenes from the couple's 14-month marriage, including their appearances at various events and awards shows. Despite the split, Brand's comments suggest a level of mutual respect and a desire to keep things amicable.

This website, dedicated to the alleged "framing" of Joe Paterno, argues that the media created a false narrative around the Jerry Sandusky scandal, unfairly implicating Paterno in crimes he did not commit. The site claims Paterno's legacy and career were unjustly destroyed, and that Penn State and its football program were punished disproportionately. It emphasizes that the media's coverage was biased, driven by ratings, and inconsistent with the facts. The site features a documentary, "The Framing of Joe Paterno," and two books, "The Betrayal of Joe Paterno" and "Perfect Sense," all aimed at exposing what they see as a media conspiracy. It also highlights various media coverage and interviews, including those with John Ziegler and Ray Blehar, who criticize the media's handling of the case. The site argues that Sandusky himself was also wrongfully accused and that the evidence strongly suggests the alleged abuse did not occur. The summary also mentions recent developments, such as the release of emails and transcripts, and ongoing efforts to challenge the Freeh Report and support Paterno's legal actions against the NCAA.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has issued a warning that breast implants may slightly increase the risk of a rare type of cancer, anaplastic large-cell lymphoma (ALCL). The risk applies to both saline- and silicone-filled implants, and to all women who have them, whether for reconstruction or cosmetic reasons. The FDA noted that so far, about 60 cases worldwide have been linked to breast implants, which is a small number compared to the 5 million to 10 million women who have implants. The cancer usually grows in the capsule of scar tissue around the implant and is not breast cancer. Most cases can be treated by removing the implant and scar tissue, but some may require chemotherapy and radiation. The FDA stated that the risk is small, and the existing data support the continued marketing and use of breast implants. However, women considering implants should discuss the information with their doctors. The agency is asking doctors to report confirmed cases to its safety information program, MedWatch, and is working with the American Society of Plastic Surgeons to create a registry of cases.

Nevest Coleman, 49, officially returned to his former job as a groundskeeper for the Chicago White Sox on Monday, nearly three decades after being wrongfully imprisoned for a crime he did not commit. Coleman, who served 23 years in prison, expressed his pride and joy at rejoining the team he had worked for in 1994. "I was proud to come back here," Coleman told CBS News. "I love the atmosphere." His first task was to power-wash the entrance to Guaranteed Rate Field, the stadium that has undergone significant changes since his last visit. Coleman, who spent his time in prison reading books like "Game of Thrones" and "Harry Potter," and avoiding television, said, "My family was always behind me. My goal was to see everybody." Coleman's return to the ballpark was a testament to the efforts of his family and friends, including his childhood priest, who reached out to the White Sox on his behalf. The team welcomed him back, and Coleman hopes to move up to full-time staff in the future. "I don't have to worry about everybody giving me things. I can support myself now," he said. Coleman's return to the field was a bittersweet moment, as he reflected on his time in prison and the joy of being back with his family. "You get tired sitting around the house," he said. "You won’t be sitting here." Coleman's journey from wrongful imprisonment to a triumphant return to his old job is a powerful reminder of the importance of justice and the resilience of the human spirit.

The gunman who attacked Dallas police headquarters in an armored van early Saturday provided authorities with a name and a motive for the assault, but officials said definitive identification will wait until a medical examination is completed. The armored van used in the attack, which was burning, was found near the headquarters south of downtown. Police had spent hours trying to negotiate with the man, who identified himself as James Boulware, a 35-year-old with a history of family violence, before he led dozens of squad cars on a chase that ended along Interstate 45 in Hutchins. No one was injured by the man, who claimed he was going to blow up police because they "took his child and accused him of being a terrorist." Boulware's mother, Jeannine, declined to comment, while his father, Jim Boulware of Carrollton, said his son had blamed police for losing custody of his child, who is in middle school. Despite previous threats of violence, Jim Boulware said he never expected anything like Saturday's events. The suspect's father added that he had seen his son Friday night and that there were no indications of trouble. Dallas police Chief David Brown stated that the gunman said he was going to blow up police because they "took his child and accused him of being a terrorist." Concerns about explosive ordnance after pipe bombs were found near the headquarters building prevented police from recovering the man's body hours after a police sniper targeted him through the windshield of the van. Officers used a robot to safely approach the vehicle to confirm the gunman was dead and alerted the public that some planned detonations might be heard as they tried to gain entry. At least two pipe bombs were found in the vehicle, which had ports in its walls to fire guns from.

A new round of sanctions against North Korea, introduced by the U.S. and China at the United Nations, aims to impede the development of Pyongyang's nuclear and missile programs following its recent atomic bomb test. Meanwhile, in a separate agricultural crisis, a voracious pest is devouring genetically modified corn that was engineered to thwart the rootworm, raising fears of a "superbug." The western corn rootworm, a significant pest in the U.S., has shown signs of resistance to the genetically modified corn's protective toxin. Experts warn that farmers may need to resume heavy pesticide use if resistant bugs become widespread, and that current farming practices could hasten the development of resistant pests. This issue highlights the potential downside of relying heavily on genetically modified crops, as resistance to both pests and herbicides emerges. While Monsanto and other biotech companies are developing new technologies to address these issues, the problem of pest resistance may be here to stay, forcing farmers to continually adapt their practices.

President Donald Trump, speaking at the National Prayer Breakfast, vowed to "totally destroy" the Johnson Amendment, a 1954 law that prohibits tax-exempt organizations, including churches, from directly or indirectly participating in political campaigns. Trump's pledge, made during his campaign, aims to free religious groups from what he views as a restriction on their freedom of speech. However, the amendment’s removal would significantly alter the landscape of political campaigning, as it has long been a safeguard against religious organizations using their tax-exempt status to influence elections. Critics argue that eliminating the Johnson Amendment could lead to a flood of unregulated political spending by churches and other non-profits, potentially undermining the integrity of the electoral process. The amendment’s repeal would also challenge the long-standing understanding that tax-exempt organizations must remain non-partisan. While some religious leaders and conservative groups support the move, many believe it could have unintended consequences, such as increased political influence from religious groups and reduced transparency in campaign finance. The debate over the amendment highlights the broader tension between religious freedom and the separation of church and state, as well as the complex interplay between political power and religious expression in American society.

Poland’s deputy defense minister, Bartosz Kownacki, resorted to schoolyard insults against France, claiming his nation taught the French to “eat with a fork.” This came after France withdrew Poland’s invite to the Euronaval 2016 event, following a breakdown in Airbus helicopter talks. Kownacki told TVN24 news channel that “the French side officially invited us a long time ago and now they are showing us the door.” He added, “But these are the people we taught to eat with a fork a couple of centuries ago, which may explain their behavior today. This is obvious history, and I invite you to read up on that.” The canceled invitation was delivered to Warsaw via the Polish Embassy in Paris, according to media reports. While there is no actual evidence to prove that Kownacki’s claim is true, some historians believe King Henry III introduced forks to his subjects after discovering them in Poland. The snub came after Poland halted talks with French aviation company Airbus, which were aimed at the purchase of 50 Caracal helicopters by Warsaw. The suspended talks were met with a furious response from Airbus chief executive Tom Enders, who said his company had never been treated so badly by any government. The talks had been backed by Paris, and the cancellation unleashed tension between the two governments, with French President Francois Hollande postponing a visit to the Polish capital. Polish Deputy Defense Minister Kownacki’s remarks have been condemned by Poland’s liberal opposition, as well as the spokeswoman of the governing Law and Justice (PiS) party, Beata Mazurek, who described the comments as “unfortunate” and “not very diplomatic.” The snub also comes amid a continuing row over a cancelled defence contract. The Euronaval 2016 event is supported by the French Ministry of Defense and the French Navy, and is seen as one of the most important exhibitions of its kind in Europe. Poland is to buy US Black Hawks instead, and Airbus has threatened to sue. The controversy is part of a series of controversies Law and Justice has become embroiled in since taking power last November, including a retreat from a near-total ban on abortion after massive street protests by women, and criticism from the EU for taking control of state media appointments and reforms to Poland's constitutional court.

Standard & Poor’s downgraded Italy’s credit rating, causing Italian government bond yields to rise and putting pressure on euro-zone leaders to address the region’s ongoing sovereign-debt crisis. The downgrade to A from A+ and a negative outlook came amid concerns over Italy’s weak economic outlook and political gridlock. This move follows similar downgrades by Moody’s and Fitch, which had already downgraded Italy’s ratings. The yield on 10-year Italian government bonds increased, and the premium over German bunds widened. The downgrade could increase Italy’s borrowing costs, complicating its large-scale refinancing program. Analysts warn that Italy’s downgrade highlights worries about the region’s banking sector, particularly French banks, due to potential impacts from a Greek default. Italy’s economy, the third-largest in the euro zone, faces significant challenges, and the European Central Bank’s bond-buying program may need to intensify. Italy’s government reacted angrily, stating the downgrade was out of touch with reality. Meanwhile, Spain’s Treasury bills sold at higher costs, and Greece continued talks with international lenders for a potential deal to avoid running out of cash.

When chess, the centuries-old game of strategy and intellect, meets the modern era of live streaming and online engagement, a new and dynamic landscape emerges. Brian "Poshybrid" Vigneault, a World of Tanks streamer, tragically died during a 24-hour charity livestream, highlighting the physical and mental toll of marathon gaming sessions. This incident underscores the need for awareness and caution among streamers, who often push their limits to maintain audience engagement. The rise of chess on platforms like Twitch and YouTube exemplifies how traditional games are adapting to digital platforms, attracting a broader audience and fostering a more inclusive community.

Chessbrah, founded by Canadian grandmaster Eric Hansen, represents one end of this spectrum. Hansen's stream is characterized by its energetic and unapologetic approach, blending trash talk, dance music, and a laid-back atmosphere that challenges the game's traditional image. His stream attracts a diverse audience, including grandmasters like Yasser Seirawan, who lend credibility and gravitas to the channel. However, Hansen's approach has faced criticism from more conventional chess players and fans who find the mix of music and trash talk incompatible with the game's serious nature.

On the other end of the spectrum, John Bartholomew, an International Master, offers a more traditional and educational approach. His YouTube channel, Chess Fundamentals, simplifies complex concepts, making chess accessible to beginners. Bartholomew's success highlights the potential of online platforms in teaching and popularizing the game. His videos, which feature detailed analysis of his own games, have garnered significant views and support, proving that there is a demand for both traditional and innovative methods of chess instruction.

Chess.com, led by Danny Rensch, bridges the gap between these two approaches. As the Chief Chess Officer, Rensch has transformed Chess.com into a robust platform that combines original programming, competitive tournaments, and interactive lessons. The PRO Chess League, a significant part of Chess.com's strategy, has attracted top players like Magnus Carlsen and Hikaru Nakamura, bringing the game to a wider audience. The success of the PRO Chess League and other initiatives has demonstrated the potential for chess to thrive in the digital age, challenging traditional notions of the game's audience and presentation.

The inclusion of female players like Alexandra Botez in the chess streaming community has brought attention to the ongoing gender gap in the game. While there are efforts to create a more inclusive environment, the challenges faced by women in the male-dominated world of streaming highlight the need for continued advocacy and support. As chess continues to evolve, the integration of streaming and online platforms offers a promising future, one that can make the game more accessible and engaging for a broader audience.

Chef Tom Colicchio has renamed his Beekman Hotel restaurant Fowler & Wells to Temple Court after uncovering its racially charged past. The establishment, built in the mid-1800s, housed the offices of Fowler & Wells, a pair of publishers and phrenologists. Phrenology, the study of skull size and structure to determine mental abilities, was often used to justify discrimination and slavery. After learning about the namesake's beliefs, Colicchio decided to change the restaurant's name to avoid perpetuating a legacy of racism. The incident highlights the ongoing relevance of historical legacies in modern society, as Colicchio's decision to rename the establishment reflects a broader effort to address and rectify past injustices.

Phrenology, as portrayed in Quentin Tarantino's Django Unchained, was not only used to justify slavery but also to argue for its abolition. The film's character, Calvin Candie, uses phrenology to explain the submissiveness of African slaves, while real-life phrenologist Charles Caldwell, a slave owner, similarly employed the pseudoscience to support his brutal way of life. Caldwell's correspondence reveals his warped sense of morality, stating that his slaves lived more comfortably than he did. Despite its racist origins, phrenology was embraced by both slave owners and abolitionists, as it provided a pseudo-scientific rationale for their respective stances. For instance, abolitionists like Lucretia Mott and Horace Mann used phrenology to argue that the inherent weakness of Africans justified their need for protection and emancipation. This duality underscores the complex interplay between scientific racism and the fight against slavery in the 19th century.

Chinese state media announced that disgraced politician Bo Xilai, once a rising star in Chinese politics, has been expelled from the Communist Party and will face justice for a series of alleged crimes spanning his entire career. Bo, who was party chief in Chongqing, is accused of corruption, abuse of power, and improper sexual relations with multiple women. His wife, Gu Kailai, was convicted of murdering British businessman Neil Heywood and given a suspended death sentence, while his former police chief, Wang Lijun, was sentenced to 15 years in prison for defection, bribery, and abuse of power. The announcement comes as China prepares for the 18th Party Congress, which will begin on November 8 and oversee the once-a-decade leadership transition. The decision to expel Bo and launch criminal proceedings against him suggests a strong message from China's leadership to tackle corruption and abuse of power. The timing of the announcement, made just before a national holiday, raises suspicions that authorities aimed to bury the news. Bo's supporters argue that he is being framed by political enemies, but the state-run media emphasize the need to maintain the party's reputation and address public concerns about corruption. The scandal has overshadowed the upcoming leadership change, casting a long shadow over the transition.

Iranian military commander Ali Fadavi stated that Iran would retaliate against both the U.S. and Israel if attacked, Reuters reports. The comments came as the White House denied an Israeli news report that it was negotiating with Tehran to avoid a future Israel-Iran war, and as U.S. President Barack Obama faces criticism from his election rival for being too soft on Tehran. Fadavi, a naval commander in Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, said, "The Zionist regime separated from America has no meaning, and we must not recognize Israel as separate from America." He added, "On this basis, today only the Americans have taken a threatening stance towards the Islamic Republic." Iran has conducted military exercises and unveiled upgraded weapons recently, aiming to show it can defend itself against any strike against its nuclear sites. Israel, believed to be the only country in the Middle East with nuclear weapons, says the prospect of a nuclear-armed Iran would pose a threat to its existence. Iran denies it is developing weapons and says its nuclear program is peaceful. Israel would expect U.S. backing if it decided to strike Iran, but top U.S. general Martin Dempsey has warned against unilateral action, stating, "I don't want to be complicit if they choose to do it." He reinforced Washington's opposition to unilateral Israeli military action, saying such an attack would "clearly delay but probably not destroy Iran's nuclear programme." Meanwhile, Dempsey expressed concern about the implications of establishing a "humanitarian zone" inside Syria, warning that it would mean not merely establishing a no-fly zone but providing protection against Syrian missiles. He also discussed the challenges in Afghanistan, including the use of "green on blue" attacks by the Taliban and the need to help develop Afghan forces to ensure NATO troops can end their combat role by the target date of the end of 2014.

Comedian Kevin Hart launched the Hurricane Harvey Relief Challenge, donating $25,000 to the American Red Cross and urging fellow celebrities to match his donation. Among those who responded were Beyoncé, Dave Chappelle, Jay-Z, Dwayne Johnson, Chris Rock, Jerry Seinfeld, and Justin Timberlake, each pledging $25,000. Meanwhile, Sandra Bullock contributed $1 million to the American Red Cross, highlighting the need for support in the wake of Hurricane Harvey. Kim Kardashian and her family also donated $500,000 to the same cause. The efforts aim to assist those affected by the flooding and destruction in Houston, Texas.

Ryan Seacrest is joining "Live" as Kelly Ripa's new co-host, marking a new chapter for the morning show. The news was confirmed to CNN before Monday's broadcast, where Ripa and Seacrest announced the change to viewers. Seacrest, a veteran broadcaster who previously hosted "American Idol," will also serve as an executive producer on the show. The move comes as NBC introduces a new 9 a.m. show led by Megyn Kelly, directly competing with "Live." Seacrest, who lives in Los Angeles but will move to New York for the role, will continue his radio shows and other commitments. The seat next to Ripa was coveted by many, including Andy Cohen, Anderson Cooper, Jerry O'Connell, and Fred Savage. Ripa thanked the temporary co-hosts who filled in during the search and expressed excitement about the new partnership. The hosting deal may open doors for further business opportunities with ABC's parent company, Disney.

News Corporation has raised its offer to take full control of BSkyB, increasing its bid to 700p per share in cash, valuing the 61% stake at £7.8 billion. BSkyB's independent directors have called for talks to find a mutually agreeable price and address regulatory issues. News Corporation intends to fund the deal with a significant portion of its cash reserves and believes that taking full control would reduce its reliance on advertising and boost its global footprint. BSkyB's share price rose 21% in early trading. Both parties have agreed to work together to proceed with the regulatory process and facilitate a proposed transaction. BSkyB has formed a committee of independent directors and executive directors to review the proposal. News Corporation's deputy chairman, Chase Carey, believes that BSkyB becoming a wholly-owned part of News Corporation would be beneficial for both companies.

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump faced a series of foreign policy questions during a Thursday interview with conservative radio host Hugh Hewitt, which highlighted his limited knowledge on the subject. Hewitt, who will moderate the next Republican debate, pressed Trump on his familiarity with Iranian military groups and leaders, including Maj. Gen. Qasem Soleimani of the Quds Force. Trump initially appeared unsure, confusing the Quds Force with the Kurds, a Middle Eastern ethnic group. He then corrected himself, but his response about the Kurds being mistreated by the U.S. was corrected by Hewitt. The exchange underscored Trump's lack of experience in foreign policy, as evidenced by his dismissive attitude towards knowing the players behind terrorist organizations. Trump also dodged a question about potential military actions, citing his unpredictability as a strength. In contrast, Carly Fiorina, another Republican candidate, demonstrated a better grasp of the issue, correctly identifying the Quds Force and the leaders of various terrorist groups. Trump's performance in the interview, while not immediately damaging his campaign, may raise concerns among voters and the media about his preparedness for the presidency. Hewitt's questions are set to continue at the upcoming debate, where Trump may face further scrutiny on his knowledge of international affairs.

Bacon lovers, rejoice! Little Caesars is introducing a new pizza that wraps 3 1/2 feet of bacon around the crust, creating a bacon-laden culinary experience. Starting February 23, this limited-time offer will be available nationwide for $12, making it one of the priciest pizzas on the menu. Little Caesars CEO David Scrivano explains, "Every time you take a bite out of the crust, you'll get bacon," adding that the pizza also features pepperoni and bacon sprinkled on top. This innovative offering is part of the chain's strategy to capitalize on the nation's ongoing bacon craze, with domestic bacon sales hitting the $4 billion mark over five consecutive years. Bacon's popularity is driven by its status as an indulgence and a rebellious show of strength in the face of health and wellness trends. However, the added complexity of the bacon-wrapped crust could slow down kitchen operations and may not travel well. Despite these potential challenges, the timing seems favorable, given the current economic climate. "Timing is everything," says Technomic's Darren Tristano, noting that the combination of rising disposable incomes and lower gas prices could work in Little Caesars' favor. The new pizza is part of the chain's ongoing efforts to innovate and offer variety, aligning with its core strengths of value, convenience, and quality.

The Germanwings co-pilot Andreas Lubitz, who appears to have deliberately crashed the plane into the French Alps, had a history of depression, according to German tabloid Bild. Lubitz, 27, received psychiatric treatment for a "serious depressive episode" six years ago, and regular assessments were recommended in his official notes. Lufthansa, the parent company of Germanwings, stated that Lubitz's training was interrupted for several months six years ago, but he passed all subsequent tests and checks with flying colors. The airline did not specify the reason for the interruption. Internal documents and Lufthansa sources cited by Bild indicate that Lubitz spent a total of one and a half years in psychiatric treatment. The cockpit voice recorder data suggests that Lubitz deliberately started the descent as the captain was locked out of the cockpit. French Prime Minister Manuel Valls said the investigation was ongoing and that "everything is pointing to a criminal, crazy, suicidal action that we cannot comprehend." Police have searched two German properties used by Lubitz, taking away boxes and a computer. The discovery at Lubitz's Duesseldorf flat is not a suicide note, according to a police spokesman. The incident has raised questions about cockpit security procedures, with several airlines pledging to ensure at least two crew members are present in the cockpit at all times. The crash site in the French Alps remains the focus of a massive recovery operation, with families of the victims visiting the area and providing DNA samples for identification. The Westerwald flight club, where Lubitz was a member, expressed shock at the revelations about his mental history. The incident has sparked discussions about pilot mental health and cockpit safety measures globally.

A new study suggests that too much vitamin B12 may promote acne, a common skin condition that affects many teenagers and young adults. The research, led by Huiying Li from the University of California-Los Angeles, found that vitamin B12 alters the gene expression of skin bacteria, particularly Propionibacterium acnes, which is commonly linked to acne. In the presence of vitamin B12, these bacteria start producing inflammatory molecules known to promote pimples. The study involved analyzing the gene expression patterns of skin bacteria from individuals prone to acne and those with clear skin. It was observed that the pathway producing vitamin B12 was significantly altered in the skin bacteria of acne-prone individuals. To further investigate, the researchers administered vitamin B12 injections to participants with clear skin, which led to changes in their skin bacteria's gene expression, resembling that of acne patients. Additionally, experiments with P. acnes in laboratory settings confirmed that adding vitamin B12 to the bacteria resulted in increased production of compounds that promote inflammation. While the study presents a potential mechanism linking vitamin B12 to acne, it does not establish a definitive cause-and-effect relationship. Experts caution that more research is needed to confirm the findings and determine if there is a significant effect on acne development. For now, the researchers suggest that the interaction between vitamin B12 and skin bacteria could be a key factor in the development of acne in some individuals. The study highlights the complex interplay between diet, skin bacteria, and human health, potentially leading to new therapeutic approaches for acne management.

For a truly unique and spine-chilling Halloween experience, Airbnb has launched a contest to win an overnight stay in the eerie Catacombs of Paris, the final resting place of approximately six million souls. The contest, open to couples and friends, invites participants to enter by midnight on October 20th with a compelling reason why they believe they are brave enough to spend the night among the dead. The prize includes a private tour of the catacombs, a private concert with impeccable acoustics, and a storyteller who will regale guests with chilling tales of the catacombs' history, ensuring that their dreams will be haunted for days to come. The only living person to wake up in the catacombs, guests will enjoy a one-of-a-kind experience that promises to be both thrilling and unforgettable. The contest comes with a few rules: visitors must respect the catacombs as if they were their own graves and are not allowed to bring pets. However, the listing assures that a monster will be lurking under each bed. With the promise of a night to remember, this contest is sure to appeal to those seeking a truly outlandish and adventurous Halloween.

US presidential candidate Donald Trump has released an ad aimed at Indian Americans, speaking Hindi and adopting the main campaign slogan of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. The ad, which features clips from Trump's recent speech to the Indian American community in New Jersey, includes the slogan "Ab ki baar Modi sarkaar," meaning "This time, a Modi government." This move comes as Trump seeks to appeal to the Indian American community, a traditionally Democratic voting bloc. However, Trump's support among Indian Americans remains low, with only 7 percent of likely voters indicating they intend to vote for him, compared to 70 percent for Hillary Clinton.

The ad's content is not groundbreaking, as campaign outreach in various languages is not uncommon. Trump's Democratic rival, Hillary Clinton, has already run Spanish-language TV ads and radio ads in Florida for Haitian American voters. In 1988, Michael Dukakis often used Greek in his speeches. This may be the first time Hindi has been targeted in a US political ad. While a group called the Republican Hindu Coalition, led by Indian American electronics magnate Shalli Kumar, is hoping to persuade some in the community to vote for Trump, the community's support is unlikely to tip the election balance in Trump's favor, given that Indian Americans make up a small percentage of the American voting public.

The ad's message is particularly noteworthy given Trump's perceived tough stance on "radical Islamic terrorism." Trump uses these three words while a picture of the iconic Taj Mahal hotel in Mumbai, which was attacked by terrorists in 2008, burns in the background. This move aims to appeal to the fears of Indian Americans and to highlight his commitment to combating terrorism. However, the ad has not gone down well with many Indians. On the streets of Delhi, reactions have been mixed but largely negative. Many feel that Trump's approach is too narrow and ignores the diversity of India, with one student stating, "India is not just Hindus, Mr Trump." Another student added, "He can't be trusted" and "He is not the right person for the job."

The ad's release has sparked a debate about the appropriateness of using another country's campaign slogan and language in a US political context. Critics argue that it is a cynical attempt to win votes without genuine understanding of the issues. The reaction from the Indian community suggests that while some may be swayed by Trump's rhetoric, the majority remain skeptical and critical of his policies and views.

Three women who exchanged explicit messages with embattled Rep. Anthony Weiner have come forward with details of their interactions. Lisa Weiss, a 40-year-old Las Vegas blackjack dealer, revealed to RadarOnline.com that she and Weiner engaged in sexual conversations over Facebook, with one exchange described as "crazy dirty." Meagan Broussard, a 26-year-old single mother from Texas, also shared her story, stating that she exchanged dozens of sexually charged messages and photos with Weiner over a month. The social media controversy has intensified calls for Weiner's resignation, with top Republicans demanding he step down. Democrats, however, have largely refrained from defending the New York lawmaker. Amidst the scandal, Jon Stewart mocked Weiner on The Daily Show, even injuring himself during a mock press conference where he "resigned" for not being tough enough on Weiner. The segment culminated with Stewart's hand injury, adding a darkly humorous twist to the ongoing political drama.

Wells Fargo CEO John Stumpf will forfeit $41 million in bonuses as the bank investigates a scandal involving the creation of two million unauthorized accounts. The bank's independent directors announced that Stumpf, who was paid $19.3 million last year, will not receive a salary during the inquiry. Carrie Tolstedt, who headed the division responsible for the unauthorized accounts, will forfeit $19 million in bonuses and leave without a severance package. California has dropped Wells Fargo as its bond underwriter and broker-dealer due to the scandal, with sanctions taking effect immediately and lasting for a year. The state treasurer, John Chiang, criticized Wells Fargo for "fleecing its customers" and accused the bank of promoting "wanton greed." Stumpf has acknowledged the company's failure to act quickly and stated he accepts full responsibility for unethical sales practices. However, he has so far ignored calls for his resignation. Wells Fargo has fired over 5,000 staff in response to the scandal. During a Senate Banking Committee hearing, Senator Elizabeth Warren was critical of Stumpf's leadership, stating that he "squeezed his employees to the breaking point so they would cheat customers." Stumpf's decision to forfeit his bonuses and salary during the investigation is seen as a step towards addressing the scandal, though critics argue that more needs to be done. The bank is also facing a Labor Department inquiry into whether employees were unfairly fired for not meeting aggressive sales targets. Wells Fargo has launched an independent investigation into its sales practices, with Stumpf working without pay during the inquiry. The bank faces a fine of $185 million and is contacting customers to verify the authenticity of their accounts. The scandal has led to a national outcry and increased scrutiny of executive compensation in the banking industry.

Terry Jones, the controversial Florida pastor, may or may not have a deal to move the Park 51 Muslim cultural center away from its current location, which is not close to the World Trade Center. His threats to burn the Qur'an on the anniversary of September 11, which gained significant media attention, may now be subject to the law of diminishing returns. The media, including Fox News, CNN, and the Associated Press, have set guidelines to avoid covering the Qur'an burning, showing a shift in handling such events. Jones's threats and actions have sparked a broader debate on freedom of speech and religion, with the Westboro Baptist Church also planning to burn Qurans, likely drawing less attention due to their controversial nature. The incident highlights the potential for such events to gain media attention and the challenges of balancing free speech with the potential for inciting violence.

From the early days of Hitler's invasion of the Soviet Union, the propaganda on both sides of the conflict painted the struggle in stark, Manichaean terms. The totalitarian nature of both regimes made such portrayals inevitable. On one side stood Hitler, fascism, and the myth of German supremacy; on the other, Stalin, communism, and the international proletarian revolution. This Manichaean framing of the conflict was a common theme in historical accounts, as noted by Anne Applebaum in her piece for the New York Review of Books. Even in the face of the looming threat, many in the West initially hoped that the danger would simply dissipate, as Al Gore’s book, An Inconvenient Truth, suggests. The rise of fascism in Europe before World War II was a significant concern, as evidenced by the actions of a character in John Grisham’s novel, The Chamber, who collected stories about groups similar to his, including Aryans, other Nazis, and the KKK. These groups were often flagging stories from Germany and Eastern Europe, and were quite thrilled with the rise of fascism in those regions.

Meanwhile, in the digital age, the Internet Archive continues its mission to archive web pages as they are created and the pages they refer to. This effort aims to preserve links to the versions of pages that were live when they were written, ensuring that when referenced pages are changed or removed from the web, a link to the original version is still available. The Wayback Machine, a tool of the Internet Archive, adds these data after an embargo period. This process helps to fix broken links on the web and provides a companion link to allow people to see what was originally intended by a page's authors.

In a different context, the rise of the term "fascism" as a popular search term on Merriam-Webster’s website in 2016 is noteworthy. The word, which was the most-looked-up term of the year, became a focal point for Merriam-Webster’s Twitter account, which launched a campaign to encourage users to look up other words instead. The team behind the account was desperate to see a different term rise to the top, with one tweet suggesting that users look up "puppies" 523 times in 30 minutes. However, the term "fascism" remained dominant, with "flummadiddle," a word defined as "something foolish or worthless," barely making a dent in its popularity. This phenomenon reflects the ongoing relevance and concern surrounding the term "fascism" in contemporary discourse, particularly in the context of the 2016 U.S. presidential election, where terms like "Trump," "bigly," and "alt-right" also gained significant traction.

In northern Mexico, the murder of Mayor Prisciliano Rodriguez in Monterrey's Doctor Gonzalez town marks the fourth public official killed in over a month, highlighting the escalating violence. The mayor, elected last year for the Institutional Revolutionary Party, was shot dead as he drove to his ranch, 30 miles east of Monterrey, by suspected drug hitmen. Another person traveling with him was also killed. Nuevo Leon and neighboring Tamaulipas states have become major drug war hotspots since the beginning of the year. In August, President Felipe Calderon, who has led a military assault on drug cartels, condemned the killings and vowed to continue his fight, citing the violence as a sign that gangs are desperate and disorganized. The conflict between the Gulf cartel and its former armed wing, the Zetas, over smuggling routes into the United States has intensified, with both gangs increasingly targeting public officials, police, and journalists. More than 29,000 people have died in drug violence since Calderon deployed over 45,000 troops and federal police in 2006. The U.S. government has advised staff at its consulate in Monterrey to send their children out of the city, once considered one of Latin America's safest. With over 450 drug killings in Monterrey and Nuevo Leon this year, fears grow that the bloodshed could undermine tourism and investment as Mexico recovers from its worst recession since 1932.

A sea slug species, Chromodoris reticulata, has surprised scientists with its unique mating behavior, as reported in the Royal Society's journal Biology Letters. This creature, found in the Pacific Ocean, is capable of detaching, re-growing, and reusing its penis, marking the first known animal with this ability. The sea slugs, which are hermaphrodites, engage in complex mating rituals where they face each other, with one's right side aligning with the other's left, allowing their penises to fit into the female openings. After copulation, which can last from a few seconds to a few minutes, the slugs discard their penises, leaving them on the tank floor. Astonishingly, these sea slugs can regenerate their penises within 24 hours, enabling them to mate multiple times. The internal structure of the penis is a coiled, compressed juvenile organ that unfolds to replace the used part. The scientists observed that the penis is equipped with spines, which may help remove sperm from previous partners, giving the sea slug an advantage in passing on its own genes. This behavior challenges our understanding of sexual reproduction and highlights the complexity of marine life. Bernard Picton, a marine invertebrate expert, notes that such intricate biology is not uncommon among sea slugs, adding, "They do have very, very complicated biology— and a lot have awfully complicated things in terms of reproduction."

Amanda Knox's memoir, "Waiting to Be Heard," is set to be published on April 30, reigniting discussions about her time in prison. The book, according to the Daily Mail, details her experiences, including claims of sexual harassment by prison guards. Knox reportedly wrote that a guard, Raffaele Argiro, summoned her for "chitchats" in his office at night, with Argiro now denying the allegations. Knox's memoir also includes accounts of a female inmate who allegedly tried to start a lesbian affair with her. She recounts being falsely informed she was HIV positive by prison officials. These accounts contrast with her earlier writings, which portrayed her time in prison more positively. Knox's prison diary, published as "Amanda and the Others," described the staff as "really nice," with a library and television in her room. She wrote that a guard gave her a pep talk when she was crying in her cell. The discrepancies between her memoir and her earlier writings highlight the complex nature of her experiences. Knox's legal battle continues, with the Italian Supreme Court ordering a new trial, potentially putting her in the spotlight once again. Her first post-prison interview, set to air on ABC, promises to delve into her thoughts and emotions following her release.

The formal sentencing of Dzhokhar Tsarnaev for his role in the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings is set for Wednesday, with the public awaiting his potential response. Tsarnaev, 21, will be formally condemned to death, but his lawyers have not indicated whether he will address the court. During the trial, Tsarnaev remained largely silent, with Sister Helen Prejean, a death penalty opponent, noting that he expressed remorse to her. However, prosecutors played video showing Tsarnaev giving the middle finger to a security camera, suggesting a lack of remorse. Legal experts say there is little upside to Tsarnaev speaking, as the judge is required to impose the death sentence. Stephen Jones, who represented Timothy McVeigh, advises against it, stating that any statement would likely be viewed as "too little, too late." McVeigh, convicted for the Oklahoma City bombing, made a brief and unremarkable statement during his sentencing, quoting a Supreme Court case. Other convicted terrorists have used their sentencing hearings to make political statements or to complain about prison conditions. Bombing survivors, such as Celeste Corcoran, have expressed that they will not attend the sentencing, stating it would only add stress and that Tsarnaev is already "dead" to them. The defense's strategy was to admit Tsarnaev's involvement but to cast him as a subordinate to his older brother, Tamerlan, who was the driving force behind the attack. The defense aims to humanize Tsarnaev in the sentencing phase, but experts doubt he will speak, fearing it could backfire. The outcome is not in doubt, and the focus now shifts to the emotional testimonies of victims and their families during the sentencing hearing.

Actress Alyssa Milano, who was raped by Harvey Weinstein 20 years ago, expressed shock and relief at the early morning arrest of the film mogul on "Megyn Kelly Today" Friday. The arrest, which came after a long-standing silence from Hollywood, was met with widespread celebration. Meanwhile, Morgan Freeman issued an apology following accusations of harassment by multiple women who have worked on movie sets with him, worked for his production company, or interviewed him in a professional setting. In a CNN report published on Thursday, eight women alleged that the 80-year-old actor subjected them to inappropriate behavior, including unwanted touching and comments about their figure. Freeman responded to the accusations in a statement to Entertainment Tonight, saying, "Anyone who knows me or has worked with me knows I am not someone who would intentionally offend or knowingly make anyone feel uneasy," and apologized to anyone who felt uncomfortable or disrespected. However, the CNN report and interview footage from past Entertainment Tonight sit-downs with Freeman show more examples of questionable behavior. In 2015, author and activist Janet Mock, who is currently writing and producing for Ryan Murphy’s new FX series, Pose, served as an Entertainment Tonight special correspondent covering Freeman’s film, Five Flights Up. During their junket interview, Freeman addressed Mock’s appearance, saying, “I don’t know how you all manage to do that all the time.” “You got a dress halfway between your knee and your hips, and you sit down right across from me and you cross your legs,” he continued. Mock described the encounter as an exhibition of the casual nature at which men in positions of power believe that everything belongs to them, including women’s bodies as they’re merely just trying to do their job. For her, as a young woman of color, who is a reporter and a fan of popular culture, she was deeply disappointed that someone who was seen as America’s grandfather was susceptible to such disturbing behavior and felt comfortable enough to do that as cameras were rolling, and that he could take claim of her body and look at it before even looking into her eyes. Entertainment reporter Chloe Melas, who co-authored the CNN piece on the accusations against Freeman, said she began reaching out to women after experiencing what she described as her own inappropriate encounter with the actor, at a press junket for his 2017 film, Going in Style. Melas, who was six months pregnant at the time, claims Freeman looked her up and down while shaking her hand, and repeatedly said some variation of “I wish I was there,” as cameras rolled in front of his co-stars and other junket personnel. The reporter said she was later told that Warner Bros. HR could not corroborate the account because only one of Freeman's remarks was on video and the Warner Bros. employees present did not notice anything. Freeman's lawyer has since demanded CNN retract its report, claiming the story was "used to unjustly attack him" and that the piece suffered from "malicious intent, falsehoods, sleight-of-hand, an absence of editorial control, and journalistic malpractice."

A 19-year-old college student in Colorado died after consuming an entire marijuana cookie that contained 6 servings of THC, according to a new report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and the Colorado Department of Public Health and Environment. The incident highlights the potential dangers associated with the consumption of edible marijuana products. The student, who had no history of alcohol abuse, illicit drug use, or mental illness, received the cookie from a 23-year-old friend who purchased it from a store. The sales clerk instructed the friend to divide the cookie into six pieces, each containing about 10 mg of THC, the recommended serving size established by Colorado authorities. Initially, the student followed these instructions and ate just part of the cookie. However, after about 30 to 60 minutes, he did not feel any effects and consumed the entire remainder of the cookie. 

Over the next few hours, the student exhibited erratic speech and hostile behaviors. Approximately 2.5 hours after eating the whole cookie, he jumped off a balcony on the fourth floor of his building, sustaining fatal injuries. The autopsy found that marijuana intoxication was the chief contributing factor to his death, with his blood levels of THC exceeding the legal limit for driving a car in Colorado. 

This case underscores the need for improved public health messaging to reduce the risk of overconsumption of THC, especially as the use of edible marijuana products continues to grow. In 2012, Colorado legalized the recreational use of marijuana, and stores selling the products opened in 2014. The delayed effects of THC-infused edibles can lead to multiple servings being consumed in quick succession before experiencing the full effects, as reportedly occurred in this case. High doses of THC can produce serious anxiety attacks and psychotic-like symptoms. Colorado has since instituted new rules for the packaging and labeling of edible marijuana products, requiring them to contain no more than 10 mg of THC or to clearly mark each 10-mg serving. However, the new report suggests a need for further public health education to prevent overconsumption.

A woman named Sally Hootnick experienced a frustrating ordeal when she left her iPad on an American Airlines flight and later discovered it was taken. After realizing the iPad was missing, Hootnick used the MobileMe application to track its location, which led her to an address in Long Island, New York. Despite contacting American Airlines and local police, she did not receive any immediate assistance. Frustrated and determined, Hootnick sent messages to the iPad, telling the suspected thief that she knew where the device was and had contacted the police. The iPad's location began to move frequently, leading Hootnick to suspect it was being used by an airline employee. To harass the thief, she used another application to make the iPad beep every two minutes, sending messages with her address and informing the thief that she had called the police. Despite her efforts, American Airlines did not respond for a month, and Hootnick eventually contacted a consumer protection agency. After speaking with a police detective, the airline and police began an investigation. However, Hootnick's iPad was eventually replaced, and she turned off the wireless service, making it impossible to track its current location. The case remains unresolved, and the iPad's whereabouts are unknown.

Friends and colleagues had warned Kenji Goto and Haruna Yukawa to avoid the dangerous zones in Syria. Goto, a veteran war journalist, even advised Yukawa, the inexperienced loner, to stay away from the area. Now, the same friends and colleagues are praying for the safe release of Goto, 47, and Yukawa, 42, from the clutches of the Islamic State extremist group. In a video posted online on January 20, a masked man wielding a knife and standing over the two kneeling Japanese men threatened to kill the hostages unless the Japanese government pays a ransom of $200 million in 72 hours.

The two men, who met in a different hostage situation in Syria in April 2014, both dismissed the warnings and entered the war-torn country for different reasons. Yukawa told a colleague he was pursuing business opportunities in Syria. Goto entered the area controlled by the Islamic State in October for first-hand coverage, a task he has done for years to shed light on the plight of the innocent victims of conflicts.

"Kenji Goto's life work has been to cover children in conflict-torn regions with a hope to convey to the world the harsh realities that those marginalized children are facing," said Kazumasa Ito, a high school teacher from Toyota, Aichi Prefecture, who has been Goto's friend for the past decade or so. In an email sent to Ito on October 22, Goto, the operator of the video news agency Independent Press, said he would make an overseas trip and return to Japan on the morning of October 29. That was the last contact Ito had with the journalist.

Around the same time, Goto sent a column via email to the online news site Christian Today. Based on his experiences in the Iraq War, he wrote about an invisible boundary between soldiers and civilians in combat zones, saying there is no guarantee for life when the latter steps over that line. After working in the TV production industry, Goto, a native of Sendai, established Independent Press in Tokyo’s Minato Ward in 1996. Freelance journalist Takeharu Watai, the 43-year-old co-founder of the company, said Goto has covered battlefields and conflict zones with camcorders since the mid-1990s. "I admired him for his bold efforts to gather news in Syria in recent years," Watai said.

Goto has also contributed to campaigns by the Japan Committee for UNICEF to raise awareness of children's rights around the world. "He has made consistent efforts to uncover and report the realities of children who are denied the opportunity to attend school or are forced to become soldiers in developing countries and conflict-plagued areas," said Hiromasa Nakai, the organization's spokesman. "I humbly pray for his safe return home."

In April last year, Goto met Yukawa, who established a private military company called PMC in January 2014. Yukawa was being detained by the Free Syrian Army (FSA), an armed opposition group, in northern Syria. According to Nobuo Kimoto, a 70-year-old former Ibaraki prefectural assembly member and adviser to PMC, Yukawa was released thanks largely to Goto, who had connections with FSA members. The journalist translated Yukawa's words to explain that he had no purpose in Syria other than to acquire on-field experience. After returning to Japan, Yukawa told Kimoto about Goto, saying he found a good connection for business opportunities in Syria. Yukawa also told acquaintances that he received a request from an FSA general to supply medical goods and an ambulance to the group. Kimoto tried to discourage Yukawa from revisiting Syria, considering his lack of experience. But according to Kimoto, Yukawa noted that he was not married and was not afraid of dying.

Yukawa apparently re-entered Syria in July. He is believed to have been captured by the Islamic State in August. "I had been worried that he would end up like this one day," Kimoto said. Yukawa's father, Shoichi, told reporters at the family's residence in Chiba on January 20 that he cannot comment on the hostage crisis because he was concentrating on all the information coming in about his son's situation.

TOKYO—Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe said Wednesday that his government will use every possible diplomatic channel to secure the release of two Japanese hostages held by Islamic extremists. A video posted on a YouTube channel used by Islamic State’s publishing arm Tuesday showed a masked man with a knife threatening to kill two kneeling Japanese men unless the government paid a $200 million ransom within 72 hours. The Japanese government has verified the identities of the two hostages, Chief Cabinet Secretary Yoshihide Suga said, adding that Tokyo would "exert its utmost to secure the men's release." Historically pacifist and heavily dependent on Mideast oil, contemporary Japan has reiterated that its aid to the Mideast nations and their allies battling ISIS was humanitarian in nature, and meant to promote the stability of the region. "We have been aggressively contributing, for the sake of peace and to improve the welfare of the people of the Mideast," Suga said. "Japan's aid is absolutely not being used to kill Muslims, as claimed by these brutal criminals." In a video released Tuesday, ISIS demanded $200 million in exchange for the lives of the two men, and accused Japanese Prime Minister Shinzo Abe directly of donating "$100 million to kill our women and children, to destroy the homes of the Muslims ... and in an attempt to stop the expansion of the Islamic State, you have also donated another $100 million to train the (apostates)." "We will not yield to terrorism, and there is no change to our position of contributing to campaigns against terror in international society," Suga said Wednesday, reiterating remarks made immediately after the video surfaced. Japan has been at pains to emphasize that the aid announced in recent days is strictly non-military in nature. The widely circulated Asahi Shimbun newspaper said the ransom demand was more than four-times the amount of money extorted by ISIS in exchange for hostages over the past year. Japan's National Police Agency, meanwhile, said it was dispatching a counter-terrorism team, activated when Japanese citizens are abducted overseas, to Amman, Jordan. The government was also analyzing the hostage video itself -- shadows on the victims' faces and discrepancies in the way the wind is blowing their garments indicate the video may be doctored. Japan is renowned for its low crime rate. Japanese police do not carry firearms and the self-defense forces are not considered an actual military. Its remote location has largely isolated it from the terrorism that has plagued Western countries in recent years, and naiveté and miscalculations by both of the hostages apparently played a role in their abduction.
