Her hit song “Royals” has made her an international alternative music star, topping the Billboard Alternative charts and becoming the fastest charting alternative song in 17 years. The inspiration for “Royals” came from a National Geographic photo of a baseball player wearing a shirt that read “Royals,” combined with Lorde’s fascination with historical aristocracy. The song criticizes the lavish lifestyles of famous musicians. Meanwhile, a San Francisco radio station, KOIT, has banned Lorde’s “Royals” from its airwaves until the San Francisco Giants win the World Series, sparking a social media backlash from Giants fans. The station’s program director responded by removing the song from its playlist, stating, “As of 4pm today we’ve removed Lorde- Royals from our playlist until the end of the World Series. Go Giants, beat the Royals!”

President Obama ordered flags at the White House and other federal buildings to fly at half-staff in honor of five U.S. service members killed in Chattanooga last week, addressing criticism over the delay. The proclamation calls for the flags to remain at half-staff through Saturday as a mark of respect. This decision came after Speaker John Boehner ordered flags at the U.S. Capitol to be lowered. Conservatives criticized Obama for the delay, with Rep. Mac Thornberry urging immediate action. The White House and U.S. Capitol both lowered their flags by Tuesday afternoon, aligning their tributes. Despite the delay, Obama emphasized the strength of the American community in response to the tragedy.

The political dynasty of Jesse Jackson Jr. and his wife, Sandi Jackson, came to an abrupt end as both were sentenced to prison terms for their misuse of campaign funds. Jesse Jackson Jr., the former U.S. Representative, was sentenced to 30 months in federal prison for spending $750,000 from his campaign fund on personal items, while his wife, Sandi Jackson, former 7th Ward Alderman, was sentenced to one year in prison for filing false joint federal income tax returns that understated their income. The sentencing hearing, held in Washington, D.C., was marked by emotional pleas from both Jacksons, who cited personal struggles such as mental health issues and the need to care for their children. Judge Amy Berman Jackson rejected arguments for probation, stating that imposing such sentences would create a double standard. The judge emphasized that the Jacksons' actions were "knowing, organized, and repeated," and that Sandi Jackson was a "key player" in the campaign. Both Jacksons were ordered to pay significant restitution, with Jesse Jackson Jr. facing a $750,000 forfeiture. The sentencing reflects the Jacksons' once-promising political careers, which were marred by financial misdeeds, and highlights the severe consequences faced by those who misuse public funds.

A rat infestation at a government office in Kissimmee, Florida, led to the contamination of donated supplies intended for Puerto Rico hurricane victims, according to the Orlando Sentinel. The Puerto Rico Federal Affairs Administration (PRFAA) office, which was managing the donated items, did not have the budget to cover shipping costs and had previously attempted to distribute the supplies through other organizations, but these efforts were unsuccessful. The office, located in a deteriorated building, had been infested by rodents since August, just a month before Hurricane Maria devastated Puerto Rico. Despite this, the supplies, including water and food, were stored in the premises. PRFAA's executive director, Carlos Mercader, stated that the agency would soon conduct an inventory to identify suitable items for distribution to Puerto Rican evacuees in Central Florida. Mercader also mentioned that the office would be relocated to a more appropriate and dignified space. Former director Juan Hernandez Mayoral criticized the inaction of the employees, calling it government negligence. The situation highlights ongoing issues with aid distribution to Puerto Rico, which has faced criticism for administrative failures. U.S. Representative Elijah Cummings and Stacey Plaskett, the congressional delegate from the U.S. Virgin Islands, have called for the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) to be subpoenaed over its failure to provide tens of millions of dollars to Puerto Rico. Additionally, FEMA awarded a $156 million contract to a small Atlanta-based company, Tribute Contracting LLC, which delivered only 50,000 of the promised 30 million meals. Contracting owner Tiffany Brown plans to sue the government for $70 million, citing the company's struggle with smaller contracts as a reason for the failure to deliver the promised aid.

Texas teen Ethan Couch, now 18, lived a life of privilege with few consequences before he took four lives in the so-called “affluenza” DUI crash, newly-released deposition videos revealed. Couch, his mother, and father testified in the videos, admitting he had problems with alcohol and drugs. In the deposition, Couch admitted to drinking at his family’s second home in Burleson “most of the time” and listed several drugs he had tried. He barely remembers the night of the crash, where he was driving with three times the legal limit of alcohol in his system. Couch was behind the wheel of his family’s white pickup truck, which crashed into a group of people helping a stranded driver, killing four and injuring a dozen others. Couch pleaded guilty to four counts of intoxication manslaughter and two counts of intoxication assault, receiving a 10-year probation and treatment sentence, much to the outrage of the victims' families. The psychologist, Dr. G. Dick Miller, testified that Couch was a victim of “affluenza,” blaming his upbringing for his lack of responsibility. Couch’s parents, Fred and Tonya, admitted to allowing their son to stay unsupervised in the Burleson home and driving before legal age. Tonya acknowledged that she never disciplined Ethan, while Fred denied that he and Tonya were “profoundly dysfunctional” parents. The family has never spoken publicly about the case, but the deposition tapes provide a rare glimpse into their private lives and the aftermath of the tragedy. The McConnells, whose son was injured in the crash, settled their lawsuit against the Couches, but remain convinced that the accident was preventable. Couch is now working at his father’s business, Cleburne Sheet Metal, and is still on probation.

Memories Pizza in Walkerton, Indiana, a small town of about 2,144 residents, has faced intense backlash and closure due to its owners' stance on the Religious Freedom Restoration Act (RFRA). The owners, Crystal and Kevin O'Connor, have stated they would not cater a wedding for a same-sex couple, despite not having received any such requests. This decision sparked a wave of negative online reviews, threats, and harassment, forcing the restaurant to close temporarily. Crystal O'Connor has been suspended from a job and is in hiding, while her father Kevin maintains their right to uphold their beliefs. The controversy has drawn national attention, with the restaurant receiving over $600,000 in donations through a GoFundMe campaign. Despite the support, the O'Connor family decided to close the business, citing the harassment and threats. Meanwhile, some customers and local residents have praised the owners for their stance, while others criticize the restaurant's closure and the community's response. The situation highlights the complex intersection of personal beliefs, business operations, and public opinion in the face of controversial legislation.

Amazon is expanding its delivery services to include business-to-customer deliveries, aiming to compete with established players like FedEx and UPS. This new venture, dubbed "Shipping with Amazon," is set to launch in Los Angeles in the coming weeks, targeting third-party merchants selling through Amazon’s platform. The service will eventually expand to other cities, with Amazon planning to offer competitive pricing to undercut its rivals. This move could significantly enhance Amazon’s presence in the delivery market, potentially disrupting the existing landscape. Shares of FedEx and UPS saw a sharp decline in pre-market trading, reflecting investors’ concerns about the impact of Amazon’s new service. UPS, however, maintains its partnership with Amazon, stating it will continue to support the e-commerce giant and other customers, though it declines to comment on Amazon’s internal strategies. This development highlights Amazon’s ongoing efforts to diversify its services and strengthen its position in the global delivery market.

Canned foods may contain bisphenol A (BPA), which leaches from the liner into the food. Two new studies link the chemicals bisphenol A and phthalates to obesity and insulin resistance in adolescents, but experts caution that the findings do not prove a cause-and-effect relationship. In one study, researchers found that teens with higher amounts of DEHP, a phthalate found in processed foods, in their urine had increased rates of insulin resistance, a condition that can lead to Type 2 diabetes. The results held even after controlling for other risk factors such as calorie intake and weight. However, the study did not find an association between insulin resistance and other phthalates found in cosmetics and personal care products. In another study, children with the highest amounts of BPA in their urine had double the risk of being obese compared to children with the lowest urinary BPA levels. The researchers noted that BPA is found in higher concentrations in fat tissue, so it is possible that people with more body fat store more BPA from food. Both BPA and phthalates have been the focus of intense research due to concerns about their potential to act like hormones in people exposed to them through food packaging. However, studies have been inconclusive, and scientists have not reached a consensus. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration maintains that current levels of BPA exposure are low and safe, but the chemical is more highly regulated in several countries as a precautionary measure. The studies suggest that reducing exposure to these chemicals by opting for fresh foods instead of canned or plastic-wrapped foods may help mitigate the risk.

The U.S. economy grew at a modest 1.3% annualized rate in the second quarter, according to the Commerce Department, significantly lower than the 1.8% expected by economists. This slowdown, coupled with a revised downward first-quarter growth rate of 0.4% from the initial 1.9%, marks the weakest pace since the recession ended. Higher gas prices and reduced consumer spending are cited as major contributors to the tepid growth. The revisions also show that the 2007-2009 recession was even more severe than previously thought, with the economy contracting 5.1% from the start of the recession to its end in June 2009, compared to the earlier estimate of a 4.1% decline. Among the previous 10 postwar recessions, only two had greater contractions, with the 1957-58 recession at 3.7% and the 1973-1975 downturn at 3.2%. The 2009 contraction was revised to 3.5%, up from the previous 2.5% estimate. The 2008 contraction was also revised to -0.3%, compared to the unchanged previous estimate. These revisions, based on more complete data, highlight the depth of the recession and the subpar growth since then, with the unemployment rate remaining at 9.2%. The annual revisions, released each July, include updates on consumer and business spending, reflecting the economy's ongoing challenges.

A 911 call reporting shots fired at Virginia College in Spartanburg, South Carolina, on April Fool's Day morning brought out a significant law enforcement response. The call, sent by Angela Timmons to her daughter, described a shooting inside the college, prompting deputies to respond with multiple patrol cars and deputies, who were initially prepared for a serious situation like Columbine High School or Sandy Hook. Timmons had initially sent a text message to her daughter about hearing gunshots in the school and was hiding in a bathroom. Her daughter called 911, and as deputies arrived, Timmons called back, informing her daughter that it was an April Fool's joke. However, the swift and intense response from law enforcement was not taken lightly by Sheriff Chuck Wright, who expressed disappointment in Timmons' poor judgment. Timmons faces four charges, including disturbing school and aggravated breach of peace, and was released on a personal recognizance bond. The college's vice president of marketing, Diane Worthington, issued a statement apologizing for the incident and expressing disappointment in Timmons' actions. Timmons acknowledged her mistake, stating that she chose the wrong prank given the current climate of school shootings. She also mentioned that she has plans to hire an attorney to address the situation. The incident highlights the serious nature of such reports and the impact on law enforcement and the affected institution.

President Donald Trump is escalating his attacks on Attorney General Jeff Sessions, suggesting the embattled official should have intervened in investigations of two popular Republican congressmen to help Republicans in the upcoming midterm elections. In a tweet, Trump criticized the Justice Department for bringing well-publicized charges against two GOP congressmen, Duncan Hunter and Chris Collins, just before the midterms, calling it "good job Jeff......" Trump's comments highlight his disregard for the Justice Department's independence, as he frequently views it as a tool for his personal and political interests rather than a law enforcement agency. The indictments of Hunter and Collins, who were both under investigation for separate charges, have raised hopes for the opposition party. Hunter, facing charges that included spending campaign funds for personal expenses, and Collins, accused of insider trading, have both proclaimed their innocence. The Hunter investigation began in June 2016, while the Collins case involved behavior from 2017. Sessions' chief of staff has stated that Sessions has no intention of resigning, despite Trump's constant criticism. The tension between Trump and Sessions has been ongoing, with Trump previously pressuring Sessions to investigate his perceived enemies and accusing him of failing to take control of the Justice Department. Sessions has maintained that the Department of Justice will not be improperly influenced by political considerations. Some Republican members of Congress have advised Trump that firing Sessions before the midterm elections would be damaging to the party, but Trump may consider a change after the elections. The situation underscores the complex relationship between the president and his attorney general, with Trump's desire for political expediency clashing with the Justice Department's traditional independence.

Israeli airstrikes and tank shells pounded parts of Gaza on Tuesday, killing a 4-year-old girl and injuring several others, after a Gaza sniper killed a Muslim Israeli man near a border fence. The Israeli military confirmed launching tank and air attacks on Gaza, targeting weapons facilities and terror infrastructure. The strikes hit a house near an al Qassam camp in central Gaza, killing the 4-year-old girl and injuring three of her relatives. The al Qassam Brigades claimed the slain Israeli was a soldier, but the Israeli military stated he was a civilian. Israeli Defense Minister Moshe Ya'alon said Israel holds Hamas responsible for the shooting, warning of a severe response to any attack on Israeli sovereignty. U.N. Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon condemned the killing and expressed concern over the violence. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu characterized the incident as a very severe incident, stating Israel would not let it go unanswered. The cross-border shooting comes after a series of attempts by Palestinians to plant explosives along the security fence. Israel tightened restrictions on Gaza workers near the fence, citing security concerns. Defense Minister Ya'alon advised Hamas to exercise its authority to prevent further attacks on Israel. President Shimon Peres urged Hamas and the Islamic Jihad to stop aggressions against Israel. Opposition leader Isaac Herzog stated the recent wave of terror is meant to sabotage peace talks, while some on the right criticized the government's policies, calling for an end to the release of terrorists from prison. The Israeli military also reported a Palestinian youth approaching the border fence, who was shot in the leg and taken to a Gazan hospital.

The captain of the Costa Concordia, Francesco Schettino, apologized for the accident that led to the deaths of as many as 32 people and acknowledged his responsibility as the ship's captain. In his first full television interview since the January 13 disaster, Schettino admitted to being distracted and blamed himself for the incident. He stated that he thought constantly about the victims and that the captain is identified when an accident occurs. Schettino, who is charged with multiple manslaughter, causing the accident, and abandoning his ship, was freed from house arrest but must remain in his hometown. He insisted that he was not in command when the ship struck the rocks and capsized near the island of Giglio, off the coast of Tuscany. Schettino claimed that the ship's officer was in charge at the time. However, investigators criticized his handling of the disaster, accusing him of bringing the 290-meter-long vessel too close to the shore, delaying the evacuation, and losing control during his departure from the ship. Schettino denied that the ship was too close to the island to show off his seamanship skills and also denied that a young woman on the ship's bridge was his lover. He broke down when asked about the youngest victim, a five-year-old girl. Schettino argued that he had saved many lives by steering the stricken vessel into shallow water. A pre-trial hearing was held in March, and investigations also target several other officers and officials of the ship's owner, Costa Cruises, a unit of the world's largest cruise operator, Carnival Corp.

Protests and arrests erupted at a "March 4 Trump" rally at the Minnesota State Capitol, where supporters of President Donald Trump clashed with counterprotesters in the Capitol rotunda. Among those arrested was Linwood Woody Kaine, the son of Democratic vice presidential nominee Tim Kaine. The incident began when masked individuals, including Kaine, allegedly threw a smoke bomb inside the Capitol, disrupting the rally. Kaine, clad in black and wearing a mask, resisted arrest, prompting three officers to subdue him with a knee strike and chemical spray. Five masked individuals were arrested on suspicion of second-degree riot, while a sixth person was cited for disorderly conduct. The Ramsey County attorney’s office declined to file felony charges, stating there were insufficient facts to prove a felony-level riot. However, the case remains under investigation for possible misdemeanor charges. Counterprotesters, some with apparent anti-fascist and anarchist leanings, used air horns, whistles, and chants to disrupt the event, while Trump supporters responded with similar tactics. The Pioneer Press reported that neither Kaine nor the four others arrested with him has been charged, and police have not specified who they believe threw the smoke bomb. Tim Kaine released a statement supporting his children’s right to peacefully express their views, while Republican Party Chairman John Krenik accused the county attorney’s office of political bias. The incident raises questions about the handling of the case and the role of political connections in legal proceedings.

German police have recovered over 100 items stolen from John Lennon's estate, including three diaries, two pairs of his signature round glasses, a cigarette case, and a handwritten music score, reports the BBC. The items were displayed at Berlin police headquarters, alongside a tape recording of a Beatles concert and other memorabilia. The stolen goods were first discovered in July 2017 when a bankruptcy administrator for the Berlin auction house Auctionata contacted police, having found the items in the company's storage. Police confiscated the items and arrested a 58-year-old German businessman of Turkish origin, raiding his home and cars. They also searched the home of another suspect, who is currently living in Turkey, and found additional Lennon memorabilia hidden in a briefcase under the spare tire in the trunk. The suspects, including Yoko Ono's former chauffeur, are suspected of handling stolen goods from Lennon's estate, with one having a previous conviction in New York related to the stolen items. The recovered items, including a leather jacket believed to have been worn by Lennon, which sold for £10,400 at an auction in England in February, and an original handwritten score for The Beatles' song "Eleanor Rigby," are expected to be returned to Yoko Ono. The last entry in one of Lennon's diaries, made on the morning of December 8, 1980, a few hours before his death, includes a note on the famous Annie Leibovitz photo shoot that same day. The exact timeline and conditions for returning the items to Ono's estate are still being determined.

North Korea launched an unidentified projectile from its capital Pyongyang that flew over Japan, officials said, escalating tensions in the already anxious region. Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff on Tuesday stated that the South Korean and U.S. militaries were analyzing the launch, but did not immediately confirm the projectile's range. Japanese officials reported that the missile flew over the northern Japanese island of Hokkaido and landed in the Pacific Ocean, with no reported damage. The launch occurred days after North Korea fired three short-range ballistic missiles into the sea and a month after its second flight test of an intercontinental ballistic missile, which analysts say could reach deep into the U.S. mainland when perfected. North Korea typically reacts with anger to U.S.-South Korean military drills, which are currently underway, often staging weapons tests and releasing threats to Seoul and Washington in its state-controlled media. The animosity is higher than usual following threats by U.S. President Donald Trump to unleash "fire and fury" on the North, and Pyongyang's stated plan to consider firing some of its missiles toward Guam. Pyongyang regularly argues that the U.S.-South Korean military exercises are an invasion rehearsal, while the allies claim they are defensive and meant to counter North Korean aggression. North Korea's U.N. ambassador, Ja Song Nam, wrote recently that the exercises are "provocative and aggressive" when the Korean peninsula is "like a time bomb." The launch is likely to further strain relations and heighten concerns over North Korea's nuclear and missile programs, as it comes amid ongoing diplomatic efforts to address the growing threat.

The New York State legislature is nearing a deal on a DNA database expansion, which would require DNA samples from all convicted criminals, potentially including those with minor offenses. This agreement is part of a broader legislative session that includes budget negotiations, redistricting, and a new pension plan. The current database, created in the mid-1990s, has been expanded three times, most recently in 2006, and now covers fewer than half of the crimes codified in state law. The Manhattan district attorney, Cyrus R. Vance Jr., has advocated for expanding the database, citing its effectiveness in identifying suspects in serious crimes. However, the defense bar argues that courts often restrict access to evidence, making it difficult for defense lawyers to run tests against the database. The Assembly speaker, Sheldon Silver, has pushed for defendants to have access to the database. The Senate majority leader, Dean Skelos, supports access provisions but opposes broader wrongful conviction protections. Meanwhile, the debate over the DNA database is intertwined with budget negotiations, where the governor proposes a new pension plan that would reduce retirement benefits for future public employees. The article also highlights the case of Bennett Barbour, who was wrongfully convicted of rape in 1978 and only exonerated nearly two decades later through DNA testing. Barbour's experience underscores the broader issue of wrongful convictions and the state's failure to notify those cleared by DNA testing. The Virginia Department of Forensics has conducted a DNA testing program since 2004, but the process has been criticized for its secrecy and inefficiency, with many potentially innocent individuals never informed of their exoneration.

The Union Street Guest House in Hudson, NY, has garnered a reputation for poor service and questionable business practices, as evidenced by numerous negative reviews. Guests have complained about dirty conditions, noisy neighbors, and unhelpful staff. One couple stayed for a wedding and was charged $468.95, only to see the charge incorrectly inflated to $4,689.50 on their Amex statement. Despite multiple attempts to resolve the issue, the owners failed to correct the error. Another guest had to pay for a second room at full price due to a last-minute room change, but never received a refund for the first room. The establishment also threatens to deduct $500 from guests' deposits if they post negative reviews online, a policy that has sparked outrage among customers. The guest house, which prides itself on its unique, vintage decor, has been criticized for its lack of cleanliness and poor maintenance. Guests have reported peeling paint, malfunctioning equipment, and cheap, outdated furniture. The owners' refusal to refund overcharged amounts and their aggressive stance towards negative feedback have led many to warn others against staying at the Union Street Guest House.

Hillary Clinton has intensified her criticism of FBI Director James Comey, accusing him of making an "unprecedented" and "deeply troubling" decision to announce the examination of new emails related to Anthony Weiner's investigation just days before the election. At a rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, Clinton urged Comey to provide more information, stating that voters deserve "full and complete facts." Her campaign chairman, John Podesta, and campaign manager Robby Mook accused Comey of being "light on facts" and "heavy on innuendo," and called for immediate transparency. They emphasized that the FBI's actions could be seen as an attempt to influence the election, violating established protocols. Meanwhile, Donald Trump capitalized on the controversy, questioning whether Clinton's close aide Huma Abedin should remain in her administration. The FBI's investigation into the emails uncovered on Weiner's laptop, which may be duplicates, has become a focal point in the final days of the campaign. Clinton aides defended Abedin, noting her cooperation with the FBI during previous investigations. The situation highlights the political tensions surrounding the FBI's actions and their potential impact on the election outcome. As the campaign enters its final stretch, both sides are using the controversy to their advantage, with Clinton focusing on Comey's actions and Trump questioning Clinton's loyalty.

Scarlett Johansson and Ryan Reynolds, who recently announced the end of their two-year marriage, were spotted sharing a friendly dinner at Blue Ribbon restaurant in New York City. They laughed and smiled, aiming to show "love and kindness" even as they ended their marriage. A source says, "They just wanted to connect and have a friendly chat, being civil and friendly." Despite the media speculation, they are not reconciling. This dinner highlights their mutual intention to maintain a respectful relationship post-split, proving that exes can still be friends.

Travelers can now enjoy a more restful sleep with the Gravity blanket, a high-tech weighted blanket designed to reduce stress and anxiety by simulating the sensation of being hugged. This innovative product, which has raised over $3 million on Kickstarter, claims to harness the power of "deep touch pressure stimulation" to increase serotonin and melatonin levels, decrease cortisol, and promote a deeper REM sleep cycle. The Gravity blanket, available in three weight sizes (15 lbs, 20 lbs, and 25 lbs), is made with high-density plastic poly pellets and a soft micro plush fleece cover, ensuring it is both comfortable and breathable. The blanket is intended to be around 10% of the user’s body weight, providing a gentle, soothing pressure that mimics the feeling of a parent swaddling their child. Users can enjoy the benefits of the Gravity blanket not just during sleep but also while reading, relaxing, or meditating. 

However, the scientific evidence supporting the blanket’s claims is limited. A 2015 study published in the Journal of Sleep Medicine and Disorders suggested that weighted blankets could provide a beneficial calming effect, especially in clinical disorders, while another study from 2008 in Occupational Therapy in Mental Health indicated that weighted blankets were effective for those suffering from anxiety. Despite these findings, the blanket’s creators have faced scrutiny over their promotional language, which violated Kickstarter’s rules by making claims that the product can treat various conditions, including insomnia, post-traumatic stress disorder, and obsessive-compulsive disorder. After being prompted by STAT, the company updated its Kickstarter page to remove these medical claims, stating that the blanket can be "used" for these conditions rather than treated them. 

The Gravity blanket is expected to be available for delivery in September and October, priced from $169. The product has garnered significant attention, with over 15,000 donors contributing to the Kickstarter campaign. However, experts in the field of sleep medicine and psychiatry caution that the blanket may only be beneficial in a small subset of patients and that more robust research is needed to fully understand its potential benefits. Despite the limited evidence, the Gravity blanket represents a promising step in the development of wellness products that aim to address common issues like stress and anxiety through natural, non-invasive methods.

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump delivered a scathing critique of Hillary Clinton during a 40-minute speech, accusing her of lacking the temperament and experience to lead the country. Trump's assault on Clinton, who is the presumptive Democratic nominee, came after she had previously criticized his handling of foreign policy issues. In his speech, Trump cited several instances where he believed Clinton's policies had failed, including her role in the Middle East and her handling of the U.S. ambassador to Libya's death in 2012. He also disputed her plans for resettling refugees, stating that her policies would be "disastrous" and create "open borders." Clinton, in turn, had previously called Trump "temperamentally unfit" for the presidency, citing his controversial statements and actions. Her foreign policy speech in San Diego had highlighted his incoherent ideas and questioned his experience and knowledge of global issues. Trump's claims were fact-checked, revealing numerous inaccuracies and exaggerations. For instance, he claimed Clinton had "almost single-handedly destabilized the entire Middle East," which was a misrepresentation of her role. He also exaggerated her role in the Benghazi attack, stating she "left the ambassador to die," when in fact, Clinton had no direct involvement in military decisions related to the incident. Additionally, Trump's assertion that Clinton accepted millions in jewelry from Brunei was incorrect; she had turned over the gift to the U.S. government. Despite these inaccuracies, Trump maintained that Clinton's policies would be detrimental to the country. The article also highlighted Trump's economic claims, such as his assertion that the U.S. is the highest-taxed nation, which was contradicted by data showing the U.S. has one of the lowest tax burdens among developed countries. Trump's promises of massive tax cuts and repeal of Obamacare were also scrutinized, with economists noting the potential negative impacts on the deficit and interest rates. Overall, the article presented a detailed analysis of the inaccuracies and exaggerations in Trump's critique of Clinton, while also examining his own policy claims.

A Texas couple, Forrest Sanco and Donna Grant, both 56, who reconnected and fell in love after high school, went missing on a private plane trip to the Bahamas. Their plans included flying to the Bahamas, then back to Fort Worth as a married couple. They were last seen on Instagram enjoying the Bahamian sunrise on September 26. Their flight plan was to land in North Eleuthera, then proceed to Rum Cay, but they never arrived at their final destination. 

Forrest’s friend and fellow pilot, Jason Fox, noticed a lack of communication but did not raise concerns until the couple failed to return to Fort Worth. The Sanco couple had recently purchased a Cessna 150 for their trip, and Forrest had been corresponding with Fox via email throughout the journey. No one realized they were missing until their absence was noticed by their families. 

Family members, particularly Forrest’s niece, LeeAnn Burger, have been actively searching for the couple through GoFundMe donations, hiring private search crews, and pilots. The couple was renting a holiday home in Rum Cay, where their absence was reported to local authorities. The Bahamas Air and Sea Rescue Association (BASRA) Operations Manager, Chris Lloyd, confirmed that Forrest officially closed his flight plan at 4:58 pm on September 26, indicating he was nearing his destination. However, they never arrived, and no reports were made until October 6, about 10 days after their expected return.

The search for Forrest and Donna has been challenging, with debris spotted on Cat Island initially thought to be related to their plane but later ruled out. The United States Coast Guard and the Royal Bahamas Defence Force are leading the search efforts, but family members have expressed frustration with the lack of resources and cooperation. Despite the difficulties, the family remains hopeful and determined to find answers, even if it means searching until they find something.

Caitlyn Jenner, the 67-year-old former Olympic gold medalist and reality TV star, has finally undergone gender reassignment surgery as part of her transition from male to female, as detailed in her new memoir, "The Secrets of My Life," which will be released on April 25. In the book, Jenner reveals that she had the "Final Surgery" in January 2017, nearly two years after publicly announcing her identity as a trans woman in an interview with Diane Sawyer. "The surgery was a success, and I feel not only wonderful but liberated," she writes, adding that she decided to be open about the surgery to stop the constant inquiries from fans. "I am telling you because I believe in candor," she explains. "So all of you can stop staring. You want to know, so now you know. Which is why this is the first time, and the last time, I will ever speak of it."

Jenner, who confirmed her transition in June 2015, had previously undergone breast augmentation and facial feminization surgery in March 2015. "I am going to live authentically for the first time in my life," she recalls thinking in the hours after those surgeries, following an initial freak-out. "I am going to have an enthusiasm for life that I have not had in 39 years since the Olympics, almost two-thirds of my life." The memoir, which earned Jenner a $4 million advance, also includes candid revelations about her past struggles and the support she received from family and friends.

A popular over-the-counter heartburn medication, proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), may accelerate the aging of blood vessel cells in laboratory settings, according to new research presented at the American Heart Association conference in New Orleans. This finding could help explain recent reports linking long-term use of PPIs to various serious illnesses, including heart disease, kidney disease, and dementia. However, clinical studies are still needed to confirm if PPIs damage blood vessel cells within the human body.

PPIs reduce stomach acid production and are among the most prescribed drugs in the United States, often used for treating acid reflux and heartburn. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration estimates that 1 in 14 Americans have used PPIs. Recent evidence has associated long-term PPI use with several serious health issues, prompting researchers to investigate the mechanisms behind these potential risks.

Researchers at Houston Methodist Research Institute found that long-term exposure to PPIs accelerated the aging of human endothelial cells, which line the inside of blood vessels. Healthy endothelial cells create a Teflon-like coating that prevents blood from sticking, while older and diseased cells become more like Velcro, allowing blood elements to stick and form blockages. Additionally, PPI exposure impaired the acid production by lysosomes in the cells lining blood vessel walls, leading to the buildup of waste and rapid cellular aging.

The study tested two different PPIs, with only one (esomeprazole, brand name Nexium) commercially available. It did not fully explain how PPIs impair lysosome acid production, and the findings were conducted in a laboratory setting, raising questions about their direct application to human physiology. The research also did not address the safety of other types of antacid drugs, such as H2 antagonists.

Lead author John P. Cooke, M.D., Ph.D., emphasized that PPIs should be used only for short-term relief of symptoms of gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) and suggested that other approaches, such as H2 antagonists, lifestyle modifications, and surgical interventions, might be considered for long-term treatment. Cooke also called for the pharmaceutical industry and regulatory agencies to re-evaluate the specificity and safety of PPIs.

While the study provides a potential mechanism for the adverse effects of PPIs, it is important to note that the findings are preliminary and require further clinical trials to confirm their relevance to human health. The researchers acknowledged that PPIs can be effective for short-term use but should not be used for extended periods without medical supervision.

During the U.S. women's soccer team's victory in the Women's World Cup final against Japan, some Twitter users began to relate the win to Japan's 1941 attack on Pearl Harbor, sparking a heated debate. The hashtag "Pearl Harbor" became one of the top trends in the U.S., with thousands of tweets referencing the historical event. Some users suggested that the victory was "payback" for the attack, while others referenced the atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki, adding, "Someone forgot to tell our US women's team that we already avenged Pearl Harbor." This tweet gained significant traction, with over 8,500 retweets and 11,000 favorites. However, many Twitter users condemned the negative reaction, stating, "Pearl Harbor isn't funny. Hiroshima isn't funny. Nagasaki isn't funny." They argued that this was a women's soccer match in 2015, not a time for such references. Defenders of the Japanese fans emerged, with one user stating, "Pearl Harbor? I thought the atomic bomb was enough reaction for that." The controversy highlighted the sensitivity of historical events and the need for empathy in social media discussions.

Last year, Harvard University appointed its first female president, marking a historic change. Now, the university is set to celebrate another milestone: the installation of the first black female as dean of Harvard College. Evelynn Hammonds, a professor of history of science and African-American studies, will take on the role, making her the first female and first black person to hold this position. Hammonds' appointment comes as Yale University is also working to increase racial diversity among its top administrative ranks. Harvard President Drew Gilpin Faust, who became the first woman to lead the university, praised Hammonds' academic values and leadership. Hammonds, who previously worked on faculty diversity and development, will oversee academic affairs, student life, and general administration of Harvard College. Her appointment follows Harvard's long history of breaking gender barriers, having waited 371 years to appoint its first female president. However, Hammonds' tenure as dean was marred by controversy, including the authorization of email searches to investigate a cheating scandal. Despite this, Hammonds is stepping down to focus on her research, leaving a legacy of promoting diversity and academic integrity at Harvard.

Fifteen former members of the Church Committee, the 1970s congressional inquiry into illegal activities by the CIA and other intelligence agencies, have penned a letter to President Obama and Attorney General Loretta Lynch advocating for leniency towards Edward Snowden, the NSA whistleblower. The letter, spanning eight pages, argues that Snowden's disclosures have led to significant public awareness and subsequent reforms, including changes to the Patriot Act and enhanced privacy protections for foreigners. The authors, who were involved in the groundbreaking investigation that exposed numerous abuses by intelligence agencies, contend that Snowden's actions, while illegal, were motivated by a genuine desire to spur reform. They cite examples of leniency shown to other officials who broke secrecy laws, such as former CIA Director David Petraeus, who received a lenient sentence for his role in the affair with his biographer. The letter emphasizes that Snowden's disclosures have had a positive impact, leading to bipartisan legislative changes and a broader public discussion on the proper scope of government surveillance. The authors also highlight the risk of prolonged exile for Snowden, which they argue benefits no one. They urge the Obama administration to negotiate a plea agreement with Snowden, suggesting that this approach would balance the public benefits of his disclosures with the need for fair legal outcomes. The letter concludes by expressing hope that the government can find a settlement that both sides can accept, recognizing the complex nature of the case and the potential for further reform in the wake of Snowden's revelations.

A new national investigation by The Atlanta Journal-Constitution has revealed that 450 doctors were disciplined for sexual misconduct or sex crimes in 2016 and 2017, yet nearly half of them remain licensed to practice medicine. Even some doctors who were criminally convicted have returned to their medical practices. The investigation highlights a system that often forgives doctors, with punishments often consisting of short suspensions paired with mandatory therapy, treating sexually abusive behavior as a symptom of an illness or addiction. Despite decades of complaints about the leniency of the physician disciplinary system, little change has been made. The #MeToo movement and increased accountability in other American workplaces have not sparked a change in how medical boards handle physicians who sexually abuse patients or staff. Examples of problematic behavior are widespread, including a gynecologist who placed a chair against the exam room door, inserted his fingers into a woman's vagina, and exposed his erect penis. Another doctor told a patient he couldn't stop staring at her breasts and recounted a dream in which he performed oral sex on her. The harm of sexually abusive doctors is exacerbated by the personal nature of the doctor-patient relationship. In Florida, a doctor convicted of misdemeanor battery and found guilty of "lack of good moral character" and "lack of worthiness" to practice medicine was allowed to continue practicing. Similarly, in Arkansas, a doctor facing multiple criminal charges for rape was allowed to keep his family practice open, so long as he's chaperoned. In Idaho, a child and adolescent psychiatrist who lost his license after being accused of having sexual relationships with four former patients was reinstated by the state board. The leniency of penalties for sexually abusive doctors sometimes frustrates even those who administer the discipline. Administrative law judges are blamed for tying their hands from seeking harsher punishments. Hospitals' reluctance to report abusive doctors, the private, interstate system meant to flag them to future employers, and patients' reluctance to challenge medical professionals all contribute to the problem. The article concludes that the current system is insufficient in addressing the issue of sexual misconduct among doctors.

Pope Francis, the 266th Supreme Pontiff, has captivated the world since his election in March 2013, embodying a pastoral and compassionate approach to the Catholic Church. His humble origins and daily acts of charity, such as paying his own hotel bill and visiting slums, have endeared him to millions. As the first non-European pope in over 1,200 years, Francis has brought a fresh perspective to the institution, emphasizing mercy, transparency, and social justice. His exhortation, "Evangelii Gaudium," calls for a church that serves the poor and broken, rather than one focused on doctrinal policing. Francis has halted the practice of granting the monsignor title to curb careerism and promote pastoral ministry. He has also appointed dynamic figures like Archbishop Konrad Krajewski to the Vatican Almoner, instructing him to engage directly with the needy outside the Vatican walls. Through his actions, Francis challenges the status quo, encouraging a more inclusive and compassionate church. His approach, while conservative on key issues like abortion and gay marriage, resonates with a global audience seeking a more relevant and accessible faith. As he continues his papacy, Francis faces the monumental task of reforming a sprawling institution steeped in tradition, yet his humility and commitment to the marginalized offer a beacon of hope.

Lena Dunham is proud of her body and has recently thanked Glamour magazine for not Photoshopping her cellulite out of their February 2017 cover. In an Instagram post, Dunham shared a photo from her Glamour shoot with her Girls costars, reflecting on her past and the culture that once made her feel ashamed of her appearance. She wrote, "Throughout my teens I was told, in no uncertain terms, that I was f--king funny looking," and that she "didn't hate what [she] looked like" but "hated the culture that was telling [her] to hate it." Dunham has been vocal about her imperfections and frequently strips off on her HBO show, but she notes that "my body isn't fair game. No one's is, no matter their size, color, gender identity, and there's a place for us all in popular culture to be recognized as beautiful." The actress thanked the magazine for letting her be real, and added, "Haters are gonna have to get more intellectual and creative with their disses in 2017 because none of us are going to be scared into muumuus by faceless basement dwellers, or cruel blogs, or even our partners and friends."

In the cover photo, Dunham is seen in a pair of purple metallic booty shorts and platform heels, alongside her Girls costars Jemima Kirke, Zosia Mamet, and Allison Williams. The final season of Girls premiered on HBO on February 12, 2017, at 10 p.m. ET. Dunham has been a vocal advocate for women's rights and has used her platform to support Planned Parenthood and other causes. She has also been open about her struggles with endometriosis and has become an advocate for women's reproductive health. Dunham's Instagram post has received widespread support, with over 100,000 likes in its first hour. Her message resonates with many who appreciate her body-positive approach and her willingness to be open about her experiences.

Truckers are planning to protest the federal government by backing up the Capital Beltway around Washington, D.C., aiming to draw attention to their frustrations with regulations and the overall political climate. The "Truckers for the Constitution" group, which includes independent truckers, is backing up the 64-mile Capital Beltway to highlight their dissatisfaction with the Obama administration's regulations, high gas prices, and government spying. They see this as a necessary step to get the attention of lawmakers and demand that they operate lawfully and constitutionally. The truckers are distributing a flyer that names President Obama, Secretary of State John Kerry, and Senators John McCain and Lindsey Graham as "domestic enemies." The group claims that the truckers keep commerce flowing for the benefit of the central government and that cutting off their "money-flow" would cut off the "life-blood" of politicians. They are not seeking impeachment but are demanding the arrest of government officials who have violated their oath of office. The truckers are also upset about Environmental Protection Agency fuel efficiency standards, high diesel fuel costs, and perceived violations of their Fourth Amendment rights. While the protest is intended to be peaceful, the truckers say they will not hesitate to take more drastic action if necessary.

A new report from the Syrian Centre for Policy Research (SCPR) paints a grim picture of the Syrian conflict, with 470,000 deaths—twice the UN’s previous estimate of 250,000—attributed to the war, directly and indirectly. The SCPR’s findings, which are based on rigorous research methods, indicate that 11.5% of Syria’s population has been killed or injured since the crisis began in March 2011, with 1.9 million wounded. Life expectancy has plummeted from 70 in 2010 to 55.4 in 2015. The report estimates overall economic losses at $255 billion. The humanitarian situation in Aleppo, Syria’s largest city, is worsening, with 50,000 people fleeing due to intensifying fighting, according to the International Red Cross. Talks in Munich on Thursday between U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov will be closely watched for any sign of an end to the deadly impasse. UN-brokered peace talks in Geneva are scheduled to resume in two weeks but are unlikely to succeed without a significant shift in policy. An opposition spokesman, Salim al-Muslet, has called on President Obama to stop Russian attacks, saying, “If he is willing to save our children, it is really the time now to say ‘no’ to these strikes in Syria.” Moscow has reportedly sent a letter to Washington proposing to stop bombing on March 1. Of the 470,000 war dead, about 400,000 were directly due to violence, while the remaining 70,000 fell victim to lack of adequate health services, medicine, especially for chronic diseases, lack of food, clean water, sanitation, and proper housing, especially for those displaced within conflict zones. The SCPR’s author, Rabie Nasser, emphasized the importance of considering indirect deaths, stating, “We use very rigorous research methods and we are sure of this figure. Indirect deaths will be greater in the future, though most NGOs and the UN ignore them.” The report notes that the mortality rate has increased from 4.4 per thousand in 2010 to 10.9 per thousand in 2015. The UN high commissioner for human rights stopped counting Syria’s dead in mid-2014, citing lack of access and diminishing confidence in data sources. The SCPR, which was based in Damascus until recently, conducted research across Syria. Despite not criticizing the Syrian government or its allies, the findings are shocking. The report highlights the “catastrophic impact” of the conflict on Syria’s national wealth, infrastructure, and institutions, with 45% of the population displaced, 6.36 million internally and more than 4 million abroad. Health, education, and income standards have all deteriorated sharply, with poverty increasing by 85% in 2015 alone. The rest of the world has been slow to wake up to the dimensions of the crisis, with global attention to human rights and dignity for Syrians intensifying only when the crisis had a direct impact on developed countries. The conflict continues to destroy the social and economic fabric of the country, with international interventions deepening polarisation among Syrians. Human development, rights, and dignity have been comprehensively ruined. The report is entitled “Confronting Fragmentation.” Previous titles in the series track the unfolding of the world’s biggest humanitarian disaster: “Syrian Catastrophe,” “War on Development,” “Squandering Humanity,” and “Alienation and Violence.”

A new study from the University of Southern California (USC) challenges the notion that electronic cigarettes (e-cigarettes) merely substitute for traditional cigarettes among teenagers. The study, published in the journal Pediatrics, analyzed data from 5,490 high school seniors who graduated between 1995 and 2014. It found that while the rate of current cigarette smoking among 12th graders decreased from 19.1% in 1995 to 7.8% in 2014, the combined rate of current cigarette or e-cigarette use in 2014 was 13.7%, which was higher than the 9.0% rate of current cigarette use in 2004, when e-cigarettes were not available. This suggests that e-cigarettes are not merely replacing traditional cigarettes but are also attracting a new group of users who would not have smoked otherwise.

The study, conducted by Jessica Barrington-Trimis and colleagues, used data from the Southern California Children’s Health Study, which has followed multiple cohorts of high school students over two decades. The researchers found that the combined prevalence of cigarette or e-cigarette use in 2014 was higher than the smoking rates in 2001, when smoking rates were at their historical peak. This indicates that e-cigarettes are not merely substituting for cigarettes but are introducing a new group of users.

The findings have significant implications for public health. E-cigarettes are perceived as less harmful and less dangerous than traditional cigarettes, which could lead to nicotine experimentation among youth who have never used any other tobacco products. The study also found that older adolescents who had experimented with e-cigarettes were six times more likely to try regular cigarettes within a year. This suggests that e-cigarettes may be a gateway to smoking for youth who would not otherwise have smoked.

The researchers caution that e-cigarettes may pose health risks, including the potential for nicotine addiction and adverse effects on cognitive development. They also note that the long-term consequences of e-cigarette use are not yet known. The study highlights the need for further research to understand the role of e-cigarettes in nicotine addiction and whether they are contributing to a new wave of tobacco use among youth.

The findings of this study are part of a broader debate in public health about the role of e-cigarettes. While some experts argue that e-cigarettes could help smokers transition away from traditional cigarettes, others are concerned that they could lead to a new generation of nicotine addicts. The study underscores the importance of regulating e-cigarettes to prevent their use among non-smokers and to ensure that they do not become a gateway to traditional smoking.

A Blue Angels F/A-18 fighter jet crashed near Nashville, Tennessee, on Thursday, killing the pilot just days before a weekend air show performance, officials said. The pilot, Marine Captain Jeff Kuss, was the only casualty, and no civilians on the ground were hurt. The Navy stated that the pilot was beginning to take off during an afternoon practice session when the crash happened. Five other F/A-18 jets landed safely moments after the crash. "My thoughts and prayers go out to the family and friends of the Blue Angels after this tragic loss. I know that the Navy and Marine Corps Team is with me. We will investigate this accident fully and do all we can to prevent similar incidents in the future," Admiral John Richardson, the Navy's top officer, said in a Facebook post.

The crash occurred just hours after a U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds jet crashed in Colorado, with the pilot ejecting safely. Kuss, a native of Durango, Colorado, joined the elite acrobatics team in 2014 and had accumulated more than 1,400 flight hours. He had previously served in Afghanistan before joining the Blue Angels.

In Smyrna, Tennessee, residents witnessed the tragic event. Brenda Lewis, a retired teacher, and her 21-year-old grandson had spent much of the day in her backyard near the airport, watching the Blue Angels perform. Lewis described the incident, saying, "They looked like they were having such a good time playing up there." She went inside to bake a chocolate pie when she heard a loud boom. She didn't think too much of it at first because the airport is just on the other side of her tree line, but then she heard sirens and went around the corner. She saw the smoke rising and police cars arriving. She went inside because she didn't want to see any more.

Phil Dennis, a manager at Auto Masters of Smyrna, was standing on the business' back deck with another employee watching the planes practice above. He described the moment the plane went down, saying, "I was so worried. I thought maybe he'd have time to recover, but he didn't." A massive fireball erupted from behind the trees. "I felt it down my spine. It shocked me, I paused for a minute and questioned whether it really happened. I thought it can't be real."

The crash site was in a residential area, and the Blue Angels were scheduled to perform at a weekend air show. The Navy is investigating the cause of the crash, and the investigation will likely include a thorough examination of the crash site and the F/A-18 jet. The Blue Angels team is known for their precision and skill, and this tragic event has left many in the aviation community and the public deeply saddened.

CNN White House correspondent Jim Acosta faced backlash after sending a direct message with a vulgar response to a GOP consultant and former aide to Melania Trump, Justin Caporale, who had mocked him on Twitter. Acosta apologized for his response, tweeting, "Hey buddy I thought you were an old friend from the campaign days. I’m so sorry. Hope I didn’t offend you. Have a good night and take care." The incident began when Acosta tweeted about the loud music at a Trump campaign rally, which Caporale responded to with a sarcastic tweet, "Dear Diary…..". Acosta then sent Caporale a direct message with the message "F– You", before blocking him. The exchange drew criticism from conservatives, who mocked Acosta on social media. Acosta has long been a frequent target of criticism from Trump supporters, with the president himself disparaging him as "fake news" during live TV appearances. His interactions with Sarah Sanders, the White House press secretary, have also frequently made headlines. The controversy highlights the ongoing tensions between the media and the Trump administration.

Dennis Rodman, the former NBA star turned amateur diplomat, has recently found himself in legal trouble, arrested for driving under the influence (DUI) in Newport Beach. According to TMZ, Rodman was driving at around 11 PM on Saturday when he was pulled over for a traffic violation. After a failed field sobriety test, he was handcuffed, placed in a patrol car, and taken to the police station. Rodman, who has a history of alcoholism, cooperated with the officers and submitted to a breathalyzer test, which revealed he was over the legal limit of 0.08. He remained in jail for seven hours before being released once the officers determined he was sober enough to care for himself.

This is not the first time Rodman has faced legal issues related to alcohol. In 1999, he was also arrested for DUI. In an exclusive statement to TMZ, Rodman's representative acknowledged that alcoholism has been a struggle for the former athlete, on and off, for the past 15 years. The rep added that Rodman has been dealing with some "tough personal issues" and plans to discuss the possibility of returning to rehab with him. Rodman's arrest comes at a time when he has been urging President Donald Trump to call him and ask about Kim Jong Un, the North Korean leader, noting that Trump has never met him or his people. Rodman expressed his desire for a more personal and direct conversation with the president, stating, "I would love for Donald Trump to call me and say, 'What is he like?' He’s never met him, he’s never talked with his people. You can say [Kim] is crazy, but what has he done to you? What has he done in general?"

In a groundbreaking move, the Obama administration has set a national goal to reduce food waste by 50% by 2030, aiming to address environmental, economic, and social challenges. Agriculture Secretary Tom Vilsack and EPA Administrator Gina McCarthy announced this initiative, which involves a partnership with charitable organizations, businesses, and local governments to combat food waste. This effort is part of the administration's broader strategy to tackle climate change and enhance food security. Food waste in the U.S. accounts for about 31% of the overall food supply, equivalent to 133 billion pounds, and has significant environmental impacts, including methane emissions from landfills, which are the third-largest source of methane in the U.S. Reducing food waste by just 15% could feed over 25 million Americans annually, addressing food insecurity. The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) are launching a consumer education campaign to inform people about food waste and provide tips on reducing it. They also plan to work with food service companies, institutions, and grocery stores to set ambitious goals for waste reduction. The USDA has already initiated the U.S. Food Waste Challenge, which has over 4,000 active participants, surpassing its initial goal of 1,000 by 2020. The initiative includes efforts to educate consumers about food date labels and safe storage practices, as well as research on innovative technologies to reduce food loss. By reducing food waste, the administration aims to boost the economy, protect public health, and preserve natural resources, aligning with the Obama administration's commitment to environmental sustainability.

A tense standoff between federal land managers and supporters of Nevada cattle rancher Cliven Bundy appeared to end on Saturday when the Bureau of Land Management (BLM) abruptly halted a cattle roundup, returning about 300 head of cattle to the open range to avoid potential violence. The BLM cited "serious concerns" for the safety of employees and the public, while hundreds of protesters, some armed, gathered near the roundup site to support Bundy. The BLM had begun the cattle gather a week earlier, claiming Bundy owed about $1 million in back fees for grazing on federal land. Bundy, who has been ranching in Nevada since the 1800s, has long disputed federal authority over grazing rights and the charges. The dispute drew armed militia groups from across the country, leading to a weeklong confrontation. On Saturday, supporters forced a temporary shutdown of northbound lanes of Interstate 15 near Bundy's ranch, causing traffic backups. U.S. Senator Dean Heller appealed for calm, urging supporters to return home and allowing the BLM to depart without interference. The BLM's decision to end the roundup came amid escalating tensions and a video of a scuffle between protesters and federal rangers. The BLM's director, Neil Kornze, stated that the decision was made to avoid violence and restore order. Nevada Governor Brian Sandoval praised the BLM for its willingness to listen to state concerns. The conflict highlights the ongoing debate over federal land management and the rights of ranchers in the West.

A high-ranking North Korean diplomat who served as the country's deputy ambassador to the United Kingdom has defected to South Korea, marking the highest-ranking North Korean official to do so in nearly two decades. Thae Yong-ho, 55, who had been living in London for a decade, was the ambassador's deputy and had been tasked with promoting a positive image of the North Korean leadership. He and his family are now under South Korean government protection. Thae had reportedly come under pressure from his government to suppress growing criticism of North Korea's human rights record. In London, Thae had enjoyed a comfortable life, playing tennis and dining at Indian restaurants, and had even chaperoned a brother of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un to an Eric Clapton concert. He had previously argued that the British were brainwashed by their ruling class into believing "shocking, terrifying" lies about North Korea. South Korean spokesman Jeong Joon-hee stated that Thae defected due to his disgust with Kim Jong-un's regime, admiration for South Korea's free, democratic system, and concerns for his family's future. His defection comes as North Korea faces increasing criticism and sanctions, and as the country's leadership continues to consolidate power through purges and executions.

In his first interview since facing accusations of inappropriate behavior on set, veteran actor Jeffrey Tambor of "Transparent" and "Arrested Development" opens up about his alleged sexual harassment scandal. Tambor, now back onscreen in "Arrested Development," admits to being mean and difficult on set but denies sexually harassing his accusers. His firing from "Transparent" came after his former assistant, Van Barnes, and actress Trace Lysette accused him of inappropriate and abusive behavior. Barnes alleged that Tambor made "butt pats" and "why aren't I taking care of him sexually" comments, while Lysette claimed he made unwanted advances and thrusts during a scene. Tambor maintains he was volatile and ill-tempered but not a predator, and he blames the politicized atmosphere for his ousting. He has received support from some castmates but faces criticism from others. Tambor acknowledges his behavior has changed, becoming more patient and gentlemanly, and he is grappling with the loss of the role of Maura Pfefferman. The #MeToo movement has brought to light the complexities of sexual harassment allegations, with Tambor's case raising questions about the intersection of gender and power in the entertainment industry. Despite the controversy, Tambor remains committed to his craft and his family, focusing on reading bedtime stories to his children and working on "Arrested Development." His story highlights the challenges faced by high-profile figures in the wake of the #MeToo movement, as they navigate public scrutiny and personal growth.

Tyra Banks will host the 12th season of "America's Got Talent," taking over from Nick Cannon after eight years. NBC announced that the supermodel and Emmy-winner will join the competition series alongside returning judges Simon Cowell, Mel B, Heidi Klum, and Howie Mandel. Contestants will showcase a variety of talents for a chance at a $1 million prize, with episodes airing live this summer from the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles. Banks expressed excitement to connect with the dreamers and encouraged them to "smize" for the audience. The show, which features a diverse array of acts, aims to continue its popularity with a new host leading the way.

The World Anti-Doping Agency (Wada) has revealed that its database was breached by a Russian hacking group, Fancy Bear, which posted confidential medical data of several American Olympic athletes online. The hackers disclosed records of Therapeutic Use Exemptions (TUEs) for four female American athletes: tennis stars Serena and Venus Williams, gymnastics champion Simone Biles, and basketball player Elena Delle Donne. These documents detail the athletes' permission to use certain banned substances for legitimate medical reasons. However, the hackers accused the athletes of doping, claiming that the TUEs amounted to "licences for doping." 

In response, US Anti-Doping Agency (Usada) chief Travis Tygart stated that the athletes had followed all global rules for obtaining permission to use medications on the Wada banned drugs list. Wada's director general, Olivier Niggli, expressed deep regret over the situation, emphasizing the threat it posed to athletes' confidential information. Wada believes the hack was executed through a spear-phishing attack, where hackers tricked users into revealing passwords. 

This incident adds to the ongoing doping scandal, with Russian athletes facing bans and investigations. The Russian track and field team was banned from the Rio Olympics due to evidence of a state-sponsored doping program. The hackers' actions are seen as an attempt to undermine the global anti-doping system and the trust in Russian athletes. Wada has confirmed that one of the victims whose password was stolen was Yuliya Stepanova, a whistleblower who exposed widespread doping in Russian athletics. 

The hackers have pledged to release more confidential records from other national Olympic teams, potentially leading to further controversy and privacy breaches. This event raises questions about the security of Wada's systems and the broader anti-doping community. The incident has also been linked to the broader geopolitical tensions, as the hackers are believed to be associated with the Russian military intelligence agency, GRU, and are suspected of involvement in cyberattacks against government and corporate targets.

The Israeli military launched a ground operation into Gaza, stepping up its 11-day-old military campaign against Palestinian militants. Troops and tanks entered Gaza to deal a significant blow to Hamas, Israel said, with 14 "terrorists" reportedly killed overnight. Gaza's health ministry reported 24 deaths and 200 injuries since the ground offensive began, including a five-month-old child. Israel suffered its first military fatality, with one soldier killed. The operation aims to destroy tunnels Hamas has dug under the border with Israel. Palestinian security sources claim airstrikes killed seven children. Israeli forces have called up 18,000 more reservists, bringing the total to 65,000. Hamas condemned the Israeli action, stating it would "pay a heavy price" and that the operation was "destined to fail." Prime Minister Netanyahu ordered the invasion after days of rocket fire and air strikes. Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas called for an end to the ground operation, warning it would lead to "more bloodshed." The ground offensive follows a temporary ceasefire on Thursday to allow Palestinians to stock up on supplies and aid workers to distribute water, food, and hygiene kits. Israel has carried out more than 1,960 attacks on Gaza since July 8, while militants have fired some 1,380 rockets at Israel. The UN reports at least 1,370 homes destroyed and 18,000 people displaced in recent hostilities. The ground operation comes after failed attempts in Cairo to negotiate a new ceasefire. Israel's goals are to diminish Hamas' military force and show it cannot attack Israel with impunity. Hamas is prepared to capture Israeli soldiers to use in prisoner swaps. The conflict continues with heavy clashes reported along Gaza's eastern border and in northern towns.

Donald Trump's Republican National Convention lineup for Tuesday includes not just one, but two actors famous for their daytime television roles: Kimberlin Brown of The Young and the Restless and The Bold and the Beautiful, and Antonio Sabato Jr. of General Hospital. Brown, who has managed to secure a prime-time slot, will be introduced by neurosurgeon and Republican presidential candidate Ben Carson. Brown's career highlights include playing the devious character Sheila Carter in the 1990s and currently hosting Dramatic Designs on The Design Network. She is also a small business owner through her role as a stylist and eBoutique owner on MK Collab. Her excitement for the convention is evident from her recent Instagram posts. The inclusion of soap opera stars as speakers is part of Trump's unconventional approach, aiming to emphasize his connection with the working class and small business owners. Dana White, president of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, and professional golfer Natalie Gulbis will also speak, adding a touch of celebrity to the lineup. The theme of the night, "Make America Work Again," will focus on Trump's business acumen and his ability to revitalize the economy. This unconventional choice of speakers reflects Trump's desire to broaden his appeal beyond traditional political figures and connect with a wider audience, including those who may not typically engage with politics.

The controversy surrounding Sandra Bland's death in a Texas jail cell continues to intensify, with some social media circles questioning whether she was already dead in her mugshot taken three days after her arrest. Forensic experts, including Dr. Michael Baden, who conducted a private autopsy for the family of Michael Brown, dismiss these theories as "ridiculous." Bland, a 28-year-old from Illinois, was arrested for failing to signal a lane change and allegedly assaulting a state trooper. She was found hanging in her cell on July 13, with the cause of death ruled a suicide by hanging. However, the family and supporters are skeptical, pointing out inconsistencies in Bland's booking documents, dashcam footage, and the circumstances of her death. The Waller County Sheriff's Department has released video of Bland during her booking process, which shows her walking and posing for her mugshot, but questions remain. Bland's second mugshot, taken from a side angle, was released later, further fueling speculation. The case has drawn national attention amid ongoing scrutiny of police interactions with black individuals. Despite the release of evidence, the family's attorney, Cannon Lambert, emphasizes the need for a thorough investigation, stating, "We understand that she was stopped, but we understand that she felt that she was handled very harshly." The investigation, involving the Texas Rangers and the FBI, is ongoing, with the family calling for transparency and an independent autopsy. The case highlights the complex and often contentious nature of police-citizen interactions and the challenges in determining the circumstances of a death in custody.

Donald Trump faced backlash over a tweet featuring a photo of Hillary Clinton with a Star of David and the phrase "Most Corrupt Candidate Ever!" The tweet, which Trump later deleted, was traced to a white supremacist message board, sparking accusations of anti-Semitism. The House Speaker, Paul Ryan, condemned the image, stating that anti-Semitic images have no place in a presidential campaign. Trump's social media director, Dan Scavino, claimed the image was sourced from an anti-Hillary Twitter user, but critics questioned the campaign's failure to attribute the original source. Trump's former campaign manager, Corey Lewandowski, defended the tweet, arguing it was a simple star often used by sheriffs. The Anti-Defamation League criticized the tweet as further evidence of extremist sympathies within the Trump campaign. The Clinton campaign's director of Jewish outreach, Sarah Bard, accused Trump of using a blatantly anti-Semitic image to promote his campaign. Trump's supporters argued the image was a simple star and not a Star of David, while his social media director blamed the campaign's social media team for the controversy. The incident raised concerns about the campaign's sourcing of memes and its handling of anti-Semitic content.

President Obama uses his weekly radio address to address the tragic shooting at Sandy Hook Elementary School in Connecticut, where 26 people, including 20 children, were killed. He urges the nation to take "meaningful action" to prevent such tragedies, emphasizing that "any of these neighborhoods could be our own." While Obama does not specify any particular actions, he calls for a united response to gun violence. New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg criticizes the administration for lacking leadership and calls for immediate action. House Speaker John Boehner cancels the Republican weekly address to show respect for the victims. Obama's speech is emotional, with him wiping away tears, and he stresses the need for support for the families affected. The tragedy reignites the debate over gun control in the U.S., where a strong gun lobby has historically hindered significant legislative changes. Obama's call for action comes as the nation grapples with the "fiscal cliff" and other pressing issues, making the timing uncertain for any legislative push.

The youngest son of the late shah of Iran, Prince Alireza Pahlavi, was found dead in his Boston home on January 4, 2011, after struggling for years with the loss of his sister and father. His brother, Reza Pahlavi, announced the death, stating Alireza had "struggled for years to overcome his sorrow." Alireza, 44, died from a single gunshot wound that was apparently self-inflicted. He had lived in the South End neighborhood for many years but kept a low public profile. Boston police found him around 2 a.m. and confirmed the identity of the body. Alireza's sister, Leila, had died in 2001 from an accidental overdose of prescription drugs. Neighbors described him as a reserved man who rarely ventured out of his home. His death came as a shock to those who had known him, including Dr. Daniel Shannon, who recalled Alireza as a curious child during the shah's reign. The Pahlavi family, once a prominent figure in Iran, has largely stayed out of politics since the 1979 revolution, with Reza taking a more public stance against the current regime. The family's loss has been mourned by the Iranian-American community, with Trita Parsi of the National Iranian American Council expressing sympathy. No funeral arrangements have been made, and the family wishes to mourn privately.

Vice President Joe Biden officiated the first same-sex wedding at the Naval Observatory, marrying longtime White House staffers Brian Mosteller and Joe Mahshie. Biden obtained a temporary certification to perform the ceremony, which was attended only by the grooms' families. His wife, Jill, tweeted "Love is love!" in support. This event marks Biden's public endorsement of same-sex marriage, which he supported in 2012. The White House has not commented on the matter, but the incident highlights Biden's evolving stance on LGBTQ rights.

Poland has summoned the U.S. ambassador and demanded an apology over comments on the Holocaust by FBI director James Comey. The foreign ministry stated that Comey's suggestion in a Washington Post article that some Poles were accomplices to Nazi Germany was an "insult to thousands of Poles who helped Jews." President Bronislaw Komorowski and Prime Minister Ewa Kopacz both emphasized that Poland was a victim of World War Two, not a perpetrator. The U.S. ambassador, Stephen Mull, clarified that the U.S. believes "Nazi Germany alone" was responsible for the Holocaust. However, Mull acknowledged that the broader message of Comey's article was that many people, including in the U.S., aided the Nazis or did not do enough to respond to atrocities.
