The Polish ambassador to Washington has protested, and the U.S. ambassador to Warsaw has apologized profusely. The article highlights the tension between the U.S. and Poland over historical narratives and the responsibility for the Holocaust. It also underscores the importance of accurate historical accounts in shaping national identities and international relations.

Gigi Hadid, the 22-year-old supermodel, has been named one of Glamour's 2017 Women of the Year, joining a roster that includes Nicole Kidman, Solange Knowles, Patty Jenkins, and Maxine Waters. This recognition comes after Hadid's meteoric rise to fame, which includes commercial success with brands like Victoria's Secret, Sports Illustrated's Swimsuit Issue, and a collaboration with Maybelline New York, as well as industry acclaim such as the Vogue cover and her runway debut for Tom Ford. Her followers, numbering 36 million on Instagram, are a testament to her influence. Hadid's work ethic and kindness are often praised, and she has used her platform to speak out on issues ranging from gun control to women's personal safety. Her ability to maintain a positive public image and her dedication to her craft have made her a role model for many.

However, Hadid's latest claim to fame is a video posted by Glamour, which features her staring into the camera for an entire four minutes. The video, described as "weirdly mesmerizing," has sparked debate. While some find it intriguing and engaging, others question its value as content. The video's simplicity—Hadid simply staring, sometimes blinking and smiling—raises questions about the future of digital media and the strategies employed by traditional magazines to adapt to the digital age. The video's creators suggest it could be used as background entertainment during holiday parties, but many find it more unsettling than relaxing. This phenomenon highlights the ongoing challenge for media outlets to innovate and engage audiences in a digital landscape where content is increasingly diverse and interactive.

Scientists have uncovered evidence that up to 25 percent of people infected with Ebola show no symptoms, challenging the understanding of the virus's transmission and impact. This finding, based on a study in the village of Sukudu, Sierra Leone, suggests that the 2013-2016 West African Ebola epidemic may have been more widespread than previously thought. The study, published in PLOS Neglected Tropical Diseases, tested 187 individuals who had been in close contact with confirmed Ebola cases but had not been identified as cases themselves. Among these, 14 tested positive for Ebola antibodies, indicating past infection, with 12 of them reporting no symptoms during the outbreak. This implies that a significant portion of Ebola transmission events may have gone undetected during the epidemic. The researchers caution that their findings cannot be directly extrapolated to other affected areas without further study. The discovery has implications for the definition of Ebola survivorship and the development of future vaccines, as it highlights the need to consider minimally symptomatic infections in public health strategies. This study underscores the complexity of containing and understanding the spread of Ebola, emphasizing the importance of more comprehensive surveillance and diagnostic tools to better manage future outbreaks.

A dead goose fell from the sky and struck a waterfowl hunter, knocking him unconscious during a hunting party near the Miles River in Dorchester County, Maryland. The incident occurred around 5 p.m. as the group was hunting. Robert Meilhammer, a 51-year-old resident of Crapo, was part of the hunting party when the goose fell, striking him and causing head and facial injuries. He was airlifted to Maryland Shock Trauma for treatment. Candy Thomson, a Maryland Natural Resources Police spokeswoman, stated that it is unclear which hunter fired the shot that killed the goose. The event highlights the unexpected dangers that can occur during hunting activities, emphasizing the importance of safety measures and awareness. Meanwhile, unrelated events such as the Orthodox Saturday morning service, which recognizes "the first resurrection of our savior and lord Jesus Christ," and the release of the annual State of Downtown Baltimore report by business and civic leaders, continue to take place in the community.

Six people were shot dead in the Russian city of Belgorod on Monday afternoon, with a 14-year-old girl among the victims, reports RIA Novosti. A gunman, identified as 32-year-old Sergey Pomazun, opened fire near an arms shop, then fled in his vehicle. Police have deployed special forces to search for the suspect, who is described as armed with a gas pistol and a semi-automatic rifle. Pomazun has a criminal record, having been convicted four times, primarily for thefts. The attack left four men aged between 28 and 45, and two schoolgirls dead, with one 16-year-old girl dying later in hospital. The city administration declared April 23 and 24 days of mourning, covering funeral expenses and providing financial aid to the families of the victims. Psychological support teams were sent to the city. The suspect's father, Aleksandr Pomazun, is reportedly cooperating with investigators, though conflicting reports suggest there may have been two suspects involved. The incident has sparked panic among residents, with police urging them to stay indoors.

Pope Francis, during a press conference aboard the papal plane returning from Armenia, addressed the issue of apologies from the Catholic Church, particularly to the gay community. He emphasized that Christians should apologize to those who have been marginalized by the church, including the poor, women, and children exploited for labor, as well as to those who have been offended or exploited by the church. Francis stated, "I repeat what the Catechism of the Catholic Church says: that they must not be discriminated against, that they must be respected and accompanied pastorally," and added, "The Church must ask forgiveness for not behaving many times — when I say the Church, I mean Christians!"

The Pope's remarks were seen as a significant step forward by some, with the Rev. James Martin, a Jesuit priest and editor at large of America magazine, calling it a "groundbreaking moment." Martin highlighted that while St. John Paul II had apologized to several groups in 2000, no pope had ever apologized to the LGBT community for the harm religious traditions have caused. Francis has not changed the church's doctrine, which calls homosexual acts sinful, but has shown a more merciful approach to people on the margins, including gays and lesbians.

In response to a German cardinal who said the Catholic Church should apologize for being "very negative" about gays, Francis reiterated that one could condemn certain behaviors but not for theological reasons, but for reasons of political behavior. He emphasized, "But these are things that have nothing to do with the problem. The problem is a person that has a condition, that has good will and who seeks God, who are we to judge? And we must accompany them well."

The Pope's comments were part of a broader discussion during the press conference, which also included questions about Brexit, former Pope Benedict XVI, and the use of the term "genocide" to describe the mass killing of Armenians during World War One. Francis defended his use of the term, stating that it would have sounded strange not to use it again after his time in Argentina and the previous statements by Pope John Paul II. He also expressed hope for the European Union to recover from the UK's decision to leave, suggesting that unity is superior to conflict and that the EU should seek creative solutions to strengthen its roots.

A long-term study of more than 400 men, spanning over 20 years, challenges the notion that chronic marijuana use during adolescence leads to significant physical or mental health issues later in life. The research, published in Psychology of Addictive Behaviors, analyzed data from the Pittsburgh Youth Study (PYS), which followed a group of boys from the 7th grade (1987-1988) until their mid-30s. The study divided participants into four groups based on their marijuana use patterns: those who rarely or never used marijuana, those who mostly used it in their teens, those who started using in adulthood, and those who were chronic users throughout their teenage years and beyond.

The findings revealed that chronic marijuana users did not exhibit more physical or mental health problems, such as depression, psychotic symptoms, or asthma, compared to the other groups. The study controlled for factors like tobacco use and socioeconomic status, ensuring a more accurate comparison. Researchers noted that there were no significant differences in adult health outcomes among the marijuana use trajectory groups, even when potential confounding factors were not accounted for.

Lead researcher Jordan Bechtold, a psychology research fellow at the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center, expressed that the results were somewhat surprising, as they contradicted some previous studies that suggested a link between chronic marijuana use and mental health issues. However, the study's unique strength lay in its longitudinal nature, providing a more comprehensive view of the participants' health over time.

Despite the findings, the researchers acknowledged that the study had limitations. It only included male participants, did not cover the full spectrum of health issues, and did not extend to conditions like cardiovascular disease. Additionally, the study did not definitively rule out the possibility that a subset of individuals might be more susceptible to the negative effects of long-term marijuana use.

Bechtold emphasized that policymakers and stakeholders should consider the results of this study in the context of the broader body of research on the potential adverse consequences of early-onset chronic marijuana use. The study highlights the need for further research, particularly to understand the long-term effects on women and the full range of health outcomes associated with marijuana use.

This afternoon, a Mountain View Police Department traffic officer noticed traffic backing up behind a slow-moving car traveling in the eastbound #3 lane on El Camino Real, near Rengstorff Avenue. The car was moving at 24 mph in a 35 mph zone. Upon approaching, the officer realized the vehicle was a Google Autonomous Vehicle. The officer stopped the car and engaged with the operators to understand how the car selects speeds and to educate them about impeding traffic. The Google self-driving cars operate under the Neighborhood Electric Vehicle Definition per 385.5 of the California Vehicle Code and can only be driven on roadways with speed limits at or under 35 mph. In this case, the car was lawfully traveling on El Camino Real, which has a 35 mph speed limit. The Mountain View Police Department regularly meets with Google to ensure their vehicles operate safely in the community. No ticket was issued, and the officer's interaction with the operators highlighted the unique challenges and questions surrounding autonomous vehicles. The Google Self-Driving Car Project acknowledged the humorous situation, explaining that their prototype vehicles are capped at 25 mph for safety and to ensure they feel friendly and approachable. They have never been ticketed during 1.2 million miles of autonomous driving, which is the human equivalent of 90 years of driving experience.

When and how long a baby looks at other people’s eyes offers the earliest behavioral sign to date of whether a child is likely to develop autism, according to a new study. Researchers using eye-tracking technology found that children who were later diagnosed with autism at age 3 looked less at people’s eyes when they were babies than children who did not develop autism. The difference emerged between 2 and 6 months of age and was not apparent at birth. The study, published in the journal Nature, involved 110 babies, from 2 months to 2 years of age, who were assessed 10 times while watching videos of friendly women acting like playful caregivers. Eye-tracking technology traced when the babies looked at the women’s eyes, mouths, and bodies, as well as toys or other objects in the background. At age 3, the children were evaluated for autism. Ultimately, researchers used data from 36 boys, 11 of whom developed autism. The researchers found that children who developed autism paid more attention to mouths and sustained attention to bodies past the age when typical children became less interested. They also looked more at objects after the first year, while typical children’s interest in objects declined. Dr. Warren R. Jones, director of research at the autism center, said that these eye-tracking differences are not something parents and pediatricians would be able to perceive without the technology and expertise of an autism clinic. He emphasized that parents should not be concerned if their babies aren't looking at them 100 percent of the time, but if they do have persistent concerns, they should talk to their child’s pediatrician. The study suggests that early interventions could be developed to address these behaviors. Dr. John N. Constantino, a child psychiatrist and pediatrician at Washington University in St. Louis, said the study showed that babies who develop autism are for the most part doing an awful lot of things right for the first few months. Perhaps the genes that drive autism begin to derail typical development after that, so that "what you are looking at moment by moment, day by day, second by second, is completely different from what other children are looking at, and the cumulative experience is what sends you off into the trajectory of autism." The findings raise hope for early interventions and could help illustrate the need for therapies to increase social engagement among very young infants. Dr. Sally Ozonoff, vice chairwoman for research in psychiatry and behavioral sciences at the MIND Institute of the University of California, Davis, said that eye contact was "just one very important channel." She continued, "I think we’d see the same things if we were measuring a child’s social reciprocity via touch or auditory listening preferences, but those are harder to measure." The researchers found that children who developed autism had shown a steady decline in attention to the eyes of other people from the age of two months onwards, when watching videos of natural human interactions. The study provides an insight into the timing of atypical social attention in children who might go on to develop autism and highlights the need for more research to confirm these findings on a larger scale.

The seed for this crawl was a comprehensive list of every host in the Wayback Machine, a project aimed at archiving the web. This particular crawl was conducted at a detailed level 1, capturing not only the URLs of the hosts but also their embedded content, as well as the URLs of all outbound links and their respective embeds. This extensive process ensures that even the most minute details of web pages are preserved, providing a robust archive for future reference. Although the WARC files associated with this crawl are not currently accessible to the public, the effort underscores the commitment to maintaining an accurate historical record of the internet.

More than 200 people attended an unveiling ceremony for a new Confederate monument in Alabama's Crenshaw County on a Sunday afternoon. The modest stone marker, located in a Confederate memorial park, commemorates the "unknown Confederate soldiers" who died in the Civil War but have been forgotten by history, particularly those from Crenshaw County and the surrounding area. The memorial stands among existing monuments, replica cannons, and tall flagpoles flying Confederate and other flags. The event was organized by David Coggins, a Sons of Confederate Veterans member who operates both the RV Park and the adjacent memorial park. Coggins emphasized the importance of remembering the soldiers who lost their lives fighting for the Confederacy and supporting the ongoing movement to honor them. Attendees, many of whom wore Confederate T-shirts, black-leather motorcycle jackets, or period costume dresses, waved Confederate flags and banners. About 10 members of the right-wing Three Percenters militia movement stood in the back, armed with large guns, as a precaution. The ceremony began with speeches, a flag-raising, and a period of calling out names of Confederate veterans who lost their lives in battle. The unveiling stage was marked by the firing of blanks from multiple replica Civil War cannons. The monument, resembling a standard stone gravestone, bears the words "Unkown AL Soldier CSA" and the quote "Mother, I have been found, I am home." Despite the recent wave of cities tearing down and relocating Confederate monuments, the organizers of the ceremony claimed it was not planned in response to the events in Charlottesville, Virginia, earlier this month. The ceremony was scheduled months ago, and the monument was ordered last year. Members of the Sons of Confederate Veterans and the Daughters of the Confederacy attended the event, along with re-enactors dressed in period clothing. Attendees expressed pride in their heritage and the importance of remembering their history, stating that forgetting one's heritage would lead to repeating it.

A 106-year-old Virginia McLaurin, celebrating #BlackHistoryMonth, danced joyfully with President Barack Obama and First Lady Michelle Obama at the White House. McLaurin entered the room, squealing with delight and telling Obama, "It's an honor, it's an honor." Michelle Obama hugged and danced with McLaurin, exclaiming, "No, you are not! [Obama] is 106!" The trio laughed and danced in the Blue Room, with McLaurin saying, "I thought I would never live to get in the White House. And I tell you. I am so happy: A black president." The sweet video of the encounter captures McLaurin's vivacious spirit and the Obamas' joy in sharing this moment.

When the Islamic State made a significant push through northern Iraq, tens of thousands of Iraqis, particularly the Yazidis, fled their homes before the Sunni militants arrived. The Yazidis, an ancient religious minority, were especially terrified as the Islamic State, known for its brutal methods, considers them "devil worshippers" and a prime target for execution. The Islamic State's offensive captured three towns and a fifth oil field, advancing to Iraq's largest dam, marking the group's most significant territorial gains since the fall of Saddam Hussein. Many Yazidis, fearing for their lives, fled to surrounding mountains, but not all managed to escape. Reports indicate that about 50 people were killed in Sinjar after the Sunni militants arrived, with 20 killed in the defense of the town, leaving the fate of the others unclear. The Yazidis, who are part of the Kurdish minority, faced a dire situation, with many children dying of thirst or hunger. The United Nations Children's Fund (UNICEF) reported that 40 children had died in the 48 hours preceding the summary, with some bodies buried in shallow graves due to the lack of resources. The U.S.-trained Iraqi army largely collapsed during the offensive, leading Kurdish fighters, known as peshmerga, to step in. However, the Islamic State's superior weaponry and tactics overwhelmed the Kurds, forcing them to retreat. As a result, thousands of civilians, mostly Yazidis, were trapped on Mount Sinjar, facing the grim choice of descending to certain death or staying and risking dehydration and starvation. The situation became dire, with children dying and families struggling to survive. The Iraqi government attempted to airdrop supplies, but the effort was insufficient, reaching only a few of the stranded civilians. The plight of the Yazidis and other minorities highlighted the failure of Iraq's political leaders to form a unified government capable of addressing the crisis. The Islamic State's advance and the subsequent humanitarian disaster underscored the urgent need for international intervention and cooperation to protect civilians and restore stability in Iraq.

A California judge has dismissed a $42 million lawsuit filed by R&B artist Jesse Graham, who records as Jesse Braham, against Taylor Swift, ruling that the pop star did not steal his lyrics for her hit song "Shake It Off." The lawsuit alleged that 92% of Swift's song came from Braham's 2013 composition "Haters Gone Hate," with both songs featuring the phrase "Haters gonna hate, players gonna play." However, U.S. District Court Judge Gail Standish, in a cheekily worded ruling, invoked lyrics from other Swift songs, including "We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together," "Blank Space," and "Bad Blood," to emphasize the court's dismissal. Standish noted that Braham did not provide sufficient factual evidence and that his allegations were speculative. She wrote, "At present, the Court is not saying that Braham can never, ever, ever get his case back in court. But, for now, we have got problems, and the Court is not sure Braham can solve them." The judge also quoted lyrics from "Shake It Off" itself, stating, "At least for the moment, Defendants have shaken off this lawsuit." Braham was given the opportunity to file a new complaint if he could address the deficiencies in his lawsuit. The case highlights the ongoing legal battles surrounding songwriting and copyright, with Swift's legal team using her own lyrics to make a point.

Neiman Marcus disclosed a data breach that affected customer information, including payment cards and email addresses, but did not compromise Social Security numbers or birth dates. The breach, which began in July and was not fully contained until January, was only publicly acknowledged after facing inquiries from a security journalist. Neiman Marcus defended its decision to wait to disclose the breach, stating it needed to confirm evidence. The company offered free credit monitoring services to affected customers. The breach was similar to the one at Target, involving malware that targeted point-of-sale systems, but Neiman Marcus did not collect PINs. State attorneys general are investigating both the Target and Neiman Marcus breaches, suspecting a connection between the two attacks, which appear to have been committed by criminal groups in Eastern Europe. A 17-page report from a computer firm hired to investigate the Target breach revealed that the malware used was highly sophisticated and innovative, capable of evading network controls and forensic tactics. The report suggested that such breaches would likely continue due to the significant financial rewards for cyber criminals.

Vincent van Gogh's vibrant colors, once so vivid, have faded over time, a discovery revealed by a recent research project at the Van Gogh Museum in Amsterdam. This revelation, showcased in the exhibition "Van Gogh at Work," highlights how some of the artist's favorite paints have deteriorated, altering the appearance of his masterpieces. The museum's study, employing advanced non-invasive techniques, has meticulously examined the microscopic structure of the artworks, revealing the extent of color changes. These changes, primarily due to light exposure, have made some of his works appear more muted and less intense than when first created.

The exhibition delves into various aspects of van Gogh's artistic practice, including the types of canvases he used, his interactions with contemporaries such as Paul Gauguin and Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, and his habit of reusing canvases. For instance, a flower painting conceals a wrestling scene by van Gogh, while two brown studies for his early work "The Potato Eaters" have vibrant self-portraits on their reverse sides. These insights bring viewers closer to understanding the artist's working methods and the physical process of creating his paintings.

The research also underscores the impact of environmental factors on the longevity of van Gogh's colors. The vibrant reds in his "Wheat Stack Under a Cloudy Sky" are slowly transforming into white, a phenomenon explained by the chemical degradation of red lead (minium) under light exposure. Scientists from the University of Antwerp have identified a previously unknown mineral, plumbonacrite, as the key to this process. This discovery provides a clearer understanding of the chemical pathway leading to the whitening of minium, allowing for better conservation strategies to preserve van Gogh's works.

While the color changes might seem to diminish the brilliance of van Gogh's art, they do not detract from his genius. The exhibition's findings offer a deeper appreciation of the artist's work, revealing the dynamic nature of his creations. Visitors can even examine the microscopic details of van Gogh's paintings through an interactive electronic microscope, providing a unique perspective on the physical composition of his masterpieces. The inclusion of van Gogh's palette and three tubes of paint used by the artist further personalizes the experience, bringing the viewer closer to the material life of the artist.

In conclusion, the research and exhibition offer a nuanced view of van Gogh's art, highlighting both the enduring brilliance and the gradual changes over time. This approach not only preserves the legacy of the artist but also enriches the understanding and appreciation of his work for future generations.

Kanye West reportedly earned millions to perform at a private wedding in Kazakhstan for the grandson of President Nursultan Nazarbayev. The concert, held at the Royal Tulip Hotel in Almaty, featured West's hit "Can't Tell Me Nothing." While the exact amount is unclear, it was likely in the millions. Kazakhstan's president, known for his alleged corruption and dictatorship, has amassed a fortune through oil resources. The wedding involved one of Nazarbayev's daughters, Dinara, who is married to Timur Kulibayev, the third richest person in Kazakhstan. This performance, taking place during Labor Day weekend, highlights West's global appeal and the financial opportunities in countries with questionable political climates.

Death Valley National Park shattered records in July 2017, recording an average temperature of 107.39 degrees, making it the hottest month ever at a single location in U.S. history, according to the National Weather Service. This surpasses the previous record of 107.2 set in 1917. The average daily high temperature was a staggering 119.6 degrees, and nights provided little relief, with the temperature not dropping below 89 degrees for the entire month. On July 7, the mercury hit 127 degrees, a mark it also achieved on two June days. The park, known as the hottest, driest, and lowest of all U.S. national parks, saw three days where the overnight low was over 100 degrees. This extreme heat prompted several other cities in the West, as well as Miami, to set record warm months. The National Weather Service reported that Death Valley's July 2017 average monthly temperature of 107.4 broke the previous record. Christopher Burt, a Weather Underground weather historian, noted that while this was a U.S. record, the world record for the warmest average monthly temperature was set in August 2015 in King Khaled, Saudi Arabia, with an average temperature of 107.44 degrees. The extreme heat in Death Valley has significant implications for the region, with no permanent residents except for a few park service staff and rangers. The heat also underscores the ongoing challenges of climate change and its impact on extreme weather events.

A white sample bag used by Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to collect the first samples of lunar rock during the Apollo 11 mission has become the center of a legal dispute. The bag, mistakenly sold at a government auction in 2015, is now the subject of a federal lawsuit filed by Nancy Carlson, an Illinois resident, against NASA. The bag, which contains lunar material embedded in its fabric, was discovered in 2003 during a search of the garage of Max Ary, the founder and former director of the Kansas Cosmosphere and Space Center, who was convicted in 2005 for stealing and selling space artifacts. The government called the bag a "rare artifact, if not a national treasure," and it was sold at a government auction for $995 to Carlson in February 2015. NASA, unaware of the sale, later refused to return the bag when Carlson sent it for authentication. Federal prosecutors are now seeking to rescind the sale and refund Carlson, arguing that the sale was due to a clerical error where two separate lunar bags were given the same inventory identification number. The other bag, from the Apollo 17 mission, was sold by Ary in 2001 and later recovered. Ary, who served three years in prison and paid $132,274 in restitution, has maintained his innocence, claiming accidental mixing of museum and private artifacts. The legal battle highlights the complex ownership and preservation of historical space artifacts, with Carlson expected to decide the bag's future, possibly for public display.

Phillip Boyle and Jamie Blyth, two lads from Middlesbrough, found themselves in a wild predicament after a night of heavy drinking led to an impromptu trip to Thailand. The story, first reported by The Gazette, details how the pair, who started their Friday night at The Southern Cross in Marton with a 'quiet pint,' ended up jetting out to Thailand in a drunken haze. Phillip, a 33-year-old company director from Nunthorpe, admits, "It was around the bend there," referring to the holiday resort of Pattaya. Despite a few moments of hesitation as the alcohol wore off, the pair had the time of their lives, with Phillip noting, "We went out for meals and to bars and didn’t really sleep that much." Jamie, a 33-year-old rigger from Marton and the instigator of the trip, echoed this, saying, "It’s been great."

Phillip’s initial packing was minimal, with him stuffing a few T-shirts and boxer shorts into a carrier bag. However, he managed to upgrade his gear, purchasing a new backpack and a pair of trainers during their stay. Unfortunately, the trainers were stolen, leaving Phillip to wear his work shoes for the remainder of the trip. Phillip’s journey to Pattaya was a whirlwind, with the pair only staying for a couple of days. They landed in Abu Dhabi for a layover, where they sobered up and questioned their decision, but ultimately decided to make the most of it. Phillip admitted, "We were a bit confused in Abu Dhabi at the stop over but just thought ‘We’re here now so we should just make the most of it.'”

Jamie, who has a new girlfriend, said, "She was a bit annoyed, but it was only two days - a short break. She’s just been laughing about it and thought we were daft." Phillip, however, is not regretting the decision, stating, "I would recommend it - it’s been brilliant fun." The pair’s story has gone viral, with many people sharing their own similar experiences of spontaneous travel due to excessive drinking. The moral of the story seems to be, as Phillip puts it, "Don’t drink in the north of England." At least, not without packing a bag first.

After President Trump and Republicans in Congress spent much of the year trying to repeal the Affordable Care Act (ACA) and cut spending on Medicaid, a half-century-old entitlement program that covers one in five Americans, the pro-expansion side in Maine is hoping to benefit from energized public support for Medicaid expansion. The main challenge is voter turnout, as there are no national or statewide races to drive people to the polls this year. Governor Paul LePage, who has a consistent stance against Medicaid expansion, has attacked Maine’s hospitals for supporting the ballot measure, which would provide free healthcare to about 70,000 low-income Mainers. He argues that hospitals are benefiting financially “on the backs” of Maine taxpayers and that Medicaid expansion would burden the state’s taxpayers. However, the state’s Office of Program and Fiscal Review estimates that state taxpayers would be on the hook for $54 million per year, while the federal government would provide $525 million annually for Medicaid expansion.

Advocates for Medicaid expansion argue that it would result in numerous benefits, such as making the population healthier and more likely to access preventive care, creating 4,000 jobs in the healthcare industry, and driving down the uninsured rate. The uninsured rate in Maine was 9.1% in 2016, according to Gallup polling. LePage has vetoed five attempts by the Legislature to approve Medicaid expansion but would not be able to do so if voters approve the referendum on November 7. The governor’s relationship with Maine hospitals has soured considerably since 2013, when he fought a successful battle with the Legislature to pay off $105 million in unpaid MaineCare reimbursements to hospitals. The money came from a bond financed with state revenues from a new wholesale liquor contract. LePage has characterized the payoff as an investment in jobs because of the capital it would provide to hospitals.

Maine Medical Center responded to the governor’s criticism by stating that while they do not share his point of view, they understand his consistent position regarding Medicaid expansion. Medicaid expansion would put struggling rural hospitals on more solid financial footing and help them with workforce shortages to attract doctors and nurses. The federal government is paying 90% or more of the cost of covering the expansion population, and Maine is one of 19 states – and the only one in New England – that hasn’t approved Medicaid expansion. Instead, the state has reduced Medicaid eligibility since LePage took office in 2011, cutting off Medicaid for childless adults and tightening eligibility for parents. Medicaid expansion would not take away care for the elderly and disabled, as states have some leeway on how to spend Medicaid money, and expanding Medicaid would not hamper programs for the elderly or intellectually disabled.

Tesla has filed a patent for an automated turn signal system that could remind drivers to use their signals by detecting the car's steering angle and the driver's intended lane change or turn. This technology, which leverages Tesla's Autopilot hardware, could potentially reduce the frequency of accidents caused by drivers forgetting to signal. While the system is not intended for fully autonomous driving, it could be a useful feature for manual drivers. Tesla has not yet confirmed when or if this technology will be implemented in their vehicles. The patent application describes the system as capable of activating the turn signal if the car's processor determines the driver intends to change lanes or turn based on the steering angle. This could be a significant improvement for drivers who frequently forget to use their turn signals, enhancing road safety.

Indoor tanning beds are not just a fashion statement but a significant financial burden, according to a recent study published in the Journal of Cancer Policy. The research reveals that skin cancers linked to indoor tanning cost the U.S. healthcare system approximately $343 million annually. This figure does not account for the broader economic impact, including lost productivity and early deaths, which the study estimates to exceed $127 billion over the lifetime of those diagnosed with these cancers. The study, co-authored by Hugh Waters of the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, analyzed the costs associated with treating melanoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and basal cell carcinoma, which are linked to the use of tanning beds. Using data on the prevalence of tanning device use and the increased cancer risk associated with indoor tanning, researchers calculated the number of skin cancer cases attributable to tanning beds in 2015. The findings indicate that tanning beds were linked to 8,947 cases of melanoma, more than 168,000 cases of squamous cell carcinoma, and at least 86,000 cases of basal cell carcinoma. The average cost of treating melanoma was estimated at $5,054 per case, while the typical cost for other skin cancers was $1,168. Additionally, the study factored in the economic loss over the lifetime of individuals diagnosed with these cancers, based on the value of a lost year of life, resulting in a reduction of gross domestic product (GDP) of $55,266 per year of life lost. While the study provides a comprehensive look at the financial impact of indoor tanning, it acknowledges potential underestimation due to the exclusion of long-term medical and productivity costs. Critics argue that the study may overestimate the economic costs associated with indoor tanning, as the health risks and costs of natural sun exposure may be higher. Nonetheless, the findings underscore the significant health and financial burden associated with indoor tanning and highlight the need for continued efforts to reduce its use.

Julian Assange, the founder of WikiLeaks, has expressed strong disapproval of the new DreamWorks film "The Fifth Estate," starring Benedict Cumberbatch as Assange. Assange wrote a letter to Cumberbatch, declining to meet with the actor and criticizing the film's accuracy and intentions. In his letter, Assange states, "I believe you are a good person, but I do not believe that this film is a good film," and warns that the film will "bury good people doing good work" and "smother the truthful version of events." He argues that the film is based on "deceitful" books and is a "work of political opportunism, influence, revenge, and, above all, cowardice." Assange is concerned that the film will negatively impact his and his organization's reputation and the truth of their work. He also expresses worry about the film's potential to harm people who may be affected by its portrayal. Cumberbatch, in a courteous response, admitted that aspects of the script troubled him. Assange's letter highlights his ongoing conflict with the U.S. government and its allies, who are pursuing him and his sources through "a whole of government investigation" under espionage laws. Assange fears that the film will be used to further the campaign against him and his organization.

Twitter is exploring the development of an in-house video-hosting service, according to sources, aiming to enhance user experience and better control content. This move aligns with Twitter's trend of integrating more features in-house, such as photo hosting, to improve consistency and user interaction. While Twitter expects most users to continue sharing videos via external platforms like YouTube and Vimeo, the potential in-house solution could offer better monetization opportunities and a richer media experience, particularly for promoted tweets. However, this change could impact third-party hosting services, which currently benefit from official Twitter app integration. The decision is still under consideration, and if implemented, it would likely be introduced quietly in a future update.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved Plan B One-Step emergency contraception for over-the-counter sale to women 15 years and older, with a prescription required for those younger. This decision partially complies with a federal judge's ruling from April, which mandated the removal of all age restrictions. The FDA stated that research showed women 15 and older could understand and use the product correctly, and it does not prevent sexually transmitted diseases. However, the age limit of 15 means women still need to present identification to purchase the pill, and the FDA noted that it does not address the challenges faced by women without ID or during late hours. Senator Patty Murray praised the decision, calling it a step towards science-based policies, while the Center for Reproductive Rights expressed dissatisfaction, arguing that the ruling should have been fully implemented. The FDA's move aims to reduce unintended pregnancies, but critics point out that barriers remain for women seeking emergency contraception.

President Donald Trump's personal attorney, Michael Cohen, has been under criminal investigation for months due to his business dealings, according to court documents obtained by ABC News. Federal prosecutors in New York conducted raids on Monday, searching Cohen's home, office, safety deposit boxes, and two cellphones. Cohen's attorneys have filed a temporary restraining order to prevent prosecutors from using some of the seized records, arguing that at least some of the documents are subject to attorney-client privilege. The prosecutors assert that Cohen "is in fact performing little to no legal work and that zero emails were exchanged with President Trump," based on a privilege review of previously obtained emails. Cohen has not been charged with any crime and has declined to comment. The Southern District of New York prosecutors have set up a "taint team" to filter out privileged material, but Cohen's lawyers are requesting to review the material themselves or for a "special master" to decide what is relevant. The hearing on the matter was initially scheduled without notice, but news organizations successfully argued for most of the hearing to be held in public. Judge Kimba Wood ordered the parties to return to court on Monday for another hearing, where Cohen must be present.

A senior North Korean official has dismissed remarks by US Vice-President Mike Pence as "stupid," casting further uncertainty about a planned meeting between the two countries' leaders. Choe Son-hui, a top aide to Kim Jong-un, said the North would not "beg" for dialogue and warned of a "nuclear showdown" if diplomacy failed. This comes amid recent tensions, with both sides indicating the 12 June Trump-Kim summit could be delayed or even called off. North Korea insists it will not give up its nuclear weapons unilaterally. Choe's statement, published by the state news agency KCNA, criticized Pence's comparison of North Korea to Libya, where the Gaddafi regime was overthrown and its leader killed after renouncing nuclear weapons. Choe warned that the US could "taste an appalling tragedy it has neither experienced nor even imagined" if the summit is canceled. The North Korean official stated, "Whether the US will meet us at a meeting room or encounter us at nuclear-to-nuclear showdown is entirely dependent upon the decision and behavior of the United States." Meanwhile, North Korea is pressing ahead with plans to dismantle its only nuclear testing facility later this week. The Punggye-ri site, located in a remote part of the north-west of the country, is set to be dismantled, with a group of international journalists invited to observe the event. The planned summit has faced several speed bumps, with both sides trading barbs and taking tougher positions. Despite the insults and defiant rhetoric, officials from the two sides are reportedly planning to meet in Singapore this weekend to further discuss the agenda and logistics. The North Korean statement reflects a growing tension between the two countries, with North Korea pushing back against perceived insults and hard-line comments suggesting it may end up like Libya if it doesn't move forward with concrete measures to get rid of its nuclear weapons.

In a recent break-in at Sandra Bullock's home, the 39-year-old intruder, identified as Joshua Corbett, may have been obsessed with the Oscar-winning actress, law enforcement sources tell Today. Corbett, arrested on suspicion of burglary after rummaging through Bullock's personal belongings, might have even kept a diary devoted to her. The incident occurred just hours after Bullock celebrated her win at the Spike TV Guys' Choice Awards. Officers responded to the call of a prowler around 6:30 a.m., finding Bullock unharmed and fine inside her home with her 4-year-old son Louis. This event raises concerns about the level of obsession the intruder had towards Bullock, given her stringent security measures.

A Texas man scheduled to be executed next week for murdering his 2-year-old daughter has been granted a stay of execution by the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals. The court's decision, based on a recent state law, allows legal challenges based on new scientific evidence potentially pointing to wrongful convictions. Robert Roberson, 49, was convicted in 2002 of killing his daughter, Nikki Curtis, after taking her to the hospital with fatal head injuries. His lawyers argue his conviction was based on "junk science" and "false, misleading, and scientifically invalid testimony." They contend new scientific evidence shows his conviction was unjust, as the injuries could have been caused by a fall, a fever, or other medical conditions. Prosecutors originally claimed Roberson sexually abused his daughter, but dropped that charge during the trial. The court sent Roberson's case back to the trial court for further review. The case highlights the controversial use of shaken baby syndrome as evidence in criminal cases, as medical consensus has shifted, and new research suggests such injuries can result from accidental falls or other factors. The execution has been postponed indefinitely, pending the outcome of the appeal.

John Roberts, in a surprising move, upheld the Affordable Care Act (ACA) as a tax, joining the liberal wing of the Supreme Court while simultaneously rolling back the Commerce Clause. This decision, while preserving the ACA, marks a significant shift in federal regulatory powers. The article argues that Roberts' move was strategic, designed to limit Congress' ability to regulate in the future, rather than a simple act of upholding the ACA. The piece contrasts Roberts' more approachable demeanor with that of his conservative colleagues, who are portrayed as more ideologically driven. It suggests that Roberts' decision, while celebrated by some, opens the door for future challenges to other federal regulations. The summary highlights the complex political and legal implications of Roberts' ruling, noting that it may not be seen as judicial activism but rather as a calculated move to limit federal power.

A woman in Taunton, Massachusetts, narrowly escaped her home moments before it exploded and burst into flames on Sunday. Laurie Beliveau, 52, was attempting to repair her gas-fueled hot water heater and removed the gas shut-off valve, which caused gas to pour into the basement. An unknown ignition source ignited the gas, leading to a powerful explosion. Neighbors reported feeling the ground shake and seeing smoke billowing from the rooftop. Beliveau's neighbor, Paul Saltalamacchia, said she ran two doors down to his home screaming for help, where he and his son provided her with sandals and a glass of water. Saltalamacchia recounted that Beliveau was hysterically talking to the fire department about a gas fireplace and lamented that her pet cockatoo was still inside. The fire department's Lieutenant Kevin C. Farrar said the incident was a graphic reminder to homeowners not to attempt repairs unless by a qualified person. The explosion leveled the home, with everything caving in, leaving nothing salvageable. Taunton Deputy Fire Chief Scott Dexter said an ongoing investigation suspects a gas leak caused the blast. Columbia Gas of Massachusetts, which has not yet commented on the incident, advises residents to leave their homes immediately and avoid operating any utilities in the event of a leak. The Northern Bristol County Registry of Deeds has an affidavit filed in August regarding a foreclosure of Beliveau's home, though it is unclear if this is related to the incident.

A federal judge in Hawaii issued a nationwide temporary restraining order on the Trump administration's revised travel ban just hours before it was set to take effect, sparking immediate criticism from the president. U.S. District Judge Derrick Watson's ruling, which came less than two hours before the executive order was to go into effect, stated that a reasonable, objective observer would conclude the ban was issued with a purpose to disfavor a particular religion. President Trump, speaking at a rally in Nashville, denounced the decision as an "unprecedented judicial overreach," accusing the court of being motivated by "political reasons." He expressed his intention to fight the ruling, vowing to take the case as far as necessary, including up to the Supreme Court, to protect the nation's security. Trump also criticized the revised order, calling it a "watered-down version" of the first, which was previously blocked by a federal judge in Washington state. The president emphasized that steps were taken to defend the order against further legal challenges, stating that the new order was tailored to the "dictates" of the 9th Circuit's ruling. Despite the setback, Trump maintained his commitment to keeping the country safe, asserting, "We are going to win. We are going to keep our citizens safe and regardless, we are going to keep our citizens safe, believe me." The day before the ruling, Trump honored the 250th anniversary of Andrew Jackson's birth, praising the former president as "one of our great presidents" and drawing parallels between their populist stances. The visit to Jackson's home in Nashville, Tennessee, was described by Trump as "inspirational," reflecting his ongoing efforts to connect his presidency with historical figures who embody his political ideology.

The British Royal Air Force has sparked controversy by sending a message to ISIS, reportedly scrawling "Love From Manchester ❤" on the exterior of a bomb. The image, confirmed by the Ministry of Defence, has been circulating on social media, drawing mixed reactions. Jeremy Corbyn, the Labour leader, has used the incident to criticize the UK's foreign policy, linking it to the recent terrorist attack in Manchester. He argues that the "war on terror" has not effectively kept the country safe and suggests that the UK's military involvement abroad may contribute to the conditions that foster extremism. Corbyn's comments come as the Labour leader calls for a reevaluation of the UK's approach to military intervention, citing the Chilcot enquiry which highlighted the increase in terrorism threats following the Iraq invasion in 2003. He emphasizes the need to ensure police resources, reduce the threat through foreign policy, and protect civil liberties. The Labour leader's stance contrasts with the sentiment expressed on the bomb, which many find disrespectful and insensitive to the victims of the Manchester attack. Humanitarian aid workers, like those working in Syria and Iraq, echo Corbyn's concerns, pointing out the devastating impact of foreign military actions on innocent civilians. They argue that such actions do not bring comfort to the victims or help the city heal, and instead, they question the morality and effectiveness of using bombs to combat terrorism. The controversy surrounding the bomb message highlights the complex relationship between military intervention and the rise of extremism, prompting a broader discussion on the UK's foreign policy and its impact on global security.

The Comedy Central Roast of Justin Bieber, featuring a star-studded panel including Hannibal Buress, Chris D'Elia, Snoop Dogg, Natasha Leggero, Ludacris, Shaquille O'Neal, Jeff Ross, Martha Stewart, and roasting master Kevin Hart, aimed to hold the teen idol over an open flame. However, the event felt more like a networking opportunity than a roast, with many participants seemingly more focused on their own careers than Justin Bieber's. Hannibal Buress's candid comments hinted at the underlying tension, stating he was only there for the opportunity to appear likable. The roast's humor was often tasteless, with Chris D'Elia's set being particularly offensive, touching on taboo subjects like rape and ISIS. Despite the attempts to rehabilitate his image, Justin Bieber seemed uncomfortable throughout, with the event feeling more like a missed opportunity to deliver a genuine roast. The night's highlights included Pete Davidson's heartfelt opening monologue and Snoop Dogg's animated rant about a racial slur, but overall, the roast failed to live up to its potential.

German Chancellor Angela Merkel and U.S. President Barack Obama discussed the reported U.S. spying on European allies during a phone call, with Merkel expressing her concerns over the alleged surveillance. Merkel stated that she believed Obama took the matter seriously and hoped for answers through upcoming high-level bilateral talks and planned EU-U.S. discussions on intelligence and privacy issues. German Interior Minister Hans-Peter Friedrich is scheduled to travel to the U.S. to address the issue. Following a poll showing a decline in trust in the U.S. among Germans, Merkel emphasized that spying on EU institutions is unacceptable. The White House assured Merkel that the U.S. would provide information on the allegations. Meanwhile, European lawmakers approved an in-depth inquiry into U.S. surveillance programs, and the issue dominated EU ambassadors' discussions ahead of upcoming talks on a U.S.-EU trade deal. France called for a delay in the trade negotiations, but the European Commission stated that the talks would proceed. Der Spiegel reported that the U.S. National Security Agency (NSA) had bugged EU offices in Washington and New York and conducted an electronic eavesdropping operation in an EU building in Brussels. The European Commission plans to sweep its offices for security breaches. The potential U.S.-EU trade deal, if successful, could add significant economic benefits to both regions.

Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) has stated he will no longer support Richard Mourdock, the Indiana Senate candidate, unless Mourdock apologizes for his recent comments on rape. McCain told CNN's Anderson Cooper that he would reconsider his support if Mourdock apologized, saying, "If he apologizes and says he misspoke and he was wrong and he asks the people to forgive him, then obviously I’d be the first." However, Mourdock has not apologized, instead clarifying that he regretted his words had been misinterpreted. Meanwhile, President Obama criticized Mourdock's comments, calling them wrong and stating that "rape is rape." The Obama campaign has used Mourdock's remarks to pressure Mitt Romney to distance himself from the candidate, with press secretary Andrea Saul maintaining that "Gov. Romney disagrees with Richard Mourdock, and Mr. Mourdock's comments do not reflect Gov. Romney's views." Other Republicans, including Sen. John McCain, are also considering their stance on Mourdock, with McCain's support contingent on Mourdock's actions. The Romney campaign has not asked Mourdock to stop using an ad featuring Romney, but still distances itself from his statements. The controversy has intensified, with Mourdock's comments potentially impacting the Indiana Senate race and the broader political landscape.

A tragic wedding turned into a nightmare in Bhopal when a 30-year-old cousin shot dead his 26-year-old first cousin, a doctor, during the reception. Anurag Namdeo, who had bought a pistol the day before, planned the murder for 20 days after discovering Jayshree Namdeo's engagement on Facebook. Jayshree, the only child of her parents, worked at Gandhi Medical College. Her family disapproved of Anurag's interest, but he repeatedly threatened them. On the night of the wedding, Anurag entered the hall, masked his face, and climbed onto the dais. He shot Jayshree just below her throat, narrowly missing the groom, Rohit Namdeo. Anurag attempted to shoot himself but was overpowered by guests. Jayshree was rushed to a nearby hospital but was pronounced dead. Anurag was severely injured and hospitalized. His father had passed away, and he worked as a bank supervisor. Anurag's cousin, Shailendra, revealed that Anurag had threatened relatives who tried to dissuade him. He had posted threatening messages and photos on Facebook. Jayshree's father, Ghanshyam Das, expressed shock at the incident, stating they had never thought Anurag would go that far. The shooting left one guest injured, and the police intervened, taking Anurag away. The incident highlights the deep-seated issues of family honor and the lengths some individuals will go to protect it.

New regulations aimed at reducing Brazil's high rate of Cesarean sections took effect, with the government hoping to steer the country away from its status as a global leader in C-section births. The rules and a campaign called "Childbirth is normal!" address what Health Minister Arthur Chioro has dubbed an "epidemic" of Cesareans, currently accounting for more than half of births in Brazil. About 84 percent of Brazilian mothers on private health care undergo the operation, often for no other reason than convenience, with 40 percent of births in public hospitals also being C-sections. This still tops the 32 percent rate in the United States and is massively higher than the World Health Organisation's recommendations of 10 to 15 percent. The new rules require doctors and hospitals to share information with patients, notably the number of C-sections they have already carried out. When they fail to provide requested information, health insurance companies face fines of up to $8,000. Making patients better informed will help diminish the rush for C-sections, health officials say. "Childbirth is one of the most important moments in the life of a woman and her family," said Jose Carlos de Souza Abrahao, director of ANS, a specialized health ministry agency. "By informing her of the risks that could come with an unnecessary surgical procedure, she will be more sure in her decision regarding the delivery, choosing what's best for her health and for her baby's health." Mass Cesareans are Brazil's "international shame," pediatrician Luciana Herrero told AFP. Ignorance and desire for convenience drive Brazilian mothers-to-be to the operating table, said the author of the just published book "Diario de Bordo do Parto," or "Guide to Childbirth." Even when fees for a Cesarean and normal birth don't vary, the surgical option is still more profitable for hospitals because it can be scheduled to the minute and has little of the unpredictability— and possibly long working hours—of natural labor. Cesareans may be convenient but can also be dangerous for the mother and potentially pose grave future health consequences for the baby, ranging from an increased risk of obesity to chronic illness. However, the latest government effort is still insufficient. "I believe the solution must include other sectors of society and be discussed openly with all involved... so that together we can put births in Brazil onto a new path," said Herrero. The office of a private maternity clinic in Sao Paulo is described as immaculate, with sterile, white, modish plastic furniture and green plants. The list of services at the clinic is long, but one thing they rarely do here is preside over a vaginal delivery. Dr. Alexandre Sasaoka struggles to remember the last time he assisted at one. And he's not alone. Brazil has one of the world's highest rates of cesarean deliveries: Some 80 to 90 percent of women in private hospitals in the country give birth via cesarean section. Much higher than the U.S. rate of 30 percent and 1 in 4 women in Britain. But Brazil's economic boom of the past decade has dragged some 40 million people into the middle class. The emphasis on status begins at birth— and cesarean deliveries are the Louis Vuitton of the maternity world. Women in Brazil want C-sections, says Sasaoka. They like them because they prefer being able to schedule their delivery and better organize their busy lives. Doctors like Sasaoka say they also recommend them. He says he doesn't think they are necessarily better, but that a woman needs to consider more than just the medical aspect of birth, such as the impact on her and her family. Of course, he says, there are many advantages to a natural birth; C-sections are a major surgery, after all. But he says women ask for C-sections, and they also allow doctors to be better organized. For example, he says, doctors don't have to interrupt what they are doing with other patients to assist a natural birth. Pressure from doctors is another factor. New mother Mariana, who doesn't want her last name used for fear of offending her doctor, says often women feel bullied into it. She says she wanted to have a vaginal delivery. "My doctor said to me he'd have more control in a C-section than in a natural birth," she says. He also told her he would almost certainly have to do an episiotomy—a procedure where the vaginal opening gets cut to allow for delivery. She was terrified. She says her doctor kept telling her that C-sections were better, and that she felt pressure to have one. Still, Mariana decided to try to give birth naturally. Then two weeks before her due date, her blood pressure spiked. And her doctor said she needed to have a C-section after all. The next day she was in the operating room. To this day she wonders if it was really necessary. She says that's the legacy of all the intervention here. "I don't know. I think he was right," she says. "But the problem in Brazil is we lack the trust between doctor and patient." Brazil has a two-tiered medical system. The C-section rate in public hospitals is much lower, the result of a government push to reduce medical costs associated with C-sections. But in private hospitals, cesarean deliveries are seen as status symbols. And that, say natural childbirth advocates, has to change. While doulas—or birth coaches—are a regular presence in many maternity wards these days in the U.S., they are still uncommon in Brazil. But they are the first port of call for couples looking to have a natural birth. Doula Mariana de Mesquita talks to a couple who say they are having trouble finding a doctor who is willing to deliver their baby vaginally. She says her profession basically disappeared with the rise of C-sections. And she says one of the most important roles she has these days is education. "Most women don't even know how long labor can last, the basics," de Mesquita says. "So I teach them what a normal birth is like, what they can expect." Brazil essentially copied the North American obstetric model, which is very interventionist, she says. De Mesquita adds that doctors do get paid more for C-sections, which is another reason for their prevalence. But she also blames women here. She says Brazilian women aren't afraid of surgery. There is a lot of plastic surgery, for example. "Women put themselves at risk for very little," de Mesquita says. She says people in Brazil see C-sections as a sign of women's liberation, but she sees them as "a sign of their submissiveness to a violent medical system."

An elderly man in Plano, Texas, died early Thursday when he rushed back into a burning home to retrieve his cell phone, according to local fire officials. The fire, which broke out shortly after 1 a.m. in the 800 block of Haggard Street, initially trapped three adults—two men and a woman—in the house. All three managed to escape, but the two men decided to re-enter the burning building to retrieve their phones to call 911. Plano Fire and Rescue Capt. Peggy Harrell stated that the house was fully engulfed in flames when firefighters arrived, three minutes after the initial call. The unidentified companion managed to escape, but 72-year-old Rex Benson was unable to re-emerge alive. Harrell emphasized the danger of re-entering a burning building, noting that around 90% of people who attempt to do so do not survive. Benson lived in the one-story brick house with his adult daughter and an unidentified roommate. Neighbors expressed shock and sadness over the incident, with one neighbor, Scott Hampton, stating, "Great guy, willing to help anyone who needed a hand; and to hear he made that big of a mistake and the loss of life because of something as simple as a cellphone seems sad." The cause of the fire remains under investigation, with no suspicion of foul play.

A murder suspect, Jayveon Caballero, remains at large following a shooting in Montpelier that left Markus Austin, 33, dead. Caballero, a former Vermont Frost Heaves basketball player, is wanted for second-degree murder. The shooting occurred early Sunday morning outside an apartment complex in Montpelier. Caballero and Austin had been involved in an altercation at Gustos bar in Barre, where Austin allegedly assaulted Caballero's girlfriend, Desiree Cary. Caballero later confronted Austin outside his apartment and shot him. Caballero's girlfriend, 22-year-old Cary, was arrested on unrelated drug charges and is in custody. Caballero is believed to have boarded a bus in White River Junction, possibly headed for New York City, as police continue to search for him. The shooting marks the first murder in Montpelier, a city of about 7,500 residents, in nearly a century. Caballero's girlfriend was taken into custody in Barre and is facing charges of selling crack cocaine and heroin. Caballero's apartment was searched early Monday, but he was not found. The search for Caballero continues, with police urging anyone with information to contact them.

Apple CEO Tim Cook has reshuffled the company’s management to focus on improving its user experience, particularly following the disastrous launch of the Maps application. Cook, known for his meticulous attention to detail and operational efficiency, has taken a more direct role in overseeing the evolution of the user interface. Scott Forstall, who was in charge of iOS and had been a vocal proponent of the Maps app, was reportedly let go due to his inability to sign Apple’s public apology for the app’s shortcomings. Cook’s move signals a shift towards a more unified and focused approach, with Jony Ive, the company’s chief designer, taking over responsibility for human interfaces across all Apple products. This change is part of a broader strategy to ensure that Apple’s products meet the high standards expected by its customers. Cook’s letter to employees emphasized the company’s commitment to excellence, stating, “Everything we do at Apple is aimed at making our products the best in the world.” The reshuffle is also part of a larger organizational restructuring, with Bob Mansfield leading a new group focused on fostering innovation in wireless technologies and semiconductors. This move suggests Apple is preparing for future technological challenges and opportunities, particularly in the realm of smart home devices, where it aims to leverage its existing technologies to create new business opportunities.

Pope Francis, the first Latin American and Jesuit pope, officially inaugurated his papacy with a Mass in St. Peter's Square, marking a new era of humility and service for the Catholic Church. The Mass, attended by up to 200,000 people, including dignitaries from 132 countries and international organizations, was notably simpler and shorter than that of his predecessor, Benedict XVI, reflecting Francis’s commitment to a more modest and accessible leadership style. In his homily, Francis emphasized the importance of protecting the poor, the weak, and the environment, drawing inspiration from the 13th-century St. Francis of Assisi, from whom he took his papal name. He warned against the consequences of failing to care for one another and the environment, urging leaders to be protectors of humanity and nature. The new pope’s humility was evident in his interactions with the crowd, as he stopped to kiss babies and bless a disabled man, and in his choice of black shoes instead of the red loafers worn by Benedict. His inaugural address also highlighted his desire for the Church to return to its mission of service, stating, “Let us not forget that hatred, envy, and pride defile our lives. Being protectors, then, also means keeping watch over our emotions, over our hearts.” Francis’s election has been widely welcomed by Catholics, with 85 percent of those surveyed in the United States expressing a favorable view of him. The new pope’s first official act was to call his compatriots in Buenos Aires, thanking them for their prayers and urging them to walk together. His selection as pope sent a powerful message that the future of the Church lies in the Global South, home to the bulk of the world’s Catholics. As he begins his papacy, Pope Francis faces the challenges of a Church mired in scandals, including a sexual abuse crisis and allegations of corruption, but his emphasis on service and humility has already resonated with many.

The Weinstein Company, once a powerhouse in Hollywood, has filed for bankruptcy, marking a significant turn in the company's tumultuous journey. The move comes as the studio attempts to address the fallout from numerous allegations of sexual misconduct against Harvey Weinstein, who was the company's co-founder. The bankruptcy filing, which was submitted to Delaware's bankruptcy court, positions Lantern Asset Management as the potential buyer of the company's assets, with an offer from an affiliate of Lantern Capital Partners. This offer, which sets the floor for higher and better bidders, is part of a court-supervised auction process. The company's bankruptcy filing lists between $500 million to $1 billion in assets and liabilities, with an estimated $500 million to $1 billion in liabilities. 

Crucially, the company's board has taken a significant step towards justice for victims by releasing all employees from non-disclosure agreements, stating, "No one should be afraid to speak out or coerced to stay quiet." This move, which was long sought by New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman, who filed a lawsuit against the company on behalf of its employees, is seen as a "watershed moment." Schneiderman expressed satisfaction with the decision, tweeting, "The Weinstein Company's agreement to release victims of and witnesses to sexual misconduct from NDAs will finally allow voices that have too long been muzzled to be heard—something my office has sought from the start."

The bankruptcy filing comes after the company's attempts to sell its assets to an investor group led by former Obama administration official Maria Contreras-Sweet fell through. The deal was terminated when the group discovered that the company had more liabilities than previously disclosed. Other potential buyers, including Lions Gate Entertainment Corp and the Qatar-owned film company Miramax, were also interested in the company's assets. The bankruptcy filing provides immediate relief by pausing pending civil matters, including Schneiderman's lawsuit and other cases now being pursued by others. The company's chairman, Bob Weinstein, stated, "While we had hoped to reach a sale out of court, the Board is pleased to have a plan for maximizing the value of its assets, preserving as many jobs as possible, and pursuing justice for any victims."

The bankruptcy process will likely face scrutiny from creditors, including those in the entertainment industry who are owed residual payments, female accusers, and investors. The possibility of criminal cases against Weinstein could also impact the proceedings. As the company navigates this complex landscape, the hope is that the bankruptcy filing will provide a path towards justice and closure for those affected by the company's past actions.

North Korea's leader, Kim Jong-un, reportedly ordered the execution of two high-ranking officials in early August, according to South Korea’s JoongAng Ilbo newspaper, citing unnamed sources. Ri Yong-jin, a senior official in the education ministry, was arrested for dozing off during a meeting with Kim and charged with corruption before being killed. Former Agriculture Minister Hwang Min was purged over a proposed project seen as a direct challenge to Kim’s leadership. If true, these executions would mark the first such actions by Kim from outside his party or the military. A spokesman at South Korea’s Unification Ministry could not immediately confirm the report. Since taking power in 2011, Kim has carried out a series of executions, including the most high-profile case of his uncle, Jang Song-thaek, who was executed in 2013 for treason. In 2014, Kim had about 50 officials executed on charges ranging from graft to watching South Korean soap operas. Robert Kelly, a political science professor at South Korea’s Pusan National University, noted that the charges were likely trumped up and that promotions or demotions often work in totalitarian states without legitimate opposition venues.

The JoongAng Ilbo’s report suggests that these executions aim to generate fear among the regime's elite after recent high-level defections. South Korean President Park Geun-hye stated that the defections signal a "serious fracture" within the North Korean regime and raise the prospects of fresh provocations as Kim seeks to maintain control. However, Professor Kelly at Pusan University argued that the isolated state is probably more stable than many people think, given that China keeps the economic lifelines flowing to Pyongyang. The executions, if confirmed, could be seen as a new reign of terror in North Korea, intended to reinforce loyalty among the elite in response to recent defections.

Robert B. Sherman, half of the sibling songwriting duo the Sherman Brothers, passed away at 86 in London. Known for crafting memorable tunes for Disney films and theme parks, Sherman's work includes "Mary Poppins," "The Jungle Book," and "It's a Small World." His songs, like "A Spoonful of Sugar," are both complex and instantly recognizable, bringing joy to millions. Sherman's legacy, alongside his brother Richard, spans over 150 songs and multiple awards, including the National Medal of Arts. His unique approach to writing, ensuring songs resonated with all ages, contributed to their enduring popularity.

President Barack Obama is set to become the first sitting U.S. president to visit Cuba in nearly 90 years, marking a significant milestone in the normalization of relations between the two countries. Obama announced the March 21-22 trip via Twitter, tweeting, "Next month, I'll travel to Cuba to advance our progress and efforts that can improve the lives of the Cuban people." The visit, part of a broader Latin American trip, aims to continue the progress made since Obama and Cuban President Raul Castro began normalizing ties in 2014. The White House has already made significant strides, including reopening embassies and restoring commercial air travel. Obama will meet with Cuban President Raul Castro, as well as entrepreneurs and members of Cuban society, to discuss further reforms and opportunities for U.S. businesses and travelers. First Lady Michelle Obama will accompany the president on his trip to Cuba, followed by a visit to Argentina. The move has drawn criticism from Republican presidential candidates, with Florida Senators Marco Rubio and Ted Cruz denouncing the visit as premature. Rubio called the Cuban government an "anti-American communist dictatorship," while Cruz stated, "Probably not going to invite me." Despite opposition, Obama sees the visit as a step forward in improving the lives of the Cuban people and charting a new course for U.S.-Cuban relations. The trip is seen as a continuation of Obama's broader foreign policy strategy of engaging with traditional U.S. foes to achieve concrete results. The last sitting U.S. president to visit Cuba was Calvin Coolidge in 1928, and since then, the relationship has been marked by decades of hostility. With less than a year left in office, Obama is eager to cement the rapprochement with Cuba, though the lifting of the U.S. economic embargo remains a sticking point. The visit is expected to provide a lasting illustration of Obama's belief that diplomacy can yield positive outcomes, even with adversaries.

A tragic incident occurred on a roof in River Falls, Wisconsin, where a four-man crew was working on replacing shingles. According to the complaint, Miguel Navarro, one of the workers, allegedly cut his co-worker, Juan Valles-Flores, with a circular saw, causing Valles-Flores to fall backward onto the garage roof. Witnesses reported that Navarro continued to cut Valles-Flores after he fell, while the other two co-workers reportedly jumped off the roof and hid until police arrived. The complaint notes that there was no apparent argument leading up to the attack, but Valles-Flores had reportedly been teased and felt he was not being paid fairly, and possibly drugged to work more. Valles-Flores died on the garage roof, sustaining 10 sharp force injuries across his face, neck, back, and lower and upper extremities, as well as a transection of the jugular vein and carotid artery, according to a provisional autopsy. Navarro was charged with first-degree intentional homicide, which carries a life sentence, and an additional charge of mayhem, which carries a maximum sentence of 40 years in prison and a $100,000 fine. Navarro was being held in Pierce County Jail on a $500,000 cash bond.

In Brussels, the family of Najim Laachraoui, a suspected suicide bomber involved in the March 22 attacks, expressed shock and disbelief at his alleged radicalization. Laachraoui, a 25-year-old Belgian, was one of the suicide bombers at the airport, according to security sources. His brother, Mourad, described Najim as a "nice, intelligent boy" who showed no signs of radicalization before leaving for Syria in 2013. Mourad said the family had warned the police about Najim's departure to Syria and that the police had visited their home. Mourad, a taekwondo athlete, emphasized that his brother was a "very good student" and had never failed a class during his six years at the Institut de la Sainte Famille d'Helmet, a Catholic school in Brussels. The family remains in the dark about what led Najim to radicalize, with Mourad stating, "You don't choose your family." The federal prosecutor confirmed that Laachraoui was the bomber seen on security camera footage, pushing a luggage trolley containing a bomb. He is suspected of being the bomb-maker involved in the November 2015 Paris attacks, with his DNA found on explosive devices at the Bataclan music venue and the Stade de France. Laachraoui also used the false name Soufiane Kayal and was with Salah Abdeslam in Hungary in September 2015. The family's lawyer, Philippe Culot, expressed the family's grief and their determination to prevent their other siblings from becoming radicalized. The family has not received official confirmation of Najim's death, and they are devastated by the news.

As pressure mounts on American retailers to join a landmark safety plan for Bangladesh factories, newly discovered documents reveal that Wal-Mart had been producing jeans at one of the operations in the Rana Plaza building, which collapsed last month, killing over 1,100 workers. The Bangladesh Center for Worker Solidarity provided The New York Times with photos of documents from the rubble, showing that a Wal-Mart contractor had produced jeans at the Ether Tex factory, located on the fifth floor of the collapsed building. Wal-Mart acknowledged the documents but denied any knowledge of the production and emphasized that the documents dated back a year. The company announced new safety measures, promising to conduct in-depth safety inspections at 100% of its 279 factories in Bangladesh and publicize the results online.
