Eva Longoria has given birth to her first child, a son named Santiago Enrique Bastón, with her husband José "Pepe" Bastón. The baby, weighing 6 lbs. 13 oz., was born on June 19 at Cedars-Sinai Medical Center in Los Angeles. Eva and José, who began dating in 2013 and were married in 2016, are excited about their new addition. Santiago will join Bastón’s three children from his previous marriage. Eva, 43, stayed active during her pregnancy and supported the Time's Up movement. She celebrated her baby’s arrival with a pajama party-themed baby shower in May. José is the president of Televisa, the largest media company in Latin America. Santiago’s arrival marks the couple’s two-year wedding anniversary.

Russian skier Maria Komissarova, 23, underwent a successful 6.5-hour surgery after breaking her back during a training crash at the Sochi Olympics. Komissarova, a skicross racer, crashed while training at Rosa Khutor Extreme Park and was immediately taken to Krasnaya Polyanskaya Hospital No. 8 for emergency surgery. Russian President Vladimir Putin visited her in the hospital. The operation was successful, but the extent of her recovery remains unclear. Komissarova, who won a World Cup silver in 2012, is ruled out of competition. The incident highlights the dangers of freestyle skiing, a discipline that debuted in the Winter Olympics in 2010.

Global financial markets received a boost Wednesday as major central banks coordinated to ease liquidity strains amid Europe's debt crisis. The European Central Bank, U.S. Federal Reserve, Bank of England, Bank of Canada, Bank of Japan, and Swiss National Bank took action to provide U.S. dollar liquidity to banks, reducing the cost of temporary dollar loans by 50 basis points. This move aimed to support the supply of credit to households and businesses, mitigating potential economic impacts. The central banks also established temporary bilateral liquidity swap arrangements to ensure banks could access ready money in any currency if needed. These actions came as fears of a credit crunch intensified, with some European banks already relying on central bank loans to fund daily operations. Stock markets reacted positively, with Germany's DAX and Dow futures in New York trading significantly higher. The coordinated efforts underscored the ongoing challenges posed by Europe's debt crisis and the global financial system's vulnerability to such strains.

In Valrico, Dustin Snyder, a 19-year-old with a rare form of cancer, is set to have his dying wish come true this weekend. Diagnosed with synovial sarcoma a day before his 18th birthday, Snyder has been battling the disease since 2016. After surgery to remove his lung and chemotherapy, doctors initially reported the cancer was in remission. However, the cancer returned three times, spreading to his stomach and pelvis, rendering surgery impossible. Snyder now receives hospice care, with a pain pump connected to his heart.

On Monday, Snyder and his girlfriend Sierra Siverio, who met in middle school and reconnected at a Steak 'n Shake, began discussing marriage. Snyder, who has weeks or a month to live, proposed after dinner on Thursday. The couple, overwhelmed by the support from strangers, decided to plan a wedding despite the circumstances. Snyder’s sister, Brittany Hails, posted their story on Facebook, seeking a donated ring and tuxedo. Offers poured in, including a diamond ring, tuxedos, a wedding dress, and even a venue from The Big Red Barn in Plant City. A GoFundMe page raised nearly $13,000 by Friday, with the leftover funds to be used for other expenses, including costs when the day comes for Dustin to be at rest.

Dustin and Sierra have been inseparable since rekindling their relationship, with Sierra by his side through the cancer battle. She believes that God will decide his fate and that they will be together again eventually. Dustin, focusing on making his life the best it can be, shares this optimistic outlook. The couple’s wedding, scheduled for Sunday, January 28, 2018, at The Big Red Barn, will be a celebration of love and support from the community.

Zynga Inc., the social game maker, priced its initial public offering at $10 per share, signaling strong investor demand. The company will begin trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ZNGA. Zynga is the latest in a series of high-profile Internet IPOs this year, following LinkedIn and Groupon. The deal values Zynga at $8.9 billion, far less than the $20 billion expected earlier this year. Zynga's games, including "CityVille" and "FarmVille," are played primarily on Facebook, with about 227 million average monthly users. For the nine months ended Sept. 30, Zynga reported total revenue of $828.9 million, up from $401.7 million in the same period last year. The company plans to use the proceeds for general corporate purposes and possible acquisitions.

Barack Obama's former Harvard Law professor, Roberto Unger, has publicly declared that the President must be defeated in the 2012 election, despite their close relationship during Obama's time at the university. Unger, a respected Brazilian politician and author, argues that Obama has failed to advance the progressive cause and has spent trillions of dollars to rescue moneyed interests, leaving workers and homeowners to their own devices. His video, posted on YouTube, lists several criticisms of Obama's policies, including the belief that the President has subordinated economic and educational opportunity to healthcare reform. Unger, who advised Obama during the 2008 campaign, now sees the President as evoking a politics of handholding rather than leading with a fight. He suggests that only a political reversal can allow the voice of democratic prophecy to speak once again in American life. Unger's scathing critique comes at a time when Obama faces challenges in maintaining his support, especially after recent policy decisions and fundraising controversies. While Unger acknowledges that a Republican victory would come with its own set of risks, he firmly believes that Obama's re-election would be detrimental to the progressive agenda.

South African forensic technology has been used to analyze tobacco pipes found in the garden of William Shakespeare, revealing the playwright's smoking habits and the plants he may have smoked. Pipes from Shakespeare’s Stratford-upon-Avon garden, including 24 fragments, were examined using gas chromatography mass spectrometry, a sophisticated technique sensitive to residues even after 400 years. The analysis identified several substances, including cannabis, nicotine, and cocaine, indicating a diverse range of smoking materials used in early 17th-century England. Notably, eight of the pipes tested contained cannabis, while two showed evidence of cocaine. The Shakespeare Birthplace Trust provided the artefacts for the study, which was published in the South African Journal of Science.

Literary connections hint at Shakespeare's potential awareness of the effects of these substances. Sonnet 76 suggests he might have preferred cannabis, noting "invention in a noted weed," possibly referring to cannabis as a creative writing tool. The sonnet also hints at a preference for avoiding "compounds strange," potentially alluding to cocaine. These findings raise questions about the atmosphere in which Shakespeare wrote, possibly in a smoke-filled environment with his contemporaries, including Sir Francis Drake and Sir Walter Raleigh, who were known to introduce various New World plants to England.

The study underscores the potential interplay between literary analysis and scientific investigation, offering insights into the substances that may have influenced Shakespeare's work. It also poses intriguing questions about the impact of these substances on the creative process and the atmosphere of the Elizabethan court where Shakespeare performed his plays.

Only about 2 percent of commercials feature men doing domestic tasks, suggesting a persistent gender divide in household responsibilities. According to Arlie Hochschild, author of The Outsourced Self and The Second Shift, cleaning is not just physical labor but emotional work, providing a sense of safety and order. However, women often bear the brunt of this emotional labor, even when they work full-time. Hochschild argues that women feel more pressure to maintain a clean home, as they are the ones judged more harshly for a messy one. When Hochschild lived with two female roommates, she was more of a slob, but after marriage, she became more concerned about the state of their home, insisting on cleaning for visitors. This suggests that societal expectations and judgments can influence women's domestic responsibilities more than men's.

In contrast, men in dual-earner relationships often do less housework, even when they are the primary breadwinners. David Michael Perez, the publisher and editor of Kindling Quarterly, notes that while he does more decorating and cleaning, he is often not credited for it. This lack of recognition can discourage men from taking on more domestic tasks. Hochschild suggests that couples should sit down and discuss their household responsibilities, but this can be daunting and impractical. Philosophy professor Alexandra Bradner proposes using economic theory to divide tasks based on comparative advantage, where men might excel at certain chores and women at others. However, this approach requires a willingness to delegate and recognize each partner's strengths.

Another solution is for women to lower their standards of cleanliness, recognizing that a certain level of mess is acceptable. For instance, a woman might not need to clean up as much when coming home from a night out, as long as the basic hygiene is maintained. This approach can be challenging, especially with children, as maintaining a clean home becomes more critical. Magary, a writer, suggests making cleaning more fun by using gadgets and tools, such as the Swiffer, to make the task more enjoyable.

The article concludes by questioning the assumption that there is a single correct level of cleanliness in a household, which is often determined by the female partner. It suggests that a more culturally relativist approach might be beneficial, allowing couples to find a balance that suits their preferences and lifestyles. This approach emphasizes the importance of recognizing the different types of work involved in household management, such as childcare, paid work, and domestic tasks, and finding a fair distribution that works for both partners.

Bruce Jenner's transition to Caitlyn Jenner, revealed in a Vanity Fair article, marks a significant chapter in his life. Jenner, once a celebrated Olympic athlete and reality TV star, now faces a new identity after years of internal struggle. The article details Jenner's journey, including his first transition attempt in the 1980s and his eventual decision to fully transition in 2015. Jenner underwent extensive facial-feminization surgery and hormone therapy, with the process taking about 10 hours. His children, particularly his stepchildren from the Kardashian family, have mixed feelings about the upcoming E! reality series documenting his transition. Despite initial support, they fear the show could overshadow the serious issues Jenner aims to address. Jenner remains committed to using her platform to raise awareness about transgender issues and plans to participate in various public events, including accepting the Arthur Ashe Courage Award at the ESPYs. Her story, while personal, also highlights broader societal challenges and the complex dynamics within her family.

Hurricane Maria’s devastation in Puerto Rico left significant communication infrastructure in ruins, and the Project Loon team has been working closely with authorities to restore internet access. Thanks to support from the U.S. and Puerto Rican governments, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC), the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), and FEMA, Project Loon is now collaborating with AT&T to provide emergency internet service to the hardest-hit areas of the island. Two Project Loon balloons, HBAL199 and HBAL237, are currently delivering basic internet services, including text messages and web access, to AT&T customers with 4G LTE-enabled devices. These balloons, more than 60,000 feet above the ground, use advanced algorithms to navigate and stay in optimal positions to maximize signal strength, relying on solar power during daylight hours. Additional balloons are on their way from Nevada, with permission from the FCC to deploy up to 30 balloons to serve the affected regions.

Project Loon, a network of stratospheric balloons designed to deliver internet connectivity to rural and remote areas, has been operational since 2013. This is the second time the technology has been used post-disaster, following a similar deployment in Peru in 2017. The balloons are experimental, and while they have shown promise, Project Loon acknowledges that their effectiveness is still being evaluated. The current deployment aims to provide essential communication tools to the approximately 3.4 million residents of Puerto Rico, many of whom are still struggling with the aftermath of Hurricane Maria, including limited electricity and functioning cell towers. While Project Loon’s efforts are commendable, other tech companies like Cisco, Facebook, and Tesla have also stepped in to offer assistance and support.

In recent days, Democratic strategists have urged President Barack Obama to regain control of a series of public relations crises that threaten to undermine his second-term agenda. Darrell Issa calling for the president to apologize and cooperate with Congress. The controversies, while significant, are seen as tier one issues, involving serious matters like the Benghazi attack and IRS targeting, compared to the Justice Department’s AP phone records seizure, which is considered a secondary concern. The article concludes by warning against the temptation for Republicans to rely solely on scandal for electoral gains, emphasizing the need for a balanced approach that includes a positive agenda.

Pop star Justin Bieber recently FaceTimed with Malala Yousafzai, the 17-year-old Pakistani activist for girls' education rights, according to an Instagram post. Bieber, 20, wrote, "She has such an incredible story. I can't wait to meet her in person and talk about how I can support her and the @malalafund #love." A distant star named KIC 8462852 has been the subject of much speculation and scrutiny, particularly after it exhibited unusual and dramatic fluctuations in brightness. Initially, the irregular dimming of the star's light, which could reach up to 22 percent, raised the possibility of an alien megastructure or a series of catastrophic events like a planetary collision. However, a new study by researchers at Iowa State University, published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, suggests a more mundane explanation: a swarm of comets.

The researchers, led by Massimo Marengo, used data from NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope to analyze the star in infrared light. They found no significant excess of infrared light, which would have been expected if the dimming were due to a collision or a dusty cloud of debris. Instead, they propose that the star's irregular dimming is the result of a family of comets traveling on a long, eccentric orbit around the star. At the head of this pack is a large comet that passed in front of the star in 2011, causing the initial dimming. Later, in 2013, the rest of the comet family, a band of varied fragments, passed in front of the star, causing a subsequent dimming event. By 2015, when the Spitzer observations were taken, the comets had moved far enough away to no longer block the star's light, leaving no trace of excess infrared emissions.

This explanation aligns with the behavior of comets, which can produce irregular dimming as they pass in front of a star. The researchers note that this is a very strange star, reminiscent of the discovery of pulsars, which initially emitted odd signals and were speculated to be caused by "Little Green Men." However, pulsars turned out to be natural phenomena, and the same may be true for KIC 8462852. While the alien megastructure theory remains untested, Marengo emphasizes that the star's unusual behavior makes it an intriguing subject for further study. The mystery of KIC 8462852 continues to captivate astronomers and the public alike, highlighting the enduring allure of the search for extraterrestrial life.

Trend-chasing coffee giant Starbucks is diving headfirst into the Lisa Frankenfoods craze with the upcoming release of a unicorn-themed Frappuccino, set to debut on April 19th. Baristas have been buzzing about this pink-and-blue creation on Reddit for days, and early taste-testers describe it as a "sour raspberry" flavor reminiscent of "fresh fruit" mixed with a "horrible sour syrup," likening it to Tropical Skittles. The drink, which is reportedly only available to those who "believe," is generating excitement and skepticism on social media, with users sharing their reactions and speculations. As Starbucks continues to experiment with whimsical and colorful drinks, this unicorn Frappuccino is likely to spark both delight and disappointment among its diverse customer base.

Sen. John McCain’s opposition to the latest Republican ObamaCare repeal bill has dealt a significant blow to the seven-year effort to dismantle the Affordable Care Act, raising questions about its future. Some Republicans still push for repeal, hoping to scrape together enough votes before the September 30 deadline that prevents a filibuster. Vice President Pence and President Trump remain undeterred, signaling their commitment to the repeal effort. However, the likelihood of a new stage in the debate seems more probable. Democrats are pushing for bipartisan talks in the Senate Health Committee, which Republicans had previously shut down. McCain’s opposition, along with potential opposition from Sens. Rand Paul and Susan Collins, suggests that the repeal bill faces significant challenges. The key issue in these talks is addressing cost-sharing reductions, payments that help insurers provide coverage to low- and middle-income people. Trump has threatened to cancel these payments, potentially destabilizing the insurance markets. While Democrats accuse Trump of threatening to sabotage the law, Standard & Poors found that ObamaCare markets are stabilizing. Democrats remain cautious, viewing repeal as a “very real threat” and warning of potential long-term harm to the exchanges. McCain’s opposition is a major setback, almost certainly dooming the current legislation. The possibility of pairing repeal with tax reform under a new budget resolution is discussed, but this plan would put tax reform at risk. Rep. Mark Meadows, chairman of the conservative House Freedom Caucus, expressed disappointment but did not criticize McCain. Democrats are maintaining a dual mission, staying vocal about the dangers of the bill while pushing for bipartisan solutions. Liberal groups are pressing ahead with rallies and ad campaigns, urging Democrats to stay vigilant. Despite the setback, Democrats are optimistic about resuming bipartisan talks led by Sens. Lamar Alexander and Patty Murray. The article concludes with a call from Pelosi for a bipartisan effort in the House to improve and update the Affordable Care Act.

Thousands of documents purportedly leaked from inside ISIS paint a detailed picture of the terror group's recruitment process and the personal information of thousands of potential and actual fighters. NBC News was among several media organizations to obtain these documents, which include a 23-question form that applicants must fill out before being inducted into ISIS. The questions range from basic personal information such as name, date of birth, and education to more sinister inquiries about previous fighting experience, blood type, special skills, and whether the applicant is interested in becoming a suicide attacker or a fighter. The forms also ask about countries traveled to, who can vouch for the recruit, and the applicant's level of obedience.

The documents, which are believed to be authentic by German intelligence officials, contain information on more than 22,000 jihadis from at least 51 nationalities, including the UK, France, Germany, and the United States. Among the names are well-known jihadis like Abdel Bary, a Londoner who joined in 2013 after visiting Libya, Egypt, and Turkey, and Junaid Hussain, the former head of ISIS's media wing. The leak could offer critical information to intelligence agencies, including routes taken by foreign fighters, previously unknown recruits, and recruiters. The documents also reveal that some of the telephone numbers on the list are still active, potentially providing a means to contact jihadis directly.

German Interior Minister Thomas de Maizière believes the documents provide a great chance for furnishing proof and the participation of Germans in terror activities. "With this, we also better understand the structures of this terror organization and it will possibly function as a deterrent for some young radical people," he said. The leak and its origin deal a blow to ISIS, signaling weakness at a time when the organization is under increasing pressure from U.S. airstrikes and other counter-terrorism efforts. The documents could be of significant intelligence value, helping to identify and track potential threats and disrupt future terrorist activities.

In 1994, Pizza Hut's PizzaNet became one of the earliest examples of online commerce, allowing consumers to order pizza through the internet. Although it wasn't the first, PizzaNet's launch marked a significant step in integrating food delivery with the burgeoning World Wide Web. Customers could customize their orders and transmit them to the nearest Pizza Hut via the internet, with local restaurants verifying orders over the phone. This innovative approach, while seemingly simple, foreshadowed the future of e-commerce and online ordering. Despite its early nature, PizzaNet's concept laid the groundwork for modern online ordering systems, influencing the way businesses interact with customers in the digital age.

About 10 people fell ill after a suspicious package arrived in the mailroom of a large IRS building in downtown Kansas City, Missouri, on Friday, according to a Kansas City Fire Department spokesman. The Fire Department isolated the package and checked for gases and fumes but has not yet determined its contents. Two individuals were taken to St. Luke's Hospital, where they are reported to be in good condition. The building remained operational, and the investigation has been handed over to the IRS and other federal authorities.

Mainstream sponsors like Gillette and Accenture have distanced themselves from Tiger Woods, but now even the insular golf community is showing signs of distancing. Golf Digest announced it would suspend monthly articles by Woods until he returns to the PGA Tour, respecting his decision to focus on his family. This move, surprising given athletes' usual support during controversies, highlights the widespread impact of Woods' scandal. His status as a $110 million annual endorsement powerhouse has been significantly damaged, with key sponsors like Accenture, Gatorade, and Gillette pulling back. Woods' Golf Digest contract, reportedly worth $3 million annually, remains intact, but the magazine's decision to pause his bylined articles signals a shift in their stance. Despite this, Tag Heuer stood by Woods, re-posting his image on their website with a supportive message, maintaining their "strictly professional" relationship. The golf community's response underscores the complex interplay between personal scandals and corporate endorsements.

The U.S. Under-23 national team was eliminated from Olympic qualifying, suffering a 3-3 tie to El Salvador in a match that saw the Americans take a one-goal lead into stoppage time but ultimately fall short. Needing a win to advance from Group A, the U.S. took an early lead through Brek Shea, but struggled to establish possession against a strong El Salvador side. Keeper Bill Hamid suffered an ankle injury in the first half, leading to a substitution that El Salvador capitalized on, scoring two quick goals. The U.S. equalized through Terrence Boyd and Joe Corona, but El Salvador's Jaime Alas scored the decisive goal in the final minute of extra time. The U.S. had a chance to run out the clock but failed, leaving them out of the Olympics for the second time in three years. Coach Caleb Porter expressed disappointment, stating, "This is probably the worst feeling I've ever felt in my life so far as a pro athlete." The El Salvador team, which had less than two weeks to prepare, advanced to the semifinals.

A new study from the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, published in the British Medical Journal, reveals that more than half of terminally ill cancer patients receive chemotherapy in the last few months of their lives, despite evidence suggesting that such treatment does not significantly extend survival. The research, involving 386 patients, found that those who received chemotherapy were more likely to die in an intensive care unit, hooked to a ventilator, rather than at home as they had preferred. Chemotherapy recipients were also less likely to have discussed their end-of-life wishes with their oncologists compared to those who did not continue chemotherapy. The study highlights a significant gap in communication between doctors and patients, as many oncologists avoid discussing the topic of dying, which can lead to patients receiving aggressive treatments that do not align with their wishes. The findings suggest that doctors may be hesitant to discuss end-of-life care, fearing that it might make patients feel that their doctors are giving up on them. This reluctance can result in a medicalized death, with patients receiving intensive care and ventilator support, rather than the peaceful, home-based death they may prefer. The study underscores the need for more open and honest conversations between doctors and patients about end-of-life care, to ensure that patients' wishes are respected and that they can die with dignity.

Syrian rebels have reportedly used the nerve agent sarin, according to U.N. human rights investigators, who gathered testimony from victims and medical staff. However, there is no concrete proof yet, as the evidence is still being verified. The United Nations independent commission of inquiry on Syria has not found evidence of government forces using chemical weapons, which are banned under international law. The investigation into the alleged use of chemical weapons in Syria has stalled. President Bashar al-Assad's government and the rebels accuse each other of carrying out chemical weapon attacks, with three incidents reported: one near Aleppo, another near Damascus, and a third in Homs. The civil war, which began in March 2011, has claimed an estimated 70,000 lives and forced over 1.2 million Syrian refugees to flee. The United States has varying degrees of confidence that sarin has been used by Syria's government. President Barack Obama declared that the use or deployment of chemical weapons by Assad would cross a "red line." Meanwhile, Israel has carried out air strikes near Damascus, targeting shipments of Iranian-made guided missiles bound for Hezbollah in Lebanon. Israel sought to reassure Syrian President Assad that these strikes were not aimed at weakening him in the face of the rebellion. Damascus accused Israel of belligerence meant to bolster the rebels. Israel has deployed Iron Dome missile interceptors near the Syrian and Lebanese borders as a precaution. Israel's public security minister, Tzachi Hanegbi, stated that the Netanyahu government aimed to avoid increasing tension with Syria by making clear that any attacks were only against Hezbollah, not the Syrian regime. Israel's actions could potentially lead to proxy attacks through Lebanon, where Israel fought an inconclusive war against Hezbollah in 2006. Tehran denied Israel's attack was on arms, and Hezbollah did not comment. The conflict has seen Israel strike areas in and around Damascus multiple times, causing damage and casualties, as documented by various news agencies.

Courtney Stodden, 21, has announced her pregnancy with her first child, confirming the news to FOX411 after a video surfaced showing the reality star with a positive pregnancy test. The video, sent to Stodden's closest friends and family, was recorded by her husband Doug Hutchison, 55, who appears to be filming his wife in their bathroom. Stodden, who is only four weeks along, expressed that the video was an "invasion of privacy." Her estranged mother, Krista Keller, revealed that she was unaware of her daughter's pregnancy until media reports broke the news. The situation has added another layer of complexity to Stodden's already tumultuous relationship with her mother, who has been trying to gain custody of Stodden for years. 

The Mother/Daughter Experiment: Celebrity Edition, a reality show that aired on Lifetime, featured a particularly awkward and cringe-worthy moment when Stodden's mother admitted to having feelings for her husband, Doug Hutchison. During the episode, Krista confronted her daughter about her feelings for Doug, raising the question, "Why don't you ask your husband what his fantasy was!" This revelation has sparked further tension in the already strained relationship between Stodden and her mother. 

Stodden and Hutchison, who are 34 years apart in age, tied the knot in 2011 when Stodden was just 16 years old. The couple briefly split in 2013 but reconciled the following year. Stodden's pregnancy comes as an early anniversary present for the couple, as their wedding anniversary is on May 20. Despite the challenges in her personal life, Stodden expressed that she is "dealing with a lot of stress and emotions surrounding life and its ups and downs." She added, "Doug is wonderful," highlighting his supportive role in her life.

British scientists from Imperial College London have made significant strides in understanding the genetic basis of human intelligence, suggesting that intelligence may be influenced by two distinct networks of genes, possibly controlled by a master regulatory system. This research, published in Nature Neuroscience, indicates that about 40% of intelligence variation is due to genetic inheritance, with the remaining factors still under investigation. The study, led by Michael Johnson, a consultant neurologist, and colleagues, identified two networks, M1 and M3, each containing hundreds of genes, which play roles in neurodevelopmental disorders such as epilepsy, schizophrenia, and autism. These networks do not overlap in function, and their specific roles in intelligence are yet to be fully elucidated.

The researchers employed a comprehensive approach, analyzing 100 mouse brains, 122 human brain samples, and 102 postmortem whole human brains. They also utilized data from the "Generation Scotland" family health study, which tracks thousands of volunteers, and the Lothian Birth Cohort 1936, involving 1,003 healthy individuals who volunteered for cognitive assessments. By combining genetic information from people who had taken IQ tests, those with autism spectrum disorder and intellectual disabilities, and individuals who underwent neurosurgery for epilepsy, the scientists were able to identify a genetic connection between intelligence and neurodevelopmental disorders.

According to Dr. Johnson, the findings highlight the importance of understanding the genetic mechanisms underlying human intelligence, as this knowledge could potentially lead to new therapeutic approaches. "The idea of ultimately using drugs to affect cognitive performance is not in any way new. We all drink coffee to improve our cognitive performance," he noted. "It's about understanding the pathways that are related to cognitive ability both in health and disease, especially disease, so one day we could help people with learning disabilities fulfill their potential. That is very important."

The research underscores the complexity of intelligence, which is a composite measure of various cognitive abilities distributed in a population. While the genetic networks identified are promising, the scientists emphasize that much work remains to be done. "Traits such as intelligence are governed by large groups of genes working together—like a football team made up of players in different positions," Dr. Johnson explained. "We found that some of these genes overlap with those that cause severe childhood-onset epilepsy or intellectual disability."

The ultimate goal of this research is to provide new insights into better treatments for neurodevelopmental diseases such as epilepsy and to ameliorate or treat cognitive impairments associated with these conditions. This study represents a significant step forward in the field of cognitive genetics, potentially opening up new avenues for understanding and addressing cognitive disorders.

Sen. Ben Cardin, a Maryland Democrat, has linked President Trump's trade policies to General Motors' recent decision to close five facilities and cut 15% of its North American salaried workforce, affecting up to 14,000 employees. Cardin's comments echo those of Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, who suggested that GM's restructuring was a consequence of the tariffs on steel and aluminum between the two countries. "I do think the way the president has gone about the trade policies, imposing tariffs—there’s a consequence, there’s a domestic consequence," Cardin told Fox News Sunday. "And clearly General Motors' decisions are in part based upon the tariff issue, so yes it has an impact, and it costs us jobs here in America." The GM closures and model discontinuations, including the Chevrolet Cruze and Buick LaCrosse, drew Trump's ire, leading him to threaten to cut all subsidies for the largest American automaker. However, Cardin expressed optimism about the 90-day trade truce between the U.S. and China, which brings a temporary halt to new tariffs, and the newly signed United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA). "Clearly, it is encouraging to see that we're talking with the Chinese on the trade front," Cardin said. "China has created many problems with trade, many obstacles for free trade. My concern about the president's trade policy is that his first action was to take tariffs against our closest allies based upon national security exceptions. We lost the unity that we needed in dealing with China." Missouri Republican Sen. Roy Blunt agreed that the news was positive but called for more details on the China truce. "People like me who have really been concerned about the president's stated trade policy can take some encouragement in what happened in the last couple of days, the signing of the U.S. Canada and Mexico agreement— that’s a big step that 6 months ago or even just a few weeks ago we were concerned that we would not be making that kind of progress," Blunt said. The White House has bipartisan support for hitting back at Chinese intellectual property theft, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., agreeing that China "takes total advantage" of the U.S. Trump appeared to be in a hurry to leave Argentina, as he was filmed seemingly leaving President Mauricio Macri abruptly on-stage as he lingered awkwardly for a group photo.

International Women’s Day on March 8th is a time for celebrating women’s achievements and advocating for gender equality, yet it also brings a flurry of corporate efforts to align with the pro-woman narrative. Brands are leveraging the occasion with ads, product launches, and social media campaigns. Mattel introduced 17 new “role model” Barbies, honoring figures like Amelia Earhart and Wonder Woman director Patty Jenkins. Nike’s ad featuring Serena Williams emphasized that women can be “the right kind of woman” despite criticism. Uber and Facebook have created themed content, while McDonald’s flipped its iconic arches to form a “W” for women. These efforts, however, have faced criticism for being superficial. Mattel’s dolls were criticized for their uniform body shapes, and McDonald’s W was panned as an odd symbol. The ongoing #MeToo and Time’s Up movements have raised the bar for brands, pushing them to move beyond inspirational messaging and towards actionable steps. Brands must be mindful of their messaging, as the conversation around women’s equality has shifted to demand more than just feel-good content.

Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov blamed Western governments for encouraging the fighting in Ukraine, warning that the situation was "getting out of control." Protesters in Kiev faced off against police, with clashes leaving vehicles burning and protesters using stones and gasoline bombs. Opposition leaders, including Vitali Klitschko, refused to meet with Ukrainian President Viktor Yanukovych, who has signed laws to curb public protests. Klitschko criticized the government for giving free rein to more radical protesters while trying to scare moderate ones. Meanwhile, Russian state television showed footage of clashes, underlining the need for the tough legislation. Lavrov criticized the protesters' use of violence and called their behavior a "complete violation of all European standards of behavior." Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov said the government would use force if clashes do not cease. Protesters, including young women clearing debris and middle-aged men and women producing a drumbeat of protest, continued to camp outside government buildings, facing off with helmeted riot police.

A former nurse in Germany, identified only as Niels H, is now suspected of being responsible for at least 84 additional murders, bringing the total number of victims to 86, according to police. Niels H, who is 40 years old, was already serving a life sentence for two murders and two attempted murders. His crimes involved administering lethal drug doses to patients at hospitals where he worked. The nurse's victims received heart medication that caused heart failure or circulatory collapse. Niels H admitted during his 2015 trial that he intentionally brought about cardiac crises in about 90 patients at an intensive care clinic in Delmenhorst, doing so to win approval by resuscitating them. The investigation into his crimes began after he was convicted of attempted murder in another case. Authorities subsequently exhumed 134 bodies to test for drug residues, but many patients were cremated, making it impossible to gather evidence in some cases. Oldenburg police chief Johann Kuehme stated, "Eighty-four killings... leave us speechless," and warned that the actual number of victims could be much higher. Kuehme criticized local health authorities for not acting more quickly on their suspicions, noting that if authorities had been alerted earlier, Niels H could have been stopped sooner. The crimes spanned from 2000 to 2005, during which time he worked at clinics in Oldenburg and Delmenhorst. Despite the significant number of suspected victims, future convictions will not affect Niels H's life sentence due to Germany's judicial system. The identities of the suspected 84 victims have not been released, and there has been no immediate comment from the families of the victims.

President-elect Donald Trump's election offers congressional Republicans their best chance in years to eliminate the estate tax, known as the "death tax," which could deliver a multibillion-dollar bonanza to America’s wealthiest families, including Trump himself and his administration nominees. The estate tax, which applies only to estates worth more than $5.45 million for individuals and $10.9 million for couples, would save over $20 billion annually for those affected. Trump, who campaigned as a champion of the working class, may find it challenging to reconcile his populist image with a tax break for the rich. The estate tax affects only a small percentage of estates, with just 0.2% of estates subject to it in 2015. Eliminating the tax would benefit several Trump administration nominees, including Wilbur Ross, who might save $545 million, and Betsy DeVos, whose father-in-law, Richard DeVos, could save $900 million. The estate tax repeal would also benefit Treasury Secretary nominee Steven Mnuchin and Gary Cohn, Trump’s choice for chief economic policy adviser, who would leave Goldman Sachs with $266 million in stock and awards.

Democrats overwhelmingly oppose reducing the estate tax, with Hillary Clinton campaigning on raising its rate to 65% for couples worth $1 billion. However, the politics of repeal may depend on how the public perceives the tax. A Gallup poll found that 54% of Americans favored eliminating the estate tax when told it’s a tax paid when a person dies. The debate may be an early test of how Republicans handle the electorate’s populist mood. Some conservatives caution that upper-end tax breaks are politically problematic and suggest that Trump should focus on delivering tangible gains to middle-income voters.

The White House also unveiled a sweeping tax overhaul plan, which would benefit high-income earners like Trump. The plan includes a 20% corporate tax rate, a 25% tax rate for small businesses, and the elimination of the alternative minimum tax, which could save Trump $31 million. The proposal also includes a 35% top tax rate, a doubling of the standard deduction, and an increase in the child tax credit. However, the plan would increase the national debt by approximately $2.2 trillion and could lead to a reduction in social programs. The plan’s lack of detail makes it difficult for policy experts to estimate its impact accurately.

Thom Hartmann argues that the Second Amendment was ratified to preserve slavery, citing Patrick Henry, George Mason, and James Madison as key figures who were concerned about federal control over state militias. The article details how slave patrols in southern states were regulated by state laws, with the fear that federal control could lead to the emancipation of slaves. Hartmann emphasizes that the amendment's primary purpose was to ensure a "free state," protecting citizens from tyranny, including their own government. He draws parallels between historical restrictions on gun ownership in countries that turned on their people, suggesting that the current debate over assault rifles and magazine sizes is relevant to the amendment's broader intent. Hartmann also points out that President Obama's upcoming gun control proposals could put Democrats up for re-election in 2014 in difficult positions, especially in pro-gun states. The summary highlights the ongoing debate over the Second Amendment's true purpose and its application in modern contexts, including the potential for future amendments to address contemporary concerns.

Senate Democrats faced a significant setback as a key procedural vote on a defense authorization bill containing a repeal of the "Don't Ask, Don't Tell" policy failed, falling 57-40 short of the 60 votes needed to advance the bill for debate. The vote, which was held without reaching a procedural agreement with moderate Republican Senator Susan Collins of Maine, who supports repeal but wanted greater openness for the process, likely dealt a final blow to advocates hoping to overturn the 17-year-old ban on gays and lesbians serving openly in the military during this session. Despite Majority Leader Harry Reid's attempt to move the bill forward, Collins expressed disappointment, stating that negotiations were "going well" and accusing Reid of walking away. Reid promised to support a stand-alone repeal bill introduced by Senators Joe Lieberman and Susan Collins, which they plan to bring to the floor before the end of the lame duck session. President Obama expressed disappointment, urging the Senate to revisit the issue during the lame duck session. The failure of the repeal effort has raised concerns about the potential impact of a hasty implementation if the courts overturn the policy first. Advocates criticized the vote, arguing that political squabbles had put the needs of the military and the American people at risk. The vote also highlights the challenges of advancing such legislation in a politically divided Congress, where a minority of senators can effectively block important measures.

Secret files revealing evidence of widespread suspected match-fixing at the top level of world tennis, including at Wimbledon, have been uncovered by the BBC and BuzzFeed News. Over the past decade, 16 players who have ranked in the top 50 have been repeatedly flagged to the Tennis Integrity Unit (TIU) over suspicions they have thrown matches. Despite this, all of the players, including winners of Grand Slam titles, were allowed to continue competing. The TIU, which was set up to police the sport, claims it has a zero-tolerance approach to betting-related corruption. However, Chris Kermode, who heads the Association of Tennis Professionals, acknowledged that evidence of match-fixing within tennis exists but insisted it is at an "incredibly small level." The cache of documents passed to the BBC and Buzzfeed News includes the findings of an investigation set up in 2007 by the ATP, which was triggered by a game involving Nikolay Davydenko and Martin Vassallo Arguello. Both players were cleared of violating any rules, but the investigation developed into a much wider inquiry looking into a web of gamblers linked to top-level players. The documents reveal that betting syndicates in Russia, northern Italy, and Sicily made hundreds of thousands of pounds betting on matches investigators thought to be fixed. Three of these matches were at Wimbledon. In a confidential report for the tennis authorities in 2008, the investigation team said 28 players involved in these matches should be investigated, but the findings were never followed up. Tennis introduced a new anti-corruption code in 2009 but, after taking legal advice, were told previous corruption offenses could not be pursued. As a result, no new investigations into any of the players who were mentioned in the 2008 report were opened. In subsequent years, there were repeated alerts sent to the TIU about a third of these players. None of them was disciplined by the TIU. A group of whistle blowers inside tennis, who want to remain anonymous, recently passed the documents on to the BBC and Buzzfeed News. Mark Phillips, one of the betting investigators in the 2007 enquiry, told the BBC that they discovered repeated suspicious betting activity about a clear group. "There was a core of about 10 players who we believed were the most common perpetrators that were at the root of the problem," he said. He has never spoken publicly about the material he gathered, which he said was as powerful as any he had seen in over 20 years as a betting investigator. "The evidence was really strong," he added. "There appeared to be a really good chance to nip it in the bud and get a strong deterrent out there to root out the main bad apples." The BBC and Buzzfeed were also passed the names of other current players the TIU have repeatedly been warned about by betting organizations, sports integrity units, and professional gamblers. Many of these players have been on the radar of the tennis authorities for involvement in suspicious matches going back to 2003. The BBC and Buzzfeed News have decided not to name the players because, without access to their phone, bank, and computer records, it is not possible to determine whether they may have been personally taking part in match fixing. However, tennis' integrity unit does have the power to demand all this evidence from any professional tennis player. "There is an element of actually keeping things under wraps," said Benn Gunn, a former police chief constable who conducted a major review of betting in tennis that led to the creation of the Tennis Integrity Unit. "If they were really serious about dealing with this, then they really need to create an integrity unit with teeth," he said. The European Sports Security Association, which monitors betting for leading bookmakers, flagged up more than 50 suspicious matches to the TIU in 2015. The organization declared that tennis attracts more suspicious gambling activity than other sports. While he welcomed the support of the betting industry, Nigel Willerton, director of the TIU, said "it is not the role of betting companies to make judgements about corrupt activity." He added: "All credible information received by the TIU is analysed, assessed, and investigated by highly experienced former law-enforcement investigators." The problem of suspicious betting and match-fixing is not going away. Eight of the players repeatedly flagged to the TIU over the past decade are due to play in the Australian Open, which starts on Monday, January 18.

A cyclospora outbreak linked to prepackaged salad mix has sickened 397 people across 16 states, according to the CDC. Iowa and Nebraska have identified prepackaged salad mix as the likely source, but the exact culprit remains unknown. The parasite, Cyclospora cayetanensis, causes severe diarrhea and other symptoms like fatigue, anorexia, and bloating. While the investigation is ongoing, the FDA and CDC are working to determine if the prepackaged salad mix is the definitive source of the outbreak. The investigation has faced criticism for its pace, with some experts calling for a quicker resolution. In Iowa, health officials traced the outbreak to a specific brand of prepackaged salad mix, but they cannot disclose the name due to state laws protecting agricultural producers. The laws prevent public disclosure of potential contamination sources unless there is an ongoing outbreak posing a public health risk. Despite the efforts, the contaminated product is believed to have been removed from the market, and the investigation continues. The CDC advises people to be cautious about their food sources and to seek medical attention if they experience symptoms. The case highlights the challenges in tracing foodborne illnesses to their exact origins, especially when dealing with prepackaged, mixed ingredients.

Rolling Stone, the iconic magazine co-founded by Ralph Gleason in 1967, is now for sale, according to a report by The New York Times. Publisher Jann Wenner, 71, stated that he loves his job and enjoys it, but selling the magazine is the "smart thing to do." Over the past half-century, Rolling Stone has been synonymous with the history of rock 'n' roll, featuring some of the most important political and investigative writers of the last 50 years, including Hunter S. Thompson, Joe Klein, P.J. O'Rourke, and Tom Wolfe. However, the magazine's reputation has suffered significantly, particularly after a 2014 article "A Rape on Campus," which detailed a gang rape at the University of Virginia, was retracted due to fundamental journalistic failures. A damning report by the Columbia Graduate School of Journalism highlighted these failures, leading to three libel lawsuits against Rolling Stone, with one resulting in a $3 million jury award. The financial situation has also been bleak, with Wenner selling a 51 percent stake in the magazine to Wenner Media in 2013 and selling Us Weekly and Men's Journal to American Media Inc. in 2018. Despite these challenges, Wenner Media's president and COO, Gus Wenner, is optimistic about the future, stating that the company will find the right home to build on its strong foundation and grow the business exponentially. However, the sale of Rolling Stone marks the end of an era for Wenner, who rose from a Berkeley dropout to a media mogul, investing $7,500 of borrowed money to start the magazine. The financial and reputational struggles of Rolling Stone underscore the changing landscape of media, where print advertising revenue and newsstand sales have declined, and the web has become the primary source of news and entertainment for many readers.

The leaders of the Republican and Democratic national committees offered differing views on the possibility of Michael Bloomberg entering the 2016 presidential race as an independent candidate. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, the chairwoman of the Democratic National Committee, suggested that Bloomberg's priorities are already "well cared-for" in the Democratic platform, while Reince Priebus, the Republican National Committee leader, welcomed the idea, framing Bloomberg as a potential spoiler who would draw votes away from the eventual Democratic nominee. Bloomberg, a billionaire and former New York City mayor, recently criticized the quality of the political discourse, stating that he was "looking at all the options" for a run. His entry would significantly alter the election landscape, as experts believe he would help the Republican nominee by drawing support from Democrats due to his liberal stances on issues like gun control and the environment. Bloomberg's potential candidacy comes as Donald Trump and Bernie Sanders dominate their respective parties, with Trump leading in New Hampshire and Sanders currently leading in the Democratic race. Bloomberg's advisers have noted that his entry could provide an opening, as the anti-establishment campaigns of Trump and Sanders have already disrupted the traditional election process. However, Bloomberg faces significant challenges, as polls indicate low favorability among both Republican and Democratic voters. His entry would also reshape the political landscape, with potential implications for the general election's outcome, particularly if no candidate secures a majority of electoral votes, forcing the decision into the hands of the House of Representatives.

Older fathers appear to have geekier sons, according to a new study that analyzed data from over 30,000 twins. By the age of 12, boys with older fathers scored higher on a "geek index" that measures non-verbal IQ, focus on subjects of interest, and social aloofness. The older the father, the higher the geek index score, with the effect being most pronounced after the father was 45. This suggests that there are evolutionary advantages for men having children later in life, potentially due to genetic factors or the extended career and educational pursuits of older fathers.

The study, published in the journal Translational Psychiatry, found that geeky boys performed better in school exams, especially in STEM subjects, indicating they might be more successful in their careers as adults. However, the researchers caution that the geek effect may not extend beyond secondary education and future success, noting that traits like flexibility and social awareness may be more beneficial in the work environment. They also suggest that the geek effect was only seen in boys, possibly because the study's measure of geekiness may not fully capture how it manifests in girls.

The findings also imply a link between advanced paternal age and autism, as some of the genes relating to geekiness and autism overlap. The researchers propose that some children may inherit a "higher dose" of these genes, potentially leading to a higher risk of autism. However, they emphasize that these findings should not influence individual decisions about parenthood. The study's lead author, Magdalena Janecka, states that paternal age should not be the main focus when considering the risks of parenthood, and individual families should not base their decisions on these results.

Scientists from King's College London and the University of Sheffield noted that while the idea of a "geek gene" is intriguing, the dangers of older parenthood, such as increased risks of infertility, miscarriage, and genetic disorders, should not be overlooked. Professor Allan Pacey from the University of Sheffield suggested that the trend towards delayed parenthood might lead to a future society of geniuses capable of solving the world's problems. However, he advised against delaying family plans specifically to increase the likelihood of having a child with geek-like qualities.

The study's limitations include the inability to determine whether the geek effect extends beyond secondary education and future success, and the possibility that the measure of geekiness may not fully capture how it manifests in girls. The researchers also noted that the genetic and environmental factors underlying the association between paternal age and geekiness remain to be fully elucidated.

Bernie Sanders, now 77, is considering another presidential run in 2020, driven by his belief that his ideas are now mainstream and supported by a majority of Americans. His 2016 campaign left him as the most popular politician in the country, but his path is fraught with challenges. Sanders is frustrated with the Democratic establishment, viewing it as dismissive and unappreciative of his contributions. He has been working to build relationships with powerful party members, particularly Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, to gain influence. Sanders uses his large social media following to pressure the party and the president on issues like health care and tax reform. Despite his popularity, his 2020 campaign faces significant hurdles, including a potentially large field of candidates and the need to address his age and past criticisms. His advisers caution that another run will be costly and negative, but Sanders remains confident he can still win. The decision to run or not will likely hinge on whether he believes he is the best candidate to defeat Donald Trump.

The passenger in the car with Walter Scott before he was shot by a South Carolina police officer has spoken out, stating that he doesn't understand why Scott ran from the officer but knows he did not deserve to die. Pierre D. Fulton, who was identified as Scott's passenger during the April 4, 2015, incident, released a brief statement through his lawyer, calling Scott a "dear friend" who had helped him become a better man. Fulton emphasized that Scott's death was unjust and asked for prayers for both Scott and his family. The statement, however, did not provide any insight into why Scott ran from the officer during the traffic stop. Meanwhile, former North Charleston police officer Michael Slager, 33, remains charged with murder in Scott's death, which was captured on video showing Scott being shot eight times as he ran away. Slager has not entered a plea and his attorney has declined to comment publicly, except to say they are conducting their own investigation.

Michael Bloomberg, the founder and CEO of Bloomberg LP, has stepped forward to address the financial shortfall caused by the United States’ withdrawal from the Paris Climate Agreement. Bloomberg has pledged to provide $15 million to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the coordinating agency of the Paris accord, to make up for the $15 million in funding that the U.S. was expected to contribute. Bloomberg’s offer comes in the form of a “parallel” pledge, indicating that leadership in the fight against climate change in the United States has shifted from the federal government to lower levels of government, academia, and industry. Bloomberg believes that non-state actors, such as cities, states, businesses, and civil society, will be able to achieve the United States’ 2025 emissions reduction target without federal government support.

Christiana Figueres, a former top United Nations climate official, has stated that there is currently no formal mechanism for entities that are not countries to be full parties to the Paris accord. However, Figueres suggested that Bloomberg’s submission could be included in future reports the United Nations compiles on the progress made by signatories of the Paris deal. Bloomberg’s offer is seen as a significant move, as it underscores the commitment of non-state actors to the Paris accord and highlights the potential for these entities to drive climate action in the absence of federal government support.

The announcement of Bloomberg’s pledge has been met with approval from other business leaders who have publicly denounced Trump’s withdrawal from the Paris accord. Tesla CEO Elon Musk and Disney CEO Bob Iger both left the President’s advisory council in protest, while corporations such as Google and Shell have criticized the president’s move online. Bloomberg’s commitment to the Paris accord, despite the U.S. government’s decision to withdraw, reflects the growing recognition among non-state actors of the importance of climate action and the potential for these entities to play a critical role in addressing the global challenge of climate change.

A 3-year-old boy, Levi, tragically drowned during a family vacation in Fort Morgan, Alabama, in June 2018, highlighting the silent and swift nature of drowning, which can occur in less than one minute and often away from swimming areas. His mother, who had always taken water safety seriously, was left devastated, as she had found her son face down in the deep end of the pool just moments after they had shared a brownie. Despite immediate medical intervention, including CPR and intubation, Levi could not be saved. Levi's death prompted his mother to delve into the statistics of drowning, which revealed that it is the leading cause of death for children aged 1-4 and the second leading cause for ages 1-14. She discovered that 69% of drowning cases involve children who were not expected to be in the water. Levi's mother, now determined to prevent such tragedies, founded a non-profit organization called Levi’s Legacy, aiming to eradicate drowning completely. She emphasizes the importance of water safety, particularly during non-swimming times, and advocates for more comprehensive water safety information to be provided to parents, especially those with children in the 1-4 age range. Levi’s Legacy’s mission is to educate and raise awareness about the silent and swift nature of drowning, urging parents to take water safety seriously and to be vigilant at all times. The organization seeks support from the American Academy of Pediatrics to ensure that water safety is given the same priority as other critical health topics. Through her advocacy, Levi’s mother hopes to prevent other families from experiencing the pain and loss she has endured.

A 40-year-old woman, Andrea Giesbrecht, faces six charges of concealing the bodies of infants after the remains of six babies were found in a U-Haul storage locker in Winnipeg. The discovery was made when U-Haul employees went to clear out the locker due to delinquent rental payments. Initially, police believed there were three or four bodies, but the number was later raised to six. The infants are believed to have been newborns, in various states of decomposition. Giesbrecht, who has a gambling addiction and a history of fraud, was arrested outside her home. She is also charged with breaching probation related to a 2012 case where she defrauded a 73-year-old woman of several thousand dollars. Giesbrecht's lawyer described her as bewildered. Police say it could take months to determine the identities of the infants, the cause of their deaths, and how long they had been in the locker. The forensic investigation will be extensive, and no suspects other than Giesbrecht have been identified. The case remains under investigation, with no homicide charges filed at this time.

Austrian daredevil Felix Baumgartner, known as "Fearless Felix," was set to attempt a record-breaking skydive from an altitude of nearly 23 miles (37 kilometers) above southeastern New Mexico. The jump, part of the Red Bull Stratos project, aimed to break the sound barrier, set the longest-duration freefall record, and reach the highest manned balloon flight altitude. However, Baumgartner's attempt was postponed to Tuesday due to unfavorable weather conditions, including gusty winds and a cold front. The 43-year-old skydiver, who has completed over 2,500 jumps, will ascend in a 55-story-tall helium balloon, carrying a 2,900-pound capsule. If successful, Baumgartner will step out of the capsule, freefall for about 20 minutes, and deploy his parachute at 5,000 feet. The mission, involving engineers, doctors, and pilots, has spent five years preparing for this event. Baumgartner's safety depends on the integrity of his specially designed pressurized suit, which can withstand extreme temperatures and the risk of ebullism, a condition where liquids in the body rapidly vaporize due to the low atmospheric pressure. The jump, if successful, will not only break records but also provide valuable data for future space suits and emergency rescue techniques.

Star Wars creator George Lucas is mourning the loss of his longtime friend and leading lady, Carrie Fisher, who died on December 27 at the age of 60 after suffering a heart attack during a flight from London to Los Angeles. Fisher, known for her role as Princess Leia, was in stable condition when her family announced the news, with her mother, Debbie Reynolds, tweeting that the actress was "in stable condition" and thanking fans for their support. Fisher had completed filming for "Star Wars: Episode VIII" before her death, with the official "Star Wars" Twitter account confirming the wrap of production in July 2016. The film, set for release on December 15, 2017, will now need to be reassessed in light of Fisher's passing, particularly regarding the role of Princess Leia in "Episode IX." Fisher's death has touched the entire "Star Wars" community, with co-stars Mark Hamill and Peter Mayhew sharing their grief. Hamill tweeted, "No words #Devastated," alongside a photo from their Star Wars years, while Mayhew wrote, "There are no words for this loss. Carrie was the brightest light in every room she entered. I will miss her dearly." Fisher's legacy extends beyond "Star Wars," with a string of roles in films like "Shampoo," "Scream 3," and "Sex and the City." Her wit and humor, as well as her contributions to the "Star Wars" franchise, will be deeply missed by fans and colleagues alike.

Four U.S. senators are betting on the outcome of the NBA Finals, with each pair of senators wagering on their home teams: California Senators Kamala Harris and Dianne Feinstein are backing the Golden State Warriors, while Ohio Senators Sherrod Brown and Rob Portman are rooting for the Cleveland Cavaliers. The stakes are high: if the Warriors win, Brown and Portman will have to deliver a case of beer to Harris and Feinstein, and a case of California Chardonnay from Feinstein. Conversely, if the Cavaliers triumph, Harris and Portman will receive a case of beer from Anchor Brewing and a case of Great Lakes Brewing from Brown. The series is closely watched, as the teams have met in every NBA Finals since 2015. In Game 1, the Warriors narrowly defeated the Cavaliers, 124-114, with a costly mistake by J.R. Smith and a disputed foul call involving LeBron James. The game featured a 51-point performance by James and a strong showing by Stephen Curry. The Cavaliers, led by James, showed resilience, but the Warriors capitalized on their opponent's blunders. The series continues with Game 2 on Sunday, with the Warriors holding a significant home-court advantage.

The US military's takeover of emergency operations in Haiti has sparked diplomatic tensions with countries and aid agencies, as flights were redirected, causing frustration and delays. Brazil and France lodged official protests, with Brazil warning it would not relinquish command of UN forces in Haiti and France complaining the airport had become a "US annex." The Red Cross and Médecins Sans Frontières also complained about diverted flights. Amid the chaos, aid was reaching some of the hundreds of thousands of people in desperate need of water, food, and medicine six days after the earthquake, which killed over 100,000 people according to Haitian authorities. The UN was feeding 40,000 people and hoped to increase that to 1 million within a fortnight. However, the security situation worsened, with looters fighting for rice, clothing, and other goods. The Haitian government, paralysed by the destruction of the presidential palace and ministries, signed a memorandum of understanding formally transferring control of Toussaint L'Ouverture airport to the US. Former President Bill Clinton said he would travel to Haiti to deliver emergency supplies. The US military was taking a leading role, with over 1,000 troops on the ground and 12,000 expected by Monday. The World Food Program finally landed flights of food, medicine, and water, but faced challenges due to a damaged port, blocked roads, and widespread fuel shortages. Coordination was a critical challenge, with the US prioritizing securing the country over humanitarian aid. The US Agency for International Development was helping choose sites and clear roads for food and water distribution centers. Despite progress, problems remained, including fuel shortages and a lack of drivers to move aid into the city. The UN mission, which had a 9,000-strong peacekeeping force in Haiti, seemed stunned by its own losses, with three of its most senior officials killed in the quake. The Haitian government, itself under siege, struggled to coordinate efforts, with the prime minister's office compound serving as a makeshift aid hub.

The Chronicles of Narnia: The Voyage of the Dawn Treader, directed by Michael Apted, is a largely dreary installment in the Narnia franchise, with a new cast of characters and a generally bland, expository plot. Will Poulter, known for his aggressive, chatterbox performance in "Son of Rambow," plays Eustace Scrubb, a cousin of the Pevensie siblings, adding unexpected depth to the film. The movie follows the children as they journey to Narnia, where they encounter King Caspian and a talking mouse, among other fantastical creatures. Despite some well-executed action scenes and moments of emotional resonance, the film struggles with its balance between faith-based messages and escapist entertainment, leaving a mixed impression. Apted's direction is generally reliable but fails to elevate the material beyond its generic, formulaic nature, making "The Voyage of the Dawn Treader" a forgettable entry in the series.

The recent assault on the National Security Five, a group of Republican Congress members, highlights the fear within the elite class about discussing and understanding radical Islamists, according to a commentary. This fear is evident in the intense pushback against inquiries into national security concerns, as seen in the case of Rep. Michele Bachmann and others questioning Huma Abedin, a Muslim aide to Hillary Clinton. The author argues that this rush to silence questions is reminiscent of the Cold War era, where unpleasant truths were uncovered, such as the FBI's Robert Hanssen and CIA's Aldrich Ames being spies. The author contends that today's political correctness and reluctance to ask tough questions about national security are a departure from the rigorous investigations of the past. The desire to avoid an honest discussion about radical Islamism stems from the fear that such a discussion might lead to a more confrontational strategy, which could alienate the public. The article also mentions that Politico's recent defense of Michele Bachmann and Newt Gingrich's Op-Ed, which criticized Muslim Brotherhood infiltration, further exemplifies the media's reluctance to engage in a serious dialogue about national security. The author concludes by highlighting the exclusion of Israel from the Global Counterterrorism Forum and the U.S. government's engagement with the Taliban, both of which underscore the complex and politically charged nature of national security discussions in the current climate.

Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau, known for his sunny disposition and diplomatic approach, has faced a humorous challenge from former Friends star Matthew Perry, who once beat up the young Trudeau in elementary school. The incident, which occurred when Trudeau's father was prime minister and security was lax, reportedly pushed the future leader into politics. In a playful tweet, Trudeau expressed his desire for a rematch, joking, "I've been giving it some thought, and you know what, who hasn't wanted to punch Chandler? How about a rematch Matthew Perry?" While Perry has not responded, the idea of the two fighting, even in a video game-like scenario, has sparked public interest, with many suggesting they should pay-per-view the match to raise charity funds. The incident highlights the personal and sometimes unexpected factors that can influence political careers, even for a leader as polished as Trudeau.

Norwegian Air Shuttle ASA aims to revolutionize transatlantic travel by offering one-way tickets to Europe for $69 in 2017, targeting smaller U.S. airports with low international fees. CEO Bjørn Kjos envisions flights to cities like Edinburgh, Birmingham, and Bergen, Norway, from airports such as New York's Westchester County Airport and Connecticut's Bradley International Airport, which currently lack extensive international service. These routes are expected to have average round-trip prices of around $300, significantly lower than Norwegian's current fares due to reduced airport fees. The strategy is part of Norwegian's broader plan to challenge traditional flag carriers by providing nonstop services to smaller cities, thereby cutting costs.

Kjos believes that within five years, the landscape of transatlantic travel will change dramatically, posing a significant threat to established airlines like Lufthansa. Norwegian's 100 Boeing 737 MAX jets, which are designed to cross the Atlantic, will play a crucial role in these new routes. These planes are more fuel-efficient and better suited for smaller airports, making them ideal for direct flights to cities like Birmingham. However, regulatory approval will be necessary to establish customs stations at U.S. regional airports to handle international traffic, a challenge that Kjos is optimistic about overcoming.

While other airlines, such as Iceland's Wow Air and Lufthansa's Eurowings, are also exploring low-cost long-haul flights, Kjos dismisses the threat posed by widebody planes like the Boeing 767, arguing that they are less fuel-efficient and have a smaller range compared to the 737 MAX. Norwegian's recent success in filling 96% of long-haul seats in September has bolstered its confidence in expanding its operations across the Atlantic. The airline's strategy hinges on leveraging its fleet of 737 MAX jets and operating from smaller airports to offer competitive prices and nonstop services, potentially reshaping the transatlantic travel market.

Support for the death penalty in the United States has dipped below 50% for the first time in nearly half a century, according to a new Pew Research Center poll. Just 49% of Americans now favor capital punishment, marking a seven-point decline from the previous year and the lowest level since 1971. This decline follows a steady trend since 1994, when support peaked at 80%. The poll also reveals significant political divides, with 72% of Republicans favoring the death penalty, compared to only 34% of Democrats. Independents now split evenly, with 44% supporting and 45% opposing the death penalty.

The drop in support may be linked to recent negative publicity surrounding lethal injection executions. In 2014, multiple inmates on death row experienced botched executions, with some struggling for an hour or more before being declared dead. Since then, the US federal government has yet to establish a widely accepted alternative to lethal injection, leading to a decline in overall executions. In 1999, 98 people received the death penalty, but only 15 met that fate in 2018.

The shift in public opinion is evident across various demographic groups. Men are more likely to support the death penalty than women, with 55% of men favoring it compared to 43% of women. White Americans are more supportive than black and Hispanic Americans, with 57% of whites backing the death penalty, compared to 29% of blacks and 36% of Hispanics. Younger adults (18-29) are less likely to support the death penalty (42%) than older age groups (51% of those 30 and older).

Religious differences also play a role, with white evangelical Protestants backing the death penalty by a wide margin (69% favor, 26% oppose). White mainline Protestants are also more likely to support (60%) than oppose (31%) the death penalty. Among Catholics and the religiously unaffiliated, opinions are more divided, with 43% of Catholics and 40% of the religiously unaffiliated supporting the death penalty, while 46% of Catholics and 46% of the religiously unaffiliated oppose it.

Despite the decline in support, a more detailed study found that 63% of the public still believed the death penalty was morally justified. However, majorities also acknowledged the risk of executing an innocent person (71%) and that the death penalty does not deter serious crime (61%).

Hostess Brands, LLC is voluntarily recalling 710,000 cases of snack cakes and donuts due to possible undeclared peanut residue from their supplier, Grain Craft. The affected products, including Ding Dongs, Zingers, and Chocodiles, were made with the recalled flour and may contain low levels of peanut allergens. While the risk is considered minimal, anyone with a peanut allergy should discard or return the products for a refund. The recall covers single-serve, multipack, and bagged donuts sold nationwide. Hostess has received reports of two allergic reactions related to the recalled items. For more information, consumers can contact Hostess at 1-800-686-2813 or visit their website.

In recent years, an increasing number of meat lovers in the United States and around the world have developed a life-threatening allergy to meat, known as alpha-gal syndrome. This condition is triggered by a bite from the Lone Star Tick, which spreads the allergy through its saliva. The allergy is caused by a sugar called galactose-alpha-1,3-galactose (alpha-gal), which is found in mammal meat, including pork and beef. When the sugar enters the body, it triggers an immune response, leading to a massive release of histamines, similar to other allergic reactions.

The condition was first identified in the southeastern United States, where people are 10 times more likely to be allergic to cetuximab, a cancer drug that contains alpha-gal. Researchers at the University of Virginia, led by immunologist Thomas Platts-Mills, discovered that the alpha-gal antibodies in affected patients matched those found in the drug. This led them to investigate the connection between the drug and meat allergies. Platts-Mills and his team found that 80% of meat allergy patients reported being bitten by a tick, and tick bites led to a 20-fold increase in alpha-gal antibodies.

The exact mechanism by which the Lone Star Tick spreads the allergy is still unclear. Scientists are investigating whether it is a molecule in the tick's saliva, a microbe, or residual proteins from the tick's previous blood meals. The condition is lifelong and can be life-threatening, as anaphylaxis can cause airway swelling and lead to death. Symptoms include itching, hives, stomach cramping, and difficulty breathing, often appearing a few hours after consuming meat.
