The spread of the allergy has been documented in new areas, including Pennsylvania and New York, raising questions about whether the tick's range is expanding or if other tick species have developed the ability to confer the allergy. Researchers are working to trace the spread of the condition, understand the mechanism behind the allergy, and develop potential treatments. For now, the best advice is to take precautions when spending time in tick-infested areas and to seek immediate medical attention if symptoms arise after consuming meat.

Turkish state-run news agency Anadolu reports that prosecutors are seeking more than four years in prison for NBA player Enes Kanter on charges of insulting President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Kanter, a center for the New York Knicks, faces trial in absentia for a series of tweets posted in May and June 2016, which prosecutors deemed insulting. Despite the potential indictment, Kanter remains unfazed, stating, "I'm in America. I'm good. My focus right now is just going out there, playing basketball, having fun with my teammates and just winning, and just thinking about playoffs. I don't really think about all this stuff, whatever. They can do whatever they want to do." Kanter, who grew up in Turkey, is a vocal supporter of Fethullah Gulen, the U.S.-based cleric blamed by Turkey for last year's failed military coup. Kanter was detained in Romania on May 20 due to his canceled Turkish passport but was able to return to the United States after American officials intervened. The Knicks center expressed his hope that the situation in Turkey can change, saying, "The only thing you can do is just pray for all these innocent people in Turkey." He added, "If we make playoffs, then that will drive him crazy, so that's what I'm really focused on right now, just make the playoffs and drive this dude crazy." Kanter also criticized the Turkish government, stating, "That dude is maniac. Think about it. I mean, America ... you've got freedom of whatever you want to say. I mean, it's a free country. But it's not like that in Turkey. You cannot criticize or you cannot even say nothing bad about the dude, Erdogan. Just, like, say he's a bad guy and you're in a prison. It's politics. People can choose or say whatever they want to say. I think right now the situation there is pretty messed up."

Donald Trump's campaign has been marked by his relentless attacks and refusal to back down, a trait that has both propelled him to the top of the Republican field and landed him in controversy. In a Rolling Stone cover story, writer Paul Solotaroff provides an intimate look at the candidate, revealing his unfiltered comments and the strategies behind his success. Solotaroff notes that Trump's ability to "attack, attack, attack" has been both his blessing and his curse, as it has earned him a lead in the polls but also drawn criticism for his personal attacks. A particularly contentious moment came when Trump was watching a newscast and saw Carly Fiorina, saying, "Look at that face! Would anyone vote for that?" He added, "I mean, she's a woman, and I'm not supposed to say bad things, but really, folks, come on. Are we serious?" This comment sparked controversy on social media, with some arguing that it was a personal attack while others defended it as fair game in a political race. Solotaroff's piece also highlights Trump's business acumen and his refusal to spend money on advertising, instead relying on his own media presence and the constant stream of controversy. Despite the backlash, Trump remains confident, stating, "I don't start these fights, but I sure as hell win them." His campaign promises and policies, while controversial, have resonated with a portion of the Republican base, particularly those disillusioned with the establishment. As the primary season heats up, Trump's ability to maintain his lead and navigate the challenges ahead will be closely watched.

CNN is under scrutiny for alleged inaccuracies in a report by its chief medical correspondent, Dr. Sanjay Gupta, following an earthquake in Nepal. The report, which aired two days after the 7.8 magnitude quake that killed over 8,000 people, claimed that Gupta had performed a life-saving operation on an eight-year-old girl with a life-threatening brain injury. However, an investigation by the Global Press Institute revealed that the girl in question had not sustained serious injuries, and that Gupta had actually assisted in an operation on a different patient, a 14-year-old. The institute also reported that CNN had initially published a text story with accurate details about the patients, which was later altered to match the broadcast report. Dr. Gupta acknowledged the discrepancy on CNN's morning news program, New Day, stating that he may have been involved with a different patient than originally reported. He explained that the chaotic conditions in the hospital after the earthquake might have led to confusion. However, Cristi Hegranes, founder of the Global Press Institute, criticized the reporting errors, emphasizing that such mistakes should not be excused, especially when the journalist was also performing a medical intervention. The incident has sparked discussions about the role of celebrity journalists in covering the developing world and the potential conflicts of interest in their reporting. CNN defended its coverage, stating that Gupta had helped save a young life during the earthquake and that the network was committed to verifying the details. Dr. Rajiv Jha, the senior neurosurgeon who conducted the operation, confirmed that Gupta had requested to assist but was only allowed to help for a short time. The controversy highlights the ethical challenges faced by physician-journalists and the importance of accurate reporting in crisis situations.

Apple is expected to announce a new subscription plan for newspapers, which hope tablets like the iPad will provide a new source of revenue as media companies struggle with declining print circulation and advertising. Apple is likely to take a 30 percent cut of all subscriptions sold through the App Store, and as much as 40 percent of the advertising revenue from publications' apps. Publishers are concerned about Apple's terms, as they must use Apple as an intermediary with subscribers and cannot offer app editions as part of subscription bundles that include print versions of the paper. While a handful of national papers already offer app subscriptions to iPad users, major metropolitan papers are preparing to roll out their own publication apps and have been in discussions with Apple. The iPad and future tablets will provide a new digital palette for publications to create sophisticated and lucrative ads, which could benefit Apple as well. However, there is some concern that readers could drop print editions for app versions too quickly, and most publishers don't want to see a rapid migration to apps without a comparable growth in advertisement revenue from tablet editions. Apple's secrecy and the high demand for any news about the company make it challenging for news organizations to maintain their standards when reporting on Apple.

On "A Day Without Immigrants," a nationwide protest, 18 employees at Bradley Coatings, Incorporated in Tennessee were fired after joining the movement, while a dozen Hispanic workers at I Don’t Care Bar and Grill in Catoosa, Oklahoma lost their jobs for skipping work to support the protest. The fired Tennessee employees, who were team leaders, stated they were unfairly terminated by their boss, who informed them they could not return to work. Bradley Coatings, Inc., a family-owned business, maintains that it terminated the employees due to the time-sensitive nature of their work assignments, emphasizing that the reason for their absence—participating in a peaceful demonstration—had no bearing on the decision. The company's attorney stated that the termination was consistent with previous communications to all employees and that the business will review its procedures to avoid similar issues in the future. Meanwhile, the Oklahoma restaurant owner, Bill McNally, justified the firings by his "zero tolerance policy for no show/no call incidents," despite the employees' long tenure and previous good standing. The fired workers expressed disappointment but did not harbor resentment, understanding the potential consequences of their actions. Both incidents highlight the complex interplay between employee rights, employer policies, and the challenges faced by immigrant communities in the United States.

Brown University has imposed sanctions on two fraternities in connection with incidents of sexual misconduct, highlighting the university's efforts to address and prevent such issues. In a letter to the campus community, senior officers Russell Carey and Margaret Klawunn detailed the sanctions and announced a comprehensive review of alcohol policies and social event regulations. The sanctions include probation and suspension of social and university privileges for Sigma Chi, a fraternity that hosted an unregistered party where a student reported an incident of non-consensual contact. Phi Kappa Psi, another fraternity, faced severe sanctions for hosting a party where two students reported receiving an alcoholic drink containing a date-rape drug, leading to non-consensual sexual contact. Both fraternities were found responsible for creating environments that facilitated sexual misconduct and inadequate security measures. The sanctions reflect a growing recognition that the status quo of social events that place students at risk is unacceptable. The university plans to review alcohol policies and social event regulations to promote a safer environment, prohibiting parties with alcohol service in residential areas. Approved events must be registered and have appropriate security measures in place. The sanctions underscore the university's commitment to preventing sexual assault and ensuring a safe campus climate.

Comedian Bill Cosby is alive despite rumors making rounds on the internet, with "Bill Cosby died" trending as the number one topic on Twitter and "is Bill Cosby dead" as the number two topic on Google Trends. Cosby, 73, took to his Twitter account to address the rumors, writing, "Again, I'm rebutting rumors about my demise." This isn't the first time Cosby has had to deal with such news; in February, he tweeted, "As you well know, a dead person cannot rebut. Therefore, I am rebutting to tell you that when I heard the news I immediately began rebutting and went into denial." He acknowledged that "rebutting" isn't a verb but added, "I don't care, because I'm alive."

Violence has erupted again in South Sudan's capital, Juba, with hundreds dead and thousands displaced. The conflict, which began on Thursday, saw fierce clashes between forces loyal to President Salva Kiir and those supporting Vice-President Riek Machar, raising fears of a full-scale civil war. Aid workers report that the fighting has led to a humanitarian crisis, with 36,000 people displaced and seeking shelter at various locations, including UN compounds. The UN has called for swift, safe, and unhindered humanitarian access to all those in need. Despite the violence, some see signs of hope. Jeremiah Young, a World Vision aid worker, notes the resilience of the South Sudanese people, who continue to seek peace and better lives for their children. However, the situation remains dire, with ongoing threats to civilians and humanitarian facilities. The UN has also called for an arms embargo and sanctions against those involved in the fighting. Meanwhile, the international community, including the US, has begun evacuating its citizens, highlighting the growing instability. The conflict's roots lie in a historic rivalry between Kiir, a Dinka, and Machar, a Nuer, with deep mistrust and ethnic tensions fueling the violence. Despite a peace agreement signed in August 2015, the current fighting threatens to undermine the fragile stability achieved. As the situation in Juba remains volatile, the international community and regional bodies like IGAD and the African Union are urging all parties to engage in dialogue and uphold the peace agreement. The crisis in South Sudan, which has already displaced millions and devastated the economy, underscores the urgent need for a lasting solution to the ongoing conflict.

The Las Vegas Strip became a scene of deadly violence early Thursday when a confrontation in a hotel valet area escalated into a car-to-car attack, leaving three people dead and at least six injured. At around 4:20 a.m., someone in a black Range Rover opened fire on a Maserati, sending it crashing into a taxi that burst into flames. The Maserati driver, Kenneth Wayne Cherry Jr., 27, and the taxi driver, Michael Boldon, were killed. Cherry's passenger was shot and taken to University Medical Center. The Range Rover fled the scene, prompting a manhunt involving police in three neighboring states. Las Vegas Boulevard near Flamingo Road, the site of several major casinos, was shut down for hours. Six vehicles were involved in the crash, including the taxi and Maserati. The shooting was not a rolling gun battle; the cars were stopped at a light when gunfire was exchanged. Police were investigating whether the altercation might have started in a nightclub. The incident marked the latest in a series of violent events on the Strip, including a shooting at a parking garage and a stabbing in an elevator. Despite the violence, Las Vegas officials emphasized the city's safety measures and reassured visitors that the Strip is among the safest travel destinations in the world.

Guinness is set to become vegan-friendly for the first time in its 256-year history, as the company plans to stop using isinglass, a by-product of the fishing industry, in its filtration process. According to a spokesman, the firm will introduce a new filtration plant that avoids the use of isinglass, which has been used for clarification since the 19th century. While isinglass is effective, large quantities are filtered out, leaving traces of fish bladders in the final product. This change follows a long-standing campaign and several online petitions from beer-loving vegans who have highlighted the lack of transparency regarding isinglass use. Guinness has already announced that its new filtration system will be implemented by late 2016, marking a significant shift in the company's approach to vegan-friendly brewing. The transition aims to ensure that all Guinness products, including draught and canned versions, are suitable for vegans, addressing the concerns of consumers who wish to enjoy the iconic stout without compromising their dietary principles.

Spring allergies are particularly bothersome this year, with Louisville, Kentucky, topping the Asthma and Allergy Foundation of America's list of 2014 Spring Allergy Capitals. The city's higher-than-average pollen counts and increased use of allergy medications, alongside a shortage of allergy specialists, contribute to its ranking. Dr. Gerald Lee, an allergist in Louisville, attributes the city's high pollen levels to its river basin effect and favorable climate, which encourages pollen growth. Dr. Nancy Snyderman, chief medical editor for NBC News, explains that a longer growing season and new plant growth exacerbate seasonal allergies, affecting about 40 million Americans. She advises avoiding outdoor activities when pollen is high and suggests running early in the morning when dew keeps pollen down. Other cities in the South, including Memphis, Baton Rouge, Oklahoma City, Jackson, Chattanooga, Dallas, Richmond, Birmingham, and McAllen, also rank among the worst for spring allergies. Residents in these areas may experience symptoms such as coughing, sneezing, itchy eyes, a runny nose, and a scratchy throat.

San Francisco is grappling with a severe car break-in problem, with over 31,000 incidents reported in 2017, and only 2% resulting in arrests, according to SFGate. To shed light on the issue, Inside Edition sent a crew to Alamo Square, a popular tourist spot, to set up a bait car with a $250 speaker and a Michael Kors purse, both rigged with GPS trackers. The bait car was parked, and Inside Edition’s Chief Investigative Correspondent, Lisa Guerrero, left the scene to monitor the situation. Soon, a couple approached the car, and one of them smashed the window to grab the purse, tossing it to a woman who was with him. The man then grabbed the speaker and walked away, unaware that the entire incident was captured on hidden cameras. Guerrero and her team tracked the suspects using the GPS devices and pursued them through the city. The suspects eventually boarded a bus and tried to enter a BART station, but Guerrero confronted them, warning, "Five million people are gonna see you steal that." The man put down the speaker and walked away, while Guerrero recovered the purse from a nearby trash can. However, the story took a twist when, during the interview, the Inside Edition camera crew van was broken into, resulting in two broken windows and the theft of thousands of dollars worth of equipment. This incident was also caught on surveillance footage. The crew's experience highlighted the prevalence of smash-and-grab thefts in the area, with one resident noting that such incidents occur every day. The shocking double theft underscored the severity of the car break-in problem in San Francisco.

The murder-suicide at UCLA and the subsequent discovery of a "kill list" in Minnesota have added a chilling twist to the case. On Wednesday, former UCLA student Mainak Sarkar, 38, shot and killed engineering professor William S. Klug, 39, before taking his own life. The motive, according to Los Angeles Police Chief Charlie Beck, was Sarkar's belief that Klug had stolen his intellectual property. Sarkar had left a note at the scene asking authorities to check on his cat, leading police to his apartment in St. Paul, Minnesota, where they found a "kill list" with the names of two UCLA professors and a woman. Ashley Hasti, 31, was found dead in her Brooklyn Park home, believed to have been killed before the UCLA shooting. The "kill list" also included the name of the second professor, who was safe. Sarkar, who had two semi-automatic pistols and multiple rounds of ammunition, had driven from Minnesota to California, and authorities are searching for his 2003 Nissan Sentra with the license plate 720KTW. The grandmother of the slain wife, Ashley Hasti, described her granddaughter as a kind, smart, and talented student who was pursuing a medical career. The discovery of the "kill list" and the deaths of both the professor and his wife have raised questions about Sarkar's mental state and the nature of his disputes. The case has left the UCLA community in shock and mourning, with a candlelight vigil held for Professor Klug. The university has resumed operations, but the tragedy has cast a shadow over the campus.

Edward Snowden's father, Lon Snowden, recently arrived in Moscow to visit his son, who is currently residing in Russia after leaking classified information about government surveillance programs. Lon Snowden expressed gratitude for Russia's decision to grant his son temporary asylum, stating he hopes his son remains in Russia. Edward Snowden, 30, was granted asylum in August after spending weeks in a transit zone at Moscow's Sheremetyevo airport. He faces espionage charges in the U.S. and has not disclosed his exact location in Russia. His father met with his son's Russian lawyer, Anatoly Kucherena, and later visited his son, though their meeting details were kept secret for security reasons. Kucherena said Snowden is living modestly, relying on savings and donations, and may seek employment in IT or human rights. The younger Snowden has received the Sam Adams Associates for Integrity in Intelligence award from former U.S. security officials. Lon Snowden defended his son, calling him a whistleblower who exposed injustices in the U.S. system, and expressed uncertainty about his son returning to the U.S. The elder Snowden praised Russia for taking his son in and thanked the Russian people and President Putin. Edward Snowden's father plans to return to Russia multiple times, maintaining a close relationship with his son despite not knowing his exact whereabouts.

The new head of the British Army, General Mark Carleton-Smith, has warned that Russia now poses a greater threat to the UK's national security than Islamist extremist groups such as al-Qaeda and Islamic State (IS). In an interview with The Daily Telegraph, Carleton-Smith emphasized the need for Britain and its allies to remain vigilant against Russia's threats, which extend beyond conventional military capabilities into non-conventional areas like cyber and space warfare. He highlighted Russia's systematic efforts to exploit Western vulnerabilities and called for a shift in focus from the reduced threat of Islamist groups in the Middle East to the growing threat from Russia. Carleton-Smith's comments come amid heightened tensions between the West and Russia over various issues, including Russia's actions in Ukraine, alleged election meddling, cyberattacks, and the poisoning of a Russian double agent and his daughter in Salisbury, England. The Russian Embassy responded to Carleton-Smith's remarks with a tweet, mocking his assessment and suggesting that the British Army chief's strategic vision is lacking. Meanwhile, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov also dismissed the accusations, stating that the British government's decisions regarding its military leadership are not subject to Russian influence. The UK government has consistently blamed Russia for the nerve-agent attack on former spy Sergei Skripal and his daughter, Yulia, in Salisbury, while Moscow denies any involvement. The incident, which involved the use of a Soviet-made military nerve agent known as Novichok, has further strained relations between the two nations.

Embedding Twitter content on your website or app requires agreement to Twitter's Developer Agreement and Developer Policy. If there's an issue connecting to the server, try again or include the basic tweet and media. Despite the agreement, some users face challenges with server connection, prompting repeated attempts and inclusion of essential elements. By following these guidelines, developers can ensure smooth integration of Twitter content into their digital platforms.

Reeva Steenkamp, Oscar Pistorius' girlfriend, expressed her fears about him in a text message sent to him just weeks before her death, the athlete's murder trial has heard. The message, dated January 27, 2013, reveals that Steenkamp was concerned about Pistorius' behavior, describing him as "nasty" and "quick to act, cold and off-ish when you are unhappy," according to the Guardian. She also accused him of being "tutored" by an acting coach, suggesting that his emotional outbursts in court might be rehearsed. Pistorius, in a reply, apologized for his behavior but admitted he was "tired and sick" and that this was not an excuse for his jealous actions. The texts also show that Steenkamp felt Pistorius was "picking on" her and that he got upset if she mentioned her ex-boyfriend. Pistorius referred to Steenkamp as "Angel," while she called him "Baba," indicating a close, but troubled, relationship.

The trial has also heard from a neighbor, Annette Stipp, who woke up around 3 a.m. on Valentine's Day 2013, the night Steenkamp was killed. She reported hearing three gunshots, followed by a woman's "terrified screaming." Moments later, she heard a man and woman screaming simultaneously, followed by a second set of gunshots, and then silence. Stipp noted that Pistorius' bathroom lights were on from the moment she awoke, and the screams did not sound muffled or as if they were coming from an enclosed space. The defense attempted to discredit Stipp's testimony, suggesting that the second set of gunshots might have been the sound of a cricket bat being used to break down the bathroom door.

The texts and Stipp's testimony are part of the prosecution's case, which is expected to conclude this week. Pistorius, who faces charges of premeditated murder, illegal possession of ammunition, and shooting a gun in public, is likely to be the first witness for the defense. The trial, originally expected to last for three weeks, has been extended until the middle of May, as only 18 of 107 possible witnesses were heard in the first three weeks. The extension was agreed upon by both sides to allow for a more thorough examination of the evidence.

In 1527, rioters smashed Michelangelo's David, and in 1991, a man attacked its toe with a hammer, but the world-famous statue has now faced its most significant indignity to date. An advertisement by the 60-year-old American small arms engineering company ArmaLite has sparked outrage in Italy, depicting the 16th-century marble statue brandishing an AR-50A1 rifle. The ad, part of ArmaLite's "A Work of Art" campaign, shows David preparing to take on Goliath with the large rifle instead of his traditional sling and stones. The image has caused such a stir that Italy's culture minister, Dario Franceschini, demanded the advertisement be "immediately" withdrawn. Florence, the home of both the statue and the new prime minister, Matteo Renzi, has expressed particular indignation. The superintendent for the city's historical heritage and fine arts board, Cristina Acidini, has issued a legal notice to ArmaLite, demanding the image be withdrawn. Cultural critic Sergio Givone described the depiction as "a real abuse," stating it is "an act of violence towards the sculpture; like taking a hammer to it and perhaps, actually, even worse." However, art critic Philippe Daverio downplayed the controversy, comparing the ad to tongue-in-cheek images of the Mona Lisa with a moustache. The Accademia Gallery director called the ad "in bad taste" and "completely illegal." ArmaLite is currently running a "McArmaLite March Sale" featuring the image of a leprechaun wielding one of its assault rifles, which may not sit well with Italian sensibilities.

Journalists were granted a rare glimpse of North Korea's preparations for a controversial rocket launch, marking the 100th anniversary of the birth of Kim Il Sung, the founder of the Communist state. The launch, set for between April 12 and 16, has been met with international skepticism, as Pyongyang insists it is for peaceful purposes, while Japan, the United States, and South Korea view it as a cover for a long-range ballistic missile test. The rocket, 30 meters long and white with some red and blue paint, was shown to visiting journalists at the Sohae Satellite Launching Station in Tongchang-ri, North Korea. North Korea has invited foreign reporters and experts to observe the launch, with more than 20 media firms represented. The satellite, which will be launched, is claimed to gather information on forestry resources, natural disasters, crop estimates, weather forecasts, and natural resources. Despite these assurances, the launch has raised tensions, with the U.S. suspending a food aid deal and Japan warning it will shoot down any part of the rocket that enters its territory. North Korea has also been preparing for a potential nuclear test, with satellite images showing construction of a new tunnel at the Punggye-ri nuclear test site in the northeast of the country. The tunnel, believed to be in its final stage, could be used for a third nuclear test, possibly involving highly enriched uranium. The launch is timed to coincide with the "Day of the Sun," a key public holiday in North Korea, and is seen as a show of strength amid persistent economic hardship. The international community remains closely watching the situation, with concerns over the potential for further escalation.

This month, the term "Blue Moon" will be invoked twice, as the second full moon of July 2015 will occur on July 31, 2015. This phenomenon, which happens roughly once every 2.7 years, is not related to the moon's color but rather to the calendar. The Blue Moon is defined as the second full moon in a month, with the first full moon occurring on July 2. The term "Blue Moon" has a long history, with its origins in an old English term meaning "betrayer," and it was used in the Maine Farmers' Almanac to describe the third full moon in a season with four. The Blue Moon on July 31 will be visible around the world, with the exact moment of fullness occurring at 6:43 a.m. EDT (10:43 GMT). Despite the name, the moon will not appear blue, and its color will depend on atmospheric conditions. The Blue Moon is a byproduct of the contrast between the calendar month and the lunar month, which averages 29.530589 days, shorter than every calendar month except February. This year, 2015, will have 13 full moons, with one extra moon in July, making the Blue Moon of July 31 a rare event. The next Blue Moon will not occur until 2018. For skywatchers, the Blue Moon will be a spectacular sight, but it's important to note that it's not the only celestial event of interest. The full moon on July 31 is also a "supermoon," meaning it will appear up to 14% larger and 30% brighter than usual, due to its proximity to Earth during its orbit. This supermoon will be visible in the early morning hours of July 31 for much of the world, with the best viewing times varying by location. The Blue Moon and supermoon together create a unique and rare celestial event, making it a must-see for astronomy enthusiasts.

Fifty-seven people, including 22 crew members and 35 passengers, are stranded aboard the Russian-operated Akademik Shokalskiy, an ice-strengthened vessel built in 1984, which has become stuck in the ice about 1,500 nautical miles from Hobart, Tasmania. The ship, on a Spirit of Mawson voyage commemorating the centenary of Douglas Mawson's exploration, issued a satellite distress call early Christmas morning. The Australian Maritime Safety Authority (AMSA) reports that the vessel is not in immediate danger and that the passengers are in good spirits, tweeting, "All are well and spirits are high. Happy Christmas." Rescue efforts are underway, with three icebreakers dispatched from different locations, but it will take at least two days for the nearest vessel to reach the remote location. The expedition, led by Australian climate change professor Chris Turney, includes a trip to Mawson's Huts, which had been inaccessible for many years due to an iceberg. Despite the storm and heavy ice, the team celebrated Christmas and continued their scientific work, collecting samples and conducting research. The expedition is using the Inmarsat satellite system to provide live communications while in the field.

Inorganic mercury, used to lighten skin in creams, poses significant health risks, including kidney damage, skin rashes, and central nervous system issues. Despite being banned, illegal mercury-containing skin creams are widely available, particularly in communities catering to Latino, Asian, African, and Middle Eastern populations. These products, often marketed as skin lighteners or anti-aging treatments, can be purchased online or brought from other countries. Mercury is absorbed through the skin, with the amount varying based on the cream's ingredients and usage frequency. The body slowly excretes inorganic mercury, leading to potential long-term health issues. Children are at risk of mercury exposure through contact with users or contaminated household items. Symptoms include irritability, tremors, vision changes, and depression. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advises avoiding such products and warns that their use can result in mercury poisoning. Consumers should wash hands and other exposed areas thoroughly, seek medical advice if symptoms arise, and properly dispose of suspected products. The FDA has an import alert to intercept such products but emphasizes the need for consumer awareness of the dangers. At least 60 Californians have suffered mercury poisoning from these creams, with some cases involving children. Parents and caregivers are urged to be vigilant and avoid using these potentially harmful products.

Texas Governor Rick Perry, known for his controversial "Oops" moment during a 2011 presidential debate, announced on July 8, 2013, that he will not seek re-election for a fourth term as governor. Speaking at a Caterpillar dealership in San Antonio, Perry said he will spend the next 18 months focusing on job creation, innovation, and state leadership before deciding his future path. He left open the possibility of running for president in 2016. Perry's decision clears the way for Texas Attorney General Greg Abbott, who is expected to run for governor. Abbott's campaign had already been gaining momentum, with a larger war chest than Perry's. Despite Perry's strong record on job creation and budget management, a recent poll showed that 60% of Texas voters did not want him to run for re-election. Perry's career, marked by his long tenure as governor and his controversial statements, has seen him rise to near-front-runner status in the 2012 presidential race before a disastrous performance. His decision not to seek re-election could have significant implications for Texas politics in the coming years.

Mitt Romney's defense of Obamacare in a recent speech in Ann Arbor, Michigan, drew criticism from conservatives and pundits. Romney argued that the individual mandate, which is now a contentious feature of Obamacare, was designed to address the "free-rider" problem. However, this justification echoes the same rationale behind the mandate in Obamacare, which conservatives oppose as an infringement on individual freedom. Romney's defense of his Massachusetts health-care plan, Romneycare, as a model for the nation was met with skepticism, as he failed to highlight any unique aspects of the Massachusetts health-care environment that are not present in other states. His claim that Romneycare and Obamacare are fundamentally different was also challenged, with critics pointing out that both plans share the same core concept of an individual mandate. Romney's speech also included a defense of the French health-care system, which drew further criticism for its incompatibility with conservative principles. The speech was seen as a poor strategy, as it made Romney appear more articulate in favor of the individual mandate than President Obama, potentially exacerbating conservative opposition to his candidacy. His opponents, like Rick Santorum, criticized Romney for his support of Romneycare and its similarities to Obamacare, arguing that both plans infringe on individual freedom and increase government healthcare costs. The speech highlighted Romney's lack of self-awareness and understanding of the current Republican primary electorate, as it is unlikely to win him support from conservative voters.

Online ticketing sites for "Star Wars: The Force Awakens" faced significant challenges as users rushed to secure presale tickets for the highly anticipated film. Fandango and Movie Tickets experienced technical issues, with some users encountering "site maintenance" messages or "unknown error" screens. The film, directed by J.J. Abrams and featuring a cast including Oscar Isaac, Daisy Ridley, and John Boyega, was set to open in theaters on December 18, 2015. The first full trailer premiered during halftime of ESPN's Monday Night Football, offering a glimpse of new characters like Poe Dameron and Finn, as well as returning favorites such as Han Solo and Chewbacca. The trailer hinted at the conflict between Kylo Ren and Finn, and the mysterious role of Rey, while Luke Skywalker's presence remained ambiguous. Despite the technical hiccups, the film's release date arrived, and the excitement surrounding "Star Wars: The Force Awakens" continued to grow, with fans eagerly awaiting the film's debut.

Mike Evans, a Tampa Bay Buccaneers wide receiver, donated $11,000 to the family of Gregory Hill, who was shot and killed by a St. Lucie County Sheriff's Office deputy in 2014. The jury found Hill 99 percent responsible for his death and the department 1 percent responsible, awarding the family just $4, with $0.04 actually received. Hill, 30, was shot by Deputy Christopher Newman while officers responded to a complaint about loud music. Tests showed Hill was intoxicated and an unloaded gun was found in his pocket. Evans, who signed a five-year, $82 million extension earlier this year, stated his charity plans would help "a lot of people." His donation helped raise nearly $100,000 on a GoFundMe page. Gregory Hill's family filed a wrongful death lawsuit, and despite the low award, they continue to seek justice.

Nintendo Co. President Satoru Iwata announced a 25 billion-yen annual loss due to poor sales of the Wii U console, marking a third consecutive annual loss for the company. Iwata said Nintendo is considering a new business model, possibly incorporating smart devices, to address the decline in family-focused content appeal. The company cut its Wii U console sales forecast to 2.8 million units from 9 million and its game sales to 19 million units from 38 million. Nintendo's shares fell 17% in New York, their biggest decline since 2001. The company also cut its forecast for operating income to a 35 billion-yen loss from the prior 100 million-yen profit. Projections for its handheld 3DS player were cut to 13.5 million units from 18 million, and for 3DS games to 66 million units from 80 million. Nintendo posted a quarterly loss of 8 billion yen in October after cutting the price of the console. Iwata is trying to attract casual gamers from Apple and Samsung, but the market has shifted towards smartphones and tablets. The company reduced its planned dividend for the fiscal year to 100 yen from 260 yen. Nintendo's market capitalization is about $20 billion, less than Samsung’s capital expenditures. Iwata emphasized the need to adapt to the changing market and questioned the traditional business model of selling consoles and games.

Zynga, the social gaming company that has struggled since its 2011 IPO, has replaced its founder and CEO Mark Pincus with Don Mattrick, the former head of Microsoft’s Xbox division. Pincus will remain as chairman and chief product officer. Mattrick, who will join the Zynga board, brings extensive experience in the gaming industry, having overseen the expansion of Xbox’s audience and introduced the Kinect motion-sensor. Zynga’s stock rose nearly 9% on the news. The move follows a series of layoffs and office closures as Zynga attempts to transition to mobile gaming, an area where it has struggled. Pincus, who has long sought a seasoned manager to lead the company, expressed confidence in Mattrick’s ability to revitalize Zynga. However, Mattrick’s lack of mobile gaming experience may pose a challenge in helping Zynga succeed in this critical market.

European scientists have determined the "perfume" of comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko, using data from the Rosetta spacecraft's onboard instrument, ROSINA. The aroma, which would be quite unpleasant for humans, includes the odors of rotten eggs (hydrogen sulphide), horse stable (ammonia), formaldehyde, and bitter almonds (hydrogen cyanide). This surprising mix of volatile compounds, detected in the comet's coma, is a result of the Rosetta Orbiter Sensor for Ion and Neutral Analysis (ROSINA) analyzing the gases released as the comet approaches the Sun. The detection of such a rich variety of molecules, including ammonia, methane, hydrogen sulphide, hydrogen cyanide, and formaldehyde, has been a pleasant surprise for the scientists, as they initially expected only the most volatile molecules, carbon dioxide, and carbon monoxide, to be released at this distance from the Sun.

The team, led by Kathrin Altwegg of the University of Bern, has been using ROSINA to 'sniff' the comet's fumes since early August, with the goal of understanding the comet's composition and chemical makeup. As the comet gets closer to the Sun, the release of these gases will increase, making the aroma more pronounced. This information will help scientists gain insights into the fundamental chemical make-up of the solar nebula from which our Solar System and, ultimately, life itself, emerged. The mission aims to compare 67P/C-G with other comets, such as those from the Kuiper Belt and the distant Oort cloud, to determine how they differ and what this tells us about the origins of comets and the Solar System. The Rosetta mission, spearheaded by the European Space Agency with support from NASA, is set to land its Philae lander on the comet's surface on November 12, 2014, to conduct on-the-spot scientific tests. The lander's findings will complement the orbiter's observations, providing a comprehensive understanding of the comet's structure and composition.

Former Subway pitchman Jared Fogle is challenging his 15-year, eight-month prison sentence, arguing that he is being punished for his fantasies rather than his actions, according to court papers obtained by Reuters. Fogle's lawyers are appealing the sentence on several grounds, claiming the judge had no right to exceed the maximum sentencing guideline of around 13 years. They note the judge who sentenced Fogle said, "This defendant is obsessed with child pornography and having sex with minors. He fantasized about it in telephone conversations." Fogle's attorneys say fantasies should not form the basis of a criminal sentence, quoting another court decision that states, "We are loath to give the government the power to punish us for our thoughts and not our actions." Fogle's lawyers argue that the fantasies and "requests to third parties" were never acted upon by Fogle, yet they were relied on by the judge in imposing the sentence. Fogle wants the appeals court to give him another sentencing hearing, where his actions—rather than his thoughts—are the focus. The appeal calls the judge's decision "unreasonable" and asks the Seventh Circuit Court of Appeals in Chicago to throw out the prison term and order a resentencing. Fogle's attorneys argue that the child pornography was on a thumb drive that Fogle received from his co-conspirator Russell Taylor and viewed, but that does not amount to a contention that Fogle actively sought, collected, and distributed images of 6-year-olds. Fogle, who was once a national sensation and appeared in a Super Bowl ad, is now serving his sentence at the Federal Correctional Institution Englewood in suburban Denver, Colorado. His case highlights the complex legal and ethical issues surrounding the punishment of individuals for their thoughts and fantasies.

Steve Carell hosted Saturday Night Live, bringing his usual listlessness to the show, which struggled with a lack of engaging sketches and jokes. Carell's monologue was peppered with former Office cast members urging him to reboot the show, but the actual attempt at a new series was a non-starter. The highlight was Carell's Jeff Bezos impersonation, where he mocked Trump's wealth, Twitter habits, and business failures. Weekend Update focused on Fox News' Laura Ingraham, who was portrayed as a smirking white supremacist, while Amazon's new HQ2 locations in New York and Virginia provided a vehicle for more Trump-bashing. The episode was marred by a poorly executed space station sketch with dead monkeys and a clueless dad character that over-explained its premise. Ella Mai performed two numbers, including a song about her ex, with the stage fog from a previous sketch. The overall episode felt listless and failed to capitalize on the rich material available, particularly the post-election landscape.

President Trump's former campaign manager, Paul Manafort, is facing a contentious trial preparation process as he awaits his July 25th criminal trial for charges including money laundering and bank fraud. Court documents reveal that Manafort is being held in solitary confinement for 23 hours a day at a Virginia jail, purportedly to ensure his safety. His legal team argues that this harsh confinement, combined with his distance from legal counsel, is impeding his ability to adequately prepare for the upcoming trials. They have appealed the judge's decision to revoke his bail, citing the challenging conditions. However, prosecutors from Robert Mueller's office maintain that the limitations Manafort faces are common for defendants awaiting trial and that his alleged witness tampering, even if done through covert persuasion, is damaging to the justice system. Despite calls from former President Trump lawyer John Dowd to release Manafort, the prosecutors assert that he does not deserve special treatment. Manafort's current living conditions, described as part of the "VIP" section of the Northern Neck Regional Jail, have sparked debate over the fairness of his confinement.

Acting DEA Administrator Chuck Rosenberg issued a memo to DEA employees on Saturday, rebuking President Donald Trump's comments from a speech in New York, where Trump suggested police officers should be "rough" when arresting suspects. Rosenberg's memo emphasized the DEA's commitment to maintaining core values of respect and compassion when dealing with suspects, stating, "The President, in remarks delivered yesterday in New York, condoned police misconduct regarding the treatment of individuals placed under arrest by law enforcement." Rosenberg further clarified that he did not intend to advance any political or personal agenda, but rather to reaffirm the DEA's commitment to upholding the highest standards of law enforcement. He wrote, "We have an obligation to speak out when something is wrong. That's what law enforcement officers do. That's what you do. We fix stuff. At least, we try." This memo comes in the wake of Trump's controversial remarks, which were met with criticism from law enforcement agencies. Attorney General Jeff Sessions, speaking at the National Organization of Black Law Enforcement Executives, pledged to hold officers accountable for any abuse of authority. Sessions stated, "We all know the cases of the last several years where, in confrontations with police, lives have been cut short. Just as I am committed to defending law enforcement who used deadly force while lawfully engaged in their work, I will also hold any officer responsible for breaking the law." The DEA's stance highlights the tension between law enforcement officials and the Trump administration over issues of police conduct and the appropriate treatment of suspects.

Americans consume an astounding 52 quarts of popcorn per person annually, according to the American Popcorn Board, making microwave popcorn a convenient yet potentially risky snack. DIY microwave popcorn is a simple alternative that eliminates exposure to harmful chemicals and trans fats found in store-bought varieties. However, the process involves using diacetyl, a synthetic butter flavoring that can cause severe lung disease when inhaled. Major brands have begun phasing out PFOA from their packaging, but many still contain trans fats and saturated fats. Sodium levels can also be excessive, with one serving containing up to 380 milligrams. Homemade popcorn offers a healthier option, allowing for custom seasoning and avoiding harmful chemicals. Despite the allure of the buttery aroma, the potential health risks associated with microwave popcorn highlight the importance of making informed choices.

President Barack Obama delivered a fiery speech at the Congressional Black Caucus Foundation dinner, urging African-Americans to vote for Hillary Clinton in the upcoming election. His impassioned plea came as he addressed the looming threat posed by Donald Trump, whom he characterized as a "nasty, hateful charlatan" selling a false message that jeopardizes the progress made during his presidency. Obama’s speech was a stark contrast to the cautious tone he usually maintains, as he went beyond the prepared remarks to deliver a robust defense of his legacy and a stern warning against Trump.

In his address, Obama emphasized that the progress of the African-American community is at stake, and he declared that he would consider it a personal insult to his legacy if black voters fail to support Clinton. He highlighted several issues, including tolerance, democracy, and justice, stating that they are all on the ballot. Obama’s tone was both mocking and scathing, particularly when he addressed Trump’s birther controversy, which Obama said was resolved just before the speech. He used sarcasm to highlight the absurdity of Trump’s claims, noting that “ISIL, North Korea, poverty, climate change — none of those things weighed on my mind like the validity of my birth certificate.”

Obama’s critique of Trump extended beyond the birther issue. He accused Trump of perpetuating a narrative that African-Americans have never had it worse, a claim that Obama found insulting given the history of slavery and Jim Crow. He urged the audience to educate Trump on this civics lesson, referencing the new Smithsonian African-American Museum opening in Washington, D.C. Obama also emphasized the importance of voting and getting more voters registered, warning that anyone who supports voter ID laws aimed at suppressing black voters is part of the problem. He highlighted the irony of Republicans who oppose gun control measures while supporting voter suppression, arguing that this shows their fear of the ballot box.

The speech was not without lighter moments. Obama joked about the “birther” controversy, saying, “There’s an extra spring in my step tonight. I don't know about you guys, but I am so relieved that the whole 'birther' thing is over.” He also referenced the upcoming implementation of the Iran nuclear deal, stating, “As we speak, Iran has rolled back its nuclear program, shipped out its uranium stockpile, and the world has avoided another war.” However, he did not mention the recent detention of 10 U.S. sailors by Iran, which occurred just before the speech.

Obama’s call to action was clear: vote for Clinton to ensure that the progress of the African-American community is not jeopardized. He emphasized that the choice in November is not about golf course promotions or birth certificates but about who will fight for the forgotten. Obama’s speech was a powerful reminder of the stakes involved and a rallying cry for the black community to remain engaged and active in the political process.

Donald Trump's business ventures, particularly the defunct Trump University real estate seminar program, have faced significant legal challenges, including three separate lawsuits. Two class-action suits in California were filed by former students, alleging that Trump University engaged in deceptive practices, such as falsely claiming that Trump personally handpicked instructors and promising access to private financing. The third lawsuit, filed by New York's Attorney General Eric Schneiderman, seeks $40 million in restitution, accusing the program of persistent fraud and illegal business practices. Former employees and students have come forward, detailing aggressive sales tactics and unqualified instructors, with some claiming they were coerced into giving positive reviews. Trump's legal team has consistently denied the allegations, arguing the lawsuits are baseless and politically motivated. Despite losing a few legal battles, including a defamation case against Tarla Makaeff, Trump has refused to settle and has suggested the cases could drag on for years. The trials, including a November 28th hearing in one of the California cases, are expected to continue, potentially impacting Trump's presidential campaign. Meanwhile, the Better Business Bureau has noted that Trump University currently lacks an A rating, reflecting ongoing consumer concerns.

Canada experienced a series of shocking attacks this week, with the latest incident occurring on Wednesday when an armed assailant shot and fatally wounded Cpl. Nathan Cirillo, 24, at the National War Memorial before storming the Parliament buildings. Moments after Cirillo was shot, MPs and witnesses reported hearing 30 to 50 shots fired inside Parliament. The gunman was later shot dead by the House of Commons sergeant-at-arms, Kevin Vickers, and RCMP officers. CBC News has identified the suspect as Michael Zehaf-Bibeau, a Canadian born in 1982 with a criminal record in Quebec and B.C. Zehaf-Bibeau had a history of drug-related charges and threats. Prime Minister Stephen Harper condemned the attacks, stating, "For the second time this week, there has been a brutal and violent attack on our soil." He vowed, "But let there be no misunderstanding — we will not be intimidated, Canada will never be intimidated." NDP Leader Tom Mulcair and Liberal Leader Justin Trudeau also condemned the attacks and pledged support for the government. Harper met with his cabinet and the Conservative caucus, who were in lockdown until late Wednesday. The attacks came two days after a Quebec soldier was killed in a hit-and-run by a man described as an "ISIL-inspired terrorist." The soldier's family received condolences from Harper. Ottawa police Chief Charles Bordeleau asked witnesses to come forward, and Ottawa Civic Hospital confirmed four people were taken to the hospital, with three released after minor injuries. Despite earlier reports of shots fired near the Rideau Centre, police later said no incident occurred there. CBC video and cellphone footage showed a chaotic scene inside Parliament, with MPs and staff scrambling for safety. Kevin Vickers, the sergeant-at-arms, was credited with shooting the attacker. The attack prompted heightened security across Canada, including at government buildings, provincial legislatures, and military bases. U.S. President Barack Obama condemned the shootings and offered assistance to Canada. The attacks have led to increased security measures and a stronger resolve to fight terrorism both at home and abroad.

In Illinois, a dangerous synthetic cannabinoid product, often called K2, spice, or fake weed, has caused severe bleeding in 38 people, with one death reported. The Illinois Department of Public Health warns that these items are sold by convenience stores and dealers or obtained from friends. They advise against using these products and urge those experiencing severe, unexplained bleeding to seek medical attention immediately. The state division has issued an advisory: "If you have purchased any of this product in the past month, do not use it. If you have used any of these products, and start experiencing severe, unexplained bleeding or bruising, please have someone take you to the hospital immediately or call 911. Do not walk or drive yourself. Tell your health care providers about the possible link between your symptoms and synthetic cannabinoid use."

Synthetic cannabinoids are human-made, unregulated mind-altering chemicals that fall under a drug category called new psychoactive substances (NPS). They are sprayed on dried plant material for smoking or sold in liquid form for vaporizing devices. These substances are marketed as being able to mimic the effects of cannabis but are significantly more potent and can be life-threatening. The consumption of synthetic cannabinoids has previously caused serious health problems such as seizures and kidney failure, but the side effect of severe bleeding is tied to the recent outbreak. According to Dr. Patrick Lank, a medical toxicologist, three of the hospitalized people tested positive for brodifacoum, a rat poison. Rat poison contains ingredients that have anticoagulant properties, preventing blood from clotting effectively. Once someone loses their ability to clot, a cascade of untoward events follows, potentially leading to shock, stroke, cardiac events, loss of consciousness, and death.

Efforts to liken synthetic cannabinoids to marijuana are misleading. These "products" contain many highly potent, dangerous chemicals, and using them poses significant risks. The Illinois Department of Public Health now reports 2 deaths, 56 cases, and expects these numbers to rise. The Bausch Foundation, a philanthropic arm of Valeant Pharmaceuticals, donated nearly 800,000 vitamin K tablets to treat the poisonings. Health officials are working to find a way to place no financial burden on patients tied to the synthetic cannabinoids outbreak.

A 34-year-old Alaska man, Justin Schneider, pleaded guilty to assaulting a woman in Anchorage, Alaska, on August 15, 2017, and was sentenced to two years with one year suspended, plus three years of probation, according to CNN. Schneider, who had lost his job as an air traffic controller due to the case, acknowledged in court that he had strangled the woman until she lost consciousness and then sexually assaulted her, saying he needed her to believe she was going to die so he could be sexually fulfilled. The woman, who did not know Schneider, had been at a gas station looking for a ride to her boyfriend's home when Schneider offered her a ride. Instead of taking her to her destination, Schneider drove her to another location and attacked her. He told her he would kill her if she screamed and then strangled her, causing her to lose consciousness. When she regained consciousness, Schneider was zipping up his pants and offered her a tissue. The woman used her phone to call the police and report the vehicle's license plate number. The prosecutor, Andrew Grannik, emphasized that this was Schneider's "one pass" and warned him that such an incident must never happen again. The victim was not present in court. Schneider's guilty plea and sentence were seen as lenient by some, given the severity of the assault.

Spain's Crown Prince Felipe was formally proclaimed the new King of Spain on Thursday, following his father, Juan Carlos, abdicating after nearly four decades on the throne. The new monarch, dressed in a military uniform, promised to lead a changed monarchy "for new times" in an address before Spain's Parliament. Felipe, 46, and his wife, Queen Letizia, a former TV presenter, appeared before the parliamentary chamber and the Spanish people, with Felipe paying tribute to his father's "extraordinary" legacy, including his role in shepherding Spain into democracy after the death of dictator Francisco Franco. The new King emphasized the need for unity and cooperation with Spain's political leaders, particularly in light of the growing independence movement in Catalonia. His ascension comes at a time when many Spaniards are struggling with high unemployment rates and economic woes, prompting the new king to focus on modernizing and meeting the challenges of a globalized world. The proclamation ceremony was marked by a lack of pomp, with no state banquet or foreign dignitaries, reflecting a desire for austerity in the face of public financial concerns. The new King faces the challenge of maintaining the monarchy's relevance and unity in a country where some call for a republic, but recent polls suggest a majority still supports the monarchy with Felipe as king.

A 23-year-old Illinois man, Gregory Arthur Weiler II, has been charged with plotting to bomb nearly 50 churches in Oklahoma after authorities found bomb-making materials and a handwritten journal detailing his plan in a Miami motel. Weiler, who has a history of mental illness, was arrested last week after a hotel maintenance worker discovered bottles and other suspicious items in a trash bin. The items included 50 brown glass bottles with cloth wicks attached by duct tape, a funnel, and a 5-gallon gasoline can. Among the documents found in Weiler's room were a list of churches, a hand-drawn map, and instructions for making Molotov cocktails. One of the journal entries read, "Self-Promote for the next 4 years while beginning list of goals written out in Oklahoma having to do with destroying and removing church buildings from U.S., a tiny bit at a time -- setting foundation for the years to follow." Weiler, who has been held without bond, is due in court on October 22. His family said he has battled drug addiction and a history of mental illness, including a suicide attempt in the eighth grade. Weiler's cousin, Johnny Meyers, said his cousin had been out of touch for several years after leaving Illinois. A pastor at a homeless shelter in Missouri said Weiler showed no violent tendencies but was clearly troubled. The community in Miami, Oklahoma, has not changed anything and is praying for Weiler.

A 220-pound meteorite, known as the Fukang meteorite, has sparked a legal dispute over ownership, turning into a cosmic legal battle. The meteorite, estimated to be worth up to $1 million, was discovered in the Gobi Desert of China in 2000 and has since become a prized possession among collectors. Stephan Settgast of Novato, California, claims the meteorite is his rightful property, while a Massachusetts couple, Lawrence Stifler and Mary McFadden, argue they paid $425,000 for it and should retain ownership. Settgast canceled the sale when he discovered the couple was planning to display the meteorite in a museum in Maine, which violated the terms of the sale, according to him. Stifler and McFadden counter that Settgast's decision to reclaim the meteorite was due to seller’s remorse and that no museum clause was part of the agreement. Settgast sued in federal court to invalidate the sale, while the couple countersued, alleging theft. The meteorite, a pallasite, is valued for its unique greenish crystals and is believed to be 4.5 billion years old. The dispute involves a New York meteorite expert, Darryl Pitt, and Kansas rock polishers, Keith and Dana Jenkerson, who claim they are entitled to a share of the meteorite's value. The case, which has garnered attention due to its extraterrestrial nature, is set for a hearing in June, with the outcome potentially determining the fate of the rare space rock.

On February 27, President Donald Trump hosted a meeting with leaders of historically black universities and colleges in the Oval Office. During the event, White House counselor Kellyanne Conway made a peculiar move when she knelt on the couch to take a candid picture, allowing her heels to touch the cushions. This moment quickly became a subject of ridicule and meme-making, as Conway's casual and unorthodox behavior during a formal meeting was highlighted by the internet's penchant for finding humor in the administration's actions.

The incident sparked a wave of jokes and memes, with users on social media and online forums finding humor in Conway's unprofessional behavior. The cringe-worthy moment was particularly noteworthy because it occurred in the Oval Office, a space typically reserved for more formal and dignified interactions. The juxtaposition of Conway's casual pose with the grandeur of the space created a stark contrast that many found amusing.

While the internet's reaction was largely lighthearted, it also served as a reminder of the need to hold the administration accountable for its actions, no matter how minor they may seem. Critics pointed out that such incidents, while perhaps trivial in comparison to broader policy issues, still reflected poorly on the administration's standards and conduct. The meme culture surrounding the event underscored the public's interest in scrutinizing the administration's behavior, even in seemingly insignificant moments.

Conway's actions were not the first nor the last time she has been the subject of ridicule. Her previous encounters with the media and her public statements have frequently been the source of jokes and memes. The incident at the Oval Office was no exception, with users creating and sharing humorous images and captions that highlighted Conway's behavior.

Despite the lighthearted nature of the reactions, it is important to recognize that such moments can contribute to a broader narrative about the administration's approach to professionalism and decorum. The internet's response to Conway's actions serves as a microcosm of the public's ongoing scrutiny of the Trump administration, highlighting both the lighter and more serious aspects of political discourse in the digital age.

In an effort to reclaim their live performances and reduce distractions, a growing number of artists and venues are turning to the Yondr pouch, a smartphone lock designed by San Francisco-based startup Yondr. The pouch, which resembles a security tag from a clothing store, allows users to store their phones in a locked state until the end of the event. This system has been adopted by artists such as Alicia Keys, Dave Chappelle, Louis C.K., and Chris Rock, who have found that their performances are more engaging when audience members are not constantly filming or texting. The pouches are also being used at schools like Mercy High in Burlingame, California, where Mr. Offield's English class requires students to lock their phones in the pouches during class to encourage more in-the-moment interaction. 

Founder Graham Dugoni, a former college soccer star, created Yondr after observing the negative impact of smartphone use at music festivals. He believes that the pouches help create a more authentic experience for both performers and attendees. “By separating something that's primarily for their social life, I'm hoping that it brings them more in the moment,” Offield said. For some students, the experience of locking their phones away was a mental adjustment. Ally Ick, a senior at Mercy High, found that the Yondr pouch helped her focus more on the present. “Maybe if there's something going on on social media, I could be really tempted to want to check my phone every second, but then with the Yonder pouches, it takes away that feeling and you don't have to worry about it so much,” she said. 

However, not everyone is on board with the idea. Some concertgoers argue that their phones are a vital tool for recording and sharing memories. Gerard Little, 24, said, “In this day and age, my phone is how I keep my memory. Chris Brown. Jason Derulo. I have their footage on my phone. If you don’t want your music heard, then don’t perform it.” Others worry about the potential security risks of not having immediate access to their phones. Jackie Coward, 53, expressed concern, “It’s annoying when people have their phones out, lights blaring. They can’t stop texting. It’s disrespectful, and I like Alicia Keys. I don’t need to put out her stuff early. They should do this in more places.” Despite these concerns, the pouches have proven effective in creating a more immersive experience for both performers and audiences. As Dugoni notes, “If you haven’t been to a phone-free show, you just don’t know what you’re missing. There’s something about living in real life that can’t be replicated.”

In her first mainstream media interview since winning the Republican nomination for the U.S. Senate race, Sharron Angle softened her rhetoric on some issues but remained firm on others. Angle admitted her pre-primary language about the electorate resorting to "Second Amendment remedies" if conservatives didn't win was "a little strong" and changed her rhetoric to "defeat Harry Reid." She also moderated her stance on Social Security, suggesting existing benefits should be protected, more money should be invested, and younger workers should have the choice between a personal account or traditional benefits. However, Angle stood firm on opposing the extension of unemployment benefits, arguing that jobs exist that those on benefits should be taking. She also restated her opposition to abortion, maintaining that the government should not be involved in the issue, and that the separation of church and state is a doctrine meant to protect the church. Angle tried to pivot to attacking Harry Reid, blaming him for high unemployment, expanding the federal deficit, and bailing out big businesses. Despite her attempts to moderate her stance, Angle's core conservative beliefs on social issues remained intact. Her interview was significant as she had been previously seen as avoiding mainstream news organizations. The article also mentions that former Republican congresswoman Barbara Vucanovich, the first woman from Nevada to hold federal office, may not even vote for Angle due to her "rigid" positions.

Former Daily Show host Jon Stewart returned to late-night television on Tuesday, delivering a scathing critique of President Trump’s first 10 days in office. Stewart and Colbert shared a comedic segment where Stewart impersonated Trump, outlining what he predicted would be the next three executive actions. The first order focused on the controversial wall proposal, with Stewart quipping, "I hereby direct that to secure our border, China shall immediately and without hesitation send us their wall. Done. Boom!" The second order declared the official language of the United States to be "bull—-," with Stewart stating, "I, Donald J. Trump, have instructed my staff to speak only in bull—-." The final order simply affirmed, "I, Donald J. Trump, am exhausting," as Stewart lamented, "It has been eleven days, Stephen. Eleven f---ing days. Eleven. The presidency is supposed to age the President, not the public. The reason that I am exhausting is that every instinct and fiber of my pathological self-regard calls me to abuse of power."

Stewart’s visit to "The Late Show with Stephen Colbert" underscored the ongoing collaboration and friendship between the two comedians. The segment was met with laughter from both the audience and Colbert, highlighting the comedic chemistry between them. Stewart’s presence seemed to serve as a reminder of the resilience and strength of the American people in the face of the tumultuous early days of the Trump administration. He called for "relentless stamina and vigilance and every institutional check and balance this country can muster" to contain the President, given the policy agenda and behavior demonstrated since his inauguration. Stewart’s visit also raised questions about the status of his deal with HBO to produce topical content, as no material had surfaced since his return to late-night television. Despite the lack of new content, Stewart remains committed to the HBO deal, working on a venture to produce timely animated programming using cutting-edge technology.

Confident Donald Trump told supporters on Saturday that he's not changing his pitch to voters, a day after his chief adviser assured Republican officials their party's front-runner would show more restraint while campaigning. "You know, being presidential's easy — much easier than what I have to do," he told thousands at a rally in Bridgeport, Connecticut. "Here, I have to rant and rave. I have to keep you people going. Otherwise you're going to fall asleep on me, right?" Trump declared to the crowd that he has no intention of reversing any of his provocative policy plans, including building a wall along the length of the Southern border. "Everything I say I'm going to do, folks, I'll do," he said.

Trump's new chief adviser, Paul Manafort, met Thursday with top Republican officials and told them his candidate, known for his over-the-top persona and brashness, has been "projecting an image." "The part that he's been playing is now evolving," Manafort said. At a rally in Waterbury, Connecticut, earlier Saturday, Trump joked about how it's easy to be presidential, making a series of faux somber faces. But he said told the crowd he can be serious and policy-minded when he has to be. "Paul was down in Florida and he said, 'You know, Donald might be changing a little bit over a period of time and he — maybe he'll tone it down, maybe he won't, but who knows what happens?'" Trump told a crowd in Waterbury, before rejecting this notion. "I sort of don't like toning it down," he said. "Isn't it nice that I'm not one of these teleprompter guys?"

The Republican front-runner and most of his rivals in both parties were out campaigning Saturday across the quintet of Northeastern states holding primaries on Tuesday, including Pennsylvania, Delaware, Maryland, Rhode Island, and Connecticut. For the Republicans, in particular, the stakes are high as Trump looks to sweep the remaining contests and reach the required 1,237 delegates needed to clinch the nomination, while his rivals Ted Cruz and John Kasich look to thwart his efforts and force the race into a contested convention. Trump revived his birther criticism of rival Cruz, which he has previously used to suggest the Texas senator is ineligible to run for president. "Rafael! Straight out of the hills of Canada!" he declared, referring to Cruz by his given name.

Cruz, in Pennsylvania on Saturday, addressed around 1,000 supporters in a high school outside Pittsburgh, and though the reception was raucous, the crowd didn't know how to react to the Texas senator's opening by saying, "Let me say something that is profoundly painful for someone who grew up as a fan of the Houston Oilers, God bless the Pittsburgh Steelers." Cruz said Tuesday "is going to be a pivotal day," but he also traveled on Saturday to Indiana, which doesn't vote until next month. Trump is thought to be favored in Pennsylvania, while Cruz's deep evangelical roots could give him a boost in Indiana.

Cruz also rebuked Trump's recent suggestions that building separate transgender bathrooms is "discriminatory" and costly, saying Saturday that it should be "the choice of the given location, of the given local government to allow that, to provide for that." Democratic front-runner Hillary Clinton also campaigned in Connecticut on Saturday. At a round-table event, she discussed ways to raise wages, promote early childhood education, and reduce the pay gap between men and women with some of New Haven's working families. "Equal pay — we shouldn't be talking about it in 2016. It is almost embarrassing," Clinton said. Clinton heard workers describe their struggles with employers, home foreclosure, and low wages. Clinton said it was "way past time that we have a raise in the nationwide minimum wage" of $7.25 an hour and said the nation should support cities and states like New York and California "that are willing to put a higher floor under low-wage workers."

Bernie Sanders, meanwhile, spoke to a boisterous crowd of mostly young people in Baltimore where he railed against big banks and highlighted his differences with Clinton on everything from the minimum wage to free trade agreements. "I oppose every one of these disastrous trade agreements. She supported almost every one of them," he said, referring to Clinton, to a chorus of cheers. As Trump prepares for a general election, his campaign seems to be in a state of flux, with his advisers suggesting he might tone down his rhetoric, while Trump himself remains resolute in his approach.

A Roman-era shipwreck off the Greek island of Antikythera, famous for yielding the Antikythera Mechanism—an ancient analog computer—has once again provided a bounty of artifacts. The 2017 expedition, led by the Greek Ephorate of Underwater Antiquities and Lund University, uncovered a bronze arm, among other items, from the wreck, which sank in 1 BC. The arm, encrusted and stained green, was discovered under half a meter of sediment on the boulder-strewn slope where the ship and its cargo now rest. The vessel, estimated to be 50 meters long, was sailing from Asia Minor to Rome when it met its fate near the tiny island between Crete and the Peloponnese.

The team also used a bespoke underwater metal detector to find large metal objects buried under the seabed, suggesting the presence of at least seven more bronze statues, potentially nine in total. The boulders that overlie these metal objects, weighing several tonnes, may have tumbled onto the wreck during a massive earthquake that shook the area in the 4th century AD. The bronze recycling industry was significant in classical times, leading to the destruction of countless statues and other artifacts, making any bronze relics from this period exceptionally rare.

Among the other artifacts recovered were a patterned slab of red marble, a silver tankard, sections of joined wood from the ship’s frame, and a human bone. The divers also found a skull, teeth, ribs, and other bones of an individual who perished on the wreck. DNA analysis of the skull has revealed the individual’s sex and place of origin, though the results have not yet been published. The person is known as Pamphilos, after divers found the name, meaning “friend of all,” carved on a buried cup decorated with an erotic scene.

The Antikythera wreck first came to light in 1900 when Greek sponge divers discovered the scene in 50 meters of water. Since then, spectacular bronze and marble statues, ornate glass and pottery, stunning pieces of jewellery, and the Antikythera Mechanism have been recovered. The latest excavations also uncovered a bronze disc that may be a missing part of the ancient device. The disc, measuring about eight centimeters across, has four metal arms with holes for pins, initially thought to be related to the Antikythera Mechanism but now believed to be a decorative object adorned with the image of a bull.

The recovery of the bronze arm and the metal detector findings have significantly boosted the number of bronze statues suspected to be at the site. The team is optimistic about the potential to find more treasures, including the missing planetary gearing from the Antikythera mechanism or even a new piece of mechanism. The next expedition is planned for the spring of 2018, with the archaeologists planning to explore the hold of the sunken ship. The Antikythera wreck continues to yield fascinating discoveries, making it a site of immense archaeological interest.

A survey of Harvard's incoming Class of 2017, conducted by The Harvard Crimson, reveals concerning levels of academic dishonesty among freshmen. According to the survey, 10% of the incoming class admitted to cheating on tests, 42% on homework, and 17% on papers or take-home assignments. Athletes were more likely to cheat, with 26% of recruited athletes reporting cheating on papers or take-home assignments, compared to 16% of non-recruits. Men were also more likely to admit to cheating. Despite these findings, 84% of freshmen ranked academics as their top priority for college. The survey also highlighted that 59% of freshmen plan to pursue a secondary field, and 36% a language citation. Interestingly, 23% intend to pursue both. The results suggest a mix of high academic ambition and potential challenges in maintaining integrity.

Russell Brand was arrested at LAX airport after allegedly attacking photographers who were allegedly trying to shoot up Katy Perry's skirt, sources tell TMZ. Brand, who was making his way through security with Perry, reportedly lashed out at the paparazzi, pushing one photographer and striking several others. A victim performed a citizen's arrest, and Brand was booked for a misdemeanor charge of simple battery before being released on $20,000 bail. Katy Perry, who was with Brand, tweeted, "If you cross the line & try and put a lens up my dress, my fiancé will do his job & protect me." The incident meant they missed their flight to Las Vegas, where they were celebrating their first anniversary. Brand is currently in New York filming the remake of Arthur.

Hailey Glassman, Jon Gosselin's girlfriend, reveals in a tearful interview on "The Insider" that she fears Jon may have suicidal thoughts if their relationship ends.
