The experimental treatment is not covered by insurance, and the family has set up a crowdfunding page to help cover the costs. They are also planning a golf outing and spaghetti dinner to raise funds for Russell’s medical expenses, travel, and lodging. The family’s journey is not just about saving Russell’s life; it is also about raising awareness and support for mitochondrial disease, a condition that affects many individuals and families without much public recognition.

Russell’s parents emphasize that they are fighting for their son’s life and for the lives of other children with the same condition. They hope that by sharing their story, they can help others facing similar challenges and contribute to the development of better treatments and support systems for those affected by mitochondrial diseases. Their determination and resilience in the face of such a daunting diagnosis are an inspiration to many, highlighting the importance of perseverance and community support in the battle against rare and complex medical conditions.

The parents of Olympic swimmer Ryan Lochte are facing foreclosure on their Florida home due to significant debt, according to a lawsuit filed in Volusia County. CitiMortgage claims the Lochtes, who took out a $258,000 mortgage in 2007, stopped making payments in February 2011 and now owe $242,239 plus interest. Ileana Lochte, Ryan's mother, filed a motion to dismiss the case in May, but a ruling has not yet been made. The lawsuit highlights the financial struggles of the parents of a successful Olympic athlete, while Ryan competes in London. His parents recently traveled to London to support him, and they have since divorced.

Emma Coronel Aispuro, the wife of notorious Mexican drug lord Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzmán, has given her first-ever interview to Telemundo, expressing deep concerns for her husband's wellbeing and safety since his recent recapture. In the exclusive interview, which aired as part of a news special titled "The Queen of El Chapo," Coronel Aispuro stated that she has not seen her husband since he was recaptured on January 8 and fears for his life, questioning the conditions he is living in at the Antiplano prison. She believes the Mexican government is responsible for his health and fears that he is not receiving the basic necessities he needs. Coronel Aispuro also discussed her relationship with Kate del Castillo, who reportedly arranged a secret meeting with Guzmán while he was on the run, and her family life, including her relationship with her twin daughters. The interview, conducted by Mexican journalist Anabel Hernández, was produced in association with the Investigative Reporting Program at UC Berkeley (IRP). Hernández revealed that the interview took place on February 12th in the state of Sinaloa, Mexico. Coronel Aispuro expressed that she has never seen her husband fearful or agitated, describing him as "very intelligent," though he lacks formal education. She also mentioned that Guzmán had long wanted to collaborate on a film about his life to counter what he viewed as untruths and sensationalism. The interview highlights the complex personal and professional relationships surrounding the drug lord and his family, adding to the ongoing narrative of his life and the impact of his criminal activities.

Angelina Jolie wowed the crowd at Comic-Con in San Diego, California, where she joined co-star Liev Schreiber for a panel discussion on their upcoming film "Salt." The 35-year-old actress, dressed in a skintight leather jacket, form-fitting black pencil skirt, and open-toe black heels, delighted fans. Jolie revealed she fell on set and was initially worried about a potential concussion, only to realize she had forgotten to remove her earplugs during a gun scene. She also shared that she got to use a variety of weapons, including a fire extinguisher, during filming. Comparing "Salt" to her previous action films like "Wanted" and "Tomb Raider," Jolie said, "My style got meaner and harder and darker, it wasn't as pretty. I think this is a better action movie than the ones I've done." Meanwhile, Jolie and Pitt's legal team secured a settlement from the British tabloid News of the World, which had published false and intrusive breakup rumors. The couple's attorneys accepted an undisclosed settlement, earmarked for charity, after the newspaper failed to retract the allegations and apologize. This marks the end of the legal battle, bringing temporary peace to the Brangelina rumors.

A 3-year-old Hawaii girl, Finley Puleo Boyle, died during a dental procedure at Island Dentistry for Children in Kailua, according to an autopsy report from the Honolulu Chief Medical Examiner. Finley, who was previously healthy, suffered a heart attack during the December 2013 visit and slipped into a coma, eventually passing away a month later. The medical examiner concluded that the sedatives and local anesthesia administered were likely the cause of her death. Finley received five drugs, including Demerol and hydroxyzine, along with laughing gas and a local anesthetic. The dentist, Dr. Lilly Geyer, has since closed her office. Parents Ashley and Evan Boyle filed a negligence lawsuit, alleging that Finley was not properly monitored while sedated. The lawsuit claims that Finley’s oxygen levels were not checked for 26 minutes, and no CPR was administered until a doctor from another office was called. The medical examiner classified the death as an accident, and no criminal charges have been brought against Geyer. New state rules tightening oversight of dental sedation in Hawaii took effect in January, following this tragic incident.

More than three dozen Pennsylvania college students spending spring break in Kentucky on a mission trip were safe Friday after becoming lost for hours when a sightseeing mountain hike unexpectedly stretched into the night, officials said. The group, made up of 37 students and three staff members from La Salle University on an annual mission trip called Project Appalachia, was helping build houses in Harlan, about a half-hour from Whitesburg, and had gone on a hiking trip that was made every year on the trip. Rescuers were able to find the group, hungry and cold, after an hours-long effort in rough terrain and freezing temperatures. Most of the hikers were seen in the emergency room at Appalachian Regional Hospital in Whitesburg, with one woman admitted and listed in good condition. The group got disoriented when it got dark while hiking near Bad Branch Falls, an area on the Bad Branch Nature Preserve. A search began about 7 p.m. Thursday, and it took until 3:30 a.m. Friday to get the entire group off the mountain. The trail, lined with hemlock trees and rhododendron bushes, takes hikers immediately into the deep woods. A sign at the trail head warns hikers to stay on the trail. The group was not dressed for the weather, with most of them wearing just sneakers, jeans, and light jackets as temperatures began dropping into the 20s. Only a few of the students had flashlights. The group had to be walked down the mountain using an alternate route that had fewer obstacles but took more time. The hikers were treated for possible hypothermia, dehydration, and exhaustion. One hiker remained hospitalized Friday morning, but was expected to be released Saturday. The group was expected to return to Pennsylvania on Saturday as scheduled.

The number of Americans driving to work alone is on the rise, leading to increased traffic and higher costs. To identify the worst cities for car ownership, SmartAsset analyzed factors such as traffic hours, annual traffic costs, motor vehicle theft rates, repair shops, parking garages, and non-driving options. Coastal cities dominate the list, with Newark, New Jersey, at the top due to heavy traffic and high theft rates. San Francisco and Washington, D.C., follow, experiencing significant traffic costs. Oakland, California, ranks fourth, plagued by crime and traffic. Arlington, Virginia, and Portland, Oregon, also make the top 10, facing traffic and repair challenges. Anaheim, California, and New York, New York, round out the list, with New York benefiting from extensive public transportation. These cities present substantial challenges for car owners, making alternative transportation more appealing.

The global obesity epidemic continues to spread, with the United States leading the world in obesity numbers, but no country has seen a decline in obesity rates over the past three decades, according to a new report published in the Lancet. The study, which analyzed data from 188 countries over the past 33 years, found that the number of overweight or obese individuals worldwide increased from 857 million in 1980 to 2.1 billion in 2013, representing nearly 30% of the world's population, up from about 20%. In the USA, 87 million people, or 13% of the global obese population, are considered obese, despite the country accounting for only 5% of the world's population. Obesity rates are particularly high in some countries, with men in Tonga and women in Kuwait, Kiribati, Micronesia, Libya, Qatar, Samoa, and Tonga having obesity rates exceeding 50%. The report also highlights that obesity is a growing problem in both developed and developing countries, with increases in obesity rates among both men and women. Among children, 22% of girls and 24% of boys in developed countries and 13% of boys and girls in developing countries are overweight or obese. While the rate of increase in obesity has slowed in developed countries, it is accelerating in developing nations. The study does not examine the causes of obesity but suggests possibilities such as increased calorie intake, changes in diet composition, decreased physical activity, and changes in the gut bacteria that live in humans. The World Health Organization has launched a commission to study rising childhood obesity and suggest solutions, with a report due in early 2015. The increasing burden of obesity is a significant public health issue, with chronic complications of weight contributing to about 3.4 million adult deaths annually.

A 3-year-old child fell into a jaguar exhibit at the Little Rock Zoo, resulting in injuries that required hospitalization, according to a statement from the Arkansas Children's Hospital. The child is reported to be stable and expected to improve. Zoo staff initially responded to a call for help, with one worker using a fire extinguisher to keep the jaguars away while another lowered a ladder into the exhibit. The father and grandfather witnessed the child's fall from the railing and attempted to distract the jaguars with items. The child was eventually retrieved and taken to an ambulance waiting at the zoo's back gate. The child suffered extensive scalp lacerations, a depressed skull fracture, and minor puncture wounds, though doctors stated the wounds were not life-threatening. Zoo officials stated that staff followed training procedures and responded quickly and efficiently. The incident is under investigation, and the zoo remains open. The Little Rock Zoo was last accredited by the Association of Zoos and Aquariums (AZA) in 2012 and is currently accredited until 2016. The U.S. Department of Agriculture has not found any violations during inspections since October 2013.

A former day care operator in Bend, Oregon, named January Irene Neatherlin, 32, was sentenced to 21 years and four months in prison for abandoning numerous young children at her unlicensed day care, drugging them with melatonin, and leaving them alone while she went to a tanning salon or to work out. The case, which garnered significant media attention, involved multiple children under her care, with some suffering severe injuries. During the sentencing hearing, which lasted an entire day, numerous parents and family members of the children Neatherlin had left unattended testified about the lasting emotional, physical, and financial damage caused by her actions. Prosecutors had initially sought a 35-year sentence.

Neatherlin's illegal day care, Little Giggles, was operating for about four years before her arrest in March 2017. Deschutes County police, based on tips from a former boyfriend and a former roommate, conducted surveillance and found Neatherlin leaving the house multiple times while children were in her care. On one occasion, she was seen at a local tanning salon, and on another, she was at a gym. During these absences, Neatherlin had given melatonin to the children to make them sleep, allowing her to leave them unattended.

The children Neatherlin had left unattended included a 11-month-old girl who was rushed to the hospital with head injuries consistent with shaken baby syndrome. Another child suffered burns from overheated milk. Neatherlin's criminal history, which included multiple theft and identity theft convictions, was also brought up during the hearing. She had repeatedly lied to parents about being a registered nurse and had created a fake certificate to support this claim. Additionally, she had approached other inmates and asked them to claim they had worked for her, attempting to manipulate the system.

During the sentencing hearing, Neatherlin apologized to the families, stating, "I failed you all. I let you all down. I let all of you down that trusted me, and no one is at fault but me." However, the judge, Wells Ashby, rejected her explanation for the head injuries, stating, "There is something broken and something missing in you. It is the court's hope that you can make yourself whole again." The judge also noted the "carnage" left by the case, including the loss of trust among parents and the potential long-term impacts on the children.

The judge's decision to sentence Neatherlin to 21 years and four months was influenced by the severity of the crimes and the potential danger to the community. However, some parents and grandparents called for a longer sentence, with one father stating, "In my opinion, your honor, 100 years would not be enough." The case highlighted the risks associated with unlicensed day cares and the importance of thorough background checks and proper licensing for child care providers.

Israeli forces continued their ground offensive in Gaza, expanding their operations and encountering resistance from Hamas militants. The conflict, now in its 12th day, showed no signs of a diplomatic breakthrough, with both sides maintaining their positions. Israeli troops uncovered more than a dozen cross-border tunnels and engaged in gunbattles with militants, killing two soldiers and thwarting a second tunnel infiltration attempt. Despite the military's claims of significant damage to Hamas' arsenal, militants fired more than 90 rockets into Israel on Saturday, killing a man and wounding four people in a southern Bedouin village. The Palestinian death toll rose above 330, including 70 children, with 61,500 people seeking refuge in UN shelters. Israeli bulldozers worked along Gaza's eastern frontier, uncovering 13 tunnels, while the military urged civilians to evacuate an expanding area of Gaza. The Israeli death toll remained low, with three soldiers killed and two wounded. Diplomatic efforts to secure a ceasefire failed, with Hamas rejecting Egypt's proposal and demanding the lifting of the blockade. The conflict's humanitarian impact was severe, with continuous explosions and sirens in Gaza and southern Israel. The international community, including the UN and France, expressed concern over civilian casualties and called for an end to the fighting. As the situation escalated, both sides prepared for potential further military action, with Israel warning of a possible two-week offensive and Hamas declaring its readiness for a prolonged conflict.

Jay-Z's streaming service Tidal secured a lifeline through a deal with Sprint, which will acquire a 33% stake for an undisclosed amount, likely around $200 million. This investment will provide Tidal with access to Sprint's 45 million customers, a dedicated marketing fund of $75 million annually, and a board seat for Sprint CEO Marcelo Claure. Tidal, which has struggled to compete with established giants like Spotify and Apple, now gains a significant customer base and marketing boost. Jay-Z emphasized the cultural importance of Tidal, aiming to revolutionize the music industry by allowing artists to connect directly with fans. With this new partnership, Tidal hopes to maintain its position as an underdog in the streaming market, offering high-quality content and exclusive experiences.

A man has pleaded guilty to the murder of an 82-year-old retired nun, Mary Greco, in Schenectady, New York, in December 2012. Michael Briggs, 38, admitted to strangling Greco in her apartment, which was discovered on New Year's Day 2013. Briggs had shoveled snow for Greco around the time of the murder, according to officials. At the time of the killing, Briggs was on parole for a burglary and robbery in Long Island. Evidence linking Briggs to the crime included fingerprints on the toilet seat, coffee mug, and glass in the kitchen, as well as his DNA on the blanket covering Greco's body. Surveillance footage showed Briggs leaving his home and walking towards Greco's just before the murder. The retired nun was a parishioner at St. Luke's Roman Catholic Church and had recently received a rosary and crucifix as gifts. Briggs' defense attorney struck a plea deal after seeing the video evidence for the first time, and Briggs will be sentenced to 30 years to life. The case highlights the extensive evidence collected, including fingerprints, DNA, and surveillance footage, that led to Briggs' guilty plea.

Sean Penn's controversial meeting with Joaquin "El Chapo" Guzmán, the world's most notorious drug lord, has come under scrutiny as Netflix releases a documentary series titled "The Day I Met El Chapo." The series, which focuses on Mexican actress Kate del Castillo's role in facilitating the meeting, has faced criticism from Penn's camp. A spokesman for Penn, Mark Fabiani, dismissed claims that Penn tipped off the U.S. Department of Justice about the meeting, stating, "The notion that Mr. Penn or anyone on his behalf alerted D.O.J. to the trip is a complete fabrication and baldfaced lie. It never happened, nor would there have been any reason for it to have happened." Del Castillo's team argues that the series presents a "profoundly false, foolish, and reckless narrative," while Netflix maintains that the events surrounding the meeting have been well-covered, and the series aims to give del Castillo a chance to tell her side of the story. Del Castillo met with producer David Broome, who sought to explore her perspective, which had not been previously told. Broome and Netflix attempted to involve Penn, but he did not participate. After Penn viewed the documentary, he requested an interview and demanded changes, asserting that the series puts him in physical danger. The controversy highlights the complex and often contradictory narratives surrounding the infamous encounter between Penn and Guzmán, and the challenges of telling such a story from multiple viewpoints.

A lifeguard in Australia has received a unique thank you from the Danish royal family after he rescued the 10-year-old heir to the Danish throne, Prince Christian, from a dangerous rip current at Mermaid Beach on the Gold Coast. Lifeguard Nick Malcolm, who was unaware of the prince's identity, rushed into the water after spotting the boy struggling in the surf. He paddled back with the prince and returned him to the care of his father, Prince Frederick, and mother, Princess Mary, who was born in Australia. The incident highlights the importance of swimming in patrolled areas, as Prince Christian was caught in a "flash rip," a type of current that can occur during wave surges. Lifeguard supervisor Stuart Keay praised Mr. Malcolm's quick action, stating, "We got him before it got too serious, but he wouldn't have come back in." Despite the international attention, Mr. Malcolm has remained humble, saying, "Oh, ok" when informed of the prince's identity. The Danish royal family, including Prince Christian and his three younger siblings, has been holidaying in Queensland and will travel to Tasmania to visit Princess Mary’s family. The 43-year-old princess, formerly Mary Donaldson, became a member of Denmark's royal family after meeting her husband at a bar during the Sydney Olympics in 2000. The incident has brought attention to the dangers of rips, which kill about 20 people each year in Australia, with 78 people drowning at beaches in Queensland over the past decade.

Apple has finally unveiled the eagerly awaited white iPhone 4, which will hit shelves tomorrow. The device, available through Apple, Verizon, AT&T, and authorized resellers, comes in 16- and 32-gigabyte versions priced at $199 and $299 respectively, with a two-year wireless contract. Apple's senior vice president of Worldwide Product Marketing, Philip Schiller, expressed excitement over the release, stating, "The white iPhone 4 has finally arrived and it’s beautiful." This long-awaited color option has been a source of anticipation for many iPhone users. Meanwhile, Apple has also addressed concerns over the gathering and use of location information by iOS devices. The company clarified that it has never tracked and will never track the location of an iPhone, attributing any confusion to a lack of user education on the technical aspects of location services. Apple identified several bugs, including a caching issue that stored location data for an extended period, and promised to release a free software update to address these concerns. The update will reduce the size of the cached Wi-Fi hotspot and cell tower database, encrypt and stop backing up this data, and delete it entirely when Location Services are turned off. This move aims to alleviate privacy concerns raised by researchers and regulatory bodies in multiple countries.

A teenage girl died after being thrown from a spinning carnival ride at St. Thomas Aquinas Catholic Church in El Paso, Texas, during the church's Dia De Los Niños Fiesta. Local police confirmed the incident, stating that two other teenagers were also on the ride when the accident occurred. One of the other teens was hospitalized with non-life-threatening injuries, while the third girl was not injured. El Paso Police Department Sgt. Enrique Carrillo said the accident remains under investigation, and its cause is yet to be determined.

The Sizzler ride, which is part of the carnival, spins people around a central point and also spins them in their seats. Sgt. Carrillo mentioned that the ride was operating with three teenagers on board when the incident happened. According to the aunt of the girl who was not ejected, the three had informed the ride operator that the seat belt wouldn't buckle. The operator reportedly told the girls that they were fine. The aunt also stated that only two people were supposed to be inside the ride at a time, but her niece held on to the seat belt for her life.

The girl who died was taken to Del Sol Medical Center, where she later succumbed to her injuries. The second teen was taken to University Medical Center with non-life-threatening injuries. The El Paso Police Department's Crime Against Persons unit has been called in to investigate the incident. The company in charge of the carnival rides is Playtime Amusements Inc., and the carnivals are regulated by state statutes. Sgt. Carrillo noted that inspections are required, but it's unclear if this vendor has been up to par with those regulations.

In August 2014, two El Paso teenagers were injured when they fell off a mechanical ride at the St. Anthony Bazaar, but the company involved in that incident was not the same as the one used in the St. Thomas Aquinas carnival. The Sizzler ride, manufactured by a company with about 200 units operating in the United States, has been in use for some time. Friends of the deceased girl, Sam Aguilar, described her as a sweet, nice girl who lived life to the fullest and played softball and track at Hanks High School. A GoFundMe page has been set up to support the family.

A controversial email sent by a Georgia Tech fraternity member offers pledges advice on how to seduce women with the help of alcohol, sparking outrage and investigation. The email, sent to Phi Kappa Tau pledges, outlines tactics for success, including giving women alcohol and referencing rape. "If anything ever fails, go get more alcohol," the email instructs. If pledges succeed in taking a girl home, the email tells them to "Expunge" (send her out of the room). The fraternity CEO issued a statement saying the email is "extremely inappropriate and does not reflect the values of the fraternity." The chapter has suspended the member who sent the email and placed itself on suspension as Georgia Tech investigates. The university does not condone this type of behavior and is working to determine the facts. The email has spread widely, with students finding it offensive and alarming. The Phi Kappa Tau national office is working with chapter leadership to resolve the matter.

The case of Brock Turner, a former Stanford swimmer convicted of sexually assaulting an unconscious woman, has sparked intense debate and controversy, particularly over the lenient six-month jail sentence handed down by Judge Aaron Persky. A letter from Leslie Rasmussen, a childhood friend of Turner, defending him and blaming the victim for drinking too much alcohol, has drawn widespread criticism and led to the cancellation of performances for Rasmussen’s band, Good English. Rasmussen’s letter, read in court and widely circulated, argued that Turner was not a monster and that his actions were a “huge misunderstanding.” She wrote, “Where do we draw the line and stop worrying about being politically correct every second of the day and see that rape on campuses isn’t always because people are rapists.” Her statement was seen as perpetuating rape culture and victim-blaming, leading to an apology from Rasmussen, who acknowledged the “enormous pain” of the victim and expressed regret for her comments. The letter was part of a package of character references submitted to the judge, which included a statement from Turner’s father arguing that his son was paying a “steep price” for “20 minutes of action.” Prosecutors and victim advocates criticized the judge’s leniency, highlighting Turner’s prior concerning behavior, including aggressive interactions with other women and evidence of drug and alcohol use. The case has reignited discussions about sexual assault, victim-blaming, and the justice system’s handling of such cases, with many calling for stricter sentencing and a more victim-centered approach.

Trevor Noah, the newly appointed host of "The Daily Show," is facing criticism over old tweets that contained offensive jokes about Jews, Israelis, and women. Noah, a 31-year-old South African comedian, was chosen to replace Jon Stewart, and his appointment has generated controversy, especially after his past tweets resurfaced. Comedian Roseanne Barr publicly criticized Noah, urging him to stop making sexist and anti-Semitic jokes. Comedy Central defended Noah, stating that his comedy often pushes boundaries and that judging him based on a few jokes is unfair. Noah himself addressed the controversy by tweeting that reducing his views to a handful of jokes that didn't land was not a true reflection of his character or his evolution as a comedian.

The backlash against Noah's tweets highlights the challenges faced by comedians who make controversial statements, particularly when those statements are brought to light after they have gained prominence. Noah's tweets range from anti-Semitic jokes, such as suggesting that behind every successful rapper is a rich Jewish man, to fat-chick jokes, like "Oh yeah the weekend. People are gonna get drunk & think that I'm sexy!" These tweets have sparked discussions about the appropriateness of certain types of humor and the responsibility comedians have to their audiences.

Comedy Central's decision to hire Noah has been met with mixed reactions. While some see his appointment as a refreshing change, given his unique background and perspective, others are concerned about the offensive material he has posted in the past. The controversy has raised questions about the vetting process and the balance between artistic freedom and maintaining a certain standard of respect and inclusivity.

Noah's appointment has also sparked debates about the role of comedy in society and the expectations placed on comedians to address sensitive issues. Some argue that Noah's hiring is a form of basic-cable performance art, a bold move to shake up the status quo. Others believe that Comedy Central's haste in making the decision, without thoroughly vetting Noah, could alienate a significant portion of their audience. The controversy surrounding Noah's tweets underscores the complex and often contentious nature of comedy and the challenges comedians face in navigating the fine line between humor and offense.

Pippa Middleton, the sister of the Duchess of Cambridge, found herself at the center of a controversial incident in Paris when she was photographed laughing as a male companion in her car pointed a gun at a paparazzo. The incident occurred on a Sunday as Middleton and three male friends were driving in an Audi convertible. The gun, which appeared to be a semi-automatic, was allegedly used in a joke, but the image captured Middleton looking back at the photographer with a grin as the driver reached for the weapon. Despite the initial reports of potential criminal charges, a spokesperson for the fashion company Vicomte A, where Middleton was a guest at a costume birthday party, confirmed that the gun was fake, stating it was "just a stupid joke." However, the Paris police are investigating the incident, and Middleton could face questioning by authorities. The incident has raised concerns, especially given the recent spate of high-profile shootings in France, and could overshadow the Queen's Diamond Jubilee celebrations. The Royal Family, while not directly representing Middleton, has remained silent on the matter, leaving many to speculate about the potential impact on her public image and the challenges she faces as a public figure.

California regulators have determined that Nestlé may have to cease extracting a substantial portion of the water it bottles from the San Bernardino National Forest, due to alleged lack of proper permits. According to the State Water Board, Nestlé may only have valid rights to approximately 8.5 million gallons of the 62.6 million gallons it claims to have extracted from the San Bernardino spring between 1947 and 2015. This conclusion stems from a nearly two-year investigation initiated in response to complaints during California's recent drought, including a 2015 report by the Desert Sun newspaper. The allegations against Nestlé ranged from claims that the company lacked full rights to the water it was selling to assertions that its operations were harming the natural environment and its inhabitants. Nestlé has argued that it monitors its spring sites to ensure they do not cause problems, but the Water Board's report was less conclusive on these points. The board's report suggests that while Nestlé may be able to claim a valid basis of right to some water, a significant portion of the water currently diverted by the company appears to be extracted without a valid basis of right. In response, the Water Board issued a letter summarizing its findings, urging Nestlé to apply for a new permit and ensuring that all of its water diversions comply with California regulations. The company was given 60 days to submit a compliance plan and 90 days to submit an investigation and monitoring plan. Nestlé expressed satisfaction that the report reaffirmed its valid rights to "a significant amount" of water, stating it would continue to operate lawfully according to these existing rights and comply fully with California law. This decision has been welcomed by activists who have long sought to halt Nestlé's water extraction, arguing that the company's operations lack proper permits and could harm the environment and wildlife, particularly during the state's ongoing drought. The court had previously ruled that Nestlé could continue its operations while its application to renew its permit was pending.

In a seaside sand dune in Peru, archaeologists have uncovered the remains of 42 ancient sacrifice victims, including children and young llamas, dating back 600 years. Tulane University physical anthropologist John Verano, who has spent 30 years excavating in Peru, describes this as an unusual discovery, especially on the coast of Peru. In June, Verano and Peruvian archaeologist Gabriel Prieto expanded the excavation at the site in Huanchaquito, where in 2011, Prieto found 42 children and 76 llamas sacrificed in a religious ceremony. The area was once part of the Chimú state, which controlled coastal Peru from 1100 to 1470 A.D., before being conquered by the Inca empire. The latest excavation uncovered numerous additional victims, allowing for a more detailed reconstruction of this unusual event. The researchers believe the sacrifice may have been an offering to the sea or a response to severe flooding brought on by an El Niño event. The llamas, they think, may have been intended to transport the victims to the afterlife. Located on a sandy ridge 100 yards from the beach, the site was disturbed by erosion and construction, leading villagers to notice bones emerging from the sand. Verano notes that his previous discoveries in Peru have revealed adults who were held captive and killed, but not usually children. Multiple laboratories are analyzing bones and teeth found at the site, with more details to come. Verano remains uncertain about the exact meaning of the discovery but considers it an exciting find.

In 2008, Hillary Clinton faced an uphill battle against the relatively untested Barack Obama. Clinton was renowned for her policy acumen, drawing on a network of top Democratic policy experts. However, her candidacy was marred by instances where she appeared to prioritize public opinion over sound policy. One such example was her proposal to suspend the federal gas tax for the summer travel season, a move criticized by economists as a short-term, politically motivated ploy. Obama, meanwhile, was often accused of policy opportunism, notably when he excluded the individual mandate from his health-care plan, a decision that initially favored Clinton but ultimately backfired.

Today, Clinton is once again seen as a candidate who puts poll numbers ahead of policy. She has recently opposed the Cadillac tax, a policy widely supported by health economists, and the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) trade deal, despite her past endorsements of both. Critics argue that these positions are inconsistent with her history and suggest that she is more concerned with political expediency than with sound policy. Her stance on the TPP, in particular, has raised questions about her commitment to long-term strategic goals, given her previous praise for the deal.

Clinton's reputation as a policy wonk is unassailable, but her critics point to her past decisions, such as the gas tax and the Iraq War, as evidence of her willingness to compromise on principle. Her critics argue that she has a history of being swayed by public opinion and interest groups, rather than adhering strictly to policy considerations. This perception is exacerbated by her recent opposition to the Cadillac tax and the TPP, which many see as politically motivated rather than a genuine shift in policy stance.

Clinton's political strategy is to appeal to the Democratic base, particularly labor unions, by taking positions that are popular with the left. However, this approach risks undermining her credibility as a policymaker who can be trusted to make tough, unpopular decisions for the greater good. Her critics argue that her willingness to change positions based on political considerations, rather than policy, is a weakness that could harm her presidency. Ultimately, the question remains: is Clinton truly committed to sound policy, or is she more focused on winning votes and maintaining her political viability?

MTV's "Rob & Big" star Christopher "Big Black" Boykin, 45, passed away on Tuesday, his representative confirmed to Variety. No official cause of death has been reported yet, but TMZ sources believe it was a heart attack. Boykin was best friends and bodyguards to Rob Dyrdek, starring alongside him in "Rob & Big" for three seasons from 2006 to 2008. The show, which featured the duo's day-to-day adventures, was a fan favorite. Boykin also appeared in episodes of Dyrdek's follow-up shows "Fantasy Factory" and "Ridiculousness." Before his television career, Boykin served in the U.S. Navy and launched a clothing line named "Do Work" in 2007. His daughter, Isis, is 9 years old. MTV expressed condolences, stating, "MTV is deeply saddened to learn the news of Christopher 'Big Black' Boykin's passing. He was a long-time and beloved member of the MTV family and will be greatly missed. Our thoughts and prayers go out to his family and friends at this time." Fellow cast member Chanel West Coast tweeted, "RIP Big Black. My heart is crushed. I'll remember all the times you made me laugh and my prayers go out to your family."

The wife of Israel's interior minister, Judy Shalom Nir-Mozes, faced intense backlash on social media after posting a racist joke about President Barack Obama. Nir-Mozes, a popular radio host and former UNICEF Israel chief, tweeted, "Do you know what Obama coffee is? Black and weak," which quickly garnered hundreds of critical comments. Many users called her "arrogant," "a disgrace," and "explicitly racist," especially in light of the recent racially motivated shooting of nine African Americans in South Carolina. Nir-Mozes swiftly deleted the tweet and issued multiple apologies, first saying it was a "stupid joke somebody told me" and later directly addressing President Obama, stating, "I like people no matter about their race and religion." In a lighthearted attempt to mitigate the damage, she joked, "Sorry if I caused any offense to anyone. I hope I will stay married when my husband will land and hear what I did." This incident comes after Nir-Mozes was accused of trolling Obama last month, tweeting, "well come, I hope u 'll write from the heart of Barack, and not from the head of Rrsedent Obama." The tweet was later deleted, but journalist Tal Schneider took a screenshot and pointed out the typo. Nir-Mozes' previous involvement in social-media controversies, including supporting Israel's military actions in Gaza, further complicated her situation. The tweet about Obama hit particularly sensitive nerves, given the ongoing discussions about race in the United States following the Charleston church shooting.

A bill in Washington D.C. aims to lower the voting age from 18 to 16, making D.C. the first municipality in the United States to allow minors to vote in all elections, including presidential races. The bill, introduced by Councilmember Charles Allen, passed a committee vote with a unanimous 3-0 decision and is set to be placed on the agenda for the full D.C. Council for a final vote. This move would enfranchise approximately 10,400 16- and 17-year-olds, the majority of whom are youth of color. Advocates of the bill, such as Chloe Ifill from Vote16DC, argue that young people vote at higher rates than adults when given the chance and are more likely to develop a lifelong habit of voting. The coalition has been working to mobilize community support and educate council members on the benefits of the bill. If passed, D.C. would become the fifth US city to have a voting age of 16, and the only jurisdiction where this age group could vote in federal elections. The bill must undergo a 30-day congressional review period before becoming law. Councilmember Allen, inspired by student protests against gun violence, believes that 16-year-olds shoulder adult responsibilities and burdens, making them eligible to participate in the political process.

Archaeologists have uncovered a stone tool at an ancient rock shelter in eastern Oregon that could potentially be older than any known site of human occupation in western North America. The tool, a hand-held scraper chipped from orange agate, was found about 8 inches below a layer of volcanic ash from a Mount St. Helens eruption dated to 15,800 years ago, at a depth of 12 feet below the surface. If the age of the site holds up to scrutiny, it would be the oldest west of the Rockies and predating the Clovis culture, which is generally believed to be the first people to migrate from Asia into North America. The earliest Clovis artifacts, known for distinctive and elegant stone points, are dated to about 13,000 years ago. University of Oregon archaeologist Patrick O'Grady, who supervises the dig, described the find as "tantalizing," but noted that they want to continue digging this summer to see whether the volcanic ash covers the entire area. Skepticism from the scientific community is expected, with Donald K. Grayson, a professor of archaeology at the University of Washington, stating that extreme skepticism is warranted until the site is fully published. The site, known as the Rimrock Draw Rockshelter, has also yielded other artifacts, including stemmed points and tooth enamel fragments believed to belong to a prehistoric camel. Blood residue analysis of the tool revealed animal proteins consistent with bison, suggesting the tool was used for scraping animal hides, butchering, and possibly carving wood. The find has the potential to significantly alter our understanding of the first human migrations into North America.

An 11-year-old girl from Northern California, Paige Warner, died during a family Thanksgiving trip to Hawaii, leaving her parents and sister to grapple with the mystery of her fatal allergic reaction. Paige, who had a history of food allergies and environmental sensitivities, was excited to visit Hawaii for the first time. On the day of the incident, she and her younger sister Violet, along with a friend, swam in a pool. Shortly after, Paige complained of a burning nose and swelling in her throat, which her mother, Karin Carpenter, recognized as a severe allergic reaction. Despite her mother's attempts to manage the situation, Paige's condition worsened, and she was rushed to the hospital where she received CPR for about an hour before her heart started again. Paige was later admitted to a coma and placed on life support. Despite intensive care, she succumbed to her injuries on December 4th, 2014, at 9:25 a.m. The exact cause of the reaction remains unclear, with theories ranging from the flight, environmental changes, cat populations, and pool chemicals. The family set up a GoFundMe page to raise funds, which has so far collected over $28,000. Paige's mother detailed the events leading up to her daughter's death, expressing her gratitude for the support from friends and community members. Paige's mother also shared her hope that her daughter's story would raise awareness about the seriousness of severe allergies and the importance of carrying an EpiPen. Paige's sister Violet, who was also present during the incident, has since helped her parents heal by insisting on putting up Christmas decorations, as Paige loved the holiday season. The family plans to hold a funeral for Paige in January, where they will remember her for her talent in art and her positive influence on those around her.

Bowe Bergdahl, the former U.S. Army soldier who was captured by the Taliban in Afghanistan and later exchanged for five senior Taliban officials held at Guantanamo Bay, found himself unexpectedly in the middle of a California marijuana raid. On Tuesday, sheriff's deputies raided a property in Redwood Valley, seizing 181 marijuana plants and arresting several individuals. Bergdahl, who was visiting old friends and had an Army pass allowing him to be in the area, was taken in for a field interview. Despite not being charged, he was treated as a witness and released. Sheriff Tom Allman of Mendocino County praised Bergdahl's behavior, noting that he was "very polite" and "not resistant at all." Bergdahl, who was scheduled to return to his duty station near Washington, D.C., was escorted back to the Army by a military escort. He remains on active duty at Fort Sam Houston, where he is currently stationed and performing administrative duties. The incident, which occurred as Bergdahl awaited his military court-martial for desertion, highlighted the unexpected and sometimes confusing circumstances surrounding his presence in California. Bergdahl, who was captured while AWOL in 2009 and later exchanged for the Taliban prisoners, faced charges of desertion and misbehavior before the enemy, with his case currently awaiting an article 32 hearing, the equivalent of a grand jury hearing.

Vili Fualaau, 33, has filed for legal separation from Mary Kay Letourneau, 55, according to court records. However, Fualaau claims the move is to protect his business interests, particularly his plans to become a distributor for "Cigaweed" marijuana cigarettes, as background checks would be required, and Letourneau's past would need to be vetted. "It’s not necessarily what you think," Fualaau told RadarOnline.com. "Everything is fine between us. All the rumors that you hear between us. It’s fine. Of course, we are still in love. A piece of paper doesn’t break someone’s feelings!" Letourneau, who served over seven years in prison for having sex with Fualaau when he was her sixth-grade student in 1996, married him in 2005 and they have two children together. Letourneau has four children from a previous marriage. She has since filed a petition to dismiss the separation, though Fualaau's lawyer says he will move forward with the petition. The couple's legal and emotional status remains uncertain.

It's uncertain whether the current flu season, which may continue until May, will result in more pediatric deaths than usual. As of January 13, 30 flu-associated fatalities in children had been reported by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). However, the actual number might be higher, as it can take a few weeks for the CDC to gather the information, and not all states report flu deaths consistently. The CDC will release updated data on pediatric deaths on January 26. Dr. John Williams, a professor and division chief of pediatric infectious diseases at the Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh, stated that every year in the U.S., between 100 to 300 pediatric deaths from the flu are reported, likely an underestimate. He noted that the best way to protect children from catching the flu is to vaccinate them, as even partial protection is better than none. The vaccine this year is not a perfect match, with its effectiveness at preventing a particularly severe strain estimated to range from 10 to 30 percent. However, it can still lessen symptoms in those who end up getting the flu. According to CDC spokeswoman Kristen Nordlund, 80 to 85 percent of children who died from the flu in past years were not vaccinated. Despite concerns, the CDC reports that there is plenty of vaccine available for the season. Providers may not be able to get the specific brand or presentation they want and may need to select something else or purchase vaccine from another source. The Cleveland Clinic states that around 930 people have been hospitalized so far this season for the flu, the largest amount they've seen since the worst flu season in recent memory in 2014-2015. The CDC still recommends vaccination as the best option to reduce the chances of getting the virus by up to 60 percent, though it can take up to two weeks to become effective. Dr. Susan Rehm, Vice Chair of the Department of Infectious Disease at the Cleveland Clinic, advises that a fever that does not go away or one that comes back after going away, difficulty breathing, or trouble staying awake are symptoms that should lead people to seek care. The mystery remains about when the widespread and deadly flu season will end, and if the worst is over yet. Several more weeks of information are needed to determine how long it will last.

AFAJP President Stephen Forbeck recently appeared on ABC Nightly News, where he was interviewed about the organization's campaign to support an Onion Pulitzer. The video, uploaded to YouTube, highlights Forbeck's cool and determined leadership as he advocates for the recognition of the satirical news organization. The interview, while taken with a lighter tone by the ABC reporter, underscores the growing awareness of AFAJP's mission. This campaign aims to garner public support for the creation of an Onion Pulitzer, a prestigious journalism award for satirical news. Forbeck emphasizes the importance of spreading the word and encourages viewers to sign the petition and upload their own videos in support. The video serves as a testament to AFAJP's increasing visibility and the potential for a significant impact on the journalism-award landscape.

This week, several celebrities and individuals have seen their "virtual stock" rise due to various online and offline events. AshleyMadison, the website for extramarital affairs, experienced a significant boost in revenue and membership after sponsoring Tiger Woods' Miss Mistress Pageant, highlighting the power of celebrity endorsements in the digital age. Conan O'Brien's random Twitter interactions have also proven lucrative, with Sarah Killen, a struggling bride, receiving numerous gifts and free services after being followed by the late-night host. Meanwhile, Corey Feldman's stock has unexpectedly risen following the tragic death of his friend Corey Haim, as he has become a sought-after source for interviews and tributes. Lastly, a teenager named Steve Holmes gained nearly 400,000 Twitter followers after being randomly selected by Kanye West, leading to an overwhelming influx of messages and attention. These examples underscore the unpredictable and often serendipitous nature of fame in the digital era.

The Los Angeles County Coroner's office is awaiting toxicology results before determining the cause of Brittany Murphy's death, which occurred due to a sudden cardiac arrest. An internal bleed was noted, and Murphy was reportedly taking prescription drugs for medical conditions. The LAPD concluded there were no signs of foul play, and charges were not filed. The coroner's office expects to make a final determination in about two months.

Two mysterious stone rings found deep inside a French cave were likely constructed by Neanderthals around 176,500 years ago, according to a study published in the journal Nature. The structures, discovered in 1990, consist of hundreds of pillar-shaped mineral deposits, or stalagmites, broken to a similar length and laid out in two oval patterns up to 40 centimeters high. The discovery challenges the long-held assumption that Neanderthals were incapable of complex behaviors, such as working underground and constructing elaborate structures. 

Archaeologist Jacques Jaubert of the University of Bordeaux, France, led a team that used sophisticated dating techniques to determine the age of the stalagmites. The results indicate that the rings were built around 176,500 years ago, making them among the oldest known well-dated constructions made by humans. The presence of these structures 336 meters from the entrance of the Bruniquel Cave suggests that Neanderthals had mastered the underground environment, marking a significant step in human modernity.

The researchers ruled out the possibility that the structures were created by chance or by animals like bears and wolves, whose bones were found near the entrance. The carefully constructed rings, which show traces of fire, indicate that Neanderthals had a "project" to go deep into the cave where there was no natural light. They likely explored underground as a group and cooperated to build the rings, using fire to illuminate the cave. 

The purpose of the oval structures, measuring 16 square meters and 2.3 square meters, remains a mystery. However, they may have served some symbolic or ritual purpose. Paola Villa, an archaeologist at the University of Colorado at Boulder, suggested that this was a common meeting place for some type of ritual social behavior. 

Wil Roebroeks, a Neanderthal expert at the University of Leiden, noted that the structures in Bruniquel may represent only the tip of the iceberg of Neanderthal culture, as most relics would have been made of organic material and decayed long ago. Roebroeks emphasized that the fact that similar rings haven't been found anywhere else makes it difficult to test any theory about their origin. 

The discovery of these structures challenges the traditional view of Neanderthals as simple and primitive, suggesting that they were capable of sophisticated behaviors and social complexities. The findings provide strong evidence of the great antiquity of such structures and contribute to a new understanding of Neanderthal societies.

Canadian pop star Justin Bieber and his entourage were asked to leave the Mayan archaeological site of Tulum in Mexico after reportedly attempting to climb onto the ruins. According to an anonymous Mexican official from the National Institute of Anthropology and History, Bieber was visiting the seaside ruins when the incident occurred. While the official did not specify which structures Bieber allegedly climbed, he confirmed that the singer was "asked to leave." The official noted that visitors can climb some pre-Hispanic pyramids in Mexico, but officials rope off or place 'no entry' signs on some ruins that are considered vulnerable or unstable. This is not the first controversy involving Bieber in Latin America; he has been involved in several incidents in the region in recent years.

GQ Magazine has sparked controversy by releasing a list of "21 Books You Don’t Have to Read," including classics such as The Bible, The Catcher in the Rye, Lonesome Dove, The Old Man and the Sea, Adventures of Huckleberry Finn, and The Lord of the Rings. In an introduction, GQ editors argue that while we've been told all our lives that we must read the Great Books, many of these works have not aged well, being either racist, sexist, or just plain boring. Instead, GQ recommends alternative titles, such as Agota Kristof's The Notebook, The Rise and Fall of the Third Reich by William L. Shirer, and Ursula K. Le Guin's Earthsea Series. The list has drawn ire from Christians, who argue that the Bible has been read by 3.9 billion people in the last 50 years and is a powerful and necessary text. Evangelist Franklin Graham called the inclusion "foolish and a shame," suggesting that GQ editors need to read the Bible again. Social media users have responded with outrage, calling GQ "The Most Overrated Magazine Of All Time!" and slamming the magazine for its "epic fail." The backlash highlights the ongoing debate over which books are essential reading and the role of popular culture in shaping literary taste.

A 35-year-old female Aldabra giant tortoise named Abuh, who escaped from Shibukawa Animal Park in Okayama Prefecture, Japan, has been found safe and sound just 140 meters from the zoo after two weeks. Abuh, weighing 55 kilograms and measuring about one meter in length, was allowed to roam freely within the park during opening hours. Zookeepers initially offered a reward of ¥500,000 for her safe return but were relieved when a local family spotted her in nearby shrubbery. Abuh, known for her gentle disposition, was found by a family from Okayama city and brought back to the zoo. She was doing well, eating pears and watermelon, and had a healthy appetite after her two-week adventure. The zookeeper expressed relief and stated they would implement new measures to prevent such incidents in the future. This was the second escape attempt for Abuh in less than a month, highlighting the challenges in managing such large, slow-moving animals. Despite her freedom, Abuh’s maximum speed is only about 1 kilometer per hour, suggesting she could have traveled a significant distance, though she remained close to the zoo.

A new study from the University of Nottingham and the Finnish National Institute for Health and Welfare has revealed that airport security plastic trays are the biggest culprits for spreading germs in airports. The team monitored germ levels on various surfaces at Helsinki-Vantaa airport in Finland during the winter of 2016 and found evidence of viruses on 10% of all the surfaces tested. The plastic trays used at airport security checkpoints harbored the highest levels of viruses, with further viruses detected on shop payment terminals, staircase rails, passport checking counters, children's play areas, and in the air. The most common virus found was rhinovirus, which causes the common cold, but the swabs also picked up the influenza A virus. Interestingly, no respiratory viruses were found on toilet surfaces. This study supports the case for improved public awareness of how viral infections spread and emphasizes the importance of hygienic hand washing and coughing into a handkerchief, tissue, or sleeve, especially in public places. The findings add weight to previous studies showing that microbes are commonly found on surfaces in public transport vehicles and will strengthen public health advice in preparation for future flu pandemics. The results provide new ideas for technical improvements in airport design and refurbishment, suggesting that airports could provide "hand sanitization opportunities where intense, repeat touching of surfaces takes place such as immediately before and after security screening." Additionally, the study suggests that the trays and other frequently touched surfaces could be cleaned more regularly. The research was part of a larger EU-funded research project called PANDHUB, which explored the role of airports and other traffic hubs in the spread of serious infections.

In a legal battle reminiscent of "David vs. Goliath," the Walton family and Walmart are suing the widow of a photographer, Helen Huff, to reclaim over 200 photos taken of the family between 1950 and 1994. The dispute centers on the ownership of these images, with the Waltons arguing they own the intellectual property rights, while Huff claims she holds the copyright. The photos, taken by Robert and David Huff at their Fayetteville, Arkansas, studio, include portraits of the Walton family, the original Wal-Mart board of directors, and the Wal-Mart visitor’s center. The Waltons contend the photos were taken under their supervision, making them works-for-hire. However, Huff asserts her husband and father-in-law were independent contractors, using their own equipment and processes, and providing copyright notices to the Walton family. The case has garnered attention from the Professional Photographers of America (PPA), which supports Huff, arguing that without written agreements, the photographers own the copyrights. The PPA cites a similar case where Oprah Winfrey lost a copyright dispute due to the absence of a work-for-hire contract. Walmart and the Walton family have offered $2,000 for the negatives and proofs, but this offer has not been confirmed by Huff’s attorneys. A federal judge in the Western District of Arkansas will hear the case on July 7, with Walmart seeking a declaratory judgment that they and the Walton family own the photographs and preventing Huff from making commercial use of them. The outcome of this case could set a significant precedent regarding the ownership of photographs taken for large corporations.

A suspected British prankster, operating under the Twitter handle @SINON_REBORN, has managed to deceive several high-ranking White House officials, including Anthony Scaramucci, into responding to him by posing as various members of the Trump administration. The prankster initially convinced homeland security adviser Tom Bossert to reply to him after impersonating Jared Kushner, leading Bossert to share his personal email address. In a series of emails, the prankster, pretending to be Reince Priebus, the former White House chief of staff, engaged in a heated exchange with Scaramucci, accusing him of hypocrisy and questioning his ethics. Scaramucci defended himself, referencing Shakespeare's Othello, and stated that he knew what the prankster had done. The White House confirmed it was investigating the matter, emphasizing the seriousness with which they treated cyber-related issues. The prankster, described as a "lazy anarchist," maintained that his actions were meant to be humorous rather than malicious, stating, "I’m not trying to get the keys to the vault or anything like that." He also admitted to tricking other officials, including former White House Communications Director Anthony Scaramucci, former Ambassador to Russia-designate Jon Huntsman Jr., and President Donald Trump's son, Eric Trump. The incidents highlight the vulnerability of government officials to spear-phishing attacks and the potential for such pranks to create tension within the administration.

Scientists have reconstructed the history of global sea levels over the past 3,000 years, revealing that the rate of increase experienced in the 20th century was "extremely likely" to have been faster than during nearly the entire period. The study, led by Bob Kopp from Rutgers University and published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, analyzed a global database of relative sea-level reconstructions from 24 locations around the world, combined with 66 global tide gauge records. The findings indicate that global sea levels rose about 14 centimeters from 1900 to 2000, at a rate of 1.4 millimeters per year, compared to the current rate of 3.4 millimeters per year, suggesting ongoing acceleration. The researchers attribute the anomalous 20th-century rise to global warming, estimating that without human-induced climate change, sea levels would have risen by between 3 centimeters and 7 centimeters during the century. The study also forecasts that 21st-century sea level rise will still greatly outstrip what was seen in the 1900s, with low emissions scenarios projecting a rise between 24 and 61 centimeters, and high emissions scenarios potentially leading to a rise as high as 4.29 feet. The methods used to project these totals may not fully capture the dynamics of the 21st century, as they are primarily based on thermal expansion and glacier melting, with the role of ice sheets in Greenland and Antarctica remaining uncertain. The research underscores the significant impact of human-caused climate change on sea levels and highlights the urgent need for mitigation and adaptation strategies.

Spencer West, a 31-year-old American born with a genetic disorder that left him without legs, has achieved an extraordinary feat by climbing Africa's tallest mountain, Mount Kilimanjaro, on his hands. This accomplishment, which took eight days and 20,000 "steps," underscores his belief that "nothing is impossible" and serves as a powerful inspiration for others to redefine their own possible. West, who was born with sacral agenesis and had his legs amputated below the pelvis at the age of five, has led a remarkably normal life despite the initial prognosis from doctors that he would never be a functioning member of society. His journey to the summit began with a realization during a trip to Kenya with the charity Free the Children, where he was confronted by a young girl who had never seen a white person with his condition. This encounter motivated him to use his story as a career and to help others. West's climb was part of his campaign called "Redefine Possible," aiming to raise $750,000 for clean water projects in Kenya. He and his two best friends trained for a year, facing challenges such as altitude sickness and physical exhaustion, but ultimately reached the summit, where West described the moment as "bittersweet and incredible." His climb highlights the power of perseverance and the potential for overcoming seemingly insurmountable obstacles.

George Zimmerman, acquitted of second-degree murder in the death of Trayvon Martin, sought to purchase a bulletproof vest and an infrared home security system while out on $1 million bond, according to records released by the Seminole County, Florida, Sheriff's Office. The log, spanning from July 2012 to July 2013, shows that Zimmerman regularly checked in with deputies every two days and moved at least three times during this period. He was required to stay within Seminole County except to visit his attorneys in a neighboring county and wear a GPS monitoring device. When a sales representative contacted authorities about Zimmerman's interest in a bulletproof vest and infrared security device, he claimed the items were for his protection. Additionally, deputies reviewed security footage from a sporting goods store where Zimmerman visited, ensuring he did not enter areas selling firearms. The records also indicate that Zimmerman and his wife, Shellie, changed their phone numbers after media obtained their old one.

Iowa police are distributing colorful thumb bands with the message "TXTNG KILLS" to combat texting while driving, part of a statewide "X the TXT" campaign. These bands, handed out at events like the Iowa State Fair and high school football games, aim to raise awareness about the dangers of texting behind the wheel. For the first year, police can only issue warnings; fines will be imposed next year. Despite the initiative, Iowa deputies find it challenging to catch offenders, as texting drivers often notice the police and stop. The state has ordered 30,000 bands and plans to distribute them further. Similar campaigns by national groups like Allstate Corp. have seen success, with over 100,000 people pledging to stop texting while driving. As of 2008, nearly 6,000 people died in crashes involving distracted driving, including cellphone use. In Iowa, 16 fatalities have occurred in accidents involving cellphones since 2001.

A federal government shutdown looms as conservative activists intensify pressure on House Republicans to reject a Senate bill restoring funding for Obamacare. Speaker John Boehner faces calls to resign if he agrees to fund the Affordable Care Act, with conservative activists warning that his credibility is on the line. Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, however, says Boehner will be responsible for a shutdown if he makes any changes to the stopgap bill that the Senate passed. Conservative groups launched a national grassroots lobbying campaign, directing 10,000 calls a day to Senate offices. Rep. Tom Graves (R-Ga.) proposed an amendment delaying ObamaCare until 2015, garnering 61 supporters. Despite Senate passage, a shutdown appears increasingly likely, with both sides unwilling to make concessions. President Obama warned Republicans to "think about who you’re hurting" by letting the government shut down, while Boehner faces pressure from his tea party and conservative colleagues to stop Obamacare’s implementation. The White House and Senate Democrats remain firm, refusing to negotiate on Obamacare-related provisions. The Treasury Department warned that the federal government will hit its borrowing limit on October 17, adding another high-stakes showdown. House Republicans are considering adding provisions to the Senate bill, including a one-year delay of the individual mandate, an end to government contributions to health care for lawmakers and staff, and the elimination of the Independent Payment Advisory Board. However, Reid has already warned he will block any House GOP funding bill with Obamacare-related provisions. The last few weeks have been a game of whack-a-mole for Boehner, Majority Leader Eric Cantor, and Majority Whip Kevin McCarthy, as they cycle through strategies to fund the government and lift the debt limit, but each time, the party’s conservative wing shoots it down and demands a new plan. The House and Senate leadership aides acknowledge the likelihood of a shutdown, with the federal government preparing for the possibility of closing for the first time in over 17 years.

Max Lomas, a friend who lived with Bobbi Kristina Brown and her boyfriend Nick Gordon in the weeks before her death, has passed away from a drug overdose. Lomas, who discovered Brown unconscious in her bathtub on January 31, 2015, and administered CPR with Gordon until help arrived, was reportedly found unconscious in a friend's bathroom and later died in a Mississippi hospital. Brown, the daughter of Whitney Houston and Bobby Brown, was in a coma for six months before passing away in hospice care at age 22 on July 26, 2015. Despite Gordon's denial of abuse, Lomas described a tumultuous relationship marked by drug use and fights. Brown's family won a $36 million wrongful death civil suit against Gordon, while no charges were ever filed against Lomas.

General Studies student Joel Davis, a sexual assault prevention activist, has been arrested for child pornography and attempting to sexually exploit children as young as two years old. Davis, who founded Youth to End Sexual Violence and served as chairman of the International Campaign to Stop Rape and Gender Violence, confessed to officers that he had sexually abused a 13-year-old boy in the past and kept child pornography on his phone. His arrest and confession have raised questions about the hypocrisy of someone who advocates against sexual exploitation now being accused of engaging in such acts. Davis, a columnist for Spectator, had previously written about his own experiences with sexual assault, adding a layer of complexity to his current situation. Federal Bureau of Investigation Assistant Director-in-Charge William F. Sweeney, Jr., stated that Davis displayed "the highest degree of hypocrisy" by his alleged attempts to sexually exploit multiple minors. Davis faces up to 70 years in prison. His case has sparked discussions about the challenges and complexities faced by nontraditional students at Columbia, especially those who have experienced trauma and are navigating the transition between their personal histories and the traditional college experience. The article highlights the tension between wanting to have a regular college experience and the fear of being judged more harshly due to one's background. It also touches on the support systems and communities that nontraditional students form to help each other navigate their unique challenges.

Pope Francis' actions during a Mass in St. Peter's Square on Sunday have sparked debate over whether he performed an exorcism. The incident involved a 43-year-old Mexican man who was wheelchair-bound and appeared to react dramatically when the Pope laid his hands on his head and prayed. According to the Italian bishops' conference television station, several exorcists confirmed that the Pope either performed an exorcism or a prayer to free the man from the devil. However, the Vatican denied this, stating that the Pope did not intend to perform an exorcism but merely prayed for a suffering person. The case gained further attention when a leading exorcist, Gabriele Amorth, claimed the man was possessed by four demons and had performed his own exorcism on the man. The incident highlights Pope Francis' frequent references to the devil in his homilies and the growing demand for exorcisms among the faithful. Experts suggest that the increase in exorcisms may reflect a broader weakening of Christian faith and an upswing in the devil's influence. The Vatican has emphasized the importance of prudence in such cases, ensuring that the individual is not merely psychologically ill.

An American Airlines flight attendant on American Airlines Flight 2332 at Dallas/Fort Worth International Airport began ranting over the intercom system about the plane crashing and alluding to the 9/11 terrorist attacks, causing a commotion before the plane could take off for Chicago. Passengers restrained the flight attendant, and the aircraft returned to the gate where it was met by airport police and TSA. Two flight attendants were injured and taken to a local hospital, but no passengers were harmed. The flight eventually departed for Chicago about an hour late. The incident raised concerns about the mental state of the flight attendant, with reports that she had bipolar disorder and had not taken her medication. Passengers and crew worked together to ensure the safety of everyone on board.

White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel, 50, on Monday revealed his interest in running for mayor of Chicago, stating on the "Charlie Rose" show that "one day I would like to run for mayor of the city of Chicago." Emanuel made this comment while discussing potential future government roles, adding that he would support Mayor Richard M. Daley if he seeks re-election but would run for mayor if Daley does not. The mayor of Chicago, Daley, is expected to seek re-election next February, but his decision has not yet been confirmed. Emanuel, who moved his family to Washington D.C. and enrolled his children in local schools, gave up a safe House seat to serve as Obama's chief of staff. Despite his aspirations, Emanuel faces competition for the mayoral position, as evidenced by the potential candidates mentioned, including former U.S. Secretary of Commerce William Daley, former White House Chief of Staff Ron Klain, and others. Emanuel emphasized his desire to reconnect with constituents, missing the direct interaction with the public that he experienced while in Congress. While he currently serves as Obama's chief of staff, Emanuel has signaled he may extend his tenure if Obama requests it.

Local federal agents arrested a 19-year-old man, Sergio Morales Soto, just before he tried to leave the country on a flight to Guatemala on April 5. Due to severe weather delays, agents were able to locate Soto on board the aircraft and apprehend him, according to Gregory Wiest, Deputy Special Agent in Charge of Homeland Security Atlanta. Soto will face six felony sex assault charges in Maryland. Wiest stated that agents can quickly identify suspects within the airport, even on a plane, and that Customs Border Protection arrests over 20 suspects daily. "This is the place we are going to get you," said Carey Davis, Port Director of U.S. Customs Border Protection.

The relationship between Wall Street and the Obama administration, often portrayed as adversarial, is more complex than it appears. Despite Obama's public stance against Wall Street, he has, in fact, received substantial financial support from the industry. This is evident in the contributions from financial services professionals to Obama and Democratic candidates, including House Financial Services Committee member Gary Ackerman, who received significant funding from Wall Street despite his tough stance during the Bernie Madoff scandal. Similarly, Senator Kirsten Gillibrand, a Democrat from New York, has received substantial support from the securities and investment industry, which is unlikely to abandon her for Mitt Romney, a fellow Republican. The financial industry's contributions to both sides of the aisle suggest a pragmatic approach, prioritizing political influence over party loyalty. This dynamic challenges the notion of mutual antagonism between Obama and Wall Street, revealing a more nuanced and mutually beneficial relationship.

Hillary Clinton's choice of Tim Kaine as her running mate for the 2016 election has garnered mixed reactions from the Democratic Party, with some progressive groups expressing disappointment. Kaine, a Virginia senator and former governor, was unveiled as Clinton's pick during the Democratic National Convention, drawing praise from labor unions and women's rights groups for his strong records on workers' issues and support for women's rights. However, liberal organizations such as the Progressive Change Campaign Committee and Democracy for America criticized Kaine for his support of trade deals like the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP) and his stance on financial regulations. Kaine's selection was seen as a strategic move by Clinton to appeal to moderate voters and swing states, particularly Virginia, where he is a senator. His background as a former mayor, governor, and chairman of the Democratic National Committee adds to his experience and appeal. Despite some concerns from progressive supporters, Kaine's pick was generally well-received by Clinton's inner circle and the Democratic Party. His acceptance of gifts during his time as governor and lieutenant governor has been a point of criticism, but Kaine maintains a strong track record on issues such as climate change and immigration. The choice of Kaine as Clinton's running mate underscores the importance of Virginia in the upcoming election, as the state has become a crucial swing state for Democrats. While Kaine may not generate the same level of enthusiasm as a progressive or first-ever Latino pick, his selection is seen as a balanced and pragmatic choice for the general election.

Virginia Attorney General Ken Cuccinelli sent a tweet that quickly went viral, sparking confusion and speculation. Cuccinelli wrote, "How much would I give to be one of the 72 Virginians Osama is 'hanging out' with since Sunday?" This tweet referenced a joke about bin Laden's death, where he is supposedly greeted by American founding fathers and other historical figures at the gates of heaven, only to be told he will face 72 virgins. The tweet's humor was lost on many, leading to widespread misunderstanding and a flurry of questions about Cuccinelli's intentions. Huffington Post writer Jason Linkins humorously speculated that Cuccinelli might have been wishing he had been part of the Virginia-based Navy SEAL unit that killed bin Laden, but noted this was an odd way to express such a wish. Cuccinelli later clarified his tweet, emphasizing the typo and the joke's context. The incident highlighted the potential pitfalls of social media, where a simple typo or misinterpreted joke can lead to public ridicule.

A six-member medical board has decided to start a multi-stage plastic surgery on the hands of Abul Bajandar, a 26-year-old Bangladeshi man known as the "Tree Man" due to massive bark-like warts covering his hands and feet. The warts, which have smothered his hands and feet, weighing up to four kilograms each, have left him unable to perform any functions. The surgery, planned for about three weeks from now, aims to remove extra flesh from his thumb and index fingers to restore some functionality. Doctors will also conduct medical examinations, including blood tests and biopsies, to ensure the surgery can be performed without damaging major nerves or causing other health issues.

Abul, from the southern district of Khulna, first noticed the warts when he was a teenager, but they began spreading rapidly four years ago. He was diagnosed with epidermodysplasia verruciformis, a rare genetic skin disease that makes individuals susceptible to skin growths. The condition, also known as "tree-man disease," is extremely rare, with only three known cases worldwide, including Abul's. The Bangladeshi government has waived the costs of his treatment, and foreign doctors and researchers have expressed interest in helping find a solution to his incurable skin disorder.
