The Menil Collection, which acquired the Picasso in 1956, has taken appropriate security measures to prevent future incidents.

When a crime occurs in the physical world, investigators search for specific types of evidence. In the case of the massive distributed denial of service (DDoS) attack that jammed the internet on Friday, Dyn, the domain name service provider hit, hasn't revealed much about its investigation. However, researchers have unearthed new leads that may point to the perpetrators. The attack, which involved 10s of millions of IP addresses, was so massive that the results of the investigation may not help prevent another attack. The investigation points to attention-seeking hackers, as the attack's nature and source are still under investigation. Flashpoint, a cybersecurity firm, released more information on Tuesday, suggesting that the hacker or group of hackers who attacked Dyn also targeted a video game company. They believe the attack was similar to recent DDoS attacks against the security blog Krebs on Security and OVH, a French internet service hosting provider. The attack involved devices that were separate and distinct from the devices used in the other digital assaults, with malware used to hijack digital video recorders and cameras. The malware, called Mirai, was released earlier this month on hackforums.net, making it accessible to anyone. The attack was similar to recent DDoS attacks against the security blog Krebs on Security as well as OVH, a French "internet service hosting provider." Flashpoint has said similar types of attacks often originate from users of hackforums.net. The attack involved millions of "Internet of Things" (IoT) devices such as DVRs and video recorders, and had those devices flood Dyn with data. Dyn doesn't control those cameras, and experts said many of those devices can't be patched, meaning someone can simply hack them again and again to launch new assaults. This is the internet of largely un-patchable things, and unless you take them out of service, these devices can be repeat offenders for the life of the internet. The size of the attack makes it unclear how useful the company's post-mortem will be, as it likely can't bolster its cyber defense quickly enough to prevent such a massive assault. Companies might be able to do a few things to mitigate the damage, but they can't stop manufacturers from making hackable devices, and they can't singlehandedly educate the public about enhancing the security of every device hooked up to the IoT. Until many IoT device owners get on top of security, we should all expect some more slow days on the internet.

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump ignited controversy by suggesting women who have illegal abortions should face punishment, a stance that drew swift rebukes from his rivals and party leaders. Trump’s comments came as he faced increasing pressure to unify the Republican Party, which has seen a series of candidates and supporters denounce his inflammatory remarks. His rivals, including Ted Cruz, John Kasich, and Ben Carson, swiftly distanced themselves, emphasizing the importance of women’s dignity and the sanctity of life. Cruz highlighted the need to support women, stating, “Of course we shouldn’t be talking about punishing women; we should affirm their dignity and the incredible gift they have to bring life into the world.” 

The fallout extended beyond Trump’s rivals. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, chairwoman of the Democratic National Committee, seized the opportunity to tie Trump to the broader Republican agenda, arguing that the party’s policies on women and their health are “dangerously wrong.” She emphasized the need to stand up for women, stating, “The real issue is a Republican party—led by Mitt Romney and Paul Ryan—whose policies on women and their health are dangerously wrong.”

Trump’s comments also reignited debates about his evolution on social issues. In a CNN town hall, Trump claimed he had “evolved” from being pro-choice to pro-life, drawing parallels to Ronald Reagan’s evolution on abortion. However, a closer look at his past statements revealed that Trump had previously expressed support for abortion rights. In 1999, he told NBC’s “Meet the Press,” “I’m very pro-choice,” and “I hate the concept of abortion. … But still, I just believe in choice.” His recent pivot to a hardline pro-life stance, while consistent with his current rhetoric, contrasts sharply with his earlier positions.

The controversy underscored the deep divisions within the Republican Party. While Trump’s base rallied behind him, many party leaders and establishment figures expressed concern. John Kasich, for instance, criticized Trump’s comments, stating, “Of course women shouldn’t be punished.” The situation highlighted the challenge for the Republican Party in maintaining unity, especially as the party’s nominee could face significant obstacles in the general election. 

The broader context of the Republican primary race also came into focus. Trump’s lead in delegate counts, while substantial, is not insurmountable. A Marquette University Law School poll showed Ted Cruz leading Trump by 10 points in Wisconsin, a state crucial for the Republican nomination. This poll, along with other state-level contests, underscored the potential for a contested convention, where Trump’s supporters might not rally behind him if he falls short.

The controversy also brought to the forefront the Republican Party’s struggle to present a united front. Party leaders, including Steve Munisteri, former chairman of the Republican Party of Texas, emphasized the importance of coming together, stating, “At the end of it, we’re supposed to all come together. That includes the people who were not successful in getting there.” However, the risk of a third-party bid loomed, with Trump’s supporters potentially backing an alternative candidate if he does not secure the nomination.

The Republican Party’s soul-searching continued as it grappled with the implications of Trump’s comments. Party leaders faced the difficult task of setting an example and bringing the party together, recognizing that a divided party could be a significant liability in the general election. As the race progressed, the challenge for the Republican Party to unify behind a nominee, especially one as polarizing as Trump, became increasingly clear.

A terrifying Halloween night in Nashville turned into a real nightmare when a group of friends playing at a haunted house were unknowingly handed a real knife by someone believed to be one of the house's actors. The incident occurred on a Friday night at Nashville Nightmare, a popular Halloween attraction in Madison, according to Metro Police. The group, consisting of four friends, had already gone inside the haunted houses and were playing carnival-type games when they were approached by a thin figure with a straw hat. The figure, dressed and speaking in character, accused one of the women's friends of "fucking around" with her and handed the woman a knife, telling her to stab the friend. The woman, thinking the knife was a prop, stabbed her friend, 29-year-old James Yochim, in the left arm. When she pulled back, she realized the knife was real and the victim's arm was gushing blood. Yochim was taken to a nearby hospital for treatment. The person who handed the knife to the woman is now believed to be an employee of the haunted house, and has been placed on leave. Nashville Nightmare, which has hosted the attraction for 8 years without any security incidents, is investigating the incident and has stated that their safety and security protocols will be reviewed. The group involved is seeking legal action. (Metro Nashville Police Department, WZTV)

A 25-year-old Israeli woman was allegedly gang-raped in the early hours of Sunday near the town of Manali in Himachal Pradesh, India, after accepting a ride in a vehicle from strangers who had offered her a lift to Manali, where she planned to catch a taxi to a nearby town. According to police, the woman was hitching a ride to Kaza in the Spiti Valley of Himachal Pradesh when a car without license plates picked her up, promising to take her to Manali. The woman alleged that two of the six men in the car raped her at an unspecified location. After the assault, she was dropped off in Manali, where she reported the incident to the police around 10 am with a friend. The Kullu superintendent of police, Padam Chand, stated that a medical examination had been conducted and sent to Mandi for expert opinion. The woman is currently being treated in a hospital.

The incident is the latest in a series of rape cases involving foreign tourists in the Kullu district. In June 2013, a 29-year-old American woman was gang-raped by three Nepalese men after hitching a ride from Vashisht to Manali, where she was also robbed of her money and cellphone. In May 2012, a 22-year-old Australian woman was allegedly raped by a Chandigarh man she had befriended on Facebook in Kasol village, after being drugged and assaulted in her hotel room. Police are confident of solving the case as the area is covered by CCTV cameras, including some with night-vision capabilities. The Israeli Foreign Ministry has confirmed the rape complaint but has not yet received further details.

The case highlights the ongoing issue of sexual violence against women in India, despite increased punishments for rapists following a 2012 fatal gang-rape in New Delhi that brought widespread attention to the problem. The police are currently examining CCTV footage to identify the suspects and have arrested two men so far. The Kullu district, known for its scenic beauty and popularity among foreign tourists, continues to grapple with the issue of sexual violence, with incidents occurring almost every day.

In an effort to resonate more with younger consumers, luxury handbag maker Coach has announced its intention to acquire its smaller rival, Kate Spade & Co., in a deal valued at $2.4 billion. This move is seen as a strategic step for Coach to broaden its customer base and appeal to the millennial market. CEO Victor Luis highlighted Kate Spade's unique brand positioning and strong awareness among consumers, especially millennials, as key factors in the decision. The deal is expected to close by the end of the third quarter of 2017 and is anticipated to add to Coach's adjusted earnings in fiscal 2018. Shares of Kate Spade surged more than 8% following the announcement, while Coach's stock ended the day up almost 5%. Analysts view this acquisition positively, noting that it aligns with Coach's goal of becoming a global, multi-brand luxury company. The deal is expected to generate $50 million in annual savings through combined inventory management and supply chain operations, which will help boost profitability. However, it also means that Kate Spade's brand independence will be preserved, and key staff will be retained. This acquisition comes as Coach continues to work on turning around its business, having already acquired popular shoe maker Stuart Weitzman in 2015. Kate Spade, on the other hand, has seen better days, with its shares hitting a three-year low before takeover rumors began to swirl. Coach's latest strategy to cut back on discounting products in the U.S. is finally paying off, as evidenced by the retailer's financial performance. The acquisition is seen as a significant step in Coach's journey to become a more diversified luxury brand portfolio.

The parents of a 20-year-old University of Alabama student, Megan Rondini, who died by suicide in 2016, have filed a federal wrongful death lawsuit against the alleged rapist, university officials, and law enforcement. The lawsuit alleges that the university and law enforcement mishandled the case, leading to Rondini's mental breakdown and eventual suicide. According to the lawsuit, Rondini was sexually assaulted by T.J. Bunn Jr. in July 2015 after a night out with friends. Bunn, a wealthy man with strong ties to the Tuscaloosa community, was never charged with a crime. The lawsuit claims that Tuscaloosa Sheriff's Department deputies were dismissive and focused on questioning Rondini about her actions rather than investigating the alleged assault. It also accuses the university of failing to provide adequate psychological support and accommodations to Rondini. Specifically, the lawsuit states that Rondini was denied counseling services until she began taking anxiety medication and that university officials failed to address her safety concerns after she saw Bunn's car outside her apartment and on campus. The lawsuit seeks to hold the university, law enforcement, and Bunn accountable for their roles in Rondini's death, hoping to prevent similar cases in the future. The Rondinis' attorney, Leroy Maxwell Jr., emphasized that the family is not seeking financial compensation but rather to bring attention to the systemic issues that led to their daughter's tragic death. The University of Alabama has previously stated that it provided support to Rondini and that the BuzzFeed News story "ignored some significant facts." The lawsuit highlights the complex and often inadequate response to sexual assault cases, particularly when the alleged perpetrator is from a prominent local family.

In South Carolina, the investigation into the case of Todd Kohlhepp, a man accused of a series of brutal killings, continues to expand. Kohlhepp, a 45-year-old real estate agent, was initially charged with the kidnapping of a woman found chained in a metal storage container on his 95-acre property near Woodruff. His arrest led to his confession regarding the 2003 quadruple homicide at Superbike Motorsports in Chesnee, where he allegedly killed the owner, service manager, mechanic, and bookkeeper. He was denied bond during a brief court appearance on four murder charges for those killings. Kohlhepp's case has now expanded, with investigators searching other properties he owns or used to own, not limited to South Carolina. The FBI and Department of Homeland Security are also involved in the investigation. On Sunday, human remains were uncovered at one of the sites Kohlhepp pointed out as potential gravesites, but the identity and cause of death of the victims remain unknown. The search for more remains will continue on Monday, with the process of removing them being meticulous and time-consuming. The investigation has brought closure to some families, such as the Lucas family, whose son Brian was one of the victims. Kohlhepp's criminal history includes a 1987 conviction for kidnapping and sexually assaulting a 14-year-old girl, which led to his registration as a sex offender. Despite this, he maintained a seemingly normal life, obtaining a real estate license in 2006. The community is grappling with the revelation of these crimes, with some expressing a mix of relief and sympathy for Kohlhepp's family. The ongoing investigation aims to uncover the full extent of Kohlhepp's alleged crimes and bring justice to the victims and their families.

Mitt Romney secured a second consecutive victory in the Nevada caucuses, defeating his rivals and demonstrating his strength as the Republican front-runner. The caucuses, which drew little attention in the primary race, are expected to be crucial battlegrounds in the general election against President Barack Obama, who faces high unemployment in Nevada. Romney's victory, which came after his win in the Florida primary, solidified his lead with 87 of the 1,144 delegates needed for the Republican nomination. His campaign focused on attacking Obama's economic policies, stating that they have prolonged the tough times for Americans. Romney's victory was significant as it came in a state with a high Mormon population, where he received strong support. Newt Gingrich and Ron Paul finished in second and third place, respectively, while Rick Santorum trailed behind. Despite the setback, Gingrich announced plans to campaign in Ohio, and Santorum urged Republicans to give his campaign another chance. Ron Paul's campaign, which spent $350,000 on television ads, hoped for a better showing but finished second to Romney. The results indicate that Romney is maintaining his momentum and tightening his grip on the Republican nomination, while his rivals struggle to keep pace.

Get ready for a celestial event on Tuesday night as the moon and the bright star Aldebaran play a game of hide-and-seek. For observers in portions of Mexico, Central America, southeastern Canada, the eastern U.S., and southern Europe, the waning gibbous moon will pass in front of Aldebaran, one of the brightest and most colorful stars in the sky. This occultation, part of a series that began in January 2015 and will end in September 2018, offers a rare chance to witness the moon's edge sliding across the star's path. The event will be visible in different ways depending on your location; those in the southern and eastern U.S. have the best viewing conditions, with a "graze" visible in a narrow band running from Los Angeles to Denver and southeast of Minneapolis. Binoculars or a telescope are recommended to catch the star's gradual disappearance and reappearance. The International Occultation Timers Association has provided detailed maps and times for over 1,000 locations, including Philadelphia, to help enthusiasts plan their observations. The next similar series of Aldebaran occultations won't occur until 2033, making this a special opportunity for skywatchers.

President Donald Trump unveiled a Republican framework for tax reform on Wednesday, aiming to simplify the tax code and provide sweeping tax cuts, particularly for the middle class. The plan includes reducing the individual tax rates from seven brackets to three, with rates of 12%, 25%, and 35%. Trump also proposed doubling the standard deduction to $12,000 for individuals and $24,000 for married couples, which would allow many to avoid the complicated process of itemizing their taxes. The corporate tax rate would be slashed to 20%, making American companies more competitive with their international counterparts. Additionally, the plan would eliminate the estate tax, a move Trump described as a "revolutionary change" that would benefit the middle class. The framework also includes a new $500 credit for non-child dependents, such as elderly parents, and a significant increase in the child tax credit. However, the plan leaves some details open, such as the income ranges for the new tax brackets and the specifics of the corporate interest expense limitation. Republicans hope to use budget reconciliation rules to pass the bill with a simple majority, bypassing Democratic opposition. Trump emphasized that the plan would not benefit the wealthy, despite his own family's potential gains, and invited Democrats to support the proposal. Despite the plan's ambitious goals, critics argue that it could add significantly to the national debt and benefit the wealthy at the expense of the middle class. The framework is expected to face significant scrutiny and debate as Congress works to fill in the details and reconcile the plan with the needs of various stakeholders.

This year, U.S. News and World Report has released its annual rankings of the top colleges and universities in the United States, offering insights into the best institutions for various types of education. The rankings cover a wide range of categories, including National Universities, Liberal Arts Colleges, and more specialized types of schools. Harvard University continues to top the list of National Universities for the 27th consecutive year, followed closely by Princeton University and the University of California, Berkeley. Among Liberal Arts Colleges, Williams College retains its top spot, while smaller institutions like Amherst and Swarthmore also make the top 10. The rankings are based on a variety of factors, including academic reputation, faculty resources, student engagement, and post-graduation success. The full list includes detailed metrics and data, allowing prospective students to compare institutions based on specific criteria. This comprehensive approach aims to provide a holistic view of each college's strengths and weaknesses, helping students and families make informed decisions about their higher education choices.

RedState, an influential conservative website, fired several prominent writers on Friday, a move that appears to target those critical of President Trump. The Daily Beast confirmed that Caleb Howe, Jay Caruso, Ben Howe, Patrick Frey (writing under the pseudonym Patterico), Neil Stevens, and Susan Wright, all often critical of the president, were among those dismissed. Fired staff learned of their layoffs either through locked email accounts or a memo from Townhall general manager Jonathan Garthwaite. Garthwaite stated that RedState had to make changes, unable to support the entire current roster of writers. The layoffs reflect a shift in the conservative movement, with many viewing it as a purge of anti-Trump voices. RedState's highest-trafficked writer, Susan Wright, has been openly critical of Trump and his supporters, generating significantly less revenue than other writers who remain with the site. The dismissals also suggest an incentive for conservative outlets to protect the Republican president at all costs, as evidenced by the firing of Ben Howe, a vocal Trump critic. The decision to cut anti-Trump writers, while keeping pro-Trump ones, is seen as a cost-saving measure, with some sources noting that insufficiently partisan writers were targeted. RedState is part of Townhall Media's portfolio, owned by Salem Media Group, which has faced criticism for its treatment of radio hosts during the Trump campaign.

The homeless good Samaritan who gained national fame after the stranded motorist he gave his last $20 to raised more than $400,000 in his name is now suing her and her boyfriend, claiming the couple is committing fraud by taking more than half of the money for themselves. On Tuesday, attorneys for Johnny Bobbitt Jr. filed the lawsuit in the Superior Court of New Jersey in Burlington County against Kate McClure, 28, and Mark D'Amico, 39. Last year, Bobbitt, a 35-year-old Marine Corps veteran who was living on the streets of Philadelphia, gave McClure the last of the cash he had panhandled that day after she ran out of gas on Interstate 95, McClure wrote on a GoFundMe fundraiser she created on Nov. 10. Bobbitt even instructed McClure to get back in her car and lock the doors before returning minutes later with a red gas can. At first, McClure showed her gratitude to Bobbitt by providing him with food, clothes, and some cash. Then, more than 14,000 people who were moved by Bobbitt's generosity and his unlikely friendship with McClure donated over $402,000 to the fundraiser, but Bobbitt is now back on the streets and worried that he may never see the bulk of the money, according to the lawsuit. The couple initially provided Bobbitt with "some of the monies contributed" but have declined to provide him with access to the rest, according to the lawsuit. Bobbitt alleges that the couple has spent more than half of the funds raised, treating it like their "personal piggy bank to fund a lifestyle that they could not otherwise afford," his attorneys wrote. Bobbitt's drug addiction has relapsed and he is back on the Philadelphia streets panhandling for money after completing two stints in rehab, The Philadelphia Inquirer reported last week. D'Amico told The Inquirer that he controls the money but would rather "burn it in front of him" than give Bobbitt the remainder of the funds. Giving Bobbitt the money would be like "giving him a loaded gun," since Bobbitt is addicted to drugs, D'Amico told the local newspaper. Bobbitt's attorneys have also filed an application for an injunctive relief require McClure and D'Amico to refrain from dissipating any of the monies donated to the GoFundMe account and from using the funds for any other purpose other than to directly benefit Bobbitt, according to court documents. Chris Fallon, one of the attorneys representing Bobbitt, did not immediately return ABC News' request for comment. An update McClure had written on the GoFundMe account indicated that the couple tried to ensure the safety of Bobbitt's financial future. Two trusts were to be set up in his name, one to provide him a small "salary" each year and a retirement trust and another which was to "be wisely invested by a financial planner." A bank account had also been set up for Bobbitt with funds for his every day needs that was intended to "get him through until he finds a job," and his one planned indulgence was to buy a 1999 Ford Ranger, the "dream truck he's always wanted," and a home of his very own, McClure wrote. A formal trust for Bobbitt's benefit has not been created, according to the lawsuit. Bobbitt is seeking compensatory damages and interest, funds of counsel fees and costs of the lawsuit and accounting of all funds donated to the GoFundMe account. In addition, the lawsuit is requesting the appointment of a receiver for the funds and for the funds to be deposited with the court. McClure and D'Amico did not respond to ABC News' request for comment.

Toronto Mayor Rob Ford, embroiled in a crack cocaine scandal, has put up some of his personal items on eBay, including the tie he wore when admitting to smoking crack. The items, which also include moose print jammie pants, a size 4XL football jersey, and a poster, are being auctioned under the handle "torontorobford." The tie, in particular, has a special connection to the Ford administration, as it was worn during a shopping trip to Walmart. However, potential buyers should be wary, as the seller currently has a feedback score of 0. The auction has sparked interest, with eBay's automatic bidding system coming into play as bids increase. Despite the controversy, Ford's supporters argue that he has made significant fiscal savings for the city, such as negotiating four-year labor deals, contracting out garbage collection, and rescinding a hated vehicle registration fee. The mayor's lawyer, Dennis Morris, has called for the police to release the controversial video to the public, stating, "All I can say is we'd love to see the video. I can't say what it shows because only a few have seen it. ... Let the public see it." Meanwhile, the mayor continues to insist he was not smoking crack, and his brother Doug has called for the video to be released to the public, saying, "I'd like to see this video and let us judge for ourselves, let the people judge for themselves."

German Chancellor Angela Merkel attended a United Nations Migration Conference in Marrakech, Morocco, as nearly 164 out of 193 U.N. members adopted the "Global Compact on Migration," a non-binding agreement aimed at improving the treatment of migrants worldwide, the Associated Press reports. The pact, described as the first of its kind, seeks to ensure "safe, orderly and regular migration" by encouraging countries to work together and fight discrimination against migrants. The deal was met with opposition from at least nine countries, including the United States under President Donald Trump, which did not participate in drafting the accord. The Trump administration criticized the agreement, stating it could "impose" policies and fail to distinguish adequately between legal and illegal immigrants. Eastern European countries, Italy, and Belgium also voiced concerns. U.N. Secretary-General Antonio Guterres defended the agreement, emphasizing the obligation to respect the human rights of migrants and noting that more than 80 percent of the world's migrants move between countries "in a safe and orderly fashion." The Global Compact for Migration addresses the significant issue of unregulated migration, which has resulted in the loss of over 60,000 lives since the year 2000. Migration affects hundreds of millions of people globally, with various motivations, including economic, social, and political factors. Defenders argue that migration benefits the global economy by diversifying and rejuvenating workforces in developed countries and providing remittances to poorer nations. Opponents often fear that migration can dilute national character, import poverty or crime, reduce wages, and take jobs from tax-paying citizens. The conference marks a significant test for the U.N.-led effort to address the challenges of international migration and ensure safe, orderly, and humane migration practices.

In a significant development, prosecutors from six California counties have united to charge Joseph James DeAngelo Jr., the man suspected of being the Golden State Killer, with 13 counts of murder. DeAngelo, a 72-year-old former police officer, was arrested in a Sacramento suburb in April, bringing to an end a decades-long mystery that has haunted California law enforcement. The combined case, which also includes multiple kidnapping and weapons charges, will be tried in Sacramento, as district attorneys from the involved counties announced at a media briefing in Orange County. Anne Marie Schubert, the district attorney for Sacramento County, emphasized the importance of this unified effort, stating, "It is very fitting that this journey for justice that has been sought for over 40 years ends in Sacramento." The case, which spans the northern, central, and southern parts of the state, includes crimes committed in the 1970s and 1980s, with the last known crime in 1986. The breakthrough came when investigators obtained the unknown killer's DNA from the 1980 murders of Lyman and Charlene Smith. By reviewing rape kits and using a genealogy database, investigators built a family tree and narrowed their search to DeAngelo. Surveillance and the collection of DNA from a tissue in DeAngelo's trash confirmed his involvement in multiple crime scenes. The unified prosecution aims to deliver justice for the victims and their loved ones, marking a historic moment in the Golden State Killer case.

Harper Lee, the 87-year-old author of the Pulitzer Prize-winning novel "To Kill a Mockingbird," has filed a lawsuit in federal court in Manhattan against her former literary agent's son-in-law, Samuel Pinkus, and other defendants, seeking to reclaim the copyright to her iconic work. The lawsuit alleges that Pinkus, who took over as her agent after her former agent's illness, took advantage of Lee's declining hearing and eyesight in 2007 to get her to assign the copyright to his company. Lee, who lives in an assisted-living facility in Monroeville, Alabama, and has been increasingly deaf and blind since a 2007 stroke, claims she was unaware of the copyright transfer. The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages and the forfeiture of commissions Pinkus and his companies have received. Lee's lawyer, Gloria Phares, states that the copyright transfer was a "gross example of self-dealing" and incompatible with Pinkus's duty of loyalty. The defendants, including Pinkus's wife, Leigh Ann Winick, and journalist Gerald Posner, have not yet commented. "To Kill a Mockingbird," a story of racial injustice in the American South, has sold over 30 million copies worldwide and won a Pulitzer Prize for fiction. The case is Lee v. Pinkus, 13-3000, in the U.S. District Court, U.S. Bankruptcy Court, Southern District of New York (Manhattan).

Eliot Spitzer, former New York governor and noted pervert, choked up on Tuesday morning while discussing his “pain” over the last five years on MSNBC’s “Morning Joe.” Spitzer, asked by host Mika Brzezinski to give a heartfelt answer on how he had changed since resigning in 2008, replied, “A lot of pain. A lot of pain. … You go through that pain, you change.” His emotional response, however, was met with skepticism from other guests. Nicole Wallace, a Republican adviser, said, “They felt real to me. I was sitting there, it felt very real to me,” while MSNBC host Joe Scarborough turned the conversation back to Spitzer’s record and hopes for the comptroller office. Spitzer, 54, is vying to be the next New York City comptroller, a position that carries less public prominence than governor or attorney general but would provide him with enough power to exert influence on corporate America. As comptroller, Spitzer could play the role of activist investor while managing the city’s almost $140 billion in pension funds, pressure money managers to accept reforms if they want to do business with New York, and audit city agencies’ various dealings with financial companies. Spitzer’s surprise announcement via an interview with the New York Times on Sunday evening has made clear that he would use the city’s shareholder position to be a watchdog of corporate America. In an interview on the Brian Lehrer Show on Monday, Spitzer offered several examples of corporate principles he would advocate as comptroller, including separating the roles of CEO and board chairman at large corporations. Spitzer’s just-announced candidacy for New York City comptroller has raised questions about how he will convince people to support him in the limited time available. Spitzer, who left office in March 2008 shortly after details of his involvement in a high-end prostitution ring became public, has repeatedly compared the city comptroller’s office to the attorney general’s office, arguing that there is a real metaphor there. Spitzer’s record, including his battles with American International Group and the New York Stock Exchange, has made him a vocal critic of Wall Street. However, his history and reputation have also raised questions about his ability to win the support of voters. Journalist Sally Quinn, the veteran Washington observer, reflected on the common thread between Spitzer, Weiner, and Sanford: “The essential thing that these politicians all have is an absence of shame.” Quinn, who now writes a column on faith, said, “We keep hearing about redemption and forgiveness — these are all religious words. There’s nothing religious about what’s going on here. This is strictly about ‘me, me, me,’ and it’s a neediness that I don’t understand but we see all the time in Washington.”

Fenway Park, the storied home of the Boston Red Sox for a century, stands as "America's Most Beloved Ballpark" and the oldest in major league baseball. Its iconic features, from the classic brick entrance on Yawkey Way to the unique left-field wall with its manual scoreboard and Pesky’s Pole, have made it a destination in itself, comparable to the Freedom Trail and the swan boats. The park’s timeless appeal is evident in its frequent appearances in popular culture, including John Updike’s description of it as a "lyric little bandbox" and its role in the TV show "Cheers" and the fan film "Fever Pitch." 

Fenway’s field, with its quirky dimensions and close proximity to the stands, offers a distinctive auditory experience, from the scalpers on Brookline Avenue to the fans singing "Sweet Caroline" and the PA announcements of "Dirty Water" after victories. The park’s charm lies in its enduring unchanged nature since its opening in 1912, with only minor updates to seating and amenities. It has hosted numerous legendary moments, including Babe Ruth’s first pitch and Ted Williams’s last home run, as well as appearances by baseball greats like Christy Mathewson, Ty Cobb, Satchel Paige, Joe DiMaggio, and Hank Aaron. 

Fenway has also served as a venue for unexpected events, such as the performances of professional football teams, the Bruins and Flyers, and political figures like Franklin Delano Roosevelt. Musicians like the Rolling Stones, Paul McCartney, and Bruce Springsteen have also performed there. The park’s lore is rich with memorable incidents, from the 1934 fire that damaged the renovated park to Ted Williams’s "Great Expectoration" in 1956, Jim Lonborg’s "hero’s ride" in 1967, Carlton Fisk’s dramatic 12th-inning home run in 1975, and Bucky “Bleeping” Dent’s heartbreaking screen shot in 1978. 

Fenway’s legacy is defined by its unique charm and the countless significant moments that have unfolded within its walls, making it a symbol of Boston’s rich baseball history and a cherished part of the city’s identity.

A 30-year-old man named Shannon Miles has been charged with capital murder for allegedly ambushing and shooting Harris County Sheriff's Deputy Darren Goforth 15 times at a gas station. Miles, who was wearing a .40 caliber Smith & Wesson, allegedly shot Goforth in the back of the head, then stood over him and fired the rest of his 14-bullet clip. The prosecutor, Devon Anderson, stated that Miles' actions were "cold-blooded and cowardly." Goforth, a 47-year-old father of two, had been a deputy for 10 years. More than 1,000 people attended a vigil at the gas station, and donations for the family have topped $150,000. Miles has a history of run-ins with law enforcement, including a 2012 case where he was declared incompetent to stand trial after assaulting a man at a Salvation Army shelter. He also pleaded guilty to resisting arrest and evading arrest. The motive for the shooting remains unclear, but Sheriff Ron Hickman linked the incident to broader anti-police rhetoric. President Obama offered condolences to Goforth's family and highlighted the bravery of law enforcement. Goforth's funeral is scheduled for Friday at Second Baptist Church.

A New Hampshire jury delivered a mixed verdict in the sexual assault trial of former St. Paul’s School student Owen Labrie, acquitting him of the most serious charges but convicting him on lesser counts. Labrie, 19 at the time, was accused of raping a 15-year-old girl in a secluded room on the St. Paul’s campus in May 2014. The jury found Labrie guilty of three misdemeanor sexual assault charges, endangering a child, and using a computer to lure a minor, a felony. Labrie, who was a straight-A student and planned to study theology at Harvard, was visibly shaken when the verdict was announced, bursting into tears and shaking his head in disbelief. His mother also wept in the courtroom. The teenage victim and her mother, who described the convictions as a “measure of justice,” expressed that the verdict did not bring the closure they sought. Labrie’s lawyer, J.W. Carney Jr., argued that the jury concluded the sexual encounter was mutual and that the convictions for misdemeanor assaults were based on the victim’s age. Carney said Labrie’s comments to friends about the encounter were the “most damning” evidence against him, but he likened the conviction to a “brand” that would follow Labrie for life.

The trial revealed the sexual culture at the prestigious 159-year-old boarding school, whose notable alumni include Secretary of State John F. Kerry and “Doonesbury” creator Garry Trudeau. Labrie and his friends sought to “slay” as many girls as possible, using their status to woo underclassmen in a rite known as the “senior salute.” Labrie’s accuser tearfully testified that Labrie had sex with her over her multiple objections, ignoring her efforts to keep her bra and underwear on. Labrie described a playful, consensual encounter in which he decided against having sex after a moment of “divine inspiration.” The jury’s verdict highlighted the complex dynamics of consent and the legal challenges in cases involving teenagers. Labrie will face a maximum sentence of 11 years, including a mandatory registration as a sex offender. The school’s rector praised the victim for her “remarkable moral courage and strength,” while Labrie’s family expressed that the outcome brought no joy, as their daughter could never regain what she had lost. The case underscored the ongoing debate over how to handle such cases, particularly when the alleged victim and perpetrator are both minors.

Tesla’s plans to go private have been put on hold after a thorough review of the situation by CEO Elon Musk and the company’s board of directors. Musk announced on Twitter on August 7 that he was considering taking Tesla private, a move that would allow him to take control of the company and potentially avoid the public market’s scrutiny. However, after consulting with investors, including institutional shareholders with internal compliance issues, and retail investors who expressed reluctance to join a private company, Musk concluded that the majority of Tesla’s existing shareholders believed the company would be better off as a public entity. Additionally, the process of going private was deemed to be more time-consuming and distracting than initially anticipated, potentially detracting from Tesla’s focus on ramping up production of the Model 3 and achieving profitability. Musk stated, “Given the feedback I’ve received, it’s apparent that most of Tesla’s existing shareholders believe we are better off as a public company.” The decision to remain public was also supported by the board of directors. Musk emphasized the importance of staying focused on building products that people love and making a difference to the shared future of life on Earth, stating, “We’ve shown that we can make great sustainable energy products, and we now need to show that we can be sustainably profitable.” The team and Musk are committed to continuing this mission, despite the challenges faced by the Model 3 production. Musk expressed gratitude to all investors, customers, and employees for their support and excitement about continuing to lead Tesla as a public company.

Belgian officials are investigating whether doctors improperly euthanized a woman with autism, Tine Nys, in 2010, marking the first criminal investigation in a euthanasia case since the practice was legalized in 2002. The three doctors from East Flanders are accused of "poisoning" Nys, who was 38 and had been diagnosed with Asperger's syndrome, a mild form of autism, two months before her death. The investigation stems from a civil action brought by Nys's sister, Sophie, who alleged numerous "irregularities" in the euthanasia process, including fumbling efforts by the doctors and attempts by the doctors to block the investigation. The case highlights concerns about the criteria for granting euthanasia to those with mental illness, as Belgium and the Netherlands are among the few countries where such requests are legally permitted. Critics argue that doctors may be too quick to approve euthanasia, while supporters say it offers a humane option for those suffering unbearably. The number of euthanasia cases involving mental illness has risen, with about 40 such cases among Belgium's 2,000 yearly euthanasia deaths. The investigation has led to a debate on the need for stricter oversight and more rigorous approval procedures to protect patients and ensure that euthanasia is only granted when truly necessary.

The deadliest attack on the Jewish community in U.S. history occurred on Saturday morning at the Tree of Life synagogue in Pittsburgh, where a gunman killed 11 people and injured six, according to the Anti-Defamation League. Robert Bowers, 46, faces 29 charges, including 11 counts of using a firearm to commit murder and multiple hate crimes. The attack happened during Sabbath services, exploiting the synagogue's unlocked door for worship. Bowers told police that Jews were committing genocide and wanted all Jews to die. Four police officers were among the wounded. The FBI is leading the investigation, which will be prosecuted as a hate crime. The shooting has drawn national condemnation and raised concerns about security in houses of worship. President Trump ordered flags to be flown at half-staff in respect for the victims, while Pennsylvania Governor Tom Wolf called for stricter gun laws. Thousands gathered for a vigil, with some blaming the political climate for the attack. The shooting has prompted extra patrols in synagogues across the country. The Tree of Life synagogue houses three separate congregations, all of which were conducting Sabbath services when the attack began. The incident has reignited debates about gun control and hate crimes, with officials promising swift and severe justice.

After an emotional journey, Josh Hardy, a 7-year-old boy from Fredericksburg, Virginia, will receive a potentially lifesaving drug as he battles a severe adenovirus infection following a bone marrow transplant. His parents, Todd and Aimee Hardy, had been pleading with Chimerix, the pharmaceutical company that developed the drug brincidofovir, to provide it for Josh. The company initially declined, citing the need to expedite the drug's broader market release. However, after intense public pressure, including a social media campaign and media coverage, Chimerix agreed to make the drug available for Josh as part of a new clinical trial. The first patient to receive the drug, Josh will be the first of 20 participants in the open-label study, which is set to begin on Wednesday. The FDA has committed to work closely with Chimerix to design a pivotal Phase 3 study that will continue this pilot study. Chimerix's president, Kenneth Moch, expressed hope that this new approach would help not only Josh but also other patients in need. The Hardys' story has garnered significant attention, with thousands of supporters rallying to help their cause. The company's decision to provide the drug has been met with relief and gratitude from the family, who have been tirelessly advocating for their son's survival.

Donald Trump's feud with Fox News and its anchor Megyn Kelly intensified after her return from a 10-day vacation. Trump launched a series of tweets criticizing Kelly, including one where he referred to her as a "bimbo" and another where he questioned her performance during an interview with Cornel West. Trump's tweets reflect his ongoing dissatisfaction with Kelly's questioning style, as he tweeted, "I liked The Kelly File much better without @megynkelly. Perhaps she could take another eleven day unscheduled vacation!" He also shared retweets from followers who echoed his negative sentiments. Kelly, however, has maintained that her vacation was planned well in advance and is unrelated to the controversy. Fox News defended its star anchor, stating that Roger Ailes has consistently supported her and her tough journalistic questioning. The network emphasized that Kelly's vacation is part of a pre-planned schedule and dismissed any speculation linking it to the Trump controversy. Trump's refusal to apologize for his comments about Kelly, including his controversial statement about "blood coming out of her eyes," has further strained his relationship with Fox News. His actions have led to his exclusion from a major conservative conference, but he maintains that Kelly owes him an apology for her questions. Despite the tension, Trump continues to deny any wrongdoing and insists that his comments were misunderstood. The ongoing dispute highlights the complex dynamics between Trump's campaign and the media, particularly Fox News, as the network seeks to maintain its journalistic integrity while managing its relationship with a key political figure.

The songwriter of "Electric Slide," Neville Livingston, also known as Bunny Wailer, has clarified that the song is not about a vibrator, dispelling rumors that have spread across social media and news outlets. In a statement to EDM.com, Livingston stated, "At no time have I ever lent credence to a rumor that the song was inspired by anything other than Eddie Grant’s Electric Avenue. To state otherwise is a falsehood and offends my legacy, the legacy of the singer Marcia Griffiths, and tarnishes the reputation of a song beloved by millions of fans the world over." Despite the denial, the lyrics of the song have been examined, leading many to question the true meaning. The song's lyrics, such as "It's electric! You can't see it (it's electric!)" and "You gotta feel it (it's electric!)," have been interpreted as references to a vibrator. Fans and social media users have expressed shock and amusement at the idea, with some joking that the song makes more sense now. However, Livingston's statement remains firm, and the song's true inspiration remains the work of Eddie Grant's "Electric Avenue." The controversy has reignited discussions about the song's meaning and the legacy of its creator.

US investigators wiretapped former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort under secret court orders before and after the election, sources tell CNN, an extraordinary step involving a high-ranking campaign official now at the center of the Russia meddling probe. The government snooping continued into early this year, including a period when Manafort was known to talk to President Donald Trump. Some of the intelligence collected includes communications that sparked concerns among investigators that Manafort had encouraged the Russians to help with the campaign, according to three sources familiar with the investigation. Special counsel Robert Mueller's team, which is leading the investigation into Russia's involvement in the election, has been provided details of these communications. A secret order authorized by the court that handles the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act (FISA) began after Manafort became the subject of an FBI investigation that began in 2014. It centered on work done by a group of Washington consulting firms for Ukraine's former ruling party. The surveillance was discontinued at some point last year for lack of evidence, according to one of the sources. The FBI then restarted the surveillance after obtaining a new FISA warrant that extended at least into early this year. Sources say the second warrant was part of the FBI's efforts to investigate ties between Trump campaign associates and suspected Russian operatives. Such warrants require the approval of top Justice Department and FBI officials, and the FBI must provide the court with information showing suspicion that the subject of the warrant may be acting as an agent of a foreign power. The conversations between Manafort and Trump continued after the President took office, long after the FBI investigation into Manafort was publicly known, the sources told CNN. They went on until lawyers for the President and Manafort insisted that they stop, according to the sources. The White House declined to comment for this story. A spokesperson for Manafort didn't comment for this story. Manafort previously has denied that he ever "knowingly" communicated with Russian intelligence operatives during the election and also has denied participating in any Russian efforts to "undermine the interests of the United States." The FBI wasn't listening in June 2016, the sources said, when Donald Trump Jr. led a meeting that included Manafort, then campaign chairman, and Jared Kushner, the President's son-in-law, with a Russian lawyer who had promised negative information on Hillary Clinton. That gap could prove crucial as prosecutors and investigators under Mueller work to determine whether there's evidence of a crime in myriad connections that have come to light between suspected Russian government operatives and associates of Trump. The FBI interest in Manafort dates back at least to 2014, partly as an outgrowth of a US investigation of Viktor Yanukovych, the former Ukrainian president whose pro-Russian regime was ousted amid street protests. Yanukovych's Party of Regions was accused of corruption, and Ukrainian authorities claimed he squirreled millions of dollars out of the country. Investigators have spent years probing any possible role played by Manafort's firm and other US consultants, including the Podesta Group and Mercury LLC, that worked with the former Ukraine regime. The basis for the case hinged on the failure by the US firms to register under the US Foreign Agents Registration Act, a law that the Justice Department only rarely uses to bring charges. All three firms earlier this year filed retroactive registrations with the Justice Department. It hasn't proved easy to make a case. Last year, Justice Department prosecutors concluded that there wasn't enough evidence to bring charges against Manafort or anyone of the other US subjects in the probe, according to sources briefed on the investigation. The FBI and Justice Department have to periodically seek renewed FISA authorization to continue their surveillance. As Manafort took the reins as Trump campaign chairman in May, the FBI surveillance technicians were no longer listening. The fact he was part of the campaign didn't play a role in the discontinued monitoring, sources told CNN. It was the lack of evidence relating to the Ukraine investigation that prompted the FBI to pull back. Renewed surveillance Manafort was ousted from the campaign in August. By then the FBI had noticed what counterintelligence agents thought was a series of odd connections between Trump associates and Russia. The CIA also had developed information, including from human intelligence sources, that they believed showed Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered his intelligence services to conduct a broad operation to meddle with the US election, according to current and former US officials. The FBI surveillance teams, under a new FISA warrant, began monitoring Manafort again, sources tell CNN. The court that oversees government snooping under FISA operates in secret, the surveillance so intrusive that the existence of the warrants only rarely become public. For that reason, speculation has run rampant about whether Manafort or others associated with Trump were under surveillance. The President himself fueled the speculation when in March he used his Twitter account to accuse former President Barack Obama of having his "wires tapped" in Trump Tower. The Justice Department and the FBI have denied that Trump's own "wires" were tapped. While Manafort has a residence in Trump Tower, it's unclear whether FBI surveillance of him took place there. Manafort has a home as well in Alexandria, Virginia. FBI agents raided the Alexandria residence in July. For the moment, Mr. Mueller’s team has shown a measure of deference to White House officials, sparing them grand jury subpoenas and allowing them to appear for voluntary interviews. Those sessions are expected to begin soon. Ty Cobb, a lawyer brought in to manage the White House response to the inquiry, has told administration officials that he wants to avoid any subpoenas from the special prosecutor. Staff members have been working long hours answering Mr. Mueller’s request for 13 categories of documents, including records related to Mr. Comey’s firing and Mr. Trump’s role in drafting a misleading statement about a June 2016 meeting between campaign officials and Russian-born visitors. Nonetheless, the demand for documents has provoked at least one angry confrontation between Mr. Cobb and Donald F. McGahn II, the White House counsel, over whether certain documents should be withheld to protect the president’s right to confidentiality. But associates of both Mr. Manafort and Mr. Flynn have received more peremptory treatment. Instead of invitations to the prosecutor’s office, they have been presented with grand jury subpoenas, forcing them to either testify or take the Fifth Amendment and raise suspicions that they had something to hide. At least three witnesses have recently been subpoenaed to testify about Mr. Manafort: Jason Maloni, a spokesman who appeared before the grand jury for more than two hours on Friday, and the heads of two consulting firms — Mercury Public Affairs and the Podesta Group — who worked with Mr. Manafort on behalf of Viktor F. Yanukovych, the pro-Russia former president of Ukraine. Mr. Mueller’s team also took the unusual step of issuing a subpoena to Melissa Laurenza, a specialist in lobbying law who formerly represented Mr. Manafort, according to people familiar with the subpoena. Conversations between lawyers and their clients are normally considered bound by attorney-client privilege, but there are exceptions when lawyers prepare public documents that are filed on behalf of their client.

In recent years, Sophie the Giraffe, a 7.5-inch rubber teether shaped like a giraffe, has become a ubiquitous baby gift among the upper-middle class, despite its relatively high price point of $24.99. This toy’s journey to popularity began in 1961 when Vulli, a French toy manufacturer, produced the first Sophie. However, it wasn’t until 2000, when Hélène Dumoulin-Montgomery, an expatriate, brought the toy to the United States, that it started gaining traction. Dumoulin-Montgomery, working part-time as a realtor’s assistant, contacted Vulli and secured a license to distribute the toy in the U.S. Despite initial poor sales, Sophie’s fortunes changed in 2004 when Teri Weiss, owner of the Beverly Hills gift boutique Elegant Child, included the toy in a custom gift basket for a high-profile client. This led to a surge in demand, with Sophie becoming a staple in baby showers and a favorite among parents. Sophie’s success can be attributed to its unique properties—made of natural rubber and food-grade paint, it stands out from other teething toys. Its price point, combined with its popularity among celebrities, made it a go-to gift for affluent parents. However, Sophie’s rise has also raised concerns about its safety. Reports of mold growth inside the toy have emerged, with parents sharing disturbing images of black mold coating the inside of the toy. Pediatric dentist Dana Chianese, who had previously recommended Sophie to her patients, now warns against using the toy due to the mold issue. The toy’s manufacturer, Sophie the Giraffe, maintains that proper cleaning instructions should be followed to prevent mold growth, but the incident has sparked a debate about the safety and practicality of toys with holes that can trap moisture. Despite the controversy, Sophie remains a popular choice for parents seeking a high-quality teething toy, highlighting the ongoing tension between product safety and consumer expectations in the baby market.

Ricki Lake's ex-husband, Christian Evans, passed away on February 11, 2023, at the age of 45, after battling bipolar disorder. In an emotional Instagram post, Lake revealed that Evans had taken his own life, sharing a photo of herself with him and writing, "The world didn't understand this man, but I did. He succumbed to his lifelong struggle with bipolar disorder." Lake emphasized that she and Evans continued their relationship despite their divorce, which was finalized in 2015 due to irreconcilable differences. They had eloped in April 2012 and had been married for two years. Lake shared that Evans had been diagnosed with bipolar disorder earlier in life and had struggled with manic episodes that affected their relationship. She explained that during one of his manic episodes, Evans believed he could fly and cure cancer, which was a stark contrast to his usual demeanor. Lake and Evans had two sons together: Milo, 19, and Owen, 15, from her previous marriage to Rob Sussman. Following Evans' diagnosis, Lake and their therapist advised cutting off contact until Evans stabilized, leading to their divorce. Evans was eventually hospitalized and entered a treatment facility but was not fully stable. His mania returned in September 2022, and he moved out again. Lake was working in London when she received a text from Evans' sister about his suicide note. Evans was found two days later with a self-inflicted gunshot wound. Lake expressed that she was not surprised by his passing, stating, "The struggle was just too much for him." She plans to honor Evans by scattering his ashes on their favorite beach in Ibiza this summer and emphasized that she had no regrets, stating, "I never stopped loving that man." Lake also encouraged others to recognize and seek treatment for bipolar disorder.

China has demonstrated its ability to manipulate the internet in significant ways, according to a report from the U.S.-China Economic and Security Review Commission. In two incidents this year, China redirected traffic to 15 percent of the world's websites through its servers for about 20 minutes. The high-level hijacking included bits and bytes destined for the U.S. Senate, the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, Air Force, Department of Defense, NASA, and commercial entities such as Dell, Yahoo, Microsoft, and IBM. Researchers from McAfee compiled a list of 53,000 websites that were hijacked for 18 minutes on April 8. The report noted that while the actions could be unintentional, they demonstrate a capability that could be used for malicious purposes. China Telecom denied any hijack of internet traffic, but the incident highlights the vulnerabilities in the internet's routing system. The April incident, in particular, is concerning because it went unnoticed, suggesting that China has the capacity to handle a massive amount of data without disruption. This capability could allow for eavesdropping, manipulation of data, or even decryption of encrypted communications. The report concludes that the methods used are generally more sophisticated than those used in previous incidents. While China disputes the findings, the incidents raise serious concerns about the security and integrity of the internet, particularly in the context of the ongoing cyber cold war between China and the United States.

Henry Rayhons, a former Iowa state legislator, faces a complex legal and ethical dilemma after being charged with third-degree sexual abuse for allegedly having sex with his wife, Donna Young, while she was living in a nursing home. Donna, who suffered from Alzheimer’s disease, died four days before her 79th birthday. The Iowa Attorney General’s office claims Rayhons had intercourse with his wife when she lacked the mental capacity to consent. Rayhons, 78, pleaded not guilty. The case raises questions about the legal definition of consent in cases involving dementia and the ethical considerations surrounding intimate relationships in nursing homes.

The Rayhons had a long and loving relationship, marrying in 2007 after both had lost their first spouses. They were deeply involved in each other’s lives, with Rayhons often visiting Donna at the nursing home and even staying overnight. Donna’s daughters, Linda Dunshee and Suzan Brunes, became concerned about their mother’s deteriorating condition and Rayhons’ behavior. They eventually moved Donna into a nursing home, where she was diagnosed with severe dementia. Staff at the facility noted that Rayhons was overly affectionate with Donna, leading to increased friction with the daughters.

On May 23, Donna’s roommate reported hearing sexual noises from Rayhons’ room. A video camera captured Rayhons dropping Donna’s panties into a laundry cart. Donna was taken to a hospital for a sexual assault test, which showed no evidence of recent sexual activity. Rayhons claims he does not remember the incident and denies having sex with Donna. The case highlights the challenges of determining consent when dealing with dementia, as cognitive abilities can fluctuate and vary from day to day.

Legal experts argue that the current legal framework inadequately addresses such cases, with Iowa’s sexual assault laws failing to adequately consider the nature of the relationship and the past consent of the parties. The statute defines “mental defect” ambiguously, making it difficult to prove the necessary elements of the case. The Rayhons’ trial is scheduled to begin in January, with the prosecution likely to portray Rayhons as a sex-hungry man who took advantage of a confused and incapacitated woman.

The case has sparked broader discussions about the rights and desires of individuals with dementia, the role of nursing homes in managing intimate relationships, and the ethical boundaries of intimate care in such settings. It also raises questions about the balance between protecting vulnerable individuals and respecting the autonomy and desires of those with cognitive impairments.

Steven Avery, the subject of the Netflix series "Making a Murderer," has filed a wide-ranging appeal challenging his conviction for the 2005 murder of photographer Teresa Halbach. The appeal, filed in an appeals court in Madison, includes numerous spelling and grammar errors and is signed by Avery himself. Avery's new attorney, Kathleen Zellner, is not immediately available for comment. The appeal raises several issues, including claims that authorities improperly used a warrant and that a juror was improperly influencing other jurors. Avery also alleges that his trial judge made misleading statements and that his legal team was ineffective. Zellner, known for seeking reversals of convictions, has taken over Avery's defense and claims to have uncovered new evidence that will exonerate him, though she has not specified what this evidence is. The case has garnered significant attention, with tens of thousands of people signing petitions for Avery's exoneration. Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker has indicated he will not consider pardoning Avery, citing a previous court ruling that upheld his conviction. Avery, who was previously wrongfully convicted of a rape case and served 18 years in prison, has long maintained his innocence in Halbach's death. The case has sparked national debate and scrutiny of the legal process, with both supporters and critics of Avery's conviction weighing in.

South Korea has approved a plan to send $8 million in humanitarian aid to North Korea, despite concerns from China, the United States, and Japan. The aid, which will be distributed through the World Food Programme and UNICEF, aims to provide nutritional products for children and pregnant women, as well as vaccines and medical treatments. This decision, which marks the first aid package from South Korea since December 2015, has faced criticism, as it could be seen as a concession to North Korea at a time when international pressure is increasing. Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi warned that the situation on the Korean peninsula was becoming more serious and called for calm. South Korea's Unification Minister Cho Myong-gyon stated that the aid was separate from political issues and aimed to improve the lives of North Korean residents. Meanwhile, North Korea's foreign minister, Ri Yong-ho, dismissed Trump's threats, comparing them to "the sound of a barking dog." Ri also expressed regret for Trump's advisers. The United States and China have imposed new sanctions on North Korea following its sixth nuclear test, but the effectiveness of these measures remains uncertain. Analysts suggest that sanctions rarely have an immediate impact, and fuel shortages in North Korea could be due to regime stockpiling rather than sanctions. The upcoming meeting between US President Donald Trump and his South Korean and Japanese counterparts, scheduled for Thursday, is expected to focus on the North Korean crisis.

Loretta Lynch, President Obama’s nominee for attorney general, faced a grueling confirmation hearing on Wednesday, where she navigated a series of contentious questions from Republican senators. The hearing highlighted the tension between the Justice Department and Congress, particularly over issues like immigration and the IRS. Lynch, the first African American woman to be nominated for the post, maintained a composed demeanor, emphasizing her commitment to upholding the rule of law and fostering better relationships with lawmakers. She declined to disavow actions taken by the Justice Department under Eric Holder, instead positioning herself as a career prosecutor dedicated to the principles of justice. Despite her efforts to distance herself from the controversial policies of the previous administration, some senators, including Jeff Sessions and David Vitter, expressed dissatisfaction with her responses, particularly on immigration. Lynch’s performance was largely well-received by Democrats, with Sen. Chuck Schumer praising her qualifications. However, she faced challenges in addressing issues like the legality of marijuana and the NSA’s surveillance programs. Her nomination comes at a critical time, as the country grapples with strained relations between law enforcement and minority communities. Lynch’s opening remarks highlighted her personal values and family history, emphasizing her dedication to the promise of America. While the committee is not expected to vote on her nomination for several weeks, her confirmation is seen as a significant milestone for diversity in the highest-ranking law enforcement position.

Mitch McConnell's political fortunes took a significant hit on Tuesday, with Alabama's Senate race delivering a decisive victory to Roy Moore over Luther Strange. The loss for Strange, who had Trump’s backing, was seen as a setback for the establishment and a win for the Trumpian base, who believed the president truly supported Moore. The race was not just a personal blow to McConnell; it also marked a failure in his long-term strategy to repeal Obamacare, as he pulled the plug on the latest repeal attempt. The loss for Strange, who was appointed by a controversial governor, was attributed to his base’s belief that Trump was only going through the motions. Moore, who has a history of defying federal edicts and openly criticized McConnell, now faces Democrat Doug Jones in the general election. The loss was particularly painful for McConnell, as he had poured significant resources into Strange’s campaign and even had Strange campaign against him. Trump, who had initially distanced himself from the race, now openly criticized McConnell at a private dinner with conservative activists, dubbing him “weak” for failing to pass the health care bill. Despite the setback, McConnell vowed to support Moore in the general election, emphasizing shared frustration with the pace of legislative progress. However, the loss has raised questions about the relationship between Trump and McConnell, with some Republicans distancing themselves from the Senate leader. McConnell’s colleagues, while maintaining personal loyalty, criticized each other rather than him, recognizing the complexity of his position. The loss in Alabama is seen as a broader reflection of the challenges facing the Republican Party, with Trump’s base increasingly at odds with the establishment.

A new study published in the journal Psychology and Aging suggests that older adults perform better on cognitive tasks in the morning compared to the afternoon, highlighting the importance of testing time when assessing cognitive function. Researchers from the Rotman Research Institute at Baycrest Health Sciences and the University of Toronto conducted a series of memory tests on 16 younger adults (aged 19-30) and 16 older adults (aged 60-82) between 1:00 and 5:00 pm. The tests involved studying and recalling picture and word combinations, with irrelevant words and pictures appearing as distractions. Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) was used to monitor brain activity during the tests.

The results showed that older adults were 10% more likely to focus on the distracting information compared to younger adults, who successfully blocked out this information. Additionally, the fMRI scans revealed that older adults showed significantly less activity in the attentional control areas of the brain in the afternoon, indicating that they were having difficulty focusing. This "idling" behavior suggests that older adults may have trouble concentrating during the later part of the day.

However, when another group of 18 older adults was tested in the morning between 8:30 and 10:30 am, they performed significantly better. They focused on fewer distracting items and closed the age difference gap in performance with younger adults. Importantly, these morning-tested older adults activated the same brain areas as young adults to ignore the distractions, indicating that the time of day can greatly influence cognitive performance.

Lead author John Anderson, a doctoral candidate in psychology at the University of Toronto, recommends that older adults schedule their most mentally challenging tasks for the morning. This includes activities such as doing taxes, taking tests, seeing doctors, or cooking unfamiliar recipes. Anderson states, "Time of day really does matter when testing older adults. This age group is more focused and better able to ignore distraction in the morning than in the afternoon."

The study provides strong evidence that there are noticeable differences in brain function across the day for older adults. Dr. Lynn Hasher, senior author on the paper, notes that ignoring the time of day when testing older adults on certain tasks may create an inaccurate picture of age differences in brain function. She adds, "Since older adults tend to be morning-type people, ignoring time of day when testing them on some tasks may create an inaccurate picture of age differences in brain function."

These findings have significant implications for researchers and practitioners who study cognitive function in older adults. They suggest that the timing of cognitive tests can significantly affect the results and should be carefully considered. The study highlights the importance of aligning testing times with the natural circadian rhythms of older adults to ensure accurate assessments of their cognitive abilities.

Toronto Mayor Rob Ford's defiant behavior continued as he walked up to the podium to honor war veterans, only to face a backlash from a World War II veteran who refused to shake his hand, calling him a "druggie." Ford's refusal to resign over his admitted drug use has left Toronto's City Council grappling with how to proceed. Allies and opponents alike agree that a series of revelations, including smoking crack cocaine and threatening to kill someone, have consumed the city's politics and impacted the City Council's ability to tackle other challenges. The embattled mayor's powers are already limited compared to those of many large U.S. cities, as he is just one voting member in the council and his authority stems mostly from his ability to build consensus and set the agenda. However, his authority has evaporated in the wake of the crack scandal. Councilors have introduced motions to call on Ford to take a leave of absence, apologize, and cooperate with police. If he refuses, the council would ask the provincial government to intervene and remove him from office. Another motion would curtail his powers, suspending his authority to appoint and dismiss the deputy mayor and his executive committee. Despite the growing calls for Ford to step down, his core supporters remain steadfast in their support. Ford's refusal to resign has left the city in a state of political chaos, with efforts to confront challenges such as developing public transit service and reducing commutes being hindered. The mayor's influence has eroded, and councilors are now openly scornful of him, creating a power vacuum that needs to be filled. Ford's brother, Doug, has been a vocal supporter, stating that he will stand by his brother and face the potential public backlash. The embattled mayor's actions and words continue to polarize the city, with hundreds lining up to purchase bobblehead dolls of him, a testament to his enduring presence in Toronto's political landscape.

Professor Will Brooker, a film and cultural studies expert at Kingston University, is embarking on a unique project to gain a deeper understanding of David Bowie’s life and work through a method he calls "The Method." This involves a transformative immersion into Bowie’s experiences, habits, and creative processes. Brooker listens to music Bowie listened to, adopts his hair and outfit styles, watches films that influenced Bowie, and even eats and drinks what Bowie ate and drank. For instance, he has been eating red peppers and drinking milk, and plans to visit places significant to Bowie’s life, including Brixton, Bromley, and Beckenham, and is scheduled to travel to Berlin next.

To fully embody Bowie’s personas, Brooker has already transitioned away from the 1974 Philadelphia soul period and from wearing thick blue eye shadow and orange hair. He has also been wearing bright yellow suits, black waistcoats, and large collared white shirts, which required him to visit a tailor. Brooker’s wardrobe now includes a variety of outfits that he sources from online marketplaces. He is preparing for the 1980s bleached perm, which Bowie himself described as a scrambled egg sitting on his head.

The academic is also immersing himself in the literature Bowie read, including works by William Burroughs, Aleister Crowley, and Michael Moorcock, as well as ideas about the death of God and existentialism by Friedrich Nietzsche. He plans to watch films Bowie would have seen and listen to songs Bowie would have heard. Brooker has even submitted himself to sleep deprivation and, on some weekends, has only consumed red peppers and milk. He listens to Bowie’s music exclusively and has been known to dream up new Bowie songs in his sleep.

Brooker’s project is part of a larger research endeavor to write a monograph titled "Forever Stardust." He is spending months at a time experiencing different points in Bowie’s career, from the early 1970s to the 1980s. He has already visited Brixton, Bromley, and Beckenham, and plans to travel to Berlin next. His approach is to inhabit Bowie’s headspace at various points in his life and career, while maintaining a critical and objective perspective. He believes this method will provide a unique insight into Bowie’s mind and work.

Brooker’s project has been met with curiosity and amusement from his students, who have not seen him teach since he began his Bowie immersion. He hopes that Bowie, if aware of his project, would be interested and amused by his research. Brooker acknowledges that no one could truly be Bowie again, but he believes that by experiencing Bowie’s life and work, he can gain a deeper understanding of the pop icon.

A 32-year-old woman, Cherie Amoore, has been charged with kidnapping a 7-week-old baby from the King of Prussia Mall, and the baby was found safe after a tense search. Amoore, who claimed to be pregnant, approached the baby's mother, Malika Hunter, and engaged in a conversation that led to the alleged abduction. According to police, Amoore took the baby from his stroller and fled the mall, leaving Hunter and her other children in shock. Amoore was seen on surveillance video leaving the mall with the baby, and police launched an extensive search involving mall security, local law enforcement, and the FBI. The baby, Ahsir Simmons, was found in a car seat inside a home in Tredyffrin Township, Chester County, where Amoore was taken into custody. Amoore confessed to taking the baby, saying, "I don't know why I did it. I can't explain it. I held him, and all those feelings rushed back. I just wanted my baby. I felt like I was holding my son again. It felt so good. I didn't want to lose that feeling. I was crazy. I never intended to do anything like this." Amoore faces felony kidnapping, unlawful restraint, false imprisonment, and other related charges. The ordeal left Malika Hunter and her family deeply shaken, with Hunter expressing fear about taking her children outside again. Amoore's case has drawn attention due to her daughter, Renee Amoore, being the deputy chairman of the Republican Party of Pennsylvania. The incident has raised questions about the mall's security protocols and the delay in issuing an Amber Alert. While the search for the baby was swift, the delay in the Amber Alert notification process has sparked discussions on the efficiency of the system.
