The bulletin does not identify the states in question but sources familiar with the document say it refers to the targeting by suspected foreign hackers of voter registration databases in Arizona and Illinois. In the Illinois case, officials were forced to shut down the state’s voter registration system for 10 days in late July, after the hackers managed to download personal data on up to 200,000 state voters, Ken Menzel, the general counsel of the Illinois Board of Elections, said in an interview. The Arizona attack was more limited, involving malicious software that was introduced into its voter registration system but no successful exfiltration of data, a state official said. The FBI bulletin listed eight separate IP addresses that were the sources of the two attacks and suggested that the attacks may have been linked, noting that one of the IP addresses was used in both intrusions. The bulletin implied that the bureau was looking for any signs that the attacks may have targeted even more than the two states. The FBI is requesting that states contact their Board of Elections and determine if any similar activity to their logs, both inbound and outbound, has been detected. This is a big deal, said Rich Barger, chief intelligence officer for ThreatConnect, a cybersecurity firm, who reviewed the FBI alert at the request of Yahoo News. Two state election boards have been popped, and data has been taken. This certainly should be concerning to the common American voter. Barger noted that one of the IP addresses listed in the FBI alert has surfaced before in Russian criminal underground hacker forums. He also said the method of attack on one of the state election systems — including the types of tools used by the hackers to scan for vulnerabilities and exploit them — appears to resemble methods used in other suspected Russian state-sponsored cyberattacks, including one just this month on the World Anti-Doping Agency. The FBI did not respond to detailed questions about the alert, saying in a statement only that such bulletins are provided "to help systems administrators guard against the actions of persistent cyber criminals." Menzel, the Illinois election official, said that in a recent briefing, FBI agents confirmed to him that the perpetrators were believed to be foreign hackers, although they were not identified by country. He said he was told that the bureau was looking at a "possible link" to the recent highly publicized attack on the Democratic National Committee and other political organizations, which U.S. officials suspect was perpetrated by Russian government hackers. But he said agents told him they had reached no conclusions, and other experts say the hackers could also have been common cybercriminals hoping to steal personal data on state voters for fraudulent purposes, such as obtaining bogus tax refunds.

Bernie Sanders has called the revelations in the Paradise Papers a stark illustration of the growing global influence of a tiny elite of billionaires, with the documents exposing the offshore financial dealings of numerous political figures, celebrities, and corporate giants. Sanders, who came in second in the Democratic presidential primary, emphasized that the Paradise Papers highlight the rapid movement toward an international oligarchy, where a few wealthy individuals and companies use tax havens to amass and protect vast fortunes, often at the expense of the broader public. He criticized both Congress and the Trump administration, particularly Secretary of Commerce Wilbur Ross, for facilitating tax breaks that allow super-wealthy individuals and corporations to avoid paying their fair share of taxes by shifting profits and assets to offshore jurisdictions. Sanders argued that this not only exacerbates income inequality but also undermines the ability of governments to fund essential services and address pressing issues like the national debt.

The Paradise Papers, which consist of 13.4 million leaked documents from offshore services firms and corporate registries, have revealed the intricate web of financial transactions that enable the wealthy to evade taxes and avoid scrutiny. For instance, Wilbur Ross, Trump’s commerce secretary, has maintained business ties with the son-in-law of Russian President Vladimir Putin, despite being under US sanctions. Ross’s investment in a shipping company, Navigator, which has a partnership with the Russian gas giant Sibur, is now under intense scrutiny. Sibur is partly owned by Kirill Shamalov, Putin’s daughter’s husband. This revelation has sparked calls for a thorough investigation into Ross’s actions and whether he has been fully transparent about his business dealings.

Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal, who sat on the Senate commerce committee during Ross’s confirmation, has demanded a clear and compelling explanation from Ross. Blumenthal, along with Senator Tammy Baldwin, has called for a Commerce Committee hearing and an Inspector General investigation to address the unanswered questions surrounding Ross’s financial interests. They argue that the lack of transparency and the potential conflict of interest warrant a more rigorous examination.

The Paradise Papers also highlight the broader issue of tax avoidance by multinational corporations. The case of Nike, one of the world’s largest and most recognizable brands, exemplifies how companies can exploit complex legal structures to minimize their tax liabilities. Nike has managed to shift significant profits from Europe to Bermuda, an offshore tax haven with zero tax, through a series of intricate financial maneuvers. This has allowed Nike to reduce its global tax rate from 34.9% in 2007 to 13.2% in recent years, despite the company’s massive profits. Nike’s use of such schemes has drawn criticism from tax authorities and campaigners, who argue that such practices are unfair and undermine the tax base of countries that rely on corporate taxes to fund public services.

In a separate revelation, the Paradise Papers have exposed the tax avoidance strategies employed by Formula One champion Lewis Hamilton. Hamilton, who is one of the world’s richest sportspeople, has used an Isle of Man scheme to avoid paying European taxes on his private jet. The scheme, which involved setting up seemingly artificial leasing businesses, has been described as potentially “abusive” by tax experts. HM Revenue and Customs is now investigating 231 tax refunds issued to private jet owners since 2011, as part of a $1 billion VAT giveaway. Hamilton’s use of offshore companies in the British Virgin Islands, the Isle of Man, and Guernsey to avoid taxes on his jet and motorhome has drawn scrutiny, with experts questioning the legitimacy of the scheme.

The Paradise Papers have also revealed that Apple, the world’s most profitable firm, has sidestepped a 2013 crackdown on its controversial Irish tax practices by moving its most significant untaxed offshore cash to Jersey, a Channel Island with a 0% corporate tax rate for foreign companies. Apple’s legal advisers sent a questionnaire to Appleby, an offshore finance law firm, to explore the benefits of different offshore jurisdictions. The company chose Jersey to continue avoiding billions in taxes, despite claims that its tax payments have not decreased. The revelations have sparked a broader debate about the fairness of the global tax system and the need for reforms to ensure that the wealthy and corporations pay their fair share.

President Donald Trump defended his upcoming executive orders to suspend the U.S. refugee program and halt issuing visas to citizens of certain countries, citing security concerns. "We can't take any chances," he told Fox News' Sean Hannity, emphasizing the need for caution given ongoing FBI terrorism investigations. A draft order would halt the refugee program for 120 days and ban citizens from Iran, Iraq, Libya, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, or Yemen from obtaining U.S. visas for 30 days. Trump questioned the vetting process, stating, "We’ve taken in tens of thousands of people. We know nothing about them. They can say they vetted them. They didn’t vet them, they have no papers."

Trump also defended his executive order to construct a wall along the U.S.-Mexico border, a key campaign promise. "The wall is necessary," he said, "that’s not just politics, and yet it is good for the heart of the nation because people want protection and a wall protects." He referenced Israel as an example, adding, "All you’ve got to do is ask Israel."

In the interview, Trump attacked the media, calling it "very hostile" and "very angry," and "very dishonest." He accused the media of making up stories, labeling them "fake news." He specifically mentioned the New York Times, CNN, and NBC, noting they had used the term "liar" to describe him. Trump also criticized their reporting on Martin Luther King Jr.'s bust in the Oval Office, saying, "Because they’re not saying the bust was taken out. What they’re saying is that I’m a racist."

Regarding his executive order on torture, Trump stated, "Look, I spoke with people who were in this world that we’re talking about. They said, ‘Absolutely, it works.’ Now, General Mattis said that he doesn’t intend to use it. I’m with him all the way. Do I believe it works? Yes, I do." He also defended his nominee to the U.S. Supreme Court, saying he had decided on a choice "pretty much in my mind" and would announce it soon.

Trump criticized Democrats for threatening to hold up his nominee and said he would use the "nuclear option" if necessary, allowing a simple majority to confirm his Supreme Court pick. He also discussed the case of Navy sailor Kristian Saucier, who was sentenced to a year in prison for taking photos of parts of a submarine's nuclear propulsion system. Trump contrasted Saucier's treatment with the FBI's decision not to charge Hillary Clinton for using personal email while secretary of state, saying, "How can you have somebody else get away with such a tremendous amount and then this person who takes a picture of his desk on an old submarine?"

Trump's comments on the media and his executive orders highlight his ongoing efforts to address perceived threats to national security and his approach to governance, while also showcasing his continued criticism of the press.

Three train enthusiasts died and over 70 others were injured when an Amtrak train derailed on a bridge over Interstate 5 in DuPont, Washington, on Monday morning. The train, which was on a new route aiming to reduce travel times, was reportedly traveling at 78 mph as it approached a curve with a 30 mph speed limit. The engineer had previously warned the crew about an over-speed condition six seconds before the derailment. The train was not equipped with positive train control, a system designed to prevent derailments caused by excessive speed. Preliminary data from the train's event data recorder and onboard cameras showed the crew bracing for impact just before the crash. The National Transportation Safety Board's full investigation, which is expected to take up to two years, will analyze the train's speed, the condition of the tracks, and the crew's actions. The three victims were identified as Jim Hamre, 61, and his friend Zack Willhoite, 35, both from the Tacoma area, and Benjamin Gran, 40, of nearby Auburn, all known train buffs.

Wisconsin Governor Scott Walker announced his withdrawal from the Republican presidential race on Monday, urging other candidates to follow suit to ensure a positive, conservative message can rise to the top. Walker cited the need to clear the field and focus on a limited number of candidates who can offer a conservative alternative to the current front-runner, Donald Trump. His decision came after a series of setbacks, including poor debate performances and a significant drop in poll numbers. Walker's campaign had struggled with fundraising, particularly hard money, and his message of being an outsider and champion of conservative values was overshadowed by the more dynamic and media-savvy candidates like Trump. His exit marks the second major Republican candidate to drop out, following former Texas Governor Rick Perry, and leaves 15 candidates still competing for the nomination. Walker's abrupt decision, communicated via a brief press conference, has already sparked a scramble among his staff and financial supporters. His network of major contributors, who had backed him in his battles against public unions, is now being courted by other campaigns. Walker's supporters, including long-time donors like Stanley Hubbard, expressed disappointment but acknowledged the harsh realities of the campaign. The governor's sudden departure highlights the challenges of running a successful presidential campaign in an era where public opinion polls and debate performances can quickly shift the landscape.

A Brenham veterinarian accused of killing a cat with a bow and arrow will not face charges at this time after an Austin County grand jury returned a "no-bill" in the case. The incident, which occurred in April, involved the vet posting a picture to Facebook of herself holding a dead cat with an arrow through its head, boasting about her kill. The cat was named Tiger, and his pet sitter, Amy Hemsell, recognized the cat in the photo. Many people protested outside the Austin County Courthouse, demanding the grand jury indict the veterinarian for animal cruelty. The vet, Dr. Kristen Lindsey, has since been fired from her job at the Washington Animal Clinic in Brenham. She was accused of acting to protect her pets from a "potentially rabid stray cat," according to the Austin County Sheriff's Office. However, investigators were unable to determine where or when the incident took place, lacking probable cause to obtain a search warrant for any Austin County properties. Subpoenas to Facebook failed to produce usable evidence as the vet's account had been deleted prior to the Sheriff's Office learning of the incident. The American Veterinary Medical Association guidelines include a "bolt to the head" as a humane form of euthanasia, which could have been the case here. The Washington Animal Clinic condemned Lindsey's actions and stated they do not allow such conduct. The case highlights the challenges in prosecuting such incidents when the only evidence is a single Facebook photo.

A convicted white-collar criminal, Shannon Egeland, had his jail sentence extended by three years and ten months after he orchestrated a staged shooting to delay his prison term and benefit from a fraudulent disability insurance policy. Egeland, 43, was serving a 10-year sentence for his role in a mortgage fraud scheme that involved raising millions from local banks through false business plans and loan applications. On July 31, 2014, Egeland directed his 17-year-old son, Rylan, to shoot him in the leg with a shotgun near Caldwell, Idaho, in an attempt to fake an injury and claim disability benefits. The teenager left the scene, and Egeland called 911, claiming he was attacked while helping a pregnant motorist. Egeland falsely applied for a disability insurance policy seven days before the shooting, stating he had no criminal record. The fraud was quickly uncovered, but the incident led to the amputation of Egeland's left leg. During his sentencing, Egeland expressed remorse, stating, "What bothers me the most is my son—the pain is on him. The pain that he has shouldn't be there... I've had 3 ½ years to recognize I am broken... If I could take it all back, I would, but I can't... That will haunt me the rest of my life." Egeland's lawyer, Ryan O'Connor, argued for a two-year sentence, noting Egeland's existing 10-year sentence and his need for mental health treatment. Assistant U.S. Attorney Scott Bradford described Egeland as a "menace to society" and a "self-absorbed, opportunistic narcissist" who had a history of criminal activity. Egeland was also ordered to pay $90,011 in child support and was urged to seek mental health treatment while in prison. The judge emphasized the psychological and emotional impact on the teenager, stating, "If Egeland had died in the stunt, the minor child would have been left to deal with the consequences."

As the debate over privacy and data collection intensifies, a new app has emerged, offering users the choice to receive daily email notifications for content from Michele Munz. The app promises to deliver notifications only once a day and only if there are new updates. However, users face a challenge if their zip code is not within the service's deliverable area, as they must either re-enter a valid zip code or opt for digital access instead. The app's functionality hinges on the user's ability to save their notification preferences successfully, though occasional technical issues may arise, such as notifications not being saved or problems with saving. Despite these minor hitches, the app aims to keep users informed about Michele Munz's latest content, providing them with a convenient way to stay updated without overwhelming their inboxes.

It was a day of unexpected twists for Cleveland Browns fans after their team's first win of the season on Christmas Eve. Initially, the fans had planned a 'Perfect Season Parade' to celebrate the team's hypothetical 16-0 record, but the parade was canceled when the Browns actually won a game. The $10,000 raised for the parade was donated to the Greater Cleveland Food Bank, and the Browns matched the donation with another $10,000. Cleveland Pizza contributed to the cause, bringing the total to over $8,000. The GoFundMe campaign, originally set up to cover the parade's expenses, surpassed its $1,999 goal quickly. The Browns' win not only ended their long losing streak but also turned a potential celebration of futility into a real opportunity to support those in need, demonstrating the community's resilience and generosity.

The National Association of Theatre Owners (NATO) is considering a significant shift in the American movie theater industry by launching an off-night discount experiment, which could begin in a single U.S. state by the end of the year. NATO chief John Fithian revealed that the initiative, which has been successful in Latin America and Canada, is being carefully planned to avoid antitrust issues. The experiment would involve theaters offering discounted tickets on non-peak days, a move that could potentially increase overall attendance and revenue. NATO's cautious approach includes limiting the scope of the experiment to one state and a brief duration, reflecting the industry's reluctance to change long-standing practices. Fithian emphasized that studios must approve the concept, as any discount would directly impact their revenue shares. This development marks a notable concession from theater owners, who have historically been resistant to ticket discounting, fearing it could devalue movie tickets and reduce overall box office sales. The potential success of such a program could reshape the landscape of movie theater pricing and attendance strategies, offering a new avenue for theaters to boost their bottom lines and potentially address the issue of declining ticket sales.

Martha Stewart has introduced a new flavor of Triscuits, a cracker that has been around since 1901. Her toasted coconut and sea salt version is now available in stores and is expected to become a "habit-forming" snack. Stewart, known for her meticulous approach to food, spent time experimenting with different flavors before settling on coconut and sea salt, which she believes is both savory and sweet. While she's not a frequent snacker, she keeps crackers in her pantry for their salt content. The cracker can be enjoyed on its own or used in various recipes, such as an elevated s'more. The launch of this flavor coincides with current food trends, including avocado and s'mores, and features a partnership with artisanal food producers. Despite being a mass-produced snack, Triscuits are appreciated by serious food enthusiasts for their simplicity and quality.

Customer service representatives at Netflix were reportedly told to expect a surge in angry calls the day before the company announced its price hike, indicating an anticipated backlash from subscribers. According to reports, Netflix added extra staff to handle the anticipated volume of calls, but many callers still faced long wait times. A Wall Street analyst, Rich Greenfield from BTIG Research, tested the company's customer service and found that representatives were unprepared, suggesting to those threatening to cancel their subscriptions to wait until the new pricing took effect in September. Greenfield criticized the lack of promotional offers to retain customers. Meanwhile, Netflix is attempting to mitigate subscriber dissatisfaction by adding new content, such as films like "Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind" and "The Motorcycle Diaries," and TV shows including "The Office" and "Law and Order: SVU." Despite these additions, the new pricing structure, which starts at $15.98 for both streaming and DVD rentals, has sparked significant discontent among subscribers. Netflix maintains that the price increase is necessary, but the company's handling of customer service and the content additions may not be enough to placate its user base.

Injuries continue to plague the Broadway musical "Spider-Man: Turn Off the Dark," with a stunt double falling from a platform into a pit during a Monday night performance. The 31-year-old actor, whose harness failed, was taken to Bellevue Hospital but was not in critical condition. Audience members described a 20- to 30-foot plunge, with the performer's empty harness swinging over seats. This incident comes after two other accidents involving broken bones and a concussion during previews. The animosity between Ted Cruz and his GOP rivals, particularly Donald Trump, has been well-documented, but the article delves into a broader narrative of how Cruz is viewed by a wide array of political figures and institutions. Bush campaign, express strong dislike and even contempt for him, citing his insufferable personality and inability to be a team player. Four black students from Florida A&M University were waiting to enter their friend’s apartment building late Saturday night when a white man claiming to be a resident allegedly accosted them, leading to a tense confrontation that was captured on video and has since gone viral. Isaiah Butterfield, one of the students, recorded the 10-minute incident, which has been retweeted nearly 6,000 times. The video shows the man, identified as Don Crandall, a manager at the Baymont Inn & Suites by Wyndham Hotels, initially refusing the students entry to the building, claiming they needed a key. An altercation ensued, with Crandall pulling out a gun in an apparent attempt to stop the students from using the elevator. Another man, identified as Chad, intervened on the students’ behalf, pushing back against Crandall. The incident has sparked outrage, with the Pax Hotel Group firing Crandall and issuing a statement condemning his actions. The management of the Stadium Centre, the apartment complex where the incident took place, has also issued a statement, stating that firearms are prohibited on their property and that they are committed to creating a diverse and inclusive community. The students, who were not armed, were shaken by the encounter and described the experience as a personal one, with one saying, "We are sick of the discrimination never thought I’d have a personal experience with racism like this." The management of the apartment complex has apologized to those affected by the actions of the former employee, emphasizing their commitment to inclusivity. The incident has drawn attention to the ongoing issues of racial discrimination and the use of excessive force by individuals, even in non-law enforcement contexts.

In a recent radio interview, Senate Majority Leader Tom Patton, who is running for the Ohio House of Representatives, made controversial remarks about his primary opponent, Jennifer Herold, a 30-year-old mother of two young children. Patton questioned Herold's suitability for the position, stating, "The gal that's running against me is a 30-year-old, you know, mom, mother of two infants. And I don't know if anybody explained to her we've got to spend three nights a week in Columbus. So, how does that work out for you? I waited until I was 48 and my kids were raised, and at least adults, before we took the opportunity to try." His comments were widely criticized as discriminatory and insulting. Herold, who has two sons, ages 1 and 3, issued a statement calling Patton's remarks "insulting and discriminatory," and highlighted the example of former Alaska Governor Sarah Palin, who ran for Vice President in 2008 with five non-adult children, including a newborn. Other women who have served in office while raising a family include Ohio Lt. Gov. Mary Taylor and state Rep. Christina Hagan.

Herold emphasized that her experience as a mother is a strength, not a liability, and that there are numerous examples of working parents who have successfully balanced their careers and family life. She called on the Cuyahoga County Republican Party, the Ohio Republican Party, and other organizations to reconsider their endorsement of Patton, as his comments reflect an "anti-working parent mentality." In a statement, Patton acknowledged that his words were "misplaced" and that he did not intend to suggest that young mothers could not serve ably in the legislature. He apologized for his choice of words, stating that raising young children and working is tough, and that he would be judged on his work and advocacy for working families.

The primary race for Ohio House District 7 is scheduled for March 15, with the winner facing Democrat David Thurau in the general election in November. Herold's statement garnered significant support, with many people signing a petition and using the hashtag #ISupportJen to show their backing. Herold encouraged those who denounce Patton's comments to make their voices heard and to hold candidates accountable for their remarks.

The search for Luka Rocco Magnotta, a suspected porn actor accused of dismembering his acquaintance and mailing body parts to Ottawa, intensified as police uncovered a headless torso in Montreal. Magnotta, 29, is also known as Eric Clinton Newman and Vladimir Romanov, and has a history of online notoriety, including allegations of cat torture and a connection to Karla Homolka, a notorious sex killer. The torso, foot, and hand found in Montreal and Ottawa are believed to be from the same victim, with the suspect known to have rented a second-floor apartment in Montreal. Neighbors described Magnotta as a quiet, anti-social individual who seemed to keep to himself. The gruesome discovery of the torso in a garbage pile and the subsequent mailing of body parts to political offices in Ottawa shocked the nation, prompting a nationwide manhunt for Magnotta. His online presence, including a website and various social media profiles, offers a glimpse into his disturbing mindset, with articles on how to completely disappear and tips on entering the porn industry. The case has raised questions about how a man with such a history could remain undetected for so long, and the police are urging the public for help in locating the suspect.

Scientists have demonstrated that bumblebees can learn and transmit a novel foraging technique to their peers, a finding that challenges the notion that only large-brained animals possess the cognitive capacity for cultural transmission. In a groundbreaking study published in PLOS Biology, researchers from Queen Mary University of London showed that individual bees can be trained to pull a string to retrieve a food reward, and that this skill can then be passed on to other bees through observation. The team first trained a small group of bees to pull a string to access a hidden reward, a process that took about 5.5 hours per bee on average. These trained bees, known as demonstrators, were then placed in separate cages to observe untrained bees. Astonishingly, 60% of the untrained bees were able to learn the string-pulling technique after watching the demonstrations, even if they had never seen the string before. This social learning was observed in two out of three test colonies, with the technique spreading across multiple generations of bees. The researchers also found that the more experienced the demonstrator, the more likely the observer was to learn the task. However, bees did not cooperate to pull the string more efficiently; instead, they often hindered each other's efforts. The study suggests that cultural transmission, previously thought to be exclusive to humans, can occur in insects with relatively small brains. This finding not only challenges the traditional view of insect cognition but also opens new avenues for understanding the evolutionary origins of cultural transmission. The ability of bees to learn and transmit complex behaviors could have significant implications for our understanding of the cognitive processes underlying cultural evolution, potentially providing insights into how such phenomena might emerge in simpler systems.

One of the oldest names in the Hollywood talent business, William Morris Endeavor Entertainment (WME), is set to merge with IMG Worldwide, a global leader in sports, fashion, and media representation, in a deal that will reshape the entertainment industry landscape, according to a joint press release. The transaction, while financial details were not disclosed, is expected to create a powerful global platform, combining WME's extensive client roster in film, television, music, and digital media with IMG's market leadership in college and professional sports, event management, and fashion. WME Co-CEOs Patrick Whitesell and Ariel Emanuel expressed excitement about the strategic value of the partnership, noting the strong complement of IMG's global reach and management team to their business. The combined entity will operate across North America, Europe, Asia, South America, and Africa, with a broad client roster and unparalleled resources. Silver Lake, a global leader in technology investing, will support the transaction, with Egon Durban, Managing Partner of Silver Lake, emphasizing the potential for growth and digital expansion. Mubadala Development Company will be a minority investor. WME and IMG's combined client base will include award-winning global creative agency Droga5, providing unique advertising, brand integration, and marketing opportunities. The deal represents a significant shift in the industry, reflecting the evolving dynamics of talent representation and media management.

A former Austin police officer, James Miller, was sentenced to 10 years of probation and six months in jail for the 2015 stabbing death of Daniel Spencer, 32, after a jury found him guilty of criminally negligent homicide. Miller, 69, faced a potential two to 10 years in prison or 10 years of probation. The case garnered attention due to the "gay panic" defense Miller used, which claimed he acted in self-defense after Spencer allegedly made a sexual advance. The prosecution argued the evidence did not support this claim, pointing out that blood evidence at the scene did not match Miller's account. Marsha Spencer, the victim's mother, expressed profound grief over her son's death, describing the loss as a "huge hole in her heart." The defense, led by attorney Charlie Baird, maintained that Miller's actions were a result of self-defense and a "gay panic" reaction to Spencer's advances. The jury found Miller not guilty of murder and manslaughter but guilty of criminally negligent homicide. As a result, Miller will serve six months in jail, complete 100 hours of community service, pay $11,000 in restitution, and use a portable alcohol monitoring service for at least a year. The verdict and sentence have sparked outrage among LGBT advocates, who argue that the "gay panic" defense perpetuates harmful stereotypes and second-class treatment of non-straight individuals. The case highlights ongoing debates about the validity and ethical implications of such legal defenses.

A group of caring individuals is rallying to help a family who lost their dog, Jade, in Yellowstone National Park on July 23, 2015. Jade's parents, David Sowers and Laura Gillice, and their daughter, Angie Sowers, have made multiple trips from Denver, Colorado, to the park, a 550-mile journey, to search for their beloved pet. They have also left a car in the area in hopes that Jade will approach it. David Sowers was involved in a severe head-on collision in the park, suffering multiple injuries that required immediate medical attention, and Jade bolted from her crate during the rescue operation. Despite multiple sightings and ongoing efforts to catch Jade using live traps and other methods permitted by the park, she remains missing. The family's determination to find Jade is evident, as they continue to travel to the park and send her familiar scents. The group is seeking donations to assist the family and support their search for Jade, who is believed to be alive and thriving in the wild. Every contribution, no matter the size, is appreciated, and visitors to the park are encouraged to join the efforts to bring Jade home safely.

Rupert Murdoch, 82, and Wendi Deng Murdoch, 44, have filed for divorce, despite living increasingly separate lives, especially in recent months, according to sources. Rupert Murdoch has a history of divorces, with his second marriage to Anna Maria Torv costing him $1.7 billion. The divorce has reignited interest in the Murdochs' relationship, including rumors of a romantic affair with Tony Blair and potential conflicts of interest.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet has been donating their daily crawl data to the Internet Archive, which are then added to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. This effort aims to archive pages as they are created and the pages they refer to, ensuring that when referenced pages are changed or removed, a link to the version live when the original page was written is preserved. The Internet Archive hopes to fix all broken links on the web through these "No More 404" crawls. Charlie Hunnam, born in Newcastle, England on April 10, 1980, began his acting career at 16 with a guest appearance in Byker Grove and gained fame in Britain for his role as Nathan Maloney in Queer as Folk. He has since appeared in independent films, television series, and even turned down a million-dollar role in Star Wars: Episode II - Attack of the Clones to focus on long-term career opportunities. Hunnam's acting philosophy emphasizes selecting roles that are right for his long-term career rather than taking money for short-term gains.

The U.S. government contractor working on behalf of USAID distributing cellphones and laptops to Cuban activists has been arrested in Cuba, raising tensions between the U.S. and Cuba. The contractor, employed by Development Alternatives Inc., was detained on December 5th, and U.S. consular officers are seeking access. The Cuban government's charges remain undisclosed, but under Cuban law, foreigners can be arrested for "dangerousness." The incident comes as the Obama administration has been cautiously improving relations with Cuba, with concrete steps like freeing political prisoners and expanding digital access seen as potential reciprocations. The detention highlights the ongoing challenges in U.S.-Cuba relations, with some experts suggesting it shows Raúl Castro's administration has not abandoned hard-line tactics. The case also raises questions about the Obama administration's approach to promoting democracy in Cuba, with critics pointing to past controversial spending and methods.

A 16-month-old girl named Sabriya Towels was found in cardiac arrest in a parked Ford F-150 in Lansdowne, Maryland, and later died at the hospital. The incident occurred around 1 p.m. on McDowell Ln. A relative, not a parent, was supposed to drop her off at the Highland Village Head Start Center but instead drove to their home on South Paca St. to sleep. Four hours later, the relative went to pick up the child and found her in the truck. At this point, police do not believe it was intentional. The temperature was 88 degrees outside, and the interior of the black car would have been even hotter. The Office of the Chief Medical Examiner will determine the cause of death. Employees at the Head Start Center did not comment on the case. The relative has not been named, and no criminal charges have been filed. In a separate incident, an Alexandria woman named Zoraida Magali Conde Hernandez has been charged with felony child neglect after her 8-month-old baby died due to being left in a hot parked car in Arlington. The mother had intended to drop the child off at daycare on her way to work in Arlington but apparently forgot and went to work. She only noticed the child was in the vehicle when she left work and immediately drove to Inova Alexandria Hospital, where the child was declared dead at about 4:20 p.m. The high temperature on that day was 90 degrees.

Students across the country staged protests on March 4, 2010, to voice their outrage over deep education funding cuts. At the University of Wisconsin-Milwaukee, 15 protesters were arrested after students threw ice and punches, and blocked university gates. At the University of California, Berkeley, a small group formed a human chain to block a main gate, while hundreds later gathered for a peaceful rally. In California, students blocked major gates at UC Santa Cruz and smashed a car window. At the University of Illinois, professors marched to protest furloughs and pay cuts. In Washington, a group of protesters carried a coffin emblazoned with "R.I.P. Education" and were ejected from the state Capitol after singing a protest song. Nationwide, thousands of students, teachers, and parents participated in marches, strikes, teach-ins, and walkouts, highlighting the financial strain on public education due to state budget deficits and reduced funding. The protests aimed to pressure lawmakers to restore funding and ensure the quality of education.

The penny, long a staple of American currency, may soon face elimination due to its high production costs. In 2016, the cost to produce a penny exceeded its face value for the first time, reaching 1.5 cents, up from 1.43 cents in 2015 and 1.66 cents in 2014. This trend, driven by rising zinc prices, has led to significant financial losses for the U.S. Mint, which reported a $69 million loss on penny production in 2015, the largest in nine years. Meanwhile, nickels have also become more expensive to produce, costing about seven cents each, due to increased copper and nickel prices. Despite these costs, dimes and quarters remain cheaper to make, helping to offset the losses. The U.S. military, which operates bases overseas where the lowest denomination is the nickel, has already stopped using pennies. President Obama and Congress have considered phasing out the penny as a way to cut the budget, with the potential to save millions of dollars. The argument for eliminating the penny is compelling, but its cultural significance and the potential for inflation remain concerns.

Interior Secretary Ryan Zinke has recommended cutbacks or other changes to nearly half of the 27 geographic national monuments he recently reviewed at the request of President Donald Trump, according to a report sent to the White House and reviewed by The Wall Street Journal. The report suggests reducing the boundaries of the Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante preserves in Utah, and reopening hundreds of thousands of square miles of protected oceans in both the Pacific and Atlantic to commercial fishing. Zinke's memo to President Trump, which has not been officially released, recommends changes to several other monuments as well, including Nevada's Gold Butte and Oregon's Cascade-Siskiyou. Trump ordered the review earlier this year after complaining about improper "land grabs" by former presidents, including Barack Obama. National monument designations add protections for lands revered for their natural beauty and historical significance, with restrictions not as stringent as for national parks. The monuments under review were designated by four presidents over the last two decades, including Mojave Trails in California, Grand Staircase-Escalante in Utah, and Bears Ears, which is on sacred tribal land. No other president has tried to eliminate a monument, but some have trimmed and redrawn boundaries 18 times, according to the National Park Service. Zinke told The Associated Press last month that unspecified boundary adjustments for some monuments designated over the past four decades will be included in the recommendations submitted to Trump. None of the sites would revert to new ownership, he said, while public access for uses such as hunting, fishing, or grazing would be maintained or restored. He also spoke of protecting tribal interests and historical land grants, pointing to monuments in New Mexico, where Hispanic ranchers have opposed two monuments proclaimed by Obama. A spokeswoman for Zinke referred questions to the White House, which did not offer immediate comment. If Trump adopts the recommendations, it would quiet some of the worst fears of his opponents, who warned that vast public lands and marine areas could be lost to states or private interests. However, significant reductions in the size of the monuments, especially those created by Obama, would mark the latest in a string of actions where Trump has sought to erode his Democratic predecessor's legacy. The recommendations cap an unprecedented four-month review based on Trump's claim that the century-old Antiquities Act had been misused by past presidents to create oversized monuments that hinder energy development, grazing, and other uses. The review raised alarm among conservationists who said protections could be lost for areas that are home to ancient cliff dwellings, towering sequoia trees, deep canyons, and ocean habitats. They've vowed to file lawsuits if Trump attempts any changes that would reduce the size of monuments or rescind their designations.

A rare collection of photographs of Adolf Hitler, taken in the final years of World War II, has recently been auctioned for a significant sum, sparking interest from collectors and historians worldwide. The photographs, believed to have been taken by someone close to Hitler, were part of Eva Braun’s personal album, which was found in the bunker of Hitler and Braun in April 1945. The album changed hands several times after it was auctioned by a British Fleet Street photographer, Edward Dean, who obtained it from a Russian soldier who discovered it in Braun’s bunker bedroom shortly after the couple’s suicide. The photographs, mostly from the early to mid-1930s, depict Hitler in a more relaxed and candid manner, walking down a path at his Berghof headquarters in the Bavarian Alps, with his guards also shown in various poses. The bidding for the photographs was highly competitive, with interest from collectors in Britain, the United States, and other countries such as Germany, China, and South Africa.

The auction highlights the ongoing fascination with Nazi memorabilia, with experts noting that buyers are typically historians rather than individuals with Nazi sympathies. The photographs, while historically significant, also raise ethical questions about the ownership and display of items related to Nazi history. The auction also underscores the scarcity of such artifacts in the open market, especially those with concrete provenance dating back to the time of their liberation. The photographs, which were carefully controlled by the Nazi regime, offer a rare glimpse of Hitler in a more casual setting, making them particularly valuable to collectors.

The article also touches on the broader issue of the ethical implications of owning and displaying Nazi-related items. It mentions that some art collectors have taken steps to determine whether their collections were looted from Jewish families, and highlights the efforts of memorials dedicated to preserving the historical context of the Holocaust to gather personal items from survivors. The director of the Auschwitz-Birkenau memorial, Dr. Piotr M. A. Cywinski, has called on the public to donate documents, photos, personal letters, and other materials that are in private hands, emphasizing the importance of mutual effort in understanding the mechanisms of hatred and the full picture of the history of Auschwitz and the Holocaust.

Peaches Geldof's 11-month-old son Phaedra was with her when she died, according to RadarOnline.com. Geldof's husband, Thomas Cohen, who had spent a night away with their eldest child, Astala, asked a friend to check on her at their home in Wrotham, Kent, when she failed to answer her phone. The socialite's body was found with Phaedra playing nearby. "The hope is that Phaedra is so young he wasn’t aware of what was going on—the most important thing is that he’s OK," a source told the UK Sun. "It is devastating for Tom that he wasn’t there but it couldn’t have been avoided." Geldof was an advocate of attachment parenting, meaning she was rarely without her young son by her side. This detail offers some comfort to her family, as it suggests she wasn’t alone when she died. Geldof's own mother, Paula Yates, was found dead at her London home in 2000, with her baby daughter, Tiger Lily, also nearby. Geldof's father, Bob Geldof, was seen visiting her home on Thursday, where he was greeted by Tom's parents, Keith and Susan. The two men spent 20 minutes talking in the garden before the rocker entered the house, leaving two hours later with some of his daughter's belongings. Geldof's body has now been released by coroners so plans for her funeral can be made, while her cause of death remains unexplained. In the weeks leading up to her death, Geldof's "worringly skinny" body had raised concern among fans and experts. She had attributed her weight loss to a dangerous diet, including a juice cleanse and miso soup. U.K. doctor/TV personality Dr. Chris Steele suggested that Geldof's death could have been caused by complications from a long-term eating disorder, such as bulimia, which can lead to heart issues. His observations included darkened and enlarged knuckles, indicative of purging behavior. The exact cause of death is still under investigation, with toxicology tests expected to take multiple weeks to complete.

Cancer is the second leading cause of death among women globally, with breast, colorectal, lung, and cervical cancers being the top four fatal forms of the disease. A report from the American Cancer Society and Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, highlights the increasing impact of cancer on women in low- and middle-income countries, predicting a significant rise in cancer-related deaths among women by 2030. The report, titled "The Global Burden of Cancer in Women," underscores the preventable or early-detectable nature of these cancers, emphasizing the need for increased education and prevention efforts. By 2030, the number of women dying from cancer is expected to increase by more than 57% from 2012 levels, reaching 5.5 million deaths, with a substantial portion of this increase projected in low- and middle-income countries. The economic burden of cancer is also highlighted, with the global cost estimated at about $286 billion in 2009, much of which is attributed to the premature death of workers. This economic impact is particularly pronounced in the United States, where the loss of productive years due to cancer in women is estimated at $82 billion.

The report advocates for a collaborative approach between the public and private sectors to address the growing global health crisis. It calls for increased prevention and early detection efforts, which can significantly improve outcomes. The American Cancer Society's All of Me Young Scholars program is highlighted as a key initiative aimed at educating and cultivating young health and civil society professionals in Brazil, Mexico, Colombia, and India, to drive meaningful change in the prevention and early detection of cancers among women in low- and middle-income countries. This program is part of the broader Healthy Women, Healthy Economies initiative, which links women's health and well-being to economic growth, advocating for policies that promote women's health to enhance their economic participation.

The report identifies several modifiable risk factors for cancer, including tobacco use, which is the leading global risk factor for cancer mortality. It also emphasizes the importance of participating in cancer screening tests, such as Pap smears for cervical cancer and mammograms for breast cancer, as well as maintaining a balanced and healthy diet, engaging in regular physical activity, and protecting the skin from sun damage. These preventive measures can significantly reduce the risk of certain types of cancer. The American Cancer Society and Merck KGaA, Darmstadt, Germany, are committed to raising awareness and advocating for the health and well-being of women worldwide, recognizing that improving women's health has a positive ripple effect on communities and economies.

Some movies struggle to attract audiences, leading to significant financial losses for studios. Notable flops like Cowboys & Aliens, The Lone Ranger, Final Fantasy: The Spirits Within, and The Adventures of Pluto Nash failed to draw crowds, despite substantial budgets. These films often miss the mark due to poor property choices, casting mismatches, or overly ambitious budgets that make box office recovery challenging. The article highlights recent underperformers, including Unforgettable, starring Katherine Heigl, which debuted to a disappointing $4.8 million, marking a career low for the actress. The Christian Bale-starrer The Promise, costing $100 million, opened to just $4.1 million, raising concerns about its financial viability. Other films like Free Fire and Phoenix Forgotten also underperformed, grossing $1 million and $2 million, respectively. Despite these disappointments, The Fate of the Furious continued its strong run, grossing $163.6 million domestically and $908.4 million globally. Meanwhile, Born in China, a nature documentary, performed well, earning $5.1 million. These examples illustrate the risks and uncertainties in the film industry, where even high-profile projects can fall flat.

Babies cry more in Britain, Canada, Italy, and the Netherlands than in other countries, according to new research by the University of Warwick. Psychologists have created the world’s first universal charts for the normal amount of crying in babies during the first three months. On average, babies around the world cry for about 2 hours per day in the first two weeks, with crying peaking at 2 hours and 15 minutes at six weeks, before gradually reducing to 1 hour and 10 minutes by the twelve-week mark. The highest levels of crying were found in the UK, Italy, Canada, and the Netherlands, while the lowest levels were in Denmark, Germany, and Japan. The research involved almost 8,700 infants from countries including Germany, Denmark, Japan, Canada, Italy, the Netherlands, and the UK. The study also found that the highest rates of colic—defined as crying more than 3 hours a day for at least 3 days a week—were reported in the UK (28% of infants at 1-2 weeks), Canada (34.1% at 3-4 weeks of age), and Italy (20.9% at 8-9 weeks of age). In contrast, the lowest colic rates were reported in Denmark (5.5% at 3-4 weeks) and Germany (6.7% at 3-4 weeks).

The research, led by Professor Dieter Wolke, aims to provide new universal guidelines for modern parents and health professionals to assess normal and excessive levels of crying in babies. Wolke comments that German and Danish parents are less likely to get worked up and will wait a bit before intervening to see if the baby can self-soothe. He suggests that the new chart of normal fuss/cry amounts in babies across industrialized countries will help health professionals reassure parents whether a baby is crying within the normal expected range in the first three months or shows excessive crying which may require further evaluation and extra support for the parents.

The study also reveals that around 40% of infant crying is inconsolable, and many new mothers and fathers are unduly stressed by some "unscientific" parenting books which offer bogus solutions. Wolke states that concern in Britain over crying babies costs the NHS an estimated £70 million each year, with stressed-out parents more likely to reinforce a pattern of crying. He emphasizes the importance of adult well-being, suggesting that if parents are not relaxed, they are less likely to be useful to their babies. The research, published in The Journal of Pediatrics, highlights the need for a more nuanced understanding of infant crying and the importance of cultural factors in how parents respond to their babies.

Stanford psychologists have challenged the notion that altruism is an innate human trait, revealing that brief reciprocal interactions can significantly influence children's willingness to help others. In a series of experiments, researchers found that 1- and 2-year-olds who engaged in reciprocal play with an experimenter were far more likely to help a new person in need compared to those who engaged in parallel play. This finding suggests that social cues and experiences play a crucial role in shaping altruistic behavior. The study involved 34 children, randomly assigned to either a reciprocal or parallel play condition. In the reciprocal condition, the experimenter and child rolled a ball back and forth, while in the parallel condition, each played with their own ball. After the play session, the experimenter knocked an object off a table, and the children's willingness to help was observed. Children in the reciprocal play condition were three times more likely to help than those in the parallel play condition. This pattern was consistent even when the experiment was repeated with older children, showing that a brief reciprocal interaction can foster altruism in preschoolers. The researchers also found that these reciprocal interactions led children to expect benevolence from others, suggesting that such interactions can shape children's perceptions of social norms. The study, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, challenges the prevailing view that early altruism is an automatic and innate response, instead highlighting the importance of social experiences in shaping children's behavior. The findings have implications for parenting and education, suggesting that fostering reciprocal interactions could be an effective way to promote altruism in children.

Vice President Mike Pence spoke at the Capitol on Friday, where the late Sen. John McCain, R-Ariz., was lying in state. Pence, representing President Donald Trump, who was not in attendance, honored McCain’s service during the Vietnam War, where he was captured and tortured. McCain, a six-term Republican senator, had requested Trump not attend his funeral, reflecting their combative relationship. The flag-draped casket was carried into the Capitol by members of America's military services, with family members watching from the steps. Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell praised McCain, calling him a hero. House Speaker Paul Ryan highlighted McCain’s support for limited government, tax reform, and the military. The ceremony was the first of two days of services in Washington honoring the Arizona senator, who served in Congress for 35 years. On Saturday, McCain’s procession will pause by the Vietnam Memorial before heading to the Washington National Cathedral for a formal funeral service. Two former presidents—Democrat Barack Obama and Republican George W. Bush—will speak. The procession highlighted McCain’s military service and his more than five years as a prisoner of war, contrasting with Trump’s style and priorities. Other officials, including Defense Secretary Jim Mattis, White House Chief of Staff John Kelly, and U.N. Ambassador John Bolton, were among those in attendance. Former Secretary of State Henry Kissinger, former Connecticut Sen. Joe Lieberman, and actor Warren Beatty also paused at McCain’s casket. McCain’s widow, Cindy, is expected to lay a wreath at the Vietnam Veterans Memorial. The ceremony began in Arizona, where McCain and Cindy raised their family, and former Vice President Joe Biden, who is considering challenging Trump in 2020, provided a preview of the tributes to come. Biden, who did not mention Trump, advised McCain’s friends and family to remember snapshots of him, such as a glance or a touch, and the pure joy he felt about taking the stage on the Senate floor. The article concludes with the casket being wheeled out of the church to "My Way," a tribute to a politician known for following his own path.

A Moscow judge found three members of the feminist punk group Pussy Riot guilty of hooliganism for their anti-Kremlin protest in Moscow’s main cathedral, sentencing them to two years in jail. The case has sparked international outrage and highlighted the divide between Putin’s secular critics and his conservative supporters. Supporters outside the courthouse chanted "Shame" and called it Putin's "personal revenge." The U.S. and EU condemned the sentence as disproportionate. Despite the women’s support from celebrities like Madonna, Paul McCartney, and Sting, opinion polls show few Russians sympathize with them. The judge declared the women guilty of hooliganism motivated by religious hatred, storming the altar of Moscow's Christ the Saviour Cathedral to protest Putin's close ties with the Orthodox Church. The trio's defense lawyers plan to appeal, while the Church urged mercy. The case has become one of Russia's most high-profile since the Soviet Union's collapse, with Putin's critics seeing it as part of a broader crackdown on dissent. However, opposition leaders plan no major rallies, and Putin's supporters say he had no influence over the court's decision. The verdict could backfire on Putin if seen as too harsh, risking public backlash.

Former prosecutor Marcia Clark is expressing skepticism and concern regarding the recent discovery of a knife on property once owned by O.J. Simpson, as reported by Entertainment Tonight. Clark, who was the head prosecutor during Simpson’s 1995 murder trial, is unsure about the authenticity and significance of the knife. She acknowledges that the knife could be a hoax or planted, but hopes that the Los Angeles Police Department (LAPD) will thoroughly test it. Clark emphasizes the potential for DNA recovery, citing advancements in modern forensic technology. She notes that if the knife is indeed connected to the murders of Nicole Brown Simpson and Ron Goldman, it could provide insights into the crime, possibly even revealing the identity of someone who helped bury the evidence. However, Clark is realistic about the slim chances of this leading to a new prosecution, given Simpson’s previous acquittal. Clark’s comments reflect her ongoing involvement in the case and her desire for the truth to come to light, while also expressing empathy for the victims’ families. The knife’s discovery has reignited interest in the case, with experts suggesting it could have been used to inflict the fatal wounds on the victims. The knife was reportedly found by a construction worker in 2002 and kept by a retired LAPD officer, who only turned it over to the police when he wanted to engrave the case number on a grim keepsake. Forensic tests are currently underway to analyze the knife for fingerprints, hair, and DNA, though the passage of time may limit the usefulness of these tests. Despite the symbolic importance of the knife, legal experts confirm that Simpson cannot be retried for the murders due to the principle of double jeopardy. The case continues to capture public interest, with ongoing efforts to determine the knife’s relevance and potential to uncover new information about the tragic events.

The U.S. stock market, now eight years old, continues to defy expectations and skepticism, marking a significant milestone since the depths of the Great Recession. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, having more than tripled since its nadir in March 2009, now stands at record levels, with the broader S&P 500 index also showing impressive gains. Despite the market's robust performance, debates persist over its true age, with some arguing that the bull market began later, perhaps in 2011, 2013, or even 2016, following significant market corrections and economic challenges. These alternative start dates highlight the subjective nature of defining market cycles, with no clear consensus on when a bull market truly commences or concludes.

Critics of the current bull market argue that it is overvalued, pointing to high price-to-earnings ratios and the potential for a correction. The S&P 500's price-to-earnings ratio of over 26, compared to historical averages, suggests that the market may be reaching a peak. Additionally, the Federal Reserve's gradual increase in interest rates poses a risk, as historically, rising rates have often coincided with market downturns. Analysts like Andrew Smithers warn that while the market is not in a speculative bubble, it is near its previous peaks of overvaluation, raising concerns about future volatility.

Despite these warnings, the market's resilience and continued gains have been fueled by a combination of factors, including low interest rates, strong corporate earnings, and the Trump administration's pro-business policies. The Dow's recent performance, particularly since the 2016 election, has added over 2,500 points, reflecting investor optimism. However, the market's lack of volatility and the absence of significant corrections have raised questions about whether investors are becoming complacent. The low volatility index (VIX) near 11, compared to its historical average, suggests that investors are underestimating the risk of a market downturn.

Moreover, the market's performance has been uneven, with some sectors outperforming others. Consumer discretionary stocks, including companies like Home Depot and Nike, have seen significant gains, benefiting from a strong economy and consumer spending. In contrast, energy companies have struggled, reflecting the broader economic and geopolitical challenges facing the sector. The inclusion of newer companies, such as Apple and UnitedHealth Group, has also contributed to the market's growth, while traditional stalwarts like Exxon Mobil have lagged behind.

The debate over the bull market's longevity and the potential for a correction remains ongoing. While many investors remain bullish, driven by the current economic environment and the promise of further stimulus, others caution that the market's high valuations and lack of historical precedent suggest a higher risk of a downturn. The market's ability to continue its upward trajectory will depend on various factors, including the effectiveness of Trump's policies, the Federal Reserve's monetary policy, and global economic conditions. As the bull market approaches its ninth year, the challenge for investors will be to navigate the balance between optimism and caution, recognizing that even the longest bull markets eventually come to an end.

Miami rapper Pitbull, also known as Armando Christian Perez, is set to embark on an unexpected adventure if a Walmart marketing campaign goes according to plan. As part of the deal, Pitbull will visit the Walmart store that garners the most "likes" on its Facebook page by July 16th. A humorous twist was introduced by David Thorpe, a writer for the Boston Phoenix and the humor website SomethingAwful.com, who encouraged fans to "like" the remote Walmart in Kodiak, Alaska, making it a frontrunner. The Kodiak Walmart's Facebook page had amassed over 35,000 "likes," significantly more than the town's population. Despite the lead, Walmart shoppers from other locations still have a chance to rally support for their local stores. Pitbull, currently touring Europe, expressed his willingness to go wherever his fans want him to, tweeting about the potential for bear repellant in Kodiak. The contest not only highlights the power of social media but also showcases the unexpected places a celebrity might end up, all for the sake of a marketing stunt.

Celebrity dermatologist Dr. Fredric Brandt, known as the "Baron of Botox," was found dead in his Miami home on Sunday at the age of 65. Friends and family attributed his death to an illness he couldn't overcome, with his publicist Jacquie Tractenberg stating that he suffered from depression. Dr. Brandt, who had practices in Coral Gables and New York City, was a dermatologist who pioneered skin care products and worked with numerous high-profile clients, including Madonna, Kelly Ripa, and Stephanie Seymour. His death was ruled a suicide by Miami police, with his friend John Joseph Hupert finding him hanging in the garage. Dr. Brandt had been devastated by a character on Tina Fey's Netflix series, Unbreakable Kimmy Schmidt, which parodied his appearance and demeanor, but his publicist denied that the show was the cause of his suicide. Dr. Brandt's legacy as a dermatologist and innovator in anti-aging treatments will be remembered by his clients and colleagues, who praised his kindness and generosity. His death has been mourned by many in the entertainment industry, with celebrities like Kelly Ripa and Joy Behar expressing their sadness. Dr. Brandt is survived by his brother and the dogs he cherished.

Pierce Brosnan, the former James Bond actor, faced an embarrassing moment at Burlington International Airport in Vermont when he attempted to board a plane with a 10-inch hunting knife in his carry-on luggage. TSA officials confiscated the blade, which was discovered during screening, and Brosnan, 62, reportedly felt embarrassed and angry about the situation. The incident occurred on Sunday, and Lieutenant Shawn Burke from the Burlington Police Department informed that Brosnan was encountered by TSA at one of their checkpoints but was allowed to continue his journey after resolving the issue. The ban on knives was introduced following the September 11 terror attacks, and all sharp objects, except for rounded or plastic butter knives, are prohibited in plane cabins. Despite the incident, Brosnan recently expressed his affection for Ireland, his home country, in a series of Instagram posts and tweets, sharing that he was "goodbye my sweet home of Ireland" and looking forward to returning. The Associated Press noted that Brosnan's publicist did not return messages seeking comment on the matter.

Crystal Mason, a 43-year-old woman from Rendon, Texas, was sentenced to five years in prison for attempting to vote while on supervised release for a previous felony conviction. The case has sparked controversy and debate over the complex and often confusing laws surrounding voting rights for felons in Texas. Mason cast a provisional ballot in the 2016 presidential election, unaware that she was prohibited from voting as a convicted felon. Her name was not on the voter rolls, and she was given an affidavit to sign, which she did without fully understanding its implications. After election officials flagged her vote, Mason was arrested for voter fraud and sentenced to five years in prison. The sentence, handed down by conservative Republican Judge Ruben Gonzalez, drew criticism from Mason’s defense attorney, Alison Grinter, who argued that the punishment was disproportionate to the crime. Grinter pointed out that a white woman in Iowa who attempted to vote twice for Donald Trump received a much lighter sentence, including probation and a $750 fine.

The case has highlighted the disparities in how felons are treated under the law, with some states requiring individuals to apply to regain their voting rights, while others automatically restore these rights upon completion of their sentences. Mason’s conviction has also brought attention to the broader issue of mass incarceration and its disproportionate impact on communities of color. The Sentencing Project, a criminal justice reform advocacy group, estimates that approximately 6.1 million Americans are disenfranchised due to felony convictions. In Texas, one in five African-Americans is disenfranchised, a statistic that underscores the racial disparities in the criminal justice system.

The case has garnered significant attention, with a petition to have all charges against Mason dropped collecting over 38,000 signatures. Many supporters argue that Mason’s sentence is an example of the harsh and disproportionate treatment of felons in the criminal justice system. Mason’s defense team has appealed the case, hoping to secure a new trial or a reduced sentence. The appeal is based on the argument that the federal Voting Rights Act provides a pathway for individuals to cast provisional ballots, shifting the burden of proof to the state. Despite the efforts, State District Judge Ruben Gonzalez denied Mason’s motion for a new trial, reaffirming the original five-year prison sentence.

The controversy surrounding Mason’s case has sparked discussions about the need for clearer and more consistent laws regarding voting rights for felons. Advocates argue that such laws should be designed to ensure that individuals are fully informed of their rights and responsibilities, reducing the risk of unintentional violations. The case has also highlighted the broader issue of how the criminal justice system intersects with voter suppression efforts, raising questions about the fairness and equity of the legal system.

At a UFO conference in Mexico City, two photographs of what are claimed to be alien remains from the 1947 Roswell crash were unveiled, generating significant buzz among UFO enthusiasts. The images, purportedly taken by geologist Bernard Ray between 1947 and 1949, were found in a box containing other photographs in the attic of a house in Sedona, Arizona. Former journalist Adam Dew, who verified the film as being from the late 1940s, presented the photos, which depict a small, humanoid figure in a display case. Skeptics argue that the photos are likely of a mummified human child, given the figure's large head relative to its body, a characteristic of children. The figure's appearance in a display case with a sign further suggests it is not an alien but a mummified specimen. Critics point out that the photos lack context, such as captions or dates, making it difficult to verify their authenticity or origin. The images were reportedly authenticated by Kodak experts, but this only confirms the film's age, not the subject's identity. UFO researcher Jaime Maussan emphasized the importance of the photos, stating they show extraterrestrial visits are a reality. However, Richard Dolan, a leading UFO researcher, claims the photos could not be a model or a mummy, suggesting a highly sophisticated understanding of comparative anatomy among species. Despite the claims, the photos remain controversial, with NASA and the U.S. government maintaining no formal recognition of extraterrestrial life. The authenticity and origin of the images remain subjects of debate, leaving the mystery of the Roswell crash unresolved.

Madonna has applied to adopt two more children from Malawi, according to a government spokesman. The 58-year-old singer appeared in court in Lilongwe on January 25 and must wait a week to find out if the court will grant the adoption order. Madonna already has two children from Malawi: David, adopted in 2006, and Mercy, adopted in 2009. Both are 11 years old. Her other children are Lourdes, 20, from a relationship with Carlos Leon, and Rocco, 16, by her former husband Guy Ritchie. Lilongwe High Court officials confirmed Madonna appeared before Justice Fiona Mwale. The singer flew into Malawi fresh from the Women’s March in Washington, D.C. Her relationship with Malawi dates back to 2006, when she established the Raising Malawi charity to improve children's lives. The charity has funded schools and scholarships and is currently building the country’s first pediatric intensive care unit at the Queen Elizabeth Central Hospital in Blantyre. Madonna’s application for the adoptions has sparked controversy, with some questioning the appropriateness of her involvement in the country’s adoption process.

Until recently, the exact number of lakes on Earth remained a mystery, with estimates ranging widely. Now, a new study published in the journal Geophysical Research Letters has provided a more accurate count, revealing that there are approximately 117 million lakes globally. This number is significantly higher than the 304 million lakes estimated in a 2006 study, marking a 46% increase. The findings were made possible through the use of high-resolution satellite data and supercomputers, which allowed researchers to analyze every cloudless pixel, thus identifying smaller lakes that were previously overlooked. The study, led by David Seekell from Umea University, found that most of the world's lakes are located in the far North, with a majority at low altitudes. Notably, 90 million of these lakes are small, measuring 0.5 to 2.5 acres each, which is roughly the size of a country house lot or a large farm pond. These small lakes, despite their size, play a crucial role in global environmental issues, including the carbon budget, as they can both release and store greenhouse gases. The researchers also discovered that the total surface area covered by lakes is 3.7% of Earth's land, a figure that surpasses previous estimates. The study's findings have significant implications for climate science, as lakes influence greenhouse gas levels in the atmosphere. However, the role of these lakes is difficult to assess without an accurate count. The study excluded major bodies of water like the Caspian Sea and Antarctica's ice-covered lakes, focusing instead on smaller, more numerous lakes. The researchers plan to make their lake database freely available and intend to update it with higher-resolution data from the Landsat 8 satellite. As climate change continues to affect the landscape, the study highlights the importance of understanding the dynamics of these lakes, especially in regions where permafrost is thawing, leading to the drying up of small lakes. The loss of these water bodies can have severe consequences, including public health hazards and changes in local climate conditions.

A passenger was forced to land a light aircraft at Humberside Airport after the pilot fell ill mid-flight, according to reports. The plane, a Cessna 172, had taken off from Sandtoft Airfield and was returning to Sandtoft when the pilot collapsed in the cockpit. The passenger, identified only as "John," was left to make an emergency landing with the assistance of two flying instructors. The landing was described as "beautiful" by one of the instructors, who praised the passenger's calm and professional handling of the situation. Eyewitnesses reported seeing sparks as the plane landed, and the incident caused delays for two incoming flights. The passenger completed four circuits of the airport before successfully landing the aircraft at about 19:30 BST. Humberside Police stated that a post-mortem would be conducted to determine the cause of death of the pilot, who was the only person on board. The pilot's identity and the exact cause of death have not been released, in accordance with the family's wishes. A friend of the pilot and passenger, Richard Tomlinson, described the passenger as "nothing short of a hero" and praised his experience and professionalism. The incident highlights the potential risks and challenges faced by pilots, even in light aircraft, and the importance of having trained individuals on board to assist in emergencies.

A senior economic adviser to Sen. Barbara Boxer (D-Calif.) resigned after being arrested for attempting to bring marijuana into the Hart Senate Office Building, according to U.S. Capitol Police. Marcus M. Stanley, who has worked for Boxer since 2009, was stopped by a police officer Tuesday morning when he allegedly tried to "remove and conceal" a leafy green substance from his pocket during a security screening. The substance tested positive for marijuana, and Stanley resigned shortly after. This incident comes amid ongoing debates over marijuana legalization, including California's Proposition 19, which would legalize and tax cannabis. Boxer and her GOP rival, Carly Fiorina, both oppose the measure. The arrest marks the fourth Hill aide to be arrested by Capitol Police this year, highlighting the persistent issue of marijuana possession on Capitol grounds.

The 23-year-old victim of a gang-rape in New Delhi remains in critical condition at Mount Elizabeth Hospital in Singapore, battling significant brain injury, lung and abdominal infections, and other severe injuries. Doctors are working tirelessly to stabilize her condition, with her family receiving support from the Indian High Commission. Meanwhile, in Punjab, authorities have suspended and fired police officers for their alleged negligence in the case of another gang-rape victim who committed suicide. This incident has sparked renewed calls for better protection of women and harsher penalties for rapists in India, with protests in New Delhi demanding reforms. The government has promised to bring the perpetrators to justice and provide the best possible medical care to the victim. However, some politicians have faced criticism for comments that minimized the seriousness of the protests, with one national lawmaker apologizing for his remarks. The case has highlighted ongoing issues of police indifference and societal pressure on victims in India.

Refugees and migrants are navigating new routes in Europe amid growing tensions and border closures. On Wednesday, hundreds of migrants crossed into Croatia from Serbia, opening a new path to northern Europe after Hungary sealed its border with Serbia. At the Serbian-Hungarian border, Hungarian riot police used water cannons, batons, and tear gas to repel migrants, resulting in a clash that left some injured. Croatia, an EU member, is prepared to receive migrants or direct them to their intended destinations, mainly Germany. However, the situation has exposed deep divisions within Europe over how to handle the crisis. Serbia’s minister, Aleksandar Vulin, criticized Hungary’s border closure, arguing it is unsustainable. Meanwhile, the EU is grappling with the influx of over 500,000 migrants this year, with many fleeing conflict and poverty, especially from Syria. The crisis has led to new challenges, such as landmine warnings in Croatia, and has strained relations between countries. The United Nations Secretary General, Ban Ki-moon, condemned Hungary’s actions, calling them unacceptable. Neighboring countries like Croatia have pledged to help migrants pass through, but the overall response remains fragmented. The situation highlights the need for a coordinated European approach to manage the unprecedented migration crisis.

President Donald Trump and French President Emmanuel Macron met at the White House for a state visit, with two notable moments of awkward hand-holding.
