During a military welcome ceremony on the White House South Lawn, Trump repeatedly tried to hold Melania's hand, only to be rebuffed by his wife, who resisted his attempts. This was not the first time Melania has shown reluctance to hold Trump's hand; previous instances include a trip to Israel and a visit to Ohio. The moment was captured on video and widely shared on social media, with many users finding it amusing. In the Oval Office, Trump attempted to brush a piece of dandruff off Macron's shoulder, joking that they had a "very special relationship" and needed to make Macron "perfect." Macron seemed initially taken aback but soon smiled and laughed at the interaction. These awkward moments of hand-holding and personal interaction have become a recurring theme in the Trump administration, with Trump's attempts to hold hands with both his wife and other world leaders often met with resistance or reluctance. The incidents have sparked numerous jokes and memes on social media, highlighting the tension and discomfort that can arise in the public eye.

Sen. Orrin Hatch, the senior senator from Utah and chairman of the Senate Judiciary Committee, has a long and storied career spanning several decades. From his early days in the Senate, Hatch has been a key figure in numerous legislative battles, notably as a proponent of conservative policies and as a voice of the Republican Party. His interactions with various presidents, including Ronald Reagan and Donald Trump, have been marked by both support and occasional disagreement. Hatch's role in the Senate has been pivotal, from his involvement in the confirmation of Supreme Court justices to his work on major legislation. His relationship with Mitt Romney, a fellow Republican and former presidential candidate, has been complex, with Romney both supporting and criticizing Hatch during his time in office. Hatch's influence extends beyond the Capitol, as he has been honored with an honorary degree from the University of Utah and has been a central figure in Utah's political landscape. As he approaches his 40th year in the Senate, Hatch's legacy is one of significant political influence and a long-standing commitment to conservative values. His future remains uncertain, with speculation surrounding his potential retirement and the possibility of a new challenger, such as Romney, stepping into his shoes. The dynamics of Utah's political scene, with its strong Mormon community and shifting political allegiances, will play a crucial role in determining the future of this Senate seat.

President Donald Trump criticized Nike for featuring former NFL quarterback Colin Kaepernick in a new ad campaign, calling it a "terrible message." Trump, who has been vocal against players protesting during the national anthem, said, "I think it’s a terrible message that they’re sending and the purpose of them doing it, maybe there’s a reason for them doing it, but I think as far as sending a message, I think it’s a terrible message and a message that shouldn’t be sent." Despite his disapproval, Trump acknowledged that companies have the right to make their own business decisions. Nike’s stock fell in early trading, dropping 2 percent, following the announcement. Kaepernick, who began a wave of protests by NFL players two seasons ago, kneeling during the national anthem to protest police brutality and racial inequality, now has a new deal with Nike. The deal, which was renegotiated into a multi-year contract, will make him one of the faces of Nike's 30th anniversary "Just Do It" campaign. The NFL and Nike extended their partnership in March to run through 2028, with Nike providing all NFL teams with game-day uniforms and sideline apparel that bears the swoosh logo. Meanwhile, NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell issued a statement, calling Trump's comments "divisive" and saying they "disrespect" the players and the good work the league does. Other NFL players and owners have also weighed in, with some, like Jets owner Woody Johnson, expressing disappointment. The controversy has reignited the debate over the NFL's response to player protests and the league's relationship with its billionaire owners and the president.

Denis Finley, the executive editor of the Burlington Free Press, found himself in a public relations quagmire after a series of tweets that many found insensitive and tone-deaf. Finley's tweet in response to Vermont's plan to offer a third gender option on driver's licenses, stating "Awesome! That makes us one step closer to the apocalypse," sparked widespread outrage and claims of canceled subscriptions. This incident highlights the challenges journalists face in the digital age, where the line between being provocatively engaging and tone-deaf can be thin. Finley's previous tweets, including a response to an AP tweet about Frank Lloyd Wright's office building, and another about Netflix, further underscored the perils of journalists opining on everything. Critics argue that Finley's tweets reflect a lack of awareness of his audience and the potential consequences of his words. The incident also raises questions about the role of editors and newsroom leaders in managing social media presence and the impact of their words on their organization's reputation. Meanwhile, the broader issue of declining readership for traditional media, particularly local newspapers, continues to be a concern. The New York Times' "The Truth is Hard" campaign, unveiled during the Golden Globes, aims to reaffirm the newspaper's commitment to truth and accuracy, but faces the challenge of connecting with audiences in an era of declining TV news viewership. The article concludes with a reflection on the evolving landscape of journalism, including the challenges of maintaining credibility and relevance in the digital age, and the importance of critical thinking and fact-checking in an era of misinformation.

Shark sightings have become a frequent occurrence along the Massachusetts coastline, particularly in Cape Cod, leading to beach closures and heightened concerns among beachgoers. In July, a man was bitten by a great white shark while swimming off Ballston Beach in Truro, Massachusetts, marking the first known attack in those waters in over 75 years. This incident, combined with recent sightings, has raised questions about the reasons behind the increased shark presence. Biologist Simon Thorrold suggests that the sharks are likely responding to a significant increase in the grey seal population, which has been protected since the 1970s by the federal Marine Mammal Protection Act. A family captured dramatic video of a shark attacking a seal off Monomoy Island, further highlighting the sharks' diet and the potential for more interactions with humans. Beachgoers are advised to stay alert and avoid the water during dawn and dusk, when sharks are more active. Despite the increased sightings, the sharks are expected to migrate to warmer waters in the coming months, providing a temporary respite for beach enthusiasts.

A female Suncor Energy employee was killed by a bear at the company's oil sands base camp site near Fort McMurray, northern Alberta, on Wednesday afternoon. The large male black bear attacked the woman in a busy part of the sprawling industrial complex. Suncor executive vice president Mark Little expressed shock and sorrow, urging everyone to focus on personal safety and be vigilant. The bear was put down, and Suncor is conducting a thorough investigation into the incident. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police and Alberta Environmental and Sustainable Resource Development responded, setting up traps and cameras. This is the third employee death on Suncor's oil sands site this year, though the other two were work-related. Suncor is reminding all workers to be especially vigilant in dealing with wildlife as bears are coming out of hibernation. The incident has left the victim's family and co-workers devastated, with Suncor offering support and privacy.

Anthony Bourdain, the celebrated chef and television personality who died by suicide in a French hotel room on June 8, had no narcotics in his system at the time of his death, according to a local prosecutor. Bourdain, known for his brash and opinionated personality, had previously spoken openly about his struggles with drug and alcohol addiction. The toxicology report revealed only a "trace of a nonnarcotic medicine in a therapeutic dose" in his system. Bourdain, 61, was working on an upcoming episode of his CNN series "Parts Unknown" with his close friend, French-born chef Eric Ripert, when he was found dead in his hotel room in Kaysersberg, France. The French prosecutor, Christian de Rocquigny de Fayel, stated that there was no evidence of foul play or violence involved in Bourdain's death, and a medical expert did not find any signs of violence on his body. 

Bourdain's ex-wife, Ottavia Busia-Bourdain, shared a photo of their 11-year-old daughter, Ariane, on Instagram, calling her "so strong and brave" just days after Bourdain's death. The photo, taken at the DROM music venue in New York City, showed Ariane dressed in all black and tall studded boots, clutching a microphone. In the caption, Busia-Bourdain wrote, "Our little girl had her concert today. She was amazing. So strong and brave. She wore the boots you bought her. I hope you are having a good trip, wherever you are." 

Bourdain's girlfriend, Asia Argento, also struggled to cope with his loss. In an Instagram post, she shared a photo of herself and Bourdain smiling in front of a teal-blue body of water, captioning it, "Two weeks without you." Argento, who had been dating Bourdain for over a year, supported him in his advocacy for the #MeToo movement and was present when he lauded her speech at the Cannes Film Festival. She wrote, "Anthony gave all of himself in everything that he did. His brilliant, fearless spirit touched and inspired so many, and his generosity knew no bounds. He was my love, my rock, my protector. I am beyond devastated. My thoughts are with his family. I would ask that you respect their privacy and mine." 

The loss of Bourdain, who had a significant impact on the culinary world and popularized travel and food exploration through his television series, has left a void that is difficult to fill. His death came three days after the suicide of fashion designer Kate Spade, and the two deaths have sparked discussions about mental health and the pressures faced by public figures.

President Donald Trump’s significant reduction in Obamacare advertising has left U.S. health insurers in many states scrambling to inform consumers about 2018 enrollment, which opened last week. Independence Blue Cross, a Pennsylvania-based insurer, has taken the initiative by commissioning a tractor-trailer truck to bring insurance consultants to shopping centers and other neighborhood spots around Philadelphia. Meanwhile, Centene Corp, known for its Medicaid health insurance, is expanding its TV and print advertising in three new states: Kansas, Missouri, and Nevada. Tech-savvy newcomer Oscar Health has launched four different TV commercials in six states, including Texas and Ohio, emphasizing “easy health insurance” with video shots of patients text-messaging with Oscar. Trump’s $90 million cut in advertising and outreach spending for the 2018 enrollment period, part of his strategy to let the Affordable Care Act “implode” until Congress can repeal it, has left a significant gap. The government’s advertising budget is now just $10 million for the 39 states relying on the federal Healthcare.gov website for enrollment, while the 11 states running their own exchanges set their own budgets. Insurers, like Anthem Inc, have raised monthly premiums on the most popular Obamacare plans to account for reduced government funding or have pulled out of dozens of U.S. counties, forcing many Obamacare customers to change health plans for 2018. The Congressional Budget Office expects 2018 enrollment to reach 11 million people, down from about 10 million this year, due to Trump’s threats and the cut in estimated $10 billion in government subsidies to insurers. Despite fears from Democrats that enrollment would fall due to reduced outreach and advertising, a record number of people signed up for ObamaCare in the first few days of open enrollment this year, with more than 200,000 people selecting a plan on the first day alone, compared to about 100,000 last year. While it is still early in the process, the spike in sign-ups is a positive development for supporters of the health-care law, who have been concerned about its fate under Republican control.

Three House Republicans, Reps. Matt Gaetz (R-Fla.), Andy Biggs (R-Ariz.), and Louie Gohmert (R-Texas), introduced a nonbinding resolution calling for the resignation of special counsel Robert Mueller, alleging "obvious conflicts of interest." The move comes as Mueller issued his first indictments in the Russia probe, including charges against former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort and his deputy Rick Gates, as well as a guilty plea from George Papadopoulos. The resolution, which states, "That House of Representatives expresses its sense that Robert Mueller is compromised and should resign from his special counsel position immediately," reflects growing frustration among Trump’s allies. While most Republicans, including leadership, are not on board with dismissing Mueller, the conservative push has alarmed some on the left, who are urging Democratic lawmakers to defend Mueller. Other conservatives, like Reps. Trent Franks (R-Ariz.) and Ron DeSantis (R-Fla.), have also called for Mueller’s departure. DeSantis has even pushed an amendment to curtail Mueller’s probe within six months and limit its scope. The resolution also includes a broader criticism of the FBI, citing its role in a 2010 uranium deal approved by US government agencies under Mueller’s watch. Gaetz argues that the FBI withheld information from Congress and the American people about Russian corruption of American uranium companies, and that Mueller’s impartiality is compromised. Despite the growing pressure, many of Gaetz’s Republican colleagues have previously expressed support for Mueller and his investigation. Senate Republicans have introduced bills to create a barrier between Trump and Mueller in the event the president attempts to fire him. The resolution highlights the intensifying political tensions surrounding the Russia probe and the ongoing efforts to influence its outcome.

Although marijuana has a reputation for being a relatively harmless drug, a new case report from Germany links it to the deaths of two young men, raising concerns about its potential cardiovascular risks. The report, based on postmortem investigations, concluded that both men were under the influence of cannabis when they died, with traces of THC, the main active ingredient in marijuana, found in their blood and brain tissue. In the first case, a 23-year-old man without a history of health problems suddenly collapsed while using public transportation and died after 40 minutes of unsuccessful resuscitation efforts. The man had a small amount of marijuana in his pockets when found. In the second case, a 28-year-old man was found dead at home by his girlfriend. An ashtray, rolling paper, and a sealable plastic bag containing marijuana remnants were discovered. The man had occasionally used cannabis and had a history of abusing alcohol and drugs such as amphetamines and cocaine. Both deaths were related to cardiovascular complications, with the researchers suggesting that smoking cannabis may have triggered arrhythmias. However, they noted that the men might have been predisposed to cardiovascular risks. Nikolas P. Lemos, a chief forensic toxicologist, acknowledged that there have been confirmed cases of marijuana having harmful effects on the heart. He emphasized that the risk of cardiovascular effects from marijuana use in the general population is low but higher in those with existing cardiovascular issues. The report highlights the growing risk of marijuana-associated adverse cardiovascular effects, especially in young people, and stresses the importance of considering marijuana use as a potential cause in patients with cardiovascular disorders. Researchers urge the medical community to be aware of these potential health complications and to collect specimens and test for cannabis in post-mortem fluids. The findings underscore the need for increased awareness and further research into the potential health risks of marijuana use.

Dinesh D’Souza, a controversial conservative writer and filmmaker, was recently pardoned by President Donald Trump, drawing attention to his past legal troubles and evolving career. D’Souza, known for his provocative and often racially charged rhetoric, has faced criticism from both conservative and liberal quarters. His 2012 conviction for campaign finance fraud, where he was sentenced to eight months of community confinement and five years of probation, was seen as a significant setback. In his defense, D’Souza has claimed selective prosecution by the Obama administration, but the judge rejected this argument. His pardon by Trump, who has a history of criticizing D’Souza, has been met with mixed reactions. D’Souza's career has seen him transition from a respected conservative intellectual to a figure associated with conspiracy theories and political provocations. His 2016 film, "Hillary’s America," which Trump is now praising, has been criticized for its racist and conspiratorial content. D’Souza's ability to generate controversy and maintain a significant following, despite his legal troubles, highlights the shifting dynamics within the conservative movement. His pardon, coming at a time when Trump is facing criticism for his pardon power, has sparked debates about political favoritism and the use of pardons.

A British woman named Kay Longstaff survived 10 hours in the Adriatic Sea after falling from the Norwegian Star cruise ship, approximately 60 miles off Croatia's coast. Longstaff, a 46-year-old from Brighton, was found by Croatian coast guard rescuers who spotted her waving her hands from the water. The captain of the rescue vessel, Lovro Oreskovic, stated that Longstaff told the crew she practiced yoga and sang to stay awake and alert. She was taken to a hospital in Pula, Croatia, where she was reported to be in good health, having suffered only stress. The Norwegian Cruise Line confirmed that Longstaff was found alive and in stable condition, and would soon be reunited with her family. The exact circumstances of the incident are under investigation, and the British embassy in Croatia has been informed. Meanwhile, the Norwegian Star continued its journey to Venice, Italy, after launching a search mission in the area where Longstaff was believed to have fallen. The warm waters of the Adriatic Sea are believed to have contributed to her survival. The incident comes weeks after a cruise ship worker fell overboard while traveling on the Norwegian Getaway, and a search was called off in May after an 80-year-old Australian man fell off the Sun Princess cruise ship while journeying from Indonesia to Malaysia.

The War on Christmas appears to be waning, according to recent data. Retailers are increasingly embracing the term "Christmas" in their marketing, with 80% now using it, up from 20% just five years ago, reports AdAge. The American Family Association, a vocal proponent of using "Christmas" in retailer messaging, predicts its campaign could conclude within the next year or two. Dick's Sporting Goods, which promotes a "Holiday Shop," is now the target of the AFA's annual boycott, urging supporters to avoid the retailer until Christmas Eve. Retailers have responded swiftly to boycotts and media scrutiny, with some renaming their "Family Trees" to "Christmas Trees" and others issuing press releases highlighting the use of "Merry Christmas." Economic pressures and the desire not to alienate customers have driven this shift. The National Retail Federation's survey shows 91% of consumers plan to celebrate Christmas, compared to 5% for Hanukkah and 2% for Kwanzaa. As the pendulum swings back, retailers are making conscious decisions about holiday messaging, with conversations now taking place at the highest levels.

Several multi-vehicle crashes, involving as many as 100 cars and dozens of tractor-trailers, stretched over several miles of icy Pennsylvania Turnpike between Willow Grove and Bensalem, PA, causing the highway to be shut down for most of the day. The eastbound lanes were particularly affected, with approximately 75 cars and several tractor-trailers involved in one crash area, while the westbound lanes were closed to allow emergency vehicle access. According to the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission, 30 people were injured and transported to local hospitals, with five of the injuries classified as serious but none life-threatening. At Doylestown Hospital, one victim was in stable condition, while Abington Hospital was treating 16 people, St. Mary’s Medical Center in Langhorne was treating seven, and Temple University Hospital was treating one. Dr. John Kelly, chief of staff at Abington Hospital, stated that the injuries were primarily soft tissue and bone type, with no fractures reported to date. The incident began around 8:30 am in the eastbound lanes, with another crash closer to the Route 1 exit involving approximately 30 cars and a jackknifed tractor-trailer. Chopper 3 footage showed at least four cars stuck under the jackknifed tractor-trailer. The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission reported that around 3:30 pm, the tractor-trailer blocking all eastbound lanes was moved to allow trapped vehicles to pass and continue eastbound on I-276. Crews were also removing small portions of the concrete median to allow drivers to U-turn onto the westbound lanes and exit the turnpike. The turnpike was reopened just before 4 pm, about 7.5 hours after the first crash. Investigators blamed icy conditions and sun glare as likely causes of the pileup. Drivers reported that road spray on windshields and the sun low in the sky may have hindered visibility, leading to sudden collisions. The crashes left dozens of drivers stranded in the cold, with up to 50 cars involved in the pileups. Rob Liepziger’s tow yard in Bristol, Bucks County, alone reported 75 cars and trucks, including six tractor trailers, with many having front-end and back-end damage, some of which were totaled.

In a rare case, a Vietnamese couple brought their fraternal twins to a genetic analysis center in Hanoi for DNA testing, after relatives noticed the children looked very different from one another. The results revealed that the twins had different fathers, a phenomenon known as heteropaternal superfecundation or bipaternal twins. Nguyen Thi Nga, director at the Center for Genetic Analysis and Technologies (CGAT), reported receiving numerous phone calls from concerned fathers across Vietnam, all seeking advice on similar cases. The first recorded case of heteropaternal twins in northern Vietnam was covered by Tuoi Tre (Youth) newspaper, prompting a wave of inquiries. The father of the twins in question, from Hoa Binh Province, was initially pressured by his relatives to undergo the DNA test due to doubts about one of the twins' real father. The results showed that he was the biological father of only one of the two babies, while his wife was the mother of both. Despite the father's initial reluctance, the DNA test confirmed the unusual situation. 

Nga emphasized that while heteropaternal twins are extremely rare, fraternal twins can look different from each other due to genetic and environmental factors. The phenomenon occurs when two ova from the same menstrual cycle are fertilized by sperm from separate acts of sexual intercourse with two different males. According to experts, the probability of such occurrences is extremely low, but not impossible. The director of the National Hospital of Obstetrics and Gynecology, Vu Ba Quyet, explained that a woman can release two ova during the same menstrual cycle, and if fertilized by sperm from different fathers, the resulting twins can have different appearances, genders, and even skin colors. Nga advised families with such doubts to avoid DNA testing, as the uncertainty can be devastating to family ties. 

The case of the Vietnamese twins has sparked interest and concern among families in Vietnam, with many fathers calling the genetic analysis center to inquire about their own children. The incident highlights the rare but real possibility of heteropaternal superfecundation and the importance of understanding the complexities of human reproduction.

At the Professional Business Women of California conference in San Francisco, Hillary Clinton highlighted the indignities faced by women in the workplace, particularly journalists and women of color. She defended April Ryan, a White House journalist, against accusations of pushing an agenda and criticized Fox News host Bill O'Reilly for making a racist comment about Rep. Maxine Waters's hair. Clinton emphasized that women, especially those of color, often endure such indignities. She urged Silicon Valley to improve diversity and inclusion, citing Uber's recent sexual harassment scandal as an example of a company struggling with these issues. In contrast, Salesforce and the Gap were praised for their commitments to equal pay and paid family leave. Clinton stressed that corporate feminism must be complemented by concrete solutions to address the broader challenges women face.

Hawaii's endangered Hawaiian monk seals are facing a significant threat from cat feces, which may be washing into the ocean and causing fatal infections. Conservationists are concerned about the feral cat population, estimated at 300,000 to 400,000 on the island of Maui alone. These cats, which are not native to Hawaii, carry a common bacterial parasite, Toxoplasma gondii, which can be deadly to monk seals. The parasite is spread through cat feces and enters the ocean via polluted runoff and sewage. Since 2001, at least eight monk seals have died from toxoplasmosis, with the latest suspected case involving a stillborn pup in January. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) estimates that the parasite has killed four monk seals in the main Hawaiian islands over the past ten years, with potential cases possibly reaching six.

The Hawaiian monk seal, an endangered species with only about 1,100 individuals left, is facing a decline in population at a rate of about 4.5 percent annually. The primary cause of death for young seals is starvation, but the threat of disease and contaminants is increasing. The seals' habitat is becoming more crowded with humans, and interactions with diseases and pollutants are becoming more frequent. The state Division of Forestry and Wildlife estimates that 300,000 to 400,000 free-ranging cats live on Maui alone, with nearly 40 percent of 67 cats captured from the slopes of Mauna Kea testing positive for toxoplasmosis. The parasite has also been found in a wide range of marine mammals, including whales, dolphins, and sea lions, and has killed seabirds and endangered Hawaiian crows and geese.

The spread of toxoplasmosis in Hawaii is a complex issue. While domestic cats are considered the main source, feral cats in remote areas also transmit the disease. In a 2007 study, 40 percent of 67 cats captured from the slopes of Mauna Kea tested positive for toxoplasmosis. The state's water quality is often impaired by pathogens and pollutants, with runoff from densely populated watersheds on Maui and Oahu likely containing pathogens. Sewage is also a significant source of pathogens, as tropical storms overwhelm aging transmission pipes and inadequate treatment systems. Injection wells on Maui have created giant wastewater plumes at some popular beaches.

Efforts to mitigate the impact of toxoplasmosis on monk seals include hunting for the pathogen and looking for signs of infection, such as swelling of the brain, lymph nodes, or lungs. NOAA is partnering with the California Marine Mammal Center to build a monk seal hospital in Kona. However, generating the political will to control cats is challenging. The Hawaiian monk seal recovery coordinator, Angela Amlin, argues that cats are not part of Hawaii's native ecosystem and should be controlled. Animal welfare advocates, such as the Hawaiian Humane Society, oppose the euthanasia of healthy felines and advocate for trapping, neutering, and spaying to control the cat population. The state's Division of Forestry and Wildlife is considering adopting a ban on feeding stray cats on state land, but this proposal was abandoned due to strong objections. The overall population's core has long been in the remote, largely uninhabited Northwest Hawaiian Islands, but more and more, conditions there are killing the seals. The greatest need for seals right now is fostering the co-existence of seals and people, as this is the most immediate threat to population growth in the main Hawaiian islands.

The number of babies born with syphilis in the United States has surged to 918 cases in 2017, marking a 46% increase from the previous year and a 20-year high, according to a report from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). This alarming rise in congenital syphilis cases highlights a broader sexually transmitted disease (STD) crisis, as total diagnoses of chlamydia, gonorrhea, and syphilis reached a record 2.3 million cases in 2017, a 200,000-case increase from the year before. The surge in syphilis diagnoses, particularly among women, has been linked to a decline in STD prevention funding and a reduction in condom use. Gay and bisexual men continue to be disproportionately affected, but the rate among reproductive-age women has increased by 143% since 2013, leading to a corresponding rise in congenital syphilis cases. The CDC reports that 37 states saw cases of congenital syphilis in 2017, with Louisiana having the highest rate. The increase in cases is attributed to a failure in ensuring women are tested for syphilis at the appropriate times during pregnancy and a lack of access to prenatal care, particularly among marginalized populations. The opioid epidemic has also contributed to the problem, as women who use drugs are more likely to engage in risky sexual behavior and less likely to receive proper treatment. Dr. Gail Bolan, director of the division of STD prevention, emphasizes that syphilis is easily curable with penicillin, and the high number of cases represents a "systemic public health failure." The National Coalition of STD Directors is calling for a public health emergency declaration and increased funding to address the issue.

Flint, Michigan, continues to grapple with the aftermath of its water crisis, as the state's governor, Rick Snyder, faces criticism for his handling of the situation. Snyder admitted that none of the corroded lead pipes, which were at the heart of the crisis, have been removed, despite reports from NBC News. The pipes, which poisoned the water supply, are still in use, raising concerns among residents about the trust issue. Snyder stated that removing the pipes isn't on his short-term agenda, focusing instead on using phosphates to coat the corroded pipes and prevent lead from leaching into the water. However, Flint Mayor Karen Weaver emphasized the urgency of pipe replacement, stating that it is "the first thing" the government needs to address to restore residents' trust. The project, estimated to cost $55 million, aims to replace 15,000 lead lines, prioritizing high-risk households. The plan, known as the Fast Start, involves collaboration between the city, state, and federal officials, with funding expected from the Michigan legislature and Congress. Snyder's commitment to the project remains uncertain, with Weaver urging him to partner with the city. The crisis began when the city switched to the Flint River as a temporary cost-saving measure, but the water was not properly treated, leading to lead contamination. The state has advised residents to use filters and drink bottled water, and the FBI is investigating the contamination. The crisis has sparked numerous lawsuits and calls for Snyder's resignation, highlighting the severity of the public health issue and the ongoing struggle for trust and accountability in Flint.

In 2019, U.S. News & World Report evaluated 41 popular diets to rank the best options for various health goals, including weight loss, diabetes management, and heart health. The DASH diet emerged as the overall top-ranked diet, excelling in short-term and long-term weight loss, nutritional completeness, and heart disease management. It was followed closely by the Mediterranean Diet, which also ranked well for preventing or managing diabetes. For weight loss specifically, the Weight Watchers and Jenny Craig diets were highly recommended. The Raw Food Diet was noted for its effectiveness in weight loss as well. The rankings considered seven key categories: short-term and long-term weight loss, diet ease, nutritional completeness, diabetes prevention and management, and heart disease management. Each diet was also assessed in five specific categories: overall diet, commercial diet plan, weight loss, diabetes, and heart-healthy diets. The DASH diet was particularly praised for its heart-healthy benefits, with the Ornish Diet topping the heart-healthy diet category. The magazine highlighted that while exercise is crucial, the primary focus of a diet is on the food choices. With 34% of U.S. adults being overweight or obese, finding the right diet can significantly impact health outcomes.

People who love horror movies often say they enjoy the unexpected adrenaline rush of gruesome, surprising scenes, often described by critics and fans as "bloodcurdling." A metaphor that may have more truth to it than previously thought, according to researchers at Leiden University Medical Center in the Netherlands. The study, published in the British Medical Journal, tested the physiological effects of horror movies on a group of volunteers, finding that fear inspired by a horror movie increased levels of clotting agents in viewers' blood. While the researchers noted this doesn't mean people's veins will start clogging while watching "Freddy Krueger" or "Saw," it does mean the term is somewhat literal. The researchers recruited 24 healthy volunteers from the hospital under age 30, showing 14 the movie "Insidious" followed by a documentary called "A Year in Champagne" separated by a week, while the other 10 were shown both movies a week apart in the reverse order. The researchers took blood samples from each participant 15 minutes before and after watching each movie. "Insidious" was found to be more frightening by viewers than the documentary, and levels of coagulating factor VIII increased in 57 percent of participants, as opposed to just 14 percent of participants' levels going up during "A Year in Champagne." During the documentary, 86 percent of the participants' levels decreased, compared to 43 percent during the horror movie. The researchers said they think the increase in the clotting factor is the body preparing to heal itself as a physical response to fear—similar to if a person is running from an animal attack but is caught, the body's preparation could help stop bleeding faster. "We suspected that fear might speed clotting in the blood," said Nemeth Banne, a researcher at Leiden University Medical Center, in a press release. "Damaged tissue gives off tissue factor, which triggers the coagulation really, but that's probably faster if there are more clotting factors in the blood." The study's findings suggest that the term "bloodcurdling" is more than just a metaphor, as fear does indeed cause the body to prepare for potential blood loss.

John Lasseter, co-founder of Pixar and Walt Disney Animation Studios, has left his position as Disney's chief creative officer, marking a significant shift in the animation industry. The decision to part ways with Lasseter was complex, with his supporters arguing that he had been unfairly swept up in the broader movement against sexual misconduct, while others felt that retaining him would divide employees and create an unsafe environment. Lasseter's departure comes amid growing criticism of Pixar's culture, which has been described as a "boys' club" where women and people of color do not have an equal creative voice. Women in Animation President Marge Dean emphasized that "misconduct" is no longer tolerated in the workplace, and the safety of all employees has become a priority for the industry. Despite the controversy, Lasseter remains dedicated to the art of animation and inspired by the creative talent at Pixar and Disney. His supporters argue that his return would be an insult to the current contributions of hundreds of employees and would demonstrate that such behavior would be tolerated by Disney-Pixar. Jennifer Lee, director of Frozen, is expected to be promoted at Walt Disney Animation, while Pete Docter, director of films like Up and Monsters, Inc., may take on greater responsibilities at Pixar. The decision to part ways with Lasseter has sparked a #LoseLasseter campaign on social media, with some employees threatening to quit if he were to return. Lasseter will serve in a consulting role at Disney throughout the end of the year, after which he will look for new creative challenges. The last six months have provided an opportunity for Lasseter to reflect on his career and personal priorities, and he remains committed to the art of animation and the creative talent at Pixar and Disney.

U.S. stocks closed lower Wednesday but recovered from session lows, with the S&P 500 holding a key technical level. Small-cap stocks and biotech firms led the initial recovery, halving their earlier intraday losses. The major averages remain in correction territory, down more than 9% year-to-date and over 10% below their 52-week intraday highs. The Dow Jones industrial average fell about 250 points, with IBM contributing significantly to declines. UnitedHealth Group made the largest positive contribution. The S&P 500 ended near 1,859, its lowest level since April 2014. The Russell 2000 closed slightly higher, while the Dow transports declined. The Nasdaq composite closed lower, its lowest since October 2014. Biotech stocks showed a late-day recovery, reversing a decline of over 3%. Veteran investor Mark D. Cook believes the market is in a bear market, citing issues with oil and gas and China's economic health. He describes four psychological stages investors go through during a bear market, currently in the denial stage. The market's heavy trading volume and sharp one-day fluctuations indicate ongoing uncertainty and volatility.

Michael James Rogan, 42, tragically lost his life in a car accident on April 17, 2015, while driving his pregnant wife Niki and their seven children to the hospital for the birth of their eighth child. The accident occurred on a rural highway in Marathon County, Wisconsin, when an oncoming vehicle struck a deer, which was then thrown into the Rogans' van, causing it to crash. Michael was pronounced dead at St. Joseph's Hospital in Marshfield, while Niki gave birth to their son, Blaise, hours later. The children, ranging in age from 2 to 15, suffered only minor injuries.

Michael, a former U.S. Marine Corps corporal, was known for his strong faith and dedication to his family. He was actively involved in his local church, singing in the choir and leading a boys' group. After his father-in-law's death, Michael took over the family's organic seed and fertilizer business. His wife, Niki, is a stay-at-home mom who homeschools the children. The family's support system is rallying to help them through this difficult time, with fundraising efforts underway to cover funeral and medical expenses, as well as to provide a safety net for the future.

Michael's death has left a profound impact on his community, with friends and family stepping forward to offer support. The family's fundraising campaign, led by Dominic and Cecilia Gruetzmacher, aims to assist in the purchase of a replacement vehicle, cover funeral and medical expenses, and create a financial buffer for the family's future needs. Donations can be made online or by mailing checks to the Rogan Fund, PO Box 5132, Wausau, WI 54402-5132. The community's response to the Rogans' loss has been overwhelming, with numerous media outlets covering the story and offering condolences and support.

Jared Fogle, the former Subway pitchman now serving a 15-year sentence for child pornography, is attempting to use the case of Larry Nassar, the disgraced former USA Gymnastics doctor, to argue for a more lenient sentence. In a legal filing, Fogle questions why Nassar, who was convicted of similar crimes, was not charged with the same travel-related offenses that Fogle was. Fogle argues that Nassar was not charged with "travel for the purpose of engaging in illicit sexual conduct," despite allegedly engaging in unlawful acts with young women. Fogle claims he was unfairly targeted with this charge, suggesting it was part of a broader effort by prosecutors to force him to plead guilty to avoid financial ruin. He also accuses his legal team of pressuring him into a guilty plea and cites his own "alcohol and sex addictions" as factors in his criminal behavior. Fogle is now seeking to withdraw his guilty plea, arguing that the courts have made a "grave error of the law." His motion highlights the disparity in treatment between himself and Nassar, who received a 175-year sentence, and suggests that similar charges should have been applied to both. The court has yet to respond to Fogle's motion, but his argument raises questions about the fairness of his original plea deal and the application of the law in high-profile cases.

Justin Bieber's behavior continues to anger passengers and neighbors alike. During a 12-hour flight from his recent Down Under promotional tour, Bieber and his entourage were overheard using profanity, much to the annoyance of a female passenger. The mother of two approached Bieber, asking him to "stop yelling curse words and using that kind of language on a plane. It's not appropriate." Embarrassed, Bieber quickly apologized and attempted to serenade the woman with an a cappella version of "Boyfriend," though the plan didn't come to fruition. Meanwhile, across the ocean, Bieber's new neighbors, actors Kristen Bell and Dax Shepard, are not fans of the pop star. They recently moved into a house behind Bieber's, and the constant noise and parties have made their lives difficult. Shepard humorously compared their new neighborhood to "living in Lebanon now." Bell, while diplomatically noting they can't pinpoint the exact source of the music, acknowledges that since Bieber moved in, the music has been blaring. Both incidents highlight the challenges Bieber's fame presents to those around him.

A treasure trove of rare gold coins discovered by a California couple while out walking their dog has gone on sale, with one coin selling for $15,000 on Tuesday. The coins, dating from 1847 to 1894, have been valued at $11 million. Don Kagin, a numismatist handling the sale, says most of the remaining 1,400 coins had gone on sale on Amazon.com and Kagins.com after the auction. The couple, a middle-aged husband and wife, found the coins last year buried under the shadow of a tree on their rural Northern California property. They plan to keep a few of the coins themselves and use the money from the rest to pay off bills and donate to local charities. Money from Tuesday's auction will benefit the effort to turn the Old Mint into a museum. Experts say the coins are extremely rare and valuable, as paper money was illegal in California until the 1870s, and most of the coins are in mint condition. Kagin says the coins were minted at the San Francisco Mint, but it's unclear who put them in the ground or how they were obtained, as theories linking the coins to stagecoach bandit Black Bart, outlaw Jesse James, and a theft at the San Francisco Mint have not panned out. The collection consists of four $5 gold pieces, fifty $10 gold pieces, and 1,373 $20 double eagles, with the crown jewel being an 1866-S No Motto $20 gold piece valued at more than $1 million. This coin find is called the largest such discovery in U.S. history, surpassing previous finds such as the $1 million worth of coins uncovered by construction workers in Jackson, Tennessee, in 1985, and the $7.3 million worth of silver dollars found in the home of a Reno, Nevada, man who died in 1974.

The United Nations Security Council unanimously passed Resolution 2371 on Saturday, imposing stringent sanctions on North Korea for its continued intercontinental ballistic missile (ICBM) testing and violations of UN resolutions. The sanctions target North Korea’s primary exports, including coal, iron, iron ore, lead, lead ore, and seafood, as well as other revenue streams such as banks and joint ventures with foreign companies. These measures are expected to reduce North Korea’s annual export revenue by over a third, amounting to approximately $1 billion. The resolution represents the strongest sanctions ever imposed in response to a ballistic missile test, according to a statement from the US ambassador to the UN.

In response, North Korea’s state-run newspaper, Rodong Sinmun, warned that the US mainland would face an “unimaginable sea of fire” if it dared to touch the country. The UN Security Council’s resolution also bans countries from hiring additional North Korean workers, a move designed to cut off another source of hard currency for the regime. Nine people and four business entities, including a major North Korean bank, were placed on a UN blacklist, facing asset freezes or travel bans.

The resolution was passed with the support of the United States, China, and Russia, despite China’s opposition to more severe restrictions. The sanctions are expected to significantly impact North Korea’s economy, potentially causing significant damage to the foreign currency income of North Korean elites and potentially undermining Kim Jong Un’s leadership. However, experts suggest that the regime is likely to prioritize its military spending and may not be deterred by economic sanctions alone. The United States and China remain at odds over the approach to North Korea, with China urging dialogue and the US emphasizing the need for continued pressure.

The sanctions are part of a broader effort by the international community to address North Korea’s nuclear and missile programs. The resolution also includes a call for North Korea to halt its nuclear and missile tests and to return to the negotiation table. While the sanctions are a significant step, experts are skeptical that they will be enough to compel North Korea to abandon its nuclear program, given the regime’s determination to remain nuclear and its history of prioritizing military spending over economic development.

A new study published in Molecular Psychiatry suggests that genes linked to an increased risk of schizophrenia may also predispose individuals to use cannabis more frequently. Researchers from King's College London analyzed genetic data from over 1,000 cannabis users and found that those with genetic markers associated with schizophrenia were more likely to use cannabis and use it in greater quantities. This finding challenges the traditional view that cannabis use alone can lead to schizophrenia, suggesting instead that common genetic factors might influence both behaviors. The study indicates that people genetically predisposed to schizophrenia might be more inclined to use cannabis, highlighting the complex interplay between genetics and environmental factors. However, experts caution that this does not rule out the possibility that cannabis use can increase the risk of developing schizophrenia in those who are already genetically predisposed. The results underscore the need for further research to understand the precise nature of the relationship between cannabis use and schizophrenia, emphasizing the importance of considering genetic overlap when evaluating the health and economic impacts of cannabis use.

Republican legislation allowing states to deny federal family planning money to Planned Parenthood and other abortion providers narrowly passed the Senate on Thursday, thanks to a tie-breaking vote by Vice President Mike Pence. The bill, which erases a regulation imposed by former President Obama, was passed with a 51-50 vote, with two GOP senators, Alaska's Lisa Murkowski and Maine's Susan Collins, joining Democrats in opposing the measure. The legislation, which has already been approved by the House, will now go to President Donald Trump for his signature. The move is seen as a victory for anti-abortion groups and Republicans, who have long sought to give states more freedom to decide how to spend family planning funds. The federal family planning program, established in 1970, serves 4 million clients at nearly 4,000 clinics, with most recipients being women and two-thirds having incomes at or below the federal poverty level. Democrats criticized the measure, calling it an attack on women's health care. The Congressional Review Act allows lawmakers to undo regulations enacted in the last months of the Obama administration with a majority vote. The vice president's tie-breaking vote was necessary after two Republican senators defected, and the measure was passed just days after the Republican health care overhaul failed in the House. The vote was seen as a significant political statement, with Vice President Pence's appearance in the Senate chamber marking the second time he has cast a tie-breaking vote to move legislation. The measure is expected to face further challenges as Democrats vow to fight efforts to strip federal dollars from Planned Parenthood through other means.

Eating a small amount of chocolate every week may reduce the risk of atrial fibrillation, a common and serious type of irregular heartbeat, according to a new study from Denmark. Researchers found that people who ate chocolate one to three times per month were about 10 percent less likely to be diagnosed with atrial fibrillation than those who ate it less than once a month. The study, published in the journal Heart, analyzed data from 55,502 people in Denmark who were between 50 and 64 years old when they entered a long-term study between 1993 and 1997. The researchers linked this dietary data to Denmark’s national health registries to track atrial fibrillation diagnoses over an average of 13.5 years. They found that those who ate one serving, about 1 ounce (28.35 grams), of chocolate per week were 17 percent less likely to be diagnosed with atrial fibrillation by the end of the study than those who ate it less than once a month. Similarly, those who ate 2 to 6 ounces per week were 20 percent less likely, while those who ate more than an ounce daily were 16 percent less likely to have the condition. The strongest risk reduction was observed in women who ate one serving per week and in men who ate two to six servings per week.

Lead author Elizabeth Mostofsky, a researcher at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health and Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center, noted that moderate chocolate intake as part of a healthy diet is a heart-healthy snack choice. The study suggests that the flavanols in chocolate, which have anti-inflammatory, blood vessel-relaxing, and antioxidant properties, may help prevent atrial fibrillation. However, the study cannot definitively say that chocolate was the cause of the reduced risk, and other factors such as physical activity and overall diet may play a role. Dr. Alice Lichtenstein, director and senior scientist at the Cardiovascular Nutrition Laboratory at Tufts University, emphasized that a healthy diet, regular physical activity, and not smoking are essential for optimal health. She noted that while chocolate may be a part of a heart-healthy diet, it should not be seen as a quick fix. Dr. Sean Pokorney and Jonathan Piccini, cardiologists at Duke University Medical Center, wrote in an accompanying editorial that the study’s findings are interesting and warrant further consideration, but a double-blind randomized controlled trial is needed to evaluate the true efficacy of chocolate for preventing atrial fibrillation.

In the late 20th and early 21st century, Brazil significantly reduced deforestation rates, becoming a global leader in forest conservation. However, these gains are now at risk due to the proposed environmental policies of Jair Bolsonaro, the far-right candidate poised to become Brazil’s next president. Bolsonaro has pledged to dismantle Brazil’s environmental ministry, relax environmental law enforcement, and open indigenous reserves to mining. His policies could lead to unprecedented Amazon deforestation, contributing to global climate instability. An economic modeling study suggests that without environmental protections, the average annual loss of primary forest in the Amazon could rise to 25,600 square kilometers per year, a 268% increase from 2017. This would equate to the deforestation rates seen at the beginning of the 2000s and could result in the loss of 46,300 square kilometers of protected areas within a decade. Bolsonaro's policies could also make it all but impossible for Brazil to meet its international climate commitments. The loss of biodiversity and climate regulation from such dramatic changes would have global consequences, pushing the Amazon closer to a tipping point where it could transition to a savanna-like ecosystem. This transition would release massive amounts of carbon dioxide, exacerbating climate change. Environmentalists warn that deforestation is likely to become more acute under Bolsonaro, with dire consequences for the Amazon and the world.

During Donald Trump's inauguration, former President George W. Bush faced a unique challenge: putting on a poncho. He discussed this humorous moment on The Ellen DeGeneres Show, where he joked, "Yeah, it looks like it." His mother, former first lady Barbara Bush, had also struggled with the poncho at an inauguration. Bush's friendship with Michelle Obama, the former first lady, has been widely publicized. They frequently sat together at official events and shared genuine moments of camaraderie, such as hugging during the dedication ceremony for the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture. Bush expressed interest in working with the Obamas to help military personnel and families. His candid comment, "That was some weird shit," about the inauguration, reflects the surreal nature of the event.

Harold Hayes, now 98, was one of the first medics added to the 807th Medical Air Evacuation Transport Squadron in Catania, Sicily, in 1943. On November 8, 1943, Hayes and 29 others boarded a transport plane to Bari, Italy, but the plane crashed in Nazi-occupied Albania. For months, Hayes and the group traversed treacherous terrain, dodged German troops, and faced extreme hunger and illness. They were aided by Albanian partisans and villagers, but were forbidden from discussing their experiences for decades. Hayes, the only surviving member of the group, recounts their harrowing journey in Cate Lineberry's book, "The Secret Rescue."

The group's flight was cut short when they encountered a storm, causing their plane to crash-land in a marsh. They were initially guided by Albanian partisans, but soon found themselves in a dangerous situation, caught between rival partisan groups and German forces. The Americans were forced to walk for miles, often in circles to avoid German patrols, and faced harsh winter conditions. They were eventually rescued by British and American forces, but three nurses remained behind in Berat, Albania, until they were brought to safety in March 1944.

Hayes, a medic from Indianola, Iowa, and the youngest of the group at 21, played a crucial role in their survival. Despite the dangers, he helped treat injuries and illnesses and maintained morale. The group's ordeal lasted 63 days, and upon their return to Allied lines, Hayes struggled with nightmares and rarely spoke about his experiences. His story, along with those of the other survivors, has been preserved in Lineberry's book, which highlights the bravery and resilience of these American heroes.

Eastern Ghouta, a rebel-held enclave near Damascus, is facing a humanitarian catastrophe as forces loyal to Syria's Bashar al-Assad intensify airstrikes and shelling, killing almost 200 civilians in two days. Amnesty International described the situation as a "flagrant war crime" on an "epic scale," with seven hospitals bombed and medical facilities struggling to treat the injured. The White Helmets, a volunteer rescue group, reported the death of one of their members, Firas Juma, while responding to a bombing. The UN expressed outrage, warning that the targeting of civilians in Eastern Ghouta "must stop now." Meanwhile, pro-government forces are also expected to enter the northern Kurdish-controlled enclave of Afrin, where Turkish troops have been on the offensive for a month. The UN's Regional Humanitarian Coordinator for the Syria Crisis, Panos Moumtzis, emphasized the urgent need to halt the senseless human suffering. The relentless bombardment has forced thousands of civilians to flee their homes, seeking refuge in makeshift shelters or basements. The situation in Eastern Ghouta is described as akin to the "day of judgment," with medical workers and residents alike expressing despair and fear for their lives. The humanitarian crisis has escalated, with medical facilities struggling to cope and the death toll rising. The UN and aid organizations warn that the situation could unfold into the worst atrocity of the war so far, potentially eclipsing past atrocities in the seven-year conflict.

On August 29, 2015, a series of shooting incidents occurred along Interstate 10 in Phoenix, Arizona, over a three-day period, raising concerns among drivers and prompting authorities to intensify their investigation. The first incident happened eastbound on I-10 at 11:03 a.m., where a sport utility vehicle was struck, and a 13-year-old female passenger sustained a minor injury to her right ear. The second shooting took place westbound between 35th Avenue and 59th Avenue at 11:09 a.m., involving a passenger-type bus with only the driver on board, who was not injured. The third shooting occurred eastbound near 16th Street at approximately 10:15 p.m., where a vehicle's passenger side was damaged by bullet holes, though the driver did not inspect the vehicle until Sunday. The fourth and final shooting was reported eastbound near 24th Street at 4:25 a.m. on August 31, 2015, where a man driving a work truck heard a loud bang, thinking a rock had struck the vehicle. Upon inspection, a bullet had damaged the driver's side front headlamp. 

Arizona State troopers are investigating these incidents, which spanned a 24-hour period and involved multiple vehicles. The shooter's motive remains unclear, and authorities are seeking public assistance to identify the suspect. The Arizona Department of Public Safety is offering a $10,000 reward for information leading to an arrest. Drivers are advised to remain vigilant and report any suspicious activity. The incidents highlight the ongoing concern for public safety and the need for increased awareness among motorists.

Scientists have uncovered what they believe to be the oldest evidence of life on Earth, potentially dating back 3.7 billion years. This discovery, led by University College London PhD student Matthew Dodd, involves tiny tubes and filaments found in rocks from Quebec's Nuvvuagittuq belt, one of the oldest rock formations on the planet. These structures, embedded within iron minerals that formed near ancient hydrothermal vents, are reminiscent of iron-oxidizing bacteria found in modern vents. The researchers argue that the consistent size and shape of these structures, along with the presence of carbon-rich material and specific isotopic ratios, strongly suggest a biological origin. However, the findings are not without controversy, as many experts remain skeptical. Martin J. Van Kranendonk, a geologist from the University of New South Wales, refers to these patterns as "dubiofossils," indicating that while they may be fossil-like, their biological nature is not definitively proven. The discovery, if confirmed, would push back the known timeline of life on Earth by millions of years and support the idea that hydrothermal vents could have been the cradle of life. This finding also opens up new possibilities for the search for life on other planets, as hydrothermal vents are now considered prime targets for exploration. Despite the skepticism, the multiple lines of evidence presented by the researchers make a compelling case, and the scientific community will likely continue to debate the findings for years to come.

While detectives in California struggled to identify the Golden State Killer, one of his distant relatives was likely busy constructing a family tree. The suspect, Joseph James DeAngelo, 72, was arrested on suspicion of a reign of terror that spanned 1976 to 1986, including 12 homicides, 45 rapes, and over 100 residential burglaries. The key to his identification came from a genealogical website called GEDmatch, which allows users to voluntarily share their genetic profiles for free. Lead investigator Paul Holes, a retired Contra Costa County District Attorney inspector, began his search six years ago and eventually used GEDmatch to identify a potential suspect. The site returned a list of relatives, with names and emails, based on shared single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Third and fourth cousins, related to DeAngelo's great, great, great, great grandfather dating back to the 1800s, provided crucial information. Holes and his team built out more than 25 different family trees, eventually linking to the Golden State Killer. The process involved a painstaking search, including ethnicity, height, and location, supplemented by surveillance and new evidence such as saliva on a restaurant dish or a discarded beer can, cigarette, or Kleenex. The case highlights the potential for genealogical websites to be used by law enforcement, even when individuals have never submitted their DNA directly to a law enforcement database. The openness of GEDmatch, which contains 900,000 DNA files, makes it a valuable tool for investigators. However, it also raises concerns about the privacy of genetic information. While major companies like 23andMe and Ancestry.com require a court order for law enforcement access, GEDmatch does not have such restrictions. The arrest of DeAngelo demonstrates the potential of this technology but also underscores the need for legal and ethical considerations. The case has reignited debates about genetic privacy and the use of genetic information in criminal investigations.

Defense Secretary Ash Carter faced criticism from lawmakers during a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing when he reported that the $500 million program to train and equip "moderate" Syrian rebels had yielded only 60 vetted candidates as of July 3, far below the goal of 5,400 fighters in the first year. Republicans, including Senate Armed Services Committee Chairman John McCain, used this to argue that President Barack Obama’s strategy for defeating the Islamic State is ineffective. Democrats, such as Senate Armed Services Committee ranking member Jack Reed, defended the program, noting that the vetting process is rigorous and that the number of recruits is expected to increase as the program matures. Carter acknowledged that the vetting process is slowing down the recruitment, but emphasized that the program is in its early stages and that the U.S. is learning more about the opposition groups, which will help in attracting recruits. However, McCain and other Republicans were unconvinced, arguing that the U.S. needs to provide more direct support, such as air cover, to the Syrian fighters to ensure their safety and effectiveness. The debate highlights the challenges of engaging local partners in the fight against the Islamic State and the need for a more comprehensive strategy.

The House of Representatives, in a week of deliberate inaction, is focused on a bill to rename the Dryden Flight Research Center after Neil A. Armstrong, the first man to walk on the moon. This seemingly trivial matter, however, is being used by Republicans as a way to highlight their strategy of inaction in the face of the looming sequester. The sequester, automatic across-the-board spending cuts, is set to take effect on Friday, but House Republicans are embracing it, as it will result in a 2.5% cut in federal spending without requiring any tax increases. President Obama is advocating for tax increases and alternative spending cuts to replace the sequester, but House Republicans are sticking to their guns, with Speaker John Boehner instructing Obama to "sit down with Harry Reid tonight and work with Senate Democrats." The House has been in session for only 20 of the 56 days so far in 2013, with most of those days consisting of pro-forma sessions or with very little legislative activity. The chamber is scheduled to be out of town on Friday, when the sequester is set to take effect, and is planning another recess at the end of March, when the federal government is due to shut down for lack of funding. The irony of the situation is not lost on some, as Rep. Donna Edwards noted, "We will do our renaming today, and then we will take an ax hammer to NASA’s budget on March 1, at the end of this week, taking out $894 million from an already strapped budget." The sequester, designed to be so horrible that both parties would recoil from it, is being embraced by Republicans, who are using it to avoid another deal like the one in December that raised taxes. The only thing that is not being cut under the sequester are the salaries of senators and representatives, which will continue to roll in, even as other areas of the budget are slashed.

A 95-year-old New York City man, Jakiw Palij, believed to be a former guard at a labor camp in Nazi-occupied Poland, has been deported to Germany after being arrested and deported by U.S. immigration authorities. Palij, who served as a guard at the Trawniki Labor Camp, where about 6,000 Jewish men, women, and children were shot dead on November 3, 1943, was taken to an elderly home in the western town of Ahlen, some 130 kilometers northeast of Düsseldorf. Born in what is now Ukraine, Palij emigrated to the United States in 1949 and became a U.S. citizen in 1957. However, he concealed his Nazi service and involvement in human rights abuses, claiming he had worked on a farm and in a factory during World War II. In 2001, Palij admitted to training at the Nazi SS Training Camp in Trawniki in 1943. The White House stated that by serving as an armed guard and preventing the escape of Jewish prisoners, Palij played an indispensable role in ensuring the Trawniki Jewish victims met their fate at the hands of the Nazis. A federal judge revoked his U.S. citizenship in 2003, and he was ordered to be deported in 2004, but no European country would accept him until Germany agreed to take him in. 

In Germany, being a member of a criminal organization like the SS is not enough to be prosecuted. Even being trained at a camp is not sufficient; the participation in or facilitation of a murder must be proven. Germany has a mixed record on convicting Nazi war criminals, with critics arguing that it let many high-ranking Nazis and SS members escape justice while focusing on their juniors. Between 1945 and 2005, West German courts convicted 6,656 Nazi criminals out of more than 36,000 investigations into over 170,000 suspects. Germany's Central Office for the Investigation of Nazi Crimes in Ludwigsburg is still investigating individuals, inspired by the 2011 conviction of Sobibor death camp guard John Demjanjuk, which showed that involvement in a camp was sufficient to be found culpable even without proof of a specific crime. The office is currently unable to prove where, when, and which unit Palij was in after his training, leaving the possibility of prosecution uncertain.

California water officials are considering a proposal that could end the state's mandatory water conservation rules, allowing local communities to set their own water use targets. This shift, proposed by the State Water Resources Control Board, aims to give cities and water districts more flexibility in managing their water supplies, especially as the state experiences a relatively wet winter. The proposal would let local areas compare their water supplies with anticipated needs if the drought persists for three more years, enabling them to set conservation targets accordingly. This regional approach is seen as a positive move by some, such as Greg Gritters, a Southern California landscaper, who believes local water officials are better equipped to manage water use. The Irvine Ranch Water District in Orange County has led the push for this regional approach, confident that districts will carefully assess their supply and demand ratios. Bans on water waste, such as washing sidewalks with a hose or washing cars without a shut-off nozzle, would remain in place. Despite the potential lifting of statewide mandates, Max Gomberg, a senior climate scientist for the state water board, remains optimistic that Californians will continue to conserve water. The proposal, which is set to extend until January, reflects the state's ongoing struggle with drought and the need for adaptable water management strategies.

Ben Friberg, a Tennessee musician, has achieved the first solo paddleboard crossing of the Florida Straits from Cuba to the Florida Keys, covering 110 miles in 28 hours, with his father watching from a support boat. Friberg, 35, aimed to promote peace and understanding between the United States and Cuba, as well as a healthy lifestyle. He stood on his 14-foot-long board for most of the journey, sitting only for quick snacks. The support boat included a medic and a navigator. Friberg wore protective gear, including a long-billed cap, a close-fitting long-sleeve shirt, gloves, and special socks. He broke the record for the longest stand-up paddleboard journey in 24 hours last year, traveling 238 miles on Canada's Yukon River. At least two Cubans have made the trip by surfboard, with Cuban-born doctor Ernesto Barral completing the journey in 1992, and Miami lifeguard Cynthia Aguilar making the crossing in 2011. Only Australian swimmer Susan Maroney has succeeded in crossing the straits without a shark cage. Friberg's journey highlights the growing popularity of long-distance paddleboarding and the challenges faced by endurance athletes in achieving their goals.

Massachusetts Republicans are facing a daunting challenge in their quest to field a candidate for the special Senate election to replace outgoing Democratic Senator John Kerry. Following Scott Brown's decision to pass on the race, the party found itself in a scramble to identify a viable alternative. However, a veritable who’s who of local GOP bigwigs have been avoiding the race, leaving the party with a short list of little-known contenders, if any at all. “It reminds me of the Three Stooges episode where the sergeant says ‘I need volunteers for a dangerous mission. Step forward,’ and they all step back,” said Sen. Robert Hedlund (R-Weymouth). Among those who have ruled themselves out are Tagg Romney, Mitt Romney’s eldest son, who told the Daily News on Monday that he will not launch a bid for the Senate seat. Tagg, who got campaign experience speaking on his father’s behalf during last year’s presidential race, said he is currently committed to his business and to spending as much time as he can with his wife and children. The timing is not right for him, he added, but he is hopeful that the people of Massachusetts will select someone of great integrity, vision, and compassion as their next US Senator. The Boston Herald reported early Monday that Tagg was considering a bid for Kerry’s seat, after Brown’s decision left Republicans scrambling for an alternative. Tagg Romney, the wealthy founder of a private equity firm, was a visible surrogate for his father’s campaign in the closing days of last year’s race. There were also reports that Tagg, frustrated that his father was being caricatured as a hopelessly unlikeable plutocrat, was taking a more aggressive role in running the campaign. But those reports infuriated Tagg, and he told associates at the time that he'd never run for any public office. William “Mo” Cowan, a former aide to Massachusetts Governor Deval Patrick, is filling Kerry’s Senate seat until a special election decides his long-term replacement in June.

In 2012, Anthony Hensley, a 37-year-old father from Villa Park, Illinois, drowned after being attacked by a swan while kayaking in a retention pond at the Bay Colony condominium complex in Maine Township. The aggressive swan, which had been nesting, continued to attack Hensley as he attempted to swim to shore. His widow, Amy Hensley, filed a wrongful death lawsuit in Cook County Circuit Court against the property management companies that owned and operated the complex, seeking at least $50,000 in damages. The lawsuit alleges the companies and homeowners/condominium associations were negligent in keeping the dangerous swans on the premises. Hensley had a history of tending to the swans, which were brought in to control the geese population. The lawsuit contends the companies should have known the swans' dangerous nature and should be held liable for their actions. The case highlights the risks associated with wildlife management practices, particularly when animals are kept on residential properties. The death was ruled an accident, but Hensley's family remains heartbroken, and the incident has left a gap in the community. The lawsuit seeks to hold the property management companies accountable for the swans' actions, emphasizing the need for better safety measures in such situations.

In a dramatic rescue, DeKalb County firefighter Robert Sutton caught a baby tossed from the second floor window of a burning apartment building in Decatur, Georgia. The father, desperate to save his child from smoke and flames, threw the baby to Sutton, who was among the first firefighters on the scene. Sutton, a 10-year veteran, credited his training and being in the right place at the right time. The baby and his family escaped without injury. Master plumber Larry Carter recorded the rescue on video, capturing Sutton's swift action. Captain Tom Burrell praised Sutton's heroism, emphasizing the importance of training and situational awareness. Sutton, a father himself, remained humble, deflecting credit to his crew. The incident highlights the bravery and quick thinking of firefighters in critical situations.

U.S. researchers have developed a method to detect Alzheimer's through antibodies in the blood, potentially leading to a blood test within months. The study, published in Cell, found that three peptoids reacted strongly with antibodies in the blood of six Alzheimer's patients but not in healthy controls. This approach, which screens for antibodies rather than specific antigens, could be applied to other diseases. Thomas Kodadek of the Scripps Research Institute licensed the technology to OPKO Health Inc., which plans to develop diagnostic kits. These tests could help pharmaceutical companies in patient stratification for clinical trials. While the test shows promise, it needs further validation in larger populations and early-stage patients. Early diagnosis is crucial for developing effective treatments, though some patients may not want to know years ahead of time they are at risk.

Pro-democracy activists in Hong Kong vowed to bring the financial hub to a standstill after China's parliament rejected their demands for the right to freely choose the next leader in 2017. The Standing Committee of the National People's Congress (NPC) endorsed a framework that limits the number of candidates to two or three, all of whom must first obtain majority backing from a nominating committee likely to be stacked with Beijing loyalists. This decision, while hailed by Chief Executive Leung Chun-ying as a significant step forward, is seen as a setback by pro-democracy groups, who fear it makes it almost impossible for opposition democrats to get on the ballot. Founders of the Occupy Central civil disobedience movement, including academic Chan Kin-man, academic Benny Tai, and Reverend Chu Yiu-ming, prepared to stage a small protest late on Sunday to formally launch a campaign of civil disobedience, aiming to culminate in a blockade of Hong Kong's Central business district. Leung Chun-ying said Beijing's decision represented a major step forward in Hong Kong's development, but political reform has been a constant source of friction between the pro-democracy movement and mainland China since the city's return to Chinese rule in 1997. The United States responded cautiously, supporting Hong Kong's "traditions and Basic Law protections of internationally recognized freedoms, including the freedom of peaceful assembly and freedom of expression," while warning that the legitimacy of the chief executive will be greatly enhanced if the election provides the people of Hong Kong a genuine choice of candidates representative of the voters’ will. Despite the NPC's decision, some democrats said Beijing was pushing a Chinese-style version of "fake" democracy. The proposed electoral framework still needs approval by two-thirds of Hong Kong's 70-seat legislature, which is likely to be shelved due to the presence of pro-democracy lawmakers. In nearby Macau, another special administrative region, leader and sole candidate Fernando Chui was "re-elected" by a select panel of 400 largely pro-China loyalists, prompting thousands of residents to demand universal suffrage. The election took place a day after an unofficial seven-day "civil referendum" in which 95% of 8,688 residents voted in favor of universal suffrage for the 2019 election. While Macau's mini-constitution makes no mention of universal suffrage as a goal, calls for democracy have been growing. Chui acknowledged shortfalls in his first term, focusing on economic diversification away from the gambling sector, which generates more income in the former Portuguese enclave than anywhere else in the world. The re-election of Chui and the NPC's decision on Hong Kong's 2017 election framework have raised concerns about the future of democracy in both regions, with activists and observers closely watching the developments.

Bloodied bodies line the streets and basements of Dariya, a Damascus suburb, where a pro-government offensive has left at least 320 people dead, opposition activists report. Video footage shows groups being buried in a mass grave, and activists claim many victims were executed after being taken prisoner. The Syrian Observatory for Human Rights estimates over 1,400 people have been killed in the Damascus suburbs since March. The government denies responsibility, blaming "terrorists," while opposition groups accuse the military of summary executions and house raids.
