UN Secretary-General Ban Ki-moon demands an independent inquiry into the reported massacre. The UN and world leaders condemn the killings, with France calling it an "atrocity on a new scale." The conflict continues, with reports of shelling and clashes in various Damascus districts.

Belgium's royal family will start paying taxes for the first time, marking a significant change as they align with other monarchies in Europe, reports Reuters. The Belgian government approved a reform, effective from 2014, which will see the royal family lose some state allowances and exemptions from income and value-added tax. Queen Fabiola, the widow of King Baudouin, will see her annual allowance cut sharply to about 450,000 euros from 1.3 million euros. Crown Prince Philippe's siblings, Princess Astrid and Prince Laurent, will continue to receive allowances set at about half the amount received by their older brother. The king, Albert II, will remain exempt from the changes due to constitutional restrictions. The reform aims to bring the Belgian royal family into line with other European monarchies, which have also been facing budget cuts.

A kayaker fishing for salmon off Waukegan Harbor on Monday morning stumbled upon an unexpected visitor in Lake Michigan—a 4-foot-long American alligator. David Castaneda, a Chicago resident, had been paddling for about four hours when he noticed something floating in the water. Thinking it was a dead salmon, he approached and discovered an alligator head. Castaneda called 911, and Waukegan’s Animal Control responded. The alligator, with its mouth taped shut, was taken to the Wildlife Discovery Center in Lake Forest, where Rob Carmichael, the curator, assessed its condition. Carmichael stated that the alligator was likely to survive only a couple more weeks due to the cooling waters of Lake Michigan. An investigation into whether the animal was abandoned, a crime, will be conducted. The city initially reported the animal as a caiman but later confirmed it to be an American alligator. The discovery of exotic animals in Lake Michigan is rare, as state regulations have made it more difficult to own such species without permits. In the past, similar incidents involved a 14-foot Burmese python found near Waukegan Harbor in 2012 and an alligator found in the Chicago River in 2010.

Another schoolgirl kidnapped by Boko Haram in 2014 was released on Thursday, two days after Amina Ali Darsha Nkeki was found by a vigilante militant group. The Nigerian military reported that Serah Luka had been "rescued" on Thursday morning, along with 96 other women and children held captive by Boko Haram. An army spokesman, Sani Kukasheka Usman, said that 35 Boko Haram fighters had also been killed in "clearance operations." If the claim is accurate, Serah Luka would be the second of the Chibok girls to escape a Boko Haram camp in Sambisa forest within two days. The first girl, Amina Ali Darsha Nkeki, met President Muhammadu Buhari on Thursday, having been found by members of a vigilante group on Tuesday. She had been a student at the Chibok school at the time of the abduction and hailed from Madagali, Adamawa State. Luka was found with a man who claimed to be her husband, Mohammed Hayatu, whom the army suspects is a Boko Haram fighter. Hayatu was not present at the presidential villa but was being investigated. The president pledged to continue the search for the remaining Chibok girls and promised Luka "the best care" that the Nigerian government could afford, including medical, psychological, and educational support. In her first two days of freedom, Luka met with dozens of Nigerian dignitaries. She was briefly allowed home so that her family could identify her before being airlifted to Maiduguri, the capital of Borno state, for medical checks and trauma counseling. She and her baby had further medical examinations and were then flown to Abuja to meet Buhari. The Nigerian army's claims of rescue have been criticized for attempting to claim credit and for parading the girl at a press conference. Activists and residents of Chibok dispute the army's account, stating that the rescued girl was actually kidnapped from her home elsewhere. The army's statements about the Chibok girls have been inconsistent, having claimed to have freed over 100 of them before later backtracking. The first of the Chibok girls, Amina Ali Nkeki, was found trying to hide from the vigilantes after running away from the Boko Haram camp. She was with a man who claimed to be her husband, Mohammed Hayatu, whom the army suspects is a Boko Haram fighter. Hayatu was not at the presidential villa but was being investigated. Buhari held the baby Amina gave birth to while a captive of the terror group, and expressed deep sadness at the horrors the young girl had endured. The Nigerian army has been trying to win public support following criticism for its inability to bring back the schoolgirls, despite rescuing thousands of Boko Haram captives. The army's focus on the Chibok girls' fate has been criticized as using their release as a measure of success in the fight against Boko Haram. The abduction of 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in April 2014 gained international attention through the #BringBackOurGirls campaign, supported by figures such as US First Lady Michelle Obama and Pakistani activist Malala Yousafzai. Boko Haram, based mainly in Nigeria's northern states, has pursued a campaign of terror, including the kidnapping of thousands of women and girls, and has been responsible for numerous attacks in neighboring countries.

A Detroit couple, Rosita and Johnny Toaster, have been searching for their missing 28-year-old daughter, Crissita Cage-Toaster, since her disappearance in October 2009. Crissita's car was found abandoned on Belle Isle, with her purse, ID, and cellphone inside. The Toasters, who now live in Atlanta, reported her missing and provided a detailed description of their daughter, including a distinctive tattoo of a large red rose with their nicknames. Despite their efforts, they received no updates until April 2017, when the National Institute of Justice contacted Detroit police after the Toasters urged them to focus on the tattoo. Police then made the connection between a body found in the Detroit River in 2010 and Crissita's case.

Crissita's body was pulled from the river five months after she was reported missing, but it was never linked to her case. The Wayne County Medical Examiner's Office and Detroit police records listed her ethnicity as Caucasian or Hispanic, despite her being black. The body was buried in an unmarked grave at Knollwood Cemetery in Canton Township, where it remained for over six years. The Toasters, who were notified of the exhumation plans, are frustrated with the handling of the case, believing that the tattoo could have been used to identify the body much earlier. They claim that the Detroit Police Department and the Wayne County Medical Examiner's Office are at fault for the mix-up, and that the body was never properly investigated or identified.

Detroit Police Lieutenant Kenneth Gardner stated that the team today was able to connect the dots in 24 hours, but the Toasters argue that the inconsistencies in the case are too numerous to be explained by simple oversight. They believe that the cause of death, which was ruled as undetermined, is more than just a mix-up and that there may be more to the story. The Toasters are seeking a proper burial for their daughter and hope to retrieve her personal belongings, which were reportedly destroyed by the police. The case highlights the importance of thorough and accurate record-keeping in missing persons and unidentified remains investigations.

Survivors of one of Australia's deadliest wildfires, which killed 119 people and destroyed over 2,000 homes in 2009, are to receive nearly 500 million Australian dollars ($470 million) in a class action settlement, the largest such compensation in the nation's history. The fire, part of a series of blazes that swept through the southern state of Victoria, occurred on Black Saturday, February 7, 2009. More than 5,000 people joined the lawsuit against electricity provider SP AusNet, alleging negligence due to inadequate maintenance of power lines that sparked the fire. The group also sued Utility Services Corporation Ltd., which maintained the lines, and the Victorian government for insufficient prevention measures. The settlement, totaling AU$494.7 million, still requires final court approval and will take 12 to 18 months to distribute. Attorney Andrew Watson stated, "No amount of money will ever compensate those affected by the fire for the losses they have suffered, but this settlement represents a measure of justice and some real compensation that will ease the financial burden of their suffering." SP AusNet, however, maintained that the conductor that broke and sparked the fire was damaged by lightning, compromising its fail-safety design. The company did not admit liability, and the settlement came without an acknowledgment of fault. Lead plaintiff Carol Matthews expressed, "There is so much pain that is still very real, but today there is also a sense of justice." The 2009 Royal Commission found that the fire began when an electricity line failed between two poles, causing arcing that ignited vegetation.

Bristol Palin, 26, and her husband Dakota Meyer are expecting their second child, following the birth of their daughter Sailor Grace last December. The couple, who recently reconciled and married in June after a bitter custody battle, shared their excitement with Entertainment Tonight, saying, "God has blessed us so much; we are thankful for His grace and new beginnings. A springtime baby in the Meyer home and we can't wait!" This upcoming addition will be Palin’s third child, as she also shares a 7-year-old son, Tripp, with ex-fiancé Levi Johnston. Palin previously expressed gratitude to Meyer on Father's Day, writing, "Thank you for putting our family first, working so hard, and giving our kids the most solid foundation, we love you so much."

A bizarre sequence of events in Fresno, California, unfolded after a jury mistakenly signed a not-guilty verdict for Bobby Pearson, a defendant in a burglary case. Pearson, 37, walked out of jail a free man, only to be stabbed to death in a fight shortly after. The incident began when the jury, unable to reach a unanimous decision, was instructed to send a note to the judge if they were deadlocked. Instead, they mistakenly signed a not-guilty verdict, leading Judge W. Kent Hamlin to release Pearson. The jury's confusion stemmed from the forms, which included one for a guilty verdict and another for a not-guilty verdict, without a clear option for a hung jury. Pearson's release was too late, as he was found dead after a fight with his sister's boyfriend, Willie Gray, who had a history of conflicts with Pearson. Gray, who was arrested at an apartment complex about a mile away from the murder scene, faces murder charges. The fight ended with Pearson stabbed, and police believe a gunshot may have been involved. An autopsy is scheduled to determine the exact cause of death. The incident highlights the potential flaws in the jury system and the critical importance of clear instructions. Prosecutors argue that despite the bizarre circumstances, Pearson did not deserve to die in such a manner. The case has sparked discussions on jury instructions and the need for more explicit guidance to prevent such misunderstandings in the future.

The polar vortex, which has been a frequent topic in recent winters, is showing signs of irregularity this year, potentially leading to a milder start but a colder end to winter, according to experts. The polar vortex, a high-speed, high-altitude wind system that typically keeps Arctic cold confined, is currently stronger than average and expected to keep the extreme cold from moving southward into the Capital Region through the early part of the winter season. However, as the winter progresses, the vortex could become more unstable, increasing the likelihood of late-season cold snaps and snowfall. This instability is linked to the retreat of sea ice around the North Pole, which is weakening the polar vortex's structure.

The polar vortex's strength at the start of winter is a significant factor in determining the winter's overall pattern. Meteorologist Andrea Lang, an assistant professor at the University of Albany, explains that while the vortex is currently strong, it could weaken later in the season, leading to colder temperatures and snowfall. This instability is particularly pronounced from late December through February, when the vortex is typically at its weakest and prone to wandering, potentially sending cold air and snow to southern regions.

The irregularity in the polar vortex's behavior is not unique to the Capital Region. National long-range weather forecasts, which credit a stronger El Nino effect in the Pacific Ocean, also predict a warmer winter for much of the country. However, the potential for the polar vortex to become more volatile later in the season suggests that the winter could be more unpredictable and variable than initially anticipated.

Despite the forecasted colder end to the winter, energy experts predict that heating bills for propane, heating oil, and natural gas users will be lower than in previous years. Propane inventories are at record highs, and prices are near record lows, which should provide some relief to homeowners. This abundance of propane is largely due to increased production in the Marcellus Shale region, particularly in Pennsylvania, which has significantly boosted supplies.

While the polar vortex's behavior remains a subject of scientific interest and study, the irregularity observed this year underscores the complex and sometimes unpredictable nature of weather patterns. Meteorologists like Judah Cohen, who directs seasonal forecasting for Atmospheric and Environmental Research, emphasize the importance of monitoring the polar vortex's behavior throughout the winter to predict potential cold spells and snowfall. Cohen's unique approach, which involves analyzing Siberian snow cover to predict winter weather in North America and Europe, highlights the interconnectedness of global weather systems and the challenges of long-range forecasting.

A rare chain reaction crash involving a black bear and three separate vehicles left three people dead and eight injured on a dark, remote road in Florida's Everglades on Sunday evening, authorities said. The initial incident occurred when a woman driving a Cadillac SUV hit a 300-pound black bear on Snake Road in Alligator Alley, near mile marker 49 on the Big Cypress Seminole reservation, according to Seminole Tribe spokesman Gary Bitner. The bear died after being struck by the SUV. The woman in the SUV, along with at least three other passengers, suffered injuries but managed to walk away unscathed, despite the SUV being totaled. Bitner stated, "I have never heard of a case of a bear being in a traffic accident," adding that Florida panthers have been involved in car accidents before but not black bears. 

Shortly after the first crash, a group of three people in a separate car pulled over to assist the stranded passengers. However, as they were getting out of their vehicle, a third car, a Mercedes, plowed into the disabled SUV and then struck the three good Samaritans, killing them. The identities of the victims were not immediately released. The third car had a total of six passengers, including a 45-year-old man, a 14-year-old son, a daughter, and a grandchild, who sustained various degrees of injury. Six patients were transported to Broward Health Medical Center in Fort Lauderdale, while two others were taken to Memorial Regional Hospital in Hollywood. 

The Florida Fish and Wildlife Commission confirmed that the Everglades is the natural habitat of black bears. This incident highlights the rare and dangerous encounters that can occur between humans and wildlife in the region. The chain reaction crash underscores the unpredictable nature of such events and the potential for tragedy when multiple vehicles are involved.

In the small Illinois town of Cahokia, a single mother named Ebony Conner faced an unusual and harsh consequence for failing to maintain her yard. Conner, who has five children, was briefly jailed for not mowing her lawn and cleaning up her yard, according to a local CBS affiliate. The incident highlights a broader issue of municipal code enforcement that has led to the arrest of several residents for minor infractions. In Prichard, Alabama, a 70-year-old woman was arrested for not mowing her lawn, though she did not receive a ticket prior to her arrest. Similarly, in Riesel, Texas, a 75-year-old woman was issued a warrant for her arrest after she was accused of not responding to a letter to appear in court for failing to mow her lawn.

The town of Pagedale, Missouri, has faced similar issues, where residents can be fined for a wide range of minor offenses, including chipped paint, mismatched curtains, and walking on the left side of a crosswalk. From 2010 to 2014, the number of non-traffic tickets issued to residents increased by 495 percent, and in 2013, nearly 20 percent of the city's revenue came from fines and fees. This has created a profit incentive for law enforcement, leading to a cycle of perpetual harassment and fines for residents who cannot keep up with the city's demands.

Residents like Vincent Blount, who has accumulated $2,800 in fines, and Valarie Whitner, who was arrested in front of her home, are caught in this cycle. Blount's home, which is not even his, is the subject of some of his tickets and fines, while Valarie has received generic tickets for "house not up to code" without further explanation. Mildred Bryant, an 84-year-old woman, faces similar challenges, with the city threatening legal action if she does not comply with demands that are beyond her physical and financial abilities. The city has demanded that she touch up or repaint her entire two-story home, including the foundation, and has asked for matching curtains, slats, or other such window treatments.

These experiences are not isolated incidents. They represent a broader pattern of unconstitutional treatment of residents in Pagedale, where the city's ticketing practices have led to a never-ending cycle of fines, imprisonment, and threats of demolition for those who cannot keep up with the city's demands. The IJ (Institute for Justice) has teamed up with some Pagedale residents to challenge the city's practices in a class-action lawsuit, aiming to put an end to this unconstitutional treatment of all residents. The lawsuit seeks to address the harm to Pagedale residents, who find themselves in a perpetual cycle of fines and fees that prevent them from making the necessary changes to comply with the city's demands.

The Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs, Colorado, announced on Tuesday that a racial slur posted outside the dorm rooms of five black students at the academy's prep school was written by one of those students, the academy said. The prep school, located on the academy grounds but not part of the four-year academy program, helps promising students meet the academy's entrance requirements. The academy's superintendent, Lt. Gen. Jay Silveria, had previously given a stern speech to cadets shortly after the slurs were reported, warning that racists were not welcome at the school. In his speech, Silveria said, "If you can't treat someone with dignity and respect, get out," and insisted that everyone in the audience take out their phones and record him so his message was clearly heard. The slurs appeared in the aftermath of racial violence in Charlottesville, Virginia, and amid a debate about NFL players kneeling for the national anthem. Silveria, a veteran fighter pilot who directed the air war in the Middle East, took command at the school in August and has repeatedly told cadets and staff that his highest priority is ensuring a climate of dignity and respect. The academy, which has about 4,000 students, has struggled with sexual misconduct problems several times in recent years but few racial incidents have been made public. The student responsible for the slurs is no longer at the school, and a spokesman declined to say whether the student withdrew or was expelled, citing privacy laws. The student's name was not released.

A 3-year-old North Carolina girl named Mariah Woods has been missing since her mother put her to bed Sunday night in their Jacksonville home, according to local officials. Mariah’s mother, Kristy Woods, reported her daughter missing at approximately 6:45 a.m. the following morning, and authorities have been searching for the little girl ever since. The Onslow County Sheriff’s Department and the FBI have been conducting ground and air searches, and have released surveillance pictures taken Monday morning at a North Carolina Walmart, attempting to determine if the child in the pictures is Mariah. Authorities are asking for the public’s assistance in identifying both the woman and the child in the images. 

Onslow County Sheriff Hans Miller stated that investigators are especially interested in speaking to anyone who has had contact with the family since Sunday, and that any clue, such as children’s clothes, can be helpful. The sheriff also mentioned that authorities are using every available resource to search for Mariah, including drones and helicopters provided by the Marine Corps, the North Carolina State Highway Patrol, and a neighboring sheriff’s department. 

Mariah’s mother, Kristy Woods, pleaded to be reunited with her child, saying, “I love her and I’ll never let her go again. I just want to hold her tight and see her smile.” She also mentioned that Mariah wears braces on her legs to help her walk and expressed disbelief that her daughter would have walked away from their house on her own. 

An Amber Alert was issued for Mariah soon after she was reported missing, and she is described as a white female with brown hair and blue eyes, about 2 feet 9 inches tall and weighing 30 pounds. Mariah’s biological father, Alex Woods, expressed skepticism about his daughter’s disappearance, questioning how someone could have taken her without any noise or witnesses. 

The search for Mariah continues, with investigators expanding their search radius and conducting interviews with family members and neighbors. The case remains under investigation, and authorities are working to find the little girl and determine what happened to her.

The family of Dennis Lee Thian Poh, a 47-year-old businessman from Kuala Lumpur who went missing during a trek in Ampurna, Nepal, on April 5, is hoping he will return in time for his second wedding anniversary on Saturday. Lee, an avid trekker, was last seen between Ghorepani and Ghundrung on the afternoon of April 5, as his group made their descent from Khopra Danda, heading to Bayeli. The weather conditions in the Himalayas have worsened, intensifying search efforts in the areas between Khopra and Bayeli, as well as Dobasto and Tadatani. SAR Dogs Nepal, an independent Nepali search-and-rescue team, has posted photographs of poor weather conditions from their base camp in Bayeli, stating that thick fog forces their teams to work carefully. Lee’s family has engaged SAR Dogs Nepal, alongside many villagers and Sherpas, but they need more people on the ground to help cover the vast area. Lee’s wife, Jennifer Peters-Lee, who flew to Nepal to follow the search, hopes they will be able to celebrate their second wedding anniversary together. The Annapurna Conservation Area, where Lee was trekking, is known for its dangerous terrain, with frequent rain, hail, and snow. The region is also one of Nepal's most dangerous for trekkers, with narrow, slippery, and unstable paths. Lee’s group guide started searching for him immediately after he disappeared, but the company waited 48 hours to alert local authorities, the dog teams, and Lee’s family. Dennis’ trekking guide and SAR Dogs Nepal have identified four spots where Lee was, including a boulder marking his last location on the main trail halfway to Bayali. However, large boulders, heavy fog, and rain have made it impossible for the team to see down the ravine, and poor visibility has blocked helicopter assistance. Snow and hail have kept nighttime temperatures below freezing, and the trail is a slippery mud morass. Dennis’ wife, Jennifer, is desperate for any information that could help locate him and has made fliers with his picture, offering a reward, to be distributed to local Nepali villagers.

A prominent Iranian lawmaker suggested that Tehran no longer needs to produce 20 percent-enriched uranium, a key point in ongoing negotiations between Iran and Western powers. Hossein Naqvi Hosseini, a spokesman for the Iranian parliament's national security and foreign policy committee, stated that Iran has sufficient fuel for its Tehran reactor and is prepared to address concerns over its stockpile of enriched uranium. However, he did not specify whether Iran would stop enrichment. Western nations, particularly the United States, have been pushing for Iran to halt 20 percent enrichment, as this level of uranium can be quickly converted to weapons-grade material. Iran currently operates over 10,000 centrifuges and possesses nearly 200 kilograms of 20 percent-enriched uranium, enough to produce a single nuclear weapon. The next round of talks between Iran and the six powers is scheduled for November 7-8 in Geneva. Despite progress, significant obstacles remain, including Iran's close relationship with Syria and the internal political dynamics within Iran. The Obama administration has been working to persuade Congress not to impose new sanctions, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu continues to advocate for a more stringent approach. The talks aim to ease crippling economic sanctions on Iran in exchange for curbs on its nuclear program, but the ultimate success and sustainability of any agreement remain uncertain.

Blake Lively and Ryan Reynolds, co-stars in "Green Lantern," are reportedly getting more serious, despite denying rumors of a relationship during Reynolds' marriage to Scarlett Johansson. Sources say Lively, 24, visited Reynolds, 34, on his film set in Boston, while Reynolds reciprocated by visiting Lively on the "Gossip Girl" set in New York. The couple was spotted having a romantic dinner at Mistral Bistro in Boston, with Lively reportedly picking up the check. Lively also shopped for Reynolds at Bergdorf Goodman's men's store. The article notes that Johansson, 26, and Reynolds, 34, finalized their divorce in July, with Johansson citing impatience and overcriticism as issues. Despite their private nature, the pair's relationship is heating up, with Lively's actions suggesting a strong connection.

The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) has filed a civil lawsuit against Goldman Sachs for alleged fraud in the creation and marketing of a collateralized debt obligation (CDO) known as Abacus 2007-AC1. The SEC claims that Goldman failed to disclose that a hedge fund, Paulson & Co., played a significant role in selecting the assets for the CDO while simultaneously betting against its success. Goldman Sachs has denied the allegations, stating that the charges are "completely unfounded in law and fact." This case is part of a broader pattern of investment banks allegedly creating CDOs with hidden conflicts of interest, a practice that contributed to the financial crisis. The SEC's suit highlights the complex and often opaque nature of financial products and the potential for conflicts of interest in the financial industry. While the SEC did not sue Paulson & Co., the case has reignited debates about transparency and accountability in the financial sector.

Alibaba Group executive chairman Jack Ma addressed the World Economic Forum in Davos, highlighting the United States' failure to distribute the benefits of globalization properly. Ma argued that the U.S. has squandered the wealth generated by globalisation, citing the $14.2 trillion spent on 13 wars over the past three decades, instead of investing in infrastructure and supporting workers. He emphasized that the issue lies in the strategy of wealth distribution, rather than blaming China for job losses, which he suggested are a result of the U.S. not spending money on its people in a proper way. Ma met with President-elect Donald Trump, expressing optimism about globalisation and suggesting that both the U.S. and China could benefit from a more inclusive form of globalisation where the gains are more widely shared. He urged the international community to give Trump time to develop his trade policies, warning that a trade war between the world's largest and second-largest economies would be disastrous. Ma also discussed his meeting with Trump, noting that they discussed how Alibaba could help small American businesses sell their products in China and Asia, potentially creating jobs. Ma's comments reflect a nuanced view of globalization, acknowledging its benefits while advocating for a more equitable distribution of its benefits.

WikiLeaks has released a significant cache of documents detailing the CIA's extensive cyber-hacking capabilities, including methods to turn everyday devices into surveillance tools. The first part of the series, titled "Year Zero," comprises 8,761 documents from an isolated, high-security network within the CIA's Center for Cyber Intelligence in Langley, Virginia. The documents suggest the CIA has developed a vast arsenal of malware, viruses, and "zero day" exploits, with the potential to target a wide range of devices, including smartphones, smart TVs, and even anti-virus software. The source of the leak, described as a current or former CIA contractor, claims the archive was circulated among former U.S. government hackers and contractors, one of whom provided WikiLeaks with portions of the archive.

The documents reveal that the CIA has created a sophisticated hacking division, the Engineering Development Group (EDG), which operates under the Center for Cyber Intelligence (CCI) and the Directorate for Digital Innovation (DDI). This division has produced over 5000 registered users and more than a thousand hacking systems, trojans, viruses, and other "weaponized" malware. The scale of the operation is such that by 2016, the CIA had utilized more code than that used to run Facebook. This division effectively created an "own NSA" with less accountability and without public oversight.

The release of these documents has sparked concerns about the security, creation, use, proliferation, and democratic control of cyberweapons. The source, who wishes to initiate a public debate, raises questions about whether the CIA's hacking capabilities exceed its mandated powers and the need for public oversight. Julian Assange, WikiLeaks editor, stated that there is an "extreme proliferation risk" in the development of cyber weapons, drawing comparisons to the global arms trade.

WikiLeaks has redacted and anonymized some identifying information, such as names and IP addresses, to avoid the distribution of "armed" cyberweapons. The group plans to publish substantive CIA documentation while avoiding the release of fully formed, usable code until a consensus emerges on the technical and political nature of the CIA's program. This includes redacting lists of CIA surveillance targets and attack machines, which include targets and machines in Latin America, Europe, and the United States.

The documents detail a range of hacking tools, including "Weeping Angel," which can turn Samsung smart TVs into covert microphones. The CIA is also reportedly studying whether it can infect vehicle control systems to conduct "nearly undetectable assassinations." The Mobile Devices Branch has developed malware to control and steal information from iPhones, with a particular focus on the iPhone's popularity among social, political, diplomatic, and business elites. The CIA also targets popular phones running Google's Android, with 24 "weaponized" Android "zero days" as of 2016.

The release of these documents has raised questions about the U.S. government's commitment to the Vulnerabilities Equities Process, which requires the disclosure of serious vulnerabilities to technology manufacturers. The documents suggest that the CIA has breached this commitment, hoarding vulnerabilities and potentially leaving the population at large and critical infrastructure at risk. The proliferation of cyber weapons is seen as a serious risk, as they can be easily copied and used by adversaries, including foreign intelligence agencies and cyber criminals.

The U.S. Consulate in Frankfurt, Germany, is revealed to be a covert CIA hacker base, operating under diplomatic cover. The documents also detail specific projects, such as UMBRAGE, which collects and maintains a library of attack techniques "stolen" from other states, and Fine Dining, which provides a standardized questionnaire for CIA case officers to transform operational needs into technical requirements for hacking attacks.

The release of these documents has alarmed cybersecurity experts, who note that while the CIA's methods may be legitimate, the potential for these tools to be misused is significant. The CIA's classification regime has been criticized for making its cyber arsenal unclassified, which could lead to the unauthorized use of these tools by adversaries. The documents also highlight the CIA's efforts to evade forensic detection and anti-virus software, with successful attacks against most well-known anti-virus programs.

In conclusion, the release of "Vault 7" by WikiLeaks has exposed the CIA's extensive cyber-hacking capabilities and raised critical questions about the security and oversight of these tools. The documents provide a rare glimpse into the CIA's covert operations and the potential risks they pose to individuals and infrastructure.

As the second open enrollment season for HealthCare.gov begins, Secretary Sylvia Burwell of Health and Human Services announced that the website is stable and functioning well, marking a significant improvement from last year's technical issues. Burwell expects strong growth, aiming for an additional 2 million enrollees, bringing the total to about 9 million for 2015. The Congressional Budget Office projects 13 million enrollees. In the first days, 100,000 new applications were submitted, compared to just a handful last year. Additionally, 500,000 existing customers logged in, and 1 million people "window-shopped" for plans. President Obama praised the improvements, stating, "HealthCare.gov works really well now." However, some returning customers faced issues, possibly due to remembering user names and passwords. Call centers received 100,000 calls, indicating high consumer interest. Despite the progress, experts warn of potential cost increases for some customers, and the administration faces pressure to avoid another website meltdown with Congress now fully controlled by Republicans.

Mark Herzlich, a New York Giants rookie linebacker, stepped off the plane in Indianapolis to play in Super Bowl XLVI, tweeting, "2 yrs ago I was told I might never walk again. Just WALKED off plane in Indy to play in The #SuperBowl. #TakeThatSh*tCancer." His journey from battling Ewing's sarcoma, a rare form of bone cancer, to playing in the Super Bowl is a testament to his resilience. Diagnosed in 2009, Herzlich faced three potential outcomes, including amputation or losing his football career. He chose aggressive chemotherapy and radiation, which allowed him to return to Boston College in 2010 and eventually sign with the Giants as an undrafted free agent. Herzlich's story, shared at Media Day, inspires many, especially those facing similar health challenges. He acknowledges the support from Boston fans, who rooted for the Giants despite their usual allegiance to the Patriots. For Herzlich, the Super Bowl is more than just a game; it's a symbol of his victory over cancer and a reminder of the importance of perseverance.

Prosecutors in southern Minnesota are pursuing a rare charge of murder against Long Vang, who is accused of driving his partner Jessica Haban to take her own life through years of relentless physical and emotional abuse. Vang, 34, is charged with third-degree murder, second-degree manslaughter, and stalking in connection with Haban’s suicide on December 16, 2015. Haban, the mother of Vang’s two children, died by suicide after enduring a decade of abuse, including being knocked unconscious, having her hair pulled, and being thrown against walls. Vang allegedly continued to harass Haban even after a court order forbade contact, pressuring her to leave inpatient mental health treatment and threatening to institutionalize her and take away custody of their children. Haban was hospitalized three times due to the abuse but was discharged just three days before her death. County Attorney Mark Ostrem stated, “I believe Mr. Vang’s conduct directly contributed to the death of his partner. Mr. Vang was clearly aware of the precarious state of his partner’s emotions following her hospitalizations and he continued the relentless contacts until her death.” Ostrem’s office is facing scrutiny over this unprecedented case, with experts noting the rarity of such charges. The case highlights the severe impact of domestic violence on mental health and suicide risk. Haban’s mother, Rita Prinzing, expressed relief that Vang would be held accountable, stating, “There is finally going to be some justice for Jessica. While we know that it won’t bring her back, he will be held accountable.” The charges against Vang raise complex legal questions and may set a precedent for similar cases involving domestic abuse and suicide.

President Obama is continuing his efforts to reform the criminal justice system by promoting rehabilitation and reintegration for formerly incarcerated individuals. In Newark, New Jersey, he highlighted the reentry process and announced several new initiatives aimed at helping Americans who have paid their debt to society. The Administration is providing $8 million in education grants to support educational attainment and reentry success for individuals who have been incarcerated. This grant program seeks to build evidence on effective reentry education programs and demonstrate that high-quality, appropriately designed, integrated, and well-implemented educational and related services in institutional and community settings are critical in supporting educational attainment and reentry success. The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) will release guidance to Public Housing Authorities and owners of HUD-assisted housing regarding the use of arrests in determining who can live in HUD-assisted properties. This guidance will clarify the Department’s position on “one strike” policies and include best practices from Public Housing Authorities. The President is directing the Office of Personnel Management (OPM) to modify its rules to delay inquiries into criminal history until later in the hiring process for most competitive federal jobs. Exceptions will be made for law enforcement, national security, and other sensitive positions. The TechHire initiative is expanding tech training and jobs for individuals with criminal records, with new commitments from Memphis, TN, and New Orleans, LA, to support people with criminal records. Newark, NJ, will offer training through the Art of Code program in software development with a focus on training and placement for formerly incarcerated people. New Haven, CT, will launch a pilot program to train and place individuals with criminal records, and will start a program to train incarcerated people in tech programming skills. Washington, DC, partners will train and place 200 formerly incarcerated people in tech jobs. The Department of Labor and Department of Justice will partner to establish a National Clean Slate Clearinghouse to provide technical assistance to local legal aid programs, public defender offices, and reentry service providers to build capacity for legal services needed to help with record-cleaning, expungement, and related civil legal services. The Department of Housing and Urban Development and the Bureau of Justice Assistance at the Department of Justice have launched an $8.7 million demonstration grant to address homelessness and reduce recidivism among the justice-involved population. The Pay for Success (PFS) Permanent Supportive Housing Demonstration will test cost-effective ways to help persons cycling between the criminal justice and homeless service systems, while making new Permanent Supportive Housing available for the reentry population. The Department of Justice awarded $3 million to provide technology-based career training for incarcerated adults and juveniles. The Department of Labor awarded a series of grants in June that are aimed at reducing employment barriers, including the Face Forward program, which gives youth a second chance to succeed in the workforce by removing the stigma of having a juvenile record through diversion and/or expungement strategies. The Department of Labor also awarded $10 million in pilot grants for programs that place One Stop Career Center/American Job Centers services directly in local jails to prepare individuals for employment while they are incarcerated. The Training to Work program focuses on training opportunities that lead to industry-recognized credentials and job opportunities along career pathways. The Departments of Education and Justice announced the Second Chance Pell Pilot Program to allow incarcerated Americans to receive Pell Grants to pursue postsecondary education and trainings that can help them turn their lives around and ultimately get jobs and support their families. The Small Business Administration published a final rule for the Microloan Program that provides more flexibility to SBA non-profit intermediaries and expands the pool of microloan recipients, making small businesses that have an owner who is currently on probation or parole eligible for microloan programs. The Corporation for National and Community Service (CNCS) and the Office of Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention at the Department of Justice announced a new round of Youth Opportunity AmeriCorps grants aimed at enrolling at-risk and formerly incarcerated youth in national service projects. The Department of Labor partnered with the Department of Defense’s National Guard Youth ChalleNGe program and awarded three $4 million grants in April to provide court-involved youth with work experiences, mentors, and vocational skills training that prepares them for successful entry into the workforce. The Department of Justice announced $6 million in awards under the Second Chance Act to support reentry programming for adults with co-occurring substance abuse and mental disorders. The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA) at HHS announced the winners of its reintegration toolkit challenge to develop software applications aimed at transforming existing resources into user-friendly tools with the potential to promote successful reentry and reduce recidivism. The Social Security Administration (SSA) finalized written statewide prerelease agreements in September with the Department of Corrections in Iowa and Kansas, ensuring continuity of services for returning citizens. The Department of Labor's Veterans' Employment and Training Service announced the award of $1.5 million in grants to help once incarcerated veterans considered "at risk" of becoming homeless. The Department of Veterans Affairs (VA) developed a web-based system – the Veterans Reentry Search Service (VRSS) – that allows prison, jail, and court staff to quickly and accurately identify veterans among their populations and connect them with services. The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) took action to make it easier for incarcerated individuals to stay in touch with their families by capping all in-state and interstate prison phone rates. The Department of Justice announced new grant awards to fund mentoring services for incarcerated fathers who are returning to their families. The Office of Juvenile Justice and Delinquency Prevention at the Department of Justice awarded $1 million to promote and expand services to children who have a parent who is incarcerated in a Federal Bureau of Prisons (BOP) correctional facility. The Center for Employment Opportunities (CEO) has committed to more than doubling the number of people served from 4,500 to 11,000 across existing geographies and 3-5 new states. Cengage Learning will roll out Smart Horizons Career Online Education in correctional facilities in up to four new states over the next 12 months, providing over 1,000 new students with the opportunity to earn a high-school diploma and/or career certificate online. These initiatives aim to reduce barriers to employment, increase access to education and enrichment, expand opportunities for justice-involved youth to serve their communities, and improve opportunities for children of incarcerated parents and their families.

Paying for college is increasingly a luxury, prompting many to question its worth. Compensation data site PayScale analyzed nearly 700 colleges and universities to determine the return on investment (ROI) for each, comparing tuition costs to graduates' average earnings. The California Institute of Technology tops the list with an ROI of $1,713,000, while Shaw University has the lowest at $15,480. PayScale's comprehensive list helps identify which institutions offer the best value, providing a clearer measure of a school's true worth. BusinessWeek also offers a state-by-state breakdown of the data, highlighting the best-value school in each. This analysis aims to guide students in making informed decisions about their higher education investments.

The U.S. Justice Department has filed a lawsuit against California and two of its top officials, alleging that state laws are interfering with federal immigration enforcement efforts. The lawsuit, filed in federal court in Sacramento, highlights the ongoing conflict between the Trump administration and California, which has taken a stance opposing federal immigration policies. The lawsuit specifically targets three California laws: one that bars private employers from voluntarily cooperating with federal immigration officials, another that restricts state and local law enforcement from sharing information with federal authorities about undocumented individuals in their custody, and a third that covers state inspections of detention facilities holding noncitizens. Attorney General Jeff Sessions, a long-time proponent of strict immigration controls, is set to speak to California law enforcement officials, emphasizing the administration's commitment to making their jobs safer and reducing crime. In response, California Governor Jerry Brown criticized the federal lawsuit, calling it a "political stunt" and expressing his opposition to the federal government's actions. The case is seen as a test of the Trump administration's ability to force state and local authorities to cooperate with federal immigration enforcement, reflecting the administration's limited tolerance for states that choose to pursue different policies.

A wealthy du Pont heir, Robert H. Richards IV, was spared jail time for raping his 3-year-old daughter, a decision that has drawn criticism from criminal justice authorities in Delaware. Superior Court Judge Jan Jurden sentenced Richards to probation and ordered him to participate in a sex offenders' treatment program, stating that he "will not fare well" in prison. This lenient sentence has raised questions about the appropriate punishment for such crimes, especially when considering the unique circumstances of the case. Richards, who is unemployed and supported by a trust fund, owns a 5,800-square-foot mansion in Greenville and a home in the exclusive North Shores neighborhood near Rehoboth Beach. His great-grandfather is Irenee du Pont, and his father is Robert H. Richards III, a retired partner in the Richards Layton & Finger law firm. The case became public after his ex-wife, Tracy Richards, filed a lawsuit seeking compensatory and punitive damages for the abuse of their two children. The lawsuit alleges that Richards also sexually abused his 3-year-old son between 2005 and 2007. In 2009, Richards was initially indicted on two counts of second-degree rape of a child, which carry a mandatory 10-year prison term. However, he accepted a plea deal for a single count of fourth-degree rape, which carries no mandatory minimum time. Judge Jurden's decision to sentence Richards to probation, rather than prison, has been criticized as unusual and potentially lenient. Delaware's Sentencing Accountability Commission (SENTAC) typically recommends that prison be reserved for violent offenders, including rapists. However, Judge Jurden cited Richards' "strong family support" and "significant treatment needs" as factors in her decision. Defense attorneys and prosecutors have expressed surprise at the judge's rationale, with some arguing that prison is the appropriate punishment for such crimes. The case highlights the complex challenges faced by judges and prosecutors in handling cases involving wealthy defendants and the potential for leniency in such cases.

In the wake of the deadly attack on the French satirical magazine Charlie Hebdo, which left 12 people dead, hundreds of thousands of people across France and around the world gathered in silent vigils to show solidarity and support. Tens of thousands of people in Paris, including Place de la République, held candles and left pens and pencils in small memorials, with many holding signs reading "Je Suis Charlie." Similar vigils took place in cities worldwide, such as London, Madrid, Berlin, Brussels, and Washington D.C. The hashtag #JeSuisCharlie trended on social media, with users sharing images of the Eiffel Tower and messages of support. In San Francisco, about 100 people gathered outside the French Consulate, holding signs and lighting candles. In Manhattan's Union Square, about 1,000 people assembled with signs in English and French, chanting "We are not afraid" and "We are Charlie." The Newseum in Washington displayed the hashtag on its atrium screen. In Madrid, about 200 people gathered outside the French Embassy, holding pens and chanting "Freedom of Expression." In Stockholm, about 100 people organized to lay flowers and candles in front of the French Embassy. The attacks on Charlie Hebdo, which had previously faced threats for its controversial depictions, sparked a global response, with people from various backgrounds coming together to defend freedom of speech and press. The swift and coordinated response demonstrated the resilience of the French people and the international community in the face of terrorism.

Professional line-sitting has become a lucrative business in New York City, where Same Ole Line Dudes Founder & CEO Robert Samuel offers his services for a fee to reduce his clients' wait times for various events and products. With over 8 million residents and 56 million tourists annually, lines in New York can be notoriously long, making the line-sitting service highly sought after. Robert Samuel, who was laid off from his job in 2012, launched SOLD, an acronym for Same Old Line Dudes, as a line waiting service. Since then, the business has grown into an enterprising start-up that views time as a precious commodity, with clients ranging from middle-class to super-wealthy individuals. Samuel's clients hire him for a variety of tasks, including waiting in line for iPhones, designer sample sales, tech releases, and even brunch waitlists. He charges $25 for the first hour and $10 for each additional half-hour, with prices potentially increasing if multiple people are hired for multiple orders.

One of Samuel's most notable jobs was waiting in line for 48 hours outside the Apple store in the Meatpacking District to secure the first iPhone 6s. He slept in a fold-up cot for two nights, had pizza delivered to his spot, and managed to secure $1000 for the gig. His business has faced competition from other share economy start-ups like TaskRabbit and Agent Anything, where the young and underemployed can be purchased to do any variety of small tasks. Despite the growing competition, Samuel continues to work full-time as a security guard for a financial services company, balancing his line-sitting business.

However, Samuel's business is not without its challenges. He has faced tension with Chinese men and women who sell the iPhones to middlemen for export to China, as well as difficulties with clients who fail to secure the desired products. For instance, during a recent attempt to secure limited-edition game wristbands, Samuel and his group were five people short of the available spots. Despite this, Samuel decided to give a partial refund to his customers, recognizing the importance of maintaining good customer relations. His mother remains skeptical about his career choice, suggesting that he should return to school. Nevertheless, Samuel's business continues to thrive, offering a unique service that caters to the time-strapped and wealthy individuals in New York City.

In the days leading up to the second US presidential debate, the choice of attire for First Lady Melania Trump became a focal point of discussion. She opted for a Gucci fuchsia "pussy-bow" blouse, a style that has a complex history and has recently resurfaced in fashion due to Gucci's influence. The debate took place just two days after a 2005 video surfaced, in which Donald Trump, the Republican nominee, boasted about grabbing women's genitals and kissing them. The choice of the "pussy-bow" blouse was not made intentionally, according to the Trump campaign, but it did not go unnoticed. Critics pointed out the irony of the choice, given the controversy surrounding Trump's comments. The style, which has a mixed reception among feminists, was seen as a sartorial reference to the 2005 scandal. Margaret Thatcher, Britain's prime minister in the 1980s, also popularized the style as a contrast to her tough persona. Despite the controversy, Melania Trump defended her husband, stating that his remarks were "unacceptable and offensive." The debate highlighted the ongoing challenges of navigating fashion and politics in a highly charged political environment.

SCHERTZ, Texas - The Bexar County Sheriff's Office is investigating a tragic accident involving a 6-year-old boy, Kameron Prescott, who was fatally shot during a deputy-involved incident. The shooting occurred in a mobile home park in Schertz, Texas, after deputies were pursuing a suspect, Amanda Lene Jones, who was a wanted felon and car-theft suspect. Sheriff Javier Salazar reported that the deputies found Jones in a closet, where she allegedly stated, "I have a weapon, I'm gonna shoot you." She fled on foot, and the deputies pursued her into a wooded area. After losing sight of her, the deputies called for backup. Later, they found Jones on a porch, where she was threatening several witnesses, leading the deputies to believe she was armed. A bullet from the deputies' gunfire struck Kameron Prescott, who was living in the home, in the abdomen. The boy was rushed to a hospital but could not be saved. Salazar stated that the deputies fired at Jones because they believed she was posing a direct threat to their lives. Kameron's teacher, Shanda Ince, described him as a kind-hearted, joyful child who loved to make everyone laugh. The Schertz-Cibolo-Universal City Independent School District expressed its deepest condolences to Kameron's family and friends. A memorial fund has been established to assist the family with expenses. The investigation continues, with the local district attorney involved. Salazar emphasized that the deputies complied with policies but acknowledged the tragic outcome, describing it as a "tragic accident" that led to Kameron's death.

The U.K. has become the first country to allow the erectile dysfunction drug Viagra to be sold over the counter and without a prescription, marking a significant shift in how the drug is accessed. Pfizer, the U.S. drug giant, has been working for nearly a decade to secure this over-the-counter (OTC) status for Viagra, which will be sold under the name Viagra Connect. The OTC version will be available for about £19.99 for a pack of four pills and £34.99 for an eight-pack at pharmacies, with pharmacists assessing the suitability of each individual. This move aims to reduce the embarrassment associated with seeking treatment for erectile dysfunction and potentially decrease the market for counterfeit drugs. In 2018, the OTC version of Viagra will be available in the U.K., but Pfizer will continue to offer the drug by prescription. Globally, Pfizer reported $1.6 billion in Viagra sales in 2016, though sales have declined as patents expire and generics enter the market. The U.K. decision follows a public consultation and is expected to reduce the number of people purchasing counterfeit versions of the drug, which can pose serious health risks. Mick Foy, the MHRA’s group manager in vigilance and risk management of medicines, emphasized the importance of quality and legitimate care, stating, "It’s important men feel they have fast access to quality and legitimate care, and do not feel they need to turn to counterfeit online supplies which could have potentially serious side effects."

Army Ranger veteran Peter Kassig, who moved to the Middle East for humanitarian work, has been taken hostage by the Islamic State (ISIS) and is potentially the next victim, according to a video released by ISIS. Kassig, a 26-year-old from Indianapolis, began his humanitarian efforts in 2012 by founding a small medical relief organization called Special Emergency Response and Assistance (SERA) in Gaziantep, Turkey. His journey started as a U.S. Army Ranger in 2006, where he deployed to Iraq in 2007 before being medically discharged. After a brief marriage and divorce, Kassig sought a "game changer" and traveled to Beirut in 2012 to learn about the Syrian crisis firsthand. His experiences there led him to establish SERA, which aimed to provide medical assistance and supplies to Syrian refugees.

Kassig's passion for helping Syrians was evident in his words: "This is what I was put here to do. I guess I am just a hopeless romantic, and I am an idealist, and I believe in hopeless causes." His humanitarian work included distributing food and medical supplies across the Syrian border and providing primary trauma care to civilian casualties. His parents, Ed and Paula Kassig, stated that Kassig converted to Islam while in captivity and took the name Abdul-Rahman. They also mentioned that his faith provided him comfort during his long captivity.

Kassig's parents maintained silence about his capture until recently, working with friends and colleagues to secure his release. However, his family confirmed that he was detained on October 1, 2013, while traveling to Deir Ezzor in eastern Syria. The Kassigs expressed their gratitude for the efforts made by those who worked to secure his freedom. His work with SERA and his direct exposure to the Syrian conflict transformed his perspective, leading him to understand the complexities and resilience of the Syrian people.

Kassig's humanitarian efforts were not without impact. He bonded with doctors and patients, witnessing both the brutality of the conflict and the resilience of the Syrian people. His work with Louliya, a 24-year-old Syrian woman who was paralyzed after being run over by a military jeep, highlighted the human cost of the conflict. Kassig's story is one of a man who found purpose in helping others, even as his own life hung in the balance. His parents' statement reflects their hope that Kassig's work and experiences will help bridge the gap between understanding and compassion in the face of conflict.

Armed assailants, including some disguised as women, carried out brazen attacks on Iran’s parliament and the mausoleum of Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, the founder of the Islamic Republic, on Wednesday, leaving 12 people dead and 46 wounded. The attacks, which lasted for hours, stunned Iran’s elite security forces and shattered the country’s image of calm. The six known attackers were killed, and five suspects were reported detained, according to official news media. Brig. Gen. Hossein Salami, deputy commander of the Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, vowed that Iran would avenge the blood of the martyrs. The attacks targeted two potent symbols of Iranian ideology, the parliament and the tomb of the Islamic Republic’s founder, and were claimed by ISIS, marking the first ISIS attack in Iran. The attacks have significant implications, stoking tensions with Saudi Arabia, Gulf states, and the United States. Iran’s hardline Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps accused Saudi Arabia of being behind the attacks, while Iran’s foreign minister, Javad Zarif, condemned the attacks as a threat to the homeland. The attacks come at a time of heightened regional tensions, with Saudi Arabia and other Sunni powers cutting ties with Qatar over its alleged support for Iran and militant groups. The attacks also exacerbate tensions within Iran between the more moderate forces, which claimed victory in the recent reelection of President Hassan Rouhani, and conservative hard-liners. The attacks will likely increase public support for the Revolutionary Guards, who are viewed as protectors of the country, and boost Iran’s efforts to combat ISIS. However, Iran’s involvement in Iraq and Syria is already extensive, and the country does not have unlimited resources to spare. The attacks could also push Iran toward a harsher regional policy. ISIS has regularly threatened Iran, one of the powers leading the fight against the militants’ forces in neighboring Iraq and Syria. The group has upped its anti-Iran propaganda and aimed to recruit from Iran’s Sunni minority community. The attacks will significantly boost ISIS morale and are expected to lead to more attacks outside Iraq and Syria. The attacks will also increase calls for revenge and make it more difficult for President Rouhani’s administration to reduce the country’s involvement in Iraq and Syria.

Indian authorities have decided to put on hold efforts to retrieve the body of American missionary John Allen Chau, who is believed to have been killed by the Sentinelese tribe on North Sentinel Island. Chau, 27, reportedly ventured to the island to convert the tribe to Christianity, despite the fact that outsiders are banned from even approaching the island. His body is still on the island, and attempts to recover it have been unsuccessful. On Monday, a senior official called a meeting of senior officials from the police, tribal welfare, forest, and anthropological departments, where it was decided to put the search for the body on hold. The decision was made to avoid disturbing the protected Sentinelese tribespeople. The official stated that a boat was sent to the area on Tuesday morning to check the situation, but they only saw tribesmen on the beach armed with bows and arrows. The authorities are consulting experts to decide on the best course of action, as the exercise is considered too risky. Rights group Survival International has called for the search to be abandoned, as it is "incredibly dangerous" for both the Sentinelese and officials. In 2006, the Sentinelese killed two Indian fishermen who had tried to sneak onto the island, and officials were unable to retrieve their bodies. The Sentinelese are known to resist contact with outsiders and have been hostile to anyone who comes near their island. Chau's family has said they forgive those who killed him. The Sentinelese have lived in complete isolation on North Sentinel Island for tens of thousands of years, and India has protected the island for decades to prevent the tribe from contracting modern illnesses and to keep outsiders safe. People are not allowed to go within five nautical miles of the island by Indian law, and the Indian Navy patrols it day and night. At least 15 Sentinelese could be living on the island, according to India's census estimates from 2011.

For decades, physics students have been taught that falling through a tunnel drilled through the Earth's center would take 42 minutes. However, a more realistic analysis, taking into account the varying density of Earth's layers, has revealed a shorter time of 38 minutes and 11 seconds. Alexander Klotz, a physics graduate student at McGill University, used seismic data to model Earth's density and calculated the time accurately. Interestingly, Klotz also found that assuming a constant gravitational field throughout the journey would yield the same result of 38 minutes. This finding highlights the importance of considering Earth's layered structure in such calculations. The traditional 42-minute estimate, while simple, is now known to be slightly longer than the actual time. This research adds a new dimension to the classic gravity tunnel problem, making it more accurate and intriguing for physics students and enthusiasts.

Israeli security forces have thwarted a large Hamas terror network in the West Bank, arresting at least 30 members and seizing weapons and explosives, according to the Shin Bet, Israel's security agency. The network, run from Hamas headquarters in Turkey, was planning a range of attacks, including car bombings, kidnappings, and shooting and bombing attacks against Israeli traffic and military targets. The intended targets included Jerusalem's Teddy soccer stadium and light rail system, as well as Israeli communities and traffic. The plot involved multiple terrorist cells in the West Bank, with recruits trained in Jordan, Syria, and the Gaza Strip, and then smuggled back into Israel. The Shin Bet revealed that the network was funded and directed by Hamas leaders in Turkey, with Saleh Aruri, a senior Hamas commander, at the helm. The arrests came after a failed roadside attack in August, which alerted security forces to the plot. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu praised the security services for preventing potentially deadly attacks, emphasizing the ongoing covert operations against Hamas. The Shin Bet also mentioned an earlier thwarted plot in August, which involved over 90 operatives and aimed to topple Palestinian Authority President Mahmoud Abbas. The arrests and uncovering of the terror network highlight the persistent threat from Hamas and the ongoing efforts to counter it.

A mysterious piece of space junk, designated WT1190F, is set to collide with Earth on Friday, November 13, 2015, creating a rare opportunity for scientists to study its descent. First glimpsed by a telescope in early October, this object, estimated to be three to six feet long and likely man-made, is expected to plunge into the Indian Ocean off the southern tip of Sri Lanka. NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory calculates it will burn up in the atmosphere, but caution that one should avoid fishing directly underneath. The object, orbiting beyond the moon and previously unidentified, could be a spent rocket or debris from a recent moon mission. Scientists hope to gather spectral information to identify the object and coordinate observations from ships or aircraft. This event highlights the need for better tracking of distant space debris, as current efforts focus primarily on near-Earth objects.

Phil Mickelson, a three-time Masters champion, was not criminally charged after the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) alleged he profited from an insider trading tip provided by sports gambler Billy Walters. Mickelson, who was not charged but was designated as a relief defendant, agreed to repay $1.03 million, including interest, to the SEC. The SEC's case against Walters, who was arrested and charged with insider trading, centered on his receipt of confidential information from Dean Foods chairman Thomas Davis, which he then passed on to Mickelson. Walters used the information to make a $17.1 million profit in 2012 by trading on Dean Foods' impending spin-off of WhiteWave-Alpro. Mickelson, who had a debt to Walters, used the Dean Foods stock to repay the gambler. The SEC also targeted Dean Foods and Thomas Davis, who was cooperating with the investigation and had already pleaded guilty to charges including perjury and obstruction of justice. Mickelson, despite his history of gambling and a previous money laundering case, has not been charged with a crime in this matter. His representatives emphasized his commitment to high professional and ethical standards, while sponsors like Barclays and KPMG expressed disappointment but accepted his statement of responsibility. The case highlights the ongoing challenges in prosecuting insider trading, especially in light of recent legal rulings that have limited the government's ability to secure convictions.

A Colorado animal sanctuary faced a heartbreaking decision after Elbert County commissioners denied their request to relocate due to flooding concerns, leading to the euthanasia of 11 animals, including five bears, three lions, and three tigers. Lion’s Gate Animal Sanctuary in Agate announced the tragic news, stating that the animals were euthanized due to the inability to continue operations safely at their current location. Co-owners Peter Winney and Joan Laub blamed the Elbert County Commissioners for the decision, alleging that the denial was the catalyst for the animals' euthanasia. However, Elbert County Chairman Danny Wilcox refuted this, stating that the decision was based on safety concerns regarding the proposed new location, which was more densely populated. Wilcox emphasized that the sanctuary was assured they would continue operating at their current site, and alternative facilities had offered to take in the animals.

The sanctuary’s owners have a history of legal issues involving unlicensed animals. Winney was convicted once for bringing two lion cubs into the state without proper documents and was charged three times with having unlicensed animals. Laub’s records were sealed in 2004, citing privacy concerns. Despite these challenges, the sanctuary had operated for over a decade in their current location. The denial of their relocation request came after a public hearing where residents expressed concerns about safety, property values, and the potential disturbance to nearby livestock and wildlife. The Elbert County Commissioners were shocked by the sanctuary’s decision to euthanize the animals, as they believed the sanctuary would continue operating as they had for the past decade. The decision has sparked controversy and criticism, with some neighbors and animal welfare advocates questioning the handling of the situation.

A 91-year-old Illinois man, Walter Thomas, fulfilled a long-held dream by backing an SUV through his garage door, a feat he had always wanted to experience. The event took place in Woodstock, Illinois, on a Sunday afternoon, with the help of his three grandchildren and a donated 1998 Isuzu Rodeo. Walter Thomas, who has a passion for automobiles and owned four separate gasoline stations in Woodstock over the past 50 years, had always admired race car driving and harbored the unconventional wish to back a car through the garage door.

The idea to make this dream a reality came from his granddaughter, Becky Goers, a physical education and driver’s education teacher at Woodstock High School. She shared the story with her brother, Andrew Thomas, an accident reconstruction officer for the McHenry County Sheriff’s Office, who was eager to help his grandfather. Andrew Thomas found an old car headed to the junkyard and located a suitable garage for the stunt. Brian Thomas, Walter’s great-grandson, and his friends, Nick and Jamielynn Wedoff, agreed to participate, as their one-car garage was scheduled for demolition.

With a small crowd of family and friends watching, including his wife of 70 years, Dorothy, Walter Thomas donned a race car driver’s helmet for safety and climbed into the driver’s seat. Andrew Thomas, also wearing a helmet, sat in the passenger seat. On the "go" signal, Walter Thomas hit the gas pedal, and the sound of screeching tires preceded the moment when the maroon Isuzu burst through the wooden garage doors. The noise and subsequent crash caused one of Thomas’ great-granddaughters to burst into tears, but the rest of the family applauded and cheered.

Although the noise and impact caused a few shattered chunks of wood to litter the driveway, only the garage door came down, and the door frame remained unscathed. Walter Thomas expressed his gratitude to his grandchildren for making his dream come true, stating, "I appreciate the kids getting together. It’s kind of nice of them to think of old grandpa." The event not only fulfilled Walter Thomas’s unusual bucket list dream but also brought the family closer together.

A Paleo diet cookbook for babies and toddlers, co-authored by celebrity chef Pete Evans, nutritionist Helen Padarin, and blogger Charlotte Carr, has been put on hold after health officials raised concerns that its recipes could be potentially dangerous for infants. The controversial cookbook, titled "Bubba Yum Yum: The Paleo Way For New Mums, Babies and Toddlers," was scheduled for release but was delayed by its publisher, Pan Macmillan Australia, amid warnings that some of its recipes might be harmful. One of the most contentious recipes is a "homemade formula" for infants up to six months old, called the "Baby Building Broth," which is made from chicken bones, feet, and apple cider vinegar. Health experts argue that this recipe is not only potentially dangerous but also nutritionally inadequate, as it lacks essential nutrients like breast milk or commercial infant formula. Professor Heather Yeatman from the Public Health Association of Australia stated, "There appears to be recommendations not to use either breast milk or an approved infant formula, but to provide other foods to infants under six months of age, and that really is a big health risk." The Federal Health Department is investigating the publication, expressing concerns about the inadequate nutritional value of some of the recipes, particularly those intended for infants. The book includes other recipes that health officials consider unsafe or inappropriate for children, such as those containing runny eggs and added salt, which contravene national health guidelines for babies. While Evans and his co-authors defend the Paleo diet, health experts warn that it may not be suitable for infants and could lead to serious health risks. The book's disclaimer states that relying on the information provided may not give the desired results or cause negative health consequences. As the controversy continues, the fate of the cookbook remains uncertain, with health officials urging parents to follow tested feeding guidelines for their children.

An obese state parole judge, Robert Beltrani, 53, faced arraignment Tuesday for a bizarre incident where he allegedly assaulted a Legal Aid lawyer, Sam Roberts, after drunkenly boasting about his violent nature. The incident occurred on October 20th at a party in Chelsea celebrating a new law firm. Beltrani, visibly intoxicated, approached Roberts and loudly proclaimed, "Yeah, I’m the judge. I do justice and I f---ing kill people!" As Roberts turned away, Beltrani allegedly struck him, causing Roberts to lose consciousness and suffer a black eye and a separated shoulder. Beltrani, who weighs nearly 300 pounds, also fell and knocked into Roberts, sending both tumbling to the sidewalk. The judge fled the scene in his car, but was later tracked down and arrested. He appeared in Manhattan Criminal Court, where he was charged with misdemeanor assault, attempted assault, and harassment. Beltrani was released without bail and an order of protection was issued in Roberts' favor. The judge, who oversees state parole cases at Rikers Island, was placed on administrative leave pending an investigation. His lawyer, Daniel Ollen, declined to comment. The incident, captured on security video, has sparked outrage and raised questions about the judge's fitness for duty.

A school bus carrying 36 sixth-grade girls from Pembroke Hill in Kansas overturned near Kansas Highway 32 around 1 p.m., sending 22 girls to area hospitals with minor injuries. The driver, Elmer Scott Jr., 66, was trapped and later extricated, sustaining serious but stable injuries. Multiple agencies responded, and the cause of the crash remains under investigation. The field trip to Tall Oaks camp was canceled, with uninjured students taken to Bonner Springs High School. Safety is Durham School Services' top priority, and they are working with authorities to determine the cause.

Laverne Cox, star of Orange is the New Black and the first transgender person to be nominated for an Emmy, will be immortalized as Madame Tussauds' first transgender wax figure. The figure, unveiled in San Francisco ahead of the city's Pride Festival, honors Cox's achievements and serves as an inspiration. "I am so deeply honored to have been asked to be part of the Madame Tussauds legacy," Cox stated. "This honor feels even more improbable and extraordinary, and I hope that this will be a source of inspiration for everyone who encounters it." The museum's spokeswoman noted that the choice reflects the San Francisco Pride 2015 theme of equality without exception. Cox's figure will be unveiled on June 26, coinciding with the start of the Pride Celebration & Parade.

A man from Hunan province, identified only by his surname Yuan, was unmasked as a playboy who had relations with 17 women, each of whom believed they were his girlfriend or wife. Yuan, who had a middle school education and falsely claimed to be a university graduate in civil engineering from a top university in central China, was hospitalized after a car accident. His deception was exposed when his 17 "girlfriends" from the ages of 20 to 40, all of whom had been in relationships with him for varying lengths of time, including one who had even given birth to his child, met in his hospital ward. They discovered through WeChat that they were all in love with the same man. Yuan's case is being charged as a criminal fraud. One of his partners, Xiao Li, expressed her shock and disbelief, saying she had been with him for a year and a half and had cried so much she had no more tears. Another partner, Wang Fang, revealed that they had a child together and that she no longer loved Yuan but still cared for their son. Xiao Ting, another of Yuan's partners, admitted that she had believed in him as her "Mr. Right" and had even started planning their wedding. Over 6,000 comments have been posted on social media, with some admirers praising Yuan for his charm and others criticizing the women for not recognizing his deceit. Yuan's case highlights the complexities of relationships and the ease with which deception can be maintained in a digital age.

Jeremy Lin's meteoric rise in the NBA has reached new heights, as he outplayed Kobe Bryant and led the New York Knicks to a 92-85 victory over the Los Angeles Lakers.
