Meanwhile, the Bush administration's decision to shut down a criminal investigation of BP has raised questions about the lack of accountability in the oil industry. The debate over the oil spill and its aftermath continues to highlight the political tensions and differing perspectives on energy policy between the two parties.

A 16-year-old girl from Montbello, Denver, has been charged as an adult for the murder of her 7-year-old nephew, Jordan Vong. According to court documents, the girl intentionally killed Jordan on August 6th after a fight with her girlfriend. She instructed Jordan to go upstairs but instead, he sat on her bed, upsetting her. She pushed Jordan off the bed, causing him to hit his face on the floor. When Jordan began to cry, she placed her hand over his mouth and nose, holding him down until he stopped moving. The girl then wrapped Jordan's body in a blanket and hid it in a portable closet in her basement bedroom. Jordan was reported missing the afternoon of August 6th, and a search was launched by police and neighbors. Two days later, Jordan's body was found in the closet. The Denver District Attorney's Office charged the girl with first-degree murder after deliberation and child abuse resulting in death. She did not inform her family of her actions out of fear.

The French presidential election is set to be a historic event, with four candidates vying for the presidency in a two-round system. The top contenders are far-right leader Marine Le Pen, centrist Emmanuel Macron, conservative François Fillon, and far-left firebrand Jean-Luc Mélenchon. This election marks a significant departure from the traditional two-party system, as no established party candidate is expected to make it to the second round. Le Pen, who heads the far-right National Front, has surged in popularity, with 22% of the vote, while Macron, who founded his own centrist movement, is close behind with 21%. Fillon, a conservative, and Mélenchon, a far-left candidate, both have 19% support. The election is a reflection of the growing dissatisfaction with mainstream politics, as indicated by the low turnout intentions, with only 66% of voters certain to cast their ballots.

Le Pen has positioned herself as a defender against Islamic fundamentalism and globalization, while Mélenchon has criticized the labor law and called for a stronger left-wing coalition. The far-right candidate’s rise has prompted concerns about the potential impact on France and Europe, with Le Pen promising to hold a referendum on the EU and close "extremist" mosques. Mélenchon, on the other hand, has accused the Socialist candidate Benoît Hamon of not doing enough to address the issues, particularly the labor law. Hamon, who has called for a united left, is currently polling at 16-17%, behind Le Pen and Macron.

Facebook has taken steps to combat misinformation, targeting 30,000 fake accounts linked to France ahead of the election. The social media giant is working with French media to run fact-checking programs and has partnered with other companies to establish a news integrity nonprofit. These efforts are part of a broader strategy to address the spread of false news and misinformation, which has been a concern following the U.S. election. The French election is of particular interest to the international community, as it could signal the extent of the "populist wave" that has swept through Europe. The outcome of this election will not only determine the future of France but also have implications for the broader European political landscape.

Tom Petty's family and former Heartbreakers bandmates compiled a four-CD box set, "An American Treasure," to be released on September 28th by Reprise Records. The set features 60 previously unreleased tracks, alternate versions, and live performances spanning Petty's career. His daughter Adria and wife Dana, along with Heartbreakers Mike Campbell and Benmont Tench, curated the collection. The first single, "Keep a Little Soul," is a previously unreleased 1982 recording. The set will be available in multiple formats, including a standard 2-CD edition, a 4-CD deluxe edition, a 4-CD super deluxe limited edition, and a 6-LP vinyl edition. The deluxe and super deluxe editions include detailed liner notes and additional photographs, while the vinyl edition will be released later. This collection marks the first posthumous release of Petty's music since his death in October 2017.

Dennis Oland, the only son of a prominent New Brunswick beer magnate, is facing a second-degree murder trial for the 2011 bludgeoning death of his father, Richard Oland. The packed courtroom heard from the accused on Wednesday, as he testified in his own defense, insisting he had nothing to do with his father's "rage killing." Richard Oland, 69, was found dead in his Saint John office, with 45 sharp and blunt force injuries to his head, neck, and hands. No weapon was ever found. The trial, which began in mid-September, has seen nearly 50 witnesses and 47 days of testimony. Dennis Oland, 47, who was the last known person to see his father alive, has been under intense scrutiny due to his financial troubles and his father's extramarital affair. His defense team abruptly closed its case on Thursday, leaving the fate of Dennis Oland in the hands of the jury. The jury will deliberate on the case, which includes allegations of police corruption and incompetence, the two-year delay in laying charges, and the absence of a murder weapon. The trial is one of the longest criminal trials in New Brunswick history. Dennis Oland's mother, sister, wife, and other family members have testified on his behalf, but the defense ended up calling only two other witnesses: a bloodstain analyst and a forensic computer expert. The judge warned the jury that deliberations would be "mentally exhausting" and "emotionally draining." With the holiday season approaching, the judge urged jurors to make good use of their week off and get some rest. The extra juror was in place as a precaution, given the length of the trial. The trial is expected to wrap up earlier than expected, possibly as soon as Friday, after which the jury will consider all the factors and reach a verdict. If found guilty, Dennis Oland's world-class legal team will likely appeal the decision all the way to the Supreme Court. The Oland dynasty, once synonymous with ice-cold beer, is now brewing some of the hottest gossip Atlantic Canada has ever known.

Snap Inc., the parent company behind the popular messaging app Snapchat, is set to go public, potentially raising up to $3.4 billion. The company has priced its shares at $17 each, giving it a market valuation of about $24 billion, more than double the size of rival Twitter and the richest valuation in a U.S. tech IPO since Facebook in 2012. The initial public offering (IPO) is expected to be the biggest technology IPO since Alibaba in 2014, and it comes at a time when the market for tech IPOs has slowed down, making it a significant event. Despite concerns about its lack of profits and voting rights, the IPO has been well-subscribed, with the book more than 10 times oversubscribed. The company plans to use the funds raised to expand its user base and develop new products, particularly in the realm of cameras and hardware.

Snap's revenue has grown significantly, increasing by 589 percent last year, though the company is still not profitable. Its daily active user base has risen to 158 million, up from 107 million the year before, although the growth has slowed in recent quarters. The slowing user growth could be a real issue, as competition from larger rivals like Facebook has intensified. Facebook's Instagram launched its own stories platform, which appeared to be a knock-off of Snapchat, and this, combined with performance issues on Android phones, has contributed to the deceleration. Additionally, Snap is spending a significant amount on cloud-hosting costs, which could eat up a large portion of its projected revenue. Goldman Sachs estimates that Snap could hit approximately $2 billion in revenue by 2018, and the company is expected to price its IPO within a range of $17 to $18, giving it a market cap of $20 billion.

Snap's unique three-share class structure will give co-founder Evan Spiegel and chief technology officer Bobby Murphy tight control over the company's stock, with Spiegel holding a roughly 17 percent stake valued at $4.05 billion. The company has emphasized how important Snapchat is to its users, how long they spend on the app, and the revenue potential of the emerging trend for young people to communicate with video rather than text. Snap has been vague on its plans to monetize image-driven conversations, but it has suggested that investors put faith in the vision of its co-founder Evan Spiegel. The company's ambitions around cameras and hardware products, such as the Spectacles, are also on the minds of investors. Despite the high valuation and concerns about slowing user growth, the IPO is expected to be a "phenomenal trade" and its stock to soar when it comes public.

The gap between the pay of America’s top CEOs and their workers has widened dramatically, according to a new report from the Economic Policy Institute. In 2017, the average CEO of the top 350 U.S. companies earned 312 times more than the typical worker, up from 270 times in 2016. This marks a significant increase from the 1960s, when CEOs earned about 20 times more than the average worker. The report highlights that the surge in CEO pay is primarily driven by stock-related components, such as stock options and awards, rather than salary or bonuses. In 2017, the value of exercised stock options accounted for 78.9% of the year-over-year growth in CEO compensation, while the value realized on options exercised fell by over 15% between 2013 and 2016. The SEC now requires publicly owned firms to disclose the CEO-to-worker pay ratio, but the report argues that these ratios have limitations and suggests using the EPI methodology, which compares CEO compensation to the median worker in the firm’s key industry. The data show that CEO compensation has grown far more rapidly than the wages of the top 0.1% of earners, casting doubt on the argument that high CEO pay is driven by the market for skills. Instead, the report concludes that substantial rents are embedded in executive pay, reflecting the power of CEOs to extract concessions. The sharp rise in CEO compensation has contributed to the growth of top 1% incomes, with 58% of the expansion of income for the top 1% of households and 67% for the top 0.1% attributed to nonfinance executives and financial sector workers. To address this trend, the report suggests implementing higher marginal income tax rates at the very top, setting corporate tax rates higher for firms with higher CEO-to-worker ratios, and changing corporate governance to limit executive pay growth.

Consumer review website Yelp Inc. made a strong market debut on its initial public offering (IPO), closing 64% higher at $24.58, surpassing its initial price range of $12 to $14. At the closing price, Yelp's valuation reached approximately $1.47 billion, nearly 17 times its 2011 revenue. Analysts attribute Yelp's success to the positive sentiment surrounding Facebook's upcoming IPO and the broader trend of successful tech IPOs. However, Yelp's profitability remains a concern, as it has yet to turn a profit since its 2004 founding. The company generates revenue through advertising from local businesses, with 25 million reviews and 66 million unique monthly visitors as of the end of 2011. Yelp's unique visitor growth accelerated in the past year, and it forecasts solid growth over the next few years. Despite its success, Yelp faces competition from Google, Facebook, and other review sites like Angie's List, which charges for memberships and saw its stock fall 5.4% on the same day as Yelp's IPO. Yelp's CEO, Jeremy Stoppelman, believes the company can become the "Amazon of local advertising," but analysts are cautious about its long-term prospects, particularly in the face of potential competition and the need to demonstrate profitability. The IPO window for tech and Internet companies is open, and Yelp's performance may influence future offerings.

A rare and mysterious marine phenomenon has gripped the west coast of America, with millions of tiny, tubular creatures known as pyrosomes swarming in unprecedented numbers. These translucent, bumpy organisms, often referred to as "sea pickles" or "fire bodies," have washed up on popular beaches and ruined fishermen's nets, leaving scientists scrambling to understand the cause and impact of this bloom. Pyrosomes, typically found in tropical waters, have been spotted as far north as Sitka, Alaska, and are so densely packed that fishers report their nets being filled with the creatures instead of their intended catch. Graduate student Olivia Blondheim, part of a new research team studying the bloom, explains, "Right now we are scrambling to learn as much as possible while we have the opportunity. If we continue to see this many, what impact will it have on the ecosystems here, and what economic impact on the fisheries? There are so many unknowns at this point, it really is a remarkable bloom." 

These pyrosomes, which can grow up to two feet long and are actually colonies of tiny animals, have been spotted in massive clusters stretching as far as the eye can see. The unusual presence of pyrosomes in the Pacific Ocean has left marine scientists puzzled. Dr. Lisa-ann Gershwin, a marine biology expert, notes, "Because they aren’t wanted, and people really aren’t used to seeing them – they really do impact fisheries and catch a lot of attention." The bloom's cause remains unknown, with possibilities ranging from climate change to changes in the pyrosomes' diet or unusual sea currents. Researcher Hilarie Sorensen, who has been monitoring the situation, observes, "Why they’re here now is unknown at this point. We’ve had warm ocean conditions over the past couple years, and something has brought them here. They’re just flourishing. It’s just very unusual to find them so close to shore, so evenly distributed, and so abundant." 

Scientists are now racing to study these pyrosomes, including their feeding habits, swimming speed, and vertical orientation in the water. The potential impact of the bloom is also a concern, as the sudden death of such a large number of pyrosomes could lead to oxygen depletion in the ocean, creating dead zones for marine life. As the phenomenon continues, researchers hope to gain more insights into the reasons behind this unusual occurrence and its broader implications for the marine ecosystem.

Facebook disclosed on Wednesday that a likely Russia-based group spent $100,000 on political ads promoting divisive social and political messages over a two-year period. The ads targeted a wide range of topics, including LGBT matters, race issues, immigration, and gun rights. Facebook identified 3,300 ads and 470 "inauthentic" accounts and pages, which it now has suspended. About one-quarter of the ads were geographically targeted, though Facebook declined to specify the locations. The findings align with U.S. intelligence agency conclusions that Russia interfered in the 2016 election, including by using paid social media trolls to spread fake news. Facebook stated that it did not find a direct link to any presidential campaign, and the ads were mostly national in scope, not targeting key swing states. The company said it is cooperating with federal inquiries and has taken action to block fake accounts linked to election meddling in France and Germany. Facebook's chief security officer, Alex Stamos, emphasized the need to stay vigilant against misuse of the platform. The disclosure comes amid ongoing investigations by congressional committees and special counsel Robert Mueller into Russian interference in the U.S. election. Rep. Adam Schiff, the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, called the findings "deeply disturbing" and consistent with intelligence community assessments. Facebook also reported another $50,000 in potentially politically related ads, likely by Russians, bringing the total to $150,000. Despite the significant amount of money spent on political ads during the 2016 campaign, Facebook's findings represent a small fraction of overall spending. The company's decision to share this information with congressional investigators and special counsel highlights the growing scrutiny of social media's role in election interference.

Two men who worked as managers at various Hooters locations, including Hollywood, Costa Mesa, and downtown Los Angeles, are suing the restaurant chain and their former male boss, alleging years of sexual harassment. Their attorney, Jason Oliver, claims that the boss, Rick Leukert, subjected them to repeated, intense acts intended to cause mental harm, humiliate, and undermine them. According to the lawsuit, filed in Los Angeles Superior Court, Leukert allegedly threw one of the men, Paul "PJ" Cagnina, down to the parking lot ground and forcibly engaged in a simulated sodomy. Cagnina's lawsuit also accuses Leukert of touching his buttocks when standing behind him. Both men say they confronted Leukert about the behavior, and the company investigated him. Within months, Leukert was fired with no explanation. However, soon after, Scott Peterson was also let go, which his attorney argues was in retaliation. "When they stood up to him, they paid the price. They were punished even more in terms of other types of mistreatment," Oliver said. Hooters released a statement saying, "This matter involves a franchised location and its employees in California. We have no independent knowledge of the facts and are therefore unable to comment." The lawsuit seeks unspecified damages and a court order directing Hooters to stop allowing sexual harassment and retaliation in the workplace.

A Trinidadian national, Bernard Charles, was caught at John F. Kennedy International Airport for attempting to smuggle nearly two pounds of heroin hidden in his underwear, authorities said. Charles, 42, stepped off Caribbean Airlines flight No. 520 on April Fool's Day and immediately drew attention from Customs and Border Protection officers due to his "awkward" gait. During a pat-down, officers discovered two clear packages in his groin area, which tested positive for heroin. The drugs, with a street value of over $70,000, were seized, and Charles was ordered held without bail. He faces up to 10 years in prison if convicted of drug smuggling. "This seizure is just another example of our Customs and Border Patrol officers being ever vigilant in protecting the United States from the distribution of these illegal drugs," said New York Field Operations Director Robert Perez. Bernard Charles's nervous behavior and unusual gait during the inspection process alerted the officers to his suspicious activity, leading to his arrest. The incident highlights the ongoing efforts of border protection agencies to prevent the illegal entry of drugs into the country.

President Donald Trump's longtime confidant, Keith Schiller, privately testified to congressional investigators that he rejected a Russian offer to send five women to Trump's hotel room during their 2013 trip to Moscow for the Miss Universe pageant, according to sources from both political parties. Schiller told the House intelligence committee that he took the offer as a joke and shared it with Trump, who laughed it off. Schiller left Trump's hotel room after several minutes, as his standard practice as Trump's security guard. The House lawmakers raised the matter due to salacious allegations in the Christopher Steele dossier, which detailed alleged ties between Trump and Russians. During a closed-door hearing, Schiller denied knowing about the dossier's claims and was asked about meetings between Trump associates and Russians, but denied having knowledge of many of those interactions. Schiller also denied knowing about the deliberations around the firing of FBI Director James Comey, saying he was only called into deliver a letter with the news to the FBI. Schiller's attorney, Stuart Sears, criticized the House Intelligence Committee for leaking information and defaming cooperative witnesses. Trump has long denied the dossier's allegations, stating that he was cautious about hotel rooms in Russia due to potential cameras. The FBI has corroborated some information in the dossier, using it as justification to obtain a surveillance warrant on Trump campaign foreign policy adviser Carter Page. Schiller's testimony comes as part of ongoing investigations into potential Russia collusion.

Cindy McCain arrived at the Arizona Capitol on Wednesday, August 29, 2018, to honor her late husband, Senator John McCain, R-Ariz., escorted by her sons Jimmy and Jack. The public viewing of McCain’s flag-draped casket began at 2 p.m., with hundreds of people waiting in the summer heat to pay their respects. Among them was Kassandra Morales, a Democrat who brought her sons to see a “real hero.” The 44-year-old has always admired McCain, even though she is a member of a different political party. 

The morning began with a private ceremony at the Capitol, where family and politicians gathered to mourn the 81-year-old senator. Cindy McCain laid her cheek on the casket, and her children, including Meghan, Jack, and Jimmy, touched it, weeping. Governor Doug Ducey, former Senator Jon Kyl, and Senator Jeff Flake gave speeches, praising McCain’s contributions to national security and his ability to unite people across political divides. Kyl highlighted McCain’s instincts in asserting U.S. power and said he would miss the senator. Flake offered a prayer, emphasizing McCain’s commitment to his country.

The public viewing attracted a diverse crowd, including veterans and constituents. Judith Hatch, a veteran, distributed flags and expressed her loss, saying, “We definitely have lost a strong advocate, so we'll need someone who is going to step up to the plate.” Many attendees, like Kassandra Morales, brought flowers and shared stories of why McCain was a hero to them. The viewing continued throughout the afternoon, with volunteers providing water and ice to the waiting crowd.

The day marked the first appearance of McCain’s family members since his death, and it was clear that his passing had touched many hearts. The public viewing was just the beginning of a series of memorials, with a procession through Phoenix, a memorial service at North Phoenix Baptist Church, and a final viewing at the U.S. Capitol. The events underscored the significant impact Senator John McCain had on Arizona and the nation, and the respect and admiration he commanded from people of all backgrounds.

NASA's Curiosity rover has delivered its most significant findings yet, revealing that ancient Mars could have supported life as we know it for long periods. The rover's exploration of Gale Crater has uncovered evidence of an ancient lake, which existed about 3.7 billion years ago, suggesting habitable environments on Mars more recently than previously thought. This lake, likely fed by streams from surrounding mountains, could have supported chemolithoautotrophs, a class of microbes that obtain energy by breaking down rocks and minerals. The lake's calm waters contained key chemical ingredients for life, including sulfur, nitrogen, hydrogen, oxygen, phosphorus, and carbon. Curiosity's analysis of fine-grained sedimentary rocks, obtained by drilling into Yellowknife Bay outcrops, revealed clay minerals formed in the lake's sediments. The lake may have existed for tens of thousands to millions of years, possibly with ice covering it periodically. While Curiosity was not designed to hunt for signs of life, the findings make the possibility of Martian life significantly more plausible. The mission has also provided insights into the planet's radiation environment, which could damage organic compounds, complicating the search for Martian organics. The rover's detour to Yellowknife Bay turned out to be a gold mine of data, confirming and extending the landmark discovery that Gale Crater could have supported microbial life. These findings are detailed in six separate papers published in the journal Science, offering a more complete picture of early Mars and its potential to support life.

President Barack Obama eulogized Nelson Mandela as a man who "took history in his hands and bent the arc of the moral universe toward justice," reflecting on Mandela's profound impact on his life and the world. Mandela's death at 95, with his family by his side, marks the end of an era. Obama, who considers Mandela a personal hero, emphasized the importance of learning from Mandela's example, particularly in striving for a future guided by love and the belief in the power of one individual to make a difference. Obama ordered American flags to be flown at half-staff in honor of Mandela, a close friend of the United States and an incomparable liberator for South Africa. The president's statement highlighted Mandela's influence on his thinking and his political journey, noting that their paths crossed only once, in a brief meeting in 2005. Obama's visit to South Africa this summer, which was overshadowed by Mandela's health, included a poignant visit to Robben Island, where Mandela spent 18 years in prison, and a meeting with Mandela's family. Mandela's legacy, encapsulated in songs and tributes from artists like U2, Public Enemy, and Santana, continues to inspire musicians and fans worldwide. His three-syllable name remains a symbol of equality, freedom, and revolution, serving as a beacon of hope and a call to action.

Two Ohio men, Ricky Jackson and Wiley Bridgeman, who were wrongly convicted of murder in 1975, were released after spending nearly four decades in prison. Jackson, 57, and Bridgeman, 60, were convicted along with Bridgeman’s brother, Ronnie, in the 1975 shooting death and robbery of Harold Franks, a Cleveland-area money order salesman. The case relied heavily on testimony from a 12-year-old witness, Edward Vernon, who recanted his testimony, revealing that he was coerced by detectives. Vernon wrote in a 2013 affidavit that he never saw the murder take place and was manipulated by police. The Ohio Innocence Project took up the case and worked to exonerate the men. After Vernon’s recantation, Cuyahoga County Prosecutor Timothy McGinty dropped the charges against Jackson and Bridgeman, allowing for their release. Jackson, who had been in prison since he was 18, was the longest-held U.S. prisoner to be exonerated. He expressed gratitude to the Ohio Innocence Project and the prosecutor, stating that the bitterness was over. Bridgeman, who had been on death row, was also released. Both men expressed a desire to move forward and focus on the future, acknowledging the courage it took for Vernon to come forward. The case highlights the importance of reliable evidence and the impact of coerced testimony on the criminal justice system.

Investigators are probing whether Prince died from an overdose and if a doctor was involved in prescribing him drugs in the weeks before his death, according to a law enforcement official. The official stated that among the things under investigation is whether a doctor was on a plane that made an emergency landing in Illinois less than a week before Prince's death. Law enforcement sources have also confirmed that prescription drugs were found at Prince's Paisley Park home, though it's unclear if they were prescribed to him. The official mentioned the possibility of powerful painkillers like Percocet being involved. Prince's plane made an emergency stop in Moline, Illinois, on April 15, and first responders administered a "save shot" of Narcan, which is used in suspected opioid overdoses. The incident occurred as Prince returned to Minneapolis following a performance in Atlanta. An autopsy has been performed, but results are expected in three to four weeks. The investigation is ongoing, and it's unclear if criminal charges will be filed. A search warrant for Prince's Paisley Park home and studio was sealed to prevent compromising the investigation. The incident report from the Carver County Sheriff’s Office, released a week after Prince's death, provided little new information, only confirming that Prince was alone when he died and that neither foul play nor suicide was suspected. Prince had canceled concerts in Atlanta due to health concerns and was suffering from physical issues, including hip and knee problems, according to his longtime friend and collaborator Sheila E. The search warrant and related documents were sealed by a Carver County judge to avoid compromising the investigation and to protect innocent people.

In the wake of Harvey Weinstein's downfall, the stories of women who have accused him of sexual harassment and assault have revealed a disturbing pattern of behavior spanning decades. Alice Evans, Katherine Kendall, and Tomi-Ann Roberts, three women who have come forward, shared their experiences in a conversation, highlighting the pervasive nature of Weinstein's alleged misconduct. Alice Evans recounted her encounter at Cannes in 2002, where Weinstein made inappropriate advances, though not as harrowing as the experiences of Kendall and Roberts. Kendall described a 1990s incident where Weinstein invited her to a movie screening, then to his apartment, where he made increasingly inappropriate requests, culminating in a sexually charged encounter. Roberts shared her 1980s experience, where Weinstein invited her to his hotel room, leading to a traumatic rape. These women's stories, along with many others, have sparked a broader conversation about the culture of sexual harassment and assault in Hollywood, and the systemic failures that allowed Weinstein to continue his alleged behavior for so long. The women expressed a mix of anger, shame, and a determination to speak out, despite the potential consequences. They also discussed the challenges of navigating these situations, often feeling trapped and unable to fully assert their boundaries. The conversation underscored the importance of supporting victims and the need for systemic changes to prevent such abuses in the future.

Ohioans will vote on Nov. 3 on whether to legalize marijuana under an oligopoly, with cultivation limited to 10 farms, making the Buckeye State the sixth to legalize. The private investor group ResponsibleOhio spent over $2 million to gather the necessary signatures, aiming to create a billion-dollar industry. However, a legislative initiative, Issue 2, also on the ballot, seeks to prevent monopolies, potentially leading to legal battles. Despite opposition from the Ohio Farm Bureau Federation and some activists, a Quinnipiac University poll found 52% support for legalization. The measure, if passed, would generate significant tax revenue and provide economic benefits, but critics argue it unfairly benefits wealthy investors.

A Montana police officer, Grant Morrison, was cleared of wrongdoing in the April 2014 shooting death of Richard Ramirez, an unarmed man high on methamphetamine. Morrison testified that he feared for his life during a 30-second encounter with Ramirez, believing the man was reaching for a gun. Video footage showed Morrison repeatedly ordering Ramirez to raise his hands before firing three shots into the car, killing him. The jury deliberated for about an hour before determining that Morrison's actions were justified. Morrison had previously been cleared of wrongdoing in a 2013 shooting incident. Ramirez's family expressed disappointment with the ruling, alleging racial profiling and excessive use of force. The incident was part of a series of police killings of unarmed suspects that have heightened scrutiny of law enforcement nationwide. Morrison was placed on paid administrative leave after the shooting and is now assigned to a task force investigating prescription drug crimes. The case was heard during a coroner's inquest, which is mandatory under Montana law whenever someone is killed by law enforcement. Morrison's actions were supported by testimony that Ramirez had a small amount of methamphetamine and a syringe near his seat, though Ramirez's family argued that his drug use was irrelevant. Morrison's emotional breakdown after the shooting, captured on dashcam footage, showed him sobbing and breathing heavily as colleagues comforted him, saying, "You're ok, I got you." Morrison stated, "I thought he was going to pull a gun," and "I couldn't take that risk. I wanted to see my son grow up." The inquest was held in the context of increased scrutiny of police use of force following incidents in Ferguson, Missouri, and New York City.

The Dutch government thwarted a Russian cyber-attack on the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons (OPCW) headquarters in The Hague, just weeks after the Salisbury novichok attack, according to new revelations. Four Russian intelligence officers, believed to be from the GRU's Unit 26165, were apprehended with hacking equipment and other incriminating evidence, including a laptop and cash, in their possession. The suspects had diplomatic passports and arrived in the Netherlands on April 13, 2018, and were immediately expelled. The OPCW was investigating the attempted assassination of Sergei and Yulia Skripal in the UK and a chemical attack in Syria at the time. British officials claim the same GRU unit had also targeted the investigation into Malaysia Airlines Flight 17, which was shot down over Ukraine in 2014, and had attempted to hack the World Anti-Doping Agency during a conference in Switzerland. The U.S. government announced criminal charges against the intelligence officers for computer hacking, wire fraud, and aggravated identity theft. The Dutch and British governments have vowed to step up their efforts against the GRU, with British Prime Minister Theresa May and Dutch Prime Minister Mark Rutte condemning the Russian military's "disregard for the global values and rules that keep us all safe." NATO Secretary General Jens Stoltenberg warned Russia to halt its "reckless" behavior, while U.S. Secretary of Defense Jim Mattis emphasized that NATO would "be exposing" Moscow's nefarious acts. Russia dismissed the allegations as "big fantasies," with Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova calling the charges "Russiaphobic."

China's highest-paid movie star, Fan Bingbing, has been placed last in an academic report ranking A-list celebrities on their social responsibility. Fan, known for her roles in Hollywood blockbusters like "X-Men: Days of Future Past," has not been seen in public since July, leading to speculation about her whereabouts. The report by Beijing Normal University evaluated celebrities based on professional work, charitable actions, and personal integrity, with a pass requiring a score of over 60%. Only nine celebrities made the cut, with actor Xu Zheng topping the list at 78%. Fan's score of zero has sparked controversy, with many defending her on social media platforms like Weibo. The report comes amid ongoing investigations into alleged tax evasion and "yin-yang" contracts in the entertainment industry. Fan's studio denied any wrongdoing, but the actress's low score has raised questions about the criteria used by the report's authors. The 2017 Forbes China Celebrity List, published in the latest edition of Forbes China, ranks Fan at the top with 300 million yuan in earnings, followed by Lu Han, Yang Mi, and Zhao Liying. Despite Fan's high earnings and international success, her social responsibility score has drawn criticism, highlighting the complex relationship between celebrity status and social expectations in China. The report emphasizes the need for celebrities to be more socially responsible and to promote positive values, suggesting that Fan's low score may be a result of the allegations against her. As the Chinese government continues to crack down on tax evasion and excessive pay in the entertainment industry, the social responsibility rankings could become a significant factor in determining a celebrity's standing and influence.

House Majority Whip Steve Scalise (R-La.) faced a significant backlash after admitting he spoke at a white supremacist group’s event in 2002, an incident that resurfaced as Republicans prepared for full control of Congress. Scalise acknowledged speaking to the group created by former Ku Klux Klan leader David Duke, but maintained he was unaware of the group’s white-supremacist leanings and that his appearance was part of his efforts to garner support for his policies. His office stated that Scalise had spoken to numerous groups during his time as a state representative, focusing on issues like eliminating slush funds and opposing a tax increase on middle-class families. Scalise’s office emphasized that he had never been affiliated with the group and that his beliefs were in stark contrast to the group’s hateful ideology.

The revelation caused a stir among conservative commentators and political opponents. Influential conservative blogger Erick Erickson questioned Scalise’s claim of ignorance, noting that by 2002, everyone knew Duke was a white supremacist. Erickson suggested that Scalise’s appearance at the event was “insulting and ludicrous.” Scalise’s defense was met with skepticism from some Louisiana Democrats, who called his explanation “ridiculous” and demanded answers about who invited him and why he did not know about the group’s history. Louisiana Governor Bobby Jindal, however, defended Scalise, stating he was a “good man who is fair-minded and kind-hearted.”

The controversy came at a critical time for Scalise, who had recently been elevated to the third-ranking House Republican position following the primary defeat of former Majority Leader Eric Cantor. Scalise’s leadership role now faces scrutiny, and his colleagues are closely watching how he handles the situation. While some conservative supporters expressed frustration with Scalise’s past voting record, others, like Rob Maness, a former Louisiana Senate candidate, defended him, calling the incident an “isolated mistake.” The incident also highlights the challenges Republican leaders face as they seek to maintain their party’s image and address concerns about their members’ past associations.

During a terrifying 90-minute ride in his car, Tamerlan Tsarnaev, one of the Boston Marathon bombing suspects, interrogated the victim about his heritage and family, while his younger brother, Dzhokhar, followed in another vehicle. After the carjacking, Tamerlan claimed responsibility for the bombings and the killing of a campus police officer. The victim, identified only as Danny, described Tamerlan as talkative and aggressive, while Dzhokhar was quieter and more compliant. Danny managed to escape when Dzhokhar left the vehicle to pay for gas, running to a nearby Mobil station and alerting authorities. The victim's Mercedes SUV, which sustained 32 bullet holes, was used by police to track the brothers and ultimately led to the shootout that killed Tamerlan and captured Dzhokhar. Danny's account reveals the brothers' spontaneous plan to travel to New York with their remaining explosives, with Danny hearing the word "Manhattan" during the ride. His testimony highlights the stark contrast in behavior between the two suspects and underscores the harrowing experience of the carjacking victim.

President Obama's press conference aimed to intensify the political battle with Republicans over tax cuts for the wealthy, framing it as a moral and economic necessity. He emphasized that maintaining high-end tax breaks would force cuts in essential programs like education, medical research, and food safety, and suggested that Republicans were prioritizing the interests of the wealthy over the broader good. Obama’s aggressive stance included highlighting the $3 billion tax break for corporate jet owners, which he argued was trivial compared to the impact on critical services. His strategy was to portray Republicans as unwilling to make balanced sacrifices and as defenders of the wealthy at the expense of the public good. Obama also addressed the Medicare issue, stating that any deficit reduction deal must not shift costs to seniors, indicating a firm stance against cost-shifting. While he stopped short of explicitly rejecting a deal that did not include high-end tax hikes, his press conference made it clear that he would continue to advocate for such measures, positioning the debate as a test of moral and political priorities. The summary of the conference highlighted Obama’s intention to use the issue as a central theme in the upcoming campaign, emphasizing the need for a balanced approach to deficit reduction that includes tax increases on the wealthy.

The Court of Arbitration for Sport (CAS) has overturned the lifetime Olympic bans of 28 Russian athletes who competed in the 2014 Sochi Olympics, dealing a significant blow to the International Olympic Committee's (IOC) anti-doping efforts. This decision, made just days before the start of the 2018 Winter Olympics in Pyeongchang, South Korea, has sparked outrage and concern among anti-doping advocates. The IOC expressed disappointment, warning that the ruling could undermine the global fight against doping. Among those whose bans were overturned are medalists in events like men's skeleton and 50-kilometer cross-country skiing. The CAS ruling was based on insufficient evidence to prove anti-doping rule violations, despite the IOC's investigation into state-sponsored doping in Russia. This has led to accusations that the CAS used a higher standard of proof than in previous doping cases, potentially emboldening future cheaters. Russian officials celebrated the decision, with Deputy Prime Minister Vitaly Mutko stating that the athletes' good names had been restored and that they should be allowed to compete in Pyeongchang. However, the IOC maintained that not being sanctioned does not automatically confer the privilege of an invitation. The decision also means that the 28 athletes will have their Sochi results reinstated, potentially returning Russia to the top of the medal table. Meanwhile, 11 other Russian athletes had their lifetime bans reduced to a ban only from the Pyeongchang Games. This complex situation has left the IOC grappling with how to handle the 28 athletes who now want to compete, with some legal challenges expected. The case highlights the ongoing struggle between enforcing strict anti-doping measures and the potential for legal loopholes that could undermine the integrity of the Olympic Games.

The official Badlands National Park Twitter account tweeted climate change statistics on Tuesday that were later deleted, potentially contradicting the Trump administration's stance on the issue. The tweets stated, "Today, the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere is higher than at any time in the last 650,000 years. #climate." A National Park Service spokesperson blamed a former employee for the tweets, which the NPS removed voluntarily. The statement noted that the park was not ordered to delete the tweets but chose to do so after realizing the account had been compromised. The National Park Service now advises its social media managers to continue using Twitter for public safety and park information posts, but to avoid content related to national policy issues. This isn't the first time park accounts have tweeted climate change information that was subsequently deleted, highlighting the ongoing tension between federal policies and local park management.

A remarkable discovery by a high-school student in 2009 has shed new light on the growth and development of Parasaurolophus, a distinctive duck-billed dinosaur that lived in southern Utah over 75 million years ago. Kevin Terris, a 17-year-old at the time, stumbled upon a baby Parasaurolophus skeleton, which was initially overlooked by two professional paleontologists who had passed by the site just days earlier. The fossil, named "Joe" in honor of Joe Augustyn, a long-time supporter of the museum, turned out to be the smallest, most complete, and youngest Parasaurolophus specimen ever found. This unique find, now on display at the Raymond M. Alf Museum of Paleontology in Claremont, California, offers unprecedented insights into the growth patterns and development of this iconic dinosaur.

The team of researchers, led by Andrew Farke, meticulously excavated the fossil, which was encased in 800 pounds of rock, and transported it by helicopter to the laboratory. After four years of careful preparation, the skeleton was finally unveiled, revealing a 6-foot-long juvenile Parasaurolophus that was less than a year old when it died. The fossil's leg bone analysis showed that the young dinosaur had not yet developed any growth rings, indicating rapid growth to a quarter of adult size within a year. This finding suggests that Parasaurolophus had a unique growth strategy, developing its distinctive crest early in life.

The discovery also revealed that the baby Parasaurolophus had a small crest bump, which would have grown into the characteristic tube-like crest of adult Parasaurolophus. This finding challenges previous assumptions about the timing of crest development and suggests that Parasaurolophus had a unique "tweeter" vocalization, contrasting with the "woofers" of adult dinosaurs. The researchers used advanced imaging techniques, including CT scans, to create a 3D digital model of the skeleton, making it accessible for study and public viewing through the DinosaurJoe website.

Kevin Terris, now an aspiring paleontologist at Montana State University, expressed his excitement about the discovery, which has not only contributed to scientific understanding but also inspired his future career path. The study, published in the journal PeerJ, highlights the importance of continued fieldwork and the unexpected discoveries that can come from the keen eyes of amateur paleontologists. This remarkable find underscores the ongoing importance of fossil research in unraveling the mysteries of ancient life.

On a Sunday morning, Luis Lopez Gallegos and his wife Perla Avina were returning home from shopping for ingredients to prepare Perla's popular posole for a Raiders game when a tragic incident occurred. The couple was driving in the southbound lanes of 98th Avenue in East Oakland when an unknown motorist opened fire, striking Perla Avina in the head from the passenger seat. Gallegos, a 33-year-old auto mechanic, drove the short distance to their home, where emergency responders performed CPR but were unable to save her. Perla Avina, a 30-year-old medical receptionist, was the mother of four children, ranging in age from 1 to 14. The shooting happened around 12:30 p.m., leaving the family and neighbors in shock. Gallegos, who described the shooter as a "coward with a gun," stated that the couple had been driving normally when shots were fired. A neighbor, Dwayne Jackson, witnessed the aftermath, helping to remove Perla from the car and performing CPR. The Oakland Police Department is offering a $30,000 reward for information leading to the arrest of the shooter. The couple's family and friends are mourning the loss, with Gallegos vowing to stay strong for his children. The incident has left the community in disbelief and a call for justice.

Three months ago, a Harvard student named Aran Khanna launched a browser extension called Marauder’s Map, which mapped the locations of Facebook Messenger users based on their messages. The app, which Khanna posted on Medium and other platforms, quickly gained traction, with over 85,000 downloads. Facebook, aware of the privacy implications, swiftly responded by disabling the extension and tweaking its code to prevent the transmission of location data to browsers. However, the company did not change the default settings for the Messenger app, which still shares locations by default on Android and with user permission on iOS. Khanna’s project brought to light the extent of location data collection by Facebook Messenger, which had been sharing users’ locations with anyone they messaged since 2011. The extension highlighted the ease with which such data could be accessed and visualized, prompting Facebook to tweak its privacy settings and issue a press release announcing a new feature requiring users to opt-in to sharing their locations. Khanna’s work demonstrated the potential for transparency and public pressure to drive changes in privacy practices, even in a company known for its “hacker culture.” The incident also raised questions about the balance between user convenience and privacy, as well as the role of transparency in addressing privacy concerns.

Manspreading might make you the villain of the morning L train, but a new study suggests it could also make you lucky in love. People who adopted expansive postures—widespread limbs and a stretched-out torso—in speed-dating situations garnered more romantic interest than those who folded their arms in closed postures, the researchers found. In her recent paper, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Tanya Vacharkulksemsuk, a post-doctoral research fellow at the University of California, Berkeley, performed two studies. First, she and her team watched videos of 144 speed-dates and correlated them with the participants’ ratings of each other. People who sat in expanded postures were deemed more attractive, and for both men and women, postural expansiveness nearly doubled their chances of getting a "yes" response to a second date. Even laughing and smiling didn’t work as well as spreading out, Vacharkulksemsuk found.

Next, Vacharkulksemsuk posted pictures of people in open and closed postures on a dating site. Again, those in the expansive postures were about 25 percent more likely to generate interest from another user. However, this strategy worked much better for men than women. Men, overall, received far fewer bites than women did, but 87 percent of their "yeses" came in response to an open posture. For women, meanwhile, 53 percent of "yes" responses came when they were in an expansive posture. In a separate test, Vacharkulksemsuk found that both the male and female "expansive" photos were considered more dominant than the "closed" photos. That dominance might suggest an abundance of resources and a willingness to share those resources. When potential romantic partners are evaluating each other for just a few seconds, in other words, money talks—mainly through bodily breadth.

So should you rush to change your Tinder picture to something a little less pouty and a little more Backstreet Boys circa Millennium? Like with almost every study, there are reasons to be skeptical. "Power poses" made a big splash in 2010 when it was found that adopting them could tweak hormone levels—then sparked controversy after a follow-up study failed to replicate the effect.

Abdul Raziq, the acting chief of police in Kandahar, has been accused of involvement in a massacre of civilians and ongoing human rights abuses. Raziq, a young and powerful warlord, was appointed to his position in June 2006, following the assassination of his predecessor. His men have been implicated in killings, torture, and illegal detentions, yet Raziq has been showered with U.S. training, equipment, and financial support. Despite credible allegations of a 2006 massacre of 16 men, Raziq has been promoted and praised by both U.S. and Afghan officials. The U.S. has trained Raziq’s forces through private military firms and provided them with salaries through international funds. While U.S. officials have downplayed the abuses, a 2006 State Department report reveals evidence of Raziq’s involvement in the massacre. The article raises questions about whether U.S. assistance to Raziq and his men may have violated a 1997 law prohibiting aid to foreign military units involved in human rights violations. The situation highlights the complex challenges of training and supporting local forces in conflict zones.

Barack Obama's foreign policy has evolved from his early days as a state legislator and senator, influenced by his reading and interactions with various experts. Obama sought to learn from the mistakes of the Bush administration, particularly the Iraq War, and to avoid the pitfalls of idealism. His approach, described by one adviser as "leading from behind," reflects a pragmatic stance that acknowledges the decline of American power and the need to work within international institutions. This strategy involves a cautious and sometimes reactive approach to global challenges, such as the Libyan intervention, where the U.S. took a backseat role. Critics argue that this approach has led to indecision and a failure to assert American leadership, evident in the handling of Iran, Syria, and the broader Middle East. Some, like Charles Krauthammer, contend that this policy is a retreat from American exceptionalism and a sign of weakness. The Obama administration's response is that the U.S. faces a new reality where its power is declining, and it must adapt its approach to international relations. However, this strategy has been criticized for its perceived passivity and for not effectively addressing global challenges. The debate over Obama's foreign policy doctrine continues, with some arguing that it is a coherent response to a changing world order, while others see it as a sign of American decline and a failure to lead.

Jeb Bush's presidential campaign, once seen as a sure bet, ended in a disappointing fourth-place finish in South Carolina, marking the end of the Bush family's political dynasty in national politics. Bush's campaign, initially viewed as the frontrunner, struggled to connect with the Republican electorate, which was more interested in anger and change than policy and experience. Despite raising over $100 million, Bush failed to dominate the field, and his strategy of focusing on his record as Florida governor and avoiding direct confrontation with rivals like Donald Trump proved ineffective. Bush's campaign was also criticized for its lack of adaptability, as it failed to address the rise of Trump and his populist message. The Bush campaign's reliance on a "playbook" that underestimated the threat of Trump and other rivals, combined with Bush's own perceived lack of charisma and political savvy, contributed to his downfall. The campaign's internal disagreements, particularly over how to respond to Trump, further weakened its position. Ultimately, Bush's candidacy was seen as a mismatch for the political environment of 2016, where voters were seeking a more confrontational and less establishment candidate. The end of Jeb Bush's campaign marks the end of the Bush family's significant role in American politics, leaving behind a legacy defined more by their failures than their successes.

Just in time for holiday cookie season, a surprising ingredient has been discovered in your vanilla-flavored treats: castoreum, a substance derived from beaver anal excretions. This sticky, brown goo, secreted from a beaver’s castor sacs, is used to mark territory and has a musky, vanilla scent, making it a popular additive in perfumes and foods for over 80 years. According to Joanne Crawford, a wildlife ecologist at Southern Illinois University, “I lift up the animal’s tail, and I’m like, ‘Get down there, and stick your nose near its bum.’” “People think I’m nuts,” she adds, “but it’s beavers; it smells really good.” The process of extracting castoreum involves anesthetizing the beaver and “milking” its nether regions, which is both unpleasant for the animal and the human. Due to its unique production method, castoreum consumption is relatively small, with only about 292 pounds used annually. Despite its FDA label as “generally regarded as safe,” manufacturers may not list castoreum on ingredient lists, instead referring to it as “natural flavoring.” This raises concerns for consumers who might be ingesting beaver-bum goop without realizing it. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration considers it safe, but the process of obtaining it is anything but.

A 14-year-old boy, Stephen J. Brumby, tragically died in an accidental shooting at the High Noon Gun Range in Sarasota, Florida, on July 3rd, 2016. The incident occurred around 3:15 p.m. when his father, William C. Brumby, 64, was firing a round in the last shooting lane. The spent shell casing struck the wall, deflecting and falling into the back of William's shirt. While trying to remove the casing with his right hand, which was holding the gun, William inadvertently pointed the firearm behind him and accidentally fired, striking his son. Stephen was transported to Sarasota Memorial Hospital but later succumbed to his injuries. The investigation, based on witness statements and video evidence, confirmed that William Brumby was responsible for the fatal accident. At the time of the incident, William was also accompanied by his 24-year-old son and 12-year-old daughter, both of whom were unharmed. The family has set up a GoFundMe campaign to assist with expenses related to Stephen's death, raising over $20,000 in less than 24 hours. William Brumby expressed his remorse and responsibility for the tragedy, stating, "The gun didn't kill my boy. I did. Every round in the gun is your responsibility. When it fires you need to stand to account for it." The family's only comfort is knowing that Stephen is now with his Lord and Savior, sharing his hope with others.

Taylor Swift's new album "1989" is projected to become the first to sell over a million copies in its first week, marking her third consecutive million-selling debut. This would make Swift the first artist in pop history to achieve this feat, with "1989" joining "Speak Now" (2010) and "Red" (2012) as her third million-selling album. Industry sources now forecast "1989" to sell at least one million copies, potentially becoming the fastest-selling album since "Red" debuted in 2012. "1989" is also expected to be the first album released in 2014 to reach the million-seller mark. Swift has been actively promoting the album, making appearances on various TV shows and participating in iHeartRadio's "Taylor Swift's 1989 Secret Session with iHeartRadio." Final sales figures are expected to be released by Nielsen SoundScan on November 5, with "1989" likely to debut atop the Billboard 200 albums chart.

An anesthesiologist, Dr. George Doodnaught, was sentenced to 10 years in prison for sexually assaulting 21 sedated women during surgeries, a judge called "reprehensible" and "extremely" condemnable. Doodnaught, 65, took advantage of the extraordinary trust his patients placed in him, exploiting their vulnerability during operations. The assaults left victims with lasting emotional damage, including feelings of betrayal, anger, and distrust of doctors. Many of the victims, including the one who sparked the investigation, testified about the profound psychological impact of the physical violations and the emotional trauma of being assaulted by a medical professional in a place of ultimate trust. Doodnaught’s lawyer argued that his client was modest, caring, and a supportive mentor, but the judge noted that Doodnaught had widespread support from family, former colleagues, and patients. The hospital where the assaults took place, North York General Hospital, has since made changes to address and track patient complaints more effectively. Doodnaught’s medical license was suspended, and he faces a disciplinary hearing with the Ontario College of Physicians and Surgeons. His victims expressed disappointment with the sentence, believing it to be too lenient given the severity of the crimes.

In an evening press conference, NYPD Commissioner Bill Bratton, Mayor Bill de Blasio, and Brooklyn Borough President Eric Adams gathered to announce the arrest of Daniel St. Hubert, the suspect accused of stabbing two young children in an elevator of their NYCHA building in East New York. The children, Prince Joshua "P.J." Avitto, 6, and Mikayla Capers, 7, were fatally and critically injured, respectively, after being stabbed repeatedly. St. Hubert, a 27-year-old black male with nine prior arrests and a recent parole status for a domestic violence incident, is described as "armed and dangerous." He is believed to have changed his appearance, making him resemble a different photo. St. Hubert has been charged with assaulting a police officer and a correction officer, which is the reason for his current parole status. The NYPD used a cell phone trace and DNA evidence to track down St. Hubert in Queens, where he was apprehended shortly after 8 p.m. Mayor de Blasio urged the public to contact 1-800-577-TIPS if they have any information about St. Hubert or call 911 if they see him. St. Hubert's arrest comes after a citywide manhunt, and he is also suspected of being involved in the fatal stabbing of 18-year-old Tanaya Grant Copeland, four blocks away from the Boulevard Houses. The NYPD has increased its presence in public housing developments, with Commissioner Bratton indicating that new recruits will be deployed to assist in keeping residents safe. The community has expressed relief and gratitude for the NYPD's efforts, with P.J.'s mother, Aricka McClinton, thanking the police for their work.

BP has agreed to show live video of the "top kill" procedure aimed at stopping the Gulf of Mexico oil spill, as requested by the Obama administration. The "top kill" involves pumping heavy drilling mud and cement into the leaking well. BP will display the video, following discussions with Coast Guard Adm. Thad Allen, after pressure from the administration to provide transparency. The procedure, which may take up to two days, could provide a significant change in the appearance of the leak but will not definitively indicate its success. BP will report on the operation's progress and outcome. Meanwhile, multiple ROVs from various vessels are providing live streams of the operation, though these streams may freeze or be unavailable at times.

The Australian couple David and Wendy Farnell, who left behind their twin with Down syndrome, Gammy, in Thailand, have spoken publicly for the first time, defending their actions. The Farnells told Australian television they felt they had no choice but to leave Thailand with Gammy's healthy twin sister, Pipah, after the surrogate mother, Pattaramon Janbua, threatened to involve the police if they tried to take Gammy. Janbua, who was already a mother of five, said doctors, the surrogacy agency, and the baby's parents knew about Gammy's condition when she was four months pregnant but did not inform her until the seventh month, when the agency asked her to have an abortion. The Farnells, who have 22 child sex convictions, including those of girls as young as five, deny asking for an abortion and say they were angry that the agency did not conduct tests early enough. They claim they wanted to take both babies home but were forced to leave Gammy behind. The case has sparked international outrage and calls for an overhaul of Australian surrogacy laws, with Thailand preparing to ban commercial surrogacy. An online campaign has raised over $241,000 for Gammy's medical treatment and care. The Farnells insist they did not abandon their son and want to get him back, while Janbua has stated she refused to give Gammy up and threatened to keep both children. The case has drawn attention to the lack of regulation in international surrogacy and the potential risks involved.

Amazon founder Jeff Bezos' spaceflight company, Blue Origin, achieved a significant milestone on Monday by landing its New Shepard rocket back on Earth after flying to space for the first time. The reusable rocket, which reached an altitude of 100.5 kilometers and traveled at Mach 3.72, marked a crucial step towards reducing the cost of space travel. "Rockets have always been expendable. Not anymore," Bezos wrote in a blog post, emphasizing the potential of full rocket reusability. The successful landing, which involved the rocket's engine reigniting at 5,000 feet and deploying landing legs, demonstrated the viability of vertical takeoff and landing (VTOL) technology. The capsule, designed to eventually carry six people to suborbital space, safely landed via parachutes. This achievement comes as other companies, like SpaceX, have also been working towards reusable rockets. However, SpaceX has focused on ocean landings, and their attempts to land first stages after reaching orbit have not yet been successful. Blue Origin's success in landing the first stage on land validates their vehicle architecture and design, setting the stage for future suborbital flights and potentially orbital missions. Bezos envisions a future where millions of people can live and work in space, and reusable rockets are a key component of that vision. The reusable rocket concept could significantly lower the cost of space access, making it more feasible for both commercial and governmental space endeavors. While SpaceX's CEO, Elon Musk, offered congratulations, he also noted the difference between suborbital and orbital missions, highlighting the challenges and differences in energy requirements. Blue Origin's achievement is a significant step in the ongoing race to develop more sustainable and cost-effective space transportation systems.

Miranda July, the filmmaker and author, confesses to a history of shoplifting in a recent New Yorker article, revealing a series of incidents that span from her college days to her time in Portland. Her first offense involved stealing Neosporin at Zanotto’s store, an experience that left her humiliated when she wet her pants. July continued to shoplift, even from Goodwill, questioning the concept of money and feeling a sense of obligation to steal. In Portland, she perfected her technique, using a large, rigid purse to fill it with groceries and household items, often using magnets to reset copy machine counters and scissors to remove alarm tags. She even went so far as to encourage friends to steal from their luggage at the airport, taking a cut of the insurance money. Her experiences at Goodwill, where she would put "Sold" tags on items and then remove them, led to a close call with legal trouble. July’s narrative is a candid exploration of her rebellious nature and the thrill of breaking rules, reflecting on how these acts became a form of self-expression and rebellion against societal norms. She eventually quit, seeing art as a more dangerous and fulfilling form of rebellion. Her story resonates with the universal feeling of being an adult and the desire to be seen as an authentic individual.

Voters in Colorado and across the country are making their voices heard on a variety of issues, with some measures passing with strong support and others facing opposition. In Colorado, a measure to tax marijuana, which was legalized for recreational use last year, has been overwhelmingly approved. With nearly all votes counted, 65% of voters supported the new tax, which will impose a 15% excise tax on marijuana to fund school construction and a 10% sales tax for marijuana-related law enforcement efforts. The measure is expected to generate nearly $70 million in additional state tax revenue next year, bolstering its strong support. However, opponents argue that it unfairly singles out marijuana for higher taxation compared to other products like beer.

In other states, voters are considering a range of ballot measures. In Washington, voters are debating a measure that would require labeling all foods containing genetically modified ingredients. The measure has garnered significant attention from both consumer advocates and large agribusinesses, with 53% opposing and 47% supporting the labeling. In New Jersey, voters are considering whether to amend their constitution to raise the state minimum wage to $8.25 per hour, with future annual increases tied to changes in the cost of living. Eighteen states already have a minimum wage that exceeds the federal requirement. Meanwhile, in New York, voters are being asked to revise their constitution to allow the legislature to authorize seven casinos, with the goal of generating new revenue for public schools and potentially cutting property taxes.

In a more local issue, 11 counties in northern Colorado are considering the question of secession from the state. Ten counties in conservative, rural northeastern Colorado would theoretically form a 51st state known as North Colorado, with Moffat County becoming a panhandle for neighboring Wyoming. While the measure has no chance of becoming reality, it would require statewide and congressional approval. The measure has garnered 42% support in Weld County, the most populated county of those trying to secede, but it is still too early to call the race. The secession movement reflects growing grassroots conservative anger toward a more liberal Denver-based Democratic establishment, which has taken up controversial measures related to gun control, gay rights, and green energy.

The influx of outside funding in ballot measures, particularly in Washington's GMO labeling initiative, has raised concerns about the influence of out-of-state interests. In SeaTac, a $15 local minimum wage proposal has drawn nearly $2 million in contributions, with large contributions from out-of-state groups. In Whatcom County, state and national environmentalists have contributed about $300,000 to County Council races, met by more than half that from international-coal corporations. These trends highlight the growing influence of outside money in local and state politics, potentially threatening the core promise of the initiative process and representative democracy.

Nicole "Snooki" Polizzi, 26, officially tied the knot with fiancé Jionni LaValle, 27, at The Venetian in Garfield, New Jersey, on Saturday, November 29, reports Us Weekly. The Great Gatsby-themed wedding, which celebrated the couple's two young children, Lorenzo, 2, and Giovanna Marie, 3 months, featured two dresses for the bride: a traditional lace gown for the ceremony and a more fun, Gatsby-themed party dress by Ines DiSanto for the reception. Bridesmaids, including BFF Jenni "JWoww" Farley, wore black gowns with bows. After exchanging vows, the bridal party and family and friends danced to music from an 18-piece band. Polizzi, who got engaged in March 2012, told Us, "It’s not that hard to plan a wedding. For me, it’s just that I don’t let myself get stressed out. I just enjoy the moment and I try to be positive about everything."

President Donald Trump is advocating for a boycott of Harley-Davidson in response to the company's decision to shift some motorcycle production to facilities outside the United States. The move, prompted by European Union tariffs imposed in retaliation for U.S. steel tariffs, has drawn the ire of the U.S. president. Trump, who met with "Bikers for Trump" supporters at his golf course in New Jersey, expressed his support for potential consumer boycotts of Harley-Davidson. In a tweet, he wrote, "Many @harleydavidson owners plan to boycott the company if manufacturing moves overseas. Great! Most other companies are coming in our direction, including Harley competitors. A really bad move! U.S. will soon have a level playing field, or better." This stance contrasts with Harley-Davidson's stance, which has blamed the decision on the EU tariffs and stated that the move is not its preference but a necessary one to maintain affordability for EU customers. The company expects the tariffs to cost it as much as $100 million annually. Despite Trump's backing of the potential boycott, Harley-Davidson has not responded to requests for comment. The situation highlights the complex and often contentious nature of U.S. trade policies and their impact on American businesses and consumers.

Former Winnipeg broadcast personality and journalism instructor Steve Vogelsang, 53, has been charged with two counts of robbery for allegedly robbing two banks in Medicine Hat, Alberta, in October 2018. Vogelsang, who was a longtime sports anchor and news director at CTV Winnipeg and a journalism instructor at Red River College, was arrested at a hotel in Medicine Hat on Saturday morning. According to police, the suspect walked into a Royal Bank and a Bank of Montreal on consecutive days, demanding money and leaving with undisclosed amounts. Vogelsang's financial struggles, including a failed attempt to sell a home in Winnipeg and a dispute with his ex-wife over property, have been highlighted. He is also facing charges related to a protection order issued against a former student and allegations of sexual assault. Vogelsang has denied the charges and claims his ex-wife has been trying to discredit him. His arrest and charges have shocked some of his former students, who remember him as a tough but fair teacher. The case is expected to continue as Vogelsang faces multiple charges and legal proceedings.

Another New York lawyer has been caught on video making racially charged comments and physically assaulting a fellow subway passenger, drawing parallels to a previous incident involving a Manhattan lawyer. The video, which has gone viral, shows Anna Lushchinskaya, a 40-year-old woman, shouting expletives, spitting, and attacking a fellow passenger, including kicking and hitting her with an umbrella and keychain. Lushchinskaya, who is white, used racial slurs, particularly targeting an Asian passenger, and referred to a man with dark skin as "Muhammad." The incident occurred during the morning rush hour on a D train in Brooklyn. Lushchinskaya was arrested and faces felony assault charges, though she has pleaded not guilty. The viral video has sparked outrage and comparisons to the earlier incident involving Aaron Schlossberg, a Manhattan lawyer who made a racist rant in a restaurant. Schlossberg's video led to intense backlash and a referral to attorney disciplinary authorities. While it’s unclear if Lushchinskaya will face similar consequences, her criminal charges could potentially lead to disciplinary action by the New York State Bar. The incident has also highlighted the ongoing issues of racism and violence in public spaces.

South Korean film legend Choi Eun-hee, who once captivated audiences in the 1960s and 1970s and later faced a harrowing ordeal in North Korea, passed away at the age of 92 on Monday. Her eldest son, director Shin Jeong-gyun, confirmed her death to Yonhap News Agency. Born in Gwangju, Gyeonggi Province, in 1926, Choi began her film career in 1947 with the movie "A New Oath." She quickly rose to stardom, starring in iconic films such as "The Sun of Night" (1948) and "A Hometown in Heart" (1949), alongside Kim Ji-mi and Um Aing-ran, who were also celebrated actresses of that era. In 1954, she married Shin Sang-ok, a prominent film director, and together they established Shin Film, producing numerous films that propelled the Korean film industry during the 1960s and 1970s. Their joint career ended in divorce in 1978.

Choi's life took a dramatic turn in 1978 when she was kidnapped by North Korean agents in Hong Kong. Shin Sang-ok, her estranged husband, was abducted six months later. North Korea's then-leader, Kim Jong-il, reportedly confided that he had brought her to North Korea because she was his favorite actress. In North Korea, the couple was forced to make films for the state, with Choi winning the Best Actress award at the Moscow Film Festival in 1985 for her role in "Sault." After eight years, they escaped to the United States and returned to South Korea in 1999. Choi's health deteriorated, and she passed away after a long battle with kidney disease. She is survived by two sons and two daughters. Her autobiography, "Confessions," was published in 2007, detailing her experiences in North Korea. The kidnapping of Choi and Shin has been a significant event in South Korea's history, with their story inspiring a film titled "The Lovers and the Despot."

Former U.S. president Jimmy Carter received medical attention for dehydration while working on a Habitat for Humanity home in Winnipeg. Carter, 92, was rehydrated in St. Boniface Hospital, with his wife Rosalynn by his side. He had been working in the sun for about an hour when he appeared to feel faint, prompting his motorcade to rush him to the hospital for precautionary observation. Carter informed build leaders he was feeling "OK" and encouraged volunteers to continue their work. The Carters are longtime supporters of Habitat for Humanity, helping with builds in Winnipeg and across Canada as part of the organization's 34th Jimmy and Rosalynn Carter Work Project, which aims to construct 150 homes to commemorate Canada's 150th anniversary.

An Ohio man, Matthew B. Matheny, 40, was found alive on Wednesday on the flank of Mount St. Helens, nearly a week after he went missing on a day hike. Matheny, who was not familiar with the terrain, got lost and survived by eating berries and bees, his parents told reporters. He was in good condition, talking and did not appear to have suffered life-threatening injuries but was flown to a hospital to spend the night as a precaution, the Cowlitz County Sheriff's Office said. His parents, Linda and Carney Matheny, described their son as a former Boy Scout who is interested in fitness and nutrition. They said he was in the free forest at the time of his discovery, having lost the trail and fallen down a steep back. Matthew borrowed a friend's Subaru Outback to drive to the mountain and go hiking. His friends reported him missing when he did not return, prompting a search. About 30 search-and-rescue personnel, assisted by helicopters, tracking dogs, and a drone, searched for him daily. Searchers on Tuesday focused on a 1-square-mile area based on cellphone signals and a computer model that predicted Matheny's movements. Matthew was found about three miles away from the Subaru by a Skamania County-based rescue crew. He had not seen another person since Thursday and was without water for days, his mother said, but the fluids from the berries may have been enough to keep him going. Bees chased after Matheny as he moved about on the mountain, so he killed and ate some. "He knew it was a tough situation," said Linda Matheny, who arrived in Washington with her husband on Sunday. "But everyone who has encountered him have told us it's remarkable the condition he's in." The parents thanked all the emergency responders, volunteers, and his friends who aided in helping find their son. They said they were ecstatic to get their son back and in shock.

Mitt Romney faced a hostile reception from the NAACP during his speech at their annual convention, where he criticized President Obama and pledged to repeal the Affordable Care Act. Romney's assertion that he, not Obama, could best represent the African-American community drew boos and jeers. He argued that his policies would better serve black families, citing high unemployment rates and poor economic conditions under Obama. Despite the negative reaction, Romney's campaign viewed the speech as a bold move, aimed at appealing to black voters and demonstrating his willingness to speak candidly. His speech included tough policy positions, such as attacking teachers' unions and defending traditional marriage, which were met with mixed reactions.
