New Jersey Governor Chris Christie has been working on economic policies to address income inequality, blaming federal policies for the issue. However, Tepper's move underscores the challenges of balancing tax policies and economic growth. The state's budget forecasters are now grappling with the potential loss of Tepper's substantial tax contributions, emphasizing the need for alternative revenue sources. The move also raises questions about the effectiveness of high-tax policies in retaining wealthy residents and the broader implications for state budgets and economic strategies.

Chicago Mayor Rahm Emanuel and other city officials are set to declare Chicago an immigrant sanctuary city, a move that defies President-elect Donald Trump’s vow to cut off funding to sanctuary cities. The city’s stance is part of a broader effort by several cities, including New York, Los Angeles, Seattle, Philadelphia, and San Francisco, to maintain their sanctuary status. Sanctuary cities typically limit local law enforcement’s cooperation with federal immigration authorities, thereby protecting undocumented immigrants from deportation. Mayor Emanuel’s office released a statement directing residents with questions or needing legal resources to call 311. “Chicago is and will remain a sanctuary city,” Emanuel said. “Chicago has been a city of immigrants since it was founded. We have always welcomed people of all faiths and backgrounds, and while the administration will change, our values and our commitment to inclusion will not.”

In a “60 Minutes” interview, Trump vowed to deport 2 million to 3 million undocumented immigrants, with a focus on those with criminal records. He stated, “What we are going to do is get the people that are criminal and have criminal records, gang members, drug dealers, where a lot of these people, probably 2 million, it could be even 3 million, we are getting them out of our country or we are going to incarcerate.” Trump also emphasized the importance of securing the border before making any determinations about the remaining undocumented immigrants. He added, “After the border is secure and after everything gets normalized, we’re going to make a determination on the people that they’re talking about who are terrific people, they’re terrific people but we are gonna make a determination at that.”

The issue of sanctuary cities and the potential deportation of millions of undocumented immigrants has sparked concern among young immigrants who received protections under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program. President Barack Obama urged Trump to “think long and hard” before endangering the status of young undocumented immigrants, calling them “kids, who were brought here by their parents, they did nothing wrong. They’ve pledged allegiance to the flag.” Trump has pledged to end DACA, calling it “one of the most unconstitutional actions ever undertaken by a president.” Over 700,000 young immigrants were shielded from deportation and received work permits under Obama’s 2012 executive actions.

The election results have left many undocumented immigrants in a state of panic. In California, radio stations reported widespread concern among farmworkers, with one worker stating, “I’m really scared. Me and my roommate already have our truck loaded and ready to leave.” In Los Angeles, protesters shouted, “Aqui estamos y no nos vamos,” or “We are here and we are not leaving.” The day after the election, a group of protesters in downtown Los Angeles voiced their opposition to the president-elect, expressing fear for their families and their status in the country.

While Trump’s mass deportation plan is seen as implausible, many experts believe he is more likely to reverse DACA, which granted legal status and work permits to immigrants who entered the country illegally prior to their 16th birthday. The paper trail associated with DACA workers would make them easy targets for deportation. The United Farm Workers, a Latino agricultural union, will leverage its deep ties in Washington to block Trump’s deportation efforts. UFW President Arturo Rodriguez stated, “Making progress will be more difficult, but our practice of organizing for the long term will let us continue to win justice… We reaffirm our confidence in the American people and in our Si Se Puede! attitude.”

Despite the challenges, the UFW remains committed to organizing for the long term and ensuring that all farm workers and low-income working families receive the opportunities and respect they deserve. As the new administration takes shape, the fate of millions of undocumented immigrants hangs in the balance.

Los Angeles Lakers owner Jerry Buss, hospitalized for several months with an undisclosed form of cancer, has passed away at the age of 80. Buss, known for his showmanship and strategic acquisitions, led the Lakers to 10 NBA championships. His impact on the game extended beyond basketball, transforming the Lakers into a global brand. Buss purchased the Lakers in 1979, and under his ownership, the team featured legendary players like Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Magic Johnson, and Kobe Bryant. Buss was also involved in the ownership of the Los Angeles Kings and a ranch. His legacy includes not only the Lakers' success but also his innovative approach to team branding and marketing. Kobe Bryant, a key player during Buss's tenure, praised his owner, emphasizing Buss's role in shaping the Lakers' identity and the broader impact on the NBA. Buss's passing marks the end of an era in NBA history, leaving a lasting impression on the sport and its fans.

The coverage of the Steubenville rape case verdict by CNN drew widespread criticism for its focus on the convicted rapists and their families, rather than the victim and her family. On Sunday, CNN's anchor Candy Crowley and correspondent Poppy Harlow reported that the guilty verdict had a devastating impact on the lives of the convicted rapists, Trent Mays and Ma'lik Richmond. Crowley described the scene as "incredibly emotional," with the convicted rapists breaking down in tears. Harlow highlighted the "promising futures" of the boys, who were star football players and good students, and the "sobbing" of Richmond as he received his sentence. 

Legal expert Paul Callan added that the convicted rapists would be labeled as registered sex offenders, a label that would "haunt them for the rest of their lives." He emphasized the lasting impact on their futures, including difficulty in finding employment and housing. However, the coverage largely ignored the victim's experience. Her mother's statement, which expressed pity for the convicted rapists, was aired, but the emotional and psychological effects of the rape on the victim were not thoroughly addressed.

Critics argued that CNN's focus on the convicted rapists' emotions and futures was inappropriate and reflected a broader issue of rape culture. The victim's identity had been protected, and her family was not shown in tears, which led to accusations of victim-blaming. Journalists and social media users criticized CNN for sympathizing with the convicted rapists and downplaying the severity of the crime. Other networks, such as MSNBC and Fox, also aired the victim's name, further highlighting the media's failure to provide balanced coverage.

The Steubenville case has been a focal point for discussions on rape culture and the treatment of victims in the media. While the convicted rapists' futures were discussed extensively, the long-term impact on the victim and the broader societal implications were often overlooked. The case has sparked debates about the role of social media in exacerbating the issue and the need for more nuanced and empathetic reporting on sexual assault cases.

German actress Nastassja Kinski has praised her half-sister Pola for her courage in reporting that their late father, Klaus Kinski, abused her as a child. Pola, who is 19 years younger than Nastassja, stated in an interview with Stern magazine that she was abused between the ages of five and 19 by their father, who died in 1991. Nastassja, 60, expressed shock at the revelations but also pride in her sister's decision to speak out. Pola's book, Kindermund, aims to help "all the children, adolescents and mothers who fear their father and swallow this fear to hide it in the depths of their souls." Nastassja Kinski, who has starred in films such as Roman Polanski's Tess and Wim Wenders' Paris Texas, said she had read Pola's words and wept, describing her sister as a "heroine" for freeing her heart and soul from the burden of the secret. The revelations come as Klaus Kinski, known for his role in notable films such as Aguirre, the Wrath of God and Nosferatu the Vampyre, was also famous for his numerous sexual liaisons with adults. His daughter's allegations add to the complex legacy of the actor, who was revered for his film work and simultaneously reviled for his alleged abuse of his daughter. Klaus Kinski's unique genius for providing an unobstructed glimpse into his disturbed soul has long fascinated and repelled audiences. His films, including those with director Werner Herzog, are now seen as more powerful and authentic, retroactively authenticated by the depravity of their lead actor. The conflicting emotions of admiration and revulsion towards Kinski's work and character have been explored in Herzog's documentary, My Best Fiend, which depicts the physical and psychological violence Kinski exhibited on set. The documentary's ending, which portrays a gentler side of Kinski, is now seen as "horribly unbearable" in light of the new revelations.

Apple has filed a patent for a system designed to protect electronic devices, particularly iPhones, from damage when dropped. The patent, titled "Protective Mechanism for an Electronic Device," suggests a mechanism that would detect when a device is falling and then reorient the device mid-air to land on a less vulnerable part, such as the edge rather than the screen. To achieve this, the system could use various methods, including moving a weighted mass within the device, extending aerodynamic foils, or using a small gas-propulsion device. The patent also considers scenarios where cables might pull the device onto the ground and proposes solutions like forcibly ejecting cables. While the technology seems far from implementation, it showcases Apple's ongoing efforts to enhance device safety.

Lance Armstrong will give his first television interview since being stripped of his Tour de France titles to Oprah Winfrey, her network announced. The 90-minute "no-holds-barred" interview will air at 9 p.m. ET on January 17 and will be simulcast on Oprah.com. Winfrey will ask Armstrong to address the U.S. Anti-Doping Agency's report, which said there was overwhelming evidence he was directly involved in a sophisticated doping program. Armstrong, 41, has been competing in Ironman triathlons and has been working out in Hawaii. The New York Times reported that Armstrong was contemplating publicly admitting he used illegal performance-enhancing drugs, which might lead to his reinstatement. Armstrong has repeatedly denied using banned performance-enhancing drugs and illegal blood transfusions during his cycling career. The U.S. Anti-Doping Agency's 202-page report detailed Armstrong's alleged use of performance-enhancing drugs and blood transfusions, and his former teammates testified about how they beat tests or avoided them. Armstrong has been an icon for his cycling feats and celebrity, raising millions via his Lance Armstrong Foundation to help cancer victims and survivors. Armstrong was stripped of his titles and banned from cycling in October 2012, and he stepped down from the board of his foundation, Livestrong, weeks later. The interview will take place at Armstrong's home in Austin, Texas. Armstrong's interview comes as the Oprah Winfrey Network is a joint venture with Discovery Communications, the broadcaster that sponsored Armstrong's team in 2005, adding a layer of irony to the situation.

President Obama's ambitious bid to complete one of the largest free trade pacts in U.S. history moved forward Thursday when the Senate introduced bipartisan legislation that would grant his administration vast new powers to finalize the Trans-Pacific Partnership (TPP). The fast-track trade bill, drafted by Sens. Orrin G. Hatch (R-Utah) and Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), would allow the president to present a final agreement to Congress for an up-or-down vote without lawmakers being able to amend the terms. A similar bill, crafted by Rep. Paul Ryan (R-Wis.), is expected to be introduced in the House in the coming weeks. The TPP, a 12-nation trade and regulatory deal in the Asia Pacific, was signed in 2015 after more than five years of negotiations. Obama has touted it as a cornerstone of his second-term agenda, arguing that it would help ensure U.S. competitiveness in the face of a rising China. However, the deal faces fierce opposition from many Democrats, labor unions, and environmental groups, who claim it will kill U.S. jobs and benefit large, multinational corporations. The AFL-CIO announced a six-figure ad buy to fight the fast-track bill, targeting 16 senators and 36 House members. The fast-track legislation, formally known as "trade promotion authority," was negotiated for months between Hatch and Wyden, with the Democrat under increasing pressure from liberal groups not to sign onto the legislation. The bill includes provisions aimed at ensuring greater public transparency in the trade negotiations and a key provision that would allow the Senate to turn off the fast-track authority if the Obama administration fails to meet certain requirements during the negotiations. Politically, the legislation places Obama squarely against a majority of House Democrats and a large bloc of Senate Democrats, many of whom believe previous trade deals have hurt U.S. workers. In a sign of how difficult the fight will be, Sen. Charles E. Schumer (D-N.Y.), who is expected to take over as leader of his party in the Senate in 2017, said he was skeptical of the TPP because it lacks protections against currency manipulation. With most Senate Republicans likely to support the fast-track legislation, the House, where the margins are incredibly narrow, will be the main battleground. Obama would need to deliver more than 30 Democrats to win passage, a task that insiders on both sides of the aisle say is not guaranteed. "This is wrong, and members of Congress will not stand for it," said Rep. Rosa L. DeLauro (D-Conn.), who has led the liberal opposition to trade deals.

On Independence Day, the United States relies heavily on China for its fireworks, despite a growing "Buy American" sentiment. For the past 35 years, China has dominated the U.S. market, supplying nearly 98 to 99 percent of the consumer fireworks and 75 percent of the professional-grade pyrotechnics used in large public shows. The fireworks industry's shift to Chinese production began shortly after the U.S. and China reestablished trade ties in 1979. By 2013, the U.S. was importing $213 million worth of fireworks, almost all from China. The trend is unlikely to change anytime soon, according to fireworks industry experts.

The U.S. fireworks industry acknowledges that Chinese imports are necessary due to the labor-intensive nature of fireworks production, which is still largely done by hand. The industry has worked closely with China to improve the quality of fireworks, with the American Fireworks Standards Laboratory inspecting tens of thousands of shipments each year. While China has faced criticism for imported products like tires and agricultural goods, the fireworks industry maintains a positive relationship with its Chinese counterparts.

The quality of fireworks has improved significantly, but challenges remain, particularly in creating a true blue color. The U.S. military, through its Picatinny Arsenal, has been working on more environmentally friendly formulations for colored signals, which could enhance neighborhood fireworks displays. The Army has developed greener fireworks that burn brighter and produce less smoke, and is aiming to spin off these innovations to the commercial sector.

Innovations in fireworks include creating shapes in the sky, such as letters and numbers, and integrating technology like video projections. For example, Disney's "Frozen" spectacular will feature a video countdown of parkgoers' selfies. Despite the reliance on Chinese imports, the U.S. fireworks industry continues to innovate, driven by both the military and theme parks. The key to a successful fireworks display lies in a well-paced show with variety and drama, ensuring a memorable experience for all.

A dessert called 'Roofie Colada' at The Phunky Elephant in Staten Island was taken off the menu after social media backlash. The drink, a dessert-drink hybrid with coffee ice cream, Kahlua, vanilla vodka, and topped with donuts and whipped cream, was named after a joke on the cartoon "Family Guy." The restaurant received complaints for months but only faced significant pressure recently. Critics argued that the name trivialized date rape, making it unacceptable. The restaurant owner, Patricia Gaja, acknowledged the backlash but defended the name as a homage to the show. After more complaints, the dessert was removed from the menu, and the restaurant issued an apology, promising to be more sensitive in the future. The incident sparked a debate about the appropriateness of using potentially offensive humor in a business context, with some supporting the name and others calling for greater respect toward sensitive issues.

Bell's Two Hearted Ale was crowned the number one beer in the 15th annual Best Beers in America survey by Zymurgy magazine, marking an end to Russian River Brewing Company's eight-year reign with Pliny the Elder. Homebrewers and beer enthusiasts from the American Homebrewers Association (AHA) selected the top 20 beers from a wide range of options, with Bell's Two Hearted Ale leading the pack. The survey, conducted online, highlights the preferences of discerning beer drinkers and homebrewers. Bell's Brewery, founded by Larry Bell, celebrates this achievement, acknowledging the homebrewing community that inspired its beginnings. Other top-ranked beers and breweries are also listed, with Stone Brewing topping the list of breweries and Bell's Brewery leading in the number of top-ranked beers. The complete list is available on the AHA's website, and the AHA offers clone recipes for homebrewers interested in replicating these winning beers. This recognition underscores the quality and popularity of craft beers among homebrewers and beer enthusiasts.

The Connecticut Supreme Court ruled that authorities can forcibly medicate a mentally ill doctor, Lishan Wang, accused of killing a Yale University physician, to make him competent to stand trial. Wang, a Chinese citizen, is charged with the 2010 murder of Dr. Vajinder Toor and attempted murder for shooting at Toor’s pregnant wife. The court confirmed that it is substantially likely that Wang would become competent with medication and unlikely to suffer significant side effects. It also found no less-intrusive option and deemed the drugs in Wang’s best interest. The decision came after Wang refused to take the medication, arguing it would violate his constitutional rights. The case stems from a 2008 workplace dispute Wang had with Toor and other doctors at Kingsbrook Jewish Medical Center in New York City, where Wang was fired after a series of confrontations. In November, a lower court judge ruled that state officials could forcibly medicate Wang to make him competent to stand trial. The main issue in the appeal was whether prosecutors showed that it was "substantially likely" that forcing medication on Wang would restore him to competency. The Connecticut Supreme Court set the "substantially likely" standard as "more likely than not, or a greater than 50 percent probability." Wang's public defender argued that a projected success rate of mid-50s to 70 percent did not meet this threshold. The ruling has raised concerns about the balance between protecting the rights of the accused and ensuring a fair trial.

For years, the European Union has been a perennial contender for the Nobel Peace Prize, and in 2012, the bloc finally received the honor. The decision to award the prize to the EU is a recognition of its significant contributions to peace and reconciliation in Europe, particularly in the aftermath of World War II. The European Union, a unique supranational body where national governments share some of their powers, has facilitated the integration of diverse countries, including former military dictatorships and communist states, into a unified market and political structure. This integration has fostered a sense of unity and cooperation among its member states, reducing the likelihood of conflict.

The European Union's peace project is rooted in the lessons learned from the catastrophic events of the 20th century. It has successfully united Germany and its former enemies, a feat that was once unimaginable. Despite the ongoing financial and sovereign debt crisis, which poses one of the most serious challenges in the EU's history, the bloc has managed to maintain its unity and resilience. Critics often point out the EU's bureaucratic nature and lack of transparency, but the laws it enacts generally support integration, and citizens have a structured way to seek legal redress.

The Nobel Committee's decision to award the prize to the EU is seen as a morale boost for the continent, which is currently grappling with economic turmoil and the fragility of the euro. However, the timing of the award has drawn mixed reactions. While some view it as a timely reminder of the EU's achievements, others argue that it seems premature given the current economic crisis. The prize, worth $1.2 million, is a symbolic gesture that underscores the EU's role in promoting peace and stability in Europe. It also highlights the unique nature of the EU as an organization that has brought about a lasting peace in a continent that has historically been plagued by conflict.

The decision to award the prize to the EU was leaked and reported early by Norway's NRK public radio, despite Norway's non-EU status and its twice-rejected appeals to join the bloc. This revelation adds an interesting twist to the story, as it underscores the unpredictability of the Nobel Committee's choices. The EU's 27 member states and 500 million citizens are the true winners of the prize, as they have supported integration, reforms, and enlargement, and have borne the costs of this process. The prize serves as a reminder of the EU's enduring commitment to peace and the potential for cooperation and unity in the face of adversity.

U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo embarked on a three-hour meeting with North Korean officials in Pyongyang on Friday, aiming to flesh out details on dismantling the North’s nuclear program and recovering the remains of U.S. troops missing from the Korean War. Pompeo’s visit, his third to North Korea since April, comes as tensions simmer over the country’s nuclear capabilities and the implementation of the Singapore summit agreement. Kim Yong Chol, a key North Korean official, played a pivotal role in arranging the summit between U.S. President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. The talks, held at the Park Hwa Guest House, were Pompeo’s first overnight stay in North Korea, signaling a deeper engagement. During the meeting, Pompeo expressed optimism about Kim’s commitment to denuclearization, stating, “The President told me he believes that Chairman Kim sees a different, brighter future for the people of North Korea. We both hope that’s true.” However, U.S. officials and experts remain skeptical, noting that North Korea has yet to demonstrate concrete actions toward denuclearization. The U.S. seeks to define the terms of final denuclearization, including an initial list of nuclear sites and an inventory that could be verified against available intelligence. The issue of U.S. soldiers’ remains, agreed to be returned by North Korea, remains unresolved, with the U.S. awaiting delivery of 100 coffins. Additionally, discussions will cover the dismantlement of the Tongchang-ri missile engine test site and the possibility of U.S. monitors observing the process. Despite the progress, the U.S. faces challenges in verifying North Korea’s commitments, given the lack of a high-confidence accounting of the North’s nuclear arsenal. Pompeo’s visit is closely watched, with expectations that it will build trust and maintain momentum toward implementing the Singapore summit’s agreement. His meetings in Pyongyang and Tokyo will be crucial in shaping the future of U.S.-North Korea relations.

This web-wide crawl, conducted from March 9, 2011, to December 23, 2011, utilized Heritrix (3.1.1-SNAPSHOT) software and included the Alexa top million websites. The data set comprises 2.7 billion captures of 2.3 billion unique URLs across 29 million hosts. Due to operational issues with the new HQ software, some embedded objects were not fully crawled, and repeated Argentinian government site crawls skewed results. The data is available for experimentation, but access requests may be limited.

Scientists from the University of Granada have discovered that lying can cause a rise in the temperature of the nose, dubbing this phenomenon "The Pinocchio Effect." This effect, observed through the use of thermal imaging cameras, highlights how anxiety from lying can make the tip of the nose heat up. Interestingly, making a significant mental effort can help cool the nose down. The researchers also found that sexual desire and arousal can be detected through changes in body temperature, with increases in chest and genital areas indicating heightened arousal. Their work extends beyond deception and desire, as they identified specific thermal footprints for various activities, such as different types of dance. For instance, Flamenco dancers experience a decrease in temperature in their buttocks and an increase in their forearms. The insular cortex, involved in body temperature regulation, plays a crucial role in these findings, as its activity correlates with temperature changes. This research, detailed in their doctoral thesis, offers a unique insight into the physiological responses to emotional states and activities, potentially providing a non-invasive method for detecting deception and arousal.

Chicago has been crowned America's funniest city, according to a study by the University of Colorado at Boulder. Researchers from the Humor Research Lab evaluated several data sets, including the number of comedy clubs, famous comedians born there, humorist tweets, and traveling comedians' ratings of local audiences. They also surveyed over 900 residents from the top 10 cities, asking about their sense of humor and favorite jokes. Despite ranking as the funniest city, Chicagoans reportedly struggle to come up with jokes, preferring to derive humor from their everyday experiences. The study revealed that Boston, Atlanta, Washington, Portland, New York, Los Angeles, Denver, San Francisco, and Seattle also made the Top 10 list. Indianapolis, Detroit, and Milwaukee were ranked 25th, 34th, and 39th, respectively. The project was led by Peter McGraw, an associate professor of marketing and psychology, and his co-author Joel Warner. Their findings offer a unique insight into the humor profiles of America's top cities, highlighting the distinct comedic styles of each metropolis.

The explosion in Manhattan's Chelsea neighborhood on Saturday night injured 29 people, prompting an investigation into the incident. New York Governor Andrew Cuomo, speaking near the blast site, stated there was no evidence linking the explosion to international terrorism. The blast occurred on West 23rd Street between Sixth and Seventh Avenues, and authorities found a second suspicious device a few blocks away on West 27th Street. This device, described as a pressure cooker with wiring and a cellphone attached, was safely removed. Most of the 29 injured victims have been released from hospitals, though one was in serious condition. Mayor Bill de Blasio ruled out any terror connection but called the blast an "intentional act." Surveillance videos from the scene showed the same man near both the explosion site and the second suspicious device, raising questions about potential motives. Law enforcement officials are investigating the similarities between the devices found in New York and New Jersey, but no definitive link has been established. The incident has led to increased police presence in the city, with 1,000 additional New York State Police officers and National Guard troops deployed to key locations as a precaution. The explosion, which sent panicked people fleeing the area, has left the neighborhood on edge, with residents expressing concern about potential further threats.

The controversial ending to the Monday Night Football game between Green Bay and Seattle, where replacement officials ruled a last-minute touchdown for the Seahawks, sparked widespread outrage and financial repercussions. The call, which gave Seattle a 14-12 victory, shifted bets and potentially cost gamblers $150 million, with estimates ranging up to $1 billion. This incident, part of a series of officiating controversies, intensified calls for the return of regular officials. NFL spokesman Brian McCarthy stated, "Officiating controversies have always been a part of sport," but the league has been negotiating with the referees union for a week, aiming to resolve the issue. State Senate President Stephen Sweeney of New Jersey, whose Packers lost, announced plans to introduce legislation prohibiting the use of replacement officials, citing player safety concerns. The incident also affected the Packers' Super Bowl odds, with their chances dropping from 7-1 to 9-1. President Obama, who had been critical of the replacement officials, echoed the sentiment, calling it "terrible" and emphasizing the need for regular officials. The controversy highlighted the ongoing tension between the NFL and its officials, with the potential for further disruptions to the season.

Erik Prince, founder of the controversial private military firm Blackwater, reveals his covert role as a CIA asset, orchestrating targeted assassinations and clandestine operations for the U.S. intelligence agency. In a Vanity Fair article, Prince details his involvement in a program to assassinate Al Qaeda financier Mamoun Darkazanli, conducted by a Blackwater team in Germany. This revelation contradicts statements by CIA Director Leon Panetta that the program was never operational. Prince's account, which includes his own admission to being "thrown under the bus" politically, adds a new layer of complexity to the relationship between private military contractors and government intelligence operations. His story, marked by a mix of ambition and perceived betrayal, challenges the public perception of Blackwater and its role in modern warfare.

A violent altercation in a recreation yard at Clinton Correction Facility five days before two inmates escaped highlighted potential security lapses that may have contributed to their brazen breakout. The fight, which involved two groups of inmates, one Muslim and the other suspected of being part of the Bloods gang, occurred on June 1, with correction officers using chemical agents to quell the disturbance. An inmate suffered a broken leg, and part of the prison was temporarily locked down the following day. However, only the yard and two cellblocks were thoroughly searched, rather than the entire facility, which houses about 3,000 inmates. This limited search, combined with the inmates' placement on an "honor block," which provided them with more liberties, may have facilitated their meticulous escape plan.

The escapees, Richard Matt, 48, and David Sweat, 34, used a small electrical saw, powered by extension cords, and a sledgehammer to cut their way out of the maximum security prison. They cut through the back walls of their adjacent cells on an "honor block" tier, creating holes that led to a cavernous utility bowel inside the prison. There, they spliced an electrical cord into a light fixture to power the saw, which they then used to cut a large hole in a 24-inch steam pipe that led to a sewer outside the prison. Matt and Sweat used the sewer to escape, carrying their tools in a guitar case that they kept in one of their cells. A law enforcement source said State Police investigators are probing whether the inmates may have received the small hand-held saw and other tools from a female civilian employee who had developed a relationship with Matt. The employee, Joyce Mitchell, worked in the prison tailor shop and is now charged with aiding the inmates' escape.

The inmates' meticulous plan included piling clothing and other items under their bed linens to make it appear they were sleeping. They were on the honor block, which allowed them to wear and keep regular clothing other than their prison uniforms. The loose restrictions on the honor block tier may have contributed to their ability to carry out their escape plan. Matt and Sweat used a 20-pound sledgehammer to break the lock on a manhole cover, which they used to exit the prison. They climbed out of a sewer hole near the prison around midnight Friday and were initially on foot, leading to a focused search in a tight radius around the prison.

A massive manhunt continues in the heavily forested areas around the prison in Dannemora, with the FBI assisting in the search. The investigation has zeroed in on Joyce Mitchell, who worked in the prison tailor shop and is now charged with aiding the inmates' escape. State Police believe the escapees could still be within a five- or 10-mile radius of the prison. The escape raises questions about the security measures at the prison, particularly the limited search of the facility and the placement of inmates on the honor block. The case has also brought to light the troubled history of Richard Matt, the father of a 23-year-old son who finds it hard to believe his father could have escaped. The search for the escapees continues, with a $100,000 reward for information leading to their capture.

The race between Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump has tightened, with Clinton's lead over Trump now at 4 or 5 percentage points, according to the FiveThirtyEight polls-only forecast. This tightening has come gradually over the past few weeks, with evidence of a shift becoming more widespread, particularly in polls that surveyed the race just after the conventions. Fox News’s national poll, for instance, had Clinton up by 9 points just after the conventions and now has her up by 2 points. The recent shift in the polls has not guaranteed Trump's continued improvement, as the race remains close, with Clinton still ahead by 74 percent according to the polls-only model and 70 percent according to the polls-plus model. 

However, the tightening of the race raises concerns for Clinton, as it could potentially impact her swing states. At her peak, Clinton had a double-digit lead in Wisconsin, but by Wednesday morning, the model's trend line adjustment had reduced her lead to an estimated 7 points. This adjustment, which reflects shifts in the overall race, has been particularly evident in Wisconsin, where recent highly rated, traditional telephone polls showed Clinton up by just 3 to 5 points. 

The model's adjusted polling averages for swing states indicate a narrowing of Clinton's projected leads. For example, in Arizona, her lead has shrunk from 1.6 percentage points to -3.9, and in Florida, from 6.3 to 3.1. These numbers suggest that Clinton's swing state leads are not significantly different from her national numbers, which are currently at 4 to 5 percentage points. 

The model's expectations for Clinton are lower with a tighter race, meaning that a new poll showing her up by 5 or 6 points in Florida or Ohio could be a significant improvement for her. However, the plan to get to 270 electoral votes remains unclear, with the battleground state deployment plan still in development. The Trump campaign is also facing challenges, including a slowing of big donor contributions and confusion over who is in charge. 

Late last week, Jared Kushner, Trump's son-in-law, met with Republican National Committee (RNC) officials to discuss the campaign's infrastructure in swing states. The meeting highlighted the campaign's struggles in deploying field staffers and establishing offices in battleground states. The absence of a clear plan has affected the campaign's path to 270 electoral votes, with the current plan dividing states into four tiers, but it is unclear if this plan is being implemented. 

The reluctance of the party's biggest contributors to support Trump has also impacted the campaign's finances. The RNC convention committee remains in debt, and major donors are expressing misgivings about the nominee. This reluctance has led to a focus on competitive House and Senate races rather than the presidential race. However, recent polling has shown Trump closing the gap with Clinton, who has faced negative headlines regarding her email practices and family foundation. 

Despite these challenges, the Trump campaign has made strides, with Trump sticking more closely to his message and recent swing state and national polling showing him making gains. The campaign is also working to improve its surrogate operations, with changes coming to the process for determining who can represent the campaign on TV news programs. However, the campaign remains unstable, with a confusing work environment and unclear leadership. Staffers describe a constant lack of clarity about who is in charge, with some saying it's Kellyanne Conway and Steve Bannon, while others point to Jared Kushner and the Trump family. 

Overall, the race remains tight, with both campaigns facing significant challenges. Clinton's lead is narrowing, and Trump's campaign is struggling with infrastructure and donor support. The final months of the campaign will be crucial for both candidates as they work to secure the 270 electoral votes needed to win the presidency.

Justice Antonin Scalia downplayed recent criticism of his colleagues over the Supreme Court's landmark health care reform ruling, stating it offends him to hear such criticism. In an exclusive interview with CNN's Piers Morgan, Scalia argued that the court is not a political institution and that his colleagues do not vote for political reasons. He emphasized that personal disagreements among the justices are not reflective of the court's internal dynamics. Scalia also discussed his legal philosophy, calling it "textualism," which focuses on the actual text of laws and the Constitution, and warned against squishy, unprincipled decision-making. He expressed his views on abortion, supporting the idea that it should be left to states to decide, and on capital punishment, arguing that it should be a democratic choice. The interview also touched on Scalia's role in major cases, such as Bush v. Gore, and his frustration at being on the losing side of many cases. Despite his conservative stance, Scalia maintained that he is a peaceful man and that his harsh rhetoric is a result of his intellectual approach to the law. The summary concludes by noting that Scalia has no plans to retire and remains a prominent figure in the Supreme Court, with his new book, "Reading Law: The Interpretation of Legal Texts," further cementing his influence on legal interpretation.

Groupon has faced a series of setbacks in September, including lawsuits from employees alleging unpaid overtime. The latest lawsuit, filed in Chicago, involves 50 "deal vetters" who claim they were not paid for working more than 40 hours per week. This comes on the heels of a similar class action filed in August by over 1,000 salespeople seeking overtime pay. The deal vetters' lawsuit was filed in a federal court, with the plaintiffs' lawyer, Doug Werman, representing them. The salespeople's lawsuit was recently amended to include additional facts, such as a sample work contract showing a starting salary of $32,000. Groupon has not commented on these lawsuits. These legal challenges follow a string of staff departures, the shelving of its IPO, and other issues that have plagued the company.

Fiat Chrysler Automobiles (FCA) faces a significant challenge as the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) accuses the company of illegally using hidden software in some of its diesel vehicles, potentially leading to a fine of up to $4.6 billion. The EPA's notice of violation affects approximately 104,000 vehicles, including 2014 to 2016 Jeep Grand Cherokee and Ram pickups with 3-liter diesel engines. FCA's shares plummeted more than 16% after the news, with the maximum fine being about $4.6 billion. The EPA and California Air Resources Board both issued notices of violation, believing the undisclosed software allowed vehicles to emit excess pollution, violating the Clean Air Act. FCA's CEO, Sergio Marchionne, vehemently denied any wrongdoing, characterizing the dispute as a failure to disclose software that protects the engine. He emphasized that the company never attempted to create software to cheat emissions rules and was planning updated software to address EPA concerns. Marchionne also suggested that regulators had a "belligerent" view of automakers, stating, "We don’t belong to a class of criminals," and that "the way that it has been described, I think, has been unfair to FCA." The company has no plans to stop selling 2016 U.S. diesel models. New York Attorney General Eric Schneiderman expressed concern and stated his office would investigate the claims against FCA. The EPA's investigation comes amid closer scrutiny of automakers following the Volkswagen emissions scandal, where VW agreed to pay a $4.3 billion fine and plead guilty to criminal charges. The EPA has ongoing reviews of other automakers' emissions systems, but it is unclear if they have found any additional wrongdoing. The incident could significantly impact FCA's financials and reputation, especially as it faces the transition of its CEO, who plans to step down in 2018.

A 25-year-old Tempe mother, Alaina Marie Limpert, was arrested for allegedly allowing her almost-two-year-old daughter to ingest THC butter while eating macaroni and cheese, according to a police report. Limpert was booked on one count of child abuse. The Department of Child Safety was notified by someone in the home that the child had consumed THC butter during a meal with her father. Instead of seeking immediate medical care, the parents reportedly laughed about the child's side effects and then placed her in the backyard pool to use cold water as a "shock" treatment. It wasn't until two days later that the Department of Child Safety intervened, taking custody of all three children living in the home. Hospital officials later confirmed THC was found in the infant's system. Limpert admitted to making the mac and cheese with THC for her husband but did not realize her daughter had ingested it. Limpert is due back in court on April 19. Upon searching the home, police found two marijuana grow tents in the garage, along with mushrooms, bongs, pipes, containers of hash oil, and other drug paraphernalia. In the refrigerator, they discovered three large tubs of THC butter. The incident highlights the dangers of THC-laced food and the potential for accidental ingestion by young children.

A Tulane Medical School student, Peter Gold, is fighting for his life after being shot while trying to stop an attempted abduction in New Orleans. Security cameras captured the incident, showing a man dragging a woman, who was reportedly drunk, to a nearby SUV at 4 a.m. on Friday. Eyewitnesses say that Peter Gold, a 25-year-old fourth-year medical student, noticed the woman being dragged and pulled over to help. The man, who was wearing a dark hooded jacket, jumped out of the SUV with a semi-automatic weapon and shot Gold once in the stomach. The suspect then aimed at Gold's head, trying to shoot him three more times, but the gun jammed each time. The suspect took the woman's purse and fled the scene. Tulane University is offering a $10,000 reward for information leading to the arrest and indictment of the suspect. New Orleans police have identified the suspect as 21-year-old Euric Cain, who is wanted for attempted first-degree murder, second-degree kidnapping, and armed robbery. Surveillance footage shows Cain's SUV, and police are asking the public for help in identifying him. Peter Gold is in guarded condition at the hospital, while the woman involved in the incident was treated for minor injuries and released. The New Orleans Police Department is offering a $12,500 reward for information leading to Cain's arrest.

A veteran Boston police officer has been arrested and charged with assault and battery after an alleged overnight attack on an Uber driver in South Boston, authorities said. Officer Michael Doherty, 40, of South Boston, a 16-year veteran, was placed on paid administrative leave after the incident, and the department’s Anti-Corruption Unit is investigating. According to the police report, Doherty, who had hired an Uber car, became agitated with the driver at 2:45 a.m. because he thought he was in the wrong location. Doherty allegedly used racial slurs, including a derogatory term for Latinos, and began hitting the driver when he stopped at East Second and M Streets. The driver got out of his car and was chased around it by Doherty, who then got into the Uber vehicle and drove off. The driver flagged down a good Samaritan for help, and Doherty approached both the driver and the good Samaritan, using another racial slur and swinging at both parties, according to Doherty’s arrest report. Doherty fled the scene but turned himself in about 11 a.m. the next day. He faces two counts of assault and battery while using a racial slur and using a motor vehicle without authority. Doherty’s lawyer, Kenneth Anderson, argues his client was the real victim, citing Doherty’s black eye and torn bicep tendon. Uber has barred Doherty from using their service and stated they are ready to assist law enforcement in the investigation. The incident has raised concerns about the use of racial slurs by law enforcement and the handling of such incidents.

Jackson Odell, best known for his role as Ari Caldwell in ABC’s “The Goldbergs” from 2013 to 2015, has passed away at the age of 20. Found unresponsive in his Tarzana residence in San Fernando Valley on June 8, the cause of death is pending an autopsy with no foul play suspected. Odell’s career included roles in “The Fosters,” “Modern Family,” “iCarly,” and the 2011 film “Judy Moody and the Not Bummer Summer.” He was also a singer-songwriter, contributing original songs to the soundtrack of the 2018 romantic drama “Forever My Girl,” including “Wings of an Angel,” which “American Idol” contestant Lauren Alaina performed for the film. Odell shared several covers and original songs on his YouTube channel, showcasing his musical talent.

A new Canadian study, published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal (CMAJ), suggests that artificial sweeteners, commonly found in diet drinks and other food products, do not help with weight loss and may even contribute to weight gain and an increased risk of diabetes. Dr. Meghan Azad and her team from the University of Manitoba conducted a meta-review of 37 previously published studies involving over 400,000 people to investigate the long-term effects of artificial sweeteners. The team found no strong evidence that regular consumption of artificial sweeteners leads to weight loss. In fact, longer observational studies indicated a link between artificial sweeteners and higher risks of weight gain, obesity, high blood pressure, and diabetes.

The study highlights the lack of rigorous research on artificial sweeteners, with only seven of the 37 studies being randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that followed participants for a median period of six months. The other 30 studies, which followed participants for an average of 10 years, were observational and could only show correlations rather than establish causation. Among the RCTs, regular consumption of artificial sweeteners had no significant effect on weight loss. However, the observational studies suggested that regular use of these sweeteners was associated with an increased risk of type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure, as well as modest increases in weight and waist circumference.

Dr. Azad emphasizes the need for more research, particularly long-term studies comparing different artificial sweeteners to determine if any are better than others. She advises consumers to be cautious about relying on artificial sweeteners, especially on an everyday basis, as there is no clear evidence of long-term benefits and potential harm. The findings suggest that consumers might consider choosing water instead of artificial sweeteners, especially given the lack of evidence supporting their use for weight management.

Some experts, like Dr. Sean Wharton, an internal medicine specialist in Toronto, caution that the studies do not definitively prove that artificial sweeteners cause Type 2 diabetes. He notes that people who use artificial sweeteners might lose weight temporarily but may gain it back due to other factors, such as psychological issues or other medical conditions. However, the study's findings raise concerns about the potential long-term effects of artificial sweeteners on health.

The article also mentions that artificial sweeteners are widely consumed, with over 40% of adults reporting regular use. These sweeteners are found in various food and drink products, including diet soda, yogurt, sauces, dressings, and baked goods. The study's results challenge the common belief that artificial sweeteners are a healthier alternative to sugar and suggest that consumers might want to reconsider their use, particularly for weight management and overall health.

Balearic techno, a dance music genre born on the tropical shores of Ibiza, is designed to put people in a trance, making it an ideal vehicle for hidden messages. Polish cybersecurity researcher Krzysztof Szczypiorski saw potential in this music, creating a system called StegIbiza, which uses slight changes in tempo to encode Morse code-like messages. Essentially, a "dot" is represented by a slight increase in tempo, while a "line" is a slight decrease. This method can be implemented by DJs using tempo slides on their controllers, making the changes nearly imperceptible to the average listener. In a controlled experiment, 20 participants, half with musical backgrounds, were unable to detect the tempo changes. Szczypiorski also tested his system at an open-air party, where he had to halt the experiment due to the partygoers' dissatisfaction with the DJ's constant tempo adjustments. The ease of implementation and the difficulty of detection make this method a promising tool for covert communication. However, the practicality of using this technique in a live setting remains questionable, as it may disrupt the experience for the majority of the audience. The practice of hiding messages in music is not new, with historical examples dating back at least 500 years. Despite its potential, the challenge lies in maintaining the integrity of the music while ensuring the message is conveyed effectively.

British restaurant chain Pret a Manger faces further controversy after a second customer died from an allergic reaction to a sandwich containing an allergen not noted on the label. The incident, which occurred in December 2017, involved a supposed dairy-free product that contained dairy protein, leading to the death of a customer in Bath. Pret a Manger blamed the death on a supplier of its dairy-free yoghurt, CoYo, claiming it had been mis-sold dairy-containing yoghurt. In response, Pret a Manger promised full ingredient labelling on all freshly made products following the tragic death of 15-year-old Natasha Ednan-Laperouse, who died in 2016 after eating a baguette containing sesame seeds. The parents of Ednan-Laperouse, who have been campaigning for stronger allergen warnings, expressed deep sadness over the second death. Pret a Manger withdrew all affected products and ended its contract with CoYo, stating that subsequent testing found traces of dairy protein in the yoghurt. CoYo, however, disputed Pret's claims, accusing the sandwich chain of hindering its investigation by failing to provide batch codes. The company recalled its yoghurts in February 2018 due to dairy traces, but denied any connection to the death. Pret a Manger offered its condolences to the bereaved family and vowed to assist them. The incident highlights ongoing issues with food labelling and the potential dangers for customers with severe allergies.

The Senate passed a sweeping tax overhaul early Saturday morning, marking a significant legislative achievement for Republicans and President Donald Trump. The bill, which includes approximately $1.4 trillion in tax cuts, would lower the corporate tax rate to 20% from 35%, reshape international business tax rules, and temporarily lower individual taxes. It also touches on other Republican goals, including opening the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil drilling and repealing the individual mandate from the Affordable Care Act. The 51-49 vote came after Senate Republicans navigated internal divisions and made concessions to win over holdouts. Sen. Bob Corker of Tennessee was the only Republican to oppose the measure, while Democrats harshly condemned the legislation and the way it came together. The bill includes provisions that would allow taxpayers to continue writing off property taxes, albeit with a $10,000 limit, and an expanded deduction for medical costs. It also increases a tax deduction for pass-through businesses from 20% to 23%, a boost financed by increasing a proposed one-time tax on multinational corporations’ offshore earnings. These changes brought the Senate bill closer to the House measure, which the House passed in November. However, the House and Senate still need to settle their differences before Trump can sign a final bill. The passage of the bill is seen as a crucial step for Republicans to retain their legislative majorities in the upcoming midterm elections, despite polls showing public disapproval. The bill's permanent reduction in corporate income tax rates from 35% to 20% is contrasted with smaller individual tax breaks that would end in 2026. Critics argue that the bill's reductions for many families would be modest and that by 2027, families earning under $75,000 would on average face higher, not lower, taxes. The bill's passage is also seen as a significant economic and political milestone for Republicans, despite its potential to worsen federal budget deficits.

A 6.5 magnitude earthquake struck Eureka at 4:30 p.m. Saturday, leaving much of the city without power and causing damage reports. The quake, lasting 30 seconds, caused power poles to sway and several businesses to report broken ceiling lights and floor tiles. Eureka's Bayshore Mall was closed, and several employees reported seeing ceiling chunks fall. Residents were out of their homes in panic. Fortuna and Arcata had power, but McKinleyville reported damage. Fortuna Police received reports of gas leaks and items falling from shelves. Eureka resident Paul Knaak experienced the largest quake in his life, with broken water pipes and scattered belongings. Mike Hagedorn from Winco described a mess with items off shelves. The earthquake was felt across a wide area, including as far as Willow Creek. Six aftershocks occurred, none as strong as the main quake. Power outages affected 27,000 PG&E customers, with crews working to restore power. No major injuries were reported, but about 30 people visited hospitals for minor injuries. The epicenter was 20 miles west-northwest of Ferndale, and the quake was felt as far as central Oregon.

A mountain lion broke into a home in Boulder, Colorado, and killed the family's cat named Klondike, according to CBS4. The incident occurred when Kayla Slaughter returned home late Thursday night to find the big cat inside the living room. Neighbors witnessed the mountain lion wandering around the house, even going upstairs, as the family was not home. Officers tried to haze the animal using bean bags but were unable to capture it. The cat appeared to have pushed through a screen and could not get back out. Despite the concern over the big cat potentially returning, officers assured Slaughter that it likely wouldn't. The mountain lion was eventually scared out of the house and made its way into the wilderness near Boulder Canyon. Slaughter and her family plan to be more vigilant about keeping windows shut at night to avoid similar incidents in the future. The break-in highlighted the need for residents to secure ground-level doors and windows, especially in areas near open space.

Rutgers University, New Jersey’s premier public university, is grappling with rising tuition and fees, which will increase by 2.3% or approximately $300 for the 2015-2016 academic year, according to a plan approved by the university’s board. This hike, affecting both undergraduate and graduate students, is necessary to cover rising costs, including new union contracts and a 3.7% cut in state funding. The average in-state undergraduate living on the New Brunswick campus will face a total bill of $26,185, up from $25,559, while the typical in-state graduate student will see a $300 increase in tuition and fees. Despite the tuition hike, Rutgers continues to have one of the highest tuition rates among state universities, with in-state undergraduates receiving a 45% reduction in tuition through grants and scholarships. The university also approved a 3.2% increase in its financial aid program, allocating $32.5 million to assist low-income students with the tuition increase. This move comes amid a broader trend of high student debt, with a new study from the Center for American Progress revealing that just 20 universities received one-fifth of the total federal student loan debt for graduate students in 2013-2014, despite educating only 12% of all graduate students. Notably, these schools include pricey private institutions and for-profit colleges, with Walden University topping the list for the most debt. The study highlights that while many graduate students pursue degrees in fields like journalism and fine arts, which may not promise high salaries, they still face significant financial burdens. Rutgers, like other public universities, has had to increase tuition to make up for reduced state funding, making higher education increasingly unaffordable for many students.

Today’s jobs report from the Labor Department reveals that the U.S. economy added 160,000 new jobs in April, significantly below market expectations of 205,000. The unemployment rate remained unchanged at 5%, but this figure may not fully reflect the current state of the labor market, as the labor force participation rate dipped to 62.8%, its lowest level since March 1978. The weak job growth in April follows a period of relatively strong employment gains over the past three months, with an average of 200,000 new jobs added each month.

The report also shows that hourly earnings grew 2.5% over the past 12 months, indicating a modest improvement in wage growth. This is a positive sign, as it suggests that employers are not cutting wages despite the weak job market. However, the labor market is at a crossroads, with conflicting signals from various economic indicators. On one hand, the number of long-term unemployed is declining, and more people are confident enough to quit their jobs, as evidenced by the recent low in initial jobless claims. Additionally, the labor differential, which measures the perception of job availability, shows that more people now believe jobs are plentiful rather than hard to get.

On the other hand, the bond market is signaling caution, with the yield on 10-year Treasury bonds dropping to 1.8% from over 2% at the start of the year. This suggests that investors are seeking the safety of government debt, which is more desirable in times of economic uncertainty. Furthermore, while crude oil prices have rebounded from their lows, the overall economic growth remains tepid, as the economy grew at an annual rate of only 0.5% in the first quarter of 2016. This growth rate, coupled with persistently low inflation, has muted expectations for future economic expansion.

These mixed signals have led the Federal Reserve to hold off on raising interest rates, despite having done so for the first time in nearly a decade last December. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) acknowledged the unevenness in the economy, noting that while labor market conditions have improved, growth in economic activity has slowed. The FOMC’s statement highlighted that household spending has moderated, although real income has risen at a solid rate and consumer sentiment remains high.

With another jobs report scheduled before the next FOMC meeting in June, the economic outlook remains uncertain. If the upcoming report is as mixed as the past few, the Federal Reserve’s decision-making process will be complicated. The markets, Wall Street, and Washington are all closely watching these developments, as the health of the job market is a key factor in determining the future path of monetary policy and overall economic stability.

At least 153 people, including men, women, and children, have perished after an overturned oil tanker burst into flames near Bahawalpur, Pakistan, as hundreds rushed to collect leaking fuel, reports The Associated Press. The tanker, en route from Karachi to Lahore, lost control and crashed on the national highway, prompting a local mosque's loudspeaker to alert villagers to the fuel spill. Despite warnings from highway police, villagers, armed with jerry cans, motorcycles, and cars, rushed to the scene. When the fire erupted, the same loudspeaker called for villagers to help extinguish the blaze. Eyewitnesses described a horrific scene with victims trapped in the fireball, screaming for help. As the fire subsided, the field was strewn with bodies, and nearby were the charred remains of motorcycles and cars that had carried villagers to the accident site. The death toll is likely to rise, with many victims suffering extensive burns. At the Victoria Hospital in Bahawalpur, a state of emergency was declared, and doctors and nurses were called in to handle the emergency. Twenty-two of the most severely burned patients were airlifted by C-130 aircraft to hospitals in Lahore. DNA testing may be required to identify some of the victims. The incident occurred on the eve of the Muslim holiday of Eid al-Fitr, which marks the end of the fasting month of Ramadan. Pakistan's Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif, who was in London, immediately returned to the country to respond to the incident. The cause of the fire is believed to have been a cigarette lighter, but the exact circumstances remain unclear.

A video of a passenger being forcibly removed from a United Airlines flight in Chicago on Monday morning has sparked outrage and raised questions about airline overbooking practices. The incident, captured by a United passenger, shows a man being dragged from the plane by airport security after he refused to be bumped from the flight. United’s initial response, which focused on the overbooking situation and avoided details about the passenger, left the airline in a state of shame. CEO Oscar Munoz’s statement, which included doublespeak about the airline’s responsibility, only exacerbated the situation. Munoz’s follow-up letter to employees, which defended the airline’s ground staff and described the passenger as “disruptive and belligerent,” further undermined the argument that the flight was overbooked. The airline’s contract of carriage does not clearly address the situation of forcibly ejecting a passenger already seated to make room for a company employee. The video highlights the broader issue of passenger treatment in the United States, where airlines can overbook flights and passengers have limited rights when involuntarily bumped. The Department of Transportation acknowledges that airlines have great latitude in setting their own priority rules for bumping travelers, but compensation rules are in need of updating. The incident also brings to light the pattern of bad behavior by United Airlines, including refusing to allow passengers to board due to clothing choices and treating autistic passengers poorly. These incidents, coupled with the airline’s consistent ranking as one of the worst for customer service, have led to calls for a boycott. The article concludes by emphasizing the importance of stopping giving United your money and supporting airlines that treat passengers with respect and dignity.

The National Park Service (NPS) is proposing significant increases in entrance fees at 17 highly visited national parks to fund infrastructure improvements. These parks, including popular destinations like Yosemite and Yellowstone, would see entrance fees rise to $70 during peak seasons, a substantial increase from the current $25 to $30. Motorcycle fees would increase to $50 from $15 to $25, and pedestrian or cyclist fees would rise to $30 from $10 to $15. The annual America the Beautiful pass, which grants access to all federal lands, would remain at $80. The proposed fee hikes are expected to generate $70 million annually, a 34% increase over 2016 revenue. The peak season for each park would be defined as its busiest five-month period, with the new fee structure set to take effect in 2018. The NPS is seeking public comments on the proposal, which will be accepted until November 23, 2017, via a dedicated website and mailing address. Secretary of the Interior Ryan Zinke emphasized the need for these fee increases to ensure the preservation and maintenance of national parks for future generations. However, the National Parks Conservation Association criticized the proposal, arguing that it could make parks unaffordable for some families and that the administration should address the maintenance backlog through other means. The proposal aims to fund critical infrastructure projects, including roads, bridges, campgrounds, and waterlines, to enhance the visitor experience and protect these natural treasures.

One of the three conductors aboard the Amtrak train that derailed in Philadelphia reported hearing the locomotive's engineer say the train had been struck by an object, according to National Transportation Safety Board member Robert Sumwalt. Sumwalt said the assistant conductor believed she overheard radio transmissions made by Amtrak engineer Brandon Bostian and the engineer of a Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority (SEPTA) train. The SEPTA engineer reported to the train dispatcher that he had either been hit by a rock or shot at and had a broken windshield, placing his train into an emergency stop, and the assistant conductor also believed she heard Bostian say something about his train being struck by something. Bostian, 32, was interviewed for the first time since the derailment and told investigators he had no recollection of anything that happened once the train passed the North Philadelphia station, where he rang the required train bell. He suffered a concussion and other injuries in the crash. The locomotive's windshield was shattered in the derailment, but there is particular damage to the lower portion of the windshield that the FBI will examine, described by Sumwalt as a "circular pattern that emanates out just a bit." The NTSB will reassemble the train to connect its brake lines and test the braking system. The crash, which killed eight people and injured over 200, has raised questions about the effectiveness of positive train control, a technology that could have prevented the accident if installed. The NTSB is also investigating whether the SEPTA and Amtrak trains were struck by projectiles, as both trains reported incidents of objects hitting them shortly before the derailment. The Amtrak CEO stated that had positive train control been installed, the accident would not have occurred. The derailment has caused significant disruptions to Amtrak service, with the Northeast Corridor, one of the nation's busiest rail lines, closed between New York and Philadelphia.

A paraplegic man named Ricky Gilmore, 49, was left stranded in the New Mexico desert without his wheelchair after being abandoned by a couple he hitchhiked with. For three days, Gilmore dragged himself about four miles down a dirt road, enduring extreme conditions and physical pain. He survived on minimal resources, using his upper body to pull himself along, and found temporary shelter by curling up at night. During his ordeal, three vehicles passed by, but none stopped to help. On the third day, a motorist named Wilfred Sisco finally stopped, and Gilmore was taken to the Northern Navajo Medical Center, where he received treatment for acute kidney failure, a sprained wrist, and dehydration. His body was covered in cuts and bruises, and his jeans were tattered from the journey. Gilmore expressed relief at being found but frustration at the lack of compassion from passersby. He plans to stop hitchhiking and focus on healing. The incident has left him questioning the respect people show to those with disabilities. Gilmore is cooperating with police to identify the couple who abandoned him. His ordeal highlights the dangers faced by those who hitchhike and the importance of showing empathy and assistance to those in need.

Authorities in Thailand are facing challenges in relocating tigers from a controversial Buddhist temple, as the temple staff allegedly set some tigers free to obstruct the process. The "Tiger Temple" in Kanchanaburi Province, known for its 137 tigers that tourists can walk among and pose with, has come under scrutiny for alleged illegal breeding and trafficking of the animals. Wildlife Conservation Office (WCO) officials, armed with tranquilizer guns, have been trying to capture the tigers, but faced resistance from temple officials who initially refused to allow the WCO team entry. After a standoff lasting half a day, the wildlife officers managed to sedate and transport eight tigers, marking the beginning of a week-long operation involving approximately 1,000 state personnel. The tigers will be moved to three government animal refuges in different provinces, away from the controversial temple. The temple, a popular tourist attraction, has been criticized by animal rights activists for not properly caring for the tigers and flouting regulations. Despite the massive show of force by the authorities, temple officials initially resisted the efforts, but eventually relented after a court order was obtained. Over 300 officials remained at the temple overnight to ensure the tigers' safety and the smooth operation of the relocation. The temple had recently planned to operate as a zoo, but the government determined that the operators failed to secure sufficient resources, leading to the current situation. The operation highlights the ongoing struggle to balance tourism and animal welfare in Thailand, with the tigers' future now secured in government care.

Mariah Carey and Nick Cannon's divorce appears to be "a done deal," with sources telling TMZ that the couple separated back in May and have been living in separate houses in NYC. Divorce lawyers have been negotiating a property settlement and custody agreement for months. According to sources, the relationship soured after Nick Cannon appeared on Big Boy's radio show in March, where he named five celebrities he had slept with, including one that made Mariah insane. The couple has been drifting apart, with Nick taking on various gigs that keep him away from their children, while Mariah feels he surrounds himself with "yes men" and can't handle disagreement. Despite this, Nick maintains he's generated $75 million for the family since 2011. Meanwhile, Ronnie Magro and Sammi Giancola, stars of Jersey Shore, have called it quits for good after a tumultuous five-year romance. Magro, 28, says they were drifting apart and not spending much time together, adding that he still cares about Giancola, 27, and is not ready to date again. The couple, who had rekindled their romance several times on the show, split two months ago. Finally, Meg Ryan and John Mellencamp, who dated for more than three years, have quietly ended their relationship due to the distance between them. Ryan, 52, lives in New York, while Mellencamp, 62, resides in Indiana. Both stars have upcoming projects: Mellencamp is set to release his 22nd album, Plain Spoken, in November, while Ryan is working on her directorial debut, Ithaca, a WWII coming-of-age drama.

Austrian police have identified the cause of death of a 25-year-old woman from Colorado, Lauren Mann, who was found dead in her Vienna apartment. The body was discovered Tuesday evening after Mann's employer reported her absence from work. Police spokesman Thomas Keiblinger stated that an initial autopsy did not reveal any external injuries, and the case is currently under investigation. Mann had been working as an au pair in Vienna and had graduated in 2012 from the University of Colorado-Boulder's College of Music. The U.S. Embassy in Vienna is providing consular assistance. An autopsy conducted by the city's prosecutor Nina Bussek determined that Mann died from suffocation, but the exact circumstances remain unclear. Police are awaiting toxicological test results, which could take up to two weeks, and are speaking to Mann's neighbors and friends. The case is being treated as a homicide due to the possibility of a third party's involvement. Lauren Mann's family and friends described her as reliable, trusted, and caring. The incident has left the quiet and safe neighborhood where she lived in shock.

Norway is set to become the world's first nation to transition entirely to digital radio, marking a significant shift in broadcasting technology. The government plans to switch off FM radio channels on January 11, 2017, at 11:11:11 AM local time, as part of a broader effort to reduce costs and enhance radio quality. This move is expected to save the country approximately 200 million Norwegian Krone ($23.5 million) annually, mainly due to the lower transmission costs of digital audio broadcasting (DAB) compared to FM, which is about eight times cheaper. The transition also promises to increase the number of available radio channels and improve emergency preparedness systems, fostering increased competition and innovation.

Norway’s DAB network already supports 25 national radio channels and can accommodate up to 20 more, significantly outpacing the current five FM channels. However, the switch has faced considerable opposition, with 66% of Norwegians opposing the move, according to a recent Ipsos survey. Critics argue that the transition could result in missed emergency alerts, especially for drivers without DAB receivers or those in areas not receiving local FM signals. Additionally, the cost of purchasing DAB adaptors for existing FM car radios, which can range from 1,500 to 2,000 Norwegian Kroner ($176 to $234), poses a financial burden on many citizens.

Despite the opposition, the Norwegian government has been planning this transition for years and officially announced it in 2015, providing ample time for citizens to adapt. Radio.no, a dedicated website, has been actively informing the public about DAB and guiding them through the installation process. The criteria for the DAB network transition include covering at least 90% of the population, ensuring that at least half of all listeners tune into digital radio daily, and making radio reception in cars affordable and technically satisfactory.

Norway’s decision to go digital-only is being closely watched by other countries considering similar transitions. Britain, Switzerland, and Denmark are among those planning to follow suit by 2020. The U.S., which never adopted DAB, instead implemented HD radio, which transmits on the same frequency as AM and FM radio but offers higher quality sound when received by new radios. Old radios simply ignore the HD signal, transmitting the original, more staticky signal.

The Norwegian government believes that the transition to DAB will be a success, citing the economic benefits and the potential for increased radio diversity. However, the upcoming switch-off will be a test of public acceptance and the practical challenges of ensuring that all citizens, particularly those in rural areas, are adequately prepared.

A Chinese taxi driver who spent 24 years searching for his missing daughter will finally be reunited with her on Tuesday after she responded to his appeal for information. Wang Mingqing and his wife Liu Chengying briefly took their eyes off their daughter Qifeng, who wandered off while they were busy running their fruit stall in Chengdu, the capital of Sichuan province, in January 1994. The couple abandoned their stall to search for their daughter, but for years their efforts appeared to be in vain. Although the couple went on to have a second child, they never gave up looking for the girl. In 2015, Wang became a taxi driver. When he noticed how much his customers were using their phones, he enlisted their help by asking them to post appeals on social media in the hope his missing daughter might see them. He also printed and distributed 10,000 fliers that outlined the details of the case, including a description of how the young girl looked when she went missing in January 1994 and a local newspaper also published a report about his appeal. Over the past three years Wang had been contacted by scores of young women who suspected they might be his daughter, but DNA tests ruled this out. Two weeks ago a 27-year-old woman in Jilin province contacted the Wangs via social media after reading about his search and realizing she might be the girl in question. The woman had been told she was adopted as a child and grew up under the name Kang Ying in a town only 20 kilometers (12 miles) away from her birth parents. With the help of a non-governmental organization that helps reunite parents with their missing children, the woman, now a mother of two young children, took a DNA test that on Sunday confirmed she was Wang’s daughter. She is flying to Chengdu on Tuesday to meet her birth parents. Wang Mingqing and Liu Dengying were fruit sellers, selling their wares at a roadside stall in the southwestern city of Chengdu. On one particularly busy day, Mr. Wang ran out of change, and briefly went to a neighbouring stall to change money for a customer. When he was back minutes later, his daughter was nowhere to be found. Mr. Wang and his wife spent years searching for her in the city and surrounding areas, taking out advertisements in newspapers and setting up online appeals. The couple, who have another daughter and a son, never left Chengdu, in the hope that Qifeng would find her way back to them. In 2015, Mr. Wang decided to broaden the search by signing up as a driver with ride-hailing company Didi Chuxing.
