The agency’s total budget in 2016 was $8.6 billion, with grants and contracts totaling $11 billion. The freeze is part of a broader effort by the Trump administration to review and potentially reduce the EPA’s regulatory reach and budget.

Former New York Governor Eliot Spitzer faces two libel lawsuits totaling $90 million from former Marsh & McLennan executives over a 2010 column defending his own enforcement actions. The lawsuits, filed by William Gilman and Edward McNenney, claim Spitzer defamed them in his column, which appeared three months after their convictions for an insurance bid-rigging scandal were overturned. Spitzer, who was New York's attorney general when the investigation began, had accused Marsh of price-fixing, bid-rigging, and kickbacks. Spitzer declined to comment, while a Washington Post spokeswoman remained silent. The cases highlight the ongoing tensions between corporate executives and regulators, with Spitzer maintaining his actions were necessary to uphold justice and ethics in the marketplace.

Three men, including a California sheriff's deputy, were arrested in York County, Pennsylvania, after a major drug bust that seized 247 pounds of marijuana valued at around $2 million and $11,000 in cash. Christopher Heath, 37, a drug task force agent with the Yuba County Sheriff’s Department, was among those arrested last week in West Manheim Township. The bust was part of an ongoing investigation based on tips into law enforcement, and detectives were not aware Heath was an officer before making the arrest. Heath had his badge and service weapon on him at the time of his arrest. York County District Attorney Tom Kearney said the bust was not a routine traffic stop but part of a coordinated effort. All three men, Ryan Falsone, 27, Tyler Long, 31, and Heath, 37, have been charged with delivery of marijuana, criminal conspiracy to deliver marijuana, and possession with intent to deliver marijuana. The three men, who were arrested in the 100 block of Frogtown Road, have posted a respective $1 million bail. The operation is considered sophisticated and ongoing, with the possibility of federal charges due to the cross-state transportation of drugs.

Joe Jackson, the father and early manager of the Jackson family, passed away on June 27, 2018, at the age of 89, after a long battle with cancer, as confirmed by TMZ and CNN. Jackson, who launched the careers of his children Michael, Janet, and the Jackson 5 in the 1960s, was born in 1928 and had 11 children with his wife Katherine, whom he married in 1949. He managed his children's careers with an iron fist, often criticized for his strict and sometimes physical methods, but he maintained that his tough approach ensured their success and kept them out of trouble. Jackson's health had been a concern for some time, with reports of a stroke in 2015 and a car accident in 2017. His daughter La Toya Jackson paid tribute to him, writing, "I will always love you! You gave us strength, you made us one of the most famous families in the world. I am extremely appreciative of that, I will never forget our moments together and how you told me how much you cared."

Joe Jackson's role as a manager was pivotal in shaping the Jackson family's musical legacy. The Jackson 5, formed in 1966, became one of the most successful R&B groups, with their father initially managing their careers. As the group's success grew, Jackson managed the entire family for performances in Las Vegas. His strict parenting style was a subject of controversy, with his children recounting stories of physical discipline and harsh treatment. In a 2013 interview with CNN, Jackson defended his methods, stating, "I'm glad I was tough, because look what I came out with. I came out with some kids that everybody loved all over the world. And they treated everybody right." Despite the criticism, Jackson's efforts helped his children achieve global fame, with Michael Jackson becoming the "King of Pop" and Janet Jackson also achieving significant success as a solo artist. Joe Jackson's passing marks the end of an era for the Jackson family, with his legacy as a tough but effective manager and father continuing to be debated.

The U.S. Senate confirmed Sally Jewell, CEO of outdoor retailer REI, as the new Interior Secretary in a 87-11 bipartisan vote. Jewell, a 57-year-old former petroleum engineer and banker, will oversee the Department of Interior, which manages over 500 million acres of public lands and 1 billion acres offshore. Jewell promised to balance conservation and development, stating, "She understands there is an enormous challenge to balance these dual roles of conserving and developing." Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee Chairman Ron Wyden praised Jewell, saying she is "the right person to oversee the multitude of programs" in the Interior Department. Despite Jewell's ties to environmental groups, including her role with the National Parks Conservation Association, Senate Republicans raised concerns about her past opposition to fossil-fuel mining near national parks. Jewell, who lives in Seattle, will replace Ken Salazar, who announced his departure in January.

For centuries, Easter Island, known for its towering stone statues, has been shrouded in mystery. The prevailing narrative suggests that the Polynesian seafarers who settled the island 900 years ago, led by Hotu Matu'a, carved the giant stone heads through a society marked by infighting and resource depletion. However, a new study published in the Journal of Pacific Archaeology challenges this perspective, revealing a more complex and collaborative society than previously thought.

The research, led by Dale Simpson Jr. from the University of Queensland, analyzed the chemical composition of stone tools used to carve the statues. By examining 17 of the 1,600 toki (stone tools) recovered from excavations of four statues, the team found evidence of a sophisticated and cooperative society. The majority of the tools came from a single quarry complex, suggesting that the people worked together and shared information to produce the statues.

"This study shows how people were interacting, it's helping to revise the theory," said Laure Dussubieux, a study co-author from the Field Museum. The findings indicate that the society behind the moai (stone statues) was organized, with chiefs, priests, and guilds of workers. The complexity of the statues, numbering nearly a thousand and reaching heights of over 70 feet, points to a well-structured society capable of large-scale collaboration.

Jo Anne Van Tilburg, director of the Easter Island Statue Project, led the excavations and chemical analysis. "The near exclusive use of one quarry to produce these seventeen tools supports a view of craft specialization based on information exchange," she stated. However, Van Tilburg also cautions that the interaction may have been coercive, highlighting the complexity of human behavior.

The study's results challenge the notion of competition and collapse on Easter Island, suggesting that the society was more cooperative than previously believed. "For a long time, people wondered about the culture behind these very important statues," Dussubieux said. "This study provides insight into how the statue production industry functioned."

While the society faced challenges later on, including the arrival of colonists and the institution of slavery, the Rapa Nui culture persisted. "There are thousands of Rapa Nui people alive today—the society isn't gone," Simpson said. The research not only sheds light on the past but also offers broader insights into how societies function and interact.

Alan Rickman's portrayal of Professor Snape in the Harry Potter films is widely regarded as one of his most iconic roles. Initially cast as a villain, Rickman's nuanced performance gradually revealed Snape's complex character, transforming him into a sympathetic and tragic figure. Rickman's dedication to the role was evident, as he had to keep certain plot details secret from filmmakers and journalists, hinting at the depth of his character's backstory. In an interview with RTE, Rickman shared that he received a "little piece of information" from J.K. Rowling, which significantly influenced his portrayal. This information, though not a plot point, was crucial in shaping his understanding of Snape's character. Rickman's ability to convey the character's hidden loyalties and sacrifices made his performance a standout in the series.

Rickman's character arc in the films is a testament to his acting prowess. From the early antagonism towards Harry and his friends to the eventual revelation of Snape's true nature, Rickman's performances were marked by subtle shifts in tone and demeanor. His scenes with Daniel Radcliffe, particularly in "Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows: Part 2," showcased the depth of their on-screen chemistry and the complexity of their relationship. Rickman's final scenes with Emma Watson, where he reveals his true feelings for Harry's mother, are particularly poignant, highlighting the emotional weight of his character's journey.

Behind the scenes, Rickman's commitment to the role was evident. He had to hide his knowledge from directors and journalists, adding an extra layer of authenticity to his performance. His character's transformation from a cold and calculating villain to a hero willing to sacrifice everything for the greater good is a testament to Rickman's acting skills. The character of Snape remains one of the most memorable and complex in the Harry Potter series, and Rickman's portrayal will be remembered as a defining moment in his career.

Rickman's legacy extends beyond his work in the Harry Potter films. He was a versatile actor with a long and distinguished career, appearing in numerous films and stage productions. His final works, including "Eye in the Sky" and "Alice Through the Looking Glass," were well-received, showcasing his continued relevance as an actor. His passing at the age of 69 was mourned by the acting community and fans of his work, who celebrated his unique talent and the impact he had on the entertainment industry.

Scientists have found a link between height and cancer risk, suggesting that taller individuals have a higher likelihood of developing cancer due to having more cells in their body. This connection was explored by Leonard Nunney, an evolutionary biologist at the University of California, Riverside, who analyzed data from large cancer studies to examine the relationship between height and cancer risk. His findings, published in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B, indicate that for every 10 centimeters over the average height, a person's risk of developing any type of cancer increases by about 10%. This aligns with previous research that has also linked height to an increased risk of various health issues, including blood clots, heart problems, and diabetes.

Nunney's study involved comparing the observed cancer risk in large datasets with the expected risk based on the number of cells in the body. He found that the increased risk of cancer with height was consistent with the number of cells hypothesis, which suggests that more cells mean a higher chance of developing cancer. The analysis showed that the risk increase was more pronounced for women, with taller women 12% more likely to develop cancer compared to shorter women, while taller men had a 9% increased risk. This matches Nunney's predicted rates, which were 13% for women and 11% for men.

The study also revealed that the correlation between height and cancer risk was strongest for certain types of cancer, including colon, kidney, and lymphoma. However, there were some exceptions, such as thyroid cancer and melanoma, where the risk increase was greater than expected. Nunney speculated that other factors, such as geographical variations, might be contributing to these anomalies.

While the increased cancer risk associated with height is significant, experts emphasize that lifestyle factors such as smoking and maintaining a healthy weight play a much larger role in cancer risk. Georgina Hill from Cancer Research UK notes that the increased risk is small and that individuals can significantly reduce their cancer risk through lifestyle changes. The findings suggest that the number of cells in the body is a key factor in the height-cancer link, but they do not provide a complete explanation for why taller people have a higher cancer risk.

The research underscores the importance of understanding the underlying mechanisms that connect height to cancer risk. While the number of cells is a significant factor, other potential contributors, such as growth hormones and environmental factors, may also play a role. Further investigation is needed to fully understand the complex relationship between height, cell number, and cancer risk.

A week after Hurricane Harvey made landfall as a Category 4 storm, the remnants of the hurricane continued to unleash unprecedented rainfall, causing widespread flooding across southeastern Texas. The storm, which has displaced over 1 million people, has claimed at least 50 lives, with many more feared missing. Rescuers have answered hundreds of calls for help, with the Coast Guard alone rescuing over 3,000 people. Houston Mayor Sylvester Turner urged residents to shelter in place and stay off flooded roadways, as the city faced the threat of more rain and rising water levels. Emergency officials continued to release water from reservoirs to prevent dam failures, but the move could exacerbate flooding in surrounding areas. The National Weather Service predicted that some parts of Houston and its suburbs could receive up to 50 inches of rain, with the storm's impact extending beyond the immediate flooding. The hurricane's toll on the oil and gas industry was significant, with nearly a third of U.S. refining capacity shut down, potentially leading to higher gasoline prices. The storm also disrupted air travel, with over 1,400 flights canceled, and caused power outages for at least 1.25 million people. Insurance experts estimated that wind-damage claims could reach the low billions of dollars, with storm surges and inland flooding posing an even greater risk. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers were coordinating efforts to manage the floodwaters, with officials warning that the situation could remain dire for weeks. The Army Corps of Engineers began releasing water from the Addicks and Barker reservoirs, which had reached their peak levels, to prevent uncontrolled releases at the spillways. However, this action could lead to further flooding in nearby communities. Harris County Flood Control District meteorologist Jeff Lindner emphasized that the situation was unprecedented, with complex hydrology and multiple variables affecting the water levels. The storm's impact on the local economy was significant, with the potential for long-term consequences for the oil and gas industry and the broader U.S. economy. As the floodwaters receded in some areas, residents faced the daunting task of assessing the damage and beginning the recovery process. The storm's aftermath highlighted the need for better preparedness and response mechanisms in the face of such catastrophic events.

In real life, the most stolen car isn't an exotic sports car but a common sedan or pickup truck, according to a new report by the tracking and recovery system company LoJack. For the fifth consecutive year, the Honda Accord topped the list of most stolen vehicles, highlighting the enduring popularity of this reliable car among thieves. LoJack's 2013 Vehicle Theft Recovery Report, which analyzed data from 27 states and California law enforcement, revealed that $121 million in stolen vehicles were recovered, with the most expensive being a 2011 Porsche Panamera. Frank Scafidi, director of public affairs for the National Insurance Crime Bureau (NICB), noted that while the NICB's list and LoJack's rankings may differ, the Honda Accord's frequent appearance on the list is unsurprising due to its popularity and longevity. Honda Accords, as one of the best-selling cars in the U.S. for over three decades, are often stolen for their parts, which can be sold for three times the value of the vehicle. The company continues to equip its newer vehicles with advanced security systems, such as the Immobilizer Theft-Deterrent System, to combat theft. However, the sheer number of Accords on the road, their frequent involvement in accidents, and the demand for their parts make them a lucrative target for professional thieves. The National Insurance Crime Bureau's 2012 report also highlighted the Honda Accord as the most stolen car, with the 1996 model being the most stolen make and model, with 8,637 thefts. The LoJack report further detailed the top 10 most stolen and recovered LoJack-equipped vehicle models, with the Honda Civic, Toyota Camry, and Toyota Corolla also making the list.

Residents of Wukan, a village in Guangdong province, have reached a tentative agreement with local authorities after a prolonged standoff over land seizures and the death of a negotiator. The village, which has been in a dispute with developers since September, saw a significant escalation after the death of Xue Jinbo, a village representative who died in police custody. Villagers had planned a protest march through police barriers, but a senior provincial official met with village representatives, resulting in some demands being met. The authorities agreed to release three detained village leaders and return the body of Xue Jinbo, while also releasing the body of another detained villager. Additionally, four villagers being held by police are expected to be released over the next few days, and land from one development project will be returned to the villagers. The police withdrew their roadblocks leading into the village on Tuesday night. Despite this progress, villagers remain cautious, stating they will return to the streets if promises are not kept. This situation, which has garnered significant attention due to its scale, highlights the ongoing issue of land grabs in China, where thousands of protests occur each year.

Nearly a month after some SAT tests disappeared from Loudoun County, Virginia, officials have found the missing exams at Broad Run High School. The 236 answer sheets, which were supposed to be delivered to the College Board, were discovered at the bottom of a cart in the school's shipping area. Initially, it was reported that UPS had taken the tests out of the building, but video surveillance showed otherwise. The tests were hand-carried to Princeton, New Jersey, where they will be validated. Over 200 students in Loudoun County are relieved they won't have to retake the exam. The school system is investigating the incident and reviewing its test delivery procedures. The missing tests were found on Monday, nearly a week after the initial discovery of the missing exams.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive, contributing to the Wayback Machine. Meanwhile, a new study from Colorado College reveals that the belief in a good night’s sleep can significantly enhance cognitive performance, even if the sleep quality was not actually better. The research, involving 164 students, found that those informed they had a good night’s sleep performed better on attention and memory tests compared to those told they had slept poorly, despite both groups receiving the same cognitive exercises. Students were misled about their sleep quality, with some told they had spent 28.7% of their sleep in REM, while others were informed of only 16.2% in REM. This placebo effect, known as "placebo sleep," underscores the power of mindset in influencing cognitive states. The study, published in the Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory and Cognition, suggests that believing in the quality of one's sleep can positively impact cognitive abilities. The findings highlight the importance of maintaining a positive mindset regarding sleep, as it can serve as a powerful tool for enhancing cognitive functioning.

On March 10, 2014, aviation enthusiasts Steve Douglass and Dean Muskett, along with other photographers, gathered at the Rick Husband Amarillo International Airport in Texas. They were expecting to capture images of military aircraft, including the elusive F-22 Raptor. However, their plans took an unexpected turn when they noticed the contrails of three high-flying aircraft. Initially, the group thought the planes were B-2 stealth bombers, but upon reviewing their photos, they realized the aircraft had a unique shape that did not match the B-2's distinctive "W" trailing edge. Douglass, a journalist, described the trailing edge as "almost boomerang shaped," with a slight curve and a smooth backside. An inquiry to Whiteman Air Force Base, which houses B-2s, confirmed that no such flight took place on that day, raising further questions about the identity of the aircraft. Aviation Week and Space Technology (AW&ST) investigated the mystery and concluded that the photos likely depict a real, albeit unknown, aircraft. Douglass suggested that the aircraft might be a stealthy transport, though its exact identity remains a mystery. The incident has sparked interest in the aviation community, with some speculating that the moment might have been chosen to showcase a potential ace in the hole to a resurgent enemy, much like the F-117 did decades earlier.

Cuba's National Assembly will elect a new president on Wednesday, marking a historic political transition. The assembly is set to convene at 9 a.m. on Wednesday to select leaders of the legislature before voting for the president and other members of the Council of State, the country's highest government body. The live broadcast of the session will highlight the event's significance, as state media will cover the most crucial moments. The 86-year-old Raul Castro, who has served as president for two five-year terms, will step down, making this the first time in nearly six decades that someone from outside the Castro family will hold the country's highest office. First Vice President Miguel Diaz-Canel Bermudez, 57, is the overwhelming favorite to replace Castro, and his recent high-profile appearances on state-run television have reinforced this expectation. Diaz-Canel, a hardworking, modest-living technocrat, gained prominence as the top Communist Party official in central Villa Clara province. He has defended academics and bloggers, potentially positioning him as a potential advocate for greater openness in the system. Despite his uncharismatic image, Diaz-Canel is seen as a key figure in ensuring the continuity of Cuba's single-party system. Raul Castro's tenure has been marked by a series of economic reforms that expanded the private sector, allowing greater freedom for citizens to travel and access information. However, these changes have not significantly improved the generally unproductive state-run businesses that employ three-quarters of the workforce. State salaries remain low, averaging just $30 a month, leading to widespread economic struggles. As the new president, Diaz-Canel faces the challenge of rejuvenating the economy while maintaining the existing political structure. The transition is expected to be smooth, with all leaders selected by a government-appointed commission and receiving near-unanimous support. The Cuban government has emphasized that the system will continue, assuring citizens that no fundamental changes are occurring despite the new faces at the top. The assembly's session is scheduled to continue through the day, with the official announcement of the new national leadership expected on Thursday, the anniversary of the defeat of U.S.-backed invaders at the Bay of Pigs in 1961.

Utah man Samuel Shaffer, 34, was convicted on Wednesday on one count of rape of a child and one count of child sodomy, leading to a 15-year-to-life prison sentence. The sentence, according to Utah State Courts spokesman Geoff Fattah, means Shaffer will serve a minimum of 26 years behind bars. Shaffer was the self-proclaimed prophet of a fundamentalist offshoot of the Mormon Church, the Knights of Crystal Blade, which practices polygamy and believes in doomsday prophecies. He and another cult member, John Coltharp, were married to each other's daughters, who were minors. The case began when Coltharp’s ex-wife reported that Coltharp had kidnapped their four children. Shaffer was initially arrested on December 1, 2017, for kidnapping and was later found with two of the girls in a water barrel. The remaining two girls were found in an abandoned trailer in poor health. Shaffer’s arrest came after a December 4, 2017, Amber Alert was issued for Coltharp's daughters. Coltharp, 34, pleaded guilty on June 13 to charges of child sodomy and child bigamy, with his sentencing scheduled for August 8. A third man was also identified as an alleged follower of the doomsday group and charged with child sexual abuse. Shaffer’s case highlights the disturbing practices and dangerous living conditions within fundamentalist religious groups.

An 82-year-old Japanese man, Masafumi Nagasaki, has voluntarily lived as a castaway on the deserted island of Sotobanari in the Yaeyama Islands, Okinawa Prefecture, for nearly three decades. Nagasaki, who was 76 when he was first documented in 2012, arrived on the island in 1989, initially wearing clothes but eventually adopting a life in the buff. His decision to live on the island was driven by a desire to escape societal norms and find a place to die surrounded by nature. He told Reuters, "Finding a place to die is an important thing to do, and I’ve decided here is the place for me. It hadn’t really occurred to me before how important it is to choose the place of your death, like whether it’s in a hospital or at home with family by your side. But to die here, surrounded by nature — you just can’t beat it, can you?"

Nagasaki's routine on the island is strict and disciplined. He wakes up each day to stretch on the beach, followed by hours of beach cleaning with a pair of white gloves and a rake. He has no access to clean water, relying on rainwater collected in a system of cooking pots. His diet consists of rice cakes, which he boils in water, and he eats them whenever hunger strikes, often four or five times a day. He visits a nearby settlement once a week to buy food and water, as well as to collect the 10,000 yen sent to him by his family, on which he lives. Despite the harsh conditions, he has no regrets. "I don’t do what society tells me, but I do follow the rules of the natural world. You can’t beat nature so you just have to obey it completely," he said.

The island of Sotobanari, with its dangerous currents and lack of natural water, is rarely visited by local fishermen. Nagasaki's only companions are the wildlife, and he has developed a deep respect for nature. He stopped eating meat and fish and refused to eat the vast number of turtle eggs left by their maternal visitors, as he had seen the baby turtles being born and crawling towards the sea. "I get goosebumps every time I see that. It makes me think how wonderful life is," he said.

However, in April 2018, authorities removed Nagasaki from the island, citing his weakened state. He was taken back to civilization and is now living in a government house in the nearest city, Ishigaki, 60 kilometers away. His health is reportedly fine, but he is no longer allowed to return to the island. "They won’t allow him to return," said Alvaro Cerezo, who documented Nagasaki's life on the island. "He couldn’t even fight back because he was weak. They won’t allow him to go back any more, he cannot go there, it’s over."

Nagasaki's story is not unique. There are other voluntary castaways like him, such as the "Vietnamese Tarzan," the "Australian Hermit," and the "First Castaway Girl." These individuals have chosen to live in isolation, often driven by a desire to escape societal norms and find a sense of freedom and purpose. Nagasaki's life on Sotobanari is a testament to the human spirit's ability to adapt and find meaning in even the most challenging of circumstances.

Rescue efforts on Mount Ontake, a Japanese volcano that erupted on Saturday, have been halted due to toxic gases and ash, with five more bodies found near the summit, bringing the presumed dead to 36, according to police. The still-erupting mountain forced rescuers to abandon search operations around 1:30 p.m., as Japanese soldiers airlifted eight more bodies off the ash-blanketed peak. The latest victims were found near a shrine at the summit, the same area where other victims were reportedly discovered. The bodies were examined in a gymnasium at a small wooden elementary school in the nearby town of Kiso. More than 200 soldiers and firefighters, including units with gas detection equipment, were part of the search mission. The effort was halted due to an increase in toxic gas and ash, with rescuers reporting a strong smell of sulfur. The eruption, the first fatal one in modern times at the 3,067-meter (10,062-foot) mountain, occurred as at least 250 people were enjoying a beautiful fall day. The blast spewed large white plumes of gas and ash, blanketing the surrounding area in ash and trapping hundreds of hikers. About 40 people who were stranded overnight came down on Sunday, with many injured and some needing rescue by helicopters or carried down on stretchers. The volcano's last major eruption was in 1979, and it experienced a minor eruption in 2007. Survivors reported being pelted by rocks from the eruption, with some seeking shelter in the basement of a lodge. Family members of the missing waited at a nearby municipal hall, hoping for news. The search for victims was abandoned due to fears of toxic fumes, with the smell of sulfur strengthening at the peak.

Three people were injured in a shooting inside Washington Square Mall in Indianapolis on Wednesday night, according to police. The incident occurred around 6:30 p.m. in a corridor near the Target store, where a dispute between a known individual and the suspect escalated into gunfire. Indianapolis Metropolitan Police Deputy Chief of Operations Brian Mahone stated that the shooting was not a random act, as the suspect and the victim had a prior relationship. Two males, 25 and 26 years old, and a 20-year-old female were wounded, with one victim in serious condition. The suspect fled the scene, and police are searching for him. Eyewitness Jacob Laffey described hearing 10 to 11 shots and seeing people running. The shooting could have occurred anywhere the two individuals would have encountered each other, highlighting the unpredictable nature of such incidents. Mall property manager Adrian Lewis confirmed that a shooting occurred and that the mall's security staff and police responded quickly. The safety of shoppers and employees remains a top priority, with the mall maintaining a highly-trained staff prepared to handle emergencies. The victims and their families are receiving support during this difficult time.

A Philadelphia transit worker who found $15,200 in cash and turned it in to police has been given the money since no one ever claimed it, according to the AP. Bob Tracey, 62, found a black bag containing dozens of $100 and $20 bills in the middle of State Road in Upper Darby last March. He immediately called police and turned the money in to authorities. Upper Darby Police Superintendent Michael Chitwood was so impressed by Tracey's honesty that he said at the time the money should go to Tracey if nobody claimed the cash. However, Tracey had to petition the court under a law dealing with finders of lost property after more than a year with no claims. On Monday, Delaware County Court of Common Pleas Judge Charles Burr II ordered the money returned to Tracey. Although Chitwood believed the money should have been returned to Tracey within 90 days if the owner did not come forward, Tracey was forced to petition the courts in September to get the money returned, as was first reported by the Delaware County Daily Times. The petition stated that under state law, a finder of lost property has a valid claim for title of that property against all persons except the true owner. It's unclear why Tracey's legal battle dragged on for six months, as a listed number for him was not operational, and calls to his attorney were not immediately returned. Chitwood said the bureaucracy was a nightmare for the honest worker, who had to jump through a lot of hoops for being honest. Most people would have taken the money and kept on going.

President Donald Trump and North Korean leader Kim Jong Un held a historic summit in Singapore, signing a joint statement aimed at complete denuclearization of the Korean Peninsula. The summit, which lasted over four hours, saw the two leaders engage in numerous photo opportunities and friendly exchanges, despite the significant geopolitical tensions between their countries. Trump described the meeting as “fantastic,” while Kim stated they had “decided to leave the past behind.” The joint statement committed the U.S. to providing security guarantees to North Korea, while Kim reaffirmed his commitment to denuclearization. However, the document did not specify the nature of these security guarantees or the exact definition of “complete denuclearization.” Critics argued that the summit’s focus on friendly interactions overshadowed substantive discussions, potentially elevating North Korea’s status in the global community. Trump also mentioned his intention to invite Kim to the White House, marking a significant shift in U.S. policy towards North Korea. The summit came after North Korea had released three American detainees and halted missile tests, which Trump cited as progress. Despite the positive rhetoric, many analysts remain skeptical about the long-term prospects of a comprehensive nuclear deal, given North Korea’s historical reluctance to fully disarm. The meeting also raised concerns about the lack of transparency, as the summit was largely conducted in private with minimal public disclosure.

Eleven Secret Service agents and five military personnel were involved in a prostitution scandal in Cartagena, Colombia, before President Obama's arrival for the Summit of the Americas. The agents allegedly brought women back to their hotel rooms, with one incident escalating when an agent refused to pay a prostitute. Local police were called after a dispute, and the matter was reported to the U.S. Embassy. The Secret Service immediately launched an investigation, recalling the 11 agents and replacing them. At least one supervisor was among those involved. Five military personnel were also accused of misconduct, confined to their quarters. The scandal overshadowed Obama's diplomatic mission, with the White House maintaining the president has full confidence in the Secret Service. Rep. Peter King, head of the House Homeland Security Committee, revealed that close to all 11 agents had brought women back to their rooms. The incident highlights the potential for security risks and embarrassment, with the Secret Service emphasizing the zero-tolerance policy on personal misconduct. The military is also investigating its personnel involved in the incident, with the commander expressing disappointment. The scandal raises questions about the professionalism and conduct of federal agents and military personnel in foreign countries.

Facing criticism for its predominantly older, male, and white membership, the Academy of Motion Pictures Arts and Sciences has made a significant move to address the film industry's ongoing diversity issues. As part of a major overhaul, the Academy sent out an unprecedented 683 membership invitations, nearly half of them to women, and 41% to people of color. This initiative includes a diverse list of film industry professionals, both established and up-and-coming, from various backgrounds and nationalities. The director invitees span a wide range, including Catherine Breillat, Park Chan-wook, Lucrecia Martel, and Kiyoshi Kurosawa, among others, signaling a push towards greater representation in the directing category. The acting invitees are equally diverse, featuring actors such as Luis Guzmán, Adam Beach, and Michelle Rodriguez, reflecting the Academy's commitment to inclusivity. This move comes in the wake of the #OscarsSoWhite campaign, which was launched by April Reign, a former attorney and managing editor of BroadwayBlack.com, following the 2015 and 2016 all-white acting Oscar nominees. The campaign gained momentum when high-profile figures like Spike Lee and Jada Pinkett Smith joined the movement, prompting the Academy to make a public commitment to double the number of women and people of color in its ranks by 2020. Wednesday marked the first opportunity for the Academy to implement this commitment, with the release of the latest list of invitees, representing the largest and most diverse class to date. While this step is a positive sign, the long-term impact on the Academy's diversity and the film industry as a whole remains to be seen.

American journalist James Foley was murdered by Islamic State militants, who on August 19, 2014, publicized the killing in a graphic video uploaded to YouTube. Foley's parents received an email from his captors on August 12, 2014, stating that Foley would be "executed" as a direct result of US airstrikes in Iraq. The email, published by GlobalPost, contained factual inaccuracies and extreme rhetoric, indicating that Foley's execution was part of a broader strategy by the Islamic State to retaliate against US military actions. The terrorist group has since threatened to kill another American journalist, Steven Sotloff, if the US continues its bombing campaign in Iraq.

The execution video, dominated by the colors of orange, taupe, and black, featured a masked man with a British accent, known as "Jihadi John." Experts believe he is one of three British militants guarding the Islamic State's foreign hostages. The group has held three American hostages in Syria, including Foley and Sotloff, and has threatened to kill them if the US does not cease its airstrikes. Foley's family and GlobalPost published the email from his captors, which revealed the group's demands and motivations. The email stated that the Islamic State had given the Foleys many chances to negotiate for James's release, but the family was not given many opportunities to negotiate. The captors demanded an astronomical ransom of 100 million euros, which was likely not intended to be paid.

Foley's executioner, "Jihadi John," was reportedly an intelligent, educated, and devout believer in radical Islamic teachings. He had led negotiations with Western families for the release of their loved ones and was involved in the release of two Spanish journalists. However, Foley was singled out for torture because he was an American. His captors found pictures of his brother, a US Air Force officer, and used this information to justify his treatment. Foley was subjected to mock executions, including one in which he was "crucified against a wall."

The Islamic State's correspondence with Foley's family was different from their interactions with other Western hostages. The group demanded an absurdly high ransom, which most experts believe was not intended to be paid. Foley's family and friends described him as an extraordinary individual, a compassionate journalist who was determined to bear witness to the suffering of people in conflict. His death was seen as a martyrdom for freedom, and Pope Francis expressed his condolences to the Foleys in a heartfelt phone call.

The case of Foley and Sotloff highlights the ongoing tensions between the US and the Islamic State, and the group's use of hostages as tools of propaganda and retaliation. The threat to other Western hostages underscores the group's determination to continue its campaign of violence and intimidation.

Thai authorities are racing against time and rising water levels to rescue 12 boys and their soccer coach who have been trapped in a flooded cave for nearly two weeks. A medical assessment revealed that the group, now in a chamber where water levels are still high, is too weak to attempt a dangerous escape through the narrow, flooded tunnels. The Thai Navy SEALs have started pumping oxygen into the chamber to help maintain the boys' health. Meanwhile, water continues to be pumped out of the cave complex, with 34 million gallons removed over several days, allowing rescuers to walk through a 1.5-kilometer stretch from the entrance to the Third Chamber, where the boys are located. The Thai Navy SEALs are teaching the boys to scuba dive, but experts warn that forcing them to navigate the treacherous, murky waters could be too risky. Rescuers are also installing a fiber-optic line to connect the boys with their families and searching the mountainside for alternative entrances to the cave. The boys, aged 11 to 16, and their 25-year-old coach were found on June 23 after a soccer practice outing went awry, and heavy rains flooded the cave system. The Thai government is coordinating an international effort, with support from Australia, China, Israel, and the United States, among others. The rainy season is expected to intensify, with heavy rains forecast for the coming days, adding urgency to the rescue operation. The Thai Navy SEALs are considering bringing the boys out in phases, with the strongest or most prepared boys potentially leaving first. The situation remains tense as rescuers work to balance the boys' safety with the looming threat of rising water levels.

The California Supreme Court's recent ruling has dealt a significant blow to animal advocates seeking improved conditions for elephants at the Los Angeles Zoo. In 2007, Aaron Leider sued the zoo director and the city of Los Angeles, alleging that the zoo subjected elephants to "cruel, abusive and illegal treatment" through the use of chains, drugs, bullhooks, and electric shocks. In 2012, a Los Angeles County Superior Court judge ordered the city to stop using bullhooks or electric shocks and to exercise the elephants regularly. However, a divided appeals court affirmed the lower court's decision. The zoo's supporters argue that the city is providing top-quality care for the elephants, while animal advocates contend that the animals are suffering in captivity. Los Angeles Councilman Paul Koretz has called for the zoo to move an Asian elephant named Billy to a sanctuary, citing concerns about the elephant's health and well-being. However, the California Supreme Court has now reversed the appeals court's decision, ruling that a taxpayer action cannot be used to enforce violations of criminal law. This means that the city and its zoo director cannot be compelled to change their practices through an injunction. The court's decision has been met with disappointment from Leider's attorney, who believes that the evidence shows that elephants are dying prematurely due to conditions at the zoo. He hopes to pursue the case through the Legislature or other means to protect the elephants. The zoo, on the other hand, maintains that it provides the highest level of care for its elephants and all its animals. The court's decision has reignited the debate over the treatment of animals in zoos and the balance between public safety and the well-being of the animals.

A new study reveals that 260 million Americans cross structurally deficient bridges daily, highlighting the severity of aging infrastructure in the USA. According to the report from Transportation for America, at least 66,405 bridges, or 11% of the total, are structurally deficient, meaning they require significant maintenance, rehabilitation, or replacement. These bridges are not necessarily unsafe but are in poor condition, potentially leading to issues like potholes, weight restrictions, and lane closings. The average age of these structurally deficient bridges is 65 years, and the repair cost is estimated at $76 billion. The Federal Highway Administration warns that the situation is worsening, with 15 states experiencing an increase in structurally deficient bridges. The report projects that in 10 years, one in four bridges will be 65 years old or older. The 2018 collapse of the Interstate 5 bridge over the Skagit River in Washington state, struck by an oversized truck, serves as a stark reminder of the risks. The bridge, built in 1955, was not structurally deficient but the incident underscores the need for better maintenance and repair. The study also identifies six major bridges, each used by over 1 million vehicles daily, that are in poor condition. For instance, the Interstate 70 bridge over Havana Street in Denver, Colorado, and the I-278 approach to the Verrazano-Narrows Bridge in Staten Island, New York, both have substructures in poor condition. Transportation for America recommends raising dedicated revenues for transportation programs, making 180,000 bridges eligible for new funding, and prioritizing bridge and highway repair. While some experts argue that the overall system is improving, the report emphasizes the urgent need for increased investment to address the aging infrastructure crisis.

One of the four "Zebra Killers," responsible for a racially motivated murder spree in San Francisco during the 1970s, was found dead in his cell at San Quentin State Prison. J.C.X. Simon, 69, was pronounced dead late Thursday night after being unresponsive in his single cell. He was serving a life sentence with the possibility of parole for two counts of first-degree murder, conspiracy to commit murder, and assault with a deadly weapon. The Zebra Killers, a group of four black men, targeted white victims during a six-month period from October 1973 to April 1974, resulting in 14 deaths and seven injuries. Simon's death comes as the other three killers, Larry Green, Manuel Moore, and Jessie Lee Cooks, remain incarcerated in separate California prisons. Green is at California State Prison-Solano in Vacaville, Moore at Ironwood State Prison in Riverside County, and Cooks at Richard J. Donovan Correctional Facility in San Diego. The Zebra Killers were part of a series of racially charged killings in the Bay Area during the late 1960s and 1970s, including those by the Zodiac serial killer, the Symbionese Liberation Army, and Rev. Jim Jones. Simon's death marks the end of a notorious chapter in San Francisco's history, as the men have never been allowed to serve their sentences together.

Kim Kardashian, the queen of reality TV and a branding powerhouse, continues to captivate and command a vast consumer base. Her influence extends beyond the screen, into fashion boutiques, fitness videos, and even fragrances. Despite her rise from a sex tape to a global icon, she remains a favorite among many consumers, ranking alongside Snooki at the top of a celebrity loyalty index. Her brand, built on the reality show "Keeping Up with the Kardashians," offers a unique appeal, with each sister targeting different demographics. Khloé, the newlywed, caters to married women seeking weight loss solutions, while Kourtney, the mommy, taps into the mommy blogger market. Kim, the single sister, embodies the allure of the independent woman, resonating with single women who feel she represents their journey. Her marketing strategy is both inclusive and relatable, leveraging her personal life to create a family unit that appeals to a broad audience. The key to her success lies in her ability to project a range of images, from fashion icon to entrepreneur, and her willingness to engage directly with her fans through social media. However, her continued single status might pose a challenge, as it could dilute her brand's appeal. For now, the Kardashian empire thrives on the dynamic interplay of their individual personas, creating a diverse and compelling brand that resonates with a wide range of consumers.

People who sleep for more than eight hours a day have an increased risk of stroke, according to a study by the University of Cambridge, which suggests that this risk doubles for older people who persistently sleep longer than average. The study, published in the journal Neurology, is the first to provide detailed information about the British population and examines the relationship between a change in sleep duration over time and subsequent stroke risk. Researchers from the Department of Public Health and Primary Care at the University of Cambridge followed nearly 10,000 people aged 42 to 81 years from the European Prospective Investigation into Cancer (EPIC)-Norfolk cohort over 9.5 years. During 1998-2000 and then again four years later, they asked the cohort how many hours on average they slept in a day and whether they generally slept well.

Almost seven out of ten participants reported sleeping between six and eight hours a day, while one in ten reported sleeping for over eight hours a day. Participants who slept for less than six hours or more than eight hours were more likely to be older, women, and less active. Over the almost ten-year period of the study, 346 participants suffered a stroke, either non-fatal or fatal. After adjusting for various factors including age and sex, the researchers found that people who slept longer than eight hours a day were at a 46% greater risk of stroke than average. People who slept less than six hours a day were at an 18% increased risk, but the small number of people falling in this category meant the association was not statistically significant.

Participants who reported persistently long sleep—meaning they reported sleeping over eight hours when asked at both points of the study—were at double the risk of stroke compared to those with persistently average sleep duration (between six and eight hours a day). This risk was even greater for those whose reported sleep increased from short to long over the four years, with their risk being close to four times that of people who maintained an average sleep duration.

The study included 9,692 stroke-free participants aged 42 to 81 years from the EPIC-Norfolk cohort. The researchers also conducted a meta-analysis of combined data from 11 other studies, supporting the findings from the EPIC-Norfolk cohort study. The final analysis, including 560,000 participants from seven countries, showed that long sleep was significantly associated with an increased risk of stroke (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.46 [95% confidence interval (CI) 1.08, 1.98]) after adjustment for all covariates. The association remained robust among those without preexisting diseases and those who reported sleeping well.

The researchers say it is unclear yet why the link between sleep and stroke risk should exist. Lack of sleep has been linked with factors such as disrupted metabolism and raised levels of the 'stress hormone' cortisol, all of which may lead to higher blood pressure and increased stroke risk. However, the current study suggests that the association between longer sleep duration and higher risk of stroke was independent of normal risk factors for cardiovascular disease. The study was supported by the Medical Research Council and Cancer Research UK.

University of Missouri graduate student Jonathan Butler initiated a hunger strike, demanding the resignation of President Tim Wolfe, to address a series of racial incidents and a perceived lack of action from university leadership. Butler, a veteran of Ferguson protests, began his protest on October 26, stating he would not eat until Wolfe stepped down. His decision gained national attention, with the black members of the football team announcing they would boycott practices and games until Butler’s demands were met. This support from the football team, along with a two-day walkout by the student government, further escalated the situation. The Board of Curators, the governing body of the university, called an emergency meeting to address the unrest.

President Wolfe attempted to address the situation, but his statement did not satisfy Butler and the student activists. The resignation of both President Wolfe and Chancellor R. Bowen Loftin was announced on Monday, November 9. In response, Butler ended his hunger strike, stating, "This is only the first step! More change is to come!!" The resignations came after significant pressure from students, faculty, and even state legislators. The university system unveiled a series of initiatives to address racial tensions, including hiring a diversity, inclusion, and equity officer, providing additional support for those experiencing discrimination, and creating a task force to improve diversity and inclusion.

The protests and resignations were part of a broader movement addressing systemic issues on campus, including incidents such as the drawing of a swastika with human feces in a dormitory, the removal of Planned Parenthood services, and the denial of abortion privileges to a doctor. These events, along with the broader context of racial and social justice issues, highlighted the need for change at the university. The resignation of Wolfe and Loftin marked a significant shift, but the struggle for a more inclusive and respectful campus environment continues.

The creator of the critically acclaimed AMC drama "Mad Men," Matthew Weiner, has signed a long-term deal with Lionsgate, ensuring he will continue running the show for two more seasons, with an option for a third, taking "Mad Men" through its seventh season. The deal, worth $30 million, one of the biggest payouts of its kind in cable television, comes after months of negotiations with AMC, the network that airs the show, and Lionsgate, the production company behind it. In a compromise, the first and last episodes of each season will remain 47 minutes long, the same length as previous seasons, while the rest will be 45 minutes, allowing AMC to make more money from commercials. Weiner stated that his new contract stipulates that cast members "will not be cut for financial considerations," only for creative reasons. He also confirmed that AMC had planned for the show to skip its usual summer premiere this year, with the fifth season set to air in early 2012. Despite the negotiations, Weiner expressed gratitude for the support from fans and friends of the show, stating, "It’s been an incredible experience."

Nashville, Tennessee, is on high alert as a manhunt continues for Travis Reinking, the alleged shooter who killed four people and injured four others in a Waffle House restaurant shooting. More than 80 Nashville police officers, along with FBI, ATF, and Tennessee Highway Patrol agents, are searching for Reinking, who was last seen near his apartment complex. He was described as nearly naked, wearing only a green jacket and an assault-style rifle. The suspect's past behavior raised concerns, including a history of mental health issues and a recent move to Nashville. In July, Reinking was arrested for crossing a restricted area near the White House, where he claimed Taylor Swift was stalking him. In May 2016, he reported that people were hacking his phone and barking like dogs outside his residence. Reinking was also involved in a pool incident in Illinois, where he wore a pink woman's coat over his underwear. Authorities believe he is armed with at least one handgun and could be in an unoccupied house. A quick-thinking customer, James Shaw Jr., wrestled the gun away from the suspect, preventing further casualties. Shaw, a Nashville native who works as a wireless technician for AT&T, said he acted because "he was going to have to work to kill me." The victims include Taurean Sanderlin, a Waffle House employee, and DeEbony Groves, a 21-year-old Belmont University student. Akilah Dasilva, a 23-year-old rap artist and music video producer, and Sharita Henderson, 24, were also injured. The community is in shock, with Tia Waggoner, Dasilva's girlfriend, undergoing surgery for her wounds. The search for Reinking continues, with police urging neighbors to check on each other for safety.

Famed oceanographer Robert Ballard, known for his discoveries of the Titanic, Bismarck, USS Yorktown, and John F. Kennedy's PT-109, has added another significant find to his list: the first images in over six decades of the USS Independence, a World War II aircraft carrier scuttled in 1951 off the California coast. The 20-hour expedition, conducted by Ballard's team in collaboration with the Navy and NOAA, revealed stunning images of the carrier's flight deck, a Hellcat fighter plane, anti-aircraft guns, hatches, ladders, and even the letters of the ship's name still visible on the hull. Thousands of viewers from over 30 countries watched the discoveries live online. The Independence, a 623-foot-long light aircraft carrier, saw combat at Wake Island, Okinawa, and Leyte Gulf from 1943 to 1945 and was present at the U.S. atomic tests at Bikini Atoll in 1946. After the tests, the Navy towed the vessel to Hunter's Point Naval Shipyard in San Francisco, then towed it out to sea, placed two torpedoes in the ship, and detonated them, sinking the Independence on January 26, 1951. The ship was almost lost until 1990 when the U.S. Geological Survey found it while mapping the seafloor. Sonar scans taken by NOAA in recent years provided more detail, but until now, there were no photos or video of the Independence in its final resting place. The expedition found no trace of the unknown number of 50-gallon barrels containing low-level nuclear waste that the ship carried, which were filled with concrete and sealed in a former engine room space. Kai Vetter, a professor of nuclear engineering at UC Berkeley, stated that the ship and its contents pose virtually no risk to ocean wildlife or the public, as the half-life of the radioactive material that the steel of the ship was exposed to is seven years, meaning it degrades by half in that time period, and 70 years have passed, leaving far less than 1 percent of the original radioactivity. A scientist from Vetter's lab was on board the expedition, and the two submersibles took samples of sediments and small creatures from the ship, such as sponges, for testing. Ocean Exploration Trust plans to build a detailed 3-D digital image of the Independence from the thousands of photographs taken during the expedition.

The tragic shooting at Kerch Polytechnic College in Crimea has left the Russian city of Kerch grappling with the aftermath, as authorities search for answers. The death toll now stands at 20, with 10 critically injured being airlifted to top Russian hospitals for surgery. The 18-year-old gunman, Vladislav Roslyakov, was reportedly acting alone but Crimean authorities hinted at possible assistance from an accomplice. Roslyakov’s computer, found at his home, had been deleted, raising questions about his background. Teachers and classmates described him as shy, with few friends, and his grandmother, Taisiya Roslyakova, portrayed him as a kind boy who helped with chores. The attack, described as the deadliest school shooting in Russia since the 2004 Beslan siege, has sparked concerns about school security. Russian authorities have deployed officers and riot police to all schools and colleges in Kerch. President Vladimir Putin blamed globalization for the attack, suggesting that young people are creating false heroes through violence. The incident has reignited debates about gun control in Russia, where civilians can own hunting rifles and shotguns after undergoing significant background checks. Roslyakov had recently obtained a permit to own a shotgun and had purchased 150 cartridges. In the wake of the tragedy, Crimean residents brought flowers and toys to a makeshift memorial outside the school, while mourners lit candles in memory of the victims at a memorial stone near the Kremlin. The Kerch attack has also prompted Russian media to draw parallels with the Columbine High School shooting, highlighting the shock and disbelief in a country where such incidents were previously unheard of. The Russian government has not yet announced any plans to further restrict gun ownership, stating that they will wait for the results of the Kerch investigation. The annexation of Crimea from Ukraine in 2014 has seen Russian authorities repeatedly warn of a terrorism threat from unnamed Ukrainian nationalists and ethnic Tatars, despite the lack of violent activities from these groups in Crimea. The brutal nature of the attack, with victims’ legs and feet blown off, has left medical workers in shock, describing the injuries as "minced" with small metal objects. The incident has prompted calls for stricter security measures in schools and raised questions about the mental health support available to students.

The small town of Hurricane, Utah, has seen a significant change in its landscape after the owner of Barista's restaurant, Stephen Ward, decided to remove the prominent genitalia from a copper bull statue that had sparked controversy. The statue, which had been a point of contention for local residents, now stands without its most noticeable feature, as Ward felt it was not aesthetically pleasing. Ward, who had purchased the $130,000 bull sculpture in Las Vegas, stated that he made the decision independently of community pressure, declaring, "I told them I am not removing the penis for you or because of your complaints. I don't like you. I'm doing it for me." The removal of the genitalia was seen as a compromise, as Ward acknowledged that the original design had caused some issues, saying, "It didn't even look (right), it was in the shape of a cone — but I don't know what a weenie on a bull is supposed to look like."

The controversy surrounding the bull statue had been ongoing for weeks, with residents voicing their displeasure and even petitioning the city council to revoke Barista's business license. City Manager Clark Fawcett noted that the sign had been approved by the planning department, but he acknowledged that the dimensions of certain parts of the animal did not match the plan. Ward's decision to remove the genitalia was seen as a response to these complaints, but he maintained that it was a personal choice, not a capitulation to community pressure.

Despite the controversy, Ward stated that the removal of the genitalia had not significantly impacted his business. In fact, he noted that the attention the statue had garnered had brought in more customers, saying, "I put it up because it's an amazing piece, and I bought it as-is, but I am having fun with all the attention and it's brought in more customers." The dispute between Ward and the local community had been ongoing for years, with Ward alleging that the city had been hostile and had disrupted his business. He planned to sue the city and the man who had initiated a petition against his business, adding, "I mean, they lied. It was bolted to the parking lot for three weeks. Every person in this city saw it. It was bolted right there for three weeks to the black top."

The removal of the bull's genitalia was seen as a resolution to the controversy, but it did not fully address the underlying tensions between Ward and the local community. The incident had brought significant attention to the small town, with the story gaining widespread coverage and sparking discussions about public art and community relations. The controversy had also highlighted the complex dynamics between business owners and local residents, as well as the potential for public art to become a source of conflict.

Dennis Rodman led a team of former NBA stars in a basketball game in Pyongyang, singing "Happy Birthday" to North Korean leader Kim Jong Un. Rodman, known for his "basketball diplomacy," dedicated the game to his "best friend" Kim, who watched along with his wife and other officials. The game, played at the Pyongyang Indoor Stadium in front of 14,000 spectators, aimed to foster cultural connections despite criticism from U.S. officials and human rights groups. Rodman's team included ex-All Stars Kenny Anderson, Cliff Robinson, and Vin Baker, but his recent comments about Kenneth Bae, an American missionary imprisoned in North Korea, drew significant backlash. Bae's sister criticized Rodman for "playing games with my brother's life" and urged him to advocate for her brother's release. Rodman's trips to North Korea continue to spark controversy, with some viewing his visits as ill-advised and naive.

The Trump administration is refusing to link the release of American pastor Andrew Brunson, who has been detained in Turkey for nearly two years, with any concessions to Turkey, including relief for a major Turkish bank facing U.S. fines. The pastor's case has strained relations between the two NATO allies, with the U.S. intensifying pressure on Turkey to free Brunson, who denies any wrongdoing. The White House has tweeted that Brunson is being held "hostage" in Turkey, and U.S. officials have imposed financial sanctions and tariffs on Turkey, exacerbating the Turkish economic crisis. Turkish officials, however, are standing firm, rejecting threats and insisting they won't release Brunson. The conflict has also delayed negotiations over a separate issue involving a Turkish state bank, Halkbank, which is accused of helping Iran evade U.S. sanctions. U.S. officials have subpoenaed the bank and are pursuing an investigation that could turn into a criminal case. Despite the economic and diplomatic pressure, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan has shown no signs of releasing Brunson, maintaining that the pastor is guilty and facing up to 35 years in prison. The U.S. administration is using the case to demonstrate the effectiveness of its "strong-arm tactics" in foreign policy, while also appealing to the religious right, which has rallied in support of Brunson. The pastor's fate remains uncertain, with the feud between the two countries continuing to escalate.

Johnny Manziel's ex-girlfriend, Colleen Crowley, has provided details of an alleged assault by the former Cleveland Browns quarterback, according to a Fort Worth police report. The incident occurred early Saturday in the Dallas area, where Crowley and Manziel had spent the evening with friends at the Zaza Hotel. After the friends dispersed, Manziel and Crowley were left alone, and Crowley claims that Manziel became aggressive, striking her left ear. Manziel allegedly drove Crowley to her apartment in Fort Worth, where he continued to be verbally and physically abusive, threatening to kill them both. Crowley managed to escape and seek help from a neighbor, while Manziel fled the scene. Despite the severity of the allegations, the Dallas Police Department stated that no charges would be filed, citing the complexity of the case and Crowley's reluctance to make a formal report. The NFL acknowledged the incident but did not disclose any disciplinary actions. This latest incident adds to a long list of controversies surrounding Manziel, who was not disciplined by the NFL for a similar altercation with Crowley in Ohio in October. The Cleveland Browns, who have already stated their intention to part ways with Manziel, are limited in their ability to address the issue due to league rules. Manziel's father, Paul Manziel, expressed his ongoing concern for his son's well-being, stating, "We're trying to get our son better," but acknowledged that they are not there yet. The incident has drawn renewed scrutiny on the NFL's handling of domestic violence cases, with some critics calling for stricter measures.

Chelsea Clinton, reflecting on the 2016 election, emphasized the stark contrast between her mother Hillary Clinton and Donald Trump. "That actually I found far more upsetting … than anything they said about my mom," Chelsea said in an interview with NBC’s “Today.” She highlighted that attacks on Hillary Clinton, while difficult, were less troubling compared to Trump's insults directed at women, minorities, Muslims, and immigrants. Chelsea noted that her mother, Hillary, has years of experience in politics and can handle such criticism. "She’s tough and she can take whatever people say about her," Chelsea said.

As the Democratic National Convention approached, Chelsea expressed her excitement and emotional connection to the event, particularly as a mother. "This election is so important to me, because I'm now a mom. And as proud as I am of my mom, this election to me is fundamentally about my children, about Charlotte and Aidan," she told Matt Lauer on TODAY. She anticipated her introduction of her mother at the convention would be overwhelming, as she hoped to convey the depth of her admiration and the importance of the moment to her children.

Chelsea also addressed the challenge her mother faced in overcoming negative perceptions, especially from some in her own party. She acknowledged the need to bridge the gap between the public image of Hillary Clinton and the person she knew. "That's not the person that I know," Chelsea said. "That's not the person that I grew up with, that I'm so proud to stand beside and to introduce here in Philadelphia."

The summary of the article highlights Chelsea's support for her mother and her desire to present a positive image of Hillary Clinton to the nation. She also touched on the parallel between the conventions, noting that both she and Ivanka Trump would introduce their parents. Chelsea's comments underscored the importance of the Democratic National Convention for her and her family, as well as the broader significance of the election for her children.

AmeriCares continues to support Ebola treatment and health worker protection in Liberia, focusing on rebuilding the health system to prevent future epidemics. Since the outbreak began in early 2014, Ebola has killed over 11,100 people and infected more than 26,900, with 869 health workers infected and 507 killed. AmeriCares provided protective supplies, staffed Ebola treatment units, and offered long-term health services in Liberia, Sierra Leone, and Guinea. Current efforts include infection prevention training, medical equipment, and support for maternal and child health in Grand Bassa County. AmeriCares also partners with organizations like WFP to deliver food assistance and address the economic impact of the epidemic on local communities.

Germany's Foreign Minister Frank-Walter Steinmeier expressed frustration at the failure to secure agreement on a joint European Union action and quota system to distribute migrants from the Middle East, as up to 40,000 people might arrive this weekend, double the number welcomed last weekend. Germany now expects 800,000 migrants this year, with defense minister Ursula von der Leyen announcing 4,000 troops on standby. The German government is pushing for a fair quota distribution among EU nations, but Hungary and other Central European countries are resisting, citing national sovereignty. Prime Minister Viktor Orban of Hungary warned of stricter measures, including arrests for illegal border crossings. The Czech Republic, Slovakia, and Poland also opposed mandatory quotas, with Czech Foreign Minister Lubomir Zaoralek stating that every country has the right to decide its immigration policy. The European Commission's Jean-Claude Juncker proposed a plan for 160,000 refugees, but it faces strong opposition, especially from Eastern European countries. The United Nations supported the plan but called for all member states to participate. Meanwhile, Austria stopped rail service with Hungary, leading migrants to march toward Vienna. Macedonia faced increasing numbers of migrants, with a proposal to build a fence met with criticism. The incident involving Petra Laszlo, a Hungarian journalist, who filmed herself kicking and tripping migrants, highlights the ethical dilemmas faced by those caught in the crisis.

On May 6, 2015, Mindy Kaling appeared to send a cryptic message to her followers regarding the cancellation of her show, The Mindy Project, on Fox. Posting a video from her vacation in Montana, Kaling wrote, "Hey guys, I'm in Montana, is anything happening in LA? #themindyproject," which left fans speculating about the show's future. Shortly after Fox's announcement, Variety reported that Hulu was in talks with Universal TV to potentially save the show for multiple seasons. Kaling's smile and wink in the video seemed to hint at something positive, but the true meaning remains unclear. Fans hoped that Kaling's message was a sign that the show's cancellation might not be permanent.

The discovery of a new species of horse-sized dinosaur, named Timurlengia euotica, is providing scientists with insights into how Tyrannosaurus Rex (T. Rex) became one of Earth's top predators. Unearthed in northern Uzbekistan, Timurlengia fills a 20-million-year gap in the fossil record of tyrannosaurs, which are known to have rapidly developed huge body sizes towards the end of the age of dinosaurs. The remains suggest that tyrannosaurs evolved keen senses, including a big brain and keen hearing, long before they grew to enormous sizes. These features, which were already present in Timurlengia, likely enabled them to climb to the top of the prehistoric food chain. The iconic T. Rex, which emerged as a huge and cunning predator 80 million years ago, is believed to have evolved "head first," with its big brain preceding its colossal stature. The first tyrannosaurs lived about 170 million years ago, but remained in the shadows of larger beasts like allosaurs and spinosaurs. They emerged as giants during a 20-million-year gap in the fossil record, when the dinosaur age was coming to an end. CT scans of Timurlengia's braincase revealed that it was large for a dinosaur and had structures in the inner ear used for balancing and for hearing low-frequency sounds. These traits could have helped T. Rex in its niche as an apex predator. However, with a body mass of around 200 kilograms, Timurlengia was much smaller than T. Rex, which could weigh over 5 tonnes. The fossils support earlier proposals that T. Rex evolved "head first" – brain before bulk. The number of tyrannosaur species known has more than doubled in the past 15 years, and the discovery of Timurlengia is part of a broader effort to understand the evolution of this group of dinosaurs.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) and Tesla Motors CEO Elon Musk are both closely examining the Model S electric car following reports of battery fires after striking road debris. NHTSA opened a formal investigation into the safety of the Model S following two incidents in Washington state and Tennessee, where fires resulted from the cars hitting debris that pierced the battery compartment. A third fire in Mexico was not included in the investigation due to its jurisdictional limitations. Tesla shares initially dipped but recovered, closing 3.7% higher at $126.09.

In response to the fires, Musk announced three steps: raising the car's ground clearance to reduce the risk of hitting road debris, requesting a full investigation from NHTSA, and extending the warranty to cover damage due to fire. Musk emphasized the safety of the Model S, stating that since its introduction, there have been zero deaths or injuries due to battery fires, compared to over 400 deaths and 1,200 serious injuries from gasoline car fires in the U.S. alone. He argued that the media coverage of the Tesla fires was disproportionate and misleading, suggesting that electric cars are safer than gasoline cars.

Musk also implemented a software update to increase the Model S's ground clearance at highway speeds, aiming to reduce the likelihood of underbody impact damage. Another update in January will allow drivers to control the air suspension ride height transitions. Musk defended Tesla's vehicles, asserting that they have a lower fire risk than gasoline vehicles. He highlighted the Model S's internal firewalls and the lower combustion energy of battery packs, which limit the potential fire damage.

Despite the fires, Musk emphasized the safety record of the Model S, noting that there have been no deaths or serious injuries in any Model S accidents. He expressed confidence in the car's safety and stated that the incidents are a minor cost if the belief in the car's safety is correct. Musk's actions, including the warranty change and software updates, were intended to reassure buyers and address any misperceptions about the safety of electric cars.

In the aftermath of a failed military coup in Turkey, President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has vehemently blamed the Gülen Movement, a moderate Sunni Islamic movement with significant influence in Turkey and abroad, for orchestrating the attempted overthrow. Erdoğan, who has long accused the Gülenists of attempting to undermine his government, has demanded that the United States arrest the movement’s leader, Fethullah Gülen, who lives in Pennsylvania. Despite Gülen’s public condemnation of the coup, Erdoğan’s government has intensified its crackdown on Gülen’s supporters, including thousands of judges and prosecutors. The coup attempt, which left at least 265 people dead, including 161 civilians and police officers, and saw nearly 3,000 military personnel detained, has sparked a wave of protests and a broader political and social crisis in Turkey. Erdoğan has vowed to purge the military and other institutions of Gülenists, a move that could further polarize the country and strain its relationships with Western allies, particularly the United States. Meanwhile, the Gülen Movement, which maintains a significant presence in Turkey and the United States, has dismissed any involvement, insisting it is committed to democracy and education. The attempted coup has also raised questions about the state of Turkey’s democracy and the balance of power between the military and civilian leadership. As Turkey grapples with this internal conflict, the international community, including NATO allies and the United States, has expressed support for the country’s democratic institutions while urging restraint and a legal process in handling the crisis.

Alaska's Bureau of Land Management posted a video on its Facebook page showing a mysterious, undulating icy shape moving through the Chena River, sparking a flurry of online speculation and intrigue. The 22-second clip, filmed by an employee in Fairbanks, Alaska, showed a strange object, approximately 12-15 feet long, moving in the river's current. The Bureau of Land Management did not investigate the object, leaving the public to speculate about its nature. Viewers proposed a wide range of theories, from a giant sturgeon or lost shark to a Nessie-like sea monster, a "beavegator," and even a "zombie salmon" of unusual size. The Alaska Department of Fish and Game provided the most plausible explanation, suggesting the video shows "frazil ice stuck to a rope that is probably caught on a bridge pier." This explanation, while not as exciting as the more fantastical theories, was supported by an Alaska Fish and Game Tanana River Management Biologist, Klaus Wuttig, who explained that cold nighttime temperatures caused the ice to form on the rope, creating the illusion of movement. The Bureau of Land Management enjoyed the public's engagement and interest in the mystery, noting that the number and variety of explanations demonstrated the captivation of the natural world's mysteries.
