The vehicle stands 1.6 feet higher than the standard G-Class, offering a rugged ride. Limited to 99 units, the Maybach G650 is part of Mercedes-Benz's strategy to target ultra-wealthy customers with high-margin models, while also developing more affordable vehicles in large volumes. This move is seen as a response to the need for high research and development budgets, as Mercedes aims to compete with electric cars, autonomous driving features, and ride-sharing platforms. The Maybach G650's introduction comes after the success of the Maybach sub-brand, which has seen increased demand for luxury models. The new SUV is expected to further boost Mercedes-Benz's market position, especially in the luxury segment.

Longtime Donald Trump associate Roger Stone appeared on Infowars on Monday to refute claims of inappropriate contact with Russian intelligence during the 2016 election, donning a costume that drew attention. Stone's appearance, wearing a hot air balloon pilot outfit, came as he maintained his innocence in a series of public statements. Stone has repeatedly denied any collusion with Russian officials and has been under investigation by the FBI. He stated that he has not spoken to the bureau and is following the Senate Intelligence Committee's request to preserve documents. Stone expressed that he has been under surveillance for some time, though he does not know the probable cause or evidence behind it. He also doubled down on his assertion that former President Barack Obama had wiretapped Trump Tower, despite FBI Director James Comey's denial of such claims. Stone has long assumed he is under investigation and believes the intelligence community has become politicized. In a CBS This Morning interview, Stone defended his communications with hacker Guccifer 2.0, suggesting them to be "entirely benign." He also defended former Trump campaign chairman Paul Manafort and former national security adviser Michael Flynn, but declined to defend Carter Page, whom he had never heard of. Stone's statements about WikiLeaks and Assange have fueled suspicions of his involvement in the release of hacked emails, though WikiLeaks has denied any communication with him. Stone's public statements and appearance have continued to be scrutinized as the FBI and congressional committees investigate potential Russian interference in the 2016 election.

Ryan Reynolds has been named People's Sexiest Man Alive for 2010, just as the trailer for his role as Green Lantern hits the web. The trailer reveals more of the plot, including Reynolds' character Hal Jordan learning new powers and overcoming his fears to protect the Green Lantern Corp. from the new enemy, Parallax. It also showcases Blake Lively as Carol Ferris, a fellow test pilot and love interest, and Peter Sarsgaard as the villainous Hector Hammond. Reynolds, known for his chiseled abs and sense of humor, says the title will give his family plenty of material for teasing. His wife, Scarlett Johansson, was recently named GQ's "Babe of the Year," leading to a discussion about whether Reynolds truly deserves the honor. Despite his good looks, some argue that other stars, like Jon Hamm, exude more charisma.

CBS News chief foreign correspondent Lara Logan was brutally assaulted and sexually attacked in Tahrir Square, Cairo, on the day Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak stepped down. Logan, separated from her crew, was surrounded by a mob of over 200 people whipped into a frenzy. She was saved by a group of women and an estimated 20 Egyptian soldiers. Logan reconnected with her CBS team, returned to her hotel, and was flown back to the U.S. She is currently recovering in a U.S. hospital. The attack was one of at least 140 suffered by journalists covering the unrest in Egypt since January 30, according to the Committee to Protect Journalists. Logan, who has reported widely from Iraq and Afghanistan, joined CBS News in 2002 and has been a correspondent for "60 Minutes" since 2006. The incident highlights the dangers faced by journalists in conflict zones and the ongoing risks in Egypt, where sexual harassment of women is common. Logan's family respectfully requests privacy during this time.

When it comes to air travel in the U.S., there are two realities. Most of us—930 million passengers who flew out of a U.S. airport last year—think flying has never been worse. Seats keep getting smaller and closer together; seat cushions are getting thinner. Everything costs extra: bags, food, and even things we took to be basics, like seat assignments and carry-ons. Flights are something you endure with your knees pressed against the seat in front of you, feet jammed next to your backpack or purse, hoping you don’t get dragged off the plane against your will. “None of us fly by choice,” one disgruntled United passenger recently wrote in a pretty representative tweet. “Flying sucks, period.”

But there’s another group of people who see it differently: industry experts. These people say flying has never been better. It’s the cheapest it’s ever been, affordable for the majority of Americans. It’s safer. Your bags are less likely to get lost. On-time arrivals are hovering around 80 percent in recent years, the best it’s ever been. You’re likely to have honest-to-god internet on a damn plane.

So this is a conundrum. How can flying be both the best and the worst it’s ever been?

We have to get one thing out of the way. The experts are right. Flying is, objectively speaking, the best it’s ever been.

Saying that flying is the best it’s ever been, of course, requires knowing what it used to be. In the 1960s, if you or your company could afford to fly you somewhere, you’d first have to go to a travel agent or airline ticket desk. You’d buy your flight and try your best not to lose your ticket. On the day of the flight, ticket in hand, you’d get to the airport 20 minutes in advance, go through a metal detector, settle into one of your seats on an almost-never-full plane and get served a TV dinner-esque meal while sitting in seats more or less akin to today’s Amtrak arrangement. You could smoke in the last 10 or so rows, but since you’re in a giant metal tube, the entire plane reeked of cigarette smoke.

At some point, we were socialized to hate flying.

Until 1978, the federal government regulated which airlines could fly which routes and how much they could charge. Since airlines couldn’t compete on price, so they had to differentiate themselves in other ways: legroom, meals, service, blankets, and so on. Which is to say, airlines competed by making flying as comfortable as possible.

Prices were fixed not to keep flying affordable, but to keep airlines profitable. In 1974, it was literally illegal for an airline to charge less than $305, which would be $1,607 in 2017 dollars after adjusting for inflation, for a cross-country flight between New York and Los Angeles. Obviously, this meant far fewer Americans could afford it. In 1965, only 20 percent of Americans had ever flown on an airplane, and the portion that could afford it was overwhelmingly likely to be white.

As part of a surge of deregulation across the federal government, airlines were suddenly free to start competing in another way: by offering lower prices. At this point, basic supply and demand principles kicked in. Fares could be cheaper if they put more people on each plane. Meals are expensive to offer 30,000 feet in the air (one of my favorite airline cost-cutting stories: Northwest reportedly saved $500,000 a year by slicing its limes 16 ways as opposed to Delta’s 10). And, in the past 15 years in particular, major airlines merged to fend off bankruptcy and unbundled their products—remember when you could book a seat in the exit row which has more leg room for free?—and charged fees for everything.

But, even with the fees, flying is still cheaper and more accessible to the general public than it has ever been. That New York to Los Angeles flight that cost $1,607? The average fare, including first class and premium economy tickets, is now around $700. But you can almost certainly find a flight in economy for less than $500, maybe even under $300 if you catch a sale. And it’s not only that one route. Overall, domestic airfares have fallen by approximately 50 percent after adjusting for inflation since deregulation in 1978. If you do want extra leg room, a meal, a checked bag, or a wider seat? That’s still there, in the form of premium economy or even first class. Looking at a random one week period in February, you can fly round-trip from New York to LA for $277, or upgrade to premium economy for $543. You could even splurge and fly JetBlue’s fantastic Mint first class for $1,117, or $500 cheaper than the legally mandated price in 1978. Which is to say: even if you purchased every perk or add-on for your New York to L.A. flight, it’s still cheaper—and better—than it was before.

With the masses being able to afford to fly, anxiety about flying was more common than straight complaining. Crashes, bad turbulence, and even hijacking used to be a common fear, which was buttressed by humor. The flying experience became a frequent target for stand-up comedians and other humorists to defuse the tension. The Friar’s Club Encyclopedia of Jokes has a section on flying one-liners featuring Bob Hope, Shelley Berman, Garry Shandling, and Howie Mandel. “I’m giving up flying,” a joke by Corbett Monica went. “I was at the airport and I saw a sign: ‘Take Out Insurance.’ I thought, if the lobby’s that dangerous, imagine what it’s like in the plane.” Many of the jokes obviously predate 9/11—”Ever been frisked on a plane trip? They frisk you and then, on the plane, everybody has a steak knife!” joked Shelley Berman—and tend to deal more with safety concerns instead of lack of comfort or inconvenience.

After safety concerns became less prominent, comedians transitioned to joking about airline quality. In 1992, Saturday Night Live performed a skit with Jerry Seinfeld, Rob Schneider, Dana Carvey, and Adam Sandler called Stand-Up And Win, a mock Jeopardy! designed to poke fun at Seinfeldian prompts. The first question: “What’s the deal with airplane food?” (The “correct” answer from Schneider: “I know, could this stuff taste any worse? It’s like thanks but no thanks, I’m still stuffed from that huge bag of smoked almonds.”) “Airplanes” was also the first category on the board along with “cereals,” “commercials,” and “7-11 employees.”

It’s also not just airline companies and their policies that make us complain, but the process of flying itself. George

Rapper Malik Taylor, known as Phife Dawg, a key member of the critically acclaimed group A Tribe Called Quest, passed away at the age of 45 after complications from diabetes, according to reports. Many prominent figures in the hip-hop community took to social media to express their condolences and pay tribute to the influential artist. Jill Scott, the singer, tweeted, "So incredibly sad to hear the Great Phife Dawg of Tribe Called Quest has passed away at only 45 yrs. GREAT MC. Sincere Love and Respect." Chuck D, the rapper and founder of Public Enemy, honored Phife Dawg with the statement, "Phife-HipHop & Rap word Warrior, simple as that.Breathed it & lined rhyme into Sport. A true fire Social Narrator my bro #RIBeats ATCQforever."

To celebrate the legacy of Phife Dawg, a traffic reporter at WSB-TV Atlanta, Mark Arum, paid tribute by weaving Phife's lyrics into his traffic updates. Arum's references included: "More hits than the Braves or the Yankees," "Are things ludicrously speedy or infectious with the slow-mo?" "Track record's longer than a DC-20 aircraft," "Do that, do that, do do that that that," "Tell your mother, tell your father, send a telegram," and "One for the treble, two for the bass, you know the style." These clever inclusions not only honored Phife Dawg's contributions but also brought a touch of his unique style to the daily commute.

Additionally, the documentary "Beats, Rhymes & Life" offers a deeper look into the life and impact of Phife Dawg and A Tribe Called Quest. The group's fusion of hip-hop and jazz, as documented in the film, has influenced countless artists and remains a benchmark in the genre. Phife Dawg's role as the high-pitched, gruff vocal counterpoint to Q-Tip's smooth, mellow flow was crucial in the group's success, with their landmark album "The Low End Theory" and its follow-up "Midnight Marauders" being widely celebrated. The group's final album, "The Love Movement," released in 1998, brought their unique sound to a broader audience.

The loss of Phife Dawg is mourned by fans and fellow artists alike, with his contributions to the hip-hop community and his impact on the genre's evolution being widely recognized. His passing serves as a reminder of the importance of his work and the lasting legacy he leaves behind.

With heightened tensions and calls for military action, the Obama administration is weighing its response to a suspected chemical weapons attack in Syria, which reportedly killed over 300 people. U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry described the use of chemical weapons as a "moral obscenity" and stated that there is "very little doubt" the Syrian regime was responsible. The U.S. is consulting with allies and preparing for potential military action, including the deployment of warships armed with cruise missiles to the eastern Mediterranean. Meanwhile, the Syrian government has denied any involvement and accused rebel forces of staging the attack, while Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov warned against any military intervention, calling it a "grave violation of international law." The United Nations chemical weapons inspectors, who faced sniper fire on their convoy, are set to continue their investigation, but the Obama administration is concerned that evidence may have been destroyed due to ongoing shelling. British Prime Minister David Cameron cut short his holiday to return to London and chair a National Security Council meeting, while the U.S. is also considering recalling Parliament to debate the issue. The situation remains fraught with uncertainty, as the international community grapples with the potential consequences of military intervention in Syria.

German authorities are considering deploying software akin to a smartphone app, dubbed "Nazi Shazam," to identify neo-Nazi music swiftly, according to SPIEGEL. The interior ministers of Germany's 16 regional states will convene to discuss this innovative tool, which can recognize neo-Nazi rock in seconds, similar to how Shazam identifies music. This software, developed by the regional police office in Saxony, has the advantage of sparing resources and enabling rapid investigations. It could help police react immediately if such music is played on Internet radio or at gatherings. Currently, 1,090 pieces of music with far-right or racist content are indexed by the Federal Review Board for Media Harmful to Minors, restricting their sale and making them inaccessible to those under 18. Legal concerns, however, need to be addressed before the software can be deployed, particularly regarding whether the automatic identification of music constitutes acoustic surveillance. Advocates, like Simone Rafael of the Network Against Nazis, support the initiative, noting that music can easily recruit teenagers into neo-Nazi circles. Despite these efforts, some far-right groups have adapted by using newer folk songs or broader anti-establishment messages.

After the international manhunt, Ethan Couch, the "affluenza" teen, and his mother, Tonya, were apprehended in Puerto Vallarta, Mexico, in late December. The pair had fled to avoid facing the consequences of Ethan's 2013 drunk-driving accident that killed four people. Ethan's mother, Tonya, was arrested for hindering the apprehension of a criminal, a felony that could result in up to 10 years in prison. The mother and son were initially held in a low-rent building in Puerto Vallarta, where they had stayed after leaving a pet-friendly resort. The dog, a half-shepherd half-wolf mix named Virgil, was reported missing after the Couches were detained. Tonya Couch's attorney, Stephanie Patten, expressed concerns about her client's treatment in Tarrant County, Texas, and her primary worries were for her son's well-being and the whereabouts of their pet. Ethan Couch remains in a Mexican detention center, fighting legal delays to avoid deportation. His return to Texas is expected, with Tarrant County Sheriff Dee Anderson stating that deputies are prepared to retrieve Tonya Couch from Los Angeles. Ethan Couch faces a maximum of 120 days in jail if his case is transferred to adult court, but his mother's charges and the legal wrangling over Virgil's fate add complexity to the case. The saga continues, with legal battles and public outcry surrounding the "affluenza" teen and his mother's actions.

The parents of Otto Warmbier, a 22-year-old University of Virginia student who died after being detained in North Korea, shared harrowing details of their son's condition upon his return and called for North Korea to be listed as a state sponsor of terror. In their first television interview since Otto's death, Fred and Cindy Warmbier described the scene at the airport when they first saw their son. They heard "inhuman" howling from the plane, and upon entering, they found Otto on a stretcher, jerking violently, with a feeding tube in his nose, blind, and deaf. Cindy Warmbier said, "It looked like someone had taken a pair of pliers and rearranged his bottom teeth." Fred Warmbier accused North Korea of torturing their son, stating, "North Korea is not a victim. They're terrorists. They kidnapped Otto. They tortured him. They intentionally injured him." North Korea denied any torture and claimed Otto fell into a coma after contracting botulism and taking a sleeping pill. However, the Warmbiers and President Trump rejected these claims, with Trump tweeting, "Otto was tortured beyond belief by North Korea." Cindy Warmbier added, "We see North Korea claiming to be a victim and the world is picking on them, and we’re here to tell you: North Korea is not a victim. They’re terrorists. They kidnapped Otto. They tortured him." Doctors found Otto had suffered extensive brain damage, consistent with cardiopulmonary arrest, and was in a state of unresponsive wakefulness. He died six days after his return. The Warmbiers, devastated by the experience, called for North Korea to be listed as a state sponsor of terror, believing it should be held accountable for their son's treatment. North Korea's Foreign Ministry spokesman stated, "The fact that Warmbier died suddenly in less than a week after his return to the U.S. in his normal state of health indicators is a mystery to us as well." The State Department "strongly warns" U.S. citizens not to travel to North Korea due to the risk of arrest and long-term detention. The Trump administration is considering re-listing North Korea as a state sponsor of terrorism, a designation it lost in 2008.

Harvard University administrators revoked admissions offers to at least ten prospective members of the Class of 2021 after discovering a private Facebook group chat where students shared sexually explicit and offensive memes. The group, initially titled "Harvard memes for horny bourgeois teens," expanded to include more provocative content, with some members posting images mocking sexual assault, the Holocaust, and the deaths of children. Admissions officials found out about the chat in mid-April and informed at least ten participants that their offers had been withdrawn. The Admissions Office stated that Harvard reserves the right to rescind offers if students engage in behavior that questions their honesty, maturity, or moral character. Some students defended the decision, viewing it as a necessary action to maintain the university's standards, while others criticized it as an overreach. This incident highlights the increasing role of social media in college admissions processes, with 35 percent of admissions officers reportedly checking social media sites for information on applicants. The controversy also underscores the ongoing debates about free speech and the boundaries of acceptable behavior on college campuses.

Comedy Central's 'Roast of David Hasselhoff' turned into a night of relentless humor, with Seth MacFarlane as Roast Master leading the charge. Hasselhoff's infamous down-on-the-floor drunk, cheeseburger-chewing video from 2007 was the main focus, with Seth MacFarlane opening by saying, "He's multi-lingual, he can speak English, Spanish, German and... whatever the f--k that language was in the cheeseburger video." Comedian Jeffrey Ross added, "What a lucky break—an alcoholic that gets cast in a show about a car that drives itself!" and jokingly said, "I heard the Hoff once got so drunk he f--ked K.I.T.T. in the gashole." Hasselhoff entered the roast surrounded by dancing German beer girls while performing "Hooked On a Feeling." The night's roasters included Hulk Hogan, George Hamilton, Jerry Springer, and foulmouthed comedians Lisa Lampanelli, Gilbert Gottfried, Greg Giraldo, and Whitney Cummings. Hasselhoff gamely laughed at most of the jokes, but showed a little discomfort during a commercial break when asked about the drink in his red glass. He insisted it was water, much to the mockery of the comedians. Former Baywatch co-star Pamela Anderson also got in on the act, saying, "David, I have to say, when I saw the video of you lying on the floor -- drunk, broken down, cheeseburger meat falling from your mouth -- I felt so sad, for that cow." Despite the relentless jokes, Hasselhoff exited the show triumphantly, insisting the event was "therapeutic" and that no one had gotten him. He kept a fixed smile on his face throughout and said, "No one got me, I'm still laughing, my face hurts, I'm sorry it's over." The roast aired on August 15, with Hasselhoff addressing his greatest viral embarrassment and his longtime struggle with alcohol for the first time.

Malaysia Airlines, reeling from the loss of two jets in separate disasters in 2014, is undergoing a major restructuring that will see the carrier slash around 6,000 jobs as it struggles to stay in business. The airline's new CEO, Christoph Mueller, announced the plan, which includes a rebranding and a focus on regional traffic rather than long-haul routes. Malaysia Airlines, which is technically bankrupt, has already been poorly managed for years, slipping further into the red due to strong regional competition. The airline's performance decline began long before the tragic events of 2014, with the loss of Flight MH370 in March and the destruction of Flight MH17 by a suspected ground-to-air missile in Ukraine four months later. These incidents forced the national carrier's nationalisation and delisting from the stock market. The airline aims to "stop the bleeding" in 2015, stabilise in 2016, and start growing again by 2017. Analysts have long blamed the airline's failure to compete on poor management, unwise business decisions, government meddling, and unfavourable service and supplier contracts stemming from Malaysia's crony capitalism. The restructuring plan calls for renegotiating or resetting major contracts, and a major revitalisation of technology, training, and business operations. The airline plans to reduce its workforce to 14,000 and expects that not all of the job offers it has made to existing staff will be accepted. The rebranding, set for September, may involve a change in name, logo, or other alterations. Malaysia Airlines will continue its profitable twice-daily service from London Heathrow to Kuala Lumpur, while considering joint ventures and potential route reductions. The challenges facing the company come amid low jet fuel prices, which are expected to make this year one of the most profitable for the industry since the start of the century.

Disney's "Christopher Robin" attempts to blend the innocence of the Hundred Acre Wood with the complexities of adult life, but the result is a mixed bag of charm and confusion. The film follows Ewan McGregor as Christopher Robin, who, after surviving World War II, has grown into a harried middle manager at a luggage company. His wife, Evelyn (Hayley Atwell), and their daughter, Madeline (Bronte Carmichael), are eagerly anticipating a weekend at Christopher's childhood cottage, but he is too busy to spend time with his family. Just as they are leaving, Pooh (Jim Cummings) and his friends are mysteriously transported to London, seeking Christopher's help to find their missing friends. 

The film's first hour is a poignant exploration of lost childhoods and the struggle to reconnect with one's inner child. Pooh's presence in London is both charming and unsettling, with the animated characters' designs appearing almost creepy in their realism. Christopher's interactions with his old friends are heartfelt and nostalgic, but the transition to the adult world is jarring. The second act, set in London, is a frantic race to save the luggage factory from financial ruin, with Christopher caught between his responsibilities and his desire to return to the Hundred Acre Wood. 

The film's tone shifts abruptly, making it feel like two different movies stitched together. While the first part is a melancholic reflection on childhood, the latter half is a fast-paced, action-packed adventure. The characters' personalities remain intact, with Jim Cummings' Pooh and Brad Garrett's Eeyore delivering standout performances. However, the film struggles to reconcile its dark and light elements, resulting in a somewhat disjointed narrative. 

Despite its flaws, "Christopher Robin" offers a few moments of genuine joy and wisdom. The film's exploration of the struggle between childhood innocence and adult responsibilities resonates with both children and adults. It is a heartwarming tale that, while not revolutionary, provides a welcome break from the typical family fare.

President Obama is poised to end a 20-year ban on offering Pell grants to state and federal prisoners, potentially allowing thousands of inmates to access federal subsidies for college education. This move could come as early as this week, with Education Secretary Arne Duncan and Attorney General Loretta Lynch scheduled to visit Goucher College’s Prison Education Partnership at the Maryland Correctional Institution in Jessup to make an announcement related to federal aid. Duncan has previously stated that restoring Pell eligibility for prisoners is one way to increase college affordability. The Department of Education could circumvent the federal ban by using its experimental sites program, which provides limited exemptions to federal financial aid rules. Duncan has emphasized the need for debt-free degrees and has called for the development of experimental sites that will make Pell grants available to incarcerated adults seeking an independent, productive life after release and to adult learners enrolled in short-term certificate programs providing job-ready training. Currently, Pell grants are worth up to $5,775 per year. The Obama administration has increased total federal aid available to students by more than $50 billion and increased tax benefits and credits by an additional $12 billion, part of a total of about $150 billion annually in grants and loans for higher education. More than 2 million additional students now receive Pell grants, and the maximum Pell award has increased by more than $1,000. Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have expressed support for such a policy, and House Democrats, including education committee ranking member Bobby Scott (D-Va.), have introduced legislation to reinstate Pell eligibility for federal and state prisoners. Prisoners who participate in correctional education programs are 43 percent less likely to return to prison and 13 percent more likely to have a job after finishing their sentence. Late last year, the Education Department clarified that students in juvenile justice facilities that aren’t federal or state institutions are eligible for Pell grants. The Obama administration’s plan aims to restore federal funding for prison inmates to take college courses, a move that comes amid a broader push to reform the criminal justice system.

North and South Korea have agreed to hold another round of high-level talks following a surprise visit by a top-level North Korean delegation to the South. The delegation, led by Hwang Pyong So, the second-in-command to Kim Jong Un, included Choe Ryong Hae and Kim Yang Gon, key figures in the North Korean leadership. The visit, the first such high-level trip in over five years, comes amid speculation about the health of North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, who has not been seen in public since September 3rd. The delegation met with South Korean officials, including the unification minister and national security adviser, and agreed to resume talks, possibly before the end of the year. The visit, which included attending the closing ceremony of the Asian Games, marks a significant thaw in relations between the two Koreas, despite ongoing tensions and mutual insults. South Korean officials hope this visit signals a move towards improved inter-Korean dialogue and cooperation. The North Korean delegation's presence in the South, combined with recent diplomatic efforts, suggests a potential shift in North Korea's approach, possibly aimed at reducing its isolation and addressing its economic challenges.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer and former Director of National Intelligence James Clapper have called for a special prosecutor to lead an investigation into potential collusion between the Trump campaign and Russia, amid the ongoing controversy surrounding FBI Director James Comey's firing. Schumer stated that the Senate should refuse to confirm a new FBI director until a special counsel is appointed, while Clapper warned that the U.S. government is under assault from President Donald Trump, citing both external and internal threats. Clapper emphasized the importance of checks and balances among the three branches of government, which he believes are being eroded. The White House has not yet named a replacement for Comey, and interviews for the FBI director position are ongoing. Republican lawmakers, including Sen. Lindsey Graham, have suggested promoting an FBI agent to lead the agency, arguing that the new director should be free of political stigma. Democrats, led by Schumer, have expressed concern over the potential political influence on the investigation. Clapper also addressed Trump's controversial tweet warning Comey about leaks to the press, stating that he did not have evidence of collusion between Russia and the Trump campaign. The Senate Intelligence Committee has expressed interest in having Comey testify in an open hearing, though he has declined to do so in a closed-door session. The debate over the appointment of a special prosecutor and the selection of a new FBI director continues to be a central issue in the ongoing Russia investigation.

George Clooney's directorial effort, "Suburbicon," aims to satirize the 1950s suburban lifestyle but ultimately fails to deliver a cohesive and impactful narrative. Set in the idyllic community of Suburbicon, the film's premise is a veneer of perfect tranquility masking deep-seated issues of betrayal, deceit, and violence. However, Clooney's attempt to blend social commentary with a satirical family murder insurance scam falls flat, as the film struggles to balance its disparate elements. Julianne Moore and Matt Damon, both bringing their A-game, are unable to save the script, which is underwritten and fails to develop its characters fully. Moore's portrayal of the Stepford wife routine and Damon's doltish dork character are familiar tropes that feel recycled, lacking the freshness one might expect from such talented actors. The subplot involving the Meyers family, the first African-American residents in Suburbicon, is a condescending and uninterrogated take on old-timey racism, further detracting from the film's overall quality. The inclusion of Oscar Isaac as an insurance agent brings some levity, but the majority of the film's charm and energy come from Noah Jupe's performance as the young, hyper-vigilant Nicky. Despite the film's star-studded cast and Clooney's directorial talents, "Suburbicon" is a colossally tone-deaf misfire, with a disjointed narrative and a failure to effectively explore its social commentary. The film's R rating for violence, language, and sexuality is well-deserved, but the content is more frustrating than engaging. With a running time of 1:45, "Suburbicon" is a shoddy, shameful showing, despite its prestigious origins. Critics and audiences alike are left questioning the wisdom of Clooney's decision to tackle this subject matter, as the film's flaws far outweigh its potential.

Amid a presidential campaign marred by scandal, conspiracy theories, and the specter of a new far-right leader, disillusioned French voters have turned to an unlikely candidate: Barack Obama. A petition launched on Monday, titled "Obama17," aims to gather 1 million signatures by March 15th, hoping to entice the former U.S. president to run in this year’s French elections, which will be held in April and May. As of Friday morning, the petition had already gained 30,000 signatures, according to one of the organizers. However, the petition acknowledges the near-zero chance of Obama actually running, as French law requires presidential candidates to be French citizens. The organizers, a group of four friends in their 30s, launched the website and campaign out of frustration with the leading candidates and their campaigns. "We just wanted to say that we’ve had enough of all of these guys," one of the organizers, Antoine, told NPR. The friends, who work in creative industries, created the petition and placed 500 "Oui on peut" (Yes we can) posters around Paris, a slogan reminiscent of Obama’s 2008 campaign. The petition’s organizers emphasize that it is a joke with a serious purpose, aiming to provoke thought about the state of French politics and the possibility of a more globalized government. They argue that the world would benefit from competent leaders, rather than the same individuals who have dominated French politics for two decades. While the petition may not change French law, it serves as a reminder of the need for change in the political landscape.

Entrepreneur and coder Scott Jones, founder of ChaCha and inventor of voicemail, is opening his 27,000-square-foot Carmel, Indiana, mansion to the public for an estate sale in September. The sale will run from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on September 14-17 at 1150 West 116th St, Carmel, IN 46032. Jones, who has been residing in Hawaii for the past few years, has decided to sell his lifetime collections and household furnishings. The sale will feature a wide array of items, including a Tyrannosaurus rex skull replica for $10,000 and a Steinway grand piano for $100,000. Everything will be bar-coded for easy browsing, and Jones' publicist, John Ross, notes that the sale will offer "a nice opportunity for people to see how the other half lives."

The mansion, built in the style of an English country manor, cost $20 million and took seven years to construct. It boasts a 33-foot-high great room, an indoor treehouse, a circular mahogany slide, a 25-foot-long saltwater aquarium, and an indoor basketball court. It also includes many automation features. The home has been featured on HGTV’s Mega Mansions and MTV Cribs and has served as an incubator for members of the tech scene. Jones has amassed a collection of eclectic possessions, including high-end, original art, museum-quality antiques, custom-built furniture, Kubota tractors, and an incredible clock collection. The house itself is for sale at $4,995,000, and Jones' publicist suggests that everyday household items will be available for purchase alongside the more extravagant pieces. The sale is being managed by Aether Estate Sales Co., and more information can be found online or by calling (317) 567-2319.

Missouri Governor Eric Greitens acknowledged an extramarital affair from 2015 during his State of the State address, but denied allegations of blackmail. Greitens and his wife, Sheena, released a joint statement, stating that while Greitens was "unfaithful" in their marriage, they dealt with the issue privately and emerged stronger. Greitens' attorney, James Bennett, disputed the allegations, stating there was no blackmail and that the claims were false. The ex-husband of the woman involved provided a recording detailing a sexual encounter with Greitens and alleging that Greitens took a photograph and threatened to release it if she exposed the affair. Sheena Greitens defended their marriage, saying, "We have a loving marriage and an awesome family; anything beyond that is between us and God." Greitens maintained his innocence and asked for forgiveness, while his attorney called the allegations a "political hit piece" and a "three-year-old private matter." The controversy could impact Greitens' national political aspirations, as his 2016 campaign emphasized family values. The governor's statement and the recording have sparked a debate over the ethics and implications of the affair.

President Donald Trump's speech at the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) Friday morning deviated significantly from his prepared remarks, reflecting his typical campaign-style rhetoric. Trump, who seemed eager to engage with the crowd, abandoned his scripted speech to deliver a more off-the-cuff, candidate-like address. He emphasized his administration's accomplishments, including tax cuts, judicial confirmations, and moving the U.S. embassy to Jerusalem, though he briefly mentioned new sanctions on North Korea at the end of his nearly hour-and-a-half-long speech. Trump also criticized the media, calling it "crooked," and referenced his 2016 victory over Hillary Clinton, prompting chants of "Lock her up!" from the audience. He returned to a theme familiar from his campaign, reading the lyrics to Johnny Rivers' "The Snake," which he used to illustrate the dangers posed by undocumented immigrants. Trump warned the crowd that Democrats could take away their Second Amendment rights if they win the midterms, prompting a robust cheer from the audience. The president also called for well-trained, gun-adept teachers to carry concealed firearms, advocating for an end to gun-free school zones. He paid homage to the late Billy Graham, a longtime adviser to presidents, and emphasized the importance of maintaining conservative values. Trump urged the crowd not to become complacent and to actively support Republican candidates in the upcoming elections. His off-script approach at CPAC marked a return to the campaign-style rhetoric that defined his 2016 presidential run, indicating his strategy for rallying the conservative base ahead of the midterms.

Nevada plans to execute Scott Dozier on Wednesday using a lethal injection cocktail that includes fentanyl, a drug at the heart of the US opioid epidemic, raising questions about whether the state’s department of corrections broke the law to obtain the drug. Dozier, a double murderer, has volunteered to give up his appeals and face the execution chamber. The state intends to use a synthetic opioid, involved in over 20,000 overdose deaths in 2016 alone, to kill him after finding it difficult to obtain other drugs for Nevada’s first execution in 12 years due to opposition from pharmaceutical manufacturers. However, questions have been raised about whether Nevada’s department of corrections broke the law to obtain the fentanyl, and whether the multibillion-dollar distribution company that provided the drug ignored evidence it was to be used in an execution. Fentanyl has moved to the center of the opioid epidemic as a powerful and dangerous illicit powder, one hundred times more potent than morphine and frequently mixed with heroin or pressed into fake prescription pills. But it is also sold as a prescription painkiller, including a version for injection which can kill in higher dosages. Using fentanyl in an execution is particularly strange and confusing because of its place in the opioid epidemic, and there is a very real risk of a botched execution. Dozier will be injected with fentanyl and two other drugs, one of which is a sedative, midazolam, involved in a number of executions where the condemned man has been seen convulsing, gasping, and in evident pain before death. The Nevada authorities refused to make public how they obtained the fentanyl and other drugs, but last week the ACLU won a court ruling forcing the department of corrections to hand over invoices. They show that it placed multiple small orders over a number of months, sometimes just one day after the previous order. It is not clear if this was an attempt to avoid drawing the attention a single large order of fentanyl would bring. The drugs were ordered from Cardinal Health, one of the US’s largest pharmaceutical distribution companies, which is among wholesalers facing a barrage of lawsuits accusing them of profiteering from the opioid epidemic by delivering vast quantities of prescription painkillers to small pharmacies and ignoring evidence they were being used by people addicted to the drugs. The American Civil Liberties Union of Nevada is examining why the distributor delivered the drug to the Nevada prison authorities even after it was publicly known they intended to use fentanyl to kill Dozier. The rights group is seeking more documentation to see if the Nevada authorities “lied to Cardinal in any way.” Last year, Cardinal Health paid a $44m fine for failing to adhere to regulations intended to prevent opioids falling into the hands of those addicted to the drugs. The ACLU has also raised questions about the legality of the state’s actions in buying the drugs, as the law allows only those doctors and medical institutions with a Drug Enforcement Administration-issued license to obtain and administer scheduled medicines. It appears that the fentanyl was bought by one arm of the prison authorities with the necessary license but then passed on to the execution site where there is no such authority to handle what is supposed to be a tightly controlled drug.

Cory Monteith, the star of the hit TV show "Glee," was found dead in a hotel room in Vancouver, British Columbia, on July 13, 2013, at the age of 31. His death came as a shock to fans and colleagues, as Monteith had recently completed a stint in rehab and seemed to be making progress. Monteith's girlfriend, Lea Michele, was not with him at the time of his death, and she was devastated by the news. She released a statement through her representatives asking for privacy during this difficult time.

The circumstances surrounding Monteith's death are still being investigated, with no immediate cause of death determined. Vancouver police ruled out foul play, and an autopsy was scheduled for Monday to determine the exact cause of death. Monteith had a long history of substance abuse, having entered rehab multiple times, including a recent stint in March 2013. He had previously checked into rehab when he was 19, but his efforts to stay clean were not long-lasting. Monteith's mother had staged an intervention to help him get clean, and he had expressed gratitude for the support of his castmates and friends, particularly his girlfriend, Lea Michele.

In the days leading up to his death, Monteith was seen dining with his manager and a casting agent at a Vancouver restaurant, where he appeared relaxed and healthy. No alcohol was consumed during the meal, according to the manager. Monteith had been in Vancouver for a business trip, but the exact reason for his visit was not clear. He had been staying at the Fairmont Pacific Rim Hotel since July 6 and was due to check out on the day he died. Hotel security footage showed him returning to his room alone early Saturday morning.

Monteith's death was particularly shocking because he had recently returned from rehab and seemed to be making progress. His girlfriend, Lea Michele, had been by his side during his recovery and had expressed her support for him. Michele had been in Mexico when she received the news of Monteith's death, and she was reportedly shaken by the sudden loss. She had been planning to celebrate her birthday with a friend in Cabo San Lucas, but the tragedy overshadowed her plans.

Monteith's death had a profound impact on the "Glee" cast and crew, as well as on fans worldwide. The show's producers and castmates expressed their grief and shock at the news. Monteith's character, Finn Hudson, had become a fan favorite, and his death left a void in the show. The news of his passing also brought to light the struggles of addiction and the challenges of maintaining sobriety, especially for those in the public eye. Monteith's legacy as a talented actor and his impact on the lives of his fans and colleagues will be remembered for years to come.

A 20-year-old man from Rockaway, New Jersey, named Connor Cummings, fell to his death while climbing scaffolding at the 52-story Four Seasons Hotel in Manhattan on Wednesday evening. He and an 18-year-old friend were reportedly trying to take pictures from the hotel's exterior when Cummings slipped and fell nine stories, landing on a lower rooftop. The friend, identified as Dimitri Olivares, was not a hotel guest and was with Cummings to assist him. Cummings was a student at the University of Massachusetts Amherst and a member of the fraternity Alpha Sigma Phi, where he was known for his passion for photography. The hotel's spokeswoman issued a statement expressing sympathy to Cummings' family and emphasizing the hotel's commitment to safety. Police are investigating the incident, and no charges have been filed against the friend who witnessed the fall. Cummings' aunt expressed disbelief at the sequence of events, stating that her nephew was not a daredevil and was not drinking. The tragic incident highlights the dangers of unauthorized access to high-rise buildings and the importance of adhering to safety protocols.

A day care in San Antonio, Texas, has been shut down after an infant was allegedly bitten 27 times by another child, according to KENS 5. The incident occurred at an unlicensed home day care on Bentwood View, where state investigators found eight children in the care of the operator. The baby, whose parents asked not to be identified, was rushed to a hospital on Friday with pronounced bite marks on his body, including his eyes, cheeks, legs, stomach, and back. The parents say the day care operator waited four hours to inform them of the injuries, which did not fade away. The operator, who was not named, spoke with the KENS 5 I-Team on Tuesday morning, stating she called the parents within a few minutes of finding the bite marks. However, the parents say the operator called only after the injuries did not subside. The San Antonio Police Department’s sex crimes unit is investigating the case, though it does not appear to be a sex crime. The operator could face charges of child neglect or injury to a child by omission if the police determine something could have been done to prevent the injuries. The operator has expressed interest in getting a license and reopening the day care, but would need to complete several steps, including background checks and CPR training for all employees. The incident has raised concerns about the safety and oversight of unlicensed day cares. The case highlights the importance of proper licensing and regulation, as well as the need for parents to be vigilant in choosing a safe and reputable day care. The National Association for the Education of Young Children recommends that parents evaluate day cares based on factors such as the rate of turnover, caregiver engagement with children, and adherence to state regulations. The operator of the day care has been cited multiple times by state investigators for violations, including operating without a license, which has been in effect for eight years. The day care was shut down by the state on Monday, and the case is under investigation.

A shooting outside City Grill on Main Street in downtown Buffalo left four dead and four wounded, prompting a dramatic arrest of a parolee just two and a half weeks out of prison. Keith D. Johnson, 25, was identified as a suspect and arrested at his home, where police confiscated bloody clothing. However, after reviewing video and witness statements, Erie County District Attorney Frank A. Sedita III announced he would dismiss charges against Johnson, expressing serious reservations about his involvement. The shooting occurred as patrons left the bar, with a gunman opening fire with a 9mm handgun. Among the victims were Danyell Mackin, Tiffany Wilhite, Shawn-Tia McNeil, and Willie McCaa III, while Demario Vass, James Robbs Jr., Shamar Davis, and Tillman Ward were wounded. The incident has left the community in shock, with Police Commissioner Daniel Derenda calling it "mind-boggling." Johnson, who was involved in a 2002 drive-by shooting, had denied being the shooter, with friends and family supporting his claims. The case highlights the complexities and challenges in quickly identifying suspects in violent crimes.

Edward Snowden's decision to seek refuge in Hong Kong, a semi-autonomous Chinese territory, to unmask the extent of the National Security Agency's (NSA) surveillance programs has placed him in a high-stakes political gamble. Snowden's choice of Hong Kong, known for its press freedom and political dissent, contrasts sharply with the mainland China where he faces potential legal consequences. The United States and China's recent summit, where they reportedly agreed to differ on cybersecurity issues, adds a layer of complexity to the situation. Hong Kong's extradition treaty with the U.S. includes exceptions for political crimes and cases where extradition could harm the "defense, foreign affairs, or essential public interest or policy" of either party. This means Snowden's fate hinges on political expediency, not just in Hong Kong but in Beijing. 

Snowden's Guardian interview emphasized his commitment to free speech and political dissent in Hong Kong, despite his decision not being intended as a vote of confidence in Chinese human rights. The territory's robust press freedom and the 2003 demonstration against sedition and national security restrictions highlight the civic culture. Moreover, the tradition of commemorating the 1989 Tiananmen Square killings, banned in mainland China, is vigorously upheld in Hong Kong, further emphasizing its unique status. 

The U.S. and China's relationship, with their often testy interactions, plays a significant role in this scenario. President Obama and Chinese President Xi Jinping's agreement to differ on cybersecurity issues during their recent summit adds another layer of complexity. If Beijing decides to play this to its advantage, Snowden's extradition could be seen as a capitulation. However, the Chinese government might also consider the optics of the situation, where the U.S. might not want to put the bilateral relationship on the line over this individual. 

Snowden's legal defense group, the Progressive Change Campaign Committee, has already launched a fundraising campaign to support his legal defense. Meanwhile, his revelations have sparked a new debate about the U.S. government's collection of records of domestic telephone calls and overseas Internet activity. Supporters of the programs argue they are legal and have helped put terror plotters in prison, while critics like Glenn Greenwald contend that the leaks have exposed the extent and capabilities of the surveillance state, leading to a need for scrutiny and accountability. 

The Obama administration maintains that the programs are necessary and effective, undergoing periodic review by all three branches of government. However, Snowden's actions have brought together some liberals and conservatives to hail him as a hero, while others, like Senator Dianne Feinstein, question the extent of his access to government secrets. The debate continues, with the outcome of Snowden's case potentially shaping the balance between security interests and privacy rights.

Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Wendy Davis, who gained national attention through her 13-hour filibuster against abortion restrictions, reveals in her upcoming memoir, "Forgetting to Be Afraid," that she had two terminated pregnancies. The first, which occurred in 1996, involved a fetus with a severe brain abnormality. Doctors informed Davis that the baby would suffer and likely be incompatible with life. After consulting multiple medical opinions, Davis and her then-husband, Jeff, decided to terminate the pregnancy. They spent time with their unborn daughter, Tate Elise, and had her baptized before the baby's lifeless body was taken away. Davis writes, "She was suffering," and the experience left her "forever changed." The second pregnancy, an ectopic one in 1994, was medically necessary to avoid endangering Davis's life. Davis's memoir, priced at $27.97, is set to release next week, and she will sign copies at a Fort Worth book event. The revelation of her terminated pregnancies could further humanize Davis and complicate her opponents' attacks on her abortion stance. Davis has previously disclosed her termination of an ectopic pregnancy, which she described as "technically considered an abortion" and "heartbreaking." In her memoir, Davis writes about the decision's impact, stating, "An indescribable blackness followed. It was a deep, dark despair and grief, a heavy wave that crushed me, that made me wonder if I would ever surface." Davis's abortion story has been a significant part of her political narrative, with her filibuster in 2013 temporarily delaying new abortion restrictions. Abbott, the Republican Attorney General and her opponent, has indicated he opposes abortion, even in cases of severe fetal abnormality. Davis's memoir adds layers to her story, detailing her hardscrabble life after her father left and her journey to Harvard Law School. The book is dedicated to her daughters, Amber and Dru, and her parents, whose tumultuous relationship is also explored. Davis's decision to share her personal story in the memoir could be seen as a strategic move to connect with voters and humanize her political message.

Chicken Offsets creator Ted Frank is offering a way for Chick-fil-A lovers to support gay rights while still enjoying their chicken sandwiches. Frank's website, ChickenOffset.com, allows customers to purchase "offsets" for $1 per meal or $6 for ten, with the promise that 80% of the proceeds will go to It Gets Better and the Williams Institute, organizations that support LGBT youth. Frank, a D.C. lawyer and activist, started the site after recognizing the guilt many feel about indirectly supporting Chick-fil-A's stance on same-sex marriage. The site, launched late Saturday night, has seen modest success, with about $100 in offsets sold by Monday afternoon. Frank argues that buying an offset is more efficient than donating directly to charity, as processing fees can reduce the effectiveness of direct donations. The concept has sparked interest and debate, with some questioning the need for a middleman and others supporting the idea of guilt-free chicken consumption.

Catalonia's regional parliament voted to establish an independent Catalan Republic, declaring the region's independence from Spain in a move opposed by the Spanish government. The vote, approved with 70 in favor, 10 against, and two blank ballots, was met with celebrations outside the parliament building in Barcelona. Spanish Prime Minister Mariano Rajoy called for calm and warned that the measures to halt the region's independence bid would protect the liberties of Catalans. The Spanish Senate is set to authorize the government to take control of Catalonia's autonomous powers, including sacking the Catalan regional president and ministers, if the constitutional measures are approved. Meanwhile, thousands of protesters gathered outside the parliament, waving Catalan flags and chanting for independence. The Spanish government's response is expected to escalate the political crisis, with no international support for Catalonia's secession bid. Catalonia's independence move is opposed by all opposition lawmakers and faces legal challenges from the central government, which is prepared to invoke Article 155 of the Constitution to seize control of the region. The vote and the subsequent actions by the Spanish government highlight the deep divisions between Catalonia and the rest of Spain over the region's future status.

Two New Mexico State University students, McKinnah Sinclair, 18, and Charlie Daniels, 19, who went missing after attending a concert in El Paso, Texas, have been located by the Las Cruces Police Department in Nampa, Idaho. The students were found in a red Ford Focus, which had a fictitious license plate, driven by Daniels and occupied by Sinclair. The Nampa Police Department officer who conducted the traffic stop opted not to charge Daniels for the fake license plate, as the relationship between the students and the parents of Daniels was considered to be of a familial nature. The vehicle was reported stolen, but no charges were filed due to the circumstances.

The Las Cruces Police Department received assistance from various law enforcement agencies in New Mexico, Texas, Arizona, California, Nevada, and Idaho in locating the missing students. Sinclair and Daniels were last seen on surveillance footage at a Beverly Hills ATM on Monday, appearing to be in good condition. The driving distance from El Paso to Beverly Hills to Nampa is approximately 1,600 miles, suggesting a multi-state journey undertaken by the students. Sinclair, a member of the NMSU cheerleading squad, and Daniels, studying kinesiology, were last known to be at the Rare El Paso hip-hop concert on February 3, 2017. Their families filed missing person affidavits with the Las Cruces Police Department on Tuesday morning after the women failed to return home or contact family.

Despite attempts to reach the students via cell phone or social media, Sinclair and Daniels did not inform their families of their whereabouts or plans. The Las Cruces Police Department believes the women traveled to California and Idaho on their own, but it remains unclear why they left without informing their families or what their final destination may have been. The students' families have made arrangements to have them returned to New Mexico.

A Brazilian couple's life took a dramatic turn when they unexpectedly discovered they were brother and sister. Married for seven years, Adriana, 39, and Leandro, 37, had both been searching for their birth mothers, both named Maria, since they were infants. Adriana, a cosmetics saleswoman, had been raised by her father after her mother abandoned her. Leandro, a truck driver, found out his mother had also left him when he was eight, and his stepmother was actually his real mother. The pair met ten years ago and fell in love, moving in together and having a six-year-old daughter.

Adriana, determined to find her mother, contacted a radio show, "The Time is Now," which specializes in reuniting lost relatives. During the show, Adriana learned her mother had another son, Leandro, whom she had given up. The revelation came as a shock, as Adriana had married Leandro, and they had been together for years. The radio host, Rony Magrini, confirmed the couple's suspicions when he asked Leandro's last name, revealing that he was indeed Adriana's brother.

Despite the shocking discovery, the couple vowed to stay together. They believed their love was genuine and that their marriage was a divine arrangement. "Only death is going to separate us," Adriana said. "All this happened because God wanted it to happen." They had a family meeting and decided to continue their relationship, regardless of the circumstances. Adriana had suspected something was amiss after seeing her husband's birth certificate, which listed his mother as Maria, but she hoped the reunion would clear up any doubts.

Under Brazilian law, their marriage is technically void, as they never had it legally recognized. However, the couple stated they would remain together, emphasizing that their love and plans for the future were unbreakable.

Ladies are making waves in the world of space exploration! A set of LEGO figurines celebrating the achievements of five pioneering women in NASA's history has been selected by LEGO to become an official product. Maia Weinstock, the deputy editor of MIT News, submitted the concept to LEGO Ideas, a platform that allows enthusiasts to propose new LEGO sets. Her project, titled "Women of NASA," received 10,000 votes in just 15 days, qualifying it for official review. After rigorous testing, the set was chosen to highlight the contributions of Margaret Hamilton, a computer scientist who led the development of software for the Apollo missions; Mae Jemison, the first African-American woman in space; Katherine Johnson, a key figure in the Mercury and Apollo programs; Sally Ride, the first American woman in space; and astronomer Nancy Grace Roman, who played a crucial role in the planning of the Hubble Space Telescope. Weinstock's goal is to inspire young girls and boys to pursue careers in STEM fields, emphasizing the importance of recognizing and celebrating the historical contributions of women in these areas. By creating these LEGO figurines, Weinstock hopes to make a small but significant impact on how women are perceived and shown in books, toys, and family programming. The set, which features a diverse group of women in terms of their fields, cultural backgrounds, and ages, is set to launch, offering a unique educational experience that combines play with learning about the history of women in space exploration.

Seven-year-old Bana Alabed, who gained worldwide attention for her tweets from besieged Aleppo, has penned an open letter to newly inaugurated US President Donald Trump, appealing for his intervention in the Syrian conflict. Bana, now residing in Turkey with her family, writes, "You must do something for the children of Syria because they are like your children and deserve peace like you." Her letter, shared by her mother Fatemah, highlights the suffering of Syrian children and calls on Trump to take action. Bana recounts her experiences in Aleppo, where her school was destroyed by bombing, and friends died. She contrasts this with her current life in Turkey, where she can enjoy peace and attend school. The letter reflects Bana's hope that Trump will help end the suffering of Syrian children. Bana's plea comes as the US president's stance on Syria remains uncertain. Trump has expressed admiration for Russian President Vladimir Putin, who supports Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, and has previously stated a desire to cease aid to Syrian rebels. However, he has also spoken about establishing "safe zones" to support rebel forces. Meanwhile, a ceasefire agreement involving Iran, Russia, and Turkey is being enforced, though its sustainability remains questionable. Bana's letter underscores the ongoing humanitarian crisis in Syria, where over 300,000 people, including thousands of children, have lost their lives.

Since Flint, Michigan, switched its water supply to the Flint River in April 2014, there has been a significant increase in Legionnaires' disease cases in Genesee County, Michigan. Michigan Department of Health and Human Services (MDHHS) data from June 2014 to November 2015 show 87 confirmed cases, including 10 fatalities. This number is a stark contrast to the 6 to 13 cases reported in the previous years. While the exact cause remains unclear, Flint's water crisis, characterized by the lack of corrosion control, has been linked to the rise in Legionnaires' cases. Flint River water, without proper treatment, may have contributed to the bacteria's growth, especially in large buildings with older plumbing systems. Michigan officials have not altered their recommendations for bathing or showering, stating that the water is safe for these activities. However, the situation adds to the ongoing Flint water crisis, which has already caused widespread lead contamination, affecting thousands of residents. The crisis has led to a state of emergency, with Michigan State Police distributing bottled water and water filters. Governor Rick Snyder acknowledged the increase in Legionnaires' cases, stating that the Flint water crisis is a disaster that should never happen again. Flint residents continue to face challenges, with lead levels in some homes already decreasing, but the water remains unsafe for drinking. The crisis has sparked calls for national infectious disease specialists to investigate past outbreaks and ensure no ongoing threats. A fund has been established to address the short- and long-term needs of Flint children exposed to lead through contaminated drinking water. The ongoing Flint water crisis has not only highlighted the failure of proper water management but also raised concerns about the health impacts of contaminated water on vulnerable populations.

Fierce winds in Southern California have whipped up a rapidly growing wildfire, forcing thousands of residents to evacuate their homes and threatening a city of over 100,000 people. The blaze, which broke out Monday east of Santa Paula, a city of 30,000 about 60 miles northwest of downtown Los Angeles, has expanded to more than 15 square miles in just a few hours, consuming vegetation that hasn't burned in decades, according to Ventura County Fire Sgt. Eric Buschow. The winds are pushing the fire westward toward Santa Paula, a city with 30,000 residents, and authorities warn that the city of Ventura, 12 miles southwest with 106,000 residents, is likely to be affected soon. Ventura County Fire Chief Mark Lorenzen described the fire's growth as "absolutely exponential," emphasizing that the primary task for firefighters is to evacuate people and protect structures. Thomas Aquinas College, a school with about 350 students, has also been evacuated, with students finding shelter at their homes or those of faculty and staff. One person was tragically killed in an auto accident related to the fire, though no further details were provided. At least two structures have already been destroyed. With winds exceeding 40 mph and gusts over 60 mph, the National Weather Service is forecasting continued strong winds, which have forced the grounding of firefighting planes late Monday night. Thousands of homes in the area are currently without power, adding to the urgency and complexity of the situation.

Visiting Honolulu? Better get out of the habit of texting while walking, or at least while crossing a street. The City Council has passed a bill that bans pedestrians from looking at mobile devices in crosswalks, with fines ranging from $15 to $99 for first-time offenders. The legislation, which passed with a 7-2 vote, does not apply to talking on the phone. Mayor Kirk Caldwell is still weighing the pros and cons, but if approved, the law would take effect 90 days later. The bill, authored by Councilmember Brandon Elefante, prevents pedestrians from using cell phones, pagers, tablets, laptop computers, handheld video games, or digital cameras while crossing the street. First-time violators can receive a fine from $100 for the first offense, and up to $500 for a third citation. However, audio equipment, such as headphones, will still be allowed. Supporters of the bill say it will hold pedestrians and motorists responsible for actions on the road, while critics call the bill intrusive and an "attempt at local government overreach." HPD has expressed support for the measure. The bill now heads to Mayor Caldwell's desk. If signed into law, enforcement could begin in October. Honolulu is the first major US city to pass such a ban, and similar legislation has been considered but not passed in multiple states.

The daily hustle got you down? If so, God's Little People Cat Rescue on the Greek Island of Syros might have the perfect job for you. The organization, operating on the island of Syros, located in the Aegean Sea to the southeast of Athens, Greece, is looking to hire a live-in caretaker. The job comes with free housing and a salary, according to a post on the organization's Facebook page. "PAID JOB OFFER WITH CATS! (this is genuine and NOT a joke — friends, please feel free to verify!)," the posting reads. "A very special position and living circumstance on offer on a little Greek island called Syros (a small paradise no less!)" The job involves caring for the cats and enjoying the island's beauty. The island is described as a "small paradise," offering a unique living and working experience.

The post invites potential candidates to verify the job's authenticity and apply if interested. The organization, RESQCATS, located in Santa Barbara, California, is dedicated to rescuing, caring for, and adopting abandoned cats and kittens. It emphasizes the joy and companionship that cats can bring, highlighting their ability to sit on cold feet, greet owners in the morning, and bring presents. Cats are also noted for their ability to appreciate their owners' efforts by purring and rubbing against them.

RESQCATS takes pride in personally knowing each cat to find the "purrfect" home, considering factors such as the compatibility of the cat with young children and their socialization needs. The organization often receives calls from people who have lost their beloved cats and are seeking a new furry friend to fill the void. They encourage anyone considering adopting a cat or kitten to reach out, whether due to the loss of their own pet or the desire to give a cat a good home.

The organization's website offers a glimpse into its facilities and the cats and kittens available for adoption. Potential adopters can visit the Online RESQCATS Sanctuary to see the cats and kittens, many of whom were once or are currently part of the organization's rescue efforts. The post concludes with a quote from Jeffyne Telson, the President of RESQCATS, emphasizing that what matters most is how one sees themselves.

Honda has released an extended version of its Super Bowl commercial for the 2012 CR-V, which pays homage to the 1986 film Ferris Bueller's Day Off. In the ad, Matthew Broderick reprises his role as Ferris, calling in sick to a film shoot and enjoying a day of slacking in his new CR-V. The commercial, produced by RPA, is a delightful tribute to the classic movie, with fans spotting over two dozen references to the film. While some are obvious, others are quite subtle. This homage to the '80s classic is sure to please both car enthusiasts and Ferris Bueller fans alike, as it celebrates the original film's spirit while introducing the all-new CR-V.

A video has emerged showing bank employees in China being publicly spanked as a form of punishment during a training session, prompting suspensions and sparking a debate over the use of corporal punishment. The incident occurred at a Rural Commercial Bank in Shanxi province, where an official from a Shanghai-based leadership academy administered the spankings. The video, recorded by an audience member, shows the man, identified as Jiang Yang, using a thick stick to repeatedly strike the backsides of eight employees, including four women, for performing poorly. Jiang justified his actions, stating that physical punishment is "one of the most effective ways to raise consciousness," though he acknowledged that not everyone would agree. The bank president and another executive have been suspended, and a special task force has been established to investigate. The bank has also offered to help employees seek compensation from the trainer. The incident has drawn criticism from many, who argue that such punishment violates employees' rights. The Shanxi Rural Credit Cooperatives Union stated that the spankings were part of a "Breakthrough in Performance" training session, though some employees claim that head shaving was also used as a punishment. The video has garnered significant attention online, with many expressing outrage at the treatment of the employees.

President Obama’s appearance on "The Daily Show" with Jon Stewart Wednesday night highlighted the evolving relationship between late-night comedy and political discourse. Stewart’s interview, which lasted 22 minutes, was filled with gentle but pointed questions, challenging the president on his campaign promises and his legislative achievements. Obama, who appeared composed and engaged, defended his presidency, offering a mix of reassurances and acknowledgments of the challenges faced. Stewart’s probing questions, such as whether the economy would truly recover and if the White House had capitulated to Wall Street, underscored the show’s role in political commentary. The interview, part of the lead-up to Stewart’s "Rally to Restore Sanity" on the National Mall, aimed to engage a young, politically disenchanted audience. Stewart’s co-host, Stephen Colbert, is also involved in the rally, further emphasizing the show’s bid to harness the voices of moderates and critics of the political establishment. The event, seen as a publicity stunt for two TV shows, also reflects the blurred lines between entertainment and political engagement in the modern media landscape. Stewart’s interview with Obama, while not confrontational, served as a reminder of the power of comedy in shaping public perception and political discourse. The president’s willingness to appear on a late-night comedy show, part of his broader strategy to reach young voters, illustrates the changing dynamics of political communication in the digital age.

RAF fighter jets have been scrambled twice this month in response to potential terror threats over UK airspace, the BBC reports. Eurofighter Typhoons were dispatched from Coningsby in Lincolnshire after a United Airlines flight raised concerns about "ransom" and "hostage" over Reading, while Typhoons and Tornado F3 fighters intercepted an American Airlines plane where a passenger was reportedly trying to enter the cockpit. Both incidents turned out to be false alarms, but they highlight the heightened security measures in place following the 9/11 attacks. Procedures include alerting the prime minister, who could potentially order the destruction of a civilian airliner to prevent mass casualties. The UK's air defence control and operations centre in High Wycombe coordinates these responses, with the exact time it takes for jets to reach the scene classified. Despite the frequency of such alerts—about once a month out of three million flights annually—these incidents underscore the ongoing vigilance required to protect UK airspace.

Thirty years after the brutal murder of 14-year-old Claire Hough on Torrey Pines State Beach, San Diego homicide investigators have identified two suspects in her killing, one of whom was a former San Diego Police criminalist. Hough, a teenager visiting her grandparents, was found beaten, strangled, stabbed, and with one of her breasts severed. In November 2012, DNA evidence linked Brown, a former criminalist who worked for the San Diego Police Laboratory from 1982 to 2002, and Ronald Clyde Tatro, who died in a boating accident in 2011, to the crime. Despite the DNA evidence, homicide investigators confirmed that Brown had no connection to the evidence or the investigation. Preparations were being made to arrest Brown when he was found dead at Cuyamaca State Park, with his death initially ruled a suicide. The second suspect, Tatro, was identified as a suspect in August 2014. The case remains unsolved, with no direct evidence linking the two killings that occurred six years apart. The murder of 15-year-old Barbara Nantais in 1978, found similarly brutal on the same beach, remains separate from the Hough case. The San Diego Police Department encourages anyone with information to come forward.

On New Year’s Day, Lindsay and Lamar Austin, a couple from Concord, New Hampshire, welcomed their newborn son, Cainan, into the world. Lindsay, 26, and Lamar, 30, chose to prioritize family over work when Lindsay went into labor. Lamar, who was working as a part-time security guard for Salerno Protective Services, drove his wife to Concord Hospital, where Cainan was born at 7:44 a.m., the first baby of the year in Concord. Despite missing his shift, Lamar was determined to be present for his son’s birth, and he felt that his decision was the right one. Lindsay, a stay-at-home mom, expressed her gratitude for the support her family has received since her story went public. The couple, who met on an online dating site and have three other children, are grateful for the outpouring of support from the community and the job offers they have received. Lamar Austin, a 30-year-old Army veteran, was fired from his job after missing work to be with his family at the hospital, but he remains positive about the situation. He has received job offers, including an opportunity to apply for an electrician’s apprenticeship with the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers in Concord. Lindsay and Lamar Austin hope that their story will inspire changes in labor laws to provide better support for working parents. The family’s story has caught the attention of state legislators and labor leaders, who are considering ways to improve working conditions for employees like Lamar Austin. The couple is optimistic about the future and plans to spend as much time together as possible.

An EgyptAir flight carrying 66 passengers and crew, including 30 Egyptians, 15 French, two Iraqis, one Briton, one Canadian, one Sudanese, one Chadian, one Portuguese, one Algerian, one Belgian, one Kuwaiti, and one Saudi, disappeared over the Mediterranean Sea while en route from Paris to Cairo. The Airbus A320 vanished from radar at 2:30 a.m. Cairo time, shortly after entering Egyptian airspace, according to EgyptAir and Greek officials. French President François Hollande confirmed the plane had crashed, but the cause remains unclear. Egypt's Civil Aviation Minister Sherif Fathy suggested a terrorist attack was more likely than a technical error, though no hard evidence has emerged. Greece deployed military aircraft and a frigate to search for the plane, while France offered to send planes and boats. The French military's Falcon surveillance jet was also diverted to assist in the search. Egyptian authorities have not found any debris, contradicting earlier reports of floating objects near the Greek island of Karpathos. The search continues, with Egypt and France cooperating to uncover the circumstances behind the crash. The incident has raised concerns about Egypt's aviation safety, given recent incidents such as the hijacking of EgyptAir Flight 181 and the crash of a Russian Metrojet flight in Sinai. The families of the victims have been informed and are receiving support from the Egyptian government.

On Tuesday, October 30, 2018, in Rochester, Indiana, a tragic accident occurred at a school bus stop north of the town. Three children, 9-year-old Alivia Stahl and her twin 6-year-old brothers, Xzavier and Mason Ingle, were crossing SR 25 to board their school bus when they were struck and killed by a northbound pickup truck.
