The siblings, students at nearby Mentone Elementary School, died at the scene. An 11-year-old boy, Maverik Lowe, who was not related to the deceased siblings, was also hit by the truck and suffered multiple broken bones, undergoing surgery at a Fort Wayne hospital. The incident happened around 7 a.m., just before sunrise, as the children were crossing the southbound lane of the two-lane road from a rural mobile home community where they lived. The bus had stopped and lowered its stop-arm, but the driver of the pickup truck, Alyssa Shepherd, 24, of Rochester, did not stop. Authorities are investigating the cause of the accident, with Shepherd facing charges of three counts of reckless homicide and one misdemeanor count of disregarding a stop sign and causing injury. The Tippecanoe Valley School Corporation released a statement, deploying counselors to meet the emotional needs of students, staff, and parents, and urging the community to come together in prayer. Governor Eric Holcomb also released a statement, expressing sorrow and urging Hoosiers to send their prayers for strength. The accident has sparked discussions about school bus safety and the need for safer routes for children to cross busy roads.

Cuban authorities have confirmed the theft of at least 70 works of art from the National Museum of Fine Arts in Havana, with a total value exceeding $1 million, according to a Miami art dealer who first reported the heist to U.S. authorities. The United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) published a list of the stolen artworks, mostly paintings on canvas by Cuban artist Leopoldo Romañach, and other artists from the "Turn of the Century" period. The theft was discovered after several pieces were put on sale in Miami, home to the largest Cuban exile community. Cuban officials stated that storage facilities of the Museum of Fine Arts in Havana showed no signs of violence, and the frames were carefully repositioned, making the theft initially undetectable. The Cuban National Council of Cultural Heritage asked for help to locate the stolen works and noted that the theft is relatively rare in Cuba, where museums are tightly guarded and artwork is usually inspected before leaving the country. The theft is considered more complex than the smuggling out of Cuba, as getting the art out of the museum is very complicated. A Miami art dealer, Ramon Cernuda, first alerted law enforcement officials after purchasing a painting for $15,000, which was later confirmed to be registered to the Havana museum. Cernuda also noted that another dealer in Miami had 10 Cuban artworks for sale that appeared to have been crudely cut from their frames. The Cuban Minister of Culture, Rafael Bernal, was dismissed from his post following the theft, though no reason was given. Law enforcement officials in Cuba and the United States are investigating the case, and the Miami FBI is involved in the investigation. Despite the strained relations between the U.S. and Cuba, Cernuda expressed confidence that any recovered art would be returned to the island.

A list of alleged campus rapists has resurfaced in multiple women's bathroom stalls at Columbia University, raising concerns about vigilante justice and the handling of sexual assault allegations. The latest version, written in silver marker on the second floor of Butler, was discovered after Bwog, a Columbia student-run news site, received a tip. This is the fourth iteration of the list, with previous versions appearing in Hamilton and Lerner buildings. Each list contains the same four names, suggesting a single author. Facilities staff have removed the lists promptly, considering them acts of graffiti, which can result in disciplinary or legal consequences. Public Safety has taped up the doors of affected bathrooms but left them open, as students can enter without swiping their IDs. The incident echoes a similar event at Brown University in 1990, where lists of alleged rapists appeared in multiple bathrooms, leading to a response from administration. Bwog, in an editorial, expressed concern that publishing such a list could violate Title IX and FERPA, and questioned whether it is the best way to create a safer campus environment. The Columbia administration did not immediately respond to requests for comment, but the incident has sparked debate among students about the appropriate response to sexual assault allegations.

A new study presented at the 108th Annual Meeting of the American Sociological Association reveals that people's empathy towards victims can vary significantly based on the age and species of the victim. Contrary to the popular belief that animal suffering elicits more empathy, the research indicates that adult human victims receive less empathy compared to children, puppies, and full-grown dogs. Jack Levin, the Irving and Betty Brudnick Professor of Sociology and Criminology at Northeastern University, and Arnold Arluke, a sociology professor at the same institution, conducted the study. They surveyed 240 predominantly white, 18-25-year-old college students, who read one of four fictional news articles about a brutal beating, with the only difference being the victim's identity: a one-year-old child, an adult in his thirties, a puppy, or a six-year-old dog. Participants rated their empathy levels for the victim, and the results showed that empathy was highest for children and animals, with puppies and dogs receiving nearly the same level of empathy as children. The researchers were surprised to find that the difference in empathy for children versus puppies was statistically non-significant. They hypothesized that younger victims would receive more empathy, regardless of species, but their findings indicated that age was more influential for human victims, while species mattered more for dog victims. Levin suggested that adult dogs are perceived as dependent and vulnerable, similar to their younger counterparts and children, whereas adult humans are seen as capable of self-protection. The study also found that women exhibited higher levels of empathy towards both human and animal victims, potentially due to biological factors related to childbirth and childrearing. While the study focused on dogs and humans, Levin believes the findings would be similar for cats and other pets. The research underscores the complex nature of empathy and how it can vary based on the perceived vulnerability and dependency of the victim.

North Korea's supreme leader, Kim Jong-un, has reportedly ordered the arrest of hundreds of relatives of his recently executed uncle, Jang Song-thaek, as part of a broader purge aimed at eradicating all traces of his former mentor from the nation's history. According to a source from the North Korean capital, Pyongyang, armed men from the Ministry of State Security arrived in the Pyongchon area on the night of December 13, the day after Jang's execution, to round up a few hundred people, including distant relatives and even relatives of Jang's father. The Daily NK, a news outlet run by defectors from the regime, reported that the scale of these arrests underscores the lengths Kim Jong-un is willing to go to completely erase his uncle from North Korea's political landscape. Jang was charged with a staggering 24 crimes, including "gnawing at the unity and cohesion of the party" and "dreaming different dreams," among others, and was summarily executed for his alleged crimes. The arrests of his relatives and associates are part of a broader effort to punish those connected to Jang and to ensure that no trace of his influence remains. Some relatives have reportedly volunteered to undergo "revolutionisation" by working in mines or on farms, but the Daily NK suggests that this will not save them from severe punishment, as their crimes are categorized as "anti-party, counter-revolutionary factionalism." This move by Kim Jong-un highlights the harsh and repressive nature of North Korea's political system, where family members of those found guilty of crimes can face severe penalties, including execution or long-term imprisonment in political prison camps.

Chicago's CTA trains will implement new security measures starting November 3, as part of a federal counter-terrorism initiative. Passengers will be randomly selected to hand their bags, purses, or suitcases to a Chicago police officer for screening at some stations. The screening process involves swabbing the outside of the bags and placing the sample in a machine to check for explosive compounds. Bags will not be opened, and the test takes only about 30 seconds. Chicago Police Public Transportation Commander Nancy Lipman emphasized that the screening is a "proactive, protective measure," stating, "We know the fears and the possibilities. It's going to take 20 to 30 seconds of someone's time. While we know our commuters' time is precious, we think their safety is probably priceless." The initiative is fully funded with part of a $3.5 million federal anti-terrorism grant. However, some CTA riders expressed skepticism about the new procedure. Joseph Schwieterman, a DePaul professor specializing in transportation issues, noted the difficulty of providing airport-level security in mass transit systems. Chicago police will randomly select one rail station each day to set up the screening table outside the rail turnstiles during rush hour. A team of four to five officers will man the table, equipped with two explosives testing machines. If a rider fails the test, they will be asked to open their bag for inspection. Riders who refuse to have their bag swabbed will be ordered to leave the station and may face arrest if they attempt to board the train. The screenings will occur several times a week, with the aim of having no impact on commuters' travel times.

Actress Jamie Denbo, known for her role in Orange Is the Black, recently shared her experience with ageism in Hollywood on Twitter. At 43, Denbo was informed she was too old to play the wife of a 57-year-old actor, despite the character having an 18-year-old daughter, which would have made Denbo 25 when giving birth. Denbo pointed out that the actor's real-life wife is likely 50, making the situation even more absurd. Her tweets sparked discussions about the pervasive ageism in the industry, where older actresses are often cast as mothers of much younger characters, while younger actresses are paired with much older male co-stars. This trend, as highlighted by Helen Mirren, is seen as both "fucking outrageous" and "ridiculous." Denbo's public response has brought renewed attention to the issue, with many supporting her stance and calling for more diverse and realistic casting choices. The incident also draws attention to the work of actresses like Meryl Streep, who is funding a screenwriting lab for women over 40 to address this problem. Denbo's tweet series effectively challenged the industry norms and sparked a broader conversation about the need for more inclusive casting practices in Hollywood.

If only Andrew Stanton's John Carter had avoided the toxic buzz surrounding its production, audiences might have given it a pass as a mildly entertaining, old-school adventure. However, the movie's $250 million budget, transition from animation to live-action, and perceived rip-offs of Star Wars, Indiana Jones, and Avatar have raised expectations that the film struggles to meet. Despite these issues, the movie's visual spectacle and wonder can pull viewers in. Taylor Kitsch brings a bruised heart to the role of John Carter, a Civil War veteran who finds himself on Mars, where he must navigate a complex political landscape and fight off enemies. Willem Dafoe and Lynn Collins deliver strong performances as the Thark leader Tars Tarkas and the defiant princess Dejah Thoris, respectively. The film's action sequences, while intricate, lack real jeopardy and fail to fully utilize the Martian setting's potential. Despite its flaws, "John Carter" offers a rousing boy's adventure story, rooted in the pulp fiction of Edgar Rice Burroughs, and aims to foster a franchise. Its visual effects and imaginative world-building, while not groundbreaking, provide a unique experience that may appeal to fans of the genre.

U.S. Senator John McCain (R-AZ) expressed his frustration and disappointment with the Syrian regime’s recent complaint to the United Nations regarding his 2013 visit with Syrian rebels. McCain, who has long been a vocal critic of the Assad regime, emphasized that the international community's inaction in addressing the regime's atrocities has left a "stain on our collective moral conscience." In a statement, McCain highlighted the regime's focus on his visit, which he described as a "sad but unsurprising truth," while downplaying the significance of the regime's mass killings of over 200,000 civilians. McCain's response to the Syrian complaint was met with pride, as he claimed to have achieved a "superfecta" by upsetting regimes he opposes, including Russia, Cuba, and ISIS. The Syrian ambassador to the U.N., Bashar Ja’afari, took the opportunity to criticize not only McCain but also other individuals who entered Syria without proper authorization, such as French Foreign Minister Bernard Kouchner and former U.S. diplomat Peter Galbraith. McCain's statement underscores his unwavering support for the Syrian opposition and his belief in the importance of standing up against authoritarian regimes, even when it comes at a personal cost. The senator's response also reflects the ongoing tension between the United States and the Assad regime, highlighting the complex dynamics of international relations and the challenges faced in addressing humanitarian crises.

A South Carolina serial killer, Todd Kohlhepp, who is already serving life in prison for seven murders, claims to have two additional victims buried near Interstate 26 in Spartanburg County. Sheriff Chuck Wright said investigators are planning to lead Kohlhepp to the supposed location of the bodies. Kohlhepp, 47, admitted to killing seven people and sexually assaulting a woman who was held captive in a storage container in 2016. He confessed to the murders of Beverly Guy, Scott Ponder, Brian Lucas, and Chris Sherbert at a motorcycle shop in 2003. Kala Brown, who was rescued from a storage container on Kohlhepp’s property, told investigators she saw Kohlhepp shoot and kill her boyfriend, Charlie Carver, and that he had also killed a married couple in December 2015. Johnny Coxie and his wife, Meagan Coxie, were also found buried on Kohlhepp’s property. Kohlhepp is serving seven consecutive life sentences plus an additional 60 years in prison. Law enforcement officials are planning to search the area based on Kohlhepp’s claims, but no evidence has been found so far.

The Norwegian man charged with the deadly attacks in Oslo that killed at least 92 people left behind a detailed manifesto outlining his preparations and calling for a Christian war to defend Europe against Muslim domination. Anders Behring Breivik, 32, was identified as a right-wing fundamentalist Christian, while acquaintances described him as a gun-loving Norwegian obsessed with the threats of multiculturalism and Muslim immigration. The 1,500-page manifesto, posted online hours before the attacks, detailed months of planning and claimed Breivik was part of a small group aiming to seize political and military control of Western European countries. He predicted a conflict that would kill or injure over a million people, stating, "The time for dialogue is over. The time for armed resistance has come." Breivik was equipped with an automatic rifle and a handgun, and he was dressed as a police officer when he attacked a youth camp on Utoya Island, killing at least 85 people. The attacks raised questions about whether Norwegian security authorities had overlooked the threat from the anti-Islamic right, despite previous reports that played down the danger from right-wing and nationalist extremists. The manifesto's content and style drew comparisons to Al Qaeda declarations, with its detailed accounts of historical grievances and calls for apocalyptic warfare. The Norwegian security services are investigating whether Breivik had accomplices and whether the chemical ammonium nitrate he purchased was used in the bombing. The attacks and manifesto have sparked debates about the role of multiculturalism and the threat of right-wing domestic terrorism in Norway.

Ashley Madison, the infidelity website, has been in the spotlight again, this time for its response to a data leak that exposed highly personal details of over 30 million users. The company's executives are emphatically stating that the business fundamentals are strong and the site will continue to operate, despite the theft of private data by criminal hackers. In a statement issued early Monday, the company claimed that hundreds of thousands of new users, including 87,596 women, signed up in the week following the breach. This growth is seen as a significant counterpoint to media reports predicting the site's imminent demise. 

The company also addressed claims that the site had few genuine female users, pointing out that an analysis by tech blog Gizmodo, which concluded that very few female members had ever checked the site for messages, was based on incorrect assumptions about the meaning of fields in the leaked data. Ashley Madison executives highlighted that women sent over 2.8 million messages on the platform in the last week alone. 

In a move that adds to the company's challenges, Noel Biderman, the site's founder and CEO, left the company by mutual agreement on Friday. Internal documents and emails released by hackers revealed that Avid Life Media, the site's parent company, had been struggling to sell itself or raise funds for at least three years prior to the breach. 

Despite the negative publicity and potential legal ramifications, Ashley Madison's executives remain optimistic. They emphasize that the site is growing and that the business is resilient. The company's statement challenges media reports and aims to reassure users that the service will continue to operate.

In the wake of the Aurora, Colo., movie theater massacre, law enforcement officials suggest the gunman had likely practiced extensively before the attack. The officials based their assessment on the "unusually high" hit rate during the shooting, where 12 people were killed and 58 injured. The suspect, James Holmes, used an AR-15 assault rifle with a 100-round magazine, a 12-gauge shotgun, and a Glock .40-caliber pistol. Authorities are searching his apartment for evidence of a gun range receipt or related information, as such evidence would indicate premeditation and deliberate planning, potentially negating any insanity defense. Holmes reportedly applied for membership at a local shooting range in June but never showed up. Law enforcement officials noted his high marksmanship, considering his relative inexperience, and speculated he might have practiced on the prairie east of Aurora. The suspect displayed a high degree of marksmanship, switching weapons when the AR-15 jammed, and shooting in a dark theater with thick gas from canisters he had set off. This environment would have made precision shooting more challenging. Authorities believe he may have believed police were being drawn to an explosion at his apartment, giving him time to escape. Instead, he was arrested before reaching his car. Holmes' academic background, including his acceptance into the University of Colorado's neuroscience program and his $26,000 stipend, raises questions about his preparation and resources. University officials were shocked by his arrest, given his stellar academic credentials. The program admits just six students a year, with top grades and test scores, and does not require psychiatric evaluations. Holmes unexpectedly dropped out after failing part of his first-year final exam. His academic performance and reasons for leaving the program remain unclear. The case highlights the complexity of understanding and preventing such tragedies, as evidenced by the extensive preparations and resources the suspect had.

A new study by Stony Brook University researchers has shown that texting while walking can significantly disrupt one's gait and memory, leading to a 61 percent increase in lateral deviation and a 13 percent increase in distance traveled compared to non-texters. The study, published in Gait & Posture, found that cell phone use among pedestrians leads to increased cognitive distraction, reduced situation awareness, and increases in unsafe behavior. Participants who texted while walking veered off course, demonstrating a 61 percent increase in lateral deviation and a 13 percent increase in distance traveled. Eric M. Lamberg, co-author of the study and clinical associate professor in the Department of Physical Therapy at Stony Brook University, said, "We were surprised to find that talking and texting on a cell phone were so disruptive to one’s gait and memory recall." The findings suggest that texting while walking can interfere with working memory and result in walking errors. While the study does not advocate for a ban on texting while walking, it aims to raise awareness about the potential dangers of such behavior. In the meantime, cities like Fort Lee, N.J., have begun issuing $85 jaywalking tickets to pedestrians caught texting while walking, citing increased safety concerns. Despite the fines, some residents argue that the tickets are a financial burden and that the issue should be addressed through education rather than enforcement.

Sixteen U.S. Postal Service workers in the Atlanta area were sentenced to federal prison for accepting bribes, some as low as $250, to deliver cocaine packages on their routes, according to a statement from the U.S. Attorney's Office. The operation, which began in 2015, was part of a larger effort to dismantle a drug trafficking organization in Atlanta. Drug traffickers targeted postal workers because their jobs made them less likely to be caught by law enforcement. Federal agents learned about the scheme when a confidential source posed as a drug trafficker and approached postal workers, offering them money to deliver packages. The defendants agreed to deliver packages in exchange for bribes, and some did so multiple times. All 16 were convicted and received sentences between three and nine years in prison. The sentences included forfeiture and restitution orders. Postal workers involved included Cydra Rochelle Alexander, Aurthamis O. Burch, Kawana Rashun Champion, Eleanor Lolita Golden, Tonie Harris, Leea Janel Holt, Clifton Curtis Lee, Shakeed Anilah Magee, Horace Manson, Olivia Marita Moore, Eddie Nash, Jeffrey A. Pearson, Rodney Antwain Salter, Frank Webb, Katrina Nicole Wilson, and Harvel Donta Young. Dexter Bernard Frazier, a non-postal employee who facilitated some of the deliveries, was also sentenced to nine years in prison. The case was investigated by the Federal Bureau of Investigation, the DeKalb County District Attorney’s Office, and the U.S. Postal Service Office of Inspector General. Assistant U.S. Attorneys Garrett L. Bradford and Jill E. Steinberg prosecuted the case. The U.S. Attorney’s Office in Atlanta advises parents and children to learn about the dangers of drugs through the website www.justthinktwice.gov.

The Texas State Board of Education has approved a resolution requiring future world history textbooks to avoid a "pro-Islamic/anti-Christian bias." The resolution, passed 7-6, aims to ensure more balanced coverage of Christianity and other non-Muslim faiths, amid concerns that increased investment by Middle Easterners in the textbook publishing industry might lead to biased treatment. Board member Terri Leo argued for the resolution, stating it would send a "clear message" to publishers to avoid past biases. However, opponents criticized it as politically motivated and potentially harmful to the board's reputation. Democrats and moderate Republicans voted against the measure, with some calling it a "cosmetic exercise" and "cuckoo." The resolution warns publishers against continuing to offend Texas law with unequal coverage or demonizing religious groups.

The Democratic presidential primary campaign between Bernie Sanders and Hillary Clinton erupted into chaos on Friday after revelations that Sanders' campaign accessed and saved crucial voter data from Clinton's campaign. The controversy began when a software glitch at NGP VAN, the vendor that manages the voter database, allowed Sanders' team to access Clinton's voter files. The Sanders campaign fired one of the staffers involved, Josh Uretsky, but the incident escalated when the Democratic National Committee (DNC) cut off Sanders' access to his own voter files, a move that effectively crippled his field operation. In response, Sanders' campaign sued the DNC, alleging that the data breach was the fault of the party and its data vendor, and that the freeze on Sanders' files amounted to a breach of contract.

The Sanders campaign argued that the DNC's actions were an "inappropriate overreaction" and an attempt to sabotage their campaign. "The leadership of the Democratic National Committee is now actively attempting to undermine our campaign. This is unacceptable," said Jeff Weaver, Sanders' campaign manager. However, the DNC maintained that the Sanders campaign had inappropriately and systematically accessed Clinton's data, and that they were only acting to ensure the integrity of the voter file. Debbie Wasserman Schultz, the DNC chairwoman, said, "The Sanders campaign has now complied with the DNC’s request to provide the information that we have requested of them. Based on this information, we are restoring the Sanders campaign’s access to the voter file, but will continue to investigate to ensure that the data that was inappropriately accessed has been deleted and is no longer in possession of the Sanders campaign."

Despite the resolution, the Sanders campaign refused to drop its lawsuit against the DNC, insisting that the data breach was a result of the party's own mistakes. The dispute has reignited long-standing tensions between Sanders and the DNC, with Sanders' team accusing the party of favoritism towards Clinton. The controversy has significant implications for the upcoming Iowa and New Hampshire caucuses, as the Sanders campaign relies heavily on its voter data for outreach and organizing. The Clinton campaign, meanwhile, accused Sanders' team of "stealing" data and using it to raise money, arguing that this was an "egregious breach" of their campaign's strategy.

The incident has also raised questions about the security of the voter database and the potential for data breaches in future elections. The Sanders campaign's legal team and the DNC both emphasized the need for an independent audit to verify the actions of both campaigns. The resolution came after hours of negotiations and a court order, but the political fallout is likely to continue, with both campaigns using the controversy to their advantage in the lead-up to the upcoming debates and primary elections.

Starting in 1996, Alexa Internet has been donating their crawl data to the Internet Archive, adding to the Wayback Machine after an embargo period. In a recent issue of GQ, the preposterously good-looking stars of Glee, including Lea Michele, Dianna Agron, and Cory Monteith, posed for a racy shoot, shedding their family-friendly sensibilities and a significant amount of clothing. Michele, 24, admitted, "I've never been shot in so little clothing," while Agron echoed, "I don't know how they got me to do half the stuff I did." The cover story delves into the lives of the cast, their rise to fame, and the creation of their devoted fanbase, known as "Gleeks." Michele shared how, early in her acting career, she was advised to get a nose job, but her mother's encouragement to look up to Barbra Streisand kept her from undergoing the procedure. Monteith, 28, who dropped out of school in the ninth grade, emphasized the importance of a high school education, stating, "The last thing I want to do is kind of imply to readers in high school that you too can drop out and be an actor and get on a big show and be famous and make a s***load of money." Glee co-creator Ryan Murphy revealed his initial skepticism about creating a family-friendly show, aiming instead to produce a responsible version for young audiences. The article concludes with a memorable moment from the cast's White House Easter Egg Roll, where they performed for President Obama, feeling like they could be shot at any moment, and were moved to tears by Amber Riley's performance of the national anthem.

The National Security Agency's (NSA) continued surveillance of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Israeli leaders may have also swept up private conversations involving members of Congress, according to a report by the Wall Street Journal. Although President Obama had promised to curb eavesdropping on world leaders who are U.S. allies after Edward Snowden leaked documents revealing the extent of the surveillance, there were a few leaders the White House wished to continue monitoring, including Netanyahu. The original reason for the stepped-up surveillance of Netanyahu was the fear that he would "strike Iran without warning." By 2013, that fear had dissipated. The administration then became concerned about the Iran nuclear deal being negotiated, believing that the Israelis were spying on the negotiations and would try to scuttle the deal. Intercepted conversations between Israeli leaders confirmed Israel's knowledge of the talks and its intent to undermine any nuclear deal with Iran by leaking its details. When Netanyahu and his top aides came to Washington to lobby against the deal, the NSA was there to pick up the conversations. Senior officials told the Journal that those conversations collected by the NSA raised fears "that the executive branch would be accused of spying on Congress." However, the White House wanted the information anyway, as it "believed the intercepted information could be valuable to counter Mr. Netanyahu's campaign." To avoid leaving a trail, the White House left it to the NSA to figure out what to share, and the NSA obliged, deleting names of members and any personal attacks on the administration.

National Security Council Spokesman Ned Price wouldn't comment on the intelligence activities written about in the Wall Street Journal's story, but he said in a statement, "[W]e do not conduct any foreign intelligence surveillance activities unless there is a specific and validated national security purpose. This applies to ordinary citizens and world leaders alike." He added that the U.S. commitment to Israel's security is "sacrosanct" and "backed by concrete actions that demonstrate the depth of U.S. support for Israel." The office of Speaker of the House Paul Ryan said only that it was looking into the matter. Rep. Devin Nunes, chairman of the House Select Committee on Intelligence, said the committee would also be looking into the report. "The Committee has requested additional information from the [Intelligence Community] to determine which, if any, of these allegations are true, and whether the IC followed all applicable laws, rules, and procedures," Nunes said in a statement.

Before a campaign event in Cisco, Texas, Sen. Ted Cruz said he wasn't surprised that the administration was trying to intercept Netanyahu's communications, or even that conversations including members of Congress may have been swept up by the NSA, "because this administration views Congress, Republicans and sometimes even Democratic members of Congress as their enemy....At times, it seems like they view the American people as their enemy." The allegations "are total nonsense," a spokesman for the Embassy of Israel in Washington told the WSJ. Before Netanyahu came to address Congress, the NSA had intercepted Israeli messages that said Netanyahu wanted the "the latest U.S. positions in the Iran talks," signaling to the administration that Netanyahu intended to use his address to reveal sensitive details about the negotiations. Secretary of State John Kerry then said as much to reporters on the eve of the speech. Kerry justified his accusation by pointing to Israeli media reports, but those reports were a convenient source, given that "Intelligence officials said the media reports allowed the U.S. to put Mr. Netanyahu on notice without revealing they already knew his thinking. The prime minister mentioned no secrets during his speech to Congress," wrote the Journal.

Elton John has reignited his long-standing feud with Madonna, calling her a "f***ing fairground stripper" in an interview on the Australian TV show Sunday Night. The comments stem from Madonna's criticism of Lady Gaga, whom Elton believes Madonna has treated poorly. Elton also criticized Madonna's recent MDNA world tour, stating, "Her career is over. Her tour has been a disaster." He suggested Madonna should have focused on making "great pop records" rather than dance music. Earlier this year, Elton and his husband David Furnish had already criticized Madonna's win at the Golden Globes, with David writing, "Madonna winning Best Original Song truly shows how these awards have nothing to do with merit." The feud highlights the ongoing tension between the two, with Elton adding, "She's been so horrible to Gaga." Despite the animosity, Elton's interview with old friend Molly Meldrum was filled with fatherly pride as he discussed his young son Zachary, conceived via a surrogate mother and raised by him and David.

In a bid to combat sleep deprivation, New Yorkers are turning to a novel caffeine fix: Perky Jerky, a caffeinated beef jerky that combines the protein-packed snack with a caffeine boost. Invented by Matt Keiser and Brian Levin, the jerky hit the market in August and will soon be available at Sports Authority stores. Each 1 oz. bag retails for $2.99, while a 2 oz. bag costs $4.99, and each ounce contains 60 mg of caffeine, equivalent to a small cup of coffee. The jerky's unique flavor, a teriyaki-pepper blend with a hint of Guarana, has garnered mixed reactions. While some, like engineer Sal Bouseliman, find it effective for maintaining energy during workouts, others, such as barista Keyon Revels, find it unpalatable. Despite the taste divide, Perky Jerky positions itself as a natural, high-protein, low-fat snack, appealing to active lifestyles. The product's innovative blend of traditional jerky with a modern caffeine boost could redefine the way New Yorkers tackle their caffeine cravings.

After customers complained that a batch of the company's signature yoga pants were too transparent, Lululemon tried to make a scapegoat out of the Taiwanese company that manufactures the pants. Bad idea. Said supplier now says the pants were no different than any other batch. The Eclat Textile Company, whose clients include everyone from Gap to Under Armour, said Tuesday that Lululemon had signed off on the shipment, suggesting that Lululemon made the whole thing up. "All shipments to Lululemon went through a certification process which Lululemon had approved," Eclat's chief executive Roger Lo told The Wall Street Journal. "All the pants were manufactured according to the requirements set out in the contract with Lululemon." 

The controversy marks yet another recent stumble with products on Lululemon's store shelves. The company has now had its fourth quality-control issue in the past year, following complaints of color bleeding on some of its tops, transparency problems with some colors of swimwear shipped for last spring, and a subset of light-colored pants. Analysts expressed concern about the company's quality control, with some suggesting that Lululemon doesn't have the appropriate presence in and around its factories. 

Lululemon's shares were down almost 5% in early trading Tuesday, although they rebounded to finish at $64.08, down 2.3%, on the Nasdaq. The company's shares, after rising by about two-thirds last year, are down nearly 18% so far in 2013. The incident has left Lululemon out about $20 million in lost sales and a whole lot of yogis out of high-priced pants. The finger-pointing match has highlighted a number of questionable incidents in recent Lululemon history, with Credit Suisse analyst Christian Buss pointing out that two out of the other three issues involved the sheerness of its fabrics. The company relies heavily on a limited number of suppliers, a risk it called out in its annual report in March 2012.

Tiger Woods, the world's most notorious womanizer, has reportedly found a new love in Olympic gold medalist Lindsey Vonn, 28, and HollywoodLife.com has all the exclusive details. The 37-year-old golfer, who famously cheated on his wife Elin Nordegren with over twenty other women, has been dating Vonn since November. Their romance began through the ski community, as Vonn has been teaching Woods' children, Sam and Charlie, how to ski. Despite his chequered past, Tiger has been pulling out all the stops to win Lindsey over, and the pair spent a romantic vacation in the Caribbean island of Antigua. However, Lindsey's friends are concerned about her dating a man who has a history of cheating, and there are fears that she might be falling for one of the biggest cheaters of all time. "It took Lindsey a while to trust him because of his past," a source close to her reveals. "She was wary of him before they started dating." Tiger's marriage to Elin Nordegren famously broke down in 2010 after it was revealed that he had slept with over twenty other women while married. Now, with his children and his career in mind, Tiger is reportedly determined to be faithful this time around. "He wants to marry again and thinks Lindsey could be the woman," a source close to the golfer tells Star magazine. But will his track record of infidelity be enough to keep Lindsey from jumping ship?

Fame, fortune, and power in all its forms are celebrated in American culture, yet the powerful can swiftly fall from grace. 24/7 Wall St. compiled a list of 50 individuals who have recently experienced a significant loss in stature, showcasing a diverse range of public figures, from television personalities to CEOs and politicians. These individuals, once at the pinnacle of their careers, now face challenges that threaten their status and influence. 

Anthony Scaramucci, former White House Communications Director, held the shortest tenure in the position, lasting only two weeks before being fired. His brief stint was marked by controversy, including protocol breaches, conflicting statements, and a controversial interview. His personal life also suffered, with his wife filing for divorce during his term.

Chris Christie, former Governor of New Jersey, saw his approval ratings plummet, with many speculating that his association with Donald Trump damaged his political career. The Bridgegate scandal, in which his allies orchestrated a traffic jam on the George Washington Bridge, tarnished his reputation. Despite his political ambitions, Christie was not included in Trump’s cabinet, and his approval ratings remain at an all-time low.

James Comey, former Director of the FBI, faced intense scrutiny and criticism during the 2016 presidential election. His decision to announce an FBI investigation into Hillary Clinton just days before the election sparked controversy. Trump abruptly terminated his tenure, citing multiple conflicting reasons, despite Comey’s long-standing service under President Obama.

Mark Fields, former CEO of Ford Motor Company, was let go after a tumultuous tenure marked by declining stock prices and a failure to inspire shareholder confidence. Despite efforts to boost profits, Fields was unable to navigate the challenges of the automotive industry, particularly the rise of electric and autonomous vehicle technology.

Tiger Woods, once the top-ranked golfer in the world, has seen his career derailed by personal scandals and health issues. His infidelity and a DUI incident, coupled with his current ranking of 899, highlight the fall from grace experienced by many public figures. These examples illustrate the transient nature of power and the potential for rapid decline, regardless of one’s initial status.

The police chief in Alaska's capital city defended his department's handling of the death of newly elected Mayor Stephen "Greg" Fisk, who was found dead at home with injuries that police did not immediately rule out as natural causes. Fisk's death, which made national headlines, led to speculation about foul play. Preliminary autopsy results indicated natural causes, consistent with falling or stumbling. Police chief Bryce Johnson acknowledged that the lack of witnesses and the possibility of an assault led to a period of uncertainty. Fisk, a 70-year-old fisheries consultant, had a history of heart problems. His adult son, Ian, found his body after missing appointments. Fisk lived alone, and Deputy Mayor Mary Becker was named acting mayor. The family grieved privately, with Ian stating they had no reason to speculate on the cause of death. The case highlighted the challenges faced by police in determining the cause of death in such high-profile cases.

Lady Gaga's tribute to David Bowie at the 2016 Grammys featured a transformative performance that showcased the late artist's influence and the technological prowess of Intel. Gaga, who wore an orange wig and Ziggy Stardust-inspired outfit, performed Bowie's hits with the support of Intel's technology, including special effects and costume changes. Nile Rodgers, who produced several Bowie hits, joined Gaga for the second half of the performance, which concluded with "Heroes." The tribute was part of Intel's Experience Amazing campaign, highlighting how technology can facilitate unique experiences. Gaga's deep connection to Bowie is evident, as she thanked him for inspiration in her debut album and listed his song "Rebel Rebel" as one of her favorites. The performance was a fitting homage to Bowie, who died just days before the ceremony, leaving behind a legacy of artistic innovation and influence.

Robin Williams, who died at 63, left an indelible mark on the entertainment world, particularly on those born in the 1980s and early 1990s. His career transitioned from edgy comedy and dramatic roles to becoming a beloved voice actor in children's films, a shift that was both unexpected and deeply appreciated. Williams' performance as the Genie in "Aladdin" was a triumph, bringing a sense of imaginative expansiveness to Disney's darker story. His willingness to abandon his recognizable face and body for the role of the Genie, a blue drawing that felt more vivid and lifelike than most TV characters, was emblematic of his generosity and commitment to entertainment for kids.

Williams' career in the 1980s and early 1990s was marked by a series of films that often featured him playing characters who had been trapped in a childlike state or who were unprepared for the adult world. In "Mrs. Doubtfire," he played a voice actor who was too childlike to sustain his marriage, embodying the innocence and joy of childhood in a way that felt illicitly charged. His performance as the Genie in "Aladdin" and his role as the Genie in "Hook" were particularly memorable, as he brought a sense of fun and comfort to these stories, making them VHS classics for a generation of children.

Williams' legacy is also defined by his willingness to take on roles that were out of character for his stand-up persona. In "Jakob the Liar" and "Bicentennial Man," he played characters with complex, often abstracted backstories, which were two degrees removed from the sunny optimism of his children's films. However, for the early teens who grew up with his movies, Williams' projects were a source of joy and inspiration. His ability to give joy, even in the face of more serious adult dramas, made him a rare star who seemed genuinely excited to work on projects that resonated with his audience.

The article also recounts personal encounters with Williams, highlighting his complex and brilliant nature. As a stand-up comedian, he was known for his lightning-fast comic connections and his ability to take on different characters with ease. His confidence in his own future success, despite the overwhelming attention he was receiving, was both endearing and unsettling. Even as a formidable actor, Williams retained the same restless, exploratory spirit that defined his comedy. His final moments, captured in a stage whisper that eerily echoed the 1950s science fiction classic "The Fly," underscored the unpredictability and fragility of his life. The thought of his death made the author shudder, a testament to the profound impact Williams had on his generation.

Oakleigh Ryan Nance, a 11-month-old infant, has been battling a severe and life-threatening condition since her premature birth at just 3 pounds. Despite her small size, she has shown remarkable resilience, overcoming initial challenges in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) and breathing on her own within three days. Oakleigh's health was stable until a sudden fever spiked to 104 degrees, which was later diagnosed as a severe urinary tract infection (UTI) that likely affected her kidneys. Multiple antibiotic treatments failed to resolve the issue, leading to recurring infections and hospitalizations. 

The latest round of tests revealed that Oakleigh has stage 3 kidney reflux, a condition that is common but particularly concerning given her current health status and the antibiotic-resistant strain of Pseudomonas bacteria involved. This strain is notorious for its resistance to many antibiotics, making treatment challenging. Oakleigh's heart condition, including moderate atrial septal defect (ASD) and pulmonary stenosis, adds another layer of complexity to her medical journey. 

Oakleigh's upcoming surgery, scheduled for the end of the month, aims to address the kidney reflux by removing a pocket on the outside of her left kidney and cutting back the ureters to prevent future infections. This 4.5-hour procedure is crucial for her long-term health. Post-surgery, she will require further evaluation by a cardiologist to manage her heart condition. 

Oakleigh's family, though deeply concerned, finds solace in their faith and the support of a loving community. They have launched a GoFundMe campaign to help cover the substantial medical expenses. Oakleigh's journey is a testament to her strength and the unwavering support of her family and friends. Despite the challenges, they remain hopeful and grateful for the ongoing support and prayers from the community.

Donald Trump acknowledged in a South Carolina town hall that he "could have" supported invading Iraq during a 2002 interview with Howard Stern, though he was against the war by the time it started. Trump's stance on the Iraq War has been a point of contention, with him repeatedly claiming he opposed the invasion before it began. During the town hall, Trump criticized former President George W. Bush for launching the war, but the 2002 interview with Stern reveals he had previously expressed support for military action. Trump has been dominating South Carolina polls, and his comments on Iraq could be a risky move in a state with a strong military presence. The town hall also featured confrontations and debates between Trump and his rivals. Jeb Bush and John Kasich refused to engage in the debate between Trump and Pope Francis, with Bush stating he would not question Trump's faith. Trump continued to attack his closest competitor, Ted Cruz, calling him "problematic with the truth." Trump also defended his fast food habits, suggesting he could be more politically correct if he wanted to. The town hall also featured personal moments, such as when Governor John Kasich shared his experience of losing his parents in a car accident and how it shaped his outlook on life. The article highlights the candid and often inflammatory nature of Trump's campaign, as well as the personal and political dynamics among the candidates.

"Men in Black 3" arrives 15 years after the original and 10 years after the sequel, with a plot that involves Agent K (Tommy Lee Jones) and Agent J (Will Smith) dealing with the escape of an alien named Boris the Animal. The film's most impressive achievement is the casting of Josh Brolin as the young, 1969 version of Agent K, who looks and sounds uncannily like the original. The time travel sequences, featuring Agent J crawling out on an eagle atop the Chrysler Building, are audacious and entertaining. While the film is uneven and out of touch, it has a few saving graces, including a touching final scene and a fun run-in with Andy Warhol. Despite the creakiness of its older stars, "Men in Black 3" improves considerably with the addition of Brolin and offers a fresh take on the franchise. Critics like Kenneth Turan note that the movie's plot and characters are more engaging than in previous installments, and while it may not be a masterpiece, it is enjoyable and worth watching. The film's final sequence adds a new and touching dimension to the characters of J and K, making it a worthwhile addition to the Men in Black series.

Attorney General Eric Holder denied accusations of a "cover-up" regarding the botched "Operation Fast and Furious" gun-running program, insisting there's nothing to hide and that the probe is politically motivated. Holder told a House panel that he has nothing to hide and that no one in the Justice Department authorized the controversial tactics used in the operation. He stated that he told the field to stop the tactics and that he doesn't think the situation warranted the kind of response Republicans are giving. Holder also said that no one has been punished yet in the case, despite the fact that lost guns from the operation ended up at the crime scene where U.S. Border Patrol Agent Brian Terry was murdered. The hearing came after Issa and Grassley accused top Justice officials of covering up events surrounding the operation. Republicans also released a report claiming that Justice Department officials had much greater knowledge of, and involvement in, Fast and Furious than previously acknowledged. Holder's statements did not sit well with Republican lawmakers, who accused him of intentionally withholding key documents. Rep. Dan Burton questioned Holder's having not discussed the case with Secretary of State Hillary Clinton or Homeland Security Secretary Janet Napolitano. Issa threatened to begin a contempt proceeding against Holder to force him to release more documents. The Justice Department rejected Issa's demand for certain documents, stating that the documents show "significant misunderstanding both of the documents we recently produced and of the Department's position on the issues you raise." The showdown over the botched operation continues, with Republicans investigating how high up the operation was sanctioned, while Democrats defend Holder's testimony that he did not know about it.

President Donald Trump criticized Nordstrom for discontinuing his daughter Ivanka’s clothing line, a decision the company attributed to poor sales rather than political motives. Trump’s tweets and the White House’s retweets aimed to pressure the department store, but Nordstrom’s stock actually rose nearly 5% on the day. The controversy highlighted the tension between business and politics, with Nordstrom maintaining its stance despite the backlash. Meanwhile, T.J. Maxx also dropped Ivanka’s line, further complicating the situation. The incident underscored the potential for political influence in corporate decisions and the impact of social media on stock markets.

Larry Villarin, a 62-year-old Californian, has been America's oldest male sexual surrogate for the past 35 years, helping clients overcome sexual dysfunction through one-on-one sessions. Recognized as the leading authority on Surrogate Partner Therapy since 1973, IPSA, a non-profit organization, supports a worldwide community of professionals in this field, including surrogate partners, therapists, and individuals in need of and supportive of surrogate partner therapy. Larry's work involves helping clients, ranging in age from 22 to 75, navigate emotional and physical challenges, often paired with psychological therapy. His clients include disabled individuals, abuse survivors, those from strict religious backgrounds, and even powerful judges, all seeking to overcome sexual barriers and achieve intimacy. Larry's sessions are structured in stages, starting with emotional unloading, progressing to physical touch, and eventually, blindfolded trust walks. He employs various techniques, such as playing naked games and physical exercises, to help clients open up and overcome deep-seated anxieties. For instance, he helped a 70-year-old woman who had lived her life thinking sex was a chore, breaking through her religious guilt and achieving her first orgasm. Larry's work is not without ethical challenges, as some clients fall in love with him, pushing him into tricky emotional and ethical gray areas. Despite the legal risks, including the potential for arrest, Larry remains committed to his work, seeing it as a gateway to helping clients achieve a more fulfilling life. His clients often come to him due to milestones like birthdays, feeling the pressure to finally embrace intimacy. Larry's journey with IPSA has been pivotal, as the organization supports his work and connects clients with surrogates through psychiatrists. His dedication to his clients' emotional and physical well-being underscores the profound impact of his unique profession.

Tunisia has arrested 33 members of the ousted president's family, including his wife Leila Trabelsi and her siblings, following the popular uprising that forced Zine El Abidine Ben Ali to flee to Saudi Arabia. The arrests came amid reports of the Trabelsi clan's extensive corruption and control over various sectors of the Tunisian economy, including banking, telecommunications, and media. The family's businesses were reportedly looted and burned by angry mobs, and their assets are under investigation. Tunisian authorities have also placed Zitouna Bank, owned by a son-in-law of the former president, under the control of the central bank. The ousting of the Ben Ali regime has led to a wave of retribution against his family, with many Tunisians celebrating the downfall of a regime they saw as corrupt and oppressive.

Tunisian towns along the Libyan border have opened their homes to thousands of fleeing Libyans, providing shelter and assistance despite their own economic challenges and the strain of previous refugee influxes. Since early April, about 30,000 Libyans have sought refuge in Tunisia, with many staying with local families rather than in camps. The generosity of Tunisian residents and the government has been widely praised, though the influx is putting pressure on resources. Meanwhile, the conflict between Gaddafi loyalists and rebels has spilled over into Tunisia, with Gaddafi forces briefly occupying a border crossing. The situation in Misrata, a rebel stronghold, has worsened, with reports of larger rockets causing significant damage. Rebels blame Gaddafi forces, while Gaddafi denies targeting civilians. The international community, particularly NATO, faces criticism for its role in the conflict, with some questioning the scope and legality of the intervention.

A man who jumped the White House fence on Tuesday was apprehended by uniformed Secret Service officers who approached him with guns drawn, reports CNN. The incident, broadcast live on CNN's "John King USA" program, saw the man ordered to lie down and handcuffed before being taken into custody. A backpack thrown over the fence and lying on the ground nearby was being checked by security officers, who locked down the area as a precaution. The incident ended shortly after 9 p.m. ET when authorities issued an all-clear directive at the White House. The detained man, James Dirk Crudup, 41, is homeless and will be charged with unlawful entry and contempt of court due to a previous order to stay away from the White House. The Secret Service spokesman, Ed Donovan, said Crudup was "tackled immediately" by officers. There was no immediate information on whether the intruder had represented a security threat.

On Thursday, Jurgen Klinsmann, the coach of the United States national men’s soccer team, enjoyed a gala in Berlin where he dined with President Obama, Chancellor Angela Merkel, Nobel laureates, and astronauts. The experience, Klinsmann noted, included excellent sausages. However, by Friday, Klinsmann was facing criticism for recent losses that had harmed, but not entirely eliminated, his team's chances of qualifying for the 2018 World Cup. In a subsequent interview, Klinsmann defended his coaching record, expressing confidence in his position and stating he was not worried about being replaced. This confidence, however, was short-lived, as U.S. Soccer, the governing body of soccer in the United States, announced on Monday that Klinsmann had been fired. The decision was made after top executives Sunil Gulati and Dan Flynn met with Klinsmann at a hotel in the Los Angeles area. U.S. Soccer did not immediately name Klinsmann’s successor, but it is anticipated that Bruce Arena, a veteran of Major League Soccer who previously led the national team from 1998 to 2006, will take over through the end of the current World Cup cycle. In a statement, Gulati expressed confidence in the team's players, but acknowledged that their recent performance necessitated a change in direction. He is expected to provide more details on the rationale behind Klinsmann’s dismissal during a press conference on Tuesday.

Advisers to Mitt Romney defended his sharp criticism of President Obama, arguing that the deadly protests in the Middle East would not have occurred if Romney were in office. Romney's foreign policy team, including Richard Williamson, a top adviser, contended that the situation in Egypt, Libya, and Yemen would be different under a Romney presidency. Williamson stated, "For the first time since Jimmy Carter, we’ve had an American ambassador assassinated." They highlighted a perceived lack of American resolve and the inability to protect American property abroad. Romney's aggressive stance on foreign policy contrasted with the criticism he faced for his comments during the unrest in U.S. embassies in Egypt and Libya. 

The Obama administration faced criticism for its handling of the situation, particularly for President Obama's statement that Egypt was not an ally, which was difficult to explain. Romney's campaign defended his aggressive approach, suggesting that a Romney presidency would have taken different steps in the Middle East, such as supporting those shortchanged by the Obama administration and promoting pluralism, respect for law, and human dignity. Romney's advisers also criticized Obama's handling of Iran, Syria, and Egypt, arguing that his approach was too cautious and risk-averse.

Romney himself tried to refocus on his economic message, avoiding direct mention of Obama, but still suggested that Obama was a weak commander in chief. Romney's campaign hoped to capitalize on foreign policy as a potential advantage, given Obama's perceived weaknesses in this area. Romney's advisers emphasized the need for a clear vision for the future of the Middle East, contrasting it with Obama's approach. They also criticized Obama's handling of the situation in Syria, where 20,000 people had been killed, and suggested that a Romney presidency would have taken a more proactive stance.

In a chaotic shooting at a Tucson Safeway, four ordinary citizens—Bill Badger, Patricia Maisch, Roger Salzgeber, and Joseph Zamudio—quickly reacted to thwart the alleged gunman, Jared Loughner, saving numerous lives. Maisch, a 61-year-old grandmother, noticed Loughner reloading his gun and grabbed the magazine, creating a distraction that allowed others to subdue him. Badger, a 74-year-old retired Army colonel, described tackling Loughner and securing him on the ground. Salzgeber and Zamudio also joined in, holding down the gunman. The four heroes' actions prevented the shooter from reloading and potentially killing more. Six people died, and 14 were injured, including U.S. Representative Gabrielle Giffords. The incident highlights the importance of quick thinking and action in the face of danger. Law enforcement praised the bystanders' efforts, emphasizing the role of ordinary citizens in preventing greater tragedy. Sheriff Clarence Dupnik criticized the political climate, suggesting that the "vitriol" in rhetoric may contribute to such acts of violence.

A substitute teacher accused of being drunk at Brookland-Cayce High School in Irmo, South Carolina, was not an employee of the Lexington School District Two, according to the district's statement. On March 10, 2017, an administrator reported the substitute, Judith Elizabeth Richards-Gartee, 52, to the School Resource Officer after she was observed behaving erratically and under the influence of alcohol. The district promptly removed her from the classroom and she was later found in possession of an open container of alcohol. She was charged with disorderly conduct and released to paramedics, who took her to the hospital. The incident was handled by the Lexington County Sheriff's Department, which declined to release further details. The substitute works for Kelly Services, which contracts with the district to provide substitute teachers.

James Gandolfini, best known for his iconic portrayal of Tony Soprano on HBO's "The Sopranos," has died at the age of 51. Gandolfini, who was vacationing in Rome, Italy, passed away from a possible heart attack. The actor, a three-time Emmy winner, was set to participate in the 59th Taormina Film Festival in Sicily. "The Sopranos," which Gandolfini starred in from 1999 to 2007, was a groundbreaking series that transformed cable television and earned him widespread acclaim. His performance as Tony Soprano, a complex and flawed character, was pivotal in the show's success. Gandolfini's career extended beyond "The Sopranos," with roles in films such as "Zero Dark Thirty," "The Incredible Burt Wonderstone," and "Not Fade Away." He also produced documentaries and starred in stage productions. "We're all in shock and feeling immeasurable sadness at the loss of a beloved member of our family," HBO said in a statement. "He was special, a great talent, but more importantly a gentle and loving person who treated everyone with equal respect." Gandolfini's death has left a void in the entertainment industry, with many of his co-stars and colleagues expressing their grief and admiration for his talent and character.

President Donald Trump and North Korea’s Kim Jong Un signed a document after their historic summit in Singapore, committing both nations to work together for peace. The two leaders, who previously traded insults and threats, now shook hands and exchanged mutual compliments. Trump also took Kim on a tour of Singapore’s waterfront, including a visit to the futuristic Gardens by the Bay and the Marina Bay Sands hotel. Trump expressed optimism about the summit, stating that it had gone better than expected. However, U.S. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo cautioned that the outcome remained uncertain, emphasizing the need for North Korea to move toward complete, verifiable, and irreversible denuclearization. While North Korea’s state-run KCNA news agency heralded the summit as part of a “changed era,” experts remain skeptical about the prospects for a comprehensive agreement. Trump and Kim are expected to hold a one-on-one meeting and have lunch together on the small island of Sentosa. The summit marks a significant shift in U.S.-North Korea relations, but the path to a lasting peace and denuclearization remains fraught with challenges.

France's National Assembly approved a controversial bill allowing same-sex couples to marry and adopt, voting 329 to 229. The legislation must now pass the Senate before becoming law. This marks a significant step for French gay rights advocates, with President François Hollande's Socialist Party controlling both chambers. The bill redefines marriage as a contract between two people, aligning France with 11 other countries that have legalized same-sex marriage. However, the measure faces strong opposition from the Roman Catholic Church and social conservatives, who argue it would undermine traditional family values. Despite polls showing a majority of French people favor gay marriage, the issue remains deeply divisive. France's move is seen as a major social reform, following the abolition of the death penalty in 1981.

Family and friends of Christina Grimmie, the 22-year-old singer who was fatally shot by a deranged fan at a concert in Orlando, Florida, have expressed their gratitude for the outpouring of support and generosity they have received. In a statement, Grimmie's parents and brother, Bud, Tina, and Marcus Grimmie, wrote, "The outpouring of love and generosity that has been displayed to our family throughout these last few weeks has far exceeded anything we could have ever imagined." They also mentioned that a GoFundMe page set up by manager Brian Teefey has raised over $100,000 for funeral expenses. Adam Levine, Grimmie's coach on The Voice, offered to pay for her funeral and plane ticket, a gesture that her brother Marcus described as "blown away." The tragic incident occurred on June 10 after Grimmie had opened for the band Before You Exit at The Plaza Live. She was shot while signing autographs after the show, and her brother tackled the gunman, who then fatally shot himself. The family stated, "She will live on in our hearts forever," and they plan to take their time in determining the best ways to honor Christina moving forward.

Harrison Ford, the 72-year-old actor known for his roles in "Star Wars" and "Indiana Jones," was involved in a plane crash that occurred on March 5, 2015, at a Venice golf course. According to a publicist, Ford was piloting a vintage World War II-era plane when he reported engine trouble shortly after takeoff from the Santa Monica Airport. He attempted to return to the airport but had to make an emergency landing on the golf course. Eyewitnesses reported that the plane clipped a tree before crashing. Emergency responders, including a doctor who happened to be on the course, assisted Ford, who sustained multiple gashes to his head and was treated for moderate injuries. Ford's son, Ben, tweeted that his father was "battered, but OK" and "an incredibly strong man." The pilot was conscious and alert when taken to the hospital, where he was listed in fair to moderate condition. This incident is not the first time Ford has encountered aviation-related mishaps; he has crash-landed a vintage plane on a golf course in 2015 and a helicopter in 1999. Despite these incidents, Ford remains an experienced pilot with a history of compliance with aviation regulations.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has issued a warning letter to 23andMe, ordering the company to halt sales of its Personal Genome Service (PGS) genetic testing kit. The FDA claims the tests have not been proven effective and could mislead people about their health, potentially leading to unnecessary or ineffective treatments. Since 2009, the FDA has been working with 23andMe to comply with regulatory requirements, but the company has failed to provide the necessary scientific data to support its claims. Despite multiple meetings, emails, and detailed feedback, 23andMe has not validated the PGS for its intended uses. The company, founded by Anne Wojcicki, offers a saliva-based test that detects over 240 genetic conditions and traits, including heart disease and breast cancer. 23andMe has 15 days to respond with a plan to address the FDA's concerns or face regulatory actions such as civil fines or injunctions. The FDA's action highlights a broader debate about the regulation of direct-to-consumer genetic tests and the potential health risks associated with these unvalidated tests.

An Egyptian blogger was sentenced to three years in prison and hard labor for claiming that 45% of married women are ready for "immorality" and can cheat on their husbands, reports CNN. The controversial statement, made on a television show in December, sparked a public outcry and led to his arrest. State-run newspaper Al-Ahram reported that the court found his comments would harm public peace and damage public interest. However, prominent rights lawyer Gamal Eid argued that such criticism does not constitute a crime. This case is part of a broader crackdown on free speech in Egypt under President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi, who has overseen a series of arrests and sentences targeting artists, writers, and intellectuals. For instance, author Ahmed Naji was sentenced to two years in prison for publishing a sex scene in a literary magazine, while TV presenter Islam Behery and writer Fatma Naoot also faced imprisonment for "defaming religious symbols" and "defaming Islam," respectively. These incidents have raised concerns about the future of free expression in the country, with many activists fearing that the government is using legal and extralegal means to silence critics and control public discourse. The cases of el-Sobky and others highlight the tension between the state's efforts to maintain social order and the demands for individual freedoms and protections under the law.

Rosemont authorities have concluded their investigation into the death of 19-year-old Kenneka Jenkins, ruling her death accidental. Jenkins was found dead in a walk-in freezer at the Crowne Plaza Chicago O'Hare Hotel on September 10, nearly 24 hours after she had attended a party. The Cook County Medical Examiner's office determined her cause of death to be hypothermia, with alcohol intoxication and the use of a drug for treating epilepsy and migraines listed as significant contributing factors. Police Chief Donald Stephens III stated, "Our detectives reported no signs of foul play throughout the whole investigation. There is no evidence that Ms. Jenkins was forced to drink alcohol or consume any narcotics while at the hotel." The investigation involved retracing Jenkins' path, reviewing surveillance video, and interviewing most of the party attendees. Jenkins was last seen staggering through the hotel hallways, alone and visibly impaired, before entering a kitchen area. Surveillance footage showed her entering the kitchen but did not capture her entering the freezer. The medical examiner noted that while Jenkins was alone, the hotel kitchen had only one entrance, which was monitored by a security camera. No signs of external or internal trauma were found, and toxicology tests revealed alcohol and the epilepsy/migraine medication topiramate in her system. The release of a series of graphic postmortem photographs taken in the freezer raised questions for Jenkins' family, who called them "graphic and disturbing images" and "personal, private, and indecent." The family's attorneys accused the police of withholding information and suggested the photos raised more questions than answers. Rosemont police also identified two individuals who had booked the hotel room with a fraudulent credit card and are believed to be affiliated with a gang on the West Side of Chicago. The case remains under investigation, and authorities have released a 3D digital image of the kitchen to document the layout for potential future reference.

In a bizarre incident, a drunk passenger attempted to enter the cockpit of an Indian aircraft on the grounds of needing to charge his mobile phone, according to airline officials. The incident occurred on September 24, 2018, as the plane was preparing to depart from Mumbai for Kolkata. The unruly passenger, believed to be around 35 years old, was removed from the flight and handed over to the police station, where he was questioned but later released without charge. The airline spokesperson stated that the operating IndiGo flight 6E-395 initiated the offloading of the passenger due to security concerns. Passengers are strictly prohibited from entering the cockpit of a commercial flight.

In a similar incident, a first-time flyer on a GoAir flight from New Delhi to Patna on September 22 tried to open the plane's rear door, mistaking it for the toilet. Another passenger noticed the man's actions and alerted the crew, who managed to handle the situation safely. The man was subsequently handed over to the police after the plane landed in Patna. While it is believed he would not have been able to open the door due to the air pressure in the cabin, the incident highlights the importance of passenger compliance with standard operating procedures.

Additionally, in a separate incident last week, more than 30 passengers were hospitalized with symptoms including nosebleeds, headaches, and ear pain after crew members on a Jaipur-bound flight forgot to pressurize the cabin. This incident underscores the critical role of proper cabin pressurization in ensuring passenger safety during flights. These series of events emphasize the need for heightened security measures and the importance of passengers adhering to airline protocols.

The U.S. Olympic Committee (USOC) is set to hold a hearing that could lead to the dissolution of USA Gymnastics, the national governing body for the sport, after the organization decided not to surrender its status voluntarily. The USOC initiated a complaint 16 days ago, seeking to remove USA Gymnastics’ recognition as a national body following the sexual abuse of hundreds of female athletes by former national team doctor Lawrence Nassar. In a statement, USOC CEO Sarah Hirshland said the decision to seek revocation was not taken lightly but is necessary to ensure the organization meets the standards expected. USA Gymnastics has not voluntarily given up its status, leading to the hearing process. The next steps involve selecting a three-person panel to hear the USOC's complaint, with USA Gymnastics having the opportunity to present evidence and arguments. The panel will issue a report and make a recommendation to the USOC’s board of directors, which will make the final decision. The process could take several weeks to months. USA Gymnastics has continued to operate as usual, but if stripped of its NGB status, the USOC would take control of elite programs until a new NGB is identified. The organization has faced numerous challenges, including the departure of three CEOs since the Nassar scandal broke, and ongoing issues with sponsors and medical records. The USOC has revoked NGB status only three times before, with USA Gymnastics facing significant scrutiny for its handling of the Nassar case and other missteps.

Rocky 7, or "Creed," introduces new characters while honoring the enduring appeal of the Rocky franchise, offering a fresh take on the boxing genre. The film follows Adonis Johnson Creed, the son of Apollo Creed, as he aspires to become a boxing champion. Apollo, who died in the ring, left behind a legacy that Adonis seeks to live up to. Adonis travels to Philadelphia to reconnect with his late father’s best friend, Rocky Balboa, who is now retired. Rocky agrees to train Adonis, guiding him through the rigorous physical and mental challenges of the sport.

Michael B. Jordan delivers a compelling performance as Adonis, portraying a character who is both conflicted and determined. Adonis’s journey is marked by his reluctance to fight, stemming from the tragic death of his father in the ring. Rocky, played by Sylvester Stallone, returns to his iconic role with a touching and deeply felt performance. Stallone’s portrayal is sly and endearing, emphasizing the character’s softer side. The training montages, featuring both Adonis and Rocky, capture the natural rhythm of the sport and highlight the mentor-mentee relationship between the two.

Tessa Thompson plays Adrian, Adonis’s girlfriend, adding depth to the narrative with her honest and supportive presence. The film’s plot unfolds through a series of key fight scenes, each designed to test Adonis’s resolve and character. The climactic title fight triggers a cathartic glee, but the story’s most impactful moment comes as Rocky and Adonis slowly ascend the steps of the Philadelphia Museum of Art, evoking a nostalgic and emotional conclusion.

The film’s moral stance is clear and consistent, emphasizing the internal struggle and self-discovery that Adonis undergoes. It is a blend of classic boxing drama and modern narrative techniques, making it both familiar and fresh. The marketing department’s promise of a brutal boxing melodrama is not what viewers get, but the result is an excellent sequel that pays homage to its predecessors while introducing new elements. The film’s finale, with its stirring imagery and emotional resonance, leaves viewers with a sense of fulfillment and a renewed appreciation for the Rocky franchise.

Tiger Woods is planning to return to the PGA tour in the spring, RadarOnline.com reports. He is undergoing rehab for sexual addiction at Pine Grove Behavioral Health and Addiction Services in Hattiesburg, Mississippi, a six-week program directed by Dr. Patrick Carnes. Woods, devastated by his cheating scandal, aims to return to golf and prove he has changed. His wife Elin has not visited him at the rehab facility, fueling speculation about their marriage. Woods, linked to at least 14 women, hopes to be ready for the Masters in April. His return is seen as a way to regain trust from sponsors and fans.

The search for three missing children from the Hart family continues as authorities piece together the family's final days. The Hart family, consisting of two mothers and six adopted children, was last seen in the Newport, Oregon, area around 8:15 a.m. on March 24, about two days before their GMC Yukon SUV plunged off a California cliff, killing five family members. Surveillance footage from a Safeway in Fort Bragg, California, on March 25, shows Jennifer Hart purchasing groceries, raising questions about the whereabouts of the other family members. Authorities believe the crash was intentional, based on the absence of skid marks and data from the vehicle's software indicating a sudden acceleration. The SUV was found about 150 miles north of San Francisco, with Jennifer and Sarah Hart, both 38, inside. The bodies of three children—19-year-old Markis, 14-year-old Jeremiah, and 14-year-old Abigail—were recovered at the scene, while 15-year-old Devonte, 16-year-old Hannah, and 12-year-old Sierra remain missing. 

Neighbors and authorities have expressed concerns about the family's treatment of the children. In 2013, Alexandra Argyropoulos reported to Oregon child welfare officials that she witnessed controlling emotional abuse and cruel punishment towards the children. Argyropoulos stated that the Oregon Department of Human Services interviewed the children but found insufficient evidence to take action. More recently, Bruce and Dana DeKalb, next-door neighbors in Woodland, Washington, called Child Protective Services after Devonte, the "Free Hugs" boy, repeatedly asked them for food, alleging he was being punished by his parents. Despite these reports, authorities have not found a clear timeline of the family's movements or the exact time of the crash.
