Mayor Christian Bollwage of Elizabeth said, "If that pub was crowded and there was a lot of people there, it could have severely injured, killed and maimed many, many people." He also noted that the devices did not contain cell phones or other electronic detonators, suggesting a low-tech approach.

The discovery of the suspicious package in Elizabeth came a day after an explosion in Manhattan and an unexploded pressure cooker device found in Seaside Park, New Jersey, ahead of a Marine Corps charity run. While authorities have not definitively linked the incidents, they are investigating the possibility of a connection. New Jersey Transit service was suspended between Newark Liberty Airport and Elizabeth, and Amtrak trains were held at New York Penn Station, causing significant disruptions to the Monday morning commute.

The FBI's Newark division described the devices as "multiple improvised explosive devices," and earlier Sunday night, the FBI detained five people in Brooklyn for questioning related to the Saturday night explosion in Manhattan. Ahmad Khan Rahami, an Afghan-born American citizen, was arrested in Linden, New Jersey, on Monday after being wounded in a gunfight with police. Rahami is charged with wounding 31 people in the Chelsea bombing and planting a bomb in Seaside Park, New Jersey, which did not injure anyone. He is also accused of planting explosive devices in Elizabeth, New Jersey, which did not detonate. Rahami's defense attorney, David Patton, demanded a court appearance for his client, arguing that he has a constitutional right to a lawyer and a court appearance within two days of his arrest.

New York City Mayor Bill de Blasio and Governor Andrew Cuomo increased security measures in the city, particularly around the United Nations General Assembly, which was scheduled to convene that week. Law enforcement officials stressed that while the incidents appeared to be intentional, they were not yet ruling out the possibility of a terrorist act. The attacks in New York and New Jersey were part of a broader trend of mass attacks in the United States, including the 2013 Boston Marathon bombings and the 2016 San Bernardino and Orlando shootings. Authorities are investigating whether the attacks are connected to ISIS or other extremist groups, while also considering the possibility of lone actors motivated by similar ideologies.

As the investigation continues, the events have prompted increased vigilance and security measures in major cities, with law enforcement agencies working to identify potential threats and prevent further incidents.

The inventor of the Kalashnikov assault rifle, Mikhail Kalashnikov, who passed away in December 2013 at the age of 94, expressed deep spiritual pain and moral concerns about his creation in a letter to the head of the Russian Orthodox Church, Patriarch Kirill, before his death. In the letter, dated May 2012, Kalashnikov questioned his personal responsibility for the many lives lost due to his weapon, stating, "My spiritual pain is unbearable. I keep having the same unsolved question: if my rifle claimed people's lives, then can it be that I... a Christian and an Orthodox believer, was to blame for their deaths?" This confession came as a surprise, given his previous stance of refusing to accept responsibility for the deaths caused by his rifle. He attributed the blame to the policies of countries that acquired the weapon, rather than his own invention.

Kalashnikov, a renowned designer of assault rifles, had designed the AK-47 to defend his country during World War II, but he later expressed sadness at its use by criminals and child soldiers. The rifle, known for its simplicity and reliability, has been widely manufactured and used globally, with an estimated 100 million Kalashnikov rifles in circulation. Despite the weapon's widespread use, Kalashnikov never profited significantly from his invention, as he received numerous state honors but made little money from the rifle.

In his letter, Kalashnikov also shared that he had only recently been baptized at the age of 91, indicating a late spiritual awakening. The Russian Orthodox Church, which has been rebuilding its influence since the fall of the Soviet Union, responded to Kalashnikov's letter by stating that when weapons serve to protect the Fatherland, the Church supports both their creators and the soldiers who use them. The Church's press secretary, Cyril Alexander Volkov, emphasized that Kalashnikov had designed the rifle to defend his country, not for terrorists to use it in conflicts abroad.

Kalashnikov's legacy is complex, reflecting both the pride in his engineering achievement and the moral quandaries it raised. His letter to the Patriarch, which was published by the pro-Kremlin newspaper Izvestia, offers a rare glimpse into the personal reflections of the man who created one of the world's most iconic and widely used firearms.

In New York City, they wrote signs for four causes, including Gilda's Club, Worldwide Orphans, Youth Mentoring Connection, and Autism Speaks, and held them up for photographers to capture. Their efforts, which they undertook to draw attention to these organizations rather than themselves, have once again showcased their commitment to making a positive impact. This isn't the first time the couple has used their celebrity status to promote important causes; in 2012, they held up signs supporting cancer patients. Their message, "Good morning! We were eating and saw a group of guys with cameras outside. And so we thought, lets try this again. We dont need the attention, but these wonderful organizations do," and "Here's to the stuff that matters!" highlights their dedication to causes they believe in.

An Arkansas inmate who escaped 32 years ago from prison is now back in custody. Steven Dishman, 60, was found Sunday at a home in Springdale by the Arkansas State Police (ASP) and the Springdale Police Department and is now being held at the Varner Unit in Grady. Dishman's original term was set for seven years from December 20, 1984, when he was charged in Washington County for theft of property and burglary. He escaped on May 28, 1985, from the Benton Unit, having been held at the Cummins and Wrightsville units earlier that year. The ASP is investigating where Dishman has been since his escape and has begun questioning individuals who may have known him by another name. An anonymous tip led to his capture. Dishman will be required to finish his original sentence. Another Arkansas inmate, Joel W. Lane, was also caught Sunday after a foot chase in Pine Bluff, having escaped from a work release program while serving a sentence for simultaneous possession of drugs and a firearm and possession of a firearm by a certain person. Four prisoners remain at large as of Sunday after escaping from facilities on various dates between July 5, 1988, and Tuesday.

The body of a Massachusetts honeymooner, Josh Byrne, 30, has been recovered after he was swept away by floodwaters in Costa Rica, according to a statement from his family to NBC News affiliate WESH. Byrne and his wife, Bianca, were in Playa Dominicalito when their vehicle was caught in a flash flood while attempting to cross a bridge on Friday, October 12. Bianca managed to swim to safety, but Josh was swept away by the river. His father and brother flew to Costa Rica on Friday to assist in the search, which ended Saturday with the recovery of Josh’s remains. The family described Josh as having a "helpful and caring demeanor" and noted his ability to make friends. They expressed gratitude to the local community, Massachusetts political leaders, the Red Cross, and the U.S. Embassy and State Department for their assistance. The family has set up a GoFundMe page to help cover the costs of the proper recovery and services, and they will use the funds to pay for Josh’s services and other family matters.

David Crosby, the legendary singer-songwriter from Crosby, Stills & Nash, was involved in a car accident that injured a jogger, but the incident has a happy ending. On a Sunday afternoon, Crosby was driving his 2015 Tesla on a street near his ranch in California's Santa Ynez Valley. The 73-year-old was going the speed limit—55 miles per hour—but he was blinded by the sun, which prevented him from seeing the jogger, Jose Jimenez, 46, and his 14-year-old son. The car hit Jimenez, causing him to suffer multiple fractures, abrasions, and lacerations. Emergency responders quickly airlifted Jimenez to a hospital, where his injuries were assessed as not life-threatening. Crosby expressed his deep regret and relief that the injuries were not severe, and wished Jimenez a speedy recovery.

The incident occurred near Crosby's home, and he was reportedly devastated by the accident. According to a statement from his representative, Crosby is "obviously very upset that he accidentally hit anyone" and is "relieved that the injuries to the gentleman were not life threatening." The representative added that Crosby has been keeping a low profile in recent months, focusing on his solo career and reflecting on his past musical endeavors. The accident has brought Crosby's recent controversies back into the spotlight, including his comments about Crosby, Stills and Nash bandmate Neil Young's girlfriend, Daryl Hannah, which angered Young and led to a public rift. Crosby's representative also confirmed that Crosby, Stills and Nash would not be touring with Young again, as Young was "very angry" with Crosby and had publicly stated that he knew "at least 20 better guitar players than Neil."

The incident has sparked discussions about driver safety, particularly in areas with high sun glare, and the role of technology in modern vehicles. Crosby's accident serves as a reminder of the importance of driving safely, even in seemingly benign conditions. The singer-songwriter's representative also mentioned that Crosby had recently released a new solo album, Croz, and had been working with Crosby, Stills and Nash, though he had also been exploring new musical projects outside the group. The incident has once again thrust Crosby into the public eye, highlighting the enduring impact of his music and the controversies that often accompany it.

A mysterious earthquake that struck the center of the United States in 2013, known as the Wind River Earthquake, remains a puzzle for scientists due to its unusual depth and location. The magnitude 4.7 Mw earthquake occurred in Wyoming, a region typically quiet in terms of seismic activity. For the past 60 years, few earthquakes of magnitude 4 or higher have been recorded in the Wind River area, making this event particularly noteworthy. The earthquake's depth, estimated at 75 kilometers, is particularly striking, as it lies well within the Earth's mantle and is one of the deepest earthquakes recorded in a region covered by a stable continental crust. This depth is significantly deeper than the Earth's crust, which is typically no more than 40-50 kilometers thick in the Wyoming Craton, a cold, stable lithosphere that underlies much of North America.

Scientists from the PSL Research University in Paris and the UK’s Atomic Weapons Establishment have published a study in the journal Earth and Planetary Science Letters, detailing their findings. The earthquake's depth challenges current understanding of how the Earth's mantle behaves under such conditions. Typically, earthquakes occur along fault lines in the Earth's crust or as a result of magma movement in the mantle. However, the Wind River earthquake's characteristics suggest it might have been caused by tectonic forces rather than volcanic activity, which is unusual for such a deep event. This raises questions about the nature of the mantle's brittleness under the Wind River Craton and the forces that could cause it to fail.

The study's findings have implications for our understanding of seismic activity in stable continental regions. The Wind River earthquake's depth and magnitude suggest that the mantle might be more brittle than previously thought, potentially leading to more frequent or deeper earthquakes in such areas. This discovery could have significant implications for earthquake prediction and preparedness, especially in regions with similar geological structures. The mystery of the Wind River Earthquake highlights the ongoing challenges in understanding the complex dynamics of the Earth's interior and the potential for unexpected seismic events in stable continental regions.

The U.S. government proposed on Monday removing most of the world’s humpback whale populations from the endangered species list, marking a significant milestone in conservation efforts. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Fisheries aims to reclassify humpbacks into 14 distinct population segments, with 10 of these populations to be removed from the endangered list, while two will be listed as threatened, and two remain endangered. Assistant NOAA Administrator for Fisheries, Eileen Sobeck, emphasized the importance of focusing protection efforts on populations that need it the most. Humpback whales were listed as endangered in 1970, following the International Whaling Commission’s ban on commercial whaling in 1966. Since then, conservation efforts have led to a rebound in humpback whale numbers, with an estimated 100,000 individuals today. The proposal is part of a broader review initiated in 2010, which used genetic, morphological, and biogeographical data to identify distinct population segments. These segments rarely intermingle, each with its own independent history of whaling and recovery. For instance, the Arabian Sea population migrates between Yemen and India, while other populations make similar seasonal migrations but in different directions. Conservationists generally support the proposal, acknowledging that some populations remain at risk from threats such as fishing gear entanglement, ship strikes, energy development, pollution, climate change, and ocean acidification. However, they caution that the removal of some populations from the endangered list does not mean they are fully protected. The public has 90 days to comment on the proposed changes, with the final decision expected next year. This reclassification is seen as a conservation success story, highlighting the effectiveness of coordinated efforts to protect and recover endangered species.

Republican presidential candidate Donald Trump, whose controversial comments about Mexican immigrants have garnered significant backlash, addressed large crowds in Phoenix and Las Vegas, delivering speeches that alternated between harsh criticism of immigration policies and expressions of respect for the Mexican people. At a Libertarian gathering in Las Vegas, Trump accused Mexico of sending violent offenders to the U.S., while in Phoenix, he took a more conciliatory tone, stating, "I love the Mexican people. I love 'em." However, he quickly returned to his critical stance, emphasizing the need to secure the border and criticizing U.S. officials for being "dumb" in dealing with illegal immigrants.

Trump’s speeches were filled with insults directed at critics, including business partners such as Univision and NBC, which have dropped him in the wake of his inflammatory remarks. He also mocked other Republican candidates, including Jeb Bush, whom he called "weak on immigration," and Hillary Clinton, whom he labeled "the worst secretary of state in the history of the country." His supporters, many of whom blame illegal immigrants for crime and economic problems, rallied behind him, with one man shouting, "Build a wall!" during his Phoenix speech.

Despite the criticism, Trump’s rhetoric has resonated with a significant portion of the Republican base, particularly in states like Arizona, where anti-immigration sentiment is strong. Sheriff Joe Arpaio, known for his tough stance on illegal immigration, introduced Trump in Phoenix, praising his tough immigration policies. However, Trump’s aggressive stance on immigration has also drawn ire from party leaders, who fear that his divisive rhetoric could damage the broader appeal of the Republican nominee in the general election.

Trump’s campaign strategy seems to be centered on reinvigorating the “silent majority” and emphasizing his ability to take decisive action against illegal immigration. He has proposed a $100,000 fine per illegal immigrant and has called for a comprehensive crackdown on sanctuary cities. His supporters, like Jan Drake, 72, who lives in a retirement community outside Phoenix, believe that Trump would be a strong president who would not kowtow to anyone. Drake said, “The Republican Party will try to squeeze him out because they’re afraid of him. But he can tell them where to go — to pound sand.”

While Trump’s supporters are enthusiastic, his critics argue that his rhetoric could alienate a broader electorate. Republican strategists suggest that candidates like Jeb Bush and Marco Rubio can address the concerns of the Republican base on immigration while also appealing to a wider audience. However, as Trump continues to dominate the headlines, his impact on the Republican primary race and the party’s image remains a significant concern.

Nutrition plays a critical role in ensuring the health and success of astronauts on long-duration space missions, as highlighted in a recent publication by Scott M. Smith, Ph.D., manager for NASA's Nutritional Biochemistry Lab. The importance of proper nutrition is underscored by the fact that without it, the mission could fail. Astronauts face unique challenges in maintaining a healthy diet in space, including reduced appetite due to being busy and experiencing menu fatigue. The spaceflight environment itself also poses additional nutritional challenges, such as microgravity, higher radiation exposure, elevated carbon dioxide levels, and variations in temperature and humidity, all of which can impact health. Nutrition is vital for counteracting various effects of spaceflight, such as bone and muscle loss, cardiovascular degradation, immune function impairment, neurovestibular changes, and vision changes.

To assess the impact of spaceflight on nutrition, astronauts provide blood and urine samples before, during, and after their missions. These samples are used to create biochemical profiles that help researchers understand the changes in the body's requirements for nutrients. The Twins Study, which involves comparing Scott Kelly, who spent a year in space, to his identical twin brother Mark, who remained on Earth, provides a unique opportunity to track nutritional status over time. This study is part of a broader effort to maintain the health of astronauts during extended space missions, such as a potential journey to Mars, which could last up to 30 months or more.

Maintaining nutritional health is essential for astronauts, as it helps counteract the negative effects of space travel. However, the precise ways in which nutrition impacts the human body in space are still being studied. The research findings could also benefit Earth-based health, as they may help physicians design treatments or exercises for people with limited mobility. The future of spaceflight includes long-duration missions that require a robust understanding of how the human body adapts to microgravity and radiation. The Biochemical Profile project examines nutritional markers such as proteins, vitamins, minerals, bone markers, hormones, metabolites, immune function, antioxidants, and general chemistry to better understand these changes.

In summary, nutrition is a critical component of ensuring the health and success of astronauts on long-duration space missions. The challenges of maintaining a healthy diet in space, combined with the unique effects of the spaceflight environment, underscore the importance of ongoing research to understand and address these issues. The Twins Study and other research efforts aim to provide valuable insights that can help keep astronauts healthy during extended space missions and potentially benefit Earth-based health care.

A suspected jewelry store robber, described as a brunette, white woman in her 20s or 30s, 5-foot-8 and 130 pounds, is believed to have committed six armed robberies across Florida, Georgia, South Carolina, Tennessee, and North Carolina since April. The most recent incident occurred on Monday at a Jared Vault in Mebane, North Carolina, where she forced two employees into a back room at gunpoint, zip-tied their hands, and stole an undisclosed amount of jewelry. The total value of stolen goods exceeds $450,000. Authorities also believe a male accomplice, a black man in his 30s or 40s, 6 feet tall, and 250 pounds, was involved in three of the robberies. Both suspects are considered armed and dangerous. The FBI is urging anyone with information to contact them at 1-800-CALL-FBI (225-5324).

Microsoft's Surface, the company's first tablet, has generated mixed reactions. The device, with its sleek design and innovative features, has been praised for its industrial aesthetics and thoughtful engineering. The Surface, available in both Windows RT and Windows 8 Pro versions, offers a unique blend of tablet and laptop functionality, promising a seamless transition between the two. The 10.6-inch screen, while not as sharp as the iPad's Retina display, provides a vibrant and colorful experience. The kickstand, a clever design that allows the tablet to function as a makeshift laptop, has received positive reviews for its ease of use and stability.

The Touch Cover, a magnetic keyboard that snaps onto the tablet, has been both celebrated and criticized. While it offers a seamless integration with the device, the lack of tactile feedback and the tendency to skip letters during rapid typing have been noted. The Type Cover, a more traditional keyboard option, addresses these issues but adds bulk to the device. Both covers are designed to be easily removable, allowing users to switch between tablet and laptop modes effortlessly.

The operating system, Windows RT, presents a significant challenge. While it offers a touch-friendly interface and some familiar apps like Office, it is limited in its compatibility with traditional Windows programs and third-party apps. This restriction has led to a relatively sparse app selection, with many popular apps missing. Microsoft's promise of a more robust Windows 8 Pro version, which will run full Windows applications, has generated anticipation but also skepticism.

The hardware specifications of the Surface are impressive, with ports and jacks that exceed those of the iPad. The device's battery life, while adequate, falls short of the iPad's. The absence of a cellular version and the inability to charge from a computer's USB port are minor inconveniences. The Surface's design, with its magnesium case and kickstand, has been well-received, but the touch keyboard's lack of tactile feedback has been a point of contention.

The Surface's reception has been largely positive, with many users appreciating its innovative design and potential. However, the software limitations and the lack of a full Windows experience have dampened enthusiasm. The device's success will likely depend on the growth of the Windows Store and the development of a more comprehensive app ecosystem. For now, the Surface represents a bold step forward for Microsoft in the tablet market, but its future remains uncertain.

A dispute has erupted over access to hiking trails in Colorado, with a man named Charles D. Goodman suing media mogul Oprah Winfrey for allegedly blocking trail access to his property. Goodman claims that easements allowing residents to use the trails were erased by Winfrey's Yellow Brick Road company, the former owners Hoyt and Carol Barnett, and the town of Mountain Village, who sold the land for $10.9 million in March. Mountain Village denies the accusation, stating that the correction only cleared up ambiguities and that they wish to continue allowing trail access. Winfrey's spokeswoman, Wendy Luckenbill, said the company will work with neighbors to ensure "reasonable" access for portions of the land. The trails were established in 1989 after negotiations between Goodman and the U.S. Forest Service, which owned the land at the time. Goodman's lawsuit highlights the tension between property owners and long-time residents over access to natural resources and recreational areas. Meanwhile, Winfrey is planning to build a mansion and guest home on the property, which will require cutting down an estimated 800 to 1,000 trees to comply with the town's wildfire mitigation policies. The project is set to begin this summer, and plans for the homes have not yet been submitted. The dispute over trail access has drawn attention to the ongoing challenges of balancing property rights with the needs of local communities and the preservation of natural resources.

Syria's civil war, now in its third year, has seen a significant development with the merger between al-Qaeda's Iraqi affiliate and the most effective Syrian rebel faction, Jabhat al-Nusra, forming the "Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant." This union, announced by the leader of al-Qaeda in Iraq, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, in a 21-minute audio message, has raised concerns and complexities in the ongoing conflict. The Syrian government has seized upon this news to assert that the opposition is a foreign-backed terrorist plot. However, the merger has also complicated the Western powers' covert efforts to support more secular rebel groups and army defectors, as Jabhat al-Nusra's ties with al-Qaeda are unlikely to prompt a shift in international support for the broader Syrian opposition. The U.S. has designated Jabhat al-Nusra as a terrorist organization, and the Obama administration's non-lethal aid package for the Syrian opposition remains contentious, with the potential for weapons to fall into the hands of extremist groups. Al-Nusra's leader, Abu Mohammed al-Golani, attempted to distance himself from the merger, claiming he was not consulted and pledging allegiance to al-Qaeda's leader, Ayman al-Zawahiri, instead. This move aimed to reassure Syrians that the group remains dedicated to ousting Assad and is not beholden to non-Syrian interests. The merger has also raised fears of increased cooperation between the groups, with Iraqi officials noting shared military training compounds, logistics, intelligence, and weapons. The Syrian opposition's common goal of toppling Assad remains paramount, but the merger highlights the growing influence of al-Qaeda in the Levant and the challenges faced by the international community in supporting the Syrian rebels without exacerbating the threat of extremism.

The owner of Eva Restaurant in Los Angeles, Mark Gold, has implemented a unique policy to encourage diners to put away their phones during meals. By leaving their devices at the door, customers can enjoy a 5% discount on their bill. Gold, who runs a 40-person space with European flair, hopes this initiative will foster a more intimate and distraction-free dining experience. "For us, it's really not about people disrupting other guests. Eva is home, and we want to create that environment of home, and we want people to connect again," he explained. The policy has garnered significant attention, with the Associated Press reporting on it and leading to interviews with major outlets like CNN and Good Morning America. While the policy has not yet translated to a substantial increase in business, Gold believes it could boost sales once school resumes. The restaurant's approach to managing smartphone usage during meals has resonated with many, as evidenced by the numerous emails from other business owners expressing interest in adopting similar policies.

European airlines, including Lufthansa, Air Berlin, and Air France, extended their flight cancellations to Tel Aviv due to safety concerns amid the ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas. The U.S. Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) initially banned American airlines from flying to Tel Aviv for 24 hours after a Hamas rocket struck near the airport. The ban was extended through midday Thursday. The European Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) also recommended that airlines avoid operating flights to and from Tel Aviv. Lufthansa and Air Berlin canceled flights through Thursday, while Air France suspended flights "until further notice." KLM, Alitalia, and Scandinavian Airlines also canceled flights. British Airways, however, continued its twice-daily flights to Tel Aviv, citing the airport's security measures. The U.S. ban on flights to Tel Aviv was criticized by Michael Bloomberg, who said the airport is the most secure in the world. The U.S. Secretary of State, John Kerry, arrived in Israel on a mission to stop hostilities. The flight suspensions have left some travelers stranded in Tel Aviv, while others were forced to seek shelter during sirens. The cancellations are a significant blow to Israel's economy, particularly its tourism industry, which saw a record 1.4 million visitors in the first half of 2014. Israel's Transport Ministry opened a small airport in the far southeast of the country to accommodate some travelers. The Israeli government maintained that the security at Ben Gurion International Airport is robust, with the Iron Dome defense system effectively protecting the airport. Despite the flight cancellations, the airport is still expecting 206 flights on Wednesday, with 6,000 flights having landed and departed at Ben Gurion since the conflict began.

The New York Jets cheerleaders, known as the Flight Crew, have reached a $325,000 settlement in a class-action lawsuit against the team. The deal, approved in a New Jersey court, will provide each of the 52 squad members with $2,500 per season for the 2012-13 and 2013-14 NFL seasons. Additionally, cheerleaders who participated in photo shoots are eligible for an extra $400 per shoot. Former cheerleader Krystal C. filed the initial lawsuit in 2014, alleging that the women were paid only $150 per game and nothing for practice time. Her attorney, Patricia Pierce, argued that the actual hourly pay was well below the minimum wage, citing the required hair, makeup, and transportation expenses. The Jets denied the claims and stated that the settlement was reached to avoid the costs and distraction of litigation. State Senator Diane Savino praised the settlement and called for the Buffalo Bills to follow suit, ensuring fair pay and treatment for their cheerleaders. Savino also urged the NFL to develop uniform rules to ensure all cheerleaders receive proper employee protections. The settlement comes as other NFL teams, including the Cincinnati Bengals, Tampa Bay Buccaneers, Oakland Raiders, and Buffalo Bills, have also faced similar lawsuits.

A New Mexico obstetrician-gynecologist, Dr. Christopher Driskill, faces severe accusations and potential license revocation for multiple infractions, including having sex with patients, drinking alcohol at work, and abandoning women during labor. Driskill, 42, is a married father of four and the incoming president of the New Mexico Medical Society. The New Mexico Medical Board suspended his license, citing his actions as a "clear and immediate danger to the public."

The board's report details a series of troubling incidents. Driskill allegedly kept a stash of alcohol in his office and drank on the job, even working while under the influence. He had multiple sexual relationships with patients and former staff members, and wrote lewd notes in medical charts. In one instance, he was reportedly absent from a labor room because he was having sex with another patient, leaving a woman in labor unattended. Driskill also allegedly abandoned women during emergency C-sections, once missing a birth because he was busy with a patient.

Driskill's actions extend beyond just sexual misconduct and alcohol abuse. He failed to inform his employers, Premier Health and Lea Regional Medical Center, of his termination from Premier Health, despite requesting a leave of absence. He was fired from Premier Health in August and had not returned to work since, yet he did not disclose this information to the medical board.

The board's decision to suspend Driskill's license is based on his "sexual relationships and abuse of alcohol," which they claim have negatively impacted his practice of medicine. As the incoming president of the New Mexico Medical Society, Driskill's actions have raised significant concerns about the integrity of the medical profession. The society's representative stated that they would not comment on the matter until after the hearing, leaving the future of Driskill's medical career uncertain.

A baby with Down syndrome named Leo Forrest, born in Armenia, is being reunited with his Kiwi father, Samuel Forrest, after his mother abandoned him. Leo’s father, who works as a freelance business contractor, was given an ultimatum by his wife: either send Leo away or get a divorce. In Armenia, where families often abandon children with disabilities, it is common for parents to reject their Down syndrome babies. Leo’s mother, Ruzan Badalyan, reportedly refused to look at or touch Leo, fearing emotional attachment. The GoFundMe page set up by Samuel to help bring his son back to New Zealand has received overwhelming support, raising over $160,000 in just two hours. The New Zealand government has expedited Leo’s citizenship and passport process. Samuel, who works in Auckland, plans to move with Leo to New Zealand, where he hopes to find support from family and friends. Samuel has been working with disability awareness groups to share his story and advocate for better education and understanding of children with special needs. He emphasizes that children with Down syndrome are just as normal as any other child, despite societal labels. "After what I've been through with Leo, I'm not going to sit back and watch babies be sent to orphanages," he said. "As a child with Down syndrome, that becomes somewhat of a label. If we can get around this label, we’ll see that they’re normal. They’re a little different from us, but they’re still normal. They all have niches and I want to work hard to find out where Leo's special."

George Zimmerman's attempt to sell the gun he used to shoot and kill Trayvon Martin has taken an unexpected turn. News 6 reports that the online auction on UnitedGunGroup.com, which was open to the public and generated bids of over $120,000, was actually a fake auction. According to United Gun Group, they had at least one verified offer of $120,000 and 22 pre-qualified bidders on a private auction. The highest bid on the fake auction site was near $140,000, with 180 bids from nine online users. The winning bidder on the fake auction was listed as John Smith. United Gun Group had two auctions running simultaneously to "troll the trolls," and this time, it worked. The real auction, which was private, had 42 bids in total. Zimmerman has not yet revealed the identity of the real winner, stating that he will give an interview if his stipulations are met, which include being put up in a four-star hotel and receiving $1,000 a day. In his statement, Zimmerman thanked God for the successful auction, which raised funds for several worthy causes, and expressed gratitude to Todd Underwood and UnitedGunGroup.com for hosting the auction. He also acknowledged the support from members of UnitedGunGroup and former members of GunBroker AKA GunJoker.com who terminated their relationship with the Nazi-loving, liberal liars at Gunbroker.com. The Kel-Tec PF-9 pistol, which was used in the shooting, still carries the case number from his trial in silver permanent marker. The gun was first listed on a different website last week, prompting worldwide headlines and controversy, leading to the auction being pulled from the site. The Trayvon Martin Foundation declined to comment on the sale of the gun.

PennLive/The Patriot-News faced a backlash after announcing a policy to limit the publication of letters and op-Eds opposing same-sex marriage in the wake of the U.S. Supreme Court's decision legalizing gay marriage nationwide. Editor Seth Meyers and his team issued a statement emphasizing the importance of civil discourse, but the response was overwhelmingly hostile. Critics accused the newspaper of being "fascists" and violating the First Amendment. Meyers acknowledged that while the First Amendment is a fundamental right, it must be exercised civilly. He stressed that the policy applies to all viewpoints, including those with deeply held religious and moral objections, as long as they are expressed respectfully. The incident highlighted the ongoing tensions surrounding the issue of same-sex marriage and the challenges of fostering a civil debate in the face of strong opposition. Meyers stood by his decision, emphasizing that the Opinion pages belong to the people of Central Pennsylvania and should reflect a wide range of views, including those of his gay and lesbian colleagues. Despite the controversy, Meyers maintained that the policy was intended to promote respectful dialogue and ensure that all voices are heard.

Archaeologists have uncovered a mysterious large cavity within the Great Pyramid of Giza, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. This cavity, which stretches for at least 30 meters, lies above the grand gallery, a significant ascending corridor connecting the Queen’s chamber to the King’s chamber in the heart of the pyramid. This discovery marks the first major internal structure found in the pyramid since the 19th century. The cavity’s dimensions are comparable to the grand gallery, suggesting it may have played a structural role, such as relieving weight on the grand gallery below. However, its exact purpose remains unclear.

Scientists from Nagoya University in Japan, KEK, and CEA, France’s energy research organization, used muon detection techniques to pinpoint the cavity. Muons, particles produced when cosmic rays collide with the Earth's atmosphere, were used to sense density changes inside the pyramid. The muon detectors, placed around the Queen’s chamber and trained from the outside, confirmed the presence of a large void in the same location. The cavity is not obviously accessible, and its exact nature—whether a single chamber or a series of smaller spaces—is still unknown.

The Great Pyramid, also known as Khufu’s Pyramid or the Pyramid of Cheops, was constructed in the 4th dynasty by Pharaoh Khufu, who reigned from 2509 to 2483 BC. The monument stands 140 meters tall and contains three known chambers: a subterranean one at the base, the Queen’s chamber at the center, and the King’s chamber above. The King’s chamber houses a granite sarcophagus, but King Khufu’s mummy and any grave goods are missing, having been looted long ago.

Mehdi Tayoubi, from the HIP Institute in Paris, a non-profit organization that uses new technology to study and preserve cultural heritage, emphasized the importance of the discovery. “This big void is there; that it is impressive; and that it was not expected as far as I know by any sort of theory,” he stated. The team is now calling on experts in ancient Egyptian architecture to propose hypotheses about the cavity’s purpose, whether to relieve weight or serve as a hitherto unknown corridor.

While the cavity’s exact role remains speculative, the discovery underscores the ongoing mysteries of the pyramids. Archaeologist Mark Lehner, a panel member reviewing ScanPyramids’ work, noted that the cavity could be a space left by the builders to protect the grand gallery’s narrow roof from the weight of the pyramid. However, he cautioned that it is currently just an anomaly and more focused exploration is needed.

Further investigation could involve sending a small flying robot into the cavity, provided the Egyptian authorities approve. The non-invasive muon detection technique, which has been used to study volcanoes, glaciers, and even nuclear reactors, has provided valuable data but leaves the pyramid intact. The discovery of this large void within the Great Pyramid of Giza is a significant contribution to our understanding of this ancient wonder, prompting further questions about the pyramid’s construction and purpose.

Officers in Denver pursued a stolen tractor through the city on Friday night, leading to a dramatic end in Lower Downtown. The tractor, towing some farm equipment, swerved through busy streets and sidewalks, striking several vehicles and buildings. Police dispatched more than a dozen cars and even a helicopter to track the tractor, which was stolen from a Denver Water facility in the Lincoln Park neighborhood. The chase concluded when a police cruiser rammed the tractor, causing the airbags to deploy. An officer used a Taser to subdue the suspect, who was then placed in an ambulance. Two officers were injured but treated and released from the hospital. The suspect's identity remains undisclosed as the investigation continues. The incident could've been much worse, as one witness noted, highlighting the bravery of the officers involved.

On the Hawaiian island of Oahu, mountains are being dissolved by groundwater, potentially reducing the island to a flat, low-lying landscape similar to Midway in the future, according to research by Brigham Young University. While external erosion typically wears down mountains, on Oahu, more material is dissolving underground than being carried away by streams. This process, influenced by variable rainfall, makes the island a unique natural laboratory. Despite current growth due to tectonic forces, Oahu will eventually see its elevation decrease as groundwater continues to dissolve the volcanic rock, a phenomenon expected to take about 1.5 million years.

Americans are at an all-time low in their approval of Congress, with only 10% of people approving of the job it is doing, according to a Gallup poll. This is the lowest approval rating in nearly 40 years of Gallup polling, and it surpasses even the unpopularity of figures like Fidel Castro, Saddam Hussein, and Mark Fuhrman. The poll highlights that Americans find almost everything more favorable than Congress, including the BP oil spill during the 2010 disaster, socialism, waterboarding, abortion, President Nixon during the Watergate scandal, and even Paris Hilton. The disapproval of Congress is so severe that more people have never believed in Santa Claus than currently approve of Congress. The poll also shows that support for the Tea Party and Occupy Wall Street movements is higher than that for Congress. While the BP oil spill had a higher approval rating than Congress during the 2010 crisis, with 16% approving of BP's handling of the spill, and socialism is three times more popular than Congress, with 33% viewing it positively, waterboarding has a 50% approval rate, and 19% support abortion being legal in all cases, which is nearly double the support for Congress. President Nixon had a 24% approval rating during the Watergate scandal, which is higher than the current Congress. The disapproval of Congress is so widespread that 86% of people disapprove of it, making it the least popular institution or entity in the Gallup poll's history.

Following through on deep constitutional concerns stated in its prior Northwest Austin decision, the Supreme Court seems poised to invalidate Section 5 of the Voting Rights Act, requiring Congress to revisit the formula for requiring preclearance of voting changes. The vote is likely to be five to four, with the more liberal members pressing the narrow argument that an Alabama county was not a proper plaintiff and the broader argument that there was a sufficient record to justify the current formula. However, the more conservative majority was not persuaded by either point. The Court's conservative wing suggested that the modern South had outgrown its troubled past and that the legal burdens on the nine states were no longer justified. Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr. asked skeptically whether "the citizens in the South are more racist than citizens in the North," while Justice Anthony M. Kennedy, whose vote is crucial, asked whether Alabama today is an "independent sovereign" or must live "under the trusteeship of the United States government." Justice Antonin Scalia said the law, once a civil rights landmark, now amounted to a "perpetuation of racial entitlement." The outcome of the case will likely remain in doubt until the end of the court’s current term, in June. If the court overturns the provision, nine states, mostly in the South, would become free to change voting procedures without first getting permission from federal officials. The four members of the court’s liberal wing, citing data and history, argued that Congress remained entitled to make the judgment that the provision was still needed in the covered jurisdictions. The law passed the Senate unanimously and the House overwhelmingly, by a vote of 390 to 33, in 2006. The central provision of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 may be in peril, as the Supreme Court’s more conservative members showed tough questioning during the argument. The case, involving a challenge to the Voting Rights Act by Shelby County, Ala., highlights the ongoing debate over whether the legal burdens on the nine states are still justified.

The 26th annual Ig Nobel Prize ceremony, a celebration of scientific studies that first make people laugh and then make them think, took place at Harvard University. Nobel laureates handed out prizes to winners, including a British man who lived as a goat for three days and a German automaker that cheated emissions tests. The ceremony, which has been held for 26 years, featured a mix of serious and absurd research, including studies on rock personalities, goat and badger experiences, and the effects of polyester trousers on rat sex lives. The winners received $10 trillion Zimbabwean bills, which are nearly worthless due to hyperinflation. Among the recipients were Charles Foster and Thomas Thwaites, who spent time living as animals, and a team that investigated how rocks are perceived. The psychology prize went to researchers who asked 1,000 liars about their lying habits, while the peace prize was awarded to philosophers who studied pseudo-profound bullshit. The biology prize was given to scientists who discovered that white horses are less likely to be bitten by horseflies, and dragonflies are attracted to black tombstones. The literature award went to a Swedish author who wrote about fly collecting, and the perception prize was for investigating how things look when viewed between one's legs. The physics prize recognized a study on why white horses are more fly-proof and why dragonflies are drawn to black gravestones. The chemistry prize was awarded to Volkswagen for its emissions cheating, and the medicine prize was for a study showing that scratching an itch on one side of the body can be relieved by looking in a mirror and scratching the other side. The ceremony, known for its chaotic atmosphere, included audience members throwing paper airplanes and real Nobel laureates handing out the prizes.

Britain's terror threat level was raised to critical following the Parsons Green tube bombing, indicating a potential imminent attack, as Theresa May made a televised statement. The blast, which injured 29 people, including a young boy, occurred as a packed District line train was stationary at Parsons Green station. May condemned the attack as "cowardly" and announced armed police and military personnel would be deployed to provide extra protection. The hunt for the bomber is ongoing, with CCTV footage and images from the scene being examined. Islamic State claimed responsibility, but the device was reportedly remotely detonated, suggesting it may not have been intended as a suicide attack. The prime minister criticized US President Donald Trump's tweet, stating it was unhelpful to speculate on an ongoing investigation. The explosion happened during the morning rush hour, and many witnesses described the panic as people tried to escape. The blast was caused by an improvised explosive device (IED), and the device's initiator appeared to have worked, but the main charge did not detonate. This is the first terrorist attack in the UK this year to not result in loss of life, following two vehicle and knife attacks and a bombing in Manchester. The area around the station was evacuated, and specialist officers secured the remains of the device. The investigation is being led by Scotland Yard's counter-terrorism command, with hundreds of detectives and MI5 involved. The threat level remains at severe, but will be reviewed. London Mayor Sadiq Khan appealed for calm, stating the city would "never be intimidated or defeated by terrorism."

Facebook users are rallying around a campaign to boycott Spirit Airlines after the carrier refused to refund the cost of a dying veteran's flight. Jerry Meekins, a 76-year-old former marine, requested a refund on his $197 flight to New Jersey to visit his daughter during a surgery, as his doctor advised him not to fly due to his terminal esophageal cancer. The "Boycott Spirit Airlines" Facebook page, which initially had about 700 likes, now boasts over 18,000 likes as of Thursday morning, according to Fox News. Many of the backlash comments come from current military members and veterans, with one commenter, Robert Twigg, stating, "I believe Spirit Airlines owes a debt to the Veteran and an apology. Being a good corporate citizen seems not to be in their culture. I will not fly them because of this. I am a proud U.S. Navy Veteran." In addition to the Facebook campaign, the Veterans of the Vietnam War and the Veterans Coalition wrote a letter to Spirit Airlines on Tuesday. The airline did not respond to a request for comment. Spirit Airlines will charge a $100 fee for carry-on bags stored in overhead bins when purchased at the airport gate, starting November 6, according to a notice on the airline’s website. The current fee is $45 for both domestic and international fliers. Overall, it will cost fliers $5 to $10 more in carry-on bag fees when purchased online, at a reservation center, an airport kiosk, or counter, or as a $9 Club Fare member. The new fees will range from $25 to $100 per carry-on bag, up from $20 to $45. The new structure aims to streamline the bag fees, making them identical for domestic and international travelers.

German police are on the hunt for thieves who made off with a refrigerated trailer containing 20 tons of Nutella, Kinder Surprise eggs, and other chocolate treats, valued at up to $80,000, in a theft that occurred over the weekend in Neustadt. The police believe the perpetrators would have needed their own truck to tow such heavy cargo, suggesting a well-planned operation. This heist comes on the heels of another trailer theft in Wittenberg, where 30 tons of fruit juice vanished. In a broader context, such chocolate thefts are not unique to Germany, with similar incidents reported in Austria and the United States. For instance, in New York City, a man stole a bakery's delivery truck and distributed bread in his underwear, while a Russian crime syndicate was charged with transporting and selling 10,000 pounds of stolen chocolate. Neustadt police urge anyone offered large quantities of chocolate through unconventional means to report it to the authorities.

French warplanes and U.N. helicopters searched the northern region of Mali for the wreckage of Air Algerie flight AH5017, which crashed while carrying 110 passengers, nearly half of them French, from Burkina Faso to Algiers. French Foreign Minister Laurent Fabius suggested the plane may have encountered bad weather after the pilot requested to change direction due to a storm shortly after takeoff. However, conflicting reports emerged from Mali and Burkina Faso regarding the location of the crash. Malian President Ibrahim Boubacar Keita claimed wreckage was found between Aguelhoc and Kidal, while General Gilbert Diendere from Burkina Faso’s crisis unit reported remains in southern Mali, 50 km from the Burkinabe border. Local authorities in the nearby town of Gossi also reported finding wreckage. French President Francois Hollande, who cancelled a planned visit to overseas territories, vowed to use all military means to locate the aircraft, emphasizing that the search would take as long as necessary. The search is complicated by the vast, sparsely inhabited region, which is under the control of Tuareg separatist rebels and has a weak government presence. The area relies on French and U.N. peacekeepers for aircraft and logistical support. The crash adds to concerns over air travel, following recent incidents involving Malaysia Airlines, a TransAsia Airways crash, and flight cancellations due to the conflict in Gaza. Swiftair, the private Spanish company that owns the MD-83, confirmed the flight lost contact with Air Algerie an hour after takeoff. The passenger list included 27 Burkinabe, 51 French, eight Lebanese, six Algerians, two from Luxembourg, five Canadians, four Germans, one Cameroonian, one Belgian, one Egyptian, one Ukrainian, one Swiss, one Nigerian, and one Malian. The MD-83, part of the McDonnell Douglas MD-80 family, has a relatively clean safety record, with five accidents since 1977, two of which caused a total of eight deaths. Air Algerie’s last major accident was in 2003 when a plane crashed shortly after take-off from Tamanrasset, killing 102 people.

A male student was fatally shot at a Mississippi State University residence hall Saturday night by three suspects who fled the scene and are still at large, school officials said. Campus police arrived at the scene within one minute of being notified of the incident, and the victim, 21-year-old John Sanderson, was taken to the hospital but died about 30 minutes later. The suspects are described as three black males who fled in a blue Crown Victoria. Mississippi State University is currently operating under advisory conditions and has set up a call center for worried parents. No arrests have been made, and the university president stated that this is the first time a student has been shot on campus. Meanwhile, a 19-year-old freshman at Jackson State University died from being shot in the face at an off-campus apartment pool party in Jackson. Mississippi Governor Phil Bryant expressed his sorrow at the loss of two college students and stated that those perpetuating these crimes will be apprehended and held accountable. Both universities are known for their safe environments, with counseling centers and other resources available to assist students.

A 37-year-old Oregon man faced multiple charges after a confrontation with McDonald's workers in Sutherlin, according to the News-Review. On March 16, police arrested Jedediah Ezekiel Fulton for second-degree disorderly conduct, second-degree criminal trespass, second-degree criminal mischief, and harassment. The incident began when the restaurant declined to fulfill his order for 30 double cheeseburgers, leading Fulton to destroy a banner and attack the restaurant's iconic golden arches. A witness, fearing for their safety, pulled out a gun. It's unclear if Fulton has an attorney. The altercation highlights the tension between customers and fast-food establishments when orders are not met with satisfaction. (This customer tried to burn down a store he thought was Muslim-owned; it wasn't.)

On Monday, May 11, 2015, at 7:44 PM, Antioch Police Officers responded to a burglary in progress at the 4900 block of Ridgeview Drive. The homeowner, holding her baby, saw an intruder enter through an unlocked door and fled with her baby, leaving her 4-year-old daughter behind. Officers searched the house and found the child at the top of the stairs. She directed them to the intruder's hiding spot in her closet, where they located 21-year-old Demaria Lopez, a transient male. A brief struggle ensued, but Lopez was taken into custody without further incident. He was booked into the Martinez Detention Facility on charges of burglary and resisting arrest. The incident resulted in no injuries. Anyone with information can contact Detective McManus or text a tip using the provided keyword.

President Obama made a surprise appearance in the White House briefing room to discuss the acquittal of George Zimmerman in the shooting death of Trayvon Martin. Obama, speaking for 18 minutes, highlighted the pain and frustration within the African American community, stating, "Trayvon Martin could have been me 35 years ago." He emphasized the importance of recognizing the experiences and history that inform how the African American community interprets such events, acknowledging that racial discrimination is not a thing of the past. Obama shared personal experiences of racial prejudice, such as being followed in department stores and encountering nervous reactions from others. He also discussed the ongoing issues of racial disparities in the criminal justice system, suggesting that a young African American might have faced a different outcome had the roles been reversed.

Obama expressed respect for the jury's decision but urged Americans to engage in soul-searching to address their own racial biases. He proposed concrete policy options, including training for law enforcement to reduce racial mistrust and examining the wisdom of "Stand Your Ground" laws. The president also called for bolstering and reinforcing African American boys, noting that many need positive reinforcement. He encouraged individuals to reflect on their own biases, asking, "Am I wringing as much bias out of myself as I can?" Obama's comments reflect a more personal and expansive discussion of race relations than he has previously offered as president, aiming to foster a more honest and introspective dialogue among Americans.

The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has proposed significant new regulations to restrict the use of sunlamp products, commonly known as indoor tanning beds, for minors and to enhance safety measures for adult users. The FDA aims to protect young people from the known risks of indoor tanning, which includes skin cancer and other harmful effects. The proposed rules would ban the use of sunlamp products for individuals under 18 years old, citing the highest risk for adverse health consequences in this age group. Additionally, adult users would be required to sign a risk acknowledgment certification every six months, emphasizing the dangers of indoor tanning. The FDA also plans to implement new safety features, such as more prominent warning labels, emergency shut-off switches, and improved labeling for replacement bulbs. These measures are part of a broader effort to reduce skin cancer risks, following a 2014 Surgeon General's call to action. The proposed rules are open for public comment for 90 days, and if finalized, they could significantly impact the 1.6 million minors who use indoor tanning facilities annually.

PBS faced backlash on social media after it acknowledged splicing in video of previous years' Washington, D.C., fireworks in its live "A Capitol Fourth" broadcast on Monday night. Viewers complained that the fireworks display couldn't be live because the images were in clear weather, while Washington, D.C., was heavily overcast and foggy. Around 10 p.m., the show's social media accounts acknowledged that the "live" show was actually a combination of the best fireworks from this year and previous years. The admission sparked swift and harsh criticism online. Users accused PBS of being dishonest and questioned the patriotism of using stock footage. Some pointed out that the footage lacked the expected cloud cover and showed construction scaffolding on the Capitol building. Despite the controversy, PBS defended its decision, stating it was the "patriotic thing to do." However, many viewers were unsatisfied, with some calling for transparency and warning that such practices could lead to further criticism. The incident highlighted the tension between the desire for authentic live coverage and the challenges of broadcasting in less-than-ideal conditions.

British police are reviewing new information related to the 1997 deaths of Princess Diana and Dodi Al Fayed, who perished in a Paris car crash. The Metropolitan Police stated they are "scoping" the information to assess its relevance and credibility, emphasizing it is not a re-investigation of the case. In 2008, an inquest found the couple was unlawfully killed due to the "gross negligence" of their driver and the reckless paparazzi pursuit. The police are working with officers from the specialist crime and operations command, but declined to discuss the source of the information. The royal family and Dodi's father, Mohamed Al Fayed, have not commented on the matter. The review comes amid reports suggesting military involvement and information from an Army source. Despite the passage of 13 years, the mystery surrounding the deaths continues to intrigue, with some questioning how new information could challenge the established narrative of a tragic accident.

The Journal News published an interactive Google Map with the names and addresses of gun permit owners in New York cities following the Newtown massacre, sparking outrage and debate. Blogger Christopher Fountain responded by posting the personal information of The Journal News staff, including phone numbers and home addresses, along with a Google Maps satellite image of the publisher’s home. The Journal News defended its map as a public service, sharing critical information for community safety discussions. However, the move was criticized as potentially endangering individuals and co-opting open data for partisan purposes. The incident highlights the complex and contentious nature of transparency and privacy in the digital age, with advocates of open data struggling to maintain their utopian vision amidst partisan uses of the information.

A toxin produced by a common foodborne bacterium, Clostridium perfringens, may trigger multiple sclerosis (MS), a new study suggests. Researchers at Weill Cornell Medical College found that the epsilon toxin, produced by certain strains of C. perfringens, targets cells associated with MS, including those that form the blood-brain barrier and myelin-producing cells. The study, presented at the 2014 ASM Biodefense and Emerging Diseases Research Meeting, indicates that 13% of food products tested harbored C. perfringens, with nearly 3% positive for the epsilon toxin. MS, an autoimmune disorder affecting 400,000 Americans, is thought to be triggered by an environmental factor. The epsilon toxin could potentially be neutralized with a vaccine or drug, offering hope for prevention or treatment. The findings, while promising, require further validation in larger studies. Experts caution that more work is needed to explore the link between the toxin and MS.

An 11-year-old boy, Yonatan Daniel Aguilar, was found dead in a closet in his family's Echo Park home, weighing just 34 pounds and covered in pressure sores from the tile floor, according to court documents obtained by the Los Angeles Times. His mother, Veronica Aguilar, 39, had hidden him in a locked closet for three years, sedating him with liquid sleep medication to keep him quiet, sources close to the investigation told CBSLA. Aguilar's stepfather, Jose Pinzon, who lived in the home, was unaware of Yonatan's presence. On August 22, 2016, Aguilar told Pinzon that Yonatan had died and led him to the closet. The boy's three siblings and his mother were the only ones who knew about his secret, with two of them sleeping in the bed right outside the closet door. Aguilar had forbidden them from telling anyone. The closet was so small that Yonatan couldn't stretch his legs, and his body was covered in sores from the hard tile floor. Medicinal cups of pink and red liquid were found near his balding body. Aguilar, who had previously led people to believe Yonatan was in an institution in Mexico, is now charged with murder and child abuse causing death. She is currently jailed on a $2 million bail. The case has raised questions about the failures of the Department of Children and Family Services, which had responded to six reports of possible abuse or neglect involving the family from 2009 to 2012 and marked the boy's risk of abuse as "high" four times. Despite this, officials never formally opened a case, according to the Los Angeles Times.

An Egyptian man described as "psychologically unstable" hijacked an EgyptAir flight on Tuesday, forcing the plane to land in Cyprus and causing a six-hour standoff. The 58-year-old, identified as Seif al-Din Mustafa, used a fake suicide belt to commandeer EgyptAir Flight MS181, which was en route from Alexandria to Cairo, with 72 people on board, including 26 foreigners. Mustafa demanded to speak with his ex-wife, who was brought to the airport, but his demands were deemed incoherent and not related to terrorism. The passengers and crew were released unharmed, with only seven people—four crew members and three passengers—kept on board. Mustafa eventually surrendered, and the plane landed in Larnaca, Cyprus, where he was arrested. The incident is believed to be a family dispute, possibly stemming from a disagreement with his ex-wife. Egyptian authorities are seeking his extradition under a 1996 bilateral treaty. Mustafa's relatives have been questioned, and surveillance footage from Alexandria airport showed him being thoroughly searched, with items later used to create the appearance of the explosive belt. The Egyptian aviation industry faces renewed security concerns following the downing of a Russian plane over Sinai in October 2015, which was claimed by the Islamic State group. The EgyptAir crew was praised for their handling of the situation, with one co-pilot stating that they managed to convince the hijacker to release the passengers once the plane landed in Cyprus. The incident is expected to have a negative impact on Egypt's tourism industry, with concerns raised about the effectiveness of airport security measures.

Florida has surpassed New York to become the third-most populous state in the United States, with an estimated population of 19.9 million residents, according to the latest U.S. Census Bureau data. This growth, which added an average of 803 new residents daily, outpaces New York's slower growth rate, where the population increased by only 51,000 residents over the same period. Overall, the U.S. population grew by 0.75% to reach 318.9 million residents. Among the 44 states and the District of Columbia that saw population increases, North Dakota led with a 2.2% growth rate, largely due to an energy boom. Other fast-growing states included Nevada, Texas, Colorado, Arizona, and Utah, each experiencing growth rates above 1.3%. Texas added the most residents, with 451,000, followed by California and Florida, each gaining over 100,000 residents. Georgia reached the 10 million resident mark for the first time, joining the ranks of the eight-figure population states. In contrast, six states—Illinois, West Virginia, Connecticut, New Mexico, Alaska, and Vermont—experienced population declines, with Alaska and Vermont losing residents. Puerto Rico saw a more significant population decrease, losing 1.3% of its population, or 47,000 residents. Florida's growth was attributed to migrants from other states and countries, with ex-New Yorkers making up about 10% of new Floridians. The state's population growth contrasts with the slower pace in larger states like California and Texas, which remain the most populous with 38.8 million and 27 million residents, respectively.

A 19-year-old man who entered the headquarters of Dutch national broadcaster NOS on Thursday night, claiming to be from a "hackers' collective," demanded airtime and threatened that bombs would go off at several locations around the Netherlands if his demand wasn't met, according to a reporter who spoke to the man. Wearing a black suit, white shirt, and black tie, and carrying a pistol, the man spoke calmly to someone off-camera, stating, "We are hired in by intelligence agencies." Shortly after, police arrived with their guns drawn and ordered the man to drop his weapon and put his hands up. At least five police officers then ordered him to turn around and lie down, which he did, and he was arrested without a struggle. The suspect was identified as a 19-year-old Dutchman from the town of Pijnacker near The Hague. He was being held on suspicion of making a threat, weapons possession, and taking a hostage. No one was injured, and there were no reports of shots being fired. The incident occurred in the Media Park in Hilversum, home to many Dutch broadcasters, which has been tightly guarded for years, since populist Dutch politician Pim Fortuyn was gunned down in a parking lot there in 2002. While the broadcaster was off-air, a screen on the NOS1 channel read "Please be patient" in Dutch. All staff were evacuated from the building as the situation unfolded and remained outside nearly two hours later as police searched the building. NOS resumed broadcasting from a studio in The Hague. The man's motive was unclear; the NOS footage showed him saying, "The things that are going to be said (pause) those are very large world affairs. We were hired by the security service." Police special forces swept the building for explosives and found nothing. Dutch Minister for Security and Justice Ivo Opstelten told the ANP national news agency the man appeared to have acted alone. Security has been tightened across Europe since the jihadist attacks on the offices of the satirical weekly Charlie Hebdo and a kosher supermarket in Paris this month, as well as the killing of two gunmen in Belgium during raids on an Islamist group that authorities said were planning to attack police.

Lumberton, North Carolina police received a 911 call from a man who mistook a doll in a parked truck for an unresponsive infant, leading to the recovery of a stolen vehicle and a 3-week-old baby inside, according to the Fayetteville Observer. The dark gray 2014 Ford F-150 crew cab pickup was stolen from a home on the 1400 block of Mimosa Street, off North Roberts Avenue, around 8:55 p.m. on Monday. The mother, who had two other small children with her, was getting them inside the house when someone stole the truck, which contained the infant in a car seat. Police issued an alert, and the truck was abandoned about 10 minutes later in the parking lot of Billy Cox's Grocery and Market on N.C. 41, approximately three miles away. A man walking through the parking lot noticed a window was down, saw a baby doll on the floor, and called 911. Deputies with the Robeson County Sheriff's Office arrived and found the infant unharmed in the child-restraint seat. Police are looking for two suspects but have not released additional information. The man who saw the doll and the Sheriff's Office are credited for their quick response in reuniting the mother and her child. Anyone with information is asked to call Lumberton police Detective Deana Locklear at 910-671-3845.

U.S. customs officials at Los Angeles International Airport intercepted a significant shipment of invasive giant African snails, marking the first such large-scale interception of this pest in the United States. The snails, weighing over 35 pounds in total, were discovered in two plastic packages from Lagos, Nigeria, and were intended for human consumption. Upon arrival, CBP officials flagged the shipment, which contained 67 snails, each about 6 inches long and 2 pounds in weight, including their shells. The mollusks, known scientifically as Archachatina marginata, are commonly referred to as giant African land snails, banana rasp snails, or West African snails. These snails are considered a serious threat due to their voracious appetite for over 500 types of plants and their ability to consume stucco and paint off houses. They can also carry parasites harmful to humans, including one that can lead to meningitis. The snails were identified by USDA specialists and were subsequently transferred to a local plant inspection station for precautionary measures. Todd C. Owen, CBP Director of Field Operations, emphasized the importance of preventing the introduction of such pests, stating, "The significant interception of giant African snails is the first time this pest has been encountered in such large quantity and as a consumption entry by CBP in Los Angeles." The snails were eventually incinerated to prevent further spread, highlighting the stringent measures taken to protect U.S. agriculture, the environment, and public health from invasive species.

Tennessee state Senator Stacey Campfield faced criticism after posting a blog entry titled "Here comes Feinstein again," which featured a pressure cooker labeled with weapons-like components, one week after the Boston Marathon bombing. Campfield defended his post, stating, "People need to lighten up," and compared the reaction to the Sandy Hook shooting, where he argued that gun control was pushed by the left. In a follow-up post, he questioned the hypocrisy of those who criticize his blog while supporting gun control measures after the Sandy Hook incident. Campfield's comments drew attention to his broader stance on gun rights and his controversial history, including a bill linking academic performance to welfare benefits and statements comparing homosexuality to drug use. His defense of the post and his overall approach to gun control and social issues have sparked debate and criticism, highlighting the sensitivity surrounding the topic.

Flint's lead contamination crisis has expanded to affect animals, specifically two dogs in the Genesee County area, according to state veterinarian Dr. James Averill. These are the first confirmed cases of lead toxicity in dogs in Michigan in five years. The dogs, one a pet and the other a stray, tested positive for high lead levels in October 2015 and January 2016, though state officials have not disclosed their exact locations or further details. The state veterinarian advises pet owners to protect their animals by ensuring they only drink filtered or bottled water, as unfiltered tap water from Flint is still unsafe. Dr. Averill emphasizes that the symptoms of lead toxicity in pets can be broad and similar to those of other diseases, making it crucial for owners to monitor their pets' behavior and seek veterinary care if they notice any deviations from normal routines. The state is in contact with local veterinarians, and lab testing for lead toxicity in animals is provided free of charge. While the majority of tests for lead in dogs have been negative, the state encourages pet owners to be vigilant and take preventive measures to avoid potential health risks.

The first comprehensive map of the world's hidden groundwater was unveiled, offering a clearer understanding of the Earth's underground water resources and their potential depletion. Led by Dr. Tom Gleeson of the University of Victoria, the study, published in Nature Geoscience, utilized data and computer models to estimate the total volume of groundwater, revealing that less than six percent and perhaps as little as one percent of water found close to the Earth's surface is renewable in a human lifetime. This breakthrough provides critical insights into the sustainability of groundwater usage, highlighting the urgent need for better management and conservation.

The research team estimated a total volume of underground water to be approximately 23 million cubic kilometers, with only 0.35 million cubic kilometers younger than 50 years old. This vast reservoir of water is found beneath the Earth's surface, recharged by rain, snow, and water seeping from the bottom of lakes and rivers. Its age can range from a few months to millions of years, with some deposits as deep as 30,000 feet. The study reveals that most groundwater is located in tropical and mountainous regions, with significant deposits in the Amazon Basin, the Congo, Indonesia, and along the western borders of North and South America. Arid regions, such as the Sahara, contain the least amount of modern groundwater.

Dr. Gleeson emphasizes the importance of differentiating between old and modern groundwater. Old groundwater, found deeper in the Earth, is often used for agriculture and industry and can contain contaminants like arsenic or uranium, making it more saline than seawater. In contrast, modern groundwater, closer to the surface, is more renewable but more sensitive to climate change and human activities. It serves as a valuable buffer against climate extremes, flowing to rivers during droughts and thus playing a crucial role in water availability.

The study's findings underscore the critical need for sustainable groundwater management. With growing global demand for water, particularly in light of climate change, this research provides essential data for water managers, policymakers, and scientists from various fields to develop strategies that balance human needs with environmental sustainability. The maps generated by the study offer a quantitative estimate of modern groundwater distribution, allowing for comparisons with geochemical observations and enabling more accurate assessments of groundwater stress in regions like northern India, Pakistan, northern China, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and parts of the US and Mexico.

Dr. Gleeson's next step involves analyzing groundwater volumes in relation to usage rates to estimate how long until depletion. This will require a global-scale model, further refining our understanding of groundwater dynamics and informing policies aimed at preserving this vital resource. The study's findings highlight the complexity of groundwater systems and the urgent need for interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure the long-term sustainability of this precious resource.

A Boulder father is offering a substantial reward of $100,000 for any information that leads to the recovery of his missing son, Ryder Johnson, or to criminal charges against anyone responsible for his disappearance. Ryder, 21, was last seen on January 17 after finishing his shift at the Eldora Ski Resort near Nederland. His vehicle was found parked at the Gross Dam parking lot in Boulder, more than 20 miles away from where he was last seen. The Boulder County Sheriff's Office has not received many leads from the original scene, according to Richard Johnson, Ryder’s father. 

Johnson, along with the help of friends, has launched a search for his son and is offering the reward to find him or to identify any items his son had when he went missing. The reward will be available until January 17, 2017, which marks the one-year anniversary of Ryder’s disappearance. Johnson’s father stated, “Justice needs to be served, and I think it’s time to bring him home.” The Boulder County Sheriff’s Office has not ruled out foul play, but they believe it is more likely that Ryder disappeared on his own volition. 

Search efforts have included placing flyers near the Gross Reservoir and Walker Ranch, with the use of drones, boats, and rescue crews. Despite these extensive searches, no signs of Ryder have been found. The case remains open, and the sheriff’s office encourages anyone with information to contact them at 303-441-4444. The family continues to search for Ryder, believing that justice and his return are essential.
