Wildstein is the government's key witness in its conspiracy and fraud case against William Baroni, who served as deputy executive director of the Port Authority, and Bridget Anne Kelly, who was the governor's deputy chief of staff. The latest on the Bridgegate trial Though Christie was never charged in connection with the lane closures, the scandal is seen as contributing to his failed bid for the Republican nomination for President. Wildstein has said in his testimony that he discussed the plot with multiple members of Christie's senior staff before and during the lane closures, which he said was political retribution against Fort Lee Mayor Mark Sokolich for not endorsing the governor in his reelection campaign. Wildstein also testified that Christie was told about the gridlock at a 9/11 memorial service, as the lanes remained closed in Fort Lee. McGeady asked Brennan why he filed in Bergen County, not Mercer County, where the governor's office is located. Brennan said that it was because the lane closures took place in Fort Lee, which McGeady said was a satisfactory answer. "It's been dumped in this court's lap so this court is going to deal with it," McGeady said. Craig Carpenito, an attorney at the law firm Alston & Bird who appeared on behalf of the governor, told McGeady that Brennan's claim was "intentionally misleading" and that the governor's knowledge of the lane closures had already been thoroughly investigated. The audience in McGeady's courtroom, mostly there for minor criminal violations, applauded after he ruled. "Anything short of probable cause today would have been official misconduct on the part of the judge," said Brennan, a graduate of the Seton Hall University School of Law. "The standard is low, the evidence is heavy." McGeady said the case would now go to the Bergen County Prosecutor's Office, which would decide whether to bring an indictment against Christie. The prosecutor, Gurbir S. Grewal, a Christie appointee, would likely recuse himself, McGeady said. The Bergen County Prosecutor's Office declined to comment. In New Jersey's criminal code, a charge of official misconduct pertains mostly to public officials. "You're someone who either exercised their official function, knowing that it's unauthorized," explained James Pomaco, a former prosecutor in Passaic County who's now a criminal defense attorney. "Or you're someone who knowingly 'refrained from performing a duty which is imposed upon him by law or is clearly inherent in the nature of his office'." Pomaco said that "from a prima facie standpoint, there's enough for a charge" of official misconduct based on Wildstein's testimony that Christie was informed of the lane closures as they were occurring on Sept. 11, 2013. At the start of the Bridgegate scandal, some experts argued that state was better suited to prosecute the case overall because violations of state law were more apparent. Assemblyman John Wisniewski (D-Middlesex), who along with state Sen. Loretta Weinberg (D-Bergen), co-chaired the legislative committee that looked into Bridgegate, said "it was a very interesting development, certainly not something that I expected today." "It is a black eye for the state of New Jersey to have a judge find probable cause that the governor's actions were malfeasance in office," Wisniewski said. "Look, the testimony of David Wildstein corroborated a lot of the suspicions that the committee had during our process, that lot of people have statewide. It remains to be seen exactly what happens now that a finding of probable cause has been reached, because we know that the prosecutor has a discretion to act on that. We don't know exactly what they'll do." Weinberg said the Bridgegate panel may have to reconvene. "I believe that there are people who came before the joint committee under oath and were not exactly forthcoming, which is the kindest way I can describe. There were texts apparently that they never told us about, there were meetings that they never offered," she said.

The "Shield" actor Michael Jace, 51, is accused of fatally shooting his wife, April, at their Hyde Park home on Monday night. April Jace, a financial aid counselor at Biola University, was shot multiple times around 8:30 p.m. after returning home with their two sons from baseball practice. Neighbors, who described the couple as loving and friendly, were shocked by the allegations. Jace, who filed for bankruptcy in 2011, has a history of domestic violence, including an incident where a friend witnessed him choking and hitting his ex-wife, Jennifer Bitterman, while their infant son screamed. The couple's two sons, both under 10, were home during the shooting but unharmed. Jace was found unarmed in the doorway when police arrived. April Jace's Facebook page showed a close-knit family, with photos of her and Michael with their children. The shooting has left neighbors and the university community, where April worked, in shock. The couple's two sons were staying with family members as the investigation continued, with one neighbor describing April as a "wonderful mother." The case raises questions about the couple's public and private lives.

A former Tesla process technician, Martin Tripp, has begun tweeting internal emails, photos, and vehicle identification numbers (VINs) that he claims are evidence of flawed manufacturing practices at Tesla's battery factory, potentially putting drivers' lives at risk. Tripp, who was fired earlier this year, countersued Tesla in June, accusing the company of falsely labeling him as a hacker and initiating a smear campaign against him. Tesla responded by suing Tripp for $1 million in defamation. Tripp's tweets include photos of improperly handled cooling tubes, damaged battery cells, and graphics showing a high volume of scrap waste. He also shared a list of Tesla vehicles allegedly sold with "punctured / dented / damaged" batteries, allowing Tesla owners to check if their vehicles are on the list. Tripp's tweets have been temporarily suspended by Twitter for violating its policies against posting private information. Tesla maintains that Tripp's claims are false and that all identified VINs have safe batteries, with no battery safety issues in any Model 3 vehicles. The incident highlights the ongoing tension between Tripp and Tesla, with both parties accusing each other of misinformation and harassment. Tripp's actions mirror those of former Tesla engineer Cristina Balan, who was pushed out of the company after raising concerns about part quality and waste. Balan's experience suggests that Tesla may be attempting to silence whistleblowers and intimidate employees who speak out about quality issues.

The Supreme Court's two-day examination of the Defense of Marriage Act (DOMA) and California's Proposition 8 has revealed a divided court, with justices appearing skeptical of the law's constitutionality. On Wednesday, the court heard arguments on DOMA, which defines marriage as between a man and a woman, withholding federal benefits from legally married same-sex couples. Justice Anthony Kennedy, often the swing vote, suggested that the federal government may have overstepped its bounds by interfering with states' traditional role in defining marriage. Kennedy expressed concern that DOMA could conflict with states that have legalized same-sex marriage, noting the significant impact of over 1,100 federal laws and regulations on citizens' daily lives. Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg echoed this sentiment, questioning the law's discriminatory nature and its implications for gay couples' rights.

The Obama administration, which has declared DOMA unconstitutional, faced tough questioning from Chief Justice John Roberts. Roberts was skeptical of the idea that gay people lack political power, pointing out that political figures are actively supporting the right to same-sex marriage. The administration's decision not to defend the law in court also drew criticism from the Chief Justice, who suggested that President Obama should have stopped enforcing the law if he believed it was unconstitutional. Solicitor General Donald Verrilli Jr. argued that the law's discriminatory nature should be scrutinized more rigorously, citing the House committee's acknowledgment of "collective moral judgment" and "moral disapproval of homosexuality."

Paul D. Clement, representing House Republicans, defended DOMA, arguing that Congress was motivated by a desire for uniformity and to prevent same-sex marriage from spreading across the country. However, his arguments faced strong challenges from Justice Elena Kagan, who questioned the legitimacy of targeting a group based on prejudice. The case's procedural issues also came under scrutiny, with Harvard law professor Vicki C. Jackson arguing that the House Republicans lacked standing to defend the law, and the Obama administration was not a viable party because it agreed with the lower courts.

The second day of hearings focused on Proposition 8, which bans same-sex marriage in California. The court seemed reluctant to find a broad constitutional right to same-sex marriage, instead looking for the narrowest way to resolve the case. Justices appeared divided, with liberals more supportive of gay rights and conservatives more tolerant of government action to protect traditional marriage. Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Antonin Scalia were particularly critical of the administration's approach, questioning the administration's decision not to defend the law and suggesting that it lacked the courage to enforce its own views.

The case of Edith Windsor, who was forced to pay a federal estate tax because of DOMA, highlighted the practical implications of the law. Windsor's lawyers argued that the federal government has no role in defining marriage, which is traditionally left to the states. Lower courts have ruled in Windsor's favor, and the Obama administration agrees that the section of the law defining marriage violates the Constitution's guarantee of equal protection. However, the court may rule that the case is not properly before them, leading to a decision that Windsor wins her refund but DOMA remains on the books in states where courts have not ruled on it. Further litigation is likely, as the court's decision will have significant implications for the legal status of same-sex marriage across the country.

The Hubble Space Telescope has observed an asteroid in the asteroid belt between Mars and Jupiter, designated P/2013 P5, which is emitting six comet-like tails of dust. This unprecedented observation, captured in September, has left astronomers puzzled. The tails, believed to be caused by dust-ejection events, have shifted dramatically over just 13 days. David Jewitt, lead investigator from the University of California at Los Angeles, expressed astonishment, stating, "We were literally dumbfounded when we saw it." The tails are thought to be the result of the asteroid's rotation rate increasing to the point where its weak gravity can no longer hold it together, causing dust to slide toward the equator, shatter, and drift into space. Jessica Agarwal of the Max Planck Institute for Solar System Research modeled the asteroid's behavior, suggesting a series of impulsive dust-ejection events. The tails, formed by radiation pressure from the sun, stretch the dust into streamers. Astronomers believe this phenomenon could be common in the asteroid belt, potentially being the primary way small asteroids disintegrate. Further observations are needed to confirm the tails' formation and to understand the asteroid's history, which may include it being a fragment of a larger asteroid that broke apart in a collision about 200 million years ago.

Actress Lindsay Lohan claims she was "racially profiled" while wearing a headscarf at London's Heathrow Airport, according to a British talk show. Lohan told "Good Morning Britain" that an airport worker "opened my passport and saw 'Lindsay Lohan' and started immediately apologizing, but then said: 'Please take off your headscarf.'" The incident made her wonder "how would another woman who doesn't feel comfortable taking off her headscarf feel?" Lohan, who recently met President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Turkey, wore the headscarf out of "personal respect." She has also been photographed carrying a Quran and finds "solace" studying the Muslim holy book and other religious texts. The actress's comments come as she continues to navigate the public eye, with recent social media posts hinting at her desire to reprise the role of Ariel from The Little Mermaid. Lohan wrote on Instagram, "I will sing again, as #ariel #thelittlemermaid," alongside a side-by-side pic of her and the animated mermaid princess. She followed up with a more modest caption, "thelittlemermaid," but the image of her and Ariel side-by-side sparked a wave of online commentary. The post, which included a photo of Lohan with her mouth wide open, was met with a mix of amusement and skepticism, with some users joking that the actress might actually get the role. The incident highlights the ongoing challenges Lindsay Lohan faces in the public eye, balancing her personal beliefs with the scrutiny of the media and fans.

A mother took her case to federal court after her son, a Ladue High School junior, was not allowed to play on the Junior Varsity soccer team, despite already having played on it in the past. The Ladue School District’s rationale for not allowing the student to play on the J.V. team is to give lower grade students a chance to develop their skills, preparing them for varsity. The mother’s attorney claims the issue is age and sex discrimination, as the rules for the girls’ team are allegedly different. The coach, in a court testimony, stated that the seven juniors cut from the varsity team were not good enough to play on the J.V. team, and that he praised the student to build his self-esteem. Documents introduced by the lawyer show that the student’s performance ratings are better than some of the boys who made the varsity team. The coach admitted that there is no policy preventing juniors from playing J.V. sports, as it depends on the number of kids trying out and the team spots available, which applies to both girls and boys teams. The U.S. District Judge, John Ross, denied a request for a Temporary Restraining Order that would allow the student to play on the J.V. team, and will decide on the matter on Monday. The student’s mother wants him to play soccer and believes he should not be discriminated against based on age and gender.

Greece is poised for a pivotal referendum on Sunday, where its citizens will decide whether to accept or reject a bailout proposal from its creditors, a decision that could reshape the future of the country’s economy and the European monetary union. The situation is complex, with the Greek government and its creditors engaged in a tense standoff, and the outcome uncertain. Greece’s economy, already reeling from years of austerity measures, faces severe challenges, including high unemployment and a shrinking tax base. The Greek government, led by Prime Minister Alexis Tsipras, is advocating for a “No” vote, arguing that it will strengthen their negotiating position and potentially secure better terms for the country. However, the creditors, including the European Union, European Central Bank, and International Monetary Fund, are warning that a “No” vote could lead to Greece’s exit from the eurozone, a scenario that would be economically devastating for the country and potentially contagious, sparking fears of a broader European crisis.

The stakes are high, with Greece having already defaulted on a $1.55 billion payment to the International Monetary Fund, and its banks having been closed to prevent a run on deposits. The Greek government has imposed strict limits on cash withdrawals, allowing only €60 per day, and is considering issuing IOUs to replace euros in circulation. The IMF has warned that Greece’s debt is unsustainable, and that a debt relief package on a scale not previously considered may be necessary. However, European leaders are reluctant to provide such relief, fearing it would set a precedent for other struggling economies.

The Greek public is divided, with opinion polls showing a near-even split between those supporting a “Yes” and a “No” vote. The “Yes” campaign argues that accepting the bailout terms is the only way to ensure continued access to international funding and prevent a deeper economic crisis. The “No” campaign, supported by the Greek government and many of its allies, believes that rejecting the terms will allow for a renegotiation that could lead to more favorable conditions. The outcome of the referendum will not only determine Greece’s immediate financial future but could also have broader implications for the stability of the eurozone and the global economy.

A British couple, George Kirby, 103, and Doreen Luckie, 91, celebrated their long-awaited wedding on Saturday, becoming the world's oldest newlyweds with a combined age of 194 years. The couple, who have been together for 27 years, exchanged vows at a hotel in the seaside town of Eastbourne, southern England, in front of close friends and family. Doreen wore a white dress with blue flowers, while George, a former boxer, was dressed in a suit and tie and was in a wheelchair following a recent fall. The ceremony was officiated by a representative from the Guinness Book of World Records, making the event a historic milestone. Speaking ahead of the wedding, Doreen said, "We didn't want to bother about marriage before but eventually we did it," expressing no regrets about not tying the knot earlier. The couple has seven children, 15 grandchildren, and seven great-grandchildren between them, and they got engaged on Valentine's Day this year. George, who met Doreen at the age of 76 after divorcing, and Doreen, who became a widow three years prior after 36 years of marriage, have been living together since 1988. George, born in London in June 1912, was a talented boxer in his youth, winning all 60 of his fights. He later joined the Royal Air Force, where he worked as a physical education instructor for 25 years. After retiring, George tended Doreen's garden in Kent. Doreen, born in Brixton in September 1923, spent much of her career as a shorthand typist for the Director of Public Prosecutions. Neil Kirby, George's son, who runs the Langham Hotel where the couple lives, said, "It was a great day—everyone was so happy for them. They are such a beautiful couple." George added, "It's about time, really. Doreen keeps me young, and I can definitely say we're going to spend the rest of our lives together." The couple's wedding day was filled with joy and celebration, with Doreen having a hen party luncheon that was a "complete laugh" with her "golden girls."

Ex-EastEnder Paul Nicholls was hospitalized after falling from a jungle waterfall in Thailand and spending three days trapped in a rock pool with a broken leg. The 38-year-old actor, who played Joe Wicks in EastEnders and appeared in Law & Order: UK, survived thanks to a local villager who spotted his abandoned motorbike. Emergency services launched a search and rescue operation, which took two hours to bring Nicholls to International Koh Samui Hospital. Nicholls described his ordeal as a "great situation" but admitted he was semi-conscious and suffering from hypothermia. He revealed his kneecap was destroyed and would need complete reconstruction. Nicholls, who has battled with alcohol and drugs, was found partially submerged in a rock pool, unable to move due to his injury. The incident occurred on the island of Koh Samui, where a local tourist, Geoffrey Maui, had died after falling at the same waterfall just a month earlier. Nicholls' medical bills are expected to run into tens of thousands of pounds, and the British Embassy is considering flying him back to the UK for proper treatment.

Two lawsuits filed in federal court on Thursday aim to shut down Colorado's regulated marijuana industry, claiming that the state's recreational marijuana laws are in violation of federal law. The suits, filed by the anti-drug group Safe Streets and three other plaintiffs, target Colorado lawmakers, including Governor John Hickenlooper, Revenue Department Executive Director Barbara Brohl, and Marijuana Enforcement Division Director W. Lewis Koski. They allege that by allowing for a regulated marijuana market, these lawmakers are breaking federal law, which considers the plant illegal. The plaintiffs, including Colorado property owners Phillis Windy Hope Reilly and Michael P. Reilly, as well as New Vision Hotels Two, the corporate owner of a Holiday Inn in the state, are also seeking damages due to alleged injury brought on by legalization. The suits name participants in Colorado's marijuana industry, including various marijuana businesses and their owners, as well as several parties who have provided support for those businesses through banking, insurance, and accounting services. The suits argue that under the U.S. Constitution's supremacy clause, which states that federal law generally takes precedence over state law, Colorado's legalization of recreational marijuana is unconstitutional, because marijuana remains illegal at the federal level. Colorado state Rep. Jonathan Singer, a vocal supporter of the state's marijuana laws, called the lawsuit a "bad idea" and said that Safe Streets would see that their arguments about economic and moral decay hold no water. Colorado voters approved Amendment 64, legalizing recreational marijuana in the state, in 2012. The industry has since grown to a value of around $700 million, and the state has taken in about $60 million in taxes and fees, some of which is going toward school construction and renovation. Despite some concerns, employment numbers are up, and crime rates are down in Denver. Colorado state Attorney General Cynthia Coffman's office will defend the state's laws and clients. Kevin Sabet, president of the anti-legalization group Smart Approaches to Marijuana, applauded the legal action taken by Safe Streets, saying that the laws in Colorado and elsewhere violate federal law. However, advocates for marijuana policy reform say this week's lawsuits are misguided and doubt their success in dislodging Colorado's marijuana laws and industry.

Sarah Palin is reportedly planning to sue rapper Azealia Banks after Banks went on a very NSFW Twitter rant suggesting that the former Alaska governor should be sexually assaulted. Banks, known for her outspoken and often controversial statements, initially deleted the tweets but later issued a "sincerest" apology via Tumblr, clarifying that her "joke" tweets referred to group sex, not rape. However, Palin is not backing down, issuing a statement to People that she will take legal action against Banks "on behalf of all reasonable women of every age, race, and political leaning." Banks' apology came after a satirical news article from Newslo.com, which Banks apparently believed was real, suggested that Palin had made offensive comments about African Americans' experiences with slavery. The feud between the two has drawn attention to Banks' history of controversial statements, including declaring gay men "like the KKK" and being arrested outside an NYC nightclub. Palin, meanwhile, has accused Banks of using "double standards" and "divisive tactics" to gain attention and financial rewards. The legal battle between the two is just the latest chapter in a long-standing feud, with Banks previously calling for the rape of another public figure and Palin threatening to sue over similar accusations. The case highlights the ongoing tensions between outspoken celebrities and the public figures they criticize, and the potential consequences of such confrontations.

A Palestinian teenager was reportedly abducted and killed near his home in Jerusalem, allegedly in revenge for the deaths of three kidnapped Jewish Israelis found just hours earlier. The incident has sparked widespread condemnation and raised fears of escalating communal violence. Muhammad Hussein Abu Khdeir, 16, was reportedly forced into a car by two men on a sidewalk not far from his home in Shuafat, a Palestinian neighborhood of East Jerusalem, shortly before 4 a.m. on Wednesday. His body was later found charred in a forest on the outskirts of the city. Family members believe he was on his way to dawn prayers, as is customary during the Muslim holy month of Ramadan. His father, Hussein Saed Abu Khdeir, stated, "The settlers killed my son, they kidnapped him and killed him."

The discovery of the body led to clashes between Palestinians and Israeli forces. Stones were thrown, and police responded with foam-tipped bullets and sound grenades. Dozens of young men participated in the protest, causing significant damage to the area. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu issued a statement urging both sides "not to take the law into your own hands" and promising to "uncover quickly who is behind this despicable murder and what motivated it." A relative of one of the Jewish Israeli teens, Naftali Fraenkel, who also held U.S. citizenship, expressed his stance, stating, "If a young Arab man was murdered for nationalistic reasons, then it is a horrifying and disgusting act. There is no distinguishing blood from blood. Murder is murder, whatever the nationality or age may be. There is no justification, no forgiveness, and no atonement for any murder."

The incident has deepened the divide between the two communities. Palestinian leaders, including President Mahmoud Abbas, have accused Israel of responsibility for the abduction and murder of the Palestinian teenager. Abbas stated, "Israel bears full responsibility for this incident," and threatened to drag Israel before U.N. courts. On the ground, Palestinians express skepticism about the Israeli narrative, with many refusing to acknowledge the kidnapping and murder of the Jewish teens. They believe the incident was a form of vigilante justice for the deaths of the Jewish teens. Hussein Abu Khdeir, the father of the slain Palestinian teenager, agreed, saying, "Yes, of course, there's no other explanation."

Meanwhile, tensions are rising on both sides. Israeli authorities have begun reinforcing forces on their border with Gaza, following air strikes against the Palestinian territory early on Thursday that injured 10 Palestinians. These strikes were in response to mortar and rocket fire from Palestinian militants. The funeral of the Palestinian teenager has been delayed to allow for a post-mortem examination, which is taking longer than expected due to the severity of the burns. The family hopes the funeral can still take place on Thursday, despite the delay.

The incident has also sparked international reactions, with media and political figures expressing concern and condemnation. Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas accused Jewish settlers of killing the boy, calling for the "strongest punishment against the murderers." Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu's statement emphasized the need for a swift investigation and severe punishment for the culprits. The ongoing tensions highlight the complex and volatile nature of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, with each incident exacerbating the already fragile situation.

Donald J. Trump's immigration plan centers on three core principles: securing the southern border, enforcing immigration laws, and prioritizing the needs of American workers. Trump argues that traditional immigration reform, such as the Schumer-Rubio bill, is a giveaway to corporate interests and fails to protect American jobs. His plan emphasizes a wall along the southern border, increased interior enforcement, and a crackdown on illegal immigration. Trump believes that illegal immigration is a threat to American safety, citing cases of violent crimes committed by undocumented immigrants. He also argues that illegal immigration costs American taxpayers billions of dollars annually, and that Mexico should pay for the wall. 

To enforce immigration laws, Trump proposes tripling the number of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers, implementing nationwide e-verify, and detaining illegal aliens apprehended at the border. Trump also calls for defunding sanctuary cities and ending visa programs for Mexican CEOs and diplomats. Additionally, he aims to end birthright citizenship, arguing that it encourages illegal immigration. 

Trump's plan includes a series of policies to protect American jobs. He wants to increase the prevailing wage for H-1B visa holders, require employers to hire American workers first, and end welfare abuse. Trump also proposes a jobs program for inner-city youth and a refugee program focused on American children. 

Trump's immigration reform also includes a proposal for a permanent border wall, which he believes will significantly reduce illegal immigration. He argues that Mexico should pay for the wall, citing the billions of dollars in remittances sent by illegal immigrants back to Mexico. Trump also proposes measures to impound remittance payments, increase visa fees, and impose tariffs on Mexican imports. 

In summary, Trump's immigration plan aims to secure the border, enforce the law, and prioritize American workers. It includes a wall, increased enforcement, and a crackdown on illegal immigration, while also proposing policies to protect American jobs and reduce the number of illegal immigrants in the country.

The family of 28-year-old Grace Sung Eun Lee, a terminally ill woman with an inoperable brain tumor, is fighting to keep her on life support, despite her doctors' and court's wishes to honor her request to end life support. Lee's parents, who believe she will go to hell if she pulls the plug, have released a murky video showing her mouth moving, allegedly proving she wants to stay hooked up to breathing and feeding tubes. Lee's court-appointed lawyer, David A. Smith, claims her parents are putting her under "incredible pressure" and says she has made her wishes clear. However, the video is vague and unlikely to hold much legal weight. Lee's parents argue that removing life support would be considered suicide, which is a sin and would condemn her to burn in hell forever. The case is being handled by a four-judge Appellate Division panel, which will decide whether to let Long Island’s North Shore Hospital disconnect Lee. Despite the court ruling against Lee's parents, a hearing on her father's guardianship is still scheduled for Tuesday. Lee's lawyer contends that she has no hope for recovery and has directed him to "not let that weekend pass." The family's legal battle highlights the complex ethical and religious issues surrounding end-of-life decisions for terminally ill patients.

For the first time, a character on "Sesame Street" is experiencing homelessness, aiming to help young children grappling with the issue. Lily, a 7-year-old pink Muppet, was introduced in 2011 to address food insecurity, but now her storyline has expanded to include homelessness. As Sesame Workshop's initiative, "Sesame Street in Communities," launched this effort, Lily's family has lost their home and must stay with friends on the show. This move underscores the growing number of homeless children in the U.S., with 2.5 million experiencing homelessness, and nearly half under six years old. The initiative offers resources for children and families, including videos, storybooks, and activities, while also providing tools for professionals like teachers and social workers. Lily's story is designed to comfort and empower children, teaching them that home is more than a house and that they are not alone. The program aims to disrupt the cycle of trauma associated with homelessness, offering hope and resilience. Through Lily's journey, the initiative seeks to raise awareness and provide support for families facing this challenge.

David Blankenhorn, a long-time opponent of same-sex marriage, has shifted his stance, advocating for the legal recognition of gay marriage while emphasizing its potential benefits. In a New York Times essay and an NPR documentary, Blankenhorn explains his decision, rooted in his belief that the debate has shifted from marriage's role in parenthood to a broader issue of equality for gay and lesbian couples. He acknowledges his initial opposition was grounded in the idea that children have a right to know and be cared for by both biological parents, a stance he still holds. However, he now believes that legally recognizing same-sex relationships is a step towards basic fairness and equality. Blankenhorn also suggests a new strategy, proposing that supporters of traditional marriage and advocates for gay marriage could find common ground on issues such as the value of marriage before having children and the rights of children born through assisted reproduction. His shift has garnered mixed reactions, with some praising his intellectual honesty and others criticizing his change as a result of social pressure. The article highlights the evolving landscape of the marriage equality debate, noting the increasing public support for same-sex marriage and the broader cultural shifts it represents.

Suspected militants stormed the Kabul campus of the American University of Afghanistan on Wednesday, leading to a chaotic scene with students jumping from second-floor windows to escape gunfire and explosions, reports Reuters. The attack began around 6:30 p.m., trapping foreign staff and dozens of students in the compound. At least one person was killed, and 14 students were wounded, according to the head of hospitals in Kabul. Students described hearing a loud explosion followed by gunfire, with some sustaining injuries as they fled. Elite Afghan forces surrounded the university, and special forces entered the walled compound where gunfire had lasted for over an hour. Interior ministry spokesman Sediq Sediqqi stated that two gunmen were hiding inside the building and a clearing operation was underway. Afghan policemen wounded in the attack stood guard at the scene. The attack is the second on the university this month, with two teachers, an American and an Australian, remaining missing after being abducted on August 7. The Taliban and local offshoots of Islamic State have claimed recent attacks aimed at destabilizing the country and toppling the Western-backed government of President Ashraf Ghani. The American University of Afghanistan, established in 2006, is an elite institution with about 1,700 students and represents a symbol of cooperation between the United States and Afghanistan. The attack comes amid heightened security fears in Kabul, with American and other diplomats barred from traveling by road to their missions due to the security situation.

American gardeners can now grow a unique hybrid plant that produces both tomatoes and potatoes, thanks to the release of Ketchup ‘n’ Fries by TomTato®. This innovative grafted vegetable, developed by SuperNaturals Grafted Vegetables, LLC, combines the top part of a cherry tomato plant with the root system of a potato, allowing gardeners to maximize space and enjoy a dual harvest. The plant, which has been in development for over 15 years, was first released in the UK in 2014 and is now available in the United States through exclusive production rights held by Plug Connection in San Diego County. Home gardeners can purchase starter plants from Territorial Seed Company, which offers them in its 2015 seed catalog. The grafted process, which does not involve genetic engineering, enables the plant to produce up to 500 cherry-sized tomatoes above ground and edible white potatoes below ground, all from a single container. The Territorial Seed Company highlights the benefits of grafted plants, including increased vigor, disease resistance, and tolerance to environmental stresses, making them a popular choice among organic farmers and home gardeners. Despite initial skepticism, the TomTato has generated significant buzz and positive reviews, with some gardeners praising its unique features and others expressing disappointment. The plant's dual functionality offers a novel approach to gardening, potentially revolutionizing how we grow and utilize vegetables in our gardens.

Carey Mulligan has been cast as Daisy Buchanan in Baz Luhrmann's adaptation of "The Great Gatsby," beating out a list of other potential actresses for the role. The announcement was made by Luhrmann himself, who stated, "I was thrilled to pick up the phone an hour ago to the young Oscar-nominated British actress Carey Mulligan and say to her: 'Hello, Daisy Buchanan.'" Mulligan, who recently starred in "Wall Street: Money Never Sleeps," was chosen over other actresses including Blake Lively, Natalie Portman, and Amanda Seyfried. The casting decision was revealed at the CFDA awards in New York, an event also attended by Lively, who was reportedly a strong contender for the role. This casting choice adds to the anticipation surrounding Luhrmann's highly-anticipated adaptation of F. Scott Fitzgerald's classic novel, which is set to hit theaters.

Bristol Palin is struggling to maintain her public profile and book sales, as evidenced by a recent Craigslist ad in Washington, D.C., where she offered free, autographed copies of her memoir to attract attendees for a signing event. Her book, "Not Afraid of Life: My Journey So Far," failed to resonate with critics and the public alike, with reviewers finding her insights lacking and her brand of spectacle waning. This struggle comes after her brief stint on "Dancing with the Stars" and the initial notoriety from her mother's 2008 vice-presidential campaign, where she was revealed to be an out-of-wedlock pregnant teen. The ad for the book signing, which the conservative DC newspaper the Examiner noted was an attempt to entice fans, highlights the decline in public interest in Bristol's story.

The cast and crew of HBO's Girls express their emotions and reflections on the show's conclusion. Lena Dunham, the creator and star of Hannah Horvath, acknowledges the show's impact and the emotional journey of its characters, stating, "It’s like the family that we’ve created on this show is so close knit, and it’s so emotional to say goodbye." Allison Williams, who portrays Marnie Michaels, hopes viewers will feel compassion for Hannah and praises the season dedicated to Marnie. Jemima Kirke, playing Jessa Johansson, expresses her desire to continue exploring and refining her character. Zosia Mamet, who stars as Shoshanna Shapiro, shares her attachment to the character, noting the unique experience of playing the same part for so long. Judd Apatow, the executive producer, reflects on the show's calm and fun atmosphere despite the controversy surrounding it, and hopes the series has shown how some characters evolve while others do not. The cast's sentiments underscore the personal and professional growth experienced throughout the series.

At least three people were killed and nearly 30 hospitalized in a mass brawl at a Moscow cemetery, with up to 200 people involved, mostly migrants, reports various Russian media. The fight, reportedly a turf war over cemetery services, broke out at the Khovanskoye cemetery in southwest Moscow, where many of those involved were armed with bats, sticks, and metal bars. Eyewitnesses reported gunfire, with some suspecting the use of Kalashnikov rifles. Three bodies were discovered, and at least 29 people were hospitalized, with four in critical condition. Among those detained, 100 were reportedly involved, though estimates ranged up to 400 participants. The cemetery’s director was fired, and a private security firm responsible for security was also implicated. The conflict reportedly stemmed from a dispute between migrants from Central Asian former Soviet republics and North Caucasus regions, with the latter seeking to control the cemetery’s lucrative services. The National Guard was deployed for the first time, with 200 special forces’ servicemen participating. The incident caused massive traffic jams and raised concerns over the cemetery’s security and management.

Mitt Romney has altered his stance on the Affordable Care Act (ACA), particularly regarding the ban on insurance companies denying coverage to individuals with pre-existing conditions. In an interview with the Columbus Dispatch editorial board, Romney suggested that people who are currently uninsured should have the opportunity to obtain insurance, but those who choose not to get insured and then become ill later should not expect to receive insurance coverage. Romney argued that the uninsured can still receive necessary medical care through emergency rooms, which are required by federal law to treat patients regardless of their ability to pay. However, critics argue that this approach would leave millions of Americans without adequate health insurance, potentially leading to higher mortality rates among the uninsured. Romney's comments come as he seeks to distance himself from the Massachusetts health care law, which he previously supported, and differentiate his plan from the ACA. His position on pre-existing conditions and the role of emergency rooms in providing care to the uninsured has drawn criticism from the Obama administration and health care advocates, who point to studies showing that the uninsured face a higher risk of death due to lack of access to proper medical treatment.

Liliane Cyr, 59, has spent nearly four decades searching for her 18-month-old daughter, Yohanna, who vanished from her St-Laurent apartment in 1978. Walking down Rochon St. and Décarie Blvd., where she once lived, Cyr recounts the last time she saw Yohanna, bidding her goodbye before heading to work. Thirty-five years later, a small gathering of supporters honored Yohanna’s memory, with a new missing poster and age-processed photograph. Cyr’s daughter, Vera Sarah, sang a song for her sister, representing hope in their home.

In 1978, after working out of town, Cyr returned to find Yohanna missing. Her boyfriend initially claimed Yohanna was with his mother, but later said she had drowned and was buried. Cyr’s desperate search included contacting neighbors, hospitals, and the morgue, but no leads emerged. The taxi driver, the only witness, died a month later. Cyr brought baby photos and clothes to the police, but the file went missing a decade later. In 1994, the file was reopened, but Aaron Lewis Guay, her ex-boyfriend, denied the charges and was deported. No charges were laid, and the case went cold.

In 2013, a U.S. woman contacted the Missing Children’s Network, claiming a photo might be of Yohanna. DNA tests later revealed she was not the daughter. In 2016, a Facebook message from a U.S. woman sparked hope. She described a Y-shaped birthmark on her index finger, matching Yohanna’s. The woman claims blurry memories of being on an airplane as a child and occasional flashbacks. Cyr hopes the woman is her daughter, but remains cautious, awaiting DNA tests. Cyr’s relentless search continues, driven by the possibility of finding her daughter alive or at least knowing what happened to her.

Ahmed Mohamed's family has retained two little-known lawyers to investigate the police treatment of their 14-year-old son, who was arrested and handcuffed for bringing a homemade clock to his Irving, Texas, high school. The lawyers, Thomas Bowers and Reggie London, plan to examine Ahmed medically and investigate the city and school district's actions. Bowers, who previously represented a former stripper who sued Cowboys owner Jerry Jones, and London, who typically deals with drunken-driving charges and traffic tickets, will work on the case. Ahmed's father, Mohamed Elhassan Mohamed, has stated that his son has been humiliated and is experiencing issues since the incident. The family has also announced that they are considering legal options to regain Ahmed's science project from the Irving Police Department. Irving police had previously stated that the clock was a homemade experiment and that no charges would be filed, closing the case. However, the family's lawyers are now involved, and Ahmed's father has stated that they are no longer enrolled in the Irving school district, citing "religious persecution," and will be homeschooled instead. The Irving Police Department has released a statement, confirming that the clock was available to be picked up any weekday between 6 a.m. and 4:45 p.m. at their headquarters since September 16th, the day they announced the case was closed.

On Christmas Day in 2017, South Carolina lottery players experienced a lucky streak that was too good to be true. Between 5:51 p.m. and 7:53 p.m., a computer glitch caused gas stations and convenience stores to dispense tens of thousands of winning Holiday Cash Add-A-Play tickets, each worth up to $500. Nicole Coggins, 36, of Liberty, South Carolina, was among those who caught on to the anomaly and bought as many tickets as she could, accumulating what she thought were thousands of dollars in winnings. However, Coggins was not able to cash in her tickets. The South Carolina Education Lottery suspended the game after two hours and later announced that the error was due to a programming issue with the computer system vendor, Intralot. The lottery board of commissioners voted to reimburse the purchase price of the tickets, as mandated by state law, rather than honoring the prizes. The glitch affected approximately 71,000 tickets and led to a loss of about $35 million in potential prizes. Players who bought tickets between 5:51 p.m. and 7:53 p.m. on December 25, 2017, were eligible for a refund of the ticket price, with the South Carolina Education Lottery offering to reimburse the cost of each claim mailed in. The lottery board's decision was based on South Carolina Code Section 59-150-230(C)(3)(a), which states that prizes arising from tickets produced or issued in error must not be paid. Despite the decision, many players felt the outcome was unfair, as they had planned to use their winnings for significant purchases. Two lawsuits have been filed against the state lottery and Intralot on behalf of those denied prize money.

Special counsel Robert Mueller's investigation into the Trump campaign's potential ties with Russia continues to generate activity, with Paul Manafort, the former campaign chairman, visiting Mueller's office at least nine times in the last four weeks. These visits, occurring on most Fridays, suggest that Mueller's team is making steady progress. The quiet period before the midterm elections has seen a persistent murmur of activity, based on daily sightings of Mueller's prosecutors and sources involved in the investigation. Besides Manafort, Mueller's team has been interviewing witnesses and gathering a grand jury weekly. Discussions between the President's legal team and Mueller's office have intensified, especially after Mueller sent questions about possible collusion between the Trump campaign and the Russian government. Trump's legal team, including Jay Sekulow, Marty and Jane Raskin, and Emmet Flood, is preparing to respond to these questions, but the process may be lengthy. Manafort's cooperation is expected to aid in building potential criminal cases about coordination between the Russian government and the Trump campaign. Meanwhile, other Trump campaign officials, including Rick Gates and Michael Flynn, have also visited Mueller's office to give interviews. The flurry of interviews has left Trump's legal team somewhat in the dark about Mueller's pursuits. Expectations in Washington legal circles are growing that Mueller will issue a report soon after the November election or even before the end of the year, explaining the decisions of the Justice Department to bring or decline criminal cases. The Trump legal team believes that Mueller won't finish his work without bringing indictments closer to the Trump campaign. In other developments, Roger Stone, a Trump adviser, expects to be indicted after nine of his friends and aides spoke to Mueller's office or received grand jury subpoenas. Special counsel prosecutors have visited the federal courthouse in Washington almost daily, indicating ongoing court action. As the investigation progresses, the next potential target may be Stone himself.

After the original "Kick-Ass" inspired a new wave of self-made masked crusaders, including the Colonel Stars and Stripes and his attack dog, the sequel "Kick-Ass 2" sees Kick-Ass and Hit Girl, now in high school, struggling to balance their superhero lives with normal teenage activities. When Hit Girl is caught as Hit Girl and forced to retire, Kick-Ass teams up with the Colonel Stars and Stripes and his vigilante group to form the world's first superhero team. However, their efforts are threatened by the return of Red Mist, now known as The Mother F%&*^r. The film, directed by Jeff Wadlow and produced by Matthew Vaughn, features Jim Carrey in a prominent role as the Colonel Stars and Stripes, whose character's background and actions add depth to the story. Despite Carrey's initial enthusiasm, he withdrew his support for the film due to its violent content, a decision that has sparked debate among fans and critics. Mark Millar, the creator of the comic book series, defends the film's content, stating that the violence was always part of the script and that the movie's tone aligns with the original "Kick-Ass." Millar emphasizes that the film's action and humor are central to its appeal and that the violence is a necessary part of the story. The film, rated "R" for its graphic violence, is set for release on August 16, 2013.

EPA Administrator Scott Pruitt has broken his silence on his frequent first-class flights, attributing them to security concerns and a "toxic" political environment. During interviews in New Hampshire, Pruitt stated that he has faced "incidents" on flights since his appointment by President Donald Trump, leading to his decision to fly first class. He emphasized that these decisions are made by his security detail, not him. Pruitt's frequent premium-class travel has come under scrutiny, including a $1,641.43 first-class seat for a short flight in June from Washington to New York City, which was six times the cost of his aides' coach tickets. Federal regulations allow first-class travel when no cheaper options are "reasonably available" or if there are exceptional security circumstances, but past audits have found violations by high-ranking government officials. Pruitt's travel expenses, including first-class flights and military jets, have been detailed in reports, with taxpayers funding at least $90,000 for his and his top aides during one stretch last June. The EPA's press office has previously refused to confirm whether Pruitt was flying first class, but now admits he has been granted a waiver for such travel. EPA spokesman Jahan Wilcox stated that all of Pruitt's first-class trips were pre-approved by ethics lawyers. However, the General Services Administration (GSA) regulations require agencies to sign off on first-class travel "on a trip-by-trip basis" unless there is an up-to-date documented disability or special need. The EPA has not responded to specific requests for information about Pruitt's travel expenses, citing security concerns. The use of first-class travel by high-ranking government officials, including Pruitt, has drawn criticism from lawmakers and environmental advocates, who argue that it is a misuse of taxpayer funds. The White House's budget proposal for EPA seeks to cut $3.7 million, or 9 percent, in funding for the EPA's Office of Inspector General, which is currently investigating Pruitt's travel practices. The EPA's internal watchdog has found that Pruitt received more threats than his predecessor, Gina McCarthy, but it is unclear how many of these threats were deemed credible. The use of first-class travel by Pruitt has raised questions about the effectiveness of security measures and whether they provide any significant protection benefits compared to coach travel.

With Verizon’s long-anticipated bid to buy Yahoo finally official, speculation turns to what happens to the Internet giant’s CEO, Marissa Mayer. In a Tumblr post, Mayer wrote on Monday, “I’m planning to stay... It’s important to me to see Yahoo into its next chapter,” a position she reiterated in a CNBC interview, although she also said she was “open minded” about the future. For some, this indicates that the onetime Google wunderkind might depart after the deal is finished in the first quarter of next year. “It might be for a short period,” Morningstar equity analyst Ali Mogharabi said of the prospect of Mayer’s staying on. “They might need her input during the integration process.” After that, though, all bets are off. RBC Capital analyst Mark Mahaney said he expected AOL chief Tim Armstrong to lead the combined AOL-Yahoo company, calling him “a very seasoned internet executive,” in the CNBC interview. Ultimately, staying at Yahoo might not be Mayer’s choice to make. “She started out with just so much interest and enthusiasm and and excitement… and the last year or two have been tremendously disappointing,” said Scott Kessler, equity analyst at S&P Global Market Intelligence. Since being tapped to run Yahoo in 2012 after a scandal involving previous CEO Scott Thompson misrepresenting his credentials, Mayer initially boosted her standing with workers by bringing in Google-style staff perks like free lunch and phones. Her elimination of telecommuting in 2013 was less well received, though. Aside from running counter to the typical Silicon Valley corporate culture, which tends to encourage remote work, some charged that Yahoo’s ban was unfair to working parents, especially since it was widely reported that Mayer had a nursery built near her office to accommodate the baby boy she had a few months after taking the top spot at Yahoo. Mayer’s two-week maternity leaves, both in 2012 as well as three years later, when she had twin girls, also sparked a larger conversation about parental leave in the tech industry. “She has become the face of Yahoo, for better or worse. She has become a lightning rod,” Kessler said. Some of her choices when it came to Yahoo’s operations were also questioned, especially as the promised turnaround failed to materialize. “I would say it’s pretty much a mixed bag,” Mogharabi said. “The acquisition of Brightroll was a good one,” he said of Yahoo’s 2014 purchase of the ad platform, but he pointed out that its 2013 purchase of microblogging platform Tumblr for $1.1 billion didn’t pay off the way the company hoped. “While Marissa stabilized Yahoo during her tenure, she missed on the big trends,” Constellation Research founder and principal analyst R “Ray” Wang said via email. “Most folks would expect Marissa to leave within a year,” he noted. Leaving could be lucrative for Mayer. According to Equilar, a compensation data and research firm, she will make just under $57 million if Verizon decides not to keep her on. Through the end of last year, Equilar estimates that Mayer earned nearly $219 million, including $115 million in “realized pay,” which includes her cash earnings, value of shares vested during her tenure and gains from exercising options. That kind of money would give Mayer enough breathing room to take some time deliberating her next moves, which might be the best plan for her, Kessler suggested. “I think she would benefit from some time between what she’s doing now and what she’s going to do next,” he said. “There are a lot of options out there for her.”

On the fourth anniversary of the Sandy Hook Elementary School shooting, an organization called Sandy Hook Promise, founded by families of the victims, has released a powerful public service announcement (PSA) to raise awareness about warning signs of potential shooters. The PSA, part of the organization’s “Know the Signs” campaign, follows a typical teenager named Evan, who exchanges flirtatious messages with a secret pen pal in the school library. As Evan’s romance unfolds, an ominous figure in the background emerges, revealing an assault rifle, while viewers are subtly shown signs of another student planning a shooting. The PSA highlights behaviors such as reading gun enthusiast magazines, searching for gun videos on YouTube, and being bullied, all of which are presented as potential warning signs. The message emphasizes that while viewers were distracted by Evan’s romance, another student was showing signs of planning a shooting, but no one noticed. The PSA concludes with the text: “Gun violence is preventable when you know the signs.” Sandy Hook Promise aims to teach people how to recognize at-risk behaviors and empower them to intervene, as 80 percent of school shooters and 70 percent of individuals who killed themselves told someone of their violent plans prior to taking action, yet nobody intervened. The organization hopes that by understanding these warning signs, lives can be saved.

Officials at the Alipore zoo in Kolkata, India, are facing a peculiar challenge with their young male white tiger, Vishal, who has shown little interest in mating with his female partner, Rupa. Despite multiple attempts and the use of libido enhancers, Vishal has not responded to Rupa's advances. The zoo's senior veterinary officer, Dayanarayan Banerjee, attributes Vishal's reluctance to his "shyness" due to having been bred in captivity. Vishal, a 10-year-old male, and Rupa, an eight-year-old female, were selected for the breeding project due to their youth and vigour. However, when Rupa enters her oestrus cycle, she makes mating calls and tries to get close to Vishal, but he runs away with his tail between his legs. Medical officers administered vitamins and libido enhancers, but these efforts were unsuccessful. Experts suggest that Vishal's shyness is the primary issue, as he has never interacted with the opposite sex before. The breeding of tigers in captivity is crucial for maintaining the species, as the zoo's last successful breeding was over a decade ago. Zoo officials are considering introducing Vishal to a younger and more vigorous tigress named Rani, hoping she will succeed where Rupa has failed. The success of this breeding attempt is important for the future of the white tiger population in the zoo.

Attorney General Eric Holder, in a visit to Ferguson, Missouri, acknowledged the community's mistrust of law enforcement, drawing from his own experiences of racial profiling. Holder, speaking at St. Louis Community College, emphasized the federal investigation into the death of Michael Brown, an 18-year-old black man shot by a white police officer, and assured that the investigation would be "fair and independent." Holder recalled being stopped by police twice on the New Jersey Turnpike, accused of speeding, and having his car searched. He also recounted an incident in Washington, D.C., where he and his cousin were stopped while walking to a movie, highlighting his understanding of the community's frustration. Holder met with community leaders, the Brown family, and Missouri lawmakers, promising concrete action to address the issues. The visit came amid ongoing protests and unrest in Ferguson, with the Missouri Highway Patrol and National Guard assisting in maintaining order. Holder's presence aimed to provide reassurance and a calming influence, emphasizing the importance of dialogue and concrete action to improve relations between law enforcement and the community. The Justice Department's investigation into the shooting, involving additional autopsies and FBI agents, underscored the administration's commitment to addressing civil rights concerns. Holder's visit highlighted the administration's focus on achieving change through the Justice Department's civil rights division, with the goal of making the country a better place.

Starbucks faced backlash after inviting Irish followers to share what makes them proud to be British on Twitter as part of a diamond jubilee promotion. The tweet, intended for the UK, was mistakenly posted to the Irish account, prompting angry responses. Starbucks Ireland quickly issued an apology, stating the error was due to the tweet being erroneously posted to the Irish page. The company acknowledged the mistake and sought forgiveness from Irish customers. This incident follows a similar gaffe by Nike, which released a St Patrick's Day-themed shoe named "Black and Tan," a reference that offended Irish history. Both companies faced criticism for their lack of cultural sensitivity.

Nigeria's police have offered a $300,000 reward for information leading to the rescue of over 200 kidnapped schoolgirls, abducted by Boko Haram militants. The girls were seized from their boarding school in Borno state more than three weeks ago. Boko Haram, whose name means "Western education is forbidden," has been blamed for another attack on a town in the state on a busy market day, killing at least 150 people. The militants attacked Gamboru Ngala, on Nigeria's border with Cameroon, setting homes and shops ablaze and spraying gunfire into the market. The attack comes as the Nigerian government has accepted international offers of assistance, including from the United States, Britain, and China, to find the kidnapped girls. The U.S. plans to provide law enforcement and military consultations, while Britain is sending a small team to assist. Meanwhile, China has offered satellite and intelligence services. The international community, including high-profile figures like U.S. First Lady Michelle Obama and Pakistani activist Malala Yousafzai, has rallied behind the #BringBackOurGirls campaign, urging the Nigerian government to take more decisive action. The government has been criticized for its response, with some questioning why it has taken so long to acknowledge the kidnappings and for the reward to be offered. The attack on Gamboru Ngala highlights the ongoing threat from Boko Haram and the challenges faced by the Nigerian military in retaking control of the region.

U.S. President Barack Obama is considering military action against Syria following intelligence reports of a chemical weapons attack that killed 1,429 people, including 426 children, near Damascus on August 21. Russian President Vladimir Putin challenged the U.S. to present evidence to the U.N. of the alleged attack. Meanwhile, U.N. weapons inspectors have left Syria and are analyzing samples in The Hague, though their mandate does not include determining who used the weapons. Obama plans to seek congressional approval for any military action, aiming to deter future chemical weapon use. The U.S. has four destroyers in the eastern Mediterranean, and France's aircraft carrier is in the western Mediterranean, ready to act. However, the British Parliament voted against military action, and Russian President Putin expressed surprise at this development. The Syrian government denies responsibility and blames rebels, while the U.S. claims evidence supports their stance. The U.N. inspectors' findings could take up to three weeks to analyze, with the U.S. seeking a limited, narrow military response to send a message against chemical weapons use.

Former NFL star Chad Johnson was sentenced to 30 days in jail for a probation violation in a domestic violence case after playfully slapping his attorney on the backside in court, angering the judge. Johnson, known as Chad Ochocinco, had reached a deal with prosecutors for community service and counseling instead of jail. However, when asked if he was satisfied with his lawyer, Johnson gave the attorney a light swat, causing the judge to reject the deal. Johnson, currently undergoing therapy for domestic violence, was handcuffed and taken to jail. The judge, who noted this was not the first time Johnson had behaved this way in her courtroom, stated, "It's not the first time he's behaved that way in my courtroom." Johnson, who played for the Cincinnati Bengals and New England Patriots, has lost everything and is currently without an NFL team.

An armed man barricaded himself inside a Connect Wireless store in La Crescenta during a Black Friday standoff that lasted nearly six hours. After tactical team entry around 10 p.m., authorities found the man deceased apparently by his own hand, with no shots fired by deputies. The incident began when the man entered the store after stealing prescription drugs in an armed robbery at a nearby Rite Aid. SWAT team members and crisis negotiators attempted to persuade him to surrender. The store, located in The Marketplace Shopping Center, was evacuated and the surrounding area was secured. Foothill Boulevard was temporarily closed between Rosemont and Raymond avenues.

Federal Reserve Chair Janet Yellen faced a significant challenge during her first press conference as chair, inadvertently providing specific guidance on interest rate hikes that sent financial markets into a tailspin. Yellen was asked about the timeline for raising interest rates after the tapering of bond purchases ends. Her response: "So the language that we used in the statement is ‘considerable period.’ So I, you know, this is the kind of term it’s hard to define. But, you know, probably means something on the order of around six months, that type of thing." This statement, despite being intended to be vague, was interpreted as a clear indication that the first rate hike could come as early as April or May 2015, significantly earlier than the market had anticipated. The markets reacted negatively, with equity markets experiencing a sharp decline and interest rates rising. 

Yellen’s specificity was seen as a misstep, as the Fed had traditionally used the term “considerable period” to imply a duration of about half a year, but without being precise. Critics, including Michael Feroli from JPMorgan Chase, pointed out that Yellen’s response was inconsistent with the Fed’s usual practice of maintaining ambiguity. The market’s reaction highlighted the delicate balance the Fed must strike in communicating its monetary policy intentions. 

The change in the Fed’s forward guidance, which had previously tied the timing of rate hikes to the unemployment rate reaching 6.5%, was another factor contributing to market uncertainty. Yellen explained that the new guidance would consider a broader range of economic indicators, including inflation and financial market conditions. However, her attempt to clarify this shift was overshadowed by the market’s focus on the timing of the next rate hike. 

Yellen’s gaffe underscores the challenges she faces in navigating the complex relationship between monetary policy and financial markets. While her overall message was that the Fed would maintain a cautious approach to rate hikes, the specificity of her response on the timing of the first hike sent a mixed signal. This incident also highlights the importance of clear and consistent communication in monetary policy, as any misstep can have significant consequences for the economy and financial markets.

Police in New York City have issued a warning to residents about the potential dangers of charging cell phones under pillows or on beds, as a fire in Hamden, Connecticut, has highlighted the risks. The incident occurred when a 15-year-old boy's phone caught fire, igniting his bed and pillow. Fire Chief David Berardesca of Hamden emphasized the importance of proper ventilation for charging devices, stating that "cell phones need areas to be ventilated" and should be placed on hard surfaces to allow heat to dissipate. He also advised against blocking the air vents on the back and sides of laptops and against leaving charging devices on beds while sleeping, as bedding and pillows can block airflow and increase the risk of fire.

The New York Police Department's 33rd Precinct shared a cautionary tweet, urging people not to place their cell phones under pillows when charging. The tweet included graphic images of a burning phone and pillow, driving home the point. Fire officials recommend checking power cords and chargers regularly for damage and replacing them if they are frayed, as damaged cords can emit electrical sparks and ignite fires. Additionally, it is advised to unplug chargers that are not in use, as they continue to consume electricity even when not charging the device.

The incident in Hamden serves as a stark reminder of the potential hazards associated with improper charging practices. While the chances of a phone catching fire are relatively low, the risks are real enough to warrant caution. Fire officials across the country are using this event to educate the public about the importance of safe charging practices and the steps that can be taken to prevent such incidents.

I appreciate what PETA does, but when they take it too far, they really take it too far. They recently sent a letter to the founder of the National Buffalo Association, objecting to the use of the term "buffalo" for bison. PETA argues that using the term "buffalo" is inappropriate and perpetuates the idea that bison are related to the African buffalo, which is not true. The organization demands that the term "bison" be used instead. While I understand PETA's concern for animal welfare, I believe their campaign goes too far by targeting a long-standing term used in the industry and culture. The term "buffalo" has been used for bison for centuries and is deeply ingrained in the language and traditions surrounding bison. The National Buffalo Association has stated that they will continue to use the term "buffalo" to describe bison, emphasizing the economic and cultural significance of the term.

The MERS-CoV virus, a potentially deadly SARS-like virus, has spread to Italy, marking the first known cases in the country, the World Health Organization (WHO) announced. Of the 53 known infections worldwide, 30 have resulted in death. Symptoms, including fever and cough, can lead to severe respiratory issues and kidney failure. The virus has been found in bats and camels, raising concerns about its origin and transmission. The WHO emphasizes the virus as a global threat, highlighting the need for international cooperation to study and address the virus. In France, a 45-year-old man who recently traveled to Jordan contracted the virus, and a patient died on May 28. Health officials are still unsure of the virus's exact mode of transmission, making prevention challenging. The WHO is calling for a coordinated global response to better understand and contain the virus.
